description_generated: axon guidance is the process by which a growing axon steers toward its correct target, reading attractive and repulsive cues in the extracellular environment and translating them into directed movement of the growth cone. It builds the wiring diagram of the nervous system, and errors in it produce miswired circuits and defects in commissure formation and nerve pathfinding. Here the cues are semaphorin family ligands acting through neuropilin co-receptors, whose signals converge on cytoskeletal effectors: collapsin response mediator protein family members regulate microtubule assembly, while Rho and Ras small GTPases with focal adhesion kinase and non-muscle myosin II control actin contractility and adhesion turnover at the leading edge. Fibrillar collagens provide the substrate and mechanical context for that migration. The same machinery is reused outside the nervous system for cell migration, vascular patterning, and tumour cell invasion.

Growing axons find their targets by reading attractive and repulsive cues in the tissue they traverse, and this collection captures the guidance step where extracellular signals are converted into steering of the growth cone. Wiring of the nervous system depends on it, and comparable signalling directs migrating cells and sprouting vessels, so defects produce miswired circuits and disordered migration. A semaphorin ligand and the neuropilin co-receptor supply the directional cue; focal adhesion kinase and Ras- and Rho-family GTPases relay it to adhesion sites and the actomyosin cortex, with non-muscle myosin IIB and the CRMP family protein DPYSL3 acting on cytoskeletal dynamics to turn or collapse the growth cone. Fibrillar collagens here represent the substratum and adhesive environment through which the process occurs, linking guidance to cell-matrix interaction rather than to soluble signalling alone.

complement activation (I) is the humoral arm of innate immunity that marks pathogens and damaged cells for destruction, drives inflammation, and clears immune complexes and debris from the circulation. Loss of it leaves recurrent pyogenic infection and lupus-like autoimmunity; loss of its brakes causes hemolysis and kidney injury, as in atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome and hereditary angioedema. The genes trace the classical route from the C1q recognition subunits through the C1r/C1s proteases and C2 to cleavage of C3, alongside the alternative amplification loop supplied by factor B and factor D. Cleavage fragments engage the C3a and C5a receptors on myeloid cells to recruit and activate leukocytes, while C7 contributes to the lytic terminal complex. Regulators including factor H, factor I, CR1 and C1 inhibitor restrict activation to intended surfaces and protect host tissue.

Complement activation is the humoral arm of innate immunity that marks microbes and debris for destruction and recruits inflammatory cells to the site. The genes here trace the classical route, where the C1q recognition subunits bind antibody-coated or altered surfaces and the C1r/C1s proteases cleave C4 and C2 to build a C3-cleaving enzyme, together with the alternative route sustained by factor B and factor D. Cleavage of C3 opsonises the target for phagocytes bearing CR1, while the released C3a and C5a act through their receptors C3AR1 and C5AR1 to drive chemotaxis, vascular leak and mast cell activation; C7 contributes to the lytic membrane pore. Restraint is built in: C1 inhibitor, factor H and factor I limit activation to intended surfaces, and their loss causes hereditary angioedema, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome or macular degeneration, whereas deficiency of early components predisposes to encapsulated bacterial infection and lupus-like autoimmunity.

golgi membrane (I) groups proteins resident in or trafficking through the Golgi apparatus, where secreted and membrane-bound cargo is glycosylated, lipid-modified and sorted to its destination. This compartment determines the composition of the cell surface and the secretome, so its enzymes set the glycan and sphingolipid identity of a cell and the range of signals it can send. Here the glycosyltransferases build lactosylceramide-derived glycosphingolipids and chondroitin sulfate chains, while sphingomyelin synthase and a lysophospholipid acyltransferase remodel membrane lipids that shape Golgi structure and downstream inflammatory mediators. Other members handle cargo selection and export: sortilin routes proteins to lysosomes and regulates neurotrophin receptor traffic, WLS is the dedicated carrier that loads Wnt ligands for secretion, and PDGFC is itself Golgi-processed growth factor cargo. Defects in such Golgi steps disturb Wnt-dependent patterning, lysosomal delivery and glycolipid balance.

Proteins gathered here share residence in the Golgi membrane, the sorting and finishing station where newly made proteins and lipids are glycosylated, modified and dispatched to their destinations. The set spans the main jobs done at that membrane: glycan elaboration by B3GNT5, which extends lacto/neolacto glycolipid chains, and CSGALNACT1, which initiates chondroitin sulfate chains on proteoglycan core proteins; lipid remodelling and headgroup transfer by LPCAT2 and by SGMS2, which synthesises sphingomyelin; cargo sorting by the receptor SORT1; and dedicated secretion machinery such as WLS, the carrier that loads lipid-modified Wnt ligands for release. Also present are secretory clients and membrane proteins in transit, including the growth factor PDGFC and the endosomal nucleic-acid sensor TLR8. Together they illustrate how Golgi membrane composition determines extracellular matrix quality, membrane lipid identity and the reach of secreted signals.

enriched in monocytes (IV) is a transcriptional signature of blood monocytes and the macrophage lineage they feed, marking the myeloid cells that patrol tissue for microbes and damage, present antigen, and clear debris. Its members define what a monocyte is functionally: pattern-recognition receptors and their accessory proteins (TLR1, LY96, CARD9, LGALS3) that sense bacterial and fungal ligands; lysosomal and degradative enzymes such as CTSS, LYZ and RNASE6 that support phagocytosis; adhesion and chemotaxis machinery including CXCR2, DOCK5, MYO1F and PAK1 for migration into inflamed tissue; and inflammatory effectors and cytokine receptors such as PTGS2, PTX3, IL1R2, TNFRSF1B and TNFSF13B that shape the local response and B cell survival. Lineage transcription factors including HHEX and BCL6, together with CD4, CD68 and EMR1 surface markers, place the programme downstream of myeloid commitment. Expression of these genes rises in sepsis and chronic inflammation and falls with monocyte depletion.

A blood transcriptional module whose expression marks monocytes and closely related myeloid cells, useful as a readout of monocyte abundance and activation state in whole-blood profiling of infection, inflammation and autoimmunity. The genes describe what these cells do: pattern recognition and innate sensing through TLR1, LY96 and the CARD9 adaptor, phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation via CD68, CTSS, LYZ and RNASE6, antigen presentation components such as HLA-DMB, and receptors for cytokines and chemoattractants including TNFRSF1B, IL1R2, LTBR and CXCR2 that position the cell in inflamed tissue. Prostaglandin synthesis by PTGS2, the acute-phase pattern-recognition molecule PTX3, and lipid-handling enzymes such as ACSL1 reflect the secretory and metabolic reprogramming that follows activation, while BCL6 and HHEX contribute transcriptional control of myeloid differentiation. Together these define the circulating precursors of macrophages and inflammatory dendritic cells.

enriched in monocytes (surface) describes the plasma-membrane protein signature that distinguishes blood monocytes from other leukocytes, providing the receptors through which these cells sense infection, migrate into tissue, and mature into macrophages and dendritic cells. Its members are the handles used to identify and sort monocyte populations and to gauge inflammatory state in disease. The set is dominated by innate immune receptors and adhesion molecules: CD4 and the adhesion GPCR EMR1 mark the lineage, TNFRSF1B and LTBR transduce tumour necrosis factor family signals, IL1R2 acts as a decoy that damps interleukin-1 responses, and TNFSF13B (BAFF) is released to support B cell survival. Alongside these sit MHC class II accessory machinery for antigen presentation, an ITAM-coupled activating receptor, and lactate and sphingosine-1-phosphate transport proteins that link glycolytic metabolism and chemotactic egress to monocyte effector function.

This is a monocyte-enriched surface signature: a group of membrane proteins whose expression marks circulating monocytes and their macrophage progeny rather than lymphocytes or granulocytes. Such markers underpin the identification and sorting of monocyte subsets and define how these cells sense inflammation, migrate into tissue, and present antigen. The collection spans innate immune receptors and receptor modifiers, including a decoy interleukin-1 receptor that dampens IL-1 signalling, TNF receptor family members that transduce TNF and lymphotoxin cues, a source of the B cell survival factor BAFF, an MHC class II-associated chaperone subunit, and CD4 itself, which monocytes express at lower levels than T cells. Transporters and a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor add metabolic and trafficking capacity, linking the profile to glycolytic support of activation and to recruitment during infection, atherosclerosis, and chronic inflammation.

inositol phosphate metabolism covers the making and breaking of phosphorylated inositol lipids and soluble inositol phosphates, the signalling currency that tells a membrane which compartment it is and which proteins may bind it. It matters because phosphoinositide identity governs endocytosis, autophagosome formation, endosome maturation and synaptic vesicle recycling, and because lithium's therapeutic action converges on inositol monophosphatase, which recycles free inositol for renewed lipid synthesis. The class II and class III PI 3-kinases generate PI3P on early endosomes and nascent autophagosomes, PIKFYVE converts it to PI(3,5)P2 to drive late endosome and lysosome function, and the synaptojanin phosphatase strips phosphates to release clathrin coats after vesicle budding. Effector modules such as FYVE-domain adaptors read these marks. Loss of this balance produces neurodegeneration, myopathy and lysosomal storage-like defects in membrane traffic.

Inositol phosphate metabolism generates and recycles the phosphorylated inositol species that mark membranes for identity and release calcium-mobilising second messengers. Its outputs govern how vesicles are sorted, how endosomes and autophagosomes mature, and how receptor signalling is terminated, so cells depend on it for membrane traffic as much as for signal transduction. Lipid kinases such as PIK3C2A, the class III enzyme PIK3C3 and the 5-kinase PIKFYVE phosphorylate inositol head groups on endosomal and autophagic membranes, while the polyphosphoinositide phosphatase synaptojanin removes phosphates to drive clathrin uncoating at synapses, and inositol monophosphatase completes the cycle by freeing myo-inositol for resynthesis. Loss of this turnover is damaging in neurons in particular: synaptojanin mutations cause parkinsonism and epileptic encephalopathy, and lithium acts partly by inhibiting the monophosphatase step.

enriched in G-protein coupled receptors describes cell-surface receptor signalling through heterotrimeric G proteins, the route by which hormones, lipid mediators, chemokines and proteases are converted into second-messenger changes inside a cell. It matters because this receptor class governs vascular tone, platelet activation, inflammation and leukocyte traffic, and it is the target of a large share of prescribed drugs. The members span several arms of the system: a beta-adrenergic receptor and prostaglandin E and D receptors that raise cyclic AMP, a thrombin-activated protease receptor and a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor coupled to calcium and cytoskeletal responses, and chemokine ligands that recruit T and NK cells. Downstream effectors complete the circuit, with an inositol trisphosphate receptor releasing calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores and a phosphodiesterase terminating cyclic AMP signals, so signal termination is as much a feature here as initiation.

This grouping is organised around signalling through G-protein coupled receptors, the largest family of cell-surface sensors and the target of a large share of prescribed drugs. Ligand binding here is diverse: catecholamines at the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, thrombin cleaving the protease-activated receptor F2R, prostaglandins D2 and E2 at PTGDR and PTGER2, sphingosine-1-phosphate at S1PR5, and the chemokines CCL5 and XCL1 acting on leukocyte receptors, with GPR18 as an orphan-like lipid-responsive member. Downstream components define the second-messenger arms: ITPR3 releases calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores following phospholipase C activation, while PDE4D hydrolyses cAMP and so sets the duration of Gs-coupled responses. Together these mediate smooth muscle tone, platelet and endothelial responses to vascular injury, inflammatory mediator production, and the recruitment and trafficking of immune cells.

cell adhesion, membrane describes the junctional machinery that holds epithelial sheets together and gives them apical-basal polarity and barrier function. This organisation is what allows epithelia to line the gut, airway, breast and kidney, to separate compartments of differing composition, and to restrain cell movement; its loss during epithelial-mesenchymal transition accompanies carcinoma invasion and metastasis. E-cadherin and P-cadherin with the plakoglobin linker build adherens junctions anchored to the keratin and actin cytoskeleton, while claudins 3, 4 and 7 with the lipolysis-stimulated receptor seal tight junctions and set paracellular permeability. EPCAM and the protease inhibitor SPINT1 tune junction turnover and pericellular proteolysis, and the transcription factor EHF maintains the epithelial identity that sustains the whole program. Stratifin and BIK tie adhesion status to checkpoint control and apoptotic sensitivity, so that detached or disorganised cells are eliminated.

Epithelial sheets hold together through membrane-based cell adhesion, and this collection of junctional and surface proteins defines that organization. E-cadherin and P-cadherin with the plaque protein junction plakoglobin build calcium-dependent adherens and desmosomal contacts, while claudins 3, 4 and 7 together with the lipolysis-stimulated lipoprotein receptor seal tight junctions and set paracellular permeability; EPCAM and the keratin 19 cytoskeleton mark the epithelial state. EHF is a transcription factor that sustains this epithelial identity programme, and SPINT1 restrains membrane serine proteases that would otherwise remodel the surface. The result is a polarized, cohesive barrier separating tissue compartments, with 14-3-3 sigma and BIK linking adhesion status to proliferation and apoptosis. Loss of cadherin and claudin function underlies the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition seen in carcinoma invasion and in barrier failure of gut, lung and breast epithelium.

cell cell adhesion is the machinery that binds epithelial cells to one another and to their basement membrane, creating the sealed, polarized sheets that line skin, gut, lung and glands. Without it epithelia lose barrier function and cohesion: cells detach, tissues blister, and tumour cells acquire the migratory, invasive behaviour of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, which is why loss of E-cadherin is a classic marker of carcinoma progression. Three junction types are represented. Classical cadherins CDH1 and CDH3, linked through junctional plakoglobin to the cytoskeleton, mediate calcium-dependent homophilic contact; claudins CLDN3, CLDN4 and CLDN7 build the tight-junction strands that set paracellular permeability and apicobasal polarity; and laminin-332 with integrins β6β4 anchors basal keratinocytes to the matrix via hemidesmosomes. Mutations in the laminin-332 chains cause junctional epidermolysis bullosa, showing how directly adhesion translates into tissue integrity.

Epithelial sheets hold together and stay sealed through the adhesion machinery represented here, which keeps cells attached to their neighbours and polarised so that a tissue can act as a barrier. E-cadherin and P-cadherin mediate calcium-dependent contacts at adherens junctions, with junction plakoglobin linking the cadherin tails to the cytoskeleton, while claudin-3, -4 and -7 build the tight junction strands that control paracellular flux of ions and solutes. Laminin-332 subunits together with the integrins that bind it anchor basal keratinocytes and other epithelia to the basement membrane, so cell-cell and cell-matrix attachment are described together. Loss of E-cadherin and gain of these integrins accompanies epithelial-mesenchymal transition and carcinoma invasion, and mutations in the laminin-332 chains cause junctional epidermolysis bullosa with fragile, blistering skin.

This grouping centres on nuclear regulation of chromatin, transcription and genome maintenance, with a second arm in phosphoinositide-dependent membrane traffic and cytoskeletal signalling. The chromatin remodelling ATPase SMARCA5 positions nucleosomes for replication and repair, TLK1 couples histone chaperone activity to replication timing, and the deubiquitinase USP1 removes ubiquitin from PCNA and FANCD2 to terminate translesion synthesis and Fanconi anaemia-pathway repair; ZMYM2, ATF2 and the elongation/splicing regulators TCERG1 and SFRS12 shape transcriptional output and mRNA processing. Alongside these, PIKFYVE generates PI(3,5)P2 for endosome and lysosome maturation, ACBD3 and PLEKHF2 organise Golgi and endosomal membranes, and ROCK1 drives actomyosin contractility during cell shape change and apoptotic blebbing. Metabolic components including glycogen debranching and pantothenate kinase feed cofactor and carbohydrate supply, linking these regulatory activities to cell growth, division and stress recovery.

This grouping brings together nuclear regulators of chromatin and transcription with a smaller set of membrane and metabolic enzymes, and is best read as a broad housekeeping module supporting gene expression and genome maintenance. On the nuclear side, SMARCA5 is the ATPase of ISWI-type nucleosome remodelling complexes that space nucleosomes during replication and repair; TLK1 phosphorylates histone chaperones to couple chromatin assembly to S phase; USP1 removes ubiquitin from FANCD2 and PCNA to terminate DNA damage tolerance and interstrand crosslink repair; ATF2, TCERG1 and SFRS12 act on transcription and splicing, and ZMYM2 and RNF6 contribute transcriptional repression and ubiquitin ligation. Alongside these, PIKFYVE generates PI(3,5)P2 for endolysosomal membrane dynamics, ACBD3 organises Golgi signalling, and AGL and PANK3 serve glycogen debranching and coenzyme A synthesis. Loss of such functions impairs replication-coupled chromatin assembly, repair fidelity and basic metabolic supply.

T cell differentiation covers the developmental program that turns a thymic progenitor into a mature, antigen-responsive T lymphocyte, and the signalling machinery that decides at each step whether a cell survives, matures, or is deleted. It is what gives the body its helper and cytotoxic compartments; its failure produces immunodeficiency, while its miscalibration permits autoimmunity or T cell leukemia. The genes describe both control layers: transcriptional commitment through BCL11B and TCF7, which enforce T lineage identity and block alternative fates, and proximal receptor signalling through the tyrosine kinases ITK and TXK, the RasGRP1 exchange factor, and CD28 costimulation, which convert antigen and costimulatory input into activation. Negative regulators such as UBASH3A set the threshold for that response, and SH2D1A links receptor engagement to help delivered to B cells during antibody responses.

Thymic progenitors become functional T lymphocytes through a programme of lineage commitment and receptor-driven selection, and these genes mark that route. Its output is the naive T cell repertoire that underpins adaptive cellular immunity; failure produces immunodeficiency, while loss of the checkpoints on receptor signalling permits autoimmunity. BCL11B enforces T cell identity and prevents progenitors from diverting to other lineages, while TCF7 acts downstream of Wnt signals to sustain the naive and memory state. Signal transduction from the antigen receptor runs through the tyrosine kinases ITK and TXK and the Ras activator RASGRP1, converting receptor engagement into proliferation and differentiation decisions; CD28 supplies the costimulatory second signal and UBASH3A dampens receptor output. SH2D1A couples signalling in T cells to help for B cells, linking this developmental programme to antibody responses.

Intracellular transport covers the routing of proteins, membranes and nucleic acids between compartments, the logistics without which secretion, receptor turnover and nuclear-cytoplasmic communication all fail. The genes span the main stations of that route: signal recognition particle components and SEC63 that deliver nascent chains into the endoplasmic reticulum, clathrin adaptors and phosphoinositide kinases such as PIK3C2A and PIKFYVE that shape endosomal carriers, the ESCRT ATPase VPS4B that severs vesicles into multivesicular bodies, and exocyst subunit EXOC1 that tethers vesicles at the plasma membrane. Nucleoporins NUP107 and NUP133 form the scaffold through which macromolecules cross the nuclear envelope, while G3BP2 links transport to stress granule dynamics and mRNA localisation. Also represented are centrosomal and cytoskeletal regulators that position organelles. Disruption of these steps produces lysosomal storage, ciliopathy and secretory defects.

Moving proteins, membranes and cargo between compartments is the logistical backbone of a eukaryotic cell, and intracellular transport covers the steps by which newly made proteins enter the secretory pathway, vesicles bud and fuse, endosomes mature, and macromolecules cross the nuclear envelope. Without it, secretion and receptor turnover fail and misfolded protein accumulates. Distinct arms are represented here: a signal recognition particle subunit and the SEC63 translocon component direct cotranslational entry into the endoplasmic reticulum, where TMX1 assists oxidative folding; nucleoporins of the NUP107-133 scaffold form part of the nuclear pore for nucleocytoplasmic exchange; an exocyst subunit targets vesicles to the plasma membrane; clathrin-associated CLINT1 supports endocytic uptake. Phosphoinositide kinases PIK3C2A and PIKFYVE generate the lipid marks that specify endosomal identity, read by FYVE-domain proteins, while the AAA-ATPase VPS4B recycles ESCRT machinery during multivesicular body formation.

amino acid metabolishm and transport describes the handling of amino acids and their derivatives in the kidney proximal tubule and liver "" their reabsorption from filtrate, conjugation, and catabolism. This is the biology that keeps amino acids out of the urine and converts their carbon and nitrogen into usable or excretable forms; loss of it produces aminoacidurias such as cystinuria, caused by defects in the SLC3A1""SLC7A9 heteromeric cystine transporter, and disturbances of betaine, glycine and tryptophan metabolism. Apical and basolateral carriers for neutral and dibasic amino acids, betaine and organic anions work alongside scaffolds such as PDZK1 and collectrin that position them in the brush border. Metabolic components include betaine""homocysteine methyltransferase and dimethylglycine dehydrogenase in one-carbon and methionine metabolism, BBOX1 in carnitine synthesis, glycine and acetyl conjugating enzymes, and the kynurenine branch enzyme ACMSD, with bile acid""activated NR1H4 providing transcriptional control.

Amino acid metabolism and transport in this sense is largely the business of the liver and the kidney proximal tubule, where filtered amino acids and their derivatives are reabsorbed, conjugated, or degraded rather than lost in urine. The heterodimeric cystine and dibasic amino acid transporter formed by SLC3A1 with SLC7A9 is the clearest example: loss of either causes cystinuria and cystine stones, and TMEM27 and PDZK1 support apical transporter trafficking and scaffolding. Betaine and glycine handling appears through BHMT and BHMT2, which remethylate homocysteine to methionine, DMGDH, GLYAT and the betaine/GABA transporters SLC6A12 and SLC6A13, linking osmolyte accumulation to one-carbon metabolism. Other members degrade tryptophan and pyrimidine-derived intermediates, acylate or acetylate amino acids for excretion, and move urate, organic cations and anions across the tubular epithelium, tying nitrogen disposal to renal solute handling.

TLR and inflammatory signaling is the innate-immune sensing program of myeloid cells, principally neutrophils and monocytes, that detects microbial products and host damage signals and converts them into an inflammatory response. It underlies the first line of antimicrobial defence, and its dysregulation drives septic shock, chronic inflammatory disease and autoimmunity. Surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors, together with the LPS co-receptor MD-2, signal through MyD88 and IRAK kinases toward NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription, while IRAK3 imposes negative feedback and tolerance. Alongside them sit the effector receptors of myeloid activation: complement and formyl-peptide chemoattractant receptors that direct chemotaxis, Fc receptors and the ITAM adaptor TYROBP that trigger phagocytosis and Src-family kinase signalling, inhibitory LILR and Siglec receptors that restrain it, and NADPH oxidase and ALOX5 components that generate reactive oxygen species and leukotrienes. PADI4 links the same cells to neutrophil extracellular trap formation.

Innate immune cells detect microbial products and host-derived danger signals and convert that detection into inflammation, and this Toll-like receptor and inflammatory signalling programme is the sensing apparatus that does it. Surface and endosomal receptors for bacterial lipopeptides, lipopolysaccharide, flagellin and nucleic acids (TLR1, TLR2, TLR4, TLR5, TLR6, TLR7, TLR8) act with the LPS co-receptor MD-2 and signal through MyD88 and IRAK-family adaptors toward NF-κB-driven cytokine production; IRAK3 restrains this output to limit tissue damage and endotoxin tolerance. Alongside them sit the effector receptors of myeloid cells: complement and formyl-peptide receptors and the chemokine receptor CXCR2 that guide neutrophil recruitment, Fc gamma receptors and the DAP12 adaptor TYROBP for phagocytosis, inhibitory LILR and Siglec receptors that damp activation, plus leukotriene synthesis and the NADPH oxidase subunit NCF4. The composition reflects granulocyte and monocyte biology, host defence against infection, and the sterile inflammation underlying sepsis and autoimmunity.

Leukocyte differentiation covers the transcriptional programs that turn haematopoietic progenitors into the specialised white blood cells of innate and adaptive immunity, and that push mature cells into activated states. It determines the composition of the immune system: how many neutrophils, monocytes, dendritic cells and lymphocytes are produced, and whether they mature at all, with failures manifesting as immunodeficiency or leukaemic arrest. The genes here are largely inducible transcriptional regulators acting downstream of cytokine and antigen receptor signalling — NF-κB family members and their modulators such as NFKB2 and BCL3, immediate-early factors including JUNB, EGR2 and NR4A2, Krüppel-like factors, and the retinoic acid receptor RARA, whose disruption blocks myeloid maturation in promyelocytic leukaemia. Alongside them sit surface and secreted effectors such as CD83, ADAM8, IL1A and LIF, linking lineage decisions to inflammatory context and cell cycle exit.

Leukocyte differentiation is the process by which haematopoietic progenitors and activated immune cells commit to specialized fates anging from granulocytes and monocytes to dendritic cells and lymphocyte subsets, and it determines the composition of the immune system available to fight infection. The genes here are largely nuclear regulators that translate inflammatory and cytokine cues into lineage decisions: NF-κB family members and the IL-1-inducible modulator BCL3, immediate-early factors such as JUNB, EGR2, BTG2 and the orphan nuclear receptor NR4A2, Krüppel-like factors, and the retinoic acid receptor RARA, whose ligand drives granulocytic maturation and whose disruption by chromosomal translocation blocks it in acute promyelocytic leukaemia. Also represented are secreted signals including LIF and IL1A, the dendritic cell maturation marker CD83, the metalloprotease ADAM8, and the transcriptional coactivator MED1. Failure of this programme produces immunodeficiency or leukaemic arrest at an immature stage.

Xenobiotic metabolism is the chemical defence system by which cells modify drugs, dietary compounds and environmental toxins so they can be excreted, and it sets how long any given drug persists in the body. The genes here span the two classical arms: oxidative phase I attack by cytochrome P450 enzymes of the CYP3A family, which handle a large share of clinically used drugs and whose polymorphic expression underlies interindividual differences in drug response, and phase II conjugation by a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase that appends glucuronic acid to make metabolites water-soluble. Accompanying transporters and catabolic enzymes, including a cystine-dibasic amino acid carrier and the beta-alanine-generating pyrimidine breakdown steps of dihydropyrimidinase and ureidopropionase, place this activity in absorptive epithelia of gut, liver and kidney, where deficiencies cause fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy toxicity and impaired clearance.

Drugs, dietary chemicals and other foreign compounds must be chemically altered before they can be cleared, and xenobiotic metabolism is the set of enzymes that performs that conversion and disposal. Its capacity determines how long a drug persists, whether a pro-carcinogen is activated or detoxified, and how patients differ in response and toxicity. Two phases are represented here: cytochrome P450 monooxygenases of the CYP3A family carry out oxidative functionalisation of a broad range of substrates, while a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates sugar onto the products to make them water-soluble for excretion. Accompanying transporters and hydrolytic enzymes place this chemistry in absorptive epithelia of the intestine, liver and kidney, where amino acid and pyrimidine catabolic activities such as dihydropyrimidinase and beta-ureidopropionase overlap with handling of pyrimidine-analogue drugs. Loss of individual components shifts drug exposure and underlies inherited differences in clearance.

enriched in dendritic cells marks the transcriptional signature of myeloid dendritic cells and closely related monocyte-derived antigen-presenting cells, the sentinels that sample tissue antigen and instruct T cell responses. Its members define how these cells recognise, ingest and process what they encounter: C-type lectin receptors such as CLEC10A and CLEC5A bind glycan and pathogen ligands, FCER1A confers high-affinity IgE capture on skin and blood DC subsets, DAB2 and CAPG support endocytic uptake and actin-dependent membrane remodelling, and the lysosomal cathepsins CTSB and CTSL degrade internalised protein for peptide loading onto MHC. Additional components tune the response to the tissue environment, including IL1R1 for inflammatory cytokine sensing, JAG1 for Notch-mediated instruction of neighbouring lymphocytes, and metabolic and glycosylation enzymes that accompany maturation. Together these genes distinguish dendritic cells in immune profiling and underlie the initiation of adaptive immunity and tolerance.

This grouping marks the transcriptional signature of dendritic cells, the antigen-presenting sentinels that sample tissue, migrate to lymph nodes and set the tone of T cell responses. Several members are the surface molecules by which these cells are recognised and by which they capture antigen: the high-affinity IgE receptor alpha chain FCER1A, and the C-type lectins CLEC10A and CLEC5A, which bind glycans on pathogens and damaged cells and feed signals into innate activation. Lysosomal cathepsins B and L supply the proteolysis needed to process internalised antigen for presentation and to mature invariant chain, while DAB2 supports endocytic uptake and CAPG remodels actin during migration and phagocytosis. Others contribute cytokine responsiveness through IL1R1, Notch ligand signalling to lymphocytes via JAG1, and metabolic support for activation. The set is useful chiefly for identifying and quantifying this lineage in tissue and blood.

Hox cluster IV is a set of homeodomain transcription factors from the HOXA and HOXB clusters that assign positional identity along the head-to-tail axis of the developing embryo. Their nested, colinear expression domains tell cells in the paraxial mesoderm, neural tube and limb bud where they are, and thereby which vertebral, rib, hindbrain or skeletal structure to build; loss or ectopic expression produces homeotic shifts in vertebral formulae and limb malformations. Central members such as HOXA5, HOXB4 and HOXB5 also pattern the respiratory and gut tube, while posterior genes including HOXA9, HOXB9 and HOXA11 specify lumbosacral segments and the distal limb, and govern hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal. Retinoic acid and CDX signals set their boundaries, and Polycomb and Trithorax complexes maintain them; misregulated posterior HOXA activity drives acute leukemias.

Hox genes encode homeodomain transcription factors that assign positional identity along the head-to-tail axis of the embryo, and this grouping draws on members of the A and B clusters spanning middle to posterior paralogue groups. Their nested, colinear expression domains tell cells in the paraxial mesoderm, neural tube and lateral plate which segment they occupy, so that vertebrae, limb segments, and hindbrain rhombomeres form in the right order. Loss or misexpression shifts structures to the identity of a neighbouring segment; in humans, HOXA11 mutation disrupts radius and ulna development and kidney formation, while several of these genes are also active in haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, where HOXA9 misregulation by chromosomal translocation drives leukaemia. Retinoic acid signalling and chromatin-level repression by Polycomb complexes set and maintain the boundaries of these expression domains during development.

enriched for TF motif TTCNRGNNNNTTC groups genes that share an upstream inverted nGAAn-repeat element of the kind read by heat shock factors, and the genes themselves form a coherent stress-and-injury response program rather than a metabolic route. They are classic immediate-early and inducible transcripts: FOSB and the zinc-finger EGR3 with the orphan nuclear receptor NR4A3 provide rapid transcriptional output, CXCL3 recruits neutrophils, EDN1 constricts vessels, and PLAU drives pericellular proteolysis for matrix remodelling and cell migration. Together they describe how cells respond within minutes to proteotoxic, inflammatory or mechanical stress by remodelling their transcriptome, signalling to the immune system, and altering vascular tone and tissue architecture. PHLDA2 and GJB2 add growth-restraining and gap-junction components, tying the program to wound healing, placental and epithelial biology, and to the inflammatory activation that accompanies tumour invasion.

Genes grouped by a shared upstream promoter element, TTCNRGNNNNTTC, an inverted repeat of TTC/GAA half-sites of the kind recognised by heat shock factors and related inverted-repeat binding transcription factors. The members are dominated by immediate-early and stress-responsive transcripts: the activator protein-1 component FOSB and the nuclear receptor-family factors EGR3 and NR4A3 are themselves transcription factors induced within minutes of growth factor, cytokine or stress stimulation, while endothelin-1, the chemokine CXCL3 and the plasminogen activator PLAU are secreted effectors that drive vasoconstriction, neutrophil recruitment and extracellular matrix proteolysis. PHLDA2 and GJB2 add imprinted growth regulation and gap-junction coupling to the collection. As a motif-defined group rather than a curated mechanism, its value is as a hypothesis about shared upstream control, linking rapid transcriptional responses to inflammation, wound repair and vascular tone.

This pathway describes the surface receptors and survival machinery of circulating mononuclear leukocytes — monocytes and T lymphocytes — and the transcriptional programme that tunes their inflammatory responsiveness. Chemokine receptors CCR2 and CX3CR1 define the two major monocyte subsets and direct their exit from marrow and patrolling of the endothelium, making this biology the entry point for macrophage recruitment into inflamed tissue and atherosclerotic plaque. The GIMAP GTPases, expressed in lymphocytes, set the threshold for apoptosis and thereby peripheral T cell persistence. Signalling input arrives through the IL-1 receptor accessory protein and the TWEAK receptor TNFRSF12A, and is resolved by the immediate-early nuclear receptor NR4A3 and the MAP kinase phosphatase DUSP4, which restrains ERK and JNK output. Accompanying KRAB zinc-finger proteins, the transcriptional repressor HIC1 and the metabolic coactivator PPARGC1B shape the differentiated state, linking innate immune activation to mitochondrial and lipid metabolism.

A mixed immune-expression module centred on mononuclear leukocyte identity and trafficking, combining chemokine receptors, GTPase-of-immunity-associated proteins and transcriptional regulators. Monocyte and macrophage recruitment to inflamed tissue depends on CCR2 and CX3CR1, whose ligands direct patrolling and infiltrating cells to vessel walls and injured sites; loss of this axis blunts inflammatory monocyte egress from bone marrow and reshapes atherosclerotic and neuroinflammatory disease. The GIMAP proteins act in lymphocyte survival and homeostasis, linking the set to T cell persistence as well as myeloid function. Signalling and feedback components include the IL-1 receptor accessory protein required for interleukin-1 responses, the MAPK phosphatase DUSP4 that dampens kinase output, the TNF-family receptor FN14, and the immediate-early factor NR4A3. Numerous KRAB-type zinc finger proteins and the repressor HIC1 suggest accompanying transcriptional control, alongside metabolic and autophagy-related members.

This gene set centres on monocyte identity and chemotactic control of myeloid trafficking, the process that determines which circulating phagocytes leave the blood and where they go. CCR2 and CX3CR1 together define the two principal monocyte subsets: CCR2-high classical monocytes recruited to inflamed tissue in response to MCP-1, and CX3CR1-high patrolling monocytes that crawl the endothelium and give rise to resident macrophages and microglia. Loss of this axis blunts inflammatory recruitment in atherosclerosis, infection and neuroinflammation, while its overactivity drives chronic tissue damage. Accompanying immediate-early and orphan nuclear receptor transcription factors such as FOSL1 and NR4A3 provide the rapid transcriptional response downstream of chemokine and stress signalling, and a group of zinc-finger regulators, an immune-associated GTPase and cytoskeletal tropomodulin link this program to sustained gene control and the motility machinery migration requires.

Circulating monocytes find their way into tissue by reading chemokine gradients, and the two receptors that anchor this group, CCR2 and CX3CR1, are the pair that defines the classical and non-classical monocyte subsets and governs their recruitment to inflamed vessel walls, injured tissue and the brain, where they become macrophages or microglia. Loss or blockade of this axis limits atherosclerotic plaque myeloid influx and blunts inflammatory infiltration, which is why it is a longstanding drug target. Alongside the receptors sit immediate-early transcriptional responses, with the AP-1 component FOSL1 and the orphan nuclear receptor NR4A3 coupling receptor engagement to changes in gene expression that set monocyte activation state and survival. Additional zinc-finger factors and the immune-associated GTPase-like GIMAP6 suggest accompanying transcriptional and lymphoid-myeloid regulatory control rather than chemotaxis alone.

T cell differentiation via ITK and PKC describes the proximal signalling that converts antigen receptor engagement into T cell fate decisions, determining whether a thymocyte survives selection and which effector program a mature T cell adopts. It matters because these components set the threshold for activation: loss of ITK impairs helper T cell responses and causes an immunodeficiency with susceptibility to Epstein-Barr virus, and loss of the related adaptor SH2D1A produces X-linked lymphoproliferative disease. Mechanistically, ITK acts downstream of the T cell receptor to activate phospholipase C, generating diacylglycerol that recruits the T lineage-restricted kinases PRKCQ and PRKCH to the immunological synapse and drives transcription factors such as ETS1. Downstream outputs include BCL2-dependent survival and FASLG-mediated killing and activation-induced death, linking receptor signal strength to clonal expansion, contraction and tolerance.

T cell receptor engagement must be converted into decisions about survival, lineage identity and effector function, and the kinases ITK and the T cell-enriched protein kinase C isoforms sit at that conversion point. ITK is a Tec-family tyrosine kinase recruited to the activated receptor complex, where it drives phospholipase C-gamma activity and the calcium and diacylglycerol signals that follow; PRKCQ and PRKCH then read the diacylglycerol arm and feed NF-kB and AP-1 activation at the immunological synapse. The transcription factor ETS1 and the anti-apoptotic regulator BCL2 shape how thymocytes and peripheral T cells survive and commit to a lineage, while FASLG equips effector cells to kill and to be removed by activation-induced cell death. SH2D1A couples SLAM-family receptors into the same signalling network, and its loss causes X-linked lymphoproliferative disease; defective ITK signalling likewise produces combined immunodeficiency with poor control of Epstein-Barr virus.

muscle contraction, SRF targets describes the smooth muscle contractile program driven by serum response factor and its coactivator myocardin, the transcriptional switch that converts a mesenchymal cell into a differentiated, contractile smooth muscle cell. This program gives blood vessels, gut, bladder and airway their tone; when it is switched off, smooth muscle cells dedifferentiate into the proliferative, synthetic state that drives atherosclerotic plaque formation, restenosis and vascular remodelling. The genes are the structural output of that switch: smooth muscle myosin heavy chain and gamma-actin form the contractile apparatus, calponin, leiomodin and PGM5 organise and regulate the actin cytoskeleton, desmin builds the intermediate filament lattice, and phospholamban tunes calcium reuptake and therefore relaxation. Myocardin itself is included, since the pathway is self-reinforcing: actin dynamics feed back on SRF cofactor availability, coupling cytoskeletal state to contractile gene expression.

Smooth muscle cells maintain a contractile phenotype through a transcriptional program driven by serum response factor together with its muscle-restricted coactivator myocardin, and the genes here are the output of that program. They encode the contractile apparatus and its regulators: smooth muscle myosin heavy chain, gamma-actin, desmin, calponin, leiomodin and the calcium-handling modulator phospholamban, plus matrix and cytoskeletal components that couple force to surrounding tissue. Together they set the tone of blood vessels, airways, gut and bladder wall. Because actin polymerization itself releases the coactivators that license this transcription, the pathway acts as a feedback loop linking cytoskeletal state to contractile gene expression. Loss of the program underlies phenotypic switching of vascular smooth muscle toward proliferative, synthetic states in atherosclerosis and restenosis, while myocardin mutations impair visceral smooth muscle development.

These genes converge on myeloid and platelet regulation, the arm of innate immunity and haemostasis in which surface receptor engagement is translated into inflammatory gene expression or into control of cell activation. LYN, the Src-family kinase that both initiates and dampens signalling from immunoglobulin and integrin receptors, together with the myeloid-restricted membrane protein LST1 and the transcription factor CEBPB, marks the monocyte/macrophage and granulocyte programme: CEBPB drives acute-phase and cytokine responses and is required for emergency granulopoiesis. MRVI1 anchors the nitric-oxide/cGMP brake on platelet calcium release, linking the set to inhibition of aggregation, while PDLIM7 and CPPED1 act on actin cytoskeletal and phosphatase-dependent remodelling that accompanies activation. Additional members contribute membrane phospholipid synthesis, autophagic trafficking, tRNA splicing and nuclear export, the housekeeping capacity such secretory, high-turnover cells depend on. Dysregulation here shifts the balance toward chronic inflammation or thrombosis.

These genes converge on myeloid and platelet function, where surface signalling is translated into changes in the actin cytoskeleton and in gene expression. The Src-family kinase LYN sits at the top of immunoreceptor and integrin signalling in leukocytes and platelets, setting both activating and inhibitory tone, while LST1 is an immune-cell transmembrane protein that shapes membrane protrusions and cell-cell contact. MRVI1 couples nitric oxide-driven cGMP signalling to inhibition of calcium release from intracellular stores, a brake on platelet activation. CEBPB provides the transcriptional arm, driving inflammatory and granulocyte-macrophage differentiation programmes, and PDLIM7 and XPO6 act on actin organisation, the latter exporting actin from the nucleus. Also represented are phospholipid synthesis, autophagy-related trafficking and tRNA splicing activities that support these cells, making the group a mixture of activation signalling, cytoskeletal control and housekeeping capacity.

antigen processing and presentation is how cells display fragments of proteins and lipids on their surface so that T cells can inspect them, the step that lets the adaptive immune system distinguish self from pathogen. Without it, helper T cells are never primed, antibody responses fail, and tumour or microbial antigens go unseen. The genes centre on the MHC class II arm: HLA-DP and HLA-DQ heterodimers load peptides in the endosomal compartment of dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, while the HLA-DM chaperone catalyses removal of the placeholder CLIP peptide and edits the repertoire toward stable, high-affinity ligands. CD1D extends the same logic to lipid antigens recognised by invariant NKT cells, and WDFY4 is required for cross-presentation of cell-associated antigen by conventional dendritic cells to CD8 T cells. Variation here dominates genetic risk for autoimmune disease.

Immune surveillance depends on cells displaying fragments of what they have encountered, and this pathway covers the loading and surface display of antigen for recognition by T cells. The class II molecules here, including HLA-DP and HLA-DQ chains, present peptides taken up from outside the cell to CD4 helper T cells, an event that licenses antibody responses and macrophage activation; the HLA-DM heterodimer acts as a peptide-exchange catalyst in the endosomal loading compartment, releasing the invariant chain remnant and editing bound peptides for stability. CD1D instead presents lipid antigens to invariant natural killer T cells, and WDFY4 is required in dendritic cells for cross-presentation of cell-associated antigen to cytotoxic CD8 T cells. Variation in these loci underlies much of the genetic risk for autoimmune disease and shapes transplant compatibility, while loss of presentation lets tumours and intracellular pathogens escape detection.

Wnt signaling pathway refers to the intercellular signalling system that tells cells where they sit in a tissue, whether to divide, and which fate to adopt, and it governs stem cell maintenance, skeletal and neural patterning, and wound repair; its dysregulation drives fibrosis and cancer. The genes here emphasise extracellular tuning and mesenchymal output rather than the core destruction complex: secreted frizzled-related proteins FRZB and SFRP4 sequester Wnt ligands to set the strength and range of the signal, PDZRN3 acts as a ubiquitin ligase modulating receptor traffic and planar polarity, and YAP1 links the pathway to Hippo-dependent growth control. Matrix and guidance components such as LAMC1, LOXL2, NRP1 and CHL1, together with CXCL12 and KITLG, place this activity in the niche where migrating and differentiating cells read positional cues, with SOX4 carrying transcriptional output.

Wnt signalling tells cells where they are and what to become, controlling stem and progenitor self-renewal, body axis and limb patterning, bone mass and the mesenchymal programmes of tissue repair; its persistent activation drives cancers, while loss of tone in bone and cartilage contributes to degenerative disease. The genes here emphasise the extracellular and matrix-facing side of the pathway rather than the nuclear core: FRZB and SFRP4 are secreted Frizzled-related decoys that bind Wnt ligands and dampen receptor engagement, while laminin, LOXL2-dependent collagen crosslinking and adhesion molecules such as CHL1 and NRP1 shape the environment through which the ligand gradient is read. PDZRN3, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, tunes Wnt receptor and planar-polarity output, and SOX4 and the transcriptional coactivator YAP1 link the pathway to growth and cell-fate decisions downstream, alongside chemokine and growth-factor cues including CXCL12 and KITLG.

This pathway centers on control of cell shape, adhesion and directed migration through Rho-family GTPase signalling and actin nucleation, coupled to transcriptional programs that specify tissue identity. ARHGAP5 inactivates RhoA to loosen adhesion and permit motility, SCAI restrains invasive migration by repressing MT1-MMP transcription downstream of RhoA-mDia, and JMY acts both as an actin nucleator at the leading edge and as a p53 cofactor linking cytoskeletal remodelling to DNA damage responses. HACE1, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades active Rac1, suppresses tumour growth and reactive oxygen production, while TUBE1 seeds centriole assembly and thereby microtubule organisation. Homeodomain and NKX2-1 transcription factors impose regional and lung epithelial identity on these motile behaviours, and APP and CCL23 contribute adhesive and chemotactic cues. Together these activities govern morphogenesis, wound repair and the migratory steps that become tumour invasion when deregulated.

Cell migration and invasion are held in check by regulators that limit Rho-family GTPase activity and remodel the actin cytoskeleton, and several members here converge on that control point. ARHGAP5 accelerates GTP hydrolysis on RhoA, HACE1 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets active Rac1 for degradation, and SCAI restrains transcription-coupled invasion programmes, while JMY nucleates actin and also acts as a transcriptional cofactor for p53-dependent responses. Alongside these sit developmental transcription factors of the homeobox and NK2 families that specify regional and organ identity, notably NKX2-1 in thyroid and lung epithelium, plus APP and a chemokine ligand that influence adhesion and leukocyte recruitment. Taken together the grouping speaks to cytoskeletal and transcriptional restraint of motility and growth, biology whose loss contributes to tumour invasion and metastasis.

lysosome is the cell's acidic degradative compartment and the hydrolase set that works inside it, breaking down proteins, glycans and lipids delivered by endocytosis, phagocytosis and autophagy so their building blocks can be recycled. Its capacity matters most in macrophages and other phagocytes, where CD68 marks the lysosomal membrane and cathepsins B, L and Z digest ingested material and process antigens; it also matters in neurons, where failure of these enzymes produces storage disease. The genes cover the main functional classes: cysteine protease hydrolases, glycosidases such as alpha-L-fucosidase and glucosamine-6-sulfatase that dismantle glycoconjugates and glycosaminoglycans, the lipid-hydrolase activators prosaposin and GM2 activator protein, and sortilin, a sorting receptor that traffics newly made hydrolases from the Golgi to the lysosome. Together they link membrane turnover and nutrient recovery to immune function.

Lysosomes are the acidic degradative compartment where proteins, glycans and lipids delivered by endocytosis, phagocytosis and autophagy are broken down and their building blocks returned to the cell. The genes here cover both the hydrolases and the machinery that supports them: cathepsins B, L, V and Z carry out bulk proteolysis, fucosidase and glucuronidase-type glycosidases trim sugar chains, and prosaposin and the GM2 activator protein act as lipid-transfer cofactors that present sphingolipid substrates to their enzymes. Sortilin sorts newly made hydrolases and other cargo from the Golgi toward this compartment, while CD68 is a heavily glycosylated lysosomal membrane protein used as a marker of macrophages and other highly phagocytic cells. Loss of single hydrolases or their activators causes lysosomal storage disease, with undigested substrate accumulating and neurodegeneration a frequent consequence.

Small GTPase mediated signal transduction is the switch-like relay by which Ras-superfamily GTPases convert receptor signals into changes in cytoskeletal shape, adhesion and motility. The genes here describe a specifically hematopoietic version of that relay, built around Rho-family members RAC2, RHOG and RHOH: the exchange factors VAV1 and FGD3 load them with GTP downstream of antigen and integrin receptors, while a large complement of RhoGAPs and the dissociation inhibitors ARHGDIA/ARHGDIB terminate and spatially confine the signal. This balance sets the timing of lymphocyte activation, leukocyte migration and phagocyte NADPH oxidase assembly; loss of RAC2 or VAV1 function produces immunodeficiency with defective T cell signalling and neutrophil chemotaxis. Because activation is transient by design, the abundance of negative regulators is the point rather than an accessory feature, and their disruption drives unchecked motility and invasion.

Small GTPase mediated signal transduction converts receptor engagement into changes in the actin cytoskeleton, cell shape, adhesion and directed movement, and the genes here represent the Rho-family arm of that switching system as it operates in leukocytes. Rac2, RhoG and RhoH cycle between GDP- and GTP-bound states; a nucleotide exchange factor such as VAV1 loads GTP downstream of immune receptor signalling, while numerous Rho GTPase-activating proteins accelerate GTP hydrolysis to terminate the signal, and the guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors ARHGDIA and ARHGDIB sequester inactive GTPases in the cytosol. The balance of these opposing regulators sets how much and how long a cell can polarise, spread, phagocytose or migrate. Loss of RAC2 or VAV1 function compromises neutrophil chemotaxis, lymphocyte activation and immune synapse formation, and dysregulated Rho signalling contributes to invasive behaviour in cancer cells.

metabolism of steroids covers the enzymatic modification and disposal of steroid hormones and related lipophilic compounds, the step that terminates hormone action and allows androgens, estrogens and bile acid derivatives to be excreted in urine and bile. The dominant activity here is glucuronidation: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases of the UGT2A and UGT2B families conjugate glucuronic acid onto steroid hydroxyl groups, converting them into water-soluble products that no longer bind nuclear receptors. UGT2B15 and UGT2B17 act on testosterone and dihydrotestosterone metabolites, so their activity sets androgen tone in liver and prostate, and copy-number loss of UGT2B17 is a well-known source of variation in androgen clearance and drug metabolism. The remaining members point to the tissues where this chemistry happens — renal tubular and biliary epithelium, represented by PKHD1, HAVCR1 and myo-inositol oxygenase — linking steroid inactivation to excretory organ function and to xenobiotic detoxification more broadly.

Steroid hormones are cleared and inactivated as well as made, and this grouping centres on that disposal arm of steroid metabolism. Several UDP-glucuronosyltransferases of the UGT2B family attach glucuronic acid to hydroxysteroids, converting androgens and their metabolites into water-soluble conjugates that can be excreted in urine and bile; UGT2B15 and UGT2B17 are the main routes for testosterone and dihydrotestosterone, so their common deletion and coding polymorphisms shift circulating androgen levels and influence prostate biology and drug clearance. A related transferase acting on similar lipophilic substrates broadens the range of steroids and xenobiotics handled. The remaining members point to kidney and epithelial context, including a fibrocystin-encoding gene mutated in polycystic kidney disease, a kidney injury marker, an inositol oxygenase, a glycosyltransferase and a kinase, consistent with hormone conjugation occurring in liver and in the epithelia that complete excretion.

respiratory electron transport chain (mitochondrion) is the oxidative phosphorylation machinery of the inner mitochondrial membrane, the route by which electrons stripped from NADH and succinate are passed to oxygen and the energy released is captured as ATP. Nearly all aerobic ATP production depends on it, and loss of individual subunits causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, lactic acidosis and Leigh syndrome, with tissues of high energy demand such as brain, heart and muscle affected first. The genes span the chain from end to end: multiple accessory and core subunits of complex I, the Rieske iron-sulfur protein of complex III, a cytochrome c oxidase subunit, and subunits of the ATP synthase that converts the resulting proton gradient into chemical energy. Assembly is coordinated between nuclear and mitochondrial genomes, and the same electron flow is the principal cellular source of reactive oxygen species.

Oxidative phosphorylation is how most ATP in aerobic cells is made, and this is the mitochondrial inner-membrane machinery that does it: electrons stripped from NADH pass along the respiratory chain to oxygen while protons are pumped across the membrane, and the resulting gradient drives ATP synthesis. The genes here span several of the complexes involved — numerous accessory and core subunits of complex I (including NDUFS3, NDUFA8 and the acyl carrier subunit NDUFAB1), the iron-sulfur subunit of complex III, a cytochrome c oxidase subunit, and subunits of the F1Fo ATP synthase. Tissues with high energy demand depend most heavily on this chain, and mutations in its subunits or their assembly factors cause mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, Leigh syndrome and optic neuropathies. The same electron flow is a principal source of reactive oxygen species, tying respiration to redox signalling and to apoptotic commitment.

transcription elongation, RNA polymerase II covers the productive phase of messenger RNA synthesis, in which polymerase II, having cleared the promoter, moves processively along the gene body to complete a full-length transcript. Rates of elongation set how quickly genes respond to stimuli and influence co-transcriptional splicing and termination, so defects here distort gene expression programmes broadly. The core here is the shared small subunits of the polymerase itself — POLR2E, POLR2I, POLR2J and POLR2L, which also serve RNA polymerases I and III — together with elongin B (TCEB2), a subunit of the elongin complex that suppresses transient pausing and, in a separate role, forms part of the VHL ubiquitin ligase. Accompanying mitochondrial respiratory subunits and small redox and iron-trafficking proteins link the transcriptional output to the energetic and metabolic state of the cell.

Once RNA polymerase II has initiated at a promoter, productive mRNA synthesis depends on it moving processively through the gene body, and the elongation step is where most regulation of transcript output is exerted. Several shared small subunits of the polymerase core, including POLR2E, POLR2I, POLR2J and POLR2L, hold the enzyme together and provide surfaces for elongation and termination factors, while elongin B (TCEB2) acts as the regulatory partner of the elongin complex, which stimulates the rate of elongation and is also the substrate-recognition module co-opted by the von Hippel-Lindau ubiquitin ligase. Failure of processive elongation stalls polymerase, promotes premature termination and distorts gene expression programmes. The remaining members are small respiratory chain and mitochondrial ribosome-associated proteins, tying transcriptional output to the energetic state of the cell rather than to the polymerase machinery itself.

cell activation (IL15, IL23, TNF) describes the inflammatory activation state of myeloid and stromal cells, in which pro-inflammatory cytokines are induced together with the NF-κB machinery that drives them and the brakes that limit them. This program mobilises innate and T cell responses — IL15 sustains NK and memory CD8 T cells, IL23 supports Th17 responses, and TNF amplifies local inflammation — and its unchecked persistence underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, which is why these cytokines are major drug targets. The gene complement captures the feedback logic as much as the output: NFKB2 and BCL3 shape late transcriptional responses, MAP3K8 relays signals toward cytokine production, and TNFAIP3 terminates NF-κB to prevent runaway signalling. Accompanying matrix and acute-phase components (FN1, COL3A1, SERPING1, A2M, TF) place the response in a tissue remodelling and wound-healing context, alongside CD83 marking activated antigen-presenting cells.

Inflammatory cell activation driven by the cytokines IL-15, IL-23 and TNF, a module that links innate stimulation to sustained NF- induced gene expression and to the tissue changes that accompany chronic inflammation. IL-15 supports natural killer and memory T cell survival, IL-23 sustains IL-17-producing T cells, and TNF amplifies both, so this combination underlies the cytokine networks targeted therapeutically in psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis. Signal relay runs through MAP3K8 to the MAP kinase cascade and through NFKB2, with BCL3, TNFAIP3 and SBNO2 acting as feedback restraints that limit how long activation persists; loss of such brakes predisposes to autoimmunity. Alongside these, CD83 marks activated dendritic cells, while fibronectin, collagen III, PDGFRA and acute-phase products such as A2M, SERPING1 and transferrin reflect the stromal remodelling and systemic response that follow prolonged activation.

chromosome Y linked collects genes carried on the male-specific portion of the Y chromosome, together with their X-linked counterparts, and it defines the small set of protein-coding functions unique to male cells. Its significance is twofold: these genes underlie spermatogenesis and male fertility, and their loss from blood cells with age is associated with cancer risk and cardiovascular disease. Several members are X-Y gene pairs that escaped degeneration and act in housekeeping roles -- the RNA helicase DDX3Y, the deubiquitinase USP9Y, and the histone demethylases KDM5D and UTY, which link Y-linked dosage to chromatin regulation and transcription. Deletions in this region cause azoospermia. The set also includes noncoding RNAs of sex chromosome regulation, notably XIST and its antisense partner, which govern X inactivation and thereby the broader problem of balancing sex chromosome gene dosage between males and females.

Genes carried on the male-specific portion of the Y chromosome, together with their X-linked counterparts, define the sex-chromosome dosage differences between male and female cells. Because the Y escapes the silencing that inactivates one X in females, its surviving genes are expressed from a single copy in males only, and several are ubiquitously transcribed housekeeping factors rather than testis-specific ones: an RNA helicase, a deubiquitinase, and the chromatin regulators that remove or read histone methylation marks, each with a closely related X-encoded paralogue. Others are restricted to germ cells and underlie spermatogenesis, so deletions of Y intervals produce azoospermia and male infertility, while age-related loss of the Y in blood cells is linked to cancer and cardiovascular risk. The presence of X-inactivation regulators here marks the counterpart process that balances expression from the other sex chromosome.

This grouping centres on a primate-specific gene family and the housekeeping functions that sit alongside it. The TBC1D3 paralogues, expanded by segmental duplication in the human lineage, encode Rab GTPase-activating domain proteins that act on endosomal trafficking and growth factor receptor recycling, amplifying signalling through the EGF receptor and insulin pathways, and their overexpression is oncogenic and has been linked to expansion of cortical progenitor pools during brain development. Other members reach into unrelated but broadly used processes: an HSP90 co-chaperone-like ATPase regulator supporting protein folding, a cyclin L family member that partners with CDK11 in pre-mRNA splicing, and a deadenylase complex subunit that trims poly(A) tails to control mRNA turnover. The calcitonin/CGRP locus contributes peptide hormones governing calcium handling and vasodilation, so the collection spans membrane traffic, RNA metabolism and endocrine signalling.

This is a heterogeneous grouping rather than a coherent signalling route, and the biology it points to is best read gene by gene. Several members are primate-specific TBC1D3 paralogues, products of a hominoid-expanded segmental duplication that carry a Rab-GAP-like domain, localise to endosomal membranes and modulate growth factor receptor trafficking and macropinocytosis; their amplification has been linked to transforming activity. CALCA encodes the precursor for calcitonin and CGRP, hormones that lower blood calcium and drive potent vasodilation and nociceptive signalling. PAN2 is the catalytic subunit of the Pan2-Pan3 deadenylase that trims mRNA poly(A) tails during the first phase of mRNA turnover, while CCNL2 is a cyclin-like partner of CDK11 acting in pre-mRNA splicing, so RNA processing and decay form one recognisable thread. AHSA2 is a co-chaperone-family relative of Hsp90 activators, with additional uncharacterised loci also included.</description>

These genes converge on the control of gene expression downstream of growth and stress signalling, linking receptor-proximal regulators to the transcriptional machinery and to the ubiquitin system that limits how long transcription factors persist. CREBBP and MED1 act as coactivators bridging DNA-bound factors to RNA polymerase II, REL carries NF- inkB-family transcriptional output, DYRK1A phosphorylates transcriptional and splicing substrates, and FBXW7 targets short-lived activators such as MYC, cyclin E and NOTCH for proteasomal destruction, setting the amplitude and duration of the response. RASA2 restrains Ras signalling, MAP3K2 feeds kinase cascades into it, and the sorting nexins and ACAP2 govern endosomal traffic and Arf-dependent membrane remodelling that determine where signalling receptors go. Dosage sensitivity in this circuitry underlies neurodevelopmental disorders with intellectual disability, and its loss of restraint is a recurrent route to tumour growth.

These genes converge on the braking and tuning of growth-factor signalling as it feeds into transcription, a control layer whose loss produces overgrowth, cancer and neurodevelopmental disease. Two GTPase-activating proteins, RASA2 for Ras and ACAP2 for an Arf-family GTPase, terminate signalling at the membrane, while MAP3K2 relays kinase input downstream and sorting nexins SNX13 and SNX14 govern endosomal trafficking and receptor fate. In the nucleus, the CREBBP acetyltransferase and the Mediator subunit MED1 couple activated signals to RNA polymerase II, and the NF-kappaB family member REL drives inflammatory and lymphoid transcription. Degradative and phosphorylation-based control comes from the FBXW7 ubiquitin ligase substrate receptor, which destroys short-lived growth regulators, and the DYRK1A kinase; STRN3 links the module to striatin-containing phosphatase complexes and Hippo pathway output. Many members are recurrently mutated in developmental disorders and tumours.

enriched in nuclear pore complex interacting proteins points to the nuclear pore-interacting protein family, a primate-expanded group encoded in duplicated segments of chromosome 16 whose members associate with the nucleoporin scaffold that gates traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm. Nuclear pore complexes control the export of mRNA and ribosomal subunits and the import of transcription factors, so proteins docking at the pore influence how quickly regulatory signals reach chromatin. The set is dominated by NPIP-like genes and uncharacterised loci arising from the same low-copy repeats, alongside unrelated genes such as the pluripotency RNA-binding factor LIN28A, the histamine receptor HRH4 and the T helper 17 cytokine IL17A, reflecting the copy-number-variable, segmentally duplicated genomic neighbourhoods these sequences occupy rather than a single coherent biochemical route.

Nuclear pore complex interacting proteins are a primate-expanded family encoded near segmental duplications on human chromosome 16, and the grouping here is built around them together with a scattering of other loci. The NPIP-related members associate with the nucleoporin scaffold that forms the gateway between nucleus and cytoplasm, the channel through which mRNA, ribosomal subunits and transcription factors pass and through which nucleocytoplasmic traffic is regulated; their duplication history makes them useful markers of recent genome rearrangement rather than of a single defined biochemical step. The remaining members belong to unrelated processes — LIN28A is an RNA-binding regulator of let-7 microRNA maturation and stem cell self-renewal, IL17A a T cell cytokine driving mucosal inflammation, HRH4 a histamine receptor on immune cells — so the set is best read as a duplication-defined locus group with limited shared function.

This grouping centres on genome maintenance and the division machinery that protects it, linking interstrand crosslink repair to mitotic microtubule organisation and ubiquitin-dependent control of proliferation. Two of its members, FAAP100 and FAAP20, are accessory subunits of the Fanconi anaemia core complex, the E3 ligase assembly that monoubiquitinates FANCD2/FANCI at stalled replication forks; loss of this activity produces chromosome breakage, bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition. Alongside them sit regulators of the same cellular decisions from other angles: E4F1, an atypical ubiquitin ligase and transcription factor that couples p53 to cell-cycle arrest and mitochondrial metabolism; FBXL15, an SCF substrate adaptor; and SSNA1 and RASSF7, centrosomal and microtubule-associated proteins required for orderly spindle assembly. TBL3 adds ribosome biogenesis, tying growth capacity to the same proliferative checkpoints.

This grouping brings together proteins that have in common little more than a shared place in interaction screens, yet several of them converge on mitotic and genome-maintenance functions. SSNA1 is a microtubule-associated protein that promotes filament branching and localises to centrosomes and the midbody, and RASSF7 is likewise a centrosomal Ras-association domain protein required for orderly spindle formation and mitotic entry. Ubiquitin-dependent control is represented by E4F1, an atypical E3 ligase and transcription factor that acts on p53 and couples cell-cycle progression to metabolism, and by FBXL15, a substrate-recognition subunit of an SCF-type ligase. FAAP100 (C17orf70) belongs to the Fanconi anaemia core complex that ubiquitinates FANCD2 during interstrand crosslink repair, while TBL3 is a WD-repeat factor in small-subunit ribosome biogenesis. Together they mark proliferation-linked processes: spindle assembly, protein turnover, DNA crosslink repair and ribosome production.

These genes converge on white adipocyte biology and the endocrine control of fat storage. Adipose tissue must buffer nutrient excess by packaging triglyceride into lipid droplets and simultaneously report its own mass to the brain; failure of either function produces lipodystrophy, insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia. Leptin is the signal that adipose tissue sends to hypothalamic circuits regulating appetite and energy expenditure, while CIDEC and PLIN4 act at the droplet surface, driving droplet fusion and unilocular droplet formation and restraining lipolysis — loss of CIDEC causes partial lipodystrophy with multilocular adipocytes. CD300LG contributes to endothelial lipid handling and triglyceride clearance, TIMP4 restrains matrix metalloproteinases during adipose tissue remodelling, and heparan sulfate modification by HS2ST1 shapes lipoprotein and growth factor capture. Together the set describes adipocyte differentiation, lipid droplet architecture and systemic metabolic signalling.

These genes converge on the fat cell as a lipid-storing endocrine organ. Leptin is the adipocyte-derived hormone that reports fat mass to hypothalamic circuits controlling appetite and energy expenditure, and its loss causes severe hyperphagic obesity. CIDEC and PLIN4 act at the lipid droplet surface, the former promoting droplet fusion into the single large droplet characteristic of white adipocytes and the latter coating droplets to govern access by lipases; mutations in CIDEC cause partial lipodystrophy with insulin resistance. CD300LG is an endothelial transmembrane protein linked to triglyceride and HDL handling, TIMP4 restrains matrix metalloproteinases during adipose tissue remodelling, and HS2ST1 sulfates heparan sulfate chains that anchor lipases and growth factors to the cell surface. Together the group describes how triglyceride storage capacity, tissue expansion and metabolic signalling are coordinated, and how their failure produces dyslipidaemia and diabetes.

chemokine cluster (II) is the inflammatory chemoattractant program that recruits leukocytes out of the blood and into infected or damaged tissue. It determines which cells arrive and when: monocytes and memory T cells follow CCL2, CCL5 and CCL7 through CCR1 and CCR5, neutrophils follow CXCL5 and CXCL6, and the interferon-inducible ligands CXCL9, CXCL10 and CXCL11 draw activated Th1 cells and NK cells to sites of viral infection, while CXCL13 organises B cells into follicles and ectopic lymphoid tissue. Sustained expression of these ligands underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, tumour-associated myeloid infiltration, and, in the case of the CCR5 ligands, competition with HIV entry. Annexin A1 marks the counter-regulatory side, restraining leukocyte adhesion and promoting resolution, so the set spans both the drive and the braking of inflammatory cell traffic.

This is a coordinated inflammatory chemokine module: a set of secreted chemoattractants and two of their receptors that recruit monocytes, T cells, neutrophils and dendritic cells out of the blood and into inflamed tissue. Its output determines which leukocytes arrive where, and so shapes the character of an immune response towards acute neutrophilic inflammation, chronic mononuclear infiltration, or organised lymphoid aggregates. CCL2, CCL7 and the CCL4/CCL5 pair act through CCR1 and CCR5 on monocytes and effector T cells; the interferon-inducible CXCL9, CXCL10 and CXCL11 draw in activated Th1 cells; CXCL5 and CXCL6 mobilise neutrophils, CXCL13 organises B cell follicles, and CCL20 targets immature dendritic cells and mucosal lymphocytes. Annexin A1 supplies a counter-regulatory, pro-resolving brake. Sustained expression of these ligands drives atherosclerosis, rheumatoid synovitis and tumour-associated inflammation, and CCR5 doubles as an HIV entry coreceptor.

This pathway describes growth-factor signal transduction coupled to receptor endocytosis, the arm of cell signalling in which ligand-bound receptors are internalised and sorted so that the strength and duration of downstream kinase output is set rather than left to run unchecked. It matters for cell survival, proliferation and the cytostatic and fibrogenic responses to TGF-beta, and its imbalance underlies tumour growth and tissue fibrosis. The clathrin adaptor subunit AP2M1, the fission GTPase DNM2 and the ESCRT-0 component HGS carry cargo from the plasma membrane through endosomes toward degradation, while AKT1 with its co-chaperone CDC37 and the kinase PKN1 transmit the surviving signal; PPP2R1A supplies phosphatase-mediated damping and PSMD3 links the route to proteasomal turnover. Calcium- and lipid-binding proteins such as CPNE1 and NUCB1 tie membrane traffic to intracellular calcium, placing receptor fate at the intersection of trafficking and phosphorylation control.

This grouping centres on the coupling of clathrin-mediated receptor internalisation to intracellular kinase signalling, the step that determines how long a growth factor signal lasts and whether the receptor is recycled or degraded. Adaptor and scission components, including the AP-2 mu subunit and dynamin-2, capture cargo at the plasma membrane and pinch off vesicles, while the ESCRT-0 protein HGS sorts ubiquitinated receptors toward the lysosome. On the signalling side, AKT1 and the related kinase PKN1 transmit survival and cytoskeletal cues, CDC37 works with HSP90 to fold and stabilise client kinases, and the scaffolding subunit of protein phosphatase 2A opposes them by dephosphorylation. TGFB1 provides a ligand whose receptors are themselves controlled by endocytic trafficking. Together these activities set signal amplitude and duration, processes that when deregulated drive growth factor independence in cancer and fibrotic tissue remodelling.

inflammatory response is the coordinated reaction of innate immune cells to infection, tissue damage and modified self-molecules, producing the cytokine output and phagocytic clearance that contain a threat and then set the stage for repair.
