The genes here sit largely in the myeloid compartment: TLR4 senses bacterial lipopolysaccharide, CARD9 relays signals from C-type lectin and other pattern receptors to NF-κB, and FCER1G with its partner adaptor TYROBP couples immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs to Syk in macrophages, dendritic cells and microglia, where AIF1 marks activated states. Counterweights are present too — β-arrestin-2 dampens receptor signalling, glutathione peroxidase limits oxidative injury, and the scavenger receptor STAB1 clears modified lipoproteins and apoptotic debris. TNFSF13 links this innate activity to B cell help. Unrestrained, the same circuitry drives sepsis, atherosclerosis and chronic neuroinflammation.

The inflammatory response is the innate reaction to infection and tissue damage, in which myeloid cells detect microbial and host-derived signals, release cytokines, recruit further leukocytes, and then help resolve the reaction; too little leaves infection unchecked, too much drives chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease. The genes here are largely macrophage and dendritic-cell machinery: TLR4 senses bacterial lipopolysaccharide, CARD9 couples pattern-recognition receptors to NF- cebB-dependent cytokine transcription, and the TYROBP/FCER1G pair provides the ITAM-bearing signalling subunits shared by Fc and immunoreceptor-like receptors, with AIF1 marking activated microglia and macrophages. Counterbalancing elements are present too: arrestin beta 2 dampens receptor signalling, STAB1 is a scavenger receptor for clearance of damaged material, and glutathione peroxidase 1 limits oxidative damage from the respiratory burst. Together they span recognition, amplification, scavenging and restraint.

cytoskeletal remodeling (enriched for SRF targets) describes the contractile actin program that lets fibroblasts, smooth muscle and endothelial cells stiffen, spread, adhere and pull on their surroundings. It sets the contractile phenotype of vascular smooth muscle, drives wound closure and myofibroblast conversion, and when it runs unchecked it feeds fibrosis, vascular remodeling and tumor stroma stiffening. The members are the output of actin-MRTF-SRF signaling: filament stabilizers and crosslinkers such as tropomyosins, alpha-actinin and caldesmon, the focal adhesion protein vinculin, and myosin light chain kinase, which generates the actomyosin tension that in turn frees MRTF to sustain transcription. Secreted matrix components CTGF and thrombospondin-1 export the same program to the extracellular environment, coupling it to TGF-beta signaling, while lipid phosphatase and nuclear receptor components tune the upstream Rho and differentiation inputs. Mechanotransduction and gene expression are thereby locked in a feedback loop.

Cells that must generate or resist mechanical force keep a transcriptional programme on standby that rebuilds the actin cytoskeleton and its attachments, and this cytoskeletal remodeling module — dominated by targets of serum response factor and its actin-sensing MRTF coactivators — is that programme. Its output defines the contractile phenotype of smooth muscle cells, myofibroblasts and activated fibroblasts, and drives wound closure, vascular tone and, when sustained, fibrosis and tumour stroma stiffening. The genes encode the machinery itself rather than the signals: tropomyosins and caldesmon that tune actomyosin interaction, myosin light chain kinase that triggers contraction, alpha-actinin and vinculin that anchor filaments at focal adhesions, and secreted matrix regulators such as CTGF and thrombospondin-1 that feed force back through integrins. Because monomeric actin controls MRTF availability, the pathway is a feedback loop in which cytoskeletal state dictates its own reinforcement.

enriched in neutrophils (I) is a transcriptional signature of mature blood neutrophils, the first-responding phagocytes of innate immunity, and the genes in it define how those cells are recognised, mobilised and licensed to kill. Loss or dysfunction of these products underlies recurrent bacterial and fungal infection, while their excess drives the tissue damage of sepsis and chronic inflammation. The set is dominated by chemoattractant receptors that steer migration to infected tissue — formyl peptide receptors, the complement C5a receptor, interleukin-8 receptor CXCR1 and the platelet-activating factor receptor — alongside immunoglobulin Fc receptors that mediate opsonophagocytosis, the G-CSF receptor that governs granulopoiesis, and NCF4 of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase that generates the respiratory burst. Also present are granule and metabolic enzymes, short-chain fatty acid and niacin receptors sensing microbial metabolites, and inflammasome regulators such as NLRP12 that restrain the response.

This is a neutrophil-enriched expression signature: the genes it collects are the ones that distinguish circulating granulocytes from other blood leukocytes, and together they define how these cells are recruited, activated and armed for antimicrobial defence. Loss or dysregulation of this programme underlies impaired bacterial and fungal killing, while its overexpansion marks the inflammatory neutrophilia seen in sepsis and chronic inflammatory disease. Much of it is receptor machinery for danger sensing and chemotaxis — formyl peptide receptors, the C5a receptor, IL-8 receptor CXCR1, the platelet-activating factor receptor and short-chain fatty acid receptor FFAR2 — alongside Fc gamma receptors including the neutrophil-specific FCGR3B that drive opsonic phagocytosis, and the G-CSF receptor CSF3R that supports granulopoiesis. Additional members support the respiratory burst, leukotriene metabolism, glycogen and glycolytic fuelling, inflammasome regulation and lineage transcription, reflecting the metabolic and secretory specialisation of a short-lived effector cell.

cell division covers the machinery that duplicates a genome and partitions it faithfully into two daughter cells, the process underlying tissue growth, renewal and, when deregulated, tumour proliferation. The genes span the sequence of events: cyclin E driving the G1-to-S transition and licensing DNA replication, the BLM helicase and the nuclease partner CtIP resolving recombination intermediates and processing broken ends so that replication finishes without chromosome fusions, condensin subunits compacting sister chromatids into transportable rods, and spindle- and kinetochore-associated factors together with a nucleoporin that must be redeployed once the nuclear envelope breaks down. VRK1 kinase couples envelope disassembly and chromatin condensation to mitotic entry. Failure at any of these steps produces aneuploidy, micronuclei or mitotic arrest, and several components are hallmarks of proliferating cells used as markers of tumour growth fraction.

Cell division requires that a replicated genome be condensed, resolved into separate sister chromatids, and partitioned equally, and the genes here span those steps. Cyclin E with CDK2 drives the G1-to-S transition and licenses replication origins, setting the pace at which cells commit to a division cycle. Condensin subunits shape mitotic chromosomes, while the Bloom syndrome helicase and the CtIP nuclease cofactor resolve recombination intermediates and stalled forks so that entangled or broken DNA does not reach anaphase; loss of BLM causes chromosome instability and cancer predisposition. A microtubule-associated protein contributes to spindle function, a nucleoporin to nuclear envelope reassembly, and the VRK1 kinase to chromatin and envelope changes at mitotic entry and exit. Together these activities couple genome duplication and repair to accurate chromosome segregation, and their failure yields aneuploidy or proliferative arrest.

integrin mediated leukocyte migration describes how circulating white blood cells stick to blood vessel walls and crawl out of them into tissue, the step that delivers immune cells to sites of infection and inflammation. Without it leukocytes remain in the bloodstream and cannot mount local defence, the basis of leukocyte adhesion deficiency and recurrent bacterial infection; when it runs unchecked it drives the tissue infiltration of autoimmune disease, which is why blocking the α4 integrin is therapeutic in multiple sclerosis and inflammatory bowel disease. Mechanistically, integrins such as LFA-1 (ITGAL/ITGB2) and α4β1 engage endothelial counter-receptors including VCAM1, and inside-out activation converts chemokine and antigen receptor signals into high-affinity adhesion. The signalling module is lymphocyte-specific: TEC-family kinases ITK and TXK, PI3Kδ, PLCγ1, protein kinase Cβ and the Rho-family exchange factor VAV1 link receptor engagement to cytoskeletal remodelling and directed motility.

Leukocytes leave the bloodstream by gripping the inflamed endothelium and then crawling across it, and integrin-mediated leukocyte migration is the adhesion-and-motility step that makes this possible. Without it, immune cells circulate but cannot reach infected or injured tissue, the defect seen in leukocyte adhesion deficiency, where recurrent bacterial infection follows from failed extravasation. The pathway centres on the beta-2 integrin chain ITGB2 paired with ITGAL to form LFA-1, and on the alpha-4 integrin that binds endothelial VCAM-1; both must switch from a low- to a high-affinity conformation on cue. Antigen and chemokine receptors deliver that cue through Tec-family kinases ITK and TXK, PI3K delta, phospholipase C gamma and protein kinase C, with the Rho-family exchange factor VAV1 remodelling actin to generate traction. The same machinery is targeted therapeutically to block lymphocyte trafficking in multiple sclerosis and inflammatory bowel disease.

Rho GTPase cycle is the switching of Rho-family GTPases between active GTP-bound and inactive GDP-bound states, and here it is the mitotic face of that cycle: the spatial control of RhoA activity that positions and drives the cleavage furrow. Without it cells fail to complete cytokinesis, generating binucleate and aneuploid progeny. The centralspindlin components ECT2 and RACGAP1 pair a Rho activator with a Rho inactivator at the central spindle, where PRC1 crosslinks antiparallel microtubules and CEP55 recruits the abscission machinery to the midbody. Additional GAPs such as ARHGAP11A and ARHGAP19, together with DEPDC1 and DEPDC1B, restrict Rho signalling in time and space, while E2F2 links their expression to cell cycle entry. The whole module is a proliferation signature, and its genes are broadly overexpressed in aggressive tumours.

Rho family GTPases switch between GDP- and GTP-bound states, and the cycling itself — loading by exchange factors, inactivation by GTPase-activating proteins — is what converts signals into localized actomyosin contraction. The genes here tie that cycle to cell division: ECT2 is the exchange factor that activates RhoA at the equatorial cortex, while RACGAP1, its partner in the centralspindlin complex, provides GAP activity and helps position the cleavage furrow. PRC1 crosslinks antiparallel midzone microtubules and CEP55 recruits abscission machinery to the midbody, so the pathway spans furrow ingression through the final severing of the daughter cells. Several ARHGAP and DEPDC1 members add further inactivating or regulatory input, and E2F2 links the whole programme to S-phase entry. Loss of control here produces failed cytokinesis, binucleate cells and aneuploidy, and these genes are recurrently overexpressed in proliferative tumours.

mitotic cell cycle covers the machinery that drives a cell from DNA replication licensing through chromosome segregation and division, the process by which tissues grow, renew and repair themselves. Its control determines whether daughter cells inherit a correct genome; loss of that control produces aneuploidy and is a hallmark of tumours, which is why several of these components are drug targets. Mitotic entry is set by cyclin B/CDK1, held in check by the inhibitory kinases WEE1-family PKMYT1 and released by CDC25 phosphatases, with FOXM1 and E2F factors supplying the transcriptional wave of cyclins and mitotic kinases. Downstream, PLK1 and NEK2 organise centrosome separation and spindle assembly, PLK4 and the CEP proteins license centriole duplication, gamma-tubulin and CKAP5 build and stabilise spindle microtubules, and shugoshin protects centromeric cohesion until anaphase.

Somatic cells duplicate their chromosomes and partition them equally into two daughters, and this mitotic cell cycle module covers the commitment to division and the machinery that executes it. Getting it wrong produces aneuploidy, tetraploidy and the chromosomal instability that characterises tumours; sustained overexpression of these genes is one of the most consistent proliferation signatures in cancer tissue. Mitotic cyclins partnered with CDK1 drive entry into mitosis, opposed by the inhibitory kinases WEE1-family member PKMYT1 and reversed by CDC25 phosphatases that remove the restraining phosphates. FOXM1 supplies the transcriptional programme for the G2/M genes. Downstream, PLK1 and NEK2 coordinate spindle assembly and centrosome separation, PLK4 and centriolar proteins such as CEP152 license centriole duplication, gamma-tubulin nucleates microtubules, and shugoshin protects centromeric cohesion until anaphase.

complement and other receptors in DCs describes the surface sensing and antigen-presenting apparatus of dendritic cells and related myeloid antigen-presenting cells, the machinery by which they detect pathogens, tissue damage and dying cells and convert that detection into T cell activation. Its components span three jobs: local production of complement C1q subunits, which opsonise debris and apoptotic cells for clearance; innate pattern receptors such as TLR8 with its MD-2 cofactor and the scavenger receptor OLR1, which read microbial RNA and modified lipoproteins; and the CD11c integrin, SIRPA-TYROBP signalling module and MHC class II with CD86 and CD58, which together set the threshold for costimulation and adhesion at the immunological synapse. This combination defines dendritic cell identity in tissue transcriptomes and links innate recognition to the initiation of adaptive immunity, self-tolerance and clearance of immune complexes.

Dendritic cells sample tissue for pathogens and debris and then instruct T cells, and this receptor repertoire is what lets them do both jobs at once. Complement C1q, assembled from its A, B and C chains, binds immune complexes and apoptotic cell surfaces and marks them for uptake, while a scavenger receptor for oxidised lipoprotein and the LPS co-receptor MD-2 with endosomal TLR8 add recognition of modified self and of microbial nucleic acid. The output of that sensing is antigen presentation and costimulation: class II HLA-DQ molecules display peptide, CD86 and CD58 engage T cell CD28 and CD2. Complement receptor 2, the integrin chain CD11c, SIRP-alpha and the signalling adaptor TYROBP set adhesion, phagocytic threshold and the 'don't eat me' restraint imposed by CD47. Loss of C1q function predisposes to lupus-like autoimmunity, reflecting failed clearance of dying cells.

This pathway centers on neuronal differentiation and survival signaling, with a secondary thread of solute transport and stress defense. Neurotrophic and peptide cues dominate: pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide acts through cAMP to promote neuronal survival and neurosecretion, GFRA3 presents artemin to RET in sensory and sympathetic neurons, and ERBB4 receives neuregulin to shape interneuron migration and synapse formation. Downstream identity is set transcriptionally by POU4F2, which specifies retinal ganglion cells and sensory neurons, while GRID2 and TUBB4 support cerebellar Purkinje cell synapses and the microtubule cytoskeleton of axons; mutations in these cause ataxia and dystonia. Alongside, SLC7A11 imports cystine for glutathione synthesis and guards against ferroptosis, SLC17A1 handles phosphate and organic anion transport, and PEG3 links imprinted growth control to apoptotic signaling. Failure of these cues yields defective neural wiring and neurodegeneration.

The dominant theme here is neuronal specification and neurotrophic signalling, with several components that shape how developing neurons find their targets and survive. A secreted neuropeptide of the PACAP family acts through G protein-coupled receptors to promote neuronal survival and neuroendocrine responses to stress; a GDNF-family co-receptor transmits artemin signals in sensory and sympathetic neurons; ERBB4 receives neuregulin at synapses and in interneuron development; the delta-2 glutamate receptor subunit is a Purkinje cell synaptic organiser whose loss causes ataxia; and POU4F2 is the transcription factor that commits retinal ganglion cells to their fate. A beta-tubulin isotype supplies the microtubule lattice for axonal structure, and a cystine/glutamate antiporter links glutamate handling to glutathione synthesis and ferroptosis resistance. Other members, including an imprinted zinc-finger regulator, a Paneth cell defensin and a renal anion transporter, sit outside this neural core.

This pathway groups regulators of tissue patterning and secretory differentiation rather than a single metabolic route, centring on developmental transcription factors and receptor tyrosine kinases that shape epithelial and neural structures. TFAP2A and HOXC10 assign positional and lineage identity in neural crest, surface ectoderm and posterior axial tissues, while the imprinted regulator PEG3 links this control to growth and placental function. EPHB1 and ERBB4 transduce contact and neuregulin cues that guide axon targeting, cell sorting and epithelial morphogenesis, and NPR3 clears natriuretic peptides to set vascular tone and skeletal growth. Terminal specialised functions appear alongside: CYP11B1 completes cortisol synthesis in the adrenal cortex, DEFA5 provides Paneth cell antimicrobial defence in the small intestine, and dystrophin anchors the muscle membrane to its cytoskeleton. Loss of individual members produces craniofacial defects, adrenal steroid deficiency, or muscular dystrophy.

This is a heterogeneous grouping whose members share little beyond being tissue-restricted effectors and regulators of differentiated cell function, so it is best read as a composite of developmental patterning and organ-specific specialisation rather than a single mechanism. Transcriptional regulators dominate one side of it: TFAP2A directs neural crest and surface ectoderm derivatives such as craniofacial structures and epidermis, HOXC10 contributes positional identity along the posterior body axis, and the imprinted PEG3 acts in growth control and maternal behaviour. Receptor signalling makes up another arm, with the Eph receptor EPHB1 guiding axons and cell sorting and ERBB4 responding to neuregulins in neural and cardiac development, while NPR3 clears natriuretic peptides and thereby tunes blood pressure and skeletal growth. The remainder are terminal specialisations: dystrophin anchoring the muscle sarcolemma, CYP11B1 completing adrenal cortisol synthesis, and DEFA5 providing Paneth cell antimicrobial defence in the small intestine.

T cell signaling and costimulation covers the events by which a T cell converts antigen recognition into a decision to proliferate, differentiate, or remain quiescent, and the accessory inputs that set the threshold for that decision. It is what allows adaptive immunity to respond only to genuine antigen presentation; weakened signalling produces immunodeficiency, while unrestrained signalling drives autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation. The Src-family kinases LCK and FYN initiate phosphorylation at the engaged receptor, feeding into stress- and mitogen-activated kinase cascades through MAPK14, while cytoskeletal and adaptor proteins such as LCP1 and the Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor ARHGDIB reorganise the actin network at the contact site. Cytokine input via IL7R sustains survival and homeostatic expansion, TCF7 imposes the transcriptional programme of naive and memory states, and IL23A links the response to inflammatory T helper differentiation.

T cells commit to proliferation and differentiation only when antigen receptor engagement is accompanied by costimulatory and cytokine input, and this combination of signalling and costimulation sets the threshold for that decision. The genes here span the proximal kinases that initiate receptor signalling, LCK and FYN, which phosphorylate receptor chains and adaptors to launch downstream cascades; MAPK14 carries stress- and cytokine-driven signals into transcriptional responses. Survival and homeostatic cues arrive through the IL-7 receptor, indispensable for thymocyte development and peripheral T cell persistence, while IL23A supports inflammatory effector programmes. TCF7 acts in the transcriptional network that specifies T cell identity and sustains stem-like memory states. Cytoskeletal and membrane organisers such as LCP1, ARHGDIB and the tetraspanin CD37 shape the immune synapse and adhesion. Loss of these inputs produces immunodeficiency; their excess drives autoimmunity.

enriched in B cells (I) is a transcriptional signature of the B lymphocyte lineage: the set of genes expressed far more highly in B cells than in other blood cells, useful for identifying B cell content in tissues and tumours and for tracking B cell depletion or expansion. Its members span the antigen receptor itself and its proximal signalling apparatus — surface immunoglobulin heavy and light chains, the CD79A/CD79B module, CD19, CD22, BLK, BANK1 and STAP1 — together with the transcription factors PAX5, EBF1, SPIB and TCF4 that commit progenitors to the lineage and maintain B cell identity. Also represented are co-receptors and inhibitory regulators (CD72, BTLA, FCER2, complement receptor CR2), the follicular homing receptor CXCR5, and markers of immature and naive stages such as VPREB3 and TCL1A. Loss of these programs abolishes antibody-mediated immunity; their dysregulation underlies B cell lymphomas and autoimmunity.

This is a B lymphocyte identity signature: the genes whose expression marks cells of the B lineage and distinguishes them from other leukocytes in blood, lymph node and tumour samples. It captures what a B cell is built to do carry a surface immunoglobulin receptor, sense antigen, and mature into an antibody-secreting or memory cell and its components are the markers used clinically to type B cell leukaemias and lymphomas and the targets of depleting antibody therapy. Antigen receptor subunits and their proximal signalling adaptors appear alongside immunoglobulin heavy and light chain loci, the surface tetraspanin CD20, and co-receptors such as CD19, CD22 and CD72 that tune receptor output. Lineage commitment is enforced by the transcription factors PAX5, EBF1, BCL11A and SPIB, while CXCR5 directs homing into follicles where germinal centre responses occur.

enriched in B cells (IV) is a transcriptional signature of the B lymphocyte compartment, the set of genes whose expression in blood or tissue reports how many B cells are present and how mature they are. It matters because such modules let B cell content be read out of bulk expression data in vaccination, autoimmunity and lymphoma, where B cell abundance tracks disease activity and response to depleting therapy. The members span the antigen receptor signalling apparatus, notably the kinase BTK whose loss blocks B cell development and causes agammaglobulinaemia, the innate co-receptors CD180 and TLR10 that shape B cell activation thresholds, the MHC class II machinery CIITA and HLA-DOA underlying antigen presentation to helper T cells, the survival receptor FAIM3, the lineage transcription factor MEF2C, and immunoglobulin heavy chain transcripts marking antibody-secreting differentiation.

This is a B cell signature module: a group of genes whose expression in blood or tissue marks the presence and activity of B lymphocytes, useful for reading out humoral immune compartments from bulk expression data. Several members define B cell identity directly — BTK transmits antigen receptor signals to survival and proliferation programmes and is lost in X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, CD180 and TLR10 are innate receptors that shape B cell responses to microbial ligands, and FAIM3 encodes the IgM Fc receptor. Immunoglobulin heavy chain genes for IgA and IgG report the antibody output of plasma cells and memory B cells. Antigen presentation is also represented, with the MHC class II transactivator CIITA controlling class II gene expression and HLA-DOA modulating peptide loading, while MEF2C supports B lineage transcriptional programmes.

cell adhesion covers the molecular contacts that let cells grip the extracellular matrix, each other, and circulating blood cells, holding tissues together and letting them be remodelled. Its outputs are connective tissue integrity, vascular wall stability, leukocyte recruitment to inflamed endothelium, and platelet plug formation at sites of injury; loss of these functions produces bleeding disorders, fibrosis, and unchecked tumour invasion. The genes span the matrix itself — fibrillar and network collagens, fibronectin, laminins, nidogen, tenascin, thrombospondins and periostin — and the receptors that read it, notably the integrin αIIbβ3 and GPIb-IX complexes through which platelets bind von Willebrand factor. Endothelial and junctional components such as VCAM1, P-selectin, ESAM and JAM3, together with CXCL12 and inflammatory cytokines, couple adhesion to immune trafficking, while SNAI2 links it to epithelial-mesenchymal transition and migratory behaviour.

Cells attach to each other and to the matrix around them, and this cell adhesion programme supplies both the ligands and the receptors that make those contacts. It underlies tissue architecture, wound healing, leukocyte recruitment and platelet plug formation, and its dysregulation contributes to fibrosis, thrombosis and tumour invasion. Fibrillar and network collagens together with fibronectin, laminins, nidogen, tenascin, periostin and thrombospondins build the adhesive substrate, while integrins such as the platelet fibrinogen receptor pair ITGA2B/ITGB3, the von Willebrand factor receptor complex GP1BA/GP9, and endothelial adhesion molecules VCAM1, SELP and junctional JAM3/ESAM mediate binding under flow. Chemokines CXCL12 and IL8 and the cytokine IL1B activate these receptors on circulating cells, and SNAI2 links the same machinery to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, coupling adhesion to migration and matrix remodelling.

T cell activation (IV) describes the machinery by which a T cell recognises antigen through its receptor and converts that recognition into proliferation, cytokine output and effector differentiation. It matters because this step licenses adaptive immunity to pathogens and tumours, and because its thresholds determine whether a response is protective or autoimmune. The genes span the proximal receptor module and its tuning: the CD3 epsilon chain of the receptor complex, the Src-family kinase LCK that initiates phosphorylation, and the phosphatases PTPN6 and CD45 that set signal gain, alongside inhibitory surface receptors CD5 and LAG3 that damp overactivation. Transcriptional regulators including GATA3, GFI1 and SPI1 direct lineage choice and helper-subset commitment, while L-selectin governs entry into lymph nodes and XCL1 recruits dendritic cells. Together these define both the sensitivity and the outcome of antigen encounter.

T cells commit to an immune response only when the T cell receptor engages peptide-MHC, and this module covers the proximal machinery and transcriptional context of that activation step. It matters because the same components set the threshold between productive immunity and either anergy or autoimmunity, and several are the basis of clinical T cell markers and checkpoint blockade. Receptor-proximal signalling runs through the CD3 epsilon chain and the Src-family kinase LCK, which is regulated by the phosphatases CD45 and SHP-1 acting as brakes on tyrosine phosphorylation; LAG3 provides further inhibitory tuning, while CD5 dampens receptor sensitivity. Lineage and effector output are shaped by transcription factors including GATA3 and GFI1, with L-selectin governing lymph node entry of naive cells and the chemokine XCL1 recruiting dendritic cells to the responding T cell.

immuregulation - monocytes, T and B cells describes the crosstalk by which myeloid cells, T cells and B cells tune each other's activation, setting the threshold between productive immunity and inflammatory damage. It matters because the same molecules that amplify a response also restrain it: CTLA4 delivers the inhibitory counter-signal that terminates T cell costimulation, and CD200 engages its myeloid receptor to keep monocytes and macrophages quiescent, while IL1A, IL23A, OSM, CSF3 and the chemokine CCL4 drive recruitment, granulopoiesis and T helper polarisation. B cell identity is represented by the antigen receptor adaptor CD79A, surface IgD and the low-affinity IgE receptor FCER2, linking antibody responses to this network. KIT ties in progenitor and mast cell output. Loss of the inhibitory arm produces autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation; excess suppression permits chronic infection and tumour escape, which is why these checkpoints are drug targets.

Immune responses are tuned by signals passed between monocytes and lymphocytes, and this collection of immunoregulatory mediators spans all three compartments: B cell receptor components and surface markers, T cell inhibitory receptors, and monocyte- and macrophage-derived cytokines. Together they set the balance between activation and restraint that determines whether an encounter with antigen produces effective immunity, tolerance, or inflammatory tissue damage. CTLA4 delivers the inhibitory counterweight to costimulation and restrains T cell expansion; CD200 engages its myeloid receptor to dampen macrophage activation; CD79A and BLK carry antigen receptor signalling in B cells, while FCER2 and secreted IgD reflect their activation state. Inflammatory and growth-promoting outputs including IL1A, IL23A, CCL4, OSM and CSF3 recruit and expand myeloid cells and shape helper T cell polarisation, linking this circuitry to autoimmunity and chronic inflammation.</description>

mitotic cell division is the machinery that attaches chromosomes to spindle microtubules and delays anaphase until every attachment is correct, so that each daughter cell inherits one exact copy of the genome. When it fails, chromosomes missegregate and cells become aneuploid, a hallmark of tumours and a cause of embryonic lethality. The genes describe the kinetochore itself, from the CENP-A-marked centromeric chromatin and its inner constitutive components through the outer NDC80/NUF2 microtubule-binding complex and the SKA subunits that stabilise attachment. Layered on this are the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins BUB1, MAD2L1 and the RZZ components, which restrain CDC20 and hence the anaphase-promoting complex, and the error-correcting kinases Aurora B and PLK1 acting with the chromosomal passenger complex. Depolymerising kinesins and shugoshin-mediated cohesion protection complete the control of chromosome movement and separation.

Faithful segregation of duplicated chromosomes during mitotic cell division depends on building a kinetochore at each centromere and attaching it correctly to spindle microtubules. The genes here define that machinery: centromere-specific histone and constitutive centromere-associated proteins that mark and assemble the platform, the outer kinetochore complex including NDC80 and NUF2 that grips microtubules, and microtubule-depolymerising motors that tune attachment stability. Overlaid on this is the spindle assembly checkpoint, in which BUB1, BUB1B and MAD2L1 restrain CDC20 and thus the anaphase-promoting complex until every chromosome is bioriented. Aurora B kinase with survivin and its partners corrects erroneous attachments, while PLK1 coordinates mitotic progression. Loss of these controls produces lagging chromosomes, missegregation and aneuploidy, a route to chromosomal instability in cancer; many components are also proliferation markers and drug targets.

enriched in NK cells (receptor activation) describes the surface receptor repertoire by which natural killer cells decide whether a target cell lives or dies. NK cells patrol for virus-infected and transformed cells that have downregulated MHC class I, and this receptor set encodes both halves of that decision: inhibitory killer immunoglobulin-like receptors and CD94/NKG2A-type lectins that read self MHC and restrain killing, and activating receptors such as NKG2D and 2B4 that detect stress ligands and tumour-associated markers. Engagement is transduced through the CD3 inth-chain zeta adaptor and ZAP70, then through ITK, PKC-theta and the CARD11 scaffold toward NF-kB activation, degranulation and cytokine release. The same components serve cytotoxic T cells, and the balance of inhibitory versus activating input underlies missing-self recognition, tumour immune surveillance, and the therapeutic logic of KIR-mismatched transplantation and checkpoint blockade.

Natural killer cells decide whether to kill a target by summing activating and inhibitory signals from surface receptors, and this receptor repertoire is what defines that decision. It underlies surveillance of virus-infected and tumour cells that have lost MHC class I, and its inhibitory arm enforces tolerance to healthy self tissue. Killer immunoglobulin-like receptors read HLA class I ligands, with long-tailed forms delivering inhibition and short-tailed forms contributing activation; NKG2D paired with CD94/NKG2 family partners detects stress-induced ligands, while CD244 and CD96 tune adhesion and co-stimulation. Signals converge on ITAM-bearing CD3 zeta and the kinases ZAP70 and ITK, with protein kinase C-theta and the CARD11 scaffold linking receptor engagement to transcriptional activation and cytotoxic granule release. Skewed receptor-ligand combinations affect antiviral control, transplant outcome and susceptibility to autoimmunity.

regulation of localization covers the control layer that decides where proteins, vesicles and lipids end up inside a cell and at its surface, rather than how much of them is made. This positional control determines whether a receptor reaches the plasma membrane, whether a secretory granule fuses, and whether cholesterol is exported instead of stored, so its failure shows up as mistrafficking, defective secretion and unrestrained growth signalling. The genes here span several arms of that control: AKT1 and TSC2 couple growth-factor input to the localization of metabolic and mTOR-pathway components; SNX17 retrieves integrins and receptors from endosomes for recycling; NAPA and STXBP2 execute SNARE-dependent membrane fusion, and STXBP2 loss causes familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis through failed cytotoxic granule release; ARHGDIA, FLNA, ARAP1 and PKN1 tie Rho- and Arf-family GTPase activity to cytoskeletal anchoring, while NR1H2 governs sterol redistribution.

Cells constantly decide where proteins, vesicles and lipids should be, and this collection covers the control of that positioning rather than transport itself. The genes span several routes by which a signal changes a molecule's location: kinase signalling that drives effectors to membranes, as with AKT1 and its substrate TSC2 or the MAP2K2 arm of the MAPK cascade; small GTPase regulation, where ARHGDIA sequesters Rho GTPases in the cytosol and ARAP1 acts as a GTPase-activating protein toward Arf and Rho family members; sorting and recycling of internalised receptors through the endosomal adaptor SNX17; and membrane fusion steps needed for regulated secretion, including SNAP-alpha and the Munc18 family member STXBP2 required for cytotoxic granule release. Filamin A anchors receptors to actin, while TGFB1 and the nuclear receptor NR1H2 link extracellular and lipid cues to these placement decisions.}</description>

This pathway is the differentiated tissue macrophage program — the transcriptional and enzymatic identity that lets monocyte-derived cells phagocytose debris and pathogens, present antigen, and locally restrain T cell responses. It matters for infection control, iron and heme turnover, and the immunosuppressive myeloid states found in tumours and in the inflamed brain. The genes trace several arms of that phenotype: FCER1G with BTK and ADAP2 couple Fc and immune receptors to phagocytic and cytoskeletal responses; CYBB drives the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst whose loss causes chronic granulomatous disease; HMOX1 degrades heme to release iron and carbon monoxide; and IFI30, CPVL and CST3 handle lysosomal proteolysis for antigen processing. IDO1, KMO and KYNU run tryptophan down the kynurenine route, depleting tryptophan and generating metabolites that suppress effector lymphocytes, with MAFB reinforcing macrophage commitment."TBA" aside, this is macrophage effector biology.

These genes mark the differentiated tissue macrophage and microglial state, the resident phagocyte programme that clears debris and dying cells, handles iron and heme, and shapes local immune tone. Fc receptor gamma chain and the Tec kinase BTK couple immunoglobulin and immune-complex recognition to phagocytosis, while CYBB encodes the NADPH oxidase catalytic subunit gp91phox that generates the respiratory burst; its loss causes chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent bacterial and fungal infection. Heme oxygenase-1 degrades heme to biliverdin, carbon monoxide and free iron, linking these cells to erythrocyte recycling and to copper and amino acid transport by SLC31A2 and SLC7A7. IDO1 with KMO and KYNU carries tryptophan down the kynurenine route, producing metabolites that suppress T cell responses and, in brain, act on neurons. MAFB sustains the macrophage identity underlying all of it.

enriched in B cells (VI) is a transcriptional signature of the mature B lymphocyte, the cell type responsible for antibody-mediated immunity and antigen presentation to helper T cells. Its members are the surface proteins by which B cells are recognised and therapeutically targeted, including CD19, CD20 (MS4A1), CD22 and the complement receptor CR2, together with the antigen receptor's signalling subunits CD79A and CD79B, which couple immunoglobulin binding to intracellular kinase cascades. Also present are inhibitory co-receptors such as BTLA, CD72 and CD200 that set thresholds for activation and prevent autoreactivity, the follicular homing receptor CXCR5 that positions cells in germinal centres, and HLA-DOB, a modulator of MHC class II peptide loading. Expression of this program marks B cell content in tissue and blood, and its loss accompanies B cell depletion or immunodeficiency.

This grouping captures the transcriptional signature of mature B cells, the antibody-producing lineage of adaptive immunity, and its members are the surface proteins by which B cells are recognised and therapeutically targeted. The core is the antigen receptor complex and its immediate modulators: CD79A and CD79B transmit immunoglobulin engagement into intracellular signalling, while CD19 amplifies that signal and CD22, CD72 and BTLA restrain it, setting the threshold at which a B cell responds to antigen rather than ignoring it or reacting to self. Complement receptor CR2 links innate opsonisation to B cell activation, CXCR5 directs homing into follicles and germinal centres, and HLA-DOB tunes peptide loading for presentation to helper T cells. MS4A1, the CD20 target of depleting antibodies, and Fc receptor-like proteins complete a profile that distinguishes B cells in tissue and blood expression data.

enriched in NK cells (I) is a transcriptional signature of natural killer cells and closely related cytotoxic effector lymphocytes, the innate arm of lymphoid immunity that kills virus-infected and tumour cells without prior sensitisation and shapes the response through interferon-gamma and chemokine output. Loss of these cells leaves patients vulnerable to herpesvirus disease and impairs tumour surveillance. The genes trace the whole effector programme: granule contents and delivery machinery such as perforin, granulysin and multiple granzymes; germline-encoded recognition receptors of the killer lectin-like family including NKG2D and NKG2A that weigh activating ligands against MHC class I; proximal signalling through CD247, ZAP70 and ITK; and the transcription factors T-bet, EOMES and STAT4 that impose cytotoxic identity. Trafficking and tissue-exit cues appear as S1PR5 and the chemokines XCL1/XCL2 and CCL5, which recruit dendritic cells to sites of killing.

This is a natural killer cell signature: the transcripts that mark circulating cytotoxic innate lymphocytes and distinguish them from other leukocytes. NK cells kill virus-infected and transformed cells without prior sensitization and shape immune responses through chemokine and cytokine output, so this programme underlies antiviral defence and tumour surveillance. Much of it is the killing apparatus itself — perforin, granulysin and a set of granzymes stored in cytotoxic granules, together with FASLG for death-receptor-mediated lysis. Target recognition runs through germline-encoded activating and inhibitory receptors of the killer lectin-like family, including NKG2D and CD94/NKG2 partners signalling via CD3-zeta, ZAP70 and ITK. Transcription factors EOMES, TBX21 and STAT4, with IL-2 and IL-18 receptor subunits, set the lineage and its interferon-gamma response, while S1PR5 governs egress into blood. CCL5 and the XCL chemokines recruit dendritic cells.

T cell activation (III) covers the proximal signalling and transcriptional machinery that converts antigen recognition by the T cell receptor into proliferation, cytokine output and lineage commitment. Without it, thymocytes fail selection and peripheral T cells cannot mount effective responses, leaving both immunodeficiency and, when regulation is lost, autoimmunity. The kinase LCK initiates the cascade at the receptor, PRKCQ and RASGRP1 propagate it to NF-kB and Ras-ERK, and THEMIS tunes signal strength during positive and negative selection in the thymus. Calcium-dependent CAMK4 relays activation to the nucleus, where LEF1, ETS1, RORA and KLF12 set quiescence, survival and helper-subset identity, with chromatin readers such as ZMYND11 and GLYR1 shaping the accessible state. CD96 contributes adhesion-based costimulation. Together these define naive-to-effector transition and the thresholds that keep self-reactive cells in check.

Engagement of the T cell receptor must be converted into a decision to proliferate, differentiate or remain quiescent, and this module captures one arm of that T cell activation programme, dominated by proximal signalling and the transcriptional identity of naive T lymphocytes. LCK initiates receptor-proximal tyrosine phosphorylation, PRKCQ relays signals from the immunological synapse toward NF- theB-dependent transcription, RASGRP1 couples diacylglycerol to Ras-ERK activation, and CAMK4 transmits calcium signals into the nucleus. THEMIS sets the signalling thresholds that govern positive and negative selection in the thymus, while LEF1, ETS1 and RORA shape lineage commitment and effector differentiation. CD96 contributes adhesion and co-signalling. Loss of these functions produces immunodeficiency with impaired antigen responses, whereas failures of thresholding and selection permit autoreactive clones, linking this biology to both host defence and tolerance.

This pathway describes a set of broadly expressed housekeeping regulators that keep transcription, RNA handling, and membrane trafficking coordinated during cell growth and division. Its members touch several general control layers: chromatin and transcription (the ARID4B repressor complex component, the SP3 transcription factor, cyclin C as a partner of CDK8 in Mediator-associated transcriptional control, and the chromatin architectural protein DEK), post-transcriptional regulation (FMR1 and MBNL1 governing translation and alternative splicing of neuronal and muscle transcripts, with G3BP2 nucleating stress granules), and endomembrane dynamics (VPS4B disassembling ESCRT complexes for multivesicular body formation and abscission, SACM1L controlling phosphoinositide levels, ITSN2 and PLEKHF2 in endocytic trafficking). NEK7 links the group to mitotic spindle assembly and inflammasome activation, while PPP1R12A targets myosin phosphatase to the actin cytoskeleton. Together these activities support proliferation, cytokinesis, and cellular responses to stress.

A mixed group of broadly expressed regulators that keep housekeeping functions of the cell running: chromatin-associated and transcriptional components, RNA-binding proteins, and machinery for endosomal membrane traffic and cytoskeletal contractility. Several members act on gene expression — a chromatin-interacting subunit of a histone deacetylase-containing repressor complex, a cyclin partner of the CDK8 kinase module of Mediator, and the zinc-finger transcription factor SP3. Others control the fate of mRNAs after they are made: MBNL1 governs alternative splicing of muscle and neuronal transcripts, FMR1 represses translation at synapses and its loss causes fragile X syndrome, and G3BP2 nucleates stress granules when translation stalls. A third arm handles membranes and organelles, including the ESCRT-associated ATPase VPS4B in multivesicular body formation, a phosphoinositide phosphatase acting at the Golgi and ER, and a myosin phosphatase targeting subunit that tunes actomyosin tension.

DNA repair is the set of surveillance and correction activities that keep the genome intact as cells replicate and encounter damage, and its failure is the direct route to the mutation load and chromosomal instability that drive cancer. The genes gathered here cover the recombinational arm most closely tied to replication: the MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex that senses and resects double-strand breaks, RAD51 with BRCA1 and BRCA2 loading it onto RPA-coated single-stranded DNA for strand invasion, and the Fanconi anaemia proteins that resolve interstrand crosslinks stalling forks. Repair synthesis then reuses the replication machinery itself — PCNA, the RFC clamp loader, polymerases delta and epsilon, FEN1 and ligase I. Phosphorylated H2AX marks damaged chromatin to recruit these factors. Germline loss of BRCA1, BRCA2 or Fanconi components causes hereditary breast and ovarian cancer and bone marrow failure syndromes.

Genomes are damaged continuously by replication errors, crosslinking agents and double-strand breaks, and this DNA repair programme is the machinery that detects those lesions and restores the duplex before a cell divides. Its failure is the origin of hereditary cancer predisposition and of bone marrow failure syndromes, and its partial loss is what makes tumours sensitive to crosslinking chemotherapy and to inhibitors that force reliance on a single repair route. The genes here cover homologous recombination, with BRCA1 and BRCA2 loading RAD51 onto resected single-stranded DNA coated by replication protein A; end sensing and resection by the MRE11-RAD50 complex; crosslink repair through the Fanconi anaemia proteins FANCD2 and FANCI; and the shared synthesis and ligation steps that finish repair, using clamp loader subunits, PCNA, replicative polymerases, FEN1 and LIG1. Histone H2AX marks damaged chromatin to recruit these factors.

This pathway couples cell-surface receptor engagement to cytoskeletal and transcriptional responses in two settings that share the same wiring: lymphocyte activation and endothelial/mesenchymal adhesion. On the immune side, the B cell adaptor BLNK, the T cell receptor-associated TRAT1, the gut-homing chemokine receptor CCR9 and the transcription factor MEF2C tie antigen and chemokine sensing to survival, differentiation and tissue-selective trafficking, functions whose loss produces immunodeficiency and impaired mucosal immunity. On the adhesion side, focal adhesion kinase PTK2, the GAB1 scaffold, phospholipase C beta and a G protein gamma subunit relay integrin and growth factor input into calcium and Ras-family signalling, while endoglin and CTGF tune TGF-beta responses in vessel wall and matrix remodelling, the axis disrupted in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Glycosyltransferases such as LARGE and NDST3 modify the ligand-binding sugars these receptors depend on."TBA" is not used here.

These genes converge on receptor-proximal signalling that converts extracellular cues into changes in cell adhesion, migration and tissue remodelling. One arm is vascular and mesenchymal: endoglin acts as a TGF-beta superfamily co-receptor in endothelium, CCN2/CTGF and CRIM1 shape growth-factor availability in the matrix, and focal adhesion kinase with GAB1, PLCB1 and the Ral activator RGL1 relay integrin and growth-factor input to the cytoskeleton and to Ras-family GTPase output. A second arm is lymphoid: the adaptor BLNK couples the B cell receptor to downstream kinases, TRAT1 associates with the T cell receptor complex, the chemokine receptor CCR9 directs gut-homing of lymphocytes, and MEF2C acts as a transcriptional regulator in both haematopoietic and cardiovascular lineages. Together the members read as a module supporting vascular integrity and immune cell positioning, with LARGE-dependent glycosylation contributing basement-membrane attachment.

enriched in naive and memory B cells marks the resting, antigen-inexperienced and recirculating memory compartments of the B lineage, the cells that populate follicles and lymph node mantle zones and stand ready to respond to antigen without yet secreting antibody. The genes are the surface identity of such cells: the tetraspanin CD37 and CD20 organise membrane microdomains and receptor signalling thresholds, the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B restrains activation by immune complexes, LY86 supports innate receptor responsiveness, and the adaptor BANK1 tunes antigen receptor calcium signalling. MEF2C provides transcriptional control of B cell proliferation after receptor engagement. Together these define a state biased toward restraint and survival rather than plasma cell differentiation, and their expression distinguishes naive and memory B cells from germinal centre and antibody-secreting cells in tissue and blood profiling.

This signature marks resting B cells of the naive and memory compartments, the circulating pool that carries immunological memory and stands ready to respond to antigen without yet having become an antibody-secreting plasma cell. Its members are the surface proteins and regulators by which such cells are recognised in blood and tissue: MS4A1 (CD20), the tetraspanin CD37, the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B that raises the threshold for antigen receptor activation, the scaffold BANK1 that dampens B cell receptor signalling, and the pattern-recognition accessory molecule LY86. MEF2C supplies transcriptional control of B cell proliferation and germinal centre responses. Loss of these restraints on receptor signalling predisposes to autoimmunity, while the same markers make this population the target of depleting antibody therapy. The adhesion molecules and other regulators present suggest additional roles in homing and quiescence rather than effector secretion.

proinflammatory dendritic cell, myeloid cell response describes the activated state of dendritic cells and macrophages that converts detection of microbes or tissue damage into an inflammatory, T cell–stimulating program. This is the step that decides whether an immune response is mounted at all: the same genes drive protective host defence and, when sustained, the tissue injury of inflammatory bowel disease, arthritis and sepsis. The output is a burst of cytokines and chemokines — IL1B, TNF, CCL4 and CCL20 — that recruit neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes, alongside CD80-mediated costimulation that licenses naive T cells. IFNG and STAT4 mark the reciprocal Th1 amplification loop feeding back on myeloid cells, while GCH1 supports tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent nitric oxide production. Adenosine receptor and phosphodiesterase components set the cAMP tone that restrains the response, and TNFAIP6 and SERPINB9 limit collateral damage and self-killing.

This programme captures the proinflammatory activation state of dendritic cells and other myeloid cells as they sense microbial or tissue-damage signals and convert them into a T cell-recruiting, T cell-stimulating response. It underlies acute innate defence and the initiation of adaptive immunity, and when sustained it drives the tissue damage of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease. Activated cells secrete TNF, IL1B and the chemokines CCL4 and CCL20 to draw monocytes and lymphocytes into the site, while CD80 provides the costimulation that licenses responding T cells. GCH1 supplies tetrahydrobiopterin for nitric oxide production, SERPINB9 protects the activated cell from its own granzyme B exposure, and ADORA2A and PDE4B set cyclic AMP-dependent brakes on cytokine output. STAT4 and IFNG mark the type 1 polarised feedback loop that reinforces the response.

leukocyte migration is represented here by a coherent intestinal epithelial programme: the genes define the differentiated enterocyte and colonocyte, the polarised absorptive cell that forms the gut's selective barrier and its first line of defence against luminal microbes. Loss of this programme underlies barrier failure in inflammatory bowel disease and its reactivation marks intestinal metaplasia and colorectal cancer. The CDX1/CDX2 and FOXA3 transcription factors impose intestinal identity, driving expression of brush border and apical machinery (VIL1, MYO1A, MYO7B, PLS1, MEP1A, GUCY2C), tight junction claudins with EPCAM to seal the paracellular route, and secreted mucins and galectins that maintain the protective glycocalyx. Fucosyltransferases and GMDS glycosylate surface adhesion molecules such as CEACAM5 and GPA33, while RNF43 restrains Wnt signalling in the crypt, coupling barrier maintenance to controlled epithelial renewal, lipid handling and xenobiotic sensing.

These genes mark the differentiated intestinal and colonic epithelium, the absorptive barrier that takes up nutrients, excludes luminal bacteria and renews itself continuously from crypt stem cells. The master transcription factors CDX1 and CDX2, with FOXA3, impose hindgut identity, while EPCAM, CDH17 and the claudins CLDN3, CLDN4 and CLDN7 build adherens and tight junctions that seal the paracellular space. Brush border and apical organisation depend on villin, myosins MYO1A and MYO7B, PLS1 and POF1B; mucins MUC13 and MUC3B, galectin-4 and fucosyltransferases glycosylate the surface; FABP1 and ACSL5 handle absorbed lipid, and GUCY2C transduces guanylin signals controlling fluid secretion. RNF43 restrains Wnt activity in the crypt. Loss of this programme underlies barrier failure in inflammatory bowel disease, congenital diarrhoeas, and the aberrant expression of CEACAM5 and KRT20 seen in colorectal cancer and gastric intestinal metaplasia.

enriched in hepatocyte nuclear factors (I) describes the transcriptional program that gives endoderm-derived epithelia — liver, pancreatic duct and islet, intestine and kidney tubule — their identity and their differentiated metabolic output. It matters because these factors set up bile and lipid handling, glucose-responsive insulin secretion and intestinal absorptive character; loss-of-function mutations in HNF4A and HNF1B cause maturity-onset diabetes of the young, renal cysts and pancreatic hypoplasia, and the same regulators are re-expressed in gastrointestinal and hepatic tumours. FOXA2 and FOXA3 open chromatin at endodermal enhancers and act with HNF4A, HNF4G and HNF1B in a cross-regulating, self-reinforcing loop, while MNX1 contributes to pancreatic endocrine specification. Their downstream targets appear here as the effectors of that identity: apical mucins and glycosyltransferases such as MUC13 and GMDS, the brush-border lectin LGALS4, CEACAM5, and cytoskeletal and lipid-signalling components of polarised epithelial cells.

Hepatocyte nuclear factors are the transcriptional regulators that give liver, pancreas, intestine and kidney epithelium their identity, and this grouping centres on that circuitry: FOXA2 and FOXA3 act as pioneer factors that open chromatin at endoderm-specific enhancers, while HNF1B, HNF4A and HNF4G drive the downstream programmes of bile acid and lipid handling, glucose metabolism, and apical epithelial differentiation. The factors cross-regulate one another in a reinforcing network, so loss of a single member destabilises the whole state — heterozygous HNF1B or HNF4A mutation causes maturity-onset diabetes of the young and renal cystic disease, and MNX1 loss disrupts pancreatic beta cell specification. Accompanying targets such as the intestinal lectin LGALS4, the membrane mucin MUC13 and CEACAM5 mark the differentiated brush-border epithelium these factors specify, alongside fucose-donor synthesis by GMDS for glycan production.

B cell development covers the signals and transcriptional regulators that guide progenitors through the B lineage and shape the mature B cell compartment, the basis of antibody production and humoral memory. Its failure yields immunodeficiency with poor antibody responses, while dysregulation feeds autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy. The genes span several layers of that control: the ETS factor SPI1 (PU.1) sets haematopoietic lineage output with partners such as HHEX, CEBPE and the transcriptional corepressor CBFA2T3, while the Src-family kinase LYN transmits and dampens antigen receptor signalling, setting thresholds for tolerance. Cytokines of the TNF family, including lymphotoxin-alpha and the survival factor TNFSF13/APRIL, together with LIF, act on the stromal niches and germinal centre architecture that support maturation, and CCR7 directs migration into lymphoid tissue. TLR4 links innate recognition to B cell activation.

B cell development spans the commitment of haematopoietic progenitors to the B lineage, their maturation in bone marrow, and their positioning and activation in secondary lymphoid tissue, and it underwrites antibody-mediated immunity. Lineage-determining transcriptional regulators are represented here: SPI1 (PU.1) sets myeloid versus lymphoid output in a dose-dependent way, while HHEX and CBFA2T3 act as transcriptional regulators of early progenitor fate. Signalling contributions come from LYN, a Src-family kinase that both propagates and dampens antigen receptor output so that autoreactive responses are held in check, and from innate sensing through TLR4. Cytokines of the tumour necrosis factor family, including TNF, LTA and TNFSF13 (APRIL), support B cell survival, plasma cell maintenance and the lymphoid microenvironment, and CCR7 directs chemotactic homing to lymph node and spleen. Disruption of these steps yields immunodeficiency, impaired antibody responses, or loss of self-tolerance.

enriched in antigen presentation (III) describes the machinery by which professional antigen-presenting cells display peptides to CD4+ T helper cells, the step that licenses adaptive immune responses and antibody production. Its core is the MHC class II locus BA/DRB heterodimers, together with HLA-DM, which catalyses the exchange of invariant chain-derived CLIP peptide for antigenic peptide in the endolysosomal loading compartment. Around this sits the myeloid and lymphoid membrane apparatus needed for productive contact: the integrin LFA-1 beta chain and ICAM1 forming the adhesive ring of the immunological synapse, the phosphatase CD45 and adaptors FYB and PLEK tuning receptor signalling, and macrophage- and microglia-associated proteins such as AIF1, CD53 and LAPTM5. Expression of these genes marks tissue macrophage and dendritic cell infiltration, and their variation at the class II locus underlies susceptibility to many autoimmune diseases.

This module marks the professional antigen-presenting compartment of the immune system, where extracellular proteins are displayed on MHC class II to CD4 T cells so that helper responses, antibody production and immunological memory can be initiated. Its core is the class II locus itself — HLA-DR alpha and beta chains together with the HLA-DM chaperone that catalyses exchange of the invariant chain-derived placeholder peptide for high-affinity antigenic peptides in the late endosome. Around this sit the adhesion and signalling components that make a productive contact with the T cell and sustain it: ICAM1 with the integrin beta-2 chain, the pan-leukocyte phosphatase CD45, CD53, and the myeloid adaptors AIF1, FYB and PLEK. Expression of this programme in monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells defines their competence to present; loss of class II expression causes profound combined immunodeficiency, while its inappropriate induction contributes to autoimmunity and transplant rejection.

T cell surface signature is the set of membrane proteins that mark a cell as a T lymphocyte and equip it to read antigen and costimulatory cues. It defines the identity used to enumerate T cells in blood and tissue, and its components are the handles by which T cell responses are amplified or shut down therapeutically. The core is the T cell receptor signalling apparatus -- CD3E and CD3G, the adaptor SIT1, and the CD45-associated phosphoprotein PTPRCAP -- flanked by adhesion and costimulatory receptors CD2, CD6, CD28 and ICOS that set the threshold for activation, and by inhibitory LAG3 and SIRPG that restrain it. Chemokine receptors such as CXCR6 direct tissue homing, while MAL organises raft microdomains at the immunological synapse. Amino acid and cofactor transporters appear alongside, reflecting the metabolic reprogramming that accompanies activation and clonal expansion.

A surface signature of T lymphocytes, comprising the membrane proteins that define the lineage and set the threshold for its activation. These molecules are the basis of T cell identification by flow cytometry and the targets of both stimulatory and blocking immunotherapies. The core is the antigen receptor signalling apparatus, with CD3E and CD3G transducing T cell receptor engagement and the adaptors SIT1 and PTPRCAP tuning it at the membrane; costimulation is supplied through CD28 and ICOS, adhesion and synapse formation through CD2 and CD6, and inhibitory restraint through LAG3 and SIRPG. Chemokine and cytokine receptors including CXCR6 direct tissue positioning, while MAL and ITM2A shape raft organisation and trafficking. Coordinate expression of this module underlies antigen recognition, helper and cytotoxic function, and tolerance; its loss or depletion leaves cell-mediated immunity absent.

Single strand break repair removes nicks and gaps in one strand of the DNA duplex before they can be converted into far more dangerous double-strand breaks or stall transcription and replication. Single-strand breaks arise constantly from oxidative attack, abortive topoisomerase reactions and the incision steps of base excision repair, and cells that cannot seal them accumulate persistent damage; inherited defects in this machinery cause cerebellar degeneration and neurological syndromes, reflecting how dependent long-lived neurons are on it. Mechanistically it uses the same enzymes as base excision repair: damaged or blocked break ends are cleaned up by end-processing factors such as aprataxin and tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase, gaps are filled, and XRCC1 acts as the scaffold coordinating end processing with ligation. Related activities include glycosylase-initiated base removal, transcription-coupled repair, and chromatin and telomere contexts that shape access to lesions.

Single-strand breaks are the most frequent DNA lesion in cells, arising from oxidative attack, abortive topoisomerase action, and the incision steps of base excision repair; repairing them prevents replication fork collapse and the double-strand breaks and transcription blocks that follow. Detection recruits a scaffold, XRCC1, which organises end-processing and ligation at the nick. End-cleaning enzymes prepare chemically damaged termini: aprataxin removes abortive ligation adducts, TDP1 resolves trapped topoisomerase I-DNA intermediates, and APLF contributes nuclease and scaffolding activity, while uracil-DNA glycosylase and NEIL3 generate nicks through excision of damaged bases. Coupling to transcription is represented by the CSB and CSA proteins, which handle lesions encountered by elongating RNA polymerase. Because neurons are long-lived and highly oxidative, defects in this repair route produce hereditary cerebellar ataxias and neurodegeneration rather than cancer predisposition, and the pathway also intersects chromatin regulation and telomere protection.

regulation of mitotic recombination controls how often and how far homologous recombination proceeds in dividing somatic cells, keeping repair of broken or stalled replication forks accurate rather than allowing crossovers, loss of heterozygosity and gross rearrangements. Too little recombination leaves double-strand breaks unrepaired; too much, or recombination between the wrong repeats, drives translocations and the genome instability characteristic of cancer. The genes span the steps where that balance is set: the MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex that senses and resects breaks, the mismatch repair factor MLH1 that rejects mismatched heteroduplexes and limits recombination between diverged sequences, ANKLE1 nuclease activity resolving joint molecules late in the process, and TERF2 shielding chromosome ends from being read as breaks. ZSCAN4 links this control to telomere recombination and elongation. The pathway therefore sits within DNA damage response and chromosome maintenance rather than meiotic exchange.

Recombination between homologous sequences is a safe way to repair a broken chromosome in a dividing cell, but unrestrained exchange produces loss of heterozygosity, translocations and rearrangements between repeats. Regulation of mitotic recombination sets how often and how far such exchange proceeds during somatic cell divisions, and its loosening is a route to genome instability and cancer predisposition. The genes here act at several control points: the MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex senses and processes double-strand break ends to commit them to homology-directed repair, the mismatch repair factor MLH1 polices heteroduplex fidelity and rejects recombination between diverged sequences, TERF2 shields telomeres from being treated as broken ends, and ANKLE1 is a nuclease that resolves branched recombination intermediates late in the process. Together they link break repair, telomere protection and repeat stability to faithful chromosome transmission.

Very long-chain fatty acid metabolic process covers the synthesis and breakdown of fatty acids longer than 22 carbons, the lipids that build myelin, skin barrier ceramides, retinal photoreceptor membranes and sperm membranes. Its failure is directly disease-causing: defective peroxisomal import of these substrates underlies X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, and mutations in the elongase acting on retinal species cause macular dystrophy. Elongation proceeds by iterative cycles on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, with ELOVL enzymes setting chain-length and substrate specificity, followed by 3-hydroxyacyl dehydratase and trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase steps. Because mitochondrial beta-oxidation cannot handle such long chains, catabolism requires ATP-binding cassette transporters to deliver activated substrates into peroxisomes, where acyl-CoA oxidase, a bifunctional enzyme and thiolase shorten them. Fatty acid transport proteins and acyl-CoA synthetases supply activation, and thioesterases release free acid, linking this route to membrane lipid composition and lipid signalling.

Fatty acids longer than 22 carbons are made and broken down by a dedicated set of enzymes, and the balance between the two determines the lipid composition of myelin, skin barrier ceramides, retinal photoreceptor membranes and sperm. Elongases together with the reductase and dehydratase steps of the microsomal elongation cycle add two carbons at a time to acyl-CoA substrates, while peroxisomes handle the catabolic side: transporters of the ABCD family import very-long-chain acyl-CoAs, which are then shortened by acyl-CoA oxidase, the multifunctional D-bifunctional protein and thiolase, with acyl-CoA synthetases and thioesterases setting substrate availability. Loss of this capacity is directly pathogenic causing X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy when peroxisomal import fails, Stargardt-like macular dystrophy from elongase mutations, and ichthyosis when barrier lipids cannot be assembled.

urea cycle is the liver's route for disposing of waste nitrogen, converting ammonia generated by amino acid breakdown into urea for excretion by the kidney. Without it ammonia accumulates in blood and brain, and inherited deficiencies of any step present as hyperammonemic encephalopathy in newborns or after protein loads. The cycle spans two compartments: mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, activated by N-acetylglutamate from NAGS, condenses ammonia and bicarbonate, ornithine transcarbamylase makes citrulline, and ornithine/citrulline exchange across the inner membrane by ORNT carriers links this to the cytosolic steps in which argininosuccinate is built from aspartate, cleaved to arginine and fumarate, and hydrolysed by arginase to release urea and regenerate ornithine. The fumarate produced ties nitrogen disposal to the citric acid cycle, while arginine output feeds nitric oxide and polyamine metabolism; hepatocyte expression is set by transcription factors such as CEBPA.

Protein turnover releases ammonia, which is toxic to the brain, and the urea cycle is how the liver converts it into a harmless, excretable form. Running largely in periportal hepatocytes, the route fixes ammonia and bicarbonate into carbamoyl phosphate, condenses it with ornithine, and adds a second nitrogen from aspartate to build argininosuccinate; cleavage yields arginine and fumarate, and hydrolysis of arginine liberates urea while regenerating ornithine for another turn. Mitochondrial and cytosolic steps are linked by ornithine/citrulline exchange across the inner membrane, and flux is tuned by N-acetylglutamate, the obligatory activator of the first committed enzyme, and by transcriptional control of hepatic gene expression. Loss of any component causes an inherited urea cycle disorder, with hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy and coma. The cycle also supplies arginine and connects nitrogen disposal to fumarate entry into the citric acid cycle.

ribosomal large subunit export from nucleus is the final nuclear step of ribosome biogenesis: the newly assembled 60S subunit is escorted through nuclear pores into the cytoplasm, where it joins 40S subunits to translate mRNA. Cells depend on it to sustain protein synthesis and growth, and blocking it stalls translational capacity and triggers nucleolar stress responses that stabilise p53. The adaptor NMD3 binds the maturing 60S and presents a leucine-rich export signal to the exportin CRM1, whose cargo release is driven by the RAN GTPase gradient across the nuclear envelope; passage occurs through nucleoporin channels including NUP88. Nucleolar chaperones such as nucleophosmin and assembly factors like SDAD1 couple export competence to correct late maturation, so that only properly built subunits leave the nucleus. This links nucleolar ribosome assembly to cytoplasmic translation and to proliferative control in rapidly dividing and cancer cells.

Ribosome production begins in the nucleolus but translation happens in the cytoplasm, and export of the assembled large subunit is the step that bridges the two. Without it, pre-60S particles accumulate in the nucleus, ribosome supply falls, and cells lose the capacity to sustain growth and protein synthesis; such defects underlie ribosomopathies and impose nucleolar stress that engages p53. The adaptor NMD3 binds the maturing 60S particle and presents a leucine-rich export signal to the exportin XPO1, whose cargo release depends on the RanGTP gradient set across the nuclear envelope; passage occurs through nuclear pore channels built from nucleoporins such as NUP88, while NPM1 and SDAD1 act in nucleolar assembly and maturation of the particle before and during transit. Final maturation steps, including release of the adaptor, occur once the subunit reaches the cytoplasm.

sulfur amino acid metabolic process covers the making, breaking and recycling of methionine, cysteine and their derivatives, the chemistry that links dietary protein to methylation capacity, glutathione supply and sulfide handling. It matters because these reactions set the cell's redox buffer and its universal methyl donor: loss of cystathionine beta-synthase or methionine synthase activity causes homocystinuria and megaloblastic anemia, while failure of glutamate-cysteine ligase leaves cells unable to detoxify oxidants. The genes trace the transmethylation cycle (MAT1A, GNMT, MTR, MTRR, MTHFR, BHMT), transsulfuration to cysteine (CBS, CTH), the methionine salvage route from methylthioadenosine (MTAP, APIP, ENOPH1, MRI1), and cysteine's fates in taurine synthesis (CDO1, CSAD), glutathione assembly, and sulfurtransferase-mediated disposal of sulfide and cyanide. Cystine import by SLC7A11 ties the pathway to ferroptosis resistance and tumour redox adaptation.

Handling of the sulfur-containing amino acids methionine and cysteine underpins methylation capacity, glutathione supply and sulfide detoxification. Methionine is activated to S-adenosylmethionine by MAT1A for methyl transfer, and homocysteine is either remethylated by the folate- and betaine-dependent routes (MTR, MTRR, MTHFR, BHMT) or committed to cysteine by the transsulfuration enzymes CBS and CTH; loss of CBS causes homocystinuria, and impaired remethylation raises homocysteine with vascular and neural consequences. Cysteine obtained this way or imported by the SLC7A11 antiporter feeds glutathione synthesis via GCLC/GCLM and taurine formation through CDO1 and CSAD, linking the pathway to redox defence and bile salt conjugation. Salvage of methylthioadenosine regenerates methionine from polyamine synthesis, while sulfurtransferases such as MPST and TST dispose of cyanide and hydrogen sulfide, and MSRA repairs oxidised methionine residues in proteins.

nuclear-transcribed mRNA catabolic process, nonsense-mediated decay is the surveillance system that destroys messenger RNAs carrying a premature stop codon, preventing the accumulation of truncated proteins that would act as dominant-negative or toxic species. It sets the severity of many nonsense mutations in human disease and also tunes the normal transcriptome, clearing transcripts with upstream open reading frames, retained introns, or unproductive alternative splicing. Recognition depends on the exon junction complex deposited during splicing — EIF4A3, MAGOH, RBM8A and CASC3 — which, if it lies downstream of a terminating ribosome, recruits UPF1, UPF2 and UPF3B. The SMG1 kinase then phosphorylates UPF1, licensing SMG6 endonucleolytic cleavage and SMG5/SMG7-directed deadenylation, decapping and exonucleolytic degradation by the exosome and the SKI complex. Release factors ETF1 and GSPT1 couple the decision to translation termination itself, and mutations in UPF3B cause X-linked intellectual disability.

Messenger RNAs carrying a premature stop codon are recognized and destroyed rather than translated, and nonsense-mediated decay is the surveillance system that does it. This protects cells from truncated, dominant-negative proteins, shapes the severity of nonsense mutations in inherited disease, and also tunes the abundance of normal transcripts that contain upstream open reading frames or retained introns. Recognition depends on a stalled terminating ribosome with its release factors and the helicase UPF1 together with UPF2 and UPF3; the exon junction complex, including MAGOH, RBM8A and EIF4A3, marks spliced junctions downstream of the stop. The SMG1 kinase and the SMG5-SMG7 and SMG6 branches then commit the transcript to decay, which proceeds by decapping and 5' exonucleolysis, deadenylation, endonucleolytic cleavage, and exosome-dependent degradation. The pathway is thus coupled to splicing, nuclear export and translation termination.

protein polyubiquitination is the tagging of proteins with ubiquitin chains, the mark that commits a substrate to proteasomal destruction or, with different chain linkages, to signalling and membrane trafficking outcomes. It sets the lifetime of most regulatory proteins, so it governs cell cycle progression, DNA damage responses, quality control of misfolded proteins, and the switching on and off of inflammatory signalling. E2 conjugating enzymes of the UBE2 family work with E3 ligases of several architectures: multisubunit cullin-RING complexes with their F-box and BTB substrate receptors, the anaphase-promoting complex that degrades mitotic cyclins and securin, HECT and RBR ligases such as ITCH, NEDD4 and parkin, and RING and TRIM proteins including RNF8 and RNF168 that build chains at damaged chromatin. Linear and K63 chains assembled by RNF31, SHARPIN and TRAF6 propagate NF- influenced innate immune and IL-17 receptor signalling, while TNFAIP3 reverses them. Loss of individual ligases causes neurodegeneration, developmental syndromes and cancer.

Tagging a protein with a chain of ubiquitins rather than a single moiety is how cells mark substrates for destruction by the proteasome, and how they encode non-degradative signals such as the linkage types that drive inflammatory signalling and DNA damage responses. Protein polyubiquitination is carried out by E2 conjugating enzymes of the UBE2 family working with RING, HECT and RBR E3 ligases, including cullin-RING complexes built on CUL1-SKP1-RBX1 with interchangeable F-box or BTB substrate adaptors, and the anaphase-promoting complex that destroys cyclins and securin to allow mitotic exit. Through it, cells time cell cycle transitions, clear misfolded proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, restrain WNT and NF-kB signalling, and mark damaged mitochondria for autophagy. Loss of individual ligases causes cancer predisposition, neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease, and dysregulated immune activation, reflecting how much regulatory information is written in ubiquitin chains.

mitotic cell cycle is the ordered program by which a somatic cell duplicates its genome and divides it equally between two daughters, passing through G1, S, G2 and M. It underlies all tissue growth, renewal and repair, and its deregulation is the defining feature of cancer, while errors in chromosome partitioning generate aneuploidy. Progression is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases paired with successive cyclins, restrained by CDK inhibitors and the RB-E2F switch, and made irreversible by ubiquitin-mediated destruction through the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF ligases. Aurora and Polo kinases, the gamma-tubulin ring complex and kinetochore components including the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes build and correct the spindle, with the spindle assembly checkpoint holding anaphase until attachment is complete.
