Cohesin and condensin shape the chromosomes, ESCRT machinery severs the midbody, and ATM/ATR damage checkpoints impose delay when replication or DNA integrity is compromised.

Cell proliferation depends on an ordered progression through the mitotic cell cycle — G1, S, G2 and M — in which the genome is replicated once and then partitioned equally into two daughter cells. The programme is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases paired with successive cyclins, restrained by CDK inhibitors such as p21 and p27 and by the retinoblastoma–E2F switch that licenses S-phase entry, and reset by ubiquitin-mediated destruction of cyclins and securin through the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF ligases. Origin licensing by MCM proteins, checkpoint kinases responding to DNA damage or replication stress, kinetochore and spindle assembly checkpoint components, condensin and cohesin, centrosomal and microtubule machinery, and ESCRT-dependent abscission at the cleavage furrow each govern a distinct step. Loss of these controls produces aneuploidy, genome instability and unchecked growth, which is why the pathway is central to cancer and to development.

response to oxygen radical is the set of cellular reactions triggered by superoxide, hydroxyl and related free-radical species, allowing cells to survive the unavoidable leakage of partially reduced oxygen from respiration, phagocyte oxidases and xenobiotic metabolism. When it fails, radicals oxidise lipids, proteins and DNA, driving vascular disease, neurodegeneration and premature senescence. Detoxification is handled by the superoxide dismutases in cytosol, mitochondrion and extracellular space, with copper delivery by CCS and ATP7A, downstream peroxide removal by peroxiredoxins and thioredoxin reductase, and quinone handling by NQO1. Transcriptional adaptation runs largely through NFE2L2, which induces antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes, while PARK7 senses oxidative damage and ERCC6 links the response to repair of oxidised DNA lesions. Uncoupling proteins and endothelial nitric oxide synthase with its GCH1-dependent cofactor tie redox tone to mitochondrial proton leak and vascular signalling.

Cells detect and respond to oxygen radicals such as superoxide and hydroxyl radical, mounting a defence that limits damage to lipids, proteins and DNA and keeps redox-sensitive signalling within a usable range. The response matters because unchecked radical flux drives atherosclerosis, neurodegeneration and ageing phenotypes, and because motor neuron disease follows from mutation of superoxide dismutase. Three superoxide dismutases dispose of superoxide in cytosol, mitochondrial matrix and extracellular space, with a dedicated copper chaperone loading the cytosolic enzyme; peroxiredoxins and mitochondrial thioredoxin reductase then clear the resulting peroxide. The transcription factor NFE2L2 induces detoxifying enzymes including NQO1, while uncoupling proteins lower mitochondrial radical production, metallothionein and globins buffer metals and oxygen, and GCH1 and NOS3 tie the response to nitric oxide and vascular tone. DNA repair and PARP-linked components handle the oxidative lesions that escape.

mRNA 3'-splice site recognition is the step in pre-mRNA splicing at which the spliceosome identifies the downstream end of an intron, fixing exactly where the exons will be joined. Accurate choice of this site determines the reading frame of the mature transcript and, through alternative selection of competing sites, which protein isoform a gene produces; errors generate frameshifted or intron-retaining messages and underlie splicing-driven disease. Branch point binding by SF1 together with the SF3A subunits of the U2 snRNP defines the intron's 3' region during early assembly, while SLU7 acts later to ensure the correct AG dinucleotide is used in the second transesterification. The same logic applies to the minor U12-type spliceosome acting on its rarer introns. This is part of nuclear mRNA maturation, upstream of export and translation.

Every intron must be located precisely before it can be removed, and recognition of the 3' end of the intron is how the assembling spliceosome fixes one of those boundaries. Errors here shift the reading frame or retain intronic sequence, so the fidelity of this step determines whether a transcript yields functional protein. In both the major U2-type and the minor U12-type systems, branch-point recognition by SF1 together with the U2 snRNP-associated SF3A complex (SF3A1, SF3A2, SF3A3) commits the intron 3' region to splicing, while SLU7 acts later to ensure the correct 3'-splice site is selected during the second catalytic step. This branch-site and 3'-site selection is also where regulated alternative splicing operates, expanding proteome diversity; mutations in these components are associated with myelodysplastic syndromes and other splicing-factor diseases.

Autophagy of mitochondrion is the selective clearance of mitochondria by the autophagy machinery, the quality-control system that removes organelles that have become depolarised, damaged, or surplus to requirement. It sets mitochondrial number during erythrocyte and cardiomyocyte maturation, limits release of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and DNA, and its failure underlies recessive Parkinson disease through loss of PINK1 or the ubiquitin ligase parkin. Damage-sensing occurs on the organelle itself: PINK1 accumulates on unimported precursors, parkin ubiquitinates outer-membrane proteins, and receptors including BNIP3, BNIP3L, FUNDC1, FKBP8 and BCL2L13 recruit LC3 and GABARAP family adaptors, with OPTN and SQSTM1 bridging ubiquitin to nascent membrane. Downstream steps use the general core machinery -- ULK1 with ATG13 and RB1CC1, the ATG14-containing PI3K complex, WIPI and ATG9 lipid delivery, and the ATG7-ATG5-ATG12 conjugation cascade -- to build the engulfing autophagosome for lysosomal degradation. USP30 opposes the process.

Cells dispose of damaged or surplus mitochondria by wrapping them in autophagosomes and delivering them to lysosomes for degradation, the quality-control route known as mitophagy. It limits release of reactive oxygen species and apoptogenic factors, adjusts mitochondrial mass during differentiation and metabolic change, and clears paternal mitochondria and erythroid mitochondria during maturation. Loss of this clearance underlies recessive Parkinson disease, where the kinase PINK1 accumulates on depolarized outer membranes and activates the ubiquitin ligase parkin, tagging substrates such as VDAC1 and mitofusin for recognition by receptors including optineurin and SQSTM1; USP30 opposes this by removing ubiquitin. Receptor-mediated routes act independently of ubiquitin, with BNIP3, BNIP3L/NIX, FUNDC1 and BCL2L13 binding LC3 and GABARAP directly. Downstream, the ULK1 kinase complex, BECN1-ATG14 lipid kinase machinery, WIPI and ATG2 proteins and the ATG5-ATG12-ATG7 conjugation system build the engulfing membrane.

Mitophagy is the quality-control route by which whole mitochondria are captured in autophagosomes and delivered to lysosomes, letting cells cull organelles that are depolarised, damaged, or simply surplus. It sets mitochondrial number during reticulocyte maturation and after metabolic remodelling, and its failure allows damaged organelles to accumulate and leak reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial DNA, a defect central to autosomal recessive Parkinson disease. The best-defined arm is ubiquitin-driven: the kinase PINK1 accumulates on depolarised outer membranes, activates the ligase Parkin, and the resulting ubiquitin chains recruit OPTN and SQSTM1, with USP30 opposing the mark. Receptor-mediated arms act independently, through BNIP3, BNIP3L, FUNDC1, BCL2L13 and inner-membrane prohibitin, binding LC3 and GABARAP directly. Core autophagy machinery, ULK1 initiation, ATG conjugation, and fission by DNM1L then execute engulfment, tying this pathway to hypoxia, iron handling and metabolic reprogramming.

Mitochondria that are damaged, depolarised or simply surplus are removed by mitophagy, a selective form of macroautophagy in which an individual organelle is captured in an autophagosome and delivered to lysosomes. This is how cells keep their respiratory network functional, how reticulocytes clear mitochondria during maturation, and how neurons limit oxidative damage; its failure underlies familial Parkinson disease. The best-characterised route begins with the kinase PINK1 accumulating on depolarised membranes and recruiting the ubiquitin ligase parkin, whose ubiquitin chains -- opposed by the deubiquitinase USP30 -- recruit receptors such as OPTN and SQSTM1 to bridge the organelle to ATG8-family proteins. Receptors embedded in the outer membrane, including BNIP3, BNIP3L and FUNDC1, provide ubiquitin-independent capture under hypoxia and during development. Downstream, the core autophagy initiation, elongation and lipidation machinery builds and closes the engulfing membrane.

Cleavage in ITS2 between 5.8S rRNA and LSU-rRNA of tricistronic rRNA transcript (SSU-rRNA, 5.8S rRNA, LSU-rRNA) is a step in making the large ribosomal subunit: the single polymerase I transcript carrying 18S, 5.8S and 28S sequences must be cut apart, and this reaction separates the 5.8S end from the 28S body by an endonucleolytic incision within the second internal transcribed spacer. Ribosome output, and therefore the cell's capacity to grow and proliferate, depends on it. The genes form the PELP1-TEX10-WDR18-LAS1L complex together with the SUMO protease SENP3 and the polynucleotide kinase NOL9, which prepare the cleaved ends for exonucleolytic trimming; the AAA-ATPase MDN1 and the PES1-BOP1-WDR12 module then drive nucleolar pre-60S maturation. Defects here stall pre-rRNA processing, trigger nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation, and underlie ribosomopathy-like phenotypes.

Ribosomal RNA is transcribed as one long precursor carrying the small subunit rRNA, 5.8S and the large subunit rRNA in tandem, and the spacers between them must be removed for functional ribosomes to be made. This step is the endonucleolytic cut inside internal transcribed spacer 2, which separates the 5.8S rRNA from the large subunit rRNA and commits the pre-60S particle to maturation; blocking it stalls large subunit assembly, triggers nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation, and underlies ribosomopathy-like growth defects. The genes here form the PELP1-TEX10-WDR18 nucleolar complex together with the SUMO protease SENP3, the endonuclease LAS1L paired with the polynucleotide kinase NOL9, the AAA-ATPase MDN1 and the pre-60S factor BOP1. Their coordination links spacer processing to nucleolar quality control and to the proliferative demand for new ribosomes.

small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein complex assembly builds the box C/D and H/ACA particles that guide 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation of ribosomal RNA, and so determines whether a cell can make functional ribosomes at all. Assembly is not spontaneous: dedicated chaperones and assembly factors capture nascent core proteins before they meet RNA, with SHQ1 holding dyskerin and NAF1 placing it on H/ACA RNAs, while ZNHIT3, ZNHIT6 and NUFIP1 chaperone the box C/D core protein SNU13 onto its RNA. The AAA+ ATPases RUVBL1 and RUVBL2, together with PIH1D1 and the R2TP adaptor machinery, provide the energy-dependent remodelling that licenses these handovers. The same route supplies telomerase, which shares an H/ACA core. Loss of these factors impairs ribosome biogenesis and nucleolar function, and mutations in the pathway cause ribosomopathies and neurodevelopmental disease.

Small nucleolar RNAs do not work as bare transcripts; each must be loaded with a defined set of core proteins before it can guide modification or cleavage of ribosomal RNA, and snoRNP complex assembly is the chaperoned process that builds those particles. Because box C/D and box H/ACA snoRNPs carry out the 2'-O-methylation, pseudouridylation and pre-rRNA processing steps that precede ribosome maturation, a failure here limits ribosome production and cell growth, and telomerase — itself an H/ACA particle — depends on the same route. Dedicated assembly chaperones act on each class: SHQ1 and NAF1 hand off to H/ACA cores, while ZNHIT3, ZNHIT6 and NUFIP1 deliver C/D proteins. The R2TP machinery, comprising the RUVBL1–RUVBL2 AAA+ ATPase ring with PIH1D1 and its partners, provides the ATP-dependent remodelling that places proteins onto the RNA in the nucleolus.

Telomere maintenance via recombination keeps chromosome ends long enough to be replicated and protected when telomerase is absent or insufficient, using homologous recombination to copy sequence from one telomere to another. This is the basis of the alternative lengthening of telomeres programme that roughly one in ten cancers uses to escape replicative senescence, and it also salvages ends that have shortened or become damaged in normal cells. RAD51 and its paralogues, with BRCA2 as the loader, invade a donor telomeric repeat; the SMC5/6 complex with the NSMCE2 SUMO ligase promotes recombination-dependent telomere clustering, while ERCC1-XRCC4 nucleolytic and XRCC1-dependent repair activities process the resulting joints. TERF2 restrains inappropriate recombination at intact ends, so the pathway sits at the interface of end protection, double-strand break repair and cellular immortalisation.

Chromosome ends shorten with every division, and when telomerase is absent or insufficient cells can instead copy sequence from another telomere by homologous recombination to keep ends long enough to be protected. This break-induced replication route is the basis of the alternative lengthening of telomeres programme used by a subset of cancers, and it also determines whether cells escape crisis or enter senescence when telomeres erode. Strand invasion and repair synthesis depend on RAD51 with its paralogues RAD51C and XRCC3 and the mediator BRCA2, while the RAD50-containing nuclease complex processes ends and the ERCC1-ERCC4 structure-specific endonuclease trims recombination intermediates. The SMC5/6 complex with the SUMO ligase NSMCE2 resolves and relocalises recombining telomeres, and shelterin's TERF2 normally suppresses this activity so that ends are not treated as double-strand breaks. Failure of the balance produces telomere fusions, rearrangements and genome instability.

DNA synthesis involved in DNA repair is the gap-filling step that finishes a repair reaction: once a broken 3' end has invaded a homologous duplex, a polymerase copies the intact template to restore the missing sequence. Without it, recombination intermediates cannot be completed, double-strand breaks persist, and cells accumulate the genomic instability that drives cancer and premature ageing syndromes. The genes cover the replicative machinery redeployed for repair — polymerase alpha, delta and epsilon subunits with the clamp loader — plus translesion polymerase eta for damaged templates, ribonucleotide reductase subunits that supply dNTP precursors, and the WRN helicase-exonuclease whose loss causes Werner syndrome. Meiotic recombination components such as SPATA22, SYCP1 and TEX12 tie the same synthesis step to crossover formation during gametogenesis, while SIRT1 and CDKN2D link it to cell cycle and chromatin control.

When a double-strand break is resected to leave a 3' single-stranded end, that end invades an intact homologous duplex and is extended by new DNA synthesis — the repair-associated synthesis step that converts a strand invasion intermediate into restored sequence. Without it, homologous recombination cannot be completed, breaks are shunted into error-prone end joining, and cells accumulate translocations and chromosome loss. The polymerases that carry out this extension include the replicative enzymes Pol delta and Pol epsilon with their clamp loader subunits, alongside the primase-associated Pol alpha and the translesion enzyme Pol eta; ribonucleotide reductase subunits supply the deoxynucleotide pools required. The RecQ helicase WRN and its interacting partner WRNIP1 process and stabilise recombination and stalled fork intermediates. Several members act in meiotic recombination, where the same synthesis chemistry generates crossovers during germ cell development.

cell morphogenesis is the process by which a cell acquires and maintains its shape, size and polarity as it differentiates, and it is what distinguishes a neuron with a long axon from a hair cell with a stereocilia bundle or an epithelial cell with an apical surface. Without it tissues cannot be wired or organized, and defects produce cortical malformations, axon guidance disorders, hearing loss and neurodegeneration. The genes converge on remodelling of the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton: Rho-family GTPases with their GEFs and GAPs, WAVE/Arp2/3 regulators, formins, cofilin and myosins, together with tubulins and MAPs that build and steer growth cones. Layered on top are the guidance and adhesion systems that tell a cell which way to grow — semaphorin-plexin, ephrin-Eph, netrin-DCC/UNC5, slit-Robo, cadherins, integrins and planar cell polarity components — plus transcription factors that specify shape as part of cell fate.

Cells acquire their characteristic size and shape during development, and this morphogenetic programme is what turns an unpolarised progenitor into a neuron with an axon and dendrites, an epithelial cell with an apical brush border, or a hair cell with an ordered stereocilium bundle. Actin and microtubule machinery does the building — actins, cofilin, formins, WAVE/Arp regulators, tubulins and the microtubule-associated proteins MAP2 and MAPT — while Rho-family GTPases such as RHOA, RAC1 and CDC42 with their many GEFs, GAPs and PAK/ROCK effectors decide where protrusion and contraction occur. Guidance and adhesion cues including semaphorins with their plexin receptors, ephrins and Eph kinases, slits with Robo, netrins with DCC and UNC5, cadherins and integrins orient the process, and transcription factors plus Wnt, Notch, Hedgehog and neurotrophin signalling couple it to cell fate. Disruption underlies neurodevelopmental malformations, hereditary spastic paraplegia and syndromic deafness.

Cytokinesis is the final step of cell division, in which the cytoplasm and plasma membrane are physically split so that each daughter cell receives one genome and a working complement of organelles. Getting it wrong produces binucleate cells, tetraploidy and chromosome instability, a route toward tumorigenesis, and its controlled incompletion is what creates the intercellular bridges of germ cell syncytia. Positional information from the anaphase spindle, delivered by the central spindle kinesin and its RhoGAP partner and by the aurora kinase-containing chromosomal passenger complex, activates RhoA to assemble an actomyosin ring; septin filaments, anillin and IQGAP proteins organise the furrow cortex. Rab11 and exocyst-directed vesicle traffic then feeds membrane to the midbody, where ESCRT components recruited by CEP55 and the VPS4 ATPases sever the last connection. Phosphatases, PLK1 and cullin-based ubiquitin ligases time each transition.

Cytokinesis is the final step of cell division, partitioning cytoplasm and plasma membrane so that each daughter cell receives one genome and a complete set of organelles; when it fails, cells become binucleate or tetraploid, a route to aneuploidy and tumorigenesis, and in male germ cells its deliberate incompleteness creates the intercellular bridges of the syncytium. RhoA, activated at the equator by the ECT2/RACGAP1 module, drives assembly and constriction of an actomyosin ring built from non-muscle myosin II, anilin and septin filaments, while kinesins and PRC1 organise the central spindle. Aurora B with INCENP and survivin times the events and monitors the furrow, and Rab11 vesicle traffic plus the exocyst deliver membrane to the cleavage site. Final abscission of the intercellular bridge depends on CEP55 recruiting ESCRT components, IST1 and VPS4 ATPases, with spastin severing the residual microtubules.

regulation of mitochondrial RNA catabolic process controls how quickly transcripts made from the mitochondrial genome are destroyed, and thereby sets how much of each respiratory chain subunit a cell can build. Mitochondrial DNA is transcribed as long polycistronic units from both strands, so degradation, not initiation, is the main determinant of steady-state mRNA levels and the means of clearing antisense and double-stranded byproducts that would otherwise leak into the cytosol and trigger interferon responses. The degradosome formed by the helicase SUPV3L1 with the exoribonuclease PNPT1 performs the turnover, while GRSF1 sequesters transcripts in RNA granules and the LRPPRC-SLIRP complex stabilises and polyadenylates mature mRNAs against it. Loss of this balance depletes specific mitochondrial mRNAs and causes oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, as in LRPPRC-linked Leigh syndrome.

Mitochondrial DNA is transcribed as long polycistronic precursors, and the steady-state level of each mature transcript depends as much on how fast it is degraded as on how fast it is made; this pathway covers the control of that turnover of mitochondrially encoded RNA. It matters because the thirteen respiratory chain subunits encoded by the organellar genome must be supplied in balance with nuclear-encoded partners, and because non-coding and antisense products of the same genome would otherwise accumulate and form RNA duplexes. Degradation activity resides in a helicase-exoribonuclease pair, SUPV3L1 with PNPT1, which forms the degradosome that resolves and digests aberrant and antisense species. GRSF1 melts structured transcripts within RNA granules, while LRPPRC with its partner SLIRP binds and stabilises mature mRNAs, protecting them from this machinery; loss of LRPPRC causes a French-Canadian form of cytochrome c oxidase deficiency.

rRNA 5'-end processing trims the precursor ribosomal RNA transcript to generate the exact 5' terminus of mature rRNA, a prerequisite for building functional ribosomes and therefore for all protein synthesis and cell growth. The genes here belong to the small subunit processome, the large nucleolar assembly that folds and cleaves the 47S/45S pre-rRNA en route to 18S rRNA. UTP20 and TBL3 are core processome scaffolds, NOP14 and NOP9 are RNA-binding factors that position cleavage sites, and ABT1 associates with the transcription and early processing machinery. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on proliferation, this step is a control point coupling nucleolar activity to growth signalling; defects impair 18S maturation, trigger nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation, and underlie ribosomopathies characterised by tissue-specific developmental failure.

Ribosome production begins with a long polycistronic rRNA precursor that must be cut and trimmed at defined points, and forming the mature 5' end of rRNA is one of those steps. The genes here act in the small-subunit processome, the large nucleolar assembly that folds and cleaves the 5' portion of the pre-rRNA destined for the 40S subunit. NOP14, NOP9, TBL3 and UTP20 are processome components that bind the nascent transcript and coordinate cleavage with assembly of early ribosomal proteins, while ABT1 contributes to the same nucleolar maturation events. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on cell growth, defects in these steps stall proliferation and provoke nucleolar stress signalling; comparable processome lesions in humans underlie ribosomopathies with growth and developmental consequences.

fatty acid alpha-oxidation removes a single carbon from the front end of branched-chain fatty acids so that they can be handled by the ordinary beta-oxidation machinery. It exists because dietary phytanic acid, derived from chlorophyll, carries a methyl group at carbon 3 that blocks the dehydrogenation step of beta-oxidation; shortening the chain by one carbon shifts the branch to an even position and unblocks the route. The reactions occur in peroxisomes, where phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase introduces a 2-hydroxyl group and HACL1 cleaves the bond to release formyl-CoA and pristanal, en route to pristanic acid. Substrate entry and cofactor supply depend on peroxisomal transporters and on the import machinery of the organelle. Loss of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase causes Refsum disease, with phytanic acid accumulation producing retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral neuropathy and ataxia.

Branched-chain fatty acids such as phytanic acid, released from chlorophyll-derived dietary lipids, carry a methyl group at carbon 3 that blocks the dehydrogenation step of ordinary beta-oxidation; alpha-oxidation shortens them by one carbon so the remainder can be degraded conventionally. The chemistry is peroxisomal: a long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase activates the substrate, a 2-hydroxylase introduces a hydroxyl at the alpha carbon, and a thiamine-pyrophosphate-dependent 2-hydroxyacyl-CoA lyase cleaves off formyl-CoA, yielding pristanal and then pristanic acid for entry into beta-oxidation. Delivery of enzymes into the organelle and transport of substrates and cofactors across its membrane are part of the route, which is why generalised peroxisome biogenesis defects impair it. Loss of the hydroxylase step causes phytanic acid accumulation with retinitis pigmentosa, anosmia and peripheral neuropathy, linking this catabolic route to dietary lipid handling and neurological health.

Response to protozoan covers the host reaction to parasites such as Plasmodium, Leishmania and Toxoplasma, and it determines whether an infection is contained in the tissue or spreads systemically. It matters because these organisms live inside macrophages and other host cells, so control depends on cell-autonomous killing plus tightly balanced inflammation; too little causes uncontrolled parasitaemia, too much causes cerebral malaria and immunopathology. The genes describe both arms. Pattern recognition through Dectin-1 and MyD88 drives IL-12 and interferon-gamma-dependent programmes, and the guanylate-binding proteins then disrupt the parasitophorous vacuole to expose the parasite to killing. Transcription factors including IRF8, IRF4 and the BATF proteins set macrophage and dendritic cell activation states, while arginase-1, IL-10 and phagosomal metal transport by SLC11A1 tune the balance between nitric oxide production, nutrient deprivation and resolution of inflammation. Defensins and platelet factor 4 add direct antiparasitic activity.

Protozoan parasites such as Plasmodium, Toxoplasma and Leishmania provoke a distinctive host response, and this pathway covers the cellular and organismal changes triggered by that encounter. It matters because control of intracellular protozoa depends on interferon-driven macrophage activation rather than antibody alone, and defects here lead to uncontrolled parasite replication or, at the other extreme, immunopathology from excessive inflammation. Pattern recognition through a C-type lectin for fungal and parasite glycans and the adaptor MyD88 initiates signalling; transcription factors including IRF8, IRF4 and the BATF family drive dendritic cell and macrophage programmes and IL12B production, steering T cells toward interferon-gamma output. Guanylate-binding proteins then disrupt parasite-containing vacuoles, while SLC11A1 restricts phagosomal metal availability and arginase and IL-10 restrain the response. Antimicrobial defensins and CD40 costimulation link innate detection to adaptive immunity.

Gastric acid secretion is the release of hydrochloric acid into the stomach lumen by parietal cells, the step that lowers gastric pH enough to activate pepsin, kill ingested microbes, and liberate dietary iron and vitamin B12. Too little acid causes hypochlorhydria with bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption; too much drives peptic ulceration and reflux disease. Secretion is switched on by gastrin acting through CCKBR, by histamine through the H2 receptor, and by muscarinic input from the vagus, and restrained by prostaglandin E2 receptors, somatostatin and peptides such as secretin and ghrelin. Downstream, the proton pump is trafficked to the apical canalicular membrane in a process requiring HIP1R and SNX10, while KCNQ1 recycles potassium and SLC26A7 and SLC9A4 handle the accompanying anion and sodium fluxes. TFF2 provides mucosal protection against the acid produced.

Gastric acid secretion is the controlled release of hydrochloric acid into the stomach lumen by parietal cells, which lowers luminal pH enough to activate pepsin, kill ingested microbes and liberate dietary iron and vitamin B12. Secretion is driven by the proton pump at the apical membrane, supported by anion and cation transport that recycles chloride and potassium, with SLC26A7 supplying chloride, KCNQ1 providing potassium conductance and SLC9A4 handling sodium-proton exchange. Stimulation comes through receptors for gastrin, acetylcholine and histamine, while prostaglandin E and somatostatin-like signals restrain it; ghrelin, secretin and neuromedin U add endocrine control tied to feeding. Trafficking proteins including HIP1R and SNX10 govern the tubulovesicle rearrangements that deliver pumps to the canaliculus. Too much acid produces peptic ulceration and reflux disease, while achlorhydria causes malabsorption and bacterial overgrowth, and TFF2 marks the protective mucous response.

Cell fate determination is the step in development at which a cell stops being merely biased toward an identity and becomes irreversibly committed to it, passing that commitment to its daughters. It is what allows a single embryonic genome to generate stable, distinct cell types — neurons, muscle, endoderm, retina — and its misregulation underlies developmental malformations and the identity switches seen in tumours. The genes span the classical machinery: master transcription factors that lock in lineage programs (MYOD1 for skeletal muscle, ASCL1 and ATOH1 for neuronal and sensory fates, GATA and SOX factors for mesoderm and endoderm), pluripotency and neural progenitor regulators such as POU5F1, PAX6 and FOXG1, and the intercellular signals that assign fates within a field — Notch ligands and receptors with HES1 for lateral inhibition, plus WNT, BMP, Hedgehog and retinoic acid inputs. Commitment thus emerges from signalling converging on self-reinforcing transcriptional networks.

Once a progenitor has been steered toward a particular identity, cell fate determination locks that choice in: the commitment becomes irreversible and is inherited by daughter cells, so that neurons stay neurons and muscle stays muscle through subsequent divisions. This step converts transient positional signalling into a stable transcriptional state, and its failure produces malformed organs, mispatterned nervous systems, or cells that revert to a progenitor-like state, as in tumour initiation. The genes here span both halves of the process: secreted cues and their receivers, including Wnt, BMP and Hedgehog components, Notch receptors with their ligands Delta and Jagged, and the Hes repressors that mediate lateral inhibition; and the lineage-defining transcription factors that enact the decision, such as MyoD for skeletal muscle, the proneural factors ASCL1 and ATOH1, PAX6 and FOXG1 in the eye and forebrain, and GATA and SOX proteins in mesoderm and endoderm.

Mesodermal cell fate commitment is the step in early embryogenesis at which a pluripotent epiblast cell irreversibly chooses the middle germ layer, the source of heart, blood, skeleton, muscle and kidney. Everything built from mesoderm depends on this decision being made in the right cells at the right time; its failure or misplacement produces gastrulation arrest and severe congenital malformation. Commitment is driven by graded signalling at the primitive streak: NODAL and BMP4 acting through BMPR1A and SMAD1, WNT3A, and FGFR1, tuned by the secreted antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2 so that mesoderm is specified only where these inputs converge. Downstream transcription factors lock the state in and begin regionalising it, with MESP1 marking nascent cardiovascular mesoderm and PAX2, SIX2, EYA1 and HOX genes directing intermediate and posterior mesoderm toward nephron and limb fates.

During gastrulation, cells of the early embryo must decide irreversibly whether to join the mesoderm, and mesodermal cell fate commitment is the step that locks in that choice before any muscle, bone, blood, heart or kidney tissue can form. Failure or misdirection at this point produces embryonic lethality or malformation of the structures that derive from mesoderm. Commitment is driven by graded extracellular cues: NODAL and BMP4 acting through receptors such as BMPR1A and the SMAD1 transcriptional relay, WNT3A signalling tuned by the secreted antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2, and FGFR1-mediated input at the primitive streak. These converge on transcriptional regulators, notably MESP1 for nascent mesoderm and PAX2, SIX2, EYA1/EYA2 and FOXC2 for the intermediate and paraxial derivatives that generate the kidney and somites. The pathway therefore sits at the interface of patterning signals and lineage-restricting gene expression in the gastrulating embryo.

Formation of cytoplasmic translation initiation complex is the final commitment step of protein synthesis initiation, in which the large ribosomal subunit joins a small subunit already positioned at the start codon, yielding an elongation-competent 80S ribosome with initiator methionyl-tRNA in the P site. Because this step sets how often and which mRNAs are translated, it is the main point at which growth factor and nutrient signalling, stress responses, and viral takeover of the host ribosome exert control over gene expression. The thirteen-subunit eIF3 complex acts as the scaffold that holds mRNA, initiator tRNA and the 40S subunit together and prevents premature subunit joining, while eIF5 triggers GTP hydrolysis on eIF2 to license release of the initiation factors. Individual eIF3 subunits are recurrently overexpressed in tumours, where they bias translation toward proliferative transcripts.

Protein synthesis begins only once a ribosome has been assembled correctly on a start codon, and the formation of the cytoplasmic translation initiation complex is that final commitment step: the large 60S subunit joins the 43S/48S preinitiation complex already positioned at an AUG, initiation factors are released, and the initiator methionyl-tRNA is left seated in the P site of an elongation-competent 80S ribosome. The genes here are almost entirely subunits of eIF3, the largest initiation factor, which scaffolds the 40S subunit, binds mRNA and eIF4 components, and prevents premature subunit joining; eIF5 acts as the GTPase-activating protein for eIF2, triggering GTP hydrolysis and the start-codon commitment that precedes 60S recruitment. Because this step sets the rate of global and mRNA-selective translation, it is a control point for growth signalling, stress responses, and the translational reprogramming exploited in tumours.

Somitogenesis is the process that carves the vertebrate embryo's paraxial mesoderm into a repeating series of blocks, the somites, which go on to form the vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis. Its regularity sets the body's segmental plan, and its disruption produces congenital vertebral malformations and rib fusions such as spondylocostal dysostosis. Timing comes from a segmentation clock built on oscillating Notch signalling, with HES7, LFNG, DLL1 and DLL3 and the glycosyltransferases that modify Notch receptors setting the period, read out against opposing Wnt and FGF gradients from the tail bud. TBX6, MSGN1 and TBXT maintain the presomitic mesoderm, while MESP2 and the RIPPLY repressors define each future boundary and impose anterior-posterior polarity within a somite. Downstream transcription factors including PAX-family partners, MEOX and MYF5 then commit somite compartments to sclerotome and myotome fates.

Somitogenesis is the process that cuts the presomitic mesoderm into paired blocks along the head-to-tail axis, establishing the segmental blueprint from which vertebrae, ribs, dermis and skeletal muscle later derive. Its timing is set by a segmentation clock driven by oscillating Notch and Wnt components — HES7, LFNG, DLL1 and DLL3, with glycosyltransferases such as POFUT1 and POGLUT1 and the ubiquitin ligase MIB1 tuning ligand-receptor output — read out against posterior Wnt and BMP gradients that define where a boundary forms. MESP2, TBX6, RIPPLY1/2 and TCF15 then confer rostral-caudal identity within each somite and resolve boundaries, while MEOX and myogenic factors commit derivatives to sclerotome and myotome. Disruption of clock or boundary genes produces congenital vertebral malformation and rib fusion, as in spondylocostal dysostosis, linking embryonic patterning directly to axial skeletal anatomy.

Neutrophil homeostasis keeps the circulating neutrophil pool at a steady size, balancing granulopoietic output from the marrow against the clearance of aged and apoptotic cells so that the body has enough phagocytes for antibacterial defence without the tissue damage of unchecked neutrophilia. Its failure appears clinically as neutropenia with recurrent infection at one extreme and as persistent inflammatory infiltration at the other. Set points are read through signalling from cytokine and chemoattractant receptors, including IL6, the CCR2 axis and thrombopoietin receptor MPL, and transmitted by kinases and phosphoinositide enzymes such as BTK, PDE4B and the PI3K catalytic subunits, with SH2B3 restraining the response. The disposal arm is equally represented: XKR8 scrambles phosphatidylserine to flag dying neutrophils, and MERTK and AXL on macrophages engulf them, while annexin A1 and released HMGB1 tune whether resolution or further recruitment follows.

Neutrophils are short-lived and produced in enormous numbers, so their standing count is set by a balance between marrow output and clearance of aged cells. Maintaining neutrophil homeostasis keeps the blood supplied with phagocytes without the tissue damage that unchecked neutrophilia causes; its failure gives neutropenia and recurrent bacterial infection at one extreme, or inflammatory injury at the other. Granulopoiesis is driven by cytokine and growth-factor signalling through IL6 and thrombopoietin receptor pathways, with intracellular relays such as BTK, the class IA PI3K catalytic subunits PIK3CB and PIK3CD, and the negative regulator SH2B3 tuning progenitor expansion and cell activation. Removal depends on apoptotic-cell recognition: XKR8 scrambles phosphatidylserine to the surface of dying cells and the receptors MERTK and AXL mediate their engulfment, while ANXA1 and chemoattractant receptors including CCR2 and HCAR2 restrain and redirect trafficking so that senescent neutrophils are cleared rather than degranulating in tissue.

Type IV hypersensitivity is delayed-type, cell-mediated allergy: antigen-specific T cells recognise processed peptide, release cytokines, and recruit and activate monocytes and other leukocytes over hours to days rather than minutes. It is the basis of contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test reactivity, granuloma formation, drug eruptions and much transplant rejection, and it depends on effector T cells reaching tissue rather than on antibody. The genes trace that sequence: fucosyltransferase VII and the sialomucin CD43 build and present the selectin ligands that let activated T cells roll and adhere on inflamed endothelium, GATA3 sets the Th2 cytokine program that shapes which effector response ensues, and an IL-20 family receptor subunit couples the resulting cytokines to keratinocyte and epithelial inflammation. Zona pellucida antigen illustrates the autoimmune version, where T cell recognition of a self tissue protein drives the same destructive infiltrate.

Type IV hypersensitivity is the delayed, antibody-independent arm of immune injury: T cells recognise processed soluble or cell-associated antigen, release cytokines, and recruit and activate leukocytes over hours to days rather than minutes. It underlies contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin reactivity, granuloma formation, allograft rejection and much autoimmune tissue damage, and it is the response probed by skin testing. The genes here touch the steps that make such a reaction possible: fucosyltransferase-dependent synthesis of selectin ligands on leukocyte surface sialomucins governs rolling and extravasation into inflamed tissue, so that effector T cells reach the antigen-bearing site; GATA3 sets the transcriptional polarisation of helper T cells and the cytokines they produce; an interleukin-20 family receptor subunit links lymphocyte-derived cytokines to responses in keratinocytes and other epithelia; and a well-studied glycoprotein autoantigen provides the target recognition that initiates T cell-mediated ovarian inflammation.

Inner cell mass cell differentiation is the earliest cell fate decision in mammalian development, setting apart the pluripotent inner cell mass of the blastocyst from the trophectoderm that will build the placenta. Everything the embryo proper becomes, and the derivation of embryonic stem cells in culture, depends on this segregation and on keeping the inner cells pluripotent rather than letting them drift into extraembryonic fates. The Hippo kinases LATS1 and LATS2 read cell position and contact, restricting the trophectoderm program to outer cells, while transcriptional regulators including PRDM14, TFAP2C, NR5A2 and SOX17 establish naive pluripotency and the first primitive endoderm split. TET1-mediated DNA demethylation and PAF1 complex-dependent transcription elongation via CTR9 maintain the chromatin state that keeps these lineage genes responsive. Failure here arrests development before implantation.

In the preimplantation embryo, the inner cell mass is the pluripotent compartment set aside from the trophectoderm, and its differentiation is what commits blastomeres to becoming embryo proper rather than placenta. Getting this allocation right determines whether implantation yields a viable embryo, and the same regulatory logic underlies derivation and maintenance of embryonic stem cells. Hippo pathway kinases LATS1 and LATS2 restrain the YAP-driven trophectoderm programme in interior cells, favouring inner cell mass identity, while PRDM14, TFAP2C and the DNA demethylase TET1 shape the naive pluripotency network and its epigenetic ground state. Transcriptional elongation and ribosome biogenesis factors such as CTR9 and NLE1 support this specification, and SOX17, HNF1B and NR5A2 mark the later endodermal and lineage-restricted fates that emerge as pluripotency resolves. Disruption causes early embryonic lethality before or around implantation.

Epithelial to mesenchymal transition is the programme by which a polarised, junction-bound epithelial cell dismantles its apical-basolateral organisation, releases its neighbours, breaches basement membrane and becomes a motile mesenchymal cell. It builds the mesoderm and neural crest during gastrulation, drives palate and heart valve morphogenesis, contributes to wound repair and organ fibrosis, and is reactivated in carcinoma to grant invasiveness, stem-like properties and drug resistance. TGF-beta and BMP receptors signalling through SMAD2/3/4, canonical WNT acting via beta-catenin and LEF1/TCF7L2, NOTCH-RBPJ and receptor tyrosine kinase input converge on the transcription factors SNAI1, SNAI2, TWIST1 and ZEB-like repressors that extinguish junctional genes such as cadherins and desmogleins. Chromatin modifiers including EZH2, KDM1A and HDAC2, a large set of microRNAs led by the miR-200-like and miR-145 families, and ROCK-driven cytoskeletal remodelling set the threshold and reversibility of the switch.

Epithelial to mesenchymal transition converts a polarized, junction-bound epithelial cell into a motile mesenchymal one: apical-basolateral polarity is dismantled, cell-cell adhesions are severed, basement membrane is remodelled and the cell migrates. It builds the mesoderm and neural crest during gastrulation, drives heart valve and palate morphogenesis, and reappears in wound healing, organ fibrosis and carcinoma invasion and metastasis, where it also confers drug resistance and stem-like properties. The programme is driven by TGF-beta and BMP ligands signalling through type I and II receptors to SMAD2/3/4, by WNT-beta-catenin with LEF1/TCF7L2, and by NOTCH, FGF and HGF inputs, converging on SNAI1, SNAI2 and TWIST1 to repress epithelial genes. Chromatin modifiers such as EZH2, KDM1A and HDAC2 lock in the new state, ROCK kinases and integrin-adhesion proteins reorganize the cytoskeleton, LOXL enzymes remodel matrix, and antagonists including NOG, GREM1, SFRPs, SMAD7, OVOL2 and numerous microRNAs restrain the switch.

Neural tube formation is the earliest morphogenetic event of central nervous system development, converting the flat neural plate ectoderm into a closed tube that becomes brain and spinal cord. Failure of closure produces anencephaly and spina bifida, among the most common human birth defects, and explains why folate metabolism genes such as MTHFR, MTHFD1 and FOLR1 sit alongside the structural machinery here. Closure requires planar cell polarity signalling through VANGL2, CELSR1, SCRIB, PRICKLE1 and the frizzled receptors to drive convergent extension, apical constriction powered by actin regulators such as CFL1, PFN1 and SHROOM-like effectors, and ciliary transport (IFT proteins, MKS1, TCTN1) that tunes Sonic hedgehog patterning via PTCH1 and SUFU. BMP, Nodal and retinoic acid inputs set dorsoventral identity, while GRHL2/GRHL3 and apoptotic regulators control fusion of the apposed neural folds and remodelling of the surface ectoderm.

Neurulation converts the flat neural plate into a closed tube, the founding step of central nervous system development; failure to close leaves spina bifida, anencephaly or craniorachischisis, among the most common human birth defects. Bending and fusion of the neuroepithelium depend on planar cell polarity components such as VANGL2, CELSR1, PRICKLE1 and the Frizzled receptors, which orient convergent extension, together with actin remodelling by cofilin, profilin, VASP and Rho regulators that drive apical constriction and hinge point formation. Dorsoventral patterning signals from BMPs, Nodal, noggin and Sonic hedgehog transduction through PTCH1 and SUFU, plus primary cilium and intraflagellar transport proteins, set positional identity, while GRHL2, GRHL3 and OVOL2 govern the surface ectoderm that zips over the closing tube. Folate handling enzymes including MTHFR and MTHFD1 explain why maternal folate status modifies closure risk.

Retina homeostasis is the maintenance of a working photoreceptor layer over a lifetime: keeping rods and cones alive, renewing their outer segments, recycling visual chromophore, and matching metabolic supply to one of the most energy-demanding tissues in the body. Its failure is the molecular basis of inherited blindness — retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, Usher and Bardet-Biedl syndromes, and macular degeneration. The genes trace the structures involved: connecting-cilium and transition-zone proteins that traffic opsin into the outer segment, the visual cycle enzymes RPE65 and RDH12 acting in the pigment epithelium, ABCA4 clearing retinoid adducts, and cadherin-based tip links that also serve hearing, explaining why so many of these disorders combine retinal and cochlear degeneration. Glucose transport, oxidative defence and lysosomal or autophagic clearance of shed discs complete the survival programme.

Maintaining the retina as a working tissue means keeping photoreceptors alive and functional for a lifetime, since they are post-mitotic and cannot be replaced. The genes here define that homeostasis and, when mutated, produce the inherited retinal degenerations — retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, Stargardt disease, Usher syndrome and Bardet-Biedl syndrome — in which rods and cones die progressively and vision is lost. Much of the work is structural and transport-based: rhodopsin and its phototransduction partners must be renewed in outer segments, the visual cycle enzymes RPE65 and RDH12 regenerate chromophore in concert with the pigment epithelium, ABCA4 clears retinoid adducts that would otherwise accumulate as toxic lipofuscin, and ciliary and BBSome components move cargo through the connecting cilium. Cadherin-based tip links and CRB1-organised junctions add adhesion, while trophic and antioxidant factors set the balance between survival and cell death.

Regulation of receptor recycling controls how quickly internalised surface receptors are returned to the plasma membrane rather than degraded, and thereby sets how strongly a cell can keep responding to a hormone, neurotransmitter or lipoprotein. The balance matters directly in cholesterol homeostasis, where PCSK9 diverts the LDL receptor to lysosomal destruction instead of recycling and raises plasma LDL, and in synaptic plasticity, where the rate of AMPA receptor return to the postsynaptic membrane determines synaptic strength. The genes describe the machinery and its brakes: endocytic adaptors and cargo selectors such as EPS15 and KIF16B, Rab and Arf regulators including ARAP1, TBC1D16 and RAB29, phosphoinositide phosphatases that mark recycling endosomes, and SNARE-dependent fusion via VAMP3 and NSF. Polarity and scaffolding proteins bias delivery to particular membrane domains, linking receptor traffic to receptor sensitivity and desensitisation.

Receptors internalized by endocytosis are either degraded or returned to the cell surface, and this pathway governs how strongly the recycling arm is favoured. Setting that balance determines how many receptors a cell displays, and therefore how sensitive it remains to hormones, lipoproteins and neurotransmitters. Cholesterol handling is a clear illustration: PCSK9 diverts the LDL receptor toward lysosomal destruction rather than recycling, so its loss lowers circulating LDL while gain of function causes hypercholesterolaemia. Other members act on the trafficking machinery itself — Rab-directed regulators and TBC1D16, the kinesin KIF16B moving endosomes along microtubules, ESCRT and SNARE components including CHMP5, NSF and VAMP3 for membrane fusion, and EPS15 at the internalization step. In neurons the same logic controls surface AMPA receptor subunit GRIA1 during synaptic plasticity, linking endosomal sorting to learning, receptor desensitization and signal termination.

negative regulation of endothelial cell proliferation is the braking side of angiogenesis: the signals and repressors that keep vessel-lining cells quiescent so that capillary beds stay stable rather than sprouting continuously. It matters because unchecked endothelial growth drives tumour vascularisation, retinopathy and vascular malformation, while excessive braking impairs wound healing and collateral vessel formation. The genes span several restraining mechanisms: BMP9/ALK1 signalling through ACVRL1, ENG and TGFBR1, whose loss causes hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia; Notch ligand DLL4 and the decoy VEGF receptor FLT1, which limit tip-cell selection and sequester VEGF; matrix-derived inhibitors such as THBS1, SPARC and collagen IV fragments; the CCM complex of KRIT1 and PDCD10, mutated in cerebral cavernous malformations; and inflammatory and interferon-driven inputs including TNF, STAT1 and CXCR3. A large cohort of microRNAs, notably miR-15/16, miR-34a and miR-503, imposes post-transcriptional restraint on the same growth programme.

Blood vessels only grow when endothelial cells are allowed to divide, and this pathway is the brake: the collected signals, receptors and microRNAs that stop or slow endothelial cell proliferation and so keep the vasculature quiescent. Its loss permits pathological angiogenesis in tumours and retinopathy, while excessive or mutationally disrupted braking underlies vascular malformations. Much of the mechanism runs through BMP9/BMP10 signalling to the ACVRL1–ENG–TGFBR1 receptor complex, mutated in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, and through the KRIT1–PDCD10 module lost in cerebral cavernous malformation. Notch ligand DLL4 restrains tip-cell proliferation during sprouting, soluble VEGF receptor FLT1 sequesters ligand, and matrix and secreted inhibitors such as THBS1, SPARC, MMRN2 and vasohibin act from outside the cell. Inflammatory cytokines, caveolins, PPARG and a large complement of microRNAs add post-transcriptional and contextual control.

lymph vessel development is the construction of the lymphatic vasculature, the vessel network that drains interstitial fluid back to the blood, absorbs dietary lipids in the gut, and carries antigen and immune cells to lymph nodes. Its failure produces lymphoedema, chylous effusions and lymphatic malformations. The genes trace the sequence: SOX18, NR2F2 and PROX1 specify lymphatic endothelial identity within the embryonic vein, VEGFC acting through FLT4 with the extracellular partner CCBE1 drives sprouting and migration of those progenitors, and FOXC2 with PDPN and NPR2 governs the separation of collecting vessels from capillaries and the formation of valves. TGF-beta/BMP receptors, ephrin-B2 and TIE1 tune vessel remodelling and maturation, while podoplanin-dependent platelet aggregation through SYK and LGALS8 keeps the lymphatic and blood systems from connecting.

Lymphatic vessels drain interstitial fluid, absorb dietary lipids and carry immune cells to lymph nodes, and this pathway covers their construction from venous endothelium through to a mature, valved, hierarchically patterned network. When it fails the result is lymphoedema, chylous effusions and lymphatic malformation, and the same programme is exploited by tumours for metastatic spread. Lymphatic fate is specified by transcription factors acting in sequence, with SOX18 and the nuclear receptor NR2F2 inducing PROX1 in a subset of cardinal vein cells; PROX1 then maintains identity together with FOXC2, which also controls valve formation under shear stress. Sprouting and migration depend on VEGFC signalling through the receptor FLT4 with its collagen-binding cofactor CCBE1, while podoplanin, TIE1, EFNB2 and the adhesion protein SVEP1 shape vessel remodelling, separation from blood vessels and lumen stability. BMP and natriuretic peptide receptor inputs modulate the process.

regulation of cell-matrix adhesion controls how tightly and how transiently a cell grips the extracellular matrix, the decision that determines whether it stays anchored, migrates, or dies by anoikis. It underlies wound healing, angiogenesis, immune cell trafficking and tissue architecture, and its dysregulation permits tumour invasion, metastasis and fibrosis. The core machinery is the integrin adhesion complex: talin, kindlins and vinculin link receptors such as ITGB3 to actin, while FAK, PTK2B and SRC transduce engagement into survival and cytoskeletal signalling. Rho-family GTPases with their GAPs and effectors, including RHOA, RAC1, DLC1 and ROCK kinases, tune contractility and adhesion turnover, and phosphatases, PTEN-PI3K signalling and microtubule-tethering proteins set the timing of focal adhesion assembly and disassembly. Proteases, matricellular proteins and guidance cues such as thrombospondin, MMP14, semaphorins and ephrins modify the matrix itself, coupling adhesion strength to the surrounding environment.

Cells hold onto the extracellular matrix through integrin-based contacts, and the strength, turnover and location of those contacts are actively tuned rather than fixed. This regulation of cell-matrix adhesion determines whether a cell stays anchored, migrates, spreads or dies of detachment, and it underlies wound healing, angiogenesis, immune cell trafficking and the invasive behaviour of tumour cells. Talin, vinculin, kindlins and the integrin tail-binding proteins assemble the adhesion plaque; focal adhesion kinase, SRC, ABL1 and phosphatases such as PTPRA signal from it; and RHOA, RAC1 with ROCK kinases and cofilin set the actomyosin tension that adhesions sense. Receptor inputs from growth factors, ephrins, semaphorins, WNT and TGF-beta family ligands feed in, while matrix-remodelling proteases and secreted modulators such as thrombospondin and plasminogen activators alter the substrate itself. Loss of control produces defective migration, fibrosis and metastatic dissemination.

regulation of systemic arterial blood pressure by circulatory renin-angiotensin is the endocrine cascade that sets vascular tone, sodium balance and blood pressure over minutes to days, and it is the pathway targeted by most antihypertensive drugs. It begins when the kidney releases renin, which cleaves circulating angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme and a set of peptidases including chymase, cathepsin G and aminopeptidases then generate angiotensin II and the further fragments angiotensin III, IV and angiotensin-(1-7), while ACE2, prolylcarboxypeptidase and neprilysin degrade or redirect them. The balance of these peptides acting on angiotensin receptors determines vasoconstriction versus vasodilation, aldosterone release and renal salt retention. Mast cell proteases, the renin receptor, and sensors such as the succinate receptor on juxtaglomerular cells couple local tissue and metabolic cues into renin release. Dysregulation produces hypertension, renovascular disease and cardiac and renal remodelling.

Systemic arterial pressure is set in part by a hormone cascade that begins in the kidney, and this circulating renin-angiotensin arm is the body's main means of defending perfusion pressure and sodium balance when volume falls. Renin, released from juxtaglomerular cells and bound by its receptor, cleaves liver-derived angiotensinogen, and peptidases including angiotensin-converting enzyme, aminopeptidases such as ENPEP and ANPEP, neprilysin, prolylcarboxypeptidase and prolyl endopeptidase generate or degrade the downstream angiotensin peptides that act on vascular receptors to cause vasoconstriction, aldosterone release and thirst. ACE2 diverts the pathway toward vasodilatory products, and mast cell proteases such as chymase, cathepsin G and CPA3 provide alternative angiotensin-generating routes in tissue. Chronic overactivity drives hypertension, cardiac and renal fibrosis, which is why enzyme and receptor blockade of this axis is standard antihypertensive therapy; loss of signalling produces hypotension and renal tubular dysgenesis.

Regulation of blood volume by renin-angiotensin is the hormonal circuit that sets how much fluid the body retains, and with it arterial pressure. When renal perfusion or salt delivery falls, juxtaglomerular cells release renin, which cleaves circulating angiotensinogen; angiotensin-converting enzyme then generates angiotensin II, the effector that constricts vessels, drives aldosterone and vasopressin release, promotes tubular sodium and water reabsorption, and stimulates thirst. Signalling through the AT1 receptor accounts for most of these pressor and volume-expanding actions, while AT2 receptors and the ACE2 branch, which degrades angiotensin II to vasodilatory angiotensin-(1-7), oppose them, and NADPH oxidase-derived oxidants amplify the vascular response. Sustained overactivity of this axis produces hypertension, cardiac and renal fibrosis, and heart failure, which is why ACE inhibitors and receptor blockers are mainstays of cardiovascular therapy. The pathway links kidney sensing to systemic haemodynamics and fluid balance.

Blood volume and arterial pressure are set in part by a hormonal cascade that begins when the kidney senses reduced perfusion or salt delivery. Renin released from juxtaglomerular cells cleaves circulating angiotensinogen from the liver, and angiotensin-converting enzyme completes the conversion to angiotensin II, which acts through its type 1 receptor to constrict vessels, drive aldosterone release, promote renal sodium and water retention, and stimulate thirst; the type 2 receptor and ACE2, which degrades angiotensin II to the vasodilatory angiotensin-(1-7), oppose these effects. This axis explains why its blockade with ACE inhibitors and receptor antagonists lowers blood pressure, and why sustained activation contributes to hypertension, heart failure and progressive kidney disease. Associated NADPH oxidase and kinase signalling components link receptor engagement to oxidative stress and vascular remodelling, and tachykinin receptor signalling ties the system to fluid intake behaviour.

Chondrocyte development covers the maturation of a committed cartilage cell through proliferation, hypertrophy and matrix production, the sequence that builds the growth plate and thereby determines the length and shape of every endochondral bone. When it fails, the result is skeletal dysplasia, disproportionate short stature or premature joint degeneration. SOX9 sustains the chondrocytic program while RUNX2 and MSX2 drive the switch to hypertrophy, and the pace of that switch is set by PTHLH acting against FGF18, BMP receptor and TGF-beta receptor signalling, with WNT modulators such as AXIN2 and SFRP2 tuning the balance. The rest of the program is secretory: collagen XI and XXVII, matrilin, COMP and the enzymes that synthesise and sulfate proteoglycan chains build a cartilage matrix, whose folding and export depend on SERPINH1 and PERK-mediated stress signalling. Matrix remodelling by sulfatases and SMPD3 prepares hypertrophic cartilage for mineralisation and replacement by bone.

Chondrocyte development covers the maturation of a committed cartilage cell through proliferation, hypertrophy and the production of a cartilage matrix, and it sets the pace of endochondral bone growth and thus limb and skeletal proportion. Failure produces chondrodysplasias, short stature and joint disease, and the same programme is redeployed during fracture repair. SOX9 maintains the chondrocytic state while RUNX2 and MSX2 drive the switch to hypertrophy, with PTHLH restraining premature maturation; BMP and TGF-beta receptor signalling, FGF18 and modulators such as SFRP2 and AXIN2 tune the growth plate response. Much of the gene content is matrix and matrix-modifying: collagen XI and XXVII, COMP, matrilin-1, chondroitin and heparan sulfate biosynthetic enzymes, and the sulfatases SULF1 and SULF2, which edit heparan sulfate to alter growth factor availability. SERPINH1 and EIF2AK3 link collagen folding and secretory stress to chondrocyte survival.

Epithelial cell maturation is the final step of epithelial differentiation: after a cell has been placed in a sheet and given its shape, it must acquire the secretory, absorptive, or barrier machinery that makes it useful. This is what turns a committed progenitor into a functioning gland cell, an enterocyte with a brush border, a skin keratinocyte with a competent lipid barrier, or a hormone-secreting islet cell, and its failure leaves epithelia present but non-functional — as in barrier defects underlying atopic dermatitis or loss of insulin output. The genes point to lineage-restricted transcriptional programmes, including FOXA1 and PGR in hormone-responsive glandular epithelium, NKX6-1 in pancreatic beta cells, TFCP2L1 in kidney and stomach, and RFX3 in ciliated cells, together with XBP1-driven secretory expansion, HIF1A-sensed oxygen availability, TGFB1 signalling, and lipid and barrier components such as GPAT4 and TMEM79.

Epithelial cell maturation is the final step by which a committed epithelial cell acquires the secretory, absorptive or barrier capacity that makes a sheet of cells functional, without further change in cell shape. It determines what a given epithelium actually does: hormone-responsive glandular secretion in mammary and uterine tissue, insulin production in pancreatic islets, mucus and ion handling in airway and gut, and lipid-based barrier formation in skin. Lineage-restricted transcription factors set the terminal programme, with FOXA1 and PGR driving hormone-responsive glandular identity, NKX6-1 specifying islet beta cells, TFCP2L1 acting in kidney and secretory epithelia, and RFX3 coupling maturation to ciliogenesis. Supporting these are secretory-capacity and stress-adaptive arms, notably XBP1-dependent expansion of the endoplasmic reticulum, HIF1A-mediated responses to low oxygen, and TGFB1 signalling. Failure yields immature, poorly secreting or leaky epithelia, as in barrier defects of the skin and impaired glandular differentiation.

Extraocular skeletal muscle development builds the six small muscles that move the eye, a striated muscle group with an origin and a biology distinct from that of the trunk and limbs. It matters because these muscles must contract faster and more finely than any other skeletal muscle to keep gaze stable, and because they are selectively spared in Duchenne muscular dystrophy yet selectively vulnerable in mitochondrial ophthalmoplegia and thyroid eye disease. Arising from cranial rather than somitic mesoderm, the lineage depends on PITX2, whose loss underlies Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome with ocular and periocular defects, acting alongside FOXL2 in the surrounding periocular mesenchyme. Differentiation ends in a specialised sarcomere and excitation-contraction apparatus: an unusual myosin heavy chain complement including MYH15, the M-band protein myomesin, and the voltage sensor CACNA1S coupling depolarisation to calcium release.

Extraocular skeletal muscle development produces the six small muscles that move the eye, a lineage that arises from cranial rather than somitic mesoderm and keeps a distinctive molecular identity throughout life. This programme matters because eye movement demands unusually fast, fatigue-resistant fibres, and because these muscles are selectively spared in some dystrophies while being selectively targeted in myasthenia and thyroid eye disease; failure of their specification produces congenital strabismus and fixed ophthalmoplegia. Transcriptional control from PITX2 and FOXL2 establishes and maintains the extraocular fate, with PITX2 loss causing the ocular anomalies of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. The remaining components build the contractile apparatus itself: an unconventional myosin heavy chain contributing to the specialised fibre types, a sarcomeric M-band protein, and the voltage-gated calcium channel of the transverse tubule that couples excitation to contraction.

Regulation of receptor internalization controls how quickly cell-surface receptors are pulled out of the plasma membrane, which sets the strength and duration of nearly every signal a cell receives. Tuning this step determines whether a receptor keeps signalling from the surface, is recycled back, or is routed to lysosomes for degradation, and its failure produces sustained or blunted signalling in contexts ranging from insulin action to cholesterol handling, where PCSK9-driven internalization of the LDL receptor governs plasma lipid levels. The machinery spans clathrin adaptors and endophilin-type membrane benders, arrestins that uncouple and package G protein-coupled receptors, ubiquitin ligases and ankyrin-repeat sorting factors that mark cargo, and Rab and Arf regulators that direct the resulting vesicles. A large neuronal contingent, including PICK1, ARC and NUMB, applies the same logic to AMPA receptor removal during synaptic depression and to receptor turnover underlying plasticity.

Cells tune how many receptors sit on their surface, and the control of receptor internalization sets that number by speeding or slowing clathrin- and ubiquitin-dependent uptake into endosomes. It determines how strongly a cell responds to a hormone, growth factor or neurotransmitter, and whether that response is sustained or desensitized. Arrestins, the AP-2 adaptor and endophilin-type BAR proteins couple activated receptors to coated pits; ANKRD13 proteins and CBLB mark ubiquitinated cargo; RAB effectors and sorting factors then decide between recycling and lysosomal degradation. The targets span insulin and EGF receptors, dopamine receptors, integrins and the LDL receptor, which PCSK9 drives toward degradation and thereby raises plasma cholesterol. In neurons the same machinery removes AMPA receptors from synapses during long-term depression, linking endocytic regulation to synaptic plasticity, metabolic signalling and the attenuation of growth factor pathways.

negative regulation of receptor internalization covers the mechanisms that hold receptors at the cell surface by blocking or slowing their endocytic removal, thereby setting how long a cell can keep responding to a ligand. Because internalization is the main way signalling is terminated and receptor number is tuned, restraining it prolongs surface residence and sensitivity, and its loss blunts responses. The genes span several routes to this end: ANKRD13 family proteins bind ubiquitinated receptor tails to modulate their uptake, PCSK9 diverts the LDL receptor toward degradation rather than recycling and so governs plasma cholesterol, and scaffolds such as DLG4 and syntenin anchor receptors within postsynaptic complexes, with LRRTM adhesion molecules stabilising AMPA receptors at excitatory synapses. Additional regulators act on Rab-dependent trafficking, phosphoinositide turnover and ubiquitin handling, linking this control to synaptic strength, lipoprotein clearance and growth factor signalling.

Receptors at the cell surface are continually pulled inward by endocytosis, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that keep them there, setting how long a cell can respond to a hormone, ligand or neurotransmitter before the receptor is removed for degradation or recycling. Holding receptors at the membrane matters for sustained signalling and for synaptic strength: the scaffold DLG4 and the synaptic adhesion proteins LRRTM1 and LRRTM2 stabilise glutamate receptors in the postsynaptic density, while syntenin and NECAB2 tether receptors through PDZ and calcium-binding interactions. Other members act on trafficking machinery itself instead of the cargo, including ANKRD13 family ubiquitin-binding proteins, the RAB5 activator RIN3, the phosphoinositide phosphatase MTMR2 and the chaperone LRPAP1. PCSK9 illustrates the opposite direction, promoting LDL receptor loss, so regulation here tunes cholesterol clearance as well as neuronal and growth factor responsiveness.

Auditory receptor cell morphogenesis builds the shape of the cochlear hair cell, above all the staircase bundle of actin-filled stereocilia that converts sound-driven fluid motion into receptor current. Getting this geometry right is what makes hearing possible: mutations in these genes cause congenital deafness and, when the eye is also affected, Usher syndrome. The genes describe how the bundle is assembled and held together — cadherin-based tip and lateral links such as CDH23 and STRC, the scaffolds USH1C, WHRN and PDZD7 that anchor them, an unconventional myosin that transports cargo along stereocilia, and actin cross-linkers including PLS1 and TRIOBP that set rootlet and core stiffness. Planar cell polarity and cytoskeletal regulators orient the bundle within the sensory epithelium, while the tectorial membrane component TECTA couples it mechanically. The result is a polarized mechanotransducing cell whose form is inseparable from its function.

Hearing depends on hair cells of the cochlea acquiring and maintaining a precisely shaped apical hair bundle, and auditory receptor cell morphogenesis is the developmental programme that builds it. Stereocilia must be graded in height, tightly cross-linked, and polarised in a single direction across the epithelium, because deflection toward the tallest row is what gates mechanotransduction channels. Tip-link and upper-link cadherins, myosin motors such as MYO7A, and PDZ scaffolds including USH1C, WHRN and PDZD7 assemble and anchor the bundle, while actin-bundling and rootlet proteins like PLS1 and TRIOBP give stereocilia their stiffness and insertion into the cell body. Planar polarity and trafficking components orient the bundle relative to the organ of Corti. Mutations in these genes cause nonsyndromic deafness and Usher syndrome, in which hair bundles are disorganised, stunted or splayed and hair cells degenerate.

cytoplasmic translational elongation is the processive phase of protein synthesis in which the ribosome adds one amino acid at a time to a growing polypeptide, setting the rate at which cells convert transcripts into functional protein and thereby governing growth, secretory output and the speed of stress responses. Charged tRNAs supplied by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases such as AARS1 are delivered by elongation factor complexes, with the eEF1B subunit EEF1D recycling the GTPase and the ribosomal stalk protein RPLP2 recruiting factors to the ribosome. Elongation is also a control point: CPEB family proteins tune translation of specific mRNAs in neurons and oocytes, while NEMF surveys stalled ribosomes and marks incomplete nascent chains for degradation. Defects in these steps cause protein aggregation, ribosome collision stress, and neurological disease.

Cytoplasmic translational elongation is the processive phase of protein synthesis in which the ribosome adds one amino acid after another to a growing polypeptide, setting the rate at which cells convert transcripts into protein and therefore how quickly they grow, secrete and respond to stimuli. Charged tRNA supply comes from aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases such as the alanyl enzyme AARS1, while elongation factor subunits and ribosomal stalk proteins like RPLP2 support factor recruitment and repeated cycles of tRNA delivery and translocation. Quality control is part of the same process: NEMF recognises stalled ribosomes carrying incomplete chains and helps mark them for degradation, preventing accumulation of truncated products. Cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding proteins impose message-specific control, repressing or activating elongation on particular mRNAs, a mode of local translational regulation prominent in neurons and in synaptic plasticity.

Cytoplasmic translational initiation is the rate-limiting first step of protein synthesis, in which a small ribosomal subunit loaded with initiator methionyl-tRNA is delivered to an mRNA and positioned on its start codon. Because initiation is where most translational control is exerted, this step sets how much protein a cell makes from each transcript and is the point at which growth factor and stress signals are converted into changes in proteome output. The genes cover cap recognition and scaffolding through eIF4A/eIF4G and the nuclear cap-binding proteins, the multisubunit eIF3 complex that binds the 40S subunit and promotes scanning, the eIF2 ternary complex with its eIF2B guanine nucleotide exchange factor, and mTOR- and AKT-dependent regulation. Also present are reinitiation and non-canonical factors such as DENR-MCTS1 and eIF2D, m6A readers, and DHX29 for structured 5' leaders. Impaired eIF2B function causes leukoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter.

Translational initiation in the cytoplasm is the step at which a message is chosen for protein synthesis: the small ribosomal subunit, loaded with initiator methionyl-tRNA, is recruited to an mRNA, scans to a start codon, and joins the large subunit before the first peptide bond forms. Because it is rate-limiting, it is the main point at which growth signals and stress set the cell's protein output. The eIF3 multisubunit complex, the cap-binding and helicase activities of eIF4A/eIF4G and the nuclear cap-binding proteins, eIF5 and the eIF2 subunits with their eIF2B guanine-nucleotide exchange factor form the core machinery, and eIF2B loss causes leukoencephalopathy. mTOR-dependent signalling, phosphorylation-driven eIF2 inhibition during the integrated stress response, and m6A readers or DENR-MCTS1 for reinitiation tune which transcripts are translated; failure produces stress granules, arrested growth, and ribosomopathy-like disease.

Somatic diversification of immune receptors generates antigen receptor variety that the germline genome does not encode, so that lymphocytes can collectively recognise essentially any pathogen. It covers V(D)J recombination in developing B and T cells, and class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation in activated B cells that mature antibody affinity and switch effector isotype. Loss of these steps produces severe combined immunodeficiency or hyper-IgM syndromes; their misfiring underlies lymphoid translocations. The genes trace a deliberate DNA damage strategy: RAG1/RAG2 or AID-initiated uracil lesions processed by uracil glycosylase and mismatch repair, then resolved by non-homologous end joining and translesion polymerases, with ATM, 53BP1 and the shieldin complex directing repair choice. Cytokine and costimulatory signals such as IL-4, CD40L and TGF-beta, read out through STAT6, BATF and BCL6, determine which B cells undergo the process and which isotype they adopt.

Antigen receptor diversity is not inherited but built in each developing lymphocyte, and this somatic diversification of immune receptors is how a limited germline repertoire yields antibodies and T cell receptors against essentially any pathogen. The same DNA-breaking chemistry also switches antibody isotypes and refines affinity in germinal centres. RAG1 and RAG2 initiate V(D)J recombination, and the resulting breaks are sealed by non-homologous end joining involving DNA-PKcs, Artemis, LIG4, XRCC4 and the shieldin complex under 53BP1 control; AID deaminates cytosine in immunoglobulin loci, and uracil glycosylase plus mismatch repair factors convert those lesions into mutations or class switch recombination. Cytokine and costimulatory inputs such as IL4, CD40 ligation and TGFB1 direct which isotype is chosen. Loss of these steps produces severe combined immunodeficiency, hyper-IgM syndromes, or radiosensitivity with lymphoid malignancy.

response to molecule of bacterial origin is the cellular reaction to bacterial products such as lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides, flagellin and peptidoglycan fragments, and it is how the innate immune system detects infection before any antibody exists. It sets the tempo of inflammation: too little and bacteria disseminate unchecked, too much and the same mediators produce sepsis, tissue injury and chronic inflammatory disease. Recognition runs through surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors with their accessory proteins CD14, LBP and LY96, and through cytosolic sensors such as NOD2 and the NLRP3 inflammasome, converging on MyD88-IRAK-TRAF6 signalling to NF-kB, MAP kinases and interferon regulatory factors. The output is transcription of TNF, IL1B, IL6 and chemokines, inducible nitric oxide and antimicrobial peptides, phagocyte recruitment and antigen-presenting cell maturation. Negative regulators including A20, IRAK3, SIGIRR, ZC3H12A and several microRNAs enforce resolution and tolerance.

Host cells detect conserved bacterial products — lipopolysaccharide, lipoproteins, peptidoglycan fragments, flagellin, CpG DNA — and this response to molecules of bacterial origin converts that detection into inflammation, antimicrobial defence and tissue repair. It is the front line of innate immunity at epithelial surfaces and in macrophages and neutrophils; too little of it permits invasive infection, while too much drives sepsis, endotoxic shock and chronic inflammatory disease.
