Recognition runs through Toll-like receptors with CD14, LBP and the MD-2 partner LY96, and through the cytosolic sensor NOD2, feeding MyD88, IRAK kinases and TRAF6 into NF-κB, MAP kinase and interferon-regulatory transcription. Output includes IL-1β, IL-6, TNF and chemokines such as CXCL8, inflammasome-dependent caspase-1 processing, inducible nitric oxide synthase, and secreted antimicrobials including lactoferrin, lipocalin-2, cathelicidin and defensins. Negative regulators — TNFAIP3, IRAK3, SIGIRR, IL18BP, IL36RN, ZC3H12A and several microRNAs — restrain and terminate the reaction.

Hematopoietic progenitor cell differentiation describes how mesoderm-derived precursors and hematopoietic stem cells acquire the identity of committed myeloid and lymphoid progenitors, the step that sustains lifelong production of blood and immune cells. Its failure underlies bone marrow failure syndromes, immunodeficiency and leukemia, since the same regulators that specify progenitors are recurrently mutated in transformed blood cells. Lineage choice is set by a core transcriptional network -- TAL1, MYB, SPI1, GATA3, SOX4, MLLT3 and HOX factors such as HOXB4 -- acting downstream of niche cues delivered through KIT and its ligand, FLT3, NOTCH1, BMP4 and TGF-beta family signals. Cytokine receptors couple to LYN, PTPN6 and RAS-ERK components to control progenitor proliferation and self-renewal, while m6A writers and readers, DNA repair and replication factors, and TP53 maintain genome integrity during rapid expansion.

All blood and immune cells descend from stem cells that first commit to intermediate progenitors, and hematopoietic progenitor cell differentiation is the step in which a precursor acquires that restricted myeloid or lymphoid identity. It sets the output of the bone marrow for life; its failure underlies aplastic marrow syndromes, immunodeficiency and leukaemic transformation, since blocked or misdirected commitment is a recurring theme in myeloid malignancy. Lineage-determining transcription factors do much of the work — TAL1, MYB, SPI1, GATA3, SOX4 and the HOXB4/MLLT3 axis that sustains self-renewal — acting downstream of cytokine receptors such as KIT with its ligand KITLG, and FLT3, alongside Notch, BMP, TGF-beta/activin and Hedgehog cues from the niche. Chromatin and m6A RNA modification machinery, including METTL3/METTL14 and YTHDF2, plus genome-maintenance factors, tune how rapidly progenitors expand and differentiate.

wound healing involved in inflammatory response covers the repair of damaged tissue as it proceeds under, and is driven by, inflammation — the phase in which clotting, immune cell recruitment, and matrix remodelling are coordinated so that a breach is sealed and rebuilt rather than left open or scarred. It matters for skin and vascular injury, ulcer closure in diabetes, and fibrotic outcomes when the inflammatory phase fails to resolve. Damage-associated signals acting through TLR4 and the receptor for advanced glycation end products alert resident cells; thrombin acting on F2R links coagulation to that alert; IL1A amplifies it. Hypoxia sensing via HIF1A and the cytoprotective enzyme HMOX1 adapt cells to the wound's low-oxygen, oxidant-rich environment, while TGFB1 and TIMP1 drive fibroblast activation and restrain matrix degradation. PPARG provides an anti-inflammatory brake that steers macrophages toward resolution.

Tissue injury triggers repair and inflammation together, and this is the arm of wound healing that feeds into the inflammatory response: the events that restore barrier integrity while recruiting and instructing immune cells. It matters for how cleanly a wound closes — too little and healing stalls, as in chronic diabetic ulcers, too much and the result is fibrosis or scarring. Damage-associated signals sensed through TLR4 and AGER, together with thrombin acting on its receptor F2R, link clotting and innate immune activation to cytokine output such as IL1A. TGFB1 drives matrix deposition and myofibroblast behaviour, while TIMP1 restrains metalloproteinase-mediated matrix turnover. Hypoxia in the wound bed acts through HIF1A, and HMOX1 and PPARG temper oxidative and inflammatory tone, placing resolution alongside repair as part of the same programme.

Macrophage activation involved in immune response is the switch that turns a resting tissue macrophage into an effector cell: on encountering a cytokine, microbial product, or damage signal it changes shape, ramps up phagocytosis, and begins secreting inflammatory mediators that recruit and instruct other immune cells. This step sets the tone of innate immunity and of the tissue response that follows, and its misregulation drives chronic inflammation, sepsis pathology, and neurodegenerative microglial states. The genes cover the triggering inputs (IFNG, IL1B, IL33, HMGB1 as an alarmin, LBP delivering bacterial lipopolysaccharide), the receptors and adaptors that read them (IL1R1 with IL1RAP, TICAM1 downstream of Toll-like receptors, TREM2 signalling through TYROBP and SYK), and the phospholipase and kinase relays that convert them into transcription. TNF and IL1B are the principal outputs, while TREX1 and SBNO2 restrain the response.

Macrophages are not fixed in one state: exposure to cytokines, microbial products, damage signals or cellular ligands converts a resting tissue macrophage into an effector cell that phagocytoses, secretes inflammatory mediators and shapes the wider immune response. This activation drives host defence against infection, clearance of dying cells and debris, and the inflammatory tone of tissues, and its dysregulation underlies chronic inflammation, autoinflammatory disease and neurodegeneration. The genes here span the stimuli and their receivers: interferon gamma, TNF and IL-1 family cytokines with their receptor and accessory chains, the alarmin HMGB1 and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, the metabolite sensor SUCNR1, and the TLR adaptor TICAM1. Downstream, the TREM2/TYROBP pair signals through SYK and PLCG2 to sustain microglial and macrophage responses to lipids and damaged tissue, while granulin and TREX1 restrain excessive activation.

T cell activation involved in immune response describes how a resting T cell, on encountering peptide-MHC together with costimulation and cytokines, changes shape, proliferates, and acquires an effector programme that drives host defence. It sets the tone of adaptive immunity: too little gives susceptibility to intracellular pathogens, too much gives autoimmunity and inflammatory disease. The genes span the recognition step -- class II MHC and its chaperone, CD80/CD86 and ICOS ligands, adhesion via ICAM1 and LFA-1 -- and the signalling that follows through PI3K-mTOR, PKC-MALT1-NF-κB, and JAK1/JAK3-STAT modules. Cytokine inputs including IL-2, IL-6, IL-12, IL-18, IL-23, IL-27 and the interferons feed master transcription factors such as TBX21, GATA3, RORC, EOMES, BCL6 and FOXP3 that fix helper and regulatory lineage identity. Proteasome subunits, SOCS proteins, ZC3H12A and the roquin ligases restrain the response, and antigen processing supplies it.

When a T cell meets antigen presented on MHC together with costimulation, it changes shape, upregulates activation markers, proliferates and commits to an effector programme; this is the step that converts specific recognition into an actual immune response. The genes here span the antigen-presentation and costimulatory interface (HLA class II, CD74, CD80/CD86, ICOS and its ligand, ICAM1 and the integrin LFA-1), the cytokine and JAK-STAT circuitry that instructs lineage choice, and the transcription factors that define the resulting subsets — TBX21 for Th1, GATA3 for Th2, RORC for Th17, BCL6 for follicular helper and FOXP3 for regulatory T cells. Immunoproteasome subunits, IL-12/IL-23/IL-6 receptor components and negative regulators such as SOCS3, SMAD7 and the roquin proteins set the threshold and duration of the response. Too little yields immunodeficiency; unchecked activation drives autoimmunity and chronic inflammation.

T cell activation via T cell receptor contact with antigen bound to MHC molecule on antigen presenting cell describes the licensing step of adaptive immunity: a T cell changes shape and behaviour after its receptor engages peptide displayed on MHC by a dendritic cell, macrophage or B cell, committing it to proliferate and mount a response. Without productive contact the T cell remains naive or is tolerized, and the balance of stimulatory and inhibitory input here sets the difference between protective immunity, autoimmunity and tumour escape. The genes cover the physical side of the immunological synapse — integrin LFA-1 with ICAM-1 and the adaptor RIAM that clusters it, tetraspanin and MHC class II peptide-loading support — alongside checkpoint receptors such as TIM-3 and its galectin-9 ligand, LILRB1, and TREM2–TYROBP signalling in the presenting cell, plus semaphorin–plexin cues that tune contact duration.

T cells commit to an immune response only when their receptor engages a peptide displayed on MHC by an antigen-presenting cell, and this pathway covers the accessory contacts at that interface that decide whether the encounter activates, tunes down, or fails to move the T cell. It underlies antigen-specific adaptive immunity and, when misregulated, contributes to autoimmunity or to the exhausted, unresponsive T cells found in tumours and chronic infection. Adhesion and cytoskeletal components such as the integrin LFA-1 chain ITGAL, its ligand ICAM1, and the RAP1 effector APBB1IP stabilise the immunological synapse; HLA-DMB supports peptide loading onto class II MHC. Countering these are inhibitory inputs, notably the galectin-9/HAVCR2 axis and the MHC class I-binding receptor LILRB1, while TREM2 with its adaptor TYROBP and semaphorin-plexin contacts modulate the presenting cell side.

T-helper cell lineage commitment is the decision point at which an activated CD4-positive alpha-beta T cell locks into one of the helper fates that direct the rest of an immune response — Th1, Th2, Th17 and related subsets — determining whether the body mounts an antiviral, antiparasitic or antifungal defence, and whether that response tips into autoimmunity or allergy. Cytokines encountered at priming set the outcome: IL-12 and IL-23 receptors, IL-6 signalling through IL6R and gp130, and the JAK1/JAK3 kinases funnel into STAT3, STAT5A, STAT6 and the master transcription factors TBX21, IRF4 and BATF, which open subset-specific enhancers with the help of EP300 and BET proteins. SOCS3 restrains the same signals, while SLAM-family contacts, mTOR-dependent metabolic reprogramming and mitochondrial remodelling through OPA1 couple commitment to the energetic demands of clonal expansion and stable effector identity.

A naive CD4 T cell that has recognised antigen must choose which kind of helper cell to become, and T-helper lineage commitment is that decision: the point at which cytokine cues are converted into a stable, self-reinforcing transcriptional identity. The choice determines whether the ensuing response favours intracellular pathogens, worms and allergy, or mucosal defence, and skewed commitment underlies asthma, autoimmune inflammation and susceptibility to mycobacteria. Cytokine receptors for IL-6, IL-12 and IL-23 signal through JAK1 and JAK3 to STAT3, STAT5A and STAT6, which induce master regulators including TBX21 and IRF4; SOCS3 restrains this signalling. Chromatin readers and the acetyltransferase EP300 open the relevant cytokine loci, BATF cooperates with IRF4 at enhancers, and mTOR couples metabolic state to the outcome. SLAM-family receptors provide the T-T contact cues that accompany the decision.

Myeloid progenitor cell differentiation is the step at which a multipotent haematopoietic precursor commits to the myeloid side of blood formation, generating the progenitors that later give rise to granulocytes, monocytes and macrophages, erythrocytes, and platelets. Without it the marrow cannot replenish innate immune cells or oxygen-carrying cells, and its deregulation is the basis of myeloid leukaemias and myelodysplasia. The commitment is enforced transcriptionally by PU.1, whose dose determines myeloid versus lymphoid fate, with chromatin remodelling subunits such as DPF2 shaping the accessible enhancer landscape. Receptor tyrosine kinases KIT and FLT3, acting through RAS-RAF signalling, supply the proliferation and survival cues that expand the committed pool, which is why activating mutations in these genes drive acute myeloid leukaemia. Adhesion molecules such as JAM3 tie progenitor behaviour to the marrow niche.

Myeloid progenitor cell differentiation is the step at which multipotent haematopoietic precursors commit to the lineages that produce granulocytes, monocytes and macrophages, erythrocytes, megakaryocytes and mast cells, and it sets the supply of blood and innate immune cells for life. Two receptor tyrosine kinases, KIT and FLT3, read stem cell factor and FLT3 ligand from the marrow niche and drive progenitor survival and expansion, with BRAF carrying the signal into the MAP kinase cascade; SPI1 (PU.1) acts as the transcriptional master switch that specifies myeloid over lymphoid fate, assisted by chromatin regulators such as DPF2. Adhesive contact with the niche, mediated in part by JAM3, and regulators such as MLF1 tune whether progenitors proliferate or mature. Disruption of these signals underlies bone marrow failure, and constitutive activation of KIT, FLT3 or BRAF is a recurrent driver of myeloid leukaemia and mastocytosis.

B cell proliferation involved in immune response is the clonal expansion step that turns a few antigen-specific B cells into a population large enough to mount a useful antibody response. Without it, humoral immunity is quantitatively inadequate: germinal centre reactions fail and protective antibody titres never accumulate, while unrestrained proliferation of the same kind underlies B cell lymphomas and autoantibody-driven disease. The genes cover both the drive and the brake. Antigen receptor co-receptor CD19 and the kinase ABL1 amplify signals into cell cycle entry, and the Toll-like receptors CD180 and TLR4 provide microbial co-stimulation that lowers the threshold for division. Countering these, GAPT and the phospholipase C-like adaptor PLCL2 dampen receptor output and limit expansion, so the pathway sits at the junction of antigen recognition, innate sensing and proliferative control in the humoral arm of adaptive immunity.

Following antigen encounter, activated B cells must expand into a clone large enough to supply antibody, and this proliferative burst is what turns recognition into a useful humoral response. Its regulation sets the magnitude of antibody output; too little leaves poor protection after infection or vaccination, while unrestrained expansion contributes to autoantibody production and lymphoproliferation. The genes here sit on both sides of that balance: CD19 amplifies antigen receptor signalling to lower the threshold for division, while GAPT and PLCL2 act as brakes on B cell receptor-driven responses. CD180 and TLR4 add innate sensing of bacterial lipopolysaccharide, so microbial context can drive proliferation alongside antigen, and ABL1 kinase links receptor engagement to cytoskeletal and cell cycle machinery. The result couples antigen specificity, innate danger signals and negative feedback to clonal expansion during an immune response.

pro-B cell differentiation covers the earliest committed step of B lymphopoiesis, in which a bone marrow lymphoid progenitor takes on pro-B identity and begins joining diversity and joining segments of the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus. It sets the size and diversity of the antibody repertoire, and its failure produces arrest at the pro-B stage with absent mature B cells and immunodeficiency. Recombination intermediates are resolved by the non-homologous end joining machinery, with DNA-PKcs and DNA ligase IV sealing the coding and signal joins, so defects here cause radiosensitive severe combined immunodeficiency. Cytokine and receptor input through FLT3 and RAS activation via SOS1/SOS2 drives progenitor expansion, while Notch signalling and its HES targets bias progenitors toward or away from the T lineage. Folliculin and FNIP1 couple metabolic and mTOR-linked checkpoints to passage through this stage, and SOX4 supports the transcriptional program.

Pro-B cell differentiation is the first committed step of B lymphopoiesis, in which a lymphoid progenitor acquires pro-B identity and begins rearranging the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus by joining D and J segments. Without it there are no mature B cells and no antibody response, and the severe combined immunodeficiency caused by defective DNA repair at this stage illustrates the dependence directly: DNA-PKcs and DNA ligase IV complete the non-homologous end joining that seals the breaks made during V(D)J recombination. Cytokine input through the FLT3 receptor and the RAS exchange factors SOS1 and SOS2 drives progenitor expansion, while Notch signalling and its HES targets bias cells away from the B lineage toward T cell fates, so commitment requires that this pressure be relieved. SOX4 and the folliculin-FNIP1 nutrient-sensing module are further requirements for progression past this checkpoint.

pre-B cell differentiation is the developmental step in the bone marrow at which a pro-B cell, having rearranged and expressed an immunoglobulin heavy chain, becomes a pre-B cell and is tested for productive receptor assembly. It sets the size and diversity of the antibody repertoire, and its failure produces agammaglobulinemia and severe combined immunodeficiency. The recombinase components RAG1 and RAG2 introduce the double-strand breaks that join V, D and J segments, while ATM coordinates the DNA damage response that holds broken intermediates together and prevents translocations that would otherwise seed lymphoid malignancy. Surface expression of the mu heavy chain with surrogate light chain signals successful rearrangement and licenses proliferation and light chain recombination, with LAPTM5 and LRRC8A shaping receptor turnover and lymphocyte survival. The pathway couples programmed genome rearrangement to checkpoint control during lymphopoiesis.

Pre-B cell differentiation is the stage at which a pro-B cell rearranges its immunoglobulin heavy chain V, D and J segments and displays the resulting mu chain, the step that decides whether a developing lymphocyte can go on to make antibody. Everything downstream of it — a diverse antibody repertoire, mature B cells, humoral immunity — depends on this recombination succeeding, and its failure produces B cell aplasia and agammaglobulinaemia. The recombinase encoded by RAG1 and RAG2 introduces the double-strand breaks at recombination signal sequences, and ATM couples those breaks to the DNA damage response so that joining is completed faithfully and cells with unrepaired breaks are arrested or removed; defects here cause immunodeficiency with genomic instability. Expression of membrane IGHM marks successful rearrangement, while other components support the surface signalling and trafficking that accompany the transition.

Myeloid dendritic cell chemotaxis describes the directed migration of antigen-bearing dendritic cells out of peripheral tissues and into draining lymph nodes, the step that physically connects innate antigen capture to T cell priming. Without it, antigen stays in the periphery, lymph node T cell zones are poorly populated, and adaptive responses to infection and vaccination fail to be initiated; the same axis is exploited by tumours and by metastasising cells to reach lymphoid tissue. Mechanistically, maturing dendritic cells upregulate CCR7 and follow gradients of the lymphoid chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 produced by stromal and lymphatic endothelial cells, with receptor engagement converted into polarised actin remodelling through Rho-family exchange factors such as ARHGEF5. The myeloid identity of the migrating cell is set upstream by the transcription factor SPI1, tying leukocyte lineage specification to this trafficking programme.

Myeloid dendritic cells only present antigen usefully if they can leave the tissue where they captured it and find the T cell zones of a draining lymph node, and this directed migration is what the chemotaxis programme provides. Stromal and lymphatic endothelial cells lay down the chemokines CCL19 and CCL21, which the receptor CCR7 reads on the maturing dendritic cell surface, converting a gradient into polarized crawling toward and along lymphatic vessels. Downstream, a Rho-family guanine nucleotide exchange factor couples that signal to cytoskeletal rearrangement, while the myeloid transcription factor PU.1 specifies the cell type in which this machinery is expressed. Loss of the receptor or its ligands strands antigen-loaded cells in the periphery, blunting priming of naive T cells and tolerance induction; the same axis is exploited by tumour cells for nodal metastasis.

Antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via MHC class Ib is the display of peptides on non-classical class I molecules such as HLA-E, HLA-F and HLA-G, rather than on the classical HLA-A/B/C molecules that prime conventional cytotoxic T cells. This arm of antigen presentation speaks mainly to innate lymphocytes: HLA-E loaded with leader peptides from other class I proteins reports on the integrity of the whole presentation system to NK cell receptors, and HLA-G at the maternal-fetal interface enforces tolerance toward the trophoblast. Like the classical molecules, these heavy chains require beta-2 microglobulin and peptide delivered through the transporter associated with antigen processing. Related surface ligands of the RAET1/ULBP family are recognised by the same innate effectors as stress signals. Loss or tumour-driven remodelling of this axis lets cancers and viruses evade NK surveillance.

Non-classical MHC class Ib molecules display peptides and related ligands at the cell surface to report a cell's internal state to lymphocytes, complementing the classical class I route that presents to conventional cytotoxic T cells. Presentation via HLA-E, HLA-F and HLA-G tunes natural killer and T cell responses rather than simply flagging foreign peptides: HLA-G restrains maternal immune attack on trophoblast at the placental interface, and HLA-E signals whether normal class I synthesis is intact. All of these heavy chains require beta-2-microglobulin for assembly and depend on transporter-mediated delivery of peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum. The accompanying ULBP and RAET1 stress-induced ligands share the class I fold but engage activating NK receptors instead of presenting peptide. Loss or subversion of this axis contributes to viral immune evasion, tumour escape from NK surveillance, and pregnancy disorders.

Leukocyte mediated immunity covers the effector arms of immune defence that white blood cells actually carry out: killing infected and transformed cells, degranulating against microbes, opsonising and lysing pathogens, and secreting antibody. It is what converts immune recognition into clearance, and its failure produces immunodeficiency, uncontrolled infection and impaired tumour surveillance, while its excess drives autoimmunity and hyperinflammation. The genes span cytotoxic granule contents and their release machinery (perforin, granzymes, RAB27A, UNC13D, syntaxins and VAMPs), neutrophil azurophil proteases such as elanase and cathepsin G, the complement cascade with its regulators, Fc and NK receptor families (FCGR, KLR, KIR, NCR) signalling through SYK, BTK and ITAM adaptors, MHC and CD1 antigen presentation, and immunoglobulin loci with the class-switch and somatic hypermutation machinery. Cytokine receptors and lineage transcription factors set which effector program a leukocyte adopts.

Leukocyte mediated immunity covers the effector work that white blood cells actually perform once mobilised: killing infected and tumour cells, degranulating, phagocytosing opsonised targets, and secreting antibody and cytokines. It is what converts recognition into clearance of pathogens, and its failure produces immunodeficiency, haemophagocytic syndromes and recurrent infection, while its excess drives autoimmunity and tissue damage. The genes span several effector arms: cytotoxic granule contents and the machinery that releases them, including perforin, granzymes and the exocytosis regulators UNC13D, STXBP2 and RAB27A; activating and inhibitory receptors of NK and T cells such as KLRK1, KIR and PDCD1, signalling through SYK, LYN, BTK, VAV1 and PI3K subunits; Fc and complement receptors that couple immunoglobulin and the complement cascade to myeloid ingestion; neutrophil granule proteases; MHC class I, class II and CD1 lipid presentation; and the immunoglobulin loci with the class-switch and somatic hypermutation apparatus, AICDA and mismatch and end-joining repair factors, that diversify antibody effector function.</description>

Antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen is how a cell advertises its internal protein contents to the immune system, displaying fragments of self-made proteins on MHC class I molecules at the surface. This is the surveillance mechanism by which cytotoxic T cells detect virus-infected and tumour cells, and by which healthy cells prove their normality; loss of it allows tumours and viruses to escape killing. Proteasome-derived peptides are pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed to length by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto HLA-A, -B and -C heavy chains paired with β2-microglobulin, with tapasin holding the complex until a high-affinity peptide binds. Non-classical relatives such as HLA-E and HLA-G, together with the stress-induced ULBP and RAET1 ligands, extend the same display logic to natural killer cell recognition.

Every nucleated cell continuously advertises samples of its own protein content on its surface, and this display of endogenously derived peptides is how cytotoxic T cells distinguish healthy cells from ones harbouring a virus or expressing mutated tumour proteins. Proteasomal fragments are pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed to length by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto class I heavy chains paired with beta-2-microglobulin, with tapasin holding the complex in a peptide-receptive state. Classical HLA-A, -B and -C molecules carry the peptides to the surface, while the non-classical relatives HLA-E and HLA-G and the stress-induced ULBP and RAET1 ligands instead signal cell status to NK receptors. Loss of loading machinery lets tumours and viruses escape surveillance; particular allotypes and ERAP variants predispose to autoinflammatory disease.

peptide antigen assembly with MHC protein complex is the loading step of antigen presentation: peptides are placed into the binding groove of class I and class II MHC molecules so that T cells can inspect what a cell contains. This is what allows cytotoxic T cells to detect virally infected or tumour cells and helper T cells to recognise material taken up by dendritic cells and macrophages, and it sets the repertoire of self peptides against which tolerance is established. Class I loading depends on a peptide-loading complex in which tapasin, calreticulin and the thiol oxidoreductase ERp57 edit peptides onto HLA-A heavy chains paired with beta-2-microglobulin; class II loading requires HLA-DM to exchange the invariant chain remnant for antigenic peptide, with HLA-DO tuning that exchange. Polymorphism in these HLA genes underlies transplant matching and much of the genetic risk for autoimmune disease.

Loading a peptide into the binding groove of an MHC molecule is the step that determines what the immune system sees. Without it, class I and class II molecules reach the cell surface empty or unstable, T cells cannot be selected in the thymus or activated in the periphery, and infected and tumour cells escape recognition; the same chemistry underlies transplant rejection and the strong HLA associations of autoimmune disease. Class I assembly occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum, where beta-2 microglobulin, calreticulin, the thiol oxidoreductase ERp57 and tapasin hold the heavy chain receptive until a suitable peptide binds. Class II molecules, built from the paired alpha and beta chains of the DR, DQ and DP isotypes, acquire peptides in endosomal compartments, with HLA-DM catalysing exchange and HLA-DO tuning it. Groove occupancy thus sets both the stability and the antigenic content of surface MHC.

leukocyte differentiation is the broad developmental program by which hematopoietic progenitors commit to and mature into the white blood cell lineages — T and B lymphocytes, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, granulocytes, osteoclasts and innate lymphoid subsets. It builds the entire cellular basis of immunity, and its failure produces immunodeficiency, autoimmunity, or leukemia. Lineage choice is enforced by transcription factor networks acting in mutually antagonistic pairs, such as SPI1 and GATA1, PAX5 and EBF-driven B cell commitment, BCL11B and TCF7 in thymocytes, and CEBPA/CEBPE in granulopoiesis, with chromatin remodelers and polycomb components setting the accessible landscape. Cytokines and their receptors (IL7R, KIT, FLT3, CSF1R, TNFSF11) plus JAK–STAT and NOTCH signaling supply the instructive extrinsic cues, while antigen receptor assembly by RAG1/RAG2 and thymic selection through peptide–MHC and costimulatory molecules impose checkpoints that couple differentiation to self-tolerance.

White blood cells of every kind arise from hematopoietic precursors that progressively lose potency and acquire lineage-specific machinery, and leukocyte differentiation is the collection of programmes that make this happen. It supplies the myeloid and lymphoid cells of innate and adaptive immunity, and its disruption produces immunodeficiency, autoimmunity, or leukemia when progenitors are frozen at an immature stage. Lineage-determining transcription factors such as SPI1, GATA1, PAX5, CEBPA, FOXP3 and TBX21 set and maintain identity, acting alongside chromatin remodelling complexes and Notch, Wnt and TGF-beta inputs. Cytokines and their receptors, including IL7R, KIT, FLT3, CSF1R and the JAK-STAT machinery they engage, drive survival and expansion, while antigen receptor assembly and thymic selection impose checkpoints on lymphocyte maturation. Osteoclast-forming genes extend the same logic to bone-resorbing macrophages.

Leukocyte migration involved in inflammatory response is the recruitment step of innate immunity: the directed movement of neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes out of blood and through tissue toward a site of infection or injury. Without it, pathogens are not cleared and wounds do not resolve; in excess, it drives the tissue damage of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease. The genes trace the adhesion cascade itself — E-selectin and the fucosyltransferase that builds its glycan ligand for tethering, the beta-2 integrin chain shared by LFA-1 and Mac-1 for firm adhesion, and junctional adhesion molecules for passage between endothelial cells. Alongside these are chemoattractant systems, including the leukotriene-generating 5-lipoxygenase, short-chain fatty acid sensing, fractalkine and the CCR6 axis, plus neutrophil alarmins S100A8/A9 and granule proteases that amplify further influx. Loss of integrin function causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency with recurrent bacterial infection.

Inflammation depends on leukocytes leaving the circulation and moving into damaged or infected tissue, and this is the arm of the inflammatory response that directs that traffic. Without it, bacteria are not cleared and abscesses cannot form; in excess it drives the neutrophil-rich infiltrates of arthritis, colitis, atherosclerosis and acute lung injury. Endothelial E-selectin and the fucosyltransferase that builds its glycan ligands capture flowing cells, the beta-2 integrin subunit shared by LFA-1 and Mac-1 converts capture into firm adhesion, and junctional adhesion molecule C governs passage between endothelial cells. Chemotactic cues come from a chemokine receptor used by memory lymphocytes, a membrane-anchored chemokine, leukotriene products of 5-lipoxygenase, and a short-chain fatty acid receptor sensing microbial metabolites. Neutrophil-derived S100A8/A9 and elastase amplify recruitment, linking migration to granulocyte activation and tissue damage.

production of molecular mediator involved in inflammatory response covers how cells manufacture and release the signals that create inflammation — cytokines, eicosanoids, reactive nitrogen species and antimicrobial peptides — after an inflammatory stimulus is sensed. It is the output arm of innate immunity: it recruits leukocytes to infected or damaged tissue, and when it runs unchecked it produces the autoinflammatory syndromes, septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease that follow loss of restraint on cytokine output. Pattern recognition receptors such as TLR4, NOD2 and CLEC7A feed through MYD88, SYK and CARD9 into NF-κB and p38 signalling to drive transcription of TNF, IL6 and the IL-17 and IL-36 families; inflammasome components including PYCARD and MEFV control maturation of IL-1-family mediators, while ALOX5 with its activating protein and secreted phospholipases generate leukotrienes. Vesicle proteins mediate release, and numerous microRNAs plus ZFP36, ZC3H12A and PDCD4 impose post-transcriptional damping.

Inflammation works through diffusible messengers, and this pathway covers the making and releasing of those mediators once a cell detects an inflammatory stimulus. It sets the amplitude and duration of host defence: too little and infection goes unchecked, too much and the result is sepsis, chronic inflammatory disease, or the periodic fevers caused by mutations in genes such as MEFV. Pattern-recognition receptors including TLR4, TLR3, NOD2 and the fungal sensor CLEC7A signal via MYD88, TICAM1, SYK and CARD9 into NF-κB subunits and stress kinases, driving transcription of TNF, IL6, IL17 family members and inducible nitric oxide synthase. Lipid mediators come from ALOX5 with its activating protein and secreted phospholipases, and inflammasome adaptors process IL-1 family cytokines. Release depends on vesicle fusion machinery, while negative regulators—NFKBIA, DUSP10, ZFP36, ZC3H12A and numerous microRNAs—restrain output and resolve the response.

Platelet degranulation is the release of preformed mediators from platelet secretory granules at sites of vascular injury, converting an initial adhesion event into a self-amplifying haemostatic response. Dense granules discharge ADP, ATP, calcium and serotonin, while alpha granules deliver adhesive and growth-promoting proteins that recruit further platelets and support wound repair; blunting this step causes bleeding tendency, while excessive release drives thrombosis and vascular inflammation. The genes cover the sequence from receptor to secretion: immune receptor and collagen receptor signalling through FCER1G, the Src-family kinase LYN and SYK, purinergic ATP-gated P2RX1 and phosphoinositide-dependent calcium mobilisation, the cytoskeletal adaptor PLEK, and the SNARE chaperone STXBP1 that licenses granule membrane fusion. Loading of the granules is also represented, with TPH1 synthesising serotonin and the transporter ABCC4 concentrating nucleotides and other small mediators.

When platelets adhere at a site of vascular injury, they release the contents of preformed storage granules, and platelet degranulation is that regulated exocytosis step. The secreted cargo — serotonin, ADP, calcium, adhesive and coagulation proteins — recruits and activates further platelets, so this release amplifies a local activation signal into a stable haemostatic plug; too little causes bleeding, too much promotes thrombosis. Activation signals converge through immunoreceptor-type tyrosine kinase signalling, with the Src-family kinase LYN and the spleen tyrosine kinase SYK acting downstream of an FcR gamma-chain-coupled collagen receptor, alongside purinergic calcium entry through the P2RX1 channel. STXBP1 contributes to the SNARE-dependent fusion of granules with the membrane, while TPH1 generates the serotonin and ABCC4 transports mediators into dense granules for storage.

Positive regulation of antigen processing and presentation covers the signals that increase how much antigen a cell loads onto MHC molecules and displays to T cells, setting the strength with which adaptive immunity is initiated. It matters because T cell priming depends on dendritic cells and macrophages reaching lymphoid tissue and upregulating presentation machinery; when these inputs fail, pathogens persist and tolerance is poorly calibrated. The genes span the steps involved: chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 acting through CCR7 to bring antigen-bearing dendritic cells into lymph nodes, CD74 chaperoning MHC class II and protecting its peptide groove until loading, intracellular pattern recognition by NOD1 and NOD2 and inflammasome assembly via PYCARD that license maturation, phagosomal metal transport by SLC11A1 supporting degradation, and TREM2 tuning myeloid activation. The pathway therefore links innate sensing and cell trafficking to antigen display.

Antigen processing and presentation converts intact proteins into peptides displayed on MHC molecules for inspection by T cells, and the genes here act to increase that activity rather than to carry it out directly. Boosting presentation is how innate sensing translates into adaptive immunity: without it, dendritic cells and macrophages fail to prime naive T cells and infections are cleared poorly, while excessive enhancement contributes to autoimmunity. The chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 acting through CCR7 bring antigen-bearing dendritic cells and naive lymphocytes together in lymph node T cell zones, and CD74 chaperones MHC class II and shields its peptide groove during transit. Intracellular bacterial sensors NOD1 and NOD2, the inflammasome adaptor PYCARD, the phagosomal metal transporter SLC11A1 and the myeloid receptor TREM2 tie pathogen detection and phagosome maturation to stronger presentation.

positive regulation of dendritic cell antigen processing and presentation covers the signals that push dendritic cells to display captured antigen more effectively to T cells, the step that converts innate detection of a pathogen into an adaptive immune response. Without it, priming of naive T cells in lymph nodes fails and vaccination or infection generates weak cellular immunity. The genes span the two requirements for this to happen: chemokine guidance, in which CCL19 and CCL21 from lymphoid stroma act through CCR7 to bring antigen-loaded dendritic cells into T cell zones, and intracellular sensing, in which the cytosolic peptidoglycan receptors NOD1 and NOD2 and the phagosomal metal transporter SLC11A1 report on microbial presence and shape the maturing compartment. CD74 chaperones MHC class II and controls when peptide loading occurs, linking these cues to antigen display itself.

Dendritic cells only prime T cells effectively once they have been instructed to load and display antigen, and this pathway covers the signals that raise the rate and extent of that processing and presentation. It sits at the junction between innate detection of microbes and the onset of adaptive immunity: without it, antigen captured in tissue is never converted into productive T cell priming in lymph nodes, and tolerance or unchecked infection follows. Chemokine signalling through CCR7 with its ligands CCL19 and CCL21 draws activated dendritic cells into lymphoid tissue where presentation occurs, while the cytosolic sensors NOD1 and NOD2 detect bacterial peptidoglycan fragments and license maturation. CD74 chaperones MHC class II and controls peptide loading, and SLC11A1 acts in the phagosome, linking divalent metal transport to antimicrobial handling of ingested antigen.

regulation of immunoglobulin production sets how much antibody a B cell makes and of which class, tuning humoral immunity between protective responses and the excesses seen in allergy, autoimmunity and immunodeficiency. Control operates at several levels. T cell help through CD40-CD40L, CD28/OX40 costimulation and cytokines such as IL-4, IL-21, IL-6 and IL-10 drives activation, while IL-13/STAT6 biases toward IgE and TGFB1 toward other isotypes; inhibitory receptors CD22 and FCGR2B, together with BCL6 and FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells, damp the response. Class switch recombination requires resolution of AID-induced DNA breaks by mismatch repair and the 53BP1-RIF1-shieldin end-joining axis, so mutations here restrict the antibody repertoire. Terminal differentiation into plasma cells depends on XBP1, MZB1 and DNAJB9 expanding secretory capacity to sustain high-rate immunoglobulin synthesis and folding.

Antibody output by B cells is tuned rather than simply switched on, and the regulation of immunoglobulin production covers the signals and machinery that set how much antibody of which class a response generates. It matters for vaccine responses and mucosal defence, and its dysregulation gives hypogammaglobulinaemia at one extreme and autoantibody disease or IgE-driven allergy at the other. T cell help provides much of the input: costimulatory and TNF-family ligand-receptor pairs such as CD40 with its ligand, CD28-CD86 and OX40 engagement, together with cytokines including IL-4, IL-21, IL-6, IL-10 and TGF-beta acting through STAT6 and lineage factors like BCL6, TBX21 and FOXP3. Inhibitory receptors including CD22 and the low-affinity Fc gamma receptor IIB damp the response. Class switching and somatic diversification require double-strand break repair and mismatch repair components, notably the shieldin complex, 53BP1, RIF1 and MLH1-MSH2-PMS2, while XBP1, MZB1 and DNAJB9 support the secretory expansion of plasma cells.}

Respiratory burst involved in defense response is the surge of oxygen consumption that phagocytes mount after engulfing a microbe, converting molecular oxygen into superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and hypohalous acid inside the phagosome to kill ingested bacteria and fungi. It is the effector arm of innate cellular immunity: loss of its components produces chronic granulomatous disease, with recurrent infections and granuloma formation, while unrestrained bursts damage host tissue during inflammation. Assembly of the NADPH oxidase requires cytosolic subunits such as NCF1 and the membrane chaperone CYBC1, and is triggered downstream of Fc and pattern receptors through Src-family kinase HCK and the leukocyte PI3K isoforms p110δ and p110γ. Myeloperoxidase converts the peroxide output into more reactive oxidants, S100A9 and LBP amplify the response to bacterial ligands, and peroxiredoxin-2 with phosphatase-directed feedback restrains it.

Phagocytes kill ingested microbes by deliberately making reactive oxygen: the respiratory burst that accompanies a defense response, in which oxygen consumption rises sharply and NADPH oxidase output is converted into superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and downstream oxidants. It is the effector arm of innate antimicrobial killing by neutrophils and macrophages, and its loss produces chronic granulomatous disease, with recurrent bacterial and fungal infection and granuloma formation. Oxidase assembly at the phagosome requires cytosolic subunits such as NCF1 and the membrane chaperone CYBC1, priming signals delivered through class IB and IA PI3Ks and the Src-family kinase HCK, and modulation by TREM2, progranulin and S100A9. Myeloperoxidase uses the hydrogen peroxide produced to generate hypohalous acid, while peroxiredoxin-2 limits collateral oxidative damage. Because these oxidants also shape inflammation and tissue injury, the burst is restrained as tightly as it is triggered.

positive regulation of leukocyte chemotaxis covers the signals that recruit white blood cells out of the bloodstream and steer them toward sites of infection, injury or tumour growth. It is how inflammation is localised: without it, host defence and wound healing fail, and when it is excessive it drives chronic inflammatory disease, atherosclerosis and leukocyte infiltration of tumours. The bulk of the activity is chemokine-based, with ligands such as CCL2, CCL5, CXCL8 and CXCL12 acting through G protein-coupled receptors including CCR2, CCR7, CX3CR1 and the complement receptors C3AR1 and C5AR1. Alarmins like HMGB1, lipid and peptide chemoattractants, and growth factors of the VEGF and CSF1 families add further recruiting cues. Downstream, ERK signalling, focal adhesion kinases, Rac GTPases and the WNK-OXSR1/STK39 module remodel the actin cytoskeleton and adhesion so cells polarise and crawl up the gradient.

Leukocytes only reach infected or damaged tissue if something tells them where to go, and this pathway covers the signals and machinery that increase the rate and extent of that directed migration. It underlies inflammatory infiltration, wound healing, lymph node trafficking of dendritic and T cells, and the recruitment of monocytes and macrophages; excessive activity drives chronic inflammation, atherosclerosis and tumour-promoting myeloid influx, while loss of it leaves tissues unable to mount a cellular defence. Chemokines such as CCL2, CCL5, CXCL8 and CXCL12 act through G protein-coupled receptors including CCR2, CCR7, CX3CR1 and the complement receptors C3AR and C5AR, converting a gradient into polarised motility. Downstream, Rac GTPases, focal adhesion kinases, WNK-OXSR1-STK39 signalling and ERK activity remodel the actin cytoskeleton and adhesion, while sheddases and alarmins amplify the recruiting cues.

negative regulation of cellular extravasation restrains the exit of leukocytes from the bloodstream into tissue, setting a limit on how much inflammatory infiltrate a site receives. This braking function protects tissue from collateral damage during infection and underlies the resolution phase of inflammation; when it fails, persistent neutrophil and monocyte recruitment drives chronic inflammatory and autoimmune injury. The genes act at several levels of the recruitment cascade: chemokines such as CXCL12, CCL21, CCL25 and CCL28 can retain or redirect cells rather than promote transmigration, prostaglandin E2 acting through the EP4 receptor and phospholipase C-beta signalling dampen adhesion and integrin activation in endothelium and leukocytes, and IL-27 receptor signalling suppresses inflammatory effector programmes. MIR146A adds a post-transcriptional negative feedback loop on NF-kB-driven adhesion molecule and cytokine expression, tying this control to innate immune tolerance and vascular barrier maintenance.

Leukocytes leave the bloodstream by adhering to endothelium and squeezing between cells, and this biology restrains that step, limiting how many cells extravasate into tissue. Damping cellular extravasation keeps inflammation proportionate: without such brakes, neutrophils and monocytes accumulate in tissue and drive collateral injury, as seen in sepsis, arthritis and atherosclerotic vessel walls. The restraint comes from several directions. Chemokines such as CXCL12, CCL21, CCL25 and CCL28 pattern where cells are held or directed, and in some contexts their signalling retains cells rather than recruiting them. Prostaglandin E2 acting through the EP4 receptor raises cyclic AMP in leukocytes and endothelium to suppress adhesion, MIR146A dampens NF-κB-driven inflammatory output, and phospholipase C beta and a cytokine receptor subunit tune the downstream signalling that converts chemotactic cues into firm arrest and diapedesis.</br>

positive regulation of leukocyte mediated immunity covers the signals that amplify killing and effector activity by white blood cells, tuning how aggressively natural killer cells, cytotoxic T cells, macrophages and granulocytes attack infected or transformed targets. Its output is tumour surveillance and control of intracellular pathogens; too little leaves susceptibility to infection and malignancy, too much drives autoimmunity and cytokine-driven tissue damage. Mechanistically it combines antigen and stress-ligand display with activating receptor engagement and cytokine amplification: classical and non-classical MHC molecules plus CD1 and MR1 present peptide and lipid, NKG2D ligands of the ULBP and RAET1 families mark stressed cells, and receptors such as KLRK1, CD226, SLAMF and CD28 relay through VAV1, BTK, PLCG2 and RASGRP into degranulation and adhesion. IL-12, IL-18, IL-2 and IL-21 acting via STAT5 and TBX21 raise cytotoxic potential, while FOXP3, LAG3 and TGFB1 set the opposing brake.

Leukocyte-mediated immunity is the arm of host defence in which white blood cells directly kill infected or transformed targets and release effectors that damage pathogens, and this programme covers the signals that raise its frequency and intensity. Amplifying it clears intracellular infection and tumour cells; failure leaves cytotoxicity blunted, while unrestrained amplification drives autoimmunity and cytokine-driven tissue injury. Activating receptors on NK and T cells, including KLRK1 with its TYROBP/DAP-type adaptors, CD226 and the SLAM family with SH2D1A, sense stress ligands such as the ULBP and RAET1 proteins and engage VAV1, PLCG2 and BTK to trigger granule release, marked here by LAMP1 and vesicle SNAREs. Classical and non-classical MHC molecules, CD1 lipid-presenting proteins and MR1 supply the recognition side, while IL-12, IL-18, IL-2, IL-23 and type-defining factors TBX21 and GATA3 set the polarising cytokine context.

negative regulation of T cell mediated immunity is the set of brakes that limit how strongly and how long T cells attack, protecting tissues from collateral damage and enforcing tolerance to self and to fetal tissue. Loss of these brakes produces autoimmunity and immunopathology; their exploitation by tumours produces immune escape, which is why several members are the direct targets of checkpoint blockade. Inhibitory receptors such as PD-1, BTLA, LAG3, and the leukocyte immunoglobulin-like and NK receptor families engage ligands including PD-L1, HLA-G and HVEM to raise the threshold for activation, while phosphatases and negative regulators like CD45 and DUSP22 damp proximal receptor signalling. Regulatory T cells specified by FOXP3, together with metabolic suppression by arginase and IL4I1 and the tryptophan-sensing transcription factor AHR, impose suppression from outside the responding cell. Type I interferons and SMAD7 add transcriptional restraint on effector differentiation.

T cell effector responses must be damped once they are no longer needed, and this braking programme is what keeps cytotoxic and helper T cell activity from destroying healthy tissue. Its failure underlies autoimmunity and graft rejection, while its exploitation by tumours and by the placenta produces immune escape and maternal-fetal tolerance respectively. Inhibitory receptors on the T cell surface, including PD-1, LAG3, BTLA and CTLA-4's ligands CD80 and CD274, deliver co-inhibitory signals that raise the activation threshold; non-classical MHC molecules such as HLA-G and HLA-F engage leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptors on lymphocytes and myeloid cells. FOXP3 specifies regulatory T cells, and amino acid-depleting enzymes such as arginase and IL4I1 starve responding T cells of substrate. These are the checkpoints that antibody blockade in cancer immunotherapy is designed to release.

positive regulation of T cell mediated immunity covers the signals and surface molecules that amplify T cell effector responses against infected, transformed or foreign cells. It determines the strength of antiviral and antitumour immunity and, when overdriven, contributes to autoimmunity and inflammatory disease; several of its components are exploited therapeutically. Antigen display is the first tier: classical MHC class I and II molecules with B2M and the TAP transporter, plus the non-classical CD1 family and MR1 that present lipids and microbial metabolites. Cytokines then set the programme, with IL-12, IL-18, IL-23, IL-1 and IL-6 acting through their receptors and TRAF/MAP3K7 adaptors, while GATA3, TBX21 and FOXP3 fix helper lineage identity. Costimulatory and stress ligands including OX40L, nectins and the ULBP/RAET1 family engage NKG2D and related receptors to lower the threshold for cytotoxic killing.

T cells only attack what they are shown, and this pathway covers the events that raise the strength, speed and reach of T cell mediated immunity. It matters for clearing intracellular pathogens and tumour cells, and its excess drives autoimmunity and inflammatory tissue damage. Antigen presentation supplies the trigger: classical class I and class II molecules together with beta-2 microglobulin and the peptide transporter, plus the lipid-presenting CD1 family and the metabolite-presenting MR1 that serve unconventional T cells. Stress-induced ULBP and RAET1 ligands and nectin-family surface proteins engage activating receptors, while costimulation and cytokines including IL-12, IL-18, IL-23, IL-1 and IL-6 push differentiation toward effector states, with T-bet and GATA3 fixing helper lineage choice. Adaptor and kinase components such as MALT1, TRAF6 and MAP3K7 carry receptor engagement into transcription, and FOXP3 marks the regulatory arm that counterbalances it.

negative regulation of B cell mediated immunity is the set of brakes that keep antibody responses proportionate and self-tolerant, limiting how much antibody is made and how far complement-mediated damage proceeds. Without these restraints, autoantibody production and immune complex disease follow, which is why several of these genes are lupus and glomerulonephritis susceptibility loci. Restraint operates at three levels: inhibitory surface receptors such as FCGR2B, which raises the threshold for B cell activation by immune complexes, and the phosphatase PTPN6 that dampens antigen receptor signalling; soluble and membrane complement regulators including C4b-binding protein, CD46 and CR1, which prevent convertase amplification on host cells; and transcriptional control, where BCL6 constrains plasma cell differentiation while FOXP3 regulatory T cells and NDFIP1-directed ubiquitination suppress helper signals that would otherwise sustain the response.

Antibody responses must be damped as well as launched, and this set covers the braking processes that limit B cell mediated immunity so that self-tissue is spared and responses resolve once antigen is cleared. Several routes converge: inhibitory receptor signalling through the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B and the phosphatase PTPN6, which raises the threshold for B cell activation and drives apoptosis of low-affinity clones; complement restraint by regulators such as C4BPA/C4BPB, CD46 and CR1, which prevent amplification of the classical cascade on host membranes; and transcriptional control, where BCL6 restrains differentiation and FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells suppress help to B cells. Loss of these controls permits autoantibody production, immune complex disease and lupus-like autoimmunity, while ubiquitin-pathway regulators including NDFIP1 contribute by curbing lymphocyte activation. The biology sits at the interface of peripheral tolerance, complement homeostasis and germinal centre regulation.

cytoplasmic pattern recognition receptor signaling pathway is the intracellular arm of innate immune surveillance: sensors sitting in the cytosol detect microbial nucleic acids, peptidoglycan fragments and other conserved pathogen structures that have breached the membrane, and convert that detection into interferon production, inflammatory cytokine release and inflammasome-driven cell death. It is how cells recognise viral replication and invasive bacteria from within, and its misfiring underlies interferonopathies, autoinflammatory fever syndromes and Crohn-associated inflammation. DNA sensing runs through cGAS and STING to TBK1 and IRF3; RNA sensing through RIG-I and MDA5 to MAVS; peptidoglycan through NOD1/NOD2 and RIPK2 to NF- cB; and NLRP3, NLRP1 and pyrin assemble with ASC to activate caspase-driven maturation of IL-1 family cytokines. Layered onto these are ubiquitin editors, palmitoyl transferases, endolysosomal transporters and negative regulators such as TREX1 and A20 that keep the response from turning on self.

Intracellular sentinels detect microbial nucleic acids and cell wall fragments that have breached the plasma membrane, and this cytoplasmic pattern recognition receptor signaling underlies the first line of antiviral and antibacterial defence in essentially every cell type, not just professional immune cells. Cytosolic DNA is read by cGAS and IFI16 feeding STING, RNA duplexes by RIG-I and MDA5 feeding the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, and bacterial peptidoglycan by NOD1 and NOD2 through RIPK2, converging on TBK1-IRF3 to drive type I interferon or on TAK1-IKK-NF-κB to drive inflammatory cytokines. A parallel arm assembles inflammasomes around NLRP3, NLRP1 or pyrin with ASC, activating caspase-mediated IL-1 release and pyroptosis. Ubiquitin editing by A20, CYLD and OTULIN, TRIM ligases, palmitoylation, and nucleases such as TREX1 keep the output proportionate; loss of restraint produces interferonopathies and hereditary periodic fever syndromes, while loss of sensing leaves hosts vulnerable to infection.

regulation of T-helper 1 type immune response tunes the strength of the IFN-γ-dominated arm of adaptive immunity, the response that clears intracellular bacteria, mycobacteria and viruses by arming macrophages and cytotoxic cells. Too little of it leaves patients with disseminated mycobacterial and Salmonella infection; too much drives autoimmune tissue damage and granuloma formation. Control is exerted mostly at the point where innate cytokines instruct a naive CD4 T cell: IL-12 and IL-18, amplified by IL-1 and IL-23 and shaped by IL-27, signal through paired receptor chains and JAK-STAT to induce the lineage transcription factor TBX21, with HLX and ARID5A reinforcing commitment. Counter-regulators set the ceiling, including the decoy IL-18BP, SOCS5, and the inhibitory receptor pair TIM-3 and galectin-9 that deletes activated Th1 cells. Costimulation, chemokine-guided positioning in lymph nodes, and eicosanoid signalling complete the circuit.

Type 1 helper T cell responses drive defence against intracellular bacteria, mycobacteria and viruses, and this pathway covers the signals that raise or damp that response. Interferon-gamma-producing Th1 cells depend on it; too little leaves susceptibility to disseminated mycobacterial and salmonella infection, while too much contributes to autoimmune and granulomatous inflammation. The core mechanism is cytokine instruction of naive T cells: IL-12 and its shared receptor subunits, IL-18 with its receptor and the decoy binding protein IL-18BP, and related IL-12 family members including IL-23 and IL-27 acting through shared chains such as IL6ST and downstream JAK3. TBX21 is the lineage-defining transcription factor, with HLX reinforcing the programme and SOCS5 restraining it. Costimulation via CD80 and TNFSF4, inhibitory input through HAVCR2 and its ligand LGALS9, chemokine-guided positioning, and inflammasome-linked IL-1 signalling set the response's magnitude and its resolution.

regulation of response to tumor cell governs how strongly the immune system attacks transformed cells, setting the balance between effective tumor clearance and the tolerance that lets cancers grow. It is the biology exploited by checkpoint blockade: PD-1 with its ligand PD-L1, LAG3, TIM-3, BTLA and CD160 with the herpesvirus entry mediator, and the CD226/TIGIT axis competing for the nectin ligands PVR and NECTIN2 all tune the activation threshold of cytotoxic T and NK cells. Counterbalancing signals promote attack, including IL-12 driving type 1 differentiation, MR1-restricted and MHC class II antigen presentation, and immunogenic release of HMGB1 or gasdermin-mediated pyroptotic death. Suppressive arms act through TGF-beta, the tryptophan-metabolising IL4I1 and aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling. Ubiquitin-pathway components such as FBXO38 and KLHL22 control checkpoint receptor turnover, determining how long inhibition persists on the cell surface.

Immune recognition and killing of tumour cells is tunable, and this pathway covers the processes that set how strong that antitumour response becomes. Its components are the checkpoints exploited by cancers to escape immunity and the targets of checkpoint blockade therapy: PD-1 with its ligand PD-L1, LAG3, TIM-3 (HAVCR2), BTLA and its ligand TNFRSF14, CD160, and the nectin-family ligands PVR and NECTIN2 that engage the activating receptor CD226. Counterbalancing signals come from IL-12 subunits and HMGB1, which promote cytotoxic and NK responses, while TGFB1, AHR and IL4I1 impose immunosuppression through metabolite and cytokine cues. Regulators of checkpoint protein stability, including the ubiquitin machinery acting on PD-1, determine surface receptor levels. Also represented are intrinsic death routes such as gasdermin E-dependent pyroptosis, linking target-cell killing mode to the resulting inflammation and immune escape.

negative regulation of acute inflammatory response to antigenic stimulus is the braking system on antigen-triggered acute inflammation, the set of processes that limit how fast and how far an immediate hypersensitivity or immune-complex reaction can escalate. It matters because unchecked responses of this type produce anaphylaxis, serum sickness and tissue-damaging immune-complex disease, and because loss of these brakes predisposes to autoantibody-driven autoimmunity. The best-defined component is the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B, whose ITIM-based signalling raises the threshold for immune-complex activation of B cells, mast cells and phagocytes; sialophorin (SPN, CD43) similarly restrains leukocyte adhesion and activation. Neuropeptide Y acting through its receptors supplies neural input that dampens mast cell and leukocyte reactivity, while SELENOS links endoplasmic reticulum stress handling to cytokine output. Together these represent receptor-level inhibition, neuroimmune modulation and cytokine receptor competition converging on resolution rather than initiation of inflammation.

Acute inflammation triggered by antigen must be actively damped, or immune complexes and mast cell activation drive tissue injury, anaphylaxis and autoantibody-driven disease; the genes here restrain that response rather than initiate it. The clearest example is the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B, the only inhibitory Fc gamma receptor, which carries an inhibitory signalling motif and raises the threshold for B cell, mast cell and phagocyte activation by immune complexes; loss of its function predisposes to systemic autoimmunity. Neuropeptide Y acting through its receptors links neural output to immune tone, illustrating neuroimmune brake on local inflammatory responses, while sialophorin (SPN, CD43) shapes leukocyte adhesion and contact-dependent activation. Other members contribute cytokine receptor signalling and endoplasmic reticulum stress handling. Collectively this is the negative arm of hypersensitivity control, setting how strongly and how long an antigen-provoked inflammatory episode proceeds.

positive regulation of myeloid leukocyte mediated immunity describes the signals that ramp up the effector output of neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages and mast cells — degranulation, phagocytosis, oxidative burst and cytokine release — during infection and inflammation. Its strength sets whether pathogens are cleared efficiently or whether tissue is damaged by excessive myeloid activation, as in sepsis, vasculitis and allergic disease. The genes span the main activating inputs: Fc receptors and their shared ITAM adaptors FCER1G and TYROBP feeding into BTK-dependent kinase cascades, complement C3 and the CD11b/CD18 integrin pair driving opsonic phagocytosis and adhesion, protease-activated and neuropeptide receptors, and innate nucleic acid sensors such as RIG-I and MAVS with the TLR adaptor TICAM1. SPI1 supplies the transcriptional program that specifies myeloid identity in the first place, while STX4 supports the membrane fusion that delivers granule contents.

Myeloid effector cells — neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, mast cells — kill microbes and clear opsonised targets by degranulation, phagocytosis and oxidative burst, and this pathway covers the signals that turn that activity up. Enhanced myeloid leukocyte mediated immunity is what makes acute antibacterial and antifungal defence possible, while unchecked amplification drives tissue damage in sepsis and inflammatory disease. The genes point to several converging inputs: Fc receptor engagement of complement-opsonised or antibody-coated particles through FCGR1A with the FCER1G and TYROBP signalling chains, the CD11b/CD18 integrin pair mediating adhesion and complement receptor function, and BTK relaying these to granule release, with STX4 supplying the fusion machinery for exocytosis. Innate nucleic acid sensing via RIGI, MAVS and TICAM1 and the lineage transcription factor SPI1 set the responsiveness of these cells, while C3 and POMC-derived peptides act as extracellular modulators.

Regulation of humoral immune response tunes the arm of immunity that acts through soluble mediators — complement, antibodies and antimicrobial peptides — setting how strongly and for how long these systems attack a target. Its main business is restraint: membrane and fluid-phase complement regulators such as CD46, CD55, CD59, factor H, factor I and the C4b-binding proteins prevent the cascade from damaging host tissue, and their loss causes haemolytic disease, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and hereditary angioedema. On the other side sit activators and amplifiers, including C3, MASP1, properdin and inflammatory cytokines such as TNF, LTA, IL1B and IL-17. Antibody output itself is modulated by inhibitory receptors like FCGR2B and phosphatases PTPN6 and PTPRC, while CXCL13 and CCR7 position B cells in lymphoid follicles where responses are generated.

Humoral immunity — antibodies, complement and soluble antimicrobial factors acting in blood and mucosal fluid — must be tuned so that it clears pathogens without damaging host tissue, and this pathway covers the processes that raise or dampen its magnitude and duration. Much of the control is exerted on the complement cascade: membrane and fluid-phase regulators such as CD46, CD55, CD59, factor H, factor I and C4b-binding protein restrain C3 and C5 convertase activity and protect self cells from lysis, while properdin stabilises the alternative pathway and MASP1 initiates the lectin arm. Complement receptors CR1 and CR2 link opsonised antigen to B cell activation, and FCGR2B together with the phosphatases PTPN6 and PTPRC sets the threshold for antibody-mediated feedback. Cytokines including TNF, lymphotoxin-alpha, IL1B and IL17, plus the follicular chemokine CXCL13, shape the lymphoid environment in which antibody responses develop. Loss of these brakes underlies complement-driven haemolysis, nephropathy and autoantibody disease.

positive regulation of humoral immune response describes the processes that amplify immunity carried by soluble mediators — antibodies, complement proteins and antimicrobial peptides — rather than by direct cell contact. Boosting this arm speeds opsonisation and lysis of extracellular bacteria and helps clear immune complexes, while unchecked amplification drives autoantibody disease and complement-mediated tissue injury. The genes span several amplifying inputs: complement components and the properdin-dependent alternative pathway with its receptors CR1 and C3, inflammatory cytokines such as TNF, lymphotoxin-alpha, IL1B and the IL-17 family that promote germinal centre organisation and antibody output, chemokine-driven lymphocyte homing through CCR7, and antimicrobial effectors including cathelicidin. Regulators such as the inhibitory receptor FCGR2B and the phosphatase CD45 set the threshold at which B cells respond, tying humoral output to inflammatory and innate signalling context.

Humoral immunity is the arm of defence carried by soluble factors in blood and tissue fluids — antibodies, complement proteins and antimicrobial peptides — and this grouping covers the signals that raise its output. Enhancing it speeds opsonisation and lysis of bacteria and helps clear immune complexes; excessive drive contributes to autoantibody disease and complement-mediated tissue injury. Several members act directly in the cascade, with C3 as the central convertase substrate, C6 in the lytic terminal complex, properdin stabilising the alternative pathway, and CR1 and FCGR2B tuning how opsonised particles and antibody complexes are handled on cell surfaces. Cytokines including TNF, lymphotoxin alpha, IL1B and the IL-17 family amplify the response and support the lymphoid architecture where antibody is made, while CCR7 positions lymphocytes and dendritic cells for that encounter. Cathelicidin and haem-binding hemopexin extend the effect to direct antimicrobial and sequestering activity.

tRNA threonylcarbamoyladenosine modification installs the t6A mark at position 37, immediately 3' of the anticodon, on every tRNA that reads an ANN codon. This bulky modification stabilises codon-anticodon pairing and enforces reading-frame maintenance, so without it ribosomes misread and frameshift, translational fidelity collapses, and cells show growth and stress-response defects; in humans, loss-of-function mutations in the complex cause Galloway-Mowat syndrome, with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome and microcephaly. YRDC first makes the threonylcarbamoyl-AMP intermediate from threonine, bicarbonate and ATP, and the KEOPS complex — the OSGEP catalytic subunit with TPRKB, GON7 and their partners — transfers that moiety onto the adenine amino group in the cytoplasm and nucleus, while OSGEPL1 performs the equivalent reaction on mitochondrial tRNAs. The pathway thus links amino acid and one-carbon availability to the accuracy of protein synthesis.

Accurate decoding of ANN codons depends on a bulky modification at position 37, immediately 3' of the anticodon, and tRNA threonylcarbamoyladenosine modification is how it is installed. The mark stabilises codon-anticodon pairing and suppresses frameshifting and near-cognate misreading, so its loss degrades translational fidelity across a large share of the genetic code. Threonine, bicarbonate and ATP are first condensed into a threonylcarbamoyl-adenylate intermediate by YRDC, which then serves as donor for the transfer step carried out by the KEOPS complex: the metallo-hydrolase-fold catalytic subunit OSGEP together with the accessory subunits TPRKB and GON7, with OSGEPL1 acting on mitochondrial tRNAs. Beyond translation, KEOPS components have been tied to telomere maintenance and transcriptional regulation, and biallelic mutations in OSGEP, TPRKB or GON7 cause Galloway-Mowat syndrome, combining steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome with microcephaly and brain malformation.

developmental process involved in reproduction covers the progressive changes in germline and reproductive somatic tissues that give an organism the capacity to produce offspring, from gonad specification through gamete maturation. It underlies fertility, and its disruption causes disorders of sex development, premature ovarian insufficiency, azoospermia and teratozoospermia. The genes span sex determination and gonadal differentiation (SRY, SOX9, WT1, NR5A1, FOXL2, AMH), pituitary and steroid hormone signalling that drives puberty and gametogenesis (FSHB, LHCGR, AR, ESR1, CYP19A1, inhibins and activins), and meiotic entry and recombination (STRA8, SPO11, DMC1, SYCP1-3, MSH4, REC8). A large sperm-specific module builds the acrosome, flagellar axoneme and sperm head, compacts chromatin with protamines and transition proteins, and equips the cell for capacitation via CatSper channels. Oocyte factors, piRNA-pathway TDRD and PIWIL proteins, and imprinting DNA methyltransferases link gamete quality to the epigenetic state inherited by the embryo.

Making offspring requires more than gamete production: gonads must be specified and built, germ cells must complete meiosis, and gametes must be shaped into functional sperm and eggs. This broad developmental programme of reproduction covers sex determination and gonad morphogenesis, germline specification, meiotic recombination and gametogenesis, together with the hormonal control that coordinates them. Transcriptional regulators such as SRY, SOX9, NR5A1, WT1, FOXL2 and the DMRT family set gonadal fate, while gonadotropin and steroid signalling through FSHR, LHCGR, AR and ESR1 drive maturation. Meiosis depends on SPO11-initiated recombination and synaptonemal complex components including SYCP1-3, and piRNA factors with PIWI proteins silence transposons in the germline. Spermiogenesis contributes flagellar axoneme and outer dense fibre proteins, protamine-based chromatin remodelling, and CatSper channels for sperm motility and fertilization. Failure at any stage yields disorders of sex development, premature ovarian insufficiency, azoospermia or infertility.

heart morphogenesis is the construction of the heart during embryonic development: the specification of cardiac progenitors, their assembly into a beating tube, and the looping, chamber ballooning, septation, valve formation and outflow tract remodelling that convert that tube into a four-chambered pump. Its failure is the origin of congenital heart disease, the commonest class of birth defect, including septal defects, valve malformations and laterality-associated malposition. A core transcriptional network of NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, HAND1/2 and MEF2C reads out inductive signalling from BMP, TGF-beta/Nodal, Notch, Wnt, Hedgehog and FGF8, while left-right cues from cilia and PITX2 orient the looping heart. Downstream, sarcomeric and cytoskeletal genes such as MYH6, TNNT2 and TTN build contractile myocardium, and endothelial and neural crest contributions supply endocardium, cushions and great vessels. Cell migration, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and extracellular matrix remodelling shape each step.

Heart morphogenesis covers the shaping of the heart from mesodermal precursors into a four-chambered pump: specification of cardiac progenitors, looping of the linear tube, septation, valve formation, outflow tract remodelling and buildup of the conduction system and working myocardium. Failure at any step produces the congenital heart defects that are the commonest birth malformations, and the same genes underlie inherited cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia when they act later in life. Core transcription factors such as NKX2-5, TBX5, GATA4 and HAND1/2 set chamber identity, while BMP, Notch, Wnt, Hedgehog, TGF-beta and FGF8 signalling from surrounding endocardium, epicardium and pharyngeal mesoderm pattern the tissue; retinoic acid synthesis and cilium-dependent left-right cues fix asymmetry. Endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition builds the cushions that become valves, and sarcomeric genes including MYH6, TNNT2 and TTN give the growing chambers contractile function.

muscle system process covers the work that muscle tissue performs as an organ system: generating force in skeletal muscle for movement and posture, pumping blood through rhythmic cardiac contraction, and setting the tone of smooth muscle in vessels, airways and gut. The genes span the whole chain from excitation to force. Voltage-gated sodium, calcium and potassium channels and the neuromuscular acetylcholine receptor set membrane excitability; dihydropyridine receptors coupled to ryanodine receptors, junctophilins, calsequestrin, triadin and SERCA/phospholamban handle calcium release and reuptake; actin, myosin heavy and light chains, troponins, tropomyosins and titin form the contractile apparatus, with myosin light chain kinase and RhoA-ROCK tuning smooth muscle sensitivity. Also present are the myogenic regulators MYOD1, MYOG, MEF2A and cardiac factors such as NKX2-5 and GATA4, plus dystrophin-glycoprotein complex members and atrophy controls like FBXO32 and myostatin. Failure produces muscular dystrophy, myopathy, arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy.

Muscle system processes are the organ-level functions of contractile tissue: skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation, the cardiac beat and its rhythm, and the tone of smooth muscle in vessels, airways and gut. They underlie locomotion and posture, cardiac output, blood pressure control and visceral motility, and their failure produces myopathy, cardiomyopathy with arrhythmia, and vascular or airway dysregulation. The genes span the sarcomere itself (actins, myosin heavy and light chains, titin, tropomyosins and the troponin complexes), the calcium cycling machinery that times contraction (ryanodine receptors, SERCA pumps, calsequestrins, phospholamban, junctophilins, triadin, dihydropyridine channel subunits), and the sodium and potassium channels that shape excitability and conduction. Alongside these sit the neuromuscular junction acetylcholine receptor subunits, dystrophin-associated costameric proteins linking sarcomere to membrane, and adrenergic, endothelin and purinergic receptors that set tone, plus transcriptional and microRNA regulators that specify and remodel muscle.

regulation of systemic arterial blood pressure mediated by a chemical signal is the hormonal and locally released chemistry that sets vascular tone and blood volume, keeping perfusion pressure within limits from beat to beat and across days. Its failure produces hypertension, and with it heart failure, stroke and renal damage; several of its members are the targets of the most widely used antihypertensive drugs. The core is the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, in which renin and angiotensin-converting enzyme generate angiotensin II acting through AGTR1, while ACE2 and MAS1 form an opposing degradative arm and aldosterone synthase couples the system to sodium handling. Around it sit vasoconstrictors and vasodilators acting in parallel -- endothelins and their receptors, vasopressin, adrenergic and thrombin receptors, tachykinins, and endothelial nitric oxide synthase -- together with mast cell proteases and peptidases that process the peptide ligands, and redox enzymes that modulate endothelial responsiveness.

Systemic arterial blood pressure is set moment to moment by circulating and locally released chemical signals acting on vessel tone, cardiac output and renal salt and water handling. This hormonal, autocrine and paracrine control is what keeps perfusion adequate on standing or after blood loss, and its derangement underlies essential hypertension, pre-eclampsia and heart failure. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis dominates: renin cleaves angiotensinogen, angiotensin-converting enzyme generates angiotensin II for AT1 and AT2 receptors, while ACE2 and a Mas receptor arm oppose it and aldosterone synthase drives mineralocorticoid production.
