Vasopressin and oxytocin receptors, endothelins with their converting enzyme, adrenergic and dopaminergic receptors, substance P and tachykinin signalling, and thrombin-activated protease receptors add further inputs, balanced against endothelial nitric oxide synthase-derived vasodilation and modulated by NADPH oxidase-generated superoxide and mast cell proteases.

negative regulation of systemic arterial blood pressure covers the signals that lower arterial pressure, opposing vasoconstrictor and volume-retaining drives so that perfusion stays within a range the heart and vasculature can tolerate. Loss of this depressor arm underlies hypertension and its sequelae: left ventricular hypertrophy, stroke, and renal damage. The genes span several convergent mechanisms. Cardiac natriuretic peptides released on atrial stretch promote natriuresis and vasodilation; the angiotensin II type 2 receptor and the MAS receptor for angiotensin-(1-7) counterbalance the classical pressor arm of the renin-angiotensin system; adrenergic beta receptors, adenosine A1, and neuropeptides such as substance P and CRH act on vascular tone, renal handling, and central autonomic outflow. Smooth muscle contractility is tuned by a Rho GAP, potassium channel activity, and antioxidant control of nitric oxide availability, with Klotho linking the pathway to vascular ageing.

Blood pressure is held within a narrow range by opposing influences, and this pathway covers the arm that lowers it — reducing the force with which blood travels through the systemic arterial circulation. It matters because loss of these depressor mechanisms leaves vasoconstriction and sodium retention unchecked, the setting for hypertension and its downstream damage to heart, kidney and vessel wall. The natriuretic peptides ANP and BNP, released from stretched cardiac myocytes, promote vasodilation and renal sodium excretion; the angiotensin II type 2 receptor and MAS1 oppose the classical pressor axis of the renin–angiotensin system; adrenergic and adenosine receptors, tachykinins and MRGPRD-linked sensory signalling relax smooth muscle or damp sympathetic outflow. Also represented are regulators of vascular tone and remodelling such as ARHGAP42, BMPR2 and Klotho, tying this control to endothelial function, oxidative stress and pulmonary as well as systemic vascular disease.

regulation of glomerular filtration covers the signals that tune how fast plasma is filtered across the glomerular capillary wall into the renal tubule, setting the kidney's clearance of water and solutes and, through it, salt balance and blood pressure. Filtration rate depends on capillary hydraulic pressure and on the integrity of the podocyte-endothelial barrier, and both are targets here: adenosine acting through ADORA1 mediates tubuloglomerular feedback and afferent arteriolar constriction, thrombin and trypsin receptors F2R and F2RL1 couple coagulation proteases to mesangial and endothelial tone, PDGFB sustains mesangial cell recruitment, and gap junction connexin GJA5 propagates vasoconstrictor signals along the arteriole. Podocyte-restricted proteins such as PTPRO, CORO2B and EMP2 maintain foot process architecture and slit diaphragm function. Loss of these controls produces proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis and declining filtration rate in chronic kidney disease.

The kidney sets how fast plasma is filtered across the glomerular capillary wall, and this regulation determines urine output, solute clearance and salt and water balance across the whole body. Filtration rate is tuned both by vascular tone in the afferent and efferent arterioles and by the contractile and structural state of mesangial cells and podocytes that support the capillary loops. Adenosine acting through ADORA1 mediates tubuloglomerular feedback, constricting the afferent arteriole when distal salt delivery rises, while thrombin receptors F2R and F2RL1, PDGFB and GAS6 signal to mesangial and endothelial cells, and gap junction protein GJA5 helps propagate vasomotor signals along the arteriole. PTPRO, EMP2 and CORO2B act in the podocyte, where their loss produces foot process effacement, proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome; CYBA-dependent superoxide production modulates the same tone. Dysregulation underlies hyperfiltration injury in diabetes and hypertension.

regulation of systemic arterial blood pressure by endothelin describes how the vascular endothelium raises vascular tone and blood pressure through the endothelin peptides, one of the most potent vasoconstrictor systems in the body. It sets basal arterial resistance and is recruited in hypertension, pulmonary arterial hypertension, heart failure and chronic kidney disease, which is why endothelin receptor antagonists are used clinically. Endothelin-1 is synthesised as a precursor and activated by endothelin-converting enzyme at the endothelial surface, then acts on adjacent smooth muscle to trigger calcium entry and RhoA-dependent sensitisation of the contractile apparatus, sustaining constriction. The same pathway is balanced against endothelial nitric oxide synthase, so the net diameter of a vessel reflects opposing vasoconstrictor and vasodilator signals from the same cell layer. Related endothelin isoforms additionally act in neural crest and craniofacial development.

Endothelin is the endothelium's most potent vasoconstrictor, and its control of systemic arterial blood pressure sets vascular tone from moment to moment as well as over the long term through vessel wall remodelling. The peptide precursors encoded by EDN1, EDN2 and EDN3 are matured by the endothelin-converting enzyme ECE1 and then act on smooth muscle receptors, raising intracellular calcium and engaging RhoA-dependent contractile signalling that sensitises the myofilaments and sustains constriction. The same endothelial cells oppose this through endothelial nitric oxide synthase, so arterial diameter reflects a balance between endothelin-driven constriction and nitric oxide-driven relaxation. Loss of that balance, with excess endothelin tone, contributes to pulmonary arterial and systemic hypertension, and receptor blockade is an established therapy. Endothelin signalling also shapes neural crest derivatives during development, linking blood pressure control to craniofacial and enteric nervous system formation.

Outflow tract morphogenesis builds the exit channel of the developing heart and divides it into the aorta and pulmonary trunk, so that systemic and pulmonary circulations are separated at birth. Its failure produces the common conotruncal malformations — tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, transposition and persistent truncus arteriosus — and is the basis of the cardiac defects in 22q11 deletion and Alagille syndromes. The process depends on second heart field progenitors marked by ISL1 and TBX1 adding myocardium to the arterial pole, and on cardiac neural crest cells migrating in along semaphorin, plexin and slit-robo cues to septate the vessel and pattern the aortic arch arteries. BMP, TGF-beta, Notch, WNT and FGF8 signalling coordinate these populations with endocardial cushion remodelling, valve formation and smooth muscle differentiation, under transcriptional control by NKX2-5, GATA6, HAND2, PITX2 and TBX20.

The outflow tract is the single vessel leaving the embryonic heart that must be septated, rotated and remodelled into separate aorta and pulmonary trunk with their valves. Getting this wrong produces the common conotruncal malformations — tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, transposition, persistent truncus arteriosus — and it is the developmental step disrupted in DiGeorge/22q11 deletion through TBX1 and CRKL. Building it requires second heart field progenitors marked by ISL1 and NKX2-5, cardiac neural crest guided by SEMA3C–PLXND1 and Robo signals, and endocardial cushion cells undergoing endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition. BMP, FGF8, Notch–JAG1–RBPJ, TGF-beta, retinoic acid and non-canonical Wnt/planar polarity inputs converge on transcription factors including TBX20, HAND2, GATA6, PITX2 and TWIST1 to pattern septation, valve formation and great-artery identity.

morphogenesis of an endothelium is the shaping of the single-cell layer that lines blood vessels, lymphatics and heart chambers into a continuous, correctly patterned sheet. It determines whether a vascular tube forms a lumen of the right diameter with stable cell-cell junctions, and its failure produces the vascular malformations seen in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and cerebral cavernous malformation, where ACVRL1 and CCM2 act respectively. The genes span the inputs and effectors of this remodelling: Notch components DLL4 and RBPJ set arterial versus venous and tip versus stalk identity during sprouting, beta-catenin couples junctional adhesion to transcription, and RhoA, RhoB and the RhoGAP STARD13 drive the cytoskeletal contractility that bends and elongates cells. Growth factor and chemokine cues such as FGF1 and CXCL10 tune the process, linking endothelial architecture to angiogenesis, barrier integrity and inflammation.

Blood and lymphatic vessels work only if their endothelial lining is built into the right shape: a continuous, correctly polarized monolayer enclosing a lumen of appropriate calibre. Morphogenesis of an endothelium covers the sculpting of that layer during vascular development and remodelling, and its failure produces malformed, leaky or shunting vessels. Notch components such as DLL4 and its transcriptional partner RBPJ set tip-versus-stalk identity and restrain excessive sprouting, while ACVRL1 transduces BMP9/10 signals that stabilize arterial endothelium and is mutated in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Junctional and cytoskeletal control runs through beta-catenin, RHOA and RHOB with the RhoGAP STARD13, and CCM2 loss produces cerebral cavernous malformations by disrupting endothelial junction integrity. Additional inputs from FGF1, chemokine signalling and transcriptional regulators such as FOXP1 tune proliferation, migration and tube formation during angiogenesis and vessel maturation.

mitral valve development builds the left atrioventricular valve, the two-leaflet structure that keeps blood moving forward from left atrium to ventricle under the highest pressures in the heart. Its failure produces some of the commonest structural heart disease in humans, from myxomatous leaflet prolapse and regurgitation to atrioventricular septal defects. The process begins with endocardial cushions: BMP and activin receptor signalling through SMAD effectors, restrained by the inhibitory SMAD6, drives endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, while NOTCH1, TWIST1 and SOX4 govern cushion cell migration, proliferation and remodelling into thin fibrous leaflets. Planar cell polarity through DCHS1 orients the mesenchymal cells that lay down organised extracellular matrix, and ADAMTS19 and glycosaminoglycan turnover shape that matrix as the valve matures. The pathway therefore sits at the intersection of cardiac morphogenesis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and connective tissue patterning.

The mitral valve separates the left atrium from the left ventricle and must form leaflets thin enough to open freely yet strong enough to seal against systolic pressure; this developmental programme takes it from an endocardial cushion of the atrioventricular canal to that mature, layered structure. Its failure underlies myxomatous degeneration and mitral valve prolapse, one of the commonest causes of valve surgery, as well as congenital atrioventricular septal defects. Endocardial cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and populate the cushions under BMP receptor signalling through ACVR1, BMPR1A and BMPR2, restrained by the inhibitory SMAD6, with NOTCH1 and transcriptional regulators including TWIST1 and SOX4 driving mesenchymal identity. Planar cell polarity through DCHS1 orients the migrating cells, and later remodelling organizes extracellular matrix into the stratified leaflets and tension apparatus that give the valve its mechanical competence.

Pulmonary valve morphogenesis builds the three-leaflet valve that separates the right ventricle from the pulmonary artery and enforces one-way flow into the lungs. Errors here produce pulmonary stenosis, dysplastic or bicuspid pulmonary valves, and are part of the outflow tract malformations seen in Tetralogy of Fallot and Alagille syndrome. The valve arises from endocardial cushion tissue: NOTCH1/2 with JAG1 and the HEY family transcriptional repressors specify endocardium and restrain myocardial fate, while TGFB2, BMP4 and SMAD2 drive endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, with SMAD6 limiting it. NFATC1 and endothelial nitric oxide signalling coordinate leaflet elongation and proliferation, SLIT-ROBO guidance cues shape cushion patterning, and ADAMTS proteases including ADAMTS19 remodel the proteoglycan-rich matrix so leaflets thin into flexible cusps. TBX20 supplies the underlying cardiac transcriptional program, linking this process to outflow tract septation and general heart valve development.

The pulmonary valve guards the outflow from the right ventricle into the lung circulation, and its formation from endocardial cushion tissue determines whether blood leaves the heart in one direction only. Failure of this morphogenetic programme produces pulmonary stenosis, atresia or dysplastic thickened leaflets, lesions common in congenital heart disease and in syndromes such as Alagille. Notch receptors with their Jagged ligand and HEY-family transcriptional repressors pattern the cushion endocardium and drive endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, while TGF-beta and BMP4 signalling through SMAD2 is restrained by the inhibitory SMAD6 to set leaflet size. Calcineurin-NFATC1 signalling and endothelial nitric oxide synthase couple valve endothelium to cushion remodelling, SLIT-ROBO guidance cues shape the outflow tract, and ADAMTS proteases with versican turnover sculpt the extracellular matrix into thin, elongated leaflets. TBX20 supplies the upstream cardiac transcriptional context.

atrioventricular valve formation is the embryonic construction of the mitral and tricuspid valves, the structures that enforce one-way flow between atria and ventricles. Its failure produces some of the commonest congenital heart defects — atrioventricular septal defects, valve dysplasia, regurgitation — and milder disruption of the same program underlies degenerative mitral valve prolapse in adults. The process begins in the atrioventricular canal, where endocardial cells receive myocardial cues, undergo endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and invade the cardiac jelly to form the endocardial cushions that later remodel into thin fibrous leaflets. Notch signalling through NOTCH1 and its HEY1/HEY2 targets sets the boundary of the valve-forming region, GATA4 with its cofactor ZFPM1 and BMP/TGF-beta signals transduced by SMAD4 drive cushion mesenchyme formation, and DCHS1 governs the planar organisation and extracellular matrix of the maturing leaflet.

The mitral and tricuspid valves begin as endocardial cushions in the atrioventricular canal, and this pathway covers the steps that turn that swelling into a recognizable valve rudiment. Without it, the heart cannot separate atrial from ventricular blood or prevent regurgitation, and defects here underlie atrioventricular septal defects, valve dysplasia and myxomatous mitral valve disease. Endocardial cells overlying the cushion undergo endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invade the cardiac jelly, a decision governed by NOTCH1 signalling and its transcriptional effectors HEY1 and HEY2, by TGF-beta/BMP signals routed through the common mediator SMAD4, and by the GATA4-ZFPM1 (FOG2) transcription factor partnership that patterns the atrioventricular canal. DCHS1, a protocadherin mutated in mitral valve prolapse, orders the migration and polarity of the resulting valve interstitial cells. The programme links cardiac chamber specification to the mechanics of unidirectional flow.

cardiac chamber morphogenesis is the developmental program that carves the early heart tube into discrete atria and ventricles with walls, trabeculae and septa of the right size and shape. It determines whether a newborn has a normally partitioned four-chambered heart, and its disruption underlies much of congenital heart disease — septal defects, hypoplastic chambers, valve and outflow malformations — as well as later cardiomyopathy. Chamber identity is set by a core of transcription factors, including NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, TBX20, HAND1/2 and MEF2C, acting on regional patterning cues from BMP, TGF-beta, Notch, WNT, FGF and retinoic acid signalling. Endocardial–myocardial crosstalk through NOTCH1, JAG1, HEY2 and NRG1 drives trabeculation and compaction, while sarcomeric genes such as MYH6, MYH7, TNNT2 and MYL2 give each chamber its contractile character. Laterality and cushion genes coordinate looping with septation.

The four-chambered heart is built by carving distinct atrial and ventricular cavities out of a simple tube, and cardiac chamber morphogenesis is the programme that generates and shapes those chambers. It determines wall thickness, trabeculation, septation and the atrioventricular boundary, and its failure produces the commonest human birth defects "septal defects, hypoplastic chambers, non-compaction and valve malformations. Cardiac transcription factors such as NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, TBX20, HAND1/2 and MEF2C set chamber identity and regional gene expression, with TBX2 and TBX3 repressing chamber programmes in the canal and conduction regions. They act downstream of BMP, TGF-beta/SMAD, Notch-Jagged, Wnt/Frizzled and neuregulin signals passing between endocardium and myocardium, and converge on sarcomeric output "MYH6, MYH7, MYL2, troponins, tropomyosin " so that each chamber acquires the contractile properties its workload demands.

Atrial cardiac muscle tissue development builds the thin-walled upper chambers of the heart and gives them an identity distinct from the ventricles, including the specialized conduction tissue that sets heart rate. It determines atrial wall growth, left-right asymmetry of the atria, and the formation of the sinoatrial node; its disruption underlies atrial septal defects, atrial fibrillation, sick sinus syndrome and laterality defects such as heterotaxy. Cardiac progenitors marked by MESP1 and ISL1 are directed by NKX2-5, GATA6, TBX5 and PITX2, with PITX2 enforcing left atrial character and TBX3/SHOX2 repressing working-myocardial genes to carve out pacemaker tissue expressing HCN4. BMP10 and BMP4, tuned by the antagonist noggin and by endoglin, drive chamber myocardial proliferation, while MYH6 and gap junction and Popeye-domain proteins provide contractile and electrical coupling. The pathway sits within broader cardiac morphogenesis and cardiac conduction.

Atrial cardiac muscle tissue development covers the specification, growth and maturation of the thin-walled upper chambers of the heart, the compartment that fills the ventricles and houses the pacemaking and conduction tissue. Its outcome determines atrial identity as distinct from ventricular myocardium, marked by chamber-specific contractile and gap junction proteins such as MYH6, and it sets left-right asymmetry of the atria through PITX2 and ZIC3 activity. Transcription factors including NKX2-5, GATA6, TBX5, ISL1 and MESP1 act with BMP and WNT signals, the BMP antagonist NOG among them, to drive cardiac progenitors into atrial myocytes, while TBX3, SHOX2 and the HCN4 pacemaker channel carve out the sinoatrial node within this territory. Disruption produces septal defects, atrial isomerism, sinus node dysfunction and a predisposition to atrial fibrillation.

growth involved in heart morphogenesis is the tissue growth that gives the developing heart its shape — the expansion and remodelling of myocardium, chambers and outflow tract that turns a simple tube into a four-chambered pump. When this growth is misproportioned, the result is congenital heart disease: hypoplastic chambers, valve and septal defects, or thin, poorly trabeculated ventricular walls. The genes span the stages of that process. A mesoderm transcription factor specifies the cardiac progenitors that supply the growing heart, Notch signalling patterns endocardium and trabeculae and instructs myocardial proliferation, and sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor signalling couples vascular and endocardial cues to growth of the surrounding tissue. A cardiac-enriched ADP-ribosylhydrolase-like protein acts in the sarcomeric apparatus of growing cardiomyocytes, and a microRNA tunes proliferative output. Together they link cell cycle control in cardiomyocytes to organ-level form.

Growth that contributes to shaping the heart couples cell proliferation and tissue expansion to the sculpting of chambers, valves and outflow structures during cardiac development. Timing matters: too little growth leaves hypoplastic chambers or thin ventricular walls, while misplaced growth distorts septa and valves, and defects in this process underlie much of congenital heart disease. The genes here span the sequence from specification to remodelling. MESP1 marks the earliest cardiogenic mesoderm that gives rise to the heart tube, NOTCH1 signalling patterns endocardium and is required for valve and outflow tract formation, and S1PR1 links sphingosine-1-phosphate sensing to endothelial behaviour and vascular integrity within the growing myocardium. ADPRHL1 is a sarcomere-associated protein of developing cardiac muscle, tying contractile apparatus assembly to chamber growth, while microRNA input adds post-transcriptional control over cardiomyocyte proliferation.

Regulation of membrane depolarization governs how readily an excitable cell moves its membrane potential away from rest toward the threshold for firing, setting heart rate, neuronal excitability and the timing of action potentials. Its failure produces arrhythmia and seizure: mutations in the cardiac sodium channel and its accessory beta subunits, or in their trafficking and anchoring partners such as ankyrin-G, RANGRF and SLMAP, underlie Brugada and long QT syndromes, while the HCN family carries the pacemaker current that drives spontaneous depolarization in sinoatrial node and rhythmically active neurons. Control is exerted at several levels — channel abundance and surface delivery through NEDD4L-dependent ubiquitination, phosphorylation by CaMKII and Src, calcium- and ATP-gated conductances such as TRPM4 and P2RX7, gap junction coupling, and transcriptional programs involving TBX5 and CREB1. Mitochondrial depolarization and permeability regulators link the same term to apoptotic commitment.

Excitable cells encode information in how quickly and how far their membrane potential swings positive, and this pathway covers the processes that tune that depolarization rather than simply carrying it. Control of the rate, frequency and extent of depolarization sets heart rate, conduction velocity and neuronal firing patterns, and its derangement produces arrhythmia and seizure susceptibility. Much of the gene content converges on the cardiac sodium channel and its auxiliary beta subunits, together with trafficking and scaffolding partners such as ankyrin-G, NEDD4L, SLMAP and RANGRF that determine how much channel reaches the sarcolemma. Hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels supply the pacemaker current that drives spontaneous depolarization in sinoatrial and neuronal cells, while a T-type calcium channel, TRPM4, a chloride channel, gap junction connexin and P2RX7 shape the threshold and shift the membrane in the depolarizing direction. Transcriptional and kinase inputs, including TBX5, CREB1, CAMK2D and SRC, adjust this machinery over longer timescales.}

Ventricular septum development is the embryonic partitioning of the primitive ventricle into left and right chambers, the step that separates pulmonary from systemic circulation after birth. Its failure produces ventricular septal defects, the commonest form of congenital heart disease, and contributes to complex malformations such as tetralogy of Fallot and atrioventricular canal defects. Muscular and membranous septal components arise from coordinated myocardial growth, endocardial cushion remodelling and cardiac neural crest contribution, directed by BMP and TGF-beta signalling through BMPR1A, SMAD4 and their SMAD6/SMAD7 brakes, by NOTCH1-RBPJ and HEY2 patterning of trabecular and compact myocardium, and by Slit-Robo, planar cell polarity and Hippo inputs that guide cell movement and proliferation. Cardiac transcription factors NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5 and ZFPM2 integrate these cues, and their mutation in humans directly causes septation defects with conduction abnormalities.

Separation of the embryonic heart into left and right pumping chambers depends on formation and remodelling of the ventricular septum, the muscular and membranous wall whose incomplete closure produces ventricular septal defects, the commonest congenital heart malformation, and contributes to Tetralogy of Fallot and atrioventricular canal defects. The genes here define the transcriptional and signalling circuitry that patterns the interventricular region and drives cushion-derived tissue to fuse with the growing muscular septum. Cardiac transcription factors such as NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5 and their cofactors ZFPM2 and CITED2 set chamber identity and are recurrently mutated in human septal disease, while BMP and TGF-beta receptor signalling through SMAD4 with the inhibitory SMADs 6 and 7, Notch output via RBPJ and HEY2, planar-cell-polarity and WNT components, and SLIT-ROBO guidance coordinate myocardial growth, cushion mesenchyme and outflow alignment. The programme links early cardiac specification to postnatal circulatory separation.

Atrial septum primum morphogenesis builds the first partition between the developing atria, the crescent-shaped tissue that grows from the atrial roof toward the endocardial cushions and, after fusing with them, separates left from right heart. Its correct formation is what makes serial circulation possible after birth; incomplete or failed development leaves an atrial septal defect, one of the commonest forms of congenital heart disease and a cause of left-to-right shunting and pulmonary overcirculation. The process depends on TGF-beta and BMP-family signalling through receptors such as ACVR1 acting on cushion mesenchyme, on epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition of endocardial cells, and on cardiac transcriptional control by GATA4 and SOX4, with chromatin regulation by NSD2 linking it to the broader gene programme of cardiac chamber and valve formation.

Formation of the septum primum, the first partition to grow across the common atrium in the embryonic heart, is a step toward separating right and left atrial chambers and completing the atrial septum. Failure leaves an atrial septal defect with left-to-right shunting, a common form of congenital heart disease, and the same genes underlie broader septal and valve malformations. The programme couples TGF-beta family signalling, through the ligand TGFB2 and the type I receptor ACVR1, to transcriptional control by GATA4 and SOX4, which pattern the atrial myocardium and the adjacent mesenchyme; NSD2 contributes chromatin methylation that shapes this output. The pathway therefore ties growth-factor signalling in the endocardium and atrial wall to the coordinated cell proliferation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and tissue fusion that build a septum, and GATA4 mutations in humans cause inherited atrial septal defects.

muscle hypertrophy in response to stress is the growth of muscle cells, rather than an increase in their number, when the tissue is loaded beyond its usual demand. In the heart this is the response to pressure overload, hypertension or valve disease: myocytes enlarge, sarcomeres are added, and a fetal-like gene programme returns, marked by the switch between MYH6 and MYH7 and induction of the natriuretic peptide NPPA. Calcium handling supplies the trigger, with calcineurin and TRPC3 relaying sustained calcium signals to transcription, while chromatin and transcriptional regulators including HDAC4, EZH2, KDM4A, CAMTA2, KLF15, FOXO1 and SMAD3/4 set the size and quality of the growth response. A set of microRNAs, notably the cardiac-specific miR-208a, tunes it further. Initially compensatory, sustained activation drives pathological remodelling, fibrosis and progression to heart failure, and related regulation shapes skeletal muscle mass.

Muscle cells enlarge rather than divide when workload or injury disturbs homeostasis, and the genes here describe that stress-induced hypertrophic growth as it occurs chiefly in the heart. Pressure overload, neurohormonal stimulation and altered calcium handling converge on a transcriptional programme that increases cell size, remodels the sarcomere and reactivates fetal contractile genes such as MYH7 and the natriuretic peptide NPPA, a switch used clinically as a marker of cardiac stress. Calcium entry and cycling components including the SERCA2 pump and the calcineurin catalytic subunit relay the signal, while chromatin regulators and repressors such as HDAC4, EZH2 and HEY2, transcription factors GATA6, FOXO1, KLF15 and SMAD partners, and several microRNAs including the cardiac-specific miR-208a set the growth threshold. Initially compensatory, sustained activation drives pathological remodelling, fibrosis and progression to heart failure and cardiomyopathy.

Galactose metabolic process covers the handling of dietary and recycled galactose, the sugar released from lactose in milk, and its conversion into forms a cell can burn for energy or use to build glycans. It matters most in infancy: loss of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase or galactokinase causes classical galactosemia and cataracts, as unmetabolized galactose and its phosphate accumulate and damage liver, brain and lens. The core route runs through epimerase, kinase and transferase steps of the Leloir pathway, with mutarotase interconverting anomers and phosphoglucomutase feeding the product into glycolysis and glycogen. The remainder of the genes place galactose in glycoconjugate biology: a UDP-galactose transporter supplies the Golgi lumen, galactosyltransferase and sulfotransferase activities extend and modify N-glycans and glycolipids, and beta-galactosidases release galactose again during lysosomal turnover, linking this sugar to both nutrient catabolism and glycosylation.

Galactose metabolism handles the sugar delivered mainly by dietary lactose, converting it into forms the cell can burn or use for building glycoconjugates. The core route is the Leloir pathway: galactose mutarotase sets the anomeric configuration, galactokinase phosphorylates galactose, GALT exchanges it onto UDP, and GALE epimerises UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose so the two hexoses are interconvertible; phosphoglucomutase links the output to glycolysis and glycogen. Loss of GALT causes classic galactosemia, with cataracts, liver damage and developmental injury on milk feeding, while galactokinase deficiency produces cataracts alone. The same UDP-galactose pool, imported into the Golgi by a nucleotide-sugar transporter, supplies galactosyltransferases and sulfotransferases that build N-glycans, glycolipids and keratan sulfate, and beta-galactosidases release galactose again during lysosomal turnover s- deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme underlies GM1 gangliosidosis.

UDP-N-acetylglucosamine biosynthetic process produces the activated sugar donor that virtually all glycosylation depends on, supplying the GlcNAc used in N-linked and O-linked glycans, glycosaminoglycans, GPI anchors and nuclear O-GlcNAc modification. Its output level acts as a nutrient sensor, coupling glucose, glutamine, acetyl-CoA and UTP availability to how heavily proteins are glycosylated, and loss of flux through it causes congenital myasthenic syndromes and severe glycosylation disorders. The route begins with the committed step in which glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate transaminases divert fructose-6-phosphate out of glycolysis into the hexosamine pathway, followed by acetylation, phosphomutase conversion to GlcNAc-1-phosphate, and uridylyltransferase capping with UTP. A salvage arm phosphorylates free GlcNAc, while deaminases run the reverse direction to return amino sugars to glycolysis, balancing biosynthesis against catabolism.

UDP-N-acetylglucosamine biosynthesis supplies the activated amino sugar that nearly every glycosylation route draws on: N-linked and O-linked glycans, glycosaminoglycan and proteoglycan chains, GPI anchors, and the O-GlcNAc modification through which cells couple nutrient supply to signalling and transcription. Flux begins when glutamine:fructose-6-phosphate amidotransferase, the committed and rate-limiting step, diverts fructose-6-phosphate out of glycolysis; successive acetylation by GNPNAT1, isomerization by PGM3, and uridylylation by UAP1 complete the donor, while deacetylase and deaminase activities together with the salvage kinase NAGK feed reclaimed hexosamine back in and set steady-state pools. Because the pathway senses glucose, glutamine, acetyl-CoA and UTP availability, it acts as a metabolic gauge; loss-of-function mutations in GFPT1 and PGM3 cause congenital myasthenic syndrome and an immunodeficiency with atopy, and elevated flux is linked to insulin resistance and tumour growth.

Glycerol metabolic process handles the three-carbon backbone released when fats are broken down, deciding whether it is burned, converted to glucose, or re-esterified into new lipid. It links adipose tissue lipolysis to hepatic gluconeogenesis, and so supports blood glucose during fasting; loss of glycerol kinase activity causes glycerol kinase deficiency with hyperglycerolaemia and metabolic decompensation. Glycerol entering a cell is phosphorylated by GK and oxidised by glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, feeding the triose phosphate pool through TPI1 and the gluconeogenic step catalysed by PCK1 and PCK2. The opposite direction is also represented: monoacylglycerol and diacylglycerol acyltransferases rebuild triacylglycerol, while phospholipase and lipid-binding proteins supply and traffic the substrates. Hormonal control by leptin and ANGPTL3 ties the route to whole-body energy balance and plasma triglyceride handling.

Glycerol sits at the junction of fat storage and glucose production: released when triglycerides are broken down in adipose tissue, it travels to the liver and kidney to be phosphorylated and fed into glycolysis or gluconeogenesis, or re-esterified back into lipid. Handling it properly is how the body converts stored fat into circulating fuel during fasting, and glycerol kinase deficiency causes hypoglycaemia, acidosis and developmental problems. Glycerol kinase performs the committing phosphorylation, glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase links the product to the mitochondrial shuttle that reoxidises cytosolic NADH, and triose phosphate isomerase channels the carbons into central metabolism. Acyltransferases such as the monoacylglycerol and diacylglycerol enzymes run the opposite direction, rebuilding triacylglycerol, while PCK1 and PCK2 commit the carbon skeleton to glucose synthesis. Leptin and ANGPTL3 place the whole process under systemic control of lipolysis and lipoprotein handling.

acetyl-CoA metabolic process governs the production and consumption of the two-carbon currency that links sugar, fat and amino acid breakdown to energy generation and biosynthesis. Whether a cell burns acetyl units in the TCA cycle, stores them as fatty acids, or diverts them into cholesterol and isoprenoids determines its metabolic state; loss of control here produces lactic acidosis and neurodegeneration on the catabolic side and dyslipidaemia on the anabolic side. The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and its regulatory kinases and phosphatase form the central switch, gating glycolytic carbon entry into mitochondria. Citrate export and cleavage by ACLY supply cytosolic acetyl-CoA, which acetyl-CoA carboxylases commit to fatty acid synthesis via FASN or HMGCS1 and HMGCR commit to the mevalonate route. Ketogenesis, acetate activation, thioesterase-mediated release and sirtuin deacylation adjust the pool, which also sets the substrate supply for protein acetylation.

Acetyl-CoA sits at the junction of catabolism and biosynthesis, and the reactions that make and consume it decide whether a cell burns fuel or builds with it. Sugars enter through the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and its regulatory kinases and phosphatase, which switch oxidation of pyruvate on and off according to nutrient supply; amino acid breakdown and mitochondrial citrate export via ATP-citrate lyase, plus direct acetate activation, feed the same pool. Downstream, acetyl-CoA carboxylases commit it to malonyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis, HMG-CoA synthase and reductase route it into cholesterol and isoprenoids, and a ketogenic arm supplies fuel during fasting. Because the cytosolic and nuclear pool also supplies acetyl groups for protein acetylation, this metabolism links energy status to gene regulation. Inherited defects in the pyruvate dehydrogenase subunits cause lactic acidosis and neurological disease.

Pyruvate metabolic process covers the production and disposal of pyruvate, the hub metabolite where glycolysis meets mitochondrial oxidation, lactate production and gluconeogenesis. It determines whether a cell burns glucose aerobically or ferments it, and so underlies muscle performance, hepatic glucose output, the Warburg-like shift of proliferating and hypoxic cells, and the lactic acidosis and encephalopathy that follow enzyme deficiency. The genes span the full glycolytic chain from hexokinase and phosphofructokinase through GAPDH, enolase and pyruvate kinase, the lactate dehydrogenases and monocarboxylate transporters that export or import lactate, the mitochondrial carrier and pyruvate dehydrogenase complex with its PDK kinases and PDP phosphatases, malic enzymes, and the PCK1/FBP1 gluconeogenic exits. Layered on top is regulation: HIF1A and MYC-like transcriptional control, insulin and IGF1 input, AMPK and mTOR nutrient sensing, and sirtuin and acetylation-dependent tuning of flux.

Pyruvate sits at the junction between glucose breakdown and oxidative metabolism, and the reactions that make, consume and dispose of it determine whether a cell burns sugar aerobically or ferments it to lactate. The glycolytic chain from hexokinases through phosphofructokinases, aldolases, enolases, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and pyruvate kinase generates the pyruvate pool; lactate dehydrogenases and monocarboxylate transporters such as SLC16A1 and SLC16A3 handle its reduction and export; the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier and the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex with its dedicated kinases and phosphatase commit it to acetyl-CoA and the TCA cycle; and PCK1/PCK2 with fructose-bisphosphatase run the gluconeogenic direction. Layered on top are hypoxic, hormonal and nutrient controls through HIF1A, insulin signalling, AMPK and mTOR that set flux according to oxygen and fuel supply. Disturbance underlies lactic acidosis, inherited glycolytic enzyme deficiencies with haemolytic anaemia or myopathy, and the fermentative shift of tumour metabolism.

Oxaloacetate metabolic process governs the turnover of a four-carbon hub metabolite that sits at the junction of the TCA cycle, gluconeogenesis, amino acid interconversion and lipid synthesis. Because oxaloacetate condenses with acetyl-CoA to keep the citric acid cycle turning, its supply sets the anaplerotic capacity of mitochondria; its withdrawal by PCK1 and PCK2 into phosphoenolpyruvate commits carbon to glucose production during fasting, a step whose dysregulation contributes to hyperglycaemia in diabetes. Cytosolic and mitochondrial malate dehydrogenases and the aspartate aminotransferases GOT1 and GOT2 shuttle oxaloacetate-derived carbon and reducing equivalents across the mitochondrial membrane through the malate-aspartate shuttle, linking glycolytic NADH to respiration. ATP-citrate lyase releases oxaloacetate while generating cytosolic acetyl-CoA for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, and FAHD-family decarboxylases dispose of it, tuning mitochondrial oxidative flux.

Oxaloacetate sits at the junction of the citric acid cycle, gluconeogenesis and amino acid metabolism, and the enzymes that make and consume it decide whether carbon is burned for energy, exported as glucose, or shuttled between cytosol and mitochondrion. The reactions represented here include reversible transamination with aspartate by cytosolic and mitochondrial aspartate aminotransferases, interconversion with malate by malate dehydrogenase, and decarboxylation to phosphoenolpyruvate by the cytosolic and mitochondrial forms of PEPCK, the committed step of gluconeogenesis in liver and kidney. The malate-aspartate shuttle built from these same activities moves reducing equivalents into mitochondria and supports redox balance. Oxaloacetate decarboxylase activity of the FAHD family and ATP-citrate lyase, which cleaves citrate to acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate for lipogenesis, further tune the pool. Loss of PEPCK function causes hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis during fasting.

regulation of carbohydrate metabolic process covers the control layer that decides how fast cells make, store, and burn sugars, matching fuel use to nutritional state. It is the biology of blood glucose homeostasis: insulin, glucagon, leptin and adiponectin signalling through their receptors into IRS1/IRS2, AKT, GSK3 and mTOR complexes, with AMPK subunits and sirtuins reading energy and NAD status. Downstream, glycogen handling is tuned by the PPP1R3 family of glycogen-targeting phosphatase subunits, phosphorylase kinase subunits, and by glucokinase and fructose-bisphosphatase at the glycolytic/gluconeogenic switch, while pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases gate entry into oxidation. Transcriptional and epigenetic regulators including FOXO1, HIF1A, PPARGC1A, MLXIPL, TCF7L2 and TP53 set longer-term capacity, and microRNAs fine-tune it. Failure of this control produces insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and glycogen storage disease.

Cells and whole organisms must match glucose use and storage to fuel availability, and this collection captures the control layer over carbohydrate metabolism rather than its enzymatic steps. It sets whether glucose is burned, stored as glycogen, or made anew, and its failure underlies insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and glycogen storage disease. Hormonal inputs dominate: insulin and glucagon acting through their receptors, IRS adaptors, AKT and GSK3, opposed by glucocorticoid, leptin and adiponectin signalling. Energy-sensing arms run through AMPK subunits, mTOR with RPTOR and MLST8, and sirtuins. Glycogen phosphatase targeting subunits of the PPP1R3 family direct PP1 onto glycogen enzymes, while pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases gate entry of pyruvate into oxidation. Transcriptional regulators including FOXO1, HIF1A, PPARGC1A, MLXIPL and TCF7L2, plus several microRNAs, provide slower adjustment of glycolytic and gluconeogenic gene expression.

energy reserve metabolic process covers how cells build up and draw down stored fuel — chiefly glycogen and fat — so that blood glucose and ATP supply are maintained between meals and during exercise. It defines the metabolic behaviour of liver, muscle and adipose tissue, and its failure produces glycogen storage diseases, Lafora disease, and the impaired glucose handling of insulin resistance and diabetes. Glycogen synthesis and breakdown are carried out by glycogenin, glycogen synthase, branching and debranching enzymes and the phosphorylase kinase complex, all switched by protein phosphatase 1 targeting subunits and glycogen synthase kinase 3. Insulin, glucagon and leptin signalling through insulin receptor substrates, AKT and mTOR set the direction, while autophagy components including WIPI proteins and glycophagy receptor STBD1 deliver stored glycogen and lipid to lysosomes. Fatty acid oxidation and circadian regulators tie the process to whole-body energy balance.

Between meals or during exercise, cells draw on stored fuel rather than circulating nutrients, and energy reserve metabolism covers the making and breaking of those stores. It centres on glycogen: synthases and branching enzymes build the polymer from UDP-glucose on a glycogenin core, while phosphorylases and their phosphorylase kinase subunits, debranching enzyme and lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase release glucose again. Protein phosphatase 1 catalytic and glycogen-targeting subunits, together with glycogen synthase kinase 3, set the balance, and insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors and AKT tips it toward storage while glucagon and adrenergic signals tip it toward mobilisation. Autophagy components provide a parallel route for degrading glycogen and lipid stores in the lysosome. Leptin, POMC and clock proteins link the process to whole-body energy balance. Defects cause glycogen storage diseases, Lafora body epilepsy, hypoglycaemia and exercise intolerance.

Oxidative phosphorylation is the process that supplies most of the ATP used by human cells, coupling the oxidation of NADH and succinate to the synthesis of ATP at the inner mitochondrial membrane. Tissues with high energy demand — heart, brain, skeletal muscle — depend on it, and inherited defects in its subunits or assembly factors produce mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, Leigh syndrome and optic neuropathies. Electrons pass through complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c oxidase, pumping protons whose return through the F1Fo ATP synthase drives phosphorylation of ADP; both nuclear and mitochondrially encoded subunits are required, so the two genomes must be coordinated. Also represented are cofactor and assembly steps, iron-sulfur cluster supply through ISCU and frataxin, and regulators such as SIRT3, PINK1 and the inhibitory factor ATP5IF1 that tune output, quality control and mitochondrial apoptotic signalling.

Aerobic ATP production is completed here: electrons stripped from nutrients pass down the mitochondrial respiratory chain to oxygen, pumping protons across the inner membrane, and the resulting gradient drives ATP synthase. Nearly every energy-demanding process in the cell depends on this output, and its failure produces the mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, with tissues of high oxidative demand such as brain, heart and muscle affected first. The gene complement spans all five complexes, including the many NDUFA/NDUFB/NDUFS subunits of complex I, the succinate dehydrogenase tetramer linking the pathway to the TCA cycle, cytochrome bc1 and cytochrome c oxidase subunits, mobile cytochrome c, and the F1FO ATP synthase with its inhibitory factor. Both nuclear and mitochondrially encoded subunits appear, so assembly requires coordination between the two genomes, aided by dedicated assembly factors, metal and iron-sulfur cofactor delivery, and regulators including SIRT3 and PINK1 that tie respiration to quality control.

cAMP biosynthetic process is the generation of cyclic AMP, the second messenger that converts hormone and neurotransmitter binding at the cell surface into intracellular action through protein kinase A and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels. It sets the tone for glycogen and lipid mobilisation, cardiac contractility and heart rate, hormone secretion, olfactory and taste transduction, and the synaptic plasticity underlying memory. The core of the pathway is the family of adenylyl cyclases, which convert ATP to cAMP downstream of stimulatory and inhibitory G proteins; individual isoforms are tuned differently, some by calcium and calmodulin, and the soluble form ADCY10 responds instead to bicarbonate and is required for sperm capacitation and motility. Upstream input comes from receptors such as those for PACAP and neurotensin, together with neuropeptide ligands, which couple external cues to cAMP output. Dysregulated cyclase activity contributes to endocrine tumours, heart failure and movement disorders.

Formation of cyclic AMP from ATP is the step that converts hormone and neurotransmitter binding at the cell surface into an intracellular second messenger, setting the tone for protein kinase A activity, ion channel gating, gene transcription and metabolic switching such as glycogenolysis and lipolysis. The pathway is carried chiefly by a family of membrane adenylyl cyclases with distinct regulation -- some stimulated by calcium and calmodulin, others inhibited by it, all subject to control by Gs and Gi proteins -- plus a soluble, bicarbonate-sensitive cyclase that operates independently of G proteins and is required for sperm motility and capacitation. Upstream input comes from receptors for peptide ligands, including the pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide receptor and the neurotensin receptor. Deficient or excessive cAMP production distorts neuronal plasticity, endocrine output and cardiac contractility.

GTP biosynthetic process supplies the cell with guanosine triphosphate, the nucleotide that fuels RNA and DNA synthesis, translation elongation, G protein signalling, tubulin polymerisation and countless GTPase switches. Because proliferating cells demand far more guanine nucleotide than resting ones, this route sets a limit on lymphocyte activation and tumour growth, and its rate-limiting enzyme IMPDH is the target of immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate; mutations in IMPDH1 cause retinitis pigmentosa. IMPDH1 and IMPDH2 oxidise inosine monophosphate to xanthosine monophosphate, committing purine flux toward guanine rather than adenine, while the nucleoside diphosphate kinases of the NME family transfer phosphate from ATP to GDP to complete the triphosphate pool. These kinases act in distinct compartments, including mitochondria, coupling local GTP supply to organelle function, and NME1 additionally acts as a metastasis suppressor.

GTP biosynthesis supplies the guanine nucleotide pool that fuels RNA synthesis, protein translation, G protein and small GTPase signalling, and tubulin polymerisation, so its output sets how fast a cell can grow and divide. Two committed steps dominate here: IMP dehydrogenase oxidises inosine monophosphate to xanthosine monophosphate, the rate-limiting and feedback-controlled entry into guanine nucleotide synthesis and the target of immunosuppressive drugs used to restrain lymphocyte proliferation, while the nucleoside diphosphate kinase family transfers a phosphate from ATP to GDP to regenerate GTP, including within mitochondria and at sites of local nucleotide demand. Proliferating and secretory tissues depend on this flux; loss of the retinal IMP dehydrogenase isoform causes dominant retinitis pigmentosa, and nucleoside diphosphate kinase members double as metastasis suppressors and regulators of membrane dynamics, linking nucleotide supply to cell behaviour.

cAMP catabolic process terminates cyclic AMP signalling by hydrolysing the second messenger to 5'-AMP, and so sets how strongly and how long a cell responds to hormones, neurotransmitters and other stimuli acting through G protein-coupled receptors. Without this degradative arm, protein kinase A activity would remain switched on after the receptor signal has passed, and the spatial compartmentalisation of cAMP into discrete microdomains would collapse. The work is done by cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases with distinct tissue distributions and affinities: PDE4 family members dominate in inflammatory cells and brain, PDE8 isoforms act at very low cAMP concentrations, and PDE10A is enriched in striatal medium spiny neurons. These enzymes are drug targets in asthma and COPD, depression, and psychiatric and movement disorders, making cAMP breakdown a practical control point for tuning inflammation, cardiac contractility and neuronal excitability.

Signals carried by cyclic AMP have to be terminated as well as started, and this pathway is the off switch: cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases hydrolyse cAMP to 5'-AMP, setting how high and how long a cAMP signal rises after a receptor engages adenylate cyclase. The rate of breakdown, more than the rate of synthesis, defines local cAMP gradients and therefore how much protein kinase A activity a cell experiences. The enzymes here are the cAMP-preferring families, differing in affinity, regulation and where they sit in the cell: PDE4 isoforms dominate in inflammatory and airway cells and are the target of anti-inflammatory inhibitors, PDE10A is enriched in striatal neurons and manipulated for psychiatric and movement disorders, and PDE8 forms contribute to steroidogenic and immune cell control. Loss of this catabolism leaves cells persistently stimulated, distorting metabolism, secretion and contractility.

pyrimidine nucleobase catabolic process is the route by which uracil and thymine are dismantled rather than salvaged, converting them through dihydro intermediates and ring opening to β-alanine, β-aminoisobutyrate, ammonia and carbon dioxide. It sets the balance between nucleotide reuse and degradation in liver and other tissues, and it is the same route that clears fluoropyrimidine chemotherapeutics: loss of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity causes severe 5-fluorouracil toxicity, while inherited deficiency of this enzyme or of dihydropyrimidinase produces neurological and developmental disease from accumulated pyrimidines. The first, rate-limiting reduction is followed by hydrolytic ring cleavage and a methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase step that feeds carbon into central metabolism. Several dihydropyrimidinase-like proteins here retain the fold but not the catalytic function, acting instead as collapsin response mediators that steer axon guidance and cytoskeletal remodelling in neurons.

Breakdown of the pyrimidine nucleobases uracil and thymine disposes of bases released by nucleic acid turnover and returns their carbon and nitrogen to central metabolism as beta-alanine, beta-aminoisobutyrate, ammonia and carbon dioxide. The route runs in three steps: dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase reduces the ring, dihydropyrimidinase hydrolyses it open, and a beta-ureidopropionase step completes the degradation, with a methylmalonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase linking the thymine branch onward to propionyl-CoA. This chemistry sets how much of a pyrimidine analogue drug survives in the body, and loss of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity causes severe, sometimes fatal fluoropyrimidine toxicity, while inherited defects in the first two enzymes produce neurological and developmental disease. Several family members here, the collapsin response mediator proteins, are catalytically inactive relatives that instead regulate microtubules and axon guidance in neurons.

DNA replication is the duplication of the genome that must happen once, and only once, before every cell division, so that each daughter cell inherits a complete and accurate copy. Failure produces under-replicated or rearranged chromosomes, and the human syndromes of replication failure feature growth retardation, bone marrow failure, premature ageing and cancer predisposition. Origins are licensed by the origin recognition complex with CDC6 and CDT1, loading MCM2-7 helicase, which CDC7-DBF4 and cyclin-dependent kinases convert into an active CMG helicase at a fired origin; primase, polymerases alpha, delta and epsilon with PCNA and RFC then synthesise and mature the new strands while chromatin is reassembled behind the fork. Also here are the checkpoint and fork-protection responses -- ATR, CHEK1, RPA, TOPBP1 -- together with translesion polymerases, nucleases and helicases that restart stalled forks, plus the nucleotide supply and mitochondrial replication machinery.

Duplicating the genome once and only once each cell cycle is the task captured here, and it underwrites proliferation, tissue renewal and the faithful inheritance of genetic information; its failure produces replication stress, chromosome rearrangement and the genome instability that drives cancer and premature ageing syndromes. Origins are licensed by the origin recognition complex with CDC6 and CDT1, loaded with MCM2-7 helicase subunits, then fired under CDK and CDC7-DBF4 control, with geminin and licensing inhibitors preventing re-replication. Unwinding by the CMG helicase with GINS and CDC45 feeds primase-polymerase alpha, the processive polymerases delta and epsilon, PCNA and the clamp loader RFC, while RPA coats single strands. Also present are nucleotide supply enzymes, Okazaki maturation and ligation, chromatin assembly and cohesion factors, ATR-CHEK1 fork surveillance, translesion and fork-restart activities, and the separate mitochondrial replication machinery.

DNA replication initiation is the step that decides where and when a genome starts copying itself, licensing each origin exactly once per cell cycle so that daughter cells inherit one complete, unduplicated copy. Loss of that control produces re-replication, amplification and the genome instability that drives tumorigenesis. The origin recognition complex marks chromatin, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase as an inactive double hexamer, and cyclin E-CDK2 together with CDC45, GINS and MCM10 converts it into an active replisome that unwinds duplex DNA for priming by DNA polymerase alpha-primase. Licensing is restricted by geminin and by CRL4-DDB1-CDT2 mediated degradation of CDT1, while TOPBP1 and TICRR couple firing to checkpoint state. The same machinery is redeployed in multiciliated cell differentiation through GMNC and MCIDAS, linking origin control to centriole amplification.

Before a cell divides it must copy its genome exactly once, and replication initiation is the step that decides where and when copying starts. Origin recognition complex subunits mark origins in G1, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase to license them, and rising cyclin E-CDK2 activity together with CDC45, GINS and TOPBP1/TICRR converts licensed origins into unwound, primed forks where the polymerase alpha-primase complex lays down RNA-DNA primers. Licensing is confined to G1 by geminin, which sequesters CDT1, and by CRL4-DTL-mediated degradation of CDT1 after firing, so that no origin fires twice; loss of this restraint causes re-replication, amplification and genome instability of the kind that drives cancer. The same machinery is redeployed developmentally, as MCIDAS and GMNC direct centriole amplification in multiciliated cells.

DNA repair is the collective machinery that keeps the genome intact against damage from radiation, chemical mutagens, oxidative and alkylating byproducts of metabolism, and errors made during replication. Without it cells accumulate mutations and chromosomal rearrangements, and the human consequences are cancer predisposition, immunodeficiency, developmental syndromes and premature ageing, as seen in the excision-repair, Fanconi anaemia and helicase disorders. The genes span all of its branches: direct reversal by alkyltransferases and dioxygenases, base excision through glycosylases with APEX1, LIG3 and XRCC1, nucleotide excision with XPC and the transcription-coupled TFIIH helicases, mismatch correction by MSH and MLH complexes, translesion synthesis by Y-family polymerases, and double-strand break repair by homologous recombination with BRCA1/2 and RAD51 or by nonhomologous end joining. Overlaid are damage sensing and checkpoint signalling through ATM, ATR and TP53, chromatin remodelling, and ubiquitin and PARP-dependent recruitment that organise repair at the lesion.

Genomes are continuously damaged by radiation, chemical mutagens, endogenous oxidants and alkylating agents, and by errors made during replication; DNA repair is the collective response that restores the original sequence and keeps cells viable and non-mutagenic. Its failure produces cancer predisposition and progeria-like and immunodeficiency syndromes, as seen with mutations in BRCA1/BRCA2, the Fanconi anaemia genes, mismatch repair genes such as MLH1 and MSH2, and the nucleotide excision repair factors XPA and XPC. Distinct routes are represented: direct reversal by alkyltransferases and dioxygenases, base excision initiated by DNA glycosylases and APEX1, nucleotide excision coupled to transcription, mismatch correction, translesion synthesis by Y-family polymerases, and double-strand break repair by homologous recombination or end joining. Sensing and signalling through ATM, ATR and checkpoint kinases coordinate arrest with repair, while chromatin remodellers, ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases control access to damaged DNA.

base-excision repair is the cell's routine maintenance system for small, non-helix-distorting DNA lesions — oxidised, deaminated, alkylated or mismatched bases and the abasic sites and single-strand breaks they generate. It handles the thousands of such damages arising daily from normal metabolism, and its failure raises mutation rates: inherited defects in MUTYH or NTHL1 cause colorectal polyposis and cancer predisposition. A damage-specific glycosylase such as OGG1, UNG, TDG or MPG excises the offending base, APEX1 incises the resulting abasic site, and PNKP or the polymerase's lyase activity cleans the ends. POLB fills short patches sealed by LIG3 with XRCC1 as scaffold, while long-patch repair uses PCNA, replicative polymerases, FEN1 and LIG1. PARP1 and PARP2 detect the strand break and recruit the machinery, which is why this pathway underlies the synthetic lethality exploited by PARP inhibitors.

Base-excision repair handles the most common kind of everyday DNA damage: single bases that have been oxidised, deaminated, alkylated or mismatched, such as the 8-oxoguanine left by reactive oxygen species or the uracil left by cytosine deamination. Without it, these lesions become point mutations at every round of replication, and inherited defects in the glycosylases MUTYH and NTHL1 predispose to colorectal cancer. A damage-specific glycosylase (OGG1, UNG, TDG, MPG, SMUG1, MBD4, the NEIL enzymes) excises the base; the AP endonuclease APEX1 cuts the abasic sugar-phosphate backbone; polymerase beta fills the single-nucleotide gap, or FEN1 with PCNA and replicative polymerases performs longer-patch synthesis; and LIG3 with its scaffold XRCC1 seals the nick. PARP1 and PARP2 sense the strand break and recruit repair factors, which is why PARP inhibition is exploited therapeutically in tumours already deficient in other repair routes.

base-excision repair, AP site formation is the opening step of the pathway that removes the small chemical lesions DNA sustains constantly from oxidation, deamination, alkylation and spontaneous base loss. It matters because these damaged bases are mutagenic if left in place: loss of OGG1 or MUTYH activity lets oxidised guanine mispair and drive G:C to T:A transversions, and inherited MUTYH or NTHL1 defects cause colorectal cancer and polyposis syndromes. Each of these DNA glycosylases surveys the duplex for a particular class of altered base, flips it out of the helix, and hydrolyses the N-glycosidic bond, leaving an abasic sugar that the downstream endonuclease incises so the gap can be filled and ligated. Substrate specificities overlap and complement one another, covering uracil from cytosine deamination, thymine glycol and other ring-fragmented purines and pyrimidines, and alkylated bases, including lesions in methylated CpG contexts.

Bases in DNA are constantly damaged by oxidation, deamination and alkylation, and this first step of base-excision repair is how the offending base is found and cut out, leaving an abasic (AP) site for downstream processing. Without it, oxidised and deaminated bases persist through replication and generate point mutations; loss of the adenine glycosylase MUTYH, which removes adenine mispaired with 8-oxoguanine, causes an inherited colorectal adenomatous polyposis, and germline NTHL1 defects likewise predispose to tumours. Each glycosylase has its own substrate preference: UNG and SMUG1 excise uracil arising from cytosine deamination or misincorporation, TDG and MBD4 act on deaminated 5-methylcytosine at CpG sites, MPG removes alkylated purines, and OGG1 with the NEIL enzymes handles oxidative lesions. The resulting AP site is then incised and the gap resynthesised, linking this chemistry to genome stability, mutation avoidance and control of cytosine methylation turnover.

nucleotide-excision repair removes bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions "such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers and 6-4 photoproducts, intrastrand crosslinks and chemical adducts" by excising a short oligonucleotide around the damage and resynthesising the strand with DNA polymerase and ligase. It is the pathway that protects skin and neurons from sunlight and genotoxins; its loss causes xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome and trichothiodystrophy, with extreme skin cancer risk or neurodegeneration. Lesions are found either by XPC-RAD23 and the DDB1-DDB2-CUL4 ubiquitin ligase scanning the genome, or by stalled RNA polymerase II with CSA/CSB and UVSSA during transcription. XPA and RPA verify the damage, TFIIH with its XPB and XPD helicases opens the duplex, and ERCC1-XPF and XPG incise. SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling, histone acetylation and p53 make the damage accessible and couple repair to cell cycle arrest.

Bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, 6-4 photoproducts and chemical adducts are removed by nucleotide-excision repair, which excises a short damage-containing oligonucleotide and refills the gap by DNA polymerase and ligase action. This is the pathway that protects skin and other exposed tissues from sunlight-induced mutation; its loss causes xeroderma pigmentosum with extreme UV sensitivity and skin cancer, or Cockayne and UV-sensitive syndromes when the transcription-coupled branch fails. Damage is recognized either globally, through XPC with RAD23 partners and the DDB1/DDB2 complex acting with a CUL4-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase, or by RNA polymerase II stalling, sensed via ERCC6, ERCC8 and UVSSA. TFIIH subunits including the ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicases open the duplex, XPA and RPA stabilize the bubble, and ERCC1-ERCC4 and ERCC5 incise it. SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits and p53 make the lesion accessible and couple repair to damage signalling.

Mismatch repair corrects the base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops that DNA polymerases leave behind, acting after replication to raise the fidelity of the newly synthesised strand by orders of magnitude. Its loss produces microsatellite instability and a hypermutator phenotype, and germline defects in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 cause Lynch syndrome with its excess of colorectal and endometrial cancer; tumours lacking the system are also the ones that respond to immune checkpoint blockade. Recognition complexes built from MSH2 with MSH6 or MSH3 detect the lesion, MutL homologues license strand incision, and EXO1, RPA, PCNA, POLD and LIG1 excise and resynthesise the error-containing tract. Related activities extend the theme: MSH4 and MSH5 act in meiotic recombination, MUTYH removes oxidised-base mispairs, and the RNase H2 complex handles ribonucleotides embedded in DNA.

DNA polymerases make mistakes, and mismatch repair is the proofreading system that finds and removes them after replication, restoring the correct base by excising and resynthesizing a stretch of the newly made strand. Its loss leaves cells with microsatellite instability and a mutation rate orders of magnitude too high; inherited defects in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 cause Lynch syndrome and predispose to colorectal and endometrial cancer, while tumours that lose the system accumulate neoantigens and respond to immune checkpoint blockade. Mismatch recognition by MSH2-containing heterodimers is coupled through MLH1 partners to strand discrimination, with EXO1 excision, RPA-coated single-stranded intermediates, PCNA-dependent resynthesis by polymerase delta and ligation by LIG1. Related components act in meiotic recombination, where MSH4-MSH5 and MLH3 promote crossover formation, and in other lesion-removal routes such as oxidized-base and nucleotide excision repair.

DNA modification covers the enzymatic chemistry that changes bases in place rather than replacing them, and the machinery that reads those changes as damage. It matters because the same reactions serve two opposite ends: deliberate mutation, as when activation-induced deaminase and the APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases edit immunoglobulin genes or hypermutate viral genomes, and genome defence, as when a spectrum of DNA glycosylases excises deaminated, oxidised or alkylated bases to start base excision repair. UNG, SMUG1, TDG and MBD4 handle uracil and thymine mismatches, OGG1, NTHL1, NEIL1-3 and MUTYH handle oxidative lesions, and PARP enzymes signal the resulting strand breaks and recruit repair factors. Terminal transferase adds untemplated nucleotides during receptor assembly. Loss of control here drives APOBEC mutational signatures in cancer, colorectal tumour predisposition, and autoinflammation when cytosolic DNA is not cleared.

Covalent DNA modification, the enzymatic alteration of bases in place, is used both as a deliberate mutagenic tool and as the entry point to repair. Activation-induced deaminase converts cytosine to uracil in immunoglobulin genes to drive somatic hypermutation and class switching, while the APOBEC3 deaminases edit retroviral and retroelement DNA as an innate restriction mechanism — and, when misdirected, leave characteristic mutation signatures across many cancers. The resulting lesions are recognised by uracil and thymine DNA glycosylases such as UNG, SMUG1, TDG and MBD4, alongside oxidative-damage glycosylases OGG1, NTHL1, MUTYH and the NEIL enzymes, which excise the damaged base and commit the site to base excision repair; loss of MUTYH predisposes to colorectal adenomas. PARP enzymes add ADP-ribose at breaks to recruit repair factors, and TREX1 degrades cytoplasmic DNA. Together these activities set the balance between programmed diversification and genome stability.

Mitotic recombination is homologous recombination as it operates in dividing somatic cells, where its job is to repair double-strand breaks and collapsed replication forks using an intact sister chromatid as template. This is the high-fidelity arm of break repair, and its loss underlies chromosomal instability and cancer predisposition, most familiarly through BRCA2 deficiency and the sensitivity to PARP inhibition that follows. Mechanistically, the MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex resects broken ends, mediators load RAD51 and its paralogues onto single-stranded DNA to drive strand invasion, and structure-specific nucleases such as MUS81-EME1 and GEN1 resolve the resulting joint molecules; the SMC5/6 complex with the NSMCE2 SUMO ligase restrains and disentangles recombination intermediates. Mismatch repair proteins police heteroduplex fidelity, while a telomere-associated branch supports recombination-based telomere maintenance in cells lacking telomerase activity.

Somatic cells use homologous recombination during mitotic growth to repair double-strand breaks and collapsed replication forks accurately, copying sequence from an intact homologous duplex rather than joining broken ends. This is what keeps dividing tissues from accumulating deletions and translocations, and its loss underlies the genomic instability of BRCA2-mutant cancers and Fanconi-type repair disorders. The MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex processes broken ends, BRCA2 and RAD52 load RAD51 and its paralogues onto single-stranded DNA to invade the donor template, and structure-selective nucleases such as MUS81-EME1 and GEN1 resolve the resulting joint molecules; the SMC5/6 complex with the SUMO ligase NSMCE2 restrains and disentangles recombination intermediates. Mismatch repair proteins police heteroduplex fidelity, and telomere factors link the same machinery to recombination-based telomere maintenance.

chromatin organization covers the assembly and continual remodeling of the nucleosomal packaging of DNA, the layer of regulation that decides which genes a cell can read and how faithfully its genome is copied and repaired. It defines cell identity and differentiation, and its disruption underlies cancers, imprinting disorders and neurodevelopmental syndromes. The genes span the core and variant histones themselves, histone chaperones such as ASF1 and the CAF-1 subunits that deposit them behind the replication fork, and ATP-dependent remodelers of the SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD and INO80 families that slide and evict nucleosomes. Layered on top are the writers, erasers and readers of histone marks — acetyltransferases and HDACs, SET-domain and PRDM methyltransferases, JmjC and LSD demethylases, bromo- and chromodomain readers — together with DNA methylation machinery, Polycomb complexes, cohesin and CTCF-based genome folding, and specialized centromeric and germline-specific packaging.

Chromatin organization covers how DNA is packaged with histones into nucleosomes and how that packaging is built, moved, marked and dismantled so that genes can be read, replicated and repaired at the right time. It sets which parts of the genome are accessible, underlies cell identity and its inheritance through division, and its failure produces developmental syndromes, imprinting disorders and many cancers. Core and linker histones plus variants such as H2A.Z, macroH2A, H3.3 and the centromeric CENP-A are deposited by chaperones like ASF1, HIRA, NPM1 and CAF-1, then repositioned by ATP-dependent remodellers of the SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD and INO80/SRCAP families. Writers, erasers and readers of acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation and ubiquitylation control Polycomb and heterochromatin silencing, DNA methylation via DNMTs, TETs and UHRF1, cohesin- and CTCF-based genome folding, and the chromatin response to double-strand breaks.

DNA replication-dependent chromatin assembly rebuilds nucleosomes on daughter DNA strands as the replication fork advances, so that a newly copied genome is packaged and epigenetically re-marked rather than left as naked DNA. This coupling protects fork stability, restrains cryptic transcription, and propagates histone modification patterns to both daughter cells; when it falters, cells accumulate replication stress, DNA damage and loss of heritable gene expression states. Histone H3-H4 dimers are escorted by the chaperones ASF1A and ASF1B and the histone-binding protein NASP, then handed to the CAF-1 complex of CHAF1A, CHAF1B and RBBP4, which is recruited to the fork through PCNA and deposits the tetramer before H2A-H2B completes the particle. The same chaperones buffer soluble histone pools, linking histone supply to S-phase progression and to chromatin restoration after DNA repair synthesis.

As a replication fork passes, the DNA it leaves behind must be repackaged into nucleosomes within minutes, and replication-dependent chromatin assembly is the machinery that does it. Without it, newly copied DNA stays naked and vulnerable, forks stall, and the epigenetic state of the parent chromatin is not restored in the daughter cells. Histone H3-H4 dimers are escorted from their point of synthesis by soluble chaperones, handed to ASF1A and ASF1B, and delivered to the CAF-1 complex, whose CHAF1A and CHAF1B subunits are recruited to the fork through PCNA and deposit the H3-H4 tetramer onto nascent DNA before H2A-H2B completes the particle. RBBP4 links this histone handling to chromatin-modifying and remodelling complexes that mature the new nucleosomes. The result couples S-phase histone supply to DNA synthesis and underlies heritable chromatin organisation and genome stability.

DNA-templated transcription termination is the step that ends transcription: polymerase halts, the RNA-DNA hybrid melts, and both transcript and enzyme are released from the template. Getting this right sets where genes stop, prevents polymerase from running into neighbouring genes or replication forks, and keeps the polymerase pool available for reinitiation; failure produces read-through transcripts, R-loop accumulation and transcription-replication collisions that damage the genome. The genes cover all three nuclear polymerases plus the mitochondrial termination factors, together with the effectors that act on them: the 5'-3' exonuclease XRN2 and cleavage factor PCF11 for torpedo-style termination of protein-coding genes, the helicase senataxin for resolving RNA-DNA hybrids, TTF1 and TTF2 for ribosomal and stress-induced release, and phosphatases such as SSU72 and PP1 that reverse polymerase tail phosphorylation. Premature termination through ZC3H4 and SCAF proteins also shapes non-coding transcription.

Transcription must stop as reliably as it starts, and DNA-templated transcription termination is the step that halts elongating polymerase, releases the nascent RNA from the RNA-DNA hybrid, and recycles the enzyme for reuse. It sets the 3' boundaries of genes, prevents read-through into neighbouring transcription units, and resolves collisions between transcription and replication; failure leaves persistent R-loops and genome instability, as seen with mutations in the RNA-DNA helicase senataxin. All three nuclear polymerases are represented, together with the mitochondrial termination factors that define rRNA and mRNA ends in the organelle. Mechanistically, CTD phosphatases such as SSU72 and the PP1 holoenzyme with its PNUTS regulatory subunit, cleavage factor PCF11, the 5'-3' exonuclease XRN2, and the ATPase TTF2 cooperate to dismantle elongation complexes, linking termination to 3' end processing, chromatin state and polymerase turnover.

Transcription elongation by RNA polymerase I is the productive synthesis phase of ribosomal RNA, in which Pol I moves processively along ribosomal DNA repeats in the nucleolus after clearing the promoter. Because pre-rRNA output sets the ceiling on ribosome production, this step largely determines a cell's capacity for protein synthesis and growth, and it is throttled down under nutrient stress or DNA damage and driven up in rapidly proliferating and tumour cells. The catalytic core POLR1A/POLR1B, together with the shared subunits POLR1C, POLR1D and several small Pol II-common subunits, forms the enzyme; associated factors such as POLR1F and POLR1G couple it to the initiation machinery. Also present are the repair helicases ERCC2 and ERCC6 with a TFIIH component, reflecting how lesions in rDNA stall elongation and recruit transcription-coupled repair. Mutations in these subunits cause ribosomopathies affecting craniofacial development.

Ribosome production begins with the synthesis of the large ribosomal RNA precursor, and transcription elongation by RNA polymerase I is the processive phase in which that long transcript is actually made after the enzyme has cleared the rDNA promoter. Because rRNA output sets the ceiling on how many ribosomes a cell can build, the rate of this step is tied directly to growth capacity, nucleolar size, and the response to nutrient and growth-factor signals; it is also a pressure point exploited by drugs that block nucleolar transcription in rapidly dividing tumours. The polymerase itself is represented here by its catalytic core subunits POLR1A and POLR1B together with the subunits it shares with the other nuclear polymerases, while ERCC6, ERCC2 and GTF2H5 link elongation to the repair of lesions that stall the enzyme on ribosomal DNA.
