Defects in these components underlie ribosomopathies and craniofacial malformation syndromes.

rRNA processing converts the long primary ribosomal RNA transcripts made in the nucleolus into the mature 18S, 5.8S and 28S species that build the ribosome, and so sets the ceiling on a cell's capacity to make protein and grow. Endonucleases and exonucleases trim the precursor at defined sites, snoRNP components such as fibrillarin, dyskerin, NOP56 and NHP2 direct site-specific methylation and pseudouridylation, and DEAD-box helicases, GTPases and large scaffolds of the U3 small subunit processome remodel the pre-ribosome as assembly factors and ribosomal proteins load onto it. The exosome complex degrades excised spacers and discards defective intermediates, while parallel enzymes mature mitochondrial rRNA. Imbalance here triggers nucleolar stress and p53 activation through free ribosomal proteins, and inherited defects in factors such as SBDS or dyskerin cause ribosomopathies with bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition.

Ribosomes cannot be built until the long primary transcript made in the nucleolus is trimmed, chemically modified and folded into the mature 18S, 5.8S and 28S species, and rRNA processing is that conversion. It sets the ceiling on how many ribosomes a cell can make, so it tracks growth rate and is a major consumer of nuclear energy; when it stalls, unassembled ribosomal proteins stabilise p53 and trigger the nucleolar stress response, and inherited defects cause ribosomopathies such as Shwachman-Diamond syndrome and Diamond-Blackfan anaemia. The work is done by large small-nucleolar RNP-guided machines: pseudouridine synthases and the fibrillarin methyltransferase modify specific nucleotides, UTP-containing processome subunits and numerous DEAD-box helicases remodel the pre-rRNA, and endo- and exonucleases including the exosome complex and XRN2 make the cleavages and degrade discarded spacers. Related enzymes serve the parallel maturation of mitochondrial rRNA.

transcription elongation by RNA polymerase II covers everything that happens after polymerase II clears a promoter: the release of paused polymerase, its processive movement through the gene body, and the coupling of that movement to chromatin and RNA processing. It sets how fast and how completely genes are expressed, and its control by CDK9 within P-TEFb, restrained by the 7SK snRNP with HEXIM1 and LARP7, is the step at which many growth and developmental programmes are actually decided. NELF and DSIF impose the pause; BRD4 and Mediator recruit the kinase that lifts it; the PAF1 complex, SPT6, TFIIS and the ELL-containing elongation factors keep the enzyme moving and rescue backtracked complexes; SETD2 and the Integrator complex link elongation to histone methylation and premature termination. Loss of these controls underlies leukaemias, VHL-associated renal cancer and CDK12-mutant tumours.

After RNA polymerase II clears a promoter it typically stalls just downstream, and the transition into productive elongation is the step that decides whether a gene is actually expressed. This control point governs inducible and developmental gene programmes, and its subversion by enhancer-associated bromodomain proteins and CDK9 is the basis of transcriptional addiction in cancer. The negative elongation and DSIF factors hold paused polymerase in place; P-TEFb, itself sequestered in an inhibitory complex with 7SK RNA, HEXIM1 and LARP7, phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain and the pausing factors to release it. The PAF1 complex, SPT6, TFIIS and ELL-containing complexes then sustain processive synthesis, the Integrator complex offers an opposing route of premature termination and snRNA 3' processing, and SETD2-dependent histone methylation couples elongation to chromatin state and co-transcriptional splicing.

termination of RNA polymerase II transcription is the step that tells an elongating polymerase where a gene ends, releasing the finished pre-mRNA and clearing the template so that transcription units do not run into their neighbours. Without it, read-through transcription generates chimeric and antisense RNAs, interferes with downstream promoters, and leaves stalled polymerase and RNA:DNA hybrids that threaten genome stability. Termination is coupled to 3' end processing: cleavage factors such as PCF11 recognise poly(A) signals via the polymerase C-terminal domain, the exonuclease XRN2 degrades the downstream RNA to chase the enzyme off the DNA, and the helicase senataxin resolves R-loops at pause sites. Phosphatase activity, notably SSU72 and PP1 with its regulator PNUTS, reverses CTD and Spt5 phosphorylation to convert elongation into termination, while TTF2 strips polymerase from chromatin. The pathway also shapes gene looping, transcriptional recycling and mitotic silencing.

Ending a transcription cycle is as regulated as starting one: termination of RNA polymerase II transcription releases the polymerase and the finished pre-mRNA from the gene, defining where transcripts stop and preventing read-through into neighbouring genes or regulatory elements. It is coupled to 3' end processing, so the same events that cleave and hand off the nascent RNA also dismantle the elongation complex. Recognition of poly(A) signals and cleavage by PCF11-containing machinery is followed by exonucleolytic chase of the downstream RNA by XRN2, while the helicase SETX resolves RNA:DNA hybrids that would otherwise stall polymerase and provoke DNA damage. The phosphatase SSU72 and PP1 with its regulator PPP1R10 reset phosphorylation marks on the polymerase C-terminal domain, and TTF2 can strip stalled polymerase from chromatin. Failure produces read-through transcription, R-loop accumulation and genome instability.

transcription by RNA polymerase III produces the small untranslated RNAs that the rest of gene expression runs on — tRNAs, 5S ribosomal RNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and other short transcripts — so its output sets the ceiling on a cell's capacity for protein synthesis and growth. Output scales with nutrient and growth-factor status: mTOR signalling through raptor relieves the repressor MAF1, linking ribosome and tRNA supply to anabolic demand, and its deregulation contributes to transformation. Mechanistically the multisubunit polymerase, which shares several subunits with the other nuclear polymerases, is recruited by distinct promoter architectures: TFIIIC and TFIIIB with BRF1 and BDP1 at internal gene-type promoters, and BRF2 with the SNAPc complex plus TBP at upstream snRNA-type promoters. Chromatin remodellers, ZNF143 and assorted helicases modulate access, while RO60 surveys the resulting nascent transcripts.

Cells need a constant supply of tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and other short untranslated transcripts, and RNA polymerase III transcription is the machinery that makes them. Because these products set the ceiling on translational capacity and spliceosome assembly, output is tuned to growth: nutrient and mTOR signalling, acting through the repressor MAF1, restrains the polymerase when biosynthesis must slow, and its de-repression supports proliferation and transformation. The multisubunit enzyme, which shares several small subunits with the other nuclear polymerases, is recruited by distinct initiation routes — TFIIIC and TFIIIA with TFIIIB components BRF1 and BDP1 at gene-internal promoters, and BRF2 with the SNAPc complex and ZNF143 at upstream snRNA-type promoters — all requiring TBP. Chromatin remodellers and RNA helicases assist elongation and template access. Mutations in polymerase subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, and the transcripts are also sensors in innate immune nucleic acid detection.

mRNA catabolic process is the controlled destruction of messenger RNA, the step that sets how long each transcript persists and therefore how much protein it makes. Without it, transcriptomes cannot be remodelled during differentiation, inflammatory messages are not switched off, and faulty transcripts are translated into truncated proteins. Degradation begins with deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT and PAN2-PAN3 complexes, followed by decapping through DCP2 with LSM-PATL1 partners and 5'-to-3' digestion by XRN1, or 3'-to-5' attack by the exosome and SKI complex. Specificity comes from sequence- and modification-reading factors: AU-rich element proteins such as ZFP36 and ELAVL1, m6A writers and YTHDF readers, endonucleases of the ZC3H12 family, and microRNAs acting through Argonaute and TNRC6 scaffolds. Surveillance branches recognise premature stop codons via UPF1 and SMG proteins, or stalled ribosomes, linking decay to translation quality control, germ cell mRNA storage and immune homeostasis.

Every transcript has a lifespan, and controlled mRNA degradation sets it, determining how much protein a message yields and how fast expression can be switched off. Deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT and PAN2-PAN3 complexes initiates decay, followed by decapping through DCP2 with its LSM-PATL1 partners and 5'-to-3' digestion by XRN1, or 3'-to-5' attack by the cytoplasmic exosome and SKI complex; DIS3L2 clears uridylated targets. Quality-control arms remove faulty messages: UPF1 with SMG proteins and the endonuclease SMG6 execute nonsense-mediated decay, while PELO-HBS1L rescue stalled ribosomes. Sequence-specific recognition comes from AU-rich element binders such as ZFP36 and ELAVL1, the ZC3H12 endoribonucleases, m6A readers of the YTHDF family, and microRNAs acting through Argonaute-TNRC6 complexes. This machinery shapes inflammatory cytokine output, germ cell and oocyte transcript storage, and stress responses, and its failure underlies immune dysregulation and tumour-associated gene expression changes.

mRNA export from nucleus is the step that licenses a transcript to be translated: only fully processed, correctly packaged mRNAs are handed through the nuclear pore to the cytoplasm, so this pathway couples gene expression to quality control. Blocking it silences protein synthesis regardless of how much transcription occurs. Capping, splicing and 3' end formation leave marks that recruit the TREX complex and its adaptor ALYREF, which load the export receptor NXF1-NXT1 onto the messenger ribonucleoprotein; the exon junction complex and cap-binding proteins mark spliced transcripts, while the nuclear pore basket, TPR and NUP214, together with the helicase DDX19 and GLE1, give directionality by stripping receptors on the cytoplasmic face. Retained or aberrant transcripts are instead degraded, and the same first round of translation feeds nonsense-mediated decay through UPF1 and SMG proteins. Methylation readers such as YTHDC1 bias which transcripts leave.

Gene expression only counts once a transcript reaches the ribosome, and mRNA export from the nucleus is the licensing step that moves finished, correctly processed transcripts through the nuclear pore to the cytoplasm. It couples transcription, splicing and 3' end formation to translation: the TREX complex and its ALYREF adaptor load onto spliced mRNA, the exon junction complex (MAGOH, RBM8A, EIF4A3) marks splice sites, and the NXF1-NXT1 receptor carries the ribonucleoprotein to nucleoporins such as NUP214 and TPR, where the DEAD-box helicases DDX19A/B with GLE1 strip adaptors and impose directionality. Cap-binding proteins, methylation readers and modification enzymes bias which transcripts leave and when, while the surveillance factors UPF1 and SMG1-7 destroy those bearing premature stop codons. Defects in pore and helicase components produce motor neuron degeneration and inherited arthrogryposis, and export is a common target of viral shutoff strategies.

translation is protein synthesis itself: the decoding of mature mRNA by the ribosome into a polypeptide, together with the machinery that decides which messages are read, how fast, and when reading stops. Every cell depends on it for growth, and its regulation is where nutrient, stress and growth-factor signals converge — mTOR and the 4E-BP/eIF4E axis set cap-dependent initiation, while eIF2α kinases such as PERK and GCN2 shut initiation down during the integrated stress response. The genes span cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal subunits, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, initiation, elongation and release factors, tRNA and mRNA modification enzymes, and quality-control systems that rescue stalled ribosomes and degrade faulty nascent chains. Overlaid on this are repressive controls: microRNAs with their Argonaute–TNRC6 effectors, deadenylation by the CCR4–NOT complex, and sequence-specific RNA-binding proteins that store or silence transcripts. Defects underlie ribosomopathies, neurodegeneration and oncogenic growth.

Translation is the step where the information in a mature mRNA is read out as protein, and this collection spans the whole of it: cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal subunits, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases that charge tRNAs, initiation, elongation and release factors, and the tRNA-modifying enzymes that keep decoding accurate. Because protein synthesis consumes much of a cell's energy, it is also a major control point for growth and stress adaptation: mTOR and S6 kinases raise output, eIF4E-binding proteins restrain cap-dependent initiation, and eIF2alpha kinases such as PERK and GCN2 shut initiation down during the integrated stress response while favouring ATF4. Also represented are quality-control and mRNA-fate systems that decide whether a message is translated at all, including nonsense-mediated decay, ribosome-associated ubiquitin ligases, deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT complex, and microRNA/Argonaute repression. Defects cause ribosomopathies, neuropathies and mitochondrial translation disorders.

Protein folding is the chaperone system that gets newly made and stress-damaged polypeptides into their correct three-dimensional shapes and assembles them into complexes, the prerequisite for essentially every protein's activity. Without it cells accumulate misfolded and aggregated species, the outcome behind neurodegenerative proteinopathies, cataract, and secretory-cell stress. The genes span the major machines and their compartments: HSP70s with their DNAJ co-chaperones and nucleotide-exchange factors, HSP90 with CDC37 and the FKBP/PPI immunophilins, the cytosolic CCT/TRiC chamber with prefoldin for actin and tubulin, mitochondrial HSPD1/HSPE1, and small heat-shock proteins that hold unfolded clients soluble. In the endoplasmic reticulum, BiP, calnexin/calreticulin lectin cycles, UGGT1 quality control, and protein disulphide isomerases with ERO1 oxidases fold and proofread secretory and membrane proteins, linking this activity to the unfolded protein response, degradation triage, and collagen and antigen-presentation maturation.

Newly made polypeptides do not reach their functional shape unaided, and this is the machinery that guides them there and keeps them there. It sustains the proteome under heat, oxidative and metabolic stress, and its failure produces misfolded, aggregation-prone protein — the basis of chaperonopathies, cataract from mutant lens crystallins, and the aggregate burden of neurodegeneration. The work is done by ATP-driven chaperone families and their cofactors: HSP70s with their J-domain partners and nucleotide exchange factors, HSP90 with co-chaperones such as CDC37 and the immunophilins, the mitochondrial HSP60/HSP10 chamber, small heat shock proteins that hold unfolded clients soluble, and the CCT/TRiC and prefoldin system that folds actin and tubulin. In the endoplasmic reticulum, calnexin and calreticulin, protein disulfide isomerases and oxidases, and glycan-based quality control ensure correct disulfide bonding and release only properly folded secretory cargo. Peptidyl-prolyl isomerases and dedicated assembly factors handle rate-limiting isomerization and subunit-specific folding.

Protein deacetylation strips acetyl groups from lysine residues on histones and thousands of non-histone proteins, and in doing so sets how tightly chromatin is packed, how long transcription factors survive, and how metabolic enzymes are tuned to nutrient supply. Because acetylation is reversible, this reaction is the off switch that makes lysine acetylation a signal rather than a permanent mark; its loss deregulates gene expression, mitochondrial fuel choice, and genome maintenance, and its enzymes are drug targets in cancer. Zinc-dependent histone deacetylases such as HDAC3 and HDAC7 act within corepressor complexes on promoters, HDAC6 works in the cytoplasm on tubulin and misfolded protein cargo, and the NAD+-dependent sirtuins couple deacetylation directly to cellular energy state, with SIRT3, SIRT4 and SIRT5 acting inside mitochondria. Acetyltransferases and shared adaptor subunits are present as the opposing arm that this activity balances.

Protein deacetylation strips acetyl groups from lysine residues, reversing the marks left by acetyltransferases and thereby setting how tightly chromatin is packed, how stable and active many enzymes are, and how cells read their metabolic state. Because acetyl-CoA supplies the acetyl group and NAD+ is consumed by the sirtuin class, this chemistry links nutrient availability to gene expression, and its loss contributes to genome instability, metabolic disease and features of ageing. Classical zinc-dependent enzymes such as HDAC3 act in corepressor complexes on histones, while HDAC6 works in the cytoplasm on tubulin and chaperones and SIRT3-SIRT5 operate inside mitochondria on fatty acid oxidation and urea cycle enzymes. Counterpart acetyltransferases and their partner subunits appear here too, since deacetylation is meaningful only as one half of a reversible cycle whose balance is continuously adjusted.

Protein methylation covers the transfer of methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine onto amino acid side chains and protein termini, a modification that tunes protein interactions, stability and activity without changing sequence. It sets the histone marks that define transcriptional states — H3K9 by EHMT1/EHMT2, H3K36 by SETD2, H4K20 by KMT5A, H3K4 by SETD7 — and equally modifies non-histone substrates: arginine methylation by the PRMT family regulates Sm proteins and spliceosome assembly, actin histidine methylation by SETD3 shapes cytoskeletal function, and dedicated methyltransferases mark translation factors eEF1A, eEF2 and the release factor, chaperones, ATP synthase and respiratory complex I subunits. Related activities methylate protein N-termini, prenylated C-termini for membrane anchoring, and repair isoaspartyl damage. Loss of individual enzymes causes developmental syndromes, congenital insensitivity to pain, myopathy and cancer, reflecting how broadly gene expression, RNA processing and mitochondrial assembly depend on this chemistry.

Protein methylation is the enzymatic transfer of a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine onto amino acid side chains or protein termini, and it is one of the main ways a cell tunes a protein's interactions without changing its sequence. The genes here cover the breadth of that chemistry: lysine methyltransferases acting on histones (EHMT1/2, KMT5A, SETD2, SETD7, SMYD2) to set chromatin states and direct transcription and DNA repair; arginine methyltransferases of the PRMT family that mark histones and RNA-binding proteins, including Sm proteins of the spliceosome, and depend on methylosome partners; N-terminal and non-histone methyltransferases that modify translation factors, chaperones, respiratory chain assembly factors and ATP synthase; and prenylcysteine carboxyl methylation that completes membrane anchoring of small GTPases. TRMT112 serves as an obligate activating subunit for several of these enzymes. Loss of individual activities causes intellectual disability syndromes, mitochondrial dysfunction and cancers driven by aberrant chromatin marking.

protein O-linked glycosylation builds the sugar chains attached through serine, threonine, hydroxylysine or tyrosine hydroxyls, generating the mucin coats of epithelial surfaces, the glycosaminoglycan chains of proteoglycans, the O-mannose glycans that let dystroglycan grip laminin, and the O-fucose and O-glucose marks that tune Notch. Loss of individual steps causes congenital muscular dystrophies with brain malformation, skeletal dysplasias, bleeding and immune-cell trafficking defects, so the pathway underlies basement membrane adhesion, cartilage and bone matrix assembly, and leukocyte homing. Polypeptide GalNAc transferases initiate mucin-type cores that are elongated by C1GALT1 with its chaperone, branched by GCNT enzymes, then capped with sialic acid and fucose; xylosyltransferases and EXT enzymes start heparan and chondroitin chains, which sulfotransferases and epimerases then decorate. Nucleotide-sugar transporters supply donors, and cytoplasmic OGT and OGA add and remove O-GlcNAc as a nutrient-responsive regulatory modification.

Sugars attached to serine, threonine, tyrosine or hydroxylysine side chains give secreted and membrane proteins their bulk, charge and binding specificity, and protein O-linked glycosylation covers all of the routes by which these chains are initiated and extended. Mucin-type synthesis begins with a large family of polypeptide GalNAc transferases and the core-1 galactosyltransferase with its chaperone, then branches, sialylates and fucosylates to build selectin ligands and mucus barriers. Separate arms make O-mannose glycans on dystroglycan, whose loss causes congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and eye involvement; O-fucose and O-glucose on EGF repeats, which tune Notch; collagen galactosyl-hydroxylysine; and the xylose-primed linker that nucleates heparan and chondroitin sulfate chains, with sulfotransferases and epimerases setting their sulfation patterns. Nucleotide-sugar transporters and the nucleocytoplasmic O-GlcNAc cycle of OGT and OGA complete the picture, linking nutrient status to signalling.

N-terminal protein lipidation attaches fatty acids to the amino terminus of newly made proteins, converting soluble polypeptides into membrane-associating ones and thereby setting where they act in the cell. Its best-known outputs are N-myristoylation of hundreds of substrates by the myristoyltransferases NMT1 and NMT2, which anchors Src-family kinases, ARF GTPases and G protein alpha subunits to membranes, and N-palmitoylation of Hedgehog by HHAT, a modification without which the morphogen cannot be secreted or signal to Patched during development. The modification also creates the exposed myristoyl groups recognised during apoptotic protein relocalisation and pathogen effector targeting. Loss of this lipidation misroutes signalling proteins to the cytosol, degrades growth factor patterning, and is exploited pharmacologically, since myristoyltransferase and Hedgehog acyltransferase inhibitors are pursued as anticancer agents. It belongs to the wider set of co-translational and post-translational lipid modifications governing membrane trafficking.

Attaching a lipid to a protein's amino terminus converts a soluble polypeptide into one that docks onto membranes, and this modification determines where many signalling proteins can act. The dominant reaction is N-myristoylation, in which the N-myristoyltransferases NMT1 and NMT2 transfer myristate from myristoyl-CoA onto an N-terminal glycine exposed after initiator methionine removal; substrates include Src-family kinases, ARF GTPases and calcineurin-associated proteins, whose membrane targeting and stability depend on it. A distinct branch is N-terminal palmitoylation of Hedgehog proteins by the acyltransferase HHAT, a step required for Sonic hedgehog to signal during embryonic patterning; HHATL is a related inactive homolog. Loss of these activities misdirects proteins away from membranes, blunts developmental signalling, and myristoylation is exploited as a drug target in cancer and parasitic infection.

GPI anchor metabolic process builds and remodels the glycolipid tether that fastens a large family of proteins to the outer face of the plasma membrane, among them CD55 and CD59, alkaline phosphatases, folate receptors and prion protein. Loss of the pathway strips cells of these surface proteins: somatic mutation of PIGA in haematopoietic stem cells causes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria through complement-mediated lysis, while inherited hypomorphic defects in PIGV, PIGN or PGAP3 produce intellectual disability syndromes with raised serum alkaline phosphatase. Assembly begins on the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum with GlcNAc transfer to phosphatidylinositol, proceeds through mannosylation using dolichol-phosphate-mannose and addition of ethanolamine phosphate side chains, and ends when a transamidase complex including PIGK, GPAA1 and PIGT swaps the anchor for a protein's C-terminal signal. Subsequent lipid and glycan remodelling in the ER and Golgi determines anchored-protein sorting, raft association and stability.

Many surface proteins have no transmembrane domain and are tethered to the outer face of the plasma membrane by a glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor; the metabolic pathway that makes, attaches and remodels these anchors is what puts them there. Its products include CD59 and CD55, alkaline phosphatases, folate receptors and numerous ectoenzymes, so the pathway supports complement regulation on blood cells, nutrient uptake and membrane microdomain organisation. Stepwise glycosylation of phosphatidylinositol by the PIG enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum builds the core glycan, with mannose donated as dolichol-phosphate-mannose; a transamidase complex including GPAA1, PIGK, PIGS, PIGT and PIGU then cleaves a nascent protein's C-terminal signal and joins it to ethanolamine phosphate. Later lipid and side-chain remodelling by PGAP enzymes matures the anchor for transport. Somatic loss of PIGA causes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, while inherited defects give intellectual disability and seizure syndromes.

amino acid metabolic process covers the synthesis, interconversion and breakdown of amino acids, the reactions that let cells build protein, dispose of excess nitrogen, and feed carbon skeletons into the citric acid cycle. It underlies whole-body nitrogen balance and is the origin of many inborn errors of metabolism: phenylketonuria from PAH, urea cycle defects from OTC, CPS1 or ASS1, maple syrup urine disease from the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, and homocystinuria from CBS. The genes span transaminases and dehydrogenases such as GOT1/2 and GLUD1, serine and proline biosynthetic enzymes, tryptophan degradation through the kynurenine route, sulfur amino acid and methionine cycling, glutathione synthesis, and mitochondrial and cytosolic aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases that commit amino acids to translation. Also included are transporters and transcriptional controls such as ATF4, which link amino acid supply to stress signalling, and the decarboxylases producing neurotransmitters and polyamines.

Amino acids are the building blocks of protein, but they are also nitrogen carriers, neurotransmitter precursors and fuels, and this broad collection of reactions covers their synthesis, interconversion and breakdown. It sets how the body disposes of surplus nitrogen through urea cycle enzymes such as CPS1, OTC and ASS1, how branched-chain and aromatic amino acids are catabolised toward the TCA cycle and ketone bodies, and how serine, glycine and methionine feed one-carbon and glutathione chemistry. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases link the same pools to translation, while decarboxylases and hydroxylases generate dopamine, serotonin, GABA, histamine and nitric oxide. Loss of individual steps produces the classical inborn errors of metabolism — phenylketonuria, tyrosinaemia, maple syrup urine disease, homocystinuria, hyperammonaemia — and dedicated transporters and transcriptional regulators such as ATF4 adjust flux when particular amino acids run short.

L-tryptophan catabolic process degrades the essential amino acid tryptophan, chiefly through the kynurenine route, which both disposes of excess tryptophan and generates the precursors for de novo NAD+ synthesis. Its outputs matter well beyond metabolism: local tryptophan depletion and kynurenine accumulation suppress effector T cells and favour regulatory T cell induction, making this a checkpoint on immune tolerance at the placenta and within tumours, while neuroactive intermediates such as kynurenic and quinolinic acid influence glutamatergic signalling. The first and rate-limiting oxidation is performed by IDO1, IDO2 and hepatic TDO2, with IL4I1 offering an alternative indole route; downstream formamidase, kynureninase, KMO and HAAO steps carry flux toward quinolinate, and ACMSD diverts intermediates to complete oxidation instead. Dysregulation contributes to inflammatory neurodegeneration and to immune evasion by cancers.

Tryptophan is the only amino acid degraded largely through the kynurenine route, and this catabolic pathway both disposes of surplus tryptophan and generates the precursors for de novo NAD+ synthesis. Its first and rate-limiting step is oxidative ring cleavage, performed in liver by TDO2 and in immune and inflamed tissues by the interferon-inducible IDO1 and IDO2; downstream, formamidase, kynurenine 3-monooxygenase, kynureninase and HAAO produce kynurenine, 3-hydroxykynurenine and quinolinate, while ACMSD diverts intermediates toward complete oxidation instead of NAD+. Because depleting tryptophan and accumulating kynurenines suppress effector T cells and promote regulatory ones, this route is a major mechanism of immune tolerance in pregnancy and of immune escape by tumours, with IL4I1 contributing an alternative oxidation. The same intermediates are neuroactive, linking the pathway to excitotoxicity and neurodegeneration.

L-tyrosine catabolic process degrades the aromatic amino acid tyrosine to fumarate and acetoacetate, feeding its carbon skeleton into the citric acid cycle and ketone body metabolism. It matters most in liver and kidney, where dietary and protein-turnover tyrosine must be disposed of; blocking any step traps reactive intermediates that damage tissue rather than simply accumulating. Transamination by tyrosine aminotransferase begins the route, followed by hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, homogentisate dioxygenase, the maleylacetoacetate isomerase activity of GSTZ1, and finally fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase. Loss of these enzymes causes the classic tyrosinemias and alkaptonuria: FAH deficiency produces hepatorenal disease driven by succinylacetone, while homogentisate build-up pigments and destroys cartilage. An amino acid oxidase, IL4I1, provides an alternative immune-cell route of tyrosine deamination linked to lymphocyte regulation. The pathway ties amino acid disposal to gluconeogenic and ketogenic fuel supply.

Tyrosine catabolism disposes of the aromatic amino acid taken in from diet and protein turnover, converting it in the liver and kidney to fumarate and acetoacetate that feed the citric acid cycle and ketogenesis. The route runs through transamination to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate by tyrosine aminotransferase, dioxygenase-mediated conversion to homogentisate by HPD, ring cleavage by homogentisate dioxygenase, isomerization by the maleylacetoacetate isomerase activity of GSTZ1, and final hydrolysis by fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase. Blocks at each step cause recognizable inherited disease: HPD or FAH deficiency gives tyrosinemia with hepatorenal damage from accumulated reactive intermediates, while loss of homogentisate dioxygenase causes alkaptonuria, in which homogentisate polymerizes and pigments cartilage. IL4I1, an L-amino acid oxidase secreted by myeloid cells, oxidizes tyrosine and other aromatic amino acids in the immune microenvironment rather than for energy, linking this chemistry to local amino acid depletion and T cell suppression.

polyamine biosynthetic process builds putrescine, spermidine and spermine, the small polycations that cells require for growth, ribosome function and chromatin compaction. Proliferating tissues, spermatogenesis and wound repair depend on it, and its deregulation is a hallmark of tumours, which is why ornithine decarboxylase inhibition is pursued therapeutically. Ornithine decarboxylase commits ornithine to putrescine, while adenosylmethionine decarboxylase supplies the aminopropyl donor used by spermidine and spermine synthases. Flux is held under unusually tight control: antizymes target ornithine decarboxylase for proteasomal destruction without ubiquitin, antizyme inhibitors relieve that block, and acetylation by SAT1 followed by oxidation by PAOX or SMOX either exports or recycles the higher polyamines in a back-conversion loop. An agmatinase route offers an alternative entry from arginine. The pathway ties amino acid and methionine metabolism to translational control, including polyamine-dependent hypusination and eIF5A activity.

Putrescine, spermidine and spermine are small polycations that bind nucleic acids and stabilise chromatin, and their synthesis supports proliferation, translation, and hypusine modification of eIF5A; tumours raise this flux, and its inhibition is the basis of ornithine decarboxylase-targeted therapy. Ornithine decarboxylase (ODC1) makes putrescine, S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase (AMD1) supplies the aminopropyl donor, and spermidine and spermine synthases (SRM, SMS) extend the chain, with an alternative route from agmatine via agmatinase. Because excess polyamines are toxic, the pathway is held under unusually tight control: antizymes (OAZ1-3) direct ODC to proteasomal degradation while antizyme inhibitors (AZIN1, AZIN2) relieve that block, and acetylation by SAT1 plus oxidation by SMOX and PAOX feed a back-conversion and export cycle that sets steady-state pool sizes.

Protein targeting is the sorting problem every cell must solve: newly made proteins carry address information that must be read so each one ends up in the right membrane, lumen or organelle. Getting it right builds the secretory pathway, mitochondria, peroxisomes and lysosomes; getting it wrong causes mislocalisation diseases, peroxisome biogenesis disorders and lysosomal enzyme deficiency. The genes cover the main delivery routes: signal recognition particle and its receptor with the Sec61 translocon and signal peptidase for co-translational entry into the ER, a GET/SGTA route for tail-anchored proteins, TOM and TIM translocases with processing peptidases for mitochondrial import, PEX factors for peroxisomal matrix and membrane proteins, mannose-6-phosphate tagging and receptors for hydrolase delivery to lysosomes, and adaptor, HOPS/GARP and ESCRT complexes for vesicular sorting. ZDHHC palmitoyltransferases add lipid anchors that direct membrane association, while ubiquitin ligases and autophagy receptors clear proteins that fail to reach their destination.

Newly made proteins have to reach the compartment where they work, and protein targeting is the collection of recognition and delivery steps that gets them there, usually by reading a sorting signal built into the polypeptide. Without it, secretory and membrane proteins never enter the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and peroxisomes cannot import their proteomes, and lysosomal enzymes are secreted instead of stored. The signal recognition particle and its receptor deliver ribosomes to the Sec61 translocon, where signal peptidase removes the cleaved sequence; tail-anchored proteins use a separate insertion route; TOM and TIM translocases with matrix processing peptidases handle mitochondrial precursors; PEX proteins recognise peroxisomal targeting signals; and mannose-6-phosphate tagging routes hydrolases to lysosomes. Palmitoyltransferases, adaptor and retromer-like complexes, ubiquitin ligases and autophagy receptors then position or redirect cargo, linking targeting to organelle quality control and diseases such as peroxisome biogenesis disorders and lysosomal storage.

Protein export from nucleus moves proteins out of the nucleus through the nuclear pore, the return leg of nucleocytoplasmic transport that lets a cell decide where a regulator acts. Because localisation is itself a switch, this pathway controls transcription factor activity, cell cycle progression, tumour suppressor function and stress responses: forced nuclear retention or premature export changes gene expression without changing protein levels. Exportins including XPO1 and the CSE1L importin-recycling route capture cargo bearing leucine-rich export signals, and directionality comes from the RanGTP gradient maintained by RanGAP1, RanBP3 and NUTF2, with docking at pore components such as NUP214 and TPR. Kinases and 14-3-3 proteins including GSK3B, PRKACA and YWHAE gate export by phosphorylating cargo, while p14ARF and SMAD-linked factors tune it. XPO1 inhibition is exploited therapeutically in myeloma to trap tumour suppressors in the nucleus.

Proteins made in the cytoplasm but working in the nucleus must eventually be returned, and regulated export across the nuclear envelope is how cells control where a protein acts. It underlies signal-dependent relocalization: transcription factors, cyclin-dependent kinase regulators, and tumour suppressors are switched off by being moved out of the nucleus, and blocking this traffic is the basis of exportin-targeted cancer therapy. Cargo recognition is carried out by karyopherin-family exportins, chief among them XPO1, which bind leucine-rich export signals together with RanGTP; directionality comes from the Ran gradient, maintained by cytoplasmic RanGAP1 and its nuclear guanine-nucleotide exchange, with RanBP3 and NXT1 acting as export cofactors. Nucleoporins such as NUP214 and TPR provide the docking sites at the pore where complexes disassemble. Phosphorylation by kinases including GSK3B and PKA, and 14-3-3 binding, gate individual cargoes, linking export to growth, stress and DNA damage responses.

Cotranslational protein targeting to membrane routes newly made secretory and membrane proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being translated, the entry step for roughly a third of the proteome, including antibodies, hormones, receptors and lysosomal enzymes. As a signal sequence emerges from the ribosome, the signal recognition particle — an RNA-protein complex built on 7SL RNA with SRP9, SRP14, SRP54 and the SRP68/72 heterodimer — binds it, pauses elongation, and docks the ribosome onto the SRP receptor at the ER membrane. Translation then resumes directly through the Sec61 translocon, assisted by SEC62/SEC63, the translocon-associated signal sequence receptor subunits, TRAM proteins and the BiP nucleotide exchange factor SIL1, which drive insertion, topology and lumenal folding. Loss of these components disturbs secretory capacity and ER proteostasis, and underlies conditions ranging from Marinesco-Sjögren syndrome to polycystic liver disease and immunodeficiency.

Secretory and membrane proteins must reach the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being made, and this cotranslational targeting route is how that happens: the signal recognition particle binds an emerging signal sequence, pauses elongation, and delivers the ribosome-nascent chain complex to its receptor at the ER membrane. Handover to the Sec61 translocon channel, assisted by Sec62/Sec63, the translocon-associated signal sequence receptor subunits and the TRAM proteins, allows the chain to cross the bilayer or integrate into it, after which lumenal folding factors take over. The RNA component of the particle is contributed by 7SL genes. Everything downstream depends on it — antibody and hormone secretion, receptor and channel biogenesis, glycosylation — and failures produce ER stress and translocation disease; mutations in the main translocon subunit cause immunodeficiency and polycystic kidney disease.

SRP-dependent cotranslational protein targeting to membrane delivers nascent secretory and membrane proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being translated, and is the entry step for essentially everything a cell secretes or displays on its surface. A signal sequence emerging from the ribosome is captured by the signal recognition particle, built around the 7SL RNA and the SRP9/14, SRP19, SRP54 and SRP68/72 proteins; SRP54 binding pauses elongation until the complex docks on the heterodimeric SRP receptor at the ER membrane. The ribosome is then transferred to the Sec61 translocon, with SEC63, TRAM proteins and the translocon-associated subunits assisting insertion of transmembrane segments and translocation of soluble domains into the lumen. Loss of this route strands hydrophobic precursors in the cytosol, triggering proteotoxic stress and failure of secretion, antibody production and membrane biogenesis.

Secreted and membrane proteins must reach the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being made, and this is the route that gets them there. The signal-recognition particle, a complex of the 7SL RNA with SRP9, SRP14, SRP54 and the SRP68/72 heterodimer, binds an emerging signal sequence, pauses elongation, and delivers the ribosome-nascent chain complex to the SRPRA/SRPRB receptor on the ER membrane. The nascent chain is then transferred into the SEC61 translocon channel, with SEC63, TRAM proteins and the signal sequence receptor subunit assisting insertion and translocation of hydrophobic segments. This targeting step defines the entire secretory pathway: without it, antibodies, hormones, receptors and ion channels would be synthesised in the cytosol and degraded, and secretory cells such as plasma cells and pancreatic acinar cells could not function. Translocon mutations cause immunodeficiency and polycystic kidney disease.

SRP-dependent cotranslational protein targeting to membrane, signal sequence recognition is the first decision point in the secretory pathway: as a ribosome begins translating a protein bearing an N-terminal signal sequence, the signal recognition particle captures that sequence and commits the nascent chain to the endoplasmic reticulum. Everything a cell secretes or displays on its surface — hormones, antibodies, receptors, lysosomal enzymes — depends on this recognition step being accurate. The particle is a ribonucleoprotein built on 7SL RNA with a set of protein subunits: SRP54 binds the hydrophobic signal, the SRP9/SRP14 Alu domain transiently arrests elongation so the chain cannot fold or emerge prematurely, and the SRP68/72 core mediates handoff to the heterodimeric SRP receptor at the ER membrane, where translation resumes into the translocon. Loss of components causes ribosomopathy-like bone marrow failure and neutropenia.

Secreted and membrane proteins must be delivered to the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being made, and this step is where that decision is taken: the signal recognition particle binds the hydrophobic signal sequence as it emerges from the ribosome exit tunnel, pauses elongation, and holds the nascent chain translocation-competent until the complex docks at the ER membrane. The particle is built from the 7SL RNA scaffold together with SRP9, SRP14, SRP19, SRP54, SRP68 and SRP72, with SRP54 making the direct contact with the signal peptide and the GTPase handshake with the heterodimeric SRP receptor formed by SRPRA and SRPRB. Recognition failure misroutes secretory and membrane cargo into the cytosol, so this early sorting event underlies secretion, glycoprotein biogenesis and the composition of every downstream compartment of the secretory route.

protein targeting to mitochondrion covers the delivery of nuclear-encoded proteins to mitochondria and their translocation across the outer and inner membranes, the route by which almost the entire mitochondrial proteome is built since the organelle's own genome encodes only a handful of subunits. Cytosolic precursors bearing targeting signals are recognised by outer-membrane receptors and passed through the TOM channel, then handed to small intermembrane-space chaperones or the TIM23 translocase and pulled inward by a matrix motor; presequences are then clipped by processing peptidases and degraded, and rhomboid and AAA proteases mature or clear substrates. Import efficiency doubles as a quality-control readout: PINK1 stalled on depolarised mitochondria recruits Parkin and ubiquitin machinery to trigger mitophagy, linking this pathway to fission, apoptotic priming, and the neurodegeneration seen when import or its surveillance fails.

Nearly all mitochondrial proteins are made in the cytosol and must be delivered to the correct submitochondrial compartment, and protein targeting to the mitochondrion is the recognition-and-import step that makes this possible. Presequences are read by outer-membrane receptors and the translocation pore (TOMM20, TOMM22, TOMM40 and partners), passed to inner-membrane carriers of the TIMM family with the TIMM44 motor, and then clipped by matrix processing peptidases (PMPCA/PMPCB, MIPEP) or intramembrane proteases such as PARL and HTRA2 to yield mature protein. Import efficiency doubles as a quality-control sensor: stalled or unimported precursors stabilise PINK1 at the outer membrane, recruiting parkin and ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes to mark damaged organelles for mitophagy, alongside fission and fusion factors including FIS1, MFF and MFN2. Failures compromise oxidative metabolism and underlie neurodegenerative and neuropathic disease, including parkinsonism and Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2A.

protein processing involved in protein targeting to mitochondrion describes the proteolytic maturation steps that finish mitochondrial protein import. Most proteins made in the cytosol for mitochondria carry N-terminal targeting signals that must be clipped off after translocation, and only then do they fold, assemble into respiratory complexes, or reach their correct sub-compartment. The matrix processing peptidase, built from the catalytic PMPCB and regulatory PMPCA subunits, removes the presequence, and the mitochondrial intermediate peptidase trims a residual octapeptide from a subset of substrates; the inner membrane peptidase subunits IMMP1L and IMMP2L cleave signals from proteins sorted into the intermembrane space. UQCRC1 is a structural relative of the processing peptidase within complex III. Loss of these activities strands unprocessed precursors, impairs oxidative phosphorylation, and causes mitochondrial disease with cardiomyopathy and neurodegeneration.

Most mitochondrial proteins are made in the cytosol with an N-terminal targeting signal that must be cut off once the protein arrives, and this proteolytic maturation is what completes import and lets the mature protein fold, assemble and function. The matrix processing peptidase, a heterodimer of PMPCA and PMPCB, removes the presequence from incoming precursors, and MIPEP trims residual octapeptides from a subset of them, including subunits of the respiratory chain. The inner membrane peptidase subunits IMMP1L and IMMP2L cleave signals from proteins routed to the intermembrane space. Loss of these steps leaves unprocessed precursors that cannot mature, causing respiratory chain deficiency and neurodegenerative and ataxic disease; PMPCA and MIPEP mutations give cerebellar ataxia and cardiomyopathy. The presence of LRRK2 and the complex III core subunit UQCRC1 links this processing to mitochondrial quality control and assembly of oxidative phosphorylation complexes.

Triglyceride metabolic process covers the synthesis, storage, transport and breakdown of the triesters of glycerol that serve as the body's main energy reserve. It determines how dietary fat is absorbed, how much lipid is deposited in adipocytes and liver, and how fatty acids are released to fuel other tissues; its dysregulation underlies hypertriglyceridaemia, fatty liver disease, lipodystrophy and pancreatitis. Synthesis runs through the glycerol-3-phosphate and monoacylglycerol routes, with acyltransferases, phosphatidate phosphatases of the lipin family and the terminal diacylglycerol acyltransferases DGAT1/2 building triglyceride for packaging into lipid droplets coated by perilipins and CIDE proteins. Mobilisation depends on hormone-sensitive lipase, ATGL with its activator ABHD5, and monoacylglycerol lipase under protein kinase A control. Secreted lipoproteins and their apolipoprotein regulators, together with lipoprotein lipase and its endothelial anchor GPIHBP1, deliver plasma triglyceride to tissues, all under transcriptional control by SREBP and liver X receptors.

Triglyceride metabolism is how the body stores surplus fatty acids as neutral lipid and releases them again when fuel is needed, and it links dietary fat absorption, adipose storage, hepatic lipid handling and plasma lipoprotein transport into one continuous economy. Synthesis proceeds through glycerol-3-phosphate acylation by GPAT and AGPAT enzymes, dephosphorylation of phosphatidate by lipins, and final esterification by DGAT1 and DGAT2; monoacylglycerol acyltransferases provide the intestinal re-esterification route after pancreatic lipases digest dietary fat. Mobilisation runs the other way through ATGL (PNPLA2) with its activator ABHD5, hormone-sensitive lipase and monoacylglycerol lipase acting on perilipin-coated droplets under protein kinase A control. Circulating triglyceride is delivered by apoB-containing particles and hydrolysed by lipoprotein lipase with its APOC2 activator and GPIHBP1 anchor, while SREBF1, INSIG and liver X receptors set transcriptional tone. Defects cause hypertriglyceridaemia, lipodystrophy, hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance.

Phospholipid metabolic process covers the synthesis, remodelling and breakdown of the phosphate-containing lipids that build every cellular membrane and serve as the substrate pool for lipid signalling. It sets membrane composition, curvature and fluidity, supplies surfactant in the lung and myelin in nerve, anchors GPI-linked proteins to the cell surface, and generates the second messengers that relay receptor activation. The genes span de novo glycerophospholipid synthesis through glycerol-3-phosphate acylation and the Kennedy pathway, the Lands cycle acyltransferases and phospholipases that swap acyl chains, cardiolipin production and tafazzin-dependent remodelling in mitochondria, the stepwise assembly of GPI anchors, and the phosphoinositide kinases, phosphatases and phospholipase C enzymes that mark organelle identity and drive calcium and PI3K signalling. Also included are lipid transfer and transport proteins and lipoprotein-associated enzymes. Defects cause Barth syndrome, myotubular and Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathies, surfactant deficiency and dyslipidaemia.

Phospholipids are the structural backbone of every cellular membrane and the source of most lipid second messengers, and this metabolic programme builds, remodels, degrades and interconverts them. It sets membrane fluidity and curvature, supplies surfactant and lipoprotein lipids, and generates the signals that drive growth, secretion and inflammation; its failure underlies myotubular and Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathies, surfactant deficiency, Barth syndrome and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Glycerophosphate acyltransferases and CDP-choline/ethanolamine enzymes assemble the major classes, while lysophospholipid acyltransferases and diverse phospholipases remodel acyl chains and release arachidonate for eicosanoid synthesis. A large phosphoinositide arm—PI kinases, PIP5 and PIP4 kinases, myotubularin and INPP/OCRL phosphatases, and phospholipase C isoforms—writes and erases the lipid codes that mark organelle identity and recruit trafficking and signalling proteins. Further branches handle cardiolipin for mitochondrial function, GPI anchor assembly, sphingomyelin exchange, and lipid transfer between membranes.

Sphingomyelin catabolic process is the hydrolysis of sphingomyelin, the major sphingolipid of the plasma membrane and lysosomal membranes, into ceramide and phosphocholine. This single step converts a structural lipid into a potent signalling molecule: ceramide generated here drives apoptosis, stress responses, senescence and membrane microdomain reorganisation, and it feeds the wider sphingolipid network toward sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate. The reaction is carried out by sphingomyelinases distinguished by pH optimum and location — acid sphingomyelinase in the lysosome, neutral enzymes at the plasma membrane, Golgi and nuclear envelope, and an alkaline intestinal enzyme that digests dietary sphingomyelin. Protein kinase C signalling couples receptor stimulation to this ceramide release. Loss of the lysosomal enzyme causes Niemann-Pick disease types A and B, in which undegraded sphingomyelin accumulates with neurodegeneration and organomegaly, while the neutral enzymes shape bone mineralisation and membrane vesicle release.

Sphingomyelin catabolism converts an abundant membrane phospholipid into ceramide and phosphocholine, and because ceramide is itself a signalling lipid, the reaction couples membrane composition to decisions about stress responses, growth arrest and apoptosis. The sphingomyelinases here work in distinct settings: an acid enzyme in the lysosome, whose loss causes Niemann-Pick disease types A and B through massive sphingomyelin storage and neurodegeneration, and neutral, magnesium-dependent enzymes at the plasma membrane, Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum that generate ceramide locally in response to cytokines and stress, with roles in bone and cartilage mineralisation. Related phosphodiesterases act on the intestinal brush border to digest dietary sphingomyelin or on extracellular substrates in macrophages, and a protein kinase C isoform links receptor signalling to enzyme activation. The ceramide produced feeds onward into sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate metabolism.

Sphingomyelin biosynthetic process builds the most abundant sphingolipid of the plasma membrane, the lipid that together with cholesterol forms ordered membrane domains and gives the myelin sheath and the epidermal barrier their physical properties. It begins with serine palmitoyltransferase, whose SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 subunits condense serine and palmitoyl-CoA to commit the cell to sphingoid base synthesis; mutations here cause hereditary sensory neuropathy. Ceramide made in the endoplasmic reticulum is then carried to the Golgi by CERT1 working against VAP anchors at membrane contact sites, where sphingomyelin synthases transfer phosphocholine from phosphatidylcholine onto ceramide, SGMS1 in the Golgi lumen and SGMS2 at the cell surface. Because that reaction consumes ceramide and releases diacylglycerol, it sets the balance between two potent lipid second messengers and thereby links membrane construction to apoptosis and growth signalling.

Sphingomyelin biosynthesis produces the abundant choline-containing sphingolipid of plasma membranes and myelin, where it pairs with cholesterol to form ordered, raft-like domains and sets membrane rigidity and permeability. The route begins with serine palmitoyltransferase (SPTLC1/SPTLC2) condensing serine and palmitoyl-CoA to launch de novo sphingoid base synthesis, and ends when a sphingomyelin synthase transfers phosphocholine onto ceramide: SGMS1 acting in the Golgi and SGMS2 largely at the cell surface, with SAMD8 a related ceramide phosphoethanolamine synthase. Because ceramide is made in the endoplasmic reticulum, delivery depends on ceramide transfer by CERT1 tethered through VAPA, alongside lipid-transfer and membrane-contact roles for OSBP. The balance struck here governs how much ceramide accumulates as a pro-apoptotic signal versus being consumed; mutations in serine palmitoyltransferase subunits cause hereditary sensory neuropathy, and the pathway also feeds cellular cholesterol and choline handling.

Androgen biosynthetic process builds testosterone and dihydrotestosterone from steroid precursors, the hormones that drive masculinisation of the fetal genitalia, pubertal virilisation, spermatogenesis and the growth of prostate and hair follicles. It operates mainly in testicular Leydig cells and the adrenal cortex, with peripheral tissues finishing the job: CYP17A1 performs the hydroxylase and lyase steps that divert pregnenolone away from cortisol toward C19 steroids, 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and HSD17B3 complete testosterone synthesis, and SRD5A2 reduces it to the far more potent dihydrogenase-resistant dihydrotestosterone in target tissues. Nuclear receptor coactivation by MED1 and gonadal patterning input from WNT4 link hormone output to the transcriptional programme of the steroidogenic cell. Loss of individual enzymes causes disorders of sex development, 46,XY undervirilisation, or congenital adrenal hyperplasia, while excess flux underlies hyperandrogenism and fuels prostate cancer growth.

Androgen biosynthesis converts cholesterol-derived precursors into testosterone and dihydrotestosterone, the hormones that masculinize the fetal genital tract and drive puberty, spermatogenesis, and prostate growth. Loss of individual steps causes disorders of sex development: CYP17A1 performs the 17"a-hydroxylation and 17,20-lyase cleavage that commit pregnenolone to the C19 series, HSD3B2 supplies the adrenal and gonadal 3"b-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase activity, and HSD17B3 completes testicular testosterone synthesis by reducing androstenedione. Peripheral 5"a-reductases encoded by SRD5A1 and SRD5A2 amplify signalling by converting testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, the step blocked pharmacologically in benign prostatic hyperplasia and androgenetic alopecia. Regulatory input is represented by the nuclear receptor coactivator MED1 and by WNT4, which restrains steroidogenic differentiation during gonadal development. The route operates chiefly in Leydig cells, adrenal cortex, and androgen target tissues such as skin and prostate.

Estrogen biosynthetic process produces the C18 steroid hormones that drive female sexual development, ovarian cycling, endometrial and mammary growth, and, in both sexes, bone maturation and closure of the growth plate. Its centrepiece is aromatase, CYP19A1, which converts androgens to estrogens in granulosa cells, placenta, adipose tissue and brain and sets the local estrogen supply that feeds nuclear receptor signalling. Flanking it are the 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, which interconvert weak and potent forms: HSD17B1 generates estradiol from estrone, while HSD17B2 reverses that step, so the balance of these oxidoreductases determines hormone potency in a given tissue. Upstream 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity supplies precursors from the common steroidogenic route. Loss of aromatase causes virilisation and skeletal defects, while excess local synthesis sustains hormone-dependent breast and endometrial tumours, the rationale for aromatase inhibitors.

Estrogen biosynthesis converts androgen precursors into the C18 steroid hormones that drive female sexual development, ovarian cycling, endometrial and breast growth, and, in both sexes, bone maturation and lipid and brain function. The committed step is aromatization of androgens to estrogens by aromatase (CYP19A1), the only enzyme able to make the aromatic A ring; its loss causes estrogen deficiency with tall stature and unfused epiphyses, and its inhibition is the basis of endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. Interconversion of potency is handled by 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, with HSD17B1 favouring reduction of estrone to the more active estradiol and HSD17B2 oxidizing it back, so local ratios of these enzymes set tissue estrogen exposure. HSD3B1 and additional short-chain and aldo-keto reductases supply and recycle precursors, linking this route to the wider steroidogenic pathway from cholesterol.

NADPH regeneration replenishes the cell's pool of reducing power, the currency that supports reductive biosynthesis of fatty acids, cholesterol and nucleotides and that keeps glutathione and thioredoxin reduced against oxidative damage. Cells that cannot regenerate NADPH fail to detoxify peroxides, as in erythrocytes lacking G6PD, where oxidant stress causes haemolysis. Several routes converge on NADP+: the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway through G6PD, PGLS and PGD, with the non-oxidative transketolase and transaldolase arm recycling carbon back to glycolysis; cytosolic IDH1; mitochondrial folate-linked ALDH1L2; and the inner-membrane transhydrogenase NNT, which draws on the proton gradient. Flux is regulated rather than constitutive: p53 and its target TIGAR shift glucose away from glycolysis toward the pentose phosphate route, while mTOR complex components tie NADPH supply to anabolic growth signalling and redox demand in proliferating and tumour cells.

NADPH is the cell's reducing currency for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence, and this pathway covers the reactions that refill its pool wherever it is consumed. Without adequate regeneration, glutathione and thioredoxin cannot be re-reduced, reactive oxygen species accumulate, and fatty acid and nucleotide synthesis stall; red cells are especially vulnerable, as glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and drug-induced haemolysis illustrate. The oxidative pentose phosphate branch, with G6PD and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase, is the dominant cytosolic source, feeding a non-oxidative arm of transketolase, transaldolase and pentose isomerases that also supplies ribose for nucleotides. Cytosolic isocitrate dehydrogenase and the folate-linked ALDH1L enzymes provide additional reducing equivalents, while nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase regenerates NADPH across the mitochondrial inner membrane. Flux is tuned by p53 and its target TIGAR, and by mTOR complex components, tying redox supply to growth and stress signalling.

Vitamin A metabolic process converts dietary carotenoids and retinyl esters into the active retinoids the body needs: retinoic acid for gene regulation, and 11-cis-retinal for vision. Its failure causes night blindness and retinal degeneration, and disrupts the retinoid signalling that patterns developing limbs, heart, and nervous system. Beta-carotene is first cleaved by BCO1 to retinal, while LIPA liberates retinol from stored esters and LRAT re-esterifies it for storage in liver stellate cells and the retinal pigment epithelium. Because retinoids are hydrophobic and reactive, each intermediate is escorted by a dedicated binding protein such as RBP1, RBP2, or RLBP1. In the visual cycle RPE65 isomerizes retinyl ester to 11-cis-retinol for regeneration of rhodopsin chromophore, whereas ALDH1A2 commits retinal irreversibly to retinoic acid, the ligand for nuclear retinoid receptors controlling differentiation.

Vitamin A metabolism converts dietary carotenoids and retinyl esters into the two forms the body actually uses: retinal for vision and retinoic acid for gene regulation. Without it, animals lose photoreceptor function and develop night blindness, and embryonic patterning of the heart, hindbrain and limbs fails because retinoic acid gradients cannot be built. Beta-carotene is cleaved to retinal, esterified retinol is mobilised by lysosomal and cytosolic ester hydrolysis, and lecithin retinol acyltransferase stores retinol back as retinyl esters in liver and retinal pigment epithelium. In the visual cycle, an isomerohydrolase regenerates 11-cis-retinal for opsin, with dedicated binding proteins escorting these insoluble, reactive retinoids between compartments and cells. A dehydrogenase step commits retinal irreversibly to retinoic acid, the ligand for nuclear retinoid receptors that control differentiation of epithelia and immune cells. Mutations in the visual-cycle components cause inherited retinal dystrophies.

Porphyrin-containing compound metabolic process covers the synthesis, transport and breakdown of heme and related tetrapyrroles, the cofactors that let hemoglobin carry oxygen and let cytochromes, catalases and P450 enzymes perform redox chemistry. Erythroid precursors depend on it most heavily, and defects in individual steps cause the porphyrias, sideroblastic anemia, and jaundice from failed bilirubin handling. The eight-enzyme route runs from succinyl-CoA and glycine through aminolevulinic acid synthases and the cytosolic enzymes to ferrochelatase in mitochondria, supported by glycine and intermediate transporters and by iron delivery. Catabolism proceeds through heme oxygenases and biliverdin reductases to bilirubin, which is glucuronidated and exported by hepatic transporters. Regulation ties the pathway to iron status and to translational control of globin synthesis, so that heme and its apoproteins are made in matched amounts.

Metabolism of porphyrin-containing compounds covers the making, transport and breakdown of the tetrapyrrole ring that becomes heme, the cofactor of hemoglobin, cytochromes and catalases. Its output sets the oxygen-carrying capacity of red cells and the electron-transfer capacity of mitochondria and the cytochrome P450 system, so blocked or unbalanced flux causes the porphyrias, sideroblastic anemia and jaundice. Eight enzymes, from the rate-setting ALAS1 and erythroid ALAS2 through HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX and PPOX to ferrochelatase, build protoporphyrin and insert iron, with mitochondrial carriers such as SLC25A38 and ABCB10 supplying glycine and moving intermediates. Heme oxygenases HMOX1 and HMOX2 open the ring to biliverdin, which biliverdin reductases and UGT1A1 convert to excretable bilirubin. Related branches feed heme a synthesis for cytochrome oxidase and couple synthesis to cellular iron sensing and translational control.

Heme A biosynthetic process produces the specialized heme variant that sits in the catalytic core of cytochrome c oxidase, the terminal enzyme of the respiratory chain. Without it, complex IV cannot assemble or transfer electrons to oxygen, and cells lose oxidative phosphorylation capacity — the basis of infantile cardiomyopathy, Leigh syndrome and other mitochondrial encephalomyopathies caused by mutations in the farnesyltransferase COX10 and the monooxygenase COX15. The route begins with the shared tetrapyrrole pathway, in which succinyl-CoA and glycine are condensed by ALAS1 and successive enzymes build the porphyrin ring, ending with ferrochelatase inserting iron to give heme B. Heme B is then modified inside mitochondria: COX10 farnesylates a vinyl group to yield heme O, and COX15 hydroxylates a methyl group to give heme A. The pathway thus links iron and porphyrin metabolism directly to respiratory chain biogenesis.

Cytochrome c oxidase cannot function without heme A, a specialized heme bearing a farnesyl side chain and a formyl group, and heme A biosynthesis is the route that makes it. The pathway begins as the common porphyrin route: ALAS1 condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA, ALAD, HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX and PPOX elaborate and oxidize the tetrapyrrole, and ferrochelatase inserts iron to give heme B. Two mitochondrial inner-membrane enzymes then commit that heme to respiration, COX10 transferring a farnesyl group to form heme O and COX15 oxidizing its methyl substituent to the formyl of heme A. Without this tailoring, complex IV fails to assemble and oxidative phosphorylation collapses, causing infantile cardiomyopathy, Leigh syndrome and other mitochondrial disease, while defects in the upstream porphyrin steps instead produce porphyrias and anemia.

sulfur compound metabolic process covers the handling of sulfur in the cell, from the sulfur amino acids methionine and cysteine through glutathione, coenzyme A, thiamine, lipoate, sulfate esters and hydrogen sulfide. It supplies the reducing thiols that buffer oxidative stress, the methyl donor S-adenosylmethionine, and the acyl carrier and cofactor chemistry on which fatty acid and energy metabolism depend; its failure produces homocystinuria, cystinosis, glutathione deficiency and sulfide toxicity. The genes trace transsulfuration and methionine recycling (CBS, CTH, MAT2A, MTR), glutathione synthesis, conjugation and recycling by the glutathione transferases and gamma-glutamyl cycle, coenzyme A biosynthesis through the pantothenate kinases, sulfate activation by PAPSS1/2 with the sulfotransferases that modify hormones, xenobiotics and glycans, and sulfide clearance by SQOR and ETHE1. Much of it is transcriptionally coordinated by NFE2L2 as part of the antioxidant and detoxification response.

Sulfur compound metabolism covers the handling of the element in all its cellular forms: the sulfur amino acids methionine and cysteine, glutathione, coenzyme A and thioester acyl carriers, thiamine and lipoate cofactors, sulfate esters, and inorganic sulfide. It underwrites methylation capacity, redox buffering and detoxification, and it is why defects here produce homocystinuria, cystinosis, glutathione deficiency and sulfite oxidase disease. Transmethylation and transsulfuration link methionine through homocysteine to cysteine via CBS and CTH, feeding glutathione synthesis by GCLC/GCLM and GSS and taurine production through CDO1 and CSAD. Glutathione is then consumed by transferases and gamma-glutamyl enzymes to conjugate electrophiles, and regenerated by reductase and peroxidase activity. Sulfate activated by PAPSS1/2 supplies cytosolic sulfotransferases and carbohydrate and tyrosine sulfation, while MPST, TST and SQOR dispose of hydrogen sulfide. Coenzyme A and thioesterase reactions place fatty acid metabolism within the same thiol economy.

Phosphorus metabolic process gathers the reactions that make, break and transfer phosphate-containing compounds, the chemistry on which cellular energy currency, signalling and nucleic acid synthesis all depend. It spans ATP production by glycolytic enzymes, the mitochondrial respiratory chain and ATP synthase; nucleotide salvage and de novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis; phospholipid and inositol phosphate turnover through kinases, phospholipases and phosphatases; and sugar phosphate handling in the pentose phosphate pathway. A large share of the genes are protein kinases and phosphatases, so reversible phosphorylation of proteins is part of the same chemistry, linking this metabolism directly to growth factor and cytokine signalling, cell cycle checkpoints, and nutrient sensing through AMPK and mTOR complexes. Because phosphate transfer underlies both bioenergetics and information flow, defects in individual steps produce mitochondrial disease, metabolic disorders, immunodeficiency and cancer, and the pathway also connects to systemic phosphate homeostasis via PTH and PHEX.

Phosphorus metabolic processes encompass every reaction that makes, breaks, or transfers phosphate-containing compounds, and they underlie the chemistry of energy, information, and membranes. The nucleotide and sugar-phosphate arms shown here build purines and pyrimidines, run glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway, and feed oxidative phosphorylation through respiratory complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, and the ATP synthase, so that cells can store and spend energy as ATP. A second arm turns phosphate into a reversible regulatory mark: hundreds of protein kinases (receptor tyrosine kinases, MAP kinase cascades, AMPK and mTOR components, cyclin-dependent kinases) paired with phosphatases such as the PTP and DUSP families and PP1/PP2A catalytic subunits, governing growth, division, and stress responses. Lipid kinases, phosphoinositide phosphatases, phospholipases, and phosphatidylinositol-anchor biosynthesis enzymes generate membrane phosphate species that recruit proteins and define organelle identity. Loss of individual steps causes metabolic, neurological, and oncogenic disease.

Manganese ion transport moves manganese across membranes to keep this trace metal available as an enzyme cofactor while preventing its accumulation to neurotoxic levels. Manganese is required by mitochondrial superoxide dismutase, arginase, and the Golgi glycosyltransferases that build glycans, so cells must supply it to the right compartments; excess manganese damages the basal ganglia and produces a parkinsonian syndrome. Uptake transporters of the SLC39 family, notably SLC39A8 and SLC39A14, import manganese at the intestine and liver, while SLC30A10 exports it for biliary excretion, and loss-of-function mutations in these genes cause inherited manganese deficiency with skeletal dysplasia or hypermanganesemia with dystonia. Secretory-pathway calcium/manganese ATPases and TMEM165 load the Golgi lumen to support glycosylation, and divalent metal transporters such as SLC11A2 couple manganese handling to iron uptake, linking this pathway to systemic metal homeostasis and macrophage antimicrobial defence.

Manganese is needed as a cofactor by glycosyltransferases, mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and arginase, yet it is neurotoxic in excess, so cells and the body must move it with precision. This transport system handles uptake, compartmentalisation and disposal: divalent metal importers of the SLC11 and SLC39 families bring manganese across the plasma membrane and into hepatocytes and enterocytes, secretory-pathway calcium/manganese ATPases and TMEM165 load it into the Golgi where glycosylation enzymes use it, and SLC30A10 exports it for biliary excretion. Failure at either end causes recognisable disease: loss of efflux or of SLC39A14 produces manganese accumulation in the basal ganglia with dystonia and parkinsonism, while defective Golgi delivery gives congenital disorders of glycosylation. The pathway therefore links trace-metal homeostasis to protein glycosylation, antioxidant defence and neurological function.

neurotransmitter transport covers the whole logistical chain that moves chemical messengers where they are needed: loading them into synaptic vesicles, releasing them at the active zone, and clearing them from the synaptic cleft afterwards. Without it chemical synaptic transmission fails, and the genes involved are the ones mutated in epilepsy, dystonia, paroxysmal movement disorders and parkinsonism, and the targets of antidepressants, psychostimulants and anticonvulsants. Vesicular transporters of the SLC17, SLC18 and SLC32 families concentrate glutamate, monoamines, acetylcholine and GABA against a proton gradient; SNARE proteins with syntaxins, SNAP25 and VAMP2, together with the calcium sensors synaptotagmin and complexin and the priming factors UNC13 and STXBP1, execute regulated exocytosis; plasma membrane SLC1 and SLC6 carriers in neurons and astrocytes then recapture transmitter to terminate signalling and recycle substrate. Presynaptic scaffolds such as piccolo and RIM organise the release site, linking this pathway to synaptic vesicle cycling and calcium channel coupling.

Chemical signalling between neurons depends on moving transmitter molecules into the right compartment at the right moment, and this pathway covers both halves of that job: loading and clearing transmitters across membranes, and releasing them from synaptic vesicles. Vesicular carriers of the SLC17, SLC18 and SLC32 families concentrate glutamate, monoamines, acetylcholine and GABA into vesicles, while plasma-membrane SLC6 and SLC1 transporters recapture GABA, glycine, dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin and glutamate from the cleft, terminating signalling and protecting against excitotoxicity. Release itself runs through calcium-triggered fusion: syntaxins, SNAP25 and VAMPs form the fusion complex, synaptotagmins and complexins gate it, and Munc13, Munc18, RIMs and the active-zone scaffolds piclo and bassoon-like proteins organise vesicle priming. Loss of these components produces epilepsy, movement disorders, paroxysmal dyskinesia and neurodegeneration, and the reuptake transporters are the direct targets of antidepressants and psychostimulants.

mitochondrial transport covers the movement of metabolites, ions, proteins and whole organelles into, out of and within mitochondria, the traffic that lets a compartment sealed by two membranes participate in cellular metabolism. Carrier families dominate: the SLC25 solute carriers exchange ADP/ATP, ornithine, carnitine-acylcarnitines, citrulline and glutathione, MPC1/MPC2 import pyruvate for oxidation, sideroflexins and TMEM14C handle serine and porphyrin intermediates, and uncoupling proteins dissipate the proton gradient for thermogenesis. Outer-membrane channels VDAC1/2 and MTCH2 set the permeability that carnitine shuttle enzymes CPT1/CPT2 depend on for fatty acid oxidation. The same channels are commandeered by the BCL2 family, so permeabilization by BAX and BAK converts transport into apoptotic release of cytochrome c. Miro GTPases RHOT1/2 move mitochondria along cytoskeletal tracks, and PINK1-PRKN marks damaged ones for mitophagy; failures here underlie Parkinson's disease, neuropathy and metabolic disorders.

Mitochondria are metabolically sealed off from the cytosol, so almost everything they consume or release has to be carried across their membranes, and this transport biology covers that traffic. It supplies the matrix with pyruvate, fatty acyl groups, amino acids, serine and one-carbon units, ornithine and glycine for heme synthesis, adenine nucleotides and metal ions, and it exports ATP and metabolic intermediates back to the cell. Carrier families dominate the list: the SLC25 exchangers, the sideroflexins, the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier subunits, uncoupling proteins that dissipate the proton gradient as heat, and outer-membrane porins. Carnitine shuttle enzymes feed fatty acid oxidation. The same membranes govern release of apoptogenic proteins, so BCL2-family regulators, permeability transition components and the PINK1-parkin mitophagy pair appear alongside Miro GTPases that move organelles along the cytoskeleton. Defects cause metabolic, neurodegenerative and hematologic disease.

Tricarboxylic acid transport moves citrate and related tri- and dicarboxylic acids across membranes, linking the mitochondrial matrix, the cytosol, and the bloodstream. This traffic sets the supply of cytosolic citrate that is cleaved to acetyl-CoA for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis and for protein acetylation, and it governs how much citrate the kidney reabsorbs rather than excretes. The mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1 exports citrate in exchange for malate, while the sodium-coupled transporters SLC13A5 and SLC13A3 import citrate and succinate at the plasma membrane of hepatocytes, neurons, and renal tubule cells; SFXN5 handles citrate at the inner mitochondrial membrane. Loss of these activities has clear consequences: SLC25A1 deficiency causes combined D,L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, SLC13A5 mutations cause early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, and reduced urinary citrate promotes calcium stone formation.

Citrate and related tricarboxylic acids must cross membranes to move between the compartments that make and use them, and this transport is what couples mitochondrial oxidative metabolism to cytosolic lipid and sterol synthesis. The mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1 exports citrate in exchange for malate, supplying the acetyl-CoA and NADPH-generating steps of de novo lipogenesis; its loss causes a severe neurometabolic disorder with D-2- and L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. At the plasma membrane, sodium-dependent dicarboxylate/citrate transporters of the SLC13 family take up citrate from blood, intestine and renal tubular fluid, where SLC13A5 shapes hepatic and neuronal citrate supply and mutations cause early infantile epilepsy, while renal handling of citrate influences urinary calcium stone formation.
