A sideroflexin family member and the kidney-secreted protein uromodulin place this transport activity in both mitochondrial carrier biology and tubular solute handling.

pyruvate transport moves pyruvate across membranes, linking glycolysis in the cytosol to oxidative metabolism in the mitochondrion and allowing cells to exchange this three-carbon fuel with one another. Without it, pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle, so cells fall back on lactate production regardless of oxygen supply — the metabolic state that characterises proliferating tumour cells. Two arms are represented: the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, an inner-membrane heterocomplex of MPC1 and MPC2 that governs how much pyruvate is available for oxidation and gluconeogenesis, and plasma-membrane monocarboxylate transporters such as SLC16A1 and SLC16A3 that co-transport pyruvate and lactate with protons, supporting lactate shuttling between glycolytic and oxidative tissues. SLC5A8 adds sodium-coupled uptake in kidney and gut epithelium. Loss of carrier function causes lactic acidosis and developmental disease, and MPC activity sets the balance between glucose and fatty acid use in muscle, liver and pancreatic beta cells.

Pyruvate sits at the junction between glycolysis and oxidative metabolism, but it cannot cross membranes unaided, so its directed movement across the plasma membrane and the inner mitochondrial membrane is what decides whether a cell burns it, exports it as lactate, or shunts it elsewhere. Two families do the work here: monocarboxylate transporters of the SLC16 group carry pyruvate and lactate across the plasma membrane along proton gradients, allowing lactate export from glycolytic tissue and uptake by oxidative tissue, while the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, a heterocomplex of MPC1 and MPC2, delivers pyruvate to the matrix for oxidation by pyruvate dehydrogenase or carboxylation for gluconeogenesis. A sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporter additionally absorbs short-chain monocarboxylates in gut and kidney epithelium. Loss of carrier function causes lactic acidosis and developmental disease, and these transporters shape the metabolic flexibility exploited by tumours.

Mitochondrial calcium ion transmembrane transport moves Ca2+ into and out of mitochondria, linking cytosolic calcium signals to the control of energy metabolism, cell death and redox balance. Matrix Ca2+ activates dehydrogenases of the citric acid cycle and thereby matches ATP output to demand, while overload opens the permeability transition pore and triggers necrotic and apoptotic death, a route implicated in ischemia-reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration. Uptake occurs through the inner-membrane uniporter, a pore of MCU and MCUB with the essential regulator EMRE and the gatekeeping MICU1/2/3 subunits that set a cytosolic Ca2+ threshold, fed by VDAC1 across the outer membrane at contacts with ER release sites bearing IP3 receptors and presenilin. Efflux runs through the mitochondrial Na+/Ca2+ exchanger SLC8B1 and LETM1, and quality-control proteases such as AFG3L2 and SPG7 govern uniporter assembly and stability.

Mitochondria take up calcium from the cytosol and release it again, and this traffic sets the pace of oxidative metabolism, shapes cytosolic calcium signals, and decides whether a stressed cell survives. Uptake runs through the inner-membrane uniporter channel, whose pore subunit MCU works with the regulatory subunit EMRE and the paralogue MCUB, while MICU1, MICU2 and MICU3 act as calcium-sensing gatekeepers that keep the channel shut at resting concentrations and open it during signalling. Calcium enters the matrix down the membrane potential and stimulates dehydrogenases that feed the respiratory chain; efflux via the sodium/calcium exchanger SLC8B1 and LETM1 returns the matrix to baseline. VDAC1 and ER-resident IP3 receptors supply calcium at contact sites, and AFG3L2 and SPG7 control maturation of uniporter components. Overload triggers permeability transition and cell death, linking this transport to ischaemic injury and neurodegeneration.

Intracellular copper ion homeostasis keeps cellular copper at a level that supplies cuproenzymes without allowing free copper to catalyse oxidative damage. Copper is required by cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase, lysyl oxidase and ceruloplasmin, yet an unbuffered ion is toxic, so cells import, chaperone, store and export it along tightly controlled routes. High-affinity transporters of the CTR family bring copper across the plasma membrane, metallothioneins and the chaperone ATOX1 buffer and route it, SCO1 and SCO2 deliver it to the respiratory chain, and the P-type ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B load copper onto secreted enzymes in the Golgi and traffic to membranes for efflux when copper rises. Loss of these ATPases causes Menkes disease and Wilson disease, showing how systemic copper distribution depends on cell-level handling; the same machinery is linked to prion protein and amyloid precursor protein biology.

Copper is needed as a catalytic cofactor yet is toxic when free, so cells keep intracellular copper ion homeostasis by importing, chaperoning and exporting it without ever letting an unbound pool accumulate. The high-affinity importer SLC31A1 brings copper across the plasma membrane, metallothionein and small chaperones such as ATOX1 buffer it and hand it on, and the two copper-transporting ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B load it onto secreted cuproenzymes including ceruloplasmin or excrete the excess, with trafficking regulators shifting them between Golgi and membrane as copper rises. A separate branch delivers copper to cytochrome c oxidase through SCO1, SCO2 and COX19, linking this balance to respiration. Loss of the exporters causes Menkes disease and Wilson disease, the classic copper deficiency and copper overload disorders, and the same chemistry underlies copper-dependent cell death and the copper binding attributed to prion protein and APP.

post-Golgi vesicle-mediated transport is the sorting step that decides where newly made membrane proteins, secreted cargo and lysosomal enzymes actually end up. After the Golgi, vesicles must be budded, loaded with the right cargo, moved along cytoskeletal tracks and fused with a specific target, and this pathway supplies each of those activities: clathrin adaptor complexes (AP-1 through AP-4) and GGA proteins select cargo, ARF GTPases and their regulators such as GBF1 initiate budding, Rab GTPases with motors like MYO5A and KIF13A direct delivery, and SNAREs including VAMP2/3 with NSF drive fusion. Retromer-like and commander/retriever components recycle receptors back from endosomes. The output is cell surface polarity, regulated secretion, lysosome biogenesis and receptor recycling; sortilin-family receptors here also route neurotrophin and lipoprotein cargo, and defects cause lysosomal storage disease, pigmentation and platelet disorders, and neurodegeneration.

Cargo leaving the Golgi must be sorted into vesicles and delivered to the right destination "u2014 endosomes, lysosomes, secretory granules, or a particular face of the plasma membrane "u2014 and post-Golgi vesicle-mediated transport is that delivery system. It sustains secretion, receptor and transporter surface levels, lysosome biogenesis and the polarity of epithelial and neuronal cells; defects produce lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative disease, pigmentation and coagulation disorders. Adaptor complexes and GGA proteins recognise sorting signals and recruit clathrin at the trans-Golgi, sortilin-family receptors select hydrolase and neurotrophin-receptor cargo, and Arf and Rab GTPases with their regulators specify carrier identity. Kinesins and myosin motors move carriers along cytoskeletal tracks, while exocyst, SNARE and NSF-dependent fusion machinery completes tethering and membrane merger. Retromer-like and commander/retriever components recycle receptors back for reuse, coupling outward traffic to endosomal retrieval.

Golgi to vacuole transport is the route by which newly made hydrolases, membrane proteins and lipids are delivered from the Golgi to the lysosome (the vacuolar compartment of animal cells), building and maintaining the cell's degradative organelle. Without it, acid hydrolases are missecreted, lysosomes fail to mature, and storage disease follows. Sorting begins at the trans-Golgi network, where receptors such as sortilin capture cargo and clathrin adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-3 concentrate it into budding carriers, with GAK and the GGA-associated factor CCDC91 supporting coat assembly and uncoating. Vesicles then travel through endosomal intermediates, guided by Rab effectors including ANKFY1 and rabenosyn-5 and the GARP complex, and fuse using the SNAREs VTI1A and VTI1B. Cargo delivered this way includes LAMP1 and CLN3, whose loss causes neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, tying this traffic to lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic turnover and antigen processing.

Newly made lysosomal enzymes, membrane proteins and pigment-granule cargo leave the Golgi by carriers directed specifically to the vacuolar or lysosomal compartment, and this route is what gives a cell a functional degradative organelle. The clathrin adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-3, with their accessory factors, select cargo at the trans-Golgi network and at endosomes; sortilin acts as a sorting receptor that captures ligands for delivery and is then retrieved, while SNAREs such as VTI1A and VTI1B and retromer-associated subunits VPS52 and VPS54 handle fusion and recycling steps. LAMP1 marks the destination membrane. Failures of this traffic underlie lysosomal storage and pigmentation disorders, including the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis caused by loss of CLN3 and Hermansky-Pudlak-type defects in AP-3, and they compromise antigen processing and melanosome and platelet granule formation.

Vesicle targeting is the step that gives membrane traffic its specificity: once a transport vesicle has budded, it must be delivered to the correct destination membrane rather than any membrane it encounters. This selectivity keeps the secretory pathway organised, sustains polarised delivery to the cell surface, and underlies regulated secretion and neurotransmitter release; its failure produces broad trafficking disease, including skeletal and neurodevelopmental disorders linked to tethering-complex mutations. The genes describe the machinery involved -- COPII coat and cargo receptors such as SAR1A/B, SEC16A and the TMED p24 proteins for ER exit, the multisubunit TRAPP and exocyst tethering complexes that capture vesicles at Golgi and plasma membrane, golgins and microtubule plus-end tracking proteins that position them, and SNAREs including SNAP23, SNAP29 and YKT6 that commit tethered vesicles to fusion. Kinases, ubiquitin ligases and calcium sensors tune the process.

Vesicle targeting is the step that gives membrane traffic its specificity: a budded carrier must be steered to the one destination membrane whose cargo and identity match it, rather than fusing indiscriminately. The genes here cover the machinery that does this at successive stations. COPII budding and ER exit involve SAR1A/SAR1B, SEC16A, TFG and the p24 family cargo receptors, while ARFGAP2/3 and GBF1 govern Arf-dependent coat dynamics on Golgi membranes. The multisubunit TRAPP complexes and the exocyst act as tethers that capture arriving vesicles and license SNARE pairing, with SNAP23, SNAP29, YKT6 and synaptotagmin/complexin components carrying the process through to fusion; CLASP proteins and TRIP11 link carriers to microtubules. Phagocytosis is how macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and microglia physically eat particles cells, bacteria, dying and deliver them to lysosomes for destruction. It clears apoptotic corpses to prevent autoimmunity, removes pathogens as a first line of innate defence, and provides antigen for presentation; its failure underlies recurrent infection, chronic inflammation, defective tissue remodelling and neurodegeneration. Recognition comes from opsonins and receptors: complement components and collectins coat targets, Fc receptors and integrins bind antibody and complement, and scavenger and phosphatidylserine receptors such as MERTK, TIMD4, MFGE8 and TREM2 read "eat-me" signals, while CD47 SIRPA marks self as off-limits. Engagement drives Src-family and SYK signalling to Rho-family GTPases through VAV and DOCK ELMO modules, remodelling actin and phosphoinositides to close the cup. Rab GTPases, SNAREs and the NADPH oxidase then mature the phagosome into a degradative, microbicidal compartment.

Phagocytosis is how macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and microglia swallow microbes, dying cells and debris and route them to the lysosome for destruction. It underlies innate defence against bacteria and fungi, the silent clearance of apoptotic cells that prevents autoimmunity, surfactant and lipid turnover in the lung, and synaptic pruning in the brain. Recognition comes from opsonins and their receptors complement components with integrin partners, IgG-binding Fc receptors, collectins and pentraxins and from direct sensors of exposed phosphatidylserine such as MERTK, TIMD4 and MFGE8, while CD47 SIRPA signals self and spares healthy cells. Receptor engagement activates Src-family and SYK kinases, PLCG2, and Rho-family GTPase exchange through VAV and DOCK ELMO modules to drive actin remodelling and cup closure. Phosphoinositide turnover and a RAB cascade then mature the phagosome, coupling it to NADPH oxidase assembly, antigen presentation and cytokine output.

muscle contraction is the generation of force by actin and myosin filaments sliding past one another at the expense of ATP, the process behind every heartbeat, every voluntary movement, and the tone of blood vessels, airways and gut. The genes span all three muscle types: sarcomeric myosins, actins, troponins and tropomyosins with their scaffolds titin, desmin and dystrophin-associated proteins; the excitation-contraction coupling apparatus of dihydropyridine receptors, ryanodine receptors, junctophilins, triadin, calsequestrin and the SERCA-phospholamban pump; and the voltage-gated sodium, potassium and calcium channels that shape the action potential in cardiac and neuronal excitability. Smooth muscle is represented by myosin light chain kinase, RhoA-ROCK signalling and receptors for endothelin, adrenaline and acetylcholine that set vascular tone. Mutations here cause the cardiomyopathies, congenital myopathies, muscular dystrophies, arrhythmia syndromes and malignant hyperthermia, linking calcium handling directly to contractile output.

Muscle contraction is the conversion of chemical energy into mechanical force, shortening or stiffening skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle to move the skeleton, pump blood, and set the tone of airways, gut and blood vessels. The core machinery is the sarcomere actin and myosin heavy and light chains, titin, tropomyosin and the troponin complex whose ATP-driven cross-bridge cycling is switched on by calcium. Excitation contraction coupling supplies that calcium: voltage-gated sodium, potassium and L-type calcium channels shape the action potential, dihydropyridine receptors signal to ryanodine receptors in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and SERCA pumps with phospholamban and calsequestrin restore resting levels. In smooth muscle, myosin light chain kinase and Rho-kinase set sensitivity to calcium downstream of adrenergic, muscarinic and endothelin receptors. Mutations here cause cardiomyopathies, arrhythmias, congenital myopathies and muscular dystrophies.

Regulation of muscle contraction sets how strongly, how fast and how often cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle shorten, tuning heartbeat, vascular tone, airway and gut motility, and voluntary movement to physiological demand. Its failure produces arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, hypertension and myopathy. Control converges on calcium: voltage-gated channels and their auxiliary subunits trigger release through ryanodine receptors held in junctional membranes by junctophilins, triadin and calsequestrin, while SERCA pumps, phospholamban, sodium-calcium exchangers and calmodulin set removal and the duration of the transient. Sensitivity of the myofilaments themselves is adjusted at troponin, tropomyosin and myosin light chains through kinase and phosphatase activity. Layered on top are neurohumoral inputs -- adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, purinergic and tachykinin receptors acting via cAMP, PKA, PKG and RhoA -- plus transcriptional and microRNA programs that fix contractile phenotype, and channels including HCN4 and KCNQ1 that govern pacemaking and repolarisation.

Whether a muscle cell contracts, how strongly and how fast, is set by processes that tune calcium delivery to the sarcomere and the sensitivity of the sarcomere to it; this regulation of muscle contraction covers cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle alike. It determines cardiac output and rhythm, vascular tone and blood pressure, gut and airway motility, and skeletal muscle force, and its failure produces arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, malignant hyperthermia-type disorders and hypertension. Voltage-gated calcium and sodium channels, potassium and pacemaker channels, and the sarcoplasmic reticulum release and uptake machinery (ryanodine receptors, SERCA pumps with phospholamban, calsequestrin, triadin and junctophilins) shape the calcium transient, while troponins, tropomyosin, myosin light chains and their kinases translate it into force. Layered on top are G protein-coupled inputs from adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, purinergic and tachykinin receptors acting through cyclic nucleotides, calmodulin and RhoA, plus transcriptional and microRNA control of the contractile programme.

Smooth muscle contraction is the force-generating program of the involuntary muscle that lines blood vessels, airways, gut, bladder and uterus, setting vascular tone, peristalsis, bronchial calibre and continence. Its dysregulation underlies hypertension, asthma, vasospasm and intestinal dysmotility. Force comes from actin and a high ratio of myosin rather than sarcomeres, with contraction switched on by myosin light chain kinase acting on smooth muscle myosin, and switched off by nitric oxide-cGMP signalling through soluble guanylate cyclase and protein kinase G. Sensitivity to calcium is tuned by RhoA-ROCK and phosphatase inhibition, while calcium entry, extrusion pumps, sodium-calcium exchange and BK channels shape the underlying calcium and membrane-potential cycles. A broad set of adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, tachykinin, purinergic and prostanoid receptors provides the inputs, and myocardin with serum response factor and microRNAs such as miR-143/145 maintain the differentiated contractile phenotype.

Smooth muscle contraction generates force in the walls of blood vessels, airways, gut, bladder and uterus, setting vascular tone, peristalsis, bronchial calibre and parturition; its dysregulation underlies hypertension, asthmatic bronchoconstriction, vasospasm and intestinal dysmotility. Unlike striated muscle it lacks sarcomeres and contracts over a wide length range, using calcium-calmodulin activation of myosin light chain kinase to phosphorylate the regulatory light chain of smooth muscle myosin and drive actin-based force with ATP hydrolysis. Rho-ROCK signalling sensitises the apparatus by suppressing myosin phosphatase, while nitric oxide acting through soluble guanylate cyclase and PRKG1 promotes relaxation. Contractile tone is tuned by a large repertoire of surface receptors for adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, tachykinin, purinergic and prostanoid ligands, and by calcium handling through sodium-calcium exchange, plasma membrane pumps and large-conductance potassium channels. Myocardin and SRF, with miR-143/145, maintain the differentiated contractile phenotype.

striated muscle contraction is the force-generating program of skeletal and cardiac muscle, in which sarcomeric actin and myosin convert ATP into shortening and thereby produce movement, posture, and the cardiac output that sustains circulation. Its logic is excitation-contraction coupling: voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels and their accessory subunits depolarise the sarcolemma and T-tubules, dihydropyridine receptors signal through junctional proteins such as STAC3, junctophilins and triadin to ryanodine receptors, and released calcium binds troponin C to relieve tropomyosin inhibition of the thin filament. Relaxation follows from SERCA pumps, phospholamban, calsequestrin buffering, sodium-calcium exchange, and repolarising potassium channels. Titin, dystrophin, myosin-binding protein C and the sarcomeric myosins and myosin light chains set mechanical properties and tune contractility, while adrenergic and calmodulin-kinase signalling adjust it to demand. Mutations here cause hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies, arrhythmia syndromes, congenital myopathies, and muscular dystrophy.

Striated muscle contraction is the force-generating programme of skeletal and cardiac muscle, in which sarcomeres arranged in register shorten as myosin heads cycle on actin using ATP. It underlies locomotion, posture, breathing and the heartbeat, and its components are the genes mutated in cardiomyopathies, congenital myopathies and inherited arrhythmia syndromes. Excitation begins with acetylcholine receptors or pacemaker and sodium channel activity, spreads through voltage-gated sodium, potassium and calcium channels, and is coupled at triad and dyad junctions, where dihydropyridine receptors, junctophilins and ryanodine receptors release stored calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium binds troponin C, shifting tropomyosin to permit crossbridge formation; relaxation follows reuptake by SERCA pumps under phospholamban control and sodium-calcium exchange. Titin, dystrophin and associated costameric proteins transmit and buffer the resulting force, while adrenergic and calmodulin-kinase signalling tunes contractile strength.

Inflammatory response is the body's immediate defensive reaction to infection or tissue injury, producing the local vasodilation, plasma leakage and leukocyte influx that clear pathogens and damaged cells and set the stage for repair. Without it, hosts cannot contain microbes; when it fails to resolve, the result is chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, fibrosis and septic shock. Pattern-recognition receptors such as the Toll-like receptors, NOD proteins and NLRP inflammasome sensors detect microbial and damage signals and route through MyD88, IRAK kinases, MAP kinases and NF-kB to induce cytokines including TNF, IL-1, IL-6 and IL-17 family members. Chemokines and their receptors direct neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes along selectin- and integrin-dependent adhesion routes, while eicosanoids, complement, kinins and acute-phase proteins amplify the response. Caspase-1-driven pyroptosis, negative regulators such as A20 and IL-10, and lipid mediator switching enforce resolution.

The immediate defensive reaction of vertebrate tissue to infection or injury, marked by local vasodilation, leakage of plasma into interstitial spaces, and recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages to the site. It clears pathogens and damaged tissue and initiates repair; when it fails to resolve, the same machinery drives sepsis, autoinflammatory fevers, atherosclerosis and chronic inflammatory disease. Pattern-recognition receptors including Toll-like receptors and NOD-like sensors, acting through MYD88, IRAK kinases and NF-kB, induce cytokines such as IL1B, IL6 and TNF; inflammasome assembly on NLRP3 and PYCARD activates caspase-1 and gasdermin-dependent release of mature IL-1 family cytokines. Chemokines and their receptors direct leukocyte traffic, selectins and integrins mediate adhesion to endothelium, complement, eicosanoids, bradykinin and acute-phase proteins amplify the response, and negative regulators including IL10, IL1RN, TNFAIP3 and SOCS3 terminate it.

cellular defense response covers the effector arm of innate and cytotoxic immunity: how leukocytes detect microbes, injured tissue and abnormal cells, migrate to them, and destroy them. It is what makes neutrophil and macrophage killing, natural killer cell surveillance of virus-infected and tumour cells, and the recruitment of these cells into inflamed tissue possible; its failure produces recurrent infection, and its excess produces inflammatory tissue damage. The genes span the steps in sequence: chemokine receptors such as CCR2, CCR5 and CXCR2 with the complement receptor C5AR1 guide cells to the site; LBP and LY96 hand endotoxin to Toll-like receptor signalling, which reaches NF-κB through BCL10 and RELA; NADPH oxidase subunits NCF1 and NCF2 build the respiratory burst; and perforin, granulysin, NCR1/NCR2 and killer-cell inhibitory receptors set the threshold for granule-mediated cytotoxicity. Adhesion, phagosome acidification and autophagy components complete the killing machinery.

Cell-mediated defense against microbes and damaged or transformed cells, carried out largely by neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages and natural killer cells rather than by antibodies. Loss of these functions leaves a host prone to recurrent bacterial and viral infection and impairs clearance of infected or stressed targets. The genes cover the main effector steps: chemokine receptors such as CCR2, CCR5 and CX3CR1 that steer leukocytes to inflamed tissue; pattern and complement sensing through LY96, LBP and the C5a receptor; NADPH oxidase subunits NCF1 and NCF2 that generate the microbicidal oxidative burst; and cytotoxic granule proteins perforin and granulysin that lyse targets. Killer-cell immunoglobulin-like and NKG2 receptors with the TYROBP adaptor, together with HLA-G and NCR ligand recognition, set the activating versus inhibitory balance that licenses NK killing, while NF-kB components including RELA and BCL10 drive the accompanying inflammatory transcription.

mitochondrion organization covers everything cells do to build, shape, position and dismantle their mitochondria, and it determines whether the organelle can sustain oxidative phosphorylation, buffer calcium, and serve as the platform for apoptosis. Its breadth is reflected in the machinery involved: import translocases of the outer and inner membranes, cristae-shaping MICOS and OPA1 complexes, assembly factors that chaperone respiratory complex I, III and IV subunits into place, mitochondrial DNA maintenance and transcription factors such as TFAM and SSBP1, and quality-control proteases including LONP1, CLPP and AFG3L2. Opposing fission and fusion activities (DRP1, MFF, MFN1/2) set network morphology, while PINK1-parkin, BNIP3 and FUNDC1 mark damaged organelles for mitophagy and BCL2-family proteins govern outer membrane permeabilization. Biogenesis is driven transcriptionally through PPARGC1A. Defects here produce optic atrophies, spastic paraplegias, cardiomyopathy, and neurodegeneration.

Mitochondria are built, shaped, positioned and turned over continuously, and mitochondrion organization covers the whole of that housekeeping: import of nuclear-encoded proteins, assembly of the respiratory complexes, maintenance of cristae architecture, fusion and fission, movement along the cytoskeleton, replication of the mitochondrial genome, and selective removal of damaged organelles. Its outputs are oxidative energy supply, calcium buffering and control of apoptosis, so failures surface as mitochondrial myopathy and encephalopathy, optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy and parkinsonism. The machinery includes outer- and inner-membrane translocases, the cristae-organizing scaffold with its mitofilin and MICOS components, dedicated assembly factors for complexes I, III, IV and the ATP synthase, the dynamin-related fission GTPase with its receptors opposing the fusion GTPases mitofusin and OPA1, motor-adaptor proteins for trafficking, matrix chaperones and proteases, and the PINK1-parkin mitophagy axis. Outer-membrane BCL2-family proteins couple organelle state to permeabilization and cell death.

Inner mitochondrial membrane organization builds and maintains the folded architecture of the mitochondrial inner membrane, the surface on which oxidative phosphorylation happens. Cristae shape sets respiratory efficiency, so its loss lowers ATP output, destabilises supercomplexes, releases cytochrome c and predisposes to optic atrophy, cardiomyopathy and neurodegeneration. The MICOS complex, anchored by mitofilin and the CHCHD3/CHCHD6 subunits, holds crista junctions in place and, through SAMM50 and the metaxins, tethers the inner membrane to the outer membrane at contact sites. OPA1 and the AFG3L2/OMA1 proteases regulate crista remodelling and fusion, while the TIM22 and TIM8/13 carrier import machinery, OXA1L and TAFAZZIN insert and lipidate the membrane's proteins and cardiolipin. PINK1 links this architecture to quality control, marking damaged organelles for mitophagy.

The inner mitochondrial membrane is folded into cristae, and the shaping and maintenance of that architecture is what this pathway describes. Cristae geometry sets how densely respiratory complexes can pack, how much cytochrome c is sequestered, and therefore how much ATP a cell makes and how readily it commits to apoptosis; its collapse underlies optic atrophy, cardiomyopathy and mitochondrial encephalopathy. Central to it is the MICOS complex at cristae junctions, built around mitofilin (IMMT) with CHCHD3, CHCHD6, APOO and APOOL, tethered to the outer membrane through SAMM50 and the metaxins. OPA1 controls inner membrane fusion and junction tightness and is cleaved by the stress proteases OMA1 and AFG3L2. Carrier-pathway TIM chaperones and the insertases OXA1L and COX18 deliver membrane proteins into the bilayer, while tafazzin remodels cardiolipin, the lipid that stabilises the curvature these proteins impose.

Plasma membrane organization covers how a cell builds, shapes, repairs and remodels its outer boundary, determining cell shape, polarity, and the ability to fuse, divide, or seal a wound. Loss of these activities underlies muscular dystrophies with defective sarcolemma repair, failures of sperm-egg fusion and infertility, and defects in apoptotic cell clearance. The genes span the main machineries involved: BAR-domain and caveolar proteins (BIN1, PACSIN, CAV1-3, EHD2) that impose curvature and form membrane invaginations; ESCRT-III subunits with VPS4 ATPases that scission and patch membrane; spectrin, ankyrin and IQGAP-actin linkages that tether bilayer to cytoskeleton; scramblases and flippases (ANO6, PLSCR, XKR, ATP8B1) that control phospholipid asymmetry and phosphatidylserine exposure; and dedicated fusogens such as IZUMO1, MYMK and MYMX for gamete and myoblast fusion. Together they make the membrane a dynamic, repairable, compositionally patterned structure rather than a passive barrier.

How a cell builds, shapes and repairs its outer boundary is captured here as plasma membrane organization: the assembly, remodelling and disassembly of the lipid bilayer and its associated scaffolds. It determines cell shape and polarity, the formation of caveolae and membrane microdomains, wound resealing after sarcolemmal injury, and the membrane fusion events of myoblast and sperm-egg fusion. Caveolins and cavin, flotillin, and BIN/amphiphysin and PACSIN family proteins generate and stabilise curvature, while dynamin, sorting nexins and the ESCRT-III subunits with VPS4 ATPases sever and reseal membrane necks. Spectrin, ankyrin, plectin and myosin link the bilayer to the cortical cytoskeleton, and scramblases and flippases of the XKR, PLSCR and ATP8B/ATP10 families redistribute phospholipids to expose or conceal surface signals such as phosphatidylserine. Loss of these activities underlies muscular dystrophies, cholestasis, peripheral neuropathies and defects in fertilisation.

post-chaperonin tubulin folding pathway finishes the job of making usable tubulin: after the CCT chaperonin releases partially folded alpha- and beta-tubulin, a set of dedicated cofactors completes folding and assembles the two into the heterodimer that microtubules are built from. Everything that depends on microtubules — mitotic spindles, cilia and flagella, intracellular transport, neuronal axons — depends on this supply step, and the same cofactors also dismantle dimers, so the pathway sets the size of the free tubulin pool. Cofactors A and B capture the monomers, C, D and E form the complex in which GTP hydrolysis validates and releases the dimer, and RP2 acts as a GTPase-activating partner for TBCC. Mutations cause retinitis pigmentosa, cortical malformations, and hypoparathyroidism with encephalopathy, linking dimer quality control to neurodevelopment and photoreceptor survival.

Alpha- and beta-tubulin emerge from the chaperonin only partly folded, and this post-chaperonin step finishes the job and joins the two monomers into the heterodimer that polymerises into microtubules. Without it a cell cannot build spindles, cilia or axonal tracks, and the supply of assembly-competent dimer sets the size of the usable tubulin pool. Dedicated cofactors each capture one subunit or the other, bring them together, and then hydrolyse GTP to release a native dimer; the same cofactors can run in reverse to dissociate dimers, so the pathway also governs tubulin turnover and degradation. RP2 acts as a GTPase-activating protein for ARL3 and shares activity with the cofactor C domain, and its loss causes X-linked retinitis pigmentosa, while mutations in TBCE cause hypoparathyroidism with dysmorphism and encephalopathy, and TBCD mutations give early-onset neurodegeneration.

cell cycle covers the ordered program by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it into daughter cells, the process behind all tissue growth, renewal and repair, and the process whose deregulation underlies cancer and developmental disorders. The genes span every stage: cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases with their CDK-inhibitor brakes and E2F/RB transcriptional switches that license S phase; origin licensing and replication machinery such as MCMs, CDC45, PCNA and DNA polymerases; ATM/ATR-CHEK1/CHEK2 damage and replication checkpoints converging on p53; cohesins, condensins and kinetochore-spindle assembly checkpoint components that ensure faithful chromosome segregation; centrosome duplication, tubulins and mitotic kinases such as PLK1 and Aurora; and ESCRT-dependent abscission at cytokinesis. Ubiquitin ligases including the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF impose irreversibility by timed proteolysis. Also included is the meiotic variant, with recombination, synaptonemal complex and germ-cell factors required for gametogenesis.

Cell division requires that a cell duplicate its genome once and only once, then partition the copies equally, and this pathway encompasses the whole ordered sequence from growth-factor-driven commitment through DNA replication, mitosis and cytokinesis, including the meiotic variant used in the germ line. Progression is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases paired with successive cyclins, opposed by CDK inhibitors such as p21 and p27 and gated by the retinoblastoma protein and E2F transcription factors; ubiquitin ligases including the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF impose irreversibility by timed proteolysis. Checkpoints sensing DNA damage, replication stress or unattached kinetochores act through ATM, ATR, CHEK1/2 and p53 to delay progression, while centrosomes, spindle microtubules, kinesins, cohesin, condensin and ESCRT-dependent abscission execute segregation and division. Meiosis-specific recombination and synapsis components support gamete formation. Loss of this control underlies aneuploidy, infertility and the unchecked proliferation of cancer.

Spindle organization builds, shapes and disassembles the bipolar microtubule array that segregates chromosomes at each division, and it determines whether daughter cells inherit a correct genome and where the division plane falls. Loss of fidelity here produces aneuploidy, chromosomal instability in tumours, and, through mutations in centrosomal and spindle-pole components such as ASPM and WDR62, microcephaly from depleted neural progenitor pools. The genes cover nucleation by the γ-tubulin ring complex and the augmin/HAUS branching machinery, RAN-GTP release of TPX2 to activate Aurora A, motor-driven pole separation and antiparallel sliding by kinesins and dynein, plus-end regulation by CKAP5, CLASPs and EB proteins, kinetochore attachment through NDC80 and SKA complexes, and cortical force generation that orients the spindle. Chromosomal passenger, PLK1 and cohesin components couple spindle geometry to error correction, anaphase onset and midbody abscission.

Before a dividing cell can separate its chromosomes it must build a bipolar microtubule array, and spindle organization covers the assembly, shaping, positioning and eventual disassembly of that structure. Get it wrong and chromosomes missegregate, producing aneuploid daughters, or the division plane is misplaced, which in neural progenitors causes microcephaly. Nucleation begins at centrosomes and on pre-existing microtubules through the gamma-tubulin complex and the augmin subunits, while RAN-GTP gradients and TPX2 activate Aurora A to promote assembly near chromatin. Motors such as the kinesin KIF11 push poles apart, kinetochore-associated NDC80 and SKA modules couple chromosomes to microtubule tips, and CKAP5 and CLASP proteins regulate plus-end dynamics. Aurora B within the inner-centromere complex corrects faulty attachments, PLK1 and cyclin B-CDK1 time the whole programme, and cortical cues orient the spindle to set the axis of division.

Spindle assembly involved in female meiosis builds the microtubule apparatus that segregates chromosomes in the oocyte, the step that determines whether an egg carries the correct chromosome number. Because oocyte spindles form without canonical centrosomes and must hold chromosomes through long arrest, this process is error-prone, and its failure is the main source of aneuploid eggs, miscarriage and maternal age-related infertility; mutations in the oocyte-specific tubulin TUBB8 cause oocyte maturation arrest in women. The genes cover microtubule nucleation and pole organisation under Aurora A kinase, kinetochore-microtubule attachment through the NDC80 and SKA complexes, cohesin release by WAPL, and control of anaphase timing via cyclin B and the APC/C inhibitor FBXO5. It therefore sits at the intersection of meiotic cell cycle regulation, cytoskeletal organisation and reproductive competence.

Oocytes divide without centrosomes and must build a bipolar spindle from scratch, and spindle assembly in female meiosis is the process that does it, positioning chromosomes for the asymmetric divisions that produce a single egg and its polar bodies. Errors here are a principal source of aneuploid eggs, miscarriage and trisomy, and mutations in the oocyte-specific β-tubulin TUBB8 cause oocyte maturation arrest and female infertility. Aurora A kinase organises acentrosomal microtubule nucleation and spindle poles, while the NDC80 complex with the SKA1–SKA3 subcomplex couples kinetochores to dynamic microtubule ends. Cyclin B2 and the APC/C inhibitor FBXO5 time the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, and cohesin regulation through WAPL governs how sister chromatid linkages are resolved across two sequential divisions. The pathway sits at the intersection of cytoskeletal organisation, chromosome segregation and the oocyte-specific control of meiotic progression.

Chromosome segregation is the machinery that divides replicated genetic material equally between daughter cells, in both mitosis and meiosis. Its accuracy determines ploidy: failure produces aneuploidy, micronuclei and chromosome instability, drives tumourigenesis, and in the germline causes infertility, miscarriage and trisomic offspring. The genes cover the whole sequence — condensin-driven chromosome compaction and topoisomerase-mediated decatenation, cohesin loading and its protection at centromeres by shugoshin, assembly of the CENP-A-marked centromere and the outer kinetochore that grips spindle microtubules, and the bipolar spindle built by gamma-tubulin complexes, augmin, kinesins and dynein. Aurora and Polo kinases with the spindle assembly checkpoint license anaphase only when attachments are correct, at which point the anaphase-promoting complex destroys securin and cyclin B to release separase. A meiosis-specific arm adds synaptonemal complex formation, programmed double-strand breaks and crossover control, plus ESCRT-dependent abscission at the end of division.

Accurate partitioning of duplicated chromosomes into daughter cells is what keeps genomes stable across divisions; when it fails, cells acquire aneuploidy and structural rearrangements that drive tumourigenesis, miscarriage and developmental disorders. The genes here cover the whole sequence: condensin and cohesin complexes compact chromosomes and hold sister chromatids together, centromeric CENP proteins and the HJURP chaperone define the kinetochore platform, and the NDC80, MIS12 and SKA modules couple that platform to spindle microtubules nucleated from gamma-tubulin complexes and augmin. Aurora kinases, PLK1, BUB1 and MAD2 monitor attachment through the spindle assembly checkpoint, delaying anaphase-promoting complex activation until separase can cleave cohesin. Kinesins and dynein generate the forces that move chromosomes poleward, while ESCRT components finish abscission. A meiotic arm — synaptonemal complex proteins, SPO11, PRDM9, REC8 and the MSH4/MSH5 machinery — adapts the same problem to recombination and reductional division in germ cells.

mitotic cell cycle checkpoint signaling is the surveillance system that halts cell division until DNA is intact and chromosomes are correctly attached to the spindle, so that daughter cells receive one accurate copy of the genome. Its failure produces aneuploidy, structural rearrangements and the genomic instability that drives tumour formation, which is why several components are inherited cancer predisposition genes. Two arms dominate. Damage and replication stress are sensed by the ATM and ATR kinases with their mediators and clamp loaders, which activate CHEK1/CHEK2 and p53 to impose G1/S and G2/M arrest and stabilise stalled forks. At mitosis, kinetochore-based signalling through MAD1, MAD2, BUB1, BUBR1 and the NDC80 complex sequesters CDC20 and restrains the anaphase-promoting complex until biorientation is achieved, with Aurora B correcting faulty attachments and an abscission checkpoint delaying the final cut.

Cells that divide with damaged or unreplicated DNA, or with chromosomes not properly attached to the spindle, produce aneuploid and mutated progeny, and mitotic cell cycle checkpoint signaling is what delays division until those conditions are corrected. It underlies genome stability, and its components are classic tumour suppressors whose loss drives chromosome instability and cancer predisposition. Two broad arms are represented. Damage and replication-stress sensing runs through the ATM and ATR kinases, the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, TOPBP1, CLSPN and the CHEK1/CHEK2 effectors to p53 and CDKN1A, restraining CDK activity and origin firing. The spindle assembly checkpoint uses kinetochore components including BUB1, BUB1B, BUB3, MAD1L1, MAD2L1, the NDC80/NUF2 complex and the ROD-ZW10-Zwilch module to sequester CDC20 and block anaphase-promoting complex activity until attachments are correct. Aurora B with INCENP and survivin corrects errors, while abscission checkpoint proteins delay the final cut.

male meiosis I is the reductional division of spermatocytes, the step that halves chromosome number and shuffles parental alleles before sperm are made; when it fails, spermatocytes arrest and are cleared, producing azoospermia and male infertility. The genes trace its defining events: SPO11 introduces programmed double-strand breaks, DMC1, MEIOB, BRCA2, RAD51C and HSF2BP direct their repair by homologous recombination onto the homologue rather than the sister chromatid, SYCP3 and REC8 build the synaptonemal complex and hold cohesion until anaphase, and TRIP13 governs checkpoint release and crossover maturation. Layered on this are germline transcriptional and chromatin programmes -- MYBL1, BRDT, DNMT3L and the piRNA factors MOV10L1 and TDRD9 that silence transposons -- together with CCNA1 and HSPA2 driving the meiotic G2/M transition. The pathway thus links genome recombination, chromosome segregation and spermatogenic differentiation.

Spermatocytes halve their chromosome number in the first meiotic division, and this male-specific programme covers the events that get them through it: double-strand break formation, homologous pairing and recombination, sister chromatid cohesion, and the transcriptional switch that licenses progression. Its output is haploid, genetically recombined spermatids; failure causes spermatocyte arrest, apoptotic loss of germ cells and azoospermic infertility, and mis-segregation yields aneuploid sperm. SPO11 initiates programmed breaks that DMC1, MEIOB, BRCA2 and RAD51C resolve using the homologue as template, TRIP13 governs checkpoint turnover of repair intermediates, REC8 and SYCP3 build the cohesion and synaptonemal axis that holds bivalents together, and MYBL1 and CCNA1 drive the meiotic transcriptional and cell cycle machinery. A piRNA arm including MOV10L1 and TDRD9 silences transposons, protecting the germline genome while recombination leaves it transiently broken.

Cell adhesion covers the molecular machinery by which cells attach to one another and to the extracellular matrix, the basis of tissue architecture, epithelial barriers, immune cell trafficking, wound healing and neural wiring. Loss of adhesion control underlies metastasis, blistering skin disease, leaky epithelia and inflammatory pathology. The genes span the major adhesion receptor families — cadherins and protocadherins at adherens junctions and desmosomes, claudins and tight-junction scaffolds such as TJP1 and F11R, integrins with their talin, kindlin and paxillin-linked focal adhesion complexes, selectins and immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors (ICAMs, VCAM1, NCAM1, nectins, CADMs) used for leukocyte rolling and immune synapse formation — together with their matrix ligands: collagens, laminins, fibronectin and thrombospondins. Downstream, Src, FAK, Rho-family GTPases and catenin–actin linkages convert attachment into cytoskeletal remodelling, migration, survival signalling and transcriptional change, coupling adhesion to development and differentiation.

Cell adhesion is how cells attach to one another and to the extracellular matrix, and it underlies almost every multicellular arrangement: epithelial sheets that seal a lumen, endothelium that retains blood, synapses that pair the right neurons, and leukocytes that stick to vessel walls before entering tissue. The machinery falls into recognisable families here dash cadherins, protocadherins and catenins at adherens junctions; claudins, occludin partners and tight-junction scaffolds such as ZO proteins; desmosomal cadherins with plakophilins and desmoplakin; integrins with talin, kindlin, paxillin and focal adhesion kinase linking matrix ligands like fibronectin, laminins and collagens to the actin cytoskeleton; and selectins, ICAMs and immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors mediating immune contacts. Adhesion complexes also signal, controlling survival, polarity, migration and differentiation. Loss of adhesive integrity produces blistering skin and kidney disease, barrier failure, immunodeficiency, and the detachment and invasion that accompany tumour metastasis.

Homophilic cell-cell adhesion is the binding of a surface molecule on one cell to the same molecule on its neighbour, a like-binds-like rule that lets tissues sort themselves into layers, boundaries and compartments without any external instruction. It builds epithelial sheets and junctions, keeps endothelial barriers sealed, and in the nervous system supplies the recognition code by which axons choose partners, tile dendritic fields and avoid their own sister branches. The classical and desmosomal cadherins anchor adherens junctions and desmosomes to the cytoskeleton, while the clustered protocadherin locus generates combinatorial identities that give individual neurons a distinguishing surface signature. Immunoglobulin-superfamily members such as nectins, CADMs, DSCAM and L1CAM, and guidance receptors including the ROBO family, extend the same principle to synapse formation and axon guidance. Loss of this adhesion underlies blistering skin disease, deafness, retinal degeneration, and the invasive behaviour of carcinomas after cadherin downregulation.

Tissues hold together in part by like-binding-like: an adhesion molecule on one cell engages an identical molecule on its neighbour, so that cells of the same type sort into coherent sheets, layers and boundaries. This homophilic cell-cell adhesion underlies epithelial integrity, endothelial barrier function, and the wiring specificity of neurons, and its failure shows up as loss of epithelial cohesion in cancer invasion, blistering skin disease when desmosomal components are attacked, and neurodevelopmental disorders. The classical cadherins, including the epithelial and neural forms, couple such binding to the actin cytoskeleton at adherens junctions, while desmogleins and desmocollins anchor desmosomes. The very large clustered protocadherin families, expressed in stochastic combinations, give individual neurons a recognition identity used for self-avoidance and dendritic patterning. Nectins, CADMs, contactins, receptor tyrosine phosphatases and the atypical FAT and CELSR cadherins extend the same logic to synapse formation, planar polarity and tissue growth control.

Receptor guanylyl cyclase signaling pathway covers hormone and peptide signals that are transduced by cell-surface receptors which are themselves cyclase enzymes, generating cGMP directly rather than through G proteins. It sets blood pressure and fluid balance, controls intestinal fluid secretion, drives skeletal growth at the growth plate, and resets photoreceptors after light. Natriuretic peptides ANP, BNP and CNP bind NPR1 and NPR2 to raise cGMP and activate protein kinase G, relaxing vascular smooth muscle and promoting natriuresis; guanylin-family peptides acting on intestinal GUCY2C regulate salt and water movement and epithelial turnover; retinal GUCY2D and GUCY2F, tuned by calcium-sensing activator proteins, restore cGMP to gated channels in phototransduction. Phosphodiesterases such as PDE2A and PDE10A terminate the signal. Loss of these components causes hypertension and heart failure, secretory diarrhoea, skeletal dysplasia, and inherited retinal degeneration.

Some hormone receptors are themselves enzymes: binding of a peptide ligand to the extracellular domain switches on an intracellular guanylyl cyclase domain that makes cGMP from GTP, and this receptor guanylyl cyclase route converts that second messenger into changes in ion transport, tone and gene expression. Two arms dominate. Natriuretic peptides secreted by the heart and vasculature act through their cyclase-linked receptors to lower blood pressure, promote natriuresis and, via a separate receptor, drive the chondrocyte proliferation that sets long bone growth. An intestinal receptor responds to guanylin-family peptides to control fluid secretion and is the target hijacked by bacterial heat-stable enterotoxin in secretory diarrhoea. Retina-specific cyclases, regulated by calcium-sensing activator proteins, restore cGMP after photon absorption and are mutated in inherited retinal degeneration. Output is read by cGMP-dependent protein kinase and terminated by cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases.

cell surface receptor protein serine/threonine kinase signaling pathway is essentially the TGF-beta superfamily axis: ligands such as TGF-beta, the BMPs, activins, inhibins, nodal, GDFs and anti-Mullerian hormone binding type II receptors that recruit and phosphorylate type I receptors, which in turn phosphorylate receptor-SMADs for transport to the nucleus with SMAD4. It patterns the embryo, specifies left-right asymmetry, builds bone and cartilage, drives epithelial-mesenchymal transition and fibrosis, restrains epithelial proliferation, and sets hepcidin-dependent iron balance; its loss underlies skeletal dysplasias, vascular malformations such as hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, and tumour progression. Output is heavily tuned rather than simply transmitted: secreted antagonists like noggin, chordin, gremlin and follistatin sequester ligands, latent complexes and integrins control activation, inhibitory SMAD6/7 with SMURF ubiquitin ligases terminate signalling, and SKI/SnoN with histone deacetylase complexes and numerous microRNAs shape the transcriptional response.

Signalling through cell surface receptors that are themselves serine/threonine kinases is essentially the TGF-beta superfamily system: ligands such as TGF-beta isoforms, activins, inhibins, nodal, anti-Mullerian hormone, myostatin and the many BMPs and GDFs bind paired type I and type II receptors, whose kinase activity phosphorylates SMAD transcription factors that partner with SMAD4 and reach the nucleus to reprogramme gene expression. The outputs shape embryonic patterning and left-right asymmetry, bone and cartilage formation, muscle mass, fibrosis and extracellular matrix deposition, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, immune suppression and iron homeostasis via hepcidin control. Much of the gene content is regulatory: secreted antagonists like noggin, follistatin, gremlins and chordin, latent complex and matrix binding proteins, decoy receptors, inhibitory SMAD6/SMAD7 with SMURF ubiquitin ligases, phosphatases, corepressors such as SKI and TGIF, and numerous microRNAs. Loss of restraint underlies skeletal dysplasias, vascular malformations, pulmonary hypertension, cancer progression and organ fibrosis.

G protein-coupled receptor signaling pathway, coupled to cyclic nucleotide second messenger is the route by which hormones, neurotransmitters, chemokines and drugs change the intracellular concentration of cAMP or cGMP, converting an extracellular ligand into a graded, amplified change in kinase activity and gene expression. It sets heart rate, smooth muscle tone, steroid and thyroid hormone output, lipolysis, pigmentation, mood and nociception, and it is the target of a large share of prescribed medicines. Receptors here couple through Gs to stimulate adenylate cyclase or through Gi/Go to inhibit it, with cAMP acting mainly on protein kinase A and Epac. The membership spans adrenergic, muscarinic, serotonergic, histaminergic, opioid, cannabinoid, somatostatin, melanocortin and glycoprotein hormone receptors, so receptor pairs on the same cell can push cyclase in opposite directions and tune the response. Loss or constitutive activation of individual receptors causes endocrine and metabolic disease.

Many hormones, neurotransmitters and drugs act on cells without entering them, and this is the route by which they do it: a receptor at the surface engages a heterotrimeric G protein that turns adenylate or guanylate cyclase up or down, and the resulting change in cyclic nucleotide concentration sets protein kinase activity, ion channel behaviour and gene expression. The receptors named here span the pharmacology of the nervous and endocrine systems — muscarinic acetylcholine, serotonin, histamine, dopamine, opioid, cannabinoid, somatostatin and melanocortin receptors, together with peptide hormone receptors for thyrotropin, parathyroid hormone, luteinizing hormone and VIP. Stimulatory coupling raises cAMP and mobilises steroidogenesis, glycogenolysis or lipolysis; inhibitory coupling lowers it and damps neuronal firing and transmitter release. Because this signalling is dose-graded and reversible, it is the most heavily drugged interface in medicine, and activating receptor mutations cause endocrine hyperfunction such as familial hyperthyroidism and precocious puberty.

Adenylate cyclase-activating serotonin receptor signaling pathway is the excitatory, cAMP-raising branch of serotonin signalling, used when serotonin needs to increase rather than dampen the activity of a target cell. It governs gut motility and secretion, mood, cognition and sleep-wake regulation, and its receptors are drug targets: 5-HT4 agonists are prokinetics for constipation, while 5-HT6 and 5-HT7 antagonism is pursued for cognitive and psychiatric indications. Mechanistically, serotonin binds 5-HT4, 5-HT6 or 5-HT7, which couple through the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit encoded by GNAS to adenylate cyclase, so that ATP is converted to cAMP; the resulting rise in cAMP activates protein kinase A and alters ion channel conductance, neurotransmitter release, smooth muscle contraction and gene expression. It stands in functional opposition to the Gi-coupled serotonin receptors that inhibit the same cyclase.

Serotonin does not act through a single mechanism; one branch of its signalling raises intracellular cAMP, and that is what this adenylate cyclase-activating serotonin receptor pathway describes. Receptors of the 5-HT4, 5-HT6 and 5-HT7 classes couple through the stimulatory G protein subunit encoded by GNAS to membrane adenylyl cyclase, so that serotonin binding increases cAMP and activates protein kinase A and downstream transcriptional and channel targets. The consequences are regional: enhanced neuronal excitability and neurotransmitter release in cortex and hippocampus, modulation of mood, cognition and circadian and thermoregulatory output, and stimulation of peristalsis in the gut, where 5-HT4 agonists are used as prokinetic drugs. The same receptors are pursued as targets in depression, schizophrenia-associated cognitive deficits and irritable bowel syndrome, placing this arm of serotonergic transmission at the interface between neuromodulation and cyclic nucleotide second-messenger control.

Phospholipase C-activating G protein-coupled acetylcholine receptor signaling pathway is the excitatory arm of muscarinic cholinergic transmission, in which acetylcholine acting through Gq-coupled receptors mobilises intracellular calcium rather than altering cyclic AMP. It drives smooth muscle contraction in airway, gut and bladder, glandular secretion, and slow depolarising responses in neurons that support learning and memory; blocking it is the basis of bronchodilator and antispasmodic anticholinergic drugs. Ligand binding to M1, M3 or M5-type receptors activates Gq/G11 family alpha subunits, which stimulate phospholipase C beta to cleave PIP2 into inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol. IP3 opens receptor channels on the endoplasmic reticulum to release stored calcium, while diacylglycerol and calcium together activate protein kinase C, whose substrates carry the signal to contractile machinery, ion channels and transcriptional programs.

Acetylcholine acts through two receptor families, and this route covers the muscarinic arm that raises intracellular calcium: agonist binding to M1, M2 or M3 receptors couples to Gq-family subunits, which activate phospholipase C beta to cleave PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate. IP3 opens its receptor channel on the endoplasmic reticulum to release stored calcium, while DAG and calcium together engage protein kinase C, converging on contraction, secretion and changes in gene expression. This is the signalling underlying parasympathetic control of smooth muscle tone, glandular secretion and gastric acid release, and in the brain the M1 pathway shapes cortical and hippocampal excitability and memory. Muscarinic antagonists and agonists acting here treat overactive bladder, COPD, and glaucoma, and loss of M1-mediated signalling is implicated in cognitive decline. The presence of M2, normally Gi-coupled, reflects promiscuous coupling to Gq at high receptor density.

G protein-coupled acetylcholine receptor signaling pathway covers the slow, modulatory arm of cholinergic transmission, in which acetylcholine acts through muscarinic receptors rather than ion channels to reset the excitability, secretion and contractile tone of a target cell. It is the basis of parasympathetic control of heart rate, smooth muscle and glandular output, of cholinergic modulation of learning and memory in cortex and hippocampus, and of the actions of atropine-like and pro-cholinergic drugs. The five muscarinic receptors split by G protein coupling: M1, M3 and M5 engage Gq/G11 to activate phospholipase C-beta, releasing inositol trisphosphate, calcium through ITPR1, and protein kinase C, while M2 and M4 act through Gi to lower cyclic AMP and open potassium channels. Kinases such as GRK2 and RGS proteins terminate the signal, and receptor output feeds into transcriptional and synaptic plasticity programs.

Acetylcholine acts not only through fast ionotropic channels but also through the five muscarinic receptors, and this slower, G protein-coupled arm of cholinergic transmission sets the tone of parasympathetic control and of cortical and hippocampal circuits. It slows the heart, drives glandular secretion and smooth muscle contraction, and shapes attention, learning and memory; loss of this signalling contributes to cognitive decline, and its receptors are the targets of atropine-like antimuscarinics and of bronchodilator therapy. The odd-numbered receptors couple through Gq/G11 to phospholipase C beta, generating inositol trisphosphate that opens ITPR1 channels and releasing calcium alongside protein kinase C activation, while the even-numbered ones signal through Gi to lower cyclic AMP and act via beta-gamma subunits. Receptor kinases and RGS proteins terminate the response, and shared downstream components link the cascade to histamine and opioid receptor signalling and to transcriptional change.

Notch receptor processing converts a membrane-bound Notch receptor into a transcriptional signal by cutting it apart in a defined order, and it is the step that makes juxtacrine cell-cell communication possible. Neighbouring cells use this to decide between alternative fates during neurogenesis, somite and vascular patterning, gut and skin stem cell renewal, and T cell development; when the cleavages run unchecked the released intracellular domain drives leukaemic and other cancers, which is why the enzymes here are drug targets. Ligand binding exposes an extracellular site cut by the ADAM17 metalloprotease, and the remaining stub is cleaved within the membrane by gamma-secretase, whose catalytic presenilin subunit works with nicastrin, APH1 and PEN-2 to liberate the intracellular domain for nuclear entry. Glycosylation and ligands such as DNER modulate which cells receive the signal.

Notch is a receptor that signals by being cut apart: ligand binding triggers successive proteolytic cleavages that release its intracellular domain to travel to the nucleus and switch on transcription, so receptor processing is the activating step rather than a preliminary to it. This is how neighbouring cells make divergent fate choices, and it underlies lateral inhibition during neurogenesis, boundary formation in somites, intestinal and haematopoietic progenitor decisions, and vascular patterning; loss or gain of cleavage efficiency shifts all of these at once. A metalloprotease of the ADAM family performs the ectodomain shedding step, after which the gamma-secretase complex — presenilin as the catalytic aspartyl protease together with nicastrin, APH-1 and PEN-2 — cuts within the transmembrane region. Glycosylation of the extracellular repeats tunes ligand responsiveness. The same protease complex also processes amyloid precursor protein, linking this machinery to Alzheimer disease.

positive regulation of transcription of Notch receptor target is the nuclear endpoint of Notch signalling, the step at which contact between neighbouring cells is converted into a change in gene expression. It governs binary cell-fate decisions throughout development and adult tissue renewal — neurogenesis, T-lymphocyte specification, vascular and intestinal patterning — and its deregulation drives T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, while loss of pathway components causes vascular and skeletal malformation. After ligand binding and proteolysis, the released Notch intracellular domain enters the nucleus and binds RBPJ, displacing corepressors; recruitment of a Mastermind-like coactivator (MAML1, MAML2 or MAML3) completes a ternary complex that engages histone acetyltransferases and stimulates target transcription, including HES and HEY repressors. RBM15 links the same machinery to RNA-level control. The output is inherently transient, since the complex is rapidly phosphorylated and degraded.

When a Notch receptor is cleaved, its intracellular domain travels to the nucleus and switches on target genes, and this is the transcriptional output step of that pathway. It is how cell-fate decisions are executed during development: lateral inhibition between neighbouring cells, boundary formation, maintenance of stem and progenitor pools, and lineage choice in the nervous system, gut, skin and blood. The released Notch1 or Notch4 intracellular domain binds the DNA-binding factor RBPJ, converting it from a repressor into an activator, and recruits a Mastermind-like coactivator (MAML1, MAML2 or MAML3) to assemble the ternary complex that drives transcription of HES and HEY family targets. Because the receptor itself is the transcription cofactor, signalling is short-lived and dose-sensitive. Fusions and mutations affecting these coactivators and receptors recur in leukaemias and salivary gland tumours.

activation of NF-kappaB-inducing kinase activity describes how upstream receptors switch on NIK, the kinase that drives the non-canonical NF-kappaB route to processing of p100 into p52. This is the arm of NF-kappaB signalling that builds and maintains lymphoid tissue: lymphotoxin alpha/beta acting through the lymphotoxin beta receptor organises lymph node and spleen architecture and germinal centre stroma, and its loss leaves secondary lymphoid organs malformed. Tumour necrosis factor receptors, death receptors and Toll-like receptors feed into the same output, coupling infection and inflammatory cues to transcription of survival and chemokine genes. Activation works largely by relieving constitutive degradation, with the ubiquitin ligase ZFP91 stabilising NIK, while CARD10 and CARD14 scaffold receptor-proximal signalling in epithelium and skin, where gain-of-function mutations cause psoriasis. Sustained NIK activity is a feature of multiple myeloma and other lymphoid malignancies.

NF-kappaB-inducing kinase sits at the head of the non-canonical NF-kappaB branch, and its activation is the step that licenses processing of the p100 precursor into active p52 for genes controlling lymphoid tissue organisation, stromal chemokine production and inflammatory survival signalling. Because the kinase is constitutively degraded in resting cells, stimulation depends on receptor engagement stabilising and phosphorylating it: the lymphotoxin ligands and their receptor, TNF receptor family members including TNFRSF1A/1B and the death receptors TNFRSF10A/10B, and Toll-like receptors such as TLR3 and TLR6 all feed in, with CARD10 and CARD14 scaffolding downstream complex assembly and ZFP91 acting as a ubiquitin ligase that spares the kinase from turnover. Loss of this input compromises lymph node and Peyer's patch development and germinal centre responses, while excessive activity drives chronic inflammation, psoriatic skin disease and lymphoid malignancy.

small GTPase-mediated signal transduction covers the nucleotide-switch relays that convert receptor and adhesion cues into decisions about cell shape, movement, growth and membrane traffic. These switches set cytoskeletal architecture during neuronal outgrowth, immune cell migration and epithelial junction assembly, drive vesicle budding and endosomal sorting, and gate proliferative signalling; their deregulation underlies RASopathies, cancer and neurodevelopmental disease. The logic is uniform across families: guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as SOS1, VAV and DOCK proteins load GTP, GTPase-activating proteins including NF1, DLC1 and the ARHGAP family terminate the signal, and GDIs sequester inactive pools. Effectors then execute the output, as when RHOA acts through ROCK on actomyosin, RAC1 through WAVE complexes on lamellipodia, RAS through RAF-MEK on transcription, RHEB on mTOR-dependent growth, and RAB and ARF proteins on compartment identity. Guidance receptors, integrins and G protein-coupled receptors feed into the same cassettes.

Small monomeric GTPases act as nucleotide-dependent switches that convert receptor activation into defined cellular outputs, and this signalling cassette covers the Ras, Rho, Rap, Ral, Rab and Arf families together with the regulators that set their timing. Because these switches control cytoskeletal remodelling, cell shape and polarity, adhesion, migration, vesicle traffic and growth-factor-driven proliferation, they determine how cells crawl, divide, extend neurites and organise epithelial and vascular junctions. Activation state is governed by exchange factors that load GTP, GTPase-activating proteins that accelerate hydrolysis, and dissociation inhibitors that sequester the inactive GDP-bound form, illustrated here by large families of Rho GEFs and GAPs, DOCK-ELMO modules, SOS and RasGRP exchange factors, and NF1 and TSC2 as GAPs for Ras and Rheb. Downstream effectors include ROCK kinases, WASP/WAVE actin nucleation machinery and the RAF-MEK cascade. Mutations in these switches and their regulators underlie cancers, RASopathies, and neurodevelopmental and vascular malformation syndromes.

Acrosome reaction is the single-shot exocytotic event that licenses a sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida and fuse with the egg; sperm that cannot complete it are fertilization-incompetent, a recognized cause of male infertility. Binding to zona glycoproteins ZP2, ZP3 and ZP4 triggers calcium entry and a phospholipase-driven second messenger cascade, with progesterone acting through ABHD2 to open the CatSper-associated pathway while proton and calcium channels alkalinize and depolarize the cell. The outer acrosomal membrane then fuses with the plasma membrane using conventional SNARE and priming machinery -- syntaxin, Munc18, Munc13, synaptotagmins and RAB3A -- releasing hydrolases such as acrosin and hyaluronidase, restrained by their cognate serine protease inhibitors. Exposure of inner acrosomal and equatorial proteins including SPESP1 and EQTN remodels the sperm surface for gamete membrane fusion, linking regulated secretion to sexual reproduction.

Fertilisation requires a sperm to shed the contents of its single anterior secretory granule at the moment it meets the egg coat, and the acrosome reaction is that regulated exocytotic event. Zona pellucida glycoproteins ZP2, ZP3 and ZP4 provide the binding cue; calcium entry and lipid signalling through phospholipases, adenylate cyclase and progesterone-responsive ABHD2 convert it into membrane fusion, with the outer acrosomal membrane joining the sperm plasma membrane and releasing acrosin and hyaluronidase-type hydrolases that digest a path through the zona. The release machinery is the same SNARE and synaptotagmin apparatus used at synapses, here anchored by sperm-specific scaffolds and RAB3A. Protease inhibitors of the SPINK family and proprotein convertase processing restrain premature activation. Sperm that cannot complete the reaction, or complete it too early, fail to fuse with the oocyte, a recognised cause of male infertility and a target for contraception.

Penetration of zona pellucida is the step of fertilization in which a capacitated sperm drills through the glycoprotein coat surrounding the oocyte so that the two plasma membranes can meet. Without it fertilization fails outright, and defects in the sperm head structures involved are a recognized cause of male infertility. The work depends on the acrosome, a modified lysosome capping the sperm nucleus, whose regulated exocytosis releases hydrolases such as acrosin and hyaluronidase together with glycosidases that cleave zona sugars; a sperm-surface galactosyltransferase contributes to recognition of zona glycoproteins. Other members reflect the sperm-specific architecture that makes this possible — acrosomal and inner-acrosomal membrane proteins, the mitochondria-associated cysteine-rich protein of the flagellum that supports the motility needed for mechanical thrust, and the calcineurin subunit and protamine that mark spermatid remodelling into a fertilization-competent cell.

Fertilization requires a sperm to breach the glycoprotein coat surrounding the egg, and penetration of the zona pellucida is the step that grants access to the oocyte plasma membrane for fusion. Failure at this point is a cause of male infertility even when sperm counts and motility appear normal. The work is done largely by the acrosome, a secretory organelle derived from lysosomes that caps the sperm head and releases hydrolases on contact with the zona: acrosin, a trypsin-like protease, along with glycosidases such as beta-hexosaminidase and hyaluronidase activity that loosen the matrix. Other contributors reflect the specialized architecture and signalling of the sperm head and tail, including sperm mitochondria-associated cysteine-rich protein, acrosomal membrane proteins, a testis-specific calcineurin regulatory subunit, and the chromatin-compacting transition protein laid down during spermiogenesis.

regulation of mitotic cell cycle governs whether and how fast a cell commits to division, ensuring that DNA is replicated once and chromosomes are segregated accurately; its failure produces aneuploidy, genome instability and the unchecked proliferation typical of cancer. The controls act at several decision points: cyclin-CDK pairs with their CDK inhibitors and the RB-E2F switch set the restriction point for S-phase entry; CDC25 phosphatases opposed by WEE1 and MYT1 time mitotic entry; ATM/ATR, CHEK1/2 and p53 impose damage and replication checkpoints; and the spindle assembly checkpoint (MAD2, BUB1/BUB3, kinetochore NDC80 and KNL1 complexes) restrains the anaphase-promoting complex until attachment is complete, whereupon APC/C-CDC20 ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction of cyclin B and securin trigger sister chromatid separation. Aurora, PLK and NEK kinases, chromatin remodellers and numerous microRNAs tune these transitions to growth-factor and stress input.

Cells divide only when conditions permit, and the regulation of the mitotic cell cycle is the control layer that decides when to advance, when to pause, and when to abandon division altogether. It sets proliferation rates in development and tissue renewal, and its loosening is the route to genomic instability and cancer, which is why so many of its members are tumour suppressors and oncogenes. Cyclin–CDK pairs with their inhibitors drive the transitions, Rb–E2F gates entry into S phase, and CDC25 phosphatases oppose WEE1/MYT1 to license mitotic entry. DNA damage and replication stress feed in through ATM, ATR and CHEK1/2 to TP53, arresting progression until lesions are repaired. Spindle assembly checkpoint proteins including MAD2L1, BUB1 and the kinetochore NDC80 complex hold the anaphase-promoting complex inactive until chromosomes attach, and ubiquitin–proteasome degradation makes each transition irreversible. Chromatin remodellers, microRNAs and growth factor signalling tune the whole programme.

Gastrulation is the embryonic reorganisation that converts a simple epiblast into the three germ layers — ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm — and establishes the body axes on which all later organogenesis depends. Failure at this stage is lethal or produces axis and laterality defects such as holoprosencephaly, caudal dysgenesis and heterotaxy. The genes describe how it is run: Nodal, BMP and WNT gradients, restrained by antagonists such as CER1, NOG, DKK1 and SFRP, signal through SMAD2/3, SMAD1/4 and β-catenin to switch on primitive-streak transcription factors including TBXT, EOMES, MIXL1, GSC, FOXA2, MESP1 and SOX17, while POU5F1, NANOG and SOX2 mark the pluripotent state being exited. Cells then execute epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and directed migration, using SNAI1, planar cell polarity components, integrins, laminins and collagens, and matrix metalloproteinases to ingress through the streak and pattern the nascent mesoderm.

Gastrulation converts a simple epiblast into a three-layered embryo, generating ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm and setting up the body axes on which all later organogenesis depends. Failure at this stage is embryonic lethal, and partial defects produce axis duplication, situs abnormalities, caudal truncation and heart and node malformations. The genes here trace the signalling logic: Nodal, BMP and Activin ligands acting through type I/II receptors and SMAD2/3 or SMAD1, WNT ligands with Frizzled receptors, beta-catenin and LEF1, FGF8 through FGFR1, and secreted antagonists such as Cerberus, Noggin and DKK1 that carve out the organizer. Transcription factors including TBXT, EOMES, MIXL1, GSC, FOXA2, SOX17 and MESP1/2 specify primitive streak and germ-layer fates, while planar-cell-polarity components, integrins, laminins, collagens and matrix metalloproteinases drive the epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cell migration that physically reorganize the embryo.

endoderm development tracks the innermost germ layer from its specification at gastrulation to the mature tissues it builds — the gut tube and its derivatives, including liver, pancreas, thyroid and lung epithelium. Getting it right determines whether an embryo forms a digestive and respiratory system at all, and the same signalling logic is exploited to direct pluripotent stem cells toward hepatic and pancreatic fates. Nodal and its downstream SMAD2/3–SMAD4 relay, tuned by BMP4, GDF3, FGF8 and the antagonists NOG and DKK1, drives POU5F1/NANOG-positive epiblast cells through EOMES, MIXL1 and SOX17 into definitive endoderm, after which HNF1B, GATA4/6, ONECUT1 and NKX2-1 impose regional and organ identity. Wnt–CTNNB1 input, PAF1 complex and chromatin regulators such as SETD2 and HDAC1 set transcriptional competence, while laminins, collagens, integrins and matrix metalloproteinases provide the adhesive and remodelling context for the cell movements involved.

During gastrulation the innermost germ layer is specified and then elaborated into the epithelia of the gut tube, liver, pancreas, thyroid and lungs, and endoderm development covers that whole trajectory from germ-layer formation to organ primordia. Nodal and GDF signals acting through SMAD2/3 with SMAD4 drive the transition, opposed by the antagonists Noggin and DKK1, while BMP4 and FGF8 pattern the emerging sheet. Pluripotency and mesendoderm transcription factors including POU5F1, NANOG, EOMES, MIXL1, SOX17, GATA4/6, HNF1B and ONECUT1 hand off in sequence to commit and regionalise cells, with NKX2-1 marking thyroid and lung endoderm. Cell movement depends on integrins, laminins and fibronectin, remodelled by matrix metalloproteinases, and chromatin and transcription-elongation machinery such as the PAF complex, SETD2 and HDAC1 licenses the switches. Failure yields gastrulation arrest and malformed foregut-derived organs.
