Heart development is the program that builds a four-chambered pump from mesoderm and keeps it beating, covering cardiac progenitor specification, chamber and valve morphogenesis, conduction system patterning, and the maturation of contractile muscle. Its failure is the origin of congenital heart disease, the commonest birth defect, and of cardiomyopathies and arrhythmias that appear later. A core of transcription factors including NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, MEF2C, HAND1/2 and ISL1 acts with Notch, BMP/TGF-beta, Wnt, Hedgehog and FGF signalling to assign cells to first and second heart fields, drive endocardial cushion epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and remodel outflow tract and septa. Nodal, laterality determinants and ciliary and intraflagellar transport components set left-right asymmetry before looping. Downstream, sarcomeric and cytoskeletal proteins such as TTN, MYH6/7 and TNNT2, calcium handling machinery, gap junctions and cardiac microRNAs establish rhythmic, force-generating myocardium and its vascular supply.

Cardiogenesis takes mesodermal progenitors through specification, looping of the linear heart tube, chamber and valve formation, septation, conduction system patterning and coronary vascularization, ending in a four-chambered pump that contracts rhythmically for life. Failure at any step underlies congenital heart disease, laterality defects and cardiomyopathy. Lineage transcription factors such as NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, HAND1/2, MEF2C and ISL1 act with chromatin regulators and Notch, BMP/TGF-beta, Wnt, Hedgehog, FGF and Nodal signalling to assign chamber identity and left-right asymmetry; motile and primary cilia genes set the initial laterality cue. Endocardial cushions form by endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition and remodel through matrix proteins and metalloproteinases into valves, while neural crest and second heart field cells build the outflow tract. Differentiation converges on sarcomere assembly and excitation-contraction coupling components including MYH6, TNNT2, TTN, RYR2 and SCN5A, alongside microRNAs and Hippo-YAP control of cardiomyocyte growth.

Neuromuscular junction development builds and maintains the synapse through which motor neurons command skeletal muscle, the structure whose failure produces myasthenia, congenital myasthenic syndromes and the denervation seen in motor neuron disease. Assembly is instructed from the nerve: neurally released agrin binds the muscle receptor complex LRP4-MuSK, which through DOK7 and downstream kinase cascades clusters acetylcholine receptors and anchors them via rapsyn to the underlying spectrin and ankyrin cytoskeleton. A specialised synaptic basal lamina of laminins, collagen IV and the collagen tail that tethers acetylcholinesterase, read by dystroglycan and its glycosyltransferases, aligns pre- and postsynaptic elements. Voltage-gated calcium channel subunits and the vesicular acetylcholine transporter equip the nerve terminal for release, while ubiquitin ligases and axonal transport components prune and refine contacts. The pathway therefore couples synaptogenesis, extracellular matrix organisation and postsynaptic receptor trafficking to voluntary movement.

The synapse between a motor neuron and skeletal muscle must be built, aligned and maintained for voluntary movement to occur, and neuromuscular junction development covers its assembly, patterning and remodelling. Nerve-derived agrin binds the muscle receptor LRP4, which activates the kinase MuSK through the adaptor DOK7; rapsyn then anchors clustered acetylcholine receptors beneath the nerve terminal, while synaptic basal lamina components including laminins, collagen IV and the collagen tail that tethers acetylcholinesterase organise the cleft. Dystroglycan and its glycosylation machinery link the postsynaptic membrane to that matrix, spectrin and ankyrin scaffolds stabilise it, and ubiquitin ligases prune excess innervation. Loss of these steps produces congenital myasthenic syndromes with fatigable weakness, and the same junction is the target of autoimmune myasthenia; several genes here also underlie motor neuron degeneration and muscular dystrophy.

digestion is the coordinated breakdown of ingested food into absorbable units and their uptake across the gut epithelium, the process that converts a meal into circulating nutrients. Its failure produces malabsorption, steatorrhoea, pancreatic insufficiency and nutritional deficiency. Pancreatic zymogens and lipases such as trypsinogens, chymotrypsinogen, colipase and PNLIP, together with gastric pepsinogens and brush-border enzymes like sucrase-isomaltase, perform the hydrolysis, while transporters including SLC5A1, SLC2A5, NPC1L1 and the ABCG5/ABCG8 sterol pump, plus fatty acid handlers CD36 and FABP2, move products into enterocytes. Secretion and motility are set by gut hormones — cholecystokinin, secretin, gastrin signalling, somatostatin, ghrelin and leptin — acting alongside cholinergic receptors. Mucins, trefoil factors and tight junction proteins maintain the barrier and paracellular ion flux, bile acid synthesis and nuclear receptors such as VDR and the LXRs adjust lipid and sterol handling to intake.

Digestion is how an animal converts food into absorbable molecules, and the genes here span the whole sequence: secretion of enzymes, acidification and buffering of the lumen, motility and appetite control, mucosal protection, and transport across the intestinal epithelium. Pancreatic acinar products such as trypsinogens, chymotrypsinogen, amylase, colipase and pancreatic lipase hydrolyse protein, starch and triglyceride, while gastric pepsinogens and the H+-handling and chloride/bicarbonate transporters set luminal pH. Gut hormones including cholecystokinin, secretin, ghrelin, somatostatin and motilin-like peptides coordinate enzyme release, gallbladder and gastric emptying with feeding, acting alongside muscarinic, histamine and serotonin receptor signalling. Brush-border sucrase-isomaltase, sugar transporters, fatty acid binding proteins, NPC1L1 and the ABCG5/ABCG8 sterol exporter govern uptake of sugars, lipids and cholesterol, and trefoil factors and mucins shield the epithelium. Failure produces malabsorption, pancreatitis, ulceration and inflammatory bowel disease.

hemostasis is the body's response to vascular injury: the arrest of bleeding by plugging a damaged vessel wall while keeping blood fluid everywhere else. Its failure in either direction is clinically obvious, giving haemophilia and von Willebrand disease when clotting is insufficient and thrombosis, stroke or myocardial infarction when it is excessive. The genes cover the whole sequence: von Willebrand factor and the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V and GPVI receptors that capture platelets on exposed collagen; thrombin, tissue factor and the vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors that convert fibrinogen to fibrin; integrin αIIbβ3 with talin, filamin and the actomyosin machinery that retracts the clot; and dense- and alpha-granule secretion, which amplifies recruitment through ADP and thromboxane receptors. Balancing them are anticoagulant and fibrinolytic controls — antithrombin, protein C with thrombomodulin, TFPI, plasminogen activators and their serpin inhibitors — plus endothelial nitric oxide and ADAMTS13, which limit clot growth to the site of damage.

Hemostasis is how the body seals a breached vessel and stops blood loss while keeping the rest of the circulation fluid, and its failure produces either bleeding disorders or pathological thrombosis. Injury exposes collagen and tissue factor, so platelets tether through von Willebrand factor to the GP1b-IX-V complex, engage collagen via GP6 and integrin alpha2beta1, then spread and aggregate through integrin alphaIIbbeta3 with talin and kindlin-3 completing activation. Thromboxane, ADP acting on P2RY1 and P2RY12, and thrombin acting on PAR receptors amplify the response through G protein, kinase and phospholipase signalling and granule release. In parallel the coagulation cascade generates thrombin to convert fibrinogen into a crosslinked fibrin clot, while antithrombin, protein C with thrombomodulin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor and the plasminogen activators restrain and eventually dissolve it. Vitamin K handling by GGCX and VKORC1, and platelet granule biogenesis, keep the system provisioned.

Sensory perception covers how the nervous system detects stimuli from the outside world and converts them into neural signals the brain can interpret. It defines the specialized receptor cells of the eye, ear, nose, tongue and skin, and its failure produces the common sensory disorders: retinitis pigmentosa and macular degeneration, congenital and progressive deafness, anosmia, cataract, and inherited insensitivity or hypersensitivity to pain. Mechanistically it spans distinct transduction logics united by a common plan of receptor, ion channel and amplifying cascade -- rhodopsin and cone opsins feeding transducin, phosphodiesterase and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels in photoreceptors; a very large odorant receptor repertoire with taste and vomeronasal receptors acting through gustducin and phospholipase C; hair-cell mechanotransduction built from cadherin-23, protocadherin-15, myosins and TMC channels; and nociceptor TRP, ASIC, PIEZO and voltage-gated sodium channels. Developmental regulators such as PAX6, CRX and POU4F3 specify these cells, while ciliary trafficking and retinoid recycling maintain them.

Sensory perception covers the machinery by which the nervous system captures a physical or chemical stimulus, transduces it into an electrical signal, and encodes its quality and intensity. The gene list spans the major modalities: visual phototransduction through rhodopsin and cone opsins, transducin, cGMP phosphodiesterase subunits, cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and the retinoid cycle enzymes that regenerate chromophore; a very large olfactory receptor repertoire with its trafficking cofactors and the vomeronasal and trace-amine receptors; sweet, umami and bitter taste receptors coupled to gustducin and PLC signalling; hair-cell mechanotransduction and stereocilia architecture via myosins, cadherin 23, protocadherin 15, usherin and whirlin; and somatosensory channels such as TRPV1, TRPM8, PIEZO2 and sensory sodium channels for pain, temperature and touch. Also present are lens crystallins and eye and ear developmental transcription factors. Failure of these components produces retinal degeneration, inherited deafness, cataract, anosmia and congenital insensitivity to pain.

behavior covers the nervous-system-dependent actions an animal takes in response to internal states and external cues tion — feeding, sleep, mating, locomotion, learning, fear and social interaction — and the molecules that generate them. It matters because these outputs define an animal's fitness, and their disruption produces autism, addiction, obesity, anxiety and movement disorders. The genes span the layers that build such responses: neurotransmitter systems (dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, GABA, opioid and cholinergic receptors and their transporters), synaptic adhesion and scaffolding proteins such as neurexins, neuroligins and SHANK family members that specify circuit wiring, activity-dependent immediate-early transcription (FOS, EGR1, ARC, NPAS4) that converts firing into lasting change, and hypothalamic peptide signalling — leptin, melanocortin, orexin, oxytocin, NPY — that sets appetite, arousal and social drive. Circadian regulators and ion channels controlling excitability tie these outputs to timing and state.

Behaviour is the coordinated output of the nervous system — feeding, sleep and circadian timing, locomotion, learning and memory, social interaction, reproduction, nociception and reward — and this broad collection captures the molecules through which those actions are generated and tuned. Neurotransmitter systems dominate: dopamine, serotonin, opioid, glutamate and GABA receptors, transporters such as SLC6A3 and SLC6A4, and synthetic enzymes including TH and GAD1. Neuropeptide circuits for energy balance and arousal are prominent, with POMC, AGRP, NPY, leptin and its receptor, orexins, oxytocin and CRH acting on hypothalamic targets. Synaptic adhesion and scaffolding proteins (neurexins, neuroligins, SHANK family, SYNGAP1), activity-induced transcription factors such as FOS and NPAS4, ion channels and clock components complete the picture. Disruption of these genes underlies autism and intellectual disability, addiction, obesity, sleep disorders and neurodegenerative disease, linking molecular synaptic function to whole-organism conduct.

Copulation covers the neural, endocrine and reproductive-tract events that bring about sexual union and the delivery of sperm, a behaviour on which fertilisation and reproductive success depend. The genes span its separate layers: oxytocin and vasopressin receptor signalling together with tachykinin/substance P and its receptor set sexual arousal, mating behaviour and the smooth muscle contractions of ejaculation; purinergic receptors and endothelin signalling drive contraction of vas deferens and vascular smooth muscle underlying erectile and emission responses; and seminal proteins such as semenogelin, kallikrein 14, protein C inhibitor and serpin E2 govern coagulation and liquefaction of semen, sperm motility and capacitation. Amino acid and nucleoside catabolic enzymes modulate the neurotransmitter tone behind these reflexes. Disruption produces erectile and ejaculatory dysfunction, altered mating behaviour, and infertility arising from defective seminal plasma rather than from the sperm themselves.

Copulation, the sexual union that delivers sperm to the female tract, depends on coordinated neural, smooth-muscle and seminal-fluid events rather than on a single tissue. Genes here span the behavioural and the mechanical: oxytocin and vasopressin receptor signalling, substance P acting through its receptor, and GABA transaminase shape the central and spinal circuits controlling arousal, erection and ejaculatory reflex, while purinergic receptors and endothelin receptor signalling drive contraction of vas deferens and vascular smooth muscle that propels semen. Accessory-gland products such as semenogelin and epididymal secretory proteins, together with the serine protease inhibitors of the SERPIN family and kallikrein activity, govern coagulation and liquefaction of the ejaculate and protect spermatozoa during transit. Disruption at any level manifests as erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction, altered semen viscosity, or impaired fertility, linking reproductive behaviour to the biochemistry of the seminal plasma.

circadian rhythm is the roughly 24-hour internal clock that anticipates the day-night cycle and schedules sleep, feeding, hormone release, body temperature and metabolism accordingly. Its disruption underlies jet lag, shift-work intolerance, familial advanced sleep phase, and contributes to metabolic and mood disorders. At its core is a transcriptional feedback loop in which CLOCK/NPAS2 and BMAL1 drive expression of PER and CRY, whose proteins return to inhibit their own activators; timing is set by phosphorylation through casein kinase 1 delta/epsilon and GSK3B and by ubiquitin-mediated degradation via FBXL3 and beta-TrCP complexes. Nuclear receptors such as REV-ERB and ROR, plus chromatin modifiers, sirtuins and NAMPT, couple the loop to redox and nutrient state, while AMPK and mTOR relay feeding cues. Light input through melanopsin and retinal opsins entrains the suprachiasmatic pacemaker, which broadcasts phase to peripheral tissues via melatonin, glucocorticoid and neuropeptide signalling.

Circadian rhythm is the roughly 24-hour internal timing programme that aligns sleep and wake, hormone release, feeding and metabolism with the solar day. Its core is a transcriptional feedback loop in which CLOCK and BMAL1 drive expression of the PER and CRY repressors, which in turn shut down their own activators; kinases such as CSNK1D/E and the ubiquitin ligase adaptor FBXL3 set the period by timing repressor degradation, while nuclear receptors of the REV-ERB and ROR families and chromatin modifiers add further feedback. Melatonin synthesis and its receptors, opsins including melanopsin, and neuropeptide signalling convey light and behavioural cues to the clock, and outputs reach lipid and glucose metabolism through PPARs, SIRT1, AMPK and NAMPT. Disruption underlies sleep-phase disorders and contributes to metabolic syndrome, mood disturbance and altered drug and tumour behaviour.

tRNA processing converts newly transcribed pre-tRNAs into the mature adaptors that decode mRNA, so every round of protein synthesis depends on it. Precursors must be trimmed at both ends by the RNase P complex and by 3' endonucleases, have CCA added by a nucleotidyltransferase, and in the case of intron-containing tRNAs be cut by the splicing endonuclease and rejoined by an RNA ligase complex. Dozens of modification enzymes then decorate the body and anticodon loop — pseudouridine synthases, methyltransferases, dihydrouridine and queuosine enzymes, thiolation and wybutosine machinery, and the elongator and KEOPS complexes acting at the wobble position — tuning decoding accuracy, translational speed and tRNA stability. Both nuclear and mitochondrial tRNA pools are served. Loss of individual enzymes causes intellectual disability, microcephaly, mitochondrial disease and anaemia, and altered wobble modification reshapes codon-biased translation in cancer and stress responses.

Freshly transcribed tRNAs are not usable; they must be trimmed, tailored and chemically decorated before an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase can charge them and the ribosome can read them accurately. This maturation pathway covers 5' leader removal by the ribonuclease P complex and its protein-only mitochondrial counterpart, 3' trailer cleavage by tRNase Z enzymes, CCA addition, and splicing of intron-containing precursors by the TSEN endonuclease complex followed by RTCB-dependent ligation. Layered on top is an extensive set of base and ribose modifications — pseudouridines, methylations, dihydrouridines, queuosine and wybutosine, thiolated and adenosine-deaminated wobble bases, and threonylcarbamoyl groups added by the KEOPS/EKC and Elongator machineries — which stabilise tRNA folding and set codon reading fidelity and frameshift avoidance. Both cytosolic and mitochondrial tRNAs are substrates, so defects impair global translation and oxidative phosphorylation, causing pontocerebellar hypoplasia, intellectual disability, microcephaly, mitochondrial myopathy and altered diabetes risk.

Toll signaling pathway is the innate immune signalling module that converts recognition of microbial and damage-associated molecules at Toll-like and interleukin-1 receptors into new gene transcription, chiefly the inflammatory programme driven by NF- cappaB and interferon regulatory factors. It gives cells their first-response capacity against infection, and its miscalibration produces septic shock at one extreme and recurrent pyogenic infection at the other. Ligand binding nucleates a receptor-proximal complex in which MyD88 recruits the IRAK kinases, IRAK4 and IRAK1 acting as the activating core while IRAK3 serves as a brake; Pellino E3 ligases and TRAF adaptors then build the ubiquitin scaffolds that propagate the signal to downstream kinases. Negative regulators such as SIGIRR and NLRP12 restrain output, reflecting how tightly this pathway must be tuned to avoid chronic inflammation and autoimmunity.

Toll and Toll-like receptors detect conserved microbial structures at the cell surface and in endosomes, and the signalling cascade described here converts that detection into transcriptional programmes for inflammation and host defence. Ligand binding recruits the adaptor MyD88, which assembles a receptor-proximal complex with the IRAK kinases; IRAK4 activates IRAK1 and IRAK2, and the Pellino E3 ligases ubiquitinate IRAK substrates to propagate signalling toward NF-kB and interferon regulatory factors. Output is tuned by built-in brakes: IRAK3 is a catalytically inactive pseudokinase that dampens the cascade, SIGIRR acts as a decoy receptor restraining Toll-like receptor responses, and TRAF3 biases output toward type I interferon. Because this circuit sets the threshold for innate immune activation, too little signalling leaves patients vulnerable to pyogenic bacterial infection, while unchecked activity drives septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease.

spermidine metabolic process covers the synthesis, modification and breakdown of spermidine, the polyamine that cells depend on for translation, chromatin compaction, autophagy and proliferation. Ornithine decarboxylase and S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase supply putrescine and the aminopropyl donor, spermidine synthase joins them, and catabolism proceeds through acetylation by spermidine/spermine N1-acetyltransferase followed by polyamine oxidase, a back-conversion and export route that lets cells rapidly lower polyamine levels when they are in excess. Spermidine is also the sole donor for hypusine formation on eIF5A by deoxyhypusine synthase, linking this pathway directly to the translation of proline-rich proteins. Polyamine pools are tightly autoregulated because both depletion and excess are toxic; sustained flux through ornithine decarboxylase downstream of MYC supports tumour growth, making these enzymes long-standing chemoprevention targets. Related deacetylases act on polyamine-derived substrates and on tubulin.

Spermidine is the polyamine cells depend on for proliferation, and the reactions that make, modify and degrade it keep its concentration within a narrow window. Synthesis starts from ornithine decarboxylation, one of the most tightly regulated steps in metabolism, and requires the decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine made by AMD1 as the aminopropyl donor for spermidine synthase. Catabolism runs through acetylation by spermidine/spermine N1-acetyltransferases, which both targets the polyamine for export and feeds oxidation by polyamine oxidase, generating hydrogen peroxide. Spermidine also serves as the sole substrate for hypusination of eIF5A by DHPS, linking this metabolic process to translation elongation, autophagy and cell growth; deacetylases of the HDAC6 family contribute a further layer of polyamine-linked regulation. Dysregulated flux through these steps accompanies tumour growth, and dietary spermidine is studied for effects on autophagy and ageing.

regulation of Notch signaling pathway controls how strongly and how long the Notch receptors signal, tuning a juxtacrine system that decides cell fate between neighbouring cells. Because Notch output sets the balance between progenitor maintenance and differentiation, its regulation shapes neurogenesis, somite segmentation, angiogenesis and arterial-venous specification, T cell development and gut epithelial renewal; loss of restraint drives leukaemia and Alagille- or CADASIL-type vascular disease. Control is exerted at every step: glycosyltransferases such as POFUT1, POGLUT1 and the fringe enzymes modify the receptor to bias ligand preference, ADAM10 with its tetraspanin partners performs the activating cleavage, ligands including DLL1, DLL4, JAG1 and the non-signalling DLK1 set input strength, ubiquitin ligases DTX1, FBXW7 and WWP2 limit receptor lifetime, and HES/HEY repressors plus NRARP close feedback loops. Crosstalk with BMP, WNT, YAP and STAT3 integrates Notch with other fate decisions.

Notch signalling decides cell fate between neighbouring cells, and this collection covers the many ways its output is tuned up or down. Because the pathway has no amplification step, dose matters: small shifts in ligand or receptor availability change whether a progenitor becomes a neuron, an arterial endothelial cell, or a secretory intestinal cell, and misregulation drives T-cell leukaemia, Alagille syndrome, CADASIL and aberrant angiogenesis. Control is exerted at every level. Glycosyltransferases such as POFUT1, POGLUT1 and the fringe enzymes modify receptor EGF repeats to bias ligand preference; tetraspanins and ADAM10 govern the proteolytic release of the intracellular domain; ubiquitin ligases including FBXW7, DTX1 and WWP2 set its lifetime. Downstream, HES and HEY repressors and the feedback inhibitor NRARP shape the transcriptional response, with additional input from BMP, Wnt, Hippo and microRNA regulation.

Photoreceptor cell morphogenesis builds the elaborate architecture that lets a rod or cone capture light: the stacked outer-segment discs, the connecting cilium that links them to the cell body, and the synaptic terminal that passes the signal on. This shaping happens as an immature retinal cell acquires its sensory identity, and it must be maintained for life, since outer segments are continuously renewed. Failure produces inherited retinal degeneration — retinitis pigmentosa, cone-rod dystrophy and the retinal component of ciliopathy syndromes. The genes point to the machinery involved: ciliary trafficking and basal body components such as BBS1, TMEM216 and CFAP418, the photoreceptor-specific cadherin CDHR1 that tethers nascent discs, a calcium-binding protein organizing the ribbon synapse, and a lipid transporter supplying the docosahexaenoic acid that outer-segment membranes are built from.

Rod and cone photoreceptors are among the most elaborately shaped cells in the body, and photoreceptor cell morphogenesis is the process by which an unspecialized retinal cell builds those structures: a stacked outer segment packed with visual pigment, the connecting cilium that supports it, and the specialized synaptic terminal that passes light responses to bipolar cells. The genes here converge on ciliary and membrane architecture, with a BBSome subunit and ciliary transition-zone and cilia-associated proteins governing transport into the outer segment, a photoreceptor-specific cadherin-related adhesion protein maintaining the link between outer segment and cilium, a lysophospholipid transporter supplying the docosahexaenoic acid that outer segment membranes require, and a calcium-binding protein serving the ribbon synapse. Loss of these functions causes retinal degeneration, from cone-rod dystrophy and retinitis pigmentosa to syndromic ciliopathies with blindness.

intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to osmotic stress is the route by which a cell that has lost control of its ion and water balance commits to self-destruction from within. It matters because tissues exposed to shifting tonicity — kidney medulla, vascular endothelium, neurons during ischaemia — must eliminate cells whose volume regulation has failed rather than let them lyse and inflame the surrounding tissue. Disturbed intracellular ion homeostasis is sensed and relayed through stress kinase and Rho-GEF scaffolding to the BCL-2 rheostat, where BAD tips the balance toward mitochondrial permeabilisation, cytochrome c release and caspase-3-driven execution. Counterbalancing survival inputs, including erythropoietin receptor signalling and prostaglandin synthesis via COX-2, set the threshold, while ubiquitin-editing and RNA-binding regulators tune how readily the decision is made. It is one input branch of the mitochondrial apoptotic program.

Cells that cannot restore ion and water balance after an osmotic insult commit suicide, and this is the intrinsic route by which that decision is executed. It matters wherever tonicity swings are physiological or pathological — renal medulla, blood volume regulation, ischaemic and inflammatory tissue — because the alternative to controlled death is lytic rupture and inflammation. Disturbed intracellular ion homeostasis is sensed and converted into mitochondrial permeabilisation, with the BH3-only protein BAD tipping the balance toward cytochrome c release and caspase-3-mediated demolition. Counter-signals set the threshold: erythropoietin acts as a survival factor, bradykinin receptor and prostaglandin-synthase signalling couple osmotic and inflammatory cues, and cytoskeletal and ubiquitin-pathway regulators modulate stress kinase output. The outcome is a graded choice between osmoadaptation and elimination of cells whose volume regulation has failed.

carbohydrate transport moves sugars across membranes, the step that lets cells obtain glucose and related hexoses from blood and gut lumen and that sets whole-body glycaemic control. Its failure produces glucose-galactose malabsorption, renal glycosuria, and the insulin resistance underlying type 2 diabetes. Two transporter families carry most of the traffic: facilitative GLUT carriers (SLC2A1-14) that equilibrate glucose down its gradient, and sodium-coupled SGLTs (SLC5A1, SLC5A2) that concentrate sugar against a gradient in intestinal and kidney epithelium, alongside aquaglyceroporins that pass glycerol and sucrose-type SLC45 carriers. Much of the pathway is regulatory rather than structural: insulin acting through INSR, IRS1/2, PI3K and AKT2 triggers exocytosis of GLUT4 storage vesicles via RHOQ, STXBP4 and TBC-associated trafficking factors, while leptin, adiponectin, FGF21, inflammatory cytokines and microRNAs tune transporter abundance in muscle, adipose and liver.

Sugars cannot cross membranes unaided, so cells depend on dedicated carriers to take up glucose, fructose and related solutes and to move them between tissues. Carbohydrate transport of this kind sets blood glucose, fuels the brain and red cells, allows the intestine and kidney to absorb and reclaim dietary sugar, and fails visibly in diabetes and in inherited glucose transporter deficiencies causing seizures or renal glycosuria. Two carrier families dominate: facilitative GLUT-type uniporters that follow the concentration gradient, and sodium-coupled cotransporters that drive uptake against it, the target of modern glycosuric drugs. Much of the remainder is regulation. Insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors, PI3K and AKT triggers translocation of the storage transporter to the plasma membrane of muscle and fat, with Rab and SNARE-associated trafficking proteins executing the step, while leptin, adiponectin, growth hormone and inflammatory cytokines tune sensitivity. Aquaporin channels contribute glycerol and related permeability.

Phospholipid biosynthetic process builds the glycerophospholipids that make up cellular membranes and the signalling lipids derived from them, so it determines membrane identity, organelle shape, and the platforms on which signalling complexes assemble. Its outputs are structural (phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, cardiolipin for mitochondrial inner membranes) and regulatory (phosphoinositides that mark compartments for trafficking and autophagy). The genes cover glycerol-3-phosphate acylation and lysophospholipid acyltransferases that set fatty acyl composition, the CDP-choline and CDP-ethanolamine arms via choline/ethanolamine kinases and phosphotransferases, phosphatidylserine synthesis and decarboxylation, and the kinase-phosphatase pairs, including PI3Ks, PIP5Ks, PTEN and myotubularins, that interconvert phosphoinositide species. A large GPI-anchor branch attaches lipid anchors to surface proteins. Failures cause lipodystrophy, myopathy, neurodegeneration and inherited GPI-anchor deficiencies, and dysregulated phosphoinositide turnover drives oncogenic growth signalling.

Membranes are built from phospholipids, and this biosynthetic programme supplies them: the glycerophospholipids that form every bilayer, the phosphoinositides that mark organelle identity, cardiolipin for mitochondrial cristae, and the GPI anchors that tether proteins to the cell surface. Glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferases and acylglycerophosphate acyltransferases build the diacylglycerol backbone, which CDP-choline and CDP-ethanolamine branches convert to phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, while CDP-diacylglycerol synthases feed phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylserine and cardiolipin synthesis. Lysophospholipid acyltransferases remodel acyl chains, and a large set of kinases, phosphatases and inositol phosphate enzymes interconverts phosphoinositides to control vesicle traffic, autophagy and growth signalling. Loss of individual steps causes lipodystrophy, neuropathy, myopathy and, for GPI anchor defects, congenital disorders of glycosylation with seizures and developmental delay. Sterol and sphingolipid enzymes present here reflect coordinated membrane lipid supply.

Aromatic amino acid metabolic process covers the degradation and conversion of phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan and histidine, routes that both dispose of dietary amino acids and generate signalling molecules and cofactors. Its failure is the classic cause of inborn errors of metabolism: PAH deficiency gives phenylketonuria, FAH and HGD defects give tyrosinaemia and alkaptonuria, and HAL loss gives histidinaemia, while pigmentation genes such as TYR, DCT and OCA2 tie tyrosine catabolism to melanin synthesis and albinism. Hydroxylation by PAH, TH and TPH requires tetrahydrobiopterin, regenerated by PCBD1 and QDPR, and commits tyrosine and tryptophan instead to catecholamine and serotonin production. The kynurenine branch, opened by IDO1, IDO2 and TDO2 and continued through KMO, KYNU and QPRT, feeds de novo NAD synthesis and shapes immune tolerance. Histidine decarboxylation yields histamine, inactivated by HNMT.

Handling of the ring-bearing amino acids phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan and histidine determines whether they are burned for energy or diverted into signalling molecules and cofactors. Phenylalanine hydroxylase, with its tetrahydrobiopterin recycling partners, converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, and the downstream tyrosine catabolic route through HPD, HGD and fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase feeds carbon into the TCA cycle; blocks at these steps cause phenylketonuria, alkaptonuria and tyrosinaemia. The same tyrosine pool supplies tyrosinase, DCT and pigment transporters for melanin synthesis in melanocytes, where loss produces albinism, and tyrosine hydroxylase for catecholamine production. Tryptophan is split between serotonin synthesis by TPH1 and TPH2 and the kynurenine pathway run by TDO2, IDO1/2, KMO and KYNU, which generates immunosuppressive metabolites, neuroactive quinolinate, and de novo NAD+. Histidine degradation and histamine formation complete the set.}
