methionine biosynthetic process covers the reactions that regenerate L-methionine rather than obtain it from the diet, sustaining the supply of S-adenosylmethionine on which all cellular methylation of DNA, histones, phospholipids and small molecules depends. Two routes are represented. Remethylation of homocysteine is carried out either by the cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase with its reductase partner, drawing methyl groups from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate supplied by MTHFR and the folate one-carbon enzymes, or by the betaine-dependent transferases active in liver and kidney. The second route is the methionine salvage cycle, in which MTAP cleaves methylthioadenosine left over from polyamine synthesis and MRI1, ENOPH1, ADI1 and APIP convert the thiomethyl group back into methionine. Loss of these steps causes hyperhomocysteinaemia with vascular and neural tube consequences, and links folate, vitamin B12 and choline status to epigenetic regulation.

Humans cannot synthesise methionine from scratch, so they regenerate it, and the reactions grouped here as methionine biosynthesis are the two routes that do so. Homocysteine is remethylated either by the cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase, using 5-methyltetrahydrofolate supplied by MTHFR and the folate one-carbon enzymes and kept active by its reductase partner, or by betaine-homocysteine methyltransferases in liver and kidney, which draw a methyl group from betaine instead. In parallel, the methylthioadenosine salvage route recovers methionine from the by-product of polyamine synthesis through MTAP, MRI1, ENOPH1, APIP and ADI1. Together these keep S-adenosylmethionine available for methylation of DNA, histones, phospholipids and small molecules, and prevent homocysteine accumulation; inherited defects cause homocystinuria with neurological and vascular disease, and loss of MTAP is a common feature of tumours.

glycoprotein biosynthetic process builds the sugar coats that most secreted and membrane proteins carry, determining whether they fold, exit the ER, reach the right compartment, and are recognised by other cells. It underlies blood group and selectin ligand identity, extracellular matrix assembly, muscle membrane integrity and neural development; its failure produces the congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies from defective dystroglycan O-mannosylation, and lysosomal enzyme mistargeting. The genes cover dolichol-linked precursor synthesis and the oligosaccharyltransferase complex that transfers N-glycans, ER quality control by glucosidases and UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferases, Golgi mannose trimming and branching by mannosidases and MGAT enzymes, and terminal capping by fucosyl-, sialyl- and sulfotransferases. Parallel arms make mucin-type O-glycans through GALNT enzymes, O-fucose and O-glucose on Notch, and proteoglycan chains initiated by xylosyltransferases, all supported by nucleotide-sugar synthesis and Golgi transporters.

Most proteins that reach the cell surface or the extracellular space carry sugars, and this is the machinery that builds them. Glycoprotein biosynthesis determines protein folding and quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum, secretion, receptor half-life, cell adhesion and immune recognition; its failure produces the congenital disorders of glycosylation, with multisystem developmental, neurological and coagulation defects, and the dystroglycanopathy muscular dystrophies. Assembly begins with nucleotide- and dolichol-linked sugar donors and the lipid-linked precursor made by the ALG enzymes, which the oligosaccharyltransferase complex (STT3A/STT3B, DDOST, RPN1/2) transfers to asparagine residues; trimming by glucosidases and mannosidases feeds calnexin-cycle folding checks, then Golgi GlcNAc-, galactosyl-, fucosyl- and sialyltransferases elaborate mature branches. Parallel routes install mucin-type O-GalNAc chains, O-mannose on dystroglycan, O-fucose on Notch, proteoglycan xylose linkers with heparan and chondroitin chains, and cytoplasmic O-GlcNAc. Sugar transporters, Golgi structural proteins and ion homeostasis factors keep these compartments competent.

Nucleotide metabolic process covers the synthesis, salvage, interconversion and breakdown of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, the molecules that supply DNA and RNA precursors, carry cellular energy as ATP, and act as second messengers. Its output sets the pace of proliferation, and its failures cause hyperuricaemia and gout, immunodeficiency from adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase loss, and mitochondrial DNA depletion when deoxyribonucleotide pools are unbalanced. The genes span de novo synthesis from phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPS1, PPAT, CAD, UMPS), salvage kinases and phosphorylases (HPRT1, APRT, DCK, TK2), ribonucleotide reduction, and the nucleotidases and Nudix hydrolases that sanitise damaged nucleotides. Tightly coupled to it are glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway supplying ribose and reducing power, oxidative phosphorylation regenerating ATP, NAD biosynthesis, and cyclases and phosphodiesterases governing cyclic AMP and GMP signalling, with AMPK and mTOR reading nucleotide status.

Nucleotides are the currency of energy transfer, the substrates of DNA and RNA synthesis, and the carriers of intracellular signals, and this broad metabolic programme makes, recycles, interconverts and degrades them. It covers de novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis from ribose-phosphate through enzymes such as PPAT, GART, ATIC, CAD, DHODH and UMPS; salvage of bases and nucleosides by HPRT1, APRT, ADK, TK2 and the uridine-cytidine kinases; reduction to deoxyribonucleotides by ribonucleotide reductase; and catabolism via nucleotidases, deaminases and xanthine oxidase to urate. Interlocking with it are glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway supplying PRPP, oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthase, NAD biosynthesis, and cyclic nucleotide signalling through adenylate and guanylate cyclases opposed by phosphodiesterases. Balanced pools matter: imbalance drives mutagenesis and replication stress, and inherited defects cause immunodeficiency, gout, anaemia and neurological disease, while these enzymes are long-standing targets of antimetabolite chemotherapy and immunosuppression.

Ribonucleoside metabolic process covers the interconversion, salvage and breakdown of ribose-linked purine and pyrimidine nucleosides, the step that decides whether adenosine, inosine, guanosine and uridine are recycled into nucleotide pools or degraded to waste. It matters because it keeps nucleotide supply cheap for dividing and non-dividing cells alike, and because its failures are classic inborn errors: adenosine deaminase loss causes severe combined immunodeficiency by poisoning lymphocytes with deoxyadenosine, HPRT1 loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, and xanthine oxidase activity sets urate output and gout risk. Ecto-5'-nucleotidases and cytosolic counterparts dephosphorylate nucleotides to nucleosides, kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases run the reverse salvage arm, and phosphorylases release the ribose moiety into central carbon metabolism. Extracellular adenosine generated by CD73 also acts as an immunosuppressive signal, linking this metabolism to purinergic receptor signalling and tumour immune evasion.

Ribonucleoside metabolism covers the interconversion, salvage and breakdown of nucleosides built on ribose, and it is how cells recycle adenosine, inosine, guanosine and uridine rather than making purines and pyrimidines from scratch. This economy matters most in tissues that cannot afford de novo synthesis: loss of HPRT1 salvage causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with urate overproduction, ADA deficiency poisons lymphocytes with deoxyadenosine metabolites and produces severe combined immunodeficiency, and XDH at the end of purine catabolism sets the uric acid load underlying gout. Kinases such as ADK and DGUOK phosphorylate nucleosides back into the nucleotide pool, while 5'-nucleotidases including NT5C2 and ecto-enzyme NT5E run the reverse step, and phosphorylases PNP, UPP1 and MTAP cleave nucleosides to free bases. The extracellular arm of this chemistry generates adenosine as a signalling molecule that dampens inflammation and modulates vascular tone.

Pyrimidine nucleoside monophosphate biosynthetic process builds the UMP, CMP and dTMP units from which RNA and DNA are assembled, supplying the nucleotide pools that proliferating cells draw on during S phase and that lymphocytes expand rapidly on activation. Two routes converge here: de novo synthesis, in which the multifunctional CAD enzyme, the mitochondrial inner-membrane dehydrogenase DHODH and UMPS generate UMP from glutamine and aspartate, and salvage, in which uridine, cytidine and deoxycytidine are rephosphorylated by kinases such as UCK1/2, DCK and CMPK1. Thymidylate is made separately by TYMS using folate one-carbon units provided by SHMT1, linking pyrimidine supply to folate metabolism. Because tumour cells depend heavily on this flux, its enzymes are the targets of fluoropyrimidines, methotrexate, leflunomide and cytarabine, and inherited UMPS or dihydroorotate defects cause orotic aciduria and metabolic disease.

Pyrimidine nucleoside monophosphates are the immediate precursors of the CTP, UTP and dTTP pools used for DNA replication, RNA synthesis, phospholipid head-group activation and protein glycosylation, and this pathway is how cells make them. Two routes converge: de novo synthesis, where the multifunctional CAD enzyme, the inner-membrane flavoenzyme DHODH and the bifunctional UMPS produce UMP from glutamine, bicarbonate and aspartate, and salvage, where nucleoside and base kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases such as UCK1/UCK2, DCK and UPRT recycle uridine, cytidine and deoxycytidine. Thymidylate is generated separately by TYMS with methyl groups supplied through serine hydroxymethyltransferase and folate metabolism. Because proliferating cells depend on this output, the enzymes are classic drug targets inhibited by antifolates and fluoropyrimidines and by DHODH inhibitors used in autoimmune disease, while DCK and CDA determine activation and inactivation of nucleoside analogue chemotherapies. Imbalance distorts nucleotide pools and destabilises the genome.

nucleoside diphosphate catabolic process covers the enzymatic removal of phosphate from nucleoside diphosphates such as ADP, UDP and GDP, a step that both salvages nucleotides and terminates their signalling. Extracellular ADP and UDP are potent agonists of platelet and purinergic receptors, so the ectonucleotidases of the ENTPD/CD39 family, working with CD73, set the balance between pro-thrombotic, pro-inflammatory nucleotide signals and immunosuppressive adenosine; loss of this control drives thrombosis and inflammation, while its excess in tumours blunts T cell responses. Intracellular NUDIX hydrolases perform analogous housekeeping on modified and damaged nucleotides. The bulk of the genes here, however, are glycolytic: hexokinases, phosphofructokinases, PGK, enolases and pyruvate kinase consume and regenerate ADP, together with their insulin, AMPK, mTOR and HIF1A regulators, tying nucleoside diphosphate turnover to cellular energy charge and glucose flux.

Nucleoside diphosphates are consumed as well as made, and this catabolic branch covers their hydrolysis to monophosphates plus inorganic phosphate together with the glycolytic reactions that spend and regenerate ADP. It matters for purinergic signalling at the cell surface, where ectonucleotidases of the ENTPD family and NT5E stepwise degrade extracellular ATP and ADP to adenosine, switching an inflammatory, platelet-activating signal into an immunosuppressive one; loss of this control alters thrombosis, T cell responses and tumour immune evasion. Intracellularly, hexokinases, phosphofructokinases, aldolase, GAPDH, PGK and pyruvate kinase transfer phosphate between nucleotides and sugar intermediates, with NUDT hydrolases clearing diphosphate nucleotides and damaged species. Overlaying this are the regulators that set glycolytic flux to nucleotide supply and demand: AMP-activated protein kinase, mTOR complex components, HIF1A and insulin signalling, linking nucleotide turnover to energy sensing and growth.

nucleoside triphosphate biosynthetic process covers the reactions that produce ATP, GTP, CTP, UTP and dTTP, the energy currency and polymerisation substrates on which essentially all cellular work depends. Two arms dominate. One is oxidative phosphorylation: the complex I subunits, succinate dehydrogenase, the mitochondrially encoded ATP synthase subunits and the full F1Fo assembly, together with quality-control and assembly factors such as PINK1, PRKN and TAFAZZIN, which couple respiration to ATP output. The other is nucleotide salvage and interconversion, where adenylate and nucleoside diphosphate kinases, thymidylate kinase, uridine-cytidine kinases, CTP synthetases, IMPDH isoforms and thymidylate synthase raise mono- and diphosphates to the triphosphate level and balance the pools needed for DNA replication and transcription. Loss of the respiratory arm causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathy; the nucleotide arm sets proliferative capacity and is a longstanding target of antimetabolite chemotherapy.

Cells must continuously regenerate the triphosphorylated nucleotides that fuel work and supply the substrates for RNA and DNA synthesis, and this is the set of reactions that makes them. The dominant contribution comes from oxidative phosphorylation: complex I subunits, succinate dehydrogenase, and the F1Fo ATP synthase together convert the proton-motive force into ATP, with glycolytic enzymes providing a substrate-level route. Alongside ATP production, kinases interconvert and top up the other triphosphates, including adenylate kinases, nucleoside diphosphate kinases, thymidylate and uridine-cytidine kinases, and the CTP and IMP dehydrogenase enzymes that commit flux toward pyrimidine and purine pools. Mitochondrial quality-control and assembly factors are included because ATP output depends on intact organelles. Loss of these activities produces mitochondrial disease with lactic acidosis and neuromuscular failure, while the nucleotide-synthesizing arm is a long-standing target of antiproliferative and immunosuppressive drugs.

Nucleoside triphosphate catabolic process degrades ATP, GTP, dUTP, dCTP and their non-canonical relatives, and its main service is quality control of the nucleotide pool. Cells cannot afford to let dUTP, dITP or oxidised and halogenated triphosphates reach DNA polymerases, so hydrolases such as DUT, ITPA, DCTPP1 and the NUDT sanitising enzymes clear them before incorporation; loss of this surveillance produces uracil-laden or mutagenic DNA. A second arm sets the size of the dNTP supply itself: SAMHD1 depletes dNTPs and thereby restricts retroviral reverse transcription, and its failure causes the interferon-driven Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome. Ectonucleotidases including ENPP1 and the ENTPD family act outside the cell, stepping ATP down toward adenosine and so converting a pro-inflammatory purinergic signal into an immunosuppressive one. The same chemistry governs how thiopurine drugs are detoxified, making NUDT15 a pharmacogenetic determinant of chemotherapy toxicity.

Nucleoside triphosphate catabolism removes NTPs and dNTPs from the cell's pools, both to size those pools for accurate DNA replication and to clear damaged or non-canonical nucleotides that would otherwise be incorporated into nucleic acids. Hydrolases here act at different sites: dUTPase and dCTP pyrophosphatase limit uracil and modified cytosine misincorporation, ITPA removes deaminated inosine and xanthosine triphosphates, and NUDT15 and NUDT16 sanitise nucleotide pools, which is why NUDT15 variants cause severe toxicity from thiopurine drugs. SAMHD1 depletes cellular dNTPs and thereby restricts retroviral reverse transcription; its loss causes Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome with chronic interferon activation. Ecto-enzymes of the ENPP and ENTPD families degrade extracellular ATP and related nucleotides, terminating purinergic receptor signalling and generating adenosine, while adenosine deaminase links this catabolism to immune function.

Ribonucleoside monophosphate biosynthetic process builds the immediate precursors of RNA and of the nucleotide cofactors that power metabolism, supplying AMP, GMP, UMP and CMP to dividing cells. Proliferating tissues, lymphocytes above all, depend on it, and its enzymes are long-standing drug targets: inhibition of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase or dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is used to suppress immune responses, and thiopurines act through the salvage route. Two arms are represented. De novo synthesis starts from ribose-5-phosphate via PRPS-generated PRPP, then proceeds through the multistep purine assembly line (PPAT, GART, PFAS, PAICS, ATIC, ADSL) or the pyrimidine route through CAD and UMPS. Salvage enzymes such as HPRT1, APRT, ADK and the uridine-cytidine kinases recycle preformed bases and nucleosides far more cheaply, while deaminases and AMP deaminases balance the pools. Loss of individual steps causes gout, immunodeficiency and neurological disease.

Cells need a steady supply of ribonucleoside monophosphates as the immediate precursors of RNA, DNA and the nucleotide cofactors of metabolism, and this biosynthetic process is how they make them. Two routes converge: de novo synthesis builds purine rings stepwise on phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate through the multifunctional enzymes GART, PAICS and ATIC to reach IMP, which is then committed either to AMP via adenylosuccinate synthase and lyase or to GMP via IMPDH and GMP synthase, while CAD and DHODH feed the pyrimidine arm toward UMP. Salvage routes recycle preformed bases and nucleosides through HPRT1, APRT, adenosine kinase and uridine-cytidine kinases, and deaminases with AMP deaminases drain flux back out. Rapidly dividing cells depend heavily on this output, which is why several steps are antimetabolite drug targets; inherited defects cause gout, immunodeficiency and Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

Deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate catabolic process dismantles dNMPs back to bases and sugars, and by doing so it sets the size and balance of the deoxynucleotide pools that DNA replication and repair draw upon. Its output matters twice over: it prevents accumulation of imbalanced or damaged nucleotides that would drive mutagenesis, and it feeds salvage and terminal degradation routes that dispose of purine and pyrimidine rings. Cytosolic and mitochondrial 5'-nucleotidases strip the phosphate, phosphorylases and deaminases such as PNP, ADA, TYMP and CDA cleave or convert the resulting nucleosides, and XDH or the dihydropyrimidine enzymes complete breakdown to urate or beta-amino acids. Failure at individual steps produces severe disease -- immunodeficiency from adenosine deaminase or PNP loss, mitochondrial DNA depletion from thymidine phosphorylase deficiency -- and these same enzymes govern the activation and clearance of nucleoside analogue chemotherapeutics.

Breakdown of deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates keeps the deoxynucleotide pools that feed DNA replication and repair in balance, disposing of excess or damaged precursors and recycling their bases and sugars. The first committed step is dephosphorylation by 5'-nucleotidases acting in cytosol and mitochondria, including NT5C2 and the mitochondrial NT5M, releasing nucleosides that are then cleaved phosphorolytically by purine nucleoside phosphorylase or thymidine phosphorylase, deaminated by adenosine, cytidine or guanine deaminases, and finally degraded to uric acid by xanthine dehydrogenase or through the pyrimidine catabolic route via dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase. The balance matters clinically: loss of adenosine deaminase or of purine nucleoside phosphorylase causes severe combined immunodeficiency through accumulation of toxic deoxynucleotides in lymphocytes, thymidine phosphorylase deficiency drives mitochondrial DNA instability, and these same enzymes determine activation and clearance of nucleoside analogue chemotherapeutics.

Pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate metabolic process governs the supply and turnover of dCMP and dTMP, the immediate precursors of the cytosine and thymine nucleotides that DNA replication and repair consume. Its output sets the size and balance of the deoxynucleotide pool, and imbalance here is directly mutagenic: loss of dUTPase allows uracil misincorporation and futile excision repair, while thymidylate synthase and its serine hydroxymethyltransferase-supplied folate one-carbon units are the target of fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy. Deaminases and phosphorylases feed the salvage route by recycling cytidine, uridine and thymidine, and 5'-nucleotidases run the reverse dephosphorylation step that tunes pool levels. Catabolism through dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and dihydropyrimidinase disposes of excess bases and determines patient tolerance to 5-fluorouracil, linking this metabolism to proliferating tissues, mitochondrial DNA maintenance and drug toxicity.

Pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate metabolism governs the supply and turnover of dCMP and dTMP, the immediate precursors of the DNA building blocks dCTP and dTTP. Because DNA replication and repair stall when thymidylate runs short, this chemistry sets both the rate of proliferation and the fidelity of the genome, and it is the target of fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy. Thymidylate synthase methylates dUMP to dTMP using folate one-carbon units supplied by serine hydroxymethyltransferase, while dCMP deaminase feeds dCMP into the same node and a dUTP-hydrolysing pyrophosphatase prevents uracil misincorporation. Opposing 5'-nucleotidases and nucleoside phosphorylases dephosphorylate and degrade these monophosphates, and the pyrimidine catabolic enzymes including dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase dispose of the released bases. Loss of these steps causes nucleotide pool imbalance, mitochondrial DNA depletion, and severe toxicity from pyrimidine analogue drugs.

pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate metabolic process supplies and balances the dCTP and dTTP pools that DNA replication and repair draw on, and keeps them free of the wrong nucleotides. Its output determines whether a cell can enter and complete S phase; imbalance or contamination of these pools causes misincorporation, replication stress and mutagenesis, which is why the pathway is a target of fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy. Thymidylate synthase commits folate-derived one-carbon units to dTMP, thymidylate kinase and NME-family phosphotransferases carry it to the triphosphate, and dUTPase and dCTP pyrophosphatase act as sanitising enzymes that destroy dUTP and modified dCTP before polymerases can use them. CMPK2, induced by interferon, links this nucleotide chemistry to innate immune signalling and mitochondrial DNA maintenance. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of nucleotide biosynthesis, genome stability and proliferative control.

Metabolism of pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates supplies and polices the dCTP and dTTP used for DNA replication and repair. Balanced pools matter as much as abundance: excess dUTP leads to uracil misincorporation, and skewed dTTP/dCTP ratios drive mutagenesis and replication stress. Thymidylate synthase generates dTMP from dUMP, thymidylate kinase phosphorylates it onward, and a nucleoside diphosphate kinase completes conversion to the triphosphate, while dUTP pyrophosphatase and a dCTP pyrophosphatase sanitize the pool by hydrolysing dUTP and excess or damaged dCTP back to monophosphates. A mitochondrial cytidine/uridine monophosphate kinase contributes to nucleotide supply for mitochondrial DNA and is induced by interferon. These enzymes are classic chemotherapy targets, and inherited defects cause mitochondrial DNA depletion and neurological disease, placing the pathway at the junction of genome stability and nucleotide salvage.

Nucleotide-sugar metabolic process builds the activated sugar donors -- UDP-, GDP- and CMP-linked monosaccharides -- that every glycosyltransferase in the cell depends on, and so sets the supply line for N- and O-glycosylation, proteoglycan and glycolipid synthesis, and glycogen metabolism. Interrupting it causes congenital disorders of glycosylation: defects in phosphomannomutase and GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase produce multisystem disease and dystroglycanopathy, while loss of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase underlies galactosemia. The genes trace the individual branches -- the hexosamine route through glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate amidotransferase and PGM3 to UDP-GlcNAc, GDP-fucose synthesis by GMDS and its salvage counterpart, sialic acid production via GNE, NANS and CMAS, and UDP-glucuronate and UDP-xylose generation for glycosaminoglycan chains. Dedicated transporters then move these donors into the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum lumen, coupling nutrient flux from glucose to the glycan code displayed on cell surfaces.

Every glycan a cell makes is built from activated sugar donors, and nucleotide-sugar metabolism is the set of reactions that produces, interconverts and delivers them. It supplies UDP-GlcNAc, UDP-Gal, UDP-GlcA, UDP-xylose, GDP-mannose, GDP-fucose and CMP-sialic acid for N- and O-glycosylation, proteoglycan and glycolipid synthesis, so its output determines the composition of the cell surface and secreted proteins. Hexosamine entry is controlled by glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate transaminase (GFPT1/2) and continued through GNPNAT1, PGM3 and UAP1; parallel branches run through phosphomannomutase PMM2 and GMPPA/GMPPB to mannose and fucose donors, while CMAS activates sialic acid for transfer. Dedicated transporters such as SLC35A3 and SLC35C1 move donors into the Golgi lumen. Defects in these steps cause congenital disorders of glycosylation and congenital myasthenic syndromes, and blocked galactose handling through GALT underlies galactosemia; flux here also links nutrient supply to glycan-based signalling.

Protein lipoylation attaches lipoic acid to specific lysine residues on the handful of mitochondrial enzymes that require it, and without this modification oxidative metabolism of pyruvate, branched-chain ketoacids and glycine collapses. The recipients are the E2 subunits of the pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes plus the H protein of the glycine cleavage system, so the pathway sits directly upstream of entry into the citric acid cycle and of one-carbon metabolism. An octanoyl chain is transferred from the mitochondrial acyl carrier protein NDUFAB1 by LIPT2, sulfurated by the radical-SAM enzyme LIAS using its own iron-sulfur clusters, and finally transferred to target apoproteins by LIPT1; BOLA3 supports cluster handling. Because of this dependence, defects in these steps or in iron-sulfur cluster supply cause lipoic acid synthesis disorders with lactic acidosis, hyperglycinaemia and severe infantile neurological disease.

Four mitochondrial enzyme systems — pyruvate dehydrogenase, 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase and the glycine cleavage system — are inert unless a lipoyl group is covalently attached to a specific lysine on their carrier subunits, and protein lipoylation is the route by which that cofactor is installed. Without it, pyruvate and branched-chain amino acids cannot enter oxidative metabolism and glycine accumulates, producing the lethal infantile lactic acidosis and hyperglycinemia of lipoic acid synthesis defects. The octanoyl precursor is delivered from the mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis machinery via the acyl carrier protein NDUFAB1, transferred to the substrate lysine by LIPT2 and LIPT1, and converted to lipoate by the radical SAM enzyme LIAS, which depends on iron–sulfur clusters supplied with help from BOLA3. The pathway therefore links fatty acid synthesis, cluster assembly and central carbon oxidation.

deoxyribonucleotide metabolic process supplies and polices the dNTP pool that DNA replication and repair draw on, keeping the four precursors balanced in the right amounts at the right time. Too little limits replication fork progression; too much or too skewed a pool drives mutagenesis, and loss of individual enzymes causes mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes, immunodeficiency, or the interferon-driven autoinflammation of Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome. De novo synthesis runs through ribonucleotide reductase and thymidylate synthase with folate-linked one-carbon input, while salvage kinases such as DCK, DGUOK and TK-type activities recycle deoxyribonucleosides, notably in mitochondria. Opposing them are catabolic and sanitising enzymes -- nucleotidases, deaminases, phosphorylases, SAMHD1 and NUDT hydrolases -- that degrade excess or damaged nucleotides. The associated uracil and oxidised-base glycosylases connect pool quality to base excision repair. These enzymes also determine the activation and toxicity of nucleoside analogue chemotherapies and antivirals.

Supplying DNA replication and repair with balanced pools of the four dNTPs is the job of deoxyribonucleotide metabolism, and the size and proportion of those pools sets both the speed and the fidelity of genome duplication. Ribonucleotide reductase subunits convert ribonucleotides to their deoxy forms, thymidylate synthase and thymidylate kinase build the thymidine arm, and deoxyribonucleoside and nucleoside monophosphate kinases salvage bases from turnover. Countervailing activities keep pools in check and remove hazardous species: 5'-nucleotidases and deaminases degrade nucleotides, SAMHD1 hydrolyses dNTPs, dUTPase and pyrophosphohydrolases clear dUTP and oxidised or modified precursors, and DNA glycosylases excise the mispaired or damaged bases that escape. Imbalance here drives mutagenesis and replication stress; inherited defects cause mitochondrial DNA depletion and immunodeficiency, and these enzymes determine the activation and toxicity of nucleoside analogue and antifolate chemotherapy.

cellular response to starvation is how a cell detects that nutrients have run short and rewires itself to survive until they return. It preserves viability during fasting, ischaemia and amino acid limitation, and its failure underlies both neurodegeneration from defective autophagy and the unchecked growth signalling seen in tumours. Two sensors dominate: mTORC1 with its Rag GTPases, GATOR/KICSTOR regulators, sestrins and amino acid detectors such as CASTOR1 and SAMTOR, and AMPK, which reads falling energy charge. Their inactivation and activation converge on autophagy initiation through ULK-BECN1-PIK3C3 complexes, ATG conjugation and LC3/GABARAP lipidation, then autophagosome-lysosome fusion via STX17 and VAMP8. In parallel, GCN2-eIF2α-ATF4 and the ER stress arm reprogramme translation, TFEB drives lysosomal biogenesis, and FOXO, PPARA, p53 and SREBP outputs shift metabolism toward catabolism, gluconeogenesis and lipid droplet turnover.

When nutrients run short, cells stop building and start recycling, and this starvation response is the switch that makes that happen. It preserves viability through fasting and ischaemia, supports amino acid and glucose homeostasis at the organismal level, and when it fails cells either die or, in tumours, exploit it to survive nutrient-poor microenvironments. Two sensors dominate: the mTOR complex 1 machinery, with its Rag GTPases, GATOR and TSC regulators and sestrins reporting amino acid and energy status, and AMPK, activated when ATP falls. Their combined output releases autophagy initiation through ULK-associated ATG14, beclin and PI3KC3, drives LC3 and GABARAP lipidation, and directs autophagosome-lysosome fusion by STX17 and VAMP8. In parallel, eIF2α kinases and ATF4 reprogramme translation and induce amino acid synthesis and transport, while TFEB and FOXO transcription factors expand lysosomal and catabolic capacity.

Amine catabolic process is the set of reactions that dispose of biogenic amines and polyamines once they have acted, keeping neurotransmitter, histamine and polyamine pools within safe limits. It matters because unchecked amine signalling drives hypertension, migraine and psychiatric disturbance, while polyamine excess promotes proliferation and oxidative stress; drugs that block these enzymes, notably monoamine oxidase inhibitors, work precisely by interrupting the route. Monoamine oxidases MAOA and MAOB oxidatively deaminate dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline in the outer mitochondrial membrane, with COMT and the sulfotransferases providing parallel methylation and conjugation routes, and HNMT terminating histamine action. A second arm handles polyamines: SAT1 acetylates spermidine and spermine for oxidation by PAOX or direct back-conversion by SMOX. Choline and betaine oxidation feeds the related one-carbon and osmolyte metabolism, linking amine turnover to methyl group supply and to catecholamine reuptake by DAT.

Amine catabolism is the set of reactions that dispose of biogenic amines, polyamines and choline-derived betaines, terminating their signalling activity and preventing accumulation of reactive or toxic nitrogenous compounds. Its importance is clearest in the nervous system, where monoamine oxidases A and B oxidatively deaminate dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin and related transmitters, catechol O-methyltransferase methylates catechols, and histamine N-methyltransferase inactivates histamine; loss or variation in these steps alters mood, blood pressure and susceptibility to parkinsonism, and MAO inhibitors are used as antidepressants. Sulfotransferases of the SULT1A family conjugate phenolic amines for excretion, while spermine oxidase, polyamine oxidase and spermidine/spermine acetyltransferase run the polyamine back-conversion route that generates hydrogen peroxide and aminoaldehydes. Choline and dimethylglycine dehydrogenases feed choline degradation into one-carbon metabolism, and a dopamine transporter delivers substrate for intracellular turnover.

folic acid-containing compound biosynthetic process builds and maintains the pool of reduced folate cofactors that carry one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis and methylation. Cells cannot make the pterin ring's dietary equivalent without uptake, so this biology combines receptor- and transporter-mediated acquisition of folate (FOLR1, the proton-coupled intestinal transporter SLC46A1) with reduction by dihydrofolate reductase, polyglutamylation by FPGS to retain folates intracellularly, and interconversion of formyl, methylene and methenyl derivatives by MTHFD1 and MTHFS. GCH1 supplies GTP-derived pterin, linking the pathway to tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism. The output feeds purine synthesis directly through ATIC, thymidylate production, and methionine and S-adenosylmethionine regeneration. Insufficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neural tube defects, and the dependence of proliferating cells on this route is the basis of antifolate chemotherapy, where DHFR inhibition starves DNA synthesis of thymidine and purines.

Folate derivatives carry one-carbon units for purine and thymidylate synthesis, methionine regeneration and methylation, so the biosynthesis and interconversion of folic acid-containing compounds sets the supply of these cofactors. Mammals cannot make the pterin ring into a complete folate and must take up dietary folate, which is why a receptor and a proton-coupled intestinal transporter belong here alongside the enzymes; poor uptake or reduced activity produces megaloblastic anaemia and neural tube defects. Dihydrofolate reductase regenerates tetrahydrofolate and is the target of methotrexate, while polyglutamylation by FPGS retains folates inside cells and mitochondria. GTP cyclohydrolase I supplies dihydroneopterin triphosphate for the related pterin route, and MTHFD1 with its mitochondrial counterpart MTHFD1L generate and interconvert formyl and methylene forms that ATIC consumes during purine synthesis.

response to heat is the cell's emergency programme for surviving temperatures above its optimum, when proteins begin to unfold and aggregate. It preserves proteome integrity under thermal, oxidative and metabolic stress, and its capacity determines whether a cell recovers or dies; the same machinery is co-opted by tumours to buffer misfolded protein loads and declines with age in neurodegeneration. The core is transcriptional: HSF1, held in check by HSP90 and HSBP1, trimerises on heat shock elements to induce HSPA1A/B, HSPB1 and a large family of DNAJ co-chaperones that refold or triage damaged substrates, with CHIP/STUB1 and VCP routing the irreparable to degradation. In parallel, eIF2α and its eIF2B guanine-nucleotide exchange factor arrest bulk translation and drive stress granule assembly. Thermosensation is represented too, through TRPV1, TRPV4, TRPM2 and TRPA1 channels in sensory neurons that convert noxious heat into pain signalling.

Cells and organisms exposed to temperatures above their optimum mount a coordinated defence against protein unfolding, and this heat response is what keeps the proteome soluble and functional during fever, exercise or environmental stress. Its core is transcriptional and chaperone-based: HSF1 drives induction of inducible HSP70 family members, HSP90 isoforms, small heat shock proteins such as HSPB1 and the alpha-crystallins, and a large set of DNAJ co-chaperones that direct substrate selection, with HSPBP-like regulators and nuclear import factors controlling where chaperones act. Parallel arms suppress translation through eIF2 and its guanine nucleotide exchange factor subunits, route terminally damaged proteins to degradation via CHIP, VCP and HDAC6, and trigger antioxidant and heme oxygenase defences. Sensory thermoreception is also represented, with TRPV1, TRPV4, TRPA1 and TRPM2 channels converting heat into neuronal signalling and pain. Loss of this capacity underlies heat-sensitive myopathies and aggregation-prone neurodegeneration.

response to water covers how cells and tissues sense and react to water availability and osmotic state, the basis of body fluid homeostasis. In humans this is most visible in the kidney, where vasopressin acting through its receptor drives insertion of the aquaporin-2 water channel into collecting duct membranes to concentrate urine; loss of this axis produces diabetes insipidus and dehydration. Other members report on the mechanical and ionic consequences of water movement: polycystin channels transduce flow and osmotic cues in renal cilia and are mutated in polycystic kidney disease, uromodulin shapes tubular salt handling, and calcium pumps and cytoskeletal linkers such as plectin buffer the resulting volume and tension changes. Downstream, transcriptional and kinase signalling adjust gene expression so that transport capacity matches hydration status.

Cells and whole organisms adjust their behaviour to the presence, absence or concentration of water, and in mammals this response is largely about defending body fluid osmolality and blood volume. The kidney carries most of the burden: vasopressin receptor signalling drives insertion of the water channel aquaporin-2 into collecting duct apical membranes so that free water is reabsorbed rather than lost in urine, while uromodulin shapes salt handling and the concentrating capacity of the thick ascending limb. Osmotic and mechanical cues are also read directly, through polycystin channels of the TRPP family that sense flow and tonicity, and through calcium pump and phosphoinositide kinase activity that translate these cues into intracellular signals and altered gene expression. Failure of this water response produces diabetes insipidus, dysnatraemia, and impaired urine concentration, and the same sensing machinery contributes to cyst formation in polycystic kidney disease.

Fertilization is the sequence of events by which a sperm and an egg recognise each other, fuse, and produce a diploid zygote, the starting point of every new individual; failure at any step causes infertility or early developmental arrest. The genes trace the whole itinerary: sperm capacitation and hyperactivated motility through CatSper channels, ABHD2 and axonemal/flagellar accessory proteins; binding to and penetration of the zona pellucida built from ZP1-ZP4, aided by acrosomal proteases such as acrosin, ZAN and SPAM1; and gamete membrane adhesion and fusion through the IZUMO1-JUNO pair with TMEM95, SPACA6 and DCST1/2. After fusion, PLCZ1 triggers the calcium oscillations that release the oocyte from meiotic arrest via WEE2, while ASTL cleaves ZP2 to block polyspermy, and sperm chromatin packaged by transition proteins is remodelled by NPM2 for pronuclear formation.

Fertilization is the meeting of sperm and egg that creates a zygote, and the genes here cover the whole sequence from sperm capacitation to egg activation. Sperm must cross the cumulus and bind the zona pellucida glycoprotein coat (ZP1-ZP4), undergo the acrosome reaction to release hydrolases such as acrosin and hyaluronidase, then fuse with the oolemma through the IZUMO1-JUNO receptor pair together with SPACA6, TMEM95 and DCST1/2. Progesterone-stimulated calcium entry via CatSper channels, with ABHD2 as the lipid sensor, steers hyperactivated motility and chemotaxis. After fusion, sperm-delivered PLCZ1 triggers oocyte calcium oscillations that release the meiotic arrest maintained by WEE2, while ASTL cleaves ZP2 to block additional sperm, and protamine removal with NPM2 remodels the paternal genome. Defects in these steps are a common cause of male and female infertility and of failed in vitro fertilization.

detection of biotic stimulus is the front end of innate immunity: the sensing step by which cells recognise molecules made by microbes and other organisms and convert that recognition into an intracellular signal. It sets the threshold for inflammation, determines whether an infection is contained or becomes sepsis, and shapes what antigen is later shown to T cells. Surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors with their accessory proteins LBP and LY96 read lipopeptide, LPS and CpG DNA; C-type lectins such as CLEC7A and CLEC6A detect fungal glucans and mannans; cytosolic NOD1, NOD2 and the NLRC4 and NLRP3 inflammasomes respond to peptidoglycan fragments and to bacterial secretion systems by driving caspase-1 activation. Peptidoglycan recognition proteins and scavenger receptors bind and clear microbial ligands directly, while MHC and CD1D molecules link detection to lymphocyte presentation.

Host cells must recognise that a microbe is present before they can respond to it, and detection of biotic stimulus covers the receptors and accessory proteins that convert microbial molecules into intracellular signals. This is the sensing step of innate immunity: without it, bacterial and fungal invaders replicate unchecked, while inappropriate or excessive sensing drives septic shock and autoinflammatory disease. Surface Toll-like receptors, aided by LBP and the LY96 co-receptor, detect lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides and microbial DNA; C-type lectins such as CLEC7A and CLEC6A bind fungal glucans and mannans; cytosolic NOD1 and NOD2 sense peptidoglycan fragments; and NLRP3 or NLRC4 with NAIP nucleate inflammasomes that mature IL-1 family cytokines. Peptidoglycan recognition proteins and complement components add direct antimicrobial and opsonic activity, while MHC and CD1D molecules link recognition to lymphocyte activation and adaptive immunity.

Response to symbiont covers how a host cell or tissue changes its behaviour when it detects another organism living in close association with it, from commensal gut bacteria to invading microbes and parasites. It matters because barrier surfaces must tolerate a resident microbiota while still restraining it, and the response determines whether that relationship stays benign or becomes infection and inflammation. The genes here point to several arms of that adjustment: C4BP subunits restrain complement activation on host surfaces, a control point that microbes themselves exploit to evade lysis; glutathione peroxidase buffers the oxidative burst that accompanies microbial encounters; and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases together with the carnitine transporter SLC22A5 handle conjugation and transport of small molecules at mucosal epithelium. Together they describe host defence and detoxification tuned to microbial exposure rather than to sterile injury.

This is the host side of living with a smaller partner organism: the changes in gene expression, secretion and enzyme activity that follow contact with a symbiont or other closely associated microbe. Such responses set the terms of colonisation, deciding whether a resident microbe is tolerated, contained, or cleared, and they shape mucosal chemistry at the interfaces where microbes are encountered. The genes here point to three arms of that adjustment: restraint of complement activation on host surfaces by the C4b-binding protein subunits, which keeps an inflammatory cascade from damaging host tissue; antioxidant defence against hydrogen peroxide by glutathione peroxidase 1; and conjugative detoxification of small lipophilic compounds by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases of the olfactory and airway mucosa, alongside a carnitine and organic cation transporter that supports epithelial metabolism.

response to mechanical stimulus is how cells and tissues sense physical force — stretch, pressure, shear, touch, sound — and convert it into altered ion flux, gene expression and secretion. It underlies hearing and touch sensation, blood pressure and flow sensing by endothelium, load-dependent bone remodelling, cartilage and tendon maintenance, and the hypertrophic growth of stretched cardiac muscle; its failure produces deafness, insensitivity to pain, polycystic kidney disease and maladaptive cardiac remodelling. Force is transduced at the membrane by mechanosensitive channels such as PIEZO1/2, TRPV4, TMC1/2 and the polycystins, and at adhesions and the cytoskeleton through integrins, focal adhesion kinase, dystrophin–sarcoglycan links and titin-associated sarcomeric proteins including TCAP, CSRP3 and ANKRD1. Downstream MAPK, NF-κB and β-catenin signalling drives immediate-early transcription (FOS, JUN, MYC), inflammatory cytokine output, matrix remodelling by collagens and MMPs, and osteocyte signals such as sclerostin and osteocalcin.

Cells continually sense physical force "u2014 stretch, pressure, shear, sound and touch "u2014 and convert it into electrical, transcriptional and secretory responses; this is the response to mechanical stimulus. It underlies hearing and balance, touch and mechanical pain, blood pressure and flow sensing in vessels, bone remodelling under load, and the hypertrophic adaptation of heart and skeletal muscle. Force is transduced at the membrane by mechanosensitive channels such as PIEZO1 and PIEZO2, TRPV4, potassium channels of the two-pore family, acid-sensing channels, and the hair-cell machinery built around TMC1/TMC2 and their tip-link partners, and at adhesions where integrins, cadherins, focal adhesion kinase and the cytoskeleton relay tension inward. Downstream, MAPK cascades, NF-"u03baB and immediate-early factors such as FOS and JUN reprogram gene expression, while sarcomeric and costameric proteins including titin, dystrophin and CSRP3 report muscle load. Defects give deafness, polycystic kidney disease, cardiomyopathy and skeletal fragility.

response to gravity covers how cells and tissues sense and adapt to gravitational load, a stimulus that shapes bone mass, muscle bulk and the vestibular sense of head position. Its relevance is clearest when gravity is removed: in microgravity or during prolonged unloading, bone mineral is lost and skeletal muscle wastes, changes traceable to the mechanotransduction and endocrine components represented here. Osteocalcin marks the osteoblast response to mechanical loading, growth hormone receptor and myostatin set the anabolic and catabolic balance of muscle, and immediate-early transcription through FOS, downstream of Ras signalling, converts a mechanical cue into altered gene expression. Otopetrin 1 and an NADPH oxidase are required for otoconia formation in the inner ear, the dense particles that let the utricle and saccule register linear acceleration, with synaptic transmission relaying that information onward for balance and postural control.

Gravity is a constant mechanical and sensory input, and cells respond to it by changing gene expression, growth and signalling output. Two distinct arms are represented here. In the inner ear, the otoconia of the vestibular system transduce linear acceleration and head tilt: OTOP1 is required for otoconia formation, NOX3 supplies the oxidase activity needed for their assembly, and STX1A supports transmitter release at hair cell synapses; loss of these leaves animals unable to sense which way is down, with balance and righting defects. In bone and muscle, mechanical loading against gravity governs tissue mass, with osteocalcin marking osteoblast activity, growth hormone receptor and RAS signalling relaying anabolic cues, immediate-early FOS induction reporting the load itself, and myostatin restraining muscle growth. Unloading, as in disuse or spaceflight, causes bone loss and muscle atrophy through these same routes.

response to herbicide covers the cellular and organismal reactions triggered by exposure to plant-killing chemicals, which in humans and other animals act as xenobiotic toxicants rather than as intended targets. It matters because agricultural herbicides such as paraquat and glyphosate cause oxidative injury, dopaminergic neuron loss and porphyrin-pathway disturbance, and this response determines how much damage exposure produces. The genes trace several arms of that reaction: induction of a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that oxidises the foreign compound, changes in the first and third enzymes of heme biosynthesis, which are classic readouts of chemically induced porphyria, secretion of the iron-sequestering stress protein lipocalin-2, and the mitochondrial serine protease HTRA2, which links herbicide-driven mitochondrial stress to apoptosis. Together they place this biology at the intersection of xenobiotic metabolism, heme synthesis and mitochondrial cell death signalling.

Herbicides such as paraquat, glyphosate and the diphenyl ethers reach animal cells as xenobiotic and oxidative insults, and this grouping collects the cellular responses they provoke: altered gene expression, induction of detoxifying enzymes, and adjustments to heme synthesis and stress handling. Its relevance is toxicological rather than developmental, since herbicide exposure in humans is linked to oxidative tissue injury and, for paraquat, to dopaminergic neuron loss and parkinsonism. The members point to the mechanisms involved: a xenobiotic-inducible cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that metabolises aromatic compounds, the first and second enzymes of the heme biosynthetic route whose activity is sensitive to porphyrinogenic chemicals, a mitochondrial serine protease that participates in stress-induced apoptosis, and a secreted iron-siderophore-binding protein induced during inflammation and cellular damage.</br>

response to blue light covers the cellular changes triggered by short-wavelength visible light, from circadian timing to pigment production and metabolic adjustment. In humans this is the biology behind light entrainment of the body clock and the effects of daylight and screen exposure on sleep, mood and skin. The cryptochromes CRY1 and CRY2 sit in the core clock feedback loop, repressing CLOCK/BMAL1-driven transcription and setting the phase of downstream rhythms, while OPN3 is an opsin photoreceptor expressed outside the retina, in skin melanocytes and adipose tissue, where blue light stimulates calcium signalling. Downstream effectors include the melanogenic enzymes tyrosinase and DCT, linking irradiation to pigmentation, and CPT1B, tying photic input to fatty acid oxidation. Loss of this responsiveness disrupts sleep-wake alignment and the peripheral rhythms that follow it.

Blue light in the 440-500 nm range is the strongest entraining signal for the mammalian circadian clock and also a stress stimulus for skin and eye, and this pathway covers the cellular responses it triggers. The cryptochromes CRY1 and CRY2, core repressors of the clock's transcriptional feedback loop, and the opsin OPN3 provide light-responsive components, while tyrosinase and dopachrome tautomerase link short-wavelength exposure to melanin synthesis and pigmentation in melanocytes. Downstream consequences extend to metabolic and inflammatory output, including fatty acid oxidation capacity through the carnitine palmitoyltransferase CPT1B and secretion of lipocalin-2. Disruption of these responses contributes to misaligned sleep-wake timing, altered metabolic rhythms, and light-driven skin damage, placing blue light detection at the interface of photobiology, circadian timing and energy balance.

Response to salt stress is the set of adjustments a cell or organism makes when external salt concentration rises or falls, protecting cells from osmotic swelling, shrinkage and ionic damage. In humans this matters most in the kidney medulla, where cells routinely face extreme sodium chloride and urea gradients, and in systemic control of water balance: vasopressin release, aquaporin-mediated water permeability, and sodium transport by Na/K-ATPase regulatory subunits and cation-chloride cotransporters together set urine concentration and blood volume. Downstream responses include accumulation of compatible osmolytes through aldose reductase, mechanosensitive calcium entry via TRPV4, chaperone induction, mitochondrial calcium handling, and mRNA destabilisation programmes that reshape gene expression. When the stress exceeds adaptive capacity, apoptotic and inflammatory routes engage, linking hypertonicity to tubular cell death, cytokine release and impaired concentrating ability.

Cells and tissues exposed to changing external salt concentration must defend their volume and internal ion balance, and the response to salt stress is the coordinated set of adjustments that makes this possible. It matters most in the kidney medulla, where cells survive osmolarities that would kill other tissue by accumulating compatible osmolytes, remodelling transport, and blunting the DNA damage and apoptosis that hypertonicity provokes. Aldose reductase generates sorbitol as an organic osmolyte, aquaporin water channels and cation-chloride cotransporters move water and ions across the membrane, vasopressin drives systemic water retention, and a stretch-sensitive TRPV4 channel reports cell swelling. Mitochondrial calcium uptake components and the cell death machinery set the threshold between adaptation and loss of the cell. Failure of these adaptations contributes to renal injury and to disturbances of sodium and blood pressure homeostasis.

Carbohydrate mediated signaling covers the cellular responses triggered when a sugar or glycan is detected, whether as a nutrient or as a marker of foreign material. It links dietary carbohydrate to metabolic gene expression and links microbial sugars to innate immune activation, so its outputs range from insulin secretion and lipogenesis to antifungal defence. One arm is glucose sensing in the pancreatic beta cell and liver, where PDX1 and NKX6-1 maintain beta cell identity and glucose-responsive transcription factors such as MLXIPL and the USF proteins, acting with SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits, drive lipogenic and glycolytic programmes. The other arm is lectin-based recognition: CLEC7A binds fungal beta-glucan to initiate phagocyte signalling, while AGER responds to advanced glycation end products, tying chronic hyperglycaemia to inflammatory signalling and diabetic tissue damage.

Cells read sugars as information, and carbohydrate-mediated signalling covers the routes by which detection of a carbohydrate ligand or a rise in glucose is converted into a cellular response. Two distinct arms are represented. One is nutrient sensing: transcription factors such as MLXIPL and the USF proteins, together with chromatin remodelling subunits SMARCA4 and SMARCB1 and the islet regulators PDX1 and NKX6-1, couple glucose availability to lipogenic and beta-cell gene programmes and to insulin secretion, with adenylate cyclase amplifying the secretory signal. The other is innate recognition: the lectin receptors CLEC7A and COLEC12 and the advanced glycation end-product receptor AGER bind fungal beta-glucans, glycosylated ligands and modified sugars to trigger phagocytosis and inflammatory responses. Failure on the metabolic side underlies diabetes and dysregulated lipogenesis; failure on the recognition side impairs antifungal defence.

post-embryonic animal morphogenesis covers the shaping of anatomical structures after embryogenesis is complete, during larval, juvenile and postnatal growth when tissues continue to be patterned, remodelled and matured. It matters because many organs — retina, brain, skeletal muscle, gut-associated lymphoid tissue — acquire their final architecture only in this window, and disruption produces developmental malformation rather than early lethality. The genes point to distinct arms of that process: a chromatin remodeller required for proper growth and brain development, an apical polarity protein that maintains photoreceptor and retinal layer organisation, an immunoglobulin-family adhesion receptor guiding axon and dendrite wiring, a glycosyltransferase that matures dystroglycan for muscle and neuronal migration, a homeobox factor patterning spleen and gut lymphoid tissue, and a vesicle-trafficking subunit whose loss causes progressive motor neuron degeneration. Together they link cell adhesion, glycosylation, transcriptional control and trafficking to postnatal tissue form.

Shaping of anatomical structures does not end at birth: tissues continue to grow, remodel and organize their layers through juvenile stages, and post-embryonic animal morphogenesis covers that later construction and patterning of organs. The genes grouped here point to several arms of it. A chromatin remodeller of the SWI/SNF-like family, ATRX, sustains the transcriptional programmes behind postnatal growth and brain development, and its loss causes a syndromic intellectual disability with genital and skeletal anomalies. CRB1 maintains apical polarity and adhesion at the outer limiting membrane of the retina, where failure produces progressive photoreceptor degeneration. DSCAM guides axon and dendrite arborization and self-avoidance; LARGE1 glycosylates dystroglycan so that muscle and neurons engage basement membrane laminin, and its mutation gives congenital muscular dystrophy with brain malformation. NKX2-3 patterns gut and spleen mesenchyme, while VPS54 supports motor neuron maintenance.

anterior/posterior axis specification is the embryonic patterning program that establishes the head-to-tail axis and then elaborates it into ordered segments and organ fields. It is what allows a radially symmetric early embryo to acquire a body plan, and its disruption produces gastrulation failure, axis duplication or truncation, caudal malformations and laterality defects. The genes trace the signalling that sets it up: Nodal and BMP4 with their antagonists Lefty and Cerberus, canonical and non-canonical Wnt ligands acting through beta-catenin and Frizzled, and Sonic hedgehog from midline tissue. These inputs converge on transcription factors that read positional value — Brachyury, CDX1/2/4, OTX2 and FOXA2 for axial level, and MESP2 with the RIPPLY repressors and TBX6 for the segmentation clock that partitions presomitic mesoderm into somites. Related activities include primitive streak formation, mesoderm induction and left-right asymmetry.

The head-to-tail body plan is laid down in the early embryo, and anterior/posterior axis specification is the process that establishes it, maintains it, and elaborates it into regionally distinct tissues. Its failure produces axis duplication, truncated or missing posterior structures, and laterality defects, and the same machinery is reused later to segment the trunk. Nodal and its feedback antagonists Lefty1/2 and Cerberus-like signalling set the organiser and break symmetry, while Wnt3, Wnt8A and stabilised beta-catenin with Wnt secretion machinery drive posterior identity through the CDX factors and the mesodermal transcription factors TBXT, MESP1/2 and TBX6. Anterior character is protected by FOXA2, OTX2 and LHX1, and RIPPLY1/2 provide the periodic repression that positions somite boundaries. BMP4, SHH and Polycomb-type chromatin repression coordinate this with dorsoventral patterning and HOX gene deployment along the growing axis.

Intracellular water homeostasis keeps cell volume and osmolarity within tolerable limits, allowing cells to survive osmotic challenge without swelling, shrinking, or lysing. It matters wherever fluid moves across epithelia and membranes in bulk: kidney tubules concentrating urine, brain astrocytes buffering the perivascular space, and secretory tissues handling large water fluxes. The core machinery is the aquaporin water channels, which provide selective transmembrane pores rather than relying on slow diffusion through the lipid bilayer; AQP1 serves vascular and tubular water flow, AQP4 dominates astrocyte endfeet and shapes brain water content and oedema, and AQP11 maintains intracellular and endoplasmic reticulum compartments, with its loss producing renal cyst formation. Hormonal input from secretin and its receptor links water transport to ductal fluid secretion, while CLN3 ties lysosomal and vacuolar volume control into the same regulatory picture.

Cells must hold their water content steady against osmotic swings, because volume changes distort membrane tension, cytoskeletal organisation and solute concentrations, and unchecked swelling kills. Intracellular water homeostasis covers the channels and signals that set how fast water crosses membranes and how the cell responds to osmotic stress. Aquaporins provide the conduits: AQP1 in capillary endothelium and other absorptive epithelia, AQP4 at astrocyte endfeet where it governs brain water movement and contributes to cerebral oedema, and AQP11 in an intracellular position in kidney proximal tubule and other tissues, where its loss causes vacuolated cells and polycystic kidney disease. Hormonal input arrives through G protein-coupled receptors, including the secretin receptor, whose ligand drives fluid secretion. CLN3, mutated in juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, links lysosomal function and cell volume regulation to the same balance.

Oocyte differentiation is the maturation of a female germ cell into a fertilizable egg, the step that determines a woman's reproductive lifespan and the developmental competence of the embryo that follows. Its failure underlies premature ovarian insufficiency, oocyte maturation arrest and infertility. The genes trace the whole trajectory: transcription factors such as FIGLA, SOHLH1/2, ZGLP1 and FOXL2 commit and sustain the oocyte program; meiotic recombination and cohesion factors including DMC1, REC8, BRCA2 and ATM execute and monitor prophase I; and MOS, CCNB1, CDC25B, WEE2 and FBXO5 drive meiotic arrest and resumption downstream of NPPC-NPR2 and PDE3A control of cyclic nucleotides. In parallel, piRNA-associated TDRD proteins and maternal RNA-binding regulators such as DAZL, ZAR1, YBX2, TUT4/7 and YTHDF2 silence transposons and store, extend and time the destruction of maternal mRNAs. Granulosa communication via GDF9 and follicle growth signals couple oocyte quality to the surrounding follicle.

Oocyte differentiation is the maturation of a female germ cell into a fertilizable egg, and it determines both the size of the ovarian reserve and the quality of the maternal contribution to the embryo. Transcription factors such as FIGLA, SOHLH1/2, NOBOX-like regulators, FOXL2 and ZGLP1 commit and sustain the oocyte programme, while meiotic components including DMC1, REC8, TRIP13 and MEIOC execute recombination and chromosome cohesion. Because the growing oocyte is transcriptionally quiescent, much of the control is post-transcriptional: Tudor-domain proteins and piRNA factors silence transposons, and TUT4/TUT7, YTHDF2, YBX2 and ZAR1 manage maternal mRNA storage, tailing and timed decay. Cell-cycle arrest and release depend on CCNB1, MOS, WEE2, FBXO5 and CDC25B, with granulosa-derived signals such as GDF9, NPPC-NPR2 and IGF1 coordinating follicle growth. Defects cause premature ovarian insufficiency, oocyte maturation arrest and early embryonic failure.

response to UV-C is the cellular reaction to short-wavelength ultraviolet light, the most genotoxic part of the UV spectrum, which forms pyrimidine dimers and other helix-distorting lesions that stall replication forks and block transcription. Cells that cannot mount this response accumulate mutations and die or transform, and inherited defects in its components underlie photosensitivity and cancer-prone syndromes such as xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome and Werner syndrome. The genes span lesion removal and tolerance: the nucleotide excision repair endonuclease ERCC5 excises damaged DNA, POLH performs translesion synthesis across dimers, and BRCA2 and the WRN helicase restart or protect damaged forks. Chromatin factors including HMGN1 open damaged templates for repair, while MAP3K4 signalling and transcriptional regulators such as YY1 and BCL3 couple damage sensing to stress kinase activation, altered gene expression, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.

Short-wavelength ultraviolet light in the UV-C band is absorbed directly by DNA, producing cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and other helix-distorting photoproducts, and this response is how a cell detects that damage and decides between repair, arrest and death. What it enables is genome stability after photodamage; failure of its components underlies sun-sensitivity syndromes, premature ageing and cancer predisposition. Several members act on the lesions themselves: a nucleotide excision repair endonuclease removes damaged strands, a translesion polymerase copies past dimers that would otherwise stall replication forks, and helicase and recombination factors such as WRN and BRCA2 handle the broken or collapsed forks that follow. Alongside repair, chromatin proteins and transcriptional regulators including HMGN1 and YY1 reshape gene expression, while a stress-activated kinase cascade feeds into checkpoint and apoptotic decisions, linking photodamage sensing to cell fate.

Response to lithium ion covers the cellular and transcriptional changes triggered by exposure to Li+, the ion used therapeutically as a mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder and known for its narrow therapeutic window and effects on kidney and thyroid. The genes trace lithium's two best-understood molecular targets: glycogen synthase kinase-3, inhibited by lithium to alter Wnt and insulin signalling and downstream programs of proliferation and differentiation, and inositol monophosphatase, whose blockade depletes inositol and dampens phosphoinositide second-messenger cycling. Downstream consequences appear as altered adenylate cyclase and calcineurin-NFAT signalling, changed glutamate receptor function at synapses, and shifts in differentiation-linked transcription factors governing adipocyte, myogenic and hepatic programs. Sodium-dicarboxylate transporters and chaperone-mediated stress responses place ion handling and cellular homeostasis alongside neuronal excitability in the overall reaction to lithium.

Cells and tissues exposed to lithium ions mount a characteristic set of transcriptional and signalling changes, and this response underlies both the mood-stabilising action of lithium in bipolar disorder and its side effects on kidney, thyroid and bone. The best-understood targets appear here: glycogen synthase kinase-3 alpha, which lithium inhibits and whose inhibition reshapes Wnt, insulin and circadian outputs, and inositol monophosphatase, whose blockade depletes the inositol pool that supports phosphoinositide second-messenger cycling. Downstream consequences include altered adenylate cyclase signalling, calcineurin-NFAT-dependent transcription, glutamate receptor availability at synapses, and shifts in differentiation programmes for adipocytes, muscle and epithelium through factors such as CEBPA, MYOG, ID2 and hedgehog signalling. Dicarboxylate transporters and cell-cycle regulators round out the cellular adjustment to the ion.

Detoxification of copper ion protects cells from the redox chemistry of free copper, which catalyses hydroxyl radical formation and displaces metals from the active sites of other proteins. Cells need copper as an enzyme cofactor but can tolerate almost none of it unbound, so excess is buffered or exported. The bulk of this capacity comes from the metallothionein family, small cysteine-rich proteins induced by metal load that clamp copper in thiolate clusters and hold it in an inert pool; ATP7A moves copper out of the cytosol into the secretory pathway for efflux or delivery to cuproenzymes, and DJ-1 contributes antioxidant defence against copper-driven damage. Loss of this buffering underlies copper toxicity in liver and brain, links to Wilson and Menkes disease physiology, and modulates sensitivity to copper-dependent cell death; the same metallothioneins also handle zinc and cadmium.

Copper is needed as an enzyme cofactor but is dangerous when free, since redox cycling of the ion generates reactive oxygen species and displaces other metals from their binding sites. Detoxification of copper ion keeps the cytosolic free pool near zero by buffering the metal in high-affinity thiol-rich proteins and exporting the excess. The metallothionein family, represented here by many closely related MT1 genes along with MT2A, MT3 and MT4, provides cysteine clusters that sequester copper and zinc and are induced when metal levels rise. The ATP7A copper-transporting ATPase moves copper across membranes for efflux and for loading onto cuproenzymes; its loss causes Menkes disease, while related transport failure underlies hepatic copper overload. DJ-1 contributes an oxidative-stress-protective arm, linking metal handling to redox homeostasis and neuronal survival.

negative regulation of cell fate commitment covers the braking signals that keep progenitor cells uncommitted, delaying or blocking their assignment to a particular differentiated identity. This restraint preserves stem and progenitor pools during development and in adult tissues; losing it causes premature differentiation, exhaustion of progenitors, and patterning defects. Much of the mechanism is secreted Wnt antagonism — DKK1, SFRP2 and SOSTDC1 sequester ligands or block receptor engagement, tuning the same Frizzled receptors that drive commitment — alongside Notch-driven HES1, a transcriptional repressor that suppresses proneural and lineage-determining factors to sustain a progenitor state. Other members act in immune lineage decisions, where JAK3–STAT5 signalling and the transcription factors TBX21 and SPDEF bias helper T cell and secretory epithelial fates by repressing alternatives. The theme throughout is inhibition of differentiation programmes so that timing and position, not chance, determine identity.

Development requires not only pushing cells toward a fate but holding them back from one, and this is the repressive side of cell fate commitment: processes that block, delay or damp the rate at which progenitors lock into a particular identity, keeping pools uncommitted and boundaries between territories sharp. Several members act as extracellular brakes on Wnt signalling, with DKK1, SFRP2 and SOSTDC1 sequestering or blocking ligand-receptor engagement and so restraining fate decisions in skin appendages, bone and neural tissue. HES1 supplies the Notch-driven transcriptional repression that sustains progenitors and prevents premature neuronal or secretory differentiation. Others operate in lymphoid commitment, where JAK3-STAT5A signalling and lineage factors such as TBX21 bias helper T cell identity while suppressing alternatives. Loss of such restraint causes progenitor exhaustion, mispatterned tissue and, in adult epithelia, the aberrant differentiation seen in metaplasia and cancer.

Proteasomal ubiquitin-independent protein catabolic process is the arm of proteasome-mediated degradation that destroys substrates without first tagging them with ubiquitin chains. It disposes of oxidatively damaged, intrinsically disordered and unstructured proteins, and provides a rapid route for turning over short-lived regulators, so that protein quality control does not depend entirely on the ubiquitin ligase machinery. The genes centre on the 20S core particle itself, both the outer alpha ring that gates substrate entry and the beta ring carrying the caspase-, trypsin- and chymotrypsin-like catalytic sites, together with the immunoproteasome subunit PSMB10 and the PA200 activator. Regulators such as midnolin and ENC1 deliver or restrain specific clients, and NFE2L2 links this route to oxidative stress, being itself degraded in this manner while also driving expression of proteasome subunits during antioxidant responses.

Not every protein destroyed by the proteasome is tagged with ubiquitin first. This route covers degradation in which the 20S core particle, built from the alpha rings (PSMA1-7) and the catalytic beta subunits (PSMB1-7, plus the immunoproteasome subunit PSMB10), directly engages intrinsically disordered or oxidatively damaged substrates and hydrolyses their peptide bonds without prior ubiquitin conjugation. Activators and adaptors shape the process: PSME4 caps the core and promotes degradation of unstructured substrates, while MIDN and ENC1 deliver or present clients, and NFE2L2, the master transcription factor of the antioxidant response, is itself a well-known ubiquitin-independent proteasome substrate. The pathway matters for rapid disposal of damaged and short-lived regulatory proteins, for tuning oxidative stress responses, and for protein quality control when the ubiquitin conjugation machinery is overwhelmed or bypassed.

negative regulation of calcium ion transport into cytosol restrains the release of calcium into the cytoplasm, keeping this potent second messenger below the thresholds that trigger contraction, secretion, or death. Sustained cytosolic calcium overload opens the mitochondrial permeability transition pore and activates calpains, so damping calcium entry is one way cells survive ischaemia, excitotoxicity, and endoplasmic reticulum stress. The genes act at several control points: BCL2 and the ER membrane protein TMBIM6 limit calcium leak and IP3 receptor-mediated efflux from internal stores, tuning the ER-mitochondrial calcium transfer that commits a cell to apoptosis, while nitric oxide generated by NOS1 nitrosylates and inhibits channels including the ryanodine receptor. Circulating factors such as calcitonin gene-related peptide and erythropoietin impose the same restraint from outside the cell, linking this control to vascular tone, neuroprotection, and cell survival signalling.

Cytosolic calcium is a signal that must be kept transient, and this pathway covers the braking processes that limit how fast calcium enters the cytosol from internal stores or across the plasma membrane. Restraining that influx protects cells from the sustained calcium overload that triggers mitochondrial permeabilisation, calpain activation and death, so these activities sit upstream of apoptosis control, excitotoxic injury and cardiovascular tone. The members act by distinct routes: BCL2 at the endoplasmic reticulum dampens release through inositol trisphosphate receptors, while TMBIM6 similarly reduces ER calcium leak and buffers store content; neuronal nitric oxide synthase generates NO that feeds back on channel and receptor activity; and secreted factors including calcitonin gene-related peptide and erythropoietin signal through their receptors to lower calcium entry in target cells. Together they define the inhibitory side of calcium signalling rather than its initiation.

Negative regulation of platelet activation is the braking system that keeps circulating platelets quiescent and confines clotting to sites of genuine vessel injury. Without it, spontaneous aggregation and thrombus propagation cause arterial and venous thrombosis, stroke, and consumptive coagulopathy; healthy endothelium therefore actively suppresses the platelets flowing over it. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase supplies NO, which raises cyclic GMP and engages PRKG1 to blunt integrin activation and granule release, while thrombomodulin redirects thrombin toward protein C activation instead of platelet stimulation and serpin inhibitors quench residual protease activity.
