Because methotrexate and pemetrexed enter cells through these same carriers, transport capacity shapes antifolate chemotherapy response, and inadequate folate in pregnancy leads to neural tube defects.

Coenzyme A metabolic process builds, recycles and degrades the universal acyl carrier that makes fatty acid oxidation, the citric acid cycle, ketone and cholesterol synthesis, and countless acyl-transfer reactions possible. Cells cannot import coenzyme A intact, so they must synthesise it from pantothenate through a committed five-step route: pantothenate kinases (PANK1-4) set the rate-limiting step, PPCS and PPCDC generate pantetheine phosphate, and the bifunctional COASY completes adenylylation and phosphorylation. Balance is maintained by degradation and salvage, with Nudix hydrolases cleaving CoA and acyl-CoA esters and vanin releasing pantothenate from pantetheine, while thioesterases free fatty acids from their CoA thioesters. Genes such as ACLY, HMGCR and ACAT1 mark the biosynthetic demands that draw on this pool. Loss of PANK2 causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration, and COASY mutations produce a related brain iron accumulation disorder.

Coenzyme A is the universal carrier of acyl groups, and this is the set of reactions that make it, recycle it, and dispose of it. Nearly every route through central metabolism depends on the supply — fatty acid oxidation and synthesis, the citric acid cycle, ketone and cholesterol synthesis, and protein acetylation all run on acyl-CoA thioesters. Synthesis begins with pantothenate phosphorylation by the pantothenate kinases, continues through cysteine conjugation and decarboxylation by PPCS and PPCDC, and is completed by the bifunctional COASY. Countervailing activities set the pool size and composition: Nudix hydrolases degrade CoA and its esters, thioesterases such as ACOT7 and CROT release free fatty acids and regenerate free CoA, and vanin-1 recovers pantothenate from pantetheine. Loss of PANK2 causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, marking neurons as particularly intolerant of a failing CoA supply.

Coenzyme A biosynthetic process builds the universal acyl carrier that virtually all of intermediary metabolism depends on, from fatty acid oxidation and synthesis to the citric acid cycle, ketone body handling, amino acid catabolism and protein acetylation. Cells cannot make its pantothenate precursor and must salvage vitamin B5, so the committed step is its phosphorylation by pantothenate kinases; PANK2 acts in mitochondria and its loss causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation. Downstream, cysteine is conjugated and decarboxylated by PPCS and PPCDC to form pantetheine phosphate, and the bifunctional COASY adds and phosphorylates adenosine to complete coenzyme A; mutations here also produce childhood neurodegeneration. Flux is tuned by feedback from acyl-CoA thioesters, with thioesterases such as ACOT7 and transferases like ACAT1 setting the balance between free and acylated pools, coupling cofactor supply to lipid and energy demand.

Coenzyme A is the universal acyl carrier of intermediary metabolism, and its biosynthetic process converts dietary pantothenate into the thiol-bearing cofactor on which fatty acid oxidation, the citric acid cycle, ketone body handling, cholesterol synthesis and protein acetylation all depend. Pantothenate kinases carry out the committed first step and set the flux through the route; the pathway then proceeds by cysteine ligation and decarboxylation to yield pantetheine phosphate, with a bifunctional adenylyltransferase/kinase enzyme completing the molecule. Because the kinases are feedback-inhibited by CoA and its acyl thioesters, the pathway is tuned to the cell's own acyl load, and thioesterase activity that liberates free CoA feeds back into the same pool. Loss of the neuronally important kinase PANK2 causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, and mutations in the downstream synthase produce a related neurodegenerative disorder.

Viral process covers the whole of the host-virus interface: the host molecules a virus exploits to enter, replicate and leave a cell, and the countermeasures the cell mounts against it. It matters because these proteins set susceptibility to infection and determine whether an exposure becomes disease, and they are the targets of antiviral drugs and vaccines. Entry receptors and priming proteases such as ACE2, CD4, CCR5, NPC1, TMPRSS2, furin and the cathepsins define tropism; endosomal trafficking, glycosylation and ER-associated machinery support virion maturation; translation initiation factors, RNA-binding proteins and nuclear import carriers are commandeered for viral gene expression; and the ESCRT complexes are hijacked for budding and membrane scission. Opposing this are intrinsic and interferon-induced restriction factors -- APOBEC3 deaminases, TRIM proteins, IFITMs, tetherin, the OAS-RNase L arm and autophagy components -- which degrade viral nucleic acid, trap particles and trigger innate signalling.

Viruses cannot replicate alone, so every stage of their life cycle borrows host machinery, and this collection of host-virus interactions covers the whole of it: attachment and entry, genome replication and translation, assembly, and budding. The host factors here are the ones that determine susceptibility and tropism, including entry receptors and proteases such as ACE2, CD4, CCR5, NPC1, TMPRSS2 and the cathepsins, glycosylation enzymes that build receptor and envelope sugars, translation initiation and RNA-binding proteins commandeered for viral protein synthesis, and the ESCRT machinery with VPS4 and TSG101 that pinches off enveloped particles. Opposing them are restriction and sensing factors — APOBEC3 deaminases, tetherin, IFITMs, MX1, OAS-RNase L, TRIM proteins and RIG-I-like sensors — so the same processes underlie both permissiveness and innate antiviral defence. The balance sets whether infection is cleared, becomes persistent, or drives pathology.

Detection of bacterium is the sensing step of antibacterial immunity: the recognition of conserved microbial structures and their conversion into intracellular signals that launch inflammation. It determines whether a bacterium is tolerated or attacked, and defects in its components predispose to invasive infection or, when signalling is unrestrained, to inflammatory disease such as Crohn's disease and inherited autoinflammatory syndromes. Recognition happens in two compartments. At the surface, Toll-like receptor heterodimers of TLR2 with TLR1 or TLR6 bind lipopeptides and lipoteichoic acid, while peptidoglycan recognition proteins and scavenger-type receptors bind and in some cases directly kill bacteria. In the cytosol, NOD1 and NOD2 detect peptidoglycan fragments, and NAIP paired with NLRC4 detects flagellin and type III secretion components to assemble an inflammasome. Antigen-presenting molecules, including CD1d for bacterial lipids, hand the detected material to T cells, linking innate sensing to adaptive responses.

Host cells recognise bacteria by sensing conserved microbial structures and converting that encounter into an immune signal, the first step in mounting defence against infection. Surface Toll-like receptors, acting as TLR1/2 and TLR2/6 heterodimers, detect bacterial lipopeptides and lipoteichoic acid and trigger inflammatory gene expression, while cytosolic NOD1 and NOD2 respond to peptidoglycan fragments that reach the cytoplasm of invaded cells. NAIP and NLRC4 sense bacterial flagellin and secretion-system components to assemble an inflammasome, driving caspase-1 activation, interleukin-1 release and pyroptotic death of infected macrophages. Peptidoglycan recognition proteins bind and in some cases directly kill bacteria or degrade their cell wall, and MHC class I, class II and CD1D molecules present bacterial peptides and lipids to T cells, linking this detection of bacterium to adaptive immunity. Loss-of-function variants, notably in NOD2, predispose to Crohn's disease and other inflammatory conditions.

Vesicle organization covers how cells build, shape, load, dock and dismantle the membrane carriers that move cargo between compartments and to the cell surface. It underlies secretion, endocytic uptake and degradation, neurotransmitter release, pigment and lysosome-related organelle biogenesis, and the release of extracellular vesicles; its failure produces Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, neurodegeneration and defective immune granule secretion. The genes trace each step: COPII and TRAPP components budding carriers from the ER, clathrin adaptors and dynamins pinching vesicles from membranes, sorting nexins and Rab GTPases with their effectors specifying identity and destination, HOPS and syntaxin/VAMP SNARE pairs with synaptotagmin calcium sensors driving fusion, ESCRT subunits and the vacuolar ATPase generating and acidifying multivesicular bodies, and BLOC/HPS complexes routing cargo to melanosomes and secretory granules. Sperm acrosome formation is treated here as a specialised instance of the same vesicle-shaping machinery.

Membrane traffic depends on vesicles being built, loaded, docked and taken apart again, and vesicle organization covers that whole life cycle: budding from a donor membrane, acquisition of the right coat and cargo, tethering and fusion, and the inward budding that creates multivesicular bodies. It underlies secretion, endosome and lysosome maturation, autophagy, neurotransmitter release and the biogenesis of specialized granules such as melanosomes and platelet dense bodies. COPII components and SEC24 paralogues select cargo at the ER, adaptor complexes and sorting nexins sort at the Golgi and endosomes, dynamins pinch off buds, TRAPP and HOPS complexes tether, syntaxins with VAMPs and synaptotagmins drive calcium-triggered fusion, and ESCRT subunits with VPS4 deform membranes into intralumenal vesicles. Vacuolar ATPase subunits acidify the resulting compartments. Failure produces Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi syndromes, lysosomal storage disease, and neurodegeneration linked to LRRK2, alpha-synuclein and C9orf72.

organic acid biosynthetic process gathers the reactions by which cells build carboxylic acids — fatty acids, eicosanoids, bile acids, amino acids and their keto-acid relatives — the small molecules that serve as membrane building blocks, fuels, signalling mediators and nitrogen carriers. Its breadth explains why defects here surface as such varied disease: urea cycle enzymes such as CPS1, OTC and ASS1 prevent ammonia toxicity, PAH and CBS failures cause phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, and peroxisomal ACOX1 and ABCD1 lesions produce leukodystrophy. Fatty acid synthesis through ACACA, FASN, SCD and the ELOVL/FADS elongation and desaturation series is coordinated with lipolysis and beta-oxidation by AMPK subunits, SREBP regulators and nuclear receptors including LXR and FXR, while cytochrome P450s and the prostaglandin and leukotriene synthases convert cholesterol and arachidonate into bile acids and inflammatory lipid mediators. Together these routes tie carbon, nitrogen and one-carbon folate metabolism to nutrient sensing and immune signalling.

Organic acid biosynthesis gathers the routes by which cells build carboxylic acids and related acidic metabolites: fatty acids and their very-long-chain and desaturated derivatives, bile acids, eicosanoids, amino acids, and the intermediates of urea and one-carbon metabolism. Together these supply membrane lipids, fuel for oxidation, nitrogen disposal, dietary lipid absorption, and signalling molecules, so defects surface as urea cycle crises, phenylketonuria, hyperoxaluria, peroxisomal disease, or dyslipidaemia. Mechanistically it spans cytosolic de novo synthesis by acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase, ER elongation and desaturation steps, peroxisomal beta-oxidation and bile acid conjugation, cytochrome P450 oxidations that initiate bile acid formation from cholesterol, and prostaglandin and leukotriene generation from arachidonate released by phospholipases. Regulation runs through nutrient and lipid sensors including AMP-activated protein kinase subunits, SREBP-pathway proteins, and nuclear receptors such as the bile acid and oxysterol receptors, linking output to nutritional and circadian state.

Wnt signaling pathway is the cell-cell communication system that patterns the embryo and sustains stem cell compartments in adult tissues such as the intestinal crypt, bone and hair follicle. Secreted Wnt ligands, lipid-modified by PORCN and exported via WLS, engage Frizzled receptors with LRP5/6 or alternative co-receptors including ROR1/2, RYK and PTK7. In the canonical branch this inactivates the AXIN-APC-GSK3-CK1 destruction complex so that beta-catenin accumulates, enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF, displacing TLE corepressors to drive MYC, CCND1 and AXIN2. Non-canonical branches instead direct planar cell polarity and convergent extension through Dishevelled, VANGL, PRICKLE, CELSR and small GTPases. Tuning comes from DKK, SFRP, WIF1, NOTUM, and the RNF43/ZNRF3-RSPO-LGR module that sets receptor abundance. Loss of restraint, as in APC mutation, causes colorectal cancer, while insufficient signalling underlies bone density and limb patterning defects.

Wnt signalling tells a cell where it is, what to become, and whether to keep dividing, and it does so from embryonic patterning through to the maintenance of adult stem cells in gut, skin and bone. Secreted Wnt ligands, lipid-modified by porcupine and exported with the help of Wntless, engage Frizzled receptors together with LRP5/6 or alternative receptors such as ROR and RYK. In the canonical branch, receptor engagement disables the destruction complex built on APC, Axin, CK1 and GSK3, so beta-catenin escapes ubiquitin-mediated degradation, enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF and Pygopus/BCL9 to drive targets including MYC and cyclin D1, while Groucho/TLE repressors hold those promoters off in the unstimulated state. Non-canonical arms acting through Dishevelled, Vangl, Prickle and Rho-family GTPases orient cells during planar polarity and convergent extension. Secreted antagonists (DKKs, SFRPs, sclerostin, NOTUM) and the RSPO-LGR-RNF43/ZNRF3 module set signal strength; loss of this control underlies colorectal and other cancers, skeletal disease and developmental malformation.

diterpenoid metabolic process is, in human cells, essentially retinoid metabolism: the uptake of dietary carotenoids and vitamin A, their conversion to retinol, retinaldehyde and retinoic acid, and the disposal of excess. It supplies the visual chromophore that makes photoreception possible and the nuclear receptor ligand that patterns embryos and maintains epithelial differentiation, so its failure causes night blindness, retinal degeneration and developmental malformation. Carotenoid cleavage enzymes and lipases release retinol from esters, binding proteins and transthyretin carry it through blood and cytosol, and reversible dehydrogenase and reductase steps interconvert retinol and retinaldehyde before aldehyde dehydrogenases commit it to retinoic acid. In the eye, an esterification and isomerohydrolase cycle regenerates 11-cis-retinal for opsin. Dedicated CYP26 enzymes, other cytochromes P450 and glucuronosyltransferases then inactivate retinoic acid, keeping its concentration within the narrow range that gene regulation requires.

Vitamin A and its derivatives are the diterpenoid compounds this pathway handles, and the chemistry runs from dietary carotenoid cleavage through storage, transport, oxidation to retinoic acid, and finally inactivation. It matters because retinoic acid is the ligand for nuclear receptors that pattern the embryo and maintain epithelia, while 11-cis-retinal is the chromophore of the visual pigments. Carotenoid oxygenases split provitamin A, lecithin retinol acyltransferase esterifies retinol for storage in lipid droplets, lipases and esterases mobilise it, and retinol dehydrogenases plus retinaldehyde dehydrogenases generate the acid; CYP26 enzymes and glucuronidation terminate the signal. Binding proteins and transthyretin carry the hydrophobic ligands between compartments, and receptor-mediated uptake delivers them to cells. The visual cycle isomerase RPE65 and photoreceptor dehydrogenases place retinal regeneration in this route, so failures produce blindness, and excess or deficiency produces developmental malformation.

Diterpenoid biosynthetic process in human cells is effectively the making of retinoic acid, the vitamin A-derived hormone that patterns the embryo and maintains epithelial differentiation, spermatogenesis and immune tolerance. Deficiency causes night blindness and epithelial keratinization, while excess is teratogenic, so flux through this route is tightly controlled. Dietary carotene is cleaved by BCO1 to retinal, retinol is bound and trafficked by RBP1, and reversible oxidation by RDH10 and DHRS9 feeds the irreversible step catalysed by the aldehyde dehydrogenases ALDH1A2, ALDH1A3 and ALDH8A1, which fix the tissue-specific domains of retinoic acid production. CYP1A1 and AKR1C3 modulate the pool by catabolism and by competing carbonyl reduction. The product acts as a ligand for nuclear retinoic acid receptors, linking this metabolic pathway directly to developmental gene transcription.

In humans this diterpenoid biosynthetic route is essentially retinoid production: dietary carotenoids and retinol are converted into retinoic acid, the ligand for nuclear retinoic acid receptors that patterns the embryo and maintains epithelia, germ cells and immune tissue. BCO1 cleaves beta-carotene to retinal, cellular retinol-binding protein RBP1 delivers retinol to the oxidative steps, and dehydrogenases/reductases such as RDH10 and DHRS9 interconvert retinol and retinal; aldehyde dehydrogenases ALDH1A2 and ALDH1A3 then perform the irreversible oxidation to retinoic acid, with ALDH8A1 favouring 9-cis substrate and CYP1A1 contributing oxidative turnover. Because the retinoic acid gradient acts as a morphogen, too little or too much disrupts limb, eye, heart and neural tube development, and altered flux is linked to vitamin A deficiency, night blindness and to differentiation therapy in leukaemia.

Terpenoid catabolic process is the breakdown of isoprenoid-derived compounds, most consequentially retinoids and carotenoids, so that their signalling activity is terminated and their levels held within a narrow window. This matters because retinoic acid is a morphogen: too much or too little disrupts hindbrain patterning, limb and craniofacial development, germ cell entry into meiosis, and epithelial differentiation in the adult. The CYP26 family of cytochrome P450 enzymes performs the committed step, hydroxylating all-trans retinoic acid to 4-oxo and 4-hydroxy products destined for excretion, and their expression is itself retinoic acid-inducible, forming a negative feedback loop that shapes gradients across tissue. Carotenoid cleavage by BCO2 within mitochondria and aldo-keto reductase-mediated reduction of retinal and related carbonyls supply parallel routes, while a polyprenol phosphatase acts on longer isoprenoid chains. Loss of these clearance enzymes produces retinoid excess phenotypes.

Terpenoids, the isoprenoid-derived compounds that include carotenoids, retinoids and polyprenyl phosphates, are broken down by this catabolic route so that their signalling and cofactor activity is terminated at the right time and place. Its best-understood job is limiting retinoic acid: the CYP26 enzymes hydroxylate all-trans retinoic acid toward inactive metabolites, and the steep degradation gradients they create pattern the hindbrain, limb bud and germ cells, while their loss causes retinoid excess and severe developmental malformation. Carotenoid cleavage by BCO2 disposes of non-provitamin A xanthophylls in mitochondria, preventing their accumulation in tissue, and aldo-keto reductases reduce retinaldehyde and related carbonyls. PLPP6 dephosphorylates presqualene diphosphate, turning over an isoprenoid phosphate that restrains neutrophil signalling. Together these steps couple isoprenoid turnover to nuclear receptor signalling, vitamin A homeostasis and embryonic patterning.

Glycoside metabolic process covers the making and, mostly, the breaking of compounds in which a sugar is linked to another molecule through oxygen, sulfur or selenium. In humans this chemistry matters in two settings: turnover of glycolipids and glycoconjugates in the lysosome, and the handling of dietary and xenobiotic glycosides in liver and gut. Glycosidases here cleave specific terminal residues — glucocerebrosidase releases glucose from glucosylceramide, alpha-galactosidase A acts on globotriaosylceramide, and fucosidases and alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase trim their own linkages — and loss of these steps causes storage diseases such as Gaucher, Fabry, fucosidosis and Schindler disease. Alongside them, aldo-keto reductases and a sulfotransferase reduce and conjugate the aglycone products, tying glycoside breakdown to phase I and II detoxification, prostaglandin and steroid metabolism, and clearance of reactive carbonyls.

Glycoside metabolism covers the making and breaking of bonds between a sugar and an aglycone, and here the emphasis falls on hydrolysis of such linkages and on the reduction of sugar-derived carbonyls. Lysosomal glycosidases dominate: acid beta-glucosidase releases glucose from glucosylceramide, alpha-galactosidase A cleaves globotriaosylceramide, alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase and the two alpha-L-fucosidases trim terminal residues from glycolipids and glycoproteins. Loss of these activities causes lysosomal storage disease, with Gaucher and Fabry disease the clearest examples, and undigested substrate accumulating in macrophages, kidney and nerve. Alongside them, a family of aldo-keto reductases uses NADPH to reduce aldehydes and ketones, including glucose to sorbitol by aldose reductase, linking this chemistry to polyol formation in hyperglycaemia as well as to steroid and prostaglandin turnover and detoxification of reactive carbonyls.

vesicle-mediated transport is the cell's internal courier system: cargo is packaged into membrane-bounded vesicles, budded from a donor compartment, moved along cytoskeletal tracks, and fused with a target membrane. Nearly every aspect of cell physiology depends on it — secretion of hormones, antibodies and neurotransmitters, uptake of nutrients and receptors by endocytosis, delivery of lysosomal enzymes, recycling of plasma membrane transporters, and antigen presentation. The genes span the whole itinerary: COPII and COPI coats and TRAPP/Golgi tethers for early secretory traffic, clathrin with AP adaptors and dynamins for budding and scission, Rab GTPases with their GEFs and GAPs specifying compartment identity, SNAREs, synaptotagmins and NSF driving fusion, and retromer, WASH, ESCRT and HOPS complexes sorting cargo toward recycling or degradation. Loss of individual components causes neurodegeneration, immune deficiency, pigmentation and lysosomal storage disorders, reflecting how specialised secretory and phagocytic cells are.

Membrane traffic moves proteins and lipids between compartments inside sealed vesicles, and vesicle-mediated transport covers the whole itinerary: cargo selection, budding with a coat, movement along cytoskeletal tracks, then tethering and fusion with the target membrane. This is how secreted proteins leave the cell, how receptors are internalised and either recycled or sent to lysosomes for degradation, and how neurons release neurotransmitter and phagocytes engulf and digest microbes. The machinery here spans COPI, COPII, clathrin and adaptor complexes, Rab GTPases with their activating and inactivating regulators, SNAREs and their SM-protein and NSF partners, ESCRT subunits for multivesicular body formation, retromer and WASH for endosomal recycling, tethering assemblies such as TRAPP, HOPS, COG and the exocyst, plus motors and lipid kinases that set compartment identity. Failures produce lysosomal storage and pigmentation disorders, immunodeficiencies, neurodegeneration and defective lipoprotein and hormone secretion.

Macroautophagy is the bulk degradative route by which a cell encloses cytoplasm, damaged organelles, protein aggregates and intracellular microbes in a double-membraned autophagosome and delivers the contents to lysosomes for breakdown and recycling. It sustains amino acid supply during starvation, clears mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum that have failed quality control, and protects neurons and other long-lived cells; its decline underlies neurodegeneration, myopathy, lysosomal storage disease and defective antibacterial defence, as seen with Crohn's-associated ATG16L1 and Parkinson's-associated PINK1, PRKN and LRRK2. Nutrient and energy status converge on mTORC1, AMPK and the ULK1 initiation complex, which activate the class III PI3K with BECN1 to nucleate a phagophore; two ubiquitin-like conjugation systems lipidate LC3 and GABARAP proteins onto the growing membrane, cargo receptors such as SQSTM1, NBR1 and OPTN select ubiquitinated substrates, and SNAREs, HOPS and ESCRT machinery complete fusion with acidified lysosomes.

Macroautophagy is the bulk degradative route in which a double-membrane autophagosome engulfs cytoplasm, damaged organelles or protein aggregates and delivers them to the lysosome for breakdown and recycling. It sustains cells through nutrient starvation, clears mitochondria and other cargo that would otherwise become toxic, and its decline underlies neurodegeneration, lysosomal storage disease and impaired control of intracellular bacteria. Nutrient and stress signals converge on mTORC1 and AMPK to release the ULK1 kinase complex, which with Beclin-1-associated PI3KC3 generates phosphoinositide at the growing phagophore; ATG7, ATG3 and the ATG12-ATG5-ATG16L1 machinery conjugate LC3 and GABARAP proteins to its membrane, while ATG9A and lipid transfer proteins supply membrane. Cargo receptors such as p62, NBR1, OPTN and NDP52, together with PINK1-Parkin ubiquitination, select substrates, and SNAREs, Rab7 and HOPS-linked tethering complete fusion with acidified lysosomes.

Microautophagy is the route by which lysosomes and late endosomes swallow small portions of cytosol directly, by pinching their own limiting membrane inward rather than building a separate autophagosome around the cargo. It gives cells a low-cost, continuous way to turn over soluble proteins, organelle fragments and damaged membrane components, contributing to amino acid supply during nutrient stress and to the quality control of the endolysosomal system itself. The genes span the core autophagy machinery — the ULK1/ULK2 initiation kinases with ATG13 and RB1CC1, the ATG12–ATG5–ATG16L1 conjugation system, ATG7, the ATG4 proteases that process lipidated LC3, and the lipid-transferring ATG2 proteins with the scramblase ATG9 — together with sorting nexins and the ESCRT-associated ATPases VPS4A/VPS4B that drive membrane scission after invagination. Loss of this capacity leaves cells with impaired proteostasis and accumulating lysosomal damage.

Microautophagy delivers cytosolic material into the lumen of late endosomes or lysosomes without building a separate autophagosome: the limiting membrane of the degradative compartment invaginates directly, pinches off, and the cargo is degraded still wrapped in a single membrane derived from that invagination. It provides a route for turnover of proteins and portions of cytoplasm, and for remodelling the lysosomal membrane itself, complementing the larger-scale macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated uptake pathways in maintaining protein and organelle quality control. The machinery overlaps heavily with canonical autophagy: the ULK1/ULK2 initiation kinases with ATG13 and RB1CC1, the ATG12–ATG5–ATG16L1 conjugation system with the E1-like enzyme ATG7, ATG4 proteases that process and delipidate ATG8-family proteins, lipid-transfer proteins ATG2A/ATG2B and the transmembrane lipid scramblase ATG9A. Membrane scission draws on the ESCRT-associated AAA-ATPases VPS4A and VPS4B, and sorting nexins contribute membrane recognition.

Gap junction assembly builds the direct cytoplasmic bridges between neighbouring cells, channels that let ions, metabolites and second messengers under about a kilodalton pass while excluding proteins and nucleic acids. This electrical and metabolic coupling is what allows cardiac muscle to contract as a synchronised unit, the cochlea and epidermis to maintain ionic homeostasis, and Schwann cells to nourish myelinated axons; mutations in the connexins listed here cause deafness, palmoplantar keratoderma, X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy and cardiac conduction disease. Connexin hexamers are trafficked to the plasma membrane, docked with partner hemichannels in the apposed cell, and stabilised at junctional plaques through adherens-junction and caveolar components such as CTNNA1 and CAV1. Transcriptional regulators including TBX5, IRX3 and HOPX pattern which connexin is expressed where, setting up the fast-conducting versus slow-conducting regions of the heart.

Gap junction assembly builds the direct cytoplasmic bridges between neighbouring cells, channels that let ions, metabolites and second messengers under about a kilodalton pass freely while excluding proteins and nucleic acids. This coupling is what allows cardiac myocytes to propagate an action potential as a syncytium, Schwann cells to nourish the inner myelin layers, and cochlear support cells to recycle potassium; loss of it causes arrhythmia and conduction block, X-linked demyelinating neuropathy through connexin 32, and hereditary deafness and skin disease through connexin 26 and 30. Assembly requires connexin hexamers to be trafficked, docked with a partner hemichannel in the apposing membrane and stabilised at junctional plaques, a step that depends on adherens junction and caveolar components such as alpha-catenin and caveolin-1. Cardiac transcriptional regulators including TBX5 and IRX3 set which connexins a cell expresses, patterning conduction velocity across the heart, while inflammatory and renin-angiotensin signals remodel coupling.

phosphorylation is the transfer of phosphate onto proteins, sugars and lipids, the most widespread reversible modification cells use to switch enzymes on and off and to relay information from the cell surface to the nucleus. Nearly every regulated process depends on it: growth factor and cytokine responses, cell cycle progression, metabolic commitment of glucose, apoptosis and innate immune signalling. The genes here span the machinery that does this work — receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR, FGFRs and PDGFRs; cytoplasmic tyrosine kinases including SRC, SYK, BTK and the JAK family; serine/threonine cascades through RAF–MEK–ERK, AKT–mTOR, GSK3B and the CDKs and Aurora, PLK and NEK mitotic kinases — alongside sugar kinases such as hexokinases and phosphofructokinases, regulatory subunits and cyclins, scaffolds, and the phosphatases and inhibitors that reverse or restrain the reaction. Dysregulated kinase activity here drives much of oncogenesis and is the target of many drugs.

Attaching a phosphate group to a protein, sugar or lipid substrate is the cell's most widely used switch, and this collection spans essentially the whole enzymology of that reaction. Protein kinases dominate: receptor tyrosine kinases for growth factors and cytokines (EGFR, FGFRs, PDGFRs, KIT, INSR), the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinases and JAK family that relay them, and serine/threonine cascades running through RAF-MEK-ERK, PI3K-AKT-MTOR, the polo, aurora, NEK and cyclin-dependent kinases that time mitosis, and checkpoint kinases such as ATM and CHEK1/2. Alongside them sit metabolic phosphotransferases -- hexokinases, phosphofructokinase-2 family enzymes, galactokinase, nucleotide and sugar kinases -- that trap and commit substrates to glycolysis and other routes. Also present are the phosphatases, pseudokinase decoys and inhibitory subunits that reverse or restrain the reaction, since the biological information lies in the balance. Deregulated kinase activity underlies much of oncogenesis and is the target of a large share of modern drugs.

Dephosphorylation is the removal of phosphate groups from proteins, lipids and small molecules, the counterweight to kinase action that makes phosphorylation a reversible switch rather than a one-way mark. Without it signalling cannot be terminated or reset, and cells lose the timing that governs growth factor responses, cell cycle progression, immune activation and membrane traffic. The genes span the major phosphatase families: serine/threonine holoenzymes built on PP1, PP2A, calcineurin and PPM catalytic subunits with their regulatory partners; classical and receptor-type tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPN11, PTPN6 and CD45 that set thresholds in receptor signalling; dual-specificity enzymes that inactivate MAP kinases; and inositol- and phosphoinositide-directed phosphatases including PTEN, OCRL, myotubularins and synaptojanins that shape membrane lipid identity. Loss-of-function in individual members causes cancer predisposition, myopathies, neuropathies and autoimmunity, reflecting how broadly this chemistry is used.

Phosphate removal is the counterpart to kinase action, and this collection of dephosphorylation activities sets how long a phosphorylation signal lasts on proteins, lipids and small molecules. Serine/threonine phosphatase catalytic subunits and their regulatory partners (PP1, PP2A, calcineurin, PP5, PP6, the metal-dependent PPM family) reverse kinase marks on cytoskeletal, transcriptional and cell cycle substrates, while classical and receptor-type tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPN11, PTPN6, PTEN and CD45 tune growth factor and immune receptor signalling. Dual-specificity phosphatases inactivate MAP kinases, terminating ERK, JNK and p38 output. A large lipid phosphatase contingent — myotubularins, inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatases, synaptojanins, OCRL and phospholipid phosphate phosphatases — remodels phosphoinositides and sphingolipid phosphates to control membrane identity and trafficking. Loss of these activities underlies tumour suppression failure, Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy, myotubular myopathy, Lowe syndrome and Noonan syndrome, and unrestrained inflammatory signalling.

Protein processing covers the limited proteolytic cuts that convert inactive precursors into working proteins, a maturation step that many secreted and membrane proteins cannot bypass. It determines whether a hormone is bioactive, whether a clotting cascade fires, whether a receptor reaches the surface, and whether an imported mitochondrial protein is correctly trimmed; failures produce bleeding and thrombotic disease, hypertension, amyloid deposition and lysosomal storage phenotypes. The chemistry is carried by distinct protease families acting in defined compartments: signal peptidase and the proprotein convertases furin, PCSK1 and PCSK9 in the secretory route; ADAM and matrix metalloproteinases together with the presenilin- gamma-secretase complex performing ectodomain shedding and regulated intramembrane cleavage; trypsin-like serine proteases of the coagulation, complement and kallikrein cascades; caspases in inflammasome and apoptotic maturation; and mitochondrial processing peptidases and AAA proteases at the import site. Cleavage is thus a switch, irreversible and self-amplifying.

Many proteins are synthesised as inactive precursors and become functional only when a peptide bond is cut in the right place, and this maturation by limited proteolysis is what these genes carry out. It converts prohormones, growth factors, clotting factors and receptors into active molecules, and removes targeting sequences from newly made proteins. Signal peptidase and mitochondrial processing peptidases trim presequences after translocation; proprotein convertases such as FURIN and PCSK1/2 cleave at basic residues in the secretory pathway; and membrane-anchored serine proteases, ADAM sheddases and the gamma-secretase complex release ectodomains and intracellular fragments. The coagulation cascade, complement activation, angiotensin generation by ACE, Hedgehog ligand autoprocessing and caspase maturation during apoptosis all depend on it. Mutations in individual steps cause bleeding disorders, hormone deficiencies, iron overload and neurodegeneration, and several of these proteases are exploited by viruses for entry.

protein import into peroxisome matrix, receptor recycling is the recovery step of peroxisomal protein import: after the shuttling receptor PEX5 delivers PTS1-bearing cargo across the membrane, it must be released and returned to the cytosol so that further rounds of import can occur. Without this export step receptors become trapped in the membrane, matrix enzymes such as those for beta-oxidation of very long chain fatty acids and ether lipid synthesis fail to reach the organelle, and empty peroxisomal ghosts accumulate — the basis of Zellweger spectrum disorders. Mechanistically the RING-finger complex of PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12 ubiquitinates PEX5, and the AAA-ATPases PEX1 and PEX6, anchored by PEX26, extract it using ATP hydrolysis; deubiquitination by USP9X rescues the receptor from degradation. The logic parallels ubiquitin-driven retrotranslocation at the ER, coupling cofactor-free protein translocation to an ATP-powered recycling cycle.

Peroxisomal matrix enzymes are made in the cytosol and delivered by shuttling receptors, so the import cycle can only continue if those receptors are released from cargo and returned for reuse. Receptor recycling is that recovery step: after PEX5 deposits its cargo at the membrane it is ubiquitinated by the RING-finger ligases PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12, then extracted back into the cytosol by the AAA-ATPases PEX1 and PEX6, which are tethered to the membrane by PEX26; the deubiquitinase USP9X reverses the tag so the receptor can be used again rather than degraded. Loss of these components blocks matrix protein import altogether and produces the Zellweger spectrum disorders, with failed ether lipid synthesis and very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation, severe neurological and hepatic disease. The logic parallels ATPase-driven retrotranslocation used elsewhere in protein quality control.

poly(A)+ mRNA export from nucleus moves finished, polyadenylated messenger RNAs through the nuclear pore into the cytoplasm, the step that licenses a transcript for translation and couples gene expression to protein output. It matters because export is a quality-control checkpoint: only mRNAs that have been correctly spliced, capped and polyadenylated acquire the adaptors needed to leave, so unprocessed transcripts are retained and degraded. The TREX complex and associated adaptors such as SARNP, POLDIP3 and ENY2 load the NXF1-NXT1 export receptor onto mRNA during transcription and splicing, and the receptor then shuttles through pores built from nucleoporins including NUP93 and NUP133. At the cytoplasmic face, the DEAD-box ATPases DDX19A/B, activated by GLE1 and inositol hexakisphosphate, strip the receptor to give directionality and release the message. Loss of these steps blocks mRNA availability and causes motor neuron and developmental disease.

Polyadenylated mRNAs made in the nucleus are useless until they reach the ribosome, and this route carries them through the nuclear pore into the cytoplasm. Export is coupled to the preceding steps of mRNA maturation, so only properly capped, spliced and polyadenylated transcripts are released; retention of defective messages is part of nuclear quality control, and blocking export shuts down gene expression as effectively as blocking transcription. Transcripts are loaded with export adaptors and handed to the NXF1-NXT1 heterodimer, which shuttles cargo through the pore channel formed by nucleoporins such as NUP93 and NUP133. Directionality comes from terminal-side remodelling: GLE1 stimulates the DDX19 helicases to strip the receptor from mRNA at the cytoplasmic face, preventing return. Associated transcription-export and THO-related components link elongation and 3' end processing to release, and PABPN1 marks the poly(A) tail itself.

plasma membrane phospholipid scrambling is the collapse of the normal lipid asymmetry of the plasma membrane, moving phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine from the inner leaflet to the cell surface. That exposed phosphatidylserine is a signal read by other cells and enzymes: it marks apoptotic cells for recognition and engulfment by phagocytes, provides the catalytic surface for the coagulation cascade on activated platelets, and licenses membrane fusion events. Scrambling is energy-independent and bidirectional, carried out by distinct families of scramblases — calcium-activated anoctamins such as ANO6, whose loss causes the bleeding disorder Scott syndrome, caspase-cleaved XKR8 acting downstream of apoptotic signalling, and the phospholipid scramblases PLSCR1-5. Related lipid-mobilising proteins including ATG9A, TMEM41B and VMP1 link the same chemistry to autophagosome membrane expansion, while SERINC proteins alter viral envelope lipid composition and restrict infectivity.

A resting plasma membrane keeps phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine confined to the inner leaflet; scrambling collapses that asymmetry and moves them bidirectionally to the outer surface. The exposed phosphatidylserine is a signal read by other cells: it marks apoptotic corpses for engulfment by phagocytes, provides the catalytic surface for clotting factor assembly during platelet activation, and contributes to membrane fusion events in myoblasts and bone. The work is done by several unrelated families of energy-independent lipid scramblases, including the calcium-activated anoctamins, the caspase-activated XKR proteins that partner with the apoptotic machinery, the phospholipid scramblase family, and lipid-mobilising proteins such as ATG9A, TMEM41B and VMP1 that also support autophagosome membrane expansion. Calcium entry through purinergic and TRP channels can trigger the process acutely. Loss of the platelet scrambling route causes Scott syndrome, a bleeding disorder, while failed apoptotic exposure leaves dead cells uncleared and promotes inflammation.

peptidyl-threonine phosphorylation covers the transfer of phosphate onto threonine residues in proteins, one of the core reversible modifications by which cells encode information about their state. Threonine phosphorylation switches enzyme activity, creates or destroys binding surfaces, and marks proteins for degradation, so it sits underneath cell cycle progression, growth factor responses, stress signalling and ion transport; loss of control over the responsible kinases is a recurrent theme in cancer and in hypertension. The genes span the kinase classes that do this work: cyclin-dependent kinases such as CDK1 that drive mitotic entry, checkpoint and DNA damage kinases including CHEK1 and PRKDC, the MAP kinase cascades acting through MAPK1 and MAPK8, calcium- and lipid-activated kinases like CAMK2A and PRKCD, the AKT1 and STK11 axis of metabolic control, and WNK and STK39 kinases governing epithelial salt handling, together with substrates such as ATF2.

Adding a phosphate to a threonine residue in a protein is one of the basic switches cells use to change enzyme activity, protein interactions and localisation on a fast timescale. Peptidyl-threonine phosphorylation gathers the kinases and regulators that carry out and control this modification, and through it cell cycle progression, stress responses, growth factor signalling and ion transport are all set. The genes span several kinase families: cyclin-dependent kinases and the checkpoint kinase CHEK1 that time mitotic entry and arrest damaged cells, AKT1 and MAPK1/MAPK8 acting downstream of growth factor and stress inputs, the LKB1 kinase STK11 in energy sensing, WNK3 and STK39 in regulating cation-chloride cotransporters, and TBK1 in innate immune signalling. Substrates include transcription factors such as ATF2, linking threonine phosphorylation to changes in gene expression. Misregulation of these kinases underlies tumour growth, hypertension and impaired damage responses.

Protein hydroxylation is the enzymatic addition of hydroxyl groups to specific amino acid side chains, a modification that both stabilises structural proteins and acts as a signal reporting on oxygen availability. Most of the enzymes here are 2-oxoglutarate- and iron-dependent dioxygenases that consume molecular O2, which makes their activity an intrinsic oxygen sensor: the prolyl hydroxylases EGLN2 and EGLN3 mark HIF-alpha for degradation when oxygen is plentiful, so their inhibition in hypoxia switches on the adaptive transcriptional response driving erythropoiesis and angiogenesis. Other members hydroxylate collagen prolyl and lysyl residues, and prolyl 3-hydroxylases together with the VPS33B-VIPAS39 complex support collagen folding, crosslinking and secretion; their loss produces brittle bone and connective tissue disease. Ribosomal and translation-factor hydroxylation by OGFOD1, RIOX1/2 and JmjC-family enzymes tunes protein synthesis, linking oxygen status to ribosome function and cell growth.

Hydroxylation of amino acid side chains is a post-translational modification that tunes protein stability, folding and translation, and most of the enzymes that install it are 2-oxoglutarate- and iron-dependent dioxygenases whose activity tracks oxygen availability. That oxygen dependence is the basis of cellular oxygen sensing: prolyl hydroxylases such as EGLN2 and EGLN3 mark the hypoxia-inducible factor alpha subunits for degradation when oxygen is plentiful, so the hypoxic transcriptional response is switched on by loss of hydroxylation rather than by a ligand. Other members act on the translational apparatus and on ribosomal proteins, including OGFOD1 and the JmjC-domain and ribosomal oxygenase enzymes, while the prolyl 3-hydroxylases and the protein disulfide isomerase subunit P4HB serve collagen maturation in the endoplasmic reticulum, where defective hydroxylation produces brittle-bone and connective tissue disease. VPS33B and VIPAS39 link the pathway to lysosome-related organelle trafficking.

peptidyl-amino acid modification is the broad business of chemically altering amino acid residues after a protein has been made, which is how cells expand a fixed genome into a far larger range of protein behaviours. These marks decide whether an enzyme is active, where a protein sits, how long it survives, and which partners it binds, so signalling, chromatin regulation and metabolic control all depend on them. The genes span most of the major chemistries: tyrosine and serine/threonine kinases from growth factor and cytokine receptors through to nuclear substrates; SUMO conjugation and the SENP proteases that reverse it; lysine acetyltransferases and sirtuin deacetylases; arginine and lysine methyltransferases and demethylases; palmitoyl and myristoyl transferases that anchor proteins to membranes; tubulin glutamylation and detyrosination; prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation and collagen cross-linking; lipoylation, diphthamide synthesis, and vitamin K-dependent carboxylation. Loss of individual enzymes produces phenotypes from cancer to connective tissue and neurodevelopmental disease.

Post-translational modification of amino acid residues within proteins, covering the enzymes that add, remove and read chemical marks on polypeptides after synthesis. Such modification expands protein function far beyond the genetic code: it switches enzymes on and off, creates docking sites for partners, targets proteins for degradation, and anchors them to membranes. Represented chemistries include phosphorylation by tyrosine and serine/threonine kinases acting downstream of growth factor and cytokine receptors, reversal by phosphatases, lysine acetylation by histone acetyltransferases and its removal by sirtuins, lysine and arginine methylation, SUMO conjugation and its cleavage by SENP proteases, S-palmitoylation by ZDHHC acyltransferases, N-myristoylation, tubulin polyglutamylation and detyrosination, prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation of collagen, vitamin K-dependent carboxylation, tyrosine sulfation, lipoylation and diphthamide formation. peptidyl-histidine modification covers the enzymatic tailoring of histidine residues within proteins, a rare class of post-translational modification whose best-characterised examples are diphthamide formation on translation elongation factor 2 and histidine methylation of actin. Both alter the mechanics of the cytoskeleton and of protein synthesis. The diphthamide route proceeds through several steps: an iron-sulfur enzyme pair transfers an aminocarboxypropyl group to a single histidine of eEF2, followed by methylation and amidation, and the finished residue is the target ADP-ribosylated by diphtheria toxin. Loss of these steps disrupts translational fidelity and causes developmental disorders with microcephaly and short stature. Separately, methylation of a conserved actin histidine tunes filament polymerisation kinetics and is required for normal smooth muscle contraction, including uterine function during labour.

Modification of histidine residues in proteins is rare but decisive, and the genes here carry out the two best-characterised examples in human cells. Most of them build diphthamide, an elaborately modified histidine unique to translation elongation factor 2: a radical SAM step transfers an aminocarboxypropyl group, followed by methylation and amidation to complete the residue. Diphthamide keeps translational elongation accurate, guards against ribosomal frameshifting, and is the target attacked by diphtheria toxin and related ADP-ribosylating toxins; loss of these enzymes causes developmental disorders with microcephaly and short stature. SETD3 represents the other branch, methylating histidine 73 of actin to stabilise filaments, with consequences for smooth muscle contraction and labour. Together these reactions link an unusual post-translational chemistry to protein synthesis fidelity and cytoskeletal function.

peptidyl-serine modification covers the covalent alteration of serine residues in proteins, overwhelmingly their phosphorylation by serine/threonine kinases, which is the most common switch cells use to change protein activity, localisation and stability within seconds of a stimulus. Reversible serine phosphorylation is what allows growth factor, cytokine and stress signals to be converted into decisions about proliferation, survival, metabolism and cell death, and its deregulation underlies much of oncogenesis. The genes span the major kinase families that carry out this chemistry: RAF-MEK and AKT/mTOR effectors downstream of receptor tyrosine kinases, casein kinase 2 and GSK3 as constitutive modifiers, DNA damage-responsive kinases such as ATM, PRKDC and SMG1, mitotic and polarity kinases including AURKA and BRSK1, and inflammatory kinases IKBKB, TBK1 and RIPK1. Counter-regulators such as PTEN and SPRY2, and cytokine inputs including IL6, LIF and IFNG, place the modification within signalling networks rather than a single route.

Covalent modification of serine residues in proteins — overwhelmingly phosphorylation by serine/threonine kinases — is the most common way cells convert signals into changes in protein activity, localisation and stability. The kinases here span the major growth and stress routes: AKT1 and RPS6KB1 downstream of growth factor and mTOR signalling, RAF1, BRAF, ARAF and MAP2K2 in the MAPK cascade, GSK3B and CSNK2A1 as constitutively active multi-substrate kinases, IKBKB and TBK1 driving inflammatory transcription, ATM, PRKDC and SMG1 responding to DNA damage, AURKA and CDK2 timing mitosis and S phase, and ULK1 initiating autophagy. PTEN and SPRY2 act as brakes on the lipid and receptor inputs feeding these kinases. Because serine phosphorylation gates proliferation, apoptosis, cytokine responses and metabolic enzyme activity, misregulated kinases of this type are among the most frequent oncogenic drivers and the most heavily pursued drug targets.

Peptidyl-lysine acetylation is the transfer of acetyl groups onto lysine side chains of proteins, a reversible modification that neutralises the residue's positive charge and creates docking sites for bromodomain readers. It is the chemistry behind histone acetylation and therefore behind open chromatin and transcriptional activation, but it extends far beyond the nucleus: acetylation of tubulin by ATAT1 marks stable microtubules, and acetylation of metabolic enzymes and transcription factors tunes their activity to acetyl-CoA availability. The genes span the major acetyltransferase families, from the CREBBP/EP300 coactivators that couple signal-responsive transcription factors to the general machinery, through GCN5/PCAF and the MYST enzymes KAT5 and KAT7 that act in DNA damage response and replication licensing, to ESCO1, which acetylates cohesin to establish sister chromatid cohesion. SIRT1 provides the opposing deacetylase activity, making the mark a dynamic, nutrient-sensitive switch.

Acetylation of lysine side chains is one of the most widespread reversible protein modifications, and this pathway covers the enzymes that place the acetyl group and the factors that direct them to substrates. On histones it loosens chromatin and marks active promoters and enhancers, so transcriptional programmes for growth, differentiation and stress responses depend on it; on non-histone targets it tunes protein stability, localisation and enzyme activity. The transferases here span several families: the paralogous coactivators CREBBP and EP300, the GCN5/PCAF pair, and KAT5 and KAT7, which acetylate histones in the context of DNA damage signalling and replication licensing. ESCO1 acetylates the cohesin subunit SMC3 to establish sister chromatid cohesion, while ATAT1 acetylates α-tubulin to mark long-lived microtubules. Loss or mutation of these writers causes developmental syndromes and is recurrent in cancer, and the opposing deacetylase activity of SIRT1 keeps the mark dynamic.

viral genome replication covers the host processes that support or restrict copying of a viral genome inside an infected cell, including the nucleotide supply and RNA-handling steps replication depends on. It matters because the same machinery decides whether an infection is productive or aborted, and mutations in it shape susceptibility to hepatitis, HIV and influenza. Much of the gene content is antiviral: interferon-induced effectors such as MX1, ISG15, the OAS-RNase L system and IFITM proteins, cytosolic sensors including IFI16 and MDA5 signalling through MAVS, and the APOBEC3 and ADAR deaminases that mutate viral nucleic acid. Against these sit host factors that viruses co-opt -- cyclophilins, PCBP and PABPC1 RNA-binding proteins, VAP proteins and TMEM41B for replication-organelle membranes, SMC5/6 and topoisomerases for episomal DNA. Autophagy components and translational control through PKR link replication to broader stress responses.

Replication of a viral genome inside a host cell depends on borrowed nucleotide pools, host RNA-binding proteins and membrane platforms, and it is also the step the innate immune system works hardest to block. The genes here span both sides of that contest: cyclophilins, poly(C)-binding proteins, DDX3X, PABPC1 and membrane factors such as TMEM41B and VAP proteins that support replication complexes, alongside restriction and sensing machinery that limits it. Cytosolic sensors including IFIH1 and IFI16 signal through MAVS to induce interferon, whose effectors — the OAS–RNase L arm, MX1, IFIT and IFITM proteins, ISG15 and RSAD2 — degrade viral RNA or stall its synthesis, while APOBEC3 deaminases and ADAR edit viral nucleic acid. The balance struck here sets whether an infection is cleared, becomes persistent, or drives the mutational drift underlying viral escape.

regulation of fatty acid metabolic process covers the control layer that decides whether a cell burns fatty acids or stores and synthesises them, matching lipid flux to nutritional state. It sets the balance struck between feeding and fasting in liver, adipose tissue, heart and muscle, and its derangement produces hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance and lipotoxic cardiomyopathy. Transcriptional control dominates: the PPAR family with PGC-1α drives β-oxidation and mitochondrial fatty acid entry through CPT1A, while SREBP-1c with SCAP, INSIG proteins and ChREBP drives lipogenesis, and liver X receptors and NCOR1 tune both. Superimposed are insulin signalling through IRS-AKT, AMPK and sirtuin-dependent nutrient sensing, acetyl-CoA carboxylase and malonyl-CoA turnover, microRNAs such as miR-33a, and secreted regulators including adiponectin, ANGPTL4 and the apolipoprotein C cluster that govern lipoprotein lipase activity and fatty acid delivery to tissues.

Cells must match fatty acid synthesis, oxidation and storage to nutrient supply and energy demand, and this regulatory layer sets the balance. It matters because failure of the controls produces hepatic steatosis, dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance and lipotoxic damage to heart and muscle. Nuclear receptors and lipogenic transcription factors -- PPARA, PPARD, PPARG with its coactivator PPARGC1A, the liver X receptors, and SREBF1 under SCAP and INSIG control -- switch the transcriptional programme between fat burning and fat making. Insulin acting through IRS and AKT, AMP-activated kinase subunits, sirtuins and the CPT1A/malonyl-CoA node provide acute regulation, while secreted signals such as adiponectin, ANGPTL4 and apolipoprotein-mediated modulation of lipase activity coordinate tissues. Several microRNAs, notably MIR33A, tune the same targets post-transcriptionally, and peroxisomal import and processing components extend the control to very-long-chain fatty acid handling.

cytokine-mediated signaling pathway is how cells talk to one another during immune responses, blood cell production and inflammation: a secreted cytokine binds its surface receptor and the message is converted into changes in gene transcription, survival or motility. It defines immune cell identity and behaviour, and its failures produce immunodeficiency, autoinflammatory disease, cytokine storm and leukaemia. The genes span the major receptor families and their downstream logic — interleukin, interferon and colony-stimulating factor receptors coupled through JAK kinases to STAT transcription factors, with SOCS proteins and phosphatases such as PTPN2 imposing negative feedback; tumour necrosis factor and interleukin-1 family receptors acting through TRAF adaptors, IRAK kinases and MYD88 to activate NF-κB or caspase-8-dependent death; chemokines and their G protein-coupled receptors directing leukocyte trafficking; and inflammasome components maturing IL-1β. Hormone-like ligands including leptin, growth hormone, erythropoietin and thrombopoietin use the same receptor architecture to control metabolism and haematopoiesis.

Cells coordinate immune defence, inflammation, haematopoiesis and tissue repair by secreting cytokines and reading them at the surface, and this pathway covers that whole transmission process, from ligand binding through to changes in gene transcription. It spans the major cytokine families and their receptors — interleukins and their shared chains such as IL2RG and IL6ST, type I, II and III interferons, colony-stimulating factors, erythropoietin and thrombopoietin, chemokines with their G protein-coupled and atypical scavenger receptors, and the tumour necrosis factor superfamily. Downstream, receptor-associated JAK kinases phosphorylate STAT transcription factors, while TRAF and IRAK adaptors converge on NF-kB and MAP kinase activation; SOCS proteins, phosphatases and deubiquitinases such as TNFAIP3 and CYLD impose negative feedback. Loss of individual components produces immunodeficiency or cytopenia, whereas failed restraint underlies autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease, and the same receptors are the targets of biologic anti-cytokine therapy.

response to pheromone is the cellular detection of chemical signals released by one individual that alter the physiology or behaviour of another, the basis of social and reproductive chemosensation in mammals. In humans the pathway is largely vestigial but its parts remain: the vomeronasal type 1 receptors are G protein-coupled receptors of the sensory neuron surface, several of them pseudogenes, coupled through G protein subunits such as GNG8 to depolarisation of chemosensory neurons and transmission to the accessory olfactory system. Downstream, such signals influence hypothalamic control of mating, aggression, territorial marking and oestrous timing rather than conscious odour perception. The pathway illustrates how sensory receptor repertoires expand and decay with lifestyle, and it sits alongside olfactory and taste reception as one branch of chemical sensing coupled to neuroendocrine output.

Pheromones are chemical signals passed between members of a species, and the response to pheromone describes how a cell or animal changes its behaviour, secretion or gene expression when it detects one. In mammals this chemosensation is largely the province of the vomeronasal organ, and the vomeronasal type 1 receptors here (VN1R1 through VN1R5, plus a pseudogene relic) are the G protein-coupled detectors expressed by its sensory neurons, coupled through G protein subunits such as GNG8 to depolarising transduction cascades. Downstream, these signals reach accessory olfactory and hypothalamic circuits that govern mating, aggression, territorial marking and maternal behaviour, and can influence neuroendocrine output. In humans the system is much reduced, with most vomeronasal receptor genes pseudogenised, so this biology is best understood as an evolutionarily contracted chemosensory route for social and reproductive cues.

N-acetylneuraminate catabolic process dismantles sialic acid, the terminal sugar of most cell-surface glycans, so that its carbon can be recycled into glycolysis rather than accumulating. This matters because sialylated glycoproteins and glycolipids turn over constantly in lysosomes, and the freed sialic acid must be degraded or re-used; blocked flux through this route causes sialic acid storage and free sialic acid excretion, while the same enzymes let cells salvage amino sugars from dietary and mucosal sources. Mechanistically, an aldolase cleaves N-acetylneuraminate to pyruvate and N-acetylmannosamine, which is epimerised to N-acetylglucosamine, phosphorylated by NAGK, deacetylated by AMDHD2, and finally deaminated by glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminases to fructose-6-phosphate. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of glycan turnover, hexosamine biosynthesis and central carbon metabolism, balancing supply of UDP-sugar precursors against catabolic disposal.

Sialic acid released from turned-over glycoproteins and glycolipids must be disposed of, and N-acetylneuraminate catabolism is the route that dismantles it and returns its carbon to central metabolism. The free sugar is cleaved by an N-acetylneuraminate pyruvate lyase into pyruvate and N-acetylmannosamine; an epimerase interconverts that sugar with N-acetylglucosamine, which is phosphorylated by N-acetylglucosamine kinase, deacetylated by a GlcNAc-6-phosphate deacetylase, and finally deaminated by glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminases to fructose-6-phosphate plus ammonia, feeding glycolysis. The same intermediates are shared with amino sugar salvage and with the hexosamine pathway that supplies UDP-GlcNAc for glycosylation, so flux here sets the balance between recycling and degradation. Lysosomal or transport defects upstream cause sialic acid storage disease, and the pathway also governs how much free sialic acid is available for re-use on newly made glycans.

Phenol-containing compound catabolic process is the set of reactions that inactivate and dispose of hydroxylated aromatic molecules, a class that includes the catecholamine neurotransmitters, thyroid hormones, tyrosine-derived metabolites and many dietary and drug phenols. It matters because signalling by dopamine, noradrenaline and thyroxine is terminated by degradation rather than by dilution, and because incomplete breakdown of tyrosine catabolites is directly toxic. Monoamine oxidases and aldehyde dehydrogenase oxidise the amine side chain, catechol O-methyltransferase and the sulfotransferases mask the phenolic hydroxyl for excretion, the dopamine transporter delivers substrate into cells for turnover, and dopamine beta-hydroxylase and related copper monooxygenases interconvert the catecholamines. Iodothyronine deiodinases perform the analogous inactivation of thyroid hormone, while fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase completes ring cleavage in tyrosine degradation; its loss causes hepatorenal tyrosinemia. The pathway therefore links neurotransmitter clearance, endocrine control and xenobiotic detoxification.

Phenolic compounds — catecholamines, thyroid hormones and tyrosine-derived metabolites — must be inactivated and cleared once they have acted, and this catabolic route does that work. It terminates dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline signalling and sets how long these transmitters persist in brain and at sympathetic synapses, which is why its enzymes are targets of antidepressants and of drugs for Parkinson's disease. A dopamine transporter first retrieves the amine, monoamine oxidases A and B oxidatively deaminate it to an aldehyde that an aldehyde dehydrogenase converts to acid, while catechol O-methyltransferase caps the ring hydroxyl and sulfotransferases conjugate phenols for excretion. Iodothyronine deiodinases strip iodine from thyroxine to activate or inactivate thyroid hormone locally, and fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase closes the tyrosine degradation route — its loss causes hereditary tyrosinaemia with liver and kidney damage.

Leukotriene biosynthetic process builds the lipid mediators that drive bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, vascular leak and leukocyte recruitment, making it the pathway behind asthma and other allergic inflammation and the target of drugs such as zileuton and montelukast. It begins when phospholipases release arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, after which 5-lipoxygenase, docked at the nuclear envelope by its activating protein, converts it to the unstable epoxide leukotriene A4. That intermediate is then routed one of two ways: a hydrolase makes the chemotactic leukotriene B4, while conjugation to glutathione by leukotriene C4 synthase or related microsomal transferases yields the cysteinyl leukotrienes, which are exported by MRP1 and progressively trimmed by gamma-glutamyl transferases to LTD4 and LTE4. Expression is largely restricted to myeloid and mast cells, where receptor signalling through kinases including SYK triggers calcium-dependent enzyme translocation.

Leukotrienes are lipid mediators that drive bronchoconstriction, vascular leak and leukocyte recruitment, and their biosynthesis is the reason asthma and allergic inflammation are treated with drugs aimed at this route. Arachidonic acid is first released from membrane phospholipids by cytosolic and secreted phospholipases such as PLA2G4A, then presented by the membrane protein ALOX5AP to 5-lipoxygenase, which forms the unstable epoxide leukotriene A4. From there the pathway branches: LTA4H hydrolyses it to the chemotactic leukotriene B4, while LTC4 synthase and related microsomal glutathione transferases conjugate glutathione to make the cysteinyl leukotrienes, which ABCC1 exports and gamma-glutamyl transferases trim to LTD4. Output is largely a property of myeloid and mast cells, where receptor and kinase input including SYK couples immune activation to mediator production. Excess flux underlies aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease and chronic airway inflammation.

Alditol biosynthetic process covers the reduction of sugars to their polyol counterparts, of which the dominant human example is the production of glycerol from carbohydrate carbon. This matters for whole-body fuel handling: glycerol released by adipose tissue is a substrate for hepatic gluconeogenesis, and its synthesis in the fasting or insulin-resistant state links triglyceride turnover to blood glucose. The genes point specifically to glyceroneogenesis, in which the cytosolic and mitochondrial forms of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase divert pyruvate and amino acid carbon toward triose phosphates, aspartate aminotransferase feeds the malate-aspartate shuttle that supplies those precursors, and a glycerol-3-phosphate phosphatase completes the route by dephosphorylating the intermediate to free glycerol. Leptin signalling sets the hormonal context, tying polyol output to adipose energy stores and to the futile cycling of fatty acids that buffers lipotoxicity.

Alditols are sugar alcohols formed by reducing the carbonyl group of a monosaccharide, and the best known product of this route in mammals is glycerol, the backbone of triacylglycerols and a substrate that moves between fat and liver during fasting. The genes here point specifically at glyceroneogenesis: cytosolic and mitochondrial phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase divert oxaloacetate from non-carbohydrate precursors toward triose phosphates, aspartate aminotransferase feeds that carbon through the malate-aspartate shuttle, and a glycerol-3-phosphate phosphatase releases free glycerol. Leptin links the flux to whole-body energy status, since the balance between glycerol release and re-esterification of fatty acids in adipose tissue determines how much lipid escapes into the circulation. Distortion of this balance contributes to insulin resistance, hepatic steatosis and dyslipidaemia, placing alditol synthesis at the junction of gluconeogenic carbon flow and lipid storage.

Oxalate transport moves oxalate, a metabolic dead-end anion that the body cannot degrade, across epithelial membranes so it can be secreted into the gut and excreted in urine rather than accumulating. This matters because oxalate binds calcium avidly: when handling fails, calcium oxalate crystals form kidney stones and, in primary hyperoxaluria, deposit throughout the body and destroy renal function. The work is carried out largely by the SLC26 family of anion exchangers, which swap oxalate for chloride, sulfate or bicarbonate at intestinal and renal tubular brush borders; SLC26A6 and SLC26A1 dominate oxalate flux, while related members serve chloride, iodide and sulfate transport in thyroid, airway and cochlea. Upstream of transport, the peroxisomal enzyme AGXT limits how much oxalate is generated from glyoxylate in hepatocytes, tying this pathway to amino acid metabolism and systemic mineral balance.

Oxalate is a metabolic dead end in humans: it cannot be broken down, and it precipitates with calcium to form kidney stones, so handling it depends on moving it across epithelial membranes for excretion. This transport activity is carried largely by the SLC26 family of anion exchangers, which swap oxalate against chloride, sulfate or bicarbonate at the apical and basolateral surfaces of intestinal and renal tubular cells; SLC26A1 and SLC26A6 are the principal oxalate carriers, while other members of the family specialise in chloride, iodide or bicarbonate movement in the thyroid, airway, gut and inner ear. Alongside them, the liver enzyme AGXT limits how much oxalate is generated in the first place by transaminating glyoxylate, and its loss causes primary hyperoxaluria with progressive nephrocalcinosis. The pathway therefore links glyoxylate metabolism to epithelial anion secretion and stone risk.

catechol-containing compound catabolic process is the inactivation and clearance of catecholamines and related catechols, the chemistry that terminates dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline signalling and protects tissues from their reactive oxidation products. It sets how long a monoamine signal lasts at a synapse and how much of an ingested or circulating catechol survives first-pass metabolism, so its capacity shapes mood, movement, attention and blood pressure. Degradation proceeds by O-methylation, oxidative deamination by the outer mitochondrial membrane monoamine oxidases, and sulfonation by cytosolic sulfotransferases, with the dopamine transporter first recapturing transmitter from the extracellular space and dopamine beta-hydroxylase interconverting substrates within the biosynthetic route. Loss or variation of these steps produces monoamine excess states and behavioural phenotypes, and the same enzymes are the targets of MAO inhibitors and COMT inhibitors used in depression and Parkinson disease.

Catecholamines such as dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline must be cleared quickly once released, and the catabolism of catechol-containing compounds is how signalling is terminated and how these reactive molecules are kept from generating quinones and oxidative damage. Catechol-O-methyltransferase caps one hydroxyl of the catechol ring, monoamine oxidases A and B oxidatively deaminate the amine side chain at the outer mitochondrial membrane, and sulfotransferases of the SULT1A family conjugate sulfate to phenolic substrates including dopamine, generating excretable metabolites. A dopamine transporter provides the reuptake step that delivers transmitter back into neurons for degradation, coupling clearance to synaptic recovery. The same enzymes act on dietary catechols, catechol estrogens and drugs such as L-DOPA, which is why their inhibitors are used in Parkinson's disease and depression, and why variants affect prefrontal dopamine tone and blood pressure control.

organophosphate metabolic process is the broad set of reactions that make, interconvert and break down phosphate-bearing organic molecules — nucleotides, sugar phosphates, phospholipids, phosphoinositides, coenzymes and cyclic nucleotide messengers. Because phosphorylated intermediates are the currency of both energy metabolism and signalling, this chemistry underwrites nearly every cellular activity, and inherited defects in individual steps cause glycolytic anaemias, mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, myopathies, and lipid storage and GPI-anchor deficiencies. The genes span glycolysis and the pentose phosphate route, purine and pyrimidine synthesis and salvage, nucleoside and nucleotide kinases and phosphatases, oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthase, NAD and coenzyme A biosynthesis, glycerolipid and cardiolipin assembly, sphingolipid turnover, GPI anchor construction, and the phosphoinositide cycle with its lipid kinases, phospholipases and inositol polyphosphate enzymes. Cyclases, phosphodiesterases and AMPK/mTOR components link this flux to hormonal and nutrient control.

Organophosphate metabolic process gathers the reactions that make, modify and break down phosphate-bearing organic molecules, which is most of the chemistry a cell uses to store energy, signal and build membranes. Its breadth is reflected in the genes: glycolytic and pentose phosphate enzymes plus mitochondrial ATP synthase and respiratory complex subunits handle phosphorylated sugars and ATP turnover; nucleoside and nucleotide kinases, phosphatases and nucleotidases (adenylate kinases, NME family, 5'-nucleotidases, ribonucleotide reductase) supply and balance nucleotide pools; phosphoinositide kinases and phosphatases such as PTEN, OCRL and the myotubularins, together with phospholipases, acyltransferases and choline/ethanolamine pathway enzymes, generate membrane lipids and lipid second messengers; adenylate and guanylate cyclases with cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases set cAMP and cGMP levels. Also included are GPI anchor assembly, coenzyme A and NAD synthesis, and sulfation. Defects across these routes cause mitochondrial disease, myopathy, nucleotide-pool disorders and cancer-associated growth signalling.

GDP-mannose metabolic process supplies the activated sugar donors that glycosylation depends on, converting mannose and fructose-6-phosphate into GDP-mannose and, from it, GDP-fucose. Without this route cells cannot properly build N-linked glycans, O-mannosyl glycans or fucosylated ligands, and the consequences are the congenital disorders of glycosylation: PMM2 deficiency causes the commonest form, with cerebellar and multisystem disease, while GMPPB and GMPPA mutations produce dystroglycanopathy-type muscular dystrophy and alacrima-achalasia syndrome. The sequence runs from hexokinase and mannose phosphate isomerase through phosphomannomutase and GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase, with GMDS and GFUS diverting flux to fucose donors and a Golgi transporter importing GDP-fucose for fucosyltransferases; loss of that transporter impairs selectin ligand synthesis and leukocyte adhesion. The pathway thus links central carbohydrate metabolism to protein quality control, muscle integrity and immune cell trafficking.

GDP-mannose is the activated sugar donor that feeds nearly all protein glycosylation, and its metabolism is the supply line that keeps N-linked glycans, O-mannosylation and GPI anchors supplied with mannose. The route converts fructose-6-phosphate to mannose-6-phosphate via phosphomannose isomerase, isomerises it to mannose-1-phosphate through phosphomannomutase, and caps it with GTP using the GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase subunits GMPPA and GMPPB. A branch handled by GMDS and GFUS dehydrates and epimerises GDP-mannose into GDP-fucose, which SLC35C1 then imports into the Golgi for fucosyltransferases. Loss of these steps causes congenital disorders of glycosylation: PMM2 deficiency is the commonest form, GMPPB mutations produce dystroglycanopathy with muscular dystrophy, and defective fucose transport impairs selectin ligand synthesis and leukocyte adhesion. Hexokinase and guanylate kinase link the pathway to glycolytic and nucleotide pools.

NAD+ metabolic process covers the synthesis, recycling and consumption of the central redox coenzyme that carries electrons in glycolysis, the TCA cycle and fatty acid oxidation, and that also serves as substrate for signalling enzymes. Cells replenish it two ways: de novo from tryptophan through the kynurenine route (IDO1, KMO, KYNU, QPRT) and by salvage of nicotinamide and nicotinamide riboside via NAMPT, NAPRT, NMRK kinases and the NMNAT isoforms that act in nucleus, cytosol and mitochondria. Consumers such as PARPs and sirtuin-linked deacetylation couple NAD+ levels to DNA damage responses and metabolic gene regulation, while SARM1-driven NAD+ destruction executes axon degeneration after injury. Malate-aspartate shuttle components and glycerophosphate dehydrogenases move reducing equivalents across the mitochondrial membrane, and NADK diverts the pool toward NADP+ for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence. Declining NAD+ accompanies aging, neurodegeneration and metabolic disease.

NAD+ is the electron carrier that makes catabolism possible, and this metabolic process covers both how cells build and destroy it and how they cycle it between oxidised and reduced states. Supply comes by two routes: de novo synthesis from tryptophan through the kynurenine pathway (IDO1, KMO, KYNU, HAAO, QPRT) and salvage of nicotinamide or nicotinamide riboside via NAMPT, NAPRT, NMRK kinases and the NMNAT adenylyltransferases, with NADSYN1 completing amidation and NADK producing NADP+.
