Consumption and turnover run through ADP-ribosylation and the SARM1 hydrolase, whose activation collapses axonal NAD+ and drives Wallerian degeneration. Redox balance is maintained by malate dehydrogenases, glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenases, transaminases and mitochondrial carriers that constitute the shuttles moving reducing equivalents across the inner membrane. Falling NAD+ availability impairs oxidative metabolism, sirtuin signalling and DNA repair, and underlies pellagra and axon loss.

ribose phosphate metabolic process covers the making, interconversion and breakdown of phosphorylated ribose sugars and the nucleotides built on them, the currency that powers essentially every cellular transaction. It supplies ATP and GTP for work and signalling, purine and pyrimidine precursors for DNA and RNA, and cofactors such as NAD, FAD and PAPS. PRPP synthetases feed the de novo purine assembly line and the salvage enzymes HPRT1 and APRT, while nucleoside kinases, nucleotidases and deaminases balance synthesis against degradation toward urate. Most ATP itself comes from the glycolytic enzymes and the respiratory chain and ATP synthase subunits represented here, with adenylate kinases, NME phosphotransferases and AMPK sensing the resulting energy charge. Cyclic nucleotide cyclases and phosphodiesterases divert the same metabolites into second-messenger signalling. Defects cause gout, immunodeficiency, hemolytic anemia and mitochondrial disease.

Ribose phosphate metabolism sits at the junction of sugar breakdown and nucleotide supply: phosphorylated ribose sugars derived from glycolysis and the pentose phosphate route are activated to PRPP and used to build purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, which in turn become ATP, GTP, cyclic nucleotides and cofactors. The gene complement spans PRPP synthetases and their associated proteins, de novo purine synthesis enzymes such as PPAT, GART, PAICS, ATIC and ADSL, pyrimidine enzymes including CAD, DHODH and UMPS, and the salvage route through HPRT1, APRT, ADA and PNP. Alongside these sit the glycolytic enzymes that feed carbon in, and the machinery that produces and consumes the nucleotides themselves — respiratory complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, ATP synthase, adenylate and nucleoside-diphosphate kinases, adenylyl and guanylyl cyclases, phosphodiesterases and AMPK. Deficiencies cause gout, immunodeficiency, anaemia and neurodevelopmental disease, and the pathway is a standing target for antiproliferative drugs.

B cell mediated immunity is the effector arm of humoral immunity: the production of antibodies of appropriate class and affinity, and the downstream destruction or clearance of what those antibodies bind. It protects against extracellular bacteria, viruses and toxins, and its failure produces immunodeficiency with recurrent infection, while its misdirection produces autoantibody disease. The genes span the whole output chain. Immunoglobulin heavy and light chain variable and constant regions supply the antibody repertoire itself; AICDA acting with uracil processing, mismatch repair and non-homologous end joining factors such as UNG, MSH2, LIG4 and the shieldin complex drives somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination. T cell help through CD40, CD40LG and cytokines including IL4, IL21 and IL10, with BCL6 and BATF, licenses germinal centre reactions. Secreted antibody is then translated into effector action by Fc receptors and the complement cascade, from C1q through the membrane attack complex, under regulators such as CD55 and CFI.

B cell mediated immunity covers the effector arm of humoral defence: antibody production, isotype diversification, and the downstream systems that translate antibody binding into pathogen clearance. Immunoglobulin heavy and light chain constant and variable segments dominate here, and with them the machinery of class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation — AICDA deaminates cytosine in switched loci, uracil-DNA glycosylase and mismatch repair proteins process the lesion, and non-homologous end joining with 53BP1, RIF1 and the shieldin complex resolves the resulting breaks. Costimulation through CD40 and its ligand plus cytokines such as IL-4, IL-21 and IL-10 direct which isotype is made, while BCL6 and BATF shape germinal centre fate. Secreted antibody then engages Fcγ and Fcε receptors and the complement cascade, from C1q recognition to the lytic C5b-C9 pore, with regulators like CD55, CD46 and factor I restraining self-damage. Defects produce hyper-IgM syndromes, antibody deficiency and lupus-like autoimmunity.

Antibacterial humoral response is the soluble, secreted arm of innate defence against bacteria: the antimicrobial peptides, proteins and antibodies released into mucus, saliva, sweat, milk, seminal fluid and plasma that kill or immobilise microbes before an infection takes hold. It defines the barrier competence of skin, gut and airway epithelia and the killing capacity of neutrophil granules; its loss underlies recurrent infection, and its dysregulation contributes to inflammatory skin and bowel disease. The effectors act largely by permeabilising bacterial membranes or starving microbes of nutrients — alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin, dermcidin, lactoferrin and transferrin sequestering iron, lysosomal proteases such as elastase and cathepsin G, RNase family members, and WFDC/SLPI protease inhibitors that restrain collateral tissue damage. Secreted immunoglobulins with J chain link this fluid-phase defence to adaptive immunity, while histone and neuropeptide components broaden it further.

Body fluids and mucosal secretions carry a standing chemical defence against bacteria, and this antibacterial humoral response is that defence: soluble effectors in plasma, saliva, tears, milk, airway and gut fluid, sweat and seminal plasma that kill or restrain microbes before an adaptive response is mounted. It combines pore-forming and membrane-disrupting peptides such as the alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin and dermcidin with iron-sequestering lactoferrin and transferrin, bactericidal RNases, secretory phospholipases, and the antimicrobial and protease-inhibitory WFDC and SLPI/elafin families, alongside neutrophil granule proteases including elastase and cathepsin G. Secreted immunoglobulins and the J chain that polymerises IgA add antigen-specific opsonisation at mucosal surfaces, and several neuropeptides contribute direct antimicrobial activity. Loss of these effectors, as in impaired defensin output or SPINK5 deficiency, produces recurrent bacterial infection and barrier inflammation.

Cytolysis is the destructive rupture of a cell membrane and spilling of cytoplasm, used both as a weapon of host defence against microbes and as the terminal step by which a dying cell releases its contents. It matters because it converts an infected or damaged cell into an inflammatory signal: without controlled membrane rupture, dying cells stay intact and the alarmins and cytokines that recruit immune cells are never released. The genes cover two arms. Antimicrobial effectors such as cathelicidin, RNASE7 and the chemokine CCL28 permeabilise bacterial and fungal membranes at epithelial and skin surfaces, while interferon-inducible guanylate-binding proteins coat intracellular pathogens and their vacuoles to expose them to lysis and inflammasome activation. NINJ1 and its relative execute the final plasma-membrane break during pyroptosis and other lytic death, making rupture an actively driven event rather than passive swelling.

Cytolysis is the destruction of a cell by rupture of its membrane and spilling of cytoplasm, used both as a weapon against microbes and as the final step by which a dying host cell releases its contents. The genes here cover both sides of that outcome. Cathelicidin and RNASE7 are secreted antimicrobial effectors that permeabilise bacterial membranes at epithelial and skin surfaces, and CCL28 is a mucosal chemokine with comparable direct antimicrobial activity. Guanylate-binding proteins, induced by interferon, coat intracellular bacteria and pathogen-containing vacuoles, breaking them open and exposing ligands that drive inflammasome activation. NINJ1 acts at the end of lytic cell death, polymerising in the plasma membrane to cause the rupture that releases inflammatory contents. Together these define membrane breach as an immune mechanism, linking host defence to inflammation and, when unrestrained, to tissue damage.

Antigen processing and presentation is how cells display fragments of proteins and lipids on their surface so that T cells can inspect them, and it is the basis of adaptive immune recognition, self-tolerance, transplant rejection and tumour immune surveillance. Two routes dominate: cytosolic proteins are degraded by immunoproteasomes, trimmed by aminopeptidases, and loaded onto class I molecules in the endoplasmic reticulum with help from TAP transporters, tapasin, calreticulin and beta-2-microglobulin; endocytosed material is cleaved by cathepsins and legumain in acidified vesicles and loaded onto class II molecules after the invariant chain is removed under HLA-DM control. CD1 and MR1 proteins present lipids and metabolites instead. Rab GTPases, AP-3 adaptors and phagosome maturation machinery direct the trafficking, including cross-presentation by dendritic cells, and loss of these steps lets viruses and cancers escape detection.

T cell surveillance depends on antigen-presenting cells displaying fragments of proteins, lipids or metabolites at the surface bound to MHC and MHC-like molecules, and this pathway covers how those complexes are generated and delivered. Class I loading uses immunoproteasome subunits, the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, ERAP aminopeptidase trimming and a tapasin-calreticulin-PDIA3 chaperone step with beta-2-microglobulin; class II loading depends on the invariant chain CD74, lysosomal cathepsins and legumain, and peptide exchange catalysed by HLA-DM with HLA-DO as its modulator. CD1 family members and MR1 present lipids and microbial metabolites instead. Vesicular traffic through Rab GTPases, AP-3 and phagosomal machinery supports cross-presentation, while MARCH ubiquitin ligases tune surface MHC levels. Failures cause immunodeficiency, allow viral and tumour immune evasion, and underlie HLA-linked autoimmunity and transplant rejection.

Antigen processing and presentation of endogenous antigen is how a cell advertises what it is making inside itself, displaying peptides or lipids derived from its own cytosolic and membrane proteins on surface MHC molecules for inspection by T cells and NK cells. This is the basis of immune surveillance against viruses and tumours: cells expressing altered or foreign proteins are recognised and killed, while loss of presentation is a common route to immune escape. Mechanistically, proteasomal peptides are pumped into the ER by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto class I heavy chains with beta-2 microglobulin and tapasin. Related molecules extend the repertoire: CD1 proteins present lipid antigens, HLA-E and HLA-G modulate NK responses, and ULBP/RAET1 ligands signal stress. Autophagy machinery routes cytosolic material toward class II loading.

Cells continually advertise samples of their own protein and lipid contents on the surface, and this display of endogenous antigen is how cytotoxic T cells and NK cells distinguish healthy cells from infected or transformed ones. Peptides generated in the cytosol are pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed to length by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto class I heavy chains with beta-2-microglobulin and tapasin; lipid antigens take a parallel route on CD1 molecules. Non-classical relatives such as HLA-E, HLA-G and the ULBP/RAET1 stress-induced ligands instead tune NK cell activation and maternal-fetal tolerance, while autophagy machinery can divert cytoplasmic cargo onto class II. Loss of this surveillance lets tumours and viruses escape T cell killing, and its misdirection against self peptides underlies HLA-linked autoimmunity.

dorsal spinal cord development builds the sensory half of the spinal cord — the dorsal horn interneurons that receive input from sensory ganglia and relay touch, pain, temperature and proprioceptive information toward the brain. Without correct dorsal patterning, sensory circuits miswire and reflex and nociceptive processing fail. Roof plate signals, chiefly WNT1, WNT3A and the BMP family member GDF7, set up a dorsal-to-ventral gradient that specifies successive progenitor domains marked by PAX7, GSX1 and GSX2, while proneural ASCL1 drives them to differentiate. Combinatorial LIM-homeodomain and related transcription factors, including LHX1, LHX5, LHX3, DRGX and PROX1, then assign the distinct dorsal interneuron identities. Guidance and adhesion components such as DRAXIN, MDGA1 and GDNF steer commissural and sensory axons across and along the cord, linking neuronal specification to circuit assembly in the developing nervous system.

The dorsal half of the spinal cord is where sensory information from skin, muscle and viscera first enters the central nervous system, and its development produces the interneuron classes that sort touch, pain and proprioceptive input before relaying it onward. Patterning begins with roof plate signals — WNT1, WNT3A and the BMP family member GDF7 — which impose dorsoventral positional identity, while DRAXIN restrains axon growth across the midline. Progenitor domains are demarcated by transcription factors including PAX7, GSX1 and GSX2, and ASCL1 drives them toward neurogenesis; LHX1, LHX5, LMO4, PROX1 and TAL1 then fix the identities and settling positions of individual dorsal interneuron subtypes. Related factors such as DRGX act in the sensory ganglion neurons that supply this circuitry. Disruption skews subtype proportions and miswires sensory relay, with consequences for reflex control and nociception.

Spinal cord motor neuron differentiation is the program by which progenitors in the ventral neural tube become the motor neurons that connect the central nervous system to muscle. It establishes the final common pathway for all voluntary movement, and its disruption underlies congenital motor disorders, arthrogryposis and syndromes of abnormal eye and limb innervation. A ventral-to-dorsal Sonic hedgehog gradient, read out through Patched and Gli repressors, partitions the progenitor domains marked by OLIG2, NKX2-2 and LBX1; primary cilium and intraflagellar transport components are required for that readout. Committed progenitors then switch on the LIM homeodomain and homeobox code -- ISL1, ISL2, LHX3, MNX1 -- that fixes motor neuron identity, while HOX genes assign columnar and pool identity along the rostrocaudal axis so that axons reach the correct muscle targets. Related factors specify visceral and cranial motor subtypes.

Motor neurons of the spinal cord are born in the ventral neural tube, where graded Sonic hedgehog signalling from the floor plate patterns progenitors and assigns them a motor fate; without this programme there is no functional link from the central nervous system to skeletal muscle. Hedgehog transduction components including SHH, PTCH1 and GLI3, together with cilium and intraflagellar transport proteins, set the ventral-dorsal gradient, while OLIG2 defines the progenitor domain and NKX2-2 and LBX1 restrict neighbouring interneuron identities. Commitment and maturation then depend on LIM-homeodomain and homeobox factors -- ISL1, ISL2, LHX3, LHX4 and MNX1 -- which drive cholinergic identity and, with HOX factors such as HOXC10 and HOXD10, specify rostrocaudal columnar and pool identity for correct muscle innervation. Disruption of these steps underlies neural tube patterning defects and contributes to motor neuron vulnerability in degenerative disease.

telencephalon development builds the forebrain structures that carry out perception, movement planning, memory and cognition — the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, olfactory bulb, basal ganglia and amygdala — from the anterior neural tube. Its failure produces microcephaly, lissencephaly, heterotopia, holoprosencephaly and intellectual disability, and many of its genes are recurrent autism and schizophrenia candidates. Patterning transcription factors such as FOXG1, EMX2, PAX6, GLI3 and the DLX/GSX2 pair, acting under SHH, WNT, BMP and FGF8 signals, divide the vesicle into dorsal cortical and ventral ganglionic-eminence territories that generate excitatory and GABAergic neurons respectively. Neural progenitors then proliferate with spindle and centrosome machinery (ASPM, WDR62, MCPH1), and newborn neurons migrate along RELN–DAB1 and LIS1/NDEL1 routes to form layers specified by TBR1, BCL11B and FEZF2. Axon guidance through SLIT–ROBO, semaphorin, ephrin and NOGO receptor systems completes wiring, while glial transporters support the mature tissue.

The telencephalon is the forebrain division that gives rise to the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, olfactory structures, and the basal ganglia and other subcortical nuclei, and its development converts a patch of anterior neuroepithelium into layered, regionally specified circuitry. Patterning factors such as FOXG1, PAX6, EMX2, GLI3 and SIX3 set dorsal-ventral and area identity, with SHH, FGF8, WNT and BMP signals from local organizers; GSX2, ASCL1 and the DLX genes drive ventral progenitors toward GABAergic interneurons that migrate tangentially into cortex. Radial glial proliferation, spindle and centrosome components such as ASPM, WDR62 and MCPH1, and a RELN-DAB1-LIS1 module control neuron number and inward radial migration, while SLIT, ROBO, semaphorin and ephrin cues build axon tracts and the TBR1-BCL11B-FEZF2 hierarchy assigns laminar fate. Disruption underlies microcephaly, lissencephaly, holoprosencephaly, epilepsy and intellectual disability.

Subpallium development builds the ventral half of the telencephalon, the source of the basal ganglia and of nearly every cortical GABAergic interneuron. It matters because the structures it generates control action selection, habit and reward learning; disruption of its patterning or of the striatal projection neurons it produces underlies movement disorders, dystonia and neurodevelopmental conditions with autistic and obsessive-compulsive features. Ventralising cues from FGF8 and retinoid signalling, opposed by GLI3-dependent limits on hedgehog output, establish progenitor domains in which GSX2 and ASCL1 drive neurogenesis and the DLX1/DLX2 pair specifies GABAergic identity. Downstream, BCL11B, FOXP1 and FOXP2 differentiate medium spiny neurons into direct and indirect pathways marked by DRD1 and DRD2, while synaptic organisers such as SHANK3, SLITRK5 and CNTNAP2 assemble their circuits. Ciliary BBSome components link the pathway to hedgehog transduction in progenitors.

The subpallium is the ventral floor of the embryonic telencephalon, and its development gives rise to the basal ganglia and to the GABAergic interneurons that migrate from it into cortex, hippocampus and olfactory bulb. Without it, inhibitory tone in the forebrain and the striatal circuits controlling movement, motivation and habit learning fail to form. Patterning depends on ventralising signals opposed by dorsal cues, with GLI3 and FGF8 setting positional boundaries and GSX2 specifying progenitors that ASCL1 and the DLX1/DLX2 pair drive toward a GABAergic fate. Later steps involve striatal identity and projection-neuron programmes carried by BCL11B, FOXP1 and FOXP2 and the dopamine receptors DRD1 and DRD2 that define the direct and indirect pathways. Retinoid signalling contributes to regional identity. Mutations in members such as FOXP2, SHANK3 and CNTNAP2 link this developmental programme to speech, autism and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Optic nerve development builds the cable that carries vision from the eye to the brain, from the first retinal ganglion cells through axon outgrowth, midline decision-making at the optic chiasm, and myelinated maturation of the optic tract. Without it there is no route for visual information: failures produce optic nerve hypoplasia, atrophy, coloboma, and the abnormal chiasmal crossing seen in albinism and foveal hypoplasia. The genes cover the successive steps. ATOH7 specifies the ganglion cell fate that supplies every optic axon; PAX2 and GLI3 pattern the optic stalk and fissure; EPHB1 and EPHB2, with heparan sulfate made by EXT1, guide growth cones and set the ipsilateral/contralateral choice at the midline; SLC38A8 links to chiasmal misrouting. Potassium channel subunits tune conduction in the mature nerve, while SLC25A46 and TMEM126A tie mitochondrial function to the hereditary optic neuropathies.

Formation of the optic nerve turns retinal ganglion cell axons into an organised tract that carries visual information from the eye to the brain. It matters because vision depends on these axons leaving the retina through the optic disc, sorting correctly at the chiasm, and surviving; its disruption underlies optic nerve hypoplasia, coloboma, achiasmia and inherited optic atrophy. A proneural transcription factor, ATOH7, specifies the retinal ganglion cells that supply the axons, while PAX2, GLI3 and NKX2-2 pattern the optic stalk and disc region. Guidance at the midline involves EPHB1 and EPHB2 receptors with heparan sulfate made by EXT1, determining which fibres cross. Potassium channel subunits and cholinergic signalling shape axonal excitability and activity-dependent refinement, and mitochondrial proteins such as SLC25A46 and TMEM126A support the metabolic demands of these long projections, linking this developmental programme to optic neuropathy.

facial nerve morphogenesis builds the seventh cranial nerve, the mixed sensory and motor nerve that drives the muscles of facial expression, carries taste from the anterior tongue, and supplies lacrimal, nasal and oral secretory glands through its parasympathetic branches. Its failure produces congenital facial palsy and the branchio-oto-renal and Moebius-like syndromes in which facial weakness accompanies ear and jaw defects. The genes describe two linked layers of control: a hindbrain patterning program in which Hox factors and Egr2 assign rhombomere 4 identity and specify facial branchiomotor neurons, with Six1 required for their survival and migration, and a guidance layer in which class 3 semaphorins signalling through neuropilin and plexin receptors steer motor axons and dendrites along stereotyped exit and branching routes. Together they place cranial nerve assembly within segmental hindbrain development and axon pathfinding.

Formation of the facial nerve builds the seventh cranial nerve that drives the muscles of facial expression, carries taste from the anterior tongue, and supplies lacrimal, nasal and oral secretory glands. Its assembly depends on giving branchiomotor neurons the right hindbrain identity and then guiding their axons along stereotyped branches out of the second pharyngeal arch. Hox factors together with EGR2 specify rhombomere-level identity and the facial motor neuron programme, and SIX1 contributes to cranial placode and ganglion development, while secreted semaphorins acting through neuropilin and plexin receptors repel growing axons to keep the trunk and its branches in place. Disrupted patterning yields misrouted or hypoplastic nerves and congenital facial palsy, as seen in disorders of hindbrain segmentation affecting eye movement and facial weakness, linking axon guidance to craniofacial function.

Vestibulocochlear nerve formation is the building of the eighth cranial nerve, the sensory cable that carries hearing and balance information from the inner ear to the brainstem. Without it, sound never reaches the auditory pathway and the head cannot register its orientation relative to gravity, producing congenital deafness and vestibular dysfunction. The nerve has two branches with distinct targets: a vestibular branch supplying the maculae and cristae of the membranous labyrinth, and a cochlear branch supplying the sensory epithelium of the cochlear duct, where sound-induced fluid movement is transduced. Formation depends on the specification of statoacoustic ganglion neuroblasts from the otic placode and their outgrowth toward both peripheral hair cells and central nuclei. The proneural factor NEUROG1 commits otic progenitors to this neuronal fate, while PAX2 patterns the otic vesicle and its neurogenic domain, linking inner ear morphogenesis to neuronal identity.

Hearing and balance depend on a dedicated cranial nerve linking the inner ear to the brainstem, and vestibulocochlear nerve formation is the developmental step that builds it. Neurons delaminating from the otic epithelium and neighbouring ganglionic region must be specified, then extend peripheral processes to hair cells of the cochlear duct and the vestibular end organs while projecting centrally; failure yields congenital deafness, cochlear nerve aplasia or vestibular dysfunction, and limits the benefit of cochlear implantation, which requires surviving nerve fibres. The genes here point to early neurogenic specification: a proneural transcription factor of the neurogenin class initiates commitment of otic neuroblasts, and a paired-box transcription factor patterns the otic placode and vesicle from which both sensory epithelia and their innervating neurons derive. The process sits within cranial sensory ganglion development and peripheral neurogenesis generally.

Cerebellar granular layer morphogenesis builds the innermost layer of the cerebellar cortex, the densely packed sheet of granule neurons that relays mossy fiber input to Purkinje cells and thereby supports motor coordination and learning. Its failure produces cerebellar hypoplasia, ataxia, and intellectual disability. The process spans proliferation and inward migration of granule precursors from the external germinal zone, extension of parallel fibers into the molecular layer, and assembly of glomerular synapses with mossy fiber terminals and Golgi cell axons. Trans-synaptic bridges built from cerebellin and the delta-type glutamate receptor GRID2 with presynaptic neurexins specify parallel fiber-Purkinje cell contacts, while WNT7A shapes presynaptic terminal remodeling, PROX1 drives granule cell differentiation, and OPHN1, a Rho-GAP mutated in X-linked intellectual disability, tunes dendritic and spine architecture. Cell cycle and cytoskeletal regulators such as KIF14 control precursor expansion.

The cerebellar granular layer is the densely packed innermost sheet of the cerebellar cortex, and its morphogenesis is how granule neurons are generated, migrate inward past the Purkinje cell layer, and arrange their parallel fibres and mossy fibre glomeruli into the circuit that feeds all cerebellar computation. Getting this wrong produces hypoplastic cerebellum, ataxia and impaired motor learning. The genes here span the steps involved: proliferation and cell division control in granule precursors, transcriptional specification of the granule fate by PROX1, and synapse assembly in which secreted CBLN1 bridges neurexins to the glutamate receptor delta-2 subunit GRID2 to build parallel fibre-Purkinje cell contacts. WNT7A remodels presynaptic mossy fibre terminals, while OPHN1, a Rho-family regulator mutated in X-linked intellectual disability, links the process to dendritic and spine morphology more broadly.

Hippocampus development is the construction of the brain's memory and spatial-navigation circuitry, from patterning of the medial pallium through neurogenesis, migration and lamination to the mature dentate gyrus and Ammon's horn. Its failure produces cortical malformation, epilepsy and intellectual disability, and the same programs are redeployed in adult dentate neurogenesis. Wnt and Shh signalling with transcription factors such as EMX2, LEF1, LHX5, ZIC and PROX1 specify the hippocampal field and dentate granule identity, while NEUROD1 and NEUROD6 drive neuronal differentiation. Radial migration and layer formation depend on the Reelin pathway acting through DAB1 and LRP8 and on the LIS1-YWHAE-CDK5 cytoskeletal module, whose loss causes lissencephaly. Additional genes govern axon guidance, mossy fibre targeting and synaptic partner matching, interneuron supply from ventral progenitors, and growth control through PTEN and TSC1.

The hippocampus is built over development from a patterned region of dorsomedial telencephalon into the layered dentate gyrus and cornu ammonis fields that support spatial navigation and the encoding of episodic memory; disrupted formation underlies epilepsy, intellectual disability and lissencephaly-type malformations. The genes here span the sequence of events: transcriptional regionalisation and progenitor identity through EMX2, LHX5, ZIC factors, GLI3 and Wnt/Hedgehog signalling; dentate granule cell specification via PROX1 and NEUROD1; and radial migration governed by Reelin acting through its receptor LRP8 and the DAB1 adaptor, with CDK5 and its activators, LIS1 and tubulin providing the cytoskeletal machinery. Later steps include axon guidance by ephrin and semaphorin receptors, synaptic target selection by KIRREL3, glycosylation-dependent dystroglycan function, and mTOR restraint by PTEN and TSC1 that sets neuronal size and connectivity.

Forebrain regionalization carves the early anterior neural tube into distinct territories -- cortex, basal ganglia, hypothalamus, eye field -- each with its own identity, boundaries and migratory behaviour, so that neurons are born in the right place and project to the right targets. It is the step that determines cortical arealization and the balance of excitatory versus inhibitory progenitors; its disruption produces holoprosencephaly, septo-optic dysplasia, and cortical malformations. Opposing morphogen gradients set the coordinates: SHH ventrally, BMP and WNT dorsally and caudally, FGF8 from the anterior neural ridge, read out by GLI3 and by transcription factors that hold regional identity -- PAX6 and EMX2 in dorsal telencephalon, GSX2 in ventral progenitors, NKX2-1 in the hypothalamus and medial ganglionic eminence, SIX3 rostrally, LHX2 across the cortical primordium. Ciliary components such as TTC21B tune the SHH response, linking regionalization to cilium function.

The forebrain is not uniform tissue: before neurons are born, the anterior neural tube is partitioned into cortical, subcortical and hypothalamic territories, and forebrain regionalization is the patterning step that sets those boundaries and thereby the identity, position and migratory behaviour of the cells that arise in each. It works by opposing secreted signals — SHH ventrally, BMPs and WNTs from dorsal and rostral sources, FGF8 from the anterior neural ridge — read out by transcription factors that assign territory: PAX6 and EMX2 grading the cortical sheet, GSX2 marking ventral progenitor domains, NKX2-1 the medial ganglionic eminence and hypothalamus, SIX3 the rostral prosencephalon, with GLI3 restraining ventralizing SHH activity. Loss of these controls produces holoprosencephaly, failed arealization of the cortex, and depletion of the interneuron progenitors that migrate tangentially into it.

dorsal/ventral neural tube patterning assigns positional identity across the height of the embryonic neural tube, so that motor neurons, interneuron classes and dorsal sensory relay neurons arise in the correct order and number. It is the step that converts a uniform sheet of neuroepithelium into the blueprint of the spinal cord and brainstem; its failure produces holoprosencephaly, neural tube closure defects and loss of ventral neuronal subtypes. Sonic hedgehog from the notochord and floor plate acts through Patched, Smoothened and the primary cilium, where GPR161, TULP3 and tectonic proteins tune the strength and duration of the gradient, while RNF220 and FKBP8 restrain it. Opposing BMP4 and WNT3A signals from the roof plate set dorsal character, and the two gradients together define transcription factor boundaries such as PAX7 and FOXA1. It exemplifies morphogen-based tissue patterning during central nervous system development.

Neurons are assigned their identity according to where along the top-to-bottom axis of the neural tube they arise, and dorsal/ventral patterning of the neural tube is the process that sets up that coordinate system. It determines which progenitors become motor neurons and ventral interneurons and which become dorsal sensory relay neurons, so its failure produces holoprosencephaly, neural tube closure defects and loss of ventral cell types. Sonic hedgehog from the notochord and floor plate acts through the receptor PTCH1 and the transducer SMO, with ciliary and negative regulatory components including TCTN1, TULP3 and the repressive GPR161 tuning the strength and interpretation of that gradient. Opposing BMP4 and WNT3A signals from the roof plate, together with transcription factors such as PAX7, FOXA1 and GSC, translate graded signalling into sharp progenitor domains.

Central nervous system neuron differentiation is how progenitors in the neural tube and its derivatives stop dividing and become neurons with a defined identity, position and axonal target. It builds the cortex, spinal cord, midbrain dopaminergic and cholinergic populations and the interneurons that balance them; its disruption underlies lissencephaly, holoprosencephaly, intellectual disability and epilepsy. Patterning signals -- Sonic hedgehog, Wnts, FGF8 and BMPs -- set dorsoventral and anteroposterior coordinates that are read out by homeodomain and bHLH transcription factors such as PAX6, OLIG2, ASCL1, NKX2-1, ISL1 and NEUROD family members, while FOXG1, TBR1, BCL11B and FEZF2 assign cortical layer and projection identity. Downstream, guidance receptors and ligands including DCC, ROBO/SLIT, Ephrin receptors, plexins and neuropilins, together with cytoskeletal and migration machinery such as LIS1, NDEL1, CDK5 and tubulin, direct migration, neurite outgrowth and synapse formation.

Building the brain and spinal cord requires unspecialized neuroepithelial progenitors to commit to neuronal fate and acquire the identity, shape and connectivity of a particular neuron class. This programme sets out the layers of the cortex, the interneuron classes of the forebrain, the dopaminergic and motor neuron populations of the midbrain and cord, and its disruption underlies lissencephaly, holoprosencephaly, epilepsy and intellectual disability syndromes. Patterning morphogens including Sonic hedgehog, WNT ligands and FGFs, read out through Smoothened, Frizzled and GLI factors, position progenitors along the neural axes; proneural and homeodomain transcription factors such as ASCL1, NEUROD1, PAX6, OLIG2, the LHX and DLX families, TBR1 and FEZF2 then fix subtype identity. Newborn neurons migrate and extend processes using LIS1, NDEL1, CDK5, tubulin and microtubule regulators, while Slit-Robo, Netrin-DCC, ephrin and semaphorin cues guide axons toward their targets.

molting cycle process covers the cyclical renewal of an animal's outer covering — in mammals, the hair growth cycle in which follicles alternate between active growth, regression and rest, shedding old shafts and building new ones. It matters because it keeps skin appendages replaceable throughout life, and its disruption produces alopecia, hypotrichosis, ectodermal dysplasia and abnormal skin barrier formation. The genes trace the signalling conversation between epithelium and dermal papilla that drives each round: WNT ligands with their FZD receptors, LGR5 and the inhibitors DKK1 and SOSTDC1 set stem cell activation, while EDA–EDAR, SHH–SMO–GLI2, FGF7/FGF10 through FGFR2, and BMP/TGF-beta effectors including SMAD4 time entry and exit from growth. Transcription factors such as FOXN1, HOXC13, LHX2 and SOX9 specify follicle compartments, and hair-specific keratins with transglutaminase and desmosomal proteins build and anchor the shaft itself.

Skin appendages are not permanent: hair, feathers and cuticle are shed and rebuilt on a schedule, and the molting cycle process covers the regenerative programme that drives this periodic turnover. In mammals it corresponds to the hair follicle cycle, in which quiescent bulge stem cells marked by LGR5 and LHX2 re-enter growth, build a new fibre, then regress, so the same signalling that patterns appendages during development is reused throughout life. WNT/beta-catenin activity with its brakes DKK1, DKK4 and SOSTDC1, ectodysplasin signalling through EDA and EDAR, hedgehog output via SHH, SMO and GLI2, and FGF, TGF-beta/activin and Notch inputs set the timing, while HOXC13, FOXN1 and DLX3 drive differentiation of hair keratins such as KRT25 and KRT71. Loss of these components produces hypotrichosis, ectodermal dysplasia, and the barrier and desquamation defects seen with SPINK5 or desmosomal mutation.

positive regulation of cell-cell adhesion covers the signals and surface molecules that make cells stick together more tightly or more often, a step that underlies tissue integrity, platelet aggregation, leukocyte recruitment and, above all, the stable contacts immune cells must form to communicate. Much of the content is immunological: MHC class I and II molecules, T cell receptor components and their kinases (LCK, FYN, ZAP70, SYK), costimulatory and checkpoint ligands of the CD28/B7 and TNF superfamilies, and the selectins, integrins and glycosyltransferases that build homing receptor ligands for rolling and firm arrest on endothelium. Cytokines and chemokines amplify these contacts, while junctional and cytoskeletal proteins such as catenin, ZO-1, JAM-A, RHOA and PTK2 convert receptor engagement into mechanically stable adhesion. Chromatin remodelling and lineage transcription factors set the adhesion programme during lymphocyte development. Loss of this regulation impairs immune synapse formation, antigen priming and inflammatory cell trafficking.

Cells stick to one another on cue, and this is the set of regulators that raise the rate or extent of that sticking. Much of the biology here is immunological: antigen presentation by MHC class I and class II molecules, costimulatory and coinhibitory receptor pairs such as CD28 with CD80/CD86 and ICOS with its ligand, and the proximal T cell kinases LCK, FYN, ZAP70 and SYK that convert receptor engagement into integrin activation and stable immunological synapses. Selectins, their fucosyl- and sulfotransferase-dependent ligands, junctional adhesion molecule F11R, VCAM1 and ITGA4/ITGB2 support leukocyte rolling, firm arrest and transmigration, while chemokines including CCL19, CCL21 and CXCL13 position cells for contact. Cytokine, Wnt, Hedgehog, ephrin and TGF-beta inputs, together with SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits and lineage transcription factors, set adhesive competence transcriptionally. Such control underlies lymphocyte development, inflammation, wound repair and tissue integrity, and its dysregulation contributes to autoimmunity and tumour immune evasion.

cellular process involved in reproduction in multicellular organism covers the cell-level events that make gametes and allow them to unite, and so underlies fertility itself; loss of these functions produces azoospermia, oocyte maturation arrest, premature ovarian insufficiency and failed fertilisation. It spans germ cell specification and survival (NANOS, DAZL, DND1, KIT), the meiotic program with its double-strand break machinery, synaptonemal complex and recombination checkpoints (SPO11, REC8, SYCP1/3, DMC1, MLH1), and the piRNA and RNA-binding systems that silence transposons and store maternal transcripts. Later steps build the sperm itself: chromatin remodelling into protamines, acrosome formation, and axonemal and outer dense fibre assembly, with CATSPER channels and ABHD2 conferring the hyperactivated motility and capacitation needed to reach the egg. Fertilisation is completed by zona pellucida proteins and the IZUMO1-JUNO recognition pair, followed by egg activation and oocyte-to-embryo transition.

Sexual reproduction in animals depends on specialized cell-level programmes that build gametes and allow them to meet, and this collection covers those events from germ cell specification through meiosis, sperm and oocyte maturation, and fertilization. Loss of these functions produces infertility rather than systemic disease: azoospermia, teratozoospermia with malformed sperm heads or tails, premature ovarian insufficiency, and oocytes that fail to activate after sperm entry. Mechanistically it spans meiotic recombination and synapsis (SPO11, DMC1, SYCP1/SYCP3, REC8, MLH1), piRNA-directed silencing of transposons in germ cells (PIWIL1/2, MOV10L1, TDRD family), chromatin remodelling in which transition proteins and protamines replace histones during spermiogenesis, axonemal and flagellar assembly, and sperm motility control through CatSper calcium channels. Sperm-egg recognition and fusion requires IZUMO1 with its egg receptor and the tetraspanin CD9, while zona pellucida proteins and maternal-effect factors prepare the oocyte for embryogenesis.

ovulation cycle process covers the recurring events of the female reproductive cycle by which ovarian follicles grow, select a dominant follicle, release a mature oocyte, and remodel into a corpus luteum that prepares the endometrium for implantation. It sets fertility and cycle length, and its disruption underlies anovulation, premature ovarian insufficiency and polycystic ovary phenotypes. The genes trace the gonadotropin axis from FSHB through the FSH and LH receptors into STAT5- and steroid-receptor-dependent transcription, with ESR1, PGR, NR5A1 and FOXO3 governing granulosa cell fate and the resting follicle pool. Oocyte-derived GDF9 and BMP/TGF-beta family ligands coordinate granulosa proliferation, while NPPC-NPR2 signalling holds meiosis in arrest until the ovulatory surge. Follicle rupture and cumulus expansion require matrix remodelling by ADAMTS1, MMP2, PTX3 and TNFAIP6, and atresia of unselected follicles proceeds through caspase-mediated apoptosis. Metabolic signals such as leptin link nutritional state to cycling.

The ovulation cycle process covers the recurring events by which ovarian follicles grow, select a dominant follicle, release a mature oocyte and remodel the ovary afterwards, together with the hormone-driven changes in the uterus that prepare it for implantation. It is the basis of female fertility, and its disruption underlies anovulatory infertility, polycystic ovary syndrome and premature ovarian insufficiency. Gonadotropins acting through FSHR and LHCGR drive granulosa cell proliferation and steroidogenesis, with STAT5 signalling and nuclear receptors including ESR1, PGR and NR5A1 relaying the response; oocyte-derived GDF9 and BMP receptor signalling coordinate the surrounding somatic cells, while NPPC-NPR2 signalling holds the oocyte in meiotic arrest until the ovulatory surge. Follicle rupture requires proteolytic and matrix remodelling by metalloproteinases and the cumulus matrix proteins PTX3 and TNFAIP6, and atresia of non-selected follicles proceeds by caspase-dependent apoptosis under FOXO3 control.

regulation of anatomical structure morphogenesis covers the control layer over how tissues and organs acquire their shape during development and repair — setting how fast and how far processes like branching, tube formation, axon outgrowth and blood vessel sprouting proceed. Its outputs define body plan and organ architecture, and mis-tuning underlies congenital malformations, vascular anomalies, neurodevelopmental disorders and the aberrant angiogenesis and invasion of tumours. Mechanistically it draws together the morphogen systems that pattern tissues (WNT, BMP/TGF-beta, Hedgehog, Notch, FGF and their inhibitors such as NOG, DKK1 and SPRY), guidance cue families that steer growing axons and vessels (ephrins, semaphorins, slits, netrins, VEGF/angiopoietin receptors), and the Rho-family GTPases, actin regulators and cadherin-integrin adhesion complexes that execute cell shape change and migration. Lineage transcription factors and numerous microRNAs set the quantitative thresholds at which these programs run.

Shaping tissues and organs during development requires not only the machinery that builds them but control over how fast and how far that building goes, and this broad regulatory programme covers the modulation of anatomical structure morphogenesis. It governs how epithelia branch, how blood vessels sprout and remodel, how neurons extend and steer axons and dendrites, and how mitochondria and cell shape are reorganized to permit those movements. The effectors are correspondingly varied: Rho-family GTPases with their exchange factors and GAPs acting on the actin cytoskeleton, guidance cues and receptors such as netrins, slits, semaphorins, ephrins and their plexin, Robo and Eph partners, angiogenic ligands including VEGFA and angiopoietins with KDR, TEK and NRP1, and morphogen inputs from WNT, BMP, TGF-beta, FGF and Hedgehog families, layered with transcription factors and microRNAs that tune the response. Misregulation underlies congenital malformations, vascular anomalies and abnormal tissue remodelling in disease.

Protein to membrane docking is the first committed step by which a soluble or vesicle-borne protein is captured at the surface of its destination membrane, held there by receptors and tethers that project from the target bilayer. This initial adhesion sets the specificity of downstream events: only after docking can a cargo be inserted, translocated, or a vesicle be primed for fusion. The genes span several arenas where this occurs. Peroxisomal membrane proteins are recognised and docked by PEX16 and PEX26, without which peroxisomes fail to form and severe developmental disease follows. RAB7A and SNX3 mark late endosomal and retromer-associated membranes, recruiting effectors to define where sorting and maturation take place, while STXBP3 acts with SNARE machinery to position vesicles before membrane fusion. Together they represent the recognition and tethering stage that precedes protein insertion and vesicle fusion in intracellular trafficking.

Docking is the first committed step by which a soluble or peripherally associated protein is captured at a target membrane, held there by proteins that project from the membrane surface long enough for downstream tethering, translocation or fusion to proceed. It matters because it determines where cargo, coats and fusion machinery act: peroxisomal membrane biogenesis depends on PEX16 and the tail-anchored PEX26, which recruits the AAA-ATPase receptor-recycling complex to the peroxisome; endosomal identity and cargo sorting depend on the small GTPase RAB7A and the phosphoinositide-binding sorting nexin SNX3, which recognises PtdIns3P-rich membranes; and STXBP3, a Munc18-family SM protein, engages SNARE complexes to prepare vesicles for fusion in regulated exocytosis and glucose transporter trafficking. Loss of such docking events derails organelle formation and membrane traffic, as in the peroxisome biogenesis disorders arising from PEX gene mutations.

DNA strand elongation is the productive phase of DNA synthesis, in which polymerases extend a primed 3' end to copy the genome ahead of cell division and to complete repair patches. Without it replication forks stall and collapse, generating breaks, chromosomal rearrangements and the genome instability that underlies cancer. The genes cover the core replisome and its accessory machinery: the MCM helicase with GINS, priming by polymerase alpha, processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon on a PCNA clamp loaded by RFC, and Okazaki fragment maturation through DNA2 and ligase I. Elongation happens on chromatin, so the INO80 remodelling complex with its RUVBL ATPases repositions nucleosomes at the fork. Telomeric components, including telomerase and the shelterin protein POT1 with the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, extend and protect chromosome ends where conventional replication cannot finish.

Extending a DNA strand by adding nucleotides to its 3' end is the productive step of replication, and the machinery here covers both the polymerases that do it and the factors that keep forks moving through chromatin. Without it cells cannot duplicate their genomes on schedule, and stalled or collapsed forks become the source of the chromosomal breaks and rearrangements that drive cancer. Replicative polymerases alpha, delta and epsilon work behind an MCM helicase and GINS, with PCNA as the sliding clamp loaded by RFC subunits, DNA2 and LIG1 processing and sealing Okazaki fragments. The INO80 chromatin remodelling complex, with its RUVBL1/RUVBL2 ATPases, clears nucleosomes ahead of the fork and aids restart. MRE11-RAD50-NBN handles damaged forks, while TERT and POT1 extend and protect the chromosome ends that conventional elongation cannot finish.

Electron transport chain is the set of membrane-embedded carriers that pass electrons from NADH and FADH2 down a redox gradient to oxygen, pumping protons and building the electrochemical potential that ATP synthase uses. It supplies most of the ATP in aerobic tissues, and its failure produces the mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, lactic acidosis and exercise intolerance seen when complex I or cytochrome oxidase subunits are mutated. The core is complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c oxidase, with cytochrome c and ubiquinone as mobile shuttles, together with assembly factors, iron-sulfur and heme cofactor pathways, and the electron transfer flavoprotein route that feeds in electrons from fatty acid oxidation. Output is regulated transcriptionally through PGC-1alpha and hypoxia-responsive signals, and the same components govern superoxide production, redox stress handling and release of cytochrome c during apoptosis.

Cells recover most of the energy in nutrients by passing electrons down a chain of carriers to a terminal acceptor, and this electron transport chain is that machinery. Coupled to proton pumping, it builds the inner-membrane gradient that ATP synthase uses, so its failure collapses oxidative phosphorylation and causes the mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, lactic acidosis and neurodegeneration seen when respiratory subunits are mutated. Nuclear- and mitochondrially encoded subunits of complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c oxidase assemble with cytochrome c, ubiquinone and iron-sulfur or copper cofactors supplied by dedicated assembly and metallation factors. Flavoprotein dehydrogenases feed electrons in from fatty acid oxidation. Quality control and biogenesis regulators such as PINK1, PARK7 and the transcriptional coactivator PPARGC1A tune chain content, while leaked electrons generate superoxide, countered here by SOD2.

Microvillus assembly builds the finger-like actin protrusions that give absorptive epithelia their brush border, expanding the apical surface of intestinal and kidney tubule cells for nutrient and solute uptake and anchoring digestive enzymes and transporters at the membrane. Loss of this program flattens the apical surface and produces malabsorptive diarrhoea, as in microvillus inclusion disease. The genes describe how a parallel actin bundle is made and tethered: espin and fascin crosslink the core filaments, ezrin and radixin with the scaffold NHERF1 link that core to the overlying membrane, and the unconventional motor MYO1A slides membrane along the bundle. Upstream, a Rap GTPase module and the STE20 kinases MST4 and TNIK set apical polarity and license brush border formation, tying protrusion growth to epithelial differentiation and apical membrane identity.

Microvillus assembly builds the dense apical projections that expand the absorptive surface of epithelial cells, most conspicuously the intestinal brush border and the kidney proximal tubule. Without it, enterocytes fail to present digestive and transport machinery at the correct density, and inherited defects in apical trafficking and brush border organisation cause congenital diarrhoeal disease and cholestasis. The projections are cored by actin bundles: espin and fascin crosslink the filaments, while ezrin and its relative radixin tether the bundle to the overlying plasma membrane, with the scaffold NHERF1 anchoring transporters and receptors at that interface, and myosin-1a moving membrane along the core. A Rap GTPase module with its exchange factors and a GTPase-activating protein, together with the STE20-family kinase MST4, sets apical polarity and licenses ezrin activation, linking apical membrane identity to surface architecture and nutrient uptake.

actin filament-based movement covers the force-generating and cargo-hauling work that myosin motors perform on actin, spanning muscle contraction, cytoplasmic organelle transport, and the shape changes of migrating and polarized cells. It matters because it produces the heartbeat, moves melanosomes and vesicles, builds and maintains the hair-cell stereocilium and the intestinal brush border, and drives cytokinesis and cell crawling. Sarcomeric myosins with troponin, tropomyosin and titin convert calcium transients into shortening, while unconventional myosins such as MYO5A, MYO6 and MYO7A carry cargo and anchor membranes; nucleation promoting factors of the WASP family supply the tracks. A large cardiac contingent here reflects excitation-contraction coupling: sodium, potassium and calcium channels, ryanodine receptor and phospholamban set the electrical and calcium signal that the contractile apparatus reads. Mutations across these components cause cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, deafness and pigmentation disorders.

Actin filament-based movement covers the two ways cells use actin tracks to generate motion: myosin motors walking cargo along filaments, and myosin-driven sliding of filaments past one another to shorten a sarcomere. It underlies muscle contraction, cell migration and shape change, and the short-range transport of vesicles, melanosomes and mitochondria at the cell periphery. Conventional myosin heavy and light chains together with the troponin-tropomyosin regulatory system, titin, myosin-binding protein C and cardiac actins represent the contractile arm here, while unconventional single-headed myosins and MYO5A, MYO6, MYO7A and MYO19 handle cargo hauling, endocytic traffic, stereocilia and mitochondrial positioning. Actin nucleation regulators such as WAS and WIPF1 supply the tracks. A large complement of sodium, potassium and calcium channels, ryanodine receptor, calsequestrin and phospholamban links excitation and calcium release to force, and mutations in these components cause cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, myopathy and deafness.

Insulin processing converts the inert precursor preproinsulin into the mature two-chain hormone that pancreatic beta cells secrete to control blood glucose. Everything downstream of it — hepatic glucose output, muscle and adipose glucose uptake, lipid storage — depends on correctly cleaved, properly folded insulin, and defects here cause hyperproinsulinemia, beta cell ER stress, and diabetes. After signal peptide removal in the endoplasmic reticulum, protein disulfide isomerase and the beta cell oxidase ERO1B install the interchain disulfide bonds, and cargo export requires YIPF5. In immature secretory granules the prohormone convertases PCSK1 and PCSK2 excise the C peptide and carboxypeptidase E trims the resulting basic residues, while zinc transported by SLC30A8 lets the hormone crystallize into storage granules. HID1 helps sort cargo toward the regulated secretory route, linking maturation to stimulus-coupled release.

Pancreatic beta cells store insulin in a ready-to-release form, and insulin processing is the maturation route that converts the newly translated precursor into the active hormone. Preproinsulin loses its signal peptide on entry into the endoplasmic reticulum, folds with help from the disulfide machinery — protein disulfide isomerase P4HB and the beta-cell oxidase ERO1B install the interchain bonds — and traffics through the secretory pathway to immature granules. There the endoproteases PCSK1 and PCSK2 excise the C-peptide and carboxypeptidase E trims the resulting ends, leaving A and B chains joined by disulfides. Zinc supplied by transporters including SLC30A8 lets the product crystallize as hexamers for storage. Because glucose homeostasis depends on releasing correctly cleaved hormone, defects here cause proinsulin hyperinsulinaemia, monogenic and type 2 diabetes, and ER stress-driven beta-cell failure.

Insulin secretion is the process by which pancreatic beta cells release stored insulin into the bloodstream in proportion to nutrient load, the central control point for whole-body glucose homeostasis; its failure produces type 2 diabetes and its congenital defects cause neonatal diabetes or hyperinsulinism. The genes trace the whole stimulus-secretion coupling chain: glucose entry and phosphorylation by glucokinase, mitochondrial metabolism generating ATP, closure of the KATP channel (KCNJ11/ABCC8), calcium entry, and SNARE- and Rab-dependent granule fusion via SNAP25, STX1A, RAB3A and synaptotagmins, with proinsulin processing and zinc loading through SLC30A8. Layered on top are amplifying and restraining inputs — incretin and adrenergic receptors, somatostatin, leptin, cAMP effectors and PKA/PKC — plus the beta-cell identity transcription factors PDX1, MAFA, NKX6-1 and the HNFs, circadian clock components, and inflammatory cytokines that degrade secretory competence.

Pancreatic beta cells couple the level of circulating nutrients to the release of insulin, and this regulated secretory pathway is what keeps blood glucose within a narrow range; its progressive failure defines type 2 diabetes, while mutations in individual components cause monogenic diabetes and congenital hyperinsulinism. Glucose enters through a transporter and is phosphorylated by glucokinase, the rate-setting step, and the resulting rise in ATP closes the KATP channel formed by KCNJ11 and the sulfonylurea receptor ABCC8, depolarising the membrane and admitting calcium. Calcium then drives fusion of insulin granules through SNARE and synaptotagmin machinery including STX1A, SNAP25 and RAB3A, with cAMP acting through PKA and EPAC to amplify release. Incretin, adrenergic, somatostatin and fatty-acid receptors tune the response, and transcription factors such as PDX1, MAFA, NEUROD1 and the HNFs maintain beta cell identity, granule content and zinc-dependent insulin storage.

protein repair restores damaged proteins to working form rather than destroying them, sparing the cell the cost of degradation and resynthesis and limiting the accumulation of dysfunctional molecules that drives ageing and neurodegeneration. Its targets are the spontaneous chemical injuries that proteins suffer simply by existing: methionine residues oxidised to sulfoxides, aspartate isomerised to isoaspartate, and lysine residues glycated by sugars. Methionine sulfoxide reductases acting in cytosol, nucleus and mitochondria reverse oxidation and thereby also let methionine serve as a renewable antioxidant sink; a protein-L-isoaspartate methyltransferase reconverts abnormal isoaspartyl linkages, and its loss causes fatal seizures in mice; a fructosamine kinase deglycates sugar adducts. DJ-1 repairs glycation damage and doubles as an oxidative stress sensor whose mutation causes early-onset parkinsonism, tying protein maintenance to neuronal survival.

Proteins accumulate chemical damage simply by existing in an oxidizing, aqueous, sugar-rich cytoplasm, and protein repair is the small set of enzymes that reverse that damage rather than sending the protein for degradation. Methionine sulfoxide reductases of both stereospecificities restore oxidized methionine residues to methionine, acting in cytosol, nucleus and mitochondria and doubling as an antioxidant sink that protects catalytic and structural sites. A protein-L-isoaspartate methyltransferase recognizes isoaspartyl residues formed by spontaneous asparagine deamidation and initiates their conversion back to normal aspartate, limiting the abnormal backbone kinks that promote aggregation and loss of function. Glycation damage is countered by a fructosamine kinase that destabilizes sugar adducts, and PARK7 repairs glycation-derived glyoxal modifications; its loss causes early-onset parkinsonism. Together these activities extend protein lifespan, buffer oxidative and metabolic stress, and shape the proteostasis burden of ageing tissues.

Lymphocyte differentiation is the developmental programme that turns haematopoietic progenitors into the T, B and innate lymphoid cells of the adaptive and innate immune systems, and then into their functional subsets. It determines whether an organism can mount antigen-specific responses at all: loss of its components produces severe combined immunodeficiency, agammaglobulinaemia, autoimmunity, or lymphoid malignancy. Lineage choice is driven by transcription factors such as PAX5, EBF-associated partners, BCL11B, GATA3, TCF7, FOXP3 and the RORC/TBX21/STAT axis, acting with SWI/SNF chromatin remodellers and Polycomb to fix identity. Notch ligands, WNTs and thymic stroma provide the niche signals; RAG1/RAG2 and non-homologous end joining assemble antigen receptors, whose signalling through LCK, ZAP70, SYK, BTK and CARD11 enforces positive and negative selection. Cytokines of the IL-2 receptor common gamma chain family, JAK/STAT relays and immunomodulatory receptors then set effector, regulatory and memory fates.

Lymphocyte differentiation covers the routes by which uncommitted haematopoietic progenitors become T cells, B cells, innate lymphoid and NK cells, and then specialize further into helper, regulatory, cytotoxic and antibody-secreting subsets. It builds adaptive immunity, and its failure produces severe combined immunodeficiency, agammaglobulinaemia, autoimmunity or lymphoid leukaemia. Antigen receptor genes are assembled by RAG1/RAG2 with non-homologous end joining factors such as DCLRE1C, LIG4 and PRKDC, and the resulting receptors signal through LCK, ZAP70, ITK, SYK, BTK and CARD11 to set positive and negative selection thresholds, with AIRE and thymic proteasome subunits shaping self-tolerance. Notch ligands, Wnt and BMP cues from stroma, and cytokines acting through JAK-STAT specify lineage, while transcription factors including BCL11B, PAX5, FOXP3, TBX21, GATA3, RORC and PRDM1, together with chromatin remodelling complexes, lock in identity. Chemokine receptors then direct the mature cells to their niches.

Regulation of proteolysis governs how strongly, where and when proteins are cut, spanning the controlled destruction of intracellular proteins by the proteasome and the restraint of secreted proteases acting outside the cell. It sets the half-life of cell cycle regulators, transcription factors and signalling nodes, clears misfolded and damaged proteins, and keeps tissue-remodelling and clotting enzymes from digesting healthy matrix; its failure underlies neurodegeneration, tumour progression and inflammatory tissue damage. The machinery includes the full 26S proteasome with its activators and inhibitors, ubiquitin conjugation and chaperone-linked substrate delivery through UBQLN and VCP, deubiquitinases such as USP7 and USP14 that reverse the mark, and SUMO, NEDD8 and UFM1 modifiers that tune it. In parallel, serpins, cystatins and TIMPs inhibit plasminogen activators, cathepsins and metalloproteinases, while secretases including PSEN1 and FURIN perform regulated site-specific cleavage.

Controlled protein breakdown sets the abundance and lifetime of most regulatory proteins, and the regulation of proteolysis is the layer that decides when a peptide bond is cut and when it is spared. Its outputs include cell cycle progression, inflammatory signalling, clotting and fibrinolysis, and clearance of misfolded proteins; when it fails, cells accumulate aggregates or destroy substrates prematurely, as in neurodegeneration and cancer. Much of the activity centres on the ubiquitin-proteasome system: the full 20S and 19S proteasome subunits, ubiquitin ligases and adaptors such as MDM2, FBXW7, BTRC, SPOP and STUB1, deubiquitinases including USP7, USP14 and UCHL5, and shuttle factors such as the ubiquilins, VCP and RAD23 homologues. In parallel, secreted inhibitors -- serpins, cystatins, SPINK family members and TIMPs -- restrain proteases acting in plasma, extracellular matrix and epidermis, while calpains, cathepsins, furin and the presenilin complex perform regulated cleavage.

T cell differentiation is the developmental program that turns a bone marrow-derived lymphoid progenitor into a mature T cell bearing a rearranged, MHC-restricted T cell receptor, and then into one of the effector or regulatory subsets that direct adaptive immunity. Its failure produces severe combined immunodeficiency and thymic aplasia at one extreme and autoimmunity or T cell leukaemia at the other. In the thymus, Notch ligands and IL-7 support progenitor commitment, RAG1/RAG2 and non-homologous end joining assemble the receptor, and pre-TCR and TCR signalling through LCK, ZAP70 and CARD11 drive positive and negative selection against peptide-MHC displayed by cortical and medullary epithelium, with thymoproteasome subunits, AIRE and FOXN1 shaping self-tolerance. Lineage identity is fixed by transcription factors including BCL11B, TCF7, GATA3, RUNX3, ZBTB7B and FOXP3, while cytokine-STAT circuits and SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling specify helper, cytotoxic, regulatory and innate-like fates.

T cell differentiation covers the whole route from a bone marrow-derived precursor to a functional T lymphocyte defined by its rearranged T cell receptor, and then the further specialisation of mature cells into helper, cytotoxic and regulatory subsets. It underwrites cell-mediated immunity and self-tolerance; its failure produces severe combined immunodeficiency when receptor gene rearrangement or downstream signalling is broken, and autoimmunity when selection and regulatory commitment go wrong. Thymocytes rearrange receptor loci through RAG1/RAG2 and non-homologous end joining, express a pre-TCR chain, and are tested against peptide-MHC, with AIRE-dependent presentation and thymoproteasome subunits shaping the surviving repertoire. Notch ligands, WNT and cytokine receptors drive proliferation and stage transitions, while proximal kinases LCK and ZAP70 relay receptor engagement. Lineage identity is fixed by transcription factors including BCL11B, GATA3, TBX21, RORC and FOXP3, acting with chromatin remodelling complexes and STAT-dependent cytokine programmes.

myofibril assembly builds the contractile apparatus of striated muscle: the ordered arrays of sarcomeres that let cardiac and skeletal muscle generate force along a defined axis. It is the process that turns a differentiating myoblast or cardiomyocyte into a contractile cell, and its disruption underlies congenital myopathies, nemaline myopathy and both hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy. Assembly begins with actin thin filaments whose length is set by tropomodulins, leiomodins and nebulin, capped and remodelled with the help of cofilin-2 and WDR1, while formins such as FHOD3 nucleate new filaments. Titin and obscurin act as molecular rulers spanning the sarcomere, alpha-actinin and telethonin organise the Z-disc, myomesins the M-band, and myosin-binding proteins register the thick filaments. Transcription factors including NKX2-5, SRF and SIX4 drive the sarcomeric gene programme, linking myofibrillogenesis to muscle differentiation, mechanical load sensing and hypertrophic growth.

Striated muscle contracts only because its actin and myosin filaments are built into precisely registered sarcomeres, and myofibril assembly is the process that constructs those repeating units and links them end to end and to the cell membrane. It defines cardiac and skeletal myocytes, and its disruption underlies dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies, congenital myopathies such as nemaline myopathy, and failure of heart tube maturation. Actin isoforms are nucleated and capped at defined lengths by leiomodins and tropomodulins, with cofilin and WDR1 trimming filaments; titin, nebulin, obscurin and myomesins act as molecular rulers spanning the sarcomere; alpha-actinin, telethonin, myopalladin and CSRP3 anchor thin filaments at the Z-disc, while myosin-binding proteins and troponin-tropomyosin tune contraction. Transcriptional inputs including NKX2-5, SRF and SIX4, plus integrin and growth factor signalling, coordinate assembly with myogenic differentiation and mechanical load.

Skeletal muscle thin filament assembly builds the actin-based half of the sarcomere, the filament that myosin pulls against to generate force. Getting thin filaments to a uniform, correct length is what allows a myofibril to contract efficiently, and failure of this process produces congenital myopathies with nemaline rods, muscle weakness and hypotonia from birth. Skeletal and cardiac actins polymerise into the filament, while leiomodin-3 nucleates and elongates actin at the thin filament ends within the sarcomere; loss of LMOD3 causes severe nemaline myopathy. Titin spans the sarcomere as a molecular ruler and, with its Z-disc partner telethonin, anchors filaments and sets sarcomeric dimensions. Transcriptional input from PROX1 links assembly to the myogenic differentiation programme, so that filament construction is coordinated with fibre-type specification and myofibrillogenesis during muscle development and repair.

Skeletal muscle contracts only if its actin-based thin filaments are built to a defined length and anchored correctly within each sarcomere, and this assembly programme is what produces them. Skeletal alpha-actin polymerises into the filament core, with cardiac actin contributing in developing and regenerating fibres; leiomodin-3 nucleates new actin filaments and sets thin filament length, and its loss causes nemaline myopathy with disorganised, rod-containing fibres and severe congenital weakness. Titin spans the sarcomere as a molecular ruler and elastic element, and telethonin binds its Z-disc end to help anchor the filament lattice. The transcription factor PROX1 contributes to the myogenic gene programme that establishes fibre-type-appropriate sarcomeric components. Together these activities link myofibrillogenesis during muscle development and repair to the force-generating geometry that thick-thin filament sliding requires.

regulation of intestinal cholesterol absorption controls how much dietary and biliary cholesterol enters the body across the enterocyte brush border, and equally how rigorously plant sterols are kept out. It sets whole-body sterol balance and plasma LDL levels, and its failure is clinically visible: loss of the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimer, which pumps sterols back into the gut lumen, causes sitosterolemia with xanthomas and premature atherosclerosis. Absorption efficiency is tuned at several steps -- bile acid composition set by CYP8B1 determines micellar solubilization, sphingomyelin hydrolysis by ENPP7 and membrane phospholipid remodeling by LPCAT3 alter lipid uptake, SOAT2 esterifies cholesterol for packaging, and the apolipoproteins APOA1, APOA4 and APOA2 assemble it into chylomicrons for lymphatic export. Leptin signaling links this to nutritional state, connecting the pathway to lipoprotein metabolism and cardiovascular risk.

How much dietary and biliary cholesterol actually enters the bloodstream is set in the enterocyte, and this control point determines whole-body sterol balance and plasma cholesterol levels. Equally important is selectivity: plant sterols taken up along with cholesterol must be pumped back into the gut lumen, a job done by the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimer on the apical membrane, whose loss causes sitosterolemia with xanthomas and premature atherosclerosis. Cholesterol that is retained is esterified by SOAT2 and packaged with apolipoproteins A-I, A-II and A-IV into chylomicrons for export into lymph. Bile acid composition, shaped by CYP8B1, alters micellar solubilization efficiency, while membrane phospholipid remodelling by LPCAT3 and sphingomyelin hydrolysis by intestinal alkaline sphingomyelinase modulate uptake. Leptin signalling links nutritional status to absorptive capacity, tying this step to dietary responses in hypercholesterolemia.

negative regulation of cell growth covers the brakes cells put on their own increase in size and mass, keeping tissues at the right dimensions and blocking the unchecked expansion that underlies tumour formation. It brings together several distinct restraint systems: cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors of the CDKN family acting with RB1 and TP53 to impose arrest and senescence; TGF-β and BMP receptor signalling through SMAD3/SMAD4 to suppress proliferation; Hippo components such as NF2, LATS2 and STK3 that limit organ size; and the STK11-ULK1/2 and sestrin arm that shuts down anabolic growth when nutrients or energy are scarce. A large repellent-cue contingent — semaphorins, slits, netrin receptors including DCC, and RTN4 with its receptor — restricts neurite and axon extension. Loss of these constraints is a defining feature of cancer, and several members are classical tumour suppressors.

Cells must be told when to stop enlarging and dividing, and this collection covers the brakes: processes that halt, slow or reverse cell growth. Loss of these restraints is the permissive step in tumour formation, and many of the genes here are classical tumour suppressors — TP53, RB1, BRCA1, the CDKN2A/CDKN1A family of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, NF2, STK11 and the Hippo kinases LATS2 and STK3. Growth suppression is imposed both from outside and inside: TGF-beta and BMP ligands signalling through activin and BMP receptors to SMAD3/SMAD4, secreted Wnt antagonists such as SFRP1 and FRZB, and contact-dependent cues including cadherin-mediated adhesion. A large axon-guidance component — semaphorins, netrins, slits and their plexin, DCC and neuropilin receptors — restricts neurite outgrowth, the neuronal form of growth inhibition. Energy stress sensors including sestrins and ULK kinases couple nutrient limitation to arrest.

Negative regulation of bone mineralization is the braking system that keeps hydroxyapatite deposition confined to bone and prevents it from occurring too fast, too much, or in the wrong tissue. Its failure produces ectopic calcification of arteries and soft tissue, while excessive braking underlies rickets and osteomalacia. Circulating and matrix inhibitors do much of the work: fetuin-A binds nascent calcium-phosphate mineral in serum, ENPP1 generates pyrophosphate that poisons crystal growth, and salivary statherin blocks precipitation at mineralized surfaces. Endocrine control runs through parathyroid hormone and the bone-derived phosphaturic hormone FGF23, which lowers phosphate availability. Other members act on the osteoblast itself, with BMP antagonism by gremlin, SOX9-driven chondrogenic commitment, and hypoxic and inflammatory signals through HIF1A and chemokine receptors restraining matrix maturation. Together these set the balance between skeletal mineral accrual and vascular calcification.

Bone is not allowed to mineralize wherever calcium and phosphate happen to be available, and this negative regulation of bone mineralization is the restraint that sets where and how much mineral is deposited. Losing it produces ectopic calcification of arteries and soft tissue or over-dense bone; too much of it gives rickets-like undermineralization. Several distinct brakes converge here. Circulating and matrix inhibitors such as fetuin-A, ECM1 and salivary statherin bind mineral surfaces and block hydroxyapatite nucleation, while ENPP1 generates pyrophosphate, the principal chemical inhibitor of crystal growth. Endocrine control comes from parathyroid hormone and the osteocyte hormone FGF23, which lowers phosphate availability. Others act on the cells: gremlin-1 antagonizes BMP signalling, SOX9 and BCOR shape skeletal cell fate, and chemokine signalling through CCL3 and its receptor promotes the osteoclast side of remodelling.

negative regulation of BMP signaling pathway restrains bone morphogenetic protein signalling, the morphogen system that patterns the embryonic dorsoventral axis, drives bone and cartilage formation, and sets iron balance through hepcidin. Restraint is as informative as the signal itself: loss of the secreted antagonist noggin or of sclerostin alters skeletal mass, gremlin and chordin family antagonists shape limb and kidney patterning, and mutations affecting hemojuvelin-directed BMP input to the liver cause iron overload. Inhibition operates at every tier. Extracellular ligand traps such as chordin, noggin, cerberus and twisted gastrulation sequester BMPs before receptor contact; the pseudoreceptor BAMBI and inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 block receptor and R-SMAD activation; SMURF ubiquitin ligases and the phosphatase PPM1A degrade or dephosphorylate signalling SMADs; and SKI, SKIL and TRIM33 with a large set of microRNAs damp transcriptional output. The result is graded, spatially bounded signalling rather than an on-off switch.

Bone morphogenetic protein signals instruct skeletal patterning, joint formation, vascular development and iron homeostasis, and the cell must be able to switch them off with precision; negative regulation of the BMP signaling pathway is the collection of brakes that sets how much ligand reaches a receptor and how long the response lasts. Secreted antagonists such as noggin, chordin, gremlins, twisted gastrulation and sclerostin sequester ligands extracellularly, while a pseudoreceptor and BMPER tune receptor availability at the cell surface. Inside the cell, inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 recruit the SMURF ubiquitin ligases to degrade receptors and effectors, phosphatases reverse SMAD activation, and SKI/SKIL and TOB1 silence SMAD-driven transcription; numerous microRNAs damp component expression. Loss of these restraints produces heterotopic ossification and sclerosing bone disease, and the hepcidin-regulating arm involving hemojuvelin, erythroferrone and TMPRSS6 links the same brakes to systemic iron loading.

Regulation of axon extension controls how fast and how far a growing axon advances, setting the pace of wiring during nervous system development and limiting regrowth after injury in the adult. Neurons depend on it to reach appropriate targets at the right time; when the balance of promoting and inhibiting cues is disturbed, axon tracts are misrouted or truncated, and myelin-derived inhibitors such as MAG and Nogo acting through NGR block regeneration after spinal cord damage. The genes span the whole chain from cue to cytoskeleton: attractive and repulsive guidance ligands and receptors including semaphorins with their plexin and neuropilin partners, netrin, slit, Wnts and chemokines; adhesion molecules of the L1 family and cadherins; and downstream kinases and cytoskeletal regulators such as CDK5, GSK3B, PAK1, LIMK1, shootin-1 and microtubule-associated MAP1B and tau that lengthen or stall the growth cone.

Neurons wire the brain by extending a single long axon toward its target, and this is the control layer that sets how fast, how far and in which direction that extension proceeds.
