It underlies axon guidance and tract formation during development and limits regrowth after injury in the adult, where myelin-derived inhibitors such as MAG and RTN4 (Nogo) acting through the Nogo receptor collapse growth cones and block repair. Attractive and repulsive cues / netrin-1, slits, semaphorins with their plexin and neuropilin receptors, Wnts, CXCL12 and NGF / converge on Rho-family effectors including PAK1, LIMK1 and ABL1, and on kinases such as CDK5 and GSK3B that phosphorylate microtubule-associated proteins including MAPT, MAP1B and CLASP2 to remodel the cytoskeleton. Adhesion molecules L1CAM, NRCAM and DSCAM couple the growing tip to its substrate. Mutations in several members, including CDKL5 and PAFAH1B1, cause neurodevelopmental disease.

Triglyceride storage is the sequestration of neutral fat into cytoplasmic lipid droplets so that fatty acids are held in an inert form until the cell needs fuel or membrane lipid. It lets adipocytes act as the body's energy reserve and protects other tissues from lipotoxic free fatty acids and ceramides; when it fails, fat accumulates ectopically in liver and muscle and drives steatosis and insulin resistance. The genes here cover droplet formation and its regulation: a fat-storage-inducing transmembrane protein shapes droplet budding from the endoplasmic reticulum, while perilipins coat the droplet surface and control access to it, PLIN5 tethering droplets to mitochondria for regulated fatty acid oxidation. The same coat proteins gate ATGL-driven lipolysis, so storage and mobilisation are two settings of one system, extended in lipid-laden macrophages by TREM2 signalling.

Cells that take in more fatty acid than they immediately oxidise must sequester it as triglyceride inside lipid droplets, and triglyceride storage is the process that packages and confines these neutral lipid esters away from the rest of the cytoplasm. This buffering protects membranes and mitochondria from free fatty acid toxicity and provides a fuel reserve that can be mobilised during fasting or exercise. Droplet biogenesis machinery shapes nascent droplets at the endoplasmic reticulum, while perilipin family proteins coat the droplet surface and control access to it: PLIN5 is prominent in oxidative tissues such as heart and muscle, and PLIN2 accumulates in steatotic liver. The lipase ATGL, encoded by PNPLA2, initiates hydrolysis of stored triglyceride, so storage and release are set by competition at the droplet coat. TREM2 links this lipid handling to lipid-laden macrophage and microglial states in obesity and neurodegeneration.

negative regulation of nucleotide biosynthetic process covers the brakes cells place on the synthesis of nucleotides and the cyclic nucleotides used as second messengers, keeping energy currency and signalling molecules from being made when they are not needed. Restraint here matters because uncontrolled nucleotide production wastes carbon, nitrogen and ATP, and because sustained cyclic nucleotide signalling is itself toxic in some tissues. The genes act at several levels: ATP5IF1 clamps the mitochondrial ATP synthase to prevent futile ATP hydrolysis and resynthesis when the proton gradient collapses during ischaemia, PARP1 consumes NAD+ while modifying chromatin, and RD3 suppresses retinal guanylate cyclase activity, a control whose loss causes photoreceptor degeneration and childhood blindness. Together they link nucleotide supply to mitochondrial energy state, DNA damage responses, and sensory neuron survival.

Nucleotide pools have to be held in check as well as replenished, and this is the restraining side of nucleotide biosynthesis " processes that slow or block the formation of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides and cyclic nucleotide second messengers. Damping such synthesis conserves phosphate and energy, keeps cyclic nucleotide signals transient, and limits the deoxynucleotide supply available for replication. The genes involved act through quite different routes: an inhibitory factor that blocks the mitochondrial ATP synthase from running in reverse and consuming ATP, a DNA damage sensor whose poly(ADP-ribose) synthesis draws heavily on NAD+, a regulator of retinal guanylate cyclase activity that restrains cGMP production in photoreceptors, and an insulin-signalling modulator. Loss of such restraint contributes to photoreceptor degeneration, where excess cGMP is toxic, and to the metabolic imbalance seen when nucleotide turnover outpaces demand.

Positive regulation of nucleotide biosynthetic process covers the signals that push cells to make more nucleotides, including the cyclic nucleotide second messengers cAMP and cGMP as well as the purine and pyrimidine precursors needed for nucleic acid synthesis and energy metabolism. Raising nucleotide output supports proliferation, mitochondrial ATP production, and sensory and hormonal signalling; guanylate cyclase activators such as GUCA1A set the cGMP levels that govern photoreceptor recovery after light, while soluble adenylate cyclase ADCY10 couples bicarbonate and calcium to cAMP generation. Other members act indirectly, through growth factor and cytokine signalling via MAP2K1 and STAT3, lipid-sensing transcription by PPARA, and mitochondrial quality control by PINK1 and PRKN, which sustains the respiratory capacity on which nucleotide synthesis depends. The grouping therefore links metabolic demand and stress status to nucleotide supply.

Nucleotides are needed for energy currency, nucleic acid synthesis and second-messenger signalling, and this grouping covers the regulatory inputs that raise the rate at which cells make them. Much of it concerns cyclic nucleotide production: a soluble bicarbonate- and calcium-sensitive adenylate cyclase generates cAMP, while guanylate cyclase activating protein tunes retinal guanylate cyclase to restore cGMP after photoreceptor excitation, a step whose failure causes inherited cone dystrophy. Other members act indirectly, by controlling mitochondrial capacity and the nucleotide pools that depend on it — PINK1 and parkin direct damaged mitochondria to mitophagy, tafazzin remodels cardiolipin for inner-membrane function, and a respiratory complex I subunit contributes to oxidative phosphorylation. Transcriptional and kinase regulators such as PPARA, STAT3 and MAP2K1 couple growth-factor, cytokine and lipid signals to biosynthetic demand, linking nucleotide supply to proliferation and metabolic state.

epithelial cell differentiation describes how an unspecialized progenitor acquires the features of an epithelial cell: apical-basal polarity, junctional adhesion to its neighbours, a keratin cytoskeleton, and a tissue-specific secretory or barrier function. It builds the linings of skin, gut, airway, kidney, mammary gland, lens and inner ear, and its failure underlies ichthyoses and barrier defects, ciliopathies, deafness, nephrotic syndrome, and the loss of differentiation that accompanies carcinoma and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Lineage decisions are set by developmental signalling through WNT, BMP/TGF-beta, Notch, Hedgehog and FGF and executed by transcription factors such as GRHL2, KLF4, TP63-family and OVOL, SOX and FOX regulators, together with GATA and HOX codes that give each epithelium its regional identity. Downstream come the structural outputs: claudins and tight junction scaffolds, desmosomes and plectin links, cornified envelope proteins crosslinked by transglutaminases, and ciliogenesis programmes for multiciliated cells.

Epithelia line every body surface and duct, and this pathway covers how an unspecialized progenitor takes on epithelial identity: apical-basal polarity, junctional sealing, and the terminal specializations of skin, gut, kidney, airway, lens, hair and inner ear. Its outputs are the barrier that keeps water in and microbes out, the absorptive and secretory surfaces of the viscera, and the ciliated and sensory epithelia; failure produces ichthyosis and other cornification disorders, ciliopathies, deafness, cataract and loss of the differentiation controls whose collapse underlies carcinoma and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Lineage transcription factors such as GRHL2, KLF4, FOXA1, CDX2 and OVOL family members act downstream of Wnt, BMP/TGF-beta, Notch, Hedgehog and Hippo cues, driving keratin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope genes, transglutaminase crosslinking, claudin and tight-junction assembly, and cell-cycle exit through CDKN1A and CDKN1B.

Thyroid gland development builds the endodermal gland that makes thyroid hormone, tracing it from a midline thickening of the pharyngeal floor through migration, bilobation and differentiation into hormone-secreting follicles. Its failure causes thyroid dysgenesis — agenesis, ectopy or hypoplasia — the commonest cause of congenital hypothyroidism, with consequences for skeletal growth and brain maturation because fetal and neonatal development depends on maternal and thyroidal hormone supply. A small set of transcription factors specifies and maintains the lineage: NKX2-1, PAX8, FOXE1 and HHEX-type regulators act combinatorially to switch on thyroglobulin and the machinery of iodide organification. Pharyngeal patterning inputs from HOX genes, TBX1, SIX family factors and sonic hedgehog position the primordium, while FGF8/FGF10 and RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signalling drive precursor proliferation and survival. The same MAPK components, when mutated somatically, later transform thyroid follicular cells.

The thyroid arises from a patch of pharyngeal endoderm that buds, migrates down the neck, and differentiates into follicles capable of iodinating thyroglobulin, and this developmental programme determines whether an infant can make thyroid hormone at all. Its failure produces congenital hypothyroidism from an absent, ectopic, or hypoplastic gland, with consequences for growth and brain maturation. A combinatorial transcription factor code of NKX2-1, PAX8, FOXE1 and HHEX-like partners specifies the anlage and later drives thyroglobulin and hormone-synthesis genes, while HOX, SIX and TBX1 factors set pharyngeal arch and pouch identity around it. Sonic hedgehog, FGF8 and FGF10, endothelin signalling through EDNRA, and RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK kinases supply the mesenchymal and vascular cues guiding budding and descent. The same factors are reused in the mature gland, linking organogenesis to thyroid hormone output and thyroid tumour biology.

midbrain-hindbrain boundary development builds the isthmic organizer, the narrow strip of neuroepithelium between mesencephalon and anterior hindbrain that patterns both territories. It matters because this organizer supplies the positional signals that specify midbrain dopaminergic neurons and cerebellar precursors; when it fails to form or to hold its position, the tectum and cerebellum are lost or malformed. The mechanism is a self-stabilising boundary: reciprocal repression between the midbrain factor OTX-type program and the hindbrain gene GBX2 fixes the interface, where FGF8 and WNT1 are then expressed as diffusible organizer signals, with EN1 read out as a graded response in adjacent cells. HES1 modulates the timing and sharpness of these expression domains, and chromatin regulators such as KDM2B together with transcriptional cofactors keep the boundary genes appropriately restricted during segmentation of the neural tube.

The junction between midbrain and hindbrain in the early embryo becomes a signalling centre, the isthmic organizer, that patterns the tissue around it; midbrain-hindbrain boundary development is the sequence by which that boundary is positioned, stabilised and elaborated into mature structures. What depends on it is substantial: the dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra, the inferior and superior colliculi, and the cerebellum all arise under its instruction, and loss of the organizer deletes midbrain and anterior cerebellum. Position is set by the mutually exclusive expression of transcription factors either side of the interface, with GBX2 hindbrain-side, and the boundary then secretes FGF8 and WNT1 to maintain itself and drive proliferation and regional identity. EN1 marks and specifies the responding territory, while HES1 and chromatin regulation keep progenitors in an undifferentiated state long enough for patterning to complete.

negative regulation of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor signaling pathway restrains the principal pro-angiogenic signal in endothelial cells, setting a ceiling on sprouting, permeability and vessel density. Without such brakes, VEGF input becomes unopposed, producing leaky, disorganised vasculature of the kind seen in tumour angiogenesis, diabetic retinopathy and oedema; controlled damping is equally required for orderly vascular patterning during development. The genes act at several levels: receptor internalisation and lysosomal disposal via ubiquitin ligase and endosomal sorting components such as NEDD4, EPN2 and HGS; dephosphorylation of the activated receptor by PTPN1; extracellular sequestration and matrix-based inhibition by multimerins and EMILIN1; suppression of downstream Ras and PI3K output by DAB2IP; and transcriptional or microRNA-level limits on receptor expression through HHEX and miR-200c. Together they convert VEGF stimulation into a transient, spatially confined response rather than continuous growth.

Blood vessel growth has to be held in check as much as driven, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that damp VEGF receptor signalling in endothelial cells. Restraint here sets how much sprouting, permeability and endothelial proliferation a tissue gets, and its loss contributes to excessive or disorganised angiogenesis in tumours, retinopathy and vascular malformation. Several routes converge on the same outcome: receptor internalisation and lysosomal degradation through ubiquitin ligase and endosomal sorting components such as NEDD4, HGS and epsin family adaptors; phosphatase activity that reverses receptor autophosphorylation, as with PTPN1; a GTPase-activating protein, DAB2IP, that curbs Ras-directed downstream output; matrix and junctional proteins including EMILIN1, MMRN2 and CADM4 that limit ligand availability or stabilise quiescent endothelium; and transcriptional and microRNA-level control of receptor abundance.

response to caffeine covers the cellular and physiological changes triggered by this plant alkaloid, which humans consume daily and which acts on two distinct targets: adenosine receptors in the nervous system and calcium release channels in muscle. Its significance is both pharmacological and diagnostic — caffeine and halothane contracture testing of ryanodine receptor function underlies the assessment of malignant hyperthermia susceptibility, and RYR1 variants that sensitise the channel produce that risk. The gene membership reflects this dual pharmacology: blockade of ADORA2A relieves tonic inhibition of striatal signalling through GNAL-coupled cascades, altering arousal and locomotion, while RYR1/RYR2/RYR3, calsequestrin, TRIC channels and the sodium–calcium exchanger set the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release that caffeine potentiates. Downstream metabolic and transcriptional adjustments run through AMPK signalling, HDAC2 and glutathione transferase-mediated detoxification, linking stimulant exposure to excitation–contraction coupling and energy sensing.

Caffeine acts on cells through two main routes, and this grouping covers the responses that follow a caffeine stimulus. One route is adenosine receptor blockade: caffeine antagonises the A2A receptor, which couples through a stimulatory G protein alpha subunit to cAMP, explaining much of its arousal and striatal signalling effect. The other is direct sensitisation of ryanodine receptors, the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release channels of skeletal and cardiac muscle and of neurons; caffeine-evoked calcium release through RYR1 is used diagnostically in malignant hyperthermia testing, and partner proteins such as calsequestrin, the trimeric intracellular cation channels and the sodium-calcium exchanger shape the resulting calcium transient. Additional components include an irritant-sensing TRP channel, a chromatin deacetylase and the AMP-activated kinase catalytic subunit, linking caffeine exposure to gene expression and energy-sensing responses as well as to excitation-contraction coupling.

Exocrine pancreas development builds the acinar and ductal compartment of the pancreas, the tissue that synthesises and stores the zymogens of digestive enzymes such as trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen and releases them into the gut. Its failure produces pancreatic hypoplasia or agenesis and exocrine insufficiency with maldigestion, and the same regulators are reactivated in pancreatitis and in the acinar-to-ductal metaplasia that precedes pancreatic cancer. Lineage specification depends on a transcription factor hierarchy in which PTF1A and PDX1 mark the multipotent pancreatic epithelium and NR5A2 sustains the acinar program of digestive enzyme genes such as CELA1. Growth and expansion are driven by insulin-like growth factor signalling through the insulin receptor, while Wnt secretion contributes to morphogenesis. Because acinar cells are extreme secretory cells, the pathway also relies on secretory protein targeting and the XBP1 arm of the unfolded protein response to maintain their capacity.

The exocrine pancreas is the digestive enzyme factory of the gut: acinar cells synthesise and store zymogens such as trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen and release them into the duct system, while its failure to form or function causes exocrine insufficiency, malabsorption and pancreatitis. Its development requires progenitors from the foregut endoderm to be specified and then committed to the acinar fate, with PTF1A and PDX1 acting as lineage-determining transcription factors and NR5A2 driving acinar differentiation and digestive enzyme gene expression. Growth factor input through insulin-like growth factors and their receptor supports progenitor expansion, and Wnt secretion contributes to organ patterning. Because acinar cells are extreme secretory specialists, the pathway also draws on the machinery of protein export and secretory stress adaptation, including cotranslational targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum and XBP1-dependent unfolded protein responses that build and maintain secretory capacity.

Myosin filament organization builds and arranges the thick filaments that generate contractile force, and keeps them registered within the sarcomere or the smooth muscle contractile apparatus. Without it, muscle cells cannot transmit tension, and the resulting disarray underlies hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies as well as defects in vascular and visceral smooth muscle tone. The genes span both assembly and regulation: titin acts as a molecular ruler that templates thick filament length and anchors elasticity, telethonin caps it at the Z-disc, and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain supplies the filament itself. Regulatory input comes from kinase signalling that phosphorylates the myosin regulatory light chain to control filament activation and actomyosin contractility, with a Rho-family GDP dissociation stimulator linking small GTPase signalling to cytoskeletal remodelling. The pathway therefore connects mechanical architecture to contractile control in muscle and non-muscle cells alike.

Myosin filament organization covers the assembly, arrangement and disassembly of the thick filaments built from myosin molecules, the motor structures that generate contractile force in muscle and in non-muscle cells. Correct thick filament geometry sets sarcomere length, the register of myosin heads against actin, and thus the force a cell can produce; disruption underlies cardiomyopathies and myopathies as well as defects in smooth muscle tone. Titin, the giant elastic sarcomeric protein, and its Z-disc partner telethonin template and stabilize filament arrangement and provide passive stiffness, while smooth muscle myosin heavy chain supplies the filament subunit itself. A kinase acting on myosin regulatory light chain links signalling to filament activation and contractility, connecting this structural biology to cytoskeletal remodelling, cell shape change and vascular and visceral smooth muscle function.

regulatory ncRNA-mediated gene silencing is the sum of the mechanisms by which non-coding RNAs shut down expression of specific target genes, giving cells a sequence-guided layer of control over their own transcriptome. It sets the quantitative tuning of developmental, immune and metabolic programs, defends the germline genome against transposons, and its derangement is a recurring feature of cancer. The pathway spans biogenesis and effector steps: Drosha–DGCR8 and Dicer process hairpin precursors, exportin-mediated transport moves them to the cytoplasm, and Argonaute proteins with TNRC6 scaffolds recruit deadenylation and decapping machinery to repress translation and degrade mRNA. A parallel PIWI–Tudor branch generates piRNAs that direct DNMT3-dependent methylation and heterochromatin formation at transposon loci in germ cells. Hundreds of microRNA loci, plus long non-coding RNAs such as MEG3 and NEAT1, supply the guiding specificity, while turnover factors including ZSWIM8 and ERI1 limit their lifetime.

Small and long non-coding RNAs act as sequence-specific guides that switch target genes off, and this regulatory ncRNA-mediated silencing covers the whole route from primary transcript to repressed target. Hundreds of microRNAs are represented here alongside the machinery that makes and uses them: Drosha with its partner DGCR8 crops primary hairpins in the nucleus, exportin-5 ferries precursors out, Dicer completes maturation, and the guide strand is loaded onto an Argonaute protein with a TNRC6 scaffold, recruiting deadenylase and decapping activities of the CCR4-NOT complex to shorten poly(A) tails and block translation. A parallel piRNA arm, built around PIWI proteins, Tudor-domain cofactors and MOV10L1, silences transposons in the germline and directs DNA methylation, so failure causes infertility. Long non-coding RNAs in the set instead nucleate repressive chromatin. Turnover factors set guide RNA lifetime, and misregulated microRNAs are pervasive in cancer and developmental disorders.

pre-miRNA processing converts hairpin microRNA precursors into the short mature guides that silence hundreds of target mRNAs, setting the post-transcriptional tone of nearly every developmental and stress program. Without it, cells lose the ability to damp translation of growth, differentiation and apoptotic regulators, and its components are recurrently mutated or misexpressed in cancers such as DICER1-syndrome tumours. Nuclear Drosha with its partner DGCR8 crops the primary transcript, and cytoplasmic Dicer, aided by TARBP2 and PRKRA, makes the second cut before the duplex is loaded onto an Argonaute protein to build the silencing complex. The pathway is heavily regulated rather than constitutive: LIN28 proteins recruit terminal uridylyl transferases to block let-7 maturation, methylation and RNA editing alter precursor fate, and such control links stem cell pluripotency, metabolic state and oncogenic transformation to microRNA output.

MicroRNAs silence hundreds of mRNAs each, and pre-miRNA processing is the step that converts a hairpin precursor into the short guide strand an Argonaute protein can use. Without it, cells lose post-transcriptional control over developmental timing, proliferation and differentiation, which is why the machinery is recurrently mutated or dysregulated in cancer. Drosha with its partner DGCR8 excises the hairpin from primary transcripts in the nucleus, Dicer1 with the double-stranded RNA-binding cofactors PRKRA and TARBP2 makes the second cut in the cytoplasm, and the duplex is loaded into AGO1-AGO4 to form the silencing complex. The pathway is heavily regulated at the precursor itself: LIN28A and LIN28B recruit the terminal uridylyltransferases TUT4 and TUT7 to block let-7 maturation, BCDIN3D methylates the pre-miRNA end, and ADAR-mediated editing can redirect or abolish processing.

Regeneration is the regrowth of tissue lost to injury, disease or surgical resection, restoring both mass and function through progenitor activation, controlled proliferation and redifferentiation. It underlies liver regrowth after hepatectomy, skeletal muscle repair by satellite cells, and axon regrowth after nerve damage; where it fails, tissue is replaced by fibrosis and function is permanently lost. The genes span the steps involved: injury cytokines such as IL6, TNF and TGFB1 with JAK2 and JUN prime quiescent cells to re-enter the cycle; cyclins, PCNA and CDK inhibitors set how far that proliferation goes; and lineage factors including PAX7, MYOD1, MYF6 and the fusogens MYMK and MYMX rebuild muscle fibres. Wnt, Hedgehog, Notch and YAP1 signalling supply the positional and growth cues, while myelin-associated inhibitors and their NgR receptors mark the constraints that limit regeneration in the central nervous system.

Regeneration is the regrowth of tissue lost to injury or disease, achieved by activating resident stem and progenitor cells, driving compensatory proliferation, and remodelling the surrounding matrix until form and function are restored. It is what allows liver to regain mass after resection, skeletal muscle to rebuild fibres after damage, and peripheral axons to regrow, and its limits explain why heart, retina and spinal cord heal poorly, leaving scar instead of tissue. The genes here span satellite-cell myogenesis (PAX7, MYOD1, MYF6, and the fusogens MYMK and MYMX), cell-cycle re-entry and its brakes (CCND1, PCNA, CDKN1A), and growth-factor, Wnt, Hedgehog, Notch and YAP signalling that set proliferative scale. Inflammatory mediators such as IL6, TNF and TGFB1 initiate and then resolve the response, while myelin-associated inhibitors including MAG and Nogo receptors restrain axon regrowth in the nervous system.

neuron projection regeneration is the regrowth of axons and dendrites after injury, the process that determines whether a damaged nerve reconnects with its target or leaves permanent deficit. It explains why peripheral nerves recover while central axons largely do not: the genes include the myelin-associated inhibitors MAG and OMG together with their Nogo receptors and the chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans of the glial scar, which actively suppress regrowth, alongside permissive cues such as CNTF, pleiotrophin, laminin and tenascin. Intracellular arms run from neurotrophin receptors and integrin-like adhesion through JAK2 and the BRAF-MEK cascade to regeneration-associated transcription factors JUN and KLF4, while MAP1B, neurofilaments and axonal transport adaptors rebuild the growth cone itself. Receptor phosphatases PTPRS and PTPRF read the inhibitory matrix. Manipulating this balance is the basis of strategies for spinal cord injury, optic nerve damage and peripheral neuropathy repair.

After axons or dendrites are cut or crushed, whether they regrow determines whether function returns, and neuron projection regeneration covers the growth programme and the brakes on it. Peripheral axons regenerate reasonably well; central axons largely do not, and the genes here explain much of the difference. Myelin- and matrix-derived inhibitors including MAG, OMG and the Nogo receptor family signal through a receptor complex to collapse growth cones, while chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and tenascins in the glial scar, marked by GFAP, present a further barrier. Opposing them, neurotrophic and cytokine signals such as CNTF acting through JAK2, and the BRAF-MEK cascade, drive a regenerative transcriptional state involving JUN and KLF4, with cytoskeletal and adhesion proteins like MAP1B, NEFL and dystroglycan rebuilding the process. Failure underlies the permanence of spinal cord injury and slow recovery from nerve trauma and neuropathy.

Septin ring organization governs the assembly, positioning, and disassembly of the septin-based collar that marks the division site, giving the cell a diffusion barrier and a scaffold onto which cytokinetic machinery is recruited. Without it the cleavage furrow is mispositioned or fails to complete, producing binucleate cells and aneuploidy, and the same septin-based scaffolding supports membrane compartmentalisation in polarised cells such as sperm and neurons. The genes act at the interface between septins, the actomyosin ring, and the plasma membrane: anillin crosslinks septins to actin, myosin, and RhoA at the furrow, while rhotekin and DOCK7 tie Rho-family GTPase activity into the process and myosin VI contributes actin-based membrane trafficking. Together they place septin ring dynamics within cytokinesis and cortical organisation, downstream of Rho signalling and upstream of successful abscission.

Septins form filamentous rings and collars at the cell cortex that act as diffusion barriers and scaffolds, most conspicuously at the cleavage furrow during cytokinesis and at the base of cilia and dendritic spines. Organizing that ring means building it at the right place, holding its position, and disassembling it once division is complete; failure leaves cells unable to complete abscission and produces binucleate progeny. The genes here act on the actomyosin cortex that the septin ring is coupled to: anillin scaffolds septins together with actin, myosin and RhoA at the furrow, rhotekin binds active RhoA, and a myosin motor plus Rho-family regulatory factors contribute membrane and cytoskeletal coupling. The result links septin ring assembly to Rho GTPase signalling and cortical contractility, and so to the final steps of cell division and to the compartmentalization of plasma membrane domains.

tRNA pseudouridine synthesis installs one of the most common chemical modifications in transfer RNA, rotating selected uridines into pseudouridine so that the tRNA folds correctly, resists degradation and decodes mRNA accurately. Without it translation becomes error-prone and inefficient: loss of PUS1 causes mitochondrial myopathy with sideroblastic anemia, and PUS3 and PUS7 mutations produce intellectual disability, illustrating how sensitive protein synthesis and neurodevelopment are to tRNA quality control. The pseudouridine synthases act alone, without a guide RNA, each isomerase recognising particular positions -- the anticodon stem-loop, position 55 of the T-arm by the TruB-family enzymes -- and breaking then reforming the glycosidic bond to give an extra hydrogen bond donor that rigidifies local structure. Separate members serve cytosolic and mitochondrial tRNA pools, and some also modify rRNA and mRNA, linking this pathway to the broader epitranscriptome and to ribosome biogenesis.

Transfer RNAs carry a set of chemical modifications that stabilise their fold and tune how accurately they decode messenger RNA, and pseudouridine formation in tRNA is one of the most widespread of these. The reaction is an isomerisation rather than an addition: a pseudouridine synthase flips the uracil base of an existing uridine so that carbon rather than nitrogen joins the ribose, adding a hydrogen-bond donor and rigidifying the backbone without changing the sequence. Distinct enzymes act at distinct positions, in the cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria, with some acting on the anticodon arm and others in the TψC loop; several also modify rRNA or mRNA. Loss of individual synthases has clinical consequences, including mitochondrial myopathy with sideroblastic anaemia from PUS1 deficiency and intellectual disability linked to PUS3 and PUS7, marking translational fidelity as the function at stake.

mRNA 3'-end processing builds the mature 3' end of a transcript, cleaving the nascent RNA and adding the poly(A) tail that determines whether a message is exported, translated, and how long it survives. Every protein-coding gene depends on it, and choice among alternative cleavage sites reshapes the 3' UTR landscape, changing which microRNA and RNA-binding-protein sites a transcript retains; misregulation of this choice is a hallmark of proliferating and cancerous cells. The core machinery is the cleavage and polyadenylation complex — CPSF subunits with WDR33 and FIP1L1 recognising the AAUAAA signal, CstF binding downstream sequence, symplekin scaffolding, and PAPOLA extending the tail. Coupling to transcription runs through the RNA polymerase II CTD via CDK9, SSU72 and the PAF1 complex, so termination and processing are decided together. A separate branch, using LSM10/LSM11 and SLBP, generates the non-polyadenylated histone mRNAs of S phase.

Almost every messenger RNA must be cut at a defined point and given a poly(A) tail before it can be exported and translated, and this 3'-end processing is where that decision is made. The choice of cleavage site sets the length of the 3' untranslated region, determining which microRNA and RNA-binding protein sites a transcript keeps, so the same gene can yield messages of different stability and localisation. Cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor subunits recognise the downstream signal, a stimulation factor and cleavage factors position the endonuclease CPSF3, and poly(A) polymerase then adds the tail; a separate route ending in SLBP and the U7 snRNP proteins LSM10 and LSM11 gives replication-dependent histone mRNAs a stem-loop instead. Coupling to transcription runs through CDK9 and the Paf1 complex, with SSU72 dephosphorylating the polymerase C-terminal domain, linking termination to message maturation.

positive regulation of cyclase activity covers the inputs that switch on adenylate and guanylate cyclases, raising intracellular cAMP or cGMP and thereby setting the tone of second-messenger signalling in almost every tissue. Its outputs govern hormone responsiveness, smooth muscle tone, water reabsorption in the kidney, insulin secretion, and the recovery phase of photoreceptor light responses. Most of the members are Gs-coupled receptors for peptide and small-molecule ligands — vasopressin, GLP-1 and GIP, CGRP, endothelin, adenosine, dopamine D5, corticotropin-releasing hormone — which act through the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit encoded by GNAS to engage adenylate cyclase. A second arm is calcium-dependent: store-operated entry via STIM1 and ORAI1 and voltage-gated L-type channels supply the Ca2+ that tunes cyclase output, while guanylate cyclase activator proteins restore cGMP synthesis in retina. Loss or constitutive activation of these steps produces endocrine resistance syndromes, diabetes insipidus and retinal dystrophy.

Cyclases convert ATP or GTP into the second messengers cAMP and cGMP, and this pathway covers the inputs that switch them on, setting how strongly a cell responds to hormones, neuropeptides and light. Many members are Gs-coupled receptors whose ligands raise cAMP: vasopressin acting on renal water reabsorption via AVPR2, incretin signalling through GLP1R and GIPR to drive insulin secretion, CRHR1 in the stress axis, adenosine and purinergic receptors, and the dopamine D5 receptor. Their shared transducer is the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit GNAS, mutations in which cause hormone resistance and fibrous dysplasia. Calcium provides a parallel input, with store-operated entry through STIM1 and ORAI1 and voltage-gated channels feeding calcium-sensitive cyclase regulation, while retinal guanylate cyclase activators tune cGMP resynthesis during photoreceptor recovery. Loss of such stimulation blunts endocrine, cardiovascular and sensory signalling.

negative regulation of cell projection organization is the braking side of how cells build and retract protrusions — axons, dendrites, neurites, cilia and lamellipodia. Restraint matters as much as growth: axons must stop at their targets, growth cones must be repelled from incorrect territory, ciliogenesis must be blocked until the cell exits the cycle, and after injury inhibitory cues in myelin prevent regeneration. The genes cover the classical repulsive guidance systems — semaphorins with plexins and neuropilin, ephrins with Eph receptors, slits, netrin–DCC, RGMA and the Nogo receptor family with MAG and RTN4 — converging on Rho‐family GTPase inactivation through GAPs, LIMK2 and cofilin‐mediated actin disassembly, and microtubule destabilisation by stathmins and CRMP/DPYSL proteins. Centriolar CCP110–CEP97 suppression of axoneme extension, PTEN and Wnt antagonists, and prion and Alzheimer‐associated proteins add further inhibitory input, linking this control to neural wiring, myelin‐imposed regenerative failure and neurodegeneration.

Cells build projections — axons, dendrites, filopodia, cilia — but growth must also be restrained, retracted and terminated, and this pathway covers the braking side of that balance. Negative regulation of cell projection organization shapes neural wiring by telling growth cones where not to go, prunes exuberant branches, and sets the point at which outgrowth stops; in the injured adult CNS the same signals block regeneration. Much of the gene content is repulsive guidance: semaphorins with their plexin and neuropilin receptors, ephrins and Eph kinases, Slits, netrin acting through DCC and the repulsive receptor UNC5-like partners, and the myelin-derived inhibitors MAG and Nogo signalling through Nogo receptors and RGMA. These converge on Rho-family control through GAPs such as ARHGAP24 and ARPIN, LIM kinases, cofilin, CRMPs and stathmins to depolymerize or destabilize actin and microtubules, with PTEN, PTPRS and centriolar CP110–CEP97 restraining outgrowth and ciliogenesis.

positive regulation of prostaglandin biosynthetic process covers the signals that drive cells to make more prostaglandins, the short-lived lipid mediators that produce fever, pain sensitisation, vasodilation, platelet responses and uterine contraction. Its output is the substrate and enzyme supply for the cyclooxygenase route: phospholipase A2 activity liberates arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, and inducible COX-2 converts it to prostaglandin H2 for downstream synthases. Upstream inputs here are inflammatory and vasoactive: interleukin-1 beta, the endothelins, vasopressin acting through its V1A receptor, and the macrophage migration inhibitory factor receptor component CD74, each coupling receptor engagement to increased eicosanoid output. Because this amplification underlies inflammatory pain and inflammation-associated tumour promotion, it is the step blocked by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and selective COX-2 inhibitors, and it links hormonal and cytokine signalling to lipid mediator production.

Prostaglandins are short-lived lipid mediators that drive inflammation, pain, fever, vascular tone and smooth muscle contraction, and the signals that increase their output determine how strongly those responses are mounted. This pathway covers the inputs that raise prostaglandin synthesis: inflammatory and vasoactive ligands such as interleukin-1 beta and the endothelins, and vasopressin acting through its V1A receptor, converge on cells to boost release of arachidonic acid by phospholipase A2 activity and to induce the inducible cyclooxygenase PTGS2, the rate-limiting step that non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs block. The migration inhibitory factor receptor component CD74 links cytokine sensing to the same output. Amplification here underlies inflammatory pain and fever, renal water and salt handling, and the prostaglandin surge in labour, while chronic overactivity contributes to arthritis and to tumour-promoting inflammation.

regulation of protein modification process covers the control layer above post-translational modification itself: the kinases, ubiquitin ligases, acetyltransferases and their inhibitors, adaptors and receptors that decide when a residue on a target protein gets phosphorylated, ubiquitylated, SUMOylated, acetylated or neddylated. Because modification state sets protein activity, localisation and lifetime, this regulation is how cells convert extracellular cues into decisions about growth, division and death. The genes span growth factor and cytokine receptors feeding MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR and JAK-STAT cascades; cyclin-CDK and anaphase-promoting complex control of mitotic entry and exit; the COP9 signalosome and cullin-RING adaptors governing degradative ubiquitylation; TNF and Toll-like receptor modules that build ubiquitin chains to activate NF-kB; chaperone-linked quality control; and autophagy initiation by ULK1. Tumour suppressors such as PTEN, RB1, STK11 and FBXW7 sit here, and their loss deregulates these modification circuits in cancer.

Most signalling and most protein turnover run through covalent marks added to and removed from existing proteins, and this collection captures the upstream control of that chemistry control over how much phosphorylation, ubiquitination, acetylation or SUMOylation a substrate receives, rather than the marking reactions themselves. Regulation at this level sets the gain of growth factor and cytokine cascades, decides whether a protein is degraded or stabilised, and times cell cycle transitions. The membership spans receptor tyrosine kinases and their inhibitors, protein tyrosine phosphatases that reverse activating phosphorylations, cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors such as CDKN1A and CDKN1B, the COP9 signalosome and neddylation factors that license cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases, E2 conjugating enzymes and deubiquitinases, chaperones including HSP90 and CDC37, sirtuin and histone deacetylase activity, PIAS SUMO ligases, and adaptors of innate immune and autophagy signalling. Loss of such restraint underlies oncogenic kinase activation and failed protein quality control.

Keratinization is the terminal differentiation programme that converts living keratinocytes into the flattened, protein-crosslinked corneocytes of the stratum corneum, and the equivalent process that builds hair, nails and claws. It creates the body's outermost barrier against water loss, microbes and mechanical injury, and its failure produces ichthyoses, palmoplantar keratodermas, peeling skin and hair shaft defects, as well as the barrier leakiness that predisposes to atopic dermatitis. Keratin intermediate filaments such as KRT1/KRT10 in suprabasal epidermis and the hair keratins with their associated proteins provide the mechanical scaffold; transglutaminases crosslink loricrin, involucrin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope proteins into the rigid cornified envelope. Filaggrin and hornerin aggregate filaments, ceramide synthesis and lipid transport by ABCA12 supply the intercellular lipid seal, and kallikrein and caspase-14 activity govern desquamation and filaggrin processing.

Keratinization is the terminal differentiation programme by which the outermost epidermal cells lose their cytoplasm and organelles and become flattened, keratin-filled corneocytes, producing the stratum corneum as well as hair, nails and other hard appendages. The result is the body's barrier against water loss, microbes and mechanical injury; its failure underlies ichthyoses, palmoplantar keratodermas and the barrier defects that predispose to atopic dermatitis. Keratin intermediate filaments such as KRT1, KRT5 and KRT10, together with hair keratins and keratin-associated proteins, are bundled by filaggrin and trichohyalin, while transglutaminases crosslink involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins and late cornified envelope proteins into an insoluble cornified envelope. Lipid handling by a ceramide synthase and a lipid transporter builds the extracellular permeability seal, and proteases including kallikrein 5 and caspase-14 drive desquamation and filaggrin processing into natural moisturizing factor.

positive regulation of mRNA 3'-end processing describes factors that stimulate the cleavage and polyadenylation reactions that finish a messenger RNA, the step that sets transcript stability, export competence and translational output. Efficient 3'-end formation is also what terminates transcription, so its enhancement couples the fate of an mRNA to the release of RNA polymerase II. The nuclear cap-binding complex, NCBP1 with NCBP2, ties events at the 5' cap to distal processing, illustrating how the two ends of a nascent transcript are communicated; CDC73, a component of the polymerase-associated PAF complex, links elongation to poly(A) site cleavage; the G-quadruplex-resolving helicase DHX36 acts on structured 3' untranslated regions; and CCNB1 brings cell-cycle control to bear on transcript maturation. Together these activities determine 3' untranslated region length and thus which regulatory elements a message retains.

Nearly every mRNA must be cleaved and polyadenylated at its 3' end before it can be exported and translated, and this pathway covers the inputs that stimulate that step. Enhancing 3'-end processing links transcription termination to the production of stable, translatable transcripts, and helps set which polyadenylation site is used, a choice that alters mRNA stability and untranslated-region content. The nuclear cap-binding complex, formed by NCBP1 and NCBP2 on the 5' cap, communicates across the transcript to promote efficient cleavage and polyadenylation as well as splicing and export. CDC73, a component of the PAF1 complex, couples RNA polymerase II elongation to 3'-end formation, while the helicase DHX36 acts on structured RNA that can otherwise impede processing. Coordination of these steps ties mRNA maturation to cell-cycle-regulated gene expression.

Negative regulation of lipopolysaccharide-mediated signaling pathway is the braking system on innate immune recognition of bacterial endotoxin, limiting how strongly and how long a cell responds after TLR4 detects LPS. It matters because unchecked LPS signalling drives the cytokine storm of sepsis and sustains chronic inflammation, so these restraints set the threshold between protective host defence and tissue-damaging immunopathology. The genes act at several levels: decoy and inhibitory receptors such as SIGIRR, SIRPA and LILRA2 dampen receptor engagement; the phosphatase PTPN6 and adaptors including TRIB1 and CACTIN interrupt intracellular relay; TNFAIP3 and NFKBIL1 curb NF-κB output; and CARD8 and IL37 restrain inflammasome and IL-1 family amplification. Metabolic and secreted components contribute too, with ACOD1-derived itaconate imposing a tolerant state and lactoferrin sequestering LPS extracellularly. Together they enforce endotoxin tolerance and resolution of inflammation.

Bacterial lipopolysaccharide is one of the strongest triggers of innate immune activation, and the brakes on that response are what keep an antibacterial reaction from becoming septic shock or chronic inflammatory tissue damage. Negative regulation of lipopolysaccharide-mediated signalling covers the molecules that stop or dampen transmission from endotoxin sensing to inflammatory gene expression. Several act at the receptor itself, including a decoy-like member of the Toll/interleukin-1 receptor family, SIGIRR, and inhibitory surface receptors of the SIRP and leukocyte immunoglobulin-like families that recruit the phosphatase PTPN6. Others intervene downstream: TNFAIP3 restricts NF-kB activation through its ubiquitin-editing activity, TRIB1 and NFKBIL1 modulate the same output, and CARD-containing decoys constrain caspase-1 and interleukin-1 maturation, with IL37 acting as an anti-inflammatory cytokine. Antimicrobial and secreted factors such as lactoferrin and beta-defensins can also sequester or neutralise the ligand, while ACOD1-derived itaconate reprogrammes macrophage metabolism toward tolerance.

TOR signaling is the cell's central decision system for growth: it reads nutrient supply, amino acid levels, energy charge and growth factor input, and sets the rate of protein synthesis, lipid production, ribosome biogenesis and autophagy accordingly. When it is deregulated cells grow and divide inappropriately, which is why it is one of the most frequently activated axes in cancer, and why loss of its brakes causes tuberous sclerosis and related overgrowth and epilepsy syndromes. The mechanism converges on two kinase complexes built around mTOR with either RPTOR or RICTOR, activated at the lysosome by Rag GTPases, the Ragulator scaffold and RHEB, and restrained by the TSC1/TSC2 complex, GATOR, folliculin and amino-acid sensors such as CASTOR1 and SAMTOR. Outputs include S6 kinases, RPS6 and the eIF4E-binding proteins, with AMPK, sestrins and DDIT4 relaying stress and starvation signals inward.

TOR signaling is the cell's master decision point on whether conditions favour growth: the mTOR kinase integrates amino acid supply, glucose and energy status, oxygen and growth factor input, and converts a favourable verdict into protein synthesis, lipid and nucleotide production, and suppression of autophagy. Two complexes carry the output, one built on RPTOR that phosphorylates S6 kinases and the 4E-BP translation repressors, the other on RICTOR. Amino acids are sensed at the lysosome, where the Ragulator scaffold and Rag GTPases position the kinase, with GATOR components, FLCN and sensors such as CASTOR1 and SAMTOR tuning the response; the TSC1/TSC2 complex acts as a GTPase-activating protein toward RHEB, and AMPK and LKB1 impose energy restraint. Loss of these brakes causes tuberous sclerosis and related hamartoma syndromes, and pathway hyperactivation is common in cancer, epilepsy and metabolic disease.

negative regulation of glucocorticoid biosynthetic process describes the braking inputs that restrain cortisol and corticosterone synthesis in the adrenal cortex, setting the ceiling of the stress hormone axis. Restraint matters because sustained glucocorticoid excess drives hypertension, insulin resistance, muscle wasting, bone loss and immune suppression, while loss of these brakes contributes to adrenal hyperplasia and steroid-producing tumours. The genes point to paracrine and transcriptional control rather than to the steroidogenic enzymes themselves: BMP2 and BMP5 signal through SMAD pathways to suppress steroidogenic gene expression in adrenocortical cells, DKK3 modulates Wnt signalling that governs cortical zonation and progenitor identity, REST silences neuroendocrine transcriptional programmes, and ATP1A1 sets membrane potential and ion gradients that couple to steroidogenic output. Together they act as a counterweight to ACTH-driven stimulation, tuning adrenal hormone production to physiological demand.

Cortisol output from the adrenal cortex has to be held in check as well as driven, and this is the restraining side of that balance: processes that damp the rate and extent of glucocorticoid synthesis. Because glucocorticoids shape stress responses, gluconeogenesis, immune suppression and blood pressure, losing this brake permits hypercortisolism with its metabolic and immunological consequences, while excessive restraint limits the adrenal response to stress. The genes involved point to several routes of suppression: bone morphogenetic protein ligands acting as paracrine inhibitors of steroidogenic gene expression in adrenocortical cells, a secreted modulator of Wnt signalling that influences adrenal zonation and growth, a transcriptional repressor that silences neuronal and steroidogenic programmes, and the sodium pump alpha subunit, linking membrane ion gradients and cell excitability to steroid hormone production.

locomotion involved in locomotory behavior covers the neural control of self-propelled movement — the machinery that translates motivational state, dopaminergic tone and synaptic signalling into how much and how fast an animal moves. It matters because this output is the readout of basal ganglia function: its disruption produces hypokinesia, ataxia and the hyperactivity or catalepsy seen in Parkinsonian and psychostimulant models. Dopamine D2 receptors acting through G protein beta subunits set locomotor drive, while AMPA receptor subunit GRIA1 and calcineurin with its RCAN regulators tune the striatal synapses that gate movement initiation. Appetite- and arousal-related peptide signalling via CARTPT, the ghrelin receptor and prepronociceptin links feeding state to activity levels. Neurodegeneration genes including VPS35, CLN6 and the mitochondrial dynamics factor SLC25A46 show how loss of neuronal maintenance surfaces first as impaired gait and reduced locomotion.

Whole-body movement from place to place, as the motor output of behaviour, depends on intact motor circuitry and on the neuromodulatory signals that set how much an animal moves. The genes here point to dopaminergic and peptidergic control of activity and gait: the D2 dopamine receptor restrains movement initiation through striatal output, the ghrelin receptor and the CART neuropeptide link energy state to activity, and prepronociceptin supplies an opioid-related peptide that dampens locomotor drive. Downstream, G protein subunits, AMPA-type glutamate receptor signalling, and calcineurin with its RCAN regulators translate these inputs into excitability changes in motor pathways. Other members act on neuronal maintenance rather than signalling; loss of retromer or mitochondrial and lysosomal components such as VPS35, SLC25A46 and CLN6 produces ataxia, spasticity and neurodegenerative movement disorders, showing that locomotor behaviour reports on neuronal health as well as circuit tone.

negative regulation of NF-kappaB transcription factor activity covers the brakes on inflammatory gene expression, restraining how much and how long NF-kappaB drives transcription of cytokines, chemokines and survival genes. This restraint keeps innate immune responses proportionate and self-limiting; its loss underlies chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and inflammation-driven tumour growth, while some of these genes act as tumour suppressors in their own right. The mechanisms are varied: deubiquitinases such as CYLD and OTULIN strip the ubiquitin chains that license IKK and upstream adaptors, TRAF3 and NLRC3-type sensors dampen receptor-proximal signalling, and nuclear factors including BCL3, SETD6 and SIRT1 modify or occupy RelA to silence promoters directly. Others act as decoys, notably the pyrin-only proteins that blunt inflammasome-linked activation, or as metabolic and G-protein-coupled inputs feeding back onto the pathway. Together they define the resolution phase of immune signalling and the tolerance imposed by regulatory T cells.

NF-kappaB drives inflammatory, antimicrobial and survival gene expression, and the brakes on it are what keep that output transient rather than chronic. Negative regulation of NF-kappaB transcription factor activity collects the inhibitors that limit how strongly and how long the factor occupies target promoters; when they fail, persistent inflammation, autoimmunity and inflammation-associated tumour growth follow. The mechanisms are varied: deubiquitinases such as CYLD and OTULIN strip activating and linear ubiquitin chains from upstream signalling components, TRAF3 restrains the non-canonical arm, BCL3 and NFKBIL1 act at the level of the DNA-bound complex, and SETD6 methylates RelA to hold it in a repressed state while SIRT1 deacetylates it. Pyrin-domain proteins and NLRC3 additionally damp inflammasome-linked and innate receptor input. Several members also explain how regulatory T cells and arrestin-coupled receptor signalling suppress inflammatory transcription.

positive regulation of response to external stimulus collects the amplifying arms of how cells detect and react to things outside themselves — microbes, tissue damage, chemotactic and wound signals — and it determines how vigorously inflammation, innate immunity, coagulation and wound repair are mounted. Its failure leaves hosts unable to clear infection, while unchecked activity drives sepsis, autoinflammatory syndromes and chronic inflammatory disease. The genes trace the sensing steps and their positive feedback: Toll-like receptors with MYD88, TIRAP and IRAK kinases; cytosolic nucleic-acid sensors such as cGAS–STING1, RIGI and MAVS; NOD-like receptors and inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and CASP1; and the NF-κB, MAPK and IRF modules they converge on. Downstream effectors are the cytokines, chemokines and their receptors that recruit leukocytes, alongside complement, ficolins, defensins and S100 alarmins, plus angiogenic and clotting factors that couple immunity to tissue response, with ubiquitin ligases and microRNAs tuning the output.

Cells that meet a microbe, an injury or a chemotactic gradient must not only detect it but amplify the reaction, and this collection of positive regulators of the response to external stimuli is what raises the gain. It underpins innate immune defence, inflammation, wound healing and leukocyte recruitment, and its over-activity produces septic shock, autoinflammatory fever syndromes and chronic inflammatory disease. Pattern-recognition receptors of the Toll-like, NOD-like and RIG-I-like families feed through adaptors such as MYD88, TICAM1, MAVS and STING1 into IRAK and TBK1 kinases, NF-kB and interferon-regulatory factors, while inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and CASP1 mature IL-1B and IL-18 and drive gasdermin-mediated lytic death. Complement factors, ficolins, chemokines and their receptors, growth factors, coagulation proteins and many ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and microRNAs tune the strength and duration of the response.

Riboflavin transport moves vitamin B2 across membranes, supplying the cell with the precursor of FMN and FAD, the flavin cofactors that redox enzymes of the respiratory chain, fatty acid beta-oxidation, and folate and amino acid metabolism cannot work without. Because humans cannot synthesise riboflavin, uptake from the diet and its delivery to tissues depend entirely on dedicated carriers: SLC52A1 in placenta, and SLC52A2 and SLC52A3 in intestine and neurons. Loss-of-function mutations in the latter two cause Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome, a childhood motor neuron disease with deafness and bulbar palsy that responds to high-dose riboflavin, showing how directly neuronal survival tracks flavin supply. Efflux and tissue-specific handling add another layer, with ABCG2 exporting riboflavin and retbindin retaining it in the retina to support photoreceptor metabolism.

Humans cannot synthesise riboflavin, so vitamin B2 must be absorbed from the diet and delivered to every tissue that makes FMN and FAD, the cofactors of flavoproteins in fatty acid beta-oxidation, the respiratory chain, and folate and amino acid metabolism. Riboflavin transport carries out that delivery: the SLC52 family encodes the plasma membrane riboflavin transporters that mediate intestinal uptake, placental transfer to the fetus, and entry into neurons and other cells, while ABCG2 effluxes riboflavin, contributing to its secretion into milk. Loss-of-function mutations in SLC52A2 and SLC52A3 cause Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome, a childhood motor neuron disease with deafness and bulbar palsy that responds to high-dose riboflavin supplementation, showing how directly neuronal survival depends on flavin supply. Retbindin associates with riboflavin handling in photoreceptors, linking this transport to retinal energy metabolism.

positive regulation of synaptic transmission, cholinergic covers the mechanisms that strengthen or sustain acetylcholine signalling between neurons, the transmitter system that drives neuromuscular activation, autonomic output, and the attentional and memory circuits of the basal forebrain. Its failure is felt directly: loss of cholinergic tone accompanies the cognitive decline of Alzheimer's disease, and drugs that boost it remain a mainstay of symptomatic treatment. The genes act at several levels of the same amplification problem. SLC18A3 loads acetylcholine into synaptic vesicles and so sets how much transmitter each release event delivers, while NALCN provides the sodium leak conductance that keeps cholinergic neurons depolarised and firing. Neuromodulatory input arrives through adenosine A2A receptors and through substance P acting on tachykinin receptors, and APP and the basement membrane component LAMA2 shape synapse assembly and stability at cholinergic contacts.

Acetylcholine-using synapses drive skeletal muscle contraction, autonomic output, and cortical and hippocampal circuits that support attention and memory, and this pathway covers the influences that turn that transmission up rather than down. The regulators act at several points: a vesicular acetylcholine transporter loads the neurotransmitter into synaptic vesicles and so sets quantal content, a sodium leak channel maintains the resting excitability that determines whether cholinergic neurons fire, and substance P acting through its receptors provides neuropeptide modulation that enhances release. An extracellular matrix laminin subunit contributes to the synaptic scaffolding required at neuromuscular junctions, while adenosine A2A receptor signalling and amyloid precursor protein link cholinergic gain to purinergic tone and to synaptic maintenance. Loss of cholinergic drive underlies the cognitive decline targeted by cholinesterase inhibitors and the weakness seen in neuromuscular transmission disorders.

regulation of actin filament bundle assembly controls how cells build stress fibres, filopodia and other bundled actin arrays, and thereby sets cell shape, adhesion strength, contractility and migration speed. It matters for wound healing, endothelial and epithelial barrier integrity, neuronal process outgrowth and the mechanical properties of muscle and podocytes; its misregulation contributes to invasive tumour behaviour and vascular leak. The core logic is Rho-family GTPase signalling: RhoA/RAC1/CDC42 are switched by an array of GEFs and GAPs, and downstream ROCK1/2, PAK and LIMK phosphorylate cofilin and TESK targets to stabilise filaments, while profilins, formins such as FHOD1/3, filamin A and tropomyosin nucleate, cap and crosslink them into bundles. Junctional and adhesion proteins including paxillin, ZO-1, kindlin-2 and syndecan-4 couple bundle assembly to integrin and cell-cell contact cues, with additional input from TGF-beta, Wnt, ephrin and lysophospholipid receptors and several microRNAs.

Actin filaments are cross-linked into parallel or antiparallel bundles to build stress fibres, filopodia and the contractile arrays that let cells adhere, stiffen, migrate and pull on their surroundings; this pathway covers the inputs that set how much bundling occurs and where. Control runs largely through Rho-family GTPases and their regulators — RHOA, RAC1 and CDC42 with numerous GEFs and GAPs such as ARHGEF18 and DLC1 — converging on ROCK1/ROCK2 and LIMK1, which suppress the severing and depolymerising activity of cofilin, while profilins feed monomers to formins including FHOD1 and FHOD3. Adhesion and junction proteins (paxillin, filamin A, FERMT2, ZO-1), receptor signals from sphingosine-1-phosphate, TGF-β and ephrin systems, and several microRNAs tune the output. The balance determines endothelial and epithelial barrier tone, cytokinesis, neuronal and podocyte morphology, and smooth muscle contractility.

regulation of nucleobase-containing compound transport controls how much nucleic acid and nucleotide traffic crosses membranes and the nuclear envelope, setting the rate at which mRNA reaches the cytoplasm and at which nucleosides are taken up by cells. It matters because gene expression is limited not only by transcription but by export: transcripts retained in the nucleus are never translated, and viral and oncogenic programs exploit this control point. The genes describe the export side in detail — the cap-binding and cleavage factors that mark a transcript as ready, the TREX component THOC2 and helicases DDX39A and DHX9 that drive mRNP release, and nucleoporins TPR and NUP153 that gate the pore and enforce retention of unspliced RNA. Chromatin and RNA modification enzymes such as SETD2, ALKBH5 and NSUN2 tune export through co-transcriptional marks, while transporter regulators including RSC1A1 and WNK1 adjust nucleoside uptake at the plasma membrane.

Nucleobases, nucleotides and RNA molecules must be moved across membranes and out of the nucleus at controlled rates, and this pathway covers the factors that tune those transport events up or down. Most of the genes act on messenger RNA export: nuclear pore and basket components such as NUP153 and TPR, the TREX-associated THOC2, the export adaptors DDX39A and CPSF6, and the cap-binding subunit NCBP2 together determine which transcripts leave the nucleus and how quickly. Chromatin and co-transcriptional regulators including SETD2 and IWS1 couple transcription to export competence, while the demethylase ALKBH5 and the methyltransferase NSUN2 add RNA modification marks that alter export and localisation. Other members regulate nucleoside handling at the cell surface, notably the adenosine receptor ADORA1 and the transporter regulator RSC1A1. The balance set here shapes gene expression output, and its disruption drives nucleocytoplasmic transport defects seen in cancer and neurodegeneration.

Methylation covers the transfer of a methyl group, almost always from S-adenosylmethionine, onto DNA, RNA, proteins, lipids and small molecules, and it is the chemistry through which cells encode heritable gene silencing, tune protein activity and dispose of neurotransmitters and xenobiotics. Its failure is felt everywhere: loss of DNA methyltransferases derails imprinting and differentiation, histone methyltransferases such as the KMT2, EZH, SETD, SUV39 and PRMT families are recurrently mutated in developmental syndromes and cancer, and defects in tRNA and rRNA modification enzymes cause intellectual disability and mitochondrial disease. The genes span writers of the epigenome, cap and internal mRNA methylation that sets transcript stability and translation, ribosome and tRNA maturation, protein carboxyl and lysine methylation controlling translation factors and phosphatases, and catabolic transferases like COMT and NNMT. Methionine cycle enzymes regenerate the methyl donor, coupling all of this to one-carbon metabolism and nutrient sensing.

Transfer of a methyl group onto DNA, RNA, protein, lipid or small-molecule acceptors is one of the cell's most widely used covalent modifications, and this collection covers the enzymes that perform it. Nearly all draw the methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine, linking the reaction to one-carbon and folate metabolism. The consequences are functionally diverse: DNA methyltransferases such as DNMT1 and DNMT3A set heritable gene silencing marks; histone lysine and arginine methyltransferases including the KMT2, SETD, SUV39, EZH and PRMT families write the chromatin code that specifies cell identity; tRNA and rRNA modification enzymes tune translational fidelity and ribosome biogenesis; METTL3/METTL14 with RBM15 deposit m6A to control mRNA fate; and catechol, nicotinamide, thiopurine and histamine methyltransferases inactivate neurotransmitters, hormones and drugs. Loss or misdirection of these activities underlies overgrowth and imprinting syndromes, leukemias, and altered drug tolerance.

Gonadotropin secretion is the controlled release of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone from pituitary gonadotropes, the step that links the brain to the gonads and sets the timing of puberty, ovulation, spermatogenesis and fertility. Loss of this control produces hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, delayed puberty or anovulatory infertility. Upstream, kisspeptin acting with neurokinin B and its receptor and with dynorphin signalling through the kappa opioid receptor generates pulsatile GnRH output, while RFRP/NPVF restrains it and leptin reports metabolic sufficiency; the pituitary responds through the GnRH receptor. Feedback comes from gonadal inhibins and activins, which oppose each other on FSH synthesis via SMAD-dependent transcription, alongside the shared glycoprotein alpha subunit and gonadotrope transcription factors such as FOXL2. Gap junction coupling and stress-related corticotropin-releasing hormone further tune secretory output, placing this pathway at the centre of neuroendocrine reproductive regulation.

Gonadotropin secretion is the regulated release of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone from pituitary gonadotropes, the step that drives ovarian follicle maturation, ovulation, spermatogenesis and gonadal steroid output; its failure produces hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, delayed or absent puberty and infertility. Hypothalamic input dominates the control: kisspeptin and neurokinin B acting through their receptors, together with opioid and RFamide-related signals, shape pulsatile GnRH release, which the gonadotrope reads through its GnRH receptor. Feedback from the gonads arrives as activin and inhibin subunits signalling through SMAD-dependent transcription, selectively tuning FSH beta relative to the shared glycoprotein alpha subunit. Metabolic and stress cues enter through leptin and corticotropin-releasing hormone, linking reproductive competence to energy stores. Transcription factors including FOXL2 and TBX3 establish and maintain the gonadotrope and hypothalamic cell identities on which this endocrine axis depends.

central nervous system myelin formation is the wrapping of oligodendrocyte plasma membrane into compacted multilamellar sheaths around CNS axons, the step that makes fast saltatory conduction and metabolic support of long axons possible. Where it fails or is undone, conduction slows and axons degenerate, as in multiple sclerosis and hypomyelinating leukodystrophies. The genes point to the axon-glia interface and to lipid handling: MAG in the periaxonal membrane and CNTN1 mediate recognition and adhesion between the sheath and the axon it ensheathes, TENM4 controls oligodendrocyte differentiation and small-diameter axon myelination, and ABCA2 supports the sphingolipid and cholesterol traffic that a membrane of this size demands. The process therefore couples cell-surface signalling from the axon to a program of lipid synthesis, membrane growth and compaction during postnatal white matter development and remyelination.

Oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord extend processes that spiral around axons and compact their membrane into myelin, the insulating sheath that permits fast saltatory conduction and supports long-term axonal integrity. Central nervous system myelin formation sets conduction velocity in white matter tracts, and its failure or breakdown underlies leukodystrophies and demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis. The genes here act at several stages: recognition and adhesion between the glial membrane and the axon surface through myelin-associated glycoprotein and contactin, lipid handling and intracellular trafficking needed to build a membrane of unusual composition, and regulators that control oligodendrocyte differentiation and process outgrowth. The pathway therefore links glial cell fate and membrane biogenesis to axon-glia communication, and connects to broader programmes of neural development and white matter maintenance.

Axon ensheathment in central nervous system is the wrapping of CNS axons by oligodendrocyte membrane, the step that produces myelin and with it the fast saltatory conduction and metabolic support that central axons depend on. Loss of this process underlies leukodystrophies and demyelinating disease, and mutations in the major myelin proteins cause spastic paraplegia and Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease. The genes span the whole sequence: SOX10, MYRF, NKX6-2 and the HES5/ID4 pair specify and time oligodendrocyte differentiation; PLP1 and MAG build and compact the sheath; FA2H, B4GALT5/6 and ABCA2 supply the galactosphingolipids and cholesterol traffic that give myelin its lipid character; and CNTN1, CNTN2 and CNTNAP1 organise the paranodal junction and node so that channels such as KCNJ10 are positioned correctly. PTEN restrains the growth signalling that sets sheath thickness, linking ensheathment to axon-glia size matching.

Oligodendrocytes wrap central axons in layers of membrane, and this ensheathment programme covers both myelinating and non-myelinating glial contact with the axon in the brain and spinal cord. The resulting sheath permits saltatory conduction, supplies metabolic support to the axon, and its loss underlies demyelinating disease and leukodystrophy. Lineage transcription factors including SOX10, MYRF, NKX6-2 and the Notch effector HES5, opposed by ID4, drive oligodendrocyte specification and the switch to sheath formation. Structural output includes the major membrane proteins PLP1 and MAG, glycosphingolipid and hydroxylated fatty acid synthesis through B4GALT5/6 and FA2H, and axoglial junction components such as CNTN1, CNTN2 and CNTNAP1 that organise paranodes. PTEN restrains the PI3K signalling that sets sheath thickness, while KCNJ10 handles potassium buffering at the glial interface.

positive regulation of chondrocyte differentiation covers the signals and transcription factors that push mesenchymal progenitors to become cartilage-producing chondrocytes, the cell type that builds the fetal skeleton, the growth plate, and articular surfaces. Because most long bones form by endochondral ossification, this control determines limb and joint shape and adult stature; its failure produces chondrodysplasias, joint fusion, and degenerative cartilage loss. BMP and GDF ligands acting through BMPR1B and SMAD3, together with FGF18, converge on the SOX9-SOX5-SOX6 trio that switches on collagen II and aggrecan expression, while GLI3, HOX factors, and RUNX2 position chondrogenesis in space and set when cells progress to hypertrophy. Additional modifiers, including a cGMP-dependent kinase and matrix cross-linking and modifying enzymes, tune proliferation and matrix maturation, linking this program to skeletal patterning, growth plate output, and cartilage repair.

Cartilage forms when mesenchymal progenitors condense and commit to the chondrocyte fate, and the signals gathered here push that commitment forward. Because nearly every long bone is first laid down as a cartilage template, positively regulating chondrocyte differentiation sets limb and joint proportions, growth plate output, and ultimately adult stature; its disruption produces chondrodysplasias, brachydactyly and joint malformation, and its reactivation is a feature of osteoarthritic cartilage. BMP-family ligands and receptors such as BMP6, GDF5, GDF6 and BMPR1B, together with FGF18, feed into SMAD-dependent transcription, where SMAD3 promotes and SMAD7 restrains the response. The output converges on SOX9 with its partners SOX5 and SOX6, the master activators of collagen and aggrecan expression, while RUNX2 and GLI3 tilt cells toward hypertrophy and the transition to bone. Matrix-modifying and kinase components, including LOXL2 and PRKG2, tune growth plate maturation.

negative regulation of intracellular transport collects the braking mechanisms that limit how fast and how far cargo, ions and signalling proteins move inside a cell, keeping traffic proportionate to demand rather than continuous. Such restraint matters because unchecked movement of transcription factors into the nucleus, of receptors to the plasma membrane, or of calcium across the sarcoplasmic reticulum would decouple signalling from stimulus; loss of these controls contributes to neurodegeneration and dysregulated cholesterol handling. Several distinct arms appear: nucleocytoplasmic gatekeeping through nucleoporins and the Ran system with SUMO1 and RANGAP1; retention of NF- tkB by its inhibitor; sequestration of substrates by 14-3-3 proteins; ER-associated degradation components that divert misfolded proteins from export; sarcolipin, myoregulin and phospholamban inhibiting SERCA-mediated calcium uptake; and INSIG1 and PCSK9 curbing sterol sensor and receptor trafficking. Retromer and sorting nexins, LRRK2 and CDK5 tune endosomal and cytoskeletal transport.

Cells move cargo constantly — proteins into and out of the nucleus, calcium into stores, lipids and receptors along the endosomal route — and this grouping covers the braking side of that traffic, the processes that dampen or block directed intracellular movement. Restraint of this kind sets how much signal reaches a destination: sequestering a transcription factor in the cytoplasm, limiting calcium re-uptake, or diverting a misfolded protein away from export. The genes reflect several such brakes. Sarcolipin and myoregulin inhibit the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump, controlling muscle relaxation; NFKBIA holds NF-κB out of the nucleus; RANGAP1, NUP153 and TPR govern the nucleocytoplasmic gradient; and OS9, ERLEC1, DERL2/3 with UBE2J1 retain glycoproteins in the endoplasmic reticulum for degradation rather than forward transport. VPS35, SNX3 and LRRK2 tune endosomal sorting, a route whose failure is tied to parkinsonism.

detection of molecule of bacterial origin is the front line of innate immune surveillance: the sensing of conserved microbial structures such as lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides, peptidoglycan fragments and unmethylated CpG DNA, and their conversion into an inflammatory signal. Without it, tissue macrophages, dendritic cells and epithelia fail to register invading bacteria and infection proceeds unopposed; with it set too high, the same receptors drive sepsis and chronic inflammatory disease. Surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors, acting as TLR2 heterodimers with TLR1 or TLR6 or as TLR4 paired with the co-receptor MD-2, work alongside lipid-transfer and scavenger proteins that capture and present the ligand. Cytosolic NOD2 covers bacteria that reach the intracellular compartment, and loss-of-function variants predispose to Crohn's disease. Downstream output is NF-κB- and interferon-driven cytokine transcription, phagocyte activation and instruction of the later adaptive response.

Innate immunity begins with recognizing that bacteria are present, and this is the sensing step: conserved microbial molecules such as lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides, peptidoglycan fragments and bacterial DNA are bound and converted into an intracellular signal that triggers inflammatory gene expression. Without it, infection proceeds unopposed; with it dysregulated, the same receptors drive septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease. Surface Toll-like receptors act as heterodimeric pairs (TLR1, TLR2 and TLR6) for lipopeptides, while TLR4 with the co-receptor encoded by LY96 responds to LPS delivered by lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and scavenger-type receptors; TLR9 senses unmethylated CpG DNA in endosomes, and cytosolic NOD2 detects muramyl dipeptide, a link underlying Crohn's disease risk. TREM2 and complement components modulate the resulting macrophage and microglial response, tuning phagocytosis and cytokine output rather than initiating detection.

regulation of microvillus assembly controls how cells build the dense arrays of actin-cored surface protrusions that create absorptive brush borders in the intestine and kidney, and it determines whether that apical surface forms in the right place at all. Loss of this control underlies microvillus inclusion disease and cholestatic intestinal failure, where enterocytes internalise their brush border and cannot absorb nutrients.
