The genes describe a Rap GTPase module — activating exchange factors and a GAP that sets Rap1/Rap2 output — feeding into the STE20 kinases STK26 and TNIK, which phosphorylate the ezrin-based apical scaffold and specify where microvilli grow. Alongside these are effectors acting directly on the actin core and glycocalyx, including the bundling protein fascin and the apical marker podocalyxin, plus the aminophospholipid flippase ATP8B1 that maintains apical membrane lipid asymmetry. The pathway thus links polarity signalling to actin cytoskeletal architecture and epithelial transport function.

Microvilli are the dense actin-cored protrusions that expand the apical surface of absorptive epithelia, and the genes here tune whether and where that brush border is built. Control of microvillus assembly determines the absorptive capacity of intestinal and renal epithelium; its loss underlies severe congenital diarrhoea and cholestatic liver disease. Much of the regulation runs through Rap GTPase signalling, with Rap2A and its activating exchange factors acting upstream of the Ste20-family kinases STK26 and TNIK to shape apical actin and junctional organisation. Local membrane composition contributes too: the aminophospholipid flippase ATP8B1 maintains apical bilayer asymmetry needed for stable microvilli, podocalyxin provides an anti-adhesive apical glycoprotein that promotes protrusion, and fascin bundles actin filaments. Together these link apical polarity cues to cytoskeletal remodelling during epithelial differentiation.

Mitochondrial translation is the protein synthesis machinery that operates inside mitochondria, using its own ribosomes, tRNAs and a slightly divergent genetic code to make the thirteen hydrophobic subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Those subunits form the catalytic cores of the respiratory chain complexes and ATP synthase, so this pathway sets the ceiling on oxidative phosphorylation; its failure causes combined respiratory chain deficiency, encephalomyopathy, cardiomyopathy and Perrault syndrome. The genes cover the whole cycle: the small and large subunit mitoribosomal proteins, mitochondria-specific aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases such as AARS2 and LARS2, tRNA modification and processing enzymes, initiation, elongation and release factors including MTIF2, TUFM and TSFM, ribosome assembly GTPases, and the OXA1L insertase that threads nascent chains into the inner membrane. Translation is coupled to mRNA stability and to co-translational assembly of the complexes themselves.

The thirteen proteins encoded by mitochondrial DNA are all made inside the organelle, and mitochondrial translation is the machinery that makes them. Those products are core subunits of the respiratory chain complexes and ATP synthase, so this process sets the ceiling on oxidative phosphorylation; mutations in its components cause infantile lactic acidosis, cardiomyopathy, encephalopathy, deafness and other mitochondrial disease. The bulk of the genes encode the small and large subunits of the mitoribosome, a structurally distinct particle with its own initiation, elongation and release factors and a genetic code differing from the nuclear one. Dedicated mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge the organellar tRNAs, with glutaminyl-tRNA generated indirectly by transamidation, and several enzymes install tRNA and rRNA modifications required for accurate decoding. Membrane insertion of the hydrophobic nascent chains is handled by an insertase acting co-translationally, coupling synthesis to complex assembly.

protein transport into membrane raft describes the targeted delivery of proteins into cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich microdomains of the plasma membrane, where receptors, transporters and signalling molecules are concentrated so that they can act together. Raft residence sets the efficiency of many surface events: it clusters immune receptor complexes for productive signalling, positions ion pumps and channels for polarised transport, and provides platforms for membrane trafficking and shedding. The genes here span these roles, from raftlin, which organises raft-dependent receptor signalling in lymphocytes and innate immune cells, to the sialoglycoprotein CD24 and the Na+/K+-ATPase beta subunit ATP1B1, which depends on raft localisation for correct apical or basolateral placement in epithelia. Uromodulin, secreted from raft domains of the thick ascending limb, illustrates the physiological stakes, since mislocalisation of raft cargo underlies kidney disease and defective epithelial ion handling.

Membrane rafts are cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich microdomains that concentrate selected proteins into small, dynamic platforms, and protein transport into these domains determines which signalling and transport complexes get assembled where. Targeting a receptor or pump into a raft raises its local partner density and changes its activity and turnover, so this sorting step underlies processes from immune receptor triggering to ion handling in epithelia. The genes here illustrate the range of cargo and machinery involved: raftlin is a defining raft-resident scaffold that helps recruit signalling components, the Na+/K+-ATPase beta subunit couples pump assembly and localisation to these domains, the small GPI-anchored glycoprotein CD24 partitions into rafts on immune and tumour cells, and uromodulin is sorted through raft domains in kidney tubule cells before apical secretion. Disrupted raft partitioning alters signal strength and can mislocalise transporters, a route to epithelial and immune dysfunction.

Granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor production is the regulated output of GM-CSF, the cytokine that drives myeloid expansion and licenses inflammatory monocytes, dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages. It sets the size and activation state of the granulocyte-macrophage compartment during infection, and its excess sustains autoimmune tissue damage while its loss impairs surfactant clearance and antifungal defence. The genes here are the upstream stimuli and relays rather than the cytokine itself: pattern recognition through nucleic acid and fungal sensors feeding the SYK-CARD9 axis, and an IL-1/IL-18 and IL-23-IL-17 cytokine circuit that instructs T cells and innate lymphocytes to release GM-CSF. Costimulatory and inhibitory surface receptors tune the magnitude of the response. Functionally this sits at the interface of innate sensing, myeloid haematopoiesis and the IL-17-associated inflammatory programmes targeted in neuroinflammation and arthritis.

GM-CSF is the cytokine that drives emergency production and activation of granulocytes and macrophages, and its output is a measure of how strongly the innate immune system has been alerted. Controlled release supports antimicrobial defence and alveolar macrophage function; excess sustains the inflammatory loops behind arthritis and autoimmune neuroinflammation. Here, pattern recognition upstream of GM-CSF is well represented: a nucleic acid sensing receptor and an endosomal DNA-sensing Toll-like receptor, together with a spleen tyrosine kinase and its CARD9 adaptor relaying C-type lectin signals from fungal cell walls. The cytokine environment that licenses GM-CSF-producing lymphocytes appears as IL-1 family members, IL-18 and the IL-23 subunit with its receptor, with IL-17 family cytokines as the accompanying effector output. Costimulatory and myeloid receptor components place this in antigen-presenting-cell-to-T-cell crosstalk rather than in one lineage.

type I interferon production is the innate immune cell's decision to make interferon-alpha and interferon-beta, the cytokines that put neighbouring cells into an antiviral state. It is the front line of defence against viruses and intracellular bacteria, and its miscalibration is equally consequential: constitutive activation by self nucleic acids produces the interferonopathies and contributes to lupus, while loss of components leaves severe viral susceptibility. Detection happens on several sensor arms — endosomal Toll-like receptors, cytosolic RIG-I and MDA5 signalling through MAVS, and cGAS-STING reading double-stranded DNA — which converge on the TBK1/IKKε kinases and the IRF3 and IRF7 transcription factors that drive interferon gene transcription. Ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases, TRIM proteins and nucleases such as TREX1 set the threshold and terminate the response, coupling this pathway to autophagy, nucleic acid turnover and NF-κB-dependent inflammation.

Type I interferon production is the cell's first broadcast alarm on detecting a virus, and its output of interferon-alpha/beta primes neighbouring cells into an antiviral state while shaping the ensuing adaptive response. Sensing is compartmentalised: endosomal Toll-like receptors read viral nucleic acids through MyD88 and TRIF adaptors, cytosolic RIG-I and MDA5 signal via MAVS on mitochondria, and cGAS detects DNA and activates STING. These routes converge on the TBK1/IKKe kinases and the IRF3/IRF7 transcription factors, with TRAF3, ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and phosphatases setting the threshold. Restraint matters as much as activation: loss of nucleases such as TREX1 or of negative regulators causes chronic interferon signalling and interferonopathy or lupus-like autoimmunity, while failure of the sensors leaves severe susceptibility to viral infection. Autophagy components, Siglec and SIRP-family receptors and paracrine amplification through STAT1 tune the magnitude and duration of the response.

Interleukin-21 production describes the control of how much IL-21 a cell makes and releases, a cytokine produced chiefly by follicular helper T cells and NKT cells that drives germinal centre reactions, B cell differentiation into plasma cells, and the cytotoxic programmes of CD8 T and NK cells. Too little of it cripples high-affinity antibody responses; too much feeds autoantibody-driven autoimmunity and sustains some lymphoid malignancies. The regulators here act upstream of the cytokine rather than on its receptor: IL-6 signalling through STAT3 promotes the follicular helper programme that turns IL-21 transcription on, the transcription factor FOXP1 restrains that programme, and several microRNAs, including miR-21 and the miR-221/222 pair, tune the output post-transcriptionally. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of T cell helper fate choice and humoral immunity.

Interleukin-21 production describes the making and release of IL-21, the cytokine by which follicular helper T cells drive germinal centre reactions, B cell differentiation into plasma cells and antibody affinity maturation; too much of it is linked to autoimmunity and lupus-like pathology, while too little blunts humoral responses and antiviral T cell help. The genes here concern the upstream control of that output rather than the cytokine itself: IL-6 signalling promotes the T follicular helper programme that licenses IL-21 expression, the transcription factor FOXP1 restrains that programme, and several microRNAs tune the transcripts involved. This places the pathway at the intersection of cytokine-driven T helper cell fate decisions and post-transcriptional regulation, determining how much IL-21 reaches responding lymphocytes during an immune response.

negative regulation of interferon-beta production is the set of brakes that limit type I interferon output after innate immune sensors detect nucleic acids, keeping antiviral responses proportionate and self-limited. Restraint matters because sustained interferon-beta drives interferonopathies, autoimmunity such as lupus, and immunopathology during infection, while excessive shutdown permits viral replication. The genes act at several points along the sensing-to-transcription axis: NLRC3, NLRX1 and CACTIN dampen STING- and MAVS-dependent signalling, PPM1B and other phosphatases reverse the kinase steps that activate IRF3 and NF- inB, ATG9A links autophagy machinery to attenuation of STING trafficking, and NMI, YY1, REL and RELB adjust transcription at the IFNB1 promoter. Inhibitory surface receptors including LILRB1 and SIRPA impose cell-extrinsic restraint. Together they set the threshold, amplitude and duration of interferon signalling in innate immune cells.

Interferon-beta is the front-line antiviral cytokine induced when cytosolic sensors detect viral nucleic acid, and because sustained type I interferon is toxic — driving inflammatory tissue damage and autoimmune interferonopathies — cells maintain brakes that shut the response down. This pathway collects those brakes: negative regulation of interferon-beta production. Several members restrain the STING and RIG-I/MAVS arms from inside the cell, including the mitochondrial protein NLRX1 and the NOD-like receptor NLRC3, while ATG9A links autophagy membranes to dampening of DNA-sensing signal output. Others act on the transcriptional and phosphorylation steps that drive the interferon promoter, with a phosphatase and NF-kB family members among them, and inhibitory surface receptors such as LILRB1 and SIRPA set thresholds in myeloid cells. The net effect is resolution of antiviral signalling and tolerance of self nucleic acid, at the cost of blunted early defence when overactive.

Negative regulation of type II interferon production is the set of brakes that limit how much interferon-gamma T cells and NK cells release, keeping antimicrobial and antitumour immunity from tipping into tissue damage, autoimmunity or cytokine-driven pathology. It matters because unrestrained interferon-gamma drives macrophage hyperactivation, as seen in haemophagocytic syndromes and chronic inflammatory disease, while too much restraint permits tumour escape and persistent infection. The genes describe several converging mechanisms: inhibitory checkpoint receptors and their ligands, including PD-L1, PD-L2, TIM-3 with its galectin-9 ligand, VISTA and LILR family receptors; suppressive cytokines such as IL-10 and the IL-33 axis; regulatory T cell and Th2 transcriptional programmes driven by FOXP3 and GATA3; and post-transcriptional decay of cytokine mRNA by ZC3H12A. Together they set the threshold and duration of Th1 effector output, and they are the substrate on which checkpoint blockade therapy acts.

Interferon-gamma drives macrophage activation and Th1 immunity, so limiting how much of it is made is how tissues avoid immunopathology once an infection is controlled. This braking programme keeps T cell and NK cell output of the cytokine in check, and its loss underlies autoimmune and inflammatory tissue damage, while its excess is exploited by tumours to escape immune attack. The genes act through several converging routes: inhibitory receptor-ligand pairs such as PD-L1, PD-L2, TIM-3 with galectin-9, and VISTA deliver co-inhibitory signals to T cells; IL-10 and the IL-20 family cytokines act as suppressive cytokines; FOXP3 and GATA3 impose regulatory and Th2 transcriptional programmes that oppose Th1 commitment; and ZC3H12A degrades cytokine transcripts post-transcriptionally. Together they set the threshold and duration of type II interferon production rather than blocking it outright.

Negative regulation of interleukin-10 production restrains output of the principal anti-inflammatory cytokine, and so sets how strongly an immune response is allowed to proceed before it is damped. Because IL-10 suppresses macrophage and dendritic cell activation and antigen presentation, holding it down favours inflammatory and Th1/Th17-type immunity, pathogen clearance and antitumour responses; excessive restraint contributes to tissue-damaging inflammation and autoimmunity, while failure to restrain IL-10 underlies chronic infection and tumour immune escape. The genes act at several levels: IL-12/IL-23 subunits and their receptor drive programmes antagonistic to IL-10, inhibitory receptors such as FCGR2B, LILRB family members and VSIR together with TYROBP-coupled signalling and BTK/JAK3 kinases tune the threshold in myeloid and B cells, FOXP3 and IDO1 link the process to regulatory T cell biology, and several microRNAs including let-7 family members impose post-transcriptional limits on IL-10 messenger RNA.

Interleukin-10 is the principal brake on inflammation, so processes that restrain its production keep immune responses from being damped prematurely and allow effective clearance of pathogens and tumours. Curbing IL-10 output shifts myeloid cells and T cells toward inflammatory programmes, and excessive restraint contributes to autoimmunity and immunopathology while insufficient restraint favours chronic infection and tumour tolerance. The genes here act through several routes: the IL-12/IL-23 axis, including the p40 subunit shared by both cytokines and the IL-23 receptor, promotes inflammatory differentiation at IL-10's expense; kinases such as BTK and JAK3 couple receptor engagement to cytokine transcription; inhibitory receptors including FCGR2B, LILRB family members and their TYROBP adaptor, and checkpoint ligands like CD274 and PDCD1LG2 tune the output; and several microRNAs, among them let-7 family members, repress it post-transcriptionally. FOXP3 links the process to regulatory T cell identity.

negative regulation of interleukin-8 production restrains output of the chemokine CXCL8, the principal signal that recruits neutrophils to infected or injured tissue. Because IL-8 release is fast, self-amplifying and highly destructive when unchecked, dampening it sets the ceiling on acute inflammation and protects against tissue damage in sepsis, colitis, asthma and chronic airway disease. The brakes act at several levels: anti-inflammatory mediators such as annexin A1 and IL-10, inhibitory receptors including CD33 and the phosphatase PTPN22, and intracellular checks on NF- inkappaB signalling by BCL3, CACTIN and the deubiquitinase OTUD7B. A large complement of microRNAs, notably miR-146a and let-7 family members, adds post-transcriptional damping of Toll-like receptor and cytokine-driven transcription. Together these mechanisms tune innate immune signalling toward resolution rather than persistent neutrophilic recruitment.

Interleukin-8 is a potent neutrophil chemoattractant, and restraining its output is how tissues keep an inflammatory response proportionate and self-limiting. Negative regulation of interleukin-8 production prevents runaway neutrophil recruitment of the kind seen in sepsis, chronic airway inflammation, inflammatory bowel disease and atherosclerosis, and it also limits the tumour-promoting angiogenic effects of sustained chemokine release. Much of the control converges on NF-kB: the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL10 dampens transcription, BCL3 and the deubiquitinase OTUD7B tune NF-kB activity, and CACTIN acts as a repressor downstream of Toll-like receptor input. The glucocorticoid-inducible annexins ANXA1 and ANXA4 suppress inflammatory signalling, KLF4 acts transcriptionally, PTPN22 modulates immune receptor phosphorylation, and inhibitory receptors such as CD33 contribute. A large complement of microRNAs, notably MIR146A and let-7 family members, adds post-transcriptional braking on the same circuits.

positive regulation of type II interferon production describes the signals that drive T cells and natural killer cells to make interferon-gamma, the cytokine that arms macrophages for intracellular killing, boosts antigen presentation, and defines Th1-type immunity. Loss of these inputs leaves patients vulnerable to mycobacteria and other intracellular pathogens, while excess drives autoimmunity and macrophage activation syndromes. The genes trace the whole induction circuit: innate sensing through Toll-like receptors, CD14 and inflammasome components that release IL-1beta and IL-18; the IL-12/IL-23/IL-27 cytokine family and their receptors, which with IL-18 synergise to switch on IFNG transcription; NK and T cell activating receptors such as NKG2D, CD2 and SLAM family members alongside inhibitory counterweights like TIM-3 and galectin-9; and proteasome and MHC class I components that supply the peptides triggering cytotoxic recognition in the first place.

Interferon-gamma is the signature cytokine of type 1 cellular immunity, and this pathway covers the inputs that drive T cells and NK cells to make it. The output licenses macrophage activation, MHC upregulation and control of intracellular bacteria, mycobacteria and viruses; too little permits disseminated mycobacterial and salmonella infection, while too much fuels autoimmunity and hemophagocytic inflammation. The strongest drivers here are the IL-12 family cytokines and their receptors acting with IL-18 and its receptor chains, plus IL-2, IL-21 and IL-23 signalling. Innate sensing feeds in through several Toll-like receptors, CD14, the beta-glucan receptor CLEC7A and inflammasome adaptors, while NK and T cell surface receptors such as KLRK1, CD226, SLAM family members and antigen-presenting MHC molecules provide contact-dependent triggers. Antigen processing by the immunoproteasome, negative regulators including HAVCR2 and PTPN22, and cyclic-nucleotide phosphodiesterases set the threshold.

positive regulation of interleukin-1 alpha production covers the signals that drive cells to make and release IL-1 alpha, an alarmin cytokine that initiates sterile inflammation when epithelial or myeloid cells are damaged. Unlike its relative IL-1 beta, IL-1 alpha is preformed and can act from dying cells, so control over its output determines how strongly tissue injury converts into neutrophil recruitment, fever and downstream cytokine cascades. The genes point to danger sensing at the cell surface and its coupling to unconventional secretion: extracellular ATP acting through the P2X7 receptor, pannexin channels that amplify nucleotide release and potassium efflux, and S100A13 as a partner in the non-classical export route used by IL-1 alpha and FGF1. NLRP10 and neuropeptide and transcription factor components add inflammasome-adjacent and neuroimmune regulation, linking this arm of innate immunity to chronic inflammatory disease.

Interleukin-1 alpha is an early alarm cytokine released by damaged or stressed epithelium and myeloid cells, and this pathway covers the signals that increase its production. Because IL-1 alpha is already made as an active precursor stored in the cytoplasm, its output depends heavily on danger sensing and on unconventional release rather than on classical secretion: extracellular ATP acting through the P2X7 receptor together with the pannexin-1 channel links nucleotide leakage from injured cells to cytokine output, while an inflammasome-related NLR protein and an S100 family partner contribute to activation and to non-vesicular export. Amplified IL-1 alpha drives fever, neutrophil recruitment, and sterile inflammation after necrosis, and sustained overproduction contributes to chronic inflammatory and autoinflammatory disease. Neuroendocrine and transcriptional regulators in the same programme connect the response to peptide signalling and to cell-type-specific control of cytokine gene expression.

positive regulation of interleukin-18 production describes the signals that drive cells to make and release IL-18, a cytokine that pushes T cells and NK cells toward interferon-gamma output and shapes mucosal barrier defence. It matters because IL-18 links detection of microbes and cell damage to type 1 immunity, and its unchecked release contributes to macrophage activation syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease, while its loss leaves epithelial surfaces poorly defended against enteric viruses. Mechanistically the genes converge on the inflammasome: pattern recognition through Toll-like receptors and nucleic acid sensors, together with TNF-driven priming, raises pro-IL-18 availability, while NLRP9 and GBP5 promote assembly of caspase-1-activating platforms. Caspase-1 cleaves the precursor and gasdermin D pores permit its export, coupling cytokine maturation to pyroptotic cell death rather than conventional secretion.

Interleukin-18 is made as an inactive precursor and only becomes an active cytokine after inflammasome-driven cleavage, so upregulating its production is a step in mounting inflammatory and antiviral responses. The mature cytokine drives interferon-gamma output from T and NK cells, links innate sensing to type 1 immunity, and contributes to mucosal defence; excessive output underlies macrophage activation syndromes and inflammatory bowel pathology. Here, pattern recognition through Toll-like receptors for bacterial lipoproteins and CpG DNA, together with nucleic acid sensing and NLR-family inflammasome scaffolds, converges on caspase-1, which processes the pro-cytokine. Gasdermin D pores and guanylate-binding protein support of inflammasome assembly provide the release route and amplification, while tumour necrosis factor contributes to the surrounding inflammatory milieu. The result couples microbial detection to cytokine maturation rather than to transcription alone.

Mast cell cytokine production is the tissue mast cell's capacity to release TNF, IL-6, IL-13 and other mediators after activation, an output distinct from the immediate degranulation of histamine and proteases. It sustains the late phase of allergic inflammation, recruits eosinophils and neutrophils to mucosal and connective tissue, and contributes to asthma, chronic urticaria and helminth defence; unchecked, it drives persistent airway and skin inflammation. IgE crosslinking through the high-affinity receptor gamma chain initiates the signal, which requires the CARMA-BCL10-MALT1 complex to reach NF-kB and switch on cytokine transcription, while KIT signalling from stem cell factor sets mast cell survival and tunes the strength of the response. Transcriptional regulators including BCL6 and the immediate-early receptor NR4A3 shape which cytokines are made and for how long, linking receptor engagement to gene expression rather than to preformed granule release.

Mast cells do more than release preformed histamine and proteases; hours after activation they transcribe and secrete cytokines that sustain allergic inflammation, recruit eosinophils and neutrophils, and shape tissue remodelling in asthma and chronic urticaria. Cytokine output by mast cells is the slower, transcription-dependent arm of this response, and it is set by how strongly the cell is stimulated and by which transcriptional brakes are in place. Signalling through the IgE receptor gamma chain couples antigen crosslinking to the kinase cascades that engage an adaptor scaffold feeding NF-kB activation, while the KIT receptor for stem cell factor supplies the survival and priming input that mast cells depend on for maturation and tissue residence. Transcriptional regulators of the BCL6 and NR4A families then restrain or tune the resulting cytokine gene programme, determining whether mast cell activation resolves or drives persistent inflammation.

positive regulation of CREB transcription factor activity describes the signalling inputs that switch on CREB, the transcription factor through which cyclic AMP and calcium signals are converted into lasting changes in gene expression. This step underlies long-term synaptic plasticity and memory consolidation, hepatic gluconeogenic gene programmes, and hormone-driven transcription in endocrine tissue; its loss blunts activity-dependent transcription of targets such as BDNF and PGC-1α. Calcium-stimulated adenylate cyclases generate the cAMP that activates protein kinase A, while calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases and the MSK family kinases phosphorylate CREB at Ser133 to recruit the CBP/p300 coactivators. In parallel, the CRTC coactivators are dephosphorylated and enter the nucleus to engage CREB directly, providing a second, kinase-independent route to target-gene induction and integrating nutrient and neuronal stimuli at the same promoters.

CREB is the transcription factor that converts transient rises in cyclic AMP and calcium into lasting changes in gene expression, and this pathway covers the upstream events that switch it on. The output matters for memory consolidation and synaptic plasticity, for hepatic gluconeogenesis and gluconeogenic gene induction during fasting, and for hormone-responsive programmes generally. Calcium-stimulated adenylate cyclases ADCY1 and ADCY8 raise cAMP in neurons, a calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase and the MSK-family kinases RPS6KA4 and RPS6KA5 phosphorylate CREB at its regulatory serine, and the CREB-regulated transcription coactivators CRTC1 and CRTC2 are dephosphorylated and move to the nucleus to engage CREB at target promoters. Convergence of these inputs sets the threshold above which stimulation becomes transcription, linking neuronal activity and metabolic hormones to durable transcriptional responses.

Receptor catabolic process is the controlled destruction of signalling receptors, the step that sets how long and how strongly a cell can respond to a hormone, growth factor, morphogen or neurotransmitter. Because a receptor that is not degraded keeps signalling, this pathway is a brake on proliferation and metabolic signalling: loss of the ubiquitin ligases RNF43 and ZNRF3 leaves Frizzled receptors on the surface and drives Wnt-dependent tumours, while PCSK9 and MYLIP direct the LDL receptor to lysosomal or ubiquitin-dependent turnover and thereby set plasma cholesterol. Mechanistically, HECT and RING ligases such as NEDD4, ITCH and SMURF1 mark activated receptors with ubiquitin; sorting adaptors, ESCRT components and KIF16B route them into multivesicular bodies; and lysosomal proteases including legumain and calpain, together with the autophagy regulators BECN1, UVRAG and PIK3R4, complete degradation. Hepcidin-driven ferroportin removal and furin-family processing extend the same logic to iron and receptor maturation.

Signalling receptors are not permanent fixtures; their degradation sets how long and how strongly a cell can respond to a hormone, growth factor or ligand. This receptor catabolic process covers the routes by which receptors are marked, internalised and destroyed, chiefly ubiquitin-dependent sorting into lysosomes. HECT-domain and RING ligases such as NEDD4, NEDD4L, ITCH, SMURF1 and the Wnt-receptor ligases RNF43 and ZNRF3 tag receptors for downregulation, while MYLIP targets the LDL receptor and secreted PCSK9 drives its lysosomal disposal, a link that underlies cholesterol handling and lipid-lowering therapy. Endosomal and autophagy machinery -- BECN1, UVRAG, PIK3R4, KIF16B and ESCRT-associated MVB12A -- delivers cargo onward, and lysosomal proteases including legumain complete breakdown. Loss of this turnover leaves receptors signalling unchecked, a route to hyperproliferation, and also governs iron control through hepcidin-driven ferroportin loss.

regulation of natural killer cell activation sets the threshold at which NK cells commit to killing a target or releasing interferon-gamma, tuning innate surveillance against virus-infected and tumour cells while sparing healthy tissue. Too little restraint drives immunopathology and hyperinflammation; too much allows tumours to escape. Activation is balanced between inhibitory and activating receptor pairs "" the CD94/KLRD1 complex with KLRC1 or KLRC2 reading HLA-E, NKG2D ligands such as MICA, and FCGR3A with the TYROBP adaptor for antibody-dependent killing "" feeding into proximal signalling through FGR, RASGRP1 and the phosphatase PTPN22. Cytokine input from IL-15, IL-12, IL-18 and IL-21 acting via STAT5 sets responsiveness and survival, while checkpoint receptors like TIM-3 and AXL/GAS6 signalling dampen it. Transcriptional regulators including TOX, PRDM1, ZBTB1 and ZNF683 govern NK development and the acquired, memory-like state, and a CRL4-DCAF15 ubiquitin ligase module degrades activation substrates.

Natural killer cells must be licensed and tuned before they kill, and this collection of regulators sets how readily that activation occurs. The balance matters for clearing virus-infected and tumour cells while sparing healthy tissue; too little leaves malignancies and herpesvirus infections unchecked, too much drives haemophagocytic and autoimmune pathology. Activating and inhibitory receptor pairs read surface ligands — CD94/NKG2 family members with HLA-E, NKG2D ligands such as MICA, and the Fc receptor FCGR3A with its TYROBP adaptor — and feed into proximal signalling through kinases and RASGRP1, restrained by the phosphatase PTPN22 and checkpoint receptor HAVCR2. Cytokines set responsiveness from outside: IL-15 with its receptor alpha chain supports survival and priming, while IL-12, IL-18 and IL-21 promote interferon-gamma output via STAT5 and transcriptional regulators including PRDM1, TOX and ZNF683. A cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase module adds degradative control.

Negative regulation of natural killer cell activation is the set of brakes that keep NK cells from firing at healthy tissue, setting the threshold a target must cross before it is killed. This restraint matters for self-tolerance, for maternal acceptance of the fetus, and for limiting the collateral damage of antiviral and antitumour responses; conversely, tumours exploit the same brakes to escape immune surveillance. Inhibition acts at several levels: HLA-E displayed on normal cells engages inhibitory receptors and reports intact MHC expression, checkpoint receptors such as HAVCR2 and the inhibitory lectin CLEC12A dampen cytotoxic signalling, shed MICA blunts activating receptor engagement, and intracellular components including the kinase FGR, the adaptor CLNK and the ubiquitin-pathway regulator RHBDD3 tune signal strength downstream. Progesterone-induced blocking factor extends the same logic to pregnancy, linking innate cytotoxicity to reproductive immunology.

Natural killer cells kill without prior sensitization, so their activation has to be actively restrained to keep cytotoxicity off healthy tissue and to limit inflammatory damage during infection. This inhibitory arm sets the threshold: HLA-E signals intact self to the CD94/NKG2A receptor and licenses tolerance of normal cells, HAVCR2 (TIM-3) acts as a checkpoint receptor that dampens effector responses and marks exhausted lymphocytes, CLEC12A is an inhibitory C-type lectin receptor, and the kinase FGR and adaptor CLNK act inside the cell to tune receptor-proximal signalling. Shed ligands such as MICA can blunt activating receptor engagement, a route tumours exploit to escape NK surveillance. Pregnancy-associated and peptidoglycan-recognition factors contribute further suppression. Loss of this restraint favours autoimmunity and graft rejection; excess of it permits tumour and viral persistence, which is why several of these receptors are immunotherapy targets.

regulation of cellular pH reduction covers the control of processes that acidify the cell interior, a variable that sets enzyme activity, vesicle trafficking, and the balance between survival and death. Cytoplasmic and organellar pH must be held within narrow limits: sodium-hydrogen exchangers such as SLC9A7 and SLC9A8 extrude protons in exchange for sodium across Golgi and endosomal membranes, tuning the luminal acidity on which glycosylation and cargo sorting depend, while BCL2 opposes the intracellular acidification that accompanies mitochondrial apoptotic signalling. Hormonal input enters through vasopressin acting on its V1A receptor, linking systemic fluid and electrolyte handling to proton flux in target cells, and the ubiquitin ligase UBE3A adds post-translational control. Loss of these exchangers causes intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental disease, reflecting how tightly neuronal function is tied to organellar pH.

Cells hold their internal pH within a narrow band, and control over the processes that acidify the cytosol or intracellular compartments is part of how that band is maintained. Regulation of cellular pH reduction covers the modulation of acidifying activity, which matters because proton gradients set enzyme activity, vesicle trafficking, apoptotic sensitivity and, in the kidney, water and acid handling. The genes here point to two routes: hormonal signalling through vasopressin and its V1A receptor, which acts on renal and vascular target cells, and sodium/hydrogen exchangers of the intracellular Golgi and endosomal membranes, which trade sodium for protons and thereby limit compartmental acidification. BCL2 links pH control to mitochondrial apoptotic decisions, while the ubiquitin ligase UBE3A implies proteolytic turnover of the regulators themselves.

neurotrophin production covers the synthesis, processing and release of the growth factors that keep developing and mature neurons alive. Target tissues make neurotrophins such as NGF and BDNF in limiting amounts, so the supply set by this pathway determines which innervating neurons survive, how far their axons grow, and how synapses are strengthened during learning; reduced availability contributes to neurodegeneration, neuropathic pain and depression. The genes point to two control points. Proprotein convertases including FURIN and PCSK6 cleave pro-neurotrophins into mature ligands, a step that switches the product from a death-promoting to a survival-promoting signal at TrkA/TrkB versus p75. Trafficking and neuromodulatory inputs, via the huntingtin-associated protein HAP1, adenosine A1 receptors and neuropeptide Y, tune how much factor is packaged and secreted, linking neuronal activity and metabolic state to trophic support.

Neurons survive and extend axons only if their target fields supply trophic support, and neurotrophin production is the synthesis, processing and release of those factors — NGF, BDNF and relatives — that suppress neuronal apoptosis and drive process outgrowth. Loss of this supply during development eliminates neurons that fail to secure enough of it, and in the adult it contributes to degeneration, impaired regeneration after injury, and altered pain and mood signalling. Much of the control is post-translational: proneurotrophins must be cleaved by proprotein convertases such as furin and PCSK6 to yield the mature, TrkA/TrkB-activating ligand, since the unprocessed precursors act through p75 to favour cell death instead. Vesicular trafficking and activity-dependent secretion set how much is actually delivered, with HAP1 implicated in BDNF transport, and neuromodulators including adenosine and neuropeptide Y tuning release.

negative regulation of activin receptor signaling pathway restrains signalling through activin type I and II receptors and the SMAD2/3 branch of the TGF-beta superfamily, setting how much activin output a cell receives. This braking is what allows graded mesoderm patterning in the embryo, controls pituitary FSH synthesis, and limits activin-driven growth suppression and fibrosis in adult tissues. Restraint acts at every level: secreted follistatin and FSTL3 sequester activin dimers, inhibin alpha pairs with beta subunits to form antagonistic inhibin and competes for receptors with betaglycan, and cerberus and DAND5 block ligand in the node. Loss of these controls skews reproductive endocrine output and developmental axis formation.

Activin signalling drives mesoderm patterning, gonadal function and pituitary FSH output, and the brakes on it set how much of that signal a cell actually receives. Negative regulation of activin receptor signalling operates at every level: secreted follistatin and follistatin-like 3 sequester activin ligands, Cerberus and the DAN-family antagonists Dand5 block ligand access during early embryonic patterning, and inhibin alpha pairs with a beta subunit to form inhibin, a competitive antagonist that restrains pituitary gonadotropin release. positive regulation of activin receptor signaling pathway covers the events that turn up transmission through activin receptors, the TGF-beta family route that controls follicle-stimulating hormone output, gonadal and reproductive development, erythroid maturation, pancreatic islet and mesodermal patterning, and the balance between cell proliferation and growth arrest in epithelia. Enhancement can come from increased receptor availability and complex formation, from kinases such as casein kinase 2 that modify receptor or SMAD activity, from cooperating growth factor input including FGF9, and from RNA-binding regulators of the pathway's transcripts. Because activin signaling restrains growth in many tissues, its amplification shapes tumor suppression, wound healing, and the fibrotic and inflammatory response.

Activin signalling, a branch of the TGF-beta superfamily, controls reproductive endocrine function, mesoderm patterning and the follicle-stimulating hormone axis, and this grouping covers the influences that raise its output. Activin binds a type II receptor, ACVR2A or ACVR2B, which recruits and activates the type I kinase ACVR1B to phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3 and drive transcription of growth-inhibitory and differentiation genes. Casein kinase 2 activity and modulatory factors such as FGF9 and the zinc-finger protein ZC3H3 act as positive inputs that increase receptor complex activity or reinforce downstream transduction. Muscle cell proliferation covers the mitotic expansion of muscle cell populations — skeletal myoblasts and satellite cells, cardiomyocytes, and vascular smooth muscle cells — and the controls that decide when such cells divide rather than differentiate or remain quiescent. Muscle cell populations expand by division during development, growth and repair, and this programme covers the signals that drive or restrain that expansion in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle. It matters for heart chamber growth and cardiomyocyte cell-cycle exit after birth, for satellite-cell amplification during regeneration, and for the vascular smooth muscle proliferation that thickens vessel walls in atherosclerosis, hypertension and restenosis. Inflammatory cytokines and a large complement of microRNAs, notably the muscle-enriched miR-1 and miR-133 family, tune the response.

regulation of myeloid cell apoptotic process sets how long neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages and erythroid progenitors survive, and thereby determines both the size of the innate immune pool and how quickly inflammation resolves. Tuning myeloid cell apoptosis determines the size of the circulating granulocyte pool, the timely clearance of neutrophils that ends an inflammatory episode, and the survival of erythroblasts during red cell production; too little death gives persistent inflammation or myeloid expansion, too much gives neutropenia or anaemia. The pathway therefore links inflammation resolution, haematopoietic output and innate immune tone.

positive regulation of myeloid cell apoptotic process describes the signals that drive neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages and their progenitors into programmed death, setting the lifespan of the innate immune compartment. Because myeloid cells are short-lived by design, timely apoptosis is what allows an inflammatory episode to resolve: dying neutrophils are cleared by macrophages, further recruitment stops, and tissue repair begins. Loss of this control produces persistent inflammation, while its excess causes neutropenia and impaired host defence. The genes point to several converging inputs, including the pro-resolving mediator annexin A1, the niacin receptor HCAR2 and the adipokine adiponectin acting from outside the cell, class I PI3K catalytic subunits and SIRT1 tuning survival signalling and p53 activity from within, and CDKN2A and MEF2C linking myeloid differentiation state to death sensitivity. Myeloid cells such as neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages are short-lived by design, and signals that increase their rate of programmed cell death set how quickly an inflammatory response is terminated. Promoting myeloid apoptosis clears spent granulocytes from inflamed tissue so that macrophages can engulf them without spilling proteases and oxidants, and it limits the size of the myeloid compartment produced by the marrow; when this control fails, neutrophils persist and inflammation becomes chronic, while excessive death contributes to neutropenia. negative regulation of immature T cell proliferation in thymus restrains the expansion of thymocytes as they progress through development, setting a limit on how many immature T cells are produced and when they stop dividing to differentiate. This braking function shapes thymus size and the composition of the repertoire that leaves it; loss of such restraint permits unchecked thymocyte proliferation and predisposes to T cell lymphoblastic leukaemia, a link made explicit by the CDKN2A locus, whose p16 and p14ARF products enforce cell cycle arrest and are frequently deleted in that disease. The pathway therefore couples niche-derived instruction to intrinsic cell cycle control, tying proliferative arrest to differentiation during T lymphopoiesis.

Thymocyte expansion must be curbed as well as driven, and this pathway covers the signals that dampen proliferation of immature T cells in the thymus. Restraining the progenitor pool sets the size and timing of successive developmental stages, allowing selection to operate on a controlled number of cells; loss of such brakes contributes to thymocyte hyperplasia and lymphoid malignancy. The genes involved span secreted morphogens and cell-intrinsic cell cycle control: bone morphogenetic protein and hedgehog ligands produced by thymic stroma act on developing thymocytes to limit their expansion, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor encoded at the INK4A locus enforces cell cycle arrest, and a transmembrane regulator of Wnt responsiveness tempers proliferative signalling. Together they illustrate how niche-derived cues and intracellular checkpoints converge to balance proliferation against differentiation during T cell development.

regulation of intracellular steroid hormone receptor signaling pathway controls how strongly and for how long cells respond to steroids such as androgens, estrogens and glucocorticoids, tuning the transcriptional programs that drive sexual development, reproductive tissue growth, metabolism and bone and muscle maintenance. Because receptor output is dose- and context-dependent, its misregulation underlies hormone-driven cancers of the prostate and breast and endocrine resistance to therapy. The regulators here act largely at chromatin: coactivators and acetyltransferases such as EP300, CARM1 and MED1 versus corepressors NCOR1/2 and HDACs, pioneer factors including FOXA1 that decide which response elements are accessible, and demethylases and remodellers that reset the template. Others set receptor abundance and localisation through ubiquitin and UFMylation, chaperone and prohibitin complexes, and kinase signalling, while circadian components CLOCK, BMAL1, PER and CRY impose daily timing on hormonal responsiveness.

Steroid hormones act by binding intracellular receptors that then work as ligand-gated transcription factors, and this pathway covers the machinery that tunes how strongly and how long that transcriptional output runs. Such regulation sets tissue sensitivity to androgens, oestrogens and glucocorticoids, and its derangement underlies hormone-driven cancers: androgen receptor coactivator and corepressor balance is a central determinant of prostate cancer progression and of resistance to anti-hormonal therapy. Control is exerted by coactivator and corepressor complexes (EP300, MED1, NCOR1/2, HDAC1/2), chromatin modifiers including the demethylase KDM1A and the methyltransferase CARM1, lineage-restricting factors such as FOXA1 that dictate where receptors bind, and by ubiquitin-like UFM1 conjugation and other post-translational marks that alter receptor stability. Circadian components including CLOCK, BMAL1, CRY1/2 and PER1 impose daily rhythm, linking endocrine responsiveness to the clock.}

negative regulation of intracellular steroid hormone receptor signaling pathway is the braking system on nuclear receptor action, limiting how strongly and how long estrogen, androgen, glucocorticoid and related steroid signals are transcribed into gene expression. Steroid hormones act through nuclear receptors that bind DNA and switch on transcription, and this collection of brakes keeps that output limited in time and amplitude. Meiotic cytokinesis is the physical division of the cytoplasm that follows each meiotic nuclear division, converting one germ cell into daughter cells with halved chromosome complements. Additional components link spindle midzone and chromatin cues to the division plane, coupling chromosome segregation to correctly placed cytoplasmic cleavage in gametogenesis.

Division of the cytoplasm following a meiotic nuclear division separates the products of meiosis into distinct daughter cells, and in the female germ line it is what makes an asymmetric division possible: one large oocyte plus a small polar body, preserving maternal stores for the embryo. The gene membership points to actin-based mechanics rather than generic contractile ring biology, with the Arp2/3 subunits ACTR2 and ACTR3 nucleating branched filaments, the formin FMN2 and the Spir actin nucleators SPIRE1 and SPIRE2 cooperating to build filament networks that position the spindle and the division plane, and a WASH complex component linking membrane traffic to actin assembly. It is the target of anti-TNF biologics in rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease, and its unchecked activation underlies septic shock and chronic inflammatory tissue damage. Related receptor-ligand pairs here extend the same logic to osteoclast differentiation and B cell survival.

Iron import into cell is how cells acquire the iron they need for haem, iron-sulfur clusters, and the many enzymes of respiration and DNA synthesis, moving iron ions from the extracellular space into the cytoplasm either directly across the plasma membrane or through receptor-mediated endocytosis of iron carriers. Duodenal enterocytes depend on it for dietary iron absorption, and hepatocytes and macrophages use it to set systemic iron balance; loss of these transporters causes anaemia, while excess uptake drives tissue iron overload and oxidative damage. Ferric iron is first reduced by surface ferrireductases such as CYBRD1 and the STEAP proteins, then carried inward by divalent metal transporters including SLC11A2 and the SLC39 zinc-iron permeases. Transferrin receptor 2 links uptake to hepcidin-based hormonal control, and siderophore-binding lipocalin-2 and hypoxia-induced miR-210 tune it to inflammation and low oxygen.

Cells acquire iron from their surroundings either by pumping it across the plasma membrane or by internalising iron-loaded carriers, and this import step sets how much iron is available for haem synthesis, iron-sulfur cluster assembly and oxidative metabolism. It matters most in the duodenal enterocyte, where dietary iron enters the body, and in hepatocytes and macrophages that buffer systemic iron; too little causes anaemia, too much drives tissue iron overload. Because only ferrous iron is transported, surface ferrireductases such as CYBRD1 and the STEAP proteins reduce Fe(III) before the divalent metal transporter SLC11A2 carries it into the cytoplasm, with SLC39A8 and SLC39A14 providing additional routes shared with manganese and zinc. A transferrin receptor family member reports iron status to hepatic signalling, secreted lipocalin-2 scavenges siderophore-bound iron, and inflammatory and hypoxic inputs adjust the whole process to demand.

Actin-myosin filament sliding is the contractile event itself: myosin thick filaments pulling calcium-activated actin thin filaments past one another to shorten a sarcomere. It is what makes a heartbeat and a skeletal muscle twitch, and its regulation sets force, speed and relaxation kinetics. The genes are the sarcomere's parts list cardiac and skeletal myosin heavy chains with their essential and regulatory light chains, sarcomeric actin, tropomyosin and the troponin complex that translates a calcium transient into thin-filament activation, plus myosin light chain kinase which tunes crossbridge sensitivity. Titin and telethonin provide the elastic backbone and Z-disc anchoring against which the sliding does work, while myosin-binding protein C brakes and paces crossbridge cycling. Mutations in these components underlie hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies and congenital skeletal myopathies such as distal arthrogryposis.

Muscle shortens because myosin thick filaments pull actin thin filaments past one another, and this sliding is the contractile event underlying heartbeat, breathing and voluntary movement. The genes here build the sarcomere itself: cardiac and skeletal actin, sarcomeric myosin heavy chains of embryonic, perinatal, fast and cardiac types, essential and regulatory light chains, and the giant elastic scaffold titin with its Z-disc partner telethonin. Calcium control is imposed through the troponin complex and tropomyosin, which occlude myosin binding sites on actin until cytosolic calcium rises; myosin binding protein C and a myosin light chain kinase tune the force and kinetics of the stroke. Mutations in these components are the classic causes of hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy, distal arthrogryposis and congenital myopathy, so the pathway links sarcomere mechanics directly to cardiac and skeletal muscle disease.

geranylgeranyl diphosphate metabolic process produces and turns over the 20-carbon isoprenoid geranylgeranyl diphosphate, the lipid donor that anchors Rho, Rab and Rap GTPases to membranes and a branch point for other terpenoid products. The route runs from acetyl-CoA through HMG-CoA synthase and the rate-limiting reductase HMGCR, then mevalonate kinase, phosphomevalonate kinase and mevalonate diphosphate decarboxylase to isopentenyl diphosphate, which IDI1 isomerises and FDPS condenses to farnesyl diphosphate; GGPS1 adds a final isoprene unit, while a phosphatase step can return prenyl diphosphates toward the alcohol pool. Cholesterol synthesis via desmosterol is one of the two post-squalene routes, the Bloch pathway, in which the side-chain double bond is retained until the last step and desmosterol serves as the immediate precursor of cholesterol. The route supplies membrane sterol for growth, myelination, lipoprotein assembly and steroid hormone and bile acid production, beginning with acetyl-CoA condensation and mevalonate formation by HMGCS1 and the rate-limiting, statin-sensitive HMGCR, then isoprenoid condensation to squalene by FDPS and FDFT1, epoxidation by SQLE and cyclization by lanosterol synthase. Its failure is diabetes: loss of beta cell identity or insulin secretion, or peripheral insulin resistance, with consequences for every tissue that depends on glucose. The genes span the whole regulatory circuit — the transcription factors that specify and maintain pancreatic beta cells (PDX1, NKX6-1, NEUROD1, HNF1A, HNF4A, RFX6), the glucose-sensing and secretion apparatus (GCK, ABCC8, SLC30A8, insulin granule exocytosis), the counter-regulatory hormones glucagon, leptin, adiponectin, ghrelin and POMC-derived peptides, and the insulin receptor signalling chain through IRS1/2, PI3K, AKT and FOXO1 that drives GLUT4 trafficking. Blood and cellular sugar levels are held within narrow limits, and carbohydrate homeostasis is the coordinated set of hormonal, transcriptional and transport events that does it. Its failure produces diabetes: pancreatic beta cells fail to secrete insulin, liver and muscle stop responding, and glucose rises unchecked. Glucose entry and phosphorylation by transporters and hexokinases, including the beta-cell sensor glucokinase, sets the rate at which insulin is released, a step requiring ATP-sensitive potassium channel subunits, zinc handling and exocytic machinery. Secreted insulin and the opposing glucagon act through receptor tyrosine kinase and G-protein-coupled routes, converging on PI3K-AKT, FOXO1 and AMPK to switch between glycogen synthesis, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis via PCK1 and glucose-6-phosphatase. Lineage factors such as PDX1, NEUROD1 and NKX6-1 build and maintain the islet, while adipokines including leptin and adiponectin, circadian regulators and nutrient-stress signalling tie glucose control to whole-body energy balance and feeding.

fatty acid beta-oxidation using acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is the mitochondrial route by which fatty acids are broken down two carbons at a time to fuel ATP production and ketogenesis, and it is what sustains heart, muscle and liver during fasting or sustained exercise. Chain-length-specific flavoenzymes — very-long-, long-, medium- and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenases — introduce the trans-2 double bond that starts each cycle, and the electrons they strip are handed to electron transfer flavoprotein and its ubiquinone oxidoreductase, feeding the respiratory chain rather than NADH directly. Related dehydrogenases such as IVD and GCDH act on branched-chain and lysine catabolic intermediates, linking this machinery to amino acid breakdown. Inherited loss of MCAD, VLCAD or the electron transfer components causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and metabolic crisis on fasting, and is screened for in newborns.

Mitochondria extract energy from fatty acids by shortening them two carbons at a time, and the flavin-dependent acyl-CoA dehydrogenases catalyse the first, committed oxidation of each round, converting acyl-CoA to trans-2-enoyl-CoA. This route supplies acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle and hepatic ketone bodies during fasting and sustained exercise, so heart, skeletal muscle and liver depend on it when glucose is scarce. Chain-length-specialised enzymes divide the work between very long, long, medium and short substrates, and related dehydrogenases handle branched amino acid intermediates such as isovaleryl-CoA and glutaryl-CoA. Electrons removed at this step are not passed directly to the respiratory chain but through electron transfer flavoprotein and its iron-sulfur dehydrogenase to ubiquinone, ending as water. Loss of individual dehydrogenases causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis, while electron transfer flavoprotein defects produce multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency.

cellular response to stress is the broad umbrella covering how cells detect damaging conditions — DNA lesions, misfolded proteins, oxidants, hypoxia, nutrient shortage, heat, inflammatory and mechanical insults — and reprogram themselves to survive or die. It determines whether an injured cell repairs itself, arrests, senesces, or is eliminated, so it underlies tumour suppression, ageing, neurodegeneration, and the response to radiation and chemotherapy. Cells continuously encounter insults — DNA damage, heat, oxidants, nutrient shortage, hypoxia, misfolded protein burden — and this broad response programme is how they detect the damage, pause growth, repair what can be repaired, and die when it cannot. Its coverage here spans the DNA damage checkpoints and repair routes (ATM/ATR, p53, mismatch, nucleotide- and base-excision, homologous recombination and end joining), the heat shock chaperones and HSF1, endoplasmic reticulum stress sensors with ERAD and the integrated stress response through eIF2α kinases and ATF4, antioxidant defence via NRF2, KEAP1, superoxide dismutases and peroxiredoxins, hypoxia sensing by HIF prolyl hydroxylases, nutrient sensing through mTORC1 and AMPK, autophagy and mitophagy, and apoptotic execution. Outcomes include cell cycle arrest, senescence, or death. Deficits give genome instability and cancer predisposition, neurodegeneration, and premature ageing syndromes.

The genes here point to the redox arm of that response: catalase and mitochondrial superoxide dismutase dispose of hydrogen peroxide and superoxide, while glutathione S-transferase P1 handles conjugation of electrophilic products, together determining whether ascorbate acts as an antioxidant or, at high local iron and concentration, as a pro-oxidant. Alongside these sit an adhesion receptor for collagen and the adipokine leptin, linking vitamin C exposure to matrix interaction and metabolic signalling. The pathway thus connects micronutrient status to oxidative stress defence, connective tissue behaviour, and endocrine control of energy balance.

Cells adjust their behaviour when vitamin C is available, and this response captures the transcriptional and enzymatic changes that follow an L-ascorbic acid stimulus. Because ascorbate is both a reducing agent and, at high concentration or in the presence of transition metals, a source of hydrogen peroxide, much of the response is redox handling: catalase disposes of peroxide, mitochondrial superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to peroxide, and a glutathione S-transferase conjugates electrophilic products of oxidative damage. Alongside this antioxidant arm, changes in a collagen-binding integrin subunit and in leptin expression link ascorbate to cell-matrix adhesion and to endocrine control of energy balance. The pathway matters for how tissues use dietary vitamin C in collagen-rich matrix, adipose signalling, and defence against oxidative stress, and it frames ascorbate as a signal cells interpret rather than simply a cofactor they consume.

Response to genistein covers the cellular changes triggered by genistein, a soy isoflavone that acts both as a weak estrogen-receptor agonist and as a xenobiotic requiring detoxification. It matters because dietary isoflavone exposure alters hormone-responsive gene expression in reproductive, vascular and hepatic tissues, which is why soy phytoestrogens are studied for effects on breast tissue, coagulation and menopausal physiology. The genes trace two arms of that response: xenobiotic handling, through induction of the cytochrome P450 CYP1A1 and a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase that conjugates the compound for excretion, and estrogen-like transcriptional output, including oxytocin, coagulation factor VII and the membrane metalloproteinase MMP14 involved in extracellular matrix remodelling. Negative regulation of tissue remodeling is the braking system on structural turnover of tissues — the signals that restrain matrix degradation, bone resorption and cellular reorganisation once repair or adaptation is complete. Toll-like receptor 2 signaling pathway is the innate immune sensing route that detects bacterial and fungal cell wall components — lipoproteins, lipoteichoic acid, zymosan — and converts that recognition into inflammatory gene expression. It gives macrophages, monocytes and microglia their first response to Gram-positive bacteria and mycobacteria, and its output shapes whether infection is contained or drives septic inflammation. Acylglycerol transport moves mono-, di- and triacylglycerols across membranes and between tissues, the step that lets dietary and stored fat reach cells that burn or store it. The pathway determines plasma triglyceride levels and contributes to steatosis and atherogenic dyslipidaemia when deranged.

Lipid translocation moves lipids between the two leaflets of a membrane bilayer, and in doing so builds and breaks the asymmetry that cells use as information. Keeping phosphatidylserine on the inner face of the plasma membrane marks a cell as healthy; exposing it marks a cell as dying or a platelet as ready to clot, so this activity underlies apoptotic corpse clearance, coagulation, and bile and surfactant secretion. Related lipid-mobilising proteins support autophagosome membrane expansion and restrict enveloped viruses. Mutations cause cholestasis, harlequin ichthyosis, retinal degeneration and Tangier disease.

Membrane bilayers are built asymmetrically, and lipid translocation is the set of activities that move phospholipids and sterols across a bilayer from one leaflet to the other. Loss of individual components causes cholestasis, retinal degeneration, harlequin ichthyosis, Tangier disease and defective clearance of apoptotic cells, and the same lipid movements support autophagosome membrane expansion.

Macrophages can merge with one another to form multinucleated cells, and this pathway controls how readily that happens. The fused products are functionally distinct: osteoclasts, which resorb bone and are needed for skeletal remodelling and tooth eruption, and the multinucleated giant cells that wall off persistent foreign material and infection in granulomas.
