Endothelial cells read vascular endothelial growth factor as an instruction to sprout, migrate, survive and become permeable, and this response is how new blood and lymphatic vessels are built during development, wound healing, and tumour growth. Ligands VEGFA, VEGFB, VEGFC, VEGFD and PGF engage the receptor tyrosine kinases KDR, FLT1 and FLT4 with neuropilin and integrin co-receptors, feeding PI3K-AKT, GAB1 and p38-MAPKAPK2 branches toward cytoskeletal remodelling and transcriptional change. Notch components including DLL4 and NOTCH1 impose tip-versus-stalk cell identity so sprouting stays organised, while soluble FLT1, decorin, gremlin and SPRY2 damp the signal, and PROX1, NR2F2, FOXC1 and CCBE1 direct the lymphatic arm. A large set of microRNAs tunes the output. Excess signalling drives tumour vascularisation and retinal neovascularisation; insufficient signalling leaves tissue ischaemic and lymphatic drainage defective.

cellular response to topologically incorrect protein is the set of reactions a cell mounts when proteins fail to reach their native fold, and it determines whether that cell adapts or dies. It protects secretory tissues under heavy folding load — pancreatic beta cells, plasma cells, hepatocytes — and its failure underlies Wolfram syndrome, neurodegenerative aggregate diseases, and the vulnerability of tumours to proteotoxic stress. Three endoplasmic reticulum sensors dominate: PERK phosphorylates eIF2α to arrest translation and induce ATF4 and CHOP, IRE1 splices XBP1 mRNA to expand folding and lipid capacity, and ATF6 is cleaved by site-1 and site-2 proteases to a transcription factor. Terminally misfolded substrates are recognised by lectins and mannosidases, retrotranslocated through derlin channels, and degraded by VCP-dependent ubiquitin-proteasome routes, while cytosolic chaperones, HSF1 and autophagy receptors handle aggregates. Persistent stress switches the output to apoptosis through BAX, BAK and PUMA.

Misfolded proteins are toxic if left to accumulate, and the cellular response to topologically incorrect protein is the surveillance and corrective programme that detects them, restores folding capacity, and kills the cell if the burden cannot be cleared. It is what allows secretory tissues such as plasma cells and pancreatic beta cells to sustain heavy client loads, and its failure underlies neurodegeneration, diabetes and inherited misfolding diseases. Three endoplasmic reticulum sensors dominate: IRE1 splices XBP1 mRNA to expand chaperone and lipid capacity, PERK phosphorylates eIF2 alpha to throttle translation while inducing ATF4 and CHOP, and ATF6 is cleaved by site proteases to release a transcription factor. In parallel, mannosidase-like lectins and derlins select terminally misfolded glycoproteins for retrotranslocation, ubiquitination and VCP-driven degradation, while cytosolic chaperones, HSF1 and aggresome routing handle misfolding outside the ER. Sustained stress tips output toward BH3-only proteins and apoptosis.

Aggrephagy is the route by which cells clear protein aggregates that are too large for the proteasome, packaging them into autophagosomes for lysosomal destruction. It is the main defence against the inclusion bodies that accumulate in neurodegenerative disease, and its decline with age underlies the toxicity of aggregated huntingtin, tau and other misfolded species in neurons, which cannot dilute damage by division. Cargo is first concentrated: ubiquitin-binding receptors such as SQSTM1 and UBQLN1, the scaffold WDFY3, and the BAG3-HSPB8 chaperone module recognise misfolded protein and, with HDAC6-dependent transport along microtubules, deliver it to a perinuclear site where an autophagosome forms. ATG4 proteases and lipidated LC3 supply the membrane conjugation machinery, while casein kinase 2 phosphorylation of the receptor tunes cargo capture. The pathway sits within selective macroautophagy alongside mitophagy, coupling chaperone-based quality control to bulk membrane degradation.

Misfolded proteins that escape refolding and cannot be threaded into the proteasome are collected into inclusions and cleared by aggrephagy, the selective routing of protein aggregates into autophagosomes for lysosomal degradation. This is the main defence against proteotoxicity in long-lived cells such as neurons and muscle fibres, and its decline accompanies Huntington disease and other aggregate-associated neurodegeneration; huntingtin itself is both a substrate and a scaffold here. Ubiquitinated aggregates are recognised by receptors including p62 and ubiquilin, concentrated with the help of a chaperone-based sorting module built on BAG3, HSPB8 and the tubulin deacetylase HDAC6, which moves cargo along microtubules to the perinuclear aggresome. Large scaffolds such as WDFY3 and WDR81 organise cargo delivery, while ATG4 family cysteine proteases process and recycle LC3 proteins for autophagosome membrane formation, linking aggregate clearance to general macroautophagy and proteostasis.

endodermal cell differentiation is the specification of the innermost germ layer during gastrulation, the step that commits pluripotent epiblast cells to the lineage that will build gut, liver, pancreas, lung and thyroid. Without it no endoderm-derived organ forms, and its regulators are the same signals used to direct stem cells toward hepatocytes or beta cells in vitro. Nodal/activin signalling acting through EOMES, MIXL1, SOX17, GATA6 and HNF1B drives the transcriptional switch, while pluripotency factors POU5F1, NANOG and SOX2 must be dismantled and DKK1 tunes Wnt/beta-catenin input. Chromatin and elongation machinery, including the PAF1 complex, SETD2 and macroH2A, make the new programme heritable. The prominent collagens, laminins, fibronectin, integrins and matrix metalloproteinases reflect the cell-shape changes, basement membrane remodelling and migration by which nascent endoderm ingresses and forms an epithelial sheet.

Endodermal cell differentiation is the step by which pluripotent epiblast cells commit to the innermost germ layer, the source of gut epithelium, liver, pancreas, lung and thyroid; failure or misdirection of this choice leaves the embryo without an endoderm-derived organ programme, and its recapitulation in culture is how stem cells are steered toward hepatocytes and beta cells. Nodal and activin signalling acting through beta-catenin and DKK1-modulated Wnt input induces the definitive endoderm transcription factors EOMES, MIXL1, SOX17, GATA6 and HNF1B while pluripotency factors POU5F1, NANOG and SOX2 are extinguished. The PAF1 transcription elongation complex with CDC73, LEO1, CTR9 and RTF1, together with SETD2-dependent chromatin methylation, licenses these lineage genes. Extensive collagen, laminin, fibronectin, integrin and matrix metalloproteinase components indicate that commitment is accompanied by matrix remodelling and cell migration during gastrulation.

response to erythropoietin is what a cell does when it encounters the kidney-derived hormone that governs red blood cell production. Erythroid progenitors depend on this response for survival, proliferation and terminal maturation; without it they die by apoptosis and anaemia follows, which is why recombinant erythropoietin treats the anaemia of renal failure, and why activating changes in the same axis drive erythrocytosis. Binding of the hormone to its receptor dimerises it and activates the associated kinase JAK2, which phosphorylates STAT5 for transport to the nucleus and, with CREB1, drives transcription of anti-apoptotic and cell cycle genes. The stem cell factor receptor KIT cooperates in expanding the progenitor pool, and induced metallothioneins reflect an accompanying shift in metal handling and oxidative stress tolerance as haemoglobin synthesis ramps up. The erythroid-specific adaptor RHEX marks the receptor-proximal branch of this signalling in human progenitors.

Erythropoietin is the kidney-derived hormone that tells red cell progenitors to survive, divide and mature, and the cellular reactions to it set the rate of erythropoiesis and thus blood oxygen-carrying capacity. Loss of the response causes anaemia, as in renal failure, while constitutive activation of its signalling drives polycythaemia and myeloproliferative disease. The hormone binds a dedicated receptor whose dimerisation activates the receptor-associated kinase JAK2; phosphorylated STAT5 then enters the nucleus to switch on anti-apoptotic and differentiation genes, with CREB1 contributing further transcriptional output. An erythroid-specific JAK2 substrate, RHEX, and cooperation with stem cell factor signalling through KIT amplify progenitor expansion. Induction of metallothioneins reflects the accompanying handling of metal and oxidative stress in maturing erythroblasts, linking this hormonal axis to iron and redox physiology.

alpha-linolenic acid metabolic process is the conversion of a dietary essential fatty acid into the long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids that cells cannot make from scratch, above all EPA and DHA. It matters because humans depend on this route for the docosahexaenoic acid enriched in retinal photoreceptors, synaptic membranes and sperm, and for the substrates of anti-inflammatory lipid mediators; low conversion efficiency, worsened by variants in the desaturase locus, constrains omega-3 status on plant-based diets. Alternating desaturation by FADS1 and FADS2 and two-carbon elongation by the ELOVL family, notably ELOVL2 and ELOVL5, build progressively longer and more unsaturated chains in the endoplasmic reticulum; the final step requires a round of peroxisomal beta-oxidation, which explains the presence of ABCD1, ACAA1 and SCP2. The pathway thus links dietary lipid intake to membrane composition and eicosanoid signalling.

Alpha-linolenic acid is a dietary essential fatty acid that humans cannot synthesise, and its metabolism converts it into the long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids that cells actually use. The route matters for brain and retinal membrane composition and for the supply of precursors to lipid signalling mediators; poor flux through it leaves tissues dependent on preformed dietary long-chain omega-3 fats. Alternating desaturation and elongation steps drive the conversion: FADS1 and FADS2 introduce double bonds, while ELOVL2 and ELOVL5, with related elongases, add two carbons at a time to the growing acyl chain. The final shortening step that yields docosahexaenoic acid occurs in peroxisomes, which is why peroxisomal components including the acyl-CoA transporter ABCD1, the thiolase ACAA1, SCP2 and an acyl-CoA thioesterase belong here, linking this biosynthetic route to peroxisomal beta-oxidation and its disorders.

RNA (guanine-N7)-methylation installs a methyl group on the N7 position of guanine in RNA, a modification that marks messenger RNA caps and stabilises the folds of transfer and ribosomal RNAs. It determines whether a transcript is recognised as translatable and whether tRNAs survive to deliver amino acids, so its loss degrades protein synthesis globally. Distinct enzymes serve distinct substrates: RNMT with its activating partner RAM caps nascent mRNA co-transcriptionally, licensing export and ribosome recruitment; METTL1 with WDR4 modifies G46 in tRNA variable loops; BUD23 acts on 18S rRNA during small subunit maturation. TRMT112 serves as a shared obligate subunit that stabilises several of these methyltransferases. Hypomorphic WDR4 and METTL1 mutations cause microcephalic primordial dwarfism through tRNA fragmentation and ribosome stalling, and cap methylation is exploited by proliferating cells to sustain translation of growth-promoting transcripts.

Methylation of guanine at the N7 position marks RNA for recognition and stability, and these enzymes carry it out on three different RNA classes. RNMT, with its activating subunit RAMAC, caps messenger RNAs by methylating the guanosine added at the 5' end, the modification that licenses nuclear export, efficient translation initiation and protection from decapping-dependent decay. METTL1 with WDR4 installs m7G at position 46 of tRNA variable loops, stabilising the fold and tuning translation elongation; loss-of-function mutations in WDR4 cause microcephalic primordial dwarfism. BUD23 methylates a guanine in 18S ribosomal RNA during small subunit maturation, coupling the modification to ribosome biogenesis. TRMT112 serves as the shared obligate partner that stabilises and activates several of these methyltransferases. Collectively the pathway sits upstream of protein synthesis capacity, and its disruption is linked to developmental disorders and to tumour growth driven by altered tRNA methylation.

Swimming behavior describes stimulus-driven locomotion through water, a whole-organism readout used to score how nervous system function translates into coordinated movement, and one of the standard behavioral endpoints by which neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental damage is detected in animal models. The genes here connect that output to amyloid biology and neuronal signalling: the amyloid precursor protein and the beta-secretase that cleaves it, an executioner caspase that carries out apoptotic pruning and neuronal death, a receptor tyrosine kinase that shapes neuronal differentiation and monoaminergic tone, and the tryptophan-degrading enzyme that feeds kynurenine metabolites acting on glutamatergic transmission. Together they place motor performance downstream of amyloid processing, programmed cell death and neuroactive metabolite production, so that loss of these functions registers as impaired swimming, altered escape responses, and reduced motor endurance.

Swimming behaviour is a whole-organism locomotor response to sensory or internal cues, and it is used experimentally as a readout of neural circuit integrity, motivation and stress coping. The genes grouped here are better known for neuronal maturation and degeneration than for movement itself: a receptor tyrosine kinase with roles in neurodevelopment and monoaminergic signalling, the amyloid precursor protein together with the beta-secretase that cleaves it to generate amyloid-beta, an executioner caspase that drives apoptosis and prunes synapses, and the tryptophan-degrading enzyme that initiates the kynurenine pathway and links inflammation to neuroactive metabolites. Their shared appearance in this context reflects how amyloid processing, programmed cell death and immune-driven tryptophan metabolism alter motor output and behavioural performance, the basis for using swimming assays in models of neurodegeneration and depression-like states.

cellular response to increased oxygen levels is how cells sense and adapt to hyperoxia, the condition of oxygen tension above normal, which is both a therapeutic exposure in ventilated patients and neonates and a source of oxidative injury. Excess oxygen drives reactive species production, and cells must either detoxify, remodel damaged components, or die; failure of this balance underlies bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy of prematurity, and hyperoxic lung injury. The genes point to three linked responses: NADPH oxidase-derived superoxide generation as the proximal signal, autophagy and lysosomal acidification through ATG7 and the vacuolar ATPase subunits to clear oxidized cargo, and apoptotic and transcriptional arms through FAS and FOXO1 that commit damaged cells to death or to antioxidant and stress gene expression. Caveolin-1 and lipocalin-2 tie the response to membrane signalling platforms and iron handling.

Cells detect not only oxygen scarcity but oxygen excess, and this response covers what a cell does when oxygen levels rise above its accustomed set point. Hyperoxia raises the flux of reactive oxygen species, and the adaptive programme decides whether a cell clears damaged material and survives or commits to death, which matters in the lung and retina of oxygen-treated newborns and in reperfused tissue. Several components point to autophagy and lysosomal acidification: ATG7 drives autophagosome formation, while a set of vacuolar-type ATPase subunits together with assembly factors acidifies the lysosome so that autophagic cargo is degraded. FOXO1 provides the transcriptional arm, tuning antioxidant and autophagy gene expression, and FAS-driven death signalling offers an alternative outcome. Caveolin-1, a NADPH oxidase and the iron-sequestering protein lipocalin-2 link the response to membrane signalling and oxidative stress control.

response to increased oxygen levels is the cellular reaction to hyperoxia — the adjustments a cell or tissue makes when oxygen tension rises above what it is adapted to. It matters because oxygen excess is chemically dangerous: more oxygen means more superoxide and peroxide leaking from respiration, so lipid, protein and DNA damage follow unless detoxification keeps pace. This underlies retinopathy of prematurity and ventilator-associated lung injury, and it is the mirror image of the hypoxic response, with erythropoietin production and pulmonary vascular tone (via KCNA5) turning down as oxygen returns. The genes cover antioxidant defence (catalase, mitochondrial SOD2, thioredoxin reductase), base excision repair, NADPH oxidase as a deliberate source of signalling oxidants, and BNIP3- and ATG7-dependent autophagy and mitophagy that clear damaged mitochondria. Lysosomal V-ATPase subunits link the response to acidification and degradative turnover, alongside FOXO1-driven transcriptional adaptation, matrix remodelling and apoptotic commitment when damage cannot be contained.

Cells monitor oxygen tension in both directions, and this programme covers the adjustments made when oxygen rises — hyperoxia, reoxygenation after ischaemia, or the transition to air breathing at birth. Rising oxygen means more reactive oxygen species, so a large part of the response is antioxidant defence: catalase, mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and thioredoxin reductase limit oxidative damage, while base excision repair handles the lesions that escape. At the same time oxygen-sensitive gene expression is reversed, with erythropoietin transcription falling and the hypoxia-induced mitophagy receptor BNIP3 no longer needed, and autophagic and lysosomal acidification machinery adjusts mitochondrial content. In the pulmonary vasculature, oxygen-sensitive potassium channels and caveolar signalling couple oxygen levels to vascular tone. Failure to buffer this transition underlies reperfusion injury, bronchopulmonary dysplasia and oxygen toxicity in ventilated patients.

Interstrand cross-link repair resolves lesions that covalently tie the two strands of the double helix together, which would otherwise block the strand separation required for replication and transcription. It is the pathway lost in Fanconi anemia, where its failure produces bone marrow failure, developmental defects, chromosome breakage and cancer predisposition, and it determines cellular sensitivity to crosslinking chemotherapies such as cisplatin and mitomycin C. Stalled replication forks are sensed by the ATR checkpoint and by FANCM, which recruits the core Fanconi complex to monoubiquitinate FANCD2-FANCI; ubiquitin signalling through RNF8/RNF168 and RFWD3 then organises downstream nucleases including ERCC1-ERCC4, FAN1, SLX-type activities and NEIL3-mediated unhooking. The unhooked crosslink is bypassed by translesion or template-switch synthesis, and the resulting double-strand break is repaired by RAD51-dependent homologous recombination, with MCM8-MCM9 and protein extraction by VCP and SPRTN clearing adducts.

Interstrand cross-links covalently tether the two strands of the double helix, so they block the strand separation required for replication and transcription and must be excised before a fork can proceed. This repair route keeps replication going in the face of aldehydes, platinum drugs and other cross-linking agents, and its loss causes Fanconi anaemia, with bone marrow failure, developmental defects and cancer predisposition; the same defect underlies the clinical sensitivity of tumours to mitomycin C and cisplatin. A stalled fork recruits the core Fanconi complex, which monoubiquitinates the FANCD2-FANCI pair to license nucleolytic unhooking by structure-specific endonucleases such as the ERCC1-ERCC4 and FAN1 activities, or in some contexts glycosylase-mediated cross-link cleavage. Translesion and gap-filling synthesis follow, and the resulting double-strand break is resolved by RAD51-dependent homologous recombination under ATR-coordinated checkpoint control, with ubiquitin signalling and replisome remodelling organising factor exchange at the lesion.

response to sterol covers how cells sense and react to cholesterol, oxysterols and related lipids, adjusting gene expression, transport and enzyme activity to keep membrane sterol content within tolerable limits. It matters because sterol excess is both toxic and atherogenic: cells that cannot register it fail to export cholesterol or to shut off its synthesis, the situation underlying foam cell formation and hypercholesterolaemia. The genes span the main sensing and effector arms — INSIG1 and INSIG2 restraining sterol synthesis through the SREBP–reductase axis, the GRAMD1/Aster proteins moving accessible cholesterol from the plasma membrane, ABCA1 effluxing it to acceptors, and CYP7A1 with CYP8B1 disposing of it as bile acids. Sterols also act as signals here, via Smoothened and Patched in Hedgehog reception and the RORA/RORC nuclear receptors, linking lipid status to developmental patterning, immune tone and TGF-beta signalling.

Cells sense sterols and adjust their metabolism, membrane composition and gene expression accordingly, and this response to sterol stimulus links cholesterol abundance to transport, catabolism and signalling decisions. When cholesterol is plentiful, INSIG1 and INSIG2 hold the sterol-sensing machinery of the endoplasmic reticulum in check to shut down sterol synthesis, while ABCA1 exports excess cholesterol to nascent HDL and CYP7A1 with CYP8B1 commit it to bile acid synthesis in the liver. GRAMD1 (Aster) proteins move accessible cholesterol from the plasma membrane to the ER, and oxysterol-binding proteins provide further intracellular transfer. Sterols also act as ligands and cofactors for signalling: cholesterol and oxysterols modulate Smoothened and Patched in the Hedgehog pathway, and oxysterol-responsive RORA and RORC couple sterol status to transcription. Loss of this regulation drives cholesterol overload, foam cell formation and atherosclerosis, with additional inflammatory and TGF-beta-linked outputs represented here.

Intestinal stem cell homeostasis keeps the crypt stem cell pool at a constant size, balancing self-renewal against differentiation so that the intestinal epithelium can be replaced every few days without exhausting its progenitors or overgrowing. Loss of this balance underlies impaired regeneration after injury, defective barrier function, and the crypt hyperplasia that precedes colorectal tumorigenesis. The genes point to several inputs converging on the crypt niche: LGR4 receives R-spondin and amplifies Wnt signalling in the stem cell compartment; NOD2 senses bacterial peptidoglycan and links the microbiota to stem cell survival, a connection relevant to Crohn's disease; membrane lipid remodelling by LPCAT3 and secreted phospholipases tunes stem cell proliferation through lipid availability and Paneth cell antimicrobial output; and chromatin regulation by ZNHIT1 restrains the stem cell programme. Together they couple nutrient, microbial and mechanical cues to epithelial renewal.

The intestinal epithelium is renewed every few days from stem cells in the crypt base, and intestinal stem cell homeostasis is the balance that keeps their numbers steady — enough proliferation to replace shed enterocytes, not so much that crypts hyperplase or transform. Loss of that balance underlies impaired mucosal repair, chronic inflammation and colorectal tumour initiation. The genes here touch several inputs to that balance: LGR4 potentiates Wnt signalling from Paneth and mesenchymal niche cells, the dominant driver of crypt stem cell self-renewal; NOD2 senses bacterial muramyl dipeptide and links microbial cues to stem cell survival, with variants predisposing to Crohn's disease; membrane lipid handling through LPCAT3 and secreted phospholipases shapes crypt lipid composition and antimicrobial defence; and ZNHIT1 acts in chromatin remodelling that constrains the stem cell state. Together they place niche signalling, microbial sensing and lipid metabolism upstream of epithelial renewal.

Platelet morphogenesis is the process by which megakaryocytes build and release anucleate platelets, the cell fragments that seal vascular injury and initiate coagulation. Its failure produces thrombocytopenia and bleeding disorders, or conversely platelets of abnormal size and granule content, as in gray platelet syndrome caused by loss of NBEAL2. The pathway couples transcriptional specification of the megakaryocyte lineage — GATA1 with its cofactor ZFPM1, TAL1, MEF2C, SRF and the acetyltransferase EP300 — to thrombopoietin receptor signalling through MPL and the phosphatases PTPN11, PTPN6 and PTPRJ that set its gain. Execution depends on cytoskeletal remodelling: the β1-tubulin marginal band, non-muscle myosin MYH9, actinin, tropomyosin and WDR1 drive proplatelet extension and fragmentation, while granule biogenesis and apoptotic caspases contribute to final platelet maturation and shedding into the marrow sinusoids.

Platelets are anucleate fragments shed from megakaryocytes, and platelet morphogenesis covers the steps by which those giant marrow cells build and release them: cytoskeletal remodelling, proplatelet extension, granule loading, and final sizing of the circulating disc. Without it, bleeding follows from too few or structurally abnormal platelets, as in the macrothrombocytopenias caused by mutations in the actin-binding protein ACTN1, the nonmuscle myosin MYH9, or the platelet-specific tubulin TUBB1, and in the granule-deficient gray platelet syndrome caused by loss of NBEAL2. Thrombopoietin acting through its receptor MPL drives megakaryocyte expansion, with the transcription factors GATA1, TAL1, ZFPM1, MEF2C and SRF specifying the lineage and its cytoskeletal gene programme, while PTPN11, PTPN6 and PTPRJ tune the phosphotyrosine signalling that sets output. Caspase activity and membrane receptors such as CLEC1B and MPIG6B contribute to terminal platelet formation and marrow niche behaviour.

Sodium ion export across plasma membrane is the pumping of sodium out of the cell that sets up the electrochemical gradient nearly all other transport depends on. Because the sodium gradient powers secondary transport of glucose, amino acids, calcium and protons, and because it underlies the resting potential and the recovery of excitable cells after an action potential, its loss halts nerve conduction, cardiac rhythm and epithelial fluid handling. The core machinery is the Na+/K+-ATPase, built from catalytic alpha subunits with tissue-specific distribution in neurons, muscle and kidney, obligatory beta subunits, and FXYD proteins that tune pump kinetics locally. Related P-type pumps handle gastric acid secretion, while sodium-calcium and sodium-proton exchangers and a bicarbonate cotransporter couple sodium movement to calcium extrusion and pH control. Digitalis glycosides act here, and natriuretic peptide signalling regulates the same sodium balance systemically.

Pumping sodium out of the cell is what keeps the plasma membrane electrochemical gradient charged, and almost every secondary transport event — glucose and amino acid uptake, calcium and proton extrusion, neurotransmitter reuptake — runs on that gradient. Sodium ion export across the plasma membrane is dominated here by the Na+/K+-ATPase, built from catalytic alpha subunits (ATP1A1-ATP1A4, plus the related gastric and non-gastric proton pumps ATP4A and ATP12A) with obligatory beta subunits and a family of small FXYD regulators that tune pump kinetics in a tissue-specific way. Exchangers contribute too: SLC9A1 trades extracellular sodium for protons, while SLC8A1 uses the inward sodium gradient to expel calcium from cardiomyocytes. The alpha isoforms underlie neuronal and muscle excitability, and their mutation causes familial hemiplegic migraine, alternating hemiplegia and rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism; renal handling of sodium here also sets extracellular volume and blood pressure, with atrial natriuretic peptide as an endocrine input.

Synaptic vesicle recycling is how a presynaptic terminal reuses its vesicles: after fusion and neurotransmitter release, membrane and vesicle proteins are retrieved and reformed into release-competent vesicles. Because a bouton holds only a small vesicle pool, this retrieval sets how long a synapse can fire without fatiguing, and its failure underlies epilepsies, movement disorders and parkinsonism linked to synuclein, LRRK2, parkin, synaptojanin and auxilin. Mechanistically the genes trace clathrin-mediated endocytosis and its alternatives: AP-2 and AP-3 adaptors and cargo-specific stonins select synaptotagmin and VAMP2, BAR-domain proteins such as amphiphysin, endophilin and BIN1 bend the membrane, dynamins sever the neck, and phosphoinositide phosphatases plus Hsc70 co-chaperones uncoat the product. Actin, Rho-family GTPases and calcium-calmodulin/calcineurin signalling couple retrieval rate to activity, while Rab GTPases and SNAREs return vesicles to docking and priming.

Fast, sustained neurotransmission depends on presynaptic terminals rebuilding their vesicle supply locally, and synaptic vesicle recycling is how a fused vesicle is retrieved, refilled and returned to the releasable pool. Without it, terminals fatigue during repetitive firing and the presynaptic membrane cannot maintain its area or composition. After exocytosis, clathrin and its adaptor complexes with accessory proteins such as amphiphysin, endophilin, stonins and SGIP1 select vesicle cargo including synaptotagmin and VAMP2; dynamins sever the neck, and synaptojanin phosphoinositide phosphatases together with the uncoating chaperone auxilin strip the coat so vesicles can be re-acidified, reloaded by transporters, and docked via Rab3 and syntaxin-dependent priming. Actin and Rho-family GTPase regulators shape the endocytic membrane. Several members, notably LRRK2, synuclein, parkin, DNAJC6 and DJ-1, are Parkinson disease genes, linking failure of this cycle to dopaminergic neurodegeneration, while other mutations cause epileptic encephalopathies.

Synaptic vesicle recycling via endosome is the slower arm of vesicle reuse at the presynaptic terminal, in which membrane retrieved by clathrin-coated endocytosis is routed through an endosomal compartment before being reformed into vesicles that re-acidify and reload with neurotransmitter. This route sustains transmission during prolonged or high-frequency firing, when the local vesicle pool would otherwise be exhausted, and it also serves as a sorting station that keeps vesicle proteins and lipids correctly composed. The genes point to the machinery involved: intersectins couple endocytic coat assembly to actin and small GTPase signalling, an AP-3 adaptor subunit directs cargo sorting from endosomes into newly budded vesicles, RAB7A marks late endosomal identity and maturation, and a GRIP-associated guanine nucleotide exchange factor links the pathway to receptor trafficking. Defects impair synaptic endurance and neurotransmitter release fidelity.

Sustained neurotransmission depends on the local reuse of synaptic vesicle membrane, and one route to regeneration passes through an endosomal intermediate rather than returning directly to the releasable pool. After clathrin-mediated retrieval at the periactive zone, vesicle membrane fuses with a sorting endosome, where cargo composition is corrected before budding, re-acidification and refilling with neurotransmitter. Adaptor and small GTPase machinery gives the route its identity: an AP-3 subunit selects cargo for budding from endosomes, Rab7 marks the late endosomal compartment, intersectins couple endocytic sites to actin and GTPase regulators, and a GRIP-associated guanine nucleotide exchange factor links receptor and vesicle traffic to endosomal recycling. This slower pathway maintains vesicle protein quality and pool size during prolonged activity; its disruption is associated with impaired transmitter loading, presynaptic depression and neurodevelopmental disorders.

ERAD pathway is the quality-control system that clears misfolded and surplus proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, sending them across the ER membrane to the cytosolic proteasome. It keeps the secretory pathway from shipping defective glycoproteins and prevents accumulation of aggregation-prone material, and its overload triggers the unfolded protein response through ATF6 and XBP1; loss of individual components causes neurodegeneration, diabetes-like syndromes and immune dysfunction. Substrates are recognised by lectins and mannosidases such as OS9, ERLEC1 and the EDEM proteins that read trimmed N-glycans as a folding-failure signal, then delivered to membrane ubiquitin ligase complexes built around SYVN1-SEL1L, AMFR, MARCHF6 or RNF185. Derlins and the retrotranslocation channel pass the chain outward, and the VCP-UFD1-NPLOC4 ATPase, with UBX adaptors, deubiquitinases and ubiquilin shuttles, extracts and hands it off for degradation. The same machinery also regulates sterol metabolism and ER membrane protein abundance.

Proteins that fail to fold correctly in the endoplasmic reticulum are not simply retained there; ER-associated degradation recognises them, extracts them, and feeds them to the cytosolic proteasome. This quality-control route keeps the secretory pathway from shipping defective cargo and relieves ER stress, and its failure underlies conditions from alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency to neurodegeneration, while several viruses and toxins exploit it. Lectins and mannosidases such as OS9, ERLEC1 and the EDEM proteins read trimmed N-glycans as a signal that folding attempts have failed, with chaperones including BiP, calnexin and calreticulin upstream. Membrane-embedded ubiquitin ligases -- SYVN1 with SEL1L, AMFR, MARCHF6, RNF5 and relatives -- together with E2 enzymes ubiquitinate substrates at the membrane, and the VCP/p97 ATPase with UFD1, NPLOC4 and UBX cofactors pulls them into the cytosol, where deubiquitinases tune the outcome. Transcriptional arms via XBP1 and ATF6 expand the machinery when demand rises.

Dopaminergic neuron axon guidance is the steering of growth cones from midbrain dopamine neurons toward their forebrain targets, the step that builds the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic projections underlying movement control, motivation and reward. If these axons fail to reach the striatum or misroute along the way, the circuitry for motor initiation and reinforcement learning is never properly wired, a defect relevant to both parkinsonian motor phenotypes and neurodevelopmental disorders of reward processing. Guidance here is dominated by Wnt cues read through non-canonical, planar cell polarity-type machinery: WNT5A and WNT7B act as attractive and repulsive gradients along the anterior-posterior axis, sensed by the Frizzled receptor FZD3 and the atypical receptor tyrosine kinase RYK, with CELSR3 and VANGL2 organising polarity within the growth cone. The output is directional cytoskeletal remodelling rather than transcription, linking this pathway to axon tract formation generally.

Midbrain dopaminergic neurons must send axons along stereotyped routes to the striatum and prefrontal cortex, and dopaminergic neuron axon guidance is the steering process that gets them there. The accuracy of this wiring sets the anatomy of the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic systems that control voluntary movement, motivation and reward; mistargeting leaves dopamine release in the wrong place and is a plausible developmental contributor to motor and psychiatric dysfunction. The cues here are Wnt ligands acting through non-canonical, planar-cell-polarity-type receiving machinery: a Frizzled receptor together with the atypical cadherin CELSR3, the core polarity protein VANGL2, and the atypical tyrosine kinase receptor RYK, which reads Wnt gradients as attractive or repulsive instructions at the growth cone. Signalling converges on cytoskeletal remodelling and oriented outgrowth, linking this pathway to the broader use of polarity proteins in axon tract formation.

collagen-activated tyrosine kinase receptor signaling pathway is how cells read the collagen scaffold around them as an instruction rather than a passive support, using receptor tyrosine kinases that are switched on by triple-helical collagen itself. It sets epithelial adhesion and basement membrane responsiveness, controls cell migration and matrix remodelling in fibrosis and tumour invasion, and in platelets converts exposed subendothelial collagen at a vascular injury into aggregation and thrombus formation. The discoidin domain receptors DDR1 and DDR2 bind fibrillar and network collagens, including the type IV collagens of the basement membrane, and autophosphorylate slowly and persistently to reshape transcription and protease output. The platelet arm works through GP6 with the tetraspanin TSPAN9 and the kinase SYK, whose signalling is damped by the phosphatase UBASH3B. Loss or mutation of these receptors causes bleeding disorders, skeletal and renal defects, and altered fibrotic responses.

Cells read the collagen in their surroundings partly through receptor tyrosine kinases, and this collagen-activated signalling converts that contact into changes in adhesion, migration, matrix remodelling and gene expression. The discoidin domain receptors DDR1 and DDR2 bind triple-helical collagens, including fibrillar type I and the basement membrane type IV chains, and autophosphorylate slowly to control epithelial adhesion, branching morphogenesis, cartilage and bone growth, and fibrotic and invasive responses in tumours; DDR1 loss disrupts kidney and mammary development, and DDR2 mutation causes a short-limbed skeletal dysplasia. A parallel arm operates in platelets, where the immune-type collagen receptor GP6 signals through the tyrosine kinase SYK to trigger activation and aggregation at sites of vessel injury, with TSPAN9 supporting receptor function and UBASH3B acting as a phosphatase that restrains the response. Together these routes link extracellular matrix composition to cytoskeletal and transcriptional output.

vascular endothelial growth factor signaling pathway is the growth factor circuit that tells endothelial cells to sprout, migrate, survive and form new blood and lymphatic vessels. It drives developmental angiogenesis, wound healing and tissue responses to hypoxia, and its overactivation feeds tumour vascularisation and retinal neovascularisation, which is why VEGF and its receptors are among the most heavily drugged targets in oncology and ophthalmology. Secreted ligands VEGFA, VEGFB, PGF and the lymphangiogenic VEGFC/VEGFD, the latter activated by proteolytic processing involving ADAMTS3 and CCBE1, engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 together with neuropilin co-receptors and integrins, recruiting GAB1 and PI3K catalytic subunits to control motility and permeability. Transcriptional partners such as FOXC1, PROX1 and NR2F2 set arterial versus lymphatic identity, while decoy receptors, SPRY2, DAB2IP and several microRNAs restrain the output.

Endothelial cells decide whether to sprout, migrate and form new vessels largely on the basis of vascular endothelial growth factor signaling, which drives angiogenesis in development, wound healing and tumour growth, and lymphangiogenesis in the lymphatic bed. Ligands of the VEGF family, including VEGFA, VEGFB, placental growth factor and the lymphatic ligands VEGFC and VEGFD, engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 together with the neuropilin co-receptors NRP1 and NRP2, activating PI3K catalytic subunits and adaptors such as GAB1 to change endothelial survival, permeability, cytoskeletal behaviour and transcription. Extracellular processing matters too: ADAMTS3 and CCBE1 mature VEGFC before it can act, while decorin, gremlin and integrins tune signalling from the matrix. Downstream, PROX1, FOXC1 and NR2F2 specify lymphatic identity. Excess signalling underlies tumour vascularisation and retinal neovascular disease, making these receptors the targets of anti-angiogenic therapy; loss causes lymphoedema and vascular malformation.

Fc receptor signaling pathway is how immune cells read antibody that has already bound its target, converting immunoglobulin coating of a pathogen or immune complex into phagocytosis, degranulation, cytokine release and antibody-dependent cell killing. It is the effector arm that gives antibodies their power, underlies mast cell allergic responses through IgE receptors, and its inhibitory branch sets the threshold that prevents autoimmune tissue damage; therapeutic antibodies depend on it for activity. Receptor engagement clusters ITAM-bearing chains such as FCER1G and CD247, which are phosphorylated by Src-family kinases including LYN, FYN and HCK, recruiting SYK and BTK and assembling a signalosome with PLCG1/2, VAV guanine-nucleotide exchange factors and PI3K adaptors. Downstream output runs through protein kinase C isoforms, JNK-directed MAP kinase cascades and NF-kB activation, driving cytoskeletal remodelling for particle engulfment and transcription of inflammatory mediators. ITIM-containing receptors like FCGR2B and CD33 oppose this.

Antibodies do more than bind antigen: their constant regions are read by Fc receptors on myeloid, mast and lymphoid cells, converting humoral recognition into cellular action. This pathway couples immunoglobulin-loaded receptors to phagocytosis, antibody-dependent cytotoxicity, degranulation and inflammatory gene expression, and it is the basis of IgE-driven allergic responses as well as much of the efficacy of therapeutic antibodies. Receptor engagement clusters ITAM-bearing chains such as FCER1G and CD247, which are phosphorylated by Src-family kinases including LYN, FGR and HCK and recruit SYK; BTK, PLCG1/PLCG2, protein kinase C isoforms and VAV-family exchange factors then drive calcium flux, JNK cascade activation and cytoskeletal remodelling for particle internalisation. Inhibitory receptors, notably FCGR2B and CD33-family lectins, impose ITIM-based restraint, and loss of that balance contributes to autoantibody-mediated tissue damage and immune complex disease.

Fc-epsilon receptor signaling pathway is the route by which IgE bound to mast cells and basophils triggers their activation, and it is the proximate cause of immediate hypersensitivity: allergic rhinitis, urticaria, asthma and anaphylaxis all begin here, while the same receptors mediate protective responses to parasites. Antigen crosslinking of IgE held on the high-affinity receptor clusters its alpha and gamma chains, whose ITAM motifs recruit the Src-family kinase LYN and then SYK. SYK activates BTK and phospholipase C-gamma to raise calcium and diacylglycerol, driving granule exocytosis of histamine and proteases, while VAV-family exchange factors, SOS1 and a MAP3K-MAP2K cascade feed JNK and NF-kappaB for transcription of cytokines and eicosanoid enzymes. The low-affinity receptor CD23 provides feedback control of IgE production, tying this signalling to the regulation of allergic sensitisation itself.

Mast cells and basophils sense antigen indirectly, through IgE already bound to their surface, and this is the signalling route that converts that recognition into an allergic response. Crosslinking of IgE-loaded high-affinity receptor complexes triggers degranulation, histamine and lipid mediator release, and cytokine transcription, producing the immediate hypersensitivity of asthma, urticaria, food allergy and anaphylaxis; the low-affinity IgE receptor instead tunes IgE production and antigen capture on B cells and other cells. Receptor subunits recruit the Src-family kinase LYN and the tyrosine kinase SYK, which engage BTK and phospholipase C-gamma isoforms to mobilise calcium and activate protein kinase C, while VAV family exchange factors and SOS1 feed into a JNK cascade through MAP3K and MAP2K tiers, and TRAF6 with IKK-beta drives NF-kappaB-dependent gene expression. Blocking receptor occupancy with anti-IgE antibody is an established treatment for severe allergic disease.

ERBB2-EGFR signaling pathway describes growth factor signalling through a mixed receptor pair, in which a ligand-bound EGFR partners with ERBB2 to drive epithelial proliferation, migration and survival. It matters because ERBB2 has no ligand of its own: it acquires signalling competence only by heterodimerising with an activated family member, and this partnership is the setting in which ERBB2 amplification becomes oncogenic in breast and gastric cancer. The upstream inputs are a family of related EGF-domain ligands — EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, betacellulin and HBEGF — several of which are made as membrane-anchored precursors and released by proteolytic shedding, so ligand availability is itself regulated. Dimer formation triggers tyrosine autophosphorylation and recruitment of adaptors feeding the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT routes, coupling extracellular cues to cell cycle entry, tissue repair and epithelial development.

Epidermal growth factor family ligands drive epithelial proliferation, wound repair and developmental morphogenesis, and this branch of that system routes the signal through a mixed receptor pair rather than EGFR alone. EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, betacellulin and heparin-binding EGF each engage EGFR with distinct affinity and duration; the activated receptor then partners with ERBB2, which binds no ligand of its own and depends on heterodimerisation to be switched on. The resulting complex is a more potent and less rapidly downregulated signalling unit than the EGFR homodimer, feeding into RAS-MAPK and PI3K outputs that control cell cycle entry, survival and migration. Because ERBB2 amplification supplies an excess of dimerisation partner, this receptor combination is a central driver in breast and gastric carcinoma and a direct target of antibody and kinase-inhibitor therapy, with ligand availability shaping the response.

interleukin-11-mediated signaling pathway is the arm of gp130 cytokine signalling driven by IL-11, a member of the IL-6 family that supports megakaryocyte maturation and platelet production, bone remodelling, mucosal repair after injury, and trophoblast and decidual function in early pregnancy. IL-11 binds its non-signalling alpha receptor, IL11RA, and the complex recruits the shared transducer gp130 (IL6ST), whose associated JAK1 phosphorylates the receptor tail and activates STAT3, which enters the nucleus and drives programmes of proliferation, survival and matrix production. Because the receptor chain is shared with IL-6 and CNTF, output depends on which alpha receptor a cell expresses, and pathway components overlap with those cytokines. Loss-of-function mutations in IL11RA cause craniosynostosis with dental and skeletal anomalies, while sustained IL-11 signalling promotes fibroblast-to-myofibroblast conversion and fibrosis in heart, lung, kidney and liver, and supports gastrointestinal tumour growth.

Interleukin-11 is a gp130-family cytokine that acts on stromal and epithelial cells to drive tissue remodelling, and interleukin-11-mediated signalling is the route by which that message is read. It supports megakaryocyte and platelet production, bone turnover and mucosal repair, and when persistently active it drives fibroblast-to-myofibroblast conversion and scarring in heart, lung, liver and kidney, making it a target of anti-fibrotic drug development. Signalling begins when the cytokine engages its specific alpha receptor IL11RA and recruits the shared signal-transducing subunit IL6ST (gp130); the associated kinase JAK1 then phosphorylates STAT3, which enters the nucleus and changes transcription of proliferation, survival and matrix genes. Because gp130 and JAK1/STAT3 are held in common with interleukin-6 and ciliary neurotrophic factor receptor complexes, specificity rests on the alpha chain, and loss-of-function mutations in it cause craniosynostosis with skeletal defects.

angiotensin-activated signaling pathway is the cellular response to angiotensin II, the effector hormone of the renin-angiotensin system, and it sets systemic blood pressure, vascular tone, and renal sodium and water handling. Chronic overactivity drives hypertension, cardiac and vascular hypertrophy, and fibrotic remodelling, which is why ACE inhibitors and receptor blockers are mainstays of cardiovascular therapy. Angiotensinogen is cleaved and converted by ACE to angiotensin II, which acts mainly through the AT1 receptor to mobilise calcium and engage protein kinase C, calcium/calmodulin kinase and calcineurin, while Rho-associated kinases and Rac1 reorganise the actin cytoskeleton for smooth muscle contraction. Src links the receptor to growth-factor-like transcriptional programmes and hypertrophic gene expression. AT2 and the MAS receptor for angiotensin-(1-7) oppose these effects, and caveolin scaffolding, receptor-associated adaptors and microRNAs tune signal strength in vascular smooth muscle and renal epithelium, where transporter regulation adjusts acid-base and solute transport.

Angiotensin II is the effector hormone of the renin-angiotensin system, and this pathway covers what happens once it engages its receptors on a target cell: vasoconstriction, sodium and fluid retention, aldosterone release, and longer-term changes in gene expression that drive cardiac and vascular remodelling. Sustained signalling through it underlies hypertension, cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, which is why converting enzyme and receptor blockade are mainstays of cardiovascular therapy. Angiotensinogen is cleaved and processed by ACE to the active peptide, which acts on the type 1 receptor to mobilise calcium and activate protein kinase C, calcineurin, CaMKII, Src, Rac1 and the ROCK kinases, while the type 2 receptor and the MAS1 receptor oppose these effects. Receptor-associated and scaffolding proteins such as AGTRAP and caveolin tune output, and transporter coupling links the pathway to renal acid-base and sodium handling.

interleukin-33-mediated signaling pathway is the alarmin arm of innate immunity: IL-33 stored in epithelial and endothelial nuclei is released on tissue damage and alerts nearby cells to barrier injury. It drives type 2 inflammation, activating group 2 innate lymphoid cells, mast cells, eosinophils and Th2 cells to produce IL-5 and IL-13, and variation in this axis is among the strongest genetic risks for asthma and allergic disease; it also contributes to tissue repair and regulatory T cell maintenance. Signalling runs through the ST2 receptor with its shared accessory chain, recruiting MyD88 and the IRAK4-IRAK1 kinase module, then TRAF6 and TAK1, converging on NF-κB and MAP kinase activation and transcription of inflammatory cytokines. Because the receptor exists as a soluble decoy form, the pathway is tuned by ligand sequestration as well as by receptor expression on responding cell types.

Interleukin-33 is an alarmin released from the nucleus of damaged epithelial and endothelial cells, and the signalling it triggers alerts the immune system to barrier injury. Acting through the receptor ST2 (IL1RL1) together with the shared accessory chain IL1RAP, it drives type 2 inflammation: activation of mast cells, group 2 innate lymphoid cells and Th2 cells, with release of IL-5 and IL-13. This makes the pathway a major contributor to asthma, allergic rhinitis and atopic dermatitis, and a target of biologic therapy, while also supporting tissue repair and regulatory T cell maintenance. Mechanistically it follows the canonical interleukin-1 receptor family route, recruiting MYD88 and the kinases IRAK4 and IRAK1, then TRAF6 and TAK1 (MAP3K7), to converge on NF-κB and MAP kinase-dependent transcription of inflammatory genes.

bile acid signaling pathway treats bile acids not merely as detergents for fat absorption but as hormones, sensed by dedicated receptors that feed back on the synthesis, transport and disposal of bile acids themselves. This is how the liver and intestine keep bile acid pools within a narrow range; loss of the sensing arm leads to cholestatic liver injury, bile acid diarrhoea, and disordered lipid and glucose handling. Two routes are represented. The nuclear receptor FXR, with vitamin D receptor as an additional bile acid-responsive transcription factor, reprograms gene expression to suppress CYP7A1 and induce transporters and FGF19. The membrane receptor GPBAR1 (TGR5), coupled through Gs to cAMP, acts on enterocytes, immune cells and enteroendocrine cells to release GLP-1 and modulate inflammation. Pruritogenic G protein-coupled receptors such as MRGPRX4 link bile acid accumulation to the itch of cholestasis.

Bile acids are not only detergents for fat absorption but hormones, and this signalling route is how cells read their concentration and respond by changing transcription and second-messenger tone. It closes the feedback loop on bile acid synthesis and export in liver and intestine, and contributes to lipid and glucose handling, gut motility, and the itch that accompanies cholestasis. Sensing is split between a nuclear and a membrane arm: the farnesoid X receptor NR1H4 binds bile acids to drive gene programmes that restrain their own production, the vitamin D receptor responds to secondary bile acids such as lithocholic acid, and the G protein-coupled receptor GPBAR1 raises cyclic AMP through Gs signalling. Mas-related receptors including MRGPRX4 link bile acids to sensory neurons and pruritus. Loss of this feedback underlies progressive cholestatic liver disease and bile acid toxicity.

Establishment of mitotic spindle localization positions the mitotic spindle within the dividing cell, thereby setting where the cleavage furrow forms and whether the two daughters inherit equal or distinct fates. It decides symmetric versus asymmetric division, keeps divisions planar in epithelia, and governs the balance between proliferative and differentiative divisions in neural progenitors; its failure underlies microcephaly, disordered epithelial architecture and cystic kidney disease. Cortical force generators anchored by LGN and NuMA recruit dynein-dynactin, which pulls on astral microtubules whose plus ends are stabilised and captured through EB1, CLASP proteins and the LIS1-NDEL1 module. Centrosomal and kinetochore components such as CDK5RAP2, MCPH1, NDC80 and the spindle checkpoint proteins ZW10 and SPDL1 couple orientation to spindle assembly and chromosome attachment, while cell adhesion through integrin signalling communicates tissue geometry to the cortex.

Where a cell divides is determined by where its mitotic spindle sits, and establishment of mitotic spindle localization is the process that moves and anchors the spindle to a chosen position within the cell. This positioning sets the cleavage plane and therefore whether division is symmetric or asymmetric, which governs stem cell self-renewal, the stratification of epithelia and the expansion of neural progenitors; its failure underlies microcephaly and disorganised tissue architecture. Cortical cues captured by GPSM1/GPSM2 and NuMA recruit dynein-dynactin, with LIS1, NDE1 and NDEL1 licensing the motor to pull on astral microtubules, while CLASP1/2 and EB1 regulate microtubule plus-end behaviour at the cortex. Kinetochore and checkpoint components such as NDC80, ZW10 and SPDL1 couple positioning to faithful chromosome attachment, and centrosomal CDK5RAP2 and MCPH1 link spindle orientation to brain development.

regulation of growth rate covers the controls that set how fast cells, tissues, or a whole organism increase in mass, tuning growth to nutrient supply, hormonal cues, and the limits imposed by genome maintenance. Its importance is visible at both extremes: too little growth signalling produces short stature and wasting, too much drives hyperplasia and tumour growth, and premature loss of these controls accompanies accelerated ageing. The genes point to several arms of that regulation. Ghrelin is the gut-derived hormone that stimulates growth hormone release and appetite, linking energy intake to somatic growth. ARMC10 acts at mitochondria to couple metabolic capacity to growth, while BNIPL and RFTN1 modulate proliferative and membrane-associated signalling. The WRN helicase ties growth rate to replication fidelity, since its loss causes a segmental premature ageing syndrome with growth failure and cancer predisposition.

Growth rate regulation covers the processes that set how fast a cell, tissue or whole organism enlarges, tuning mass accumulation to nutrient supply, hormonal cues and the limits imposed by genome integrity. The genes here act at very different levels of that control. Ghrelin is the stomach-derived peptide hormone that stimulates appetite and drives pituitary growth hormone release, linking energy intake to somatic growth. WRN encodes a RecQ family helicase-exonuclease whose loss causes Werner syndrome, in which growth arrest at adolescence and premature ageing follow from unrepaired replication and telomere damage. Others modulate growth indirectly through mitochondrial dynamics, membrane raft-dependent signalling, apoptotic regulation, or cell surface proteolysis affecting proliferation. Taken together they illustrate that growth rate is not one pathway but a convergence of endocrine signalling, metabolic capacity and damage surveillance, with failure producing dwarfism, overgrowth or tumour-like expansion.

Locomotion covers the self-propelled movement of cells and organisms from place to place, the capacity that lets leukocytes reach infected tissue, endothelial tips sprout new vessels, neurons extend axons to their targets, and sperm and ciliated cells generate motion. Its failure underlies immunodeficiency, defective wound healing and malformed nervous and vascular systems, while its inappropriate reactivation drives tumour invasion and metastasis. Mechanistically it joins directional cues to cytoskeletal output: chemokines and their receptors, growth factors such as VEGF, HGF and PDGF, and guidance ligands including semaphorins, slits, netrins and ephrins converge on Rho-family GTPases, PAK, ROCK and actin regulators like cofilin, profilin and WASP. Integrins, cadherins and matrix proteases anchor and remodel the substratum so traction can be produced, and transcriptional programmes of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, together with numerous microRNAs, tune how readily a cell becomes motile.

Locomotion covers the self-propelled movement of cells and whole organisms from one place to another, and in humans it is mostly cell migration: leukocytes crossing vessel walls to reach infection, endothelial tips sprouting new vessels, neural crest and axonal growth cones navigating the embryo, keratinocytes closing a wound, and sperm swimming. Its failure leaves immunodeficiency, defective vascular and neural patterning and poor healing, while its inappropriate reactivation underlies tumour invasion and metastasis. The genes span the layers this requires: chemokines and their receptors, growth factor and semaphorin/slit/ephrin guidance cues, integrins, cadherins and matrix components that provide traction, metalloproteinases that clear a path, and Rho-family GTPases with their regulators, actin nucleators, cofilin, profilin and myosin light-chain kinase that build and retract the leading edge. Ciliary and flagellar components add motile cilia and sperm propulsion, and numerous microRNAs and transcription factors tune the whole programme.

negative regulation of multicellular organism growth covers the brakes on body size — the signals that limit how large an animal grows and when growth stops, setting adult stature rather than the growth of any single tissue. It matters because the same restraints, when lost, produce overgrowth syndromes, and when excessive produce growth failure and short stature. Several of the genes act on the growth hormone/IGF axis: SOCS2 terminates growth hormone receptor signalling and its loss causes gigantism, while stanniocalcin STC2 sequesters the proteases that liberate IGF from its binding proteins. Others impose systemic restraint through appetite and energy expenditure, including GDF15 as an anorexigenic stress signal and β-adrenergic receptors coupling to GNAS for catabolic tone. Developmental repressors such as PTCH1, and factors mutated in Bardet–Biedl and Smith–Magenis syndromes, link body-size control to hedgehog signalling, ciliary function and neuroendocrine regulation of feeding.

Body size is set not only by growth-promoting signals but by brakes on them, and this is the set of processes that limit how large an organism becomes. Its members restrain the growth hormone/IGF axis and systemic energy balance: SOCS2 dampens growth hormone receptor signalling, and its loss produces gigantism in mice, while stanniocalcin-2 inhibits the IGF-releasing protease PAPP-A, and GDF15 acts on hindbrain circuits to suppress appetite and lower body weight. Beta-adrenergic receptors and their coupling through the stimulatory G protein Gs link sympathetic tone to lipolysis and metabolic rate, and PTCH1 acts as the inhibitory receptor of Hedgehog signalling that restrains proliferative growth. Mutations here shift stature and body mass in both directions, as seen in overgrowth syndromes, Smith-Magenis syndrome from RAI1 haploinsufficiency, and the obesity of Bardet-Biedl syndrome, placing this biology at the junction of endocrine growth control and appetite regulation.

regulation of meiotic nuclear division controls when germ cells enter meiosis, how far they proceed, and when they arrest, so that oocytes and sperm emerge with a single haploid genome set. Its failure produces infertility, premature ovarian insufficiency, or aneuploid gametes and miscarriage. The genes cover several regulatory layers: STRA8 and MEIOSIN license meiotic entry downstream of retinoic acid, PRDM9 designates recombination hotspots while HORMAD1/2 and TRIP13 police synapsis and crossover checkpoints, and a spindle assembly checkpoint module with CDC20, KNL1 and ZWINT guards chromosome segregation. Oocyte arrest and reawakening depend on cAMP tone through GPR3 and PDE3A, on EMI1/EMI2-type APC/C inhibitors with FZR1, and on MOS and WEE2 kinase activity. RNA-binding regulators such as DAZL, NANOS2 and PIWIL2 impose translational and transposon control, linking germline gene expression to the meiotic cell cycle.

Meiosis must be started at the right moment and then stopped and restarted at defined arrest points, and this regulatory layer sets that timing so that a diploid germ cell yields haploid gametes. It matters for fertility: loss of control produces oocytes that fail to arrest or resume, aneuploid eggs, and spermatogenic failure. Retinoic acid-responsive entry factors such as STRA8 and its partner MEIOSIN license meiotic initiation, while DMRT1, NANOS2 and DAZL govern whether germ cells enter meiosis or stay mitotic. Prophase surveillance runs through HORMAD proteins, TRIP13 and the recombination hotspot determinant PRDM9. Oocyte arrest is maintained by cAMP signalling through GPR3 and PDE3A, and release depends on MOS kinase, WEE2, and control of the anaphase-promoting complex by CDC20, FZR1 and its inhibitors FBXO5 and FBXO43, with spindle checkpoint components monitoring kinetochore attachment.

Epigenetic regulation of gene expression is the layer of control that decides which genes a cell can read, using marks on DNA and histones rather than changes in sequence, and it is what allows one genome to specify many stable cell identities through repeated divisions. Its failure underlies imprinting disorders, loss of X inactivation, transposon reactivation in the germline, and a large fraction of cancers. The machinery here writes, reads and erases those marks: DNMT1 with UHRF1 propagates cytosine methylation at the replication fork while TET enzymes reverse it; Polycomb complexes built on EZH2, SUZ12 and RING1B compact developmental loci; SETDB1, SUV39H and the HUSH complex with TRIM28 silence repeats and retroelements; histone acetyltransferases, deacetylases and demethylases tune accessibility, and ATP-dependent remodellers reposition nucleosomes. Piwi proteins and Tudor partners extend the same logic to small RNA-guided silencing in gametes, and CTCF organizes the resulting domains.

Cells with identical genomes maintain different expression programmes because chromatin itself carries heritable information, and this is the machinery that writes, reads, erases and propagates it. Such epigenetic regulation of gene expression establishes lineage identity, silences repetitive and parasitic DNA, imprints maternal and paternal alleles, inactivates one X chromosome, and keeps the settings stable through rounds of DNA replication even after the initiating signal is gone. The components span DNA methylation writers and the TET dioxygenases that initiate demethylation, methyl-CpG readers such as MECP2 and UHRF1, histone acetyltransferases opposed by HDAC and sirtuin deacetylases, H3K9 and H3K27 methyltransferases with Polycomb and HP1 silencing complexes, ATP-dependent nucleosome remodellers, histone variants and linker histones, and a piRNA-guided arm that silences transposons in germ cells. Misdirection of these activities underlies imprinting disorders, Rett syndrome, and widespread silencing of tumour suppressors in cancer.

snRNA modification is the chemical decoration of spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs after they are transcribed, converting raw transcripts into stable, correctly folded components of the splicing machinery. Pseudouridines and 2'-O-methyl groups placed in and around the snRNA regions that base-pair with pre-mRNA branch points and splice sites tune the fidelity and efficiency of intron removal, while cap modification and 3' end binding determine whether an snRNA is protected or degraded. The genes cover both arms: the H/ACA pseudouridine synthase core of dyskerin with NHP2 and NOP10, the methyltransferases that install N6-methyladenosine and N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine marks, and the MePCE-LARP7 pair that caps and stabilises 7SK. Loss of these activities destabilises snRNPs and disrupts splicing, and dyskerin mutations cause dyskeratosis congenita with failure of telomere maintenance and bone marrow function.

Spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs are not functional as bare transcripts; they carry pseudouridines, methylated bases and modified caps that stabilize them and tune how they pair with pre-mRNA. Modification of snRNA supplies these marks and so underwrites accurate splice-site recognition and the stability of the snRNPs themselves. Pseudouridine synthase activity is contributed by the dyskerin complex together with NHP2 and NOP10, the same H/ACA machinery used on ribosomal RNA and telomerase RNA, which is why its loss produces the multisystem failure of dyskeratosis congenita. MEPCE adds the gamma-monomethyl phosphate cap to 7SK, with LARP7 binding and protecting that transcript in the complex restraining transcription elongation, while METTL16 and METTL4 introduce adenine methylation, linking U6 snRNA maturation to broader RNA methylation regulating splicing and gene expression.

Protein refolding is the cell's repair arm for damaged proteins: when heat, oxidation, or mutation unfolds a polypeptide, chaperones bind the exposed hydrophobic surfaces, prevent aggregation, and drive ATP-dependent cycles that return the protein to its native, active shape. This is what allows cells to survive proteotoxic stress instead of accumulating inclusions, and its decline underlies aggregation diseases of neurons, muscle, and the lens. The machinery here spans compartments and families: cytosolic and stress-inducible HSP70s with their DNAJ co-chaperones and nucleotide-exchange regulators such as BAG5, HSP90, the mitochondrial HSP60 chaperonin and mortalin, the endoplasmic reticulum BiP with its SDF2L1 partner, and ATP-independent small heat shock proteins including HSPB1 and the lens alpha-crystallins that hold unfolded clients in a refoldable state. Refolding competes with degradation, so these factors also triage substrates toward proteasomal disposal when repair fails.

When heat, oxidative stress or mutation leaves a protein unfolded or misfolded, chaperones can restore it to its active shape rather than let it aggregate or be degraded, and this refolding capacity is what allows cells to survive proteotoxic stress. The gene complement is dominated by the HSP70 family (HSPA1A/B, HSPA8, the endoplasmic reticulum BiP HSPA5, mitochondrial HSPA9) together with their J-domain co-chaperones DNAJA2, DNAJA4 and DNAJB2, which deliver substrates and stimulate ATP-driven cycles of binding and release; HSP90 and the mitochondrial HSP60 chaperonin provide additional folding routes, while small heat shock proteins such as HSPB1 and the lens alpha-crystallins hold partly unfolded clients soluble in an ATP-independent manner. Nucleotide exchange factors like BAG5 tune the cycle. The same activity operates in cytosol, ER and mitochondria, and its decline underlies cataract, myopathy and protein aggregation disease.

Olfactory behavior covers the responses an animal makes to odors — approach, avoidance, feeding, mating and social recognition — and therefore the whole chain from odorant detection to a motor decision. It matters because anosmia and hyposmia disrupt appetite, hazard avoidance and social interaction, and appear early in neurodegenerative and developmental syndromes. The genes point mainly to the olfactory sensory neuron and its cilium, where adenylyl cyclase ADCY3 generates the cAMP signal that opens transduction channels, and where ciliary and trafficking factors such as BBS1 and CFAP69 maintain the sensory compartment; loss of these produces ciliopathy-associated smell defects. Others act on circuit assembly and central processing, including CHD7, mutated in CHARGE syndrome with olfactory bulb hypoplasia, the transcription factor LMX1A, and the postsynaptic scaffold SHANK1. The pathway thus links chemosensory transduction to behavior.

Behavioural responses to odours depend on the machinery that lets olfactory sensory neurons detect volatile cues and relay them to the brain, and on the developmental programmes that build that circuitry. Loss of these functions produces anosmia or hyposmia, which in humans blunts appetite and flavour perception and removes a warning system for spoiled food and smoke. Odorant receptor signalling converges on adenylate cyclase 3 to raise cAMP in the cilia of sensory neurons, so ciliary assembly and maintenance genes such as BBS1 and CFAP69 are required for smell as much as the transduction enzymes are. Transcriptional regulators including CHD7 and LMX1A shape formation of the olfactory epithelium and bulb, and CHD7 mutation underlies the anosmia seen with CHARGE syndrome. Synaptic scaffolding contributes at the downstream relay, tying sensory input to behavioural output.

T-helper 1 type immune response is the arm of adaptive immunity that clears pathogens living inside host cells — intracellular bacteria, fungi and protozoa — by arming macrophages and cytotoxic effectors with interferon-gamma. Its overactivity underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease including arthritis, while loss of the IL-12/IL-23 receptor axis leaves patients susceptible to mycobacteria and salmonella. Commitment runs from dendritic cell IL-12 and IL-18 production through IL12RB1/IL12RB2 to STAT4 and the master transcription factor TBX21, with HLX and LEF1 reinforcing the program and IL-10, SOCS5, IL18BP and STAT6 restraining or diverting it. Innate priming via TLR4, HMGB1, IL-1 family cytokines, RIPK2 and TRAF6-dependent NF-kB feeds the same circuit. Immunoproteasome subunits PSMB8/PSMB9 and MHC class II reflect the antigen processing and presentation on which Th1 differentiation depends, alongside costimulation through CD80 and TNFSF4.

Clearance of pathogens that hide inside cells depends on the T-helper 1 arm of CD4 T cell differentiation, which commits naive T cells to making interferon-gamma and so licenses macrophages to kill intracellular bacteria, fungi and protozoa. The same programme, run too hard, drives inflammatory arthritis and other autoimmune tissue damage, while its loss leaves people vulnerable to mycobacteria and salmonella. Commitment is instructed by IL-12 and IL-18 from activated dendritic cells and macrophages acting through their receptor chains, and is read out by STAT4 and the lineage-defining transcription factor TBX21, with IL-27, IL-23 and IL-33 shaping the balance and STAT6, IL-10 and IL18BP restraining it. Innate sensing through TLR4 and RIPK2, costimulation by CD80 and peptide display on MHC class II together with proteasome subunits that generate those peptides supply the priming context.</description>}</invoke></function_calls></response>}</invoke>ilmiş</invoke>

positive regulation of T cell proliferation covers the signals that drive antigen-experienced T cells to expand into clones large enough to clear an infection, and that sustain the lymphocyte pools underlying adaptive immunity, vaccine responses and transplant rejection. Three inputs converge: peptide-MHC engagement of the T cell receptor complex, relayed through CD3, ZAP70, PRKCQ, CARD11 and calcineurin; costimulation by CD28, ICOS, OX40 and 4-1BB ligands presented on dendritic cells; and growth-promoting cytokines, chiefly IL-2 acting via IL2RA and STAT5, with IL-12, IL-15, IL-21 and IL-23 shaping the expanding subset. Adhesion, chemokine and actin-regulatory components such as VCAM1, CCL19 and CORO1A position cells for productive contacts. Several members are inhibitory checkpoints whose loss increases proliferation, so the same wiring sets the threshold: too little yields immunodeficiency, too much autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation.

Clonal expansion of antigen-specific T cells is what turns a handful of naive lymphocytes into an effective response, and the processes gathered here are those that drive or amplify that expansion. Antigen presentation on MHC class I and class II molecules, engagement of the TCR complex and CD4, and costimulation through CD28 with its ligands CD80 and CD86 or the TNF-family ligands OX40L and 4-1BBL set the threshold for division. Proximal signalling by ZAP70, LCK-associated adaptors, PRKCQ, CARD11 and calcineurin feeds into IL-2 production, while IL-2, IL-15, IL-12, IL-21 and IL-23 act through their receptors and STAT5 to sustain cycling. Several members are better known as brakes -- PD-L1, PD-L2, TIM-3, B7-H4, FOXP3 -- reflecting how tightly proliferative drive is balanced. Excessive output underlies autoimmunity and transplant rejection; failure leaves immunodeficiency and poor tumour control.

macrophage activation is the switch by which a resting tissue macrophage becomes an effector cell, changing shape, metabolism and secretory output in response to microbial products, cytokines or damaged host material. It sets the tone of innate immunity: too little leaves mycobacterial and other intracellular infections uncontrolled, too much drives the cytokine storms, granulomas and neuroinflammation seen in sepsis and neurodegeneration. Recognition runs through Toll-like receptors, Fc and complement receptors, formyl-peptide and purinergic sensors, and the TREM2-TYROBP-SYK axis of microglia, converging on JAK2, PLCG2 and AP-1 factors to induce TNF, IL1B, IL6 and CCL3. Opposing inputs polarise the response, with IFNG driving classical activation and IL4, IL13, IL10 and the nuclear receptors NR1H3 and RORA promoting alternative, resolving states. Brakes such as CD200, HAVCR2, ZC3H12A and VSIG4 keep activation self-limiting.

Macrophage activation is the shift in shape, gene expression and behaviour that turns a resting tissue macrophage into an effector cell, triggered by cytokines, microbial ligands or host-derived damage signals. It sets the tone of innate immunity: classical activation by interferon-gamma and Toll-like receptor agonists such as LPS drives TNF, IL-1B and IL-6 production and microbial killing, while IL-4 and IL-13 acting through IL4R and JAK2 promote the alternative, tissue-repair state, and IL-10 restrains both. Receptor sensing runs through TLR1/4/6/9 with the TICAM1 adaptor, complement and Fc receptors, and ITAM-coupled TREM2-TYROBP signalling to SYK and PLCG2, with nuclear receptors and transcription factors including NR1H3 and JUN fixing the resulting programme. Excessive or mistimed activation underlies septic inflammation and chronic inflammatory disease, while hypofunction, notably of TREM2 or GRN in microglia, contributes to neurodegeneration and failed clearance of debris.

Lipoprotein catabolic process covers the breakdown of lipid-modified proteins and lipid-carrying particles, spanning both the clearance of circulating lipoproteins and the enzymatic removal of lipid anchors from proteins. It determines how much cholesterol and triglyceride is taken out of plasma, and failure of its receptor and lysosomal arms produces familial hypercholesterolaemia, atherosclerosis, and lysosomal acid lipase deficiency. Particle clearance runs through apolipoprotein ligands such as APOB and APOE binding LDLR, followed by endocytosis and hydrolysis of cholesteryl esters by LIPA and cathepsin D in the lysosome; APOC2 tunes upstream lipolysis. A parallel set of thioesterases and hydrolases, including PPT1, LYPLA1 and the ABHD17 depalmitoylases, strips palmitate from cysteine residues, reversing S-acylation and controlling the membrane localisation and turnover of signalling proteins. NOTUM removes palmitoleate from Wnt ligands, extinguishing Wnt signalling in the extracellular space.

Lipoproteins carry cholesterol and triglyceride through plasma, and their catabolism determines how much lipid is delivered to cells and how much remains in circulation — the step whose failure produces hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis. Receptor-mediated uptake via the LDL receptor, guided by apolipoprotein B and apolipoprotein E ligands, routes particles to lysosomes, where cathepsin D degrades the protein moiety and lysosomal acid lipase hydrolyses cholesteryl esters and triglycerides to free cholesterol and fatty acids; loss of that lipase causes Wolman disease and cholesteryl ester storage disease. Apolipoprotein C-II acts instead as the cofactor that lets lipoprotein lipase strip triglyceride from circulating particles. Also represented is breakdown of protein-attached lipid itself: depalmitoylating thioesterases and serine hydrolases remove S-acyl groups from cysteines, with palmitoyl-protein thioesterase deficiency causing infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, and NOTUM removing the palmitoleate required for Wnt activity.

Modified amino acid catabolic process is the disposal arm for amino acid derivatives — conjugates, methylated and hydroxylated forms, thyroid hormones and glutathione-linked adducts — returning their carbon, nitrogen and sulfur to usable pools.
