The resulting phosphoinositide pool docks PDPK1 and Akt at the membrane, and phosphorylated Akt then suppresses apoptosis, drives glucose uptake, and releases mTOR complex activity by inactivating TSC2, linking this route to nutrient sensing and autophagy control. Opposing activities set the tone: PTEN and other inositol phosphatases degrade the lipid signal, PHLPP1 and PP2A dephosphorylate the kinase, and numerous microRNAs tune the components. Persistent activation through PIK3CA mutation or PTEN loss is among the commonest oncogenic events, while impaired signalling underlies insulin resistance.

mitochondrial DNA repair keeps the mitochondrial genome intact so that the handful of genes it encodes for the respiratory chain and mitochondrial translation remain readable. Mitochondrial DNA sits close to the site of oxidative phosphorylation and accumulates oxidative lesions, strand breaks and deletions; without repair and tolerance mechanisms these accumulate into the large deletions and depletion seen in mitochondrial myopathies, neurodegeneration and ageing tissue. The genes here cover the main routes available in the organelle: base excision repair completed by a mitochondrial ligase and PARP1-mediated break sensing, nuclease and helicase activities that trim flaps and degrade damaged linear ends, and a primase-polymerase that permits replication restart past lesions rather than repairing them outright. The pathway therefore links genome maintenance to mitochondrial replication and turnover, and its failure is registered as loss of oxidative capacity rather than as nuclear mutation.

Mitochondria carry their own small genome close to the respiratory chain, where reactive oxygen species and replication stress leave it heavily damaged, and repairing that DNA keeps oxidative phosphorylation genes intact. Loss of this capacity leads to mitochondrial DNA deletions, depletion and point mutations, and underlies mitochondrial myopathies and progressive multi-organ disease as mutant genomes accumulate with age. The proteins here cover the main routes available in the organelle: base excision repair completed by a ligase that seals nicks, nuclease and exonuclease activities that trim flaps and degrade damaged or linear mitochondrial DNA, a primase-polymerase able to reprime replication past lesions, and a poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase that senses strand breaks. Because the organelle lacks nucleotide excision repair, tolerance and degradation of damaged genomes, rather than repair of every lesion, substantially shapes mitochondrial genome maintenance and copy number.

negative regulation of DNA damage response, signal transduction by p53 class mediator is the braking system on p53 signalling, setting how much arrest, senescence or apoptosis a cell commits to after its DNA is damaged. It matters because unrestrained p53 output kills or permanently arrests cells that could be repaired, while excessive braking allows damaged cells to keep dividing — the route by which many tumours inactivate p53 without mutating it. The dominant mechanism is ubiquitin-dependent turnover through MDM2, reinforced by gankyrin (PSMD10) and other ubiquitin ligase components; deacetylation by SIRT1 and demethylation by KDM1A strip p53 of activating modifications, and DYRK kinases and the cytokine MIF, acting via CD74, damp the response from outside the nucleus. Notably, the EMT transcription factors SNAI1, SNAI2 and TWIST1 suppress p53 output, linking checkpoint attenuation to invasive and stem-like cell states.

Damage-induced p53 signalling must be switched off once repair is complete, and damping of this DNA damage response by p53-class mediators sets how readily a cell commits to arrest, senescence or apoptosis. The brake matters in both directions: too much restraint lets damaged cells proliferate and is a route to tumour formation, while too little causes excessive cell death and loss of stem and progenitor pools. MDM2 is the central ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for degradation and holds its level low in unstressed cells; SIRT1 deacetylates p53 to blunt its transcriptional output, and the demethylase KDM1A removes methyl marks that otherwise stabilise activated p53. DYRK-family kinases, the gankyrin proteasome regulator PSMD10, and the mesenchymal transcription factors SNAI1, SNAI2 and TWIST1 add further repression, linking p53 suppression to epithelial-mesenchymal transition and to signals from MIF and CD74.

regulation of neuron apoptotic process sets the threshold at which a neuron either survives or dies, and because most neurons are never replaced, where this threshold sits determines the size of the mature nervous system and the pace of neurodegeneration. During development, excess neurons are eliminated unless they receive trophic support, and the pathway is built around that competition: neurotrophins such as NGF, BDNF and NT-3 acting through TRK receptors and PI3K-AKT survival signalling, opposed by JNK-cascade kinases, CDK5, and the BCL-2 family gatekeepers BAX, BCL2L11 and MCL1 that license mitochondrial permeabilisation and caspase-3/9 activation. Stress inputs converge here too, including DNA damage sensing by ATM and p53 targets, the integrated stress response through ATF4 and CHOP, hypoxia, and glial cytokines. Many familial neurodegeneration genes, among them PINK1, PRKN, SNCA, PSEN1, APP, GRN and SOD1, act as modulators, linking this control point to Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.

Neurons are largely post-mitotic and irreplaceable, so whether one lives or dies is tightly controlled, and this regulation of neuronal apoptosis sets both the sculpting of the developing nervous system and the survival of mature circuits under stress. During development, excess neurons die unless they capture target-derived trophic support; neurotrophins such as NGF, BDNF, NT-3 and GDNF acting through TRKA, TRKB and related receptors engage PI3K-AKT and STAT3 signalling to suppress the intrinsic death machinery, while withdrawal activates JNK-pathway kinases, FOXO3 and BH3-only proteins including BIM, PUMA and HRK to permit BAX-dependent mitochondrial permeabilization and caspase-9/caspase-3 activation. BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 oppose this, and DNA damage, ER stress effectors ATF4 and CHOP, hypoxia sensing, and neuroinflammatory signals from microglia feed in. Many familial neurodegeneration genes, among them PARK7, PINK1, PRKN, SNCA, APP, PSEN1, GRN and SOD1, act here, linking dysregulated neuronal death to Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and motor neuron disease.

regulation of translation in response to stress is how cells throttle protein synthesis when conditions turn hostile, conserving energy and preventing the accumulation of misfolded or damaged protein until the insult passes. It matters because the same shutdown reprograms which mRNAs are read: global initiation falls while stress-adaptive transcripts such as ATF4 are selectively translated, driving the integrated stress response, and failure of this control underlies pancreatic beta-cell loss in Wolcott-Rallison syndrome and contributes to neurodegeneration. The core switch is phosphorylation of the initiation factor eIF2 alpha by kinases sensing unfolded protein load in the endoplasmic reticulum (PERK) or amino acid deprivation (GCN2), reversed by a phosphatase complex containing GADD34 and PP1. Additional layers act on eIF4G and ribosomal protein S6 kinases, on tRNA cleavage by angiogenin, and through stress granule assembly, linking translational arrest to nutrient sensing, redox balance and cell-fate decisions.

When cells meet heat, oxidants, amino acid shortage or misfolded protein load, they throttle global protein synthesis while selectively favouring stress-response messages, and this translational control in response to stress is that switch. It buys time for repair, conserves energy and amino acids, and drives assembly of stress granules; chronic engagement of the same circuitry underlies the integrated stress response seen in neurodegeneration, diabetes and tumour adaptation to hypoxia. The core event is phosphorylation of the eIF2 alpha subunit by kinases that sense unfolded protein accumulation in the ER or uncharged tRNA, which blocks ternary complex recycling and shuts down cap-dependent initiation. Recovery depends on a phosphatase targeting subunit that directs protein phosphatase 1 back onto eIF2 alpha, while a translational GTPase-binding inhibitor restrains kinase activation. Additional inputs act through initiation factor eIF4G, RNA helicase and RNA-binding components, an angiogenin-driven tRNA cleavage arm, and nutrient sensing via sestrin.

positive regulation of insulin-like growth factor receptor signaling pathway covers the inputs that amplify signalling through the IGF1 receptor, the axis that drives somatic growth, skeletal and muscle anabolism, and cell survival. Its output is body size: loss of the upstream hormonal steps causes short stature and growth hormone deficiency, while excess produces gigantism and acromegaly, and chronic overactivation supports tumour growth. Much of the regulation is endocrine and hierarchical, with hypothalamic GHRH acting through its receptor, and ghrelin through GHSR, to release pituitary growth hormone, which in turn induces hepatic IGF1. Availability of the ligand at the receptor is then set by binding proteins such as IGFBP3 and IGFBP5, which prolong its half-life and present it to target tissues. Androgen receptor and WNT1 signalling feed in as tissue-level potentiators, coupling growth factor sensitivity to hormonal and developmental context.

Growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor signalling drives somatic growth, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise output through the IGF1 receptor. Its strength sets body size, bone and muscle accrual, and tissue anabolism; loss of the hypothalamic-pituitary arm causes short stature and growth hormone deficiency, while excess IGF1 receptor signalling supports proliferation and survival in many tumours. The upstream components are endocrine: a hypothalamic releasing hormone acting through its own receptor and a secretagogue receptor drive pituitary growth hormone, which induces hepatic IGF1. At the tissue level, IGF-binding proteins hold the ligand in reserve and can enhance its presentation to the receptor, and additional modulators including androgen receptor and WNT1 signalling amplify the response. The net effect is potentiation of receptor-proximal growth signalling rather than a separate cascade.

negative regulation of insulin-like growth factor receptor signaling pathway covers the brakes on IGF1R signalling, the growth-factor axis that drives cell proliferation, survival, protein synthesis and body size. Restraining it matters because unchecked IGF signalling promotes tumour growth and hypertrophy, while its controlled damping allows tissues to stop growing, terminally differentiate, and remain insulin-sensitive. The mechanisms represented are diverse: secreted binding proteins such as IGFBP5 and cartilage matrix proteins sequester IGF ligands before they reach the receptor; SHIP2 (INPPL1) hydrolyses PIP3 to shut down the downstream PI3K-AKT arm; TRIM72/MG53 promotes receptor and substrate turnover in muscle; and microRNAs together with transcription factors such as NKX3-1 lower the abundance of pathway components. BMP ligands intersect from a parallel signalling route. Loss of this restraint contributes to prostate and other cancers, cardiac and skeletal muscle hypertrophy, and insulin resistance.

Insulin-like growth factor signalling drives growth, anabolic metabolism and cell survival, so it must be damped as well as switched on; the genes here restrain IGF receptor output. They act at several levels: secreted binding proteins such as IGFBP5 and the cartilage matrix protein CILP sequester or block ligand access to the receptor, TRIM72 promotes turnover of receptor-proximal components in muscle, and the inositol phosphatase INPPL1 degrades PIP3 to shut down PI3K-AKT signalling downstream. Transcriptional and microRNA inputs, including NKX3-1 and miR-29 family members, lower the abundance of pathway components, while bone morphogenetic proteins impose crosstalk from a parallel growth-factor system. Setting this brake matters for body and organ size, skeletal and muscle growth, cardiac hypertrophy and metabolic control, and its loss permits the sustained proliferative and anti-apoptotic signalling characteristic of tumour growth.

Astrocyte cell migration is the directed movement of astrocytes, the most abundant glial cells of the brain and spinal cord, toward sites where they are needed. This behaviour underlies glial scar formation after injury, the reactive astrogliosis that walls off lesions in stroke and demyelination, and the positioning of astrocyte endfeet that maintains the blood-brain barrier; it is also exploited by infiltrating glioma cells. The genes point to chemokine-driven guidance, with CCL2 and CCL3 acting through CCR2 to steer astrocytes and recruit inflammatory partners, and the oxysterol receptor GPR183 adding a lipid-sensed directional cue. Movement also requires remodelling of the surrounding matrix, provided by the membrane metalloproteinase MMP14 and lysosomal glycoside hydrolase activity, while Wnt modulation via APCDD1 tunes the response. The pathway therefore links neuroinflammatory signalling to tissue repair and barrier integrity in the central nervous system.

Astrocytes are not static support cells; they move, and directed astrocyte migration is how they populate the developing brain, tile their territories, and converge on sites of injury to form the glial scar that walls off damaged tissue. The genes here point to chemotactic guidance and matrix remodelling as the two levers: the chemokines CCL2 and CCL3 acting through CCR2 recruit and steer cells along inflammatory gradients, the oxysterol receptor GPR183 adds a lipid-sensed positional cue, and the membrane-anchored metalloproteinase MMP14 clears a path by degrading extracellular matrix at the leading edge. APCDD1, an inhibitor of Wnt signalling, links migration to developmental patterning cues. Too little of this response leaves lesions unsealed; too much contributes to reactive gliosis, chronic neuroinflammation, and the invasive behaviour of glial tumours.

Cortical microtubule organization builds and remodels the microtubule arrays that lie just under the plasma membrane, the layer where the cytoskeleton is coupled to cell adhesions and to the cell surface. This coupling sets where a cell places its spindle, how it polarizes, and how it steers during migration; when it fails, spindles misorient and tissue architecture and axon guidance suffer, as in the congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles caused by KIF21A mutation and the neuronal migration defects of lissencephaly from PAFAH1B1 loss. Mechanistically, KANK1 links talin at integrin adhesions to liprin-containing cortical platforms that capture and stabilize microtubule plus ends, while ezrin and DLG1 anchor the array to membrane and polarity complexes and KIF21A restrains excess growth. The result is a mechanically responsive interface between microtubules, adhesion sites, and cortical signalling.

Microtubules that reach the cell periphery must be captured, tethered and their growth restrained at the cortex just under the plasma membrane, and cortical microtubule organization is the machinery that does this. It sets where the microtubule array points, and with it the position of the spindle, the direction of cell migration and the polarity of epithelia; failure of individual components produces congenital eye-movement disorders and nephrotic-syndrome-like kidney disease. The genes here link the actin-based cortex and adhesions to plus ends: talin and ezrin anchor at the membrane and integrin sites, KANK1 bridges adhesion complexes to the cortical microtubule-capture apparatus, and the kinesin KIF21A acts as a brake on microtubule growth at the cortex. Scaffolds of the liprin family and a DLG1 polarity module localize these activities, while LIS1 couples captured microtubules to dynein-based pulling forces during spindle positioning and neuronal migration.

post-translational protein modification covers the covalent tagging and editing of proteins after synthesis, the step that sets a protein's stability, location, activity and partners without changing the gene that encoded it. It is how cells make decisions quickly and reversibly, and its failure underlies neurodegeneration, cancer and inflammatory disease. The genes here are dominated by the ubiquitin system: E1 activating enzymes, dozens of E2 conjugases, and the HECT, RING, TRIM, cullin-RING and anaphase-promoting complexes that select substrates, opposed by a large family of deubiquitinases such as USPs and OTUs that erase the mark. Related ubiquitin-like conjugation pathways for SUMO, NEDD8, ISG15, UFM1 and ATG8 lipidation are represented alongside acetylation, ADP-ribosylation, glycosylation, methylation and phosphorylation activities. Together these marks drive proteasomal and autophagic degradation, DNA damage responses, NF- cB and interferon signalling, cell cycle transitions and protein quality control.

Proteins acquire much of their functional information after they leave the ribosome, and post-translational protein modification covers the enzymes that add, read and remove those covalent marks. The dominant theme here is ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like tagging: activating E1 enzymes, a full complement of E2 conjugases, and E3 ligases of every architecture — cullin–RING complexes with their F-box, BTB/KLHL, DCAF and SOCS/ASB substrate receptors, HECT ligases such as the NEDD4 family, and RING and TRIM proteins — together with the deubiquitinases (USP, OTU, JOSD, MINDY families) that reverse them. Parallel branches handle SUMO, NEDD8, UFM1, ISG15 and ATG8 conjugation, alongside acetylation/deacetylation, ADP-ribosylation, glycosylation and methylation activities. These marks decide protein lifespan, localisation, complex assembly and signalling output, governing cell-cycle progression, DNA repair, NF-κB and innate immune responses, hypoxia adaptation and mitophagy; their failure underlies cancers, neurodegeneration and inflammatory disease.

host-mediated suppression of viral transcription is the arm of antiviral defence in which host factors shut down transcription from viral genomes and integrated proviruses rather than attacking virions directly. It underlies latency of retroviruses such as HIV-1, where transcriptional silencing keeps infected cells invisible to immune clearance and blocks eradication, and it limits productive replication during acute infection. The genes act mostly in the nucleus on chromatin and promoter occupancy: HDAC1 deacetylates histones at the viral LTR, REST and other repressive DNA-binding proteins recruit corepressors, BRD4 competes with viral transactivators for the elongation machinery, and TARDBP and HMGA2 bind viral regulatory RNA and DNA. Chemokines including CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5 add an extracellular layer by blocking entry and shaping the inflammatory milieu, linking this repression to broader innate immune control and to strategies aimed at reversing latency.

Host cells can silence an integrated or episomal viral genome by shutting down transcription from its promoter, and this is one route by which latency is established and maintained rather than the virus being cleared outright. Chromatin-level repression is central: a histone deacetylase removes acetyl marks from nucleosomes on the viral long terminal repeat or early promoter, and sequence-specific repressors such as REST and TFAP4 recruit corepressors to viral regulatory elements, while BRD4 competes for the elongation machinery that viral transactivators need. Chemokines produced by the host, including CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5, contribute by limiting productive infection of neighbouring cells. Other factors act as RNA-binding or transcriptional modulators of viral gene output. Failure of this restraint permits reactivation from latency and renewed viral replication, making the same machinery a target for strategies that either enforce silence or deliberately reverse it.

Glucan metabolic process covers the synthesis and breakdown of glucose polymers, which in humans means glycogen — the storage form of glucose that buffers blood sugar between meals and fuels muscle contraction during exertion. Its failure produces the glycogen storage diseases: acid maltase deficiency, McArdle disease, phosphorylase kinase and branching enzyme defects, and the polyglucosan accumulation of Lafora disease. Glycogenin primes the chain, synthases elongate it and branching enzyme shapes it, while phosphorylases, debranching enzyme and lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase mobilise it. Flux is set by hormones: insulin acting through its receptor, IRS proteins and AKT inactivates GSK3 to relieve inhibition of glycogen synthase, opposed by glucagon; protein phosphatase 1 with its PPP1R3 glycogen-targeting subunits localises this control to the granule itself. STBD1 and the autophagy machinery route glycogen to lysosomes for glycophagy, and circadian factors impose daily timing on storage.

Glucan metabolism in humans is essentially glycogen metabolism: the synthesis, branching, storage and breakdown of the glucose polymer that buffers blood sugar between meals and fuels muscle contraction during exercise. Glycogenin primes the chain, glycogen synthase and the branching enzyme extend and branch it, while phosphorylase isoforms with their phosphorylase kinase subunits and the debranching enzyme release glucose-1-phosphate, funnelled onward through phosphoglucomutase and glycolysis or, in liver, dephosphorylated for export. Control is imposed by insulin and glucagon signalling through the insulin receptor, IRS adaptors, AKT and GSK3, and by protein phosphatase 1 catalytic subunits directed to glycogen particles by PPP1R3 targeting subunits. Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase and glycophagy components clear glycogen by autophagy. Loss of individual steps causes the glycogen storage diseases, Pompe disease, and the polyglucosan accumulation of Lafora disease.

regulation of respiratory system process controls how fast and how deeply an animal breathes, tuning ventilation to metabolic demand and blood gas levels. Most of the genes here act not in the lung but in the brainstem circuits that generate and pace respiratory rhythm, which is why their loss produces central hypoventilation, apnoea and neonatal respiratory failure rather than airway disease. Transcription factors including PHOX2B, TLX3, GSX2, PBX3 and TSHZ3 specify the visceral and respiratory neurons of the medulla, while glycine receptor subunits, neuroligins and CC2D1A set the excitatory-inhibitory balance and synaptic wiring within the rhythm-generating network. Adenosine A1 receptors and the astrocytic Na+/K+ ATPase ATP1A2 couple neuronal activity and metabolic state to breathing frequency. MECP2 links the pathway to the disordered breathing of Rett syndrome, placing it at the intersection of neurodevelopment and autonomic homeostasis.

Breathing must be adjusted continuously to match metabolic demand, and this set concerns the regulation of respiratory system processes — chiefly the rate, depth and rhythm of ventilation generated by brainstem circuits. Its importance is clearest when it fails: congenital central hypoventilation, in which PHOX2B mutations disrupt development of the autonomic and chemosensory neurons that sense carbon dioxide, and the breathing pauses and apnoeas of Rett syndrome caused by loss of MECP2. Several members are transcription factors that specify medullary and pontine respiratory neurons and their neurotransmitter identity, including TLX3, PBX3, GSX2 and TSHZ3. Others tune the excitability and synaptic balance of the resulting network: glycine receptor and neuroligin components shape inhibitory transmission onto rhythm-generating neurons, adenosine signalling depresses respiratory drive, and glutaminase supplies excitatory neurotransmitter. The pathway thus links neural development to autonomic homeostatic control.

cellular response to leptin stimulus describes how cells read the adipose-derived hormone leptin, the signal that reports how much fat the body is carrying. Hypothalamic neurons use this input to suppress appetite and raise energy expenditure, while peripheral tissues adjust glucose handling and lipid storage; loss of leptin or its receptor produces severe early-onset obesity and hyperphagia, and obesity itself is characterised by resistance to the signal. Binding to the long-form receptor activates JAK-STAT signalling, with STAT3 carrying transcriptional output to targets governing feeding and metabolism, and SIRT1 and nuclear receptors such as NR4A3 shaping the response. Ciliary and BBSome components including BBS2, BBS4 and MKKS are required to traffic the receptor and sustain sensitivity, linking this hormone axis to cilium biology, and downstream effects extend to glucokinase-dependent glucose sensing.

Leptin is secreted by white adipocytes in proportion to fat mass, and the cellular response to it is how tissues read that signal and adjust appetite, energy expenditure and metabolic gene expression. Hypothalamic neurons are the best-known responders, where leptin binding to its receptor drives STAT3-dependent transcription that suppresses food intake; loss of either the hormone or its receptor causes severe early-onset obesity and hypogonadism. Trafficking of the receptor to the cell surface and its signalling competence depend on the BBS/chaperonin-like proteins represented here by BBS2, BBS4 and MKKS, explaining the leptin resistance and obesity of ciliopathy syndromes. Downstream and cooperating factors include SIRT1, nuclear receptor NR4A3 and glucokinase, linking the response to insulin sensitivity, glucose handling and lipid signalling rather than to appetite alone.

type B pancreatic cell proliferation describes the expansion of insulin-secreting beta cells within pancreatic islets, the process that sets and maintains functional beta cell mass. It matters because beta cell number determines how much insulin can be released on demand: mass expands during pregnancy, obesity and insulin resistance, and its failure to keep pace underlies the transition to type 2 diabetes, while autoimmune destruction of the same population causes type 1. The genes span growth-factor and hormonal inputs to the cell cycle, including insulin-like growth factor binding proteins, secreted regulators such as ANGPTL8 and CCN3, and the hepatic-islet protease inhibitor SERPINB1 that drives compensatory replication. Alongside these sit immediate-early and circadian transcription factors, the beta cell identity factor NKX6-1, and survival regulators such as BAD, linking nutrient sensing and metabolic demand to proliferation, differentiation state and apoptosis.

Insulin-secreting beta cells of the pancreatic islets are normally quiescent, but their number can expand during growth, pregnancy, obesity and insulin resistance; this proliferative capacity sets how much insulin a person can secrete and its loss underlies the beta cell deficit of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The genes here act as drivers and brakes on beta cell replication rather than on insulin release itself: hepatokine and secreted growth-regulatory signals, IGF-binding proteins that sequester and modulate IGF availability, a hepatocyte-derived protease inhibitor that stimulates beta cell mitosis, and apoptotic and stress regulators such as BAD that couple nutrient sensing and survival to cycle entry. Nuclear receptors of the NR4A family and a circadian factor place proliferative decisions under transcriptional and daily metabolic control, while NKX6-1 maintains the mature beta cell identity that expanding cells must retain.

Macropinocytosis is the bulk, non-selective drinking of extracellular fluid, in which the plasma membrane throws up actin-driven ruffles that close back on themselves to trap a large droplet in a macropinosome up to several micrometres across. It lets cells sample soluble antigen, scavenge extracellular protein and amino acids as a nutrient source, and internalise surface receptors in bulk; dendritic cells and macrophages depend on it for immune surveillance, and tumour cells with activated Ras exploit it to feed on serum protein. It is also the route many viruses and bacteria use to enter cells. The genes point to the actin and Rho-GTPase machinery that builds the ruffle, notably a Rac exchange factor and a capping-protein regulator, together with endosomal adaptors and sorting nexins that shape and mature the resulting vesicle, plus kinase and ion-channel inputs that control ruffling and inflammasome-linked responses.

Macropinocytosis is the bulk, non-selective drinking of extracellular fluid: the plasma membrane throws up actin-driven ruffles that close back on themselves, trapping a droplet of medium in a large, irregular macropinosome up to several micrometres across. Cells use it to sample soluble antigen, to scavenge extracellular protein and amino acids as a nutrient source, and as an entry route exploited by viruses and bacteria; in macrophages and dendritic cells it is a major contributor to immune surveillance, and in RAS-driven tumour cells it supports growth under nutrient limitation. The process depends on regulated actin remodelling at the cortex, with capping-protein regulators and a Rac-directed guanine nucleotide exchange factor shaping the ruffle, kinases downstream of stress signalling tuning cytoskeletal dynamics, and endosomal adaptors and sorting nexins together with Rab and SNARE proteins directing macropinosome closure, maturation and traffic toward lysosomal degradation.

Protein localization to cytoskeleton covers the targeting and retention of proteins on microtubules, actin filaments and the centrosome, which is how a cell decides where its machinery acts rather than merely whether it is present. Correct positioning underlies mitotic spindle assembly and chromosome segregation, centriole duplication and ciliogenesis, cell polarity and directed migration; its failure produces multipolar divisions, aneuploidy, microcephaly and ciliopathies. The genes describe the docking platforms and their cargo adaptors: centrosomal and pericentriolar scaffolds such as PCM1, CEP131 and CEP192 that recruit satellite and appendage components, microtubule plus-end tracking proteins of the MAPRE/EB family and GAS2L cross-linkers, dynactin and BICD/HOOK adaptors that load dynein cargo, and kinases including AURKA, GSK3B, CSNK1D and MARK4 that switch attachment on and off. Depalmitoylating ABHD17 enzymes and ubiquitin-pathway members add reversible membrane and turnover control to the same targeting decisions.

Getting a protein to the right place on the cytoskeleton is what gives microtubules and actin filaments their functional identity, and this pathway covers the targeting and retention steps that put cargo, regulators and scaffolds onto those filaments. It underlies centrosome and centriole composition, cilium assembly, spindle organization and directed transport, so its failure shows up as mitotic errors, microcephaly and ciliopathy. Much of the machinery here is centrosomal or satellite-associated, including several CEP proteins, PCM1 and STIL, which recruit components to the centriole and distal appendages; the end-binding proteins encoded by MAPRE1-3 mark growing microtubule plus ends and load partners such as GAS2L1 and APC there. Kinases including AURKA, GSK3B, CSNK1D and MARK4 set these interactions dynamically, while dynactin and HOOK3 link the network to motor-driven traffic and Golgi positioning.

glucose import in response to insulin stimulus is the step that lets muscle and adipose tissue clear glucose from the blood after a meal, and its impairment is the defining lesion of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Insulin signalling causes storage vesicles holding the transporter GLUT4 (SLC2A4) to translocate to the plasma membrane, raising glucose uptake many-fold without new transporter synthesis. The genes point to the machinery that builds and traffics these vesicles: TRARG1 marks GLUT4 storage compartments and promotes their insulin-responsive delivery, and the palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC7 modifies substrates that tune this trafficking, linking protein lipidation to transporter targeting. Fatty acid transport proteins couple the same stimulus to lipid uptake, and a sarcoglycan component ties the response to the muscle membrane cytoskeleton. The pathway sits downstream of the insulin receptor and PI3K-AKT cascade and upstream of glycogen and triglyceride storage.

After a meal, insulin tells muscle and fat cells to take up glucose from the blood, and this pathway is the transport step that carries out that instruction. It sets whole-body glucose tolerance: when the response is blunted, glucose stays in the circulation and insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes follow. The central effector is the GLUT4 transporter, held in intracellular storage vesicles under basal conditions and translocated to the plasma membrane when insulin signalling reaches the cell surface. TRARG1 is a component of those GLUT4 storage vesicles and supports their trafficking, while ZDHHC7 palmitoylates GLUT4 and influences its sorting. Fatty acid transport proteins of the SLC27 family link this uptake to lipid handling in the same insulin-responsive tissues, and the sarcoglycan component ties it to the muscle membrane environment in which much postprandial glucose disposal occurs.

negative regulation of protein kinase activity by regulation of protein phosphorylation describes how cells switch kinases off by controlling whether the kinase itself is phosphorylated, rather than by blocking its substrate or degrading it. This form of restraint sets the duration of signalling bursts and prevents runaway kinase output in stress responses, cell cycle progression and innate immune activation. The genes point to two convergent themes: the adenosine deaminases that edit double-stranded RNA and thereby limit activation of the RNA-sensing kinase PKR, keeping translational shutdown and interferon-driven inflammation in check; and nucleolar and cytoskeletal regulators including NPM1, CDK5RAP3 and CORO1C that damp CDK and stress-kinase activity through phosphorylation-dependent interactions. Loss of such braking permits sustained kinase signalling, and the RNA-editing arm in particular guards against autoinflammatory disease driven by misread endogenous transcripts.

Kinases are switched off as well as on, and one route to shutting them down is to alter their own phosphorylation state rather than block their catalytic site directly. This form of negative regulation of protein kinase activity keeps signalling transient, sets thresholds for stress responses, and prevents the sustained kinase output that drives inappropriate proliferation or cell death. The genes here act indirectly on kinase phosphorylation: the RNA-editing enzymes ADAR and ADARB1 limit activation of the double-stranded RNA-sensing kinase PKR by marking cellular RNA as self, thereby restraining translational shutdown and interferon-driven signalling; CDK5RAP3 and the nucleolar chaperone NPM1 modulate kinase and cyclin-dependent kinase signalling in growth and stress pathways. Loss of such restraint contributes to autoinflammatory disease and to dysregulated cell-cycle and stress kinase output in cancer.

Epigenetic programming in the zygotic pronuclei is the wholesale rewriting of DNA methylation and chromatin marks that happens in the hours after fertilization, before the one-cell embryo divides. It converts two highly specialized gametic genomes into a totipotent one, and its failure produces developmental arrest, imprinting disorders and recurrent hydatidiform mole. The paternal pronucleus is actively demethylated by TET3-driven oxidation of 5-methylcytosine, while the maternal pronucleus, marked by DPPA3 binding to H3K9me2 laid down by KDM1B and the SUV39H methyltransferases, is shielded from the same enzymes. Imprinted loci in both genomes escape erasure through ZNF445 and the maternal-effect machinery, with DNMT3L supporting the oocyte methylation that must be preserved. Subcortical maternal complex proteins such as PADI6 and TLE6 supply the oocyte-derived scaffold on which this asymmetric reprogramming depends.

Immediately after fertilization the two parental genomes sit in separate pronuclei in the same cytoplasm and are treated very differently, and this asymmetric epigenetic reprogramming is what converts two terminally differentiated gametes into a totipotent embryo. The paternal chromatin, stripped of protamines, undergoes active demethylation driven by the dioxygenase TET3, while the maternal genome is shielded: DPPA3 (Stella) binds H3K9me2-marked maternal chromatin and blocks TET3 access, with SUV39H enzymes supplying the heterochromatic methylation that defines it. Against this global erasure, imprinted loci must keep their gamete-of-origin marks, which requires DNMT3L and the zinc-finger protein ZNF445, while KDM1B removes H3K4 methylation during oocyte imprint establishment. Subcortical maternal complex components such as PADI6 and TLE6 supply the oocyte-derived scaffold. Failure produces imprinting disorders, early embryonic arrest and recurrent hydatidiform mole.

host-mediated suppression of viral proces covers the ways an infected cell or organism actively blocks steps of the viral life cycle rather than merely detecting the pathogen, and it determines whether an incoming virus establishes productive replication or is silenced. The genes span several distinct blocking strategies: soluble innate effectors such as lactoferrin and the pentraxins that neutralise particles before entry, chemokines of the CCL3/CCL4/CCL5 family that occupy the CCR5 coreceptor and shut out HIV while recruiting leukocytes, and a large nuclear arm that represses viral promoters. There, chromatin and transcription regulators including HDAC1, BRD4, REST, JUN and TARDBP act on integrated proviruses and viral enhancers to enforce transcriptional latency or restrict genome expression. Loss of this restriction favours viral reactivation and spread, and its manipulation underlies both latency-reversal and silencing approaches to antiviral therapy.

Infected cells push back against the virus that occupies them, and this collection captures host activities that interfere with viral processes rather than simply detecting the pathogen. Some members act by shutting down viral gene expression: chromatin and transcriptional regulators such as HDAC1, BRD4, REST and the repressive activity of host factors on viral promoters keep integrated or episomal viral templates silent, which is how latency is imposed and maintained. Others act extracellularly — lactoferrin and the pentraxins bind and neutralise particles or block attachment, while the CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5 chemokines occupy the coreceptor used by HIV and recruit leukocytes to the site of infection. Transcription factors including JUN and TFAP4 tie this restriction to inflammatory and stress signalling. When these defences fail, viral replication proceeds unchecked or latent reservoirs reactivate.

mitotic G1/S transition checkpoint signaling is the surveillance step that decides whether a cell in G1 is fit to begin copying its DNA, and blocks entry into S phase when it is not. It is the main guard against replicating a damaged genome, and its loss is one of the commonest routes to unchecked proliferation in cancer. The core logic runs through p53 induction of the CDK inhibitor p21, which restrains cyclin E/CDK2 and holds the retinoblastoma pathway in its repressive state; parallel inputs degrade cyclin D1 through the ubiquitin ligase substrate receptor FBXO31 and signal damage via PLK3, DNA-PK and the RPA-associated sensor RFWD3. Cytoplasmic nuclease activity such as TREX1 limits self-DNA accumulation that would otherwise trigger the response. Arrest here allows repair, or commits the cell to senescence or apoptosis rather than division.

Before a cell commits to replicating its genome it must confirm that conditions are suitable, and the G1/S transition checkpoint is the brake that holds it in G1 when they are not. Loss of this restraint allows damaged or under-resourced cells to enter S phase, propagating mutations and driving transformation, which is why several of its components are tumour suppressors and its bypass is a hallmark of cancer. The core logic couples DNA damage sensing to cyclin-dependent kinase inhibition: p53 induces the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A, which blocks cyclin D1-CDK and CDK2 activity and prevents origin firing, while replication protein A subunits and RFWD3 report single-stranded DNA and help route the response. Additional regulators direct destruction of cyclin D1 and modulate apoptotic commitment, so the checkpoint decides not only whether to pause but whether to die.

biological phase covers the timed stages that cyclical developmental programs pass through, and here the genes point to the hair follicle cycle and the epidermal appendage patterning that depends on it. Follicles alternate between growth, regression and rest, and the switch between those stages determines hair density, wound-associated regeneration and the barrier properties of skin; mutations in these components cause hair loss, palmoplantar keratoderma and skin fragility syndromes. WNT ligands with beta-catenin drive the growth phase and specify placode fate, TGFB2 signals the transition into regression, and MSX2 acts in the transcriptional program of the follicle matrix. Adhesion and cytoskeletal linkage through P-cadherin and kindlin-1 hold the specialised epithelium together, while SPINK5 restrains protease activity in the differentiating layers. Together they illustrate how phase transitions in a tissue are enforced by coupling signalling to adhesion.

Many developmental programmes run as discrete stages rather than continuously, and this set captures the regulators that define and time such a biological phase — most recognisably the cyclical phases of the hair follicle, whose growth, regression and rest periods repeat throughout life. Wnt ligands such as WNT10B and WNT5A acting through beta-catenin drive the growth phase and follicular induction, while TGFB2 signalling pushes follicles into regression, and the transcription factor MSX2 sets the timing of hair shaft differentiation. Adhesion and structural components, including P-cadherin and the focal adhesion protein encoded by FERMT1, hold the epithelial compartments together during these transitions; the protease inhibitor SPINK5 restrains proteolysis in overlying epidermis. Mutations in these genes cause hair loss and hypotrichosis, skin fragility syndromes, and Netherton syndrome, showing how stage boundaries, once mistimed, disrupt whole tissues.

Lipoprotein localization covers the routing of lipoproteins from the cells that build them to the tissues that consume them, the step that turns dietary and hepatic lipid into circulating cholesterol and triglyceride. It sets plasma lipid levels, and its failure produces abetalipoproteinemia, chylomicron retention disease and, at the receptor end, defective clearance and atherosclerosis. Assembly in the endoplasmic reticulum requires apolipoprotein B, the lipid transfer activity of MTTP, and cargo receptors such as SURF4 that load particles into COPII vesicles budded by SAR1A/SAR1B and the large-cargo TANGO1 machinery. On the receiving side, LRP1, CD36, CUBN and the scavenger receptor MSR1 capture particles for endocytosis, while PPARG and RXRA set the transcriptional tone and several microRNAs tune apolipoprotein output. Palmitoyltransferases and lipid-binding proteins support trafficking through membranes, linking secretory vesicle transport to whole-body lipid distribution.

Lipoprotein localization covers the steps that put lipoproteins where they must be: assembled and loaded in the endoplasmic reticulum, packaged into secretory carriers for export from liver and intestine, and captured at the surface of target cells for uptake. This traffic is how dietary and hepatic lipid is distributed to peripheral tissues, and its failure produces abetalipoproteinaemia and chylomicron retention disease, fat malabsorption and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, or conversely the retention of atherogenic particles in the artery wall. Apolipoprotein B is edited by a cytidine deaminase to generate the intestinal isoform, lipidated by microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, and loaded into large COPII carriers requiring SAR1B, TANGO1 and the cargo receptor SURF4. At the receiving end, LRP1, CD36, cubilin and a scavenger receptor mediate binding and endocytosis, with nuclear receptors and microRNAs setting the expression of the machinery.

Depyrimidination is the first step of base excision repair acting on damaged or mispaired cytosine and thymine: a DNA glycosylase cleaves the N-glycosidic bond and releases the offending pyrimidine, leaving an abasic sugar for downstream AP endonuclease, polymerase and ligase steps to restore. This removal is how cells cope with spontaneous cytosine deamination, oxidative pyrimidine lesions such as thymine glycol, and alkylation damage; failure raises mutation rates at CpG sites and contributes to cancer predisposition, as seen with germline defects in NTHL1 and MBD4. The genes are the pyrimidine-directed glycosylases: uracil-specific UNG and SMUG1, TDG and MBD4 acting on G:U and G:T mismatches at methylated CpGs, and NTHL1 with NEIL1 and NEIL2 handling ring-fragmented oxidation products. TDG additionally excises oxidised 5-methylcytosine derivatives, linking this repair chemistry to active DNA demethylation and epigenetic reprogramming.

Cytosine and thymine in DNA are chemically fragile: they deaminate, oxidise and pick up alkyl groups, and a mispaired or damaged pyrimidine left in place becomes a mutation at the next round of replication. Depyrimidination is the excision step that prevents this, cleaving the N-glycosidic bond between deoxyribose and a damaged or inappropriate C or T base and leaving an abasic sugar for downstream processing. The glycosylases here cover complementary substrate ranges — uracil arising from cytosine deamination or misincorporation, thymine mispaired with guanine at deaminated methylcytosine, and oxidised or ring-fragmented pyrimidines such as thymine glycol and hydantoins. The resulting abasic site is incised and repaired by the rest of the base excision repair route, so this chemistry is the entry point to that pathway. Loss of these activities raises spontaneous mutation rates; MBD4 and TDG additionally link repair to CpG methylation and epigenetic turnover.

actin nucleation is the rate-limiting birth of new actin filaments, the step that decides where and when a cell builds fresh cytoskeleton. Because filament elongation is fast but spontaneous seed formation is not, nucleators control lamellipodial protrusion, cell migration, endocytosis, phagocytosis, membrane tubule scission and sarcomere assembly; their loss produces immunodeficiency, nemaline myopathy and neurodevelopmental disease. The core machinery here is the seven-subunit Arp2/3 complex, whose actin-related subunits mimic a filament barbed end, together with the WAVE regulatory complex and WASH, WHAMM and JMY activators that recruit it to plasma membrane, endosomes and Golgi. Formins and Spire-family and leiomodin proteins nucleate unbranched filaments instead, while arpin, GMF, coronins, gelsolin and CARMIL proteins impose negative regulation and turnover, so that nucleation is spatially restricted and reversible rather than continuous.

Building a new actin filament from scratch is kinetically the hardest part of making one, and actin nucleation is the step that overcomes it: monomers are gathered into a stable seed from which rapid elongation follows. Cells depend on it for lamellipodial protrusion and migration, endocytosis, phagocytosis, junction assembly, sarcomere thin-filament length control and the fission of endosomal and Golgi membranes. The core machinery here is the Arp2/3 complex with its ARPC subunits, switched on by WAVE-family and WASH complex nucleation-promoting factors together with JMY and WHAMM, and restrained by ARPIN, coronins and GMF. Formins and the Spire proteins nucleate by a separate, profilin-linked route, while leiomodins seed thin filaments in muscle and gelsolin, scinderin and capping regulators such as the CARMILs set how many filament ends are available. Loss of these activities impairs immune cell motility, vesicle traffic and myofibril integrity, as in nemaline myopathy.

Regulatory T cell differentiation is the programme by which a naive T cell becomes a suppressive regulatory T cell rather than an effector one, and it is what keeps immune responses from turning on self tissue. Its failure causes autoimmunity and severe early-onset multi-organ inflammation, as seen when FOXP3 is mutated; its excess allows tumours to evade immune attack. Commitment depends on TGF-beta and IL-2 signalling through the common gamma chain, TCR and CD28 co-stimulation of defined strength, and induction of FOXP3 with cofactors including FOXO3, YY1 and acetyltransferases that stabilise the locus. The resulting cells enforce tolerance using CTLA-4, LAG3, VSIR and galectin-9 to restrain antigen-presenting cells and effector T cells. Proteasome subunits, including immunoproteasome components, and antigen-presentation molecules place peptide processing and MHC class II display upstream of lineage choice, while microRNA processing and ubiquitin-dependent turnover tune the decision.

Regulatory T cells are the brake on adaptive immunity, and this programme describes how an uncommitted CD4 T cell acquires that suppressive identity. Without it, self-tolerance collapses: loss of the lineage-defining transcription factor FOXP3 causes fatal multi-organ autoimmunity in humans, while excessive differentiation lets tumours evade immune attack. Commitment depends on TGF-beta together with IL-2 signalling through the shared gamma chain, costimulation via CD28, and antigen presentation on MHC class II, with FOXP3 induction reinforced by chromatin-modifying and transcriptional partners such as KAT5, YY1 and ZBTB16, and opposed by lineage factors for other helper fates including RORC and IFN-gamma. Once established, these cells restrain effector responses through CTLA-4, LAG3 and other inhibitory receptors. Proteasome subunits, SOCS1 and FOXO3 tune the stability and magnitude of the response, linking protein turnover and cytokine feedback to peripheral tolerance.

regulation of viral genome replication covers the host machinery that raises or lowers how much viral nucleic acid a cell allows to be copied, and it is the decisive layer of cell-intrinsic antiviral defence sitting between sensing an infection and clearing it. Much of the content is interferon-induced restriction: cytidine deaminases of the APOBEC3 family and the RNA editor ADAR mutate viral genomes, the OAS-RNase L arm degrades viral RNA, PKR shuts down translation, MX1, IFIT and ISG20 block replication complexes directly, and IFITM proteins and tetherin act at membranes on entry and release. Upstream sensors such as IFI16, MDA5 and MAVS drive the interferon and cytokine output that installs these effectors, while ISG15 conjugation, TRIM ligases and RNA-binding factors tune the response. Some members are instead cofactors viruses exploit, so the pathway sets the balance of permissiveness versus restriction.

Whether a virus that has entered a cell actually copies its genome is decided largely by host factors, and regulation of viral genome replication covers both the restriction machinery that suppresses it and the host proteins viruses exploit to permit it. This is the effector layer of innate antiviral defence: outcomes range from cleared infection to persistent replication and, when restriction fails, unchecked viral spread. Cytosolic sensors such as IFIH1 and IFI16 signalling through MAVS drive interferon production, and the induced effectors act by distinct chemistries — APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases mutate viral DNA intermediates, ADAR edits double-stranded RNA, the OAS enzymes activate RNase L to degrade RNA, PKR and IFIT proteins block translation initiation, MX1 and the IFITM proteins impede uncoating and entry, and BST2 tethers budding virions. Chemokines and cytokines here recruit further immune response, while cyclophilins, helicases and poly(A)-binding proteins are co-opted as replication cofactors.

Intermediate filament organization governs how keratins, vimentin, desmin, neurofilaments and their relatives are arranged into the meshworks and bundles that give cells mechanical resilience. This is the cytoskeletal system that lets epidermis resist shearing, lets muscle transmit force across sarcomeres, sets axon calibre and conduction speed, and builds the transparent cytoskeleton of the lens; its failure produces epidermolysis bullosa simplex, palmoplantar keratoderma, hair and nail defects, desmin myopathy, cataract and neurofilament-related neuropathy. Organization depends on cross-linkers and anchors rather than the filament proteins alone: plectin and epiplakin tie filaments to each other and to junctions, while desmoplakin and plakophilins couple keratin networks to desmosomes so force is distributed across an epithelial sheet. Chaperone and ubiquitin-ligase components such as DNAJB6 and KLHL24 control filament turnover, linking network architecture to protein quality control and to cell-type-specific differentiation programs.

Intermediate filaments give cells their mechanical resilience, and this pathway covers how those filaments are spatially arranged one into meshworks, bundles and anchored networks rather than dispersed subunits. The output is tissue-specific: keratin pairs build the load-bearing scaffold of epidermis, hair shaft and cornea, desmin supports muscle, GFAP and the neurofilament triplet with peripherin and alpha-internexin set axonal calibre and glial architecture, vimentin serves mesenchymal cells, and lens-specific beaded filament proteins maintain optical clarity. Organization depends on cross-linkers and anchors such as plectin, desmoplakin, epiplakin and plakophilins, which tie filaments to desmosomes and hemidesmosomes, with chaperone and ubiquitin-pathway components including DNAJB6 and KLHL24 controlling filament protein turnover. Disruption produces blistering skin disease, epidermolytic and palmoplantar keratodermas, hair and nail defects, corneal dystrophies, cataract, myofibrillar myopathy and neurodegeneration with axonal filament accumulation.

Establishment of epithelial cell apical/basal polarity is the process by which an epithelial cell defines a top and a bottom — an apical surface facing a lumen or the outside world and a basolateral surface contacting neighbours and basement membrane. This asymmetry is what makes epithelia able to form tubes, absorb and secrete directionally, and act as barriers; its loss accompanies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and carcinoma progression. Rho-family GTPase signalling through CDC42 and RHOA, tuned by regulators such as OPHN1 and SH3BP1, orients the actin cytoskeleton, while ezrin, moesin and the scaffold NHERF1 tether apical membrane proteins to cortical actin. Non-centrosomal microtubule anchoring by CAMSAP3, laminin contact with the basement membrane, planar cell polarity input via PTK7 and WNT5A, and ciliary trafficking components together position the apical domain and coordinate lumen formation during tissue morphogenesis.

Epithelial sheets only work as barriers and secretory surfaces because each cell distinguishes an apical face from a basolateral one, and establishing that apicobasal polarity is what this biology does. The axis determines where microvilli and junctions form, which direction transport runs, and how oriented divisions keep a monolayer or tubule lumen intact; its loss underlies cystic and tubulogenesis defects and features prominently in carcinoma progression. Small GTPase signalling through CDC42 and RHOA, with regulators such as SH3BP1 and OPHN1, patterns the cortex, while ezrin and moesin link apical membrane to actin and NHERF1 anchors membrane proteins there. CAMSAP3 organises non-centrosomal microtubule minus ends to give the cell a vertical array, basement membrane laminin supplies the basal cue, and WNT5A and PTK7 tie polarity to planar and ciliary signalling.

cell-cell junction organization builds, remodels and takes apart the physical contacts that hold cells together in a tissue, and it is what makes an epithelium a barrier rather than a collection of cells. Without it, sheets cannot seal, apical-basal polarity is lost, and cells detach and become invasive, as happens when E-cadherin is silenced by SNAI1/SNAI2 during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The genes span the major junction classes: classical and desmosomal cadherins with their catenin, plakin and plakophilin plaques, claudins and occludin with ZO-family scaffolds at tight junctions, nectins and JAM proteins, and connexins forming gap junctions for direct intercellular coupling. Assembly is coupled to the actin cytoskeleton through vinculin, talin and Rho-family GTPases, and is directed by PAR/Crumbs polarity complexes and by TGF-beta and Wnt signals. Consequences of failure include leaky endothelium, blistering skin disease, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and defective glomerular filtration.

Epithelia and endothelia hold together and seal off compartments through adherens junctions, tight junctions, desmosomes and gap junctions, and the assembly, remodelling and disassembly of these contacts is what this pathway covers. It sets up apical-basal polarity, creates the paracellular barrier that keeps blood separate from tissue and urine separate from filtrate, and permits electrical and metabolic coupling between neighbours. Classical cadherins and nectins mediate adhesion and link through catenins, plakophilins and desmoplakin to actin and intermediate filaments; claudins and occludin with the scaffolds ZO-1 to ZO-3 and PAR/Crumbs polarity complexes build the tight junction; connexins form channels. Rho-family GTPases, ROCK and kinases such as PRKCI tune contractility at the junctional belt, while TGF-beta signalling and SNAI1/SNAI2 dismantle it during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Loss of junctional integrity underlies deafness, skin blistering, nephrotic and cardiomyopathic disease, leaky vasculature and tumour invasion.

MHC class I biosynthetic process covers the making of the class I antigen-presenting molecules that display intracellular peptides to cytotoxic T cells and provide the self-signal read by NK cell receptors. Its output determines whether virus-infected or transformed cells are recognised and killed; loss of class I expression is a common route by which tumours and persistent viruses escape immune surveillance. Control is largely transcriptional: NLRC5 acts as the class I transactivator, working with the broader machinery shared with CIITA-driven class II expression, while type I and type III interferons and general transcription factor components such as TAF7 tune the level of induction. Chaperone and inflammatory regulators, including HSPH1 and NLRP12, modulate assembly and dampen excessive induction, linking antigen presentation capacity to innate immune activation state.

Every nucleated cell displays fragments of its internal proteins on MHC class I molecules, allowing cytotoxic T cells to detect infection or malignancy; this pathway covers the production of those molecules and the signals that set how much of them a cell makes. Expression is not constitutive but tuned: NLRC5 acts as the dedicated transactivator driving MHC class I heavy chain and peptide-loading gene transcription, with CIITA contributing as the related master regulator of the class II arm, and general transcription machinery such as TAF7 required for output. Interferons, including type I and type III members, and other cytokines raise antigen presentation during infection, while NLRP12 restrains inflammatory signalling. Loss of this induction lets tumours and viruses escape T cell surveillance, whereas excessive presentation contributes to autoimmune tissue damage.

Positive regulation of MHC class I biosynthetic process describes the signals that raise production of the class I antigen-presentation machinery, determining how much of a cell's internal protein content is displayed to CD8 T cells and how visible infected or transformed cells are to cytotoxic surveillance. Tumours and viruses that silence this output escape killing, while excessive induction contributes to autoimmune tissue damage. The core mechanism is transcriptional: NLRC5 acts as the class I transactivator, assembling with the enhanceosome at promoter modules that also serve the class II regulator CIITA, and its activity is driven by interferon and other inflammatory cues, including the interferon-lambda and IL-33 signals represented here. Chaperone support and NLR-family modulation such as NLRP12 tune the response, linking innate immune sensing to the amount of peptide-loaded MHC class I reaching the cell surface.

MHC class I molecules display intracellular peptides to cytotoxic T cells, so raising their production tunes how visible a cell is to immune surveillance. Positive regulation of MHC class I biosynthesis governs this output, and it matters most when infection or interferon exposure demands that antigen presentation be upregulated; tumours that suppress it escape T cell killing. The central component here is NLRC5, a nucleotide-binding domain protein that acts in the nucleus as a transactivator of class I heavy chain and associated peptide-loading genes, paralleling the role of CIITA at class II promoters. Interferon-lambda and the alarmin IL33 provide cytokine input, while a heat shock protein family member links the process to chaperone capacity. Because presentation depends on transcription of the whole loading pathway, this regulation sits upstream of both antiviral and antitumour cytotoxic responses.

endothelial cell differentiation is the program by which mesodermal, bone marrow or neural crest progenitors become the flattened cells that line blood vessels, lymphatics and body cavities. It sets up the vascular and lymphatic endothelium, and with it barrier function, blood fluidity, and the arterial, venous and lymphatic identities that give a circulatory tree its architecture; its failure underlies vascular malformations and defective angiogenesis. Master regulators such as ETV2, SOX17/SOX18 and NR2F2 commit and subtype the lineage, while Notch (NOTCH1, HEY1/HEY2, RBPJ), BMP/TGF-beta receptor signalling through ACVRL1 and BMPR2, and VEGFA-KDR input pattern arterial versus venous fates and PROX1 drives lymphatic specification. Much of the gene complement builds the junctional and adhesive apparatus that defines the mature cell — VE-cadherin, PECAM1, claudin-5 and tight junction scaffolds — stabilised by Rap1 and sphingosine-1-phosphate signalling, with microRNAs tuning the transition.

Blood and lymphatic vessels are lined by a single sheet of flattened cells, and endothelial cell differentiation is how mesodermal, bone marrow or neural crest precursors acquire that identity. It determines whether vessels form at all, whether they become arterial, venous or lymphatic, and whether the barrier they present to blood is tight or leaky. Lineage specification runs through transcription factors such as ETV2, SOX17/SOX18, NR2F2 and PROX1, downstream of VEGFA signalling via KDR and NRP1, Notch-Delta/Jagged input with HEY1/HEY2, and BMP/TGF-beta receptors including ACVRL1, BMPR2 and SMAD4. Maturation brings the junctional and adhesion apparatus that defines the endothelium -- VE-cadherin, PECAM1, claudin-5 and the tight junction scaffolds -- plus Rap1 and Rho-kinase control of barrier tone and numerous microRNAs tuning the programme. Failure or corruption of these steps underlies cerebral cavernous malformation, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, and pathological angiogenesis in tumours.

cell redox homeostasis keeps the thiol-disulfide balance of the cytosol, mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum within the narrow range that enzymes, transcription factors and folding intermediates require. It sets how much hydrogen peroxide and superoxide a cell tolerates as signal rather than damage, and its failure produces oxidative injury, protein misfolding and the redox stress that accompanies inflammation, ischaemia and neurodegeneration. The core machinery is the thioredoxin and glutaredoxin systems with their NADPH-dependent reductases, peroxiredoxins that clear peroxide, glutathione synthesis through GCLC, and NRF2-driven induction of NQO1 and other detoxifying enzymes. In the ER, ERO1 oxidases and ERP44 couple oxidative protein folding to this balance, while selenoproteins and nitric oxide synthases tie selenium status and nitrosative signalling into the same network, linking redox control to metabolism, immunity and vascular tone.

Cells hold their internal thiol-disulfide balance within a narrow window, and this redox homeostasis is what keeps enzymes catalytically competent, protein folding accurate, and hydrogen peroxide usable as a signal rather than a source of damage. Its collapse produces oxidative stress, protein misfolding, and the damage associated with inflammation, ischaemia and neurodegeneration. The work is done by coupled thiol systems: peroxiredoxins reduce peroxides and are recycled by thioredoxins and the NADPH-dependent thioredoxin reductases, while glutaredoxins and glutathione reductase maintain the glutathione pool whose synthesis begins with the GCLC-containing ligase. Oxidative folding in the endoplasmic reticulum depends on ERO1-type oxidases and resident selenoproteins, and BOLA-glutaredoxin partnerships link redox state to iron-sulfur cluster handling. NRF2 and NRF1 transcriptionally amplify antioxidant capacity when demand rises, with nitric oxide synthases and NADPH quinone oxidoreductase adding further redox-active chemistry.

Photoreceptor cell maintenance covers the processes that keep rods and cones alive and functional over a lifetime rather than building them in the first place, and its failure is the direct cause of inherited retinal degeneration: retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, Stargardt disease, and the retinal component of Usher and Bardet-Biedl syndromes. Photoreceptors are extreme cells, with a daily-renewed outer segment packed with phototransduction machinery, a narrow connecting cilium through which every protein must be trafficked, and constant oxidative and photic stress. The genes reflect those pressures: ciliary transport and basal body components, outer-segment structural and adhesion proteins such as PROM1, CRB1 and the Usher cadherin complex, retinoid recycling and clearance through ABCA4 and RDH12, and trophic and redox protection by the rod-derived cone viability factors. Together they sustain outer-segment renewal, ion and metabolite supply, and survival signalling.

Rods and cones are post-mitotic, metabolically strained cells that renew their outer segments daily, and photoreceptor cell maintenance is the set of activities that keeps them alive rather than letting them degenerate. Failure of these genes produces retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, Stargardt disease, and the retinal degeneration of Usher and Bardet-Biedl syndromes, making this biology the genetic basis of most inherited blindness. Several themes recur: the connecting cilium and its transport machinery, including BBS-complex subunits and nephrocystin-related proteins, deliver opsin and other cargo to the outer segment; adhesion and scaffold proteins such as USH2A, PCDH15, CDH23 and CRB1 hold photoreceptors in register with Muller cells and the pigment epithelium; and retinoid handling by ABCA4 and RDH12 clears toxic aldehyde intermediates of the visual cycle. Redox protection and glucose supply support the high energy demand.

regulation of cholesterol biosynthetic process is the control layer over sterol synthesis, setting how much cholesterol a cell makes to match what it already has. Because cholesterol is needed for membranes, steroid hormones and bile acids yet is toxic in excess, this feedback determines plasma lipid levels and underlies statin responsiveness and atherosclerosis risk. The core is sterol sensing in the endoplasmic reticulum: SCAP escorts the SREBF transcription factors to the Golgi for cleavage by site-1 and site-2 proteases, releasing factors that drive the enzymes of the mevalonate route, while INSIG1 retains the complex when sterols are abundant. Rate-limiting enzymes are also destroyed on demand by ERLIN-dependent and MARCHF6-mediated ER-associated degradation. Superimposed on this are AMPK and PKA phosphorylation, efflux transporters and apolipoproteins that alter sterol load, and a set of microRNAs that tune the transcriptional output.

Cells must make enough cholesterol for membranes and steroid precursors without accumulating a toxic excess, and this regulatory layer sets how fast the sterol synthesis route runs. Its centrepiece is sterol-sensing feedback at the endoplasmic reticulum: SCAP escorts the SREBF transcription factors to the Golgi, where the proteases encoded by MBTPS1 and MBTPS2 release their active fragments to switch on synthesis genes, while INSIG1 retains the complex when sterols are plentiful and the ERLIN proteins and the MARCHF6 ubiquitin ligase direct degradation of HMG-CoA reductase and other targets. Kinase input from AMPK and cAMP-dependent protein kinase ties output to energy status, efflux transporters and apolipoproteins report cellular sterol load, bile acid conversion by CYP7A1 provides disposal, and several microRNAs tune transcript levels. Loss of restraint here drives hypercholesterolaemia, hepatic steatosis and atherosclerotic disease.

Negative regulation of cholesterol biosynthetic process is the brake on the mevalonate pathway, the set of controls that shuts down sterol synthesis when a cell already has enough cholesterol. It keeps membrane sterol content within a narrow range and prevents the overproduction that drives hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis; it is also the node that statins and dietary sterols act through. The core mechanism is sterol-sensing feedback in the endoplasmic reticulum: when cholesterol or oxysterols accumulate, INSIG1 retains the SCAP-SREBP2 complex in the ER so the transcription factor is never processed to its active nuclear form, while INSIG1 together with the ERLIN1/ERLIN2 complex and the E3 ligase MARCHF6 targets HMG-CoA reductase for degradation. Layered on top is post-transcriptional repression by several microRNAs, and lipoprotein-mediated sterol delivery by APOE, which signals sufficiency from outside the cell.

Cells make cholesterol only when they lack it, and the braking machinery described here shuts the synthetic route down once sterol is plentiful. Its central event is sterol-dependent control of HMG-CoA reductase and of the transcription factor that drives the whole biosynthetic programme: INSIG1 retains the SCAP-SREBP complex in the endoplasmic reticulum so that SREBP is never cleaved and activated, while ERLIN1 and ERLIN2 together with the ER-resident ubiquitin ligase MARCHF6 direct reductase and other sterol-sensitive substrates to proteasomal degradation. Secreted APOE lowers the intracellular sterol demand by promoting lipoprotein uptake and efflux, and several microRNAs damp expression of biosynthetic and SREBP-pathway transcripts. Loss of this restraint leaves synthesis running against a full sterol pool, contributing to hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis; the same feedback loop is what statin therapy engages.

positive regulation of fat cell differentiation covers the signals and transcriptional programs that drive preadipocytes to become mature, lipid-storing adipocytes. This is how the body expands its capacity to buffer excess energy as triglyceride and to secrete adipokines, and its output determines fat depot size and distribution, insulin sensitivity, and susceptibility to obesity and lipodystrophy. At its core is the PPARG-CEBPA-CEBPB transcriptional cascade, reinforced by KLF5, ZBTB16 and EBF-like inputs and by insulin/AKT signalling. Much of the regulation is permissive: secreted Wnt antagonists such as SFRP1, SFRP2 and WIF1 relieve the Wnt block on adipogenesis, while BMP2 and BMP7 commit progenitors, BMP7 favouring brown fat. Hippo kinases (STK3/STK4, SAV1), sirtuin and methyltransferase chromatin modifiers, XBP1, and several microRNAs tune the rate, and mature markers like LPL, ADIRF and chemerin mark the differentiated state.

Preadipocytes become lipid-storing adipocytes through a transcriptional cascade, and this pathway collects the inputs that drive that conversion forward. It sets how much white and brown fat a body makes, and so bears on obesity, insulin sensitivity and the endocrine output of adipose tissue. At its core PPARG acts with the C/EBP factors alongside KLF5 and ZBTB16 to switch on the lipogenic and lipid-handling programme, including lipoprotein lipase for fatty acid uptake. Insulin acting through AKT1, BMP2 and BMP7, and secreted Wnt antagonists such as SFRP1, SFRP2 and WIF1, which relieve the anti-adipogenic Wnt signal, all push cells toward this fate, as do several microRNAs and Hippo kinase components. Adipokines and adipocyte-enriched products including chemerin, ADIRF and ADIG mark the differentiated state and feed back on it.

positive regulation of endothelial cell differentiation covers the signals that push progenitor and precursor cells toward an endothelial fate, the step that creates the lining of every blood and lymphatic vessel. It matters for embryonic vasculogenesis, for postnatal repair of damaged vessel walls, and for the arteriovenous patterning whose failure produces malformations: mutations in the BMP9/10 receptor arm represented here by ACVRL1 and GDF2 cause hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Mechanistically it combines BMP ligand and receptor signalling, Notch and Wnt/β-catenin input, and the master transcription factor ETV2 with helpers such as VEZF1 and ATOH8 that drive endothelial gene programmes. A large complement of microRNAs, including miR-21, miR-34a, miR-126-family relatives and miR-200c, tunes the strength and timing of that commitment, linking endothelial specification to angiogenesis, endothelial-to-haematopoietic transition and vascular homeostasis.

Blood vessels are built from mesodermal precursors that must be instructed to adopt an endothelial fate, and this pathway covers the inputs that push cells toward and reinforce that identity. It underlies embryonic vascular formation, postnatal angiogenesis and the arterial-versus-venous patterning of new vessels; when its components fail, malformed or arteriovenous-shunting vasculature results, as in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia caused by loss of the BMP9/10 receptor ACVRL1 and its signalling partners. BMP ligands such as BMP4, BMP6 and GDF2 act through this receptor axis, with TMEM100 and the transcriptional repressor ATOH8 as downstream effectors, while Notch1 signalling and Wnt-dependent beta-catenin shape arterial specification. ETV2 is the master transcription factor able to convert progenitors into endothelium, and VEZF1 supports endothelial gene expression. Several microRNAs are included as post-transcriptional tuners that raise the rate of this differentiation programme.

regulation of inner ear auditory receptor cell differentiation controls how many cochlear hair cells are made and where they sit, setting the precise mosaic of sensory hair cells and supporting cells that makes hearing possible. Because mammalian hair cells are not replaced after damage, the balance struck here determines lifelong auditory sensitivity, and its disruption produces congenital deafness or an abnormal sensory epithelium. The core logic is Notch-mediated lateral inhibition: a cell that begins to express the proneural factor ATOH1 presents DLL1 to its neighbours, activating NOTCH1 and inducing the repressors HES1, HES5 and HEY2, which extinguish ATOH1 in those neighbours and divert them to supporting-cell fates. MYCN and MYCL sustain progenitor proliferation before differentiation, while the splicing regulator ESRP1 shapes epithelial identity in the developing otic tissue. This circuitry is the target of efforts to regenerate hair cells.

Hearing depends on a fixed, non-renewable set of cochlear hair cells, and this pathway controls how many of them are made and where. It governs the decision, taken in the developing organ of Corti, between becoming a mechanosensory hair cell and becoming a supporting cell. The proneural transcription factor ATOH1 drives hair cell fate and is both necessary and sufficient for it; lateral inhibition through a Notch receptor and its DLL1 ligand restricts that fate to a spaced subset, with HES1, HES5 and HEY2 acting as repressors that damp ATOH1 in neighbouring cells. MYCN and MYCL sustain progenitor proliferation before differentiation, and ESRP1 shapes epithelial splicing programmes in the same tissue. Loss or imbalance of these regulators produces extra, missing or disordered hair cells and congenital sensorineural deafness, and reactivating the module is a central strategy in hair cell regeneration research.

regulation of T-helper cell differentiation controls how naive CD4 T cells are steered into effector fates — Th1, Th2, Th17, follicular helper or regulatory — and thereby sets the character of an adaptive immune response. Getting this wrong produces either failed defence against intracellular pathogens or autoimmune and allergic inflammation, which is why several of these genes are risk loci for inflammatory bowel disease and spondyloarthritis. Antigen presentation and costimulation through MHC class II, CD80/CD86 and OX40 initiate the decision; cytokines such as IL-12, IL-23, IL-27 and IL-2 signal through receptors and JAK–STAT to induce master transcription factors including TBX21, ZBTB7B, BCL6, FOXP3 and RORC-associated partners BATF and IRF4. Restraint is equally represented: SOCS5 and SMAD7 dampen cytokine signals, while RC3H1/2 and ZC3H12A degrade cytokine mRNAs to limit inflammatory helper programmes.

Naive CD4 T cells choose among effector fates after antigen encounter, and the control of T-helper cell differentiation sets how strongly and in which direction that choice is made. The balance determines whether an immune response clears intracellular pathogens, recruits antibody help, or restrains itself; skewing it produces autoimmunity, allergy, or failure to control infection. Cytokines and their receptors provide the instructive signals, with IL-12 and IL-23 family subunits and IL-27 acting through JAK3 and STAT5A, while co-stimulatory ligands on antigen-presenting cells and MHC class II molecules supply the context. Lineage-defining transcription factors read these inputs out: TBX21 for Th1, BCL6 for follicular helper, ZBTB7B for CD4 commitment, FOXP3 for regulatory cells, with IRF4, BATF and JUNB as shared partners. RNA-binding repressors such as ZC3H12A and the roquin proteins, together with SOCS5 and SMAD7, damp the programme once engaged.
