Transducing channels such as TRPV1 and TRPA1 open in response to heat and irritant chemicals, acid-sensing channels report tissue acidosis, and voltage-gated sodium channels including SCN9A and SCN11A set the threshold for firing and propagate the resulting action potentials; loss-of-function mutations in these genes, or in the transcription factor PRDM12 needed for nociceptor development, abolish pain sensation. Neuropeptides of the tachykinin family, NGF signalling through NTRK1, and inflammatory mediators such as TNF sensitize these endings, linking peripheral detection to inflammatory and chronic pain states.

cellular response to chemical stress is the broad set of programs a cell runs when its internal chemistry is perturbed — by oxidants, electrophiles, heavy metals, osmotic shifts or drugs — deciding whether the cell detoxifies and adapts or commits to death. It underlies tissue tolerance of inflammation and ischaemia, drug metabolism, and the neuronal vulnerability seen in Parkinson's disease, where PINK1, PRKN, PARK7 and LRRK2 act. Sensing is largely thiol-based: KEAP1 releases NFE2L2 to drive an antioxidant transcriptional program of NQO1, glutathione and thioredoxin enzymes, superoxide dismutases, peroxiredoxins and glutathione peroxidases, while cystine import through SLC7A11 sustains it. In parallel, the integrated stress response through EIF2AK3, ATF4 and DDIT3, ER stress via ERN1 and XBP1, FOXO and TP53 outputs, mTOR and AMPK metabolic rebalancing, autophagy and mitophagy, osmotic WNK signalling, and inflammasome or RIPK-dependent death pathways set the outcome.

Cells constantly meet chemical insults — reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, electrophiles, heavy metals, osmotic and redox imbalance — and this programme is the coordinated response that lets them survive or die cleanly. It underlies ageing, neurodegeneration, ischaemia–reperfusion injury and the resistance of tumour cells to oxidative and drug-induced killing. Antioxidant enzymes (superoxide dismutases, catalase, glutathione peroxidases, peroxiredoxins, thioredoxin and its reductase) detoxify oxidants, while KEAP1–NFE2L2 sensing of electrophiles drives transcription of NQO1, G6PD and the cystine importer SLC7A11 to rebuild glutathione and NADPH. Parallel arms include the endoplasmic reticulum stress branch through EIF2AK3, ERN1, ATF4 and DDIT3, FOXO and TP53-dependent transcription, mitophagy via PINK1 and PRKN, AMPK–mTOR metabolic adjustment, and osmotic signalling by WNK and STK39 kinases. Where damage exceeds repair, inflammasome activation, caspase-dependent apoptosis or RIPK3 necroptosis removes the cell.

Proton-transporting two-sector ATPase complex assembly builds the rotary proton pumps that convert an electrochemical gradient into ATP, or ATP hydrolysis into acidification of a compartment. Two related machines depend on it: the mitochondrial F1Fo ATP synthase that produces most cellular ATP, and the vacuolar V-ATPase that acidifies lysosomes, endosomes and the kidney intercalated-cell membrane. Neither assembles spontaneously; dedicated chaperones such as ATPAF1/ATPAF2 mature the F1 catalytic head, TMEM70 and TMEM242 act on membrane subunits, OXA1L inserts them into the inner membrane, and an ER-resident group including VMA21 and VMA12 assembles the V-ATPase V0 sector before delivery. Loss of these factors produces mitochondrial encephalocardiomyopathy with lactic acidosis, X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy, or distal renal tubular acidosis, illustrating that pump biogenesis limits both oxidative phosphorylation and organelle acidification.

Rotary proton-pumping ATPases — the mitochondrial ATP synthase and the vacuolar-type ATPase — must be built from many subunits and embedded correctly in a membrane before they can couple proton movement to ATP synthesis or hydrolysis, and this pathway covers that assembly. It matters because the finished machines supply most cellular ATP and acidify lysosomes and other organelles; defective assembly causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathy and, for the V-ATPase, distal renal tubular acidosis and X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy. Dedicated chaperones such as ATPAF1 and ATPAF2 escort the F1 catalytic subunits, TMEM70 and FMC1 assist assembly and stability of the complex, and OXA1L inserts membrane subunits from the matrix side. Endoplasmic reticulum factors including VMA21 and VMA12 perform the equivalent role for V-ATPase V0 subunits, linking organelle acidification to autophagic turnover.

tRNA aminoacylation for mitochondrial protein translation charges mitochondrial tRNAs with their cognate amino acids so that the organelle's own ribosomes can synthesise the thirteen subunits of the respiratory chain encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Each enzyme joins an amino acid to the 3'-hydroxyl of the terminal adenosine of its tRNA in an ATP-dependent two-step reaction, with proofreading that keeps mistranslation low in a compartment already burdened by oxidative stress. Most of these synthetases are nuclear-encoded and imported, and several, such as GARS1, are shared with the cytosolic translation apparatus. Because oxidative phosphorylation depends entirely on this step, loss-of-function mutations produce a recognisable family of mitochondrial diseases — leukoencephalopathy with brainstem involvement, sideroblastic anaemia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ovarian failure and hearing loss — with tissue specificity that reflects each tissue's reliance on mitochondrial energy production.

Mitochondria translate their own thirteen respiratory chain subunits on a dedicated ribosome, and that translation can only begin once each mitochondrial tRNA has been charged with its matching amino acid. The enzymes here are the mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which attach alanine, aspartate, glutamate, glycine, serine, threonine, tryptophan or tyrosine to the 3' end of the corresponding tRNA inside the organelle, supplying the substrates for mitochondrial protein synthesis. Because most of these genes are nuclear-encoded and imported, the pathway is a point where nuclear and mitochondrial gene expression must stay matched. Loss-of-function mutations cause a recognizable group of recessive mitochondrial diseases with combined respiratory chain deficiency and strikingly tissue-specific presentations u2014 leukoencephalopathy, cardiomyopathy, sideroblastic anemia, ovarian failure, hearing loss u2014 placing this charging step upstream of oxidative phosphorylation capacity in every tissue that depends on it.

Regulation of mitochondrial translation controls how much protein the mitochondrion makes from its own genome, tuning the supply of the thirteen core subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase to the rest of the organelle's assembly needs. Because those subunits must be produced in step with nuclear-encoded partners, defects here cause combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, with infantile lactic acidosis, cardiomyopathy and encephalopathy. The regulators act at several levels: mitochondrial tRNA and rRNA modification enzymes, including methyltransferases and pseudouridine synthases together with the RNase P subunit TRMT10C, determine decoding fidelity; ribosome assembly GTPases and an anti-association factor govern monosome and subunit maturation; LRPPRC stabilises and polyadenylates transcripts; and translational activators such as TACO1 select individual mRNAs. Others couple synthesis directly to complex assembly, delivering newly made subunits into cytochrome c oxidase and complex III. Folate one-carbon metabolism feeds in through formylmethionine and tRNA taurinomethylation.

Mitochondria translate their own handful of mRNAs, all encoding subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation complexes, and control over that translation sets how much respiratory chain a cell can build. The genes here modulate the rate and fidelity of mitoribosomal protein synthesis rather than performing peptide bond formation themselves: mitoribosome assembly GTPases and assembly factors such as MTG1, MTG2 and MALSU1 mature the large subunit, tRNA and rRNA modifying enzymes including TRMT10C, NSUN3, RPUSD3/4, TRUB2 and CDK5RAP1 tune decoding, LRPPRC stabilises and polyadenylates mitochondrial transcripts, and TACO1 acts as a translational activator for COX1. Others couple synthesis to co-translational insertion and complex assembly, as COA3 and UQCC2 do for cytochrome c oxidase and complex III. Loss of these regulators causes combined respiratory chain deficiency, lactic acidosis, encephalomyopathy and cardiomyopathy, and connects mitochondrial gene expression to cellular energy supply and one-carbon metabolism through SHMT2.

Positive regulation of mitochondrial translation describes the factors that raise the output of the mitochondrial ribosome, which synthesises the thirteen core subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation complexes encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Because those subunits must be made in stoichiometry with imported nuclear-encoded partners, boosting and coordinating this translation is what allows respiratory chain assembly to proceed, and loss of individual components causes infantile mitochondrial disease with combined complex deficiencies, lactic acidosis and encephalomyopathy. Mechanistically the group spans several layers: mitochondrial tRNA and rRNA modification enzymes such as TRMT10C, CDK5RAP1, METTL8 and the pseudouridine synthases, mitoribosome assembly factors including NGRN, MPV17L2 and RMND1, and mRNA-specific translational activators, notably TACO1, which is required for COX1 synthesis. Others, such as COA3 and UQCC2, couple nascent chain production directly to assembly of complexes IV and III, linking translation rate to respiratory demand.

Mitochondria translate their own handful of mRNAs into core subunits of the respiratory chain, and this pathway covers the factors that raise the rate and efficiency of that process. Because every one of the thirteen mitochondrially encoded proteins sits in complexes I, III, IV or the ATP synthase, boosting or sustaining mitoribosome output is directly tied to oxidative phosphorylation capacity, and loss of these activators produces combined respiratory chain deficiency, lactic acidosis and infantile encephalomyopathy. The genes act at several steps: tRNA and rRNA modification enzymes such as TRMT10C, CDK5RAP1 and the pseudouridine synthases RPUSD3, RPUSD4 and TRUB2 mature the RNA substrates, RNA-binding proteins including C1QBP, NGRN and FASTKD3 work within RNA granules and mitoribosome assembly, and translational activators such as TACO1 promote synthesis of specific messages, with COA3 and UQCC2 coupling output to assembly of complexes IV and III.

regulation of tooth mineralization controls how much calcium phosphate is deposited into enamel and dentin, and how well ordered the resulting crystal is. It is what gives teeth their hardness and wear resistance; when it fails the result is amelogenesis imperfecta, hypomineralized or hypoplastic enamel, and dentin defects seen in hereditary rickets and syndromic craniofacial disease. Ameloblasts secrete a provisional matrix of amelogenin, enamelin and amelotin that templates crystal growth, and proteinases such as MMP20 then degrade that matrix so mineral can expand to fill the space. Ion handling supports the same end: anion exchange and CFTR-dependent transport buffer the protons released as apatite forms, while DMP1 nucleates mineral in dentin. Transcriptional and signalling inputs including TFAP2A, BCOR and WNT6 set ameloblast and odontoblast identity upstream of secretion, tying this process to tooth morphogenesis and biomineralization generally.

Enamel and dentine become the hardest tissues in the body only if calcium phosphate deposition is timed and shaped by the matrix laid down before it, and this regulatory control over tooth mineralization sets how much mineral forms and where. When it fails the result is amelogenesis imperfecta, hypomineralized or hypoplastic enamel, and teeth that chip and decay. Secreted matrix proteins including amelogenin, enamelin, amelotin and the dentine phosphoprotein DMP1 template crystal growth, while the protease MMP20 degrades that matrix so crystals can expand and mature. Ion handling matters as much as protein: the anion exchanger SLC4A2 and the chloride channel CFTR support the pH buffering that ameloblasts need to neutralize protons released during mineral deposition. Transcriptional and signalling inputs such as TFAP2A, BCOR and WNT6 position and differentiate the enamel- and dentine-forming cells themselves.

Meiotic attachment of telomere to nuclear envelope tethers chromosome ends to the inner nuclear membrane during meiotic prophase so that homologous chromosomes can find each other and pair. Without it, telomeres fail to cluster into the transient bouquet, homolog synapsis and recombination are incomplete, and gametogenesis arrests — a route to infertility in both sexes. The mechanism is a dedicated cap built on the shelterin-bound telomere: TERB1 and TERB2 recruit MAJIN, which inserts into the inner nuclear membrane, and the complex couples through SUN1 to KASH partners and cytoskeletal motors that drag telomeres across the envelope to drive chromosome movement. SPDYA-CDK2 activity licenses and regulates this attachment. The pathway thus links nuclear envelope architecture, telomere biology and the chromosome dynamics that make meiotic recombination possible.

During meiotic prophase, chromosome ends must be tethered to the inner nuclear membrane so that cytoskeletal forces can move chromosomes and bring homologues into register for pairing and recombination. This telomere-to-nuclear-envelope attachment gathers telomeres into the bouquet configuration; without it, homologue pairing and synapsis fail, crossovers are not formed, and germ cells arrest, producing infertility in both sexes. A dedicated telomere adaptor complex built from TERB1, TERB2 and MAJIN caps the chromosome end, replacing shelterin contacts and anchoring the DNA directly in the membrane, where it couples to SUN1 and thence across the nuclear envelope to cytoplasmic dynein and the microtubule network. Cyclin-dependent kinase activity, acting with the meiotic activator SPDYA, times and licenses these attachments, linking envelope tethering to progression through the meiotic cell cycle.

Establishment of protein localization to telomere is the targeted delivery and loading of protective and enzymatic factors onto chromosome ends, the step that decides whether a telomere is capped or read as a broken chromosome. It sustains replicative capacity in stem and germ cells and, when hijacked, sustains cancer cell immortality; when it fails, telomeres shorten or fuse and cells enter senescence or crisis, as in telomere biology disorders such as dyskeratosis congenita. Shelterin components including TRF1, POT1 and TPP1 must be recruited to single- and double-stranded telomeric DNA, and telomerase itself must be trafficked there — TCAB1 directs the RNA component through Cajal bodies, while chaperonin subunits assist folding and USP7 controls the stability of loaded factors. Related activities bring homologous recombination and single-strand binding proteins to ends during replication and alternative telomere lengthening.

Telomeres are only protected if the right proteins are delivered to them, and establishment of protein localization to telomere covers the targeting and loading steps that put capping and elongation factors onto chromosome ends. Without it, chromosome termini are read as double-strand breaks, triggering fusions, senescence or crisis, while insufficient telomerase recruitment shortens telomeres and causes bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis syndromes. The shelterin components TERF1, POT1 and its partner ACD bind duplex and single-stranded telomeric DNA, and ACD also delivers the TERT catalytic subunit to the 3' overhang; WRAP53 traffics telomerase from nuclear bodies to chromosome ends, and USP7 acts through deubiquitination to stabilise telomere-associated factors. Chaperonin subunits assist folding of clients en route, and BRCA2 and single-stranded DNA-binding activity link the process to recombination-based telomere maintenance and replication of these fragile regions.

protein auto-ADP-ribosylation is the self-modification step by which ADP-ribosyltransferases attach ADP-ribose units from NAD+ onto their own residues, a reaction that both switches the enzyme's activity on or off and creates a docking platform for reader proteins. It matters because it sets the amplitude and duration of ADP-ribose signalling in DNA damage response, Wnt signalling and stress adaptation. PARP1 and PARP2 automodify heavily on detecting DNA strand breaks, and the resulting poly(ADP-ribose) chains recruit repair factors and then trigger the enzymes' own release from chromatin; unchecked automodification drains cellular NAD+ and drives cell death. The tankyrases automodify to promote their turnover and control axin stability, while mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases such as PARP10, PARP12, TIPARP and the membrane-anchored PARP16 use automodification in interferon-linked antiviral responses, translational stress control and unfolded protein signalling. This self-marking underlies the sensitivity of these enzymes to clinical PARP inhibitors.

Several ADP-ribosyltransferases modify themselves, transferring ADP-ribose from NAD+ onto their own residues or onto an identical subunit, and this auto-modification is how the family sets its own activity and recruits partners. The clearest case is PARP1, which on binding damaged DNA builds poly(ADP-ribose) chains largely on itself; the resulting negatively charged polymer recruits repair factors, relaxes chromatin, and then drives the enzyme off DNA, so that failure to auto-modify traps PARP1 on the lesion. PARP2 and PARP3 act similarly at breaks, while the tankyrases automodify in the course of controlling telomere protection and Wnt signalling through axin turnover. Mono-ADP-ribosylating members, including TIPARP and the PARP7-related and membrane-associated enzymes, use the same self-modification in interferon-linked and aryl hydrocarbon receptor responses. Because the reaction consumes NAD+, its scale couples DNA damage signalling to cellular energy state and underlies the sensitivity of repair-deficient tumours to PARP inhibitors.

regulation of activation-induced cell death of T cells tunes how readily an activated T cell is deleted after it has responded to antigen, the brake that ends an immune response and enforces peripheral tolerance. Without it, activated clones persist and accumulate, favouring autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation; with it set too high, effector and memory populations are lost prematurely and immunity is blunted. The genes point to two converging arms: death receptor signalling through the adaptor FADD and the kinase RIPK3, which route Fas and related TNF-family engagement toward apoptosis or programmed necrosis, and extrinsic suppressive cues, with TGF-beta and the glucocorticoid-induced regulator TSC22D3 damping activation and altering susceptibility to deletion. This places the pathway at the interface of antigen receptor signalling, glucocorticoid and cytokine control of lymphocyte homeostasis, and the contraction phase that follows clonal expansion.

Once a T cell has been activated and repeated antigen stimulation is no longer useful, it is deleted, and regulation of activation-induced cell death of T cells sets how readily that deletion happens. Tuning this threshold keeps immune responses self-limiting and helps purge autoreactive clones as an expansion resolves; too little restraint wastes effector cells prematurely, while too much allows activated lymphocytes to persist and drive autoimmunity or lymphoproliferation. The regulators here act on death receptor signalling and on transcriptional programmes that determine sensitivity to it: an adaptor coupling Fas-family receptors to caspase activation, a kinase associated with regulated necrotic death, a glucocorticoid-induced factor that mediates steroid effects on lymphocyte survival, and a TGF-beta family ligand that dampens T cell activation. The pathway sits at the contraction phase of adaptive immune responses and underlies steroid-induced lymphocyte killing.

Mucus secretion is the regulated release of the gel layer that coats the airways, gut and other mucosal surfaces, providing lubrication and a physical and antimicrobial barrier between epithelium and the outside world. Loss of it leaves epithelia exposed to pathogens and mechanical damage, while excessive or poorly hydrated mucus underlies airway obstruction in asthma and cystic fibrosis and disrupts colonic barrier integrity in colitis. The genes cover the whole arc: the gel-forming mucin MUC2 and the disulfide isomerase AGR2 needed to fold and package it, inflammasome and autophagy components in goblet cells that license granule exocytosis, purinergic, adenosine and serotonin receptors with PKC signalling that trigger release, and VAMP2/3/8 SNAREs that fuse granules with the apical membrane. Chloride and sodium channels including ANO1 and SCNN1B set the fluid and salt content that determines mucus viscosity.

Goblet cells and other mucosal epithelia release a viscous gel of mucins, salts and water that lubricates airways and gut and forms the first barrier between the body and its lumenal contents. Losing this output leaves the epithelium exposed to pathogens, abrasion and desiccation; oversecretion or dehydration of the gel obstructs airways in asthma and cystic fibrosis. The programme couples extracellular cues to granule exocytosis: purinergic and adenosine receptors, a serotonin receptor and protein kinase C signalling trigger release, VAMP2, VAMP3 and VAMP8 drive fusion of mucin granules with the apical membrane, and the calcium-activated chloride channel ANO1 with the epithelial sodium channel subunit SCNN1B set the ion and fluid flux that hydrates secreted mucin. AGR2 is required for MUC2 folding in the ER, while NLRP6 and autophagy machinery govern granule exocytosis in intestinal goblet cells.

Extracellular matrix constituent secretion covers the regulated export of collagens, proteoglycans and matrix glycoproteins from the cells that build tissue scaffolds, chiefly osteoblasts, fibroblasts and endothelium. Without it bone fails to mineralise and connective tissue loses tensile strength: loss of CREB3L1, the transcription factor that drives the collagen secretory program, or of TMEM38B, an ER cation channel needed for procollagen handling, causes recessive osteogenesis imperfecta. The genes span the whole route from instruction to release — BMP2 and NOTCH1 specify the matrix-secreting fate, TNF receptors couple inflammatory signals to matrix turnover, and RIC1, part of the RAB6 guanine nucleotide exchange complex, together with IER3IP1 supports the enlarged ER-to-Golgi carriers that bulky matrix cargo requires. The pathway therefore links secretory trafficking capacity to skeletal development, vascular remodelling and wound repair.

Matrix-producing cells such as osteoblasts, chondrocytes and fibroblasts must not only synthesise collagens, proteoglycans and matrix glycoproteins but also route them through the secretory pathway to the outside of the cell, and this regulated secretion of extracellular matrix constituents is the step that converts biosynthetic capacity into actual tissue architecture. When it fails, bone and connective tissue form poorly: loss of the transcription factor CREB3L1, which drives collagen secretory machinery, and of the ER cation channel TMEM38B each cause osteogenesis imperfecta with brittle bones. Contributing activities include ER and Golgi trafficking components, calcium and ion handling that supports procollagen folding and transport, and signals that instruct cells to secrete at all — BMP2 and Notch signalling in skeletal differentiation, TNF receptor signalling during inflammatory matrix remodelling. The pathway therefore links vesicular transport to skeletal development, wound healing and fibrosis.

N-acylethanolamine metabolic process governs the production and breakdown of a family of lipid signalling molecules that includes the endocannabinoid anandamide, the anti-inflammatory mediator palmitoylethanolamide, and the satiety factor oleoylethanolamide. Through these products the pathway tunes pain perception, feeding behaviour, energy balance, and the resolution of inflammation. Synthesis proceeds from membrane N-acyl-phosphatidylethanolamine precursors, cleaved directly by a phospholipase D-type enzyme or routed through glycerophospho-N-acylethanolamine intermediates that glycerophosphodiesterases such as GDE1, GDPD1 and GDPD3 hydrolyse to release the free acylethanolamine. Termination is equally part of the pathway: acid ceramidase-related amidase activity degrades these lipids to fatty acid and ethanolamine, setting their local concentration and therefore how strongly they engage cannabinoid receptors, PPAR-alpha and TRP channels. Because signalling here is controlled by on-demand synthesis and rapid hydrolysis rather than storage, the degradative enzymes are pursued as analgesic and anti-inflammatory drug targets.

N-acylethanolamines are lipid signalling molecules — among them anandamide, the endocannabinoid, and the anti-inflammatory mediators palmitoylethanolamide and oleoylethanolamide — and this pathway covers how they are made and destroyed. Their turnover sets the tone of cannabinoid receptor and PPAR-alpha signalling, and thereby influences pain thresholds, appetite and feeding behaviour, neuronal excitability and the resolution of inflammation. Synthesis begins with membrane N-acylphosphatidylethanolamines, which a dedicated phospholipase D releases directly as N-acylethanolamines; a parallel route proceeds through glycerophospho-N-acylethanolamine intermediates hydrolysed by glycerophosphodiesterases such as GDE1, GDPD1 and GDPD3. Degradation limits signalling duration, with the lysosomal amidase NAAA preferentially hydrolysing palmitoylethanolamide in macrophages and other immune cells. Because these lipids are produced on demand rather than stored, the balance between the synthetic and hydrolytic arms determines local signal strength, and NAAA blockade is pursued as a non-opioid analgesic strategy.

Sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ion transport is the calcium cycling that turns an action potential into a contraction and then relaxes the muscle again. It sets the strength and timing of each heartbeat and each skeletal muscle twitch, and its failure produces heart failure, arrhythmia and myopathy. Voltage-gated L-type channels and junctophilins organise the junction where the dihydropyridine receptor meets the ryanodine receptor, so that depolarisation triggers release of stored calcium into the cytosol; calsequestrin, triadin and histidine-rich calcium protein buffer and regulate the luminal side. Reuptake by SERCA pumps, tuned by the small inhibitory peptides phospholamban, sarcolipin and myoregulin and by PKA and CaMKII phosphorylation, plus sodium-calcium exchange at the surface membrane, restores the resting state. The same machinery links beta-adrenergic stimulation to inotropy, and mutations in the ryanodine receptors cause malignant hyperthermia and catecholaminergic arrhythmias.

Every heartbeat and every skeletal muscle twitch depends on calcium being released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and then pumped back in, and this transport cycle sets both the strength and the speed of contraction and relaxation. Voltage-gated L-type channels at the plasma membrane signal across the junctional gap, through junctophilins and triadin-calsequestrin complexes, to ryanodine receptors that release stored calcium; SERCA pumps encoded by ATP2A1 and ATP2A2 return it to the lumen, with phospholamban, sarcolipin and myoregulin tuning pump activity and the sodium-calcium exchanger handling extrusion. Calmodulin, CaMKII and PKA place this machinery under beta-adrenergic and calcium-dependent control. Loss of fidelity here produces malignant hyperthermia and central core myopathy through ryanodine receptor mutation, catecholaminergic arrhythmias, and the impaired calcium handling that characterises heart failure, linking store loading directly to excitation-contraction coupling.

Lens fiber cell differentiation builds the transparent bulk of the ocular lens, converting proliferating anterior epithelial cells into elongated, organelle-free fibers packed with crystallins. Transparency and refractive power depend on it, and disruption of these genes produces congenital cataract, microphthalmia and lens degeneration. Cells first exit the cell cycle under CDKN1B and CDKN1C control, then execute a transcriptional program driven by MAF, PROX1, PITX3, FOXE3, SIX3 and HSF4 that switches on alpha- and gamma-crystallins. Elongation requires cytoskeletal remodelling through the beaded filament proteins BFSP1 and BFSP2, vimentin and tropomodulin, with cell-cell adhesion and membrane organization maintained by NF2 and ephrin-EPHA2 signalling. FGF, TGF-beta and WNT inputs pattern the differentiation gradient across the lens and are tuned by SPRY and SPRED feedback inhibitors, while programmed organelle and nuclear breakdown clears light-scattering structures from mature fibers.

The transparency and refractive power of the vertebrate lens depend on this differentiation programme, in which epithelial cells at the lens equator exit the cell cycle, elongate enormously, degrade their nuclei and other organelles, and fill with crystallins. Loss of any step gives cataract or microphthalmia, and several of the genes here are classic congenital cataract loci. Cell cycle withdrawal is enforced by CDK inhibitors such as CDKN1B and CDKN1C; transcription factors including MAF, PITX3, FOXE3, PROX1, HSF4 and SIX3 drive crystallin expression and fibre elongation. FGF and TGF-beta/SMAD inputs are tuned by Sprouty and SPRED antagonists, while EPHA2-ephrin signalling and the beaded filament proteins BFSP1/BFSP2 with vimentin and tropomodulin build the specialised cytoskeleton that packs fibres together. Organelle clearance and RNA granule functions, as for TDRD7, complete the conversion to an optically clear cell.

Lens fiber cell development describes how the elongated, tightly packed cells that fill the ocular lens mature after their fate is set, producing the transparent, refractive tissue on which vision depends. Failure of this program gives cataract: loss of clarity through disordered cell packing, cytoskeletal collapse, or crystallin aggregation. Maturation involves extreme cell elongation, formation of the beaded filament cytoskeleton from BFSP1, BFSP2, vimentin and tropomodulin, massive accumulation of crystallins such as CRYAA that act as both refractive proteins and chaperones, and eventual organelle degradation to create an organelle-free zone. Ephrin-EphA2 signalling and Wnt ligands direct the precise hexagonal packing and apical-basal alignment of fibers, while PROX1 and ATF4 sustain the transcriptional program of differentiation. The pathway links cell shape control, cytoskeletal organization and protein homeostasis to an optical function.

The transparency of the eye's lens depends on fiber cells that elongate enormously, pack together with almost no extracellular space, and degrade their nuclei and organelles to eliminate light scattering. Lens fiber cell development covers that maturation programme after fate commitment, and its disruption produces cataract and lens opacities. Structural output dominates: crystallins such as CRYAA and CRYGB accumulate to extreme concentrations and act as chaperones holding the cytoplasm in a clear, refractive state, while the beaded filament proteins BFSP1 and BFSP2 together with vimentin and tropomodulin build the specialised cytoskeleton that shapes the elongating cell. Positional cues organise the process, with EPHA2 and ephrin-A5 governing fiber alignment and hexagonal packing, Wnt ligands and FRS2-linked growth factor signalling driving elongation, and PROX1 directing exit from the cell cycle and differentiation at the lens equator.

regulation of nucleotide-binding domain, leucine rich repeat containing receptor signaling pathway sets the gain on cytosolic innate immune sensing, determining how strongly NOD- and NLR-family receptors respond to bacterial peptidoglycan fragments and other intracellular danger signals. Because these receptors drive NF-κB- and inflammasome-dependent cytokine output, their tuning decides whether an infection is cleared or turns into damaging inflammation; loss of restraint here underlies Crohn's disease, Blau syndrome and other autoinflammatory conditions. Regulation acts at several levels: peptide transporters of the SLC15 family deliver muramyl peptide ligands from endosomes to the cytosol, NAGK generates the phosphorylated sugar ligand, and TLR4 signalling primes receptor expression. Downstream, the ubiquitin ligases XIAP, BIRC2 and BIRC3 assemble activating signalling complexes while the deubiquitinase TNFAIP3 and the scaffold ERBIN dampen them, with chaperones and PTPN22 modulating receptor stability and output.

Cytosolic NOD-like receptors sense bacterial cell-wall fragments and other danger signals, and the tuning of NLR signalling sets how strongly a cell mounts inflammatory NF- cB and cytokine responses to intracellular bacteria. Too little output leaves mucosal defence weak; too much drives Crohn's disease, Blau syndrome and other autoinflammatory states, which is why this arm of innate immunity is heavily regulated. Control acts at several levels. Peptide transporters of the SLC15 family, including SLC15A3 and SLC15A4, deliver muramyl peptide ligands from endosomes into the cytosol where receptors can engage them, and NAGK contributes to generating the activating sugar-peptide ligand. Ubiquitin machinery then decides signal duration: BIRC2, BIRC3 and XIAP support productive complex assembly, while TNFAIP3 restrains it. Chaperones, ERBIN, PTPN22 and TLR4 add further positive and negative input, coupling NLR output to broader pattern-recognition signalling.

nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain containing 1 signaling pathway is the cytosolic arm of bacterial sensing: NOD1 detects peptidoglycan fragments that reach the cytoplasm of epithelial and immune cells, signalling that a bacterium has breached the membrane rather than merely touched its surface. This drives NF-kB-dependent transcription of chemokines and antimicrobial peptides, shaping mucosal defence against invasive enteric pathogens and influencing susceptibility to inflammatory bowel disease and asthma-associated inflammation. Ligand binding triggers NOD1 oligomerization and recruitment of the kinase RIPK2, which together with the ubiquitin ligase XIAP builds the scaffold that activates the IKK complex; peptide transporters such as SLC15A4 and SLC46A2 deliver muropeptides to the cytosol, while IkBa and the deubiquitinase A20 restrain the output. The pathway cooperates with surface Toll-like receptor sensing, notably TLR4, to set the magnitude of the innate inflammatory response.

NOD1 is a cytosolic sensor that detects peptidoglycan fragments from bacteria that have reached the cell interior, and signalling from it lets epithelial cells and phagocytes mount an inflammatory response to invasive or intracellular microbes without any surface receptor engagement. Activation drives NF-κB-dependent transcription of chemokines and antimicrobial genes, contributing to neutrophil recruitment, mucosal defence and shaping of adaptive responses; dysregulated output contributes to inflammatory bowel disease and asthma-associated inflammation. Ligand binding promotes oligomerization and recruitment of the kinase RIPK2, whose ubiquitination by XIAP licenses downstream IKK activation; the inhibitor NFKBIA restrains NF-κB until it is degraded, and TNFAIP3 acts as a brake by removing ubiquitin marks. Peptide transporters of the SLC15 and SLC46 families deliver peptidoglycan fragments into the cytosol, and the pathway operates alongside surface sensing by TLR4.

Thrombin-activated receptor signaling pathway is how cells sense the central protease of the coagulation cascade and convert that signal into shape change, secretion and gene expression. It is what makes platelets aggregate at a wound, and what lets endothelium and inflammatory cells register vascular injury, so it sits at the junction of haemostasis, thrombosis and inflammation. Thrombin does not bind and release like a hormone: it cleaves the extracellular tail of protease-activated receptors (F2R, F2RL1, F2RL2, F2RL3), unmasking a tethered ligand that activates the receptor irreversibly through Gq, G12/13 and Gi, driving calcium release, Rho-dependent cytoskeletal contraction and granule release, with GP1BA on the platelet surface helping localise thrombin. Downstream output includes PAI-1 induction, which feeds back to restrain fibrinolysis. Overactivity promotes thrombosis and vascular inflammation, making these receptors antiplatelet drug targets.

Thrombin does more than cleave fibrinogen: it acts as a protease that signals, cutting the N-terminus of protease-activated receptors on platelets, endothelium and smooth muscle to convert a coagulation event into a cellular response. Signalling through this route drives platelet shape change, granule secretion and aggregation, endothelial permeability and inflammatory gene expression, linking haemostasis to vascular tone, wound repair and thrombosis. Thrombin (F2) is generated at sites of injury and engages PAR1 (F2R) and the related PAR2, PAR3 and PAR4 receptors, with the platelet glycoprotein Ib complex subunit GP1BA serving as a cofactor that localises thrombin at the platelet surface. The receptors couple to heterotrimeric G proteins and downstream Rho, phospholipase C and diacylglycerol kinase-dependent effectors; PAI-1 (SERPINE1) induction ties the output back to fibrinolytic control. Excessive signalling promotes arterial thrombosis, and PAR1 is a validated antiplatelet drug target.

tRNA threonylcarbamoyladenosine metabolic process covers the synthesis of t6A, a bulky modification placed at position 37 of tRNAs that read ANN codons, together with the wider set of anticodon-loop and mitochondrial tRNA modifications that keep translation in frame and accurate. t6A stabilises codon-anticodon pairing, and its loss causes ribosomal frameshifting, mistranslation and stress; in humans, defects in the KEOPS complex components OSGEP, TP53RK, TPRKB, LAGE3 and GON7 cause Galloway-Mowat syndrome, with nephrotic-range kidney disease and microcephaly. YRDC supplies the threonylcarbamoyl donor from threonine, ATP and bicarbonate, while OSGEPL1 serves the mitochondrial tRNAs. The accompanying activities — pseudouridine synthases, methyltransferases, the GTPBP3/MTO1 taurinomethyluridine pair, CDK5RAP1 and the RNase P subunits TRMT10C and HSD17B10 — place this chemistry at the heart of mitochondrial tRNA maturation and oxidative-phosphorylation capacity.

Transfer RNAs that read ANN codons carry a bulky modification at position 37, adjacent to the anticodon, and the making of threonylcarbamoyladenosine is how that mark is installed. It matters because the modification enforces correct codon-anticodon pairing: without it ribosomes slip frames and misread, protein synthesis becomes error-prone, and cells show growth and stress phenotypes. A small nuclear complex built from OSGEP, LAGE3, TP53RK, TPRKB and GON7 performs the cytoplasmic transfer, with YRDC generating the threonylcarbamoyl donor from threonine and bicarbonate, while OSGEPL1 handles the mitochondrial tRNA pool. Alongside these sit other anticodon-loop and mitochondrial tRNA modifying enzymes such as GTPBP3, MTO1, TRIT1, PUS1 and TRMT5, placing this chemistry within the broader tRNA maturation programme that supports translational fidelity. Loss of complex subunits causes Galloway-Mowat syndrome, with nephrotic disease and microcephaly.

regulation of vitamin D receptor signaling pathway controls how strongly cells respond to vitamin D, tuning the transcriptional output that governs calcium and phosphate handling, bone mineralisation, epithelial differentiation and innate immune defence. Loss of appropriate control produces rickets and osteomalacia at one extreme and hypercalcaemia at the other, and blunted responsiveness is a feature of many cancers. Regulation acts at two levels. Ligand supply is set by the renal and macrophage hydroxylase CYP27B1, which makes the active hormone. Receptor output is then set at the promoter: VDR heterodimerises with RXRA or RXRB and recruits coactivators such as MED1 and SNW1, while TRIM24, KANK2, SNAI2 and MN1 act as corepressors or competing cofactors that restrain or redirect target gene induction. This makes the pathway a case study in nuclear receptor coregulator balance rather than simple hormone availability.

Vitamin D acts as a hormone, and its effects on calcium and phosphate handling, bone mineralisation, epithelial differentiation and immune tone all depend on how strongly its nuclear receptor drives transcription. Regulation of vitamin D receptor signalling sets that gain. Ligand supply is one control point: the renal 1alpha-hydroxylase CYP27B1 converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to the active 1,25-dihydroxy form that binds the receptor. Downstream, VDR partners with retinoid X receptors and recruits coactivators such as MED1, SNW1 and TRIM24 to target promoters, while corepressor-associated factors including KANK2, MN1 and the transcription factor SNAI2 restrain or redirect the response. Tuning this axis determines intestinal calcium absorption and parathyroid feedback; loss of ligand production or receptor responsiveness produces rickets and osteomalacia, and altered coregulator balance shifts vitamin D-dependent growth control in epithelia.

Centromeric sister chromatid cohesion keeps replicated sister chromatids physically joined at their centromeres until the moment of anaphase, so that spindle attachments can be tested and the two copies of each chromosome are pulled to opposite poles. Loss of this protection produces premature sister separation, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, and in meiosis underlies the errors that generate trisomic conceptions. The core activity is protection of centromeric cohesin from cleavage: shugoshin proteins recruit a PP2A phosphatase holoenzyme to dephosphorylate cohesin locally, while BUB1 kinase marks the inner centromere to license that recruitment and links cohesion to spindle assembly checkpoint signalling. N-terminal acetyltransferase subunits and BOD1 modulate the same protective step, MEIKIN adapts it to the reductional division of meiosis I, and CTCF ties centromeric cohesin to chromatin architecture.

Sister chromatids must stay glued together at their centromeres from replication until anaphase, and centromeric sister chromatid cohesion is the process that keeps them so. It matters because premature loss of centromeric cohesion produces unequal chromosome segregation, aneuploid daughter cells and, in oocytes, the chromosome missegregation behind trisomy and age-related infertility. The shugoshin proteins SGO1 and SGO2 mark the inner centromere and recruit a PP2A phosphatase holoenzyme, whose scaffolding subunits PPP2R1A and PPP2R1B appear here, to keep the cohesin ring dephosphorylated and protected from cleavage. The kinase BUB1 phosphorylates centromeric histone H2A to place shugoshin there, linking cohesion protection to the spindle assembly checkpoint and kinetochore geometry; MEIKIN adapts the system for the stepwise, two-division cohesion loss of meiosis. N-terminal acetylation by NAA10/NAA50 and the accessory factor BOD1 tune the same centromeric machinery.

Cyclic nucleotide transport moves cAMP, cGMP and related cyclic dinucleotides across membranes, which sets how far and how long a second messenger signal reaches and provides an alternative to phosphodiesterase degradation for terminating it. Export also matters immunologically: the same carriers release cyclic di-nucleotides and take up bacterial or tumour-derived cGAMP, feeding the STING surveillance pathway that triggers interferon responses. The ABC transporters ABCC4 and ABCC5 act as ATP-driven efflux pumps for cAMP and cGMP, shaping intracellular signalling tone in platelets, vascular smooth muscle and secretory epithelia, and their activity contributes to resistance against nucleotide analogue drugs. Volume-regulated anion channels built from LRRC8 subunits provide a separate, swelling-activated conduit for cGAMP between cells, while SLC19A1 and SLC46A2 import it. Together these routes make cyclic nucleotide signalling intercellular rather than strictly cell-autonomous.

Cyclic nucleotides act as second messengers inside cells and as immune signals between them, and cyclic nucleotide transport is how they cross membranes rather than being degraded in place. Efflux pumps of the ABCC family export cAMP and cGMP from the cytosol, providing a route to terminate or tune signalling alongside phosphodiesterase hydrolysis, and ABCC4 also handles nucleotide analogue drugs. A second arm moves cyclic dinucleotides: volume-regulated anion channels built from LRRC8 subunits pass 2'3'-cGAMP between cells, while the reduced folate carrier SLC19A1 and SLC46A2 import it, allowing cGAS-derived messenger to activate STING in neighbouring and bystander cells. This transfer shapes interferon responses to cytosolic DNA, antitumour immunity and the efficacy of STING agonists, linking nucleotide metabolism to innate immune communication.

response to interleukin-6 is the set of cellular changes triggered when a cell encounters IL-6, the cytokine that drives the acute phase response, fever, emergency granulopoiesis and the switch from innate inflammation to antibody-producing plasma cell differentiation. Its chronic activation underlies rheumatoid arthritis, Castleman disease, cachexia and inflammation-associated cancer, which is why the receptor is a major therapeutic target. IL-6 binds IL6R and signals through the shared gp130 subunit, activating JAK1 and JAK2 to phosphorylate STAT3, which enters the nucleus and induces acute phase and survival genes together with NF- involvedB subunits RELA and NFKB1. Feedback restraint is built in: SOCS3 and phosphatases such as PTPN2 terminate JAK activity, and several microRNAs of the let-7 and miR-125 families tune the output. Downstream effects include hepatic and myeloid gene programmes, neutrophil antimicrobial products such as LCN2 and CAMP, and FGF23-linked mineral regulation.

Interleukin-6 is the cytokine that converts local inflammation into a systemic response, and this is the cellular reaction to it: the acute phase response in liver, fever and hepcidin-driven iron sequestration, plasma cell differentiation, and the emergency granulopoiesis that raises neutrophil output. Persistent signalling of this kind drives rheumatoid arthritis, Castleman disease and cytokine storm, which is why the receptor is a drug target. Ligand engages IL6R with the shared signalling subunit IL6ST (gp130), activating JAK1 and JAK2 to phosphorylate STAT3, with parallel input through SRC, RIPK1 and NF-κB subunits. Negative feedback is built in: SOCS3 and the phosphatase PTPN2 restrain the kinases, and several microRNAs of the let-7 and miR-125 families tune the output. Downstream transcription factors including CEBPA, SPI1, GFI1 and MYB translate the signal into myeloid and hepatic gene programmes.

protein K48-linked ubiquitination is the tagging step that commits a protein to destruction by the 26S proteasome, building ubiquitin chains linked through lysine 48 on substrates that must be removed on schedule. It sets the half-life of cell cycle regulators, misfolded secretory proteins, transcription factors and damaged mitochondrial proteins, so its failure produces aberrant proliferation, proteotoxic stress and neurodegeneration. The genes span the enzymatic cascade: E2 conjugating enzymes such as UBE2R2, UBE2G1/2 and UBE2D family members that dictate chain linkage, cullin-RING ligases assembled from CUL1, SKP1, RBX1 and F-box receptors like BTRC and SKP2, the anaphase-promoting complex that drives mitotic exit, and ER membrane ligases including SYVN1 and AMFR that execute ER-associated degradation. TRIM and HECT ligases add substrate specificity in antiviral and inflammatory signalling, where degradation of adaptors terminates the response.

Attaching a ubiquitin chain linked through lysine 48 is the canonical way a cell marks a protein for destruction by the 26S proteasome, and it underlies the timed removal of cell cycle regulators, misfolded proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, and signalling intermediates that must be switched off. E2 conjugating enzymes of the UBE2D, UBE2G, UBE2R and UBE2A/B families build the chain while cullin-RING and multisubunit E3 ligases select the substrate: SKP1-CUL1-RBX1 complexes with F-box receptors such as SKP2 and BTRC, CUL3 with BTB/kelch adaptors, the anaphase-promoting complex with its many ANAPC and CDC subunits, and RING or HECT enzymes including HUWE1, ITCH, PRKN and the ER-resident SYVN1 and AMFR that drive retrotranslocation-coupled degradation. Degradative ubiquitination of this kind governs mitotic progression, protein quality control, antiviral and inflammatory signalling, and its failure contributes to tumorigenesis and neurodegeneration.

Neutrophil-mediated killing of gram-negative bacterium is the effector step of innate antibacterial defence in which a recruited neutrophil destroys an ingested or surface-bound gram-negative organism. It underlies clearance of enteric and respiratory pathogens, and its failure leaves patients with recurrent pyogenic infection and endotoxaemia, while its excess drives tissue injury in sepsis and acute lung inflammation. The genes span chemotactic recruitment, activation and armament: a chemokine that brings granulocytes to infected tissue, thrombin and its receptor linking coagulation to leukocyte activation, and a myeloid immunoglobulin-family receptor that amplifies inflammatory responses to bacterial contact. Killing itself depends on granule contents such as neutrophil elastase, which degrades outer membrane proteins of gram-negative bacteria, alongside oxidative mechanisms generating hydrogen peroxide from amino acid substrates. The pathway thus connects chemotaxis, phagocytosis, degranulation and oxidative burst into a single microbicidal program.

Neutrophils are the first responders that clear gram-negative bacteria from infected tissue, and this pathway covers the killing step itself: recognition of the microbe followed by deployment of proteolytic and oxidative weapons within phagosomes and at the site of infection. Loss of this capacity leaves patients with recurrent pyogenic infection, while excessive or misdirected activity damages host tissue, as in the lung injury attributed to unrestrained neutrophil elastase. The genes involved span several arms of the response: the serine protease ELANE degrades bacterial outer membrane proteins and virulence factors, a chemokine recruits further neutrophils, TREM1 amplifies inflammatory activation on myeloid cells, and thrombin with its receptor PAR2 links coagulation to inflammatory signalling. D-amino acid oxidase contributes oxidative antimicrobial chemistry by generating hydrogen peroxide from bacterial D-amino acids, connecting innate defence to peroxide-dependent killing.

Positive regulation of phospholipid biosynthetic process covers the signals that push cells to make more membrane lipid, matching phospholipid supply to demand during membrane expansion, secretion, and surfactant production. It matters wherever a cell must build membrane fast: the endoplasmic reticulum expanding under secretory load, alveolar type II cells generating pulmonary surfactant, and tissues remodelling lipid stores. The transcription factor XBP1, produced by the unfolded protein response, drives ER membrane biogenesis by upregulating phospholipid synthesis enzymes, while the bile acid receptor NR1H4 links lipid synthesis to nutrient and enterohepatic signalling. Serotonin receptors of the 5-HT2 family act through phospholipase C to stimulate phosphoinositide turnover and resynthesis, and ACSL3 activates fatty acids for incorporation into glycerolipids. ADGRF5 and RAB38 tie the process to surfactant homeostasis and lamellar body trafficking in lung epithelium.

Membrane expansion, lipid droplet formation and surfactant production all require phospholipid synthesis to be turned up on demand, and this is the regulatory arm that increases the flux through those biosynthetic routes rather than catalysing them directly. Upregulation matters when a cell must build membrane quickly: secretory cells expanding the endoplasmic reticulum during the unfolded protein response, where the transcription factor XBP1 drives lipid biosynthetic gene expression, and alveolar type II cells, where ADGRF5 and RAB38 support surfactant phospholipid production and lamellar body trafficking. Other inputs are hormonal and neurotransmitter-driven: serotonin 5-HT2 receptors couple through phospholipase C to stimulate lipid turnover, and the bile acid receptor NR1H4 links sterol sensing to lipid gene programmes. Fatty acid handling proteins such as ACSL3 and FABP3 feed activated acyl chains into the pathway. Loss of this control compromises surfactant function and membrane biogenesis.

establishment of protein localization to chromatin covers the targeted delivery and loading of regulatory proteins onto chromatin, the step that converts a diffusible nuclear factor into a positioned occupant of a specific chromosomal site. This is how epigenetic states are written and maintained: without correct loading, histone variants fail to mark repressed domains, cohesin fails to encircle chromosome arms, and chromatin readers never reach their target marks. The genes span several such loading events — NIPBL as the cohesin loader that establishes sister chromatid cohesion and looping, the macroH2A variants that build transcriptionally silent chromatin including the inactive X, linker histone H1-5 that compacts nucleosome arrays, and LRWD1 which recognises repressive methylation to anchor origin recognition complex components. RUVBL2 and SGF29 contribute chaperone-like ATPase and methyl-mark reading activities within chromatin-modifying complexes, linking this process to replication licensing, transcriptional silencing and genome stability.

Chromatin is not a passive substrate: factors that read, remodel or organise it must first be delivered to defined genomic positions, and the establishment of protein localization to chromatin covers the loading and targeted deposition steps that put them there. This determines which regions are silenced, which loops form, and which promoters recruit coactivators, so it sits upstream of transcriptional control, replication licensing and chromosome architecture. The genes here span several of those routes: NIPBL loads cohesin onto DNA to build topological domains, LRWD1 recognises methylated histones at heterochromatin and origin regions, macroH2A variants are incorporated into nucleosomes to enforce repression, a linker histone compacts the fibre, and SGF29 and RUVBL2 tether acetyltransferase and remodelling complexes to chromatin. Failure of such targeting misroutes epigenetic marks and disrupts genome stability and developmental gene expression.

cellular response to manganese ion is how cells sense and adapt to manganese, a required cofactor for mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and glycosyltransferases that becomes a neurotoxin in excess. The response matters because manganese overload produces a parkinsonian movement disorder, and several of the genes here are hereditary parkinsonism genes: the lysosomal manganese transporter ATP13A2, whose loss causes Kufor-Rakeb syndrome, together with PRKN and LRRK2, linking metal handling to mitophagy and lysosomal quality control. Excess manganese accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi and triggers the PERK arm of the unfolded protein response, with EIF2AK3 phosphorylating eIF2α to slow translation and induce ATF4, while chaperones such as HSP90B1 buffer misfolded secretory protein load. Manganese also shifts amyloid precursor protein processing through BACE1, tying the response to neurodegenerative proteostasis more broadly.

Manganese is required as a cofactor for enzymes such as mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and glutamine synthetase, but in excess it is a neurotoxin, and the cellular response to manganese ion describes how cells sense and adapt to that stimulus. Chronic overexposure produces a parkinsonian syndrome, which explains why several of the genes here are Parkinson's disease loci: the lysosomal polyamine/cation transporter ATP13A2 sequesters and detoxifies manganese, while parkin and LRRK2 shape mitochondrial and endolysosomal handling of the metal. Much of the adaptive output runs through the integrated stress response, where the ER kinase PERK phosphorylates the translation initiation factor eIF2α to dampen protein synthesis and induce ATF4, alongside ER chaperone induction. Manganese also alters amyloid precursor protein processing via BACE1, linking metal overload to neurodegenerative proteostasis and to the vulnerability of basal ganglia neurons.

cellular response to cAMP covers what a cell does once cyclic AMP rises, converting hormonal and neurotransmitter signals received at G protein-coupled receptors into changes in ion transport, secretion, metabolism and gene expression. It is the effector arm of adrenergic, glucagon and vasopressin signalling, and its failure is felt in disorders of epithelial salt and fluid movement, cardiac pacemaking and hepatic fuel output. AKAP scaffolds localise protein kinase A to particular substrates, while phosphodiesterases such as PDE4D and PDE2A terminate the signal and set its spatial limits. cAMP-gated HCN channels drive the cardiac and neuronal pacemaker current; CFTR and paired SLC26 anion exchangers drive chloride and bicarbonate secretion; CRTC coactivators enter the nucleus to switch on CREB target genes, including gluconeogenic enzymes such as PCK-pathway partners FBP1, ASS1 and CPS1. Rap1 and its RAPGEF exchange factors provide a kinase-independent branch controlling adhesion.

cAMP is the second messenger through which hormones acting on G protein-coupled receptors change what a cell does, and this pathway covers the downstream responses: ion and water transport, secretion, gene expression, and electrical pacemaking. Scaffolding proteins of the AKAP family tether kinase activity to particular substrates and compartments so that a diffusible signal produces localised effects, while phosphodiesterases such as PDE4D and PDE2A terminate it. Nuclear output runs partly through CRTC coactivators, which relay cAMP to CREB-dependent transcription of metabolic genes, including gluconeogenic and urea cycle enzymes. Effectors also include cAMP-gated exchange factors that load Rap GTPases, HCN channels that set cardiac and neuronal rhythm, and the CFTR chloride channel with partnering anion exchangers, whose cAMP-driven activation governs epithelial fluid secretion and fails in cystic fibrosis and secretory diarrhoea.

Cellular response to gonadotropin stimulus covers what a target cell does when it receives pituitary FSH or LH — the step that converts a hormonal pulse into ovulation, follicle maturation, corpus luteum formation and gonadal steroid output. It is the effector end of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis, and its failure produces anovulatory infertility, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, or, with activating receptor mutations, precocious puberty. The gonadotropin receptors FSHR and LHCGR are G protein-coupled and act through cyclic AMP to reprogram granulosa and theca cell transcription, driving cell cycle entry via cyclins, steroidogenic electron transfer through cytochrome P450 reductase, and paracrine signals such as inhibin/activin subunits, endothelin and Notch that coordinate follicular remodelling and vascular change. Antioxidant glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits buffer the oxidative load of steroid synthesis, while GATA and WT1 factors set the gonadal transcriptional context in which the hormone is read.

Gonadotropins from the pituitary — FSH and LH — instruct gonadal cells to grow, differentiate and make steroids, and this describes what a target cell does once that signal arrives. The response drives follicle maturation, ovulation, luteinization and Sertoli and Leydig cell function, so its failure produces hypogonadism, anovulatory infertility and disordered sex steroid output. Hormone recognition depends on the G protein-coupled receptors FSHR and LHCGR, whose cAMP output is translated into transcriptional change through factors such as WT1, GATA6 and NOTCH1, into cell cycle entry via cyclin A2, and into steroidogenic capacity through electron supply by the P450 reductase POR. Local mediators including endothelin-1 acting on EDNRA and the activin subunit INHBA feed back on the same cells, tying gonadotropin action to paracrine control of follicular and interstitial tissue.</description>

cellular response to follicle-stimulating hormone stimulus describes what happens inside a cell once pituitary FSH binds its receptor, the step that drives ovarian follicle growth and Sertoli cell support of spermatogenesis. It sets the pace of the reproductive cycle: loss of receptor signalling causes hypogonadism and infertility, while its manipulation is the basis of ovulation induction. FSHR is the entry point, a G protein-coupled receptor that raises cAMP in granulosa and Sertoli cells and reprogrammes transcription toward proliferation, aromatase expression and steroidogenic support, with POR supplying electrons to the cytochrome P450 enzymes involved. The remaining genes show the downstream consequences rather than the receptor itself: inhibin/activin subunits that feed back on pituitary FSH output, endothelin and ephrin signalling that shape follicular vasculature and cell contacts, Notch-dependent granulosa differentiation, and glutathione synthesis enzymes that protect the follicle from oxidative damage.

Follicle-stimulating hormone acts on gonadal somatic cells to drive ovarian follicle growth and Sertoli cell support of spermatogenesis, and this pathway covers what a target cell does once the hormone arrives. Binding to the FSH receptor, a G protein-coupled receptor coupled to cAMP production, changes gene expression, steroidogenic capacity and paracrine output; loss of receptor signalling causes hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, follicle arrest and infertility, while its regulation sets the ovarian response in assisted reproduction. Downstream effectors here include the inhibin/activin subunit INHBA, which feeds back on pituitary FSH secretion, endothelin-1 with its receptor EDNRA acting on follicular and vascular tone, Notch and ephrin components mediating cell-cell contacts within the follicle, cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase supporting steroid hydroxylation, and the glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits that build glutathione against oxidative stress during follicular maturation.

cellular response to peptide hormone stimulus covers how cells detect and act on hormones secreted into the blood as peptides — insulin, glucagon, growth hormone, leptin, angiotensin, GnRH and others — and convert that endocrine signal into altered metabolism, gene expression, growth and secretion. It is the machinery of whole-body homeostasis: blood glucose control, lipid and glycogen handling, body-weight and appetite regulation, blood pressure, growth and reproductive timing, and its derangement defines insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, obesity and hypertension. Mechanistically it spans receptor tyrosine kinase signalling through IRS adaptors to PI3K–AKT–mTOR and FOXO, cytokine-type receptors acting via JAK–STAT with SOCS feedback, and G protein-coupled receptors driving adenylate cyclase, PKA and PKC. Outputs converge on gluconeogenic and lipogenic enzymes, GLUT4 vesicle trafficking to the plasma membrane, and transcription factors such as CREB, PPARG, SREBF1 and the KLF family.

Peptide hormones such as insulin, IGFs, growth hormone, glucagon, leptin and angiotensin act at the cell surface, and this pathway covers how a target cell converts that endocrine signal into altered metabolism, gene expression and growth. It underlies whole-body glucose and lipid homeostasis, somatic growth, blood pressure and salt balance, and reproductive and stress axes; its blunting is the molecular definition of insulin and leptin resistance in type 2 diabetes and obesity. Receptor tyrosine kinases signal through IRS adaptors to PI3K, AKT, mTOR and FOXO transcription factors, driving GLUT4 vesicle translocation and suppressing gluconeogenic enzymes such as PCK1 and G6PC1, while G protein-coupled receptors for glucagon, GLP-1, TSH and angiotensin work via adenylate cyclases, PKA and PKC. Cytokine-type receptors engage JAK kinases and STATs. Negative regulators including SOCS proteins, PTPN1 and TRIB3 set signal duration and sensitivity.

Cellular response to prostaglandin E stimulus describes how cells read the lipid mediator PGE2, the dominant prostanoid of inflammation, fever, pain sensitisation and mucosal protection, and convert it into changes in gene expression, secretion and motility. It matters because PGE2 is the product blocked by NSAIDs: its receptors set vascular tone, gastric mucosal defence, and the balance between immune activation and restraint. The receptors EPTGER2 and EP4 couple through GNAS and heterotrimeric G protein subunits to adenylate cyclase and cAMP, engaging PKA scaffolds, PKC and AKT, while AMPK subunits link the signal to acetyl-CoA carboxylase and lipid metabolism. In dendritic cells and lymphocytes the same signal drives CCR7 and its chemokines CCL19 and CCL21, directing migration to lymph nodes, and induces the costimulatory ligand OX40L, so PGE2 shapes adaptive immune priming as well as smooth muscle and metabolic responses.

Prostaglandin E2 is a lipid mediator released during inflammation, and this pathway covers what a cell does once it arrives: bind it, convert it into second-messenger signalling, and change migration, secretion and gene expression accordingly. The receptors EP2 and EP4 (PTGER2, PTGER4) couple through Gs heterotrimers (GNAS with beta and gamma subunits) to adenylate cyclase, raising cAMP and engaging PKA scaffolding, with additional input through PKC and AKT1 and metabolic branches via AMPK subunits and acetyl-CoA carboxylase. The immune output is prominent: CCR7 and its ligands CCL19 and CCL21 link prostaglandin exposure to dendritic cell and lymphocyte homing into lymph nodes, while OX40 ligand shapes T cell costimulation. Because PGE2 is the product of cyclooxygenase activity, these responses are what NSAIDs blunt, and they underlie inflammatory pain, fever, vasodilation and tumour-associated immune suppression.

cellular response to progesterone stimulus covers the changes a cell makes in gene expression, secretion, and behaviour when it senses progesterone, the steroid that prepares the endometrium for implantation, sustains pregnancy by quieting uterine contraction, and shapes mammary and neural tissue. Loss of responsiveness underlies implantation failure and progesterone-resistant endometrial disease. The response runs through both classical and rapid arms: nuclear receptor-dependent transcription, aided by coregulators such as TRERF1 that remodel promoters of steroidogenic and target genes, and non-genomic signalling in which the SRC tyrosine kinase couples receptor engagement to cytoskeletal and proliferative outputs. Downstream effects reach differentiation programmes controlled by SOX10 and inflammatory metabolism through ACOD1, linking hormonal state to immune tone. This places progesterone sensing within steroid hormone signalling and reproductive tissue remodelling rather than in any single metabolic route.

Progesterone acts on target cells to reprogramme gene expression and behaviour, and this response underlies the secretory transformation of the endometrium, maintenance of pregnancy, mammary development and effects on neural and immune cells. The genes here represent the cell-side machinery engaged once the hormone is sensed: SRC links steroid receptor signalling to rapid, non-genomic kinase cascades that modulate proliferation and cytoskeletal responses, while TRERF1 acts as a transcriptional regulator that can influence steroidogenic gene expression, and SOX10 marks a lineage context in which the hormonal input is interpreted. Induction of ACOD1, which produces itaconate from cis-aconitate, points to progesterone's ability to shift inflammatory and metabolic output in responding cells. Loss or distortion of such responses contributes to progesterone resistance in endometriosis and endometrial disease, and to failures of implantation.

cellular response to lipid covers the ways cells sense lipids and lipid-derived molecules and change their behaviour accordingly, from switching on transcriptional programmes for cholesterol and fatty acid handling to mounting inflammatory responses against bacterial lipids. It is how metabolic state is translated into gene expression, and its dysregulation underlies atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, and chronic inflammatory disease. Two broad arms are represented. Lipophilic ligands -- oxysterols, bile acids, fatty acids, retinoids, steroid hormones, vitamin D -- act through nuclear receptors such as PPARs, LXR, FXR, VDR, RXR partners and RAR, together with coactivators and corepressors, to control transport (ABCA1, LDLR, SCARB1, NPC1), oxidation, and detoxifying UGT and AKR1C enzymes. In parallel, lipid A and oxidised lipids engage TLR2/TLR4 with CD14, LBP and MyD88 adaptors, driving NF-κB, MAPK and inflammasome output, while eicosanoid and lysophospholipid receptors couple through G proteins and adenylate cyclases to acute cellular responses.

Lipids are not only structural and metabolic molecules but signals, and the cellular response to lipid covers how a cell changes its gene expression, secretion, metabolism and behaviour when it encounters one. It spans two broad arms. Nuclear receptors and their coregulators — PPARs, LXR, FXR, RXR partners, VDR, retinoic acid receptors, together with NCOR/NCOA complexes, SREBF1 and INSIG proteins — read sterols, oxysterols, bile acids, fatty acids and retinoids and reset cholesterol efflux, lipogenesis and fatty acid oxidation, with LDLR, ABCA1, CPT1A and CD36 among the outputs. The second arm is innate immune sensing of lipid-bearing microbial products: TLR2/TLR4 with CD14, LBP, MYD88 and TRAF6 drive NF-κB and MAPK activation, inflammasome assembly and cytokine and chemokine release. Also included are receptors for eicosanoids, lysophospholipids and free fatty acids. Failure of this signalling underlies atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, fatty liver and chronic inflammation.

cellular response to lipoprotein particle stimulus describes how cells sense circulating lipoprotein particles — LDL, oxidized LDL, and HDL — and remodel their lipid handling, gene expression and inflammatory output accordingly. It is the cell-level basis of cholesterol homeostasis and of atherosclerosis: macrophages that take up modified LDL through scavenger receptors such as CD36 and SCARB1 become foam cells, while HDL and apolipoprotein A-I acting on the ABCA1 and ABCG1 transporters drive cholesterol efflux back out. Uptake via the LDL receptor and intracellular trafficking through NPC1 feed sterol-sensing circuits that adjust SREBF2, PPARG and RXRA target genes, and oxidized lipids engage TLR4/TLR6 with MYD88 to trigger cytokine production. Microglial TREM2 and several microRNAs tune these responses. Persistent activation links dyslipidaemia to vascular inflammation, plaque formation, and lipid-associated changes in macrophage and microglial phenotype.

Cells monitor the lipoproteins around them and respond by rewiring cholesterol handling, gene expression and inflammatory output. This cellular response to lipoprotein particle stimulus is central to macrophage biology and to atherosclerosis: uptake of modified LDL through scavenger receptors such as CD36 and SCARB1 converts macrophages into foam cells, while HDL and its apolipoprotein A-I acceptor drives cholesterol efflux through the transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1. Sterol sensing feeds into the nuclear receptor pair PPARG and RXRA and into SREBP-driven transcription that tunes LDL receptor and lipase levels, and NPC1 moves sterol out of lysosomes. In parallel, lipoprotein-derived lipids engage innate immune receptors including TLR4 and TREM2 with MYD88 adaptors, coupling lipid load to cytokine production. Failure of the efflux arm produces cholesterol accumulation, plaque inflammation and cardiovascular disease.

cellular response to oxygen levels is how cells sense oxygen availability and rewire their metabolism, growth and survival to match it. It underlies adaptation to hypoxia in ischaemia, wound healing and tumour growth, and its constitutive activation through VHL loss drives clear cell renal carcinoma and polycythaemia. The core is a hydroxylation-based oxygen sensor: prolyl hydroxylases (EGLN1-3) and VHL mark HIF1A and EPAS1 for degradation when oxygen is plentiful, so that under hypoxia the HIF-ARNT heterodimer accumulates and induces glycolytic enzymes, PDK1, VEGFA and erythropoietic and angiogenic factors. Downstream branches shift ATP production away from oxidative phosphorylation, trigger BNIP3- and PINK1-dependent mitophagy and autophagy, restrain mTOR signalling and the cell cycle, and, if stress persists, engage p53-dependent apoptosis. Additional layers include microRNAs such as miR-210, sirtuins, oxidative-stress responses and pH regulation through vacuolar ATPases and NHE1.

Cells sense how much oxygen they have and reorganise their metabolism, growth and survival accordingly; this oxygen-responsive programme is what allows tissues to tolerate ischaemia, drives new blood vessel growth in wounds and tumours, and adapts muscle and brain to altitude or vascular occlusion. Its core is the hypoxia-inducible factor system: prolyl hydroxylases such as EGLN1-3 mark HIF1A and EPAS1 for VHL-dependent degradation when oxygen is plentiful, and stabilised HIF partnered with ARNT switches on glycolytic enzymes, PDK-mediated suppression of pyruvate oxidation, erythropoietic and angiogenic factors including VEGFA, and mitophagy receptors BNIP3 and BNIP3L. Overlapping arms couple low oxygen to mTOR and AMPK control of translation, to p53-dependent apoptosis, to redox defence through NFE2L2, and to oxygen-sensitive ion channels. Chronic activation supports tumour adaptation and pulmonary vascular remodelling, while failed adaptation gives infarction and cell death.

Cellular response to pH is how cells sense protons and act on that information, keeping intracellular and extracellular acid-base conditions within the narrow range that enzymes, excitability and secretion require. It matters for sour taste, nociception during tissue acidosis, renal acid handling, immune cell function in acidic tumour and inflammatory environments, and defence against ingested acid. Detection runs through several device families: acid-sensing ion channels and the capsaicin receptor depolarise sensory neurons when protons accumulate; proton-sensing G protein-coupled receptors such as GPR4, GPR65 and GPR68 signal through Gq and Gs to change gene expression; acid-inhibited two-pore potassium channels set resting membrane potential; and PKD2L1-containing channels serve taste cells. Effector arms restore balance, with the sodium-proton exchanger SLC9A1 and its regulator CHP1 extruding acid, epithelial sodium channels adjusting transport, and the voltage-gated proton channel HVCN1 supporting the respiratory burst.

Cells monitor extracellular and intracellular acidity and respond to it, and this proton-sensing capacity underlies sour taste, acid-evoked pain, immune cell function in inflamed or tumour tissue, and renal and systemic acid-base balance. Acid-gated ion channels convert a proton stimulus into electrical signalling: ASIC1 and ASIC2 open on extracellular acidification, TRPV1 is potentiated by low pH at nociceptor endings, PKD2L1 with PKD1L3 marks sour-sensing taste cells, and several two-pore potassium channels are inhibited by acid, depolarising the cell. A parallel arm uses proton-sensitive G protein-coupled receptors, GPR4, GPR65 and GPR68, signalling through Gq/11 and Gs to alter gene expression and secretion. Homeostatic effectors restore pH, chiefly the sodium-hydrogen exchanger SLC9A1 with its regulator CHP1 and the voltage-gated proton channel HVCN1, which supports the respiratory burst in phagocytes. Dysregulation contributes to chronic pain, ischaemic injury and the acidic tumour microenvironment.

cellular hyperosmotic response is the set of adjustments a cell makes when the surrounding fluid becomes too concentrated and water is drawn out of it. It protects cells against shrinkage-induced damage, and it is the basis of how the kidney medulla, whose cells work in extreme salt and urea, survives concentrating urine. Sensing feeds through the WNK1/WNK3 kinases to the downstream kinases OXSR1 and STK39, which switch on sodium- and chloride-coupled cotransport to reclaim ions and water, while the transcription factor NFAT5 drives genes for compatible osmolyte accumulation, including the sorbitol-producing aldose reductase AKR1B1, and for aquaporin water channels. Glucose transport, gluconeogenic enzymes and mitochondrial calcium and ion carriers adjust metabolism to the stress. Failure of this response causes cytoskeletal disruption, DNA damage and apoptosis, and contributes to defective urinary concentration and to hypertonicity in diabetes and dehydration.

Cells exposed to a solute concentration higher than their own shrink as water leaves, and the cellular hyperosmotic response is how they sense that loss and restore volume and ionic balance. It matters most in the kidney medulla, where interstitial osmolality is extreme by design, and its failure leaves cells with concentrated intracellular salt, protein damage and DNA breaks. Two arms dominate the gene list. A kinase cascade in which WNK1 and WNK3 activate the related kinases OXSR1 and STK39 switches on electroneutral cation-chloride transport to reaccumulate ions, while the transcription factor NFAT5 drives expression of organic osmolyte machinery, including aldose reductase for sorbitol synthesis, so that volume can be regained without raising intracellular ionic strength. Aquaporin-mediated water flux, glucose uptake, mitochondrial calcium and magnesium handling, and cytoskeletal remodelling through ARHGEF2 accompany the adaptation.

cellular response to endogenous stimulus collects the ways cells detect and react to signals generated within the body itself — hormones, growth factors, cytokines, neurotrophins, metabolites and mechanical or metabolic cues — rather than to external insult.
