Additional dedicated partners stabilise the pool: one transmembrane protein of the LHFPL family is required to retain gephyrin-dependent clusters, another is a GABA-A receptor-associated protein controlling surface trafficking, and presynaptic neurexin adhesion aligns the release site with the receptor field. The result is a matched pre- and postsynaptic apparatus for phasic inhibition.

NMDA glutamate receptor clustering concentrates NMDA-type glutamate receptors at defined postsynaptic domains rather than letting them diffuse across the membrane, which is what allows an excitatory synapse to respond reliably and to change its strength during learning. Coincidence detection by these receptors, and the calcium influx that follows, depends on their being held opposite presynaptic release sites. The genes describe how that positioning is achieved: a trans-synaptic neurexin-neuroligin adhesion pair aligns the two sides of the contact, SHANK3 scaffolds receptors within the postsynaptic density, and secreted cues including reelin and apolipoprotein E signal through neuronal surface receptors to regulate receptor composition and subunit switching during maturation. The pathway sits within synapse assembly and plasticity, and disruption of its members is recurrently linked to autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia and intellectual disability.

NMDA-type glutamate receptors only support learning-related plasticity if they are concentrated at the postsynaptic membrane opposite a transmitter release site, and this clustering process is what puts them and holds them there. It links a trans-synaptic adhesion pair, neurexin on the presynaptic side and neuroligin on the postsynaptic side, to the scaffolding of the postsynaptic density, where SHANK3 anchors receptors within a dense protein lattice. Secreted cues contribute as well: reelin signalling through lipoprotein receptors, with apolipoprotein E as a competing ligand, tunes receptor subunit composition and positioning during circuit maturation. The result is a synapse capable of coincidence detection, calcium influx and long-term potentiation. Disruption of these adhesion and scaffold components is recurrent in autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia, and the reelin and APOE arms tie the same machinery to cortical development and to synaptic loss in neurodegeneration.

neuronal stem cell population maintenance keeps a reservoir of undifferentiated neural progenitors intact across development and into adult neurogenic niches, so that neurons and glia can continue to be generated rather than the pool being exhausted in a single wave of differentiation. It sets the balance between self-renewing and differentiative divisions, and its failure produces microcephaly, depleted hippocampal and subventricular progenitors, and impaired repair. Notch signalling through DLL1, JAG1 and NOTCH1 drives HES1/HES5 oscillations that repress proneural genes and hold cells in a progenitor state, while SOX2 and REST enforce stemness transcriptionally and FOXO factors protect against oxidative stress and premature exhaustion. Centrosomal and spindle proteins including ASPM, MCPH1, PCM1 and HOOK3 control mitotic spindle orientation and cleavage plane, determining whether daughters remain progenitors, and cadherin-mediated adhesion anchors cells to the apical niche.

The nervous system is built and later replenished from a reserve of undifferentiated progenitors, and neuronal stem cell population maintenance is the set of processes that keeps that reserve intact rather than letting it differentiate away. Its balance sets brain size and the supply of neurons for hippocampal and olfactory neurogenesis; premature exhaustion depletes the niche, while excess self-renewal favours tumour growth. Notch signalling through NOTCH1 with the DLL1 and JAG1 ligands sustains the undifferentiated state via the HES1 and HES5 repressors, SOX2 and REST hold neural genes in a progenitor-appropriate configuration, and FOXO3 limits oxidative stress in quiescent cells. Adherens junctions built on CDH2 anchor progenitors in the ventricular zone, and centrosomal and spindle proteins such as ASPM, MCPH1 and PCM1 orient divisions, with their loss producing microcephaly from a prematurely spent progenitor pool.

Amelogenesis is the making of dental enamel, the hardest tissue in the body, by ameloblasts of the developing tooth. Because enamel is acellular and never regenerated, errors here are permanent: mutations in these genes cause amelogenesis imperfecta, with hypoplastic, hypomineralised or chalky enamel that chips and decays. The process runs in two phases. In the secretory stage ameloblasts extrude a protein scaffold — amelogenin, enamelin, ameloblastin and amelotin — that templates the growth of oriented hydroxyapatite ribbons, with FAM20C-family kinases phosphorylating these matrix proteins to control mineral nucleation. In the maturation stage the proteases MMP20 and KLK4 degrade and clear that scaffold while crystals thicken, a step requiring massive transepithelial ion movement and pH buffering through transporters such as SLC24A4, SLC4A2, CFTR and the V-ATPase subunit TCIRG1. Transcription factors including MSX2 and TBX1 set ameloblast identity upstream.

Amelogenesis is how ameloblasts build tooth enamel, the hardest tissue in the body, in two phases: a secretory stage in which a protein-rich matrix is laid down and crystallites elongate, and a maturation stage in which that matrix is degraded and replaced by dense mineral. Amelogenin and enamelin form the scaffold, the proteases MMP20 and KLK4 remove it on schedule, and FAM20A and FAM20C control secretory-pathway phosphorylation of matrix proteins. Mineralization demands sustained ion movement and pH buffering across the ameloblast, supplied by calcium transport, bicarbonate and chloride handling, store-operated calcium entry through STIM1, and proton pumping. Mutations across these steps cause amelophobic enamel defects — amelogenesis imperfecta with hypoplastic or hypomineralized enamel, sometimes alongside kidney, skeletal or neurological features — making this a paradigm for matrix-mediated biomineralization and for the transcriptional control of an epithelial secretory lineage.

apoptotic signaling pathway covers the routes by which a cell receives a death cue and commits to dismantling itself, from ligand binding or internal damage sensing up to the point where executioner caspases are unleashed. It is how tissues delete surplus, infected, damaged or mutated cells, and its failure permits tumour survival and autoimmunity while its overactivation drives neurodegeneration and ischaemic injury. Both principal arms are represented: death receptors such as FAS, TNFRSF1A and TRAIL receptors recruiting FADD, TRADD and caspase-8, and the mitochondrial arm in which BH3-only proteins including BID, BAD, PMAIP1 and BBC3 overcome BCL2 and MCL1 to let BAX and BAK release cytochrome c, activating APAF1 and caspase-9. Layered onto this are p53-driven damage responses, ER stress signalling through PERK, ATF4 and CHOP, kinase and ubiquitin-ligase modulators, IAP inhibition by DIABLO, and microRNAs that set the threshold for death.

Programmed cell death lets tissues delete damaged, infected, superfluous or self-reactive cells without inflaming their surroundings, and this pathway covers everything from receipt of a death signal to the point where the execution caspases are unleashed. Two routes dominate. Death ligands such as FASLG and TNFSF10 engage their receptors and assemble FADD- and caspase-8-containing complexes, which CFLAR restrains. Intracellular stress causes p53 to induce BH3-only proteins such as PMAIP1 and BBC3, which overcome BCL2 and MCL1 to let BAX and BAK1 permeabilize mitochondria, releasing cytochrome c and DIABLO for APAF1-dependent caspase-9 activation while IAPs oppose it. Unresolved endoplasmic reticulum stress feeds in through DDIT3 and its kinases. Too little of this signalling underlies tumour survival and autoimmunity; too much drives neurodegeneration, ischaemic injury and immune cell loss.

Intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway is the route by which a cell kills itself in response to its own internal alarms — irreparable DNA damage, endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative injury, growth factor withdrawal — rather than instruction from an external death ligand. It removes damaged and potentially oncogenic cells, shapes tissues during development, and its suppression is a hallmark of cancer and of resistance to chemotherapy and radiation. The decision point is the mitochondrial outer membrane: BH3-only proteins such as BID, BAD, PMAIP1 and BBC3 are induced or activated, overcome guardians like BCL2 and MCL1, and license BAX and BAK1 to permeabilize the membrane, releasing cytochrome c and DIABLO to assemble the APAF1 apoptosome and activate caspase-9 and the executioner caspases. Upstream, ATM–CHEK2–TP53 relays genotoxic stress, while PERK–ATF4–DDIT3 and IRE1–XBP1 convert unresolved protein-folding stress into the same commitment.

Cells that have sustained irreparable internal damage kill themselves, and this intrinsic route to apoptosis is how that decision is made and executed. It matters for tumour suppression, for clearing cells with DNA lesions or unresolvable protein-folding stress, and for tissue sculpting during development; its failure permits survival of damaged cells and underlies chemoresistance, while excess activity contributes to degenerative loss of neurons and other post-mitotic cells. Sensors of DNA damage such as ATM, CHEK2 and the p53 network, and endoplasmic reticulum stress arms including PERK, IRE1 and CHOP, converge on the BCL-2 family, where BAX, BAK1 and BH3-only proteins like BID, BIM, PUMA and NOXA oppose BCL2 and MCL1 to permeabilize the mitochondrial outer membrane. Released cytochrome c and SMAC then drive apoptosome assembly with APAF1 and caspase-9, activating the executioner caspases and committing the cell to dismantling.

omega-hydroxylase P450 pathway converts arachidonic acid into hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acids by oxidising the terminal end of the fatty acid chain, producing signalling lipids that set vascular tone, renal sodium handling and blood pressure. Its best-known product, 20-HETE, constricts arterioles and modulates tubular transport, and variation in the CYP4A and CYP4F enzymes that generate it is linked to hypertension and stroke risk. The same reactions serve a catabolic purpose, since omega-hydroxylation initiates the inactivation and clearance of leukotriene B4 and other eicosanoids, damping inflammation once it has served its function. Related CYP1 and CYP2C enzymes contribute overlapping oxidations of arachidonate and of xenobiotics, placing this branch of lipid metabolism alongside the epoxygenase and cyclooxygenase routes as one of three fates for released arachidonic acid, and connecting it to drug metabolism in liver and kidney.

Arachidonic acid can be oxidised at the terminal end of its chain rather than at a double bond, and the omega-hydroxylase branch of cytochrome P450 metabolism is what performs that chemistry. Its principal product, 20-HETE, constricts small arteries, modulates renal sodium handling and tubuloglomerular feedback, and contributes to blood pressure set-point and vascular tone; variants in the CYP4A and CYP4F enzymes that make it are linked to hypertension and cerebrovascular risk. The same enzymes, working with NADPH and molecular oxygen at the endoplasmic reticulum, also inactivate leukotriene B4 and so limit neutrophil-driven inflammation. Several CYP2C and CYP1 family members included here act on arachidonate as epoxygenases or mid-chain hydroxylases, so the pathway sits alongside the epoxyeicosatrienoic acid route as one of the non-cyclooxygenase, non-lipoxygenase arms of eicosanoid production, and overlaps heavily with hepatic xenobiotic oxidation.

Programmed cell death in response to reactive oxygen species is the decision a cell makes to kill itself when oxidative damage exceeds what its antioxidant defences can absorb. It sets the threshold between adaptive stress tolerance and elimination, and shapes outcomes in ischaemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, noise-induced hair cell loss and the oxidative stress of tumour cells. The components span sensing, survival signalling and execution: PARK7 and PINK1 buffer mitochondrial oxidant load and are lost in parkinsonism, HGF-MET and AKT1 signalling suppresses death while FOXO3 and stress kinases such as MAP2K4 and STK25 promote it, and endonuclease G translocating from mitochondria fragments DNA once commitment occurs. Several microRNAs, including miR-21, miR-34a and let-7b, tune this balance in cardiomyocytes and other post-mitotic cells. The pathway therefore links redox metabolism to apoptosis rather than being a separate death programme.

Oxidative stress that exceeds a cell's antioxidant capacity does not simply damage it passively; beyond a threshold it triggers programmed cell death in response to reactive oxygen species, an active suicide programme that removes irreparably oxidised cells. This decision shapes ischaemia-reperfusion injury, cardiac and neuronal loss, and the survival of tumour cells under redox stress. Survival signalling opposes it, with hepatocyte growth factor acting through its receptor MET to engage AKT1, which restrains the pro-apoptotic transcription factor FOXO3; stress kinases such as MAP2K4 and the scaffold RACK1 push the balance the other way. Mitochondria are central: PINK1 and PARK7 protect against oxidant-induced degeneration, TRAP1 buffers the organelle, and endonuclease G relocates to fragment nuclear DNA. Several microRNAs, including miR-21 and miR-34a, tune the threshold at which commitment occurs.

calcitonin family receptor signaling pathway covers the peptide hormones calcitonin, CGRP, adrenomedullin and amylin and the receptors through which they act, controlling bone turnover and calcium handling, vascular tone and permeability, satiety and glucose homeostasis, and the sensitization of nociceptors that underlies migraine. Its defining mechanistic feature is combinatorial: two class B G protein-coupled receptors, the calcitonin receptor and the calcitonin receptor-like receptor, each associate with one of three receptor activity-modifying proteins, and the RAMP partner dictates which peptide is bound and trafficked to the surface, converting two receptors into a family of pharmacologically distinct ones. Signalling proceeds largely through Gs and cAMP, relaxing smooth muscle, restraining osteoclasts and modulating sensory neuron excitability alongside channels such as NaV1.9. Adrenomedullin signalling through RAMP2 is required for lymphatic and vascular development, and CGRP receptor blockade is now standard migraine therapy.

Signalling by the calcitonin family of peptides lets cells respond to a set of related ligands — calcitonin, the calcitonin gene-related peptides, amylin, adrenomedullin and intermedin — that control bone turnover and calcium handling, vascular tone and endothelial barrier integrity, appetite and glucose homeostasis, and the sensitisation of nociceptors. Two class B G protein-coupled receptors, the calcitonin receptor and the calcitonin receptor-like receptor, generate this diversity by pairing with receptor activity-modifying proteins: association with RAMP1, RAMP2 or RAMP3 reshapes ligand preference, converting one receptor into a CGRP or amylin receptor and the other into adrenomedullin receptors, with cAMP as a principal downstream output. Loss of adrenomedullin-RAMP2 signalling causes lethal vascular and lymphatic defects, islet amylin aggregates in type 2 diabetes, and blockade of CGRP transmission is now used to treat migraine.

Double-strand break repair via classical nonhomologous end joining is the fast, template-independent route for rejoining broken chromosomes, and the one that lymphocytes depend on to seal the coding ends generated during V(D)J recombination. It operates throughout the cell cycle, including G1 when no sister chromatid is available for homology-directed repair, and its loss produces radiosensitivity, immunodeficiency and genome instability. Broken ends are captured by the KU70/80 heterodimer, held in a synaptic complex, minimally processed, and sealed by DNA ligase IV with its XRCC4 partner. Access to this route is decided upstream by chromatin ubiquitylation and reader proteins: RNF168-dependent marks recruit 53BP1, which shields ends from resection and thereby channels repair away from homologous recombination and away from the error-prone alternative end-joining that generates translocations. Additional factors such as ERCC6L2 and TOPBP1 tune end protection and checkpoint coupling.

Double-strand breaks are the most dangerous lesions a genome can carry, and classical nonhomologous end joining is the pathway that rejoins them directly, without needing a homologous template, throughout the cell cycle. It is the route used to seal the programmed breaks of V(D)J recombination, so its loss causes immunodeficiency alongside radiation sensitivity and genome instability. The Ku70 subunit encoded by XRCC6 binds broken ends and recruits the ligase IV complex that performs the final religation, while the chromatin ubiquitin ligase RNF168 and the reader 53BP1 mark damaged nucleosomes and bias repair away from homologous recombination and end resection. Additional factors here couple end joining to transcription-associated damage, checkpoint signalling through TOPBP1, and transcriptional control of repair capacity. Unlike alternative, microhomology-mediated end joining, this pathway rejoins the correct partners and does not generate chromosomal translocations.

cell surface receptor signaling pathway via STAT is the route by which cytokines, growth factors and hormones binding at the plasma membrane change gene transcription within minutes, without a second messenger relay. It is the backbone of immune communication and blood cell production: interferons, interleukins, erythropoietin, thrombopoietin, growth hormone, prolactin and leptin all act this way, and loss of its components causes severe combined immunodeficiency, mycobacterial susceptibility, and hyper-IgE syndrome, while constitutive activation drives leukemias and myeloproliferative disease. Receptor-associated JAK kinases phosphorylate STAT1 through STAT6, which dimerize, enter the nucleus and bind target promoters, with lineage outcome determined by which STAT is engaged. Negative regulation is built in and prominent here: SOCS and CIS proteins are themselves STAT targets, forming a feedback loop, while PIAS proteins and phosphatases such as PTPN2 and PTPRC set signal duration. Coactivators and microRNAs tune the transcriptional output.

Many cytokines, hormones and growth factors act on cells by routing their signal through STAT transcription factors, and this cell surface receptor signalling via STAT is the route by which immune polarisation, haematopoiesis, growth and metabolic status are translated into changed gene expression. Ligands and their receptors here span the interleukins, interferons, growth hormone, prolactin, erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and leptin; receptor engagement activates associated Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2), which phosphorylate STAT1 through STAT6, driving dimerisation, nuclear import and target promoter binding with coactivators such as EP300. Feedback and restraint are built in: SOCS and CISH proteins, PIAS1, and phosphatases including PTPN2 and PTPRC terminate the response, and several microRNAs tune it. Loss of individual components produces immunodeficiency, growth hormone insensitivity or defective antiviral defence, while constitutive STAT activity, particularly STAT3 and STAT5, supports leukaemias and solid tumour inflammation.

vascular endothelial cell response to fluid shear stress describes how the cells lining blood vessels sense the drag of flowing blood and convert it into changes in shape, gene expression and vasodilator output. This mechanosensing keeps endothelium quiescent and anti-thrombotic in regions of steady laminar flow, while disturbed or oscillatory flow at branch points and curvatures produces the inflammatory, permeable phenotype where atherosclerotic plaque forms; the same responses guide vascular remodelling and arterial adaptation to changing hemodynamics. Mechanical load is transmitted through focal adhesions and the cytoskeleton, with focal adhesion kinase, ABL1 and calpain remodelling adhesive contacts, and relayed by adenylate cyclase-generated cAMP acting on protein kinase A holoenzymes, by PI3K-PDPK1-AKT and mTOR signalling toward survival and nitric oxide production, and by phosphatases and SOCS5 that restrain the response. MIR92A1 provides flow-sensitive post-transcriptional control of endothelial activation.

Blood flow is not just a delivery system but a signal: endothelial cells lining arteries continuously read the frictional drag of moving blood and adjust their shape, alignment, permeability and gene expression accordingly. Laminar shear keeps the endothelium quiescent, anti-thrombotic and vasodilatory, whereas disturbed flow at branch points and curvatures favours inflammatory activation and is where atherosclerotic plaque preferentially forms. Mechanical force at junctions and focal adhesions is converted into chemistry through focal adhesion kinase and ABL1, the PI3K-AKT-mTOR axis with PDPK1, and phosphatases such as PPP2CA and PTPN1 that set signal duration. A large complement of adenylate cyclases with GNAS and the regulatory and catalytic subunits of protein kinase A supplies cAMP-dependent control of barrier function and tone, while miR-92a acts as a flow-sensitive brake on the atheroprotective endothelial phenotype.

response to oscillatory fluid shear stress is how vascular endothelial cells sense and react to disturbed, back-and-forth blood flow of the kind found at arterial branch points and curvatures, as opposed to the steady laminar flow that keeps endothelium quiescent. This distinction matters because oscillatory flow drives endothelial dysfunction — loss of nitric oxide output, inflammatory activation and increased permeability — and explains why atherosclerotic plaques form at predictable, flow-defined sites rather than uniformly along the vessel. Mechanotransduction here runs through focal adhesions and the cytoskeleton: focal adhesion kinase and the ABL1 tyrosine kinase are activated at sites of integrin engagement, while the phosphatases PTPN1 and PP2A set the threshold and duration of that signalling, and calpain-mediated proteolysis remodels adhesion complexes. The output is altered cell shape, alignment, and gene expression, linking hemodynamics to vascular remodelling and disease susceptibility.

Blood does not flow smoothly everywhere: at arterial branch points and curves it becomes disturbed and reverses direction with each cycle, and endothelial cells read this oscillatory fluid shear stress differently from steady laminar flow. The response matters because it is where atherosclerosis begins — disturbed-flow regions lose endothelial quiescence and barrier integrity, turn on inflammatory adhesion, and become the sites where plaques form, while laminar regions remain protected. Mechanotransduction here converges on focal adhesions and the cytoskeleton, with focal adhesion kinase and the Abl kinase transmitting force-dependent signals, calpain-mediated proteolysis remodelling adhesion components, and a phosphatase pair opposing tyrosine and serine/threonine phosphorylation to set signal duration. The result links mechanical stimulus to changes in cell shape, alignment, and gene expression, making vascular geometry a determinant of regional disease susceptibility.

ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by runaway peroxidation of membrane phospholipids rather than by caspases, and it is the vulnerability exploited to kill therapy-resistant and mesenchymal tumour cells, as well as a contributor to neurodegeneration, ischaemia-reperfusion injury and kidney damage. The balance is set by cystine supply through SLC7A11, glutathione, and GPX4, which reduces lipid hydroperoxides; parallel defence comes from FSP1 (AIFM2) and NQO1 acting on ubiquinone, and from NRF2-driven antioxidant and iron-handling genes including HMOX1 and ferritin. On the pro-death side, ACSL4 loads polyunsaturated fatty acids into membrane lipids, making them oxidisable, while labile iron and cell-cycle- and stress-linked kinases push peroxidation forward. Serine and citrate metabolism, autophagic ferritin turnover via SQSTM1, and NINJ1-dependent membrane rupture link the process to nutrient state and to inflammatory release of cell contents.

Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by runaway peroxidation of polyunsaturated membrane lipids rather than by caspases. It shapes tumour suppression, ischaemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration and the vulnerability of therapy-resistant cancer cells, which is why drugs that trigger it are of interest. The balance is set by supply and defence: the cystine/glutamate antiporter light chain SLC7A11 feeds cysteine into glutathione synthesis so that GPX4 can reduce lipid hydroperoxides, while AIFM2/FSP1 provides a parallel, glutathione-independent radical-trapping route. On the other side, ACSL4 loads polyunsaturated fatty acids into phospholipids and makes membranes oxidizable, and labile iron released via heme oxygenase or held by ferritin determines how much radical chemistry follows. NFE2L2 and its targets, together with autophagic turnover of ferritin, tune sensitivity, and NINJ1-dependent membrane rupture links the death to release of intracellular contents and inflammation.

Calcineurin-mediated signaling converts a sustained rise in intracellular calcium into changes in gene expression, and is the route by which T lymphocytes commit to activation after antigen receptor engagement — the step blocked by cyclosporine and tacrolimus in transplant immunosuppression. Calcium entry, largely through store-operated ORAI1 channels, loads calmodulin, which activates the phosphatase built from a catalytic subunit (PPP3CA/CB/CC) and a regulatory subunit (PPP3R1/R2). The phosphatase dephosphorylates NFAT family transcription factors, unmasking their nuclear localisation signals so they enter the nucleus and drive cytokine genes such as TNF. Opposing kinases including GSK3B and DYRK2 rephosphorylate and export NFAT, while RCAN1/RCAN2 and the myozenin and calsarcin-like anchors tune or localise phosphatase activity. Beyond immunity, the same module directs cardiac and skeletal muscle hypertrophy and fibre-type specification, bone and neuronal differentiation, and organogenesis, with chronic activation contributing to pathological cardiac remodelling.

Sustained rises in intracellular calcium are converted into changes in gene expression through calcineurin-mediated signaling, the route that licenses T cell activation, cardiac and skeletal muscle remodelling, and numerous developmental commitment decisions. Calmodulin loaded with calcium activates the phosphatase built from a catalytic subunit (PPP3CA, PPP3CB, PPP3CC) and a regulatory subunit (PPP3R1/R2); the phosphatase then removes phosphates from NFATC1-NFATC4, exposing nuclear localisation and allowing these transcription factors to enter the nucleus and drive target genes such as TNF. Opposing kinases including GSK3B and DYRK2 rephosphorylate NFAT to terminate the signal, while RCAN1 and RCAN2 and the sarcomeric myozenins restrain the phosphatase directly, and store-operated entry through ORAI1 supplies the calcium. This is the step blocked by cyclosporine and tacrolimus in transplant immunosuppression, and its chronic overactivity contributes to pathological cardiac hypertrophy.

de novo centriole assembly involved in multi-ciliated epithelial cell differentiation is how cells of the airway, ependyma, and oviduct mass-produce the hundreds of basal bodies each motile cilium requires. Ordinary cycling cells make two centrioles by duplicating existing ones; multiciliated cells instead build most of theirs on deuterosomes, electron-dense spherical platforms that nucleate many procentrioles at once, independently of the parental centriole. DEUP1, a paralogue of CEP63, forms the deuterosome core and recruits CEP152, which in turn docks the kinase PLK4 to seed cartwheel assembly, while CCDC78 marks and supports the structure. The amplified centrioles migrate apically, dock at the plasma membrane, and template ciliary axonemes. Failure of this program produces reduced generation of multiple motile cilia, with impaired mucociliary clearance, chronic airway infection, hydrocephalus, and infertility.

Multiciliated cells of the airway, ependyma and oviduct need hundreds of motile cilia, far more than the two centrioles a dividing cell inherits, so during their differentiation centrioles are built de novo rather than by duplication of an existing one. The nucleating platform is the deuterosome, an electron-dense cytoplasmic structure from which many procentrioles grow in parallel; DEUP1 is its defining scaffold, a paralogue of the centrosomal CEP63 that pairs instead with CEP152 to recruit the master procentriole kinase PLK4, while CCDC78 marks and supports the amplification machinery. The output is the basal body pool that anchors each cilium and sets coordinated beating, which clears mucus from the airway, circulates cerebrospinal fluid and moves the ovum. Loss of this amplification step gives too few cilia, producing mucociliary clearance defects, hydrocephalus and infertility.

cell-cell adhesion covers the molecules by which one cell physically binds another, and the intracellular machinery that turns those contacts into signals. It is what allows epithelia to form continuous sheets with sealed barriers, neurons to select and stabilise synaptic partners, and immune cells to recognise and engage each other; loss of it underlies tissue disorganisation, barrier failure, blistering skin disease, and the invasive spread of carcinoma cells. The genes span the principal adhesion families: classical and protocadherins, desmosomal cadherins and plakins, claudins and tight-junction scaffolds, integrins, nectins, selectins and their glycan ligands, and the immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors including MHC molecules and costimulatory pairs such as CD28-CD80/86. Cytoplasmic partners including catenins, talin, vinculin and actin link junctions to the cytoskeleton, while Src-family and receptor phosphatases, Rho GTPases and transcriptional regulators couple adhesion to proliferation, polarity, migration and lymphocyte activation.

Cell-cell adhesion covers the molecular attachments by which one cell binds another, holding tissues together and letting cells recognise their neighbours. It underlies epithelial sheet integrity, endothelial barrier function, synapse formation, and the transient contacts immune cells make when a lymphocyte scans an antigen-presenting cell. The machinery falls into recognisable families: classical and non-classical cadherins with their catenin and plakophilin adaptors at adherens junctions and desmosomes, claudins and junctional adhesion molecules with ZO scaffolds at tight junctions, clustered protocadherins and neurexin-neuroligin pairs giving neurons individual identity, and immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors, selectins, integrins and their ligands such as ICAM1, VCAM1 and nectins mediating leukocyte arrest and costimulation. Adhesive engagement is coupled through actin, talin, vinculin and Src-family kinases to signalling that tunes proliferation, polarity and migration. Loss of these contacts drives epithelial dedifferentiation, invasion, blistering skin disease and barrier failure.

Postsynaptic specialization assembly builds the receptive apparatus on the receiving side of a synapse — the dense scaffold beneath the postsynaptic membrane that clusters neurotransmitter receptors opposite a presynaptic release site. Getting this assembly right determines synapse number, excitatory–inhibitory balance and the capacity for plasticity; disruption of its components underlies autism, intellectual disability and schizophrenia, as mutations in SHANK3 and NRXN family members illustrate. The genes describe trans-synaptic adhesion complexes — neurexins pairing with neuroligins, LRRTMs, SLITRKs and LRFNs, and receptor phosphatases such as PTPRD and PTPRS — that nucleate scaffolds and recruit glutamate or GABA receptors. Secreted organizers including cerebellins, C1QL proteins, neuronal pentraxins and reelin specify which contacts mature, while ARHGEF9 anchors inhibitory sites and kinases such as ABL1 and PTK2B, with PTEN, tune the cytoskeletal remodelling that stabilizes the new specialization.

Synapses work only if the receiving side builds a matching apparatus directly beneath the presynaptic terminal, and assembly of the postsynaptic specialization is how that scaffold, receptor and adhesion machinery is brought together and locked in place. It sets the strength and identity of each contact — excitatory versus inhibitory, glutamatergic versus GABAergic — and its disruption underlies intellectual disability, autism spectrum conditions and cerebellar ataxia. Trans-synaptic adhesion pairs do much of the recognition work: neurexins engaging neuroligins, LRRTMs, SLITRKs and leucine-rich partners, with C1QL and cerebellin proteins bridging to receptors such as the delta-2 glutamate receptor. Receptor-type phosphatases, kinases including ABL1 and PTK2B, Rho-family regulators, and SHANK3 and CASKIN scaffolds then organise the cytoplasmic density, anchoring receptors, cytoskeleton and downstream signalling. The same machinery supports activity-dependent remodelling of existing synapses, not only their initial formation.

Inorganic ion homeostasis is the collective machinery that holds intracellular and systemic levels of calcium, iron, zinc, copper, sodium, potassium, magnesium and phosphate within narrow limits, so that membrane excitability, enzyme cofactor supply and mineral balance remain workable. Its failure produces hemochromatosis and anaemia, Wilson and Menkes disease, rickets and nephrolithiasis, cardiac arrhythmia and neurodegeneration. Mechanistically it spans pumps and exchangers (Na+/K+- and Ca2+-ATPases, NCX and NHE families), release and store-operated calcium channels (IP3 receptors, ryanodine receptors, STIM/Orai and TRP channels) with buffers such as calsequestrin and calreticulin, mitochondrial uptake through the MCU-MICU complex, and metal-specific transporters of the SLC11, SLC30, SLC31 and SLC39 families together with ferritin, transferrin receptors and metallothioneins. Hormonal control by parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, FGF23-Klotho and the hepcidin-ferroportin axis links cellular handling to whole-body mineral and iron balance.

Cells and whole organisms hold the concentrations of calcium, iron, copper, zinc, sodium, potassium, chloride, magnesium and phosphate within narrow limits, and inorganic ion homeostasis is the collection of transporters, channels, pumps, buffers and hormonal circuits that achieves it. Loss of this control underlies cardiac arrhythmia, seizures, hypertension, iron overload and anaemia, Wilson and Menkes disease, and defective bone mineralization. Plasma-membrane and organellar ATPases, exchangers and solute carriers move ions across membranes; ryanodine receptors and inositol trisphosphate receptors release calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum while sarcoplasmic pumps and a mitochondrial uniporter complex clear it; ferritin, metallothioneins and calsequestrin buffer stored metal. Systemic set-points are imposed by parathyroid hormone, vitamin D signalling, FGF23-klotho and hepcidin-ferroportin regulation of intestinal iron export.

skin epidermis development builds the stratified, keratinized barrier that separates the body from its environment, together with the hair follicles and other appendages that arise from it. Its output is a self-renewing epithelium in which basal progenitors, held in that state by TP63 and Notch-Wnt inputs, commit to terminal differentiation and produce the cornified envelope of filaggrin, keratins, transglutaminases and lipid-processing enzymes such as ABCA12 and the lipoxygenases ALOX12B and ALOXE3. Loss of these steps causes ichthyoses, Netherton syndrome and atopic barrier defects with water loss and inflammation. Appendage patterning depends on ectodysplasin-EDAR, hedgehog, FGF and WNT10A signalling, with SOX9 and LGR5 marking follicular stem cell compartments and HOXC13 and DLX3 driving hair keratin expression. The pathway therefore links epithelial stem cell fate, barrier lipid metabolism and mesenchymal-epithelial signalling during skin morphogenesis and repair.

Skin epidermis development covers the formation and maturation of the stratified, keratinized surface of the skin, together with the hair follicles and other appendages that arise from it. Its end product is the barrier that retains water, excludes microbes and withstands mechanical stress; when it fails, the result is ichthyosis, ectodermal dysplasia, defective hair, or atopic disease driven by barrier leak. Surface ectoderm is first committed and held in a basal progenitor state by TP63 and associated transcription factors, then instructed to stratify and differentiate through Notch, Wnt, hedgehog and TGF-beta/BMP signalling, with EDA-EDAR and FGF cues patterning appendage placodes. Terminal differentiation builds the cornified envelope from filaggrin and keratins cross-linked by transglutaminase, while lipid-processing and lipid-transport enzymes such as ABCA12, ALOX12B and ALOXE3 supply the intercellular lipid seal, and protease inhibitors like SPINK5 restrain desquamation.

Response to mitochondrial depolarisation is the cell's reaction to loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, the signal that an organelle has failed and must be cleared or compensated for. This surveillance keeps damaged mitochondria from leaking reactive oxygen species and pro-apoptotic factors, and its impairment underlies the accumulation of defective mitochondria seen in Parkinson's disease and in ageing tissues. Depolarisation recruits autophagy initiation machinery to the affected organelle: the Beclin-1 complex with ATG14 and the ATG13-containing initiation complex nucleate an isolation membrane, AMBRA1 links regulation of that complex to the mitochondrial surface, and the receptor SQSTM1 bridges ubiquitinated cargo to the forming autophagosome, delivering the organelle for lysosomal degradation. GPS2 adds a retrograde arm, relaying mitochondrial status to nuclear transcription. The pathway thus couples organelle quality control to autophagy and to mitochondrial biogenesis programmes.

When a mitochondrion loses its membrane potential, the cell must recognise the damaged organelle and either repair or dispose of it, and the response to mitochondrial depolarisation is that decision point. Its principal output is selective autophagy of mitochondria: loss of potential marks an organelle for engulfment, and the autophagy initiation machinery represented here — the class III PI3-kinase complex with BECN1, ATG14 and AMBRA1, the ULK1-associated subunit ATG13, and the ubiquitin-binding cargo receptor SQSTM1 — nucleates and targets the nascent autophagosome. GPS2 links the depolarisation signal to nuclear transcriptional adjustment, so the response is not purely degradative but also retrograde. Keeping this quality-control arm intact limits accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria, reactive oxygen production and apoptotic priming; its failure is a recurring theme in neurodegeneration, particularly in dopaminergic neurons, and in age-related decline of mitochondrial fitness.

intestinal lipid absorption is the route by which dietary fat, cholesterol and fat-soluble nutrients cross the enterocyte and enter the circulation, and it sets how much of a meal's lipid load the body actually acquires. Its efficiency determines plasma lipid levels and body fat accumulation, and its failure produces fat malabsorption, steatorrhoea and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins. Luminal digestion by pancreatic lipase and cholesterol esterase releases fatty acids and sterols, which enter through transporters such as CD36 and NPC1L1; ABCG5/ABCG8 pump excess and plant sterols back into the lumen, setting the net absorbed fraction. Inside the cell, FABP2 and LPCAT3 direct fatty acids toward triglyceride and phospholipid synthesis, and APOA1, APOA2 and APOA4 with LIMA1 support chylomicron assembly and secretion. Bile acid synthesis genes and leptin signalling tune the process, linking gut absorption to systemic lipid and energy balance.

Dietary fat and cholesterol enter the body across the small intestinal epithelium, and intestinal lipid absorption is the set of steps that captures them from the lumen and hands them on as lipoprotein cargo. It sets how much of a meal's fat and sterol reaches the circulation, so it underlies energy intake, fat-soluble nutrient uptake, and plasma cholesterol levels; loss of its sterol-limiting components causes sitosterolemia, while blocking cholesterol uptake at the brush border is the basis of ezetimibe therapy. Pancreatic lipase and carboxyl ester lipase release fatty acids and sterols from dietary lipid, NPC1L1 and CD36 mediate uptake at the apical membrane, ABCG5/ABCG8 pump plant sterols back into the lumen, and cytosolic FABP2 with LPCAT3 and SOAT2 direct re-esterification toward chylomicron assembly with apolipoproteins A-I, A-II and A-IV. Bile acid composition and epithelial tight junction claudins tune the process.

Cellular oxidant detoxification is the set of enzymatic defences that dispose of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide before they damage lipids, proteins and DNA. It sets the redox tone of the cell, permits aerobic metabolism and controlled oxidant signalling, and its failure drives oxidative stress in neurodegeneration, atherosclerosis, ischaemic injury and ageing. Superoxide dismutases in cytosol, mitochondria and extracellular space convert superoxide to peroxide, which catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins then reduce; thioredoxin, thioredoxin reductases, glutathione reductase and sulfiredoxin regenerate the oxidised catalysts, and glutathione S-transferases conjugate reactive electrophiles. Selenoproteins and stress-inducible sestrins extend this capacity, while NRF2 coordinates transcription of the whole antioxidant programme, including NQO1. Heme proteins such as haemoglobin, myoglobin and cytoglobin, plus scavengers like haptoglobin and ceruloplasmin, limit iron- and heme-driven radical chemistry, linking the pathway to oxygen transport and inflammation.

Aerobic metabolism constantly leaks superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, and cellular oxidant detoxification is the set of reactions that removes them before they oxidise lipids, proteins and DNA. It sets the redox tone in which signalling, proliferation and inflammation occur; its failure produces oxidative damage linked to neurodegeneration, ischaemic injury, ageing and tumour promotion. Superoxide dismutases convert superoxide to peroxide in cytosol, mitochondria and extracellular space, and catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins then reduce peroxides, with thioredoxin, thioredoxin reductases, glutathione reductase and sulfiredoxin regenerating the oxidised catalysts. Glutathione transferases conjugate reactive electrophiles, several selenoproteins support thiol chemistry, and NFE2L2 drives transcription of many of these defences. Haem and metal-binding proteins sequester the iron and copper that would otherwise catalyse radical formation, while peroxidases such as MPO and TPO use peroxide productively in host defence and hormone synthesis.

maintenance of postsynaptic specialization structure keeps the receptor-bearing side of a synapse assembled once it has formed, preserving the arrangement of scaffolds, adhesion molecules and receptor anchors that hold neurotransmitter receptors opposite the release site. Synapses are not static, so continuous maintenance determines whether a circuit retains its wiring and its capacity for stable plasticity; loss of these proteins produces spine and postsynaptic density abnormalities and is a recurring cause of intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy. The genes span the layers of that structure: PDZ scaffolds such as SHANK1, DLG1 and TANC2 that organize glutamate receptor complexes, RAPSN which clusters acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, integrin-based adhesion to the synaptic cleft, and small GTPase regulators including ARF6, GIT1, OPHN1 and SYNGAP1 that restrain actin and membrane turnover beneath the membrane.

Synapses must not only be built but held in place, and this process keeps the postsynaptic specialization intact once it has formed, preserving the size, composition and protein arrangement of the postsynaptic density over time. Stable receptor anchoring underlies the persistence of synaptic strength that long-term memory depends on, and the genes involved are recurrently mutated in intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy. Scaffolding proteins such as SHANK1, DLG1, TANC2 and the liprin PPFIA2 organize receptors and signalling enzymes beneath the membrane, while SYNGAP1 restrains Ras-family signalling that would otherwise drive premature spine maturation, and ARF6, GIT1 and OPHN1 link the specialization to membrane traffic and actin remodelling. At the neuromuscular junction the same requirement is met by RAPSN, which clusters acetylcholine receptors; its loss causes congenital myasthenia.

regulation of cardiac muscle cell action potential tunes the electrical impulse of heart muscle cells — how readily it fires, how fast it spreads, and how long each beat's depolarisation lasts. This control sets heart rate and the coordinated sequence of atrial and ventricular contraction; when it fails the result is long QT syndrome, sick sinus and conduction disease, catastrophic arrhythmia and sudden death. The genes span the machinery that shapes the waveform: L-type calcium entry through CACNA1C with calmodulin and CaMKII feedback, ryanodine receptor and SERCA-mediated calcium cycling, HCN channels generating the pacemaker current of the sinoatrial node, and TRPM4 background conductance. Others govern where channels sit and how excitation passes between cells — ankyrin-B and AKAP9 scaffolding, caveolins and BIN1 membrane organisation, connexin-40 gap junctions, and desmosomal proteins whose loss underlies arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

Every heartbeat begins with a cardiomyocyte action potential, and this pathway covers the machinery that sets its shape, duration and rate of firing rather than the depolarization itself. Its outputs are pacemaker automaticity and orderly conduction: HCN channels carry the funny current that drives sinoatrial diastolic depolarization, GJA5 forms the connexin channels through which excitation spreads, and L-type calcium entry through CACNA1C, coupled to RYR2 release and SERCA2 reuptake, links electrical activity to contraction. Calmodulin, CaMKII and NOS1AP tune channel behaviour, while anchoring and cytoskeletal proteins such as AKAP9, ANK2, BIN1 and CAV3 place channels at the membrane domains where they act. Desmosomal components including PKP2, DSP, DSG2 and JUP tie mechanical junctions to conduction. Mutations here underlie long QT and Brugada syndromes, sick sinus syndrome, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with sudden cardiac death.

regulation of cardiac muscle cell action potential involved in regulation of contraction tunes the electrical signal that tells a cardiomyocyte when and how strongly to contract, setting heart rate and the timing of excitation-contraction coupling. Its failure produces arrhythmia: long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, sinus node dysfunction and impaired contractile reserve. The genes act at several points in this control. HCN4 carries the pacemaker current that drives spontaneous depolarisation in sinoatrial cells, while FGF13 and RANGRF modulate sodium channel availability and trafficking. AKAP9 anchors kinase signalling to potassium channels so that adrenergic input shortens repolarisation, and CAMK2D phosphorylates channels and calcium-handling proteins in response to beat-to-beat calcium. Caveolins organise the sarcolemmal microdomains where these channels reside, and the SERCA2 pump links action potential duration to sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium load, coupling membrane excitability directly to force generation.

Each heartbeat begins with an electrical event, and this pathway covers the modulation of the cardiac myocyte action potential in ways that feed directly into how strongly and how often the cell contracts. Its components tune the ion currents that shape depolarization, plateau and repolarization, and thereby set excitation-contraction coupling: the SERCA2 pump encoded by ATP2A2 reloads the sarcoplasmic reticulum with calcium between beats, CAMK2D phosphorylates calcium-handling and channel proteins in response to sustained calcium signals, and HCN4 carries the pacemaker current that drives spontaneous firing in the sinoatrial node. Scaffolding and membrane-organizing proteins such as AKAP9 and the caveolins position kinases and channels together in the sarcolemma, while FGF13 and RANGRF act as accessory regulators of the cardiac sodium channel. Mutations here produce long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, sick sinus syndrome and arrhythmia-associated cardiomyopathy.

Receptor diffusion trapping is the mechanism that fixes neurotransmitter receptors in place at synapses instead of letting them wander through the plasma membrane. Receptors such as AMPA-type glutamate receptors diffuse laterally at all times; synaptic strength depends on how many are captured and held opposite a release site, so this capture step sets the gain of excitatory transmission and underlies long-term potentiation and homeostatic scaling. The TARP family of calcium channel gamma subunits and SHISA6 act as auxiliary subunits that tether AMPA receptors to PSD-95 scaffolds, while palmitoylation by ZDHHC2 and links to the actin cortex through radixin stabilise the trap. Integrin adhesion and tetraspanin microdomains provide the extracellular and membrane-organising anchors, and KCC2 couples chloride homeostasis to the same submembrane cytoskeletal corral, tuning inhibitory receptor confinement in parallel.

Receptors do not need to be synthesized anew to change a synapse's strength; they can simply be caught and held where they are needed. Diffusion trapping describes the capture of laterally mobile plasma membrane receptors within a defined domain, typically by tethering to scaffold or matrix components beneath the membrane, and it underlies how many AMPA-type glutamate receptors accumulate at postsynaptic sites during synaptic plasticity. The transmembrane AMPA receptor regulatory proteins encoded by the CACNG family, of which stargazin is the prototype, bind receptor subunits and link them to postsynaptic density scaffolds, while SHISA6 restrains receptor desensitization and mobility. Palmitoylation by ZDHHC2 and adhesion through integrin beta-3 tune how firmly receptors are immobilized, and the potassium-chloride cotransporter KCC2 ties this to inhibitory synapse organization. Loss of trapping weakens synaptic transmission and produces ataxia and epilepsy phenotypes.

Anterograde dendritic transport of neurotransmitter receptor complex delivers assembled glutamate and other neurotransmitter receptors outward along dendritic microtubules to the postsynaptic membrane, setting how many receptors a synapse can display and therefore its strength. Because synaptic plasticity, learning and memory depend on regulated receptor supply, disruption of this traffic weakens excitatory transmission and contributes to neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease; mutations in the kinesin heavy chain KIF5A cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and motor neuron degeneration. The carriers are plus-end-directed kinesins: KIF17 with its scaffold adaptors moves NMDA receptor subunit cargo, while kinesin-1 heavy chains and the kinesin-2 components KIF3B and KIFAP3 carry receptor-containing vesicles and associated cargo. This is a specialised branch of microtubule-based intracellular transport, linked to dendritic polarity, vesicle sorting from the secretory pathway, and activity-dependent remodelling of postsynaptic receptor composition.

Excitatory synapses only work if glutamate receptors reach the postsynaptic membrane, and anterograde dendritic transport of neurotransmitter receptor complexes is how they get there: kinesin motors carry receptor-bearing cargo outward along dendritic microtubules toward the postsynapse. The capacity to deliver and replenish receptors sets synaptic strength, so this traffic underlies learning-related plasticity and, when it fails, contributes to cognitive and neurodegenerative disease. KIF17 is the motor most closely tied to NMDA receptor subunit delivery, working with a scaffold adaptor complex that includes KIFAP3 and the kinesin-2 subunit KIF3B, while the kinesin-1 heavy chains KIF5A, KIF5B and KIF5C move receptor and associated cargo through dendritic shafts. Directionality matters because dendritic microtubules are mixed in orientation, so motor choice and cargo adaptors together determine where receptors are deposited. Mutations in KIF5A cause motor neuron and spastic paraplegia phenotypes, underscoring the dependence of neurons on this transport machinery.

Postsynaptic actin cytoskeleton organization builds and remodels the actin scaffold inside dendritic spines, the structural basis of how excitatory synapses change strength during learning. Spine enlargement, stabilization, or collapse all follow from this actin turnover, and its dysregulation underlies intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorders and the synapse loss of neurodegeneration. Actin monomers themselves (ACTB, ACTG1) polymerize under the control of Rho-family GTPase signalling, with RAC3 and the guanine nucleotide exchange factor FARP1 relaying adhesion and receptor cues to the WAVE complex component WASF2, which activates branched filament nucleation. Membrane-shaping and linker proteins such as SH3GL2, EZR and DBNL couple the filament network to the postsynaptic membrane and endocytic machinery, while non-muscle myosin MYH10 provides contractility and SRCIN1 and NOS1AP tie the network to postsynaptic density scaffolds and glutamate receptor trafficking.

Dendritic spines are built on actin, and remodelling that actin at the postsynaptic side is how synapses change shape and strength. Organization of the postsynaptic actin cytoskeleton underlies spine formation, enlargement and retraction, and therefore the structural component of long-term potentiation and depression; when it is dysregulated, spine density and cognitive function suffer, as seen in intellectual disability and neurodegenerative conditions. Actin monomers themselves are supplied by the cytoplasmic beta and gamma isoforms, while a Rho-family GTPase and a WASP-family nucleation-promoting factor drive branched filament assembly, and a non-muscle myosin II heavy chain provides contractile force. Adaptors and membrane-linking proteins including drebrin-like protein, ezrin, FARP1 and the endophilin SH3GL2 couple filaments to the postsynaptic membrane, receptor scaffolds and endocytic machinery, tying cytoskeletal geometry to receptor trafficking and synapse maturation.

AMPA selective glutamate receptor signaling pathway covers fast excitatory neurotransmission at glutamatergic synapses: glutamate binds AMPA-type ionotropic receptors, the channel opens to sodium and potassium flux, and the resulting depolarization drives synaptic integration and the downstream signalling and transcriptional changes that store information. This is the principal route of moment-to-moment excitation in the brain, and its regulated strengthening or weakening is the substrate of long-term potentiation, learning and memory; disturbed AMPA receptor signalling contributes to autism spectrum disorders, epilepsy and excitotoxic neuronal death. The genes here emphasize how the receptor is positioned and controlled rather than the pore itself: trans-synaptic neurexin-neuroligin adhesion aligns pre- and postsynaptic sites, SHANK1 scaffolds receptors within the postsynaptic density, MEF2C couples activity to a transcriptional program of synapse elimination, and a beta-adrenergic receptor links neuromodulatory input to receptor trafficking and phosphorylation.

Fast excitatory transmission at most central synapses runs through AMPA-type glutamate receptors, and this pathway covers what happens after glutamate binds them: cation flux depolarises the postsynaptic membrane and sets off events that reach as far as gene expression. The strength and number of these receptors at a synapse is the physical substrate of learning, and their trafficking underlies long-term potentiation and depression; too much flux contributes to excitotoxic neuronal death. The genes here emphasise the structural and regulatory context rather than the channel itself — a trans-synaptic neurexin–neuroligin adhesion pair aligns pre- and postsynaptic sides, SHANK1 scaffolds receptors within the postsynaptic density, and MEF2C links synaptic activity to transcriptional programmes that prune or stabilise connections. A β-adrenergic receptor component reflects neuromodulatory tuning of receptor phosphorylation and synaptic gain.

vesicle-mediated transport in synapse is the membrane trafficking that makes chemical neurotransmission possible: loading transmitter into vesicles, docking and fusing them at the active zone when calcium arrives, and retrieving membrane afterwards so the terminal can fire again. Without it synapses fatigue and fail, and mutations in its components cause epilepsies, movement disorders and intellectual disability. Vacuolar ATPase subunits acidify vesicles so that vesicular transporters for glutamate, GABA and monoamines can fill them; SNAREs such as SNAP25, syntaxin-1 and VAMP2, together with Munc18, Munc13, RIM and synaptotagmin calcium sensors, execute fast release, while complexins clamp it. Endocytic retrieval uses clathrin adaptors, dynamins, synaptojanin and endophilin. The same machinery governs postsynaptic receptor trafficking and dense-core vesicle release of neuropeptides, linking it to synaptic plasticity and to neurodegenerative proteins including alpha-synuclein, LRRK2 and parkin.

Chemical neurotransmission depends on a local membrane traffic cycle, and this is the pathway that runs it: synaptic vesicles are filled with transmitter, docked and primed at the active zone, fused with the plasma membrane on calcium influx, and retrieved by endocytosis for reuse. Its throughput sets synaptic strength and short-term plasticity, and receptor-containing vesicle traffic on the postsynaptic side underlies changes in synaptic efficacy. Vesicular transporters such as the glutamate and GABA carriers load transmitter using the proton gradient built by the vacuolar ATPase; synaptotagmins act as calcium sensors, SNAREs including SNAP25, syntaxin-1 and VAMP2 with Munc18 and Munc13 drive fusion, complexins clamp it, and clathrin adaptors, dynamins and synaptojanin recover membrane. Mutations here cause epileptic encephalopathies, movement disorders and intellectual disability, and alpha-synuclein and LRRK2 tie the cycle to Parkinson disease.

Presynaptic modulation of chemical synaptic transmission covers the machinery that tunes how much neurotransmitter a nerve terminal releases, rather than whether release occurs at all. This gain control sets the strength and short-term plasticity of synapses, underlies presynaptic inhibition and facilitation, and is the point of action of nicotine, caffeine, opioid-like adenosine signalling, and antipsychotics acting at dopamine and serotonin receptors. Autoreceptors and heteroreceptors on the terminal — muscarinic M2, dopamine D2, metabotropic glutamate mGluR2, adrenergic alpha-2A, adenosine and nicotinic receptors — converge on adenylate cyclase, kinases such as GSK3B, and the release apparatus itself through RAB3A, synaptotagmins and Munc18-interacting proteins. Trans-synaptic and translational regulators including neurexins and FMR1 with its paralogues adjust terminal properties over longer timescales, linking this modulation to learning, and its disruption to fragile X syndrome and addiction.

Neurotransmitter release is not fixed: receptors and regulatory proteins sitting on the presynaptic terminal raise or lower how much transmitter a given action potential releases, and this presynaptic modulation of chemical synaptic transmission is the substrate of short-term plasticity, gain control and the dampening of excess excitation. Autoreceptors and heteroreceptors dominate the list — adenosine A1-family and A2 receptors, alpha-2 adrenergic, M2 muscarinic, dopamine D1 and D2, metabotropic glutamate mGluR2, serotonin 5-HT2A, and several nicotinic subunits that facilitate release at axon terminals — converging on cyclic AMP through adenylyl cyclase 1 and on the release machinery itself via RAB3A, synaptotagmin and Munc18-interacting proteins. Additional regulators include FMR1 and its paralogues, which couple local translation to synaptic strength; loss of that control contributes to fragile X syndrome and to the imbalance of excitation seen in epilepsy and addiction.

regulation of postsynapse organization controls the size, shape and molecular composition of the receiving side of a synapse, and with it the strength of synaptic transmission. Dendritic spine formation, maturation, pruning and collapse all depend on this regulation, which is the structural basis of learning and memory; disruption of these genes recurs in intellectual disability, autism, schizophrenia and neurodegeneration. The core machinery converges on actin: Rho-family GTPases such as RAC1 and CDC42, their GEFs and GAPs, and effectors including PAK3, cofilin and WAVE/WASP-associated regulators remodel the spine cytoskeleton. Scaffolds of the SHANK, HOMER and TANC families organize glutamate receptors and their signalling partners, while adhesion molecules such as neuroligins, LRRTMs and ephrin receptors instruct postsynaptic assembly from across the cleft. Local translation, palmitoylation cycling and ubiquitin-like modification tune this architecture in an activity-dependent manner.

Excitatory synapses are not fixed structures: the size, shape and receptor content of the postsynaptic compartment change with activity, and this remodelling is the physical substrate of learning, developmental circuit refinement and synapse elimination. Regulation of postsynapse organization covers the signals that drive those changes, converging on the dendritic spine actin cytoskeleton. Rho-family GTPases such as RAC1 and CDC42 with their many activators and GAPs (ARHGAP32, ARHGAP33, DOCK4) control actin through cofilin, drebrin and WAVE-complex components, while scaffolds including SHANK3, HOMER1, TANC1/2 and BAIAP2 organize the postsynaptic density around NMDA and metabotropic glutamate receptors. Trans-synaptic adhesion molecules — neuroligins, LRRTMs, EphB receptors, cadherins — instruct where and how large a postsynapse forms, and palmitoylation cycling by ZDHHC enzymes and ABHD17 thioesterases tunes scaffold anchoring. Disruption of these components recurs in intellectual disability, autism and neurodegeneration, where spine loss tracks cognitive decline.

regulation of trans-synaptic signaling covers the control of how strongly and how reliably one neuron communicates with the next, setting synaptic gain across the nervous system. This tuning is the physical basis of learning, memory and circuit refinement, and its derangement underlies epilepsy, autism, intellectual disability, addiction and neurodegeneration. Regulation acts on both sides of the cleft: presynaptic release probability through the active zone and SNARE-associated machinery (RIMS, UNC13, synaptotagmins, complexins, STXBP1), and postsynaptic responsiveness through glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, dopamine and neuropeptide receptors held in place by scaffolds such as PSD-95, SHANK and HOMER. Trans-synaptic adhesion complexes -- neurexins with neuroligins, LRRTMs, cerebellins and teneurin-like partners -- align and specify these compartments, while calcium sensors, CaMKII, calcineurin and kinase cascades convert activity into lasting potentiation or depression. Neurotrophins, glia and neuromodulators supply additional slow, state-dependent adjustment.

Synapses do not transmit at a fixed gain; regulation of trans-synaptic signaling covers the processes that tune how much neurotransmitter is released and how strongly the postsynaptic cell responds, which is the substrate of learning, memory and circuit refinement. Presynaptic release machinery and its modulators, including syntaxins, SNAP25, synaptotagmins, complexins, RIM proteins, UNC13A and STXBP1, set vesicle priming and calcium sensitivity, while voltage-gated calcium channels and auxiliary subunits control the calcium trigger. On the receiving side, ionotropic and metabotropic glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, dopamine and neuropeptide receptors feed into scaffolds such as PSD-95, SHANK and HOMER, with CaMKII, calcineurin and kinase cascades altering receptor number and gating. Adhesion systems -- neurexins, neuroligins, LRRTMs, cerebellins and ephrin receptors -- align the two sides and specify synapse identity. Disruption produces epilepsy, intellectual disability and autism, and this machinery is degraded in neurodegeneration.

synaptic vesicle cytoskeletal transport moves synaptic vesicles and their precursors along microtubules and actin filaments so that presynaptic terminals, often far down an axon, are stocked with the vesicles needed for neurotransmitter release. Neurons depend on it because vesicle proteins are made in the soma but used at the synapse, and failures produce impaired transmission and neurodegenerative or neurodevelopmental phenotypes. The genes describe the machinery that links cargo to motors: the AP-3 adaptor complex, which sorts vesicle membrane proteins into transport carriers destined for the terminal; the BLOC-1 complex with dysbindin and snapin, which couples this sorting to vesicle biogenesis; a BORC subunit that recruits kinesins; the anterograde motor KIF1B; and microtubule-associated proteins including MAP2 and the axon-initial-segment organiser TRIM46 that define the tracks and their polarity. This connects membrane traffic, cytoskeletal organisation and synaptic function.

Neurons must deliver synaptic vesicles and their precursors from the cell body, where membrane proteins are packaged, out along the axon to distant presynaptic terminals, and this cytoskeletal transport of synaptic vesicles is how that delivery happens. Without it terminals are starved of releasable vesicles and neurotransmission fails, a defect linked to axonal neuropathy and to neuropsychiatric and pigmentation disorders. Two coat and sorting complexes dominate: the AP-3 adaptor, which routes cargo into vesicles destined for the terminal, and the BLOC-1 complex including dysbindin and snapin, which cooperates with it in cargo sorting and couples vesicles to motors. Kinesin KIF1B carries cargo anterograde along microtubules, while MAP2 and TRIM46 organise and bundle the axonal microtubule tracks that give the transport its direction. The pathway therefore ties membrane traffic to cytoskeletal polarity and to presynaptic vesicle supply.

Vesicle cytoskeletal trafficking moves membrane cargo to the right place inside a cell by attaching it to motor proteins that walk along microtubules and actin filaments. It sets where organelles, lysosomes, synaptic vesicles and pigment granules sit, and is the reason neurons can supply distant axons and synapses at all; its failure produces hereditary spastic paraplegia, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome and the transport deficits seen in Huntington disease. Kinesins such as KIF1A, KIF5B and KIF13A drive anteriograde movement, myosin V hands cargo to actin at the cell periphery, and dynein with its regulators LIS1, NDEL1 and the BICD-like and TRAK adaptors pulls cargo back toward the centre. Adaptor and biogenesis complexes, including AP-3 and BLOC-1, select which cargo is loaded, coupling sorting at the endosome directly to long-range delivery and organelle positioning.

Membrane traffic inside a cell is not diffusion: vesicles and organelles are hauled along microtubules and actin filaments by motor proteins, and this directed transport is what places synaptic vesicles, endosomes, lysosomes and pigment granules where they are needed. Long-range movement depends on kinesins such as KIF1A, KIF5A and KIF13A for outward transport and on cytoplasmic dynein with its regulators NDE1, NDEL1 and PAFAH1B1 for retrograde delivery, while myosin V handles the final actin-based capture at the cell periphery. Adaptors link the motors to particular cargo: the AP-3 complex and the BLOC-1 subunits sort lysosome-related organelle proteins, TRAK1 and TRAK2 couple mitochondria, and huntingtin with HAP1 supports axonal transport. Because neurons have the longest routes, failure here produces hereditary spastic paraplegia, axonal neuropathies and neurodegeneration; defective AP-3 and BLOC-1 function instead causes albinism with bleeding diathesis.

Inorganic ion import across plasma membrane covers the channels, pumps and carriers that bring sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, protons, phosphate and trace metals such as zinc into the cytosol, setting the electrochemical gradients on which excitability, secretion and epithelial transport depend. Loss of these activities produces cardiac arrhythmia, epilepsy, renal salt-wasting and deafness, and several members are drug targets in diabetes and hypertension. The genes span voltage-gated calcium channels, inward-rectifier and KATP potassium channels with their sulfonylurea receptor subunits, epithelial sodium channels, TRP and purinergic cation channels, sodium-potassium ATPase subunits with FXYD modulators, and cation-chloride, sodium-proton, sodium-calcium and ZIP/ZnT solute carriers. Regulation is built in: calcineurin subunits, WNK-activated STK39, NEDD4L-mediated channel ubiquitination, scaffolds such as AKAP5 and ankyrin, and microRNAs tune transport capacity to hormonal and ischaemic demand.

Cells draw sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, protons, zinc and phosphate inward across the plasma membrane, and this inward transport sets resting membrane potential, drives electrical excitability, loads intracellular calcium stores, and supplies trace metals and nutrients. The machinery spans voltage-gated and ligand-gated channels, pacemaker and inwardly rectifying potassium channels, TRP channels acting as sensors of temperature and irritants, epithelial sodium channels, sodium-potassium pumps with their FXYD modulators, sodium-coupled cotransporters and exchangers of the chloride, proton and calcium families, plus zinc importers. Coupling is the theme: energy stored in a sodium or proton gradient pays for uptake of glucose, chloride or calcium extrusion. Regulation comes through kinases, calcineurin subunits, ubiquitin ligase-mediated channel retrieval and scaffolding proteins. Failures produce long QT and other arrhythmias, epilepsy, hypertension, renal salt-wasting syndromes, deafness and disorders of insulin secretion.

Protein localization to axon is the sorting problem that makes a neuron polarized: proteins destined for the axon must be delivered there and held in place rather than diffusing back into the soma or dendrites. This positioning creates the functional domains of the axon, above all the axon initial segment and the nodes and juxtaparanodes of myelinated fibres, where clustered ion channels and adhesion molecules allow action potentials to initiate and propagate. TRIM46 organizes the parallel microtubule bundles that give the initial segment its identity, ankyrin-G anchors membrane proteins to that scaffold, and contactin and Caspr-family adhesion complexes fix components at axon-glia contact sites, with COPI coat subunits and myelin lipid enzymes supporting delivery. Loss of these anchoring and trafficking steps degrades conduction and is linked to epilepsy, neuropathy and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Neurons keep distinct protein compositions in the axon and the somatodendritic compartment, and protein localization to axon is the sorting, transport and anchoring activity that establishes and maintains that asymmetry. It underlies excitability itself: ion channels and adhesion molecules must be held at the axon initial segment, at nodes of Ranvier and along juxtaparanodes for action potentials to initiate and propagate saltatorily. Ankyrin-G provides the membrane-cytoskeletal scaffold that tethers channels at the initial segment and nodes, TRIM46 organizes the parallel microtubule bundles that define axonal identity and direct cargo entry, and contactin-family adhesion proteins with their associated CNTNAP partners position components at axon-glial contacts. Vesicular trafficking components and myelin-associated lipid and membrane proteins contribute to delivery and stabilization. Disruption affects nerve conduction and is linked to epilepsy, neurodevelopmental disorders and demyelinating neuropathy.

regulation of cardiac muscle cell membrane repolarization controls how quickly a heart muscle cell returns to its resting potential after each action potential, and therefore sets the QT interval and the refractory period that keeps beats orderly. When it fails, repolarization is delayed or dispersed and the myocardium becomes vulnerable to early afterdepolarizations and torsades de pointes, the basis of congenital and drug-induced long QT syndromes as well as short QT and Brugada phenotypes. The work is done largely by potassium channels carrying the delayed rectifier currents, KCNQ1 and KCNH2 tuned by their KCNE accessory subunits, balanced against depolarizing sodium and L-type calcium currents. Scaffolding and anchoring proteins such as ankyrin-B, AKAP9, caveolin-3 and syntrophin position these channels in the sarcolemma and couple them to kinase and nitric oxide signalling, while calcium handling and microRNA-mediated control adjust the balance beat to beat.

Each heartbeat ends with repolarization, the potassium-driven return of the cardiomyocyte membrane toward its resting potential, and the processes that tune this phase set the duration of the action potential and hence the QT interval. Control here determines refractoriness and the safety margin against arrhythmia: too little repolarizing current lengthens the plateau and invites torsade de pointes and sudden death, as in the long QT syndromes, while excess shortens it. The core effectors are the delayed rectifier channels KCNQ1 and KCNH2 together with their KCNE accessory subunits, whose gating and surface levels are modulated by the scaffold AKAP9, ankyrin-B-dependent targeting, caveolin-3 and syntrophin microdomains, and nitric oxide signalling via NOS1 and its adaptor NOS1AP. Sodium channel beta subunits, L-type calcium channel components and calsequestrin link repolarization to depolarizing and calcium-handling currents, and microRNAs add transcriptional-level tuning.</description>

mitotic nuclear membrane organization covers the breakdown of the nuclear envelope as a cell enters mitosis and its rebuilding around the two daughter nuclei at exit. Getting this right determines whether chromosomes are correctly enclosed, whether nuclear transport and chromatin organisation are restored, and whether micronuclei or envelope ruptures arise that drive genome instability. Reassembly requires clearing endoplasmic reticulum membrane tubules from the chromatin surface, a job of the REEP proteins, followed by membrane recruitment and flattening onto chromatin through BAF and the ANKLE2-dependent dephosphorylation of BAF that reverses its mitotic inactivation. Closure of the reforming envelope uses the ESCRT machinery, with VPS4A and its regulators together with spastin-mediated severing of spindle microtubules trapped in the sealing gap. SIRT2 and RCC1 tie the process to mitotic timing and to Ran-based nuclear identity.

When a cell divides, the nuclear envelope must be taken apart and then rebuilt around each daughter genome, and this mitotic nuclear membrane organization covers both halves of that job. It matters because reforming a sealed envelope is what restores nuclear compartmentalization, allows chromatin decondensation and nucleocytoplasmic transport to resume, and prevents micronuclei and DNA damage from persisting membrane holes. Barrier-to-autointegration factor tethers chromatin to inner membrane proteins during reassembly and is regulated by phosphorylation, with ANKLE2 controlling that cycle; ESCRT-associated activities including VPS4A and BROX contribute to sealing the final gaps, while the microtubule-severing enzyme spastin clears spindle microtubules trapped in the closing envelope. Membrane-shaping reticulon-like REEP proteins clear endoplasmic reticulum from the metaphase chromatin region, and SUMO conjugation and RCC1-generated Ran-GTP gradients help position these events in space and time.

intestinal hexose absorption is the step by which dietary sugars released by carbohydrate digestion cross the small intestinal epithelium and enter the blood, supplying the body with its main circulating fuel. Loss of the machinery causes osmotic diarrhoea and malabsorption, as in glucose-galactose malabsorption from defects in the sodium-glucose cotransporter, while fructose handling depends separately on the facilitative carrier GLUT5. Uptake occurs across the brush border of absorptive enterocytes, whose microvillar structure is built and maintained by villin, ezrin and plastin, greatly expanding the surface available for transport. Sodium-coupled uptake requires a continuously replenished luminal sodium supply, which claudin-2 and claudin-15 provide by making the tight junctions of the small intestine cation-permeable. The pathway thus links epithelial architecture, paracellular ion flux and transcellular transport to whole-body glucose supply and postprandial nutrition.

Dietary carbohydrate is useless until its monosaccharide products cross the intestinal epithelium, and intestinal hexose absorption is the step that moves glucose, galactose and fructose from the gut lumen into the blood. It sets the postprandial rise in blood sugar and, when it fails, produces osmotic diarrhoea and carbohydrate intolerance: loss of the sodium-glucose cotransporter SLC5A1 causes glucose-galactose malabsorption, while the facilitative fructose transporter SLC2A5 handles fructose entry. Uptake is secondarily active, driven by the sodium gradient across the brush border, so it depends on the architecture of the absorptive enterocyte surface. Villin, ezrin and fimbrin build and anchor the microvillar actin bundles that provide that surface, and the claudins CLDN2 and CLDN15 make the tight junction cation-permeable, recycling luminal sodium to sustain transport.
