The ether catabolic process here is largely the destruction of PAF: acetylhydrolases remove the acetyl group at the sn-2 position to yield inactive lyso-PAF, terminating signalling through the PAF receptor and so damping platelet aggregation, neutrophil activation, vascular leak and bronchoconstriction. The secreted and plasma-associated phospholipases in this group circulate with lipoproteins and also hydrolyse oxidized phospholipids, linking the pathway to inflammation and atherosclerosis risk. The intracellular acetylhydrolase subunits have a second life in the cell: the regulatory subunit encoded by PAFAH1B1, better known as LIS1, governs dynein-dependent nuclear migration in the developing cortex, and its loss causes lissencephaly.

ether biosynthetic process builds the ether-linked lipids of membranes, chiefly plasmalogens, in which a fatty alcohol is attached to glycerol by an ether rather than an ester bond. These lipids are abundant in myelin, heart, and immune cells, contribute to membrane fluidity and antioxidant defence, and serve as precursors of platelet-activating factor; their loss underlies peroxisomal disorders such as rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata, with skeletal, ocular, and neurological damage. Synthesis begins in the peroxisome, where dihydroxyacetone phosphate acyltransferase and alkylglycerone phosphate synthase form the ether bond using fatty alcohols supplied by FAR1, with PEX7 importing the enzymes; the ether lipid is then completed in the endoplasmic reticulum by desaturation and headgroup addition through PEDS1, SELENOI, and choline phosphotransferase. Phospholipase A2 activity releases the arachidonate and lyso-species that feed eicosanoid and PAF signalling.

Ether lipids carry an alkyl chain attached to glycerol by an ether rather than an ester bond, and their synthesis is what allows cells to make plasmalogens and platelet-activating factor. Plasmalogens are abundant in myelin, heart and sperm membranes, where they buffer oxidative stress and influence membrane fusion; loss of the peroxisomal steps causes rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata, with skeletal shortening, cataracts and severe neurological impairment. The committed reactions begin in peroxisomes, where GNPAT and the PEX7-imported AGPS build the ether bond onto a fatty alcohol supplied by FAR1, after which the intermediate moves to the endoplasmic reticulum for desaturation by PEDS1 and headgroup addition by enzymes such as SELENOI and CHPT1. The same backbone feeds inflammatory lipid signalling: phospholipase A2 release and LPCAT2 acetylation generate platelet-activating factor, linking this ether biosynthetic process to leukocyte activation.

fatty acid derivative metabolic process covers the enzymatic conversion of fatty acids into the activated, elongated, oxygenated and esterified forms that cells actually use, rather than the core beta-oxidation of fat for fuel. It supplies the very-long-chain and ether lipids of myelin and skin barrier, the wax and diacylglycerol esters of sebum, the ketone bodies that sustain brain and heart during fasting, and the eicosanoid mediators of inflammation. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases and transporters activate substrates; ELOVL enzymes with the HACD/TECR reductase steps extend chains; lipoxygenases and CYP4 omega-hydroxylases oxidise them to leukotrienes and hydroxy acids; HMGCS2 and OXCT1 run ketogenesis and ketolysis; DGAT and AWAT enzymes complete esterification. Loss of individual steps causes peroxisomal disease such as X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, ichthyosis and retinal degeneration, linking this metabolism to membrane structure, barrier function and immune signalling.

Fatty acids are rarely used as they are taken up; this metabolic programme converts them into the activated, elongated, oxygenated and esterified derivatives that cells actually need, and it links lipid supply to membrane composition, energy balance and lipid signalling. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases and thioesterases set the pool of activated fatty acids, an elongation cycle built on ELOVL enzymes with HSD17B12, HACD and TECR extends chains for sphingolipids and very-long-chain lipids, and fatty acyl-CoA reductases feed ether lipid and wax ester synthesis alongside DGAT-dependent triglyceride formation. Lipoxygenases and CYP4 omega-hydroxylases generate eicosanoid and leukotriene derivatives, with gamma-glutamyl transferases and dipeptidases processing cysteinyl leukotrienes. Ketone body enzymes such as HMGCS2, HMGCL and OXCT1 handle the oxidative fate. Defects produce peroxisomal and very-long-chain lipid disorders, ichthyosis and inflammatory signalling imbalance.

Regulation of lymphocyte chemotaxis controls how strongly and how far T, B and NK cells migrate toward chemical cues, setting the pace of immune surveillance, lymph node homing and the recruitment of effector cells into inflamed or tumour tissue. Too little and lymphoid tissue fails to organise or infection goes uncleared; too much and tissue is damaged by persistent infiltration, as in autoimmunity and graft rejection. The genes span both the signals and the machinery that tunes them: inflammatory and homeostatic chemokines such as CCL5, CCL21, CXCL13 and CXCL10 with receptors including CCR2, sheddases ADAM10 and ADAM17 that release surface ligands and receptors, and intracellular regulators of adhesion and cytoskeletal polarity including PTK2B, NEDD9, and the WNK1-OXSR1-STK39 module that couples cell volume and ion transport to motility. NK-activating receptor KLRK1 and TNFSF14 link cytotoxic recognition to directed movement.

Lymphocytes reach the tissues and lymphoid compartments where they are needed by following chemokine gradients, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower the strength of that directed migration. It determines how efficiently T, B and NK cells enter lymph nodes, home to inflamed sites, or accumulate in tumours and autoimmune lesions. Secreted attractants dominate the list — CCL2, CCL3/4/5 and CCL7 acting on CCR2-type receptors, CCL21 guiding entry into lymphoid tissue, CXCL13 organising B cell zones, CXCL10 recruiting activated T cells, and XCL1 attracting dendritic partners. Intracellular control comes from the WNK1–OXSR1/STK39 kinase module, which restrains migration while coupling it to ion transport and cell volume, and from PTK2B and NEDD9 acting on adhesion and cytoskeletal turnover. Surface proteases ADAM10 and ADAM17 tune receptor and ligand availability by shedding, and TNFSF14 and WNT5A modify the surrounding stroma.

response to ketone collects the cellular and physiological programmes triggered by ketone-bearing signalling molecules and metabolites — most prominently steroid hormones such as progesterone, corticosteroids and androgens, along with prostaglandins and ketone bodies themselves. It matters because these compounds coordinate stress adaptation, salt and water balance, reproduction and fuel switching during fasting. The genes trace several arms of that response: nuclear receptors and their coactivators (NR3C1, AR, NR1H3, NCOA1/2) driving transcriptional output; aldosterone-responsive sodium handling in the kidney through the epithelial sodium channel subunits, SGK1 and SLC12A3; prostanoid G-protein-coupled receptors feeding adenylate cyclase and PKC cascades; and ketogenic and gluconeogenic enzymes such as HMGCS2, PCK1 and FBP1 acting with AMPK subunits, SIRT1 and uncoupling proteins to reset energy metabolism. Immediate-early factors including FOS and DUSP1 provide the rapid transcriptional wave, linking hormonal exposure to lasting changes in cell behaviour.

Cells and tissues adjust their transcriptional and metabolic programmes when exposed to ketone-containing compounds, a category that spans ketone bodies generated during fasting as well as steroid and prostanoid ligands built on ketone groups. This adaptive response links nutrient scarcity and hormone exposure to gene expression, and it underlies how liver, muscle, kidney and adipose tissue survive starvation or glucocorticoid and androgen signalling. The genes involved include ketogenic and gluconeogenic enzymes such as HMGCS2, PCK1 and FBP1, the energy sensor subunits PRKAA1 and PRKAA2, uncoupling proteins that dissipate mitochondrial proton gradients, and nuclear receptors including the glucocorticoid and androgen receptors with their coactivators. Downstream effects reach immediate-early transcription factors, prostaglandin receptors, epithelial sodium channel subunits and salt-handling transporters, so the response touches fuel selection, inflammation, and renal electrolyte balance. Its dysregulation accompanies diabetic ketoacidosis, muscle wasting and steroid-driven disease.

Cellular response to ketone covers how cells detect and react to ketone-bearing signalling molecules — glucocorticoids and other steroid ketones, prostaglandins, ketone bodies and related metabolites — and convert that exposure into changes in metabolism, gene expression and transport. It matters because these are the messengers of fasting, stress and inflammation: they redirect fuel use toward gluconeogenesis and fatty acid handling, restrain protein synthesis, and adjust salt and water balance in epithelia. Mechanistically the genes span receptor-proximal signalling through prostanoid receptors, adenylate cyclases and G protein subunits to CREB, ELK1 and FOS; nuclear receptor arms via the glucocorticoid and androgen receptors with SGK1 and epithelial sodium channel subunits; and an energy-sensing arm through AMPK subunits, SIRT1, FOXO3 and the atrophy ligase FBXO32. Failure of these responses underlies steroid resistance, disordered gluconeogenesis, and muscle wasting during catabolic stress.

Cells adjust their metabolism and gene expression when exposed to ketone-containing compounds, a class that spans ketone bodies produced during fasting, steroid hormones and ketone-bearing prostaglandins. This cellular response to ketone links nutrient and hormone sensing to transcriptional output: glucocorticoid and androgen receptors together with coactivators and steroid-modifying reductases translate steroid exposure into changes in gluconeogenic and muscle-atrophy programmes, evident in the presence of PCK1 and PCK2, FBP1, FBXO32 and myostatin. A second arm is prostanoid receptor signalling through heterotrimeric G proteins and multiple adenylate cyclase isoforms to cAMP, CREB1 and immediate-early factors such as FOS and ELK1. Energy-status kinases including AMPK subunits, AKT1, RPS6KB1 and SIRT1 couple the same stimuli to catabolic versus anabolic decisions, while epithelial sodium channel subunits and SGK1 tie corticosteroid response to salt and fluid handling. Failure of these responses underlies dysregulated glucose production, muscle wasting and inflammatory imbalance.

Glycosyl compound biosynthetic process covers the reactions that build and interconvert nucleosides and related sugar-linked compounds, supplying the ribo- and deoxyribonucleosides that feed nucleotide pools for DNA replication, RNA synthesis and methyl-group metabolism. It matters because cells recycle purine and pyrimidine bases rather than making them anew: salvage kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases such as TK1, TK2, ADK, HPRT1 and APRT re-attach sugars or phosphates to free bases, while phosphorylases and deaminases including PNP, ADA and MTAP run the reverse, degradative direction and set the balance. Loss of individual steps has clear consequences, from immunodeficiency when adenosine or purine nucleoside catabolism fails to disturbed thymidine supply and mitochondrial DNA depletion. A distinct branch, the TYW enzymes with TRMT12, constructs the hypermodified wybutosine nucleoside in tRNA-Phe, linking this sugar chemistry to translational accuracy.

Glycosyl compound biosynthesis here is largely nucleoside and nucleotide chemistry: the salvage and interconversion reactions that build purine and pyrimidine ribo- and deoxyribonucleosides from free bases, sugar phosphates and recycled precursors. Salvage spares cells the cost of de novo synthesis and supplies the dNTP pools that replication and repair consume, which is why thymidine kinase and thymidylate kinase activity tracks proliferation and why loss of adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase causes severe combined immunodeficiency through toxic metabolite accumulation in lymphocytes. Hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency underlies Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, and MTAP loss is a common collateral deletion in cancer. A second arm builds the hypermodified nucleoside wybutosine on tRNA-Phe, a set of ribose- and base-modifying steps that maintain reading-frame fidelity during translation.

Nucleotide transmembrane transport moves nucleotides and nucleotide-derived cofactors across membranes that they cannot cross unaided, keeping each compartment supplied with the currency it needs. Mitochondria depend on it most visibly: adenine nucleotide translocases exchange ADP for newly made ATP across the inner membrane so that oxidative phosphorylation can power the cytosol, while related carriers import NAD+, FAD, folates, pyrimidine nucleotides and ATP-Mg/phosphate, sustaining mitochondrial DNA replication and redox balance. Other members serve secretion and signalling, including vesicular loading of ATP for purinergic transmission, ABC-type efflux of cyclic nucleotides, volume-regulated anion channels that release nucleotides and second messengers during cell swelling, and Golgi transporters supplying PAPS for sulfation. Loss of individual carriers causes mitochondrial myopathy, cardiomyopathy and progressive external ophthalmoplegia, linking this transport layer directly to energy metabolism, nucleotide salvage and extracellular signalling.

Nucleotides are charged, membrane-impermeant molecules, so their movement across membranes requires dedicated carriers, and this transmembrane transport determines where in the cell the energy currency and nucleotide cofactors are available. The largest contribution comes from mitochondrial carriers: the ADP/ATP translocases exchange cytosolic ADP for matrix ATP to complete oxidative phosphorylation, while relatives import NAD+, FAD, folate-linked and pyrimidine nucleotides or handle ATP-Mg/phosphate exchange, supplying the matrix with cofactors it cannot synthesise. Other members move nucleotide-sugar donors and PAPS into the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum for glycosylation and sulfation, load ATP into secretory vesicles for release as an extracellular purinergic signal, or export cyclic nucleotides and nucleotide analogues across the plasma membrane. Volume-regulated anion channels provide a further conduit for ATP efflux. Loss of these routes causes mitochondrial myopathy, cardiomyopathy and defects in glycosylation and nucleotide salvage.

regulation of cell proliferation involved in kidney development controls how many cells the developing kidney makes, and where, setting nephron number and the final size and architecture of the organ. Getting this wrong produces renal hypoplasia or dysplasia, reduced nephron endowment with lifelong hypertension risk, or persistent nephrogenic blastema that can give rise to Wilms tumour. The genes span the signals and transcription factors that balance progenitor expansion against differentiation: BMP4 and BMP7 gradients acting on the ureteric bud and cap mesenchyme, PDGF ligands driving mesangial and stromal cell proliferation, and the nuclear regulators WT1, PAX-partner GATA3, MYC and the stem-cell RNA-binding factor LIN28A, whose overexpression sustains proliferation and drives tumourigenesis. FLCN, CFLAR and IL6R link the process to growth-factor, survival and inflammatory inputs on nephron progenitors.

Kidney formation depends on tight control of how many cells each lineage makes and when they stop dividing, and this is the tuning of cell proliferation during renal development. Getting it wrong produces hypoplastic or dysplastic kidneys, reduced nephron endowment, and, when growth control fails outright, embryonal kidney tumours such as Wilms tumour. Bone morphogenetic proteins BMP4 and BMP7 act on the branching ureteric epithelium and the nephrogenic mesenchyme to balance proliferation against differentiation, while PDGF ligands drive expansion of mesangial and stromal populations that build the glomerulus and vasculature. Transcriptional regulators including WT1, GATA3, EGR1 and MYC set proliferative output in nephron progenitors, and LIN28A with miR-125a links progenitor self-renewal to developmental timing. FLCN and apoptotic modulators such as CFLAR further limit inappropriate growth, connecting this biology to organ size control and renal tumour suppression.

regulation of mitochondrial DNA metabolic process controls how the mitochondrial genome is copied, repaired and turned over, setting the copy number and integrity of the DNA that encodes core respiratory chain subunits. Because each cell carries many mitochondrial genomes, this regulation determines whether damaged or mutant molecules accumulate to the threshold at which oxidative phosphorylation fails, as happens in mitochondrial myopathies, depletion syndromes and age-related decline in tissue energetics. The activities represented span nicking and degradation of mitochondrial DNA by an endonuclease, sealing of nicks during base excision repair by DNA ligase III, stabilisation of the single-stranded template at the replication fork by mitochondrial single-stranded DNA binding protein, and adenine methylation that marks the genome. Together these steps couple mitochondrial genome maintenance to nuclear signals, cell death execution and metabolic demand.

Mitochondria carry their own small genome, and its copy number and integrity must be actively managed because every respiratory chain complex depends on genes encoded there. This regulatory layer tunes how fast mitochondrial DNA is replicated, repaired and degraded, and its failure leads to depletion or mutation of the mitochondrial genome and the energy deficits that follow. The proteins involved act directly on mitochondrial nucleic acid: a single-stranded DNA-binding protein stabilises unwound replication intermediates, a DNA ligase seals nicks during replication and base excision repair, an endonuclease cleaves mitochondrial DNA during cell death and turnover, and a methyltransferase marks adenine in DNA. Together they place mitochondrial genome maintenance under control that is separate from the nuclear replication and repair machinery, linking it to organelle biogenesis and oxidative metabolism.

negative regulation of post-translational protein modification collects the brakes on protein modification: the deubiquitinases, desumoylases, deacetylases, competitive inhibitors and decoy substrates that stop, reverse or slow the addition of chemical marks to proteins. Because modification marks set protein stability, localisation and activity, restraining the enzymes that write them is how cells keep signalling from becoming self-sustaining. Examples span several mark types — TNFAIP3 and USP4 removing or editing ubiquitin chains, SENP2 stripping SUMO, PIAS3 blocking STAT modification, HDAC8 and SIRT7 erasing acylation, and the mitotic checkpoint proteins MAD2L1 and FBXO5 holding the anaphase-promoting complex inactive until chromosomes align. Chaperone and autophagy adaptors such as BAG2, DNAJB2 and SQSTM1 act by shielding substrates from ligases. Loss of these constraints drives inflammatory NF-κB activation, chromosome missegregation and oncogenic stabilisation of substrates like β-catenin.

Post-translational modifications are reversible or blockable, and this pathway gathers the brakes: factors that prevent, slow or reverse the addition of ubiquitin, SUMO, ADP-ribose, phosphate, acetyl and sugar groups onto other proteins. Restraining modification matters because ubiquitin marks commit proteins to degradation, and premature or excessive tagging destabilises substrates that a cell still needs. Deubiquitinases such as USP4 and USP44, the SUMO protease SENP2, and the ubiquitin-editing enzyme TNFAIP3, which dampens NF-κB signalling, remove or trim existing marks. Others act by occlusion or by sequestering ligases and kinases: BAG and DNAJ co-chaperones, UBXN1, MAD2L1 restraint of the anaphase-promoting complex, and FBXO5 inhibition of that same ubiquitin ligase during mitosis. The theme links protein quality control, mitotic timing, inflammatory signalling and circadian feedback through PER2 and CRY1.

Dense core granule transport moves the vesicles that store neuropeptides, neurotrophins and biogenic amines from the soma, where they are made, to the axon terminals and dendritic sites where they are released. Neurons depend on it because dense core granules cannot be replenished locally; without long-range delivery, peptidergic and neuromodulatory transmission fails, and mutations in the kinesins involved cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and sensory-motor neuropathies. Transport is driven by kinesin-3 and kinesin-1 motors walking along axonal microtubules, whose polarity and organisation are set by microtubule-associated proteins such as MAP2 and the axon initial segment factor TRIM46. Scaffolds including liprin-α and TANC2 couple cargo to motors and to postsynaptic architecture, while the granule protein synaptotagmin-4 links delivery to regulated exocytosis. The pathway thus connects intracellular trafficking to synapse formation, plasticity and neuroendocrine secretion.

Neurons and neuroendocrine cells package neuropeptides, neurotrophins and biogenic amines into dense core granules at the Golgi, but release sites lie far away at axon terminals and dendritic sites, so the granules must be actively hauled there. Dense core granule transport is that directed delivery step, and it sets where and how much peptide signalling a cell can perform; when it fails, cargo such as BDNF never reaches synapses and axonal trafficking deficits follow. Kinesin motors of the KIF1 family together with kinesin-1 heavy chains provide plus-end-directed movement along microtubules, while MAP2 and TRIM46 organise and bundle the microtubule tracks that define axonal versus dendritic routing. Adaptor and scaffold proteins including PPFIA2, TANC2 and the granule-associated synaptotagmin SYT4 couple motors to cargo and to release sites. Mutations in these motors cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and sensory-autonomic neuropathies.

negative regulation of Fas signaling pathway describes the mechanisms that damp death receptor signalling through Fas/CD95, setting the threshold at which a cell commits to extrinsic apoptosis. This restraint matters most in lymphocytes, where Fas ligation is used to delete activated or autoreactive clones: too little Fas signalling permits lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity, while unchecked signalling wastes cells needed for immune memory and tissue homeostasis. Survival cytokine input is one arm of the control, with interleukin-7 acting through its receptor and the shared gamma chain to sustain anti-apoptotic programmes in developing and resting T cells that oppose Fas-induced caspase-8 activation. Additional brakes come from transmembrane BAX inhibitor motif proteins that buffer death receptor and calcium-linked apoptotic signals, and from SMAD-mediated transcriptional regulation, linking receptor-driven cell death to growth factor and cytokine context.

Fas engagement by its ligand normally commits a cell to caspase-8-dependent apoptosis, and this pathway describes the brakes that hold that decision back, damping the frequency or extent of death receptor signalling. Restraint of Fas matters most in the immune system, where activated lymphocytes carry abundant Fas and would be deleted prematurely without survival input; unchecked Fas killing depletes T cell pools, while too much restraint permits autoreactive cells to persist. Interleukin-7 acting through its receptor and the shared common gamma chain provides exactly this kind of cytokine survival signal to developing and memory T cells, opposing apoptotic commitment. Other members contribute intracellular anti-apoptotic buffering, including a transmembrane BAX inhibitor motif protein that limits death signalling and calcium-linked stress. The biology sits at the junction of cytokine-dependent survival and extrinsic apoptosis, setting lymphocyte homeostasis and immune tolerance.

cellular response to salt is the set of adjustments a cell makes when the ionic strength of its surroundings changes, as happens in the kidney medulla, in secretory epithelia, and in any tissue facing dehydration or hypertonic shock. Getting this right preserves cell volume, protein folding and genome integrity; failing it causes osmotic stress, aggregation of macromolecules, and death. The genes point to several arms of that response: HSF1 drives the heat shock transcriptional program that supplies chaperones when high salt destabilises proteins, the stress-activated kinase MAPK13 relays the osmotic signal, and HNRNPA1 together with the nuclear export factor XPO1 links tonicity to altered RNA processing and nucleocytoplasmic trafficking. DAXX and the ribonuclease ZC3H12A tie the response to apoptotic signalling and to the turnover of inflammatory transcripts, connecting osmotic stress to inflammation and cell fate decisions.

Cells exposed to high salt face osmotic stress that shrinks them, concentrates intracellular ions, damages DNA and destabilises proteins, and the cellular response to salt is the adaptive programme that follows. It matters most in tissues that routinely encounter steep solute gradients, such as the renal medulla, and in inflamed tissue where sodium accumulates and shapes immune cell behaviour. The response spans stress-activated kinase signalling through p38 family members, transcriptional reprogramming by heat shock factor 1 to bolster chaperone capacity, altered nucleocytoplasmic trafficking by exportin 1, and changes in mRNA stability and hnRNP-dependent RNA handling as transcripts are redistributed between nucleus and cytoplasm. Regulators of transcription and of inflammatory transcript decay link salt sensing to survival decisions and to cytokine output, so the same stimulus can drive either adaptation or apoptosis depending on severity and duration.

Regulation of calcium ion import into sarcoplasmic reticulum tunes how quickly muscle relaxes after a contraction and how much calcium is stored for the next beat. Cardiac output, skeletal muscle endurance, and the pace of relaxation all depend on it, and its failure contributes to heart failure, where blunted calcium reuptake leaves the cytosol loaded and the store depleted. The pathway centres on the SERCA pump, which drives calcium back across the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane at the cost of ATP, and on a family of small transmembrane micropeptides — phospholamban, sarcolipin, myoregulin and related regulins — that dock into the pump and inhibit it, each with its own muscle-type distribution. Phosphorylation of phospholamban downstream of beta-adrenergic signalling relieves that brake, linking sympathetic drive to faster relaxation, while sarcolipin uncoupling of the pump generates heat in non-shivering thermogenesis.

After each contraction, muscle relaxes only because calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and the rate of that uptake sets both relaxation speed and the size of the store available for the next beat. Regulation of calcium import into this store is largely exerted on the SERCA pump, represented here by the fast-twitch skeletal isoform ATP2A1, through a family of small transmembrane peptides — phospholamban, sarcolipin, myoregulin and a related micropeptide — that bind the pump and lower its apparent calcium affinity. Their inhibition is relieved by β-adrenergic signalling and phosphorylation, which is how catecholamines accelerate cardiac relaxation and increase contractile force. Sarcolipin-dependent uncoupling of the pump also contributes to muscle-based thermogenesis. Disturbed control at this step underlies impaired relaxation and contractile failure in heart disease, and mutations in phospholamban cause inherited cardiomyopathy.

regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to DNA damage by p53 class mediator sets the threshold at which a cell with damaged DNA decides to kill itself rather than repair and continue. This decision determines whether genotoxic stress ends in tumour suppression or in the survival of a mutated clone, and its tuning explains much of why cancer cells resist chemotherapy and radiation. The genes act on p53 itself and on the mitochondrial step it commands: acetylation-dependent control through SIRT1 and KDM1A, cofactor and coactivator input via TAF9 and ZNF385A, translational amplification of p53 by RPL26 and HNRNPK, and direct restraint of mitochondrial permeabilisation by BCL2 and TRIAP1. Others, including MIF, CD74, MUC1 and CD44, dampen the response in a way that favours survival. The pathway therefore sits where DNA damage checkpoints hand over to the mitochondrial apoptotic machinery.

When DNA damage is severe enough that repair fails, p53 commits the cell to death through the mitochondrial arm of apoptosis; the genes here tune how readily that commitment is made. Setting this threshold decides whether a damaged cell is eliminated or survives with mutations, so it sits at the heart of tumour suppression and also governs how tumours respond to genotoxic chemotherapy and radiation. Control is exerted at several levels: cofactors and chromatin regulators such as ING2, KDM1A, SIRT1 and the TAF9/TAF9B subunits shape p53 stability, modification and promoter selectivity, ZNF385A biases transcription toward apoptotic targets, and HNRNPK and RPL26 act on p53 mRNA. Downstream, BCL2 and TRIAP1 restrain mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and caspase-9 activation, while CD44, MIF and MUC1 provide survival input that dampens the death response.</description>

cellular response to reactive nitrogen species is how a cell registers and reacts to nitric oxide, peroxynitrite and related nitrogen radicals, molecules generated during inflammation and vascular signalling that both convey information and damage proteins, lipids and DNA. The response determines whether a cell adapts or dies: it governs redox-sensitive stress kinase signalling through ASK1 and TRAF2, apoptotic commitment via AIFM1 and the caspase modulator CFLAR, cell-cycle arrest through CDK2-cyclin A and FOXO1-dependent transcription, and remodelling of the extracellular matrix by MMP3. Nitric oxide is also read as a legitimate second messenger by soluble guanylate cyclase, linking this biology to vasodilation and smooth muscle tone, while methionine synthase and phosphatase targets such as PTPN1 illustrate the direct susceptibility of thiol and cobalamin centres to nitrosative modification. Persistent nitrosative stress of this kind accompanies chronic inflammation, ischaemia-reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration.

Nitric oxide, peroxynitrite and related reactive nitrogen species are both signalling molecules and sources of damage, and this is the cellular response that decides which outcome follows. It matters in inflammation, where macrophage-derived nitrogen species reach neighbouring cells, and in vascular tissue, where nitric oxide acts as a physiological messenger rather than a toxin. Part of the response is productive signalling: the soluble guanylate cyclase subunit encoded by GUCY1B1 converts nitric oxide into a cyclic GMP signal that relaxes smooth muscle. Part is stress handling, with the MAP3K5 kinase and TRAF2 relaying redox stress toward apoptosis while CFLAR restrains death receptor signalling and the mitochondrial flavoprotein AIFM1 provides a caspase-independent death route. Cysteine nitrosation and tyrosine nitration also alter enzymes such as the phosphatase PTPN1, and transcriptional output through FOXO1 shifts cell cycle and survival gene expression.

negative regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to DNA damage is the set of brakes that keep a genotoxically stressed cell alive long enough to repair its DNA instead of committing to mitochondrial apoptosis. It sets the threshold at which p53-driven damage signalling tips into cytochrome c release, and its overactivity is a common route to chemotherapy and radiation resistance in tumours. Anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members such as BCL2, BCL2L1 and TRIAP1 restrain BAX/BAK pore formation and sequester BID, while deacetylases and cofactors including SIRT1, CCAR2, KDM1A and ZNF385A tune p53 activity and its choice between arrest and death. Replication-associated factors such as ATAD5 and DDIAS limit damage generation itself, and secreted or surface signals -- CXCL12 acting through ACKR3, MIF, CD44, MUC1, clusterin -- deliver survival cues from the microenvironment. The balance shapes both tissue tolerance of damage and mutation accumulation.

When DNA damage is severe, mitochondria release cytochrome c and the cell dies; the restraint described here is the set of activities that damp or block that intrinsic apoptotic route so a damaged cell can pause, repair and survive. It matters in two directions: it protects irreplaceable cells such as neurons and stem cells from being lost to transient genotoxic stress, and when overactive it lets mutant cells persist, a route to chemotherapy and radiation resistance in tumours. Anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members hold back permeabilization of the outer mitochondrial membrane, TRIAP1 limits apoptosome assembly, and deacetylase and demethylase activities such as SIRT1 and KDM1A blunt p53-driven transcription of death genes, while CCAR2 and ZNF385A tune the same output. Chemokine and receptor components including CXCL12, ACKR3, CD44 and MIF feed extrinsic survival signals into this checkpoint.

positive regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to DNA damage describes the inputs that push a genotoxically stressed cell past the point of repair and into mitochondrial apoptosis. This is the tumour-suppressive arm of the DNA damage response: cells carrying irreparable lesions are eliminated rather than allowed to propagate mutations, and loss of this drive underlies both chemoresistance and malignant transformation. The genes act at several levels. RAD9A links checkpoint sensing to death signalling, the helicase FBH1 converts stalled replication forks into an apoptotic signal, and RPL26 and RPS3 raise p53 output by promoting its translation and transactivation. PIAS4-mediated SUMOylation and NACC2 and SKIL modulate p53 activity, while MTCH2 works at the outer mitochondrial membrane to facilitate BID-dependent permeabilization and cytochrome c release, committing the cell to caspase activation.

When DNA damage is too extensive to repair, cells commit to death from within, and this regulatory arm pushes that decision forward by amplifying mitochondrial apoptotic signalling downstream of genotoxic stress. It matters because the threshold it sets decides whether a damaged cell is eliminated or survives with mutations, making it part of tumour suppression and a determinant of how tissues respond to radiation and chemotherapy. Several of the components act through p53: ribosomal proteins can enhance p53 translation and stability, a SUMO E3 ligase modifies p53 and other damage-response factors, and a checkpoint clamp subunit links lesion sensing to downstream effectors. Others act at the mitochondrion itself, where an outer-membrane protein promotes permeabilisation and cytochrome c release, or by relieving transcriptional repression that would otherwise blunt death signalling. Loss of such positive regulation favours survival of genomically unstable cells.

positive regulation of endoplasmic reticulum stress-induced intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway describes the events that push a cell with irreparably misfolded protein load past the point of rescue and into mitochondrial apoptosis. It is the terminal arm of the unfolded protein response: when chaperone induction and translational attenuation fail to restore ER homeostasis, these factors commit the cell to death, a decision that shapes secretory cell turnover, beta cell loss in diabetes, and neuronal death in protein-misfolding disease. The transcription factor CHOP is the hub, driving expression of the BH3-only proteins PUMA, BIM and NOXA that neutralise anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members and license BAX/BAK-dependent outer membrane permeabilisation; BOK acts at the ER-mitochondrial interface. Adaptors and modifiers including NCK1/2, PTPN2, SIRT1 and the ER-resident ubiquitin ligase RNF183 tune the threshold, linking translational control and stress duration to the apoptotic outcome.

When misfolded protein accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum beyond what the unfolded protein response can resolve, cells switch from adaptation to self-destruction, and this pathway covers the events that push that switch toward death. It matters because chronic ER stress apoptosis kills secretory cells under proteotoxic load contributing to beta cell loss in diabetes, neurodegeneration, and ischaemic injury, while its blockade allows stressed tumour cells to survive. The stress-induced transcription factor CHOP is the central amplifier, driving expression of BH3-only proteins such as PUMA, NOXA and BIM that neutralise anti-apoptotic BCL-2 relatives and license mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation; BOK acts at ER-mitochondria contacts. Adaptor and regulatory components including NCK1/NCK2, PTPN2, SIRT1 and an ER-localised ubiquitin ligase tune the threshold, linking ER proteostasis sensing to the mitochondrial intrinsic apoptotic machinery and caspase activation.

positive regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway by p53 class mediator describes the inputs that push a stressed cell over the threshold into p53-driven mitochondrial death rather than repair or arrest. This is the tumour-suppressive arm of the DNA damage response: cells with irreparable genomic damage, oncogenic signalling, or ribosomal stress are eliminated instead of propagating mutations, and loss of this amplification allows transformed cells to survive genotoxic insult and chemotherapy. The genes act at several levels. Ribosomal proteins RPL26 and RPS7 bind p53 mRNA and the MDM2 axis, coupling nucleolar and translational stress to p53 output; ubiquitin supply and TP53BP1-dependent damage signalling govern p53 stability and activation at double-strand breaks; MYC and the homeobox factor MSX1 sensitise cells transcriptionally; a microRNA tunes the response. The endpoint is BAX/BAK-mediated mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation and caspase activation.

When DNA damage or oncogenic stress is severe enough that repair is not an option, p53 commits the cell to death from within, permeabilizing mitochondria and releasing apoptogenic factors. This set covers the inputs that push that decision toward death, amplifying p53-dependent intrinsic apoptosis rather than arrest or senescence. The regulators act at several levels: 53BP1 relays double-strand break recognition to p53 activation, ubiquitin supply supports the turnover that governs p53 abundance, ribosomal proteins including RPL26 and RPS7 couple nucleolar and ribosome biogenesis stress to p53 stabilization and to translation of its mRNA, and MYC and a homeobox factor bias transcriptional output toward pro-apoptotic targets. Effective suppression of this arm removes a barrier to tumour survival, which is why it is disabled in much of human cancer; conversely, excess activity contributes to tissue loss after genotoxic insult and in ribosomopathies.

regulation of chromatin organization covers the upstream controls that decide how tightly or loosely DNA is packaged, and therefore which genes a cell can express and how faithfully it replicates and repairs its genome. It matters because chromatin state is how cell identity is remembered across divisions: loss of these regulators derails lineage commitment and causes developmental disorders and leukaemias, as with rearrangements of the histone methyltransferase KMT2A and its partner MLLT3. The genes act at several levels — histone chaperone and deposition machinery such as the HIRA–UBN1/UBN2 complex and FACT subunits that place H3.3 and clear nucleosomes ahead of polymerases, writers and erasers of histone methylation including SETD1A, KDM1A and the PHF8 demethylases, variant histones like macroH2A that mark repressed domains, and kinases such as CDK1, CDK2 and TLK1/2 that couple chromatin assembly to cell cycle progression. Lineage factors including PAX7 and TAL1 recruit this machinery to tissue-specific targets.

Chromatin is continually remodelled, and this pathway covers the regulatory inputs that set how much of that remodelling happens, where, and when. Control at this level determines whether genes stay silent or become accessible, whether nucleosomes are correctly restored behind replication forks, and whether heterochromatin domains persist through division; its loss contributes to developmental syndromes and to cancers driven by epigenetic misregulation. The members act through several routes: a histone chaperone complex built around HIRA with UBN1/UBN2 and the FACT subunit SSRP1 deposit and reassemble nucleosomes, TLK1 and TLK2 phosphorylate ASF1-type chaperones in a cell-cycle-coupled manner, and CDK1 and CDK2 tie the whole process to mitotic and S-phase timing. Writers and erasers of histone marks including KMT2A, SETD1A, KDM1A, PHF2 and PHF8, along with the variant histone macroH2A1, adjust the modification landscape that downstream readers interpret.

cell cycle DNA replication initiation is the licensing and firing of replication origins that begins each S phase, ensuring the genome is copied exactly once per division. Its regulation is what prevents re-replication and the gene amplification and genomic instability that follow, and it is the point at which growth signals and checkpoint controls decide whether a cell duplicates its DNA. CDT1 loads the MCM2-7 helicase onto licensed origins, and geminin binds and inactivates CDT1 after firing so that no origin is licensed twice within a cycle. Once origins are activated, the DNA polymerase alpha-primase catalytic subunit lays down the RNA-DNA primers from which leading- and lagging-strand synthesis extends. The pathway therefore couples origin selection to the onset of processive replication, and sits at the G1-to-S transition of cell cycle control.

Before a dividing cell can copy its genome, each origin must be licensed once and only once, and this initiation step of cell cycle DNA replication is where that decision is made and executed. Getting it wrong produces under-replicated or re-replicated DNA, chromosome breakage and the genome instability that accompanies tumour formation. CDT1 loads the MCM2-7 hexameric helicase onto origin DNA during G1, and geminin binds and sequesters CDT1 after replication begins so that loaded origins cannot be relicensed within the same cycle. Once fired, the MCM ring unwinds duplex DNA ahead of the fork, and the polymerase alpha-primase catalytic subunit POLA1 lays down the RNA-DNA primers from which processive synthesis proceeds. The pathway therefore couples origin licensing to cell cycle position and is a target of checkpoint control and of replication-stress responses.

mitotic cytokinetic process is the final act of mitosis: the physical division of one cell into two after chromosomes have segregated. It ensures each daughter receives a complete genome and intact organelles, and its failure produces binucleate cells, tetraploidy and the chromosomal instability that seeds tumours. RhoA activation by the GEF ECT2 drives assembly and ingression of the actomyosin contractile ring, with IQGAP proteins and RAB11-dependent vesicle delivery supplying membrane to the furrow. The ring then compacts into an intercellular bridge, where CEP55 recruits ALIX and the ESCRT-III machinery (the CHMP proteins, IST1) with VPS4 ATPases to sever the membrane at abscission. Aurora B and PLK1 time these steps, and the Aurora B-CHMP4C abscission checkpoint delays severing while chromatin remains trapped in the bridge, linking cytokinesis to genome surveillance.

The final step of mitosis, in which one dividing cell is physically severed into two, is carried out by the mitotic cytokinetic machinery represented here. Getting it right keeps chromosome number stable; failure leaves binucleate, tetraploid cells and is one route to aneuploidy and tumorigenesis. An actomyosin ring is positioned and constricted under control of RHOA, its activator ECT2 and the IQGAP scaffolds, with AURKB and PLK1 timing events relative to chromosome segregation. Vesicle traffic through ARF, RAB11 and its effector RAB11FIP3 and the exocyst delivers membrane to the furrow. Final abscission of the intercellular bridge uses CEP55 to recruit ALIX and the ESCRT-III subunits, whose filaments are remodelled by the VPS4 ATPases; CHMP4C holds abscission back until lagging chromatin is cleared, a delay known as the abscission checkpoint. Midbody kinesins such as KIF20A and KIF20B support bridge organization.

regulation of attachment of mitotic spindle microtubules to kinetochore controls how tightly and how correctly chromosomes are gripped by the spindle before they are pulled apart, and thereby determines whether the two daughter cells inherit equal genomes. Errors here produce lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours. The core activity is the chromosomal passenger complex — Aurora B kinase with INCENP, survivin and borealin — which localises to inner centromeres and phosphorylates outer kinetochore substrates to destabilise attachments that are not under proper bipolar tension, giving the cell repeated chances to correct syntelic and merotelic errors while the spindle assembly checkpoint delays anaphase. CDK1 sets the mitotic timing in which this operates, and acetyltransferase and sirtuin activities tune centromeric chromatin and passenger complex behaviour, linking error correction to chromatin state.

Accurate chromosome segregation depends on each sister kinetochore capturing microtubules from the opposite spindle pole, and this pathway tunes how readily and how correctly those attachments form. Its output is the difference between a euploid daughter cell and one that gains or loses chromosomes, so weakening it produces the missegregation and aneuploidy typical of tumour cells. Much of the control resides in the chromosomal passenger complex, in which Aurora B kinase together with INCENP, survivin and borealin localises to inner centromeres and phosphorylates kinetochore substrates so that attachments lacking tension are destabilised and allowed to re-form. CDK1 activity coordinates this with mitotic entry and progression, while acetyltransferase and deacetylase activities such as TIP60 and SIRT1 modify centromeric chromatin and passenger proteins themselves. The pathway therefore links error correction at the kinetochore to spindle checkpoint satisfaction and genome stability.

Positive regulation of attachment of mitotic spindle microtubules to kinetochore promotes the productive capture of chromosomes by spindle microtubules, the step that decides whether sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles or missegregated. Cells that fail here arrest at the spindle assembly checkpoint or divide with aneuploid genomes, a route to chromosomal instability in tumours. Much of the activity comes from the chromosomal passenger complex, in which Aurora B kinase together with INCENP, survivin and borealin concentrates at inner centromeres, phosphorylates outer kinetochore substrates to release incorrect attachments, and thereby biases the system toward bioriented, tension-bearing connections. Acetyltransferases such as KAT5 and KAT2B contribute through centromeric chromatin and passenger complex modification, and additional factors link the process to autophagy machinery and to RNA-binding proteins acting at the centromere.

Accurate chromosome segregation depends on each sister kinetochore capturing microtubules from the correct spindle pole, and this pathway covers the activities that promote and stabilise those attachments during mitosis. Without them, kinetochores remain unattached or wrongly attached, the spindle checkpoint holds cells in mitosis, and cells that escape become aneuploid cat- a route to chromosomal instability in cancer. Four of the genes form the chromosomal passenger complex, in which Aurora B kinase partners with INCENP, survivin and borealin to localise at inner centromeres, phosphorylate kinetochore substrates and destabilise incorrect attachments so that correct ones can form. The acetyltransferases KAT2B and KAT5 contribute through chromatin and non-histone acetylation, and Beclin 1 links this biology to its broader roles in membrane trafficking and autophagy, placing kinetochore-microtubule attachment within mitotic fidelity control rather than spindle assembly alone.

L-alpha-amino acid transmembrane transport moves amino acids across membranes, the step that lets cells acquire nitrogen and carbon skeletons, sense nutrient sufficiency, and clear neurotransmitters from the synapse. It sustains intestinal and renal absorption of dietary amino acids, supplies glutamine and leucine to growing cells, and loads vesicles with glutamate; its failure produces cystinuria, lysinuric protein intolerance, Hartnup disorder and excitotoxic neuronal injury. Carriers of the SLC1, SLC7, SLC38 and SLC17 families, some as heterodimers with the heavy chains SLC3A1 and SLC3A2, work as ion-coupled symporters, obligatory exchangers or vesicular transporters, with mitochondrial SLC25 members shuttling glutamate, aspartate and ornithine for the malate-aspartate shuttle and the urea cycle. Associated proteins including PSEN1, CLN3 and accessory chaperones govern trafficking and surface delivery, and SLC38A9 links lysosomal arginine to mTORC1 activation, tying transport directly to growth control.

Amino acids cannot cross lipid bilayers unaided, so cells rely on a large family of carriers to move them into the cytoplasm, across epithelia, and in and out of mitochondria. This transmembrane transport of L-alpha-amino acids supplies substrates for protein synthesis and nitrogen metabolism, loads neurotransmitter pools, and feeds the nutrient sensing that governs growth. Members include the sodium-dependent glutamate and neutral amino acid carriers of the SLC1 family, the SLC38 system A and N transporters, heteromeric exchangers in which SLC3A2 or SLC3A1 chaperones an SLC7 light chain, vesicular glutamate transporters, and mitochondrial carriers for glutamate, aspartate and ornithine. The output is concrete: glutamate clearance at synapses, cystine import for glutathione, urea-cycle flux, renal and intestinal reabsorption. Loss of individual carriers causes cystinuria, lysinuric protein intolerance, hyperornithinaemia and epileptic encephalopathy, and SLC38A9 links lysosomal arginine to mTORC1 activation.

regulation of organelle transport along microtubule tunes how far, how fast and in which direction membrane-bound cargoes such as lysosomes, endosomes and mitochondria are hauled along microtubule tracks by kinesin and dynein motors. This control is what allows a neuron to place lysosomes at growth cones, deliver mitochondria to distant synapses, and clear autophagosomes from long axons; its loss produces cargo stalling and the axonal transport deficits seen in neurodegeneration. The genes act at several levels: BORC subunits and LAMP1 mark lysosomes for kinesin coupling, adaptors such as FEZ1 and HAP1 link cargo to motors, TRIM46 organises parallel microtubule bundles in the proximal axon that set transport polarity, and microtubule-associated proteins including MAP2 and neurofilament heavy chain modify track availability. STK11 signalling ties this trafficking to axon specification and polarity, and TRIM58 restricts transport during erythroid maturation.

Organelles do not drift to their destinations; they are hauled along microtubules by kinesin and dynein motors, and this regulatory layer sets how far, how fast and in which direction that hauling goes. It matters most in neurons, where mitochondria, lysosomes and secretory cargo must be delivered over axonal distances and where stalled or misdirected transport contributes to neurodegeneration. The genes here act as adaptors and modulators rather than motors themselves: a BLOC-one-related complex subunit couples lysosomal membranes to kinesin for outward movement, scaffolds such as FEZ1 and the huntingtin-associated protein link cargo to motor complexes, and TRIM46 organises the parallel microtubule bundles of the axon initial segment that give transport its polarity. Microtubule-associated and cytoskeletal proteins including MAP2 and neurofilament heavy chain tune track availability, while the kinase STK11 contributes through neuronal polarity signalling.

positive regulation of intracellular signal transduction collects the activating inputs that switch on and amplify signalling inside cells, converting receptor engagement at the surface into sustained cytoplasmic and nuclear responses that drive proliferation, survival, differentiation, immune activation and metabolic adaptation. Its breadth is the point: growth factor and cytokine ligands with their receptor tyrosine kinases (FGFs and FGFRs, EGFR, insulin/IGF, PDGF, TRK family), adaptors such as GRB2, SHC1, IRS1 and GAB1 feeding RAS-RAF-MAPK and PI3K-AKT, mTOR complexes with their Rag GTPase and LAMTOR amino-acid sensing machinery, TGF-beta/BMP and WNT arms, small GTPases of the Rho and RAS families, and innate immune relays through TLRs, MYD88, IRAK kinases, TRAFs and inflammasome components toward NF-kB. Kinase cascade scaffolds, ubiquitin ligases, and microRNAs set the gain. Aberrant amplification here underlies oncogenic transformation, chronic inflammation and fibrosis, which is why many of these nodes are drug targets.

This is the aggregate of activating inputs into intracellular signalling: processes and molecules that switch on, amplify or prolong the relay of information from receptors to the cytoplasmic and nuclear machinery that changes cell behaviour. It spans growth factor and cytokine receptor tyrosine kinases with their adaptors and exchange factors, feeding RAS-RAF-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and mTOR complexes together with their amino-acid-sensing Rag and lysosomal scaffolds; innate immune receptors signalling through MyD88, IRAKs and TRAFs to NF-kB; inflammasome and death-receptor modules; TGF-beta/BMP, WNT, Hippo and G-protein-coupled receptor arms; and stress-, DNA-damage- and unfolded-protein-response kinases. Positive control is exerted by kinases, ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases, small GTPases, scaffolds and secreted ligands. The output is decisions about proliferation, survival, differentiation, metabolism and inflammation, which is why persistent overactivation of these steps underlies cancer, autoinflammatory and fibrotic disease.

Regulation of receptor localization to synapse controls how many neurotransmitter receptors are delivered to, retained at, or removed from synaptic membranes, which is the physical basis of synaptic strength and its plasticity. Learning, memory consolidation and the maintenance of excitatory/inhibitory balance depend on it, and its disruption contributes to intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy. The genes span the steps involved: auxiliary and adhesion proteins such as NETO1/2, glypicans and dystroglycan that capture and stabilise AMPA, kainate and GABA receptors at the postsynaptic site; vesicular trafficking, endosomal sorting and exocytic machinery (GRIPAP1, VPS26B, STX7) that shuttle receptors to and from the surface; Rho and Ras/Rap GTPase modules with actin regulators like drebrin that remodel the spine cytoskeleton; and post-translational modifiers, including palmitoyltransferases ZDHHC2/3 and the sheddase ADAM10, that set receptor and scaffold residence times.

How many neurotransmitter receptors sit in a postsynaptic membrane, and which ones, sets the strength of a synapse, so the trafficking steps that put them there are the substrate of learning and memory. This pathway covers the controls on receptor delivery to, and retention at, synapses: vesicular transport and endosomal recycling, exocytic fusion, scaffolding and cytoskeletal anchoring, and lipid modification that tethers scaffolds to the membrane. Auxiliary subunits such as NETO1 and NETO2 govern kainate receptor composition and surface levels, GRIPAP1 and IQSEC2 act on AMPA receptor recycling and Arf-dependent trafficking, and palmitoyltransferases ZDHHC2 and ZDHHC3 modify synaptic scaffolds and receptor subunits. Small GTPase and MAPK signalling, adhesion molecules and proteolytic shedding by ADAM10 tune the process. Disruption weakens synaptic plasticity and is associated with intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy.

regulation of lens fiber cell differentiation controls when and how fast lens epithelial cells exit the cell cycle and elongate into the transparent, crystallin-packed fiber cells that form the optical core of the eye. Getting the timing right is what makes the lens clear and correctly shaped; failure produces cataract, microphthalmia and anterior segment dysgenesis. The genes describe a balance between a differentiation-promoting growth factor signal and its brakes: FGF2 acting through receptor tyrosine kinase–ERK signalling drives fiber commitment, while Sprouty and Spred proteins dampen that output to prevent premature or excessive differentiation. Withdrawal from proliferation is enforced by the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors p27 and p57, which couple cell cycle exit to elongation, and transcription factors such as FOXE3 and ZEB2 set the epithelial progenitor state upstream. The pathway thus links growth factor signalling, cell cycle arrest and terminal differentiation in an organ whose function is purely structural.

The transparent lens is built by epithelial cells at its equator withdrawing from the cell cycle and elongating into crystallin-packed fiber cells, and this pathway sets how readily and how fast that switch occurs. Getting the balance right determines lens shape and optical clarity; misregulation is associated with cataract and anterior segment malformation. Fibroblast growth factor signalling from the vitreous provides the differentiation cue, and much of the control here is restraint of it: Sprouty proteins and the Sprouty-related SPRED family dampen receptor tyrosine kinase output through RAS-ERK, tuning rather than abolishing the signal. Cell cycle exit is enforced by the CIP/KIP inhibitors p27 and p57, which couple proliferation arrest to fiber elongation, while the transcription factors FOXE3 and ZEB2 govern the lens epithelial state and the competence of cells to differentiate.

negative regulation of lens fiber cell differentiation restrains the conversion of lens epithelial cells into elongated, crystallin-packed fiber cells, so that differentiation happens only at the equatorial transition zone and not across the anterior epithelium. This brake preserves the proliferative epithelial pool that supplies new fibers throughout life, and its loss distorts lens shape and transparency, causing congenital cataract, anterior segment dysgenesis and microphthalmia. The mechanism is largely damping of growth factor input: Sprouty and Spred proteins intercept FGF- and other receptor tyrosine kinase-driven RAS-ERK signalling, the same cascade that otherwise drives fiber elongation, while the forkhead factor FOXE3 maintains epithelial identity and proliferation in the anterior lens and is itself mutated in human lens malformations. The pathway is therefore a spatial patterning device, coupling negative feedback on ERK signalling to the maintenance of an undifferentiated progenitor compartment.

The transparent lens forms only if fibre cell differentiation happens in the right place at the right time, and this pathway supplies the brake. Epithelial cells at the lens equator must be held in a proliferative, undifferentiated state until they are positioned correctly; premature elongation and crystallin accumulation distort lens architecture and cause cataract or anterior segment dysgenesis. The Sprouty and Sprouty-related SPRED proteins dampen receptor tyrosine kinase output, restraining the FGF-driven ERK signalling that would otherwise drive fibre commitment, while the forkhead transcription factor FOXE3 maintains the anterior lens epithelium and its proliferative capacity, with mutations causing congenital lens malformations. Together these factors illustrate how negative regulation of differentiation, rather than differentiation itself, sets the boundary between epithelium and fibre compartment and preserves the ordered cell arrangement on which optical clarity depends.

negative regulation of dendritic spine maintenance describes the processes that destabilise existing dendritic spines, the small postsynaptic protrusions that carry excitatory synapses. Spine loss is how circuits are pruned during refinement and learning, but it is also the structural correlate of cognitive decline: the genes here are the ones through which amyloid- cbeta and prion protein drive synapse elimination in neurodegenerative disease. Amyloid precursor protein and its processing, the APOE isoform background, and cellular prion protein converge on NMDA receptor signalling through GluN2B and the tyrosine kinase FYN, which in turn engages cofilin-dependent remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton that gives a spine its shape. A microRNA contributes post-transcriptional restraint of the same machinery. The pathway therefore links extracellular signals to actin depolymerisation, and its overactivation is the proximate cause of synaptic failure preceding neuronal death in Alzheimer's disease.

Dendritic spines are the postsynaptic compartments of most excitatory synapses, and their persistence is actively opposed as well as supported; negative regulation of dendritic spine maintenance covers the signals that destabilise and eliminate existing spines. Controlled spine loss refines circuits during development and underlies experience-dependent remodelling, but when it runs unchecked it produces the synapse loss that tracks most closely with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease. The genes here converge on that route: amyloid precursor protein and its cleavage products, the ApoE lipoprotein that governs amyloid handling, prion protein as a surface receptor, and the Fyn kinase–NMDA receptor GluN2B axis that transmits the signal inward. Cofilin acts at the endpoint, severing the actin filaments that give a spine its shape.

regulation of mitochondrial electron transport, NADH to ubiquinone controls the throughput of complex I, the entry point where electrons from NADH are passed to ubiquinone and protons are pumped to build the membrane potential that drives ATP synthesis. Tuning this step sets how much energy a cell extracts from fuel and how many reactive oxygen species escape in the process, so its misregulation contributes to oxidative damage and to the neuronal loss of Parkinson disease. The genes act at several levels: a hypoxia-induced microRNA and the alternative subunit NDUFA4L2 dampen complex I activity when oxygen is scarce, an iron-sulfur scaffold supplies the cofactors the enzyme requires, and PINK1, PARK7 and alpha-synuclein link complex I performance to mitochondrial quality control, redox defence and synaptic health. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of oxidative phosphorylation, hypoxic adaptation and neurodegeneration.

Complex I transfers electrons from NADH to ubiquinone, the entry step of the respiratory chain and the point where most mitochondrial proton pumping and much superoxide production begin; regulating its throughput sets how much oxidative phosphorylation a cell runs and how much reactive oxygen it makes. Tuning this step matters under low oxygen, when unrestrained electron flow into a poorly oxidized chain is damaging: hypoxia-induced factors including a microRNA and the complex I subunit paralogue NDUFA4L2 dampen electron entry, while ISCU supplies the iron-sulfur cofactors the enzyme depends on and its loss limits assembly. A second arm is quality control and stress protection, with PINK1 and PARK7 supporting complex I activity and mitochondrial integrity and alpha-synuclein accumulation impairing it. The convergence of these regulators explains why complex I dysfunction is a recurring feature of Parkinson's disease and of ischaemic tissue injury.

negative regulation of amyloid precursor protein catabolic process describes the brakes on cleavage of amyloid precursor protein, the step that determines how much amyloid-beta a neuron releases. Because amyloid-beta accumulation initiates the plaque pathology of Alzheimer's disease, restraint of this processing is one of the main protective axes in the brain, and several of the genes here are among the strongest genetic risk loci for late-onset disease. The mechanisms are varied: reticulon proteins bind and sequester BACE1 away from its substrate, sortilin-related receptor SORL1 and trafficking adaptors such as BIN1 and GGA3 route the precursor through compartments where secretases cannot act, lipid and lipoprotein handling by APOE, CLU and ABCA7 modulates both cleavage and clearance, and a large panel of microRNAs suppresses secretase and precursor expression. Neurotrophic signalling through IGF1 and NTRK2 feeds into the same restraint.

Amyloid precursor protein is continuously cleaved, and how much of it is routed toward the amyloidogenic secretase pathway sets the supply of amyloid-beta peptide in the brain. This set covers the braking side of that process — factors that stop or slow APP catabolism and thereby limit amyloid-beta production, a control point whose loosening is tied to Alzheimer's disease risk. Several mechanisms converge: reticulon proteins bind and sequester BACE1 away from its substrate, the sorting receptor SORL1 and the trafficking adaptors BIN1 and GGA3 divert APP and BACE1 through endosomal and retrograde routes rather than cleavage-competent compartments, and the lipid-handling and chaperone proteins APOE, CLU and ABCA7 influence both processing and clearance. A large group of microRNAs, including the miR-29 family and miR-15/16 members, represses BACE1 and related transcripts post-transcriptionally. The pathway links membrane trafficking, lipid transport and small-RNA regulation to neuronal proteostasis.

Positive regulation of amyloid precursor protein catabolic process covers the influences that push amyloid precursor protein into its proteolytic routes, increasing the rate at which it is cleaved and, in the amyloidogenic direction, the amount of amyloid-beta peptide generated. This matters because amyloid-beta accumulation is the initiating lesion of Alzheimer's disease, and most of the genes here are recognised late-onset risk factors or drug targets: APOE and clusterin as lipoprotein chaperones, PICALM in endocytic trafficking of APP to the compartments where secretases act, and GSAP as a gamma-secretase activating partner. The set links this cleavage to several upstream inputs, including inflammatory signalling through TNF, interferon-gamma and RAGE with NF-kB and SP1 as transcriptional relays, ephrin-EphA4 and cholinergic receptor signalling at synapses, kinase activity via GSK3 and ROCK2, and caspase-3 cleavage of APP itself, tying amyloid production to neuroinflammation, membrane trafficking and neuronal stress.

Amyloid precursor protein is continuously cleaved by secretases, and the balance of those cleavages sets how much amyloid-beta peptide a neuron releases; this pathway covers the influences that push APP catabolism harder, raising amyloid-beta production and deposition in Alzheimer's disease. The genes act at several levels: gamma-secretase modulation by its activating protein GSAP, kinase input from GSK3A, ROCK2 and the Src-family kinase LYN, lipid and cholesterol handling by APOE, CLU and ABC transporters, endocytic trafficking of APP and secretase components through PICALM, and transcriptional drive via SP1 and the NF-kappaB subunit RELA downstream of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and interferon-gamma acting through its receptor. Ephrin-Eph signalling and the RAGE receptor add surface-initiated regulation. Together these tie amyloidogenic processing to cholesterol metabolism, membrane trafficking and neuroinflammation rather than to a single proteolytic step.

regulation of neurofibrillary tangle assembly controls whether hyperphosphorylated tau aggregates into the paired helical filaments and tangles that accumulate in Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies. Tangle burden tracks closely with neuronal loss and cognitive decline, so the balance struck here determines how quickly a neuron's microtubule cytoskeleton and axonal transport fail. The genes act at two levels: kinases and phosphatases that set tau's phosphorylation state, including DYRK1A, the MARK family that phosphorylates tau's microtubule-binding repeats, and the PP2A catalytic subunit that reverses these marks, plus a microRNA that limits tau expression itself. The remainder are lipid and trafficking proteins of the amyloid axis — APOE, clusterin and the sorting receptor SORL1 — linking extracellular amyloid handling and endosomal sorting to intracellular tau pathology, and accounting for much of the common genetic risk for late-onset dementia.

Neurofibrillary tangles are intraneuronal aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau, and this pathway covers the influences that promote or restrain their formation, a process central to Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies where tangle burden tracks with neuronal loss and cognitive decline. Control operates largely through tau phosphorylation balance: the kinases DYRK1A and MARK2 phosphorylate tau at sites that reduce microtubule binding and favour aggregation, while a catalytic subunit of protein phosphatase 2A reverses such marks. Post-transcriptional limits on tau production are set by microRNA regulation. Lipid and trafficking factors act from the other side, with APOE isoforms, clusterin and the sorting receptor SORL1 shaping amyloid handling, endosomal trafficking and glial responses that feed back onto tau pathology. Together these determine how quickly tau shifts from a microtubule-stabilising protein to a filamentous deposit.

Regulation of opsonization controls how heavily microbes and dying cells are coated with complement proteins to mark them for phagocyte recognition and clearance. This tuning determines whether infections are cleared efficiently, whether apoptotic debris and immune complexes are removed without inflammation, and whether complement instead damages host tissue; deficiencies in these components predispose to encapsulated bacterial infection and to lupus-like autoimmunity. The genes cover the recognition arms that initiate deposition — mannose-binding lectin, ficolins and collectins acting through the MASP proteases — together with the classical pathway components C2 and C4 and the alternative pathway amplifiers factor B and properdin, all converging on C3 as the opsonin deposited on the target surface. Counterbalancing them, C4b-binding protein restrains classical and lectin pathway activation, setting the ceiling on how much C3b accumulates.

Opsonization is the coating of microbes and dying cells with complement proteins and other tags so that phagocytes can recognize and engulf them; controlling how much of this coating occurs sets the balance between clearing pathogens and damaging host tissue. The genes here build the classical and lectin routes to C3 deposition: C2, C4A/C4B and C3 itself, factor B and properdin for the alternative amplification loop, and the recognition molecules mannose-binding lectin, ficolins and collectins with their associated proteases MASP1 and MASP2. Regulation runs in both directions — properdin stabilizes the C3 convertase to boost surface tagging, while the C4b-binding protein chains restrain classical pathway convertase activity and limit deposition on host surfaces. Secreted phospholipase PLA2G5 contributes by modifying bacterial membranes. Loss of these components predisposes to pyogenic and meningococcal infection and to impaired clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris.

negative regulation of leukocyte cell-cell adhesion covers the brakes that limit how strongly immune cells stick to one another, and therefore how readily lymphocytes form stable synapses and become activated. It is the machinery of peripheral tolerance: without it, T cells engage antigen-presenting cells unchecked and autoimmunity or chronic inflammation follows, while tumours exploit the same brakes to escape immune attack. The genes are dominated by inhibitory surface receptors and their ligands, including CTLA4, PDCD1 with CD274, LAG3, TIGIT, BTLA and HAVCR2, which recruit phosphatases such as PTPN6, PTPN11 and PTPN22 to damp antigen receptor signalling and integrin avidity. Complementing these are intracellular restraints — CBL and CBLB ubiquitin ligases, SOCS proteins, CSK, proteasome subunits — plus regulatory T cell programming through FOXP3, IL10 and TGFB1, and a large set of microRNAs tuning adhesion and activation thresholds.

Immune responses have to be damped as well as started, and this collection of brakes on leukocyte cell-cell adhesion covers the processes that reduce how often and how tightly lymphocytes stick to each other and to antigen-presenting cells. Loss of these restraints permits runaway T cell activation, autoimmunity and chronic inflammation; their exaggeration in tumours produces immune evasion. Much of the content is inhibitory receptor signalling at the immune synapse, where CTLA4, PDCD1 and its ligands CD274 and PDCD1LG2, LAG3, TIGIT, BTLA, HAVCR2 and the VSIR checkpoint recruit phosphatases such as PTPN6, PTPN22 and PTPN2 to blunt kinase signalling. Complementary arms include SOCS1-mediated cytokine feedback, ubiquitin ligases CBLB, ITCH and PELI1 with the RC3H1/RC3H2 RNA-decay system, immunosuppressive mediators IL10, TGFB1, IDO1 and arginases, galectins, and FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cell identity.

negative regulation of proteolysis involved in protein catabolic process covers the braking mechanisms that protect proteins from destruction by the proteasome and lysosome, setting how long a given protein persists and therefore how strongly its signal is felt. Stabilising a substrate is as decisive as degrading it: p53 rescue by USP7, ribosomal protein RPL5/RPL11 restraint of MDM2, and CDKN2A-linked control of the nucleolar stress response all depend on blocking turnover, and their loss underlies tumour progression and neurodegeneration. Mechanisms represented here include deubiquitinases that reverse ubiquitin marks before commitment to degradation, proteasome inhibitors such as PSMF1 and shuttling cofactors like UBXN1 and SGTA that divert clients away from proteolysis, chaperone-based triage by BAG proteins and HSP90, and UFM1 pathway components. Together they tune protein quality control, developmental signalling, and stress adaptation by determining which substrates escape catabolism.

Protein degradation must be restrained as well as driven, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that spare a substrate from proteolysis during its catabolism. Stabilising a protein rather than destroying it sets the abundance of tumour suppressors, cell cycle regulators and signalling receptors, so these brakes decide the half-life of much of the proteome. Deubiquitinating enzymes such as USP7, USP9X, USP5, USP14 and UCHL5 strip ubiquitin chains before or at the proteasome, reversing the degradation signal; USP14 and the proteasome inhibitor PSMF1 act directly at the particle to damp its activity. Chaperone and cochaperone components including BAG6, SGTA, HSP90AB1 and UBX-domain adaptors triage misfolded clients away from immediate destruction, while ribosomal proteins RPL5, RPL11 and RPL23 stabilise p53 by sequestering MDM2. Loss of such restraint accelerates turnover of regulatory proteins and contributes to tumour suppressor loss and muscle atrophy.

regulation of extracellular matrix organization controls how much matrix a tissue builds, how it is cross-linked and assembled, and how fast it is broken down again. This balance determines tissue stiffness and architecture during development and wound healing, and its loss drives fibrosis of lung, liver, kidney and heart as well as the stromal remodelling that lets tumours invade. TGF-beta signalling through its receptors and SMAD3/SMAD4 is the dominant pro-matrix input, opposed by protease inhibitors such as TIMP3 and RECK that restrain metalloproteinase activity. Collagen and laminin receptors including the discoidin domain kinases DDR1/DDR2 and integrins let cells sense the matrix they have made and adjust output, while transcription factors such as SOX9, RUNX1 and PPARG set matrix programmes by cell type. Numerous microRNAs, notably the miR-29 family, tune collagen and basement membrane gene expression post-transcriptionally.

Tissues control not just how much matrix they make but how it is assembled, cross-linked and turned over, and this regulatory layer determines whether a basement membrane forms correctly, a wound heals or a tissue scars. Signals acting here include TGF-beta ligands with their receptors and SMAD3/SMAD4 effectors, BMP2, interleukin-6 acting through STAT3, and Notch, converging on transcription factors such as RUNX1, SOX9, PPARG and PRDM5 that set the expression of structural components. Collagen VI, laminin chains and nidogen represent the matrix being organized, while TIMP3 and RECK restrain metalloproteinase activity, hyaluronan synthase and heparanase modify glycan scaffolds, and collagen receptors DDR1 and DDR2 report fibril state back to the cell. Numerous microRNAs, including the miR-29 family, tune these transcripts. Dysregulation drives fibrosis, aneurysm and connective tissue disorders, and supports tumour stroma remodelling.

negative regulation of extracellular matrix organization is the braking system on matrix assembly, restraining how much collagen and other structural protein is deposited and cross-linked around cells. It matters because unchecked matrix accumulation is fibrosis: the same restraint keeps vessel walls compliant, cartilage properly composed, and healing wounds from scarring excessively, while its loss underlies organ fibrosis and tumour desmoplasia. Two kinds of control appear here. Protease and protease-inhibitor balance is set by TIMP3, RECK, cystatin C, and the surface peptidases DPP4 and FAP, which curb metalloproteinase and collagen-processing activity. Layered on top is transcriptional and post-transcriptional damping, including TGFB1 signalling through the non-signalling decoy receptor TGFBR3, PPARG-driven suppression of myofibroblast programmes, NOTCH1, TNF receptor input, and a large complement of microRNAs, notably the miR-29 family, that directly repress collagen and matrix transcripts.

The extracellular matrix is continuously built, cross-linked and remodelled, and this pathway covers the brakes on that process — the signals and inhibitors that limit how much matrix is assembled and organized.
