The induced effectors act on many fronts: OAS1 and EIF2AK2 shut down viral RNA and translation, MX1, RSAD2, BST2 and the IFITM proteins block entry, replication and release, ISG15 with UBA7 and UBE2L6 tags proteins for antiviral modification, and immunoproteasome subunits with TAP1 and MHC class I enhance antigen presentation to recruit adaptive immunity.

Type I interferon alerts cells to viral infection, and the interferon alpha response is the transcriptional programme it switches on: dozens of genes that make a cell inhospitable to virus replication and better seen by the immune system. Signalling through STAT2 and IRF9 with IRF7 amplification drives effectors that act at every stage of the viral cycle — MX1 and IFITM proteins block entry and trafficking, OAS1 and EIF2AK2 shut down viral RNA and translation, BST2 tethers budding virions, and ISG15 with its conjugation machinery (UBA7, UBE2L6, HERC6) modifies host and viral proteins, while USP18 removes the mark and restrains the response. Immunoproteasome subunits and TAP1 with HLA class I raise antigen presentation, and CXCL10/CXCL11 recruit lymphocytes. Sustained or misdirected activation of this programme underlies interferonopathies and contributes to lupus-like autoimmunity.

Interferon gamma response is the transcriptional program switched on when cells sense IFN-gamma, the cytokine released by activated T cells and NK cells to license macrophage killing and antigen display. It is what makes infected or malignant cells visible to the immune system, and its loss underlies mycobacterial susceptibility and resistance to checkpoint immunotherapy, while its excess drives macrophage activation syndromes and autoimmune tissue damage. Receptor engagement acts through JAK2 and STAT1 with IRF1 and IRF9 to induce class I and class II MHC together with the peptide-loading and immunoproteasome machinery (TAP1, TAPBP, PSMB8/9, CIITA, NLRC5), chemokines such as CXCL9-11 that recruit effector lymphocytes, antiviral effectors including OAS, MX and ISG15 conjugation, and nitric oxide and tryptophan-catabolizing enzymes. Apoptotic and inflammasome caspases, PD-L1, and SOCS feedback are induced in parallel, coupling defense to self-limitation.

Interferon gamma, released mainly by T cells and NK cells, converts responding cells into an antimicrobial and antigen-presenting state, and the genes it induces define that state. The response underlies clearance of intracellular bacteria, protozoa and viruses, drives tumour immune recognition, and when chronic contributes to autoimmunity, macrophage activation syndromes and immune checkpoint-mediated escape. Receptor engagement signals through JAK2 and STAT1 with IRF1 and IRF9 amplifying transcription, raising class I and class II MHC together with the peptide-loading machinery TAP1, TAPBP and the immunoproteasome subunits PSMB8 and PSMB9, and CIITA and NLRC5 as the transactivators that coordinate them. Downstream products include chemokines CXCL9, CXCL10 and CXCL11 that recruit lymphocytes, adhesion molecules, complement components, guanylate-binding proteins, IDO1-mediated tryptophan depletion, nucleic acid sensors, apoptotic effectors, and PD-L1 plus SOCS1 as brakes limiting the response.

KRAS signaling DN collects the genes silenced when oncogenic KRAS is switched on, and so describes what a cell gives up as it becomes RAS-transformed. Loss of this program is part of how KRAS mutation drives pancreatic, colorectal and lung tumours: differentiated identity, tissue-specific secretory and transport function, and growth restraint are extinguished in favour of proliferation. The members are accordingly the markers of specialised cells rather than of growth — keratins and cornified envelope enzymes of stratified epithelium, contractile and ion-channel proteins of muscle and neurons, hormone subunits, solute carriers and lineage transcription factors such as SOX10, PAX3 and HNF1A. Also suppressed are antiproliferative and tumour-suppressive brakes including BTG2, PTPRJ, ZBTB16 and BARD1, along with immune costimulatory and interferon-inducible genes, linking RAS activation to both dedifferentiation and reduced immune visibility. The set serves as a readout of RAS pathway output in tumour expression data.

Oncogenic KRAS activation not only drives proliferative programmes but also silences a broad swathe of differentiation-associated genes, and this collection captures that repressed arm. The genes lost are largely markers of terminal, tissue-specific identity rather than growth: epidermal keratins and cornified-envelope components such as KRT1, KRT5, SPRR3 and TGM1; striated and cardiac muscle contractile proteins including CKM, MYH7, TNNI3 and the ryanodine receptors; ion channels and solute carriers that define specialized transporting epithelia and neurons; and lineage transcription factors such as SOX10, PAX3, PAX4, HNF1A and ZBTB16. Immune effector and antigen-presentation genes, including IFNG, IL12B, CD80 and CD40LG, are likewise among the down-regulated set, consistent with the immune-cold phenotype of KRAS-mutant tumours. Loss of these programmes underlies the de-differentiation, epithelial plasticity and immune evasion characteristic of RAS-driven pancreatic, colorectal and lung cancers, and re-expression accompanies response to RAS or MEK inhibition.

KRAS signaling up is the transcriptional output of an activated RAS-MAPK pathway — the set of genes a cell turns on when KRAS is mutated or chronically stimulated by growth factor receptors. Because activating KRAS mutations drive pancreatic, colorectal and lung cancer, this program is what oncogenic RAS actually does to cell behaviour: it sustains proliferation, remodels the extracellular matrix, and recruits an inflammatory, immunosuppressive stroma. Immediate-early and feedback components are prominent, including the ETS-family effectors ETV1, ETV4 and ETV5 that read out ERK activity, together with the negative regulators DUSP6 and SPRY2 that restrain it. Downstream lie cytokines and chemokines such as IL1B, CSF2, CXCL10 and CCL20, proteases and plasminogen activators (MMP9, PLAU, PLAUR) enabling invasion, angiogenic and adhesion factors, and PTGS2-driven prostaglandin synthesis. The signature is widely used to score RAS pathway activation in tumours.

Oncogenic KRAS locks a small GTPase in its active state, and the transcriptional output that follows defines much of the behaviour of RAS-driven cancers such as pancreatic, colorectal and lung adenocarcinoma. Genes up-regulated by KRAS activation capture that output: ERK-driven ETS family factors (ETV1, ETV4, ETV5) and their feedback brakes DUSP6 and SPRY2, EGFR-family ligands such as EREG, HBEGF and BTC that sustain autocrine growth stimulation, and cyclin D2 with immediate-early stress regulators that couple the signal to proliferation. A large inflammatory and matrix-remodelling component is equally characteristic, including IL1B, CXCL10, CCL20, CSF2, PTGS2, MMP9 and the urokinase axis PLAU/PLAUR, together with complement and myeloid genes that reflect recruitment of immune cells. Angiogenic and adhesion mediators such as ANGPTL4, ENG, NRP1 and ITGA2 round out a programme that links mitogenic signalling to invasion, neovascularisation and a permissive tumour microenvironment.

Mitotic spindle covers the machinery that builds and orients the bipolar microtubule array on which chromosomes are segregated, the step that determines whether daughter cells receive a complete genome. Failure produces aneuploidy, chromosome missegregation and the genomic instability that characterises tumours, and it is the point of attack for antimitotic drugs. The genes span centrosome duplication and maturation (PCNT, CEP192, SASS6, PLK1), gamma-tubulin ring components that nucleate microtubules, plus-end tracking and crosslinking factors such as CKAP5, CLASP1 and MAPRE1, and kinesins including KIF11 and CENPE that generate spindle bipolarity and move chromosomes. Kinetochore attachment and the spindle assembly checkpoint (NDC80, BUB1, TTK) license anaphase, while separase and cohesin subunits execute it. A large Rho-family GTPase and actin-cytoskeletal contingent positions the spindle relative to cell polarity and drives the cleavage furrow at cytokinesis, coupling mitosis to tissue architecture and asymmetric division.

Every dividing cell must build a bipolar microtubule array that captures chromosomes and pulls one copy of the genome into each daughter, and this collection covers the machinery of mitotic spindle assembly together with the cytoskeletal regulators that shape the dividing cell. Its failure produces misattached kinetochores, multipolar or collapsed spindles, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, the route by which mitotic errors feed tumour development, and several members are the targets of anti-mitotic drugs. Centrosomal and gamma-tubulin complex components nucleate microtubules, TPX2 and Aurora A activity plus kinesins such as KIF11 establish and maintain bipolarity, the NDC80 complex and CENPE link microtubules to kinetochores, and BUB1 with the checkpoint apparatus delays anaphase until attachments are correct. A large Rho-family GTPase and actin-crosslinking contingent, with ECT2, RACGAP1 and anillin, couples spindle position to cortical mechanics and cytokinetic furrow formation.

MTORC1 signaling describes the transcriptional output of the cell's central growth switch, the program induced when nutrients, amino acids, growth factors and energy status permit a cell to commit to biomass accumulation and division. It matters because it sets the anabolic set point of tissues: chronic activation drives tumour growth and metabolic disease, while loss of it blocks cell size increase and proliferation. The genes trace what growth actually requires -- glycolysis and the pentose phosphate shunt (HK2, LDHA, G6PD), serine/one-carbon and amino acid supply (PHGDH, PSAT1, SHMT2, MTHFD2), nucleotide synthesis, nutrient importers such as SLC7A5 and TFRC, and the cholesterol and fatty acid arms driven by SREBP targets HMGCR, SQLE and SCD. Alongside these sit proteostasis machinery -- chaperones, proteasome subunits and an ER stress arm through XBP1, HSPA5, DDIT3 and the feedback inhibitors DDIT4 and TRIB3 that restrain the pathway.

Genes induced when mTORC1 is active, describing the growth programme a cell switches on once nutrients, growth factors and energy are sufficient. The output is anabolic: glycolytic enzymes and glucose transporters, amino acid transporters such as SLC7A5 and SLC1A5, serine and one-carbon enzymes including PHGDH, PSAT1 and SHMT2, nucleotide synthesis, and a full cholesterol and fatty acid programme through HMGCR, SQLE, SCD and the SREBP regulator INSIG1. Protein folding and secretory capacity expand in parallel, with chaperones, proteasome subunits and XBP1 supporting the increased biosynthetic load, and iron and redox supply follow via TFRC and glutathione or thioredoxin enzymes. Feedback and stress brakes are part of the same response, including DDIT4, TRIB3, CDKN1A and the integrated stress mediators DDIT3 and PPP1R15A. Sustained activity of this axis drives cell growth and proliferation and is a common feature of tumours with PI3K or TSC pathway lesions.

MYC targets V1 is the core set of genes switched on by the MYC transcription factor, and it defines what MYC actually does for a cell: it builds biosynthetic capacity so the cell can grow and divide. Because MYC is deregulated in a large fraction of human cancers, this program is the transcriptional signature of proliferative, growth-factor-independent cells, and its loss forces quiescence or differentiation. The genes concentrate on ribosome biogenesis and nucleolar function, translation initiation and elongation, spliceosome and hnRNP-mediated mRNA processing, nucleotide synthesis (CAD, IMPDH2, TYMS, RRM1), chaperonins, proteasome subunits, and DNA replication licensing through the MCM complex and PCNA. Also present are nucleocytoplasmic transport factors and glycolytic and mitochondrial enzymes, reflecting the metabolic shift that accompanies MYC-driven growth. Together these outputs couple oncogenic signalling to mass accumulation and S-phase entry.

MYC is the transcription factor cells use to scale up their biosynthetic capacity for growth and division, and this first collection of its high-confidence target genes shows what that scaling consists of. The genes read as a blueprint for ribosome production and protein synthesis — ribosomal proteins, translation initiation and elongation factors including EIF4E and EIF4A1, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, nucleolar rRNA processing factors such as FBL and NPM1 — together with spliceosomal snRNP and hnRNP components, nucleotide biosynthesis enzymes (CAD, IMPDH2, TYMS, RRM1), chaperonin and proteasome subunits, DNA replication licensing through the MCM complex and PCNA, and nuclear transport carriers. Sustained MYC activity therefore commits a cell to high ribosome biogenesis, nucleotide supply and S-phase entry, which is why its deregulation in lymphoma and many carcinomas produces relentless proliferation and a dependence on translational and metabolic capacity.

MYC targets V2 is a second, more nucleolar-weighted set of genes switched on by the MYC transcription factor, capturing how a growth signal is converted into ribosome production capacity. MYC activation drives cell growth and proliferation in normal tissue and is among the most common events in cancer, where this program supports the elevated biosynthetic demand of transformed cells. The genes are dominated by ribosome biogenesis machinery — rRNA processing and modification factors such as NOP56, NOP2, PES1 and UTP20, nucleolar chaperones like NPM1 and NOLC1, and RNA exosome and helicase components — alongside DNA replication licensing (MCM4, MCM5), mitotic and centriole kinases (PLK1, PLK4), CDK4, and metabolic enzymes for glycolysis, nucleotide supply and polyamine synthesis. Together they link nucleolar expansion to cell cycle entry, making this program a readout of MYC-driven proliferative state and a vulnerability in MYC-dependent tumours.

A second set of genes activated by the MYC transcription factor, dominated by the ribosome biogenesis programme that MYC uses to expand a cell's biosynthetic capacity before division. Growth signals converge on MYC, and its output here is nucleolar: rRNA processing and small subunit assembly factors such as NOP56, NOP2, UTP20, WDR43, IMP4 and NIP7, the nucleolar chaperone-like proteins NPM1 and NOLC1, and RNA helicases and exosome components that trim precursor transcripts. Alongside these sit DNA replication and mitotic factors (MCM4, MCM5, CDK4, PLK1, PLK4), polyamine and nucleotide metabolism (SRM, DCTPP1), glycolytic HK2, and mitochondrial chaperonins HSPD1/HSPE1. Because tumours with amplified or deregulated MYC depend on sustained ribosome production, this signature reads out proliferative drive and marks a state that translation and nucleolar stress interventions can target.

Myogenesis is the program by which mesodermal progenitors and satellite cells become skeletal muscle: they commit to the myogenic lineage, fuse into multinucleated myofibres, and switch on the contractile and energetic machinery that lets muscle generate force. It underlies limb and trunk muscle formation in the embryo and regeneration after injury in the adult, and its components are the genes mutated in muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies. Lineage determination runs through MYOG, MYF6 and the MEF2 factors, which drive expression of sarcomeric actins, myosin heavy and light chains, troponins and tropomyosins. Downstream steps assemble the dystrophin-sarcoglycan complex that couples the sarcomere to laminin-rich basement membrane, build excitation-contraction coupling via RYR1, calsequestrin and SERCA1, install the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction, and shift metabolism toward glycogenolysis, glycolysis and creatine kinase-buffered ATP supply. Growth factor and integrin signalling time withdrawal from the cell cycle before differentiation.

Skeletal muscle is built when proliferating myoblasts withdraw from the cell cycle, fuse into multinucleated fibers, and switch on the contractile and energetic machinery that lets them generate force. Myogenesis covers that whole transition, and its failure or dysregulation underlies muscular dystrophies, congenital myopathies and the limited regenerative capacity of injured muscle. Lineage transcription factors including MYOG, MYF6 and the MEF2 family drive expression of sarcomeric structural proteins — actins, myosin heavy and light chains, troponins, tropomyosins, titin-associated Z-disc components — alongside calcium-handling proteins such as RYR1, ATP2A1 and calsequestrins that couple excitation to contraction. Membrane and matrix components including dystrophin, sarcoglycans, caveolin-3, laminin and integrins anchor fibers to their basement membrane, while creatine kinases, myoglobin and glycolytic enzymes supply energy. Acetylcholine receptor subunits and agrin mark neuromuscular junction assembly, and IGF1, TGFB1 and FGF2 signaling tunes differentiation and growth.

Notch signaling is the juxtacrine communication system by which a cell instructs its immediate neighbours, and it is the main way tissues make binary fate decisions: which cell in a cluster becomes a neuron and which stays a progenitor, how the intestinal crypt divides secretory from absorptive lineages, how somite boundaries and vascular tip cells are specified. Ligands of the Delta and Jagged families engage NOTCH1-3 on the adjacent cell, the receptor is cleaved by the gamma-secretase complex, and the released intracellular domain enters the nucleus with MAML coactivators to switch on repressors such as HES1 and HEYL along with cyclin D1. Glycosyltransferase modification of the receptor and DTX ubiquitin ligases acting with SKP1-CUL1-RBX1 tune the output. Wnt and Frizzled components appear alongside, reflecting the tight coupling of these two pathways in stem cell maintenance; dysregulation drives T-cell leukaemia and other cancers.

Notch signalling lets a cell read the identity of its immediate neighbours, and it is the main way tissues decide which of two adjacent cells adopts which fate. It patterns neurogenesis, somite boundaries, intestinal secretory versus absorptive lineages and vascular smooth muscle, and its misregulation drives T-cell leukaemia, and inherited vascular and skeletal disease. Membrane-tethered ligands such as JAG1 and DLL1 engage NOTCH1-3 receptors on the apposed cell, triggering cleavage by a gamma-secretase complex that includes presenilin, APH1A and PSENEN; the released intracellular domain enters the nucleus and, with MAML coactivators and acetyltransferase activity, turns on HES and HEY repressors and cyclin D1. Fringe glycosyltransferases tune ligand preference, DTX ubiquitin ligases and SCF components set receptor turnover, and the presence of WNT and FZD genes marks the crosstalk through which the two pathways jointly control progenitor self-renewal.

Oxidative phosphorylation is the mitochondrial machinery that converts the reducing equivalents of nutrient breakdown into ATP, supplying most of the energy used by aerobic cells and setting the metabolic capacity of tissues such as heart, muscle and neurons. Electrons from the TCA cycle and fatty acid beta-oxidation feed complexes I through IV -- the many NDUF, SDH, UQCR and COX subunits here -- pumping protons across the inner membrane so that the F1F0 ATP synthase can phosphorylate ADP, with carriers such as SLC25A4/5/6 and VDAC channels exchanging substrates with the cytosol. Supporting functions are represented too: mitochondrial protein import through TOMM and TIMM translocases, mitoribosomal translation of the core catalytic subunits, heme and iron-sulfur cofactor assembly, cristae shaping by OPA1 and MICOS, and antioxidant defence. Inherited defects in these components cause mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, and the same membrane releases cytochrome c during apoptosis.

Oxidative phosphorylation is how cells convert the reducing equivalents harvested from fuel oxidation into ATP, and it supplies most of the energy used by heart, brain, and skeletal muscle. Electrons from NADH and succinate pass through complex I, the succinate dehydrogenase subunits, the cytochrome bc1 core and cytochrome c oxidase, pumping protons across the inner membrane; the resulting gradient drives the F1Fo ATP synthase, whose catalytic and membrane subunits are well represented here. Feeding it are the TCA cycle, fatty acid beta-oxidation, the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, and carrier proteins that move pyruvate, adenine nucleotides, phosphate and acylcarnitines across the membranes. Also included is the supporting infrastructure: protein import translocases, mitochondrial ribosomes, membrane shaping and fusion proteins, heme and iron-sulfur cofactor assembly, and antioxidant defences. Loss of these functions causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathies and lowers the threshold for cytochrome c release and apoptosis.

P53 pathway is the cell's central damage-response program: when DNA is broken, oncogenes are activated, or nucleotides and oxygen run short, the p53 transcription factor halts proliferation and, if the insult persists, eliminates the cell. This is the main barrier to tumour formation in humans, and its loss through TP53 mutation or MDM2 overexpression is the most common event in cancer. The genes trace the whole circuit: sensors and stabilising kinases, the MDM2 degradation loop that keeps p53 low in unstressed cells, and the transcriptional outputs. Those outputs impose arrest through CDKN1A and GADD45A, trigger apoptosis through BAX, BAK1, FAS, APAF1 and PIDD1, drive nucleotide-excision repair via DDB2 and XPC, and tune redox and metabolic state through SLC7A11, TXNIP, SESN1 and GLS2. Related outputs promote senescence, autophagy and differentiation, linking stress surveillance to cell-fate decisions.

The p53 pathway is the cell's central damage-response programme: when DNA is broken, oncogenes are activated, or oxidative and nucleolar stress accumulates, the p53 transcription factor is stabilised and imposes arrest, senescence or death rather than allowing a damaged genome to replicate. Loss of this circuit is the most common event in human cancer, and its output genes explain why. Direct targets include the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A and GADD45A for cell cycle arrest, BAX, BAK1, FAS, APAF1 and PIDD1 for apoptosis, DDB2, XPC, ERCC5 and POLH for nucleotide excision repair and damage tolerance, SESN1, TXNIP, SLC7A11 and GLS2 for redox and metabolic control, and MDM2, PPM1D and RCHY1 as negative feedback that terminates the response. Related family members TP63 and regulators such as CDKN2A and FBXW7 tie the pathway to broader tumour suppression.

Pancreas beta cells describes the identity and secretory program of the insulin-producing endocrine cells of the islets of Langerhans, the cells whose loss or dysfunction causes type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The set couples a lineage transcription factor hierarchy — NEUROG3, PDX1, NKX6-1, NEUROD1, PAX4, ISL1, MAFB, FOXA2 — that specifies endocrine progenitors and maintains beta cell fate, with the machinery of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Glucose entry through SLC2A2 and phosphorylation by glucokinase set the metabolic threshold, ATP closes the KATP channel subunit ABCC8, and depolarisation triggers exocytosis of granules whose cargo is processed by PCSK1 and PCSK2. Signal recognition particle and signal peptidase components reflect the extreme secretory load of these cells. Also present are markers of neighbouring islet lineages such as glucagon and somatostatin, and IAPP, co-secreted with insulin and deposited as islet amyloid in diabetes.

Pancreatic islet beta cells are the body's only source of insulin, and this programme defines their identity and secretory function. It links glucose sensing to hormone release: glucokinase sets the threshold for metabolizing incoming glucose, glycolytic flux closes the ATP-sensitive potassium channel built on the sulfonylurea receptor ABCC8, and depolarization triggers calcium-dependent exocytosis of insulin granules through machinery including STXBP1. Proinsulin and islet amyloid polypeptide are routed through the signal recognition particle and signal peptidase route into granules, where prohormone convertases PCSK1 and PCSK2 mature them. A transcription factor hierarchy including NEUROG3, PDX1, NKX6-1, NEUROD1, PAX4 and FOXA2 specifies endocrine progenitors and maintains the differentiated state. Loss or dedifferentiation of these cells produces type 1 and type 2 diabetes, and mutations in several of these genes cause monogenic diabetes.

Peroxisome covers the biogenesis and metabolic output of the peroxisome, the organelle that performs beta-oxidation of very-long-chain and branched fatty acids, synthesises ether phospholipids such as plasmalogens, and detoxifies the hydrogen peroxide these reactions generate. Its failure is not subtle: loss of the import receptor or docking machinery causes Zellweger spectrum disorders, while defects in the ABCD1 transporter cause X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, both with severe neurological and hepatic consequences. The genes trace the whole route -- peroxin receptors and membrane assembly factors that import matrix enzymes bearing targeting signals, ABC transporters and acyl-CoA synthetases that load substrates, the ACOX1/HSD17B4/ACAA1 oxidation core, GNPAT for ether lipid synthesis, and catalase with peroxiredoxins and superoxide dismutases for redox defence. Also represented are retinoid, bile acid and cholesterol precursor metabolism, and nuclear receptor control linking peroxisomal capacity to lipid demand.

Peroxisomes are small oxidative organelles that handle lipid chemistry the mitochondria cannot: beta-oxidation of very-long-chain and branched fatty acids, ether phospholipid (plasmalogen) synthesis, bile acid intermediate processing, and disposal of the hydrogen peroxide these reactions generate. The organelle's identity rests on import machinery — PEX5 recognises targeting signals and docks at the PEX13/PEX14 membrane complex, with PEX2 and PEX6 completing receptor recycling, while PEX11 proteins control proliferation and division. ABCD transporters deliver fatty acyl substrates across the membrane for ACOX1, the bifunctional enzyme HSD17B4 and thiolase ACAA1, and catalase with peroxiredoxins detoxifies the peroxide produced. Loss of import causes Zellweger spectrum disease; defects in single steps cause X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and related leukodystrophies. Associated retinoid, sterol and lipid-handling enzymes tie this compartment to whole-cell lipid and redox homeostasis.

PI3K AKT MTOR signaling is the growth-factor-driven circuit that tells a cell whether nutrients and mitogenic cues justify growing, dividing, and building biomass. It couples receptor tyrosine kinases and immune receptors to protein synthesis, glucose uptake, and survival, and its constitutive activation through PTEN loss or AKT amplification is among the most common events in human cancer, while its normal tuning governs insulin responsiveness and cell size. Receptor-proximal adaptors such as GRB2, PTPN11 and PIK3R3 feed lipid kinase output to AKT1 and PDK1, which inhibit GSK3B and the TSC2 brake to release mTOR complexes assembled on RPTOR and MAPKAP1; downstream, EIF4E, MKNK1/2 and RPS6KA kinases drive translation while CDKN1A, CDKN1B and E2F1 set cell cycle entry. Overlapping MAPK, AMPK, NF-κB and stress-kinase components place this network at the junction of growth, energy sensing, and apoptotic decision-making.

Growth factor and nutrient cues converge on the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis to decide whether a cell grows, divides, takes up glucose and builds lipid, or instead arrests and conserves. Transcripts induced when this axis is switched on cover the signalling relay itself and the machinery it commands: receptor-proximal adaptors such as GRB2, PTPN11 and NCK1, the AKT1 kinase with its inhibitor PTEN and the TSC2-AKT1S1 brake on mTOR, and the mTOR partners RPTOR and MAPKAP1 that define its two complexes. Downstream outputs include cap-dependent translation through EIF4E and the MKNK kinases, glucose import via SLC2A1, lipogenesis through ACACA, and cell cycle entry via CDK2/CDK4, E2F1 and the CDKN1A/CDKN1B inhibitors. AMPK subunits and stress kinases place the pathway against opposing energy-sensing and JNK/NF-kB stress arms. Hyperactivation of this circuitry, commonly by PTEN loss, drives tumour growth and underlies insulin resistance.

Protein secretion is the membrane-traffic system that moves newly made proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum through the Golgi to the cell surface or lysosome, and retrieves and recycles membrane along the way. It is what allows cells to deliver hormones, enzymes, adhesion molecules and receptors to the right compartment, and its failure underlies lysosomal storage diseases, defective coagulation factor export and disrupted receptor signalling. The genes trace each step: COPII components for ER exit, COPI and ARF/GBF1 machinery for retrograde and intra-Golgi transport, tethering by USO1, COG and ZW10, and SNARE pairs such as BET1, GOSR2, YKT6, VAMP3 and STX16 that fuse each vesicle with its target. Clathrin adaptors, RAB GTPases and ESCRT proteins extend the network into endocytosis, mannose-6-phosphate-dependent lysosomal enzyme sorting, endosome maturation and exosome release.

Protein secretion is the route by which newly made proteins move from the endoplasmic reticulum through the Golgi to the cell surface or to lysosomes, and by which cells release hormones, enzymes, matrix components and signalling molecules. Without it, cells cannot present receptors, remodel their environment, or deliver hydrolases to degradative compartments, and secretory capacity limits specialised cells such as pancreatic and immune secretory cells. The machinery here spans each step: COPI and COPII coat subunits and cargo receptors for ER exit and retrieval, ARF GTPases and their activators for Golgi traffic, clathrin and adaptor complexes for budding, Rab GTPases for compartment identity, and SNARE proteins with their SNAP fusion factors for membrane fusion. Mannose-6-phosphate receptors sort lysosomal enzymes, while ESCRT components link the pathway to endosomal sorting and extracellular vesicle release. Defects produce lysosomal storage and congenital trafficking disorders.

Reactive oxygen species pathway is the cell's antioxidant response: the genes induced when superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and related oxidants accumulate, and the enzymes that dispose of them. It sets how much oxidative stress a cell can tolerate before lipids, proteins and DNA are damaged, and its weakening underlies neurodegeneration, ischaemic injury, inflammatory tissue damage and the redox vulnerabilities exploited in cancer therapy. The members cover each detoxifying arm — superoxide dismutases, catalase, peroxiredoxins and sulfiredoxin, glutathione peroxidases including the lipid-peroxide-directed GPX4, and the thioredoxin and glutaredoxin systems with their NADPH-dependent reductases. Supporting genes supply reducing power and thiol substrates, notably glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and the glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits, alongside iron and copper handling, phase II conjugation, and respiratory chain subunits that are both a source of oxidants and a target of them.

Aerobic metabolism continually leaks superoxide and peroxide, and this reactive oxygen species response is the transcriptional program switched on to neutralize them and repair what they damage. Its output defines a cell's redox buffering capacity: loss of these defenses leaves lipids, protein thiols and DNA open to oxidation, a process implicated in neurodegeneration, inflammatory injury and aging, while tumor cells often lean on the same genes to survive oxidative stress. The members cover the main detoxifying chemistries — superoxide dismutases in cytosol and mitochondria, catalase, glutathione and thioredoxin peroxidases, peroxiredoxins with their sulfiredoxin repair enzyme, and the reductases that regenerate reduced thioredoxin and glutathione. Others supply the reducing currency and cofactors, including glutathione synthesis enzymes and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase for NADPH, alongside iron sequestration, methionine sulfoxide repair, quinone reduction and heme handling.

Spermatogenesis is the programme by which male germ cells divide, undergo meiosis, and reshape themselves into motile sperm, and it is the basis of male fertility — loss of these genes produces azoospermia, immotile sperm, or failure of fertilisation. The set spans every stage: mitotic and meiotic cell cycle machinery including CDK1, cyclin A1, BUB1 and the recombination proteins DMC1 and SYCP1; germline transcriptional and RNA-binding regulators such as DMRT1, DDX4, YBX2 and DDX25 that hold translation in check while transcription shuts down; the histone-to-protamine transition carried out by TNP1, TNP2 and PRM2; and the structural and metabolic components of the mature gamete, from outer dense fibre and tektin proteins and the fibrous sheath anchor AKAP4 to sperm-specific glycolytic enzymes PGK2, GAPDHS and LDHC. Acrosomal proteins including ACRV1, ZPBP and ADAM2 equip the sperm for zona binding and egg fusion.

Sperm production is a continuous differentiation programme in which diploid spermatogonia undergo meiosis and then reshape themselves into motile, fertilization-competent gametes; genes induced during this process account for much of the testis-specific transcriptome, and their loss is a common cause of male infertility. The set spans the successive demands of that programme: meiotic recombination and synapsis machinery such as DMC1 and SYCP1, cell cycle drivers including CDK1, CCNA1 and BUB1 that govern the meiotic divisions, and germ-cell RNA-binding regulators like DDX4 and YBX2 that hold transcripts for translation after transcription shuts down. Later stages contribute chromatin remodelling by transition proteins and protamines, acrosome components such as ACRV1 and ZPBP for egg binding, flagellar and outer dense fibre proteins, and testis-restricted glycolytic isoenzymes including PGK2, LDHC and GAPDHS that fuel motility.

TGF beta signaling is the transcriptional program switched on when cells encounter TGF-beta family ligands, a cue that halts epithelial proliferation, remodels the extracellular matrix, and directs wound healing, immune restraint and developmental patterning. Its loss or corruption underlies fibrosis, and tumours frequently escape its growth-inhibitory arm while exploiting its pro-invasive one. Ligand engages a receptor serine/threonine kinase pair, TGFBR1 with TGFBR2 or the BMP receptors ACVR1 and BMPR1A/BMPR2, which phosphorylates SMAD3 or SMAD1 for nuclear entry with co-repressors and co-activators such as SKI, SKIL, TGIF1, TRIM33 and HDAC1. Much of the output is self-limiting: inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 recruit the ubiquitin ligases SMURF1/2, PPM1A dephosphorylates activated SMADs, and PMEPA1 sequesters them. Effector genes include SERPINE1, THBS1, JUNB and the ID factors, linking the pathway to matrix deposition, differentiation blockade and cytostasis.

Cells respond to TGF-beta family ligands by halting proliferation, remodelling their adhesion and matrix, and switching on a defined transcriptional programme; the genes induced by TGFB1 trace that response. It governs epithelial growth arrest, wound healing and fibrosis, immune tolerance, and its loss is a common route to tumour progression, while germline defects in receptor components cause vascular and skeletal syndromes. Ligand engages type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors with co-receptors such as endoglin, activating SMAD3 and, on the BMP arm, SMAD1; nuclear partners including TGIF1, SKI, SKIL and TRIM33 with histone deacetylase complexes set the output. Much of the induced set is feedback machinery: inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7, the ubiquitin ligases SMURF1 and SMURF2, the phosphatase PPM1A and PMEPA1 all damp signalling, alongside effectors like SERPINE1, THBS1, JUNB and the ID proteins.

TNFA signaling via NFKB is the transcriptional program a cell runs when tumour necrosis factor engages its receptor and activates NF-kB, and it is the core of acute inflammation. Its output recruits and activates leukocytes, remodels the endothelium for adhesion and coagulation, and simultaneously blocks the apoptotic arm of TNF receptor signalling so that the responding cell survives its own inflammatory response. Chemokines such as CXCL1-3, CCL2 and CCL20, cytokines including IL1B, IL6 and TNF itself, adhesion molecules like ICAM1 and VCAM-related factors, and prostaglandin synthesis via PTGS2 form the effector output, while BIRC3, CFLAR, BCL2A1 and MCL1 provide the survival brake. Much of the set is negative feedback: NFKBIA, TNFAIP3, ZFP36, ZC3H12A, DUSP family phosphatases and SOCS3 terminate the response, and their failure yields chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease. Immediate-early transcription factors AP-1, EGR and KLF genes couple it to proliferation and stress adaptation.

The transcriptional response a cell mounts when tumour necrosis factor engages its receptor and activates NF-kB. This is the core inflammatory programme of innate immunity: it recruits leukocytes, sustains their survival at a site of infection or injury, and remodels the surrounding tissue, while simultaneously protecting the responding cell from TNF-induced death. Its output includes chemokines such as CCL2, CXCL1 and CXCL10, cytokines including IL1B and IL6, adhesion molecules like ICAM1 and CD44, prostaglandin and nitric oxide machinery, and the anti-apoptotic proteins BIRC3, CFLAR and BCL2A1. Negative feedback is built in, with NFKBIA, TNFAIP3, ZFP36 and the dual-specificity phosphatases limiting the burst so that acute signalling resolves. Overlapping immediate-early factors (FOS, JUN, EGR1) and metabolic and angiogenic genes broaden the response. Persistent activity underlies chronic inflammatory disease and inflammation-associated tumour growth.

Unfolded protein response is the endoplasmic reticulum's stress program: when secretory proteins accumulate unfolded in the ER lumen, the cell halts general translation, expands its folding and degradation capacity, and either restores proteostasis or commits to apoptosis. It determines how well secretory cells such as plasma cells, pancreatic beta cells and hepatocytes tolerate high client loads, and its failure underlies diabetes, neurodegeneration and Wolfram syndrome, while tumours exploit it to survive hypoxia and nutrient stress. All three sensor arms are represented — PERK phosphorylating eIF2alpha to drive ATF4-dependent amino acid synthesis and CHAC1, IRE1 splicing XBP1, and ATF6 — feeding chaperones such as BiP, GRP94 and calreticulin, ERAD components including EDEM1 and HERPUD1, disulfide isomerases, and signal peptidase and translocon subunits. Coupled changes in mRNA decay, exosome-mediated RNA turnover, ribosome biogenesis and cap-dependent initiation reset overall protein output alongside VEGFA-driven adaptation.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, cells mount the unfolded protein response, a transcriptional and translational programme that either restores folding capacity or commits the cell to death. It matters for any cell with a heavy secretory load — plasma cells, pancreatic beta cells, hepatocytes — and its failure underlies diabetes, neurodegeneration and the stress tolerance that lets tumours survive hypoxia and nutrient shortage. Three sensors branch from the ER membrane: IRE1 (ERN1) splices XBP1 mRNA, PERK (EIF2AK3) phosphorylates eIF2alpha to throttle translation while permitting ATF4 synthesis, and ATF6 is cleaved to a transcription factor. Their targets expand ER chaperones and redox enzymes such as BiP (HSPA5), HSP90B1, PDIA6 and ERO1A, boost ER-associated degradation via EDEM1 and HERPUD1, and reprogramme amino acid transport and biosynthesis through ASNS, PSAT1 and SLC7A5. Ribosome biogenesis, mRNA decay and signal peptide processing factors accompany the adjustment of protein flux.

UV response DN collects the transcriptional program that is switched off when cells absorb ultraviolet light, and it describes what a cell abandons while it copes with DNA damage. Ultraviolet exposure triggers a rapid shutdown of growth-factor and adhesion signalling, extracellular matrix production, and differentiated tissue maintenance, freeing the cell to arrest, repair, or die; chronic loss of these programs underlies photoaging of skin and the matrix degradation that accompanies it. The repressed genes are dominated by fibrillar collagens and matrix proteins, TGF-beta receptors and SMADs, receptor tyrosine kinases such as MET, KIT and IGF1R with their PI3K and IRS adaptors, cell junction and cytoskeletal components, and nuclear receptors including PPARG and RXRA. Downregulation of repair and tumour-suppressor genes such as MGMT and PTEN links this response to UV-driven mutagenesis and skin carcinogenesis.

Ultraviolet irradiation forces cells to suspend their normal growth and differentiation programme while damaged DNA is assessed and repaired, and this set captures the transcripts that fall as that happens. What is switched off is largely the machinery of anchored, adherent, signal-responsive cells: fibrillar collagens and laminin, fibulins and latent TGF-beta binding proteins, junction and cytoskeletal scaffolds such as ZO-1, DLG1 and connexin 43, and growth factor receptors including KIT, MET, PDGFRB, IGF1R and ERBB2 with their downstream PI3K, PKC and IRS1 relays. Also suppressed are TGF-beta/SMAD and nuclear receptor arms (TGFBR2, SMAD3, PPARG, RXRA, NR3C1) and lipid and calcium homeostasis genes. The net effect is loss of matrix production, adhesion and mitogenic responsiveness after UV exposure, relevant to photoaging of skin, impaired wound repair and the mutagenic consequences that follow when repair factors such as MGMT decline.

UV response up collects the genes induced when cells absorb ultraviolet radiation, the transcriptional arm of the response that decides whether a damaged keratinocyte or fibroblast repairs itself, arrests, or dies. Its output matters for sunburn, photoaging and the mutational load that leads to skin cancer, since failure to arrest or apoptose lets UV-induced lesions be replicated. Immediate-early transcription factors such as FOS, FOSB, JUNB, ATF3 and NR4A1 come on within minutes, followed by antiproliferative BTG family members and CDK inhibitors that impose a growth pause, DNA repair and replication components including FEN1, RFC4, PARP2 and H2AX, and apoptotic effectors BID, BAK1, BCL2L11 and CASP3. Oxidative and proteotoxic stress modules run alongside — HMOX1, SOD2, heat shock chaperones, SQSTM1 — together with NF- cB-driven inflammatory mediators such as IL6, CXCL2 and ICAM1 that recruit immune cells to damaged skin.

Ultraviolet light damages DNA and oxidizes cellular constituents, and the transcriptional programme induced by UV exposure is the cell's attempt to halt proliferation, repair the lesions, and eliminate cells too damaged to continue. Genes up-regulated after irradiation include immediate-early transcription factors such as FOS, FOSB, JUNB, ATF3 and NR4A1, antiproliferative BTG family members and CDK inhibitors that impose growth arrest, and heat shock and chaperone components (DNAJB1, DNAJA1, STIP1) that handle misfolded protein load. Oxidative stress defences such as HMOX1, SOD2 and GPX3 appear alongside DNA replication and repair factors including FEN1, RFC4, PARP2 and the H2AX histone. Apoptotic effectors BAK1, BID, BCL2L11 and CASP3 provide the death option, while IL6, CXCL2 and ICAM1 recruit inflammation. This response underlies sunburn, photoaging and the checkpoint barrier whose failure permits UV-driven skin carcinogenesis.

WNT beta catenin signaling is the canonical WNT response, in which stabilized beta-catenin escapes destruction, enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF factors to switch on a transcriptional program governing stem cell self-renewal, proliferation and cell fate choice during development and tissue turnover. Its constitutive activation, typically through loss of destruction-complex components such as AXIN1, drives colorectal and other cancers, while insufficient signaling impairs regeneration and skeletal patterning. Ligands and Frizzled receptors initiate the cascade, Dishevelled and FRAT1 restrain the CUL1/SKP2-linked degradation machinery, and CTNNB1 recruits coactivators like KAT2A in place of NCOR2 and histone deacetylases. Targets including MYC, CCND2, AXIN2 and the DKK and NKD1 feedback inhibitors set the amplitude and duration of the response. Prominent NOTCH components -- JAG1, RBPJ, HEY1 -- reflect the tight coupling of these two pathways in fate decisions.

WNT/beta-catenin signalling is the route by which secreted WNT ligands stabilise cytoplasmic beta-catenin so that it enters the nucleus and switches on transcription with TCF/LEF partners, driving stem and progenitor self-renewal, cell fate choice and tissue patterning during development and regeneration. When the pathway is held off, beta-catenin is captured by an AXIN-based complex, phosphorylated and destroyed through cullin-RING ubiquitination; when a WNT engages a Frizzled receptor, that destruction stops. Targets induced by the active state include MYC, cyclin D and the feedback inhibitors AXIN2, NKD1 and the DKK antagonists, so the output is self-limiting. Loss of this restraint produces constitutive target-gene expression and is a founding event in colorectal and other cancers. The accompanying NOTCH components -- ligands, receptors, RBPJ, HEY factors and presenilin/nicastrin -- reflect the crosstalk by which the two pathways jointly set boundaries between proliferating and differentiating cells.

Xenobiotic metabolism is the liver-centred detoxification program that converts drugs, environmental chemicals and endogenous waste into water-soluble products the body can excrete, and it sets how long a drug acts and whether it becomes toxic. Its three stages are all represented: cytochrome P450 oxidations and their electron donor POR, together with flavin monooxygenases, aldehyde and alcohol dehydrogenases, epoxide hydrolase and quinone reductase, introduce reactive handles; glutathione S-transferases, sulfotransferase and UDP-sugar enzymes conjugate them, supported by glutathione synthesis and NADPH-regenerating dehydrogenases; and ABCC transporters and organic cation carriers export the conjugates. Alongside sit the antioxidant enzymes catalase, HMOX1 and glutathione reductase that contain the oxidative stress generated. The set also reflects the hepatocyte identity in which this occurs, with HNF4A, PPARD and plasma protein, urea cycle, amino acid and gluconeogenic genes, linking biotransformation capacity to overall liver differentiation and drug-induced injury.

Detoxification and clearance of drugs, environmental chemicals and other xenobiotics is largely a hepatic function, and this programme captures the enzymes, transporters and transcriptional regulators that carry it out. Without it, reactive intermediates accumulate, drug dosing becomes unpredictable, and oxidative and electrophilic damage follows. The chemistry runs in phases: cytochrome P450 monooxygenases with their reductase partner POR, plus flavin monooxygenases, aldehyde and alcohol dehydrogenases, epoxide hydrolase and xanthine oxidase introduce or resolve reactive groups; glutathione transferases, UDP-glucose dehydrogenase and sulfotransferase-linked PAPS synthesis conjugate the products; and ABCC efflux pumps together with solute carriers such as SLC22A1 move substrates in and out. Supporting genes place this activity in a broader liver phenotype — amino acid catabolism, urea and bile acid metabolism, plasma protein and coagulation factor synthesis, glutathione and heme handling, and control by HNF4A and nuclear receptor signalling.

Interleukin-6 signaling transmits a pleiotropic inflammatory cytokine signal that drives the hepatic acute phase response, fever, antibody production, Th17 differentiation, hematopoiesis and tissue regeneration, and whose chronic activation underlies rheumatoid arthritis, cytokine storm and inflammation-associated cancer -- the reason IL-6 and its receptor are blocked therapeutically. IL-6 binds an alpha receptor subunit and recruits the shared gp130 signaling chain, used by the whole IL-6 family including IL-11, LIF and oncostatin M. Because a soluble shed form of IL6R allows IL-6 to act on cells lacking the alpha chain, trans-signaling extends responsiveness to endothelium, smooth muscle and progenitor cells and carries most of the pro-inflammatory output, while membrane receptor signaling is regenerative. gp130 activates JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 to phosphorylate STAT3 and STAT1, with parallel Ras-MAPK input; SOCS3, SHP2 and CBL terminate the response.

Interleukin-6 signaling converts a single pleiotropic cytokine into the acute phase response, fever, hepatocyte C-reactive protein production, emergency haematopoiesis and helper T cell differentiation, and its chronic overactivity drives rheumatoid arthritis, Castleman disease and cytokine storm, which is why blocking the receptor is now standard therapy. IL-6 binds an alpha receptor, IL6R, that contributes no signalling of its own; the complex then recruits the shared beta subunit gp130 (IL6ST), used by all IL-6 family cytokines. Receptor-associated JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 phosphorylate gp130 and activate STAT3 with STAT1, inducing transcription, while a parallel Ras-MAPK arm is engaged through the phosphatase PTPN11. Restraint comes from SOCS3, which is itself STAT-induced and blocks JAK activity, and from CBL-mediated ubiquitination of receptor components. Soluble IL6R allows cells lacking the alpha chain to respond, the trans-signalling route associated with inflammation rather than regeneration.

Apoptosis is programmed cell death, the controlled self-destruction that removes damaged, infected, superfluous or autoreactive cells without inflaming the surrounding tissue, and it shapes development, tissue turnover and immune tolerance. Too little of it permits tumour growth and autoimmunity; too much drives degeneration and ischaemic injury. Two routes converge on the same executioner caspases: death receptors such as FAS and the TRAIL receptors recruit FADD and caspase-8 through the extrinsic arm, while stress signals relayed by p53 and BH3-only proteins like BID, BAD, PMAIP1 and BCL2L11 tip the BAX/BAK balance against BCL2, releasing cytochrome c and DIABLO to build the APAF1 apoptosome and activate caspase-9. Downstream cleavage of lamins, cytoskeletal and adhesion proteins, plectin, spectrin and tight-junction components, plus DFFB-mediated DNA fragmentation, produces the shrunken, blebbing, chromatin-condensed corpse; XIAP, CFLAR and the ubiquitin-proteasome system set the threshold.

Apoptosis is the orderly self-destruction that removes surplus, damaged or dangerous cells without inflaming the surrounding tissue, shaping organs during development and culling autoreactive lymphocytes; too little underlies tumour survival and autoimmunity, too much drives degeneration. Two routes converge on the executioner caspases 3, 6 and 7: death receptors such as FAS and the TRAIL receptors recruit FADD and caspase-8, while stress signals relayed through p53 and BH3-only proteins like BID, BAD, PMAIP1 and BBC3 tip the BAX/BAK-versus-BCL2 balance, releasing cytochrome c and DIABLO for APAF1-caspase-9 activation. Downstream substrates define the morphology — DFFA/DFFB for DNA fragmentation, lamins, vimentin, plectin and desmosomal proteins for nuclear and junctional collapse, ROCK1 and PAK2 for blebbing. XIAP, CFLAR and ubiquitin-proteasome activity set the threshold.

Hemostasis is the body's response to vascular injury: it stops bleeding by constricting the vessel, plugging the breach with platelets, and reinforcing that plug with fibrin. Healthy endothelium normally opposes all of this, releasing nitric oxide and prostacyclin and keeping platelets quiescent; when the barrier is broken, exposed collagen and von Willebrand factor tether platelets through GP1B-IX-V and GPVI, integrin αIIbβ3 and talin-mediated activation drive aggregation on fibrinogen, and granule release of ADP, thromboxane and chemokines such as PF4 recruits more platelets. In parallel, tissue factor triggers the coagulation protease cascade through factors VII, IX, X and thrombin, restrained by antithrombin, protein C and the fibrinolytic plasminogen system. Megakaryocyte transcription factors including GATA1 and NFE2 supply the platelets themselves. Loss of any arm produces hemophilia or bleeding disorders, while unchecked activation causes thrombosis.

Hemostasis is the sequence of events that stops bleeding from a damaged vessel, and its failure in either direction produces hemorrhage or thrombosis. Loss of the endothelial barrier exposes collagen and von Willebrand factor, which tether circulating platelets through the GPIb-IX-V complex and GPVI; signalling through G protein-coupled receptors for thrombin, ADP and thromboxane, phospholipase C, calcium release and Rap1 then switches integrin alphaIIbbeta3 to a high-affinity state so fibrinogen bridges platelets into a plug. Degranulation releases stored agonists and adhesive proteins, while tissue factor initiates the coagulation protease cascade on exposed anionic phospholipid, generating thrombin and insoluble fibrin. Counterbalancing anticoagulant and fibrinolytic arms - protein C, antithrombin and serpins, plasminogen activators - limit the clot, alongside cyclic nucleotide signalling that keeps resting platelets quiescent. Megakaryocyte transcription factors and thrombopoietin signalling supply the platelets themselves.

Intrinsic Pathway for Apoptosis is the mitochondrial route to programmed cell death, used when a cell judges its own internal state to be beyond repair — DNA damage, growth factor withdrawal, endoplasmic reticulum stress, cytoskeletal or oncogenic insult. It removes damaged and potentially transformed cells, and its suppression is one of the ways tumours become immortal and resistant to chemotherapy. BH3-only sensors such as BIM, BID, PUMA and NOXA are induced or released and neutralise BCL-2 and BCL-XL, freeing BAX and BAK to permeabilise the mitochondrial outer membrane. Cytochrome c release nucleates the APAF1 apoptosome, activating caspase-9 and then the executioner caspases-3 and -7, while SMAC/DIABLO relieves XIAP inhibition. Upstream, p53 family transcription factors and 14-3-3 and AKT survival signalling set the threshold, and caspase cleavage of gasdermins can divert the outcome toward lytic death.

Cells that are damaged beyond repair, deprived of growth factors, or stressed in the endoplasmic reticulum kill themselves through the intrinsic, mitochondrial route to apoptosis, the arm of programmed cell death that shapes tissues during development and removes cells with broken genomes. Its failure permits survival of cells that should die and underlies tumour formation and resistance to chemotherapy, while excess activity drives degenerative loss of neurons and other long-lived cells. BH3-only sensors such as BID, BAD, BIM, NOXA and PUMA relay stress signals and neutralise the guardians BCL2 and BCL2L1, allowing BAX and BAK to permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane; released cytochrome c nucleates an APAF1 apoptosome that activates caspase-9 and then the executioner caspases 3 and 7, with DIABLO relieving XIAP inhibition. Transcriptional control by p53 and its relatives, and survival input from AKT and 14-3-3 proteins, set the threshold.

Translesion synthesis by REV1 is one branch of DNA damage tolerance: rather than repairing a lesion, it lets a stalled replication fork copy past it so that replication can finish and the cell avoids fork collapse and death. REV1 is a template-dependent dCMP transferase that inserts a cytosine opposite an abasic site, and its recruitment depends on monoubiquitinated PCNA at the damaged fork, with RPA-coated single-stranded DNA and the clamp loader RFC providing the replication context. REV1 then acts as a scaffold: through MAD2L2 (REV7) it brings in DNA polymerase zeta, whose catalytic subunit REV3L extends past the lesion with low fidelity and low processivity before handing back to the replicative machinery. The trade-off is mutagenesis, making this route a major source of damage-induced point mutations and a contributor to chemotherapy resistance.

When a replication fork meets a lesion it cannot copy, such as an abasic site, replication would stall and collapse unless a specialised polymerase takes over. REV1-mediated translesion synthesis is one such bypass route: REV1 acts as a dCMP transferase that inserts a C opposite the damaged template position, and also as a scaffold that recruits the extension step. Monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by the replication factor C clamp loader onto RPA-coated DNA, marks the damage site and stimulates REV1 recruitment. Handover then goes to DNA polymerase zeta, whose catalytic subunit REV3L pairs with MAD2L2 (REV7), the subunit that physically binds REV1. Polymerase zeta extends past the lesion with low fidelity and low processivity, so this pathway preserves replication and cell survival at the cost of point mutations, and contributes to damage tolerance and chemotherapy resistance.

Recognition and association of DNA glycosylase with site containing an affected pyrimidine is the first step of base excision repair, in which a glycosylase scans duplex DNA and docks onto a damaged or mismatched pyrimidine so the base can be excised and the site handed to downstream nucleases and polymerases. This surveillance keeps oxidative and deaminative base damage from becoming fixed mutations; loss of it drives the mutational signatures behind colorectal and other cancers. Uracil arising from cytosine deamination or misincorporation is removed by UNG and SMUG1, thymine and uracil in mismatches by TDG and MBD4, and oxidised pyrimidines and ring-opened lesions by NTHL1 and the NEIL enzymes. Because lesions must be found within chromatin, core histones are integral to the search, and telomere-binding proteins including POT1, TERF1 and TERF2 place this repair in the specialised context of chromosome ends.

Base excision repair begins when a DNA glycosylase scans duplex DNA, flips out an aberrant base and prepares it for removal, and this step covers recognition of damaged or mismatched pyrimidines in particular. It is the cell's main defence against the constant chemical erosion of bases by oxidation, deamination and alkylation, and its failure drives point mutation and cancer predisposition, as seen with germline defects in the uracil- and thymine-directed glycosylases. Uracil arising from cytosine deamination or misincorporation is handled by UNG and SMUG1, mismatched thymine at CpG sites by TDG and MBD4, and oxidised pyrimidines by NTHL1 and the NEIL enzymes, while OGG1 addresses oxidised purines. Because lesions must be found within chromatin, core histones and the telomere-binding shelterin proteins are part of the context in which recognition occurs, linking this repair step to nucleosome packaging and telomere maintenance.

POLB-Dependent Long Patch Base Excision Repair is the branch of base excision repair used when a damaged base leaves an end that cannot simply be replaced by a single nucleotide, so a short stretch of DNA must be resynthesised instead. It keeps oxidative, alkylation and deamination damage from becoming mutations or persistent single-strand breaks, and its failure feeds genome instability and sensitivity to alkylating agents. After APEX1 incises the abasic site, PARP1 or PARP2 mark the break and, with the flap endonuclease FEN1, license DNA polymerase beta to perform strand-displacement synthesis of two to ten nucleotides; the displaced flap is cut away and DNA ligase I seals the nick. PARG and ADPRS reverse the poly(ADP-ribose) signal so repair factors are released, coupling the ADP-ribosylation cycle to completion of repair.

Base excision repair removes damaged or inappropriate bases, and when the resulting gap cannot be sealed after a single nucleotide is added, the cell switches to a long-patch route that displaces and trims a short flap before ligation. This variant keeps oxidative and alkylation damage from persisting as single-strand breaks, which otherwise collapse replication forks and drive mutation and genome instability. After APEX1 incises the abasic site, DNA polymerase beta performs strand-displacement synthesis of roughly two to ten nucleotides; FEN1 cleaves the displaced flap and DNA ligase I seals the nick. PARP1 and PARP2 detect the break and synthesise poly(ADP-ribose) to recruit and coordinate these factors, while PARG and ADPRS reverse that modification so the repair machinery can be released. The same damage-sensing step is what PARP inhibitors exploit therapeutically.

Resolution of AP sites via the multiple-nucleotide patch replacement pathway is the long-patch branch of base excision repair, used when an abasic site left by a DNA glycosylase carries a 5'-sugar phosphate that cannot be trimmed by the lyase activity of DNA polymerase beta. Rather than replacing a single nucleotide, the cell excises and resynthesises a short stretch of DNA, keeping oxidised, alkylated and deaminated bases from becoming mutations or strand breaks. APEX1 incises 5' to the lesion, then strand-displacement synthesis proceeds either by polymerase beta with PARP1/PARP2 support, or, when replication factors are available in S phase, by polymerase delta or epsilon loaded through PCNA, RFC and RPA. FEN1 clips the displaced flap and LIG1 seals the nick. Poly(ADP-ribose) turnover by PARG and ADPRS resets the damage signal, linking this repair route to genome stability and cancer avoidance.

Abasic sites left behind when a damaged base is excised must be cut, filled and sealed, and this long-patch branch of base excision repair handles the cases the single-nucleotide route cannot: 5'-terminal sugar phosphates that resist removal. After APEX1 incises 5' of the abasic deoxyribose, polymerase beta begins synthesis without trimming the blocking sugar phosphate, displacing it into a flap. Strand-displacement synthesis then continues either through polymerase beta with PARP1 or PARP2 in support, or, when replication machinery is at hand in S phase, through the polymerase delta or epsilon holoenzymes with PCNA, RFC and RPA. FEN1 clips the displaced flap and DNA ligase I closes the nick, while PARG and ADPRS reverse the ADP-ribose signalling that accompanies repair. Loss of this capacity leaves persistent abasic lesions that block replication and drive mutation.

Resolution of AP sites via the single-nucleotide replacement pathway is the short-patch arm of base excision repair, and it handles the majority of the everyday base damage a genome accumulates from oxidation, alkylation and spontaneous deamination. Once a glycosylase has removed a damaged base, the abasic site left behind is itself mutagenic and blocks replication, so it must be excised and refilled before the next S phase. APEX1 incises 5' of the abasic deoxyribose, DNA polymerase beta removes the sugar phosphate and inserts a single correct nucleotide, and an XRCC1-scaffolded ligase III seals the nick before the complex dissociates. Loss of this route raises mutation rates and sensitises cells to oxidative and alkylating agents, which is why its components are targets in the context of DNA-damaging chemotherapy. Lesions with refractory sugar-phosphate ends are diverted to a long-patch alternative instead.

Abasic sites arise constantly, both spontaneously and as the intermediate left behind when a DNA glycosylase excises a damaged base, and they must be converted back to intact duplex DNA before replication turns them into mutations or strand breaks. Short-patch base excision repair, in which a single nucleotide is replaced, handles the majority of these lesions. The AP endonuclease APEX1 incises the backbone 5' to the abasic deoxyribose, DNA polymerase beta removes the remaining sugar-phosphate through its lyase activity and inserts the correct replacement nucleotide, and the XRCC1 scaffold delivers DNA ligase III to seal the nick before the complex dissociates. Loss of this route leaves persistent single-strand interruptions, driving genomic instability, sensitivity to alkylating and oxidising agents, and the neurodegeneration seen when XRCC1-dependent repair fails.

SLBP independent Processing of Histone Pre-mRNAs covers the 3' end maturation of the small subset of histone transcripts that are handled without the stem-loop binding protein, and it matters because histone supply must be matched to DNA replication: mis-processed histone messages give unbalanced chromatin assembly and replication stress. These intronless genes are transcribed and then cleaved at their 3' ends by the U7 snRNP, whose Sm-like ring substitutes LSM10 and LSM11 for the canonical SNRPD1/D2 subunits while retaining the shared core proteins SNRPB, SNRPE, SNRPF and SNRPG; ZNF473 acts as a U7-associated factor coupling cleavage to the transcription machinery. The nuclear cap-binding complex, NCBP1 with NCBP2, marks the capped transcript and licenses downstream processing and export. Unlike the dominant route, these transcripts acquire polyadenylated ends through a mechanism resembling that of intron-containing pre-mRNAs, linking histone gene expression to general cleavage and polyadenylation control.

Most histone genes are intronless and their transcripts are not polyadenylated but cleaved at a conserved 3' end by a specialised machinery; this route covers the processing of those pre-mRNAs independently of the stem-loop binding protein that normally couples histone mRNA metabolism to S phase. Recognition depends on the U7 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein, whose Sm-like core substitutes LSM10 and LSM11 for the canonical D1 and D2 subunits while retaining the shared Sm proteins, together with the U7-associated zinc finger protein ZNF473 and the nuclear cap-binding complex on the transcript's 5' cap. Correct 3' end formation determines how much histone protein is available to package newly replicated DNA, so that supply of nucleosomal histones stays matched to replication; failure yields misprocessed, read-through transcripts and unbalanced chromatin assembly.

BH3-only proteins associate with and inactivate anti-apoptotic BCL-2 members is the decision step of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway, where stress sensors neutralise the survival proteins that hold mitochondria intact. When a cell suffers DNA damage, growth factor withdrawal, loss of attachment or cytoskeletal disruption, BH3-only proteins such as BIM, PUMA, NOXA, BAD, BMF and truncated BID are induced or released, and their BH3 helices dock into the hydrophobic groove of BCL-2 and BCL-XL. Sequestering these guardians frees BAX and BAK to permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane and release cytochrome c, committing the cell to caspase activation. The balance set here determines lymphocyte selection, tissue involution and the response to chemotherapy; tumours that overexpress BCL-2 survive by keeping BH3-only proteins bound, which is the rationale for BH3-mimetic drugs.

Whether a stressed cell dies is decided at the mitochondrial outer membrane, and this step is the switch: BH3-only proteins such as BIM, PUMA, NOXA, BAD, BMF and truncated BID bind the hydrophobic groove of the anti-apoptotic guardians BCL-2 and BCL-XL and neutralise them. Sequestering these guardians frees BAX and BAK to permeabilise the membrane, releasing cytochrome c and committing the cell to caspase activation. Each BH3-only protein reports a different insult — DNA damage and p53 activity induce PUMA and NOXA, growth factor withdrawal and kinase signalling control BAD phosphorylation, cytoskeletal and death receptor signals act through BMF and BID — so the balance of binding partners sets the apoptotic threshold. Tumours survive by overexpressing BCL-2 or BCL-XL, and BH3-mimetic drugs work by imitating exactly this association.

Opioid Signalling is the neuronal response to endogenous opioid peptides such as the enkephalins, endorphins and dynorphins, and to the opiate drugs that mimic them. It is the route through which morphine and related analgesics suppress pain perception and produce sedation, euphoria, respiratory depression and, on repeated exposure, tolerance and addiction. Opioid peptides derived from precursors including proopiomelanocortin and prodynorphin act on Gi-coupled receptors such as the mu receptor, whose activated alpha subunits inhibit adenylate cyclases while released beta-gamma dimers and parallel Gq-phospholipase C signalling raise inositol trisphosphate and calcium. The downstream consequences are changes in cAMP tone and in the balance of protein kinase A, protein kinase C, calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases and opposing phosphatases, feeding into CREB-dependent transcription. Receptor phosphorylation by kinases such as GRK2 desensitises the response, a step central to the adaptations underlying opioid tolerance and dependence.

Opioid signalling is how endogenous peptides such as the enkephalins, endorphins and dynorphins — and the opiate drugs that mimic them — suppress pain perception, and it explains both the analgesia and the tolerance, dependence and addiction that follow repeated opioid use. The mu receptor couples through inhibitory G proteins and a full complement of beta and gamma subunits to lower adenylate cyclase output, so cAMP falls, protein kinase A activity drops, and neuronal excitability and transmitter release decline. Phospholipase C beta isoforms, inositol trisphosphate receptors and calcium release feed calmodulin-dependent kinases, calcineurin and protein kinase C, while phosphodiesterases, phosphatases and receptor kinase-mediated desensitisation set the duration of the response. Convergence on CREB and on striatal signalling proteins including DARPP-32 links acute receptor activation to the lasting transcriptional and synaptic changes of reward learning.

Calmodulin induced events describes what happens once calcium-loaded calmodulin engages its downstream effectors, converting a rise in cytosolic Ca2+ into changes in cyclic AMP, kinase activity and gene transcription. This crosstalk between the calcium and cAMP second-messenger systems underlies activity-dependent plasticity in neurons, learning and memory, and the tuning of hormone and neurotransmitter responses. Calmodulin directly regulates adenylyl cyclases, stimulating the calcium-sensitive isoforms such as AC1 and AC8 while inhibiting others, and simultaneously activates Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphodiesterases that degrade cAMP, so the net cyclic nucleotide signal is shaped in both directions. In parallel it activates the CaMKK-CaMKIV and CaMKII kinase cascades, which converge with protein kinase A and protein kinase C on CREB-dependent transcription. Loss of this integration degrades synaptic strengthening and the coupling of excitation to long-term transcriptional responses.

A rise in intracellular calcium is translated into lasting biochemical change largely through calmodulin, and the calmodulin-induced events described here are the downstream branch in which calcium-loaded calmodulin engages cyclic nucleotide machinery and kinases. Several adenylyl cyclases are calcium-sensitive, notably type 8, so calcium can raise or lower cAMP depending on which isoform a cell expresses; calmodulin-stimulated phosphodiesterases of the PDE1 family hydrolyse the same second messenger, setting the duration of the signal. cAMP then activates protein kinase A through its regulatory and catalytic subunits, while calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase II isoforms and CaMKIV, activated via the upstream CaMK kinases, phosphorylate CREB and drive activity-dependent transcription. This convergence of calcium and cAMP underlies synaptic plasticity and memory formation, hormone secretion, and the tuning of receptor responsiveness, and it links membrane excitation to changes in gene expression.

phospho-PLA2 pathway is the activation step that releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids and so licenses eicosanoid production. It sets the pace of inflammatory lipid signalling: without it, cells cannot generate the prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes that drive fever, pain, platelet aggregation, bronchoconstriction and leukocyte recruitment, and the same reaction supplies the acyl turnover that keeps membrane phospholipid composition in repair. The cytosolic, calcium-dependent enzyme cPLA2 cleaves the sn-2 ester bond, but only after ERK-family MAP kinase phosphorylates it and a calcium rise recruits it to the nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum membranes where downstream cyclooxygenases and lipoxygenases reside. This places arachidonate release downstream of growth factor, cytokine and G protein-coupled receptor input, converting surface stimulation into a diffusible lipid mediator response, and makes the step a control point exploited by anti-inflammatory therapy.

Release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids is the committed first step in making eicosanoids, and this route describes how cytosolic phospholipase A2 is switched on by phosphorylation to do it. The consequence is inflammation: the arachidonate liberated here feeds cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase routes to prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes that drive fever, pain, platelet aggregation and leukocyte recruitment, and the same activity supplies lysophospholipids for membrane acyl turnover and repair. Extracellular stimuli converge on ERK-family MAP kinase, which phosphorylates PLA2G4A; together with a rise in intracellular calcium this promotes translocation of the enzyme to perinuclear and endoplasmic reticulum membranes, where it hydrolyses the sn-2 ester bond. Because activation is a post-translational event, cells can mount a rapid lipid mediator response without new transcription, and this step is a point at which anti-inflammatory intervention acts upstream of the prostaglandin route.

Ca-dependent events covers what a cell does once cytosolic calcium rises: the steep gradient across the plasma membrane, maintained against a thousand-fold difference in concentration, lets brief Ca2+ influx act as a second messenger that reshapes enzyme activity and gene expression. This decoding underlies synaptic plasticity and learning, muscle and secretory responses, and hormone-driven changes in metabolism. Calmodulin is the central sensor, activating CaMKII isoforms, the CaMKK-driven kinase cascade, and CaMKIV, which enters the nucleus and phosphorylates CREB to switch on activity-dependent transcription. Calcium also converges on cyclic nucleotide signalling, stimulating or inhibiting particular adenylate cyclases, driving PDE1 phosphodiesterases, and thereby tuning PKA holoenzyme output; parallel branches engage conventional PKC isoforms and cytosolic phospholipase A2 for lipid mediator release. Dysregulated calcium decoding contributes to cardiac hypertrophy, excitotoxic neuronal injury, and impaired memory formation.

A rise in cytosolic Ca2+ is one of the cell's most widely used signals, and the calcium-dependent events described here are what converts that transient into lasting changes in enzyme activity and gene expression. Because free Ca2+ inside the cell is held far below the extracellular concentration, even brief influx is read as information. Calmodulin is the principal sensor: bound to Ca2+ it activates the CaMK family and the upstream kinases CAMKK1/2, stimulates or inhibits particular adenylate cyclases, and switches on Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphodiesterases that degrade cyclic nucleotides, so calcium and cAMP-PKA signalling are directly cross-wired. Downstream, CREB1 phosphorylation couples stimulation to transcription, while protein kinase C isoforms and cytosolic phospholipase A2 act on membrane lipid signalling. This logic underlies synaptic plasticity and learning, muscle and secretory responses, and hormone-driven metabolic control.

Transmission across Electrical Synapses is direct electrical coupling between neurons, in which current from one cell flows into the next through gap junctions rather than being converted into a chemical signal. Because no transmitter release or receptor binding intervenes, transmission is nearly instantaneous and bidirectional, which is what allows populations of neurons to fire in synchrony — as in the hypothalamic neurons that release hormones in coordinated bursts, in retinal circuits, and in developing networks where coupling shapes wiring. Each junction is built from two hemichannels, one contributed by each partner cell, assembled from connexins such as GJD2 and GJC1; related pannexin channels form large-pore conduits that release ATP and other signals to the extracellular space rather than joining two cytoplasms. Loss or misregulation of this coupling disrupts network rhythmicity and, for some connexins, causes inherited visual and neurological defects.

Some neurons communicate not by releasing transmitter but by passing current directly, and transmission across electrical synapses is that route. Where populations must fire together — hypothalamic neurosecretory cells, retinal networks, inhibitory interneurons — the near-instantaneous coupling it provides synchronises activity in a way chemical synapses cannot match, and it also allows small molecules and second messengers to be shared between coupled cells. The conduit is a gap junction built from two apposed hemichannels, one contributed by each cell, assembled from connexins; the neuronal connexin encoded by GJD2 forms much of the coupling in retina, while GJC1 and GJA10 contribute elsewhere. The related pannexins form single-membrane channels rather than cell-to-cell junctions, releasing ATP and other messengers into the extracellular space and linking this biology to purinergic signalling and inflammatory responses.

Neurotransmitter clearance terminates chemical signalling at the synapse, removing transmitter from the cleft so that each presynaptic action potential produces one discrete postsynaptic response rather than sustained depolarisation. Without it receptors desensitise or are overdriven, which in cholinergic synapses means depolarising block of neuromuscular transmission, and in monoaminergic circuits altered mood, arousal and reward. Two strategies are represented: enzymatic destruction, by acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase at cholinergic synapses and by monoamine oxidase, catechol-O-methyltransferase and aldehyde dehydrogenase acting on dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin; and transport, with the dopamine and serotonin reuptake carriers returning transmitter to the presynaptic terminal and organic cation transporters providing lower-affinity uptake into surrounding cells. These proteins are the targets of antidepressants, psychostimulants, MAO inhibitors and cholinesterase inhibitors, and of organophosphate poisoning, making the pathway central to neuropharmacology as well as to normal synaptic timing.
