Synaptic transmission must stop as sharply as it starts, and neurotransmitter clearance is what terminates a signal once the postsynaptic receptors have been engaged. Excess transmitter is removed from the cleft by reuptake into the presynaptic terminal or surrounding glia, by diffusion away from the synapse, or by enzymatic breakdown; without it, receptors are continuously occupied and postsynaptic cells are overdriven. Cholinesterases hydrolyse acetylcholine at cholinergic synapses and the neuromuscular junction, while catechol-O-methyltransferase and monoamine oxidase A degrade catecholamines and serotonin, with aldehyde dehydrogenase disposing of the reactive aldehydes produced. Dedicated plasma membrane carriers recapture dopamine and serotonin, and organic cation transporters provide lower-affinity uptake. These proteins are the targets of antidepressants, psychostimulants, MAO inhibitors and anticholinesterases, and their variants shape monoamine tone, mood and cognition.

Activation, translocation and oligomerization of BAX is the commitment step of mitochondrial apoptosis: the point at which a death signal becomes irreversible permeabilization of the outer mitochondrial membrane. Cells that cannot execute it survive damage they should not survive, a route to chemotherapy resistance and tumour persistence, while inappropriate activation drives excessive cell loss in ischaemic and degenerative injury. Cytosolic BAX is normally inert; cleaved BID, generated downstream of caspase-8 in receptor-initiated death signalling, engages BAX and exposes its membrane-insertion surfaces. BAX then translocates to the mitochondrion and oligomerizes into pores through which cytochrome c and other intermembrane proteins escape, seeding apoptosome assembly and caspase-9 activation. This is the node at which the extrinsic and intrinsic death pathways converge, and the step that BCL-2 family antagonists exist to restrain.

Commitment to apoptosis is decided at the mitochondrial outer membrane, and BAX activation is the step that makes the decision irreversible. In healthy cells BAX is largely cytosolic and inactive; once engaged by the activated, truncated form of BID, it changes conformation, translocates to the outer mitochondrial membrane and oligomerizes there to form the pores through which cytochrome c and other intermembrane space proteins escape into the cytosol. That release licenses apoptosome assembly and caspase activation, linking upstream death receptor and stress signals to the execution phase of cell death. Because BID is cleaved by caspase-8, this route connects extrinsic receptor signalling to the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway and amplifies it. Blocking BAX activation, whether by antiapoptotic BCL-2 family relatives or by tumour-associated loss of function, allows damaged cells to survive; excessive activation contributes to degenerative tissue loss.

Platelet degranulation is the secretory burst that turns an activated platelet into a source of clotting factors, adhesion proteins and growth factors at a site of vascular injury. It converts a mechanical plug into a biochemical hub: without it haemostasis fails and bleeding disorders such as grey platelet and storage pool disease follow, while excessive release drives thrombosis and feeds inflammation and wound repair. Alpha granules discharge fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, thrombospondin, P-selectin, PF4 and PDGF, TGF-beta and VEGF family growth factors together with protease inhibitors of the serpin group; dense granules release ADP, ATP, serotonin and calcium that recruit further platelets in an autocrine loop; lysosomal contents complete the repertoire. Fusion depends on SNARE and Munc18 machinery with Rab27 and synaptotagmin-like regulators, coordinated with integrin alphaIIb-beta3 activation, talin and kindlin, and cytoskeletal remodelling that drives granule centralisation.

When a vessel is injured, platelets not only plug the breach but empty their storage granules into it, and platelet degranulation is that secretory event. The released cargo amplifies platelet recruitment, supports coagulation, and initiates wound repair; loss of granule content or of the machinery that releases it causes bleeding disorders such as gray platelet and storage pool disease. Alpha granules supply adhesive and clotting proteins including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen chains, factor V, thrombospondin and multimerin, along with protease inhibitors of the serpin family and growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta and VEGF family members that drive angiogenesis and fibrosis. P-selectin and CD63 move to the surface as granule membranes fuse, marking activation. Fusion itself depends on SNARE and regulatory proteins including STXBP2, VTI1B, RAB27B and SYTL4, while integrin alphaIIb-beta3 and the cytoskeletal proteins talin, kindlin-3 and filamin couple activation to secretion.

ISG15 antiviral mechanism is the arm of the type I interferon response that tags host and viral proteins with the ubiquitin-like modifier ISG15, restricting virus replication and tuning the interferon response itself. Loss of its regulation causes interferonopathy: the deconjugating enzyme USP18 is the brake, and its failure leads to runaway interferon signalling and severe disease. Conjugation follows the ubiquitin logic — activation by the E1 UBA7, transfer through UBE2L6, and ligation by HERC5, TRIM25 or ARIH1 — but the substrates are innate immune sensors and effectors such as RIG-I, MDA5, PKR, MX1, STAT1 and IRF3, whose activity or localisation is thereby altered. Translation initiation factors, importins and the nuclear pore complex appear as substrates too, linking ISGylation to control of protein synthesis and nucleocytoplasmic transport during infection, and to inhibition of viral budding.

Type I interferon signalling arms cells against viruses partly by inducing ISG15, a ubiquitin-like modifier, and the antiviral mechanism described here is the conjugation of ISG15 onto host and viral proteins. ISGylation restricts virus replication by altering the activity, stability or localisation of its targets, and interfering with viral budding and release; loss of the pathway leaves cells more permissive to infection, while its excess is restrained by the ISG15-specific protease USP18. The chemistry mirrors ubiquitination: UBA7 activates ISG15 at the cost of ATP, UBE2L6 carries it, and E3 ligases such as HERC5 and TRIM25 transfer it to substrates. Targets here include the sensors RIGI and MDA5, the effectors MX1/MX2 and the kinase EIF2AK2, transcription factors IRF3 and STAT1, and JAK1, along with translation initiation factors, importins and much of the nuclear pore complex, linking the response to protein synthesis and nucleocytoplasmic transport.

Antimicrobial mechanism of IFN-stimulated genes is the effector arm of interferon responses: once type I and type II interferons signal through JAK–STAT, hundreds of induced genes encode proteins that directly attack viruses and other intracellular pathogens while shaping the adaptive response that follows. It is what makes an interferon-primed cell resistant to infection, and its loss leaves patients vulnerable to severe viral disease. Distinct effector modules appear here: OAS enzymes and RNase L degrade viral RNA, PKR phosphorylates eIF2α to shut down translation initiation, IFIT proteins sequester foreign mRNA from the eIF3–ribosome machinery, MX GTPases trap incoming nucleocapsids, and guanylate-binding proteins disrupt pathogen-containing vacuoles and license inflammasome activation. ISG15 conjugation, driven by UBA7, UBE2L6 and HERC5 and reversed by USP18, modifies both viral and host proteins, including nucleoporins and karyopherins that control nucleocytoplasmic traffic during infection.

Interferons do more than announce infection: through JAK cSTAT signalling they switch on hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes whose products attack viruses directly, and this is the effector arm of that response. Cells lacking it fail to restrict viral replication despite intact sensing, while excessive or unchecked activity drives interferonopathy and autoinflammation. Several distinct mechanisms are represented. Double-stranded RNA activates PKR, which phosphorylates the translation initiation factor eIF2α and shuts down protein synthesis, and the oligoadenylate synthetases, which generate second messengers that unleash RNase L to degrade RNA; the IFIT proteins sequester viral transcripts from the initiation machinery, MX1 and MX2 trap incoming nucleocapsids, and guanylate-binding proteins target intracellular pathogens. ISG15 is conjugated to substrates by a dedicated E1 cE2 cE3 cascade and removed by USP18, which also restrains further interferon signalling. Nuclear pore and cytoskeletal components reflect the trafficking steps these effectors intercept.

Fertilization is the union of sperm and egg that begins a new organism, and the genes here cover the final steps: sperm activation in the female tract, penetration of the egg's outer coat, and fusion of the two plasma membranes. Failure at any of these steps causes infertility, and several components are candidate targets for non-hormonal contraception. The zona pellucida glycoproteins ZP1-ZP4 form the egg coat that sperm must bind and traverse, aided by acrosomal enzymes such as acrosin and the hyaluronidase SPAM1. Hyperactivated motility depends on the sperm-specific CatSper calcium channel complex and on pH regulation through the proton channel HVCN1 and the potassium channel KCNU1. Membrane fusion itself requires sperm IZUMO1 engaging its oocyte receptor, with CD9 on the egg surface needed for fusion competence, while oviductal glycoprotein OVGP1 conditions the gametes in transit.

Fertilization is the union of sperm and egg that restores diploidy and initiates embryonic development; failure at any of its steps is a cause of infertility and a target for contraceptive design. The genes here cover the sequential encounters: zona pellucida glycoproteins ZP1-ZP4 form the egg coat that sperm must recognize and penetrate, with the oviductal glycoprotein OVGP1 modifying that coat, while acrosin and the hyaluronidase SPAM1 provide proteolytic and matrix-degrading activity for passage through the cumulus and zona. Hyperactivated motility depends on the sperm-specific CatSper calcium channel complex and on pH regulation through the voltage-gated proton channel HVCN1 and the potassium channel KCNU1. Final membrane fusion requires sperm IZUMO1 engaging the oocyte surface, with tetraspanin CD9 needed on the egg side; ADAM family proteins contribute to sperm surface maturation and adhesion.

Cell redox homeostasis is the set of reactions by which a cell keeps its thiol pools reduced and detoxifies peroxides and other reactive oxygen species generated by metabolism or by an attacking immune system. In Mycobacterium tuberculosis this capacity is what allows the bacillus to survive the oxidative and nitrosative burst inside activated macrophages, and it is therefore a persistent focus of drug discovery. Catalase and peroxiredoxins do the peroxide-destroying chemistry, but they are only regenerated by a relay of disulfide-exchange proteins such as thioredoxins and mycothiol-linked carriers, which ultimately draw electrons from NAD(P)H through reductases including TrxB and the dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase Lpd. Because the downstream peroxidases are extensively redundant, inhibition is most effective at these upstream NAD(P)H-dependent entry points, linking central carbon metabolism directly to antioxidant defence and intracellular persistence.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside macrophages by neutralising the oxidative and nitrosative burst directed at it, and cell redox homeostasis is the network that makes this possible. Catalase and peroxiredoxin-type peroxidases destroy hydrogen peroxide and peroxynitrite, but they are not self-sufficient: each is re-reduced through relays of thiol-disulfide proteins such as thioredoxins, mycoredoxins and the lipoamide-bearing components of alpha-keto acid dehydrogenases, with electrons drawn ultimately from NADH or NADPH. Maintaining a reduced cytoplasmic thiol pool also supports biosynthetic reductions and protects iron-sulfur centres and DNA from damage. Because the peroxide-detoxifying arms are heavily redundant, inhibiting any single peroxidase is unlikely to be bactericidal; attention has instead turned to the upstream NAD(P)H-dependent reductases, including thioredoxin reductase and lipoamide dehydrogenase, that feed the entire cascade. Loss of this capacity leaves the bacterium vulnerable to host-derived oxidants.

Signaling by ERBB2 describes how the receptor tyrosine kinase ERBB2 (HER2), which binds no ligand of its own, drives epithelial proliferation, survival and differentiation by partnering with ligand-bound EGFR, ERBB3 or ERBB4. It is the pathway amplified in HER2-positive breast and gastric cancer and the target of trastuzumab and lapatinib, and its output governs normal mammary, cardiac and neural development through neuregulin signalling. Inactive ERBB2 is held by HSP90 and CDC37 and localised basolaterally by ERBIN; heterodimerisation displaces these partners and permits trans-autophosphorylation of C-terminal tyrosines that recruit GRB2, SHC1, GAB1 and PIK3R1, converging on RAS-RAF-MAP kinase, PI3K-AKT and phospholipase C gamma with PKC. Signal strength is set by counteracting machinery: phosphatases PTPN12 and PTPN18, Src-family and PTK6 kinases, and ubiquitin ligases RNF41, STUB1 and CUL5 that direct receptor degradation, with USP8 opposing them.

ERBB2 is the receptor tyrosine kinase that no ligand binds directly; it works instead as the preferred partner for EGFR, ERBB3 and ERBB4 once those receptors are engaged by EGF-family ligands or neuregulins, and the resulting heterodimers drive epithelial proliferation, survival and differentiation. Because a dimerization-ready receptor needs no ligand of its own, amplification of ERBB2 forces constitutive signalling and defines an aggressive subtype of breast and gastric cancer that is the target of receptor-directed antibodies and kinase inhibitors. Inactive receptor is held by HSP90 with CDC37, while ERBIN confines it to basolateral membrane in polarized epithelium. After dimerization, trans-autophosphorylated C-tail tyrosines recruit GRB2, SHC1, GAB1 and PI3K, feeding the RAS-RAF-MAP kinase cascade, AKT signalling and phospholipase C gamma. Ubiquitin ligases including RNF41 and STUB1, deubiquitination by USP8, and phosphatases such as PTPN12 and PTPN18 set signal duration and receptor turnover.

Regulation of gene expression by Hypoxia-inducible Factor is the transcriptional arm of the cellular oxygen-sensing system, the step at which low oxygen is converted into a new pattern of gene activity. It drives erythropoietin production and red cell mass, angiogenesis through VEGFA, pH control via carbonic anhydrase IX, and a shift toward glycolytic metabolism, so tissues can survive ischaemia; constitutive activation of the same program sustains tumour vascularisation and is the basis of VHL-associated cancers. Stabilised HIF-alpha subunits (HIF1A, EPAS1, HIF3A) are imported into the nucleus, dimerise with ARNT, bind hypoxia-response elements, and recruit the coactivators CBP and p300 to build a productive transcription complex. Negative feedback through CITED2, which competes for coactivator binding, and mitochondrial targets such as HIGD1A that retune respiration, keep the response self-limiting and matched to oxygen availability.

Cells that run short of oxygen respond by rewiring transcription, and hypoxia-inducible factor is the switch that does it. When oxygen is plentiful the alpha subunits are degraded; when it falls they are stabilised, imported into the nucleus, and pair with the constitutive partner ARNT to bind hypoxia response elements, recruiting the CBP and p300 acetyltransferases to open target promoters. The output is an adaptive programme: erythropoietin to expand red cell mass, VEGFA to drive angiogenesis, carbonic anhydrase 9 to buffer pH, and mitochondrial adjustments through factors such as HIGD1A that tune respiration to available oxygen. CITED2 competes for the coactivators and damps the response, providing negative feedback. This axis governs development, wound healing and high-altitude adaptation, and its constitutive activation in kidney cancer and other tumours supplies the vascular supply that solid tumours depend on.

Cellular response to hypoxia is the transcriptional program that lets cells sense how much oxygen they have and adjust accordingly, driving erythropoietin production, angiogenesis through VEGFA, and a shift toward glycolytic metabolism. It underlies adaptation to altitude, wound healing and ischaemia, and its constitutive activation through loss of VHL causes clear cell renal carcinoma and other highly vascularised tumours. Oxygen availability is read out by dioxygenases: the prolyl hydroxylases EGLN1-3 and the asparaginyl hydroxylase HIF1AN use O2 as substrate to modify HIF1A, EPAS1 and HIF3A. Proline hydroxylation recruits a VHL-CUL2-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase, committing HIF-alpha to proteasomal destruction, while asparagine hydroxylation blocks recruitment of the coactivators p300/CBP. When oxygen falls, hydroxylation stalls, HIF-alpha accumulates, dimerises with ARNT and activates its targets; LIMD1-AJUBA scaffolds and CITED2 tune the output.

Cells must sense how much oxygen they have and adjust transcription accordingly, and this hypoxia response is the mechanism, built around the HIF-alpha transcription factors HIF1A, EPAS1 and HIF3A. It drives erythropoietin production to raise red cell mass, VEGFA-dependent angiogenesis, and a shift toward glycolytic metabolism with carbonic anhydrase 9 to manage the resulting acid load; tumours exploit it to vascularise themselves, and loss of VHL causes constitutive activation and renal cancer. Oxygen acts as a substrate for the prolyl hydroxylases EGLN1-3 and the asparaginyl hydroxylase HIF1AN: proline hydroxylation recruits a VHL-CUL2-RBX1-elongin ubiquitin ligase that marks HIF-alpha for proteasomal destruction, while asparagine hydroxylation blocks recruitment of the coactivators p300 and CBP. When oxygen falls, both reactions stall, HIF-alpha accumulates, dimerises with ARNT and activates its targets. LIMD1 and related scaffolds assemble the hydroxylase-VHL machinery.

Oxygen-dependent proline hydroxylation of Hypoxia-inducible Factor Alpha is the cell's oxygen sensor: it destroys the HIF transcription factor whenever oxygen is plentiful, and stops doing so when it is not. This switch controls erythropoietin production, angiogenesis, and the shift to glycolytic metabolism, and its failure underlies VHL disease, familial erythrocytosis, and the pseudo-hypoxic metabolic state of many tumours. Prolyl hydroxylases EGLN1/2/3 use molecular oxygen, iron and 2-oxoglutarate to modify conserved prolines in HIF1A, EPAS1 and HIF3A; cytosolic EGLN2 (PHD2) sets the basal rate. Hydroxyproline creates a binding site for VHL within a cullin-RING E3 ligase built on Elongin B/C, CUL2 and RBX1, which polyubiquitinates HIF-alpha for rapid proteasomal degradation. LIMD1-family scaffolds assemble hydroxylase and ligase together. Under hypoxia the reaction stalls, HIF-alpha accumulates, enters the nucleus and drives the adaptive transcriptional response.

This is the oxygen sensor that keeps the hypoxic response switched off when oxygen is plentiful. Prolyl hydroxylases EGLN1, EGLN2 and EGLN3 use molecular oxygen, 2-oxoglutarate and iron to hydroxylate specific prolines in the HIF-alpha subunits HIF1A, EPAS1 and HIF3A; the modified proline creates a binding site for VHL within a cullin-RING ligase containing CUL2, RBX1, ELOB and ELOC, which polyubiquitinates HIF-alpha for destruction by the 26S proteasome. Because the reaction needs oxygen as a substrate, hypoxia stalls hydroxylation, HIF-alpha escapes degradation and enters the nucleus to drive erythropoietin, glycolytic and angiogenic gene expression. LIMD1, AJUBA and WTIP scaffold the hydroxylases with VHL to sharpen the response. Loss of VHL or EGLN1 function causes constitutive HIF signalling, underlying familial erythrocytosis, paraganglioma and clear cell renal carcinoma.

Methionine salvage pathway regenerates methionine from 5'-methylthioadenosine, the sulfur-containing waste product released whenever cells make the polyamines spermidine and spermine. Because sulfur assimilation is energetically expensive, recycling this thioether lets cells sustain high polyamine synthesis and keep the S-adenosylmethionine pool available for methylation of DNA, RNA, proteins and small molecules. Six cytosolic reactions carry it out: a phosphorylase (MTAP) cleaves the nucleoside to 5-methylthioribose-1-phosphate, releasing adenine for purine salvage, then isomerase, dehydratase, enolase-phosphatase and dioxygenase steps convert the sugar to a 2-keto acid that is transaminated to methionine, largely by GOT1. Its clinical relevance is largely oncological: MTAP is co-deleted with CDKN2A in many tumours, and the resulting accumulation of the substrate creates a selective dependence exploited by PRMT5 and MAT2A inhibitors. The pathway also connects polyamine turnover to purine and one-carbon metabolism.

Polyamine synthesis consumes decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine and leaves behind 5'-methylthioadenosine, a byproduct that must be disposed of and whose sulfur is too costly to discard. The methionine salvage pathway solves both problems, running six cytosolic reactions that regenerate methionine from the methylthio group while releasing adenine back into nucleotide salvage. MTAP begins the route by phosphorolysing the thioether nucleoside; isomerase, dehydratase-enolase-phosphatase and dioxygenase steps then rearrange and oxidise the ribose-derived carbon skeleton, and a transamination by GOT1 completes methionine. Because recycling here spares the energy of assimilating sulfate, the pathway ties polyamine metabolism to the cell's methylation capacity through the methionine-S-adenosylmethionine cycle. MTAP is co-deleted with CDKN2A in many tumours, and the resulting accumulation of methylthioadenosine creates a metabolic vulnerability exploited in cancer therapy.

Mitochondrial protein import delivers the roughly 1500 proteins encoded in the nucleus and made on cytosolic ribosomes into the organelle that needs them, sorting each to the outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane or matrix. Essentially all mitochondrial function "" respiration, the citric acid cycle, metabolite exchange, heme and iron-sulfur chemistry "" depends on it, and defects in import components cause neuropathies, deafness-dystonia and cardiomyopathy. Precursors first engage the outer membrane translocase, with TOMM20 reading N-terminal presequences and TOMM70 recognising internal signals before TOMM40 forms the conducting pore. Downstream, SAMM50 inserts beta-barrels, TIMM22 handles carrier proteins such as the ADP/ATP translocases, and TIMM23 with its motor (HSPA9, TIMM44, PAM16, GRPEL) pulls presequence-bearing proteins into the matrix, where MPP peptidases trim them. Small TIM chaperones and the MIA40/GFER disulfide relay escort hydrophobic and cysteine-rich intermembrane space clients.

Almost the entire mitochondrial proteome is encoded in the nucleus and made on cytosolic ribosomes, so mitochondria depend on a dedicated import and sorting system to acquire their roughly 1500 proteins and deliver each to the correct one of four destinations: outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane, or matrix. Precursors first engage receptors such as TOMM20 and TOMM70 and cross the outer membrane through the TOMM40 channel, then are routed onward by the SAMM50 machinery for beta-barrel insertion, by TIMM22 for carrier proteins, or by the TIMM23 translocase for presequence-bearing inner-membrane and matrix proteins, with the HSPA9 chaperone and its GRPEL nucleotide exchange factors driving translocation and PMPCA/PMPCB and PITRM1 trimming targeting peptides. Small chaperone complexes containing TIMM8, TIMM9, TIMM10 and TIMM13 escort hydrophobic precursors, while CHCHD4 oxidatively traps cysteine-rich intermembrane space proteins. Defects impair respiratory chain assembly and cause neurodegenerative and metabolic disease.

Cytokine Signaling in Immune system is the collective language of immune communication: small secreted proteins that act locally and briefly at very low concentrations to coordinate immunity, inflammation, tissue repair and haematopoiesis. It determines whether an infection is cleared, how helper T cell subsets are polarised, how blood lineages expand from progenitors, and — when miscalibrated — drives autoimmunity, chronic inflammation and cytokine storm. Receptors of the interleukin, interferon, chemokine and TNF families transmit signals through JAK kinases to STAT transcription factors, through MyD88/IRAK and TRAF adaptors to NF-kB and MAP kinases, and through PI3K and Ras branches to survival and proliferation programmes. Negative regulators such as SOCS proteins, phosphatases and ubiquitin-dependent turnover terminate the response. Interferon arms additionally impose an antiviral state, inducing ISG15 conjugation, OAS/RNase L, MX and IFIT effectors, GBPs, and enhanced antigen presentation by MHC molecules.

Cytokine signaling in the immune system is the communication layer that coordinates immunity, inflammation and blood cell production: secreted interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor family ligands, chemokines and haematopoietic growth factors act briefly and locally on specific surface receptors to instruct nearby cells to proliferate, differentiate, migrate or die. Loss or excess of these signals produces immunodeficiency, autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease, cytokine storm, and the antibody or receptor blockade targeted by modern biologics. Mechanistically the receptors coupled to JAK1/2/3 and TYK2 phosphorylate STAT1-6, which enter the nucleus through nuclear pore and karyopherin machinery and are restrained by SOCS proteins and phosphatases such as PTPN6; interleukin-1 and TNF receptor arms instead route through MYD88, IRAK kinases, TRAF adaptors and NF-kB, while interferon responses induce antiviral effectors including OAS enzymes, MX proteins, GBPs and ISG15 conjugation, alongside MHC class I and II antigen presentation.

Tandem pore domain halothane-inhibited K+ channel (THIK) describes a background potassium leak conductance that sets the resting membrane potential and dampens excitability in the cells that express it. Unlike its two-pore-domain relatives, this channel is insensitive to pH and temperature, and is instead closed by volatile anaesthetics such as halothane, which links it to anaesthetic action on neuronal excitability. The gene here, KCNK13, encodes a subunit whose open leak current provides steady potassium efflux and so opposes depolarising inputs. It is prominent in microglia, where the constitutive potassium conductance supports ramified surveillance behaviour, interleukin-1beta release and inflammasome-driven signalling, making it a control point for neuroinflammation. More broadly this belongs to potassium homeostasis and the regulation of resting potential, upstream of neurotransmitter and cytokine responses rather than part of any single receptor cascade.

Two-pore domain potassium channels provide the background leak current that sets a cell's resting membrane potential, and the halothane-inhibited member of this family, encoded by KCNK13, forms such a leak channel that is insensitive to the pH and temperature cues which gate other K2P subtypes. Each subunit contributes two pore-forming domains and four transmembrane segments, with two subunits dimerising to build a single potassium-selective pore that conducts outward current across essentially the whole voltage range. Volatile anaesthetics inhibit rather than activate this channel, distinguishing it from the anaesthetic-activated K2P channels and making it a candidate contributor to anaesthetic action on excitability. The channel is prominent in microglia, where the standing potassium conductance maintains the resting potential required for process motility, surveillance of brain parenchyma and inflammasome-dependent interleukin-1β release, linking background potassium leak to neuroinflammation.

Sperm Motility And Taxes describes how mature sperm steer and change gear on their way to the egg, converting cues in the female reproductive tract into the hyperactivated flagellar beating and directional swimming that fertilization requires. Loss of these channels leaves sperm that swim but cannot penetrate the cumulus and zona, a recognized cause of male infertility. The core is the sperm-specific CatSper complex, a pH-sensitive, calcium-selective channel built from four pore subunits and auxiliary beta, gamma and delta partners in flagellar membrane domains; it admits the calcium that reshapes the beat. The proton channel HVCN1 alkalinizes the flagellum to open it, and the potassium channel KSper sets membrane potential. Progesterone released by cumulus cells acts as a short-range chemoattractant through this system, while fluid flow provides rheotactic guidance over longer distances, and the same calcium signals prime the acrosome reaction.

Sperm must change how they swim once inside the female reproductive tract, and the ion channels gathered here are what allow that switch. Their coordinated activity produces hyperactivated motility, the asymmetric high-amplitude flagellar beating needed to penetrate the cumulus mass and zona pellucida, and it underlies the steering behaviours that guide sperm toward the oocyte, whether chemotaxis toward progesterone released by cumulus cells or rheotaxis against fluid flow over longer distances. The CatSper complex, built from pore-forming subunits and accessory subunits arranged in flagellar nanodomains, is a pH-sensitive calcium-selective channel activated by progesterone and alkalinization; the voltage-gated proton channel HVCN1 extrudes protons to raise intracellular pH, while KCNU1 provides the sperm-specific potassium conductance that sets membrane potential. Loss-of-function mutations in these subunits cause male infertility and are associated with deafness-infertility syndrome.

Biogenic amines are oxidatively deaminated to aldehydes by MAOA and MAOB is the step that terminates the action of monoamine neurotransmitters and dietary amines, converting them to reactive aldehydes plus ammonia and hydrogen peroxide. It sets the tissue levels of serotonin, dopamine, noradrenaline, tyramine and phenylethylamine, and so shapes mood, arousal and blood pressure; inhibiting it is the basis of an entire antidepressant class and of adjunct therapy in Parkinson disease, while the same inhibition creates the tyramine-cheese hypertensive reaction. Two flavin-dependent isozymes anchored to the outer mitochondrial membrane do the work, MAOA favouring serotonin and dominant in fibroblasts and gut, MAOB favouring phenylethylamine and dominant in platelets and glia. The aldehyde products are handed to aldehyde dehydrogenases for excretion, linking this reaction to downstream catecholamine catabolism and to oxidative stress in ageing neurons.

Neurotransmitters and dietary amines must be cleared as fast as they are made, and oxidative deamination by the two monoamine oxidases is the main route by which that happens. Anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane as flavin-dependent enzymes, MAOA and MAOB convert primary, secondary and tertiary amines to the corresponding aldehydes, releasing ammonia and hydrogen peroxide, after which aldehyde dehydrogenases finish the job to acids such as homovanillic and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid. The two isoforms share most substrates, including dopamine, tyramine and tryptamine, but MAOA favours serotonin and noradrenaline while MAOB favours phenylethylamine. This turnover sets synaptic monoamine tone, protects against pressor amines absorbed from food, and generates peroxide that contributes to oxidative stress in ageing neurons. Inhibitors of these enzymes are used as antidepressants and in Parkinson disease, and loss of MAOA function is linked to aggressive behaviour and Brunner syndrome.

Inactivation of APC/C via direct inhibition of the APC/C complex is the braking mechanism of the spindle assembly checkpoint: it holds the anaphase-promoting complex switched off until every chromosome is correctly attached to the spindle, so that sister chromatids are not separated prematurely. Without this restraint, cyclin B and securin are destroyed too early, cells exit mitosis with unattached kinetochores, and chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy follow. Mechanistically, a cytosolic mitotic checkpoint complex of BUBR1, BUB3, MAD2 and the substrate-recognition subunit CDC20 binds the assembled APC/C directly, occluding substrate recruitment and blocking productive interaction with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S that build ubiquitin chains on its targets. The many ANAPC and CDC subunits represent the cullin-RING-like ubiquitin ligase itself, whose reactivation upon checkpoint satisfaction triggers anaphase and mitotic exit.

Cells must not separate their chromosomes until every kinetochore is properly attached, and this branch of the spindle assembly checkpoint enforces that delay by shutting down the anaphase-promoting complex outright. The APC/C is the ubiquitin ligase that, with its E2 partners UBE2C and UBE2S, marks securin and cyclin B for proteasomal destruction to trigger sister chromatid separation and mitotic exit. When attachment is incomplete, a cytosolic mitotic checkpoint complex containing BUBR1, BUB3, MAD2 and the APC/C activator CDC20 binds the ligase directly and blocks substrate recognition, so the ubiquitination of anaphase substrates never begins. The result is a metaphase arrest that buys time for correct spindle attachment. Loss of this restraint permits premature anaphase, chromosome missegregation and the aneuploidy characteristic of tumour cells, and it underlies the action of spindle poisons used as chemotherapy.

Regulation of signaling by NODAL is the brake on a TGF-beta family signal that patterns the early embryo, setting the anterior-posterior axis, specifying mesoderm and endoderm, and breaking left-right symmetry so that heart and viscera are placed correctly. Because NODAL acts as a graded morphogen, its range and duration matter as much as its presence, and the feedback antagonists encoded here supply that limit; loss of restraint produces laterality defects such as heterotaxy and congenital heart malformation. Mechanistically, LEFTY1 and LEFTY2 and the Cerberus/DAN proteins CER1 and DAND5 sequester mature NODAL in inactive heterodimers, while the LEFTYs additionally occupy the EGF-CFC coreceptors CRIPTO and CFC1 so they cannot present ligand to the activin type I and type II receptors. The result is a self-limiting reaction-diffusion circuit rather than a simple off switch.

NODAL is a TGF-beta family morphogen that patterns the early embryo, specifying mesoderm and endoderm and setting up left-right asymmetry, so the amount and location of its signalling must be held within narrow bounds. Regulation of signalling by NODAL describes how that restraint is imposed: the secreted antagonists LEFTY1 and LEFTY2 and the Cerberus/DAN proteins CER1 and DAND5 bind mature NODAL to form heterodimers that cannot engage its receptor, while LEFTY proteins additionally sequester the EGF-CFC coreceptors Cripto and Cryptic so they cannot assemble with the type I and type II activin receptors ACVR1B, ACVR1C, ACVR2A and ACVR2B. Blocking coreceptor assembly prevents SMAD2/3 activation downstream. Asymmetric expression of these inhibitors around the node converts a symmetric signal into laterality, and their loss produces midline and left-right patterning defects such as heterotaxy and situs inversus.

Collagen formation is the biosynthetic route that produces the body's most abundant protein family and the fibrils, networks and anchoring structures they build. Collagens make up the bulk of connective tissue, giving tendon, skin, bone, cartilage, cornea and basement membranes their tensile strength and their instructions to adherent cells; defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos and Alport syndromes, epidermolysis bullosa and chondrodysplasias. Alpha chains are co-translationally modified in the endoplasmic reticulum by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, collagen galactosyltransferases and the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase and chaperone activities of PPIB, P4HB and HSP47, then trimerise into procollagen. After secretion, N- and C-propeptides are removed by ADAMTS2/3/14 and BMP1-tolloid proteinases, and lysyl oxidases introduce covalent cross-links that lock fibrils together. The set also covers assembly of type IV networks, type VII anchoring fibrils, hemidesmosomal type XVII collagen with integrin alpha6beta4, plectin and laminin-332, and matrix metalloproteinase- and cathepsin-mediated turnover.

Collagen formation covers the synthesis, modification, secretion and extracellular assembly of the collagens, the most abundant proteins in the body and the structural backbone of skin, bone, cartilage, tendon, cornea, blood vessels and basement membranes. Nascent alpha chains are hydroxylated on proline and lysine by prolyl 4-hydroxylases and lysyl hydroxylases, glycosylated by collagen galactosyltransferases, and folded into triple helices with help from a dedicated chaperone complex including HSP47 and cyclophilin B; procollagen is then secreted, its propeptides trimmed by BMP1/tolloid and ADAMTS proteinases, and the resulting fibrils cross-linked by lysyl oxidases. Beyond fibril-forming types, the pathway builds basement membrane networks, anchoring fibrils and transmembrane collagen XVII within hemidesmosomes alongside laminin-332, plectin and integrin alpha6beta4. Defects give osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos and Alport syndromes, epidermolysis bullosa and chondrodysplasias, and remodelling by matrix metalloproteinases and cathepsins shapes wound healing and fibrosis.

Synthesis of CL produces cardiolipin, the signature dimeric phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane, which shapes cristae, stabilises respiratory chain supercomplexes and ADP/ATP carriers, and anchors cytochrome c until apoptotic signals release it. Cells depleted of cardiolipin lose oxidative phosphorylation efficiency and mitochondrial ultrastructure, and defects in its synthesis or subsequent remodelling underlie mitochondrial cardiomyopathies such as Barth syndrome. The committed step is carried out by cardiolipin synthase, CRLS1, an inner-membrane enzyme that condenses phosphatidylglycerol with CDP-diacylglycerol; the CDP-DAG substrate arises within mitochondria or is drawn from a pool imported from the endoplasmic reticulum, and phosphatidylglycerol phosphate formation limits the overall rate. Nascent cardiolipin is then remodelled with unsaturated acyl chains, linking this branch of glycerophospholipid metabolism to mitochondrial bioenergetics, membrane dynamics and the regulation of programmed cell death.

Cardiolipin is the signature phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane, and its synthesis there gives that membrane the curvature and charge needed to organize respiratory chain supercomplexes, the ADP/ATP carrier, and the machinery of cristae shaping, mitochondrial fusion and fission. The final committed step condenses phosphatidylglycerol with CDP-diacylglycerol, releasing CMP, and is carried out on the matrix face of the inner membrane by cardiolipin synthase; precursor CDP-diacylglycerol can be made locally or drawn from an endoplasmic reticulum pool. Newly made cardiolipin is subsequently remodelled to its mature, largely unsaturated acyl composition. Because oxidative phosphorylation, apoptotic cytochrome c release and mitophagy signalling all depend on this lipid, depletion or defective remodelling compromises bioenergetics and is associated with cardiomyopathy, neutropenia and neuromuscular disease, placing this route at the interface of lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function.

Synthesis of PA builds phosphatidic acid, the branch-point lipid from which all glycerophospholipids and triacylglycerol are made, and which doubles as a signalling lipid that recruits proteins and bends membranes. Cells that cannot make it cannot expand their membranes or store fat, and loss of the adipose-enriched acyltransferase AGPAT2 causes congenital generalized lipodystrophy. The core route acylates glycerol-3-phosphate, supplied by cytosolic and mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenases, to lysophosphatidic acid via GPAT enzymes at the endoplasmic reticulum and outer mitochondrial membrane, then to phosphatidic acid via AGPAT/LPAAT activity; the peroxisomal GNPAT route feeds ether lipid synthesis. Phospholipase D isoforms generate the same product directly from phosphatidylcholine, with PLD6 acting on mitochondrial membranes during fusion. Secreted and cytosolic phospholipases A2 together with reacylating enzymes remodel acyl chains, tailoring membrane composition and releasing arachidonate for eicosanoid production.

Phosphatidic acid is the branch point of glycerolipid metabolism: it is the precursor from which triacylglycerol and all the major phospholipids are built, and it also acts as a signalling lipid that recruits and activates effector proteins at membranes. Its synthesis begins when glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferases esterify glycerol 3-phosphate, itself supplied by glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenases, to give lysophosphatidic acid, which acyltransferases of the AGPAT family then acylate at the sn-2 position. A second route generates it directly by phospholipase D cleavage of phosphatidylcholine, while phospholipase A2 enzymes and reacylating acyltransferases feed acyl-chain remodelling cycles that set the fatty acid composition of the product. Output is tuned to nutritional state and underpins fat storage in adipocytes; loss of AGPAT2 causes congenital generalised lipodystrophy, and mitochondrial PLD6 acts in this chemistry at organelle membranes.

Glycerophospholipid biosynthesis builds the phospholipids that form every cellular membrane, and also supplies serum lipoprotein lipids, pulmonary surfactant, and the precursors of signalling molecules such as platelet-activating factor, eicosanoids and diacylglycerol. Synthesis begins from glycerol 3-phosphate, with acyltransferases and phosphatases generating lysophosphatidic acid, phosphatidic acid and diacylglycerol; branches through CDP-choline and CDP-ethanolamine give phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, while CDP-diacylglycerol feeds phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylglycerol and mitochondrial cardiolipin. Head-group exchange and methylation interconvert phosphatidylserine, ethanolamine and choline species. Because acyl chains are asymmetrically distributed, phospholipases and reacylating enzymes such as the LPCAT and MBOAT family continuously remodel membranes, setting fluidity and curvature, while transfer proteins and contact-site components distribute products between the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and endosomes. Defects cause lipodystrophy, surfactant deficiency, and cardiolipin-related cardiomyopathy including Barth syndrome.

Glycerophospholipids form the bilayer of every cellular membrane, supply the lipid backbone of serum lipoproteins and pulmonary surfactant, and serve as reservoirs for signalling molecules such as diacylglycerol, lysophosphatidic acid and eicosanoid precursors. Their biosynthesis begins from glycerol 3-phosphate, which is acylated in sequence to lysophosphatidic acid and phosphatidic acid; phosphatidate phosphatases of the lipin family divert flux to diacylglycerol for phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine production through choline and ethanolamine kinase and cytidylyltransferase steps, while CDP-diacylglycerol synthases feed phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin. Cardiolipin is made and remodelled in mitochondria, where tafazzin transfers acyl chains and its loss causes Barth syndrome. Phospholipases and lysophospholipid acyltransferases then remodel acyl chains to generate membrane asymmetry and polyunsaturate content, and transfer proteins move finished lipids between endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and other compartments. Defects disturb lipid droplet formation, adipose development and surfactant function.

Inositol phosphate metabolism generates and interconverts the soluble inositol phosphates that carry intracellular signals, beginning with the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate released when phospholipase C cleaves PI(4,5)P2 to trigger calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum. Beyond that classical second messenger, successive kinase and phosphatase steps build a large family of higher species — IP4, IP5, IP6 and the energetic pyrophosphates IP7 and IP8 — which tune insulin secretion, phosphate and iron sensing, vesicle traffic, chromatin regulation and mRNA export. The genes span the phospholipase C isozymes, the multikinases IPMK, IPPK and IP6K1-3, diphosphoinositol pyrophosphate kinases and hydrolases, and the 5-phosphatases and PTEN-family enzymes that reverse the pathway; inositol synthase and monophosphatases recycle free myo-inositol, the latter being the target of lithium. Because synthesis shuttles between cytosol and nucleus, nucleoporins appear as the transport route. Loss of individual enzymes causes Lowe syndrome, and disrupted signalling in cancer and neurological disease.

Soluble inositol phosphates are the second messengers and signalling currency generated when phospholipase C cleaves membrane PI(4,5)P2, and this metabolic network builds and dismantles them. The immediate product, inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, releases calcium from intracellular stores and so drives secretion, contraction, fertilisation and lymphocyte activation; successive kinases and phosphatases then convert it into a large family of higher species, including the energetic pyrophosphates IP7 and IP8, that regulate phosphate sensing, insulin secretion, vesicle traffic and mRNA export. Inositol trisphosphate 3-kinases, a multikinase, IPPK, IP6 kinases and diphosphoinositol phosphatases of the NUDT family set the balance, while myo-inositol monophosphatases recycle free inositol and are the presumed targets of lithium. Lipid phosphatases such as PTEN, OCRL and synaptojanin link the soluble pool back to phosphoinositide turnover; nucleoporins appear because inositol phosphate species shuttle between cytosol and nucleus and modulate nuclear transport.

Phase II - Conjugation of compounds is the second stage of xenobiotic biotransformation, in which transferase enzymes attach polar groups from cofactors onto drugs, dietary chemicals, hormones and the reactive metabolites generated by phase I oxidation, making them water-soluble and readily excreted in bile or urine. It determines drug half-life, and its failure or genetic variation causes hyperbilirubinaemia, thiopurine and irinotecan toxicity, and susceptibility to chemical carcinogens; occasionally conjugation instead bioactivates a compound. The main routes are glucuronidation by microsomal UGTs, sulfonation by cytosolic SULTs, glutathione conjugation by the GST family, methylation by COMT, TPMT and NNMT, acetylation by NAT1 and NAT2, and amino acid conjugation by glycine N-acyltransferases. Also included is the supply and recycling of the cofactors themselves — UDP-glucuronic acid, S-adenosylmethionine, and glutathione synthesis and turnover through the gamma-glutamyl cycle — which can limit overall conjugating capacity.

Drugs, dietary chemicals and endogenous metabolites are cleared from the body by attaching a water-soluble group to them, and this conjugative arm of biotransformation is where that happens. By adding glucuronate, sulfate, glutathione, acetyl, methyl or amino acid groups, transferases make lipophilic compounds excretable in bile and urine and usually abolish their activity, though some conjugates are more reactive than the parent compound. The chemistry is spread across families: microsomal UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, cytosolic sulfotransferases, glutathione S-transferases, N-acetyltransferases and methyltransferases using S-adenosylmethionine, alongside the enzymes that synthesise and recycle the cofactors themselves, including glutathione synthesis and UDP-sugar supply. Cofactor availability often limits throughput. Variation here shapes individual drug response and toxicity, as with bilirubin handling by UGT1A1 and thiopurine inactivation by TPMT, and failure to conjugate reactive intermediates leaves them free to damage protein and DNA.

Methylation is a Phase II conjugation route that caps drugs, xenobiotics and small endogenous molecules with a methyl group, altering their activity and clearance. It is quantitatively minor next to glucuronidation and sulfonation, but pharmacologically decisive: catechol O-methyltransferase terminates dopamine and catecholamine signalling and is a target in Parkinson's therapy, while thiopurine methyltransferase deficiency causes life-threatening toxicity from azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine. All the reactions draw on S-adenosylmethionine, made from methionine and ATP by methionine adenosyltransferase isoforms, and leave S-adenosylhomocysteine, which is hydrolysed to homocysteine and remethylated by the cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase system, linking xenobiotic handling to one-carbon and folate metabolism. Substrates include phenols and catechols, aliphatic and aromatic amines, thiols, nicotinamide and arsenic species, the last methylated by AS3MT during arsenic detoxification. Cytosolic monomeric transferases carry out most of this chemistry.

Methylation is a phase II conjugation route that caps nucleophilic groups on drugs, neurotransmitters and other small molecules, and although it handles less traffic than glucuronidation or sulfonation, it determines the fate of several clinically important compounds. Methionine adenosyltransferases build the universal methyl donor S-adenosylmethionine, cytosolic methyltransferases pass its methyl group to catechols, amines and thiols, and the resulting S-adenosylhomocysteine is hydrolysed by AHCY to homocysteine, which methionine synthase and its reductase partner remethylate to close the cycle. Substrate-named enzymes give the pathway its character: COMT inactivates dopamine and other catecholamines, TPMT methylates thiopurine drugs, NNMT acts on nicotinamide, and AS3MT methylates arsenic during its detoxification. Because activity depends on cofactor supply and on common variants in these transferases, the pathway links one-carbon metabolism to differences in drug tolerance, thiopurine toxicity, and catecholamine turnover.

Acetylation is a phase II drug-metabolism route in which cytosolic N-acetyltransferases transfer an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA onto the nitrogen of aromatic amines and hydrazines, converting them to amides. It is the preferred conjugation pathway for such compounds, and it determines how quickly people clear drugs including isoniazid, sulfonamides and hydralazine, as well as how they handle arylamine carcinogens from tobacco smoke and industrial exposure. Two enzymes, NAT1 and NAT2, act through a ping-pong mechanism in which the acetyl group is parked on an active-site cysteine before delivery to the substrate. Unlike glucuronidation or sulfation, acetylation masks an amine with a non-ionizable group, so products are often less water soluble than the parent. Common NAT2 variants split populations into slow and fast acetylators, a classic pharmacogenetic difference underlying drug toxicity and bladder cancer susceptibility.

Acetylation is a phase II drug-metabolising route in which cytosolic N-acetyltransferases transfer an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA onto the nitrogen of aromatic amines and hydrazines, converting them to the corresponding amides. It is the main way the body handles arylamine drugs and carcinogens, including isoniazid, sulfonamides, hydralazine and procainamide, and unlike glucuronidation or sulfation it masks a basic amine with a non-ionisable group, so products are often less water-soluble than the parent compound. Two enzymes carry the activity, NAT1 and NAT2, working through a two-step ping-pong mechanism in which a catalytic cysteine is acetylated before the acceptor amine binds. Common NAT2 variants define slow and fast acetylator phenotypes, whose frequencies differ markedly between populations and which alter both drug toxicity, such as isoniazid-related adverse effects, and susceptibility to arylamine-associated cancers. Aliphatic amines are not substrates.

Fibronectin matrix formation is the assembly of secreted fibronectin dimers into the fibrillar network that surrounds and connects cells, providing the scaffold on which much of the rest of the extracellular matrix is built. Cells cannot organise collagen or fibrillin microfibrils without it, and its loss compromises adhesion, migration, wound healing and vascular development. Assembly is cell-driven: alpha5beta1 integrin engages the RGD and synergy sites in fibronectin's type III repeats, and the resulting conformational change and applied tension expose self-association sites so that additional dimers polymerise into fibrils. The fibril then serves as a template and binding surface for interstitial and basement membrane collagens, fibrin, heparan sulfate proteoglycans and fibulin, and its turnover is set by matrix metalloproteinase activity. Alternative splicing of the extra type III and variable regions tunes which integrins and partners a given fibronectin engages, distinguishing cellular from plasma forms.

Fibronectin matrix formation is the step that converts soluble fibronectin dimers into the fibrillar network that surrounds cells and acts as the template on which the rest of the extracellular matrix is built. It matters because collagen deposition, fibrillin microfibril assembly and cell adhesion all depend on this scaffold; without it, matrix turnover accelerates and tissue architecture, wound repair and developmental morphogenesis fail. Assembly is cell-driven rather than spontaneous: FN1 dimers, joined by C-terminal disulfide bonds, engage alpha5beta1 integrin through the RGD and synergy sites, and the resulting tension and conformational change expose self-association surfaces so that further dimers add to growing fibrils. Type III modules lack internal disulfides and unfold under applied force, giving the fibril its elasticity. The polymerized network then binds and organizes fibrillar and basement membrane collagens, linking integrin-mediated mechanics to matrix composition.

Polo-like kinase mediated events describes how PLK1 drives the commitment step into mitosis, converting a G2 cell into a dividing one. Its output is the abrupt activation of cyclin B-CDK1, the switch that triggers nuclear envelope breakdown, chromosome condensation and spindle assembly; cells that cannot execute it arrest in G2, and its deregulation is a common feature of proliferating tumours. PLK1 achieves the switch by activating CDC25 phosphatases while inhibiting the opposing kinases WEE1 and MYT1, and CDK1 itself primes these substrates so that the polo-box domain can dock on them, making the circuit self-amplifying. A transcriptional arm reinforces it: PLK1 phosphorylates FOXM1, which together with MYBL2 and the MuvB core drives expression of mitotic genes including PLK1 and cyclin B, closing a positive feedback loop on the G2/M transition.

Entry into mitosis is a switch, and Polo-like kinase 1 is one of the levers that throws it. PLK1-mediated events tip the balance of activity on cyclin B-bound CDK1 from inhibited to active, committing a cell to divide; loss of this control delays or blocks mitotic entry, while excess PLK1 activity lets cells through with damaged DNA and is common in tumours. PLK1 phosphorylates and stimulates the activating phosphatase CDC25C while inactivating the inhibitory kinases WEE1 and MYT1, and CDK1 in turn creates the phosphopeptide docking sites that PLK1's polo-box domain reads, so the two kinases reinforce each other. A second loop runs through transcription: PLK1 activates FOXM1, which together with the MYBL2-MuvB complex drives expression of G2/M genes including PLK1 and the cyclins themselves.

Mitochondrial biogenesis is how a cell builds new mitochondria and matches its respiratory capacity to demand, the adaptation that lets exercised muscle gain endurance and that fails in metabolic disease, heart failure and ageing. Calcium influx and energy depletion are the initiating signals: AMPK senses a falling ATP:AMP ratio, p38 MAPK and CaMKIV respond to contraction and calcium, and both converge on the coactivator PGC-1alpha, with PGC-1beta and PPRC acting similarly. PGC-1alpha binds no DNA itself but partners with NRF1, GABP, ESRRA and nuclear receptors such as PPARA/RXRA to drive nuclear genes for oxidative phosphorylation subunits, the MICOS cristae-shaping complex, protein import machinery and antioxidant enzymes. It also switches on TFAM, TFB2M and POLRMT, coupling nuclear transcription to replication and expression of the mitochondrial genome, while sirtuins and corepressors such as NCOR1 tune the response.

Cells match their respiratory capacity to demand by building new mitochondria, and this programme is how exercise, calcium influx and energy depletion are converted into more mitochondrial protein. It underlies endurance adaptation in muscle, thermogenic and oxidative tissue function, and its blunting accompanies ageing, insulin resistance and metabolic disease. Falling ATP and rising AMP activate AMPK, while contraction-linked calcium signals act through CaMKIV and CREB and through p38 kinases; these converge on the coactivator PGC-1alpha and its relatives PGC-1beta and PPRC1, which do not bind DNA themselves but partner with NRF1, GABP, ESRRA, PPARA and RXRA to switch on nuclear genes for mitochondrial components. Targets include the mitochondrial transcription and replication machinery, TFAM, TFB1M/TFB2M, POLRMT, TWNK and SSBP1, plus ATP synthase subunits, matrix enzymes such as SOD2 and IDH2, mitochondrial sirtuins, and MICOS proteins that shape cristae during remodelling.

Gamma-carboxylation of protein precursors is the vitamin K-dependent modification that makes coagulation factors able to bind calcium and dock onto membrane surfaces, and it is the step targeted by warfarin. Without it, prothrombin, factors VII, IX and X, protein C, protein S and protein Z circulate but cannot assemble on phospholipid at a site of injury, producing bleeding disorders; loss of the carboxylase itself causes a combined deficiency of all these factors. In the endoplasmic reticulum, a single enzyme recognises a propeptide motif on the amino-terminal side of a glutamate cluster and processively converts each glutamate to gamma-carboxyglutamate before releasing the substrate. The same modification serves biology beyond clotting: osteocalcin in bone mineralisation and Gas6 in growth factor-like signalling depend on it, linking vitamin K status to haemostasis, skeletal and vascular function.

Several secreted proteins only work after a cluster of glutamate residues near their amino terminus is converted to gamma-carboxyglutamate, which creates the calcium-binding surface that lets them dock onto membrane phospholipid. This vitamin K-dependent modification of protein precursors is what makes coagulation possible: prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X, together with the anticoagulant regulators protein C, protein S and protein Z, all require it, as do the growth factor-like GAS6 and the bone matrix protein osteocalcin. A single enzyme in the endoplasmic reticulum, gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, recognises a propeptide motif on its substrates and processively carboxylates the whole cluster before release. Loss of carboxylase activity, or vitamin K deficiency, produces combined clotting factor deficiency and bleeding; pharmacological blockade of vitamin K recycling is the basis of warfarin anticoagulation.

Removal of aminoterminal propeptides from gamma-carboxylated proteins is the maturation step that converts vitamin K-dependent proteins into functional secreted factors. It matters because the proteins involved are the backbone of blood coagulation and its control -- prothrombin, factors VII, IX and X, protein C, protein S and protein Z -- along with osteocalcin in bone mineralisation and GAS6 in cell survival signalling. The propeptide is the recognition element that lets gamma-glutamyl carboxylase modify glutamate residues in the Gla domain; once carboxylation is complete the propeptide has no further use. Furin, a Golgi-resident proprotein convertase that cleaves after a basic Arg-X-Lys/Arg-Arg motif, excises it, and the trimmed proteins move on to secretion or the plasma membrane. Uncleaved precursors are still released but function poorly, so this step gates the activity rather than the output of the clotting cascade.

Vitamin K-dependent proteins acquire gamma-carboxyglutamate residues in the endoplasmic reticulum using a propeptide that serves as the recognition signal for the carboxylase; once carboxylation is complete that propeptide must be cut away, and removal of the aminoterminal propeptides from gamma-carboxylated proteins is the maturation step that makes them functional. Furin, a Golgi-localized endopeptidase that cleaves after a basic Arg-X-Lys/Arg-Arg motif, performs the cut; uncleaved precursors are still secreted but work poorly. The substrates define the output: prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X drive coagulation, protein C, protein S and protein Z restrain it, osteocalcin binds bone mineral, and GAS6 signals through TAM receptors. Because the propeptides themselves have no known onward role, this is essentially a licensing event linking post-translational carboxylation to haemostasis, bone mineralization and cell survival signalling.

Gamma-carboxylation, transport, and amino-terminal cleavage of proteins is the vitamin K-dependent maturation step that turns newly synthesized clotting factors into functional, calcium- and membrane-binding proteins. Prothrombin, factors VII, IX and X, protein C, protein S, protein Z and Gas6 all carry a glutamate-rich Gla motif near their amino termini; the ER enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase adds carboxyl groups to these residues using reduced vitamin K, after which the propeptide is removed by furin as the protein traverses the Golgi. Only the carboxylated form docks onto phospholipid surfaces at a site of vascular injury, so loss of this processing abolishes both coagulation and its anticoagulant braking arm — the basis of warfarin action and of vitamin K deficiency bleeding. The same chemistry matures osteocalcin, linking the pathway to bone mineralization and Gas6-driven cell survival signalling.

Several secreted proteins acquire calcium-binding ability only after a vitamin K-dependent modification made as they transit the secretory pathway. Gamma-carboxylation converts glutamate residues in an amino-terminal Gla motif into gamma-carboxyglutamate, which lets the mature protein bind calcium and dock onto membrane phospholipid surfaces; removal of the propeptide by a furin-type protease in the Golgi completes maturation. Most of the substrates run the coagulation cascade and its brakes — prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X, together with the anticoagulant proteins C, S and Z — so loss of the carboxylase or of its vitamin K cofactor produces bleeding disorders, and this chemistry is the target of warfarin-class anticoagulants. Other clients extend the theme beyond haemostasis: osteocalcin in bone mineralization and Gas6 in receptor tyrosine kinase signalling and apoptotic cell clearance.

IRF3 mediated activation of type 1 IFN is the terminal step by which cells that have detected foreign DNA in their cytosol switch on interferon-beta and related type I interferon genes, arming neighbouring cells with an antiviral state and shaping the ensuing adaptive response. The cytosolic DNA sensor ZBP1/DAI recruits the kinase TBK1 together with IRF3 to its C-terminal region, where IRF3 is phosphorylated, dimerises and enters the nucleus to transactivate interferon promoters; IRF7 contributes secondarily in this branch. The pathway is held in check by negative regulation of TBK1 itself, with NLRP4 delivering the E3 ligase DTX4 to target TBK1 for degradation, so that interferon output is transient. Loss of restraint here drives interferonopathy and autoimmunity, while loss of signalling leaves cells vulnerable to DNA virus infection.

Detection of cytosolic DNA from viruses or damaged cells culminates in IRF3-mediated induction of type I interferon, the transcriptional response that arms neighbouring cells against infection before adaptive immunity engages. The DNA sensor ZBP1/DAI recruits the kinase TBK1 together with IRF3 to its C-terminal region, and TBK1 phosphorylates IRF3 so that it dimerises, enters the nucleus and drives IFN-beta and IFN-alpha4 transcription; IRF7 contributes only partially in this branch. Because sustained interferon output is damaging, the response is restrained by negative regulation of TBK1 itself: NLRP4 recruits the E3 ubiquitin ligase DTX4 to mark TBK1 for degradative ubiquitination, terminating signalling. The balance between these arms determines antiviral competence on one side and, when regulation fails, interferon-driven autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease on the other.

Reverse Transcription of HIV RNA converts the single-stranded RNA genome delivered by an incoming HIV-1 particle into double-stranded DNA, the obligatory step that allows the virus to integrate into a host chromosome and establish lifelong infection; it is the target of the nucleoside and non-nucleoside inhibitors that form the backbone of antiretroviral therapy. In the cytosol of the newly infected cell, the viral reverse transcriptase heterodimer, whose active subunit carries both a primer-dependent DNA polymerase and an RNase H domain, copies the genome from a tRNA primer, degrades the RNA of the resulting hybrids, and performs two template switches so that long terminal repeats are duplicated at both ends of the product. The host contribution here is cyclophilin A, a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase recruited by the capsid that shapes core uncoating and the fidelity and timing of DNA synthesis.

Conversion of the HIV-1 RNA genome into double-stranded DNA is the step that commits a newly infected cell to harbouring a provirus, and it is the target of the largest class of antiretroviral drugs. In the cytosol of the new host cell, the viral reverse transcriptase heterodimer copies genomic RNA into a minus-strand DNA using a host tRNA primer, degrades the RNA of the resulting RNA:DNA hybrids through its RNase H activity, and completes a plus strand, with two template-switching events that duplicate the long terminal repeats at both ends of the product. The linear duplex is then available for integration into host chromatin. Host factors participate as well: the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase cyclophilin A binds incoming capsid, influencing uncoating and the efficiency of early reverse transcription, and links this stage to innate sensing of the viral core.

Synthesis of dolichyl-phosphate mannose generates the lipid-linked mannose donor that all mannose-transfer reactions in the endoplasmic reticulum depend on. Without it, cells cannot build the dolichol-pyrophosphate oligosaccharide used for N-linked glycosylation, cannot complete the glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor that tethers a large class of surface proteins, and cannot O-mannosylate alpha-dystroglycan or C-mannosylate thrombospondin repeats; loss-of-function mutations cause congenital disorders of glycosylation with muscular dystrophy-like features. Cytosolic GDP-mannose is transferred onto dolichyl phosphate at the cytosolic face of the ER membrane, after which the product flips so its mannose faces the lumen and becomes available to the glycosyltransferases there. The reaction is carried out by a three-subunit ER membrane complex in which DPM1 is the catalytic mannosyltransferase and DPM2 and DPM3 anchor and stabilise it, coupling substrate supply to membrane localisation.

Most mannose that ends up on secreted and membrane proteins arrives through a single lipid-linked donor, dolichyl-phosphate mannose, and this two-step route is how that donor is made. It feeds the lipid-linked oligosaccharide used for N-linked glycosylation, the GPI anchor precursor, and protein O- and C-mannosylation, so its output is required for essentially all glycoprotein traffic through the secretory pathway. A mannosyltransferase transfers mannose from cytosolic GDP-mannose onto dolichyl phosphate at the cytosolic face of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane; the product then flips so the sugar faces the lumen, where downstream transferases can use it. DPM1 is the catalytic subunit and DPM2 and DPM3 are membrane subunits that stabilise and localise the complex. Loss of any of the three causes congenital disorders of glycosylation with muscular dystrophy and neurological involvement, reflecting undermannosylated alpha-dystroglycan.

Macroautophagy is the bulk self-digestion route by which a cell encloses cytoplasm, protein aggregates, damaged organelles or invading microbes in a double-membrane autophagosome and delivers it to lysosomes for degradation. It buffers starvation by recycling amino acids and lipids, and also serves development, clearance of dying cells, antigen presentation and defence against toxins; its failure contributes to neurodegeneration, Crohn's disease and cancer. Nutrient and energy status is read by mTORC1 on lysosomes, through Rag GTPases, RHEB and the TSC complex, opposed by AMPK, which together set the activity of the ULK1-ATG13-RB1CC1 initiation complex. PIK3C3 with BECN1 and ATG14 makes PI3P that WIPI proteins sense, and two ubiquitin-like conjugation cascades, ATG12-ATG5-ATG16L1 and lipidated LC3/GABARAP, build and mark the growing phagophore. Cargo receptors such as SQSTM1, NBR1 and OPTN, PINK1-PRKN-driven mitophagy, dynein-microtubule transport and ESCRT-mediated closure complete the route.

Macroautophagy is the bulk self-digestion route by which a cell sequesters cytoplasm, organelles, protein aggregates and intracellular microbes into a double-membraned autophagosome and delivers them to lysosomes for breakdown, recycling amino acids and lipids during starvation and clearing damaged components at all times. Loss of this capacity underlies neurodegeneration from accumulated aggregates, contributes to Crohn's disease and to cancer, and impairs development and immune presentation. Nutrient and energy status is read by mTORC1 on lysosomes, with Rag GTPases, Ragulator and the TSC1/TSC2-Rheb module opposing AMPK to set the activity of the ULK1-ATG13-RB1CC1-ATG101 initiation complex. PI3P made by the PIK3C3-BECN1 complex recruits WIPI proteins, and two ubiquitin-like conjugation cascades (ATG12-ATG5-ATG16L1, then ATG7/ATG3 lipidating LC3 and GABARAP proteins, reversed by ATG4) build and mark the growing phagophore. Cargo receptors such as SQSTM1, NBR1 and OPTN link ubiquitinated substrates to LC3, notably in PINK1/parkin-driven mitophagy, while dynein and microtubules move autophagosomes and ESCRT subunits assist membrane closure and fusion.

Mitochondrial transcription termination sets the boundary of the ribosomal RNA transcription unit in mitochondrial DNA, and in doing so determines how much rRNA a cell makes relative to the mRNAs encoding respiratory chain subunits. Mitochondria must build their own ribosomes in vast excess over individual messages, and the imbalance is achieved partly by stopping transcription just past the 16S rRNA gene rather than letting polymerase continue along the heavy strand. MTERF1 accomplishes this by binding a short sequence within the tRNA-Leu(UUR) gene immediately downstream of 16S rRNA, blocking read-through from the upstream ribosomal promoter. Termination therefore acts together with initiation site selection to control stoichiometry of mitochondrial gene expression, upstream of oxidative phosphorylation capacity; the same tRNA-Leu region is the site of mutations associated with mitochondrial encephalomyopathy.

Mitochondrial DNA is transcribed as long polycistronic units, and the heavy strand carries two overlapping ones: a short unit covering the two rRNA genes and flanking tRNAs, and a longer one spanning nearly the whole strand. Because ribosomes must be built in far greater numbers than any single respiratory chain subunit, the rRNA unit is transcribed much more heavily, and that imbalance is set in part by where transcription stops. MTERF1 provides the stop signal: it binds a short sequence within the tRNA-Leu(UUR) gene just past the 16S rRNA gene and terminates the ribosomal unit there, so most polymerase molecules are released before entering the downstream protein-coding genes. Control of termination therefore shapes the stoichiometry between mitochondrial ribosome components and the mRNAs encoding oxidative phosphorylation subunits, linking this step to mitochondrial gene expression and respiratory capacity.

Cell Cycle is the ordered program by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, the basis of all tissue growth, renewal and, in germ cells, gamete production. Progression is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases whose partners oscillate in abundance, opposed by CDK inhibitors, the RB-E2F transcriptional switch, and phosphatases such as PP2A, with irreversibility imposed by ubiquitin ligases including the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF feeding the proteasome. Origin licensing by ORC/MCM and replisome assembly execute S phase; centrosomes, gamma-tubulin nucleated spindles, kinetochores, cohesin and condensin execute mitosis, monitored by the spindle assembly checkpoint and by ATM/ATR-CHEK damage checkpoints. Also included are nuclear envelope breakdown and reformation, telomere maintenance by telomerase, centromeric chromatin assembly, and meiotic recombination and synapsis. Loss of these controls yields aneuploidy, genomic instability and cancer.

Cell division requires that the genome be copied exactly once and then split evenly between two daughters, and the cell cycle is the ordered programme that enforces this. Oscillating cyclin-CDK activity drives the transitions: cyclin D- and E-associated kinases inactivate RB to release E2F-dependent transcription at the G1/S boundary, origin licensing and firing proceed through ORC, CDC6, CDT1 and the MCM helicase with the replicative polymerases, and mitotic CDK1-cyclin B with Aurora and Polo kinases builds the spindle, kinetochores and condensed chromosomes. Counter-regulation comes from CDC25 phosphatases, WEE1, PP2A holoenzymes, CDK inhibitors such as p21 and p27, and ubiquitin-dependent destruction by the anaphase-promoting complex, SCF and the proteasome. Checkpoint kinases ATM, ATR, CHEK1 and CHEK2 halt progression when replication stalls or spindle attachment is faulty. Related activities include telomere maintenance, nuclear envelope and pore reassembly, cytokinetic abscission, and the meiotic recombination and synapsis machinery of germ cells. Loss of this control underlies aneuploidy and cancer.

PKA activation in glucagon signalling is the step that converts a hormonal signal of fasting into intracellular kinase activity, allowing the liver to raise blood glucose when it falls. Glucagon acting through its Gs-coupled receptor releases GNAS, which stimulates adenylate cyclase to make cAMP from ATP. Protein kinase A rests as an inactive tetramer of two catalytic and two regulatory subunits; cAMP binding to the regulatory subunits releases free catalytic monomers that phosphorylate targets driving glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenic gene expression via CREB, and suppression of glycolysis and lipogenesis. The multiple adenylate cyclase and regulatory subunit isoforms give tissue-specific tuning of signal strength and duration. Because this module is the general cAMP relay, it also transmits many other Gs-coupled hormone signals, and mutations in GNAS or the regulatory subunit PRKAR1A cause endocrine tumour syndromes.

When blood glucose falls, glucagon acts on hepatocytes to mobilise stored fuel, and this step is where the hormonal signal becomes an intracellular one. The stimulatory G protein alpha subunit encoded by GNAS switches on membrane adenylate cyclases, which convert ATP into cyclic AMP. Protein kinase A rests as a tetramer of two catalytic and two regulatory subunits; cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, the complex dissociates, and free catalytic monomers phosphorylate targets that drive glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenic gene expression and lipolysis. Several adenylate cyclase and regulatory subunit isoforms exist with distinct tissue distributions and cAMP sensitivities, tuning the amplitude of the response. Loss or gain of function in this cascade disturbs glucose homeostasis, and activating GNAS mutations or regulatory subunit loss cause endocrine tumour syndromes, underscoring that cAMP output must be held within narrow limits.

Nef mediated downregulation of MHC class I complex cell surface expression describes how HIV-1 hides infected cells from cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Class I molecules such as HLA-A, paired with beta-2 microglobulin, normally display viral peptides at the plasma membrane so that CD8 T cells can kill the infected cell; the viral accessory protein Nef prevents this display, and its loss leaves infected cells far more vulnerable to immune killing, making the pathway a determinant of viral persistence and of vaccine and immunotherapy strategy. Mechanistically Nef acts as a connector in the endosomal system, linking the short cytoplasmic tail of MHC class I to the sorting adaptor PACS1 and to clathrin adaptor protein complex 1 subunits, so that internalised class I is rerouted to the trans-Golgi network and endosomes rather than recycled to the surface. It is a hijacking of ordinary intracellular protein sorting for immune evasion.

HIV-infected cells survive cytotoxic T lymphocyte surveillance in part by stripping MHC class I from their surface, and the viral accessory protein Nef is what drives this immune evasion. Class I molecules, made up of an HLA heavy chain paired with beta-2 microglobulin, normally display cytosolic peptides for CD8 T cell inspection; removing them leaves infected cells without the signal that marks them for killing, while other ligands that would trigger NK cells are left comparatively untouched. Mechanistically, Nef bridges the cytoplasmic tail of the class I heavy chain to the sorting connector PACS1 and to the clathrin adaptor AP-1 complex, whose large, medium and small subunits are all represented here. Rather than being degraded at the cell surface, the receptor is rerouted from the trans-Golgi and endosomes away from the plasma membrane, so newly synthesised molecules never reach it.

Nef and signal transduction describes how the HIV-1 accessory protein Nef rewires host T cell and macrophage signalling to make infected cells better hosts for the virus.
