This matters because Nef-mediated signalling raises T cell activation and cytokine output, recruits resting T cells to sites of infection, and contributes to the pathogenicity that distinguishes Nef-competent virus in vivo. Myristoylated Nef partitions into cholesterol-rich membrane microdomains where signalling mediators concentrate, and its proline-rich motif engages SH3 domains of Src-family kinases such as LCK, FYN and the myeloid kinase HCK. Through a DOCK2-ELMO1 guanine nucleotide exchange module it activates RAC1, and it assembles a complex that activates PAK2, feeding into actin remodelling and TCR-proximal signalling downstream of the CD247 chain. The result is altered activation thresholds, chemokine secretion and enhanced viral replication rather than a normal antigen response.

HIV-1 Nef rewires host signal transduction to make infected cells more permissive and to recruit new targets for infection. Anchored in cholesterol-rich membrane microdomains by N-terminal myristoylation and engaging SH3 domains through its proline-rich motif, Nef captures Src-family kinases such as Lck, Fyn and the myeloid kinase Hck, positioning itself at the T cell receptor complex where the CD3 zeta chain (CD247) initiates activation signalling. It also forms a complex with the serine/threonine kinase PAK2, acting through the Rac1 GTPase and its DOCK2-ELMO1 exchange machinery to remodel the actin cytoskeleton and lower the threshold for cell activation, with enhanced interleukin-2 output during T cell stimulation. In macrophages the same accessory protein co-opts CD40 ligand signalling to release chemokines that draw resting T cells into contact and infection, linking viral pathogenesis to normal lymphocyte activation and migration control.

MTOR signalling is the cell's central decision point for growth: it reads nutrient abundance, energy charge and growth factor input, and sets the balance between anabolic programmes such as protein synthesis and catabolic ones such as autophagy. Its dysregulation underlies cancer, obesity-related metabolic disease and diabetes, and the tuberous sclerosis genes TSC1 and TSC2 act here as brakes on the pathway. Amino acid sufficiency is sensed at the lysosome, where the Rag GTPases, the Ragulator complex and the transporter SLC38A9 recruit mTORC1 for activation by RHEB; energy stress acts oppositely through the LKB1-STRAD-CAB39 module and AMPK. Activated mTORC1 phosphorylates S6 kinase and 4E-BP1 to license cap-dependent translation, while AKT relays growth factor signals and feeds back on the complex. Rapamycin binding via FKBP1A inhibits this arm selectively.

mTOR signalling is how a cell decides whether conditions are good enough to grow. The mTOR kinase sits in two complexes: mTORC1, with RPTOR and MLST8, integrates amino acid availability, energy charge and growth factor input to drive protein synthesis and suppress autophagy, while a RICTOR-containing complex responds to growth factors. Amino acids act through the lysosomal Ragulator-Rag GTPase platform and the transporter-like sensor SLC38A9 to recruit mTORC1 to the lysosome, where RHEB activates it; the TSC1-TSC2 complex opposes this as a GTPase-activating protein for RHEB, and AMPK, activated by the LKB1-STRADA-CAB39 module under low energy, brakes growth. Outputs include S6K1 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation, releasing eIF4E for cap-dependent translation, plus effects on elongation via eEF2 kinase and on miRNA silencing machinery. Dysregulation underlies tumour growth, insulin resistance and hamartoma syndromes, and rapamycin selectively blocks mTORC1.

Toll Like Receptor 4 (TLR4) Cascade is the innate immune sensing route for bacterial lipopolysaccharide, the pathway that lets macrophages, dendritic cells and endothelium detect Gram-negative infection and mount inflammation; its overactivation produces the cytokine storm, coagulopathy and organ failure of septic shock. LPS is delivered to TLR4 with the help of LBP, CD14 and MD-2, and the receptor then uses two adapter arms. At the plasma membrane TIRAP and MyD88 recruit IRAK4/IRAK1, TRAF6 and the TAK1-IKK axis, driving NF-kB and MAPK/AP-1 output and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IL-6. After dynamin-dependent endocytosis, TRAM and TRIF engage TBK1/IKKe and IRF3 for type I interferon and delayed NF-kB activation. Endogenous ligands including HMGB1 and S100 proteins feed the same circuit in sterile inflammation, while SIGIRR, IRAK3, SOCS1 and ubiquitin-editing enzymes restrain it. Output also includes co-stimulatory molecules that shape adaptive immunity.

Detection of bacterial lipopolysaccharide by innate immune cells runs through the TLR4 cascade, the signalling route that converts contact with Gram-negative outer membrane into inflammation, fever and, when unrestrained, septic shock with disseminated coagulation and organ failure. LPS is delivered to the receptor by LBP, CD14 and the co-receptor MD-2 (LY96), after which TLR4 uniquely engages two adapter arms: TIRAP with MyD88 at the plasma membrane, recruiting IRAK4/IRAK1 and TRAF6 to drive IKK-dependent NF-kB activation and MAP kinase output through TAK1, p38, JNK and ERK toward AP-1 and CREB target genes; and, after dynamin-dependent endocytosis, TRAM with TRIF, which signals via TBK1/IKKe and IRF3 to induce type I interferons and a delayed NF-kB response. Endogenous ligands such as HMGB1, S100 proteins and serum amyloid A feed the same circuit in sterile inflammation, while SIGIRR, IRAK3, SOCS1, A20-binding proteins and phosphatases restrain it. Ubiquitin conjugation and SCF-mediated IkB degradation set the timing throughout.

PIPs transport between Golgi and plasma membranes describes the vesicular delivery of phosphoinositide-rich membrane from the trans-Golgi network to the cell surface, a route that sets the lipid identity of each compartment. Phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate generated on Golgi membranes by PI4-kinases recruits lipid transfer and coat proteins, drives cargo sorting into secretory carriers, and is then carried with those carriers to the plasma membrane, where it is converted onward to PI(4,5)P2. That surface pool underlies exocytosis, endocytic vesicle formation, actin attachment to the membrane, and signalling through phospholipase C and PI3-kinase. Because organelle-specific phosphoinositide gradients tell peripheral proteins where they are, disrupting this flow blurs the boundary between Golgi and plasma membrane and impairs constitutive secretion and receptor signalling. The pathway sits at the intersection of lipid metabolism and membrane traffic.

Phosphoinositides mark organelle membranes with a lipid identity code, and the movement of these species between the Golgi and the plasma membrane keeps that code aligned with vesicular traffic. Secretory carriers budding from the trans-Golgi network carry phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate with them to the cell surface, so the same lipid that recruits clathrin adaptors and lipid-transfer proteins at the Golgi becomes a substrate pool at the plasma membrane, where further phosphorylation yields PI(4,5)P2. That surface pool governs endocytosis, actin attachment to the membrane, ion channel gating and signalling through phospholipase C, while the Golgi pool governs cargo sorting and export. Because delivery and retrieval are balanced by kinases, phosphatases and membrane contact sites, disturbances in this traffic distort secretion and surface signalling rather than any single enzymatic step, linking lipid distribution directly to the organisation of the secretory pathway.

Mitochondrial Uncoupling describes how cells deliberately waste the proton gradient built by respiratory electron transport, dissipating it as heat instead of capturing it as ATP. This is the basis of adaptive thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue, which warms small mammals in the cold, protects newborns during the cold stress of birth, and drives arousal from hibernation; regulated leak also limits reactive oxygen species production and, in pancreatic beta cells, tempers insulin secretion. The carriers involved belong to the SLC25 mitochondrial transporter family, folded on the same six-helix architecture as the adenine nucleotide translocase, which itself conducts protons. UCP1 leak is held off by purine nucleotides and released by fatty acids mobilised after adrenergic stimulation, most plausibly through a fatty-acid cycling mechanism. A separate route works through the secreted enzyme PM20D1, which makes and breaks N-acyl amino acids such as oleoyl-phenylalanine that uncouple mitochondria without UCPs.

Not all of the proton gradient made by respiratory electron transport is spent on ATP synthesis; mitochondrial uncoupling deliberately leaks protons back into the matrix so that substrate oxidation continues while the energy is released as heat. This is the basis of adaptive non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue, which warms small mammals in the cold, supports newborns through the cold stress of birth, and rouses hibernators. UCP1 is the dominant carrier there, one of a family of inner-membrane transporters that includes UCP2, UCP3, the brain and kidney carriers SLC25A14 and SLC25A27, and the adenine nucleotide translocase SLC25A4, which itself conducts protons. UCP1 conductance is held down by purine nucleotides and released by fatty acids mobilised after adrenergic stimulation, most likely through fatty acid cycling. A secreted enzyme, PM20D1, makes N-acyl amino acids such as oleoyl-phenylalanine that uncouple independently of UCPs. Controlled leak also lowers reactive oxygen species output and modulates beta-cell insulin secretion, linking this biology to energy balance and oxidative stress.

Lectin pathway of complement activation is one of the three routes into the complement cascade, and the one that lets innate immunity recognise microbes directly by their sugar coats rather than by antibody. It provides antibody-independent opsonisation and lysis of bacteria, fungi and altered host cells, and contributes to clearance of apoptotic debris; deficiency of mannose-binding lectin or MASP2 predisposes to recurrent pyogenic infection in infancy, while excessive activation drives ischaemia-reperfusion and ischaemic tissue injury. Calcium-dependent collagenous lectins – MBL, the ficolins, and the CL-K1/CL-L1 heterocomplex – oligomerise and bind repetitive carbohydrate and acetylated patterns on target surfaces, triggering conformational activation of associated MASP proteases. MASP2 then cleaves C4 and C2 to build the C4b:C2a C3 convertase, converging on the same downstream cascade as the classical pathway. MASP1 amplifies this and also cross-talks with coagulation by acting on fibrinogen and factor XIII.

Innate immune recognition of carbohydrate patterns on microbes and dying cells triggers the lectin pathway of complement activation, one of three routes into the complement cascade and a first line of antibody-independent defence. Calcium-dependent recognition molecules — mannose-binding lectin, the ficolins FCN1, FCN2 and FCN3, and the collectin heterocomplex of COLEC10 and COLEC11 — circulate as oligomers bound to MBL-associated serine proteases. Binding to sugar arrays on a target surface rearranges the complex so that MASP1 and MASP2 become active; MASP2 then cleaves C4 and C2 to build the C3 convertase that deposits opsonins, recruits phagocytes and drives lytic pore formation. MASP1 additionally activates MASP2 and cross-talks with coagulation by acting on fibrinogen and factor XIII. Deficiency of MBL2 or MASP2 predisposes to recurrent respiratory infection in childhood, while COLEC10 and COLEC11 loss causes the developmental 3MC syndrome.

RNA Pol II CTD phosphorylation and interaction with CE during HIV infection describes the earliest committed step of transcript maturation on the integrated HIV provirus: marking the polymerase so that the nascent viral RNA is capped. Because the host machinery transcribes the provirus, viral messages depend entirely on this step for stability, nuclear export and translation, and its loss aborts viral gene expression. Shortly after initiation, the TFIIH-associated kinase CDK7 with its cyclin H and MNAT1 partners phosphorylates Serine 5 of the heptad repeats on the POLR2A C-terminal domain. The capping enzyme guanylyltransferase RNGTT and the cap methyltransferase RNMT dock on this phosphorylated tail, which also stimulates guanylyltransferase activity, coupling capping to elongation alongside the DSIF subunit SUPT5H. The arrangement restricts cap addition to polymerase II products and links promoter clearance to co-transcriptional RNA processing.

Newly initiated RNA polymerase II transcripts are capped while still being made, and this step links the polymerase to the capping enzymes during transcription of the integrated HIV provirus. Capping protects the nascent 5' end from exonucleases and marks the transcript for export and translation, so viral mRNAs depend on it as host mRNAs do. The mechanism runs through the heptapeptide repeats of the largest polymerase subunit: the TFIIH-associated kinase CDK7, with its cyclin H and MNAT1 partners, phosphorylates serine 5 of the C-terminal domain near the promoter, and the phosphorylated tail is bound directly by the guanylyltransferase and the cap methyltransferase, which stimulates guanylyl transfer. The elongation factor SPT5 contributes to coupling capping with early elongation. This phosphorylation mark is the timing signal that restricts capping to polymerase II products.

Transcription of the HIV genome is the step at which an integrated HIV-1 provirus becomes a productive infection: the virus has no polymerase of its own for this job and borrows the host RNA polymerase II machinery to copy its genome into mRNAs and into the RNA packaged by new virions. Blocking or failing to activate it is what distinguishes latent, therapy-resistant reservoirs from replicating virus. Initiation depends on cellular factors recruited to the 5' LTR, with TBP and the TAF-containing general machinery, TFIIH and its CDK7 kinase positioning polymerase at the promoter. The rate-limiting control is elongation: NELF and DSIF pause the polymerase shortly after initiation, and the viral Tat protein binds the nascent TAR stem-loop to deliver P-TEFb (CCNT1-CDK9), which phosphorylates SPT5 and the polymerase tail to license processive elongation, capping, and co-transcriptional splicing.

An integrated HIV-1 provirus is transcribed by the host's own RNA polymerase II machinery, so viral gene expression is essentially a hijacking of cellular transcription, and the balance between silence and activity at the viral promoter determines whether an infected cell stays latent or produces virus. Sequences in the 5' long terminal repeat recruit TBP and the TAF-containing general factors, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and the TFIIH helicase-kinase module, which positions polymerase and phosphorylates its C-terminal domain. Polymerase then pauses just downstream, held by NELF and DSIF; escape into productive elongation requires the viral Tat protein binding the nascent TAR stem-loop and recruiting P-TEFb (CDK9 with cyclin T1). Capping enzymes, the nuclear cap-binding complex, elongin and ELL elongation factors, and the FACT histone chaperone complete the cycle, yielding transcripts that serve as mRNA and as packaged genomic RNA.

Tat-mediated elongation of the HIV-1 transcript explains how HIV-1 converts a stalled polymerase at its own promoter into a productive one, and it is the step that determines whether an integrated provirus stays latent or produces virus. RNA polymerase II can initiate at the viral LTR without help, but DSIF and NELF arrest it after a few dozen nucleotides, yielding only abortive short transcripts. The viral transactivator Tat binds the TAR stem-loop in the nascent leader RNA and tethers P-TEFb (cyclin T1 with CDK9), which hyperphosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain and the SPT5 and RD subunits of the pausing factors, releasing NELF from TAR and licensing processive elongation together with elongin, ELL, FACT and capping factors. Because this switch controls proviral output, it is the mechanistic basis of latency reversal strategies and of CDK9-directed antiviral approaches.

HIV-1 cannot make full-length viral RNA on its own: polymerases that initiate at the proviral promoter stall soon after and release short abortive transcripts, so the virus depends on its Tat transactivator to convert them into processive elongation complexes. This step sets the switch between latency and productive replication, and blocking it is the rationale behind CDK9-directed antiviral strategies. Tat binds the TAR stem-loop in the nascent leader RNA and tethers the P-TEFb kinase, cyclin T1 with CDK9, to the paused polymerase. CDK9 hyperphosphorylates the RNA polymerase II carboxy-terminal domain and also modifies the SPT5 subunit of DSIF and the RD subunit of NELF, relieving their negative effect on elongation. The remaining machinery here is the host's own: the general initiation and TFIIH kinase components, elongation factors such as ELL and the elongin complex, FACT histone chaperones, and the nuclear cap-binding proteins.

Nef Mediated CD4 Down-regulation describes how the HIV-1 accessory protein Nef strips its own entry receptor from the surface of an infected cell. Removing CD4 prevents newly made Env from being captured by receptor on the producer cell, so virions are released efficiently and remain infectious, and it simultaneously blunts helper T cell signalling and superinfection. CD4 carries a dileucine-based internalization signal that is normally masked by bound Lck; Nef displaces the kinase, exposes the motif, and links CD4 to the AP-2 clathrin adaptor complex, whose alpha, beta, mu and sigma subunits together with an ARF1- and V-ATPase-associated step drive endocytosis. Internalized receptor is then routed away from recycling toward lysosomal degradation, with COPI coatomer implicated in the final sorting. The pathway is a textbook case of a viral protein hijacking clathrin-mediated endocytosis and receptor trafficking for immune evasion.

HIV-1 Nef strips CD4 from the surface of infected cells, and this down-regulation serves the virus: without CD4 on the plasma membrane the receptor cannot engage newly made Env on budding particles, so virions are released more efficiently and are more infectious, and the cell is also protected from superinfection. CD4 carries its own internalization signal in its cytoplasmic tail, but that signal is masked while the tail is bound by the Src-family kinase Lck; Nef displaces this interaction and links CD4 to the clathrin adaptor AP-2 complex, whose alpha, beta, mu and sigma subunits drive endocytosis. Internalized CD4 is then routed onward, with ARF1-dependent coat recruitment and vacuolar ATPase-dependent acidification contributing to delivery into the lysosomal degradation route. The same trafficking machinery normally handles receptor turnover, and immune evasion here is a hijacking of it.

Trafficking and processing of endosomal TLR governs how the nucleic acid-sensing Toll-like receptors TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 reach the compartment where they can work, and why they respond to viral and bacterial DNA and RNA rather than to the cell's own. Restricting these receptors to acidified endolysosomes, and requiring an irreversible activation step there, is the main safeguard against autoreactive interferon responses; loss of that control underlies lupus-like autoimmunity, while loss of the trafficking machinery itself causes susceptibility to herpes encephalitis and pyogenic infection. Newly made receptors are held in the endoplasmic reticulum with the chaperones gp96 and CNPY3, then escorted outward by the multipass membrane protein UNC93B1. In the endolysosome, cathepsins and asparagine endopeptidase cleave the TLR7 and TLR9 ectodomains, generating the fragment competent to bind ligand and signal to the cytosol.

Nucleic-acid-sensing Toll-like receptors TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 detect viral and bacterial RNA and DNA, but only after they have been delivered to acidified endolysosomes and, in some cases, trimmed by proteases. This trafficking and processing step is what keeps innate immune sensing pointed at pathogens rather than at the cell's own DNA and RNA: compartment restriction plus a requirement for proteolytic maturation means self nucleic acids released outside endosomes go unseen, and loss of that discipline contributes to lupus-like interferon-driven autoimmunity. Newly made receptors fold in the endoplasmic reticulum with the chaperones HSP90B1 and CNPY3, and UNC93B1 escorts them onward; in the endolysosome, cysteine cathepsins such as CTSB, CTSL and CTSS together with asparagine endopeptidase cleave the TLR7 and TLR9 ectodomains to yield signalling-competent receptors. Mutations in UNC93B1 abolish endosomal TLR responses and predispose to herpes encephalitis.

Toll Like Receptor 10 (TLR10) Cascade describes innate immune signalling through one of the least understood Toll-like receptors, expressed mainly on B cells and dendritic cells as a heavily N-glycosylated surface protein that homodimerizes and can pair with TLR1 and TLR2. Its ligands remain undefined, but engagement recruits the MyD88 adaptor and the shared downstream module used by most TLRs: IRAK kinases, Pellino ubiquitin ligases, TRAF6-directed polyubiquitin chains, and the TAK1-TAB complex, which branches into IKK-driven degradation of IkB inhibitors to release NF-kB, and into the p38, JNK and ERK cascades that activate AP-1, CREB, ELK1 and MEF2 transcription factors. The output is transcription of inflammatory cytokines and immune activation genes, tuned by DUSP phosphatases, PP2A and IkB-related brakes. Because TLR10 can restrain responses from other TLRs, it contributes to setting the threshold and resolution of inflammation rather than only amplifying it.

TLR10 is an innate immune receptor of the Toll-like family expressed in a restricted way, mainly on B cells and dendritic cells, whose ligands remain poorly defined; it homodimerizes and can pair with TLR1 and TLR2, and signals through the MyD88 adaptor. The downstream cascade described here is the shared MyD88-dependent route that converts receptor engagement into inflammatory gene expression: IRAK4, IRAK1/2 and Pellino ligases assemble with TRAF6 and the TAK1-TAB complex, K63-linked ubiquitin chains built by UBE2N/UBE2V1 relay the signal, and the IKK complex frees NF-kB from IkB while parallel MAP kinase branches activate p38, JNK, ERK and the AP-1, CREB, ELK1 and MEF2 transcription factors. DUSP phosphatases, PP2A subunits and deubiquitinases restrain the output. The result is cytokine production and antigen-presenting cell activation; TLR10 itself is generally regarded as a dampener of inflammatory TLR responses.

Toll Like Receptor 5 (TLR5) Cascade is the innate immune response to bacterial flagellin, the structural protein of flagella, and it lets gut epithelium, macrophages and dendritic cells detect motile bacteria that have breached the mucosal barrier. Because TLR5 sits only on the basolateral face of intestinal epithelial cells, the response is triggered by invading pathogens rather than by luminal commensals, and its loss shifts susceptibility to enteric infection and mucosal inflammation. Ligand binding recruits MyD88 and the IRAK1/IRAK4 kinases, with Pellino proteins and TRAF6-driven ubiquitin chains activating the TAK1 complex; this branches into IKK-mediated degradation of IkB and NF-kB nuclear entry, and into the p38, JNK and ERK modules that turn on AP-1, CREB, ELK1 and MEF2 to drive cytokine and chemokine transcription. Phosphatases, deubiquitinases and IkB-like inhibitors damp the output, keeping antibacterial signalling self-limiting.

TLR5 is the innate immune sensor for bacterial flagellin, the conserved building block of flagella, and its signalling cascade lets epithelium and myeloid cells raise an inflammatory alarm when motile bacteria breach a barrier. Because TLR5 sits on the basolateral face of intestinal epithelial cells, the response is triggered by invading pathogens rather than by luminal commensals, and variation in this route affects susceptibility to enteric infection and inflammatory bowel disease. Ligand binding recruits MYD88 and the IRAK kinases, which act through TRAF6-directed ubiquitin chains and the TAK1-TAB complex to split into two outputs: IKK-mediated phosphorylation and degradation of IkB, freeing NF-kB, and MAP kinase modules that drive JNK, p38 and ERK to activate AP-1, CREB and ELK1. Phosphatases, deubiquitinases and Pellino ligases shape the amplitude, keeping cytokine output proportionate and self-limiting.

Virus Assembly and Release is the final stage of the influenza replication cycle, in which newly made viral components converge at the apical plasma membrane of polarized airway epithelial cells and bud off as infectious particles. The directionality of this step matters clinically: apical release sends progeny virions into the airway lumen for transmission and spread along the respiratory tract, whereas basolateral budding used by other enveloped viruses favours systemic dissemination, so budding polarity helps set tissue tropism and pathogenesis. Envelope glycoproteins accumulate at the same polar surface from which particles emerge, effectively marking the maturation site. Before reaching it, hemagglutinin and neuraminidase must be folded and quality-controlled in the endoplasmic reticulum, and the lectin chaperones calreticulin and calnexin perform this glycoprotein-specific surveillance, linking host secretory-pathway folding machinery to the production of functional virions.

Influenza virions are built and released at the apical surface of polarized airway epithelial cells, and the site of budding helps set tissue tropism and pathogenesis: envelope glycoproteins accumulate at the same polar membrane from which particles pinch off, so the virus emerges into the airway lumen rather than into underlying tissue. Before that can happen, the viral membrane proteins must be folded and glycosylated correctly in the endoplasmic reticulum, and the lectin chaperones calnexin and calreticulin are the quality-control step that does it, binding monoglucosylated N-glycans on nascent glycoproteins and retaining them until they attain a transport-competent conformation. The host secretory pathway is therefore co-opted for assembly and release, with chaperone-assisted maturation determining how much functional hemagglutinin and neuraminidase reach the plasma membrane and thus the infectivity of progeny virions.

Influenza Viral RNA Transcription and Replication describes how influenza A virus copies its segmented negative-strand genome inside the host cell nucleus, the step that commits an infected cell to producing progeny virions and the target of polymerase inhibitors such as baloxavir. The viral polymerase subunits and nucleoprotein, imported through the nuclear pore, use genomic RNA as template both for capped, polyadenylated messenger RNAs and for full-length complementary RNA that seeds new genome copies; the balance shifts toward genome replication and export of ribonucleoprotein complexes late in infection. Because the virus cannot make its own caps or translate its own mRNAs, the pathway is built almost entirely from hijacked host machinery: RNA polymerase II and its associated factors provide capped primers, importins and the full nuclear pore complex handle traffic in and out of the nucleus, and the cytoplasmic ribosome translates the resulting transcripts.

Influenza A is a negative-strand RNA virus that, unusually, replicates in the host nucleus, and this pathway covers the synthesis of viral mRNA and the vRNA/cRNA replication intermediates that sustain infection. Because the virus encodes only a polymerase and nucleoprotein, it must borrow the cell wholesale: host RNA polymerase II supplies the capped nascent transcripts whose 5' ends are snatched to prime viral mRNA, and its largest subunit is degraded as a consequence, shutting down host transcription. Import of polymerase subunits and nucleoprotein and export of assembled ribonucleoproteins run through the nuclear pore complex and karyopherin-mediated transport, which is why nucleoporins and importins figure here, while the cytoplasmic ribosome translates the resulting viral messages. Chaperones such as HSP90 assist polymerase assembly. These dependencies are the basis of host-directed antiviral strategies and of interferon-driven restriction of viral gene expression.

NEP/NS2 Interacts with the Cellular Export Machinery describes how influenza virus gets its newly replicated genome out of the host nucleus, the step that allows progeny ribonucleoproteins to reach the plasma membrane and be packaged into virions. Influenza replicates its RNA in the nucleus, so nuclear egress is a hard requirement for the viral life cycle and a point at which the virus is entirely dependent on host machinery. The viral nuclear export protein acts as an adaptor, bridging the matrix protein M1 coating the ribonucleoprotein to the exportin XPO1/CRM1, which in turn engages RanGTP and the nucleoporins of the nuclear pore complex. The gene complement is essentially the pore itself — the Y-complex scaffold, the FG-repeat channel nucleoporins, the cytoplasmic filaments and basket, plus RAN and RAE1 — illustrating viral subversion of normal receptor-mediated nucleocytoplasmic transport.

Influenza virus replicates its genome in the host nucleus, so newly made viral ribonucleoprotein complexes must be exported to the cytoplasm before virions can assemble at the plasma membrane. The viral nuclear export protein NEP/NS2 makes this possible by acting as an adaptor: it binds the viral matrix protein M1 coating the vRNP and simultaneously engages the host export receptor CRM1/exportin-1 (XPO1), which recognises leucine-rich export signals and releases cargo in a RAN-GTP-dependent manner. The resulting complex then translocates through the nuclear pore, whose scaffold, transmembrane and FG-repeat nucleoporins, together with RANBP2, TPR and RAE1, form the permeability barrier and docking sites for receptor-cargo transit. This hijacking of a normal nucleocytoplasmic transport route is a step at which the viral life cycle can be blocked, and it illustrates how a small viral protein can redirect host machinery built for cellular RNA and protein export.

Alternative complement activation is the arm of complement that needs no antibody and no lectin to get started: it runs continuously at low level and amplifies wherever C3b lands on a surface that fails to protect itself. This makes it the immune system's default surveillance mechanism against bacteria and other foreign surfaces, and the reason host cells must actively display regulators; loss of that restraint drives haemolysis in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and renal injury in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and C3 glomerulopathy. Mechanistically, deposited C3b recruits factor B, which factor D cleaves to leave the Bb catalytic subunit as a surface-bound C3 convertase; properdin binds and stabilises this short-lived complex, and addition of a further C3b converts it into a C5 convertase that initiates the terminal lytic sequence. The loop is inherently self-amplifying, feeding back on classical and lectin activation alike.

The alternative complement pathway provides continuous, antibody-independent surveillance of surfaces, amplifying complement deposition on microbes and other targets that lack host regulatory proteins. It matters because it converts a low-level spontaneous reaction into rapid opsonisation and lytic attack, and because its dysregulation drives conditions such as atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, C3 glomerulopathy and age-related macular degeneration. Mechanistically it is a positive feedback loop centred on C3b: once C3b attaches covalently to surface sugars, factor B binds it and is cleaved by factor D into Ba and Bb, leaving the C3bBb complex as a C3 convertase. Properdin stabilises this otherwise short-lived enzyme on the target surface, and addition of a further C3b converts it into a C5 convertase that initiates membrane attack. Serine protease granzyme M is also assigned here, linking cytotoxic granule activity to this arm of innate humoral defence.

APC/C-mediated degradation of cell cycle proteins is the ubiquitin-dependent destruction programme that makes cell cycle transitions irreversible: it triggers sister chromatid separation, drives exit from mitosis, and keeps G1 free of mitotic regulators until a new round of replication is licensed. The anaphase-promoting complex is a multisubunit E3 ligase that, with E2 enzymes such as UBE2C and UBE2S, builds ubiquitin chains on substrates bearing destruction or KEN box motifs, marking them for the 26S proteasome. Securin degradation releases separase to cleave cohesin, while loss of cyclin B inactivates CDK1. Activity is timed by mitotic phosphorylation, by the exchange of the CDC20 and CDH1/FZR1 activators, by EMI1/FBXO5 inhibition, and by spindle checkpoint proteins including MAD2 and BUBR1 that sequester CDC20 until kinetochores are attached. Failure produces premature anaphase, aneuploidy and genomic instability characteristic of tumour cells.

Mitosis is irreversible because the proteins that drive it are destroyed rather than merely switched off, and APC/C-mediated degradation of cell cycle proteins is the ubiquitin ligase machinery that does the destroying. By targeting securin and the mitotic cyclins for proteasomal proteolysis, it permits separase to cleave cohesin so sister chromatids part, then lowers CDK1 activity so cells exit mitosis; continued activity through G1 keeps cyclins low until the next S phase commitment. The multisubunit core (ANAPC and CDC16/23/27 subunits) works with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S to build ubiquitin chains read by the 26S proteasome. Substrate choice is set by the exchangeable activators CDC20 and FZR1/Cdh1, which recognise destruction- and KEN-box motifs; mitotic kinases such as PLK1 and Aurora, the inhibitor EMI1/FBXO5, and spindle checkpoint proteins MAD2L1, BUB3 and BUB1B restrain activation until chromosomes are correctly attached. Loss of this timing produces aneuploidy.

Cdc20:Phospho-APC/C mediated degradation of Cyclin A removes cyclin A at the start of mitosis, an early and distinctive step in the ordered destruction of mitotic regulators that drives cells through division. Cyclin A partners CDK1 and CDK2 to drive S phase entry and mitotic commitment; its timely clearance is required for normal chromosome segregation and for resetting the licensing of the next replication cycle, and its stabilisation contributes to genomic instability in tumours. Mechanistically, mitotic phosphorylation of the anaphase-promoting complex allows Cdc20 to load and target cyclin A for polyubiquitination by UBE2C and UBE2S, followed by degradation in the 26S proteasome. Notably this happens while the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins BubR1, Bub3 and Mad2 still restrain the same ligase from destroying securin and cyclin B, making cyclin A a checkpoint-insensitive substrate and setting the sequence of mitotic exit events.

Cyclin A drives S-phase entry and early mitotic events, and must be removed before chromosomes can be segregated correctly; its timed destruction in early mitosis is what this route accomplishes. The anaphase-promoting complex, phosphorylated by mitotic kinase activity and loaded with its Cdc20 substrate adaptor, ubiquitinates cyclin A with the help of the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S, and the 26S proteasome degrades the polyubiquitinated cyclin. Notably this happens while the spindle assembly checkpoint is still engaged: checkpoint proteins such as BUBR1, BUB3 and MAD2 restrain the same ligase from destroying securin and cyclin B, so cyclin A turnover precedes anaphase. Failure to clear cyclin A leaves CDK1 activity inappropriately high, disturbing mitotic progression and the following replication cycle.

Assembly Of The HIV Virion is the late stage of the retroviral life cycle in which a new, infectious particle is built at the host plasma membrane, packaging two copies of genomic RNA, a host tRNA-Lys primer, the envelope glycoprotein, and the Gag and Gag-Pro-Pol polyproteins that carry protease, reverse transcriptase and integrase. Without it, infected cells produce no transmissible progeny, which is why this step is a drug target alongside entry and enzymatic inhibitors. The process is almost entirely dependent on borrowed host machinery: N-myristoyltransferase directs Gag to the membrane, cyclophilin A is recruited onto capsid to license later uncoating, furin matures Env, and ubiquitin together with the ESCRT-I complex of TSG101, VPS37 subunits, UBAP1 and MVB12 provides the membrane-scission activity normally used for multivesicular body formation, here hijacked to pinch off the budding virion.

Late in HIV replication, the virus gathers everything a new particle needs to be infectious: two copies of genomic RNA, a primer tRNA, the envelope glycoprotein, the Gag polyprotein and the Gag-Pro-Pol precursor carrying protease, reverse transcriptase and integrase. Assembly of the HIV virion is essentially a hijacking of host membrane and trafficking machinery at the plasma membrane. Gag is myristoylated by N-myristoyltransferase to anchor it to the inner leaflet, the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase cyclophilin A is recruited through the capsid domain and incorporated into particles, and the envelope precursor is matured by a cellular proprotein convertase of the furin family. Budding depends on the ESCRT-I complex, TSG101 with VPS28, VPS37 subunits, MVB12 and UBAP1, together with ubiquitin, normally used for sorting cargo into multivesicular bodies. Blocking these interactions traps immature particles at the cell surface, a recognised antiviral vulnerability.

Interactions of Vpr with host cellular proteins describes how the HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr subverts host machinery to help the virus replicate in non-dividing cells and to reshape the infected cell's fate. Its main partners here are the nuclear pore complex and nuclear import factors contributing to docking and translocation of the viral pre-integration complex through the nuclear envelope, alongside importin-alpha, the chromatin tethers BANF1, HMGA1 and PSIP1/LEDGF that accompany the incoming genome. A second arm engages the adenine nucleotide translocators of the inner mitochondrial membrane, promoting membrane permeabilization and release of apoptogenic factors. Vpr additionally arrests cells at the G2/M boundary by driving inhibitory Tyr15 phosphorylation of CDK1, a block that depends on PP2A and differs from the canonical DNA damage checkpoint. Together these activities link nucleocytoplasmic transport, cell cycle control and apoptosis to viral pathogenesis and CD4 T cell loss.

HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr is a small virion-packaged protein that rewires host machinery to favour infection, and the contacts it makes with cellular proteins explain three of its activities: nuclear delivery of the viral pre-integration complex, arrest of the host cell in G2/M, and induction of apoptosis. Most of the host partners here are components of the nuclear pore complex — the scaffold and linker nucleoporins, the FG-repeat channel proteins, the transmembrane ring, and the basket with TPR and NUP153 — together with an importin-alpha and chromatin-associated factors such as BANF1, HMGA1 and the integration cofactor PSIP1/LEDGF, consistent with docking of the incoming complex at the pore and transit into the nucleus. The adenine nucleotide translocases of the inner mitochondrial membrane provide a separate route, where Vpr binding promotes permeabilization and release of pro-apoptotic factors. Blocking mitotic entry via Cdk1 hyperphosphorylation prolongs a cell state favourable to viral gene expression.

Conjugation of salicylate with glycine is the main route by which the body disposes of aspirin. Once aspirin is hydrolysed to salicylate, this two-step mitochondrial pathway converts it to salicyluric acid, a water-soluble product cleared by the kidneys, and accounts for the majority of salicylate elimination. A medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetase family (ACSM2A/2B, ACSM4, ACSM5) first activates salicylate to its CoA thioester at the expense of ATP, and a glycine N-acyltransferase (GLYAT, with related GLYATL enzymes) then transfers the acyl group onto glycine, releasing free coenzyme A. Because the route has limited capacity, it saturates at high doses, which is why salicylate kinetics become dose-dependent and toxicity escalates in overdose. The same enzymes handle benzoate and other xenobiotic and medium-chain acids, linking drug detoxification to amino acid and mitochondrial acyl-CoA metabolism.

Aspirin is hydrolysed in the body to salicylate, and conjugation of salicylate with glycine is the main route by which that salicylate is disposed of, producing salicyluric acid for renal excretion and accounting for the majority of aspirin metabolites. Because the pathway saturates at higher doses, it sets the point at which salicylate elimination shifts from first-order to capacity-limited kinetics, contributing to toxicity in overdose. Two steps are required. Mitochondrial medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetases, including the ACSM2A/ACSM2B pair and related ACSM4 and ACSM5, use ATP to activate salicylate as its coenzyme A thioester, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate. Glycine N-acyltransferase then transfers the acyl group onto glycine, regenerating free CoA; the related GLYATL enzymes carry out analogous amino acid conjugations of other acyl-CoA substrates. The same chemistry detoxifies benzoate and endogenous acyl-CoAs, placing this arm of drug metabolism alongside glucuronidation and ring hydroxylation.

Conjugation of benzoate with glycine is the two-step detoxification route that turns benzoic acid, a common dietary and food-preservative compound, into hippuric acid for urinary excretion. It was among the first drug-metabolism pathways ever described, and because each molecule of hippurate carries away a nitrogen atom, sodium benzoate has been given therapeutically to drain ammonia in patients with urea cycle defects. Mitochondrial medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetases first activate benzoate to benzoyl-CoA at the expense of ATP; glycine N-acyltransferases then transfer the acyl group onto glycine, releasing the water-soluble conjugate. Related transferase family members handle other acyl acceptors and aromatic acids, linking this chemistry to bile acid and phenylacetate handling. The pathway sits within phase II xenobiotic conjugation and mitochondrial CoA-thioester metabolism, and it competes with glycine's other uses when substrate loads are high.

Benzoate, common in the diet and as a food preservative, is detoxified by conjugation with glycine to form hippuric acid, which is readily excreted in urine. This two-step route was among the first detoxification pathways ever described, and it was used clinically to drain nitrogen in patients with urea cycle defects, since each conjugate carries an amino group out of the body. Medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetases such as ACSM1 and ACSM2B first activate benzoate to benzoyl-CoA at the expense of ATP; mitochondrial glycine N-acyltransferase GLYAT then transfers the acyl group onto glycine, releasing free CoA. The related GLYATL enzymes handle other acyl donors and related amine acceptors, extending the same chemistry to bile acid and arylalkanoic conjugation. The pathway sits in hepatic and renal phase II metabolism, and its capacity limits tolerance of benzoate loads and ammonia-scavenging therapy.

SRP-dependent cotranslational protein targeting to membrane delivers newly made secretory and membrane proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being translated, and it is the entry point for the entire secretory pathway covering hormones, antibodies, receptors, and lysosomal enzymes. A hydrophobic signal sequence emerging from the ribosome is captured by the signal recognition particle, which pauses elongation and escorts the ribosome to the SRP receptor at the ER membrane; the ribosome is then handed to the SEC61 translocon, translation resumes, and the chain threads into the lumen, where signal peptidase and translocon-associated subunits complete processing and stabilise the nascent chain. Nearly the full complement of large and small ribosomal subunit proteins participates, reflecting that this is cytosolic translation redirected to a membrane. Defects impair secretion and provoke ER stress, and ribosomal protein loss causes ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

Secreted proteins, membrane proteins and the contents of the entire endomembrane system are made on ribosomes that dock at the endoplasmic reticulum, and this is the route by which they get there. Translation begins in the cytosol like any other, but once a hydrophobic signal sequence emerges from the ribosomal exit tunnel the signal recognition particle binds it, pauses elongation, and delivers the whole ribosome-mRNA-nascent chain complex to its receptor at the ER membrane. Handover to the Sec61 translocon channel reorients the growing peptide into the lumen, translocon-associated and translocating-chain accessory components stabilise the engaged ribosome, and signal peptidase subunits clip the signal sequence so elongation can finish inside the ER. The large complement of cytosolic ribosomal subunits reflects that the translating ribosome itself is part of the machinery. Loss of this targeting step strands secretory cargo in the cytosol, blocking glycosylation, disulfide bonding and onward traffic.

Vpr-mediated nuclear import of PICs describes how HIV-1 delivers its reverse-transcribed genome across the nuclear envelope, the step that allows the virus to integrate and establish infection in non-dividing cells such as macrophages that never disassemble their nuclear membrane. The accessory protein Vpr docks the pre-integration complex at the nuclear pore, apparently by binding nucleoporins directly, while importin-alpha and the host chromatin factors BANF1, HMGA1 and the tethering protein PSIP1 (LEDGF) contribute to complex stability and eventual targeting to chromatin. The gene complement is essentially the whole nuclear pore complex — the Y-shaped NUP107–160 scaffold, the central FG-repeat channel nucleoporins, the transmembrane ring, and the cytoplasmic and nuclear basket filaments RANBP2 and TPR — illustrating how a virus subverts constitutive nucleocytoplasmic transport for its own replication cycle.

HIV-1 must deliver its reverse-transcribed genome into the nucleus of a non-dividing cell, and the accessory protein Vpr contributes to that step by docking the pre-integration complex at the nuclear envelope so that its cargo can cross into the nucleoplasm. This is what allows the virus to infect terminally differentiated macrophages and resting T cells, where no mitotic breakdown of the nuclear envelope is available, and it sets up the integration that makes infection permanent. The host contribution here is essentially the whole nuclear pore complex: the structural Y-complex scaffold, transmembrane and channel nucleoporins, and the peripheral filaments RANBP2 and TPR that Vpr and importin alpha engage. Other host factors in the complex include the lens epithelium-derived growth factor PSIP1, which tethers integrase to chromatin, together with BANF1 and HMGA1.

Nef Mediated CD8 Down-regulation is one of the immune-evasion tricks by which HIV rewires host membrane traffic: the viral accessory protein Nef strips the CD8 beta-chain from the surface of infected cells, blunting the cytotoxic T lymphocyte responses that would otherwise clear them. Nef is a membrane-associated adaptor that also removes CD4, CD28 and MHC class I, and here it links the cytoplasmic tail of CD8 beta, through an FMK motif, to the clathrin adaptor complex AP-2 assembled from its alpha, beta, mu and sigma subunits, together with a V-ATPase subunit that assists Nef-dependent sorting. The receptor is thereby routed into accelerated clathrin-mediated endocytosis, while the alpha-chain is spared. The same Nef determinants required for CD4 removal are needed here, and the activity is conserved across HIV-1, HIV-2 and SIV, connecting receptor internalisation to persistence of infection.

HIV-1 uses its accessory protein Nef to strip immune recognition molecules from the surface of infected cells, and one target is the beta chain of the CD8 alpha-beta receptor on cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Loss of surface CD8 beta blunts the co-receptor function that lets killer T cells engage peptide-MHC class I efficiently, contributing, alongside Nef-driven removal of CD4 and MHC class I, to viral escape from cell-mediated immunity. Mechanistically Nef acts as a connector to the clathrin adaptor AP-2 complex, whose alpha, beta, mu and sigma subunits are all represented here, accelerating endocytosis of CD8 beta through a short cytoplasmic FMK motif; a subunit of the vacuolar ATPase participates in the trafficking step. The same Nef determinants required for CD4 removal are needed here, and the activity is conserved across HIV-1, HIV-2 and SIV.

Signaling by cytosolic FGFR1 fusion mutants describes the oncogenic signalling that drives 8p11 myeloproliferative syndrome, an aggressive stem-cell disorder presenting with eosinophilia and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma that progresses rapidly to acute myeloid leukaemia and is currently curable only by allogeneic transplantation. Chromosomal translocations at 8p11 fuse the FGFR1 intracellular kinase domain to N-terminal partners such as ZMYM2, BCR, CUX1, CPSF6, TRIM24, LRRFIP1 or centrosomal proteins, each contributing a dimerization module. The resulting cytosolic kinase dimerizes without ligand and fires constitutively, so growth factor control is lost entirely. Because the fusions lack the membrane anchor and the FRS2 docking site, output is skewed toward PI3K and JAK-STAT arms, with STAT1, STAT3 and STAT5 activation and GRB2:GAB2 recruitment sustaining anti-apoptotic, prosurvival signalling and rendering haematopoietic progenitors independent of IL3. This is a paradigm for receptor tyrosine kinase fusion-driven leukaemogenesis.

Chromosomal translocations at 8p11 fuse the intracellular kinase domain of FGFR1 to N-terminal partners that supply a dimerization module, producing cytosolic fusion kinases that signal without ligand and drive the aggressive 8p11 myeloproliferative syndrome, which presents with eosinophilia and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma and progresses rapidly to acute myeloid leukemia. Because the fusion lacks the receptor's transmembrane and extracellular regions, it sits in the cytoplasm and is constitutively dimerized by its partner, among them ZMYM2, BCR, CUX1, TRIM24, CPSF6, LRRFIP1 and centrosomal proteins. Downstream output favours phospholipase C-gamma, PI3K through its catalytic and regulatory subunits, and STAT family transcription factors including STAT1, STAT3 and STAT5, with GRB2 and GAB2 adaptors contributing weaker MAPK activation. The net effect is cytokine-independent, anti-apoptotic proliferation of haematopoietic progenitors, illustrating how loss of ligand control over a receptor kinase becomes leukaemogenic.

Synthesis of pyrophosphates in the cytosol builds the most highly phosphorylated inositol messengers, the diphosphoinositol polyphosphates IP7 and IP8, from IP5 and IP6. These molecules act as intracellular energy and phosphate sensors: they pyrophosphorylate target proteins non-enzymatically and compete with soluble inositol phosphates for binding pockets, tuning insulin secretion and sensitivity, vesicle trafficking, telomere length, phosphate homeostasis through the SPX-domain machinery, and Akt signalling. Loss of the kinases blunts these controls, and mice lacking one of them are lean and insulin-hypersensitive. Sequential kinases handle each step: IPPK and ITPK1 supply the IP6 precursor, IP6 kinases add a beta-phosphate at the 5-position, and the diphosphoinositol pentakisphosphate kinases PPIP5K1 and PPIP5K2 phosphorylate the 1-position to make IP8. A family of diphosphoinositol polyphosphate phosphohydrolases reverses the reactions, so the pool turns over rapidly and levels track cellular metabolic state.

Inositol pyrophosphates are high-energy signalling molecules made in the cytosol by adding further phosphates to the already fully phosphorylated inositol ring, giving diphospho- and triphosphoinositol species such as 5-IP7 and IP8. They act as metabolic and phosphate-status sensors, tuning insulin secretion and sensitivity, phosphate homeostasis, vesicle trafficking, telomere length and the response to DNA damage, partly by pyrophosphorylating target proteins and partly by competing with inositol phosphate binding sites on effectors such as the Akt PH domain. Inositol hexakisphosphate kinases generate IP7 from IP6, while diphosphoinositol pentakisphosphate kinases add the second pyrophosphate to make IP8; upstream, IPPK and ITPK1 supply the precursor pool. Diphosphoinositol polyphosphate phosphohydrolases of the Nudix family reverse these reactions, so cytosolic levels reflect a continuous synthesis-degradation cycle. Loss of IP6K1 in mice impairs growth, fertility and insulin signalling.

Synthesis of IPs in the nucleus builds the higher inositol phosphates inside the nucleus, generating soluble signalling molecules that act on transcription, mRNA export, chromatin remodelling and DNA repair rather than on membranes. These compounds also serve as a phosphate and energy reservoir, since the pyrophosphorylated forms can donate a high-energy phosphate directly to target proteins, coupling inositol phosphate levels to nutrient and phosphate sensing. A sequential kinase route does the work: a multikinase with relaxed specificity phosphorylates inositol trisphosphate and its products toward IP5, a dedicated 2-kinase completes IP6, and two inositol hexakisphosphate kinases add the diphosphate groups of IP7 and IP8. Output from this route influences apoptotic sensitivity, insulin secretion and telomere length control, and loss of individual kinases disturbs growth, ribosome biogenesis and nuclear RNA trafficking.

Inositol phosphates are not confined to membranes; a soluble, highly phosphorylated series is built inside the nucleus, and these molecules act as diffusible signals and phosphate donors rather than as lipid second messengers. Their production couples cellular phosphate and energy status to chromatin and RNA metabolism, with roles in mRNA export, transcriptional control, DNA repair and apoptosis, and it shapes how cells sense and store phosphate. In this nuclear branch, a multikinase phosphorylates lower inositol phosphates to IP4 and IP5, a 2-kinase completes IP6, and two inositol hexakisphosphate kinases add a high-energy pyrophosphate to generate IP7 and IP8, which can transfer phosphate to target proteins. Loss of individual kinases alters growth signalling and stress responses, and the same enzymes influence insulin secretion and tumour cell survival, placing nuclear inositol polyphosphate synthesis upstream of both gene expression and metabolic regulation.

IP3 and IP4 transport between cytosol and nucleus describes the movement of the soluble inositol phosphate second messengers inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and inositol 1,3,4,5-tetrakisphosphate from the cytoplasm into the nucleoplasm, where a distinct pool of inositol phosphate kinases and phosphatases acts on them. This matters because nuclear inositol phosphates control local calcium release, chromatin remodelling, mRNA export and transcriptional output, so calcium signalling initiated at the plasma membrane can be relayed into nuclear responses. The route is the nuclear pore complex, represented here by the full scaffold, transmembrane and FG-repeat nucleoporin repertoire together with the basket and cytoplasmic filament components. Because these metabolites are small, passage may be simple diffusion through the pore channel rather than carrier-mediated transport. The pathway thus links phosphoinositide signalling downstream of phospholipase C to nucleocytoplasmic exchange and nuclear envelope architecture.

Inositol phosphate signalling is not confined to the cytoplasm: the nucleus maintains its own pool of inositol trisphosphate and tetrakisphosphate, which feed nuclear kinases and phosphatases and influence chromatin regulation, mRNA export and calcium release from nuclear envelope stores. Movement of IP3 and IP4 between cytosol and nucleoplasm supplies that pool, and it occurs across the nuclear pore complex, whose scaffold, transmembrane and FG-repeat nucleoporins are represented here alongside the Y-complex components, the central channel proteins, the basket formed by TPR and NUP153, and cytoplasmic filament elements such as RANBP2 and NUP214. Whether these small, highly charged metabolites simply diffuse through the pore's permeability barrier or are carried by a dedicated transporter is unresolved. Pore integrity therefore sets the boundary conditions for nuclear inositol phosphate signalling, and nucleoporin defects disturb nucleocytoplasmic exchange broadly, as in triple A syndrome caused by loss of AAAS.

Cellular hexose transport is how glucose, fructose and galactose cross plasma membranes, and it sets the terms for whole-body sugar handling: dietary absorption in the small intestine, reabsorption in the kidney tubule, delivery across the blood-brain barrier, insulin-stimulated uptake into muscle and fat, and release of glucose from liver into blood. Two families do the work. The SLC2 (GLUT) proteins carry hexoses passively down their concentration gradient, with tissue-restricted isoforms such as GLUT1 for brain endothelium, GLUT2 for hepatocyte and enterocyte basolateral flux, GLUT4 for insulin-responsive tissues and GLUT5 for fructose. The SLC5 (SGLT) proteins instead couple sugar uptake to the sodium gradient, allowing enterocytes and proximal tubule cells to absorb glucose against a gradient. Intracellular phosphorylation traps the sugar, making uptake effectively unidirectional except where glucose 6-phosphatase is expressed. Mutations cause GLUT1 deficiency epilepsy, renal glycosuria and glucose-galactose malabsorption, and SGLT2 is a major diabetes drug target.

Sugars cannot cross membranes unaided, so every tissue depends on carrier proteins to move glucose, fructose and galactose into and out of cells. Cellular hexose transport covers the two families that do this work: the facilitative GLUTs of the SLC2 family, which allow sugar to follow its concentration gradient, and the sodium-coupled SGLTs of the SLC5 family, which concentrate glucose and galactose against a gradient using the sodium electrochemical potential. Together they mediate dietary sugar absorption across the intestinal epithelium, glucose reclamation from the renal filtrate, delivery of fuel to the brain across the blood-brain barrier, and insulin-regulated uptake into muscle and fat via GLUT4. Loss of individual carriers produces distinct disease: GLUT1 deficiency causes infantile epilepsy, GLUT2 mutation causes Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, and SGLT2 is the target of glucose-lowering drugs that force renal glucose excretion.

Heme degradation disposes of the heme released when red cells are broken down, several hundred milligrams a day, while salvaging its iron for reuse. It matters because free heme is a pro-oxidant and because the pathway's end product, bilirubin, must be conjugated and excreted; blocks at successive steps produce the jaundice of hemolysis, Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar syndromes, and neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. Microsomal heme oxygenases open the porphyrin ring, releasing iron and carbon monoxide and yielding biliverdin, which biliverdin reductases reduce to bilirubin. Albumin carries bilirubin in blood, hepatic organic anion transporters take it up, cytosolic binding proteins and glutathione transferases shuttle it, UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates it with glucuronic acid, and ABC-family efflux pumps export the conjugate into bile. The inducible oxygenase HMOX1 also makes this route a cytoprotective response to oxidative and inflammatory stress.

Senescent red cells release several grams of hemoglobin daily, and heme degradation is the route by which its porphyrin ring is dismantled, its iron salvaged, and the remainder excreted. Heme oxygenases HMOX1 and HMOX2 open the ring at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, releasing iron and carbon monoxide and yielding biliverdin, which biliverdin reductases BLVRA and BLVRB reduce to bilirubin. Because bilirubin is lipophilic and neurotoxic, it travels bound to albumin, is taken up by hepatocytes through organic anion transporters of the SLCO family, held by cytosolic binding proteins, conjugated with glucuronic acid by UGT1A1, and pumped into bile by ABCC2 and related efflux pumps. Loss of conjugating capacity produces the unconjugated hyperbilirubinemias, from benign Gilbert syndrome to kernicterus, while the inducible oxygenase arm also serves as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory stress response.

FGFR1 ligand binding and activation is the first step in fibroblast growth factor signalling through receptor 1, the event that converts an extracellular FGF gradient into a receptor dimer poised to fire. It governs limb and craniofacial patterning, skeletal growth, olfactory bulb and GnRH neuron development, and phosphate homeostasis; loss-of-function mutations in FGFR1 or its partner anosmin cause Kallmann syndrome and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, while activating changes drive craniosynostosis and several cancers. Which of the paracrine FGFs binds is set by alternative splicing of the receptor's third immunoglobulin domain and by heparan sulfate, with anosmin and TGFBR3 acting as accessory co-receptors and GIPC1 shaping trafficking. The endocrine ligand FGF23 instead requires Klotho, linking the receptor to renal phosphate handling. Ligand capture here dictates the downstream RAS-MAPK, PI3K and PLC-gamma responses, and FGFR1 also reaches the nucleus to influence transcription directly.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 becomes a signalling receptor when one of a large family of FGF ligands, presented with a heparan sulfate or Klotho co-receptor, binds its extracellular immunoglobulin domains and drives receptor dimerisation and kinase activation. This ligand binding and activation step sets the specificity of the whole pathway: alternative splicing of FGFR1 and the restricted expression of individual FGFs determine which cells respond, so the same downstream cascade can direct proliferation, migration, or differentiation depending on context. The biology governs limb and craniofacial patterning, skeletal growth, and, through FGF8 and the extracellular protein anosmin-1 encoded by ANOS1, the migration of GnRH neurons — loss of which causes Kallmann syndrome with hypogonadism and anosmia. FGF23 with Klotho instead signals phosphate handling. Co-receptors and adaptors such as betaglycan and GIPC1 modulate ligand availability and receptor trafficking; aberrant FGFR1 activation recurs in cancer.

FGFR2c ligand binding and activation is the ligand-recognition step of one specific fibroblast growth factor receptor splice variant, the mesenchymal 'c' isoform of FGFR2, whose engagement drives skeletal patterning, osteoblast differentiation and suture closure in the developing skull. Alternative splicing of the third immunoglobulin-like domain determines which FGFs a cell can hear, so the c isoform responds to a mesenchyme-facing panel including FGF1, FGF2, FGF4, FGF8, FGF9, FGF17, FGF18 and the endocrine ligand FGF23, while the epithelial b isoform reads a different set. Ligand binding, stabilised by heparan sulfate or by Klotho co-receptors for endocrine ligands, dimerises the receptor and triggers kinase transactivation feeding into RAS-MAPK, PI3K and PLCgamma output. Mutations that relax this isoform-restricted binding underlie craniosynostosis syndromes such as Apert and Crouzon, and aberrant FGFR2 signalling recurs in cancer.

The FGFR2c splice variant is the mesenchymal form of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2, and this step covers which fibroblast growth factors actually bind it and switch it on. Ligand selection here is what makes FGF signalling tissue-specific: alternative splicing of the receptor's third immunoglobulin-like domain gives FGFR2c a preference for FGF2, FGF4, FGF6, FGF8, FGF9, FGF17, FGF18 and related ligands, whereas the epithelial FGFR2b form responds to a different group, and the reciprocal epithelial-mesenchymal exchange of ligands drives limb outgrowth, skeletal patterning and organ branching. FGF23 acts in this family as an endocrine regulator of phosphate handling and requires a Klotho co-receptor. Binding assembles a ligand-receptor complex with heparan sulfate, dimerises the receptor and triggers autophosphorylation of its cytoplasmic kinase, initiating downstream growth and differentiation signalling. Mutations that alter FGFR2 ligand binding or activation cause craniosynostosis syndromes, and the receptor is amplified in several cancers.

Microtubule-dependent trafficking of connexons from Golgi to the plasma membrane is the delivery step that lets cells build gap junctions, the channels through which coupled cells share ions, metabolites and second messengers. Connexin hexamers assembled in the Golgi are packaged into secretory vesicles and moved outward in saltatory fashion along curvilinear microtubules, then docked at the surface where they pair with connexons on a neighbouring cell to form an open channel. The genes reflect this dependence on the tubulin cytoskeleton, with alpha- and beta-tubulin isotypes providing the tracks and connexin 43 the cargo. Because gap junction plaques turn over rapidly, continuous microtubule-based supply sets the level of intercellular coupling in heart, lens, skin and glia, and disruption of connexin delivery underlies conduction defects, cataract and hearing loss.

Gap junction channels must be delivered to the cell surface before neighbouring cells can couple electrically and metabolically, and this step carries newly assembled connexons from the Golgi to the plasma membrane along microtubules. The cargo is connexin 43 (GJA1), which oligomerises into hexameric connexons in the secretory pathway and is then moved in vesicles that travel in saltatory fashion along curvilinear microtubule tracks, docking at the membrane where they can join a partner hemichannel on an apposed cell. The remainder of the machinery is the alpha- and beta-tubulin heterodimer pool that builds those tracks. Because connexin 43 turns over within hours, continuous microtubule-based delivery sets how much coupling a tissue has, which matters for cardiac conduction, lens transparency and coordinated contraction; disrupted trafficking or connexin mutation reduces junctional plaques and produces arrhythmia and cataract.

Gap junction assembly builds the direct cytoplasmic channels that let neighbouring cells share ions, metabolites and second messengers, the basis of electrical coupling in heart and nerve, coordinated contraction, lens transparency, cochlear ion homeostasis and epidermal differentiation. Connexins are synthesised at the endoplasmic reticulum, oligomerise into homomeric or heteromeric hexameric connexons, traverse the Golgi, and are stored in trans-Golgi membranes before microtubule-based delivery to the plasma membrane; there they diffuse laterally and dock with partner hemichannels on the apposed cell, aggregating into ordered plaques. Cx43-containing junctions reciprocally capture and stabilise microtubule plus ends, which explains the prominence of alpha- and beta-tubulins alongside the connexin family here. Mutations in individual connexins cause deafness, peripheral neuropathy, congenital cataract, palmoplantar keratoderma and arrhythmia, each reflecting the tissue where that isoform carries coupling.

Gap junction assembly builds the direct cytoplasmic channels that let neighbouring cells share ions, metabolites and second messengers, giving tissues electrical and metabolic continuity dash synchronous contraction in heart and uterus, ionic recycling in the cochlea, lens transparency, and myelin homeostasis in Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes. Connexin polypeptides are made at the endoplasmic reticulum and oligomerize into hexameric hemichannels, which traverse the Golgi, are stored in trans-Golgi membranes and then delivered to the plasma membrane along microtubules, accounting for the large tubulin component here. Once inserted, connexons diffuse laterally, dock with partners on the apposing cell and cluster into plaques, and Cx43-based junctions in turn capture microtubule plus-ends. Different connexin genes serve different tissues, and their mutation causes deafness, skin disorders such as erythrokeratodermia, cataract, X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and cardiac conduction defects.

Pre-NOTCH Processing in the Endoplasmic Reticulum is the quality-control and cofactor-installation step that makes a newly synthesised NOTCH receptor competent to signal, long before it ever meets a ligand. NOTCH signalling governs cell-fate decisions across development from somite and vascular patterning to lymphocyte lineage choice and intestinal secretory differentiation so failure at this step blocks all of it. Within the ER lumen, two dedicated glycosyltransferases decorate conserved serines and threonines in the tandem EGF repeats of the NOTCH1-4 precursors: POFUT1 adds O-fucose at a C2-X(4-5)-S/T-C3 motif, and POGLUT1, the mammalian counterpart of Drosophila Rumi, adds O-glucose at a C1-X-S-X-P-C2 motif. These sugars stabilise EGF repeat folding, permit ER exit, and set the receptor's later sensitivity to Delta- and Jagged-type ligands, with the fucose serving as the substrate for Fringe-mediated tuning. Loss of POGLUT1 causes limb-girdle muscular dystrophy and Dowling-Degos disease.

Before a NOTCH receptor can respond to ligand, its extracellular EGF repeats must be sugar-modified in the endoplasmic reticulum, and this early processing step determines whether the receptor folds correctly and reaches the surface in a signalling-competent form. All four human NOTCH precursors are substrates. An O-fucosyltransferase adds fucose to serine or threonine residues at a defined position between the second and third cysteines of an EGF repeat, while an O-glucosyltransferase adds glucose to serines in a separate consensus site; the fucose later serves as the acceptor for Fringe-mediated elongation that tunes ligand preference. Loss of either modification cripples NOTCH output, with consequences for the lineage decisions, somite and vascular patterning, and progenitor maintenance that depend on NOTCH, and mutations in the glucosyltransferase cause a form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.

Digestion of dietary lipid is the extracellular breakdown of fat in the gut lumen, the step that converts triacylglycerols and cholesterol esters from food into free fatty acids, monoacylglycerols, glycerol and cholesterol that enterocytes can absorb. Without it fat passes through undigested, producing steatorrhoea, weight loss and deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins that ride along with dietary lipid; this is the defect seen in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and in cystic fibrosis. Digestion begins in the stomach with acid-stable gastric lipase and is completed in the small intestine by pancreatic triacylglycerol lipase, whose activity on bile-salt-coated emulsion droplets requires the cofactor colipase, together with carboxyl ester lipase and related pancreatic lipase-family proteins that act on cholesterol esters and other substrates. The pathway sits upstream of chylomicron assembly and whole-body lipid and energy supply.

Fat arriving in the diet is largely triacylglycerol and cholesterol ester, neither of which can cross the intestinal epithelium intact, so digestion of dietary lipid is the step that converts them into absorbable free fatty acids, monoacylglycerols, glycerol and cholesterol. Gastric lipase begins the hydrolysis in the acidic stomach, and pancreatic triacylglycerol lipase completes it in the duodenum, where colipase anchors the enzyme to the bile-salt-coated surface of emulsified fat droplets that would otherwise inhibit it. Carboxyl ester lipase broadens the range of substrates to cholesterol esters and fat-soluble vitamin esters, while the related pancreatic lipase regulatory proteins modulate this lipolytic activity. The products are taken up by enterocytes for resynthesis and chylomicron packaging. Loss of pancreatic lipase output, as in pancreatic insufficiency, produces steatorrhoea and deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins.

Viral mRNA Translation is the step at which influenza hands its transcripts to the host protein synthesis machinery, converting viral genetic information into the ten or more proteins needed to build progeny virions. Because the virus encodes no ribosome of its own, this dependence on host 40S and 60S subunits makes translation the point where infection is most exposed to antiviral defence and to therapeutic interference. Conserved viral 5' untranslated regions favour ribosome recruitment, assisted by the cellular RNA-binding protein GRSF1, while NS1 together with the host chaperone P58(IPK) keeps the stress kinase PKR inactive so that eIF2alpha is not phosphorylated and initiation continues. Host mRNA translation is simultaneously suppressed, redirecting ribosomes toward viral messages. The PB1 segment additionally yields PB1-F2 from an alternative reading frame, expanding the coding capacity of a compact genome.

Influenza virus encodes no ribosomes of its own, so every viral protein is made by the host translation apparatus; this step converts spliced and unspliced viral mRNA in the cytoplasm into the roughly ten polypeptides that build new particles, including the surface glycoproteins HA and NA, the polymerase subunits PB1, PB2 and PA, nucleoprotein, matrix proteins and NS1. The bulk of the gene content is the cytoplasmic 40S and 60S ribosomal subunit proteins that carry out initiation and elongation. Conserved viral 5' untranslated sequences favour recruitment of this machinery, aided by the host G-rich sequence factor GRSF1, while the co-chaperone P58(IPK) restrains the antiviral kinase PKR so that initiation is not shut down by the interferon-induced translational block. Host protein synthesis falls at the same time, making this the point where the virus captures a central cellular process to its own ends.

Bile acid and bile salt metabolism is the route by which the liver disposes of cholesterol by converting it into detergents that emulsify dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins in the small intestine. Roughly half a gram of cholesterol is committed to this pathway daily, making it a principal arm of whole-body cholesterol homeostasis; its failure causes cholestasis, fat malabsorption, and progressive liver injury. Synthesis begins with 7alpha-hydroxylation of cholesterol by CYP7A1, or alternatively with oxysterols made in extrahepatic tissues by CYP27A1 and CYP46A1, followed by ring modification, peroxisomal side-chain shortening, and conjugation to taurine or glycine by BAAT. Dedicated transporters then complete the enterohepatic circulation: canalicular export via ABCB11, ileal uptake by SLC10A2, and hepatic reuptake through sodium-dependent and organic anion transporters. The nuclear receptor FXR with RXRA senses bile salt levels and feeds back on synthesis and transport.

Converting cholesterol into bile salts is the body's main route for disposing of sterol and, at the same time, the way it makes dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins absorbable. Roughly half a gram of cholesterol is spent this way each day in the liver, secreted into bile, used as detergent in the small intestine, and then almost entirely reclaimed and recirculated. The classic route begins with 7alpha-hydroxylation by CYP7A1, followed by ring modification, side-chain oxidation and peroxisomal beta-oxidation, before conjugation to taurine or glycine by BAAT. Alternative routes start from oxysterols made in extrahepatic tissues by CYP27A1 or CYP46A1, contributing little to the bile salt pool but helping clear cholesterol from brain and periphery. Dedicated transporters export salts into bile and take them up again in ileum and hepatocyte, while the nuclear receptor FXR with RXRA feeds back on synthesis. Defects cause cholestasis, fat malabsorption and bile acid synthesis disorders.

Neuropilin interactions with VEGF and VEGFR describes how the neuropilin co-receptors NRP1 and NRP2 capture VEGF family ligands and present them to the signalling receptors VEGFR1 (FLT1) and VEGFR2 (KDR), tuning the strength of angiogenic signalling. This matters for the formation and remodelling of blood and lymphatic vessels during development, for wound healing, and for tumour vascularisation, where neuropilin levels help determine how strongly endothelial cells respond to a given amount of growth factor. Neuropilins have short cytoplasmic tails and no kinase activity; they work as ligand-binding cofactors, with NRP1 favouring VEGF-A165, VEGF-B and PlGF-2 and NRP2 also binding VEGF-A145 and VEGF-C, the latter linking it to lymphatic endothelium. The same receptors serve axon guidance through semaphorins, placing this module at the intersection of vascular patterning and neuronal wiring.

Neuropilins are short-tailed cell-surface receptors that bind selected VEGF family ligands and hand them to the signalling VEGF receptors, so this set describes how ligand presentation tunes endothelial responsiveness during blood and lymphatic vessel growth. NRP1 captures the heparin-binding isoform VEGF-A165 along with VEGF-B and PlGF-2, while NRP2 additionally binds VEGF-A145 and VEGF-C, and both associate laterally with KDR (VEGFR-2) or FLT1 (VEGFR-1) to raise their affinity for particular ligands rather than to signal by their own kinase activity, since they have none. The consequence is isoform-selective control of endothelial proliferation, migration and sprouting, with NRP1 weighted toward arterial and angiogenic vessels and NRP2 toward veins and lymphatics. Loss of neuropilin function disrupts vascular patterning in development, and the same co-receptor interface is exploited in tumour angiogenesis and targeted by anti-angiogenic strategies.

Degradation of beta-catenin by the destruction complex is the off-switch of canonical Wnt signalling: in unstimulated cells it continuously destroys cytoplasmic beta-catenin so that Wnt target genes stay silent. This restraint sets the threshold for Wnt-driven proliferation and stem cell renewal in tissues such as intestinal crypts, and its loss through APC or AXIN mutation stabilises beta-catenin and drives colorectal and other cancers. A scaffold of APC, axin and AMER1 presents beta-catenin to casein kinase 1 and GSK3-beta for sequential N-terminal phosphorylation, creating a phosphodegron read by the beta-TrCP-SKP1-CUL1-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase; polyubiquitinated beta-catenin is then dismantled by the 26S proteasome, with PP2A subunits and the deubiquitinase ZRANB1 tuning complex output. Absent nuclear beta-catenin, TCF/LEF factors remain bound to TLE/Groucho and CtBP corepressors, keeping targets such as MYC repressed.
