When no Wnt ligand is present, cytoplasmic beta-catenin is kept at low levels by a dedicated destruction complex, and this restraint is what prevents constitutive transcription of Wnt target genes such as MYC. The scaffolds AXIN1/AXIN2 and the tumour suppressor APC hold beta-catenin so that casein kinase 1 alpha and GSK3B phosphorylate its N-terminal degron; the beta-TrCP-containing SCF ligase, with CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1, then polyubiquitinates it for proteasomal destruction. Protein phosphatase 2A subunits and the deubiquitinase ZRANB1 tune the complex, while FRAT proteins and AMER1 act on GSK3B and Axin availability. In parallel, TCF/LEF factors sit on target promoters with TLE/Groucho and CtBP corepressors and HDAC1, holding them silent. Loss of APC or stabilizing mutations in beta-catenin break this control and drive colorectal and other cancers, linking the pathway to intestinal stem cell renewal and development.

VEGF binds to VEGFR leading to receptor dimerization is the initiating step of angiogenic signalling: secreted VEGF family ligands engage their receptor tyrosine kinases on endothelial cells, bringing two receptor chains together so their kinase domains can trans-autophosphorylate. This event sets in motion endothelial proliferation, survival, migration and increased vascular permeability, and therefore governs blood vessel formation in development, wound healing, and tumour neovascularisation, where it is the target of anti-VEGF therapeutics. Ligand identity determines the output: VEGFA and the placental growth factor PGF act through VEGFR-1 (FLT1) and VEGFR-2 (KDR), while VEGFC and VEGFD signal through VEGFR-3 (FLT4) to drive lymphatic endothelial development. Homodimers predominate, though VEGFR-1/VEGFR-2 heterodimers form, and VEGFR-2 carries most angiogenic activity in vivo while VEGFR-1 largely restrains ligand availability.

Blood and lymphatic vessels grow where endothelial cells receive a vascular endothelial growth factor signal, and that signal begins with ligand binding to a VEGF receptor and the receptor pairing up. The step initiates cascades that drive endothelial proliferation, survival, migration and increased vascular permeability, and it is the point at which tumours recruit their own blood supply and the target of anti-angiogenic drugs. Secreted ligands including VEGFA, VEGFB, placental growth factor and the lymphangiogenic VEGFC and VEGFD engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 with distinct preferences; receptors mainly form homodimers, though FLT1-KDR heterodimers occur. KDR carries most angiogenic signalling in vivo, FLT1 acts largely as a modulating or decoy receptor, and FLT4 specifies lymphatic endothelium. Loss or dysregulation underlies vascular malformations, lymphoedema and pathological neovascularisation in retinopathy and cancer.

Signaling by ALK covers the anaplastic lymphoma kinase, a neural receptor tyrosine kinase of the insulin receptor family whose activation drives proliferation and survival, and whose deregulation is one of the best-known oncogenic drivers in anaplastic large cell lymphoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, neuroblastoma and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumours. Physiologically it is expressed in the developing central and peripheral nervous system, where the ALKAL1/ALKAL2 ligands, and possibly the heparin-binding factors pleiotrophin and midkine, induce receptor dimerisation, trans-autophosphorylation and recruitment of adaptors such as SHC1, FRS2 and IRS1. From there signals flow into RAS-MAPK, PI3K and JAK3-STAT3 routes, with STAT3 turning on MYC, MYCN, HIF1A, PRDM1 repression and PD-L1 expression through cooperating chromatin regulators. Chromosomal rearrangements producing NPM-ALK or EML4-ALK fusions, or activating point mutations, make this signalling constitutive and ligand-independent, the basis for ALK inhibitor therapy.

ALK is a receptor tyrosine kinase of the insulin receptor family, expressed mainly in the developing central and peripheral nervous system, where its activation by the secreted ligands ALKAL1 and ALKAL2 contributes to neuronal differentiation; in mice and flies it also acts as a determinant of resistance to weight gain. Its importance in humans is largely oncogenic: chromosomal rearrangements that fuse the kinase domain to dimerization-competent partners, as well as amplification and activating point mutations, drive anaplastic large cell lymphoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, neuroblastoma and other tumours, making the kinase a major drug target. Ligand binding or fusion-driven dimerization triggers transautophosphorylation and recruitment of adaptors such as SHC1, FRS2 and IRS1, feeding RAS, PI3K and SRC signalling. Parallel JAK3-STAT3 activation reprogrammes transcription, inducing MYC, MYCN and HIF1A and, via chromatin repressors including HDACs, SIN3A and DNMT1, silencing genes such as PRDM1 while raising PD-L1 expression.</br>

Metabolism of nitric oxide: NOS3 activation and regulation governs how endothelial cells make nitric oxide, the diffusible messenger that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, sets blood pressure and vascular tone, and restrains platelet aggregation and leukocyte adhesion. Loss of endothelium-derived NO is the defining feature of endothelial dysfunction and contributes to hypertension and atherosclerosis. Because NO cannot be stored, output is controlled entirely at the enzyme. Calcium-loaded calmodulin binds NOS3 to permit electron flow from its reductase domain to heme, while HSP90 and AKT1-mediated phosphorylation raise activity and caveolin-1 sequestration lowers it. N-myristoylation and palmitoylation by NMT1/NMT2 and ZDHHC21, reversed by acyl-protein thioesterase, target the enzyme to caveolae and traffic it between plasma membrane, Golgi and perinuclear membranes, with NOSIP and NOSTRIN redirecting it. Cofactor supply through tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis and DDAH1-mediated clearance of the inhibitor ADMA further tune arginine turnover.

Endothelial nitric oxide synthase makes the diffusible gas that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, and this pathway covers how that enzyme is switched on, positioned and restrained. NO produced here sets blood pressure and vascular tone, damps platelet aggregation and leukocyte adhesion, and its loss defines endothelial dysfunction in hypertension and atherosclerosis. Activity requires calcium-loaded calmodulin and is tuned by phosphorylation, with AKT1 and the HSP90 chaperone promoting output while caveolin-1 sequesters and inhibits the enzyme in caveolae. Membrane targeting depends on N-myristoylation by NMT1/NMT2 and palmitoylation by ZDHHC21, reversed by the thioesterase LYPLA1, while NOSIP and NOSTRIN redistribute the enzyme away from the plasma membrane. Substrate and cofactor supply matters too: DDAH1 destroys the endogenous inhibitor asymmetric dimethylarginine, and SPR contributes to tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis, without which the enzyme uncouples.

DS-GAG biosynthesis builds dermatan sulfate, the glycosaminoglycan that gives skin, tendon, blood vessels and cornea their tensile strength and hydration, and that decorates proteoglycans controlling collagen fibril spacing, growth factor availability and neural matrix organisation. Chains of alternating N-acetylgalactosamine and uronic acid are elongated on the tetrasaccharide linker of core proteins such as decorin, biglycan, versican and the brain proteoglycans brevican and neurocan. Dermatan sulfate identity comes from epimerisation of glucuronic to iduronic acid by DSE and DSEL, followed by sulfotransferase action: CHST14 adds 4-O-sulfate to GalNAc, CHST15 makes the 4,6-disulfated form, and UST sulfates uronic acid at position 2. This sulfation pattern encodes binding specificity for heparin cofactor II and for FGF and HGF signalling. Loss of CHST14 or DSE causes musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with joint laxity, fragile skin and skeletal malformation.

Dermatan sulfate chains are built on proteoglycan core proteins and give connective tissue its tensile and hydrating properties, while also shaping growth factor and chemokine availability in the extracellular matrix. Synthesis extends the tetrasaccharide linker with alternating N-acetylgalactosamine and uronic acid, then diversifies the chain: epimerases encoded by DSE and DSEL convert glucuronic acid to iduronic acid, which is what distinguishes dermatan sulfate from chondroitin sulfate, and sulfotransferases such as CHST14, CHST15 and UST add sulfate to the 4- and 6-positions of GalNAc or to the uronic acid 2-position. The finished chains decorate small leucine-rich proteoglycans like decorin and biglycan and the large hyalectans versican, neurocan and brevican, controlling collagen fibril assembly, skin and vascular integrity, and neural matrix organisation. Defects in the epimerase or the 4-O-sulfotransferase cause a form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome with joint laxity and fragile skin.</description>

HS-GAG degradation is the lysosomal breakdown of heparan sulfate chains released from proteoglycans, the turnover arm of proteoglycan homeostasis. It matters because heparan sulfate cannot be digested by a single enzyme: exoglycosidases and sulfatases must act in strict sequence from the non-reducing end, and loss of any one step causes undegraded fragments to accumulate in lysosomes, producing the mucopolysaccharidoses — Hurler, Hunter and the Sanfilippo subtypes — with skeletal, visceral and neurodegenerative consequences. The substrates are the cell surface and matrix proteoglycans themselves: syndecans, glypicans, perlecan and agrin, whose sugar chains tune growth factor and morphogen signalling. Cathepsin L and heparanase initiate the process by shedding and internally cleaving the chains, after which iduronidase, iduronate sulfatase, sulfamidase, acetyl-CoA transferase and alpha-N-acetylglucosaminidase strip the resulting oligosaccharides residue by residue.

Heparan sulfate chains on cell-surface and matrix proteoglycans are constantly turned over, and this pathway covers their breakdown from intact proteoglycan to free sugars. Syndecans, glypicans, perlecan and agrin are internalised, their core proteins clipped by cathepsin L, and the heparan sulfate chains cut into fragments by heparanase before delivery to the lysosome. There a strictly ordered set of exo-acting enzymes works from the non-reducing end: iduronate 2-sulfatase and alpha-L-iduronidase remove iduronic acid residues and their sulfate, sulfamidase and the acetyl-CoA-dependent transferase HGSNAT handle glucosamine nitrogen, and NAGLU releases N-acetylglucosamine. Because each step requires the previous one, loss of any single enzyme halts the chain and undegraded fragments accumulate, producing the mucopolysaccharidoses — Hunter, Hurler, and Sanfilippo syndromes — with skeletal, visceral and neurological disease.

CS/DS degradation is the lysosomal breakdown of chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate chains released from extracellular matrix proteoglycans, the disposal arm of glycosaminoglycan turnover. Proteoglycans such as decorin, biglycan, versican and the brain-specific aggrecan family members brevican and neurocan are continuously internalised and dismantled, and the sugar chains must be taken apart sugar by sugar. Hyaluronidases first fragment the long polymers, then exoenzymes act in strict order: sulfatases including ARSB and IDS remove sulfate groups, and glycosidases such as GUSB, GLB1, IDUA and the beta-hexosaminidase subunits HEXA/HEXB cleave the exposed terminal residues. Because each step depends on the one before, loss of any single enzyme halts the chain and undegraded fragments accumulate, producing mucopolysaccharidoses with skeletal, corneal, visceral and neurological damage. The pathway thus links matrix remodelling to lysosomal catabolic capacity.

Chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate chains on proteoglycans such as decorin, biglycan, versican, brevican and neurocan are continuously turned over, and their final breakdown happens in the lysosome. Endoglycosidases of the hyaluronidase family cleave the chains internally, after which exo-acting enzymes strip the ends one residue at a time: sulfatases including arylsulfatase B and iduronate 2-sulfatase remove sulfate groups, while beta-glucuronidase, alpha-L-iduronidase, beta-galactosidase and the beta-hexosaminidase subunits release the terminal sugars. Because each step depends on the one before it, loss of a single enzyme halts the whole sequence and partially digested glycosaminoglycan accumulates, producing the mucopolysaccharidoses and related lysosomal storage disorders with their skeletal, visceral and neurological consequences. This catabolism supports extracellular matrix remodelling and the general homeostasis of glycoconjugate turnover.

ERKs are inactivated is the off-switch for ERK signalling, the step that converts a growth factor stimulus into a transient pulse rather than a permanent one. Because ERK output drives proliferation, differentiation and survival decisions, the duration and location of its activity determines the cellular response, and loss of shutdown contributes to unchecked growth in cancers with hyperactive RAS-RAF input. Inactivation works by removing the activating phosphates from the threonine and tyrosine of the activation loop: dual-specificity phosphatases such as DUSP6 and DUSP7 act on cytoplasmic ERK1/2, DUSP4 acts in the nucleus, and the serine/threonine phosphatase PP2A holoenzyme contributes through its catalytic and regulatory subunits, with VRK3 serving as a scaffold for nuclear dephosphorylation. Since ERK itself induces transcription of these phosphatases, the arrangement forms a negative feedback loop that sets signal amplitude and timing.

Growth factor signalling through ERK must be switched off as well as on, and this is the shut-off arm: phosphatases strip the activating phosphates from the Thr-Xaa-Tyr motif in the activation loop of ERK1, ERK2 and ERK5, returning the kinases to a resting state. Because ERK activity drives proliferation, differentiation and survival gene programmes, the duration and amplitude of the signal determine the cellular outcome, and loss of this braking step contributes to unchecked mitogenic signalling in cancer. Dual-specificity phosphatases such as DUSP6 and DUSP7, which act largely on ERK in the cytoplasm, and nuclear DUSP4, remove both phosphates, while the PP2A holoenzyme built from catalytic, scaffolding and B56 regulatory subunits contributes serine/threonine dephosphorylation; VRK3 acts as a scaffold promoting phosphatase action on ERK. Since ERK itself induces DUSP transcription, the arrangement forms a negative feedback loop.

COPII-mediated vesicle transport is the first step of the secretory pathway: it captures newly made proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum and delivers them to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment, so that everything a cell secretes or puts on its surface can leave the ER. Its failure underlies bleeding disorders through defective export of factors V and VIII, as well as skeletal and neurological disease. Cargo is concentrated at ER exit sites organised by SEC16, where the Sar1 GTPase recruits the inner SEC23/SEC24 adaptor layer and the outer SEC13/SEC31 cage to deform the membrane into a vesicle. Cargo receptors such as LMAN1 with its partner MCFD2 select specific glycoproteins, while TRAPP complexes, Rab1 and the SNAREs STX5, BET1, SEC22B and YKT6 with NSF and SNAP proteins drive uncoating, tethering and fusion at the acceptor membrane.

Everything a cell secretes or puts on its surface leaves the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated vesicles, and this pathway is the export step that starts the secretory route. Cargo is concentrated at ER exit sites organized by SEC16, where the small GTPase SAR1B recruits the inner SEC23/SEC24 adaptor layer and the outer SEC13/SEC31 cage, budding vesicles that uncoat and fuse with the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment. Selective receptors such as LMAN1 with its partner MCFD2 capture particular clients, and mutations in either cause combined factor V and factor VIII deficiency; alpha-1 antitrypsin, collagen VII and blood clotting factors all depend on this traffic. Delivery is completed by RAB1 activation through the TRAPP complex, the tether USO1, and SNARE-mediated fusion involving STX5, BET1, SEC22B and the NSF/SNAP machinery that recycles them.

Cell death signalling via NRAGE, NRIF and NADE is the apoptotic arm of neurotrophin receptor p75 (NGFR) signalling, the route by which developing neurons that fail to secure trophic support, or neurons injured in the adult nervous system, are eliminated. Mature NGF and, more potently, proneurotrophins engage p75NTR, while TrkA signalling opposes the same outcome, so the balance between the two receptors sets neuronal survival during target-field competition and after axonal damage. Death signalling proceeds through the adaptors TRAF6, NRAGE/MAGED1 and NRIF with ubiquitin-dependent steps, activation of Rac via guanine nucleotide exchange factors, and JNK-dependent induction of BIM, BAD and caspase-2/-3. Gamma-secretase cleavage of the receptor releases an intracellular fragment that carries NRIF to the nucleus for transcriptional events. Dysregulation contributes to neurodegeneration and to neuronal loss following ischaemia or trauma.

Neurons are eliminated during development and after injury when the p75 neurotrophin receptor, rather than TrkA, dominates the response to nerve growth factor or its unprocessed precursor, and this receptor-initiated death programme is what the intracellular adaptors NRAGE, NRIF and NADE carry forward. It matters because it sculpts the size of neuronal populations to match their targets and contributes to neuronal loss after axotomy and in degenerative injury. Ligand-bound NGFR recruits TRAF6 and MAGED1 (NRAGE), engages Rac1 through an array of Rho-family exchange factors, and activates JNK, converging on BAD, BIM and caspase-3 to dismantle the cell. In parallel, gamma-secretase components including presenilins and nicastrin cleave the receptor so that its intracellular domain, with NRIF, can reach the nucleus and drive transcriptional events; ubiquitin and SQSTM1 support the signalling scaffold.

p75NTR recruits signalling complexes describes how the neurotrophin receptor p75, on binding NGF, assembles an adaptor platform at the plasma membrane that turns on NF-kB and thereby favours neuronal survival. p75NTR is unusual in that the same receptor can drive apoptosis through JNK or survival through NF-kB depending on which complex it recruits, so this branch sets the balance that determines whether developing and injured neurons live, and it shapes responses to axonal damage and neurodegenerative stress. Mechanistically, the ligand-bound receptor gathers RIP2, MyD88 and IRAK1 together with the scaffold p62/SQSTM1 and atypical PKC iota, allowing TRAF6 to build polyubiquitin chains that activate the IKK complex and release NF-kB for nuclear entry. The pathway is a clear example of ubiquitin-dependent scaffolding borrowed from innate immune signalling and used in the nervous system.

Neurotrophin binding to the p75 neurotrophin receptor turns the receptor's cytoplasmic tail into a docking platform, and the complexes it recruits determine whether a neuron survives, grows, or dies. Because p75NTR has no catalytic activity of its own, everything depends on which adaptors arrive: here the assembly built around NGF-bound receptor gathers RIPK2, MYD88 and IRAK1 together with the scaffold p62 and atypical protein kinase C iota, converging on TRAF6. TRAF6 acts as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, and the polyubiquitin supplied by the ubiquitin genes in this module drives activation of the IKK complex through IKBKB, freeing NF-kB to enter the nucleus and switch on survival and inflammatory transcription. This arm of neurotrophin signalling opposes the pro-apoptotic outputs of the same receptor, and its balance shapes developmental neuronal pruning, axon growth and injury responses.

Thyroxine biosynthesis is the making of thyroid hormone by follicular cells of the thyroid, the process that sets basal metabolic rate, thermogenesis, growth and neurodevelopment throughout life; its failure causes congenital hypothyroidism, goitre and cretinism, and its dysregulation underlies common thyroid disease. Pituitary thyrotropin, a heterodimer of a shared glycoprotein alpha subunit with TSHB, drives the programme. Iodide is concentrated from plasma by the sodium-iodide symporter SLC5A5, delivered to the apical membrane, and oxidised by thyroid peroxidase using hydrogen peroxide generated by the DUOX1/DUOX2 oxidases with their maturation factors DUOXA1/2. Iodination and coupling of tyrosines occurs on thyroglobulin, which is endocytosed and degraded in lysosomes to liberate T4 and T3, while iodotyrosine deiodinase recycles iodide. In peripheral tissues the selenodeiodinases DIO1, DIO2 and DIO3 activate T4 to T3 or inactivate it, tuning local hormone action on nuclear receptors.

Thyroid hormone sets basal metabolic rate, drives growth and brain development, and its supply depends on thyroxine biosynthesis in thyroid follicular cells. Thyrotropin, the pituitary glycoprotein hormone made of a shared alpha subunit and TSHB, stimulates follicular cells to concentrate iodide from plasma through the sodium-iodide symporter SLC5A5 and to iodinate tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin at the apical membrane. Thyroid peroxidase catalyses iodination and coupling using hydrogen peroxide generated by the dual oxidases DUOX1 and DUOX2 with their maturation factors DUOXA1 and DUOXA2. Iodotyrosine deiodinase salvages iodide from uncoupled residues, while the selenoenzymes DIO1, DIO2 and DIO3 set local hormone activity by converting T4 to active T3 or to inactive metabolites. Loss of any of these steps causes congenital hypothyroidism, goitre and, untreated, irreversible developmental delay; released T3 acts through nuclear receptors to reprogramme target gene expression.

Regulation of gene expression in late stage (branching morphogenesis) pancreatic bud precursor cells describes the transcriptional program that keeps pancreatic epithelial progenitors proliferating within branching ducts while parcelling out the first endocrine cells. It sets the size of the progenitor pool from which islet beta cells eventually arise, so its failure underlies pancreatic hypoplasia and neonatal diabetes; mutations in HNF1B cause maturity-onset diabetes of the young with renal cysts. ONECUT1 sustains HNF1B and ONECUT3 expression and drives epithelial proliferation as PDX1 and NKX6-1 levels fall. Superimposed on this, Notch signalling through NOTCH1, RBPJ, mastermind-like coactivators and the histone acetyltransferases CBP/p300 and GCN5/PCAF maintains HES1, which represses NEUROG3 and enforces lateral inhibition. Cells escaping this repression accumulate NEUROG3 and exit the cycle to begin endocrine differentiation, linking chromatin-level coactivation to cell fate choice in organ development.

During the branching morphogenesis stage of pancreatic development, committed but still undifferentiated epithelial precursors in the growing ductal tree must be kept proliferating until a subset is released to become hormone-producing endocrine cells. This transcriptional programme sets that balance, and its disruption limits beta cell number, an origin of neonatal diabetes and pancreatic hypoplasia. ONECUT1 sustains expression of ONECUT3 and HNF1B, which maintain the epithelial progenitor state and duct formation, while NEUROG3 induction marks the commitment of individual cells to the endocrine lineage. Notch signalling through NOTCH1, RBPJ and Mastermind-like coactivators, with the acetyltransferases CREBBP, EP300, KAT2A and KAT2B, drives the repressor HES1 to restrain NEUROG3 and hold neighbouring cells as progenitors, so that lateral inhibition rations differentiation across the branching epithelium.

Regulation of gene expression in endocrine-committed (NEUROG3+) progenitor cells describes the transcriptional step at which a pancreatic duct-like progenitor stops being a generic epithelial cell and commits to becoming a hormone-secreting islet cell. It is the gateway to the beta, alpha, delta and PP lineages, so loss of the initiating factor abolishes islet formation altogether and causes neonatal diabetes with malabsorptive diarrhoea, since related endocrine cells of the gut depend on the same factor. Transient expression of neurogenin 3 activates a downstream tier of regulators — PAX4, NEUROD1, NKX2-2 and INSM1 — which reinforce endocrine identity, suppress alternative acinar and ductal programmes, and steer subprogrammes toward particular hormone fates; PAX4 in particular biases cells toward beta and delta rather than alpha character. This cascade sits within pancreatic organogenesis and is the template followed when stem cells are directed toward insulin-producing cells in vitro.

Pancreatic endocrine cells arise from a transient population of progenitors that switch on neurogenin 3, and this transcriptional programme is what commits those cells away from duct and acinar fates toward the hormone-producing islet lineages. Without it no beta, alpha, delta or PP cells form; loss-of-function mutations in humans cause congenital malabsorptive diarrhoea with permanent neonatal diabetes, and the same programme is the target of efforts to make beta cells from stem cells. NEUROG3 acts as a short-lived pioneer factor that directly induces a second tier of regulators, including PAX4, NEUROD1, NKX2-2 and the zinc-finger factor INSM1, which together consolidate endocrine identity, drive exit from the cell cycle, and bias progenitors toward particular hormone subtypes. The pathway illustrates how a brief pulse of one factor is converted into a stable differentiated state.

Gene Silencing by RNA covers the small non-coding RNA systems that switch off genes after transcription, giving cells a layer of control that tunes protein output, defends the genome against transposons, and shapes development and differentiation. Loss of this machinery derails stem cell programmes, causes male infertility through transposon activation in germ cells, and contributes to cancer through widespread microRNA deregulation. Mechanistically, primary microRNA transcripts made by RNA polymerase II are cropped by Drosha with DGCR8, exported by exportin-5, diced by DICER1, and loaded into Argonaute proteins with TNRC6 partners to repress translation and destabilise target mRNAs; short interfering RNAs use the same effector step. A parallel germline branch built on PIWI proteins, Tudor-domain factors, MOV10L1 and mitochondrial PLD6 generates piRNAs that silence retroelements, while angiogenin and ELAC2 cleavage of tRNAs yields a further class of regulatory small RNAs.

Small non-coding RNAs let cells repress genes sequence-specifically, tuning developmental programmes, restraining transposons and buffering gene dosage. This silencing-by-RNA biology covers how microRNAs, small interfering RNAs, PIWI-interacting RNAs and tRNA-derived fragments are made and how they act. Primary microRNA transcripts made by RNA polymerase II are cropped in the nucleus by Drosha with its partner DGCR8, exported by exportin-5, and cut by Dicer; the resulting guide strand loads onto an Argonaute protein, which with a TNRC6 scaffold blocks translation and destabilises target mRNAs, or cleaves fully complementary targets. In germ cells a separate branch loads piRNAs onto PIWIL proteins with Tudor-domain and MOV10L1 helicase cofactors, methylated at their 3' end by HENMT1, to silence retrotransposons and safeguard spermatogenesis; loss of this arm causes germ cell loss and infertility. Angiogenin-cleaved tRNA fragments add a further layer of repression.

Stimulation of the cell death response by PAK-2p34 describes how a normally growth-promoting kinase is converted, by caspase cleavage, into a pro-apoptotic effector that helps execute the morphological program of cell death. Under stress, active caspase-3 cuts PAK-2 to release the constitutively active carboxy-terminal fragment PAK-2p34, which autophosphorylates at Thr402, loses its nuclear export signal and accumulates in the nucleus, where it drives cell rounding and chromatin condensation. This makes PAK-2 unusual among p21-activated kinases: full-length PAK-2 supports survival and cytoskeletal remodelling downstream of Rac and Cdc42, while its cleaved form commits the cell to dying. The fragment is restrained by proteasomal turnover and by binding the GAP PS-GAP, which inhibits it and relocalizes it to the perinuclear region, and it may suppress cap-dependent translation initiation by phosphorylating Mnk1 during apoptosis.

Apoptotic commitment involves not only the destruction of structural proteins but the conversion of a kinase into a pro-death enzyme, and that is what happens here. Caspase-3 cleaves the p21-activated kinase PAK-2, releasing a constitutively active catalytic fragment, PAK-2p34, that drives the morphological hallmarks of dying cells: cell rounding, loss of adhesion, and condensation of apoptotic chromatin. Cleavage removes the nuclear export signal, so the fragment autophosphorylates and accumulates in the nucleus. Its activity is held in check by proteasomal turnover and by binding to a GTPase-activating protein that both inhibits the kinase and redistributes it to the perinuclear region. Downstream, PAK-2p34 has been implicated in shutting down cap-dependent translation initiation during apoptosis. The pathway illustrates how stress signalling and caspase proteolysis converge to make an ordinarily growth- and cytoskeleton-related kinase execute cell death.

Aromatic amines can be N-hydroxylated or N-dealkylated by CYP1A2 describes a hepatic phase I biotransformation step that determines the fate of arylamine and heterocyclic amine compounds taken in from tobacco smoke, cooked meat and many drugs. Its consequences cut both ways: N-dealkylation clears substrates such as caffeine, theophylline, clozapine and tacrine, while N-hydroxylation of aromatic amines generates reactive hydroxylamines that are further conjugated and can bind DNA, linking this reaction to bladder and colorectal carcinogen activation. CYP1A2 is one of the most abundant cytochrome P450s in liver, uses NADPH-derived electrons and molecular oxygen at a heme iron centre, and is induced through the aryl hydrocarbon receptor by the same polycyclic aromatic compounds it metabolizes. Variation in its activity, from genetic polymorphism, smoking or inhibitors, is a major source of interindividual differences in drug clearance and chemical susceptibility.

Aromatic amines taken in from cooked meat, tobacco smoke and industrial exposures are chemically inert until a liver enzyme attacks their nitrogen, and CYP1A2 is the cytochrome P450 that performs this step, either N-hydroxylating the amine or stripping an alkyl group from it. The consequence is double-edged: N-dealkylation generally clears drugs such as caffeine, theophylline, clozapine and tacrine, so variation in this activity sets their plasma levels and dosing, while N-hydroxylation of heterocyclic and arylamines creates hydroxylamines that are further conjugated into DNA-binding electrophiles, linking this route to bladder and colorectal carcinogenesis. The enzyme sits in hepatic endoplasmic reticulum, draws electrons from NADPH via cytochrome P450 reductase, and is strongly induced through aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling, which is why smoking accelerates clearance of its drug substrates. It also oxidizes steroids and fatty acids as part of general phase I metabolism.

Miscellaneous substrates gathers the cytochrome P450 enzymes whose in vivo substrates and physiological assignments remain unsettled, alongside a few with better-defined but hard-to-classify chemistry. These heme-thiolate monooxygenases sit in the endoplasmic reticulum, draw electrons from NADPH via P450 reductase, and oxidize lipophilic compounds, so their activities bear on drug clearance, eicosanoid turnover, and skin and vascular physiology. The group includes CYP2D6, the highly polymorphic enzyme that determines metabolism of a large share of prescribed drugs and defines poor and ultrarapid metabolizer phenotypes; CYP4F2 and CYP4A11, which omega-hydroxylate arachidonic acid and leukotriene B4 to regulate blood pressure and terminate inflammatory signalling; and CYP4F22, required for making the acylceramides of the epidermal permeability barrier, whose loss causes lamellar ichthyosis. Others, such as CYP2W1 and CYP2S1, catalyze P450-type reactions in vitro but await confirmed endogenous roles.

Cytochrome P450 enzymes acting on miscellaneous substrates are those whose oxidative chemistry is demonstrable but whose physiological substrates and regulation remain incompletely defined, so they sit outside the tidy classes of steroid, bile acid or eicosanoid metabolism. Their importance is nonetheless concrete: CYP2D6 oxidises a large share of clinically used drugs and its polymorphisms drive interindividual differences in dose response, while CYP4F2 and CYP4A11 hydroxylate arachidonic acid and related lipids to influence vascular tone and blood pressure, and CYP4F22 is required for the ultra-long-chain fatty acid processing that builds the epidermal permeability barrier, with loss-of-function causing ichthyosis. Others, including CYP2S1, CYP2U1, CYP2W1 and CYP4B1, are expressed in epithelia, brain or tumours and perform monooxygenation of fatty acids and xenobiotics whose in vivo significance is still being established.

Endogenous sterols covers the cytochrome P450 reactions that build cholesterol, convert it to bile acids and steroid hormones, and dispose of it, keeping whole-body cholesterol input and output balanced. When this balance fails, cholesterol accumulates and drives atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, while loss of individual enzymes causes bile acid deficiency, cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, adrenal insufficiency and congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Mechanistically, a lanosterol demethylase acts within the biosynthetic route, while 7alpha-, 24-, 25- and 27-hydroxylases initiate the neutral and acidic bile acid pathways and clear sterols from tissues such as brain; mitochondrial side-chain cleavage and the 11beta- and 21-hydroxylases divert cholesterol into glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and sex steroids, supported by ferredoxin and its reductase as the electron supply. Output is controlled transcriptionally through the bile acid receptor FXR with RXR and nuclear receptor coactivators, and through aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling.

Cytochrome P450 enzymes acting on endogenous sterols set the balance between cholesterol made, converted and disposed of, and that balance determines circulating lipid levels, bile flow, and the supply of steroid hormones. One branch runs biosynthesis, where a lanosterol 14-alpha demethylase step is required to reach cholesterol; another converts cholesterol into bile acids, with the classical route initiated by cholesterol 7-alpha hydroxylase and alternative routes through sterol 27- and 25-hydroxylation, feedback-controlled by the bile acid receptor FXR with RXR. A third branch, in adrenal cortex, gonads and placenta, cleaves the cholesterol side chain and hydroxylates intermediates to make glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and oestrogens, supported by adrenodoxin and its reductase as the electron relay. Brain-specific 24-hydroxylation allows sterol export across the blood-brain barrier. Loss of individual enzymes causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia, bile acid synthesis defects and hypercholesterolaemia-linked cardiovascular disease.

Epigenetic regulation of gene expression is the set of heritable chromatin states that lock in which genes a cell may express, without altering DNA sequence. It is what makes a fat cell stay a fat cell and a lineage-inappropriate gene stay silent through division, and its breakdown underlies developmental syndromes and the aberrant silencing of tumour suppressors in cancer. The machinery covers writers, erasers and readers: Polycomb complexes deposit H3K27me3 and PRC1-mediated H2A ubiquitination, DNMT1 with UHRF1 propagates cytosine methylation while TET enzymes and TDG reverse it, SET1/MLL and WDR5-containing methyltransferases and KAT2B-type acetyltransferases activate, and Sin3/NuRD and NCoR deacetylase complexes repress. Related arms tune ribosomal RNA transcription to metabolic demand, drive nuclear receptor-directed adipocyte differentiation through PPARG and coactivators, and silence retroelements via KRAB zinc fingers, TRIM28, SETDB1 and the HUSH complex.

Heritable control of which genes a cell expresses, without altering DNA sequence, is what allows one genome to produce many stable cell identities. This epigenetic regulation of gene expression writes, reads and erases covalent marks on DNA and histones: DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B transfer methyl groups to cytosine while TET1-3 with TDG reverse that mark by oxidation and base excision; PRC2 subunits EZH2/EZH1, EED and SUZ12 deposit H3K27 trimethylation, and SETDB1, EHMT2 and SUV39H1 generate H3K9 methylation for silencing. Coactivator acetyltransferases, SIN3/NuRD/CoREST deacetylase complexes, SWI/SNF remodellers, COMPASS methyltransferases with WDR5 and the Mediator complex tune promoter output, including metabolic programmes such as PPARG-driven adipocyte differentiation and nutrient-responsive ribosomal RNA transcription. KRAB zinc fingers with TRIM28, the HUSH complex and piRNA machinery keep retroelements transcriptionally silent. Loss of these activities causes developmental syndromes and is pervasive in cancer.

EGFR interacts with phospholipase C-gamma is the branch of epidermal growth factor receptor signalling that converts ligand binding at the cell surface into calcium and protein kinase C signals. It gives growth factors control over rapid, membrane-proximal events such as cytoskeletal remodelling, motility and secretion, alongside the longer-term proliferative output of the receptor, and it is one of the arms exploited when EGFR is amplified or mutated in carcinoma and glioma. Any of several ligands -- EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or HB-EGF -- dimerises and autophosphorylates the receptor, creating phosphotyrosine docking sites that recruit PLC-gamma1 through its SH2 domains. Once phosphorylated, the enzyme hydrolyses PIP2 to IP3 and diacylglycerol, releasing calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores and activating protein kinase C isoforms, thereby linking receptor tyrosine kinase activity to phosphoinositide turnover.

Growth factor binding to the EGF receptor does more than switch on kinase cascades; one branch of its output runs through phospholipid turnover, and that is what this pathway captures. Any of several ligands — EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or heparin-binding EGF — dimerises and autophosphorylates the receptor, creating docking sites that recruit phospholipase C-gamma1 through its SH2 domains. Once tyrosine phosphorylated at the membrane, PLCG1 cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, so a single receptor event raises cytosolic calcium released from internal stores and activates protein kinase C. The resulting calcium and PKC signals feed into proliferation, migration and cytoskeletal remodelling in epithelia, and inappropriate output from this arm contributes to the growth and invasiveness of EGFR-driven carcinomas.

Hyaluronan metabolism covers the synthesis, turnover and clearance of the one glycosaminoglycan that is unsulfated, unattached to any core protein, and made at the plasma membrane rather than in the Golgi. Its enormous hydrated polymers give connective tissue, skin, cartilage and joint fluid their lubrication, compressive resilience and space-filling bulk, and they also serve as a signalling matrix: fragment size determines whether hyaluronan is quiescent or pro-inflammatory and pro-migratory. Hyaluronan synthases extrude the growing chain outward, while hyaluronidases, CEMIP and lysosomal exoglycosidases such as GUSB and hexosaminidase degrade it, with acidification and sialic acid export supporting the lysosomal step. Receptors including CD44, HMMR, LYVE1 and the scavenger STAB2 mediate cell adhesion, motility and lymphatic uptake for systemic clearance. Dysregulated production accompanies tumour invasion, fibrosis and inflammatory tissue remodelling.

Hyaluronan is the one glycosaminoglycan made without sulfation and without a protein core, and its metabolism covers both its synthesis at the plasma membrane and its turnover. Because the polymer holds enormous volumes of water, it gives cartilage, skin and connective tissue their compressive resilience and lubrication, and its fragmentation into short oligosaccharides converts a structural filler into a signal that drives inflammation, angiogenesis and cell migration. Membrane synthases extrude growing chains directly into the extracellular space, while hyaluronidases and CEMIP cleave them; the receptors CD44, HMMR, LYVE1 and the scavenger STAB2 mediate binding, migratory signalling and clearance through lymphatics and liver. Internalised fragments are degraded in lysosomes by beta-glucuronidase and hexosaminidases, with the sialin transporter exporting the released sugars. Dysregulated turnover accompanies tumour invasion, fibrosis and joint degeneration.

FMO oxidises nucleophiles is a phase I drug-metabolising route that converts soft nucleophilic heteroatoms — nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus — into more polar N-, S- and P-oxides, priming xenobiotics, dietary amines and many therapeutics for conjugation and excretion. It works alongside cytochrome P450s in liver, kidney and lung microsomes but by a distinct chemistry: NADPH first reduces the bound FAD, molecular oxygen adds to give a stable C4a-hydroperoxyflavin, and this pre-activated enzyme simply waits for a substrate to present a lone pair, transferring one oxygen and releasing water. Because activation precedes substrate binding, the enzymes are broadly promiscuous and, unlike P450s, are not induced by their substrates. FMO3 dominates in adult liver, and its loss causes trimethylaminuria, in which unoxidised dietary trimethylamine accumulates and produces a strong fish-like body odour.

Flavin-containing monooxygenases make up the second major family of microsomal drug-oxidising enzymes, working alongside the cytochrome P450s to oxygenate soft nucleophiles. By adding oxygen to nitrogen, sulfur or phosphorus atoms, they convert amines, sulfides and related xenobiotics into N-oxides, S-oxides and P-oxides that are more polar and readily excreted, and they detoxify dietary and bacterially derived compounds absorbed from the gut. Catalysis runs in an unusual order: NADPH reduces the bound FAD cofactor, molecular oxygen is captured as a flavin hydroperoxide, and only then does the substrate encounter the activated oxygen, so these enzymes are neither substrate-inducible nor dependent on substrate binding for activation. FMO1, FMO2 and FMO3 carry this nucleophile-oxidising activity, with the hepatic FMO3 form dominant in adults; its loss leaves trimethylamine unoxidised and produces the fish-odour syndrome trimethylaminuria, and variation across the family shapes individual drug clearance.

NOTCH2 intracellular domain regulates transcription is the nuclear output step of NOTCH2 signalling: after ligand-induced cleavage, the released intracellular domain enters the nucleus and switches on genes that specify cell fate. It matters for bile duct and kidney development, for marginal-zone B cell identity, and for cytotoxic lymphocyte function; its dysregulation contributes to B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and, through loss-of-function, to Alagille syndrome. Mechanistically the intracellular domain converts RBPJ from a repressor into an activator by recruiting a Mastermind-like coactivator and histone acetyltransferase EP300 at RBPJ-binding elements. Targets include the HES1 and HES5 repressors shared with NOTCH1, and others that are NOTCH2-selective, notably FCER2/CD23A, whose overexpression marks leukaemic B cells and can be mimicked by Epstein-Barr virus EBNA2. At the granzyme B promoter the complex cooperates with phosphorylated CREB1 to support CD8+ T-cell killing.

Once NOTCH2 is cleaved at the membrane, its released intracellular domain travels to the nucleus and becomes a transcription factor subunit, and this step is where NOTCH2 signalling actually changes gene expression. The cleaved domain binds the DNA-binding protein RBPJ and a mastermind-like coactivator, converting RBPJ from a repressive to an activating complex on RBPJ-binding promoter elements. Direct targets include the HES1 and HES5 repressors shared with other Notch receptors, plus targets that distinguish NOTCH2: the low-affinity IgE receptor FCER2/CD23, whose overexpression is a hallmark of B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and is mimicked by Epstein-Barr virus EBNA2, and granzyme B, activated jointly with phosphorylated CREB1 and the acetyltransferase EP300 to support CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity. The same output contributes to bile duct and kidney development.

Constitutive Signaling by Aberrant PI3K in Cancer describes how tumours lock the PI3K/AKT axis into the "on" state without any growth factor being present, giving cells continuous survival, growth and metabolic signalling. Gain-of-function mutations in PIK3CA, encoding the p110alpha catalytic subunit, or in PIK3R1, encoding the p85alpha regulatory subunit, are among the most common events in breast, endometrial and colorectal cancer, and they make tumours dependent on, and treatable by, PI3K and AKT inhibitors. Helical-domain and SH2-domain mutations break the inhibitory clamp p85 normally holds on p110 while the two subunits stay bound; catalytic-domain mutations favour an active kinase conformation. Either way PIP3 is generated and AKT is engaged ligand-independently. The surrounding receptor tyrosine kinases, ligands and adaptors such as GRB2, GAB1, IRS1 and PTPN11 mark the normal upstream input that the mutant enzyme bypasses.

Class I PI3Ks normally fire only when a growth factor receptor is engaged, and the resulting PIP3 signal drives AKT-dependent growth, anabolic metabolism and survival. Gain-of-function mutations in the p110alpha catalytic subunit or the p85alpha regulatory subunit uncouple this from ligand, so the kinase produces PIP3 and activates AKT constitutively — one of the most common oncogenic events in breast, endometrial and colorectal cancer, and the rationale for PI3K and AKT inhibitors. Helical-domain and nSH2/iSH2 mutations break the inhibitory contact between the two subunits while keeping them bound, whereas catalytic-domain mutations favour an intrinsically active conformation. The surrounding machinery defines what is bypassed: receptor tyrosine kinases and their ligands from the EGF, FGF, PDGF, HGF and neurotrophin families, adaptors such as GRB2, GAB1/2, IRS1/2 and PTPN11, and Src-family and Rac components that couple receptors to lipid kinase activation.

Cellular responses to stress collects the programs cells use to survive perturbations of their internal and external environment — oxygen shortage, heat, oxidants and electrophiles, nutrient and amino acid deprivation, misfolded protein burden, heme deficiency — and to shut down proliferation permanently when damage cannot be repaired. Tissue homeostasis depends on it, and its components are the levers of ageing, tumour suppression and adaptation to ischaemia. The genes trace several coordinated arms: HIF stabilisation by prolyl hydroxylases and VHL driving hypoxic transcription; KEAP1–NFE2L2 control of glutathione, thioredoxin and peroxiredoxin antioxidant defence; HSF1 with HSP70, HSP90 and small chaperones in proteostasis and steroid receptor maturation; PERK, ATF6 and IRE1–XBP1 in the unfolded protein response; eIF2α kinases restraining translation; mTORC1 regulation by Rag GTPases and sestrins under starvation; and p53, CDK inhibitors, telomere proteins and Polycomb complexes enforcing senescence and its inflammatory secretion.

Cells constantly meet insults from outside and from their own metabolism — low oxygen, heat, oxidants, misfolded proteins, nutrient shortage, heme or amino acid deficiency — and this collection of cellular stress responses is how they adjust to survive or withdraw from the cell cycle. Its outputs maintain tissue homeostasis; its failure underlies degeneration, ischemic injury and, when senescence programmes are bypassed, tumour growth. Oxygen sensing runs through prolyl hydroxylases and VHL-dependent turnover of HIF1A/EPAS1, which switch on erythropoietin, VEGFA and glycolytic and respiratory adaptations. Heat shock factor HSF1 with HSP90, HSP70 and small chaperones restores proteostasis, while ER stress sensors ATF6, ERN1/XBP1 and PERK-family kinases converge on EIF2S1 phosphorylation, ATF4 and CHOP to throttle translation. KEAP1–NFE2L2 drives antioxidant and glutathione genes; mTORC1 with Rag GTPases, GATOR and sestrins gauges nutrients; p53, CDKN1A and polycomb–telomere components enforce senescence.</description>

Phosphate bond hydrolysis by NUDT proteins is the cell's nucleotide sanitation and housekeeping system, clearing damaged or surplus nucleotides before they can be used. Its main payoff is genome and proteome fidelity: NUDT1 (MTH1) destroys 8-oxo-dGTP and other oxidised purine nucleotides so they are never incorporated into DNA or mRNA, and NUDT15 and NUDT18 act on related oxidised or modified substrates, while NUDT16 additionally trims inosine-containing nucleotides and RNA caps. Loss of this surveillance raises mutation rates and mistranslation under oxidative stress. Other members handle metabolic intermediates: NUDT5 and NUDT9 hydrolyse ADP-ribose, preventing spontaneous non-enzymatic ADP-ribosylation of proteins and feeding nucleotide and NAD-related salvage, and ADPRM cleaves ADP-ribose-derived phosphoesters. The shared Nudix motif coordinates the magnesium ion used for catalysis. NUDT15 activity also governs how patients tolerate thiopurine drugs.

Nudix hydrolases keep the cellular nucleotide pool clean, and the phosphate bond hydrolysis they carry out is best understood as sanitation: damaged or surplus nucleotides are cleaved before they can be used as substrates. Oxidised, deaminated or methylated purine nucleoside di- and triphosphates are degraded by enzymes such as NUDT1, NUDT15 and NUDT18, preventing their incorporation into DNA as mutations or into mRNA as mistranslated protein. NUDT16 acts on inosine- and other modified guanine-containing nucleotides, while NUDT9 and NUDT5 hydrolyse ADP-ribose, limiting non-enzymatic ADP-ribosylation of proteins and the accumulation of a potent second messenger; ADPRM degrades ADP-ribose 1''-phosphate from tRNA splicing. Because these enzymes also destroy nucleotide analogues, their activity sets tolerance to thiopurine and other nucleoside-based chemotherapies, and NUDT15 variants cause severe drug toxicity.

Metabolism of ingested H2SeO4 and H2SeO3 into H2Se converts dietary inorganic selenium into the single reduced form the cell can actually use. Hydrogen selenide is the obligatory precursor for selenophosphate and thus for the selenocysteine inserted into glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases and iodothyronine deiodinases; without this reduction step, ingested selenate and selenite cannot support antioxidant defence, thyroid hormone activation or male fertility, and selenoprotein synthesis fails. Selenate is first activated by the bifunctional PAPS synthases PAPSS1 and PAPSS2, borrowing the sulfate assimilation machinery, and the adenylylated intermediate is reduced onward. Selenite is reduced more directly at the expense of NADPH-dependent thiol systems, with thioredoxin reductase 1 and glutathione reductase supplying reducing equivalents through thioredoxin and glutathione. The chemistry is redox-costly and generates reactive intermediates, which is one reason selenium is beneficial at trace levels and toxic in excess.

Dietary selenium arrives largely as inorganic selenate and selenite, but the only form the cell can use for selenoprotein synthesis is hydrogen selenide, and this reductive route makes the conversion. Without it, selenocysteine cannot be charged onto its dedicated tRNA, and the whole selenoprotein family — glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases, iodothyronine deiodinases — fails to be made, with consequences for antioxidant defence and thyroid hormone activation. Reduction proceeds stepwise: the bifunctional sulfate-activating enzymes PAPSS1 and PAPSS2 adenylate selenate as they would sulfate, a reductase step acts on the activated intermediate, and thiol-based reducing systems built on thioredoxin reductase 1 and glutathione reductase, fed by NADPH, carry selenite through to selenide. The chemistry borrows the sulfur assimilation machinery, reflecting the close similarity of selenium and sulfur. Excess selenium is toxic, so flux through this pathway also matters for handling overload.

Selenocysteine synthesis builds the 21st amino acid on its own tRNA and delivers it into growing proteins, supplying the catalytic residue of glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases and the deiodinases. Through these selenoproteins it underwrites cellular antioxidant defence, redox signalling and thyroid hormone activation; loss of the pathway causes selenoprotein deficiency syndromes with abnormal thyroid hormone metabolism, myopathy, and, for SEPSECS mutations, progressive cerebello-cerebral atrophy. Serine is first charged onto tRNA(Sec) by seryl-tRNA synthetase, phosphorylated by PSTK, and converted to selenocysteinyl-tRNA(Sec) by SEPSECS using selenophosphate from SEPHS2. Because UGA normally terminates translation, incorporation is a recoding event: SECISBP2 binds a SECIS element in the 3' untranslated region and recruits the dedicated elongation factor EEFSEC to the ribosome, so the full complement of large and small subunit ribosomal proteins is integral to the process.

Selenocysteine is the 21st amino acid and the catalytic residue of glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases and the deiodinases, so its synthesis is what allows the cell to build selenoproteins and defend itself against peroxides. Unusually, the amino acid is made on its own tRNA rather than free: seryl-tRNA synthetase charges tRNA(Sec) with serine, PSTK phosphorylates it, SEPHS2 generates the selenium donor selenophosphate, and SEPSECS converts the phosphoseryl intermediate into selenocysteinyl-tRNA(Sec). Delivery is equally specialised — the dedicated elongation factor EEFSEC and the SECIS-binding protein SECISBP2 recode an in-frame UGA codon from stop to selenocysteine, which is why the large and small ribosomal subunit proteins accompany this chemistry. Loss of SEPSECS causes progressive cerebello-cerebral atrophy, and SECISBP2 defects disturb thyroid hormone metabolism, linking selenium handling to brain development and endocrine function.

IRS-related events triggered by IGF1R describes how insulin-like growth factor signalling is converted into the two major growth-promoting cascades of the cell. Ligand-bound IGF1R phosphorylates the insulin receptor substrate scaffolds IRS1, IRS2 and IRS4, which then recruit PI3K regulatory and catalytic subunits and the GRB2:SOS complex, launching PI3K-PDK1-AKT survival and metabolic signalling alongside RAS-RAF-MAPK proliferative signalling. This axis drives somatic growth, anabolic metabolism, cell survival and tissue regeneration, and its inappropriate activation is a recurrent feature of cancers, where IGF1R and IRS levels correlate with resistance to therapy. Shared adaptors such as FRS2, GAB1/2, PTPN11 and the RAS isoforms link this route to closely related receptor tyrosine kinase inputs including FGF receptors and FLT3, while negative regulators such as TRIB3 and feedback on IRS phosphorylation set the duration of the response.

Growth factor signalling through the type 1 insulin-like growth factor receptor is routed largely through IRS scaffold proteins, and this branch is what converts IGF1 and IGF2 binding into cell growth, survival and anabolic metabolism during development and tissue maintenance. The activated receptor phosphorylates IRS1, IRS2 and IRS4 on tyrosines, creating docking sites for the PI3K regulatory subunits and for GRB2:SOS; the first arm generates PIP3 and activates AKT via PDPK1, the second loads RAS proteins to drive the RAF-MAPK cascade. Additional adaptors such as GAB1/GAB2, FRS2 and the phosphatase PTPN11 shape the output, and negative regulators including TRIB3 restrain AKT. The same adaptor logic is shared with fibroblast growth factor receptors and FLT3, which is why those ligands and receptors appear alongside. Overactive signalling here supports tumour proliferation and resistance to therapy, while impairment produces growth deficiency and insulin-like resistance.

Establishment of Sister Chromatid Cohesion is the step in S phase that converts the transient, dynamic loading of cohesin onto chromatin into a stable embrace of the two newly replicated sister chromatids. Without it sisters cannot be held together until anaphase, and chromosomes missegregate, producing aneuploidy; mutations in these components underlie cohesinopathies such as Roberts syndrome. Cohesin itself is a ring of SMC1A, SMC3 and RAD21 with a STAG1 or STAG2 subunit, and its residence on DNA reflects a tug of war between loading and the release activity of WAPL bound to PDS5A/PDS5B. Replication-coupled acetylation of SMC3 by ESCO1 and ESCO2 permits recruitment of sororin (CDCA5), which displaces WAPL and locks the ring in place. This licensing underpins faithful chromosome segregation, and also feeds into DNA repair and chromatin looping.

After DNA replication, each chromosome exists as two identical copies that must stay physically linked until anaphase, and this is how that linkage is made permanent. Cohesin — a ring of SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21 and a STAG subunit — loads onto chromatin from telophase onward but cycles on and off, with WAPL driving release. During S phase the acetyltransferases ESCO1 and ESCO2 acetylate SMC3, which together with PDS5A/PDS5B allows CDCA5 (sororin) to bind and displace WAPL, locking cohesin onto replicated DNA. Stable cohesion gives the spindle the resistance it needs to biorient sister kinetochores, so its failure produces premature sister separation, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy. Mutations in ESCO2 and cohesin subunits underlie cohesinopathies such as Roberts syndrome and Cornelia de Lange syndrome, and the same complex also shapes interphase genome architecture and supports recombinational repair.

The phototransduction cascade converts a single absorbed photon into an electrical signal in rod photoreceptors, making dim-light vision possible; mutations in its components cause retinitis pigmentosa, congenital stationary night blindness and Leber congenital amaurosis. Light isomerizes the 11-cis-retinal chromophore of rhodopsin, which activates the G protein transducin; the freed alpha subunit stimulates PDE6 to hydrolyse cGMP, closing CNGA1/CNGB1 cation channels and hyperpolarizing the outer segment. The hyperpolarization reaches the synapse, shuts voltage-gated calcium channels, and reduces tonic glutamate release onto bipolar cells. Equally represented is the shutoff and recovery arm that resets sensitivity for the next photon: rhodopsin kinase and arrestin quench the receptor, an RGS9 complex terminates transducin, and calcium sensing through recoverin, guanylate cyclase activating proteins and the NCKX1 exchanger restores cGMP synthesis. Lipid modification and N-terminal processing enzymes anchor and mature the cascade's membrane-associated subunits.

Vision begins when a photon isomerizes the retinal chromophore bound to rhodopsin, and this cascade converts that single molecular event into an electrical signal a rod photoreceptor can send to the retina. Activated opsin turns on the G protein transducin, whose alpha subunit releases the inhibitory gamma subunits of PDE6 so that cGMP is hydrolysed; cGMP-gated cation channels built from CNGA1 and CNGB1 then close and the cell hyperpolarizes, reducing glutamate release at the synapse. Equally important is shutoff and recovery: rhodopsin kinase and arrestin quench the receptor, an RGS9 complex accelerates transducin deactivation, and calcium sensed by recoverin and the guanylate cyclase activators GUCA1A/B feeds back on cyclase activity to restore cGMP and set light adaptation. Mutations in these components underlie retinitis pigmentosa, congenital stationary night blindness and Leber congenital amaurosis.

Inactivation, recovery and regulation of the phototransduction cascade is the shut-off arm of vision in rod and cone photoreceptors: after a photon has been counted, activated rhodopsin, transducin and phosphodiesterase 6 must all be quenched and cGMP restored so the CNG channels reopen and the cell can respond to the next photon. Without it photoreceptors cannot adapt to background light or recover sensitivity, and mutations in these components cause congenital stationary night blindness, Oguchi disease, cone dystrophies and Leber congenital amaurosis. Rhodopsin kinase phosphorylates the bleached pigment and arrestin caps it, with recoverin gating kinase activity as a calcium sensor; an RGS9 complex accelerates GTP hydrolysis on the transducin alpha subunit to silence PDE6; and calcium-sensitive guanylate cyclase activators drive GUCY2D to resynthesise cGMP. Lipid and terminal modifications of the subunits determine their membrane targeting and turnover.

After a rod or cone has responded to light, it must switch off and reset before it can report the next photon, and this shutoff-and-recovery arm of phototransduction is what makes vision fast, reproducible and able to adapt to background light. Activated rhodopsin is quenched by rhodopsin kinase phosphorylation followed by arrestin capping, with recoverin gating the kinase in a calcium-dependent way; the transducin-PDE6 complex is turned off by a GTPase-activating assembly of RGS9 with its membrane anchor and G-beta-5. Falling calcium through the cyclic-nucleotide-gated channel releases guanylate cyclase activating proteins to stimulate retinal guanylate cyclase, restoring cGMP and reopening the channels. Lipid modification and N-terminal processing enzymes supply the myristoylation and farnesylation that hold these components at the disc membrane. Mutations in the cyclase, its activator, arrestin or PDE6 subunits cause stationary night blindness, cone dystrophy and retinitis pigmentosa.

Interaction With Cumulus Cells And The Zona Pellucida covers the first physical encounter between a fertilizing sperm and the egg's protective coverings, the step that decides whether fertilization happens at all and whether it happens with a single sperm. The mammalian oocyte is wrapped in cumulus cells set in a hyaluronan-rich matrix and, beneath that, the zona pellucida built from the glycoproteins ZP1-ZP4. Sperm hyaluronidase (SPAM1) lets an acrosome-intact sperm penetrate the cumulus layer, after which ZP glycoproteins mediate species-restricted binding and trigger the acrosome reaction; ADAM family sperm surface proteins and the galactosyltransferase B4GALT1 contribute to adhesion, while oviductal glycoprotein OVGP1 modifies the zona in the reproductive tract. The same matrix blocks polyspermy and shields the early embryo until implantation. Defects in ZP genes cause empty follicle syndrome and female infertility.

Before a sperm can fuse with an egg it must cross two barriers, and this pathway covers those first encounters: passage through the hyaluronan-rich cumulus cell layer and binding to the zona pellucida. The zona is built from four glycoproteins, ZP1-ZP4, which mediate species-specific sperm recognition, trigger the acrosome reaction in bound sperm, block fertilization by more than one sperm, and shield the cleaving embryo until implantation. A hyaluronidase on the sperm surface, SPAM1, digests the cumulus matrix, while ADAM-family sperm proteins and glycan-modifying enzymes such as B4GALT1 and the oviduct-secreted glycoprotein OVGP1 shape adhesive recognition between the gametes. Mutations in the zona genes cause empty follicle and zona-defect infertility in women, and these same molecules are the basis of immunocontraceptive strategies and of diagnostic sperm-binding assays.

Cellular Senescence is the permanent exit from the cell cycle that a cell adopts when it sustains DNA damage, exhausts its telomeres, or experiences oncogene activation, and it is one of the body's main barriers to tumour formation. Senescent cells accumulate with age and drive tissue decline through the inflammatory secretome they release. The genes trace the routes in: telomere capping by the shelterin complex and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN sensor feeding ATM to p53, and the p16/p21 inhibitors that shut down CDK4/6 and CDK2 to keep RB1 bound to E2F. Downstream, HIRA and ASF1A restructure chromatin into heterochromatic foci while Polycomb complexes and EZH2 silence proliferative genes, and stress kinase signalling through p38 with NF-kB and CEBPB switches on the secretory programme of IL6, IL1A and CXCL8 that reinforces arrest and alters neighbouring cells.

Cellular senescence is the permanent withdrawal of a damaged or oncogene-stressed cell from the division cycle, a barrier against tumour formation that also drives tissue ageing as senescent cells accumulate. Triggers converge on two arrest circuits: the p53-p21 axis engaged by DNA damage sensing through ATM and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and by telomere uncapping when shelterin components such as TRF1, TRF2 and POT1 are lost, and the p16/p15-RB axis that keeps CDK4/6-cyclin D and E2F targets silenced. Chromatin is remodelled into senescence-associated heterochromatic foci with HIRA-ASF1A histone chaperoning, Polycomb repressors and lamin B1 loss, while stress-activated p38 and JNK kinases with NF-kB, CEBPB and STAT3 drive the senescence-associated secretory phenotype -- IL6, IL1A and IL8 among them -- which reinforces arrest locally and can promote inflammation and invasiveness in neighbouring cells.

Formation of Senescence-Associated Heterochromatin Foci (SAHF) is the chromatin remodelling step that makes cellular senescence permanent. When DNA damage or telomere attrition forces a cell out of the cycle, each chromosome condenses into a single punctate focus of facultative heterochromatin that silences proliferation-promoting genes, so the arrest cannot be reversed by growth signals; this is a barrier to tumourigenesis and a feature of ageing tissue. A conserved histone chaperone complex of HIRA, ASF1A, UBN1 and CABIN1 first accumulates in PML nuclear bodies, then relocates to the forming foci, depositing histone H3.3 and macroH2A while H3K9 methylation and HP1 mark the compacted domains. HMGA proteins and linker histone H1 redistribution drive the architectural change, and loss of lamin B1 accompanies it. Focus formation depends on intact RB1 and TP53 signalling, linking it to CDKN1A-mediated cell cycle exit.

Cells that have sustained irreparable DNA damage or critically short telomeres exit the cell cycle for good, and the assembly of senescence-associated heterochromatin foci is how that exit is made permanent. Each chromosome condenses into a single punctate focus of facultative heterochromatin bearing H3K9 methylation, with telomeric and centromeric regions pushed to the periphery, and proliferation-promoting genes driven by E2F are locked in a silent state. A conserved histone chaperone complex of HIRA, ASF1A, UBN1 and CABIN1 stages at PML nuclear bodies before relocating to the forming foci, depositing histone H3.3 and remodelling chromatin; linker H1 variants, HMGA proteins and loss of lamin B1 accompany the structural reorganisation. Formation depends on intact RB1 and TP53 signalling, with CDKN1A enforcing the arrest. This chromatin endpoint underlies tumour suppression by senescence and contributes to the altered nuclear architecture of aged tissue.

Regulation of PLK1 Activity at G2/M Transition governs the switch that commits a cell to mitosis, setting the moment at which centrosomes mature, spindle assembly begins, and the nuclear envelope breaks down. PLK1 must be turned on at the right time and place and then turned off again; failure of this timing produces spindle defects, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, and PLK1 is a target of anti-mitotic cancer drugs. Aurora A, activated on centrosomes with the help of AJUBA, phosphorylates PLK1 on T210 in a reaction requiring BORA, which PLK1 then marks for SCF/beta-TrCP-mediated destruction so that other substrates can be engaged. A negative feedback arm runs through optineurin, released from RAB8-positive Golgi membranes, which promotes activation of MYPT1-containing myosin phosphatase to dephosphorylate T210. The accompanying centrosomal, gamma-tubulin, augmin and dynein components are the machinery this control acts upon.

Entry into mitosis depends on switching on PLK1, the kinase that ripens centrosomes, drives mitotic entry and later governs cytokinesis, and this pathway describes how its activity is turned on and off at the G2/M transition. Aurora A kinase, itself activated by AJUBA-assisted autophosphorylation at the centrosome, phosphorylates PLK1 on Thr210 with BORA as a cofactor; active PLK1 then phosphorylates BORA to mark it for SCF/beta-TrCP-mediated ubiquitination and destruction, freeing the kinase for its mitotic substrates. A negative-feedback limb runs through optineurin, which leaves Golgi-associated RAB8 for the nucleus and promotes myosin phosphatase activation, dephosphorylating Thr210 to shut PLK1 down. The accompanying centriolar, gamma-tubulin, augmin and dynein components place this control on the maturing centrosome and spindle poles. Deregulation couples centrosome amplification and chromosome missegregation to tumorigenesis, and PLK1 is a drug target.

Insulin processing is the route by which a pancreatic beta cell converts newly made preproinsulin into crystalline, secretion-ready insulin granules poised beneath the plasma membrane. It defines the secretory identity of the beta cell, and defects in it produce hyperproinsulinaemia and diabetes. In the endoplasmic reticulum, P4HB and ERO1B install three disulfide bonds in proinsulin; the folded hormone traffics to the Golgi and complexes with zinc, supplied by the granule transporter SLC30A8, and calcium. Within immature granules the prohormone convertases PCSK1 and PCSK2 cleave proinsulin at two sites and carboxypeptidase E trims the ends, releasing mature insulin and C-peptide. Kinesin-1 motors move granules along microtubules and myosin Va with RAB27A and MYRIP carry them through cortical actin, after which the exocyst tethers them and syntaxin-1A with VAMP2 drives calcium-triggered fusion.

Pancreatic beta cells make insulin as an inactive precursor, and insulin processing is the sequence of folding, cleavage and packaging that converts preproinsulin into the mature hormone held ready for release. Without it, glucose cannot be cleared after a meal, and defects in the granule machinery contribute to diabetes. In the endoplasmic reticulum, disulfide bond formation assisted by protein disulfide isomerase (P4HB) and the oxidase ERO1B produces correctly folded proinsulin, which travels to the Golgi and complexes with zinc supplied by transporters such as SLC30A8. Within immature granules, the prohormone convertases PCSK1 and PCSK2 cut proinsulin and carboxypeptidase E trims the ends, liberating insulin and C-peptide, which crystallise with zinc and calcium. Kinesins and myosin Va, with RAB27A and MYRIP, move granules to the cell cortex, where exocyst components dock them and SNAREs including STX1A and VAMP2 drive calcium-triggered exocytosis.

Stimuli-sensing channels covers the ion channels that convert physical and chemical stimuli — heat, cold, acid, mechanical pressure, taste, light-driven signals — into electrical and calcium signals a cell can act on. They define sensory neurons and taste cells, set thresholds for pain and itch, and their mutation causes inherited pain syndromes, retinal degeneration, muscle disease and epithelial transport disorders. TRP family members act as polymodal detectors of temperature, capsaicin, menthol and osmotic stress, while acid-sensing channels report tissue acidification during inflammation and ischaemia. A second theme is calcium itself as the stimulus: ryanodine receptors with triadin and calsequestrin release stores for muscle contraction, and bestrophins, anoctamins and tweety homologs open calcium-activated chloride currents. Epithelial sodium channels under WNK and SGK control, chloride channels and mucolipins extend the same logic to salt handling, endolysosomal function and, through RIPK3–MLKL, membrane permeabilisation during necroptosis.

Sensation begins at the membrane, where stimuli-sensing channels convert heat, cold, acid, mechanical force, irritant chemicals, taste and light-driven signals into ionic current. TRP channels dominate this repertoire: TRPV1 responds to capsaicin and noxious heat, TRPM8 to cold and menthol, TRPA1 to reactive irritants, and TRPM5 supports taste transduction, while TRPV5/TRPV6 and TRPM6/TRPM7 handle epithelial calcium and magnesium uptake. Acid-sensing channels detect extracellular protons during inflammation and ischaemia, contributing to pain. Calcium-gated and calcium-permeable components broaden the theme, including bestrophins and anoctamins as anion channels, ryanodine receptors releasing store calcium with calsequestrin and triadin, and endolysosomal mucolipins and two-pore channels. Chloride channels, ENaC subunits with their WNK, SGK and NEDD4L regulators, and NALCN set epithelial transport and background excitability. Mutations cause pain syndromes, retinal and renal disease, and myopathies.

Abnormal conversion of 2-oxoglutarate to 2-hydroxyglutarate describes the neomorphic activity acquired by isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 when its arginine 132 residue is mutated, an event found in the majority of low-grade gliomas and secondary glioblastomas as well as in other cancers. The normal cytosolic enzyme oxidizes isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate while generating NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence; the mutant instead consumes NADPH to reduce 2-oxoglutarate to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate, which accumulates to millimolar levels. Because 2-hydroxyglutarate competitively inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, including the TET DNA demethylases, JmjC histone demethylases and prolyl hydroxylases, the metabolic lesion is transmitted to the epigenome, producing the hypermethylation phenotype and blocked differentiation characteristic of these tumours. This links central carbon metabolism directly to chromatin state, and makes the mutant enzyme a tractable drug target.

Cancer-associated mutations at arginine 132 of the cytosolic isocitrate dehydrogenase IDH1 convert a routine metabolic step into the production of an oncometabolite. Wild-type IDH1 oxidatively decarboxylates isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate while reducing NADP+, supplying both a citric acid cycle intermediate and cytosolic NADPH for redox defence and lipid synthesis. The mutant enzyme instead reduces 2-oxoglutarate using NADPH to give 2-hydroxyglutarate, which builds up to millimolar levels in the cytosol. Because 2-hydroxyglutarate closely resembles 2-oxoglutarate, it competitively inhibits dioxygenases that depend on it, including histone and DNA demethylases and prolyl hydroxylases, producing the hypermethylated, differentiation-blocked state characteristic of IDH1-mutant tumours. The alteration is frequent in gliomas and glioblastomas and also occurs in acute myeloid leukaemia, and it serves both as a diagnostic marker and as a drug target for mutant-selective inhibitors.

Nuclear Envelope (NE) Reassembly rebuilds the nucleus at the end of mitosis, enclosing the separated sister chromatids in a sealed membrane with functional pores so that each daughter cell regains a compartment distinct from the cytoplasm. Without it, nucleocytoplasmic transport cannot be re-established, chromatin is exposed to cytoplasmic surveillance, and micronuclei or aberrant nuclear shapes arise. Reassembly is driven by reversal of mitotic phosphorylation: CDK1-cyclin B activity is extinguished and PP2A dephosphorylates lamins and inner nuclear membrane proteins such as emerin, LBR and LEM-domain proteins, while BANF1, counter-regulated by VRK kinases, tethers membranes to chromatin. Nucleoporin subcomplexes reassemble around ELYS-marked chromatin, and the RAN-RCC1-RanGAP gradient with importin-β restores directional transport. ESCRT-III components with VPS4 and the microtubule-severing enzyme spastin clear spindle microtubules and anneal the membrane, completing the diffusion barrier in telophase.

At the end of mitosis each daughter cell must rebuild a nucleus, and nuclear envelope reassembly is the step that restores the boundary between chromatin and cytoplasm. Beginning in late anaphase and finishing in telophase, membrane is recruited to decondensing chromatin, inner nuclear membrane and lamina proteins such as lamins, emerin, LBR and the LEM-domain proteins reaccumulate, and nuclear pore complexes are built and inserted so that regulated nucleocytoplasmic transport and the Ran gradient are re-established. Reversal of mitotic CDK1-cyclin B phosphorylation by protein phosphatase 2A, together with the chromatin-binding protein BANF1 and VRK kinases, times lamina reattachment, while ESCRT-III subunits with CHMP7, spastin and VPS4 sever residual spindle microtubules and seal remaining holes. Incomplete sealing leaves micronuclei and ruptured envelopes, a route to DNA damage, chromosomal instability and inflammatory cytosolic DNA sensing.

SUMO is transferred from E1 to E2 (UBE2I, UBC9) is the committed handoff step of protein SUMOylation, the modification that controls nuclear transport, chromatin organisation, DNA damage responses, transcriptional repression and the integrity of nuclear bodies. Activated SUMO1, SUMO2 or SUMO3, carried as a thioester on cysteine-173 of the UBA2 subunit of the SAE1-UBA2 activating enzyme, is passed by transthiolation to cysteine-93 of UBC9. UBC9 is the sole conjugating enzyme for all SUMO paralogues, so every SUMOylation event in the cell funnels through it; substrate choice is then set by E3 ligases, or, for targets such as RanGAP1 that present a consensus motif directly to UBC9, by no E3 at all. RWDD3 (RSUME) enhances the reaction by binding UBC9 and increasing thioester formation, linking SUMO conjugation to hypoxic and stress signalling.

SUMOylation modifies thousands of nuclear proteins to control their localisation, partner binding and stability, and the step described here is the handoff that loads the modifier onto the only conjugating enzyme available for it. The activating heterodimer of SAE1 and UBA2 charges SUMO1, SUMO2 or SUMO3 as a thioester, and that thioester is passed by transthiolation from a cysteine in UBA2 to the active-site cysteine of UBC9 (UBE2I), which then delivers SUMO to substrate lysines.
