Because UBC9 is the sole E2 for this pathway, the transfer is an obligatory bottleneck for all SUMO conjugation, including substrates such as RanGAP1 that need no E3 ligase; RWDD3 stimulates the reaction. Downstream consequences include nucleocytoplasmic transport, chromosome segregation, DNA damage responses and transcriptional repression, and loss of UBC9 is not tolerated by dividing cells.

PKMTs methylate histone lysines is the writing arm of the histone methylation code: SET-domain lysine methyltransferases, plus the SET-independent DOT1L, transfer methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine onto specific lysines of histones H3 and H4, marking chromatin as active or silent. These marks decide which genes a cell can express, and thereby lineage identity, developmental patterning, X inactivation, heterochromatin integrity and meiotic recombination hotspot choice; their loss or hyperactivity underlies overgrowth syndromes, leukaemias driven by KMT2A fusions, and NSD2- or EZH2-dependent tumours. Specificity is enzyme-encoded and often complex-dependent: SUV39H1, EHMT2 and SETDB1 lay down repressive H3K9 methylation, EZH2 within Polycomb repressive complex 2 with SUZ12 and EED makes H3K27 methylation, SETD1/KMT2 enzymes with the WDR5-RBBP5-ASH2L-DPY30 core mark H3K4 at promoters, NSD proteins and SETD2 mark H3K36 over transcribed bodies, and KMT5 enzymes methylate H4K20. Several members additionally methylate non-histone substrates such as NF-κB subunits.

Histone lysine methylation is one of the main ways chromatin is marked to say whether a gene should be read, and this pathway covers the enzymes that write those marks. Protein lysine methyltransferases transfer a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine onto the epsilon-amino nitrogen of specific lysines in histones H3 and H4, mostly through a SET domain, with DOT1L as the exception. Different enzymes are strikingly selective for site and for the number of methyl groups added: SUV39H1, EHMT2 and SETDB1 deposit repressive H3K9 methylation, EZH2 within a Polycomb complex with EED and SUZ12 marks H3K27, KMT2/SETD1 complexes with WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30 methylate H3K4 at active promoters, SETD2 and the NSD proteins act on H3K36, and KMT5A-C on H4K20. The resulting marks steer transcription, heterochromatin formation, DNA repair and mitotic chromosome behaviour, and mutation or translocation of these writers is a recurrent driver of leukaemia and other cancers and of developmental overgrowth syndromes.

HDMs demethylate histones removes methyl marks from histone lysines, making methylation a reversible signal rather than a permanent one and allowing cells to switch genes on and off during differentiation, development and stress responses. Two chemically distinct enzyme families do the work: KDM1A/B are FAD-dependent amine oxidases that need a protonatable lysine amine and therefore act only on mono- and dimethylated substrates, while the larger Jumonji C family are Fe(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases that also strip trimethyl groups, releasing formaldehyde, succinate and CO2. Individual enzymes are site-specific, erasing activating H3K4 and H3K36 marks (KDM5, KDM2), repressive H3K9 marks (KDM3, KDM4) or H3K27 marks (KDM6A/B), so their balance sets promoter and heterochromatin states. Their dependence on oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate links chromatin to metabolic status, and mutations cause intellectual disability syndromes and drive cancers.

Histone methylation is not a permanent mark, and the demethylases that erase it make chromatin states reversible, allowing genes to be switched between active and repressed as cells differentiate or respond to signals. Two chemically distinct groups do the work: KDM1A and KDM1B are FAD-dependent amine oxidases limited to mono- and dimethylated lysines, while the Jumonji C family (KDM2-KDM7, PHF2, PHF8 and relatives) are iron(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases that also clear trimethyl marks, releasing formaldehyde along with succinate and carbon dioxide. Their specificities partition the histone code: KDM5 enzymes remove the activating H3K4me2/3 mark, KDM4 and KDM3 target repressive H3K9 methylation, and KDM6A/KDM6B strip H3K27me3 to lift Polycomb silencing. JMJD6 acts on methylated arginine and as a lysyl hydroxylase. Because these enzymes require oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate, they couple metabolism to transcription, and mutations in KDM6A, KDM5C and PHF8 cause intellectual disability syndromes and cancer.

Glycogen storage diseases covers the inherited failures of glycogen synthesis, branching, and breakdown that disrupt the body's main short-term glucose reserve. Because liver glycogen buffers blood glucose between meals and muscle glycogen fuels exertion, these defects present as fasting hypoglycaemia, exercise intolerance, hepatomegaly, or myopathy, with severity depending on which tissue-specific isoform is lost. The genes trace the whole cycle: glycogenin priming and glycogen synthase elongation, branching enzyme shaping the polymer, lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase degrading it, and the glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunit with its endoplasmic reticulum transporter releasing free glucose into blood. Damage also comes from what accumulates — poorly branched, insoluble polyglucosan bodies. Laforin and malin, a phosphatase and ubiquitin ligase pair that keep glycogen soluble, cause a fatal progressive myoclonic epilepsy when mutated, and G6PC3 loss produces congenital neutropenia rather than a metabolic crisis.

Glycogen is the body's rapidly mobilizable glucose store, and its regulated synthesis and breakdown keeps blood glucose stable during fasting and supplies fuel to muscle and brain during exercise and stress. Inherited defects in the enzymes that build, branch, or release glycogen cause the glycogen storage diseases, whose presentations range from fasting hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly to myopathy, cardiomyopathy and neutropenia. Loss of the liver or muscle glycogen synthases blocks storage outright; deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase or its endoplasmic reticulum glucose-6-phosphate transporter traps glucose inside hepatocytes, while loss of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase leaves undegraded glycogen in lysosomes. Defects in the branching enzyme or in glycogenin, the self-glucosylating protein that primes new chains, yield structurally abnormal or absent glycogen. Failure of the laforin-malin pair, a phosphatase and a ubiquitin ligase acting with ubiquitin on overphosphorylated glycogen, produces insoluble polyglucosan and progressive myoclonic epilepsy.

Signaling by TGF-beta Receptor Complex in Cancer describes how a growth-inhibitory pathway is dismantled during tumorigenesis. In normal epithelium, TGF-beta ligand binding brings together the type II and type I receptor kinases, which phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3; these partner with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to switch on cell cycle inhibitors such as p15 and p21, driving cytostasis, differentiation and apoptosis. Loss of this brake is one of the more common events in cancer, through SMAD4 deletion in pancreatic tumours, TGFBR2 frameshifts in microsatellite-unstable colorectal cancer, and inactivating changes in TGFBR1, SMAD2 or SMAD3. Accessory components set the threshold for signalling, with FKBP1A restraining the unliganded type I receptor and the SARA anchor presenting SMADs at the membrane. Paradoxically, tumours that survive with intact receptors exploit the pathway later, using it to induce epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invasion.

TGF-beta acting through its receptor complex normally restrains epithelial growth, driving cell cycle arrest, differentiation and apoptosis, and cancers commonly dismantle this brake. Ligand binding brings the type II receptor together with the type I receptor, whose kinase is held in check by FKBP1A until activation; the anchoring protein ZFYVE9 presents SMAD2 and SMAD3 for phosphorylation, after which they partner with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to control transcription of growth-inhibitory targets. Deletion or loss-of-function mutation of SMAD4 is the classic route to escape and is especially frequent in pancreatic cancer, while inactivating lesions in SMAD2, SMAD3, TGFBR1 or TGFBR2 disable the same axis in colorectal and other tumours. In advanced disease the residual pathway can switch roles, promoting epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invasiveness, so its output is context-dependent rather than uniformly suppressive.

SMAD2/3 Phosphorylation Motif Mutants in Cancer describes how tumours escape the growth-suppressive arm of TGF-beta signalling by destroying the site at which the pathway's messengers are switched on. Normally ligand-bound TGFBR2 recruits and activates TGFBR1, which phosphorylates the C-terminal Ser-Ser-X-Ser motif of SMAD2 and SMAD3 after the adaptor SARA presents them at the receptor; the phosphorylated proteins then trimerise with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to drive cytostatic and differentiation programmes. Cancer-associated substitutions, truncations or deletions of the two terminal serines leave SMAD2/3 receptor-bound but permanently unphosphorylated, so no active complex forms and target genes such as those enforcing cell cycle arrest are never induced. The result is loss of contact inhibition and TGF-beta insensitivity, a recurrent event in colorectal, pancreatic and other epithelial tumours where this arm behaves as a tumour suppressor.

TGF-beta signalling normally restrains epithelial proliferation, and cancers frequently escape that restraint by breaking the step at which the receptor writes its signal onto its effectors. Ligand-bound TGFBR2 recruits and activates the TGFBR1 kinase, which phosphorylates the conserved C-terminal Ser-Ser-X-Ser motif of SMAD2 and SMAD3 after the anchoring protein ZFYVE9 presents them at the membrane; phosphorylated SMAD2/3 then assemble heterotrimers with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to direct growth-inhibitory transcription. Cancer-associated mutants of this phosphorylation motif substitute, delete or truncate the critical serines, so the receptor complex can no longer activate them, the heterotrimer never forms, and the antiproliferative arm of the pathway is silenced. Loss of this input contributes to tumour growth and to the switch of residual TGF-beta signalling toward invasion, while leaving receptor activation itself intact.

Defective CUBN causes MGA1 describes what happens when the intestine cannot absorb vitamin B12. Cubilin, working with amnionless as the cubam receptor complex on the ileal brush border, binds gastric intrinsic factor carrying dietary cobalamin and internalises it by endocytosis; loss-of-function mutations in cubilin abolish this uptake and cause recessive hereditary megaloblastic anemia 1, also known as Imerslund-Gräsbeck syndrome, typically with proteinuria because the same receptor reclaims filtered proteins in the kidney proximal tubule. Cobalamin deficiency stalls methionine synthase, trapping folate as methyltetrahydrofolate and starving thymidylate synthesis, so erythroid precursors cannot replicate DNA and arrest as large immature megaloblasts. Neurological deterioration accompanies the anemia. The pathway thus links receptor-mediated nutrient transport at an epithelial surface to one-carbon metabolism and proliferation in the bone marrow, and is corrected by parenteral B12.

Dietary vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum only as a complex with intrinsic factor, and cubilin is the receptor that takes that complex up. Loss-of-function mutations in CUBN cause recessive hereditary megaloblastic anemia of the Imerslund-Grasbeck type, in which cobalamin malabsorption starves B12-dependent reactions, stalls folate cycling, and limits thymidylate supply so that erythroid precursors cannot complete DNA replication and enlarge without dividing. Cubilin works at the apical enterocyte membrane together with amnionless, whose partner protein anchors and traffics the receptor, while gastric intrinsic factor supplies the ligand; defects in any of these produce overlapping disease, and because the same receptor complex mediates proximal tubule protein reabsorption, patients often also show benign proteinuria. The condition links a single transport step to systemic one-carbon metabolism and haematopoiesis, and responds to parenteral B12.

Defective MMAA causes MMA, cblA type describes the loss of a mitochondrial chaperone that keeps the vitamin B12-dependent enzyme methylmalonyl-CoA mutase supplied with its adenosylcobalamin cofactor. That enzyme carries propionyl-CoA derived from odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol side chains and the branched-chain amino acids valine, isoleucine, methionine and threonine into the citric acid cycle as succinyl-CoA. When MMAA fails, the mutase cannot acquire or retain its cofactor, methylmalonyl-CoA is not isomerised, and methylmalonic acid accumulates in blood and urine. Infants and young children present with life-threatening metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, failure to thrive and neurological injury, with later risk of renal impairment. Because the defect lies in cofactor handling rather than in the apoenzyme itself, this form of methylmalonic aciduria is typically responsive to pharmacological hydroxocobalamin, distinguishing it from mutations in the mutase gene.

Propionyl-CoA from odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol and the branched-chain amino acids is disposed of through methylmalonyl-CoA, and the mitochondrial enzyme MMUT converts that intermediate to succinyl-CoA using adenosylcobalamin as cofactor. MMAA is the GTPase-like chaperone that delivers and maintains the cobalamin cofactor on MMUT, and loss of MMAA function leaves the mutase without a usable cofactor. The result is cblA-type methylmalonic aciduria: methylmalonic acid builds up in blood and urine, and infants and young children suffer metabolic acidotic crises with vomiting, lethargy, hypotonia and risk of death, together with longer-term renal and neurological damage. Because the defect is in cofactor handling rather than in the enzyme itself, many patients respond to pharmacological vitamin B12, distinguishing this form from mutase-deficient methylmalonic acidaemia and linking it to the broader mitochondrial cobalamin utilisation route.

Autodegradation of the E3 ubiquitin ligase COP1 is the switch that releases p53 from constitutive destruction after DNA damage, allowing the tumour suppressor to accumulate and impose cell cycle arrest, senescence or apoptosis. In unstressed cells COP1 continuously ubiquitinates p53 and keeps its levels low; loss of this restraint, or conversely COP1 overexpression in breast and ovarian cancers, distorts the damage response. The mechanism is self-directed: the damage-activated kinase ATM phosphorylates COP1 on Ser387, COP1 dissociates from p53 and ubiquitinates itself, and the polyubiquitinated ligase is delivered to the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core particle and regulatory subunits carries out the degradation. Ubiquitin precursors supply the conjugated tag. This is a case of a ligase destroying itself to stabilise its substrate, coupling genotoxic stress sensing to proteasomal control of p53 abundance.

In unstressed cells p53 is held at low levels by ubiquitin ligases that mark it for destruction, and COP1 is one of them; this route describes how COP1 itself is eliminated so that p53 can accumulate after genotoxic stress. The switch matters because it converts DNA damage sensing into a stable p53 response that drives cell cycle arrest, senescence or apoptosis, and its loss permits damaged cells to keep dividing. The damage-activated kinase ATM phosphorylates COP1 on Ser387, which triggers COP1 autoubiquitination; polyubiquitin supplied by the ubiquitin precursor genes is then read by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of 20S core and 19S regulatory subunits carries out degradation. Removing the ligase abrogates p53 ubiquitination, making this a self-limiting brake within tumour suppressor control and a point at which COP1 overexpression can blunt p53 in cancer.

Regulation of ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) is the feedback circuit that keeps polyamine synthesis in check, and it is the textbook case of ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation. ODC catalyses the committed step in making putrescine, spermidine and spermine, polyamines required for proliferation and translation; unrestrained ODC activity is transforming, and the enzyme is a downstream effector of MYC. When polyamines accumulate they promote a ribosomal frameshift that produces antizyme, which binds ODC, inhibits it, and exposes a C-terminal degron so that the 26S proteasome destroys the enzyme without ubiquitin tagging while releasing antizyme for further rounds. Antizyme also blocks polyamine uptake, and an antizyme inhibitor sequesters it to relieve the brake. The presence of the full core and regulatory particle subunits, together with NQO1, reflects how directly proteolysis and its redox-linked stabilisation set cellular polyamine levels.

Polyamines such as putrescine and spermidine are needed for growth and translation but are toxic in excess, so cells cap their supply at the committed step: ornithine decarboxylase. This feedback circuit keeps polyamine pools within a narrow range, and its loss contributes to the elevated polyamine levels characteristic of transformed and rapidly proliferating cells. When polyamines rise they promote a ribosomal frameshift that produces antizyme (OAZ1, OAZ2, OAZ3), which binds ODC1 and exposes a C-terminal degron; the heterodimer is then destroyed by the 26S proteasome without ubiquitination, the antizyme subunit being released to act again. Antizyme additionally blocks polyamine uptake, while the antizyme inhibitor AZIN1 sequesters antizyme to relieve repression. NQO1 and the proteasome activator-associated subunits shown here place the reaction in the context of ubiquitin-independent turnover of short-lived regulatory enzymes.

Amino acid transport across the plasma membrane moves amino acids into and out of cells, and it is what allows dietary protein absorbed in the intestine to be reclaimed in the kidney proximal tubule and delivered to tissues for protein synthesis, neurotransmitter and glutathione production, and nitrogen handling. Physiologists first defined these activities as transport "systems" distinguished by substrate preference, pH dependence and coupling to sodium, chloride or exchange of a counter-amino acid; the carriers are members of several solute carrier families, including sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporters, cationic transporters, proton-coupled carriers, and heteromeric exchangers built from a heavy chain such as SLC3A1 or SLC3A2 paired with a light chain. Loss of individual members causes recognisable transport diseases, including cystinuria, Hartnup disorder and lysinuric protein intolerance, while SLC7A11 and SLC7A5 link this uptake to redox balance, ferroptosis and mTORC1 nutrient sensing.

Cells cannot make protein, glutathione or neurotransmitters without first importing the relevant amino acids, and amino acid transport across the plasma membrane is the set of carriers that does this. It underlies dietary absorption in the intestine, reabsorption from the glomerular filtrate in the kidney proximal tubule, and delivery of substrates to every tissue; loss of individual carriers causes distinct aminoacidurias, including cystinuria from failure of the cystine/dibasic carrier formed by SLC3A1 with SLC7A9 and Hartnup disorder from loss of the neutral amino acid transporter SLC6A19. The transporters here span several families with different mechanisms: sodium- and chloride-coupled symporters, proton-coupled carriers, obligate exchangers such as the SLC7 members that heterodimerise with the heavy chain SLC3A2, and facilitative uniporters. Their combined activity sets intracellular amino acid pools, which in turn feed nutrient sensing and growth signalling.

Diseases associated with glycosaminoglycan metabolism covers the inherited disorders that arise when the sugar chains of proteoglycans cannot be built, sulfated, or broken down correctly. Because glycosaminoglycans attached to core proteins such as aggrecan, versican, decorin, perlecan and the syndecans and glypicans give cartilage, bone, skin and basement membranes their tensile and hydration properties and tune growth factor signalling, defects produce skeletal dysplasias, connective tissue fragility, corneal clouding and neurodegeneration. Loss of the linker-region enzymes B4GALT7, B3GALT6 or B3GAT3 causes Ehlers-Danlos-like and multiple joint dislocation syndromes; EXT1 and EXT2 mutations give hereditary multiple exostoses; sulfotransferase and sulfate transporter defects such as CHST3, CHST6, CHST14 and SLC26A2 underlie chondrodysplasias, macular corneal dystrophy and skin laxity; and hexosaminidase deficiency blocks ganglioside and GAG catabolism in Tay-Sachs and Sandhoff disease. Overgrowth syndromes follow glypican loss.

Glycosaminoglycan chains attached to proteoglycan cores fill the extracellular matrix, hold water in cartilage and cornea, and tether growth factors at cell surfaces, so inherited defects in making or breaking them produce recognisable skeletal, connective tissue and neurological disease. Failures at the linkage-region glycosyltransferases that start a chondroitin or heparan sulfate chain, such as B4GALT7, B3GALT6 and B3GAT3, cause forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia; loss of the EXT1/EXT2 heparan sulfate polymerase gives hereditary multiple exostoses. Sulfation defects are equally damaging: CHST6 mutations cause macular corneal dystrophy, CHST3 and CHST14 alter chondroitin and dermatan sulfation, and PAPSS2 and the sulfate transporter SLC26A2 limit sulfate donor supply, producing chondrodysplasias. On the catabolic side, deficiency of the HEXA or HEXB hexosaminidase subunits blocks ganglioside and GAG degradation. Affected substrates include aggrecan, perlecan, decorin, glypicans and syndecans.

Defective SLC26A2 causes chondrodysplasias describes what happens to skeletal development when cartilage cells can no longer import sulfate. SLC26A2 is the sulfate transporter that supplies chondrocytes with the intracellular SO4(2-) needed to sulfate the glycosaminoglycan chains of aggrecan and other matrix proteoglycans; that sulfation gives cartilage its fixed negative charge, water retention and compressive resilience. Loss-of-function mutations undersulfate the growth plate matrix, disorganise the extracellular matrix and derail endochondral ossification, producing a graded series of autosomal recessive chondrodysplasias from diastrophic dysplasia through atelosteogenesis type II to perinatally lethal achondrogenesis type 1B. The pathway therefore links a single anion transport step to bone elongation, joint formation and limb and thoracic proportion, and illustrates how sulfur assimilation feeds directly into extracellular matrix biosynthesis in a tissue that depends on it absolutely.

Cartilage stiffness and resilience depend on proteoglycans whose glycosaminoglycan chains are heavily sulfated, and chondrocytes obtain the sulfate for that modification by importing it from outside the cell. SLC26A2 is the sulfate transporter that performs this uptake, exchanging extracellular sulfate for intracellular anions; loss of its activity starves the cell of the substrate needed to make the sulfate donor used in Golgi sulfotransferase reactions. The result is undersulfated matrix proteoglycan, disorganised extracellular matrix, and failure of the growth plate to build normal skeletal elements. Recessive mutations therefore cause a graded family of chondrodysplasias, from diastrophic dysplasia with clubfoot and joint deformity, through atelosteogenesis type II, to lethal achondrogenesis type 1B. The biology links a single anion transport step to skeletal growth, connecting sulfur metabolism with cartilage matrix assembly.

Defective CHSY1 causes TPBS describes what happens to proteoglycan assembly when chondroitin sulfate cannot be polymerised properly, and the skeletal and neurological disease that follows. CHSY1 elongates the chondroitin chain by alternately transferring glucuronate and N-acetylgalactosamine onto core proteins such as versican, aggrecan-family lecticans (brevican, neurocan), decorin, biglycan and the cell-surface proteoglycans CSPG4 and CSPG5. These glycosaminoglycan chains give cartilage and other extracellular matrices their water-binding, load-bearing properties and steer growth-factor and Notch signalling during limb patterning and neural development. Loss-of-function mutations produce temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome, in which affected children show shortened digits with extra phalanges, growth retardation, sensorineural deafness and intellectual disability. The pathway therefore links a single glycosyltransferase step in the Golgi to skeletal morphogenesis, matrix integrity and perineuronal net formation in the nervous system.

Chondroitin sulfate chains are built by alternating addition of glucuronate and N-acetylgalactosamine onto a linker tetrasaccharide, and CHSY1 is a principal polymerizing enzyme of that reaction. When CHSY1 is defective, chain elongation fails and the proteoglycans that depend on it are left with truncated glycosaminoglycan decoration, producing temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome dash congenital anomalies with short digits, extra phalanges, sensorineural deafness, growth retardation and intellectual disability. The affected acceptors span the cartilage and nervous-system matrix: versican, biglycan and decorin in skeletal and connective tissue, brevican, neurocan and CSPG5 in brain perineuronal and interstitial matrix, and CSPG4 on pericytes and glial progenitors. Because chondroitin sulfate controls matrix hydration, growth-factor availability and Notch-dependent limb patterning, loss of its synthesis affects skeletal morphogenesis as much as tissue mechanics, linking a single glycosyltransferase step to digit formation and hearing.

TGFBR2 Kinase Domain Mutants in Cancer describes how loss-of-function missense mutations in the kinase domain of the type II TGF-beta receptor free tumour cells from the growth-suppressive arm of TGF-beta signalling. Normally, TGFB1 binds TGFBR2, which recruits and transphosphorylates TGFBR1 to activate SMAD-dependent transcription that halts epithelial proliferation; a receptor with a dead kinase domain cannot complete this step, so the cytostatic response is lost while the ligand remains present. Such mutations occur in roughly a fifth of microsatellite stable colorectal cancers, typically affecting both alleles, and in esophageal carcinoma the mutant receptor can act dominant-negatively over the wild-type protein. They are distinct from the frameshift inactivation seen in mismatch-repair-deficient tumours, and they mark an early escape from tumour suppression in epithelial carcinogenesis.

TGF-beta normally restrains epithelial proliferation, and tumours frequently escape that restraint by damaging the receptor that receives the signal. Missense changes in the kinase domain of the type II TGF-beta receptor, TGFBR2, occur in a substantial minority of microsatellite stable colorectal cancers and in esophageal carcinoma, and they abolish the growth-inhibitory response to TGFB1 while leaving the ligand and the type I receptor intact. In the normal sequence, TGFB1 binding brings TGFBR2 and TGFBR1 into a heteromeric complex in which TGFBR2 kinase activity transphosphorylates TGFBR1 to launch SMAD-dependent transcription of cell cycle inhibitors. Kinase-domain mutants cannot perform that step; some appear to act dominant-negatively by sequestering partners in a non-signalling complex. Loss of this cytostatic arm removes a tumour-suppressive brake on epithelial cells, which is one route by which colorectal and esophageal tumours acquire unchecked proliferation.

Transcriptional Regulation by TP53 is the gene expression programme a cell runs when it detects DNA damage, oncogene activation, oxidative stress or nutrient imbalance, and it is the main barrier between a damaged cell and a tumour. TP53 binds response elements as a tetramer and, with coactivators such as EP300/CREBBP and repressive complexes such as NuRD, switches on arrest genes like CDKN1A and GADD45A, apoptotic effectors including BAX, PUMA, NOXA and the TRAIL receptors, DNA repair and checkpoint factors, and metabolic regulators such as TIGAR, SCO2 and the sestrins that tune glycolysis, respiration and mTOR signalling. Its own activity is set by ATM/ATR and checkpoint kinase phosphorylation, acetylation and methylation marks, and MDM2/MDM4-mediated degradation. Loss or mutation of TP53 in roughly half of human cancers removes this coordination of arrest, senescence, repair and death.

TP53 is the transcription factor that converts cellular stress — DNA damage, oncogene activation, nutrient or oxidative imbalance — into a decision about whether a cell continues dividing, pauses, ages out, or dies. Transcriptional regulation by TP53 therefore sits at the centre of tumour suppression, and its loss through mutation in roughly half of human cancers removes the barrier that keeps damaged cells from proliferating. Damage sensors and checkpoint kinases such as ATM, ATR, CHEK1 and CHEK2 stabilise p53 against MDM2-directed degradation, while acetyltransferases, methyltransferases and prolyl isomerases tune which promoters it occupies. The output programmes are broad: CDKN1A and 14-3-3 proteins enforce cell cycle arrest; BAX, PMAIP1, BBC3 and death receptors commit cells to apoptosis; TIGAR, SCO2, glutaminase and sestrins redirect glycolysis, respiration and mTOR signalling; and DNA repair, antioxidant and miRNA-processing effectors support recovery when damage is survivable.

NCAM signaling for neurite out-growth describes how the neural cell adhesion molecule converts cell-cell and cell-matrix contact into the intracellular signals that drive axon extension, neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity. It builds and maintains nervous system wiring; loss of this adhesion-coupled signalling impairs neurite growth and activity-dependent remodelling. NCAM1 acts partly by activating FGFR1 and partly by nucleating a cytoplasmic complex with Fyn, Src and focal adhesion kinase, regulated by the phosphatase RPTPalpha, feeding through Grb2/SOS to Ras and ERK1/2 and on to MSK1 and CREB-dependent transcription of growth and survival genes. Polysialylation by ST8SIA2 and ST8SIA4 tunes adhesive strength, spectrin cytoskeletal links anchor the receptor, and collagens and other matrix components, voltage-gated calcium channels and GDNF-family ligands with their GFRA receptors act as partners and parallel inputs to the same growth programme.

Growing axons decide where to extend by reading cell-surface adhesion cues, and NCAM signalling for neurite outgrowth is one of the main routes by which that contact is converted into growth. It shapes how neurons differentiate, extend processes and remodel synapses, and it underlies aspects of learning-related plasticity and nervous system wiring. Homophilic NCAM1 engagement, modulated by polysialylation from ST8SIA2 and ST8SIA4, recruits the Src-family kinase Fyn together with focal adhesion kinase, and also transactivates FGFR1; GRB2/SOS coupling to Ras drives ERK1/2 and, via MSK1, CREB-dependent transcription of genes for axon growth and neuronal survival. RPTP-alpha supplies the dephosphorylation step that activates Fyn. Spectrin scaffolds link the receptor to the submembrane cytoskeleton, while collagens, agrin and neurocan represent the extracellular matrix context, and GDNF-family ligands with their GFRA co-receptors provide a parallel NCAM-dependent input. Voltage-gated calcium channels couple adhesion to calcium entry.

Diseases of glycosylation collects the inherited defects that disrupt attachment and elaboration of sugar chains on proteins and lipids, the congenital disorders of glycosylation. Because nearly every secreted and membrane protein is glycosylated, these defects produce multisystem disease, most often psychomotor retardation, seizures, coagulopathy and skeletal or connective tissue abnormality; N-glycosylation defects such as PMM2-CDG are the largest group and are detected by abnormal transferrin isoforms. The genes trace each affected step: nucleotide-sugar supply and galactose metabolism, dolichol synthesis and the ALG enzymes that build the lipid-linked precursor, oligosaccharyltransferase-associated processing, O-mannosylation of dystroglycan underlying muscular dystrophies, O-fucosylation that tunes Notch, and assembly of proteoglycan linkage regions on syndecans, glypicans and lecticans. Lysosomal glycan degradation defects and mucin-type O-glycosylation belong here too. Treatment remains largely supportive.

Congenital disorders of glycosylation are inherited failures to build or attach glycans, and because nearly every secreted and membrane protein is glycosylated, the consequences are multisystem: psychomotor retardation, coagulopathy, liver and skeletal disease, and in the N-linked forms a diagnostic shift in the isoelectric focusing pattern of plasma transferrin. The genes here span the routes that can break. Lipid-linked oligosaccharide assembly on dolichol and its transfer and trimming account for classic N-glycosylation defects such as PMM2-CDG and the ALG deficiencies; O-mannosylation enzymes including POMT1, POMT2 and POMGNT1 modify dystroglycan and, when lost, cause muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy; O-fucose and O-glucose modification of Notch receptors tunes Notch signalling; and defects in the xylose-galactose-galactose linker built by B4GALT7, B3GALT6 and B3GAT3 disrupt proteoglycan assembly on decorin, perlecan, syndecans and the aggrecan-versican family, producing skeletal and connective tissue fragility. Nucleotide-sugar supply, sulfation and lysosomal glycan catabolism are affected likewise. Treatment remains largely supportive.

Enzymatic degradation of Dopamine by monoamine oxidase terminates dopamine signalling after the neurotransmitter is taken back up into presynaptic terminals and glia, setting how long and how strongly dopaminergic transmission acts on motor control, reward and executive function. Monoamine oxidase A, anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane, oxidatively deaminates dopamine to 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid, which catechol-O-methyltransferase then methylates to homovanillic acid, the principal dopamine metabolite excreted in urine and measured in cerebrospinal fluid. The reaction generates hydrogen peroxide and reactive aldehydes, linking catecholamine turnover to oxidative stress in substantia nigra neurons. Both enzymes are pharmacological targets: MAO inhibitors and COMT inhibitors prolong dopamine action in Parkinson's disease and depression, while common COMT variants alter prefrontal dopamine tone and cognitive performance.

Dopamine signalling ends when the transmitter is broken down, and this route accounts for its enzymatic degradation by monoamine oxidase in neurons and surrounding tissue. Dopamine taken back up from the synapse is oxidatively deaminated by monoamine oxidase at the outer mitochondrial membrane, producing an aldehyde that is further oxidised to 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid; catechol-O-methyltransferase then methylates a hydroxyl group to give homovanillic acid, the excreted end product measured as an index of dopamine turnover. By limiting how long dopamine persists, this catabolism sets the gain of dopaminergic transmission in motor control, reward and prefrontal cognition, and its inhibition is deliberately exploited in Parkinson's disease and depression. The deamination step also generates hydrogen peroxide and reactive aldehydes, linking dopamine breakdown to oxidative stress in dopaminergic neurons; common variation in these enzymes alters catecholamine tone and behaviour.

Cytosolic tRNA aminoacylation is the step that loads each tRNA with its correct amino acid, setting the accuracy of the genetic code before a ribosome ever reads a codon. Without faithful charging, mistranslated proteins accumulate and translation stalls; inherited mutations in these synthetases cause peripheral neuropathies, leukodystrophies and multisystem developmental disease. Each enzyme activates its cognate amino acid with ATP and transfers it to the tRNA 3' end, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate, with inorganic pyrophosphatase pulling the reaction forward. Eight of the human enzymes, including the bifunctional glutamyl-prolyl synthetase and those for arginine, lysine, methionine and isoleucine, assemble with the AIMP scaffolding proteins into a multisynthetase complex that channels charged tRNAs toward elongation factors and the ribosome. Released components of that complex moonlight in angiogenesis, inflammation and stress signalling, linking translational supply to cell state.

Every round of protein synthesis in the cytoplasm begins with charging a tRNA with its matching amino acid, and cytosolic tRNA aminoacylation is the step that establishes the accuracy of the genetic code. A family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, one for most amino acids plus a bifunctional glutamyl-prolyl enzyme, activates the amino acid with ATP and transfers it to the 3' end of a nuclear-encoded tRNA, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate; a pyrophosphatase removes the latter to keep the reaction favourable. Eight of these enzymes assemble with the accessory factors AIMP1, AIMP2 and EEF1E1 into a multi-synthetase complex thought to channel charged tRNAs to translating ribosomes, and several components moonlight in angiogenesis, inflammation and DNA damage signalling. Mutations in individual synthetases such as GARS1 and AARS1 cause peripheral neuropathies and multisystem developmental disorders, reflecting how narrowly translation tolerates mischarging.

Chemokine receptors bind chemokines is the ligand-recognition step that tells leukocytes where to go. Chemokines secreted at sites of infection, injury or within lymphoid tissue form gradients, and G protein-coupled receptors on the cell surface read them, triggering intracellular calcium flux, cytoskeletal remodelling and directed chemotaxis. This underlies neutrophil recruitment to inflamed tissue, the homing of naive T cells and dendritic cells into lymph nodes via CCR7, B cell positioning in germinal centres through CXCR5, and haematopoietic stem cell retention in marrow through the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis. Ligand-receptor pairing is subfamily-restricted but highly redundant, with many chemokines binding several receptors. Atypical receptors such as ACKR2 and ACKR3 bind without conventional signalling, instead scavenging ligand to shape gradients. Misuse of these receptors permits HIV entry, and their dysregulation drives chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and tumour metastasis.

Leukocytes find their way to infection, injury and lymphoid tissue by reading gradients of secreted chemoattractant proteins, and the binding of chemokines to their G protein-coupled receptors is the recognition step that sets that migration in motion. Ligands of the CC, CXC, CX3C and XC families engage matching receptors such as CCR1-CCR10, CXCR1-CXCR6, CX3CR1 and XCR1, triggering calcium flux, integrin activation and directed chemotaxis. The pairings define immune cell behaviour: CCR7 with CCL19 and CCL21 routes dendritic cells and naive T cells into lymph nodes, CXCR4 with CXCL12 retains progenitors in bone marrow, and CXCR1/CXCR2 with CXCL8 recruits neutrophils to inflamed tissue. Atypical receptors including ACKR2, ACKR3 and ACKR4 bind ligands without conventional signalling, scavenging them to shape gradients. This signalling underlies inflammation, lymphoid organisation, HIV entry and tumour metastasis.

Loss of Nlp from mitotic centrosomes describes a switch in centrosome behaviour at mitotic entry: the interphase microtubule-anchoring factor Nlp is evicted so the centrosome can be rebuilt as a high-capacity spindle pole. This maturation step is what allows a cell to nucleate the dense microtubule arrays needed for bipolar spindle assembly and accurate chromosome segregation; when it fails, spindles are disorganised and aneuploidy or mitotic arrest follows. Mechanistically, Plk1 activated at G2/M phosphorylates Nlp, displacing it from gamma-tubulin ring complexes, while pericentriolar scaffolds such as pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, CEP192 and AKAP9 recruit gamma-TuRC through NEDD1 and the augmin (HAUS) complex amplifies nucleation. Dynein-dynactin, centrin, NEK2 and centriolar proteins including CEP135, CEP152 and PLK4 tie the process to centriole duplication and pole separation, linking it to broader cell cycle control and ciliopathy-associated centrosome biology.

As cells enter mitosis they rebuild the centrosome into a high-capacity microtubule nucleating hub, and one step in that conversion is the loss of Nlp from mitotic centrosomes. Nlp binds gamma-tubulin ring complexes during interphase and helps organize the interphase microtubule array; when Plk1 is activated at mitotic onset it phosphorylates Nlp and drives it off the centrosome, clearing the way for a mitotic scaffold that nucleates the spindle. The accompanying machinery is the pericentriolar matrix and its regulators — pericentrin, AKAP9, CDK5RAP2 and NEDD1 recruiting gamma-tubulin, centrins and the CEP proteins of the centriole wall, the augmin (HAUS) complex, and dynein–dynactin with CDK1, PLK4 and NEK2 as kinase controls. Correct handover matters for bipolar spindle assembly and accurate chromosome segregation; failure promotes spindle disorganization and aneuploidy, and mutations in these centrosomal components cause microcephaly and ciliopathies.

Metabolism of serotonin is the catabolic route that terminates serotonin signalling and clears the amine from neurons, platelets and the gut. It sets how long serotonin persists after release and how much is available to receptors, so its output influences mood, aggression, sleep, appetite and intestinal motility; the end product, 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid, is the urinary marker used clinically to gauge serotonin turnover and to detect carcinoid tumours. Monoamine oxidase A, anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane, oxidatively deaminates serotonin to 5-hydroxyindole acetaldehyde, releasing hydrogen peroxide, and mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase then oxidises that reactive aldehyde to the stable acid. Loss of MAOA function causes excess monoamine accumulation and a syndrome of impulsive aggression, and the enzyme is the target of antidepressant monoamine oxidase inhibitors, placing this pathway at the heart of neurotransmitter inactivation.

Serotonin signalling must be terminated as well as initiated, and the metabolism of serotonin is the two-step oxidative route that destroys the transmitter after reuptake and converts it into an excretable acid. Monoamine oxidase A, anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane of neurons, enterochromaffin cells, liver and platelets, oxidatively deaminates serotonin to 5-hydroxyindole acetaldehyde, releasing hydrogen peroxide and ammonia; mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase ALDH2 then oxidises the reactive aldehyde to 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid, the urinary metabolite measured clinically as an index of serotonin turnover and of carcinoid tumour burden. This clearance sets synaptic and circulating serotonin tone, which is why monoamine oxidase inhibitors are antidepressants and why combining them with serotonergic drugs risks serotonin excess. Loss-of-function of the enzyme raises serotonin and has been linked to impulsive aggression, placing amine catabolism upstream of mood and behaviour.

PERK regulates gene expression is the translational arm of the unfolded protein response, the branch that reacts to endoplasmic reticulum stress by shutting down new protein synthesis and rewiring transcription to match. It buys a stressed cell time to clear misfolded protein, and its failure underlies the diabetes and skeletal dysplasia of Wolcott-Rallison syndrome as well as the secretory cell death seen in chronic ER stress. The ER-resident kinase EIF2AK3 is released from BiP (HSPA5) when unfolded protein accumulates, dimerises, and phosphorylates eIF2alpha, globally suppressing initiation while paradoxically favouring translation of ATF4. ATF4 with CHOP (DDIT3), CEBPB/CEBPG and NFY then drives chaperone, amino acid transport and pro-apoptotic genes, including ASNS and HERPUD1. Loss of short-lived cyclin D1 arrests the cell cycle in G1, and exosome-mediated mRNA decay factors shape which transcripts survive the response.

When unfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the kinase PERK is released from the chaperone BiP, dimerizes and phosphorylates the translation initiation factor eIF2alpha on Ser52, shutting down most cap-dependent translation while permitting selective expression of stress-response genes. This arm of the unfolded protein response lowers the load of newly synthesized protein entering the ER, depletes short-lived proteins such as Cyclin D1 to stall the cell cycle in G1, and drives a transcriptional programme through ATF4 together with CHOP (DDIT3), ATF3 and C/EBP and NF-Y factors, inducing chaperones, amino acid supply enzymes such as asparagine synthetase, and inflammatory mediators. Prolonged signalling tips the outcome from adaptation toward apoptosis. mRNA decay machinery, including deadenylases and the exosome complex, shapes the resulting transcript levels. Loss of PERK function in humans causes Wolcott-Rallison syndrome with infantile diabetes, reflecting the demands of secretory cells.

Glucagon-like Peptide-1 (GLP1) regulates insulin secretion is the incretin arm of glucose homeostasis: a hormone released by intestinal L-cells after a meal reaches pancreatic beta cells and amplifies their insulin output in proportion to circulating glucose. This glucose-dependence is why the axis is exploited therapeutically in type 2 diabetes, and its blunting contributes to the impaired postprandial insulin response of the disease. GLP-1 binds its Gs-coupled receptor, freeing Gs-alpha to stimulate adenylyl cyclases and raise cAMP, which acts through two branches. PKA, anchored near its targets by AKAPs, closes potassium channels to depolarize the cell, mobilizes ER calcium through IP3 receptors, and drives PDX-1 and CREB-dependent insulin gene transcription. In parallel, the cAMP-activated exchange factors Epac1 and Epac2 signal via Rap1A to prime secretory granules for exocytosis and support beta cell proliferation and survival.

The incretin effect — why an oral glucose load releases far more insulin than the same glucose given intravenously — rests on this signalling route, in which intestinal L-cell-derived GLP-1 amplifies glucose-stimulated insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells. It is the target of the GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors used in type 2 diabetes, and its potentiation of secretion is glucose-dependent, so it raises insulin output without provoking hypoglycaemia. GLP-1 binding to its Gs-coupled receptor frees the Gs alpha subunit to stimulate adenylate cyclases, and the resulting cAMP acts through two effectors: protein kinase A, whose catalytic subunits are released from regulatory subunits and organised by anchoring proteins, and the exchange factors Epac1 and Epac2, which load GTP onto Rap1A. Downstream, potassium channel closure, IP3 receptor-mediated calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum, and granule priming drive exocytosis, while transcriptional effects support beta cell mass.

Glycogen storage disease type 0 (muscle GYS1) describes what happens to muscle when it cannot build glycogen at all. Glycogen is the fuel store that skeletal muscle draws on during bursts of contraction and that the heart uses as a metabolic buffer, so loss of muscle glycogen synthase leaves patients with exercise intolerance, syncope on exertion, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, sometimes presenting as sudden cardiac death in childhood. Normally glycogenin self-glucosylates to form the protein primer, and glycogen synthase 1 then extends that primer by adding glucose residues in alpha-1,4 linkage from UDP-glucose, with branching enzyme introducing the branch points that make the particle compact and rapidly mobilised. When the synthase step fails, the primer cannot be elongated and no particle forms, distinguishing this defect from the storage diseases in which abnormal glycogen accumulates. It sits at the anabolic end of carbohydrate metabolism, downstream of insulin signalling.

Muscle stores glucose as glycogen for rapid use during contraction, and this disease state describes what happens when that store cannot be built. Glycogenin initiates a glycogen particle by autoglucosylating itself, and glycogen synthase 1, the isoform of skeletal muscle and heart, extends the chain by adding glucose units from UDP-glucose to the growing polymer. Loss of GYS1 activity abolishes muscle glycogen synthesis, so fibres cannot draw on an internal fuel reserve when demand outstrips glucose delivery; patients show exercise intolerance, muscle pain, and a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that can cause sudden cardiac death in childhood. Unlike the liver form, fasting hypoglycaemia is not the presenting problem. The condition marks glycogen as the substrate for anaerobic glycolysis in working muscle rather than simply a systemic glucose buffer.

CD28 dependent PI3K/Akt signaling is the costimulatory arm of T cell activation: engagement of CD28 by CD80 or CD86 on antigen-presenting cells recruits PI3K and turns on Akt, converting antigen recognition into a full productive response rather than tolerance or anergy. Without this second signal a T cell that has seen antigen fails to make IL-2, does not survive or divide, and cannot mount the metabolic expansion that effector function requires; the same axis is what checkpoint molecules such as CTLA-4 and PD-1 oppose. Mechanistically, a YMNM motif in the CD28 tail binds the p85 regulatory subunit, PI3K generates PIP3, and PDK1 together with mTORC2 activates Akt, which then drives anti-apoptotic signalling, NF-kB-directed cytokine transcription, cell cycle entry, and mTOR-dependent growth and nutrient uptake. Src-family kinases LCK and FYN link this to proximal receptor phosphorylation.

A T cell that has engaged antigen still needs a second signal to commit, and CD28-dependent PI3K/Akt signalling supplies much of it. Binding of CD80 or CD86 on antigen-presenting cells to CD28 creates a phosphotyrosine motif, phosphorylated with help from the Src-family kinases LCK and FYN, that docks the p85 regulatory subunit of PI3K. The catalytic subunits then generate PIP3 at the inner membrane, recruiting PDPK1 and AKT, whose activation is completed by mTORC2 (mTOR with RICTOR, MAPKAP1, MLST8 and PRR5). Active AKT drives IL-2 transcription, blocks apoptosis, permits cell cycle entry and reprograms metabolism toward the biosynthesis a growing effector cell requires. Tuning comes from inhibitors such as TRIB3 and THEM4. Loss of this costimulatory arm produces anergy or tolerance; its blockade is the basis of costimulation-blocking immunosuppressants, while excess contributes to autoimmunity.

NADPH regeneration supplies the reducing power that biosynthesis and antioxidant defence run on, outside of the pentose phosphate pathway's canonical route. NADPH is consumed by fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, by glutathione and thioredoxin reductases that neutralise peroxides, and by cytochrome P450 reactions, so cells maintain a high NADPH:NADP+ ratio in every compartment where those reactions occur. Cytosolic and peroxisomal isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1) carries much of this load, oxidatively decarboxylating isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate while reducing NADP+; cytosolic aconitase (ACO1) feeds it by interconverting citrate and isocitrate, linking NADPH output to citrate exported from mitochondria. The same aconitase doubles as the iron-regulatory protein IRP1, tying this reducing-equivalent supply to cellular iron sensing. A parallel arm in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen sets the local NADPH balance that steroid-modifying reductases depend on.

Reducing power for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence comes largely from NADPH, and this route regenerates it outside the mitochondrion by oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate. Cytosolic and peroxisomal isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1) performs the NADP+-dependent step, while aconitase (ACO1) supplies its substrate by isomerising citrate exported from mitochondria to isocitrate. The NADPH produced supports fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, regeneration of reduced glutathione and thioredoxin, and detoxification of peroxides, which matters in peroxisomes where beta-oxidation generates oxidative load. Related NADP+/NADPH balancing in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen sustains reductive reactions there. Because IDH1 also links this chemistry to 2-oxoglutarate availability for dioxygenases, mutations that alter its catalytic output reshape cellular redox state and metabolite-dependent epigenetic signalling, as seen in gliomas and myeloid malignancies.

Post-chaperonin tubulin folding pathway completes the manufacture of the alpha/beta tubulin heterodimer, the building block from which every microtubule is assembled. Nothing about mitotic spindles, intracellular transport, cilia or neuronal axons works unless this step delivers correctly folded, GTP-competent dimers, and mutations in its cofactors cause cortical malformations and neurodegeneration. After the CCT/TriC chaperonin releases partly folded alpha and beta tubulin monomers, five dedicated cofactors take over: TBCA and TBCB capture the individual subunits, TBCE holds alpha tubulin while TBCD holds beta tubulin, and entry of TBCC into the assembled supercomplex triggers GTP hydrolysis on beta tubulin to discharge the native dimer. The small GTPase ARL2 regulates this machinery, which also acts in reverse as a tubulin-sequestering and degradation route, setting the size of the soluble dimer pool available for polymerisation.

Microtubules can only be built from correctly folded alpha/beta tubulin heterodimers, and this is the route by which those dimers are finished after the chaperonin releases partly folded monomers. Everything that depends on microtubules — mitotic spindles, intracellular transport, cilia, axonal architecture — rests on a supply of assembly-competent dimer, and on the same machinery to sequester or recycle free monomer so that unpolymerized tubulin does not poison assembly. Five cofactors act in sequence: TBCA and TBCB capture newly released beta and alpha subunits, TBCD and TBCE present them to one another, and arrival of TBCC triggers GTP hydrolysis on beta tubulin to discharge the native heterodimer, with ARL2 also binding the cofactor complex. Numerous alpha and beta tubulin isotypes are handled this way. Loss of TBCE causes hypoparathyroidism with growth retardation, and TBCD mutations produce early encephalopathy.

Striated Muscle Contraction is the force-generating cycle of skeletal and cardiac muscle, converting chemical energy into shortening of the sarcomere and thus into movement, posture and the pumping of blood. A rise in cytosolic calcium is read by the troponin complex (TNNC, TNNI, TNNT), which shifts tropomyosin off the actin filament and uncovers myosin binding sites; myosin heads then bind, pivot, release ADP and rebind ATP, ratcheting thin and thick filaments past one another. Titin, nebulin, tropomodulins, alpha-actinin and telethonin set filament length and anchor the lattice at the Z-disc, while dystrophin and desmin transmit force to the membrane and cytoskeleton. Because the geometry is so exacting, mutations in these components cause hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies, nemaline myopathy, distal arthrogryposis and muscular dystrophy, and the isoform composition here distinguishes cardiac, fast and slow fibre types.

Skeletal and cardiac muscle shorten and generate force through the sarcomere, the repeating array of thin and thick filaments that gives striated muscle contraction its name and its banded appearance. Calcium released during excitation binds the troponin complex (troponin C, I and T isoforms), shifting tropomyosin off actin's myosin-binding sites so that myosin heads can attach, pivot, release ADP and reset on a fresh ATP; repeated cycles slide the filaments past one another. Structural and scaffolding proteins set the geometry this chemistry depends on: titin and nebulin act as molecular rulers, alpha-actinin and telethonin build the Z-disc, tropomodulins cap thin filament ends, myosin-binding proteins tune crossbridge kinetics, and dystrophin and desmin transmit force to the membrane and cytoskeleton. Mutations in these components underlie hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies, nemaline myopathy and muscular dystrophy.

Diseases associated with O-glycosylation of proteins collects the congenital disorders that arise when sugars fail to be attached to serine and threonine residues of secreted and membrane proteins. O-glycosylation comes in several flavours defined by the first sugar added, and each has its own disease signature: loss of O-mannosylation of dystroglycan by POMT1, POMT2, POMGNT1, B4GAT1 or LARGE1 breaks the link between muscle fibres and their basement membrane and produces congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and eye malformation; loss of O-fucosylation and its B3GLCT-dependent glucose extension on thrombospondin repeats of ADAMTS and ADAMTSL proteins causes Peters-plus syndrome and connective tissue disease, while altered fucosylation of Notch receptors disturbs somite and vascular patterning. Mucin-type GalNAc glycosylation, built by C1GALT1 with its chaperone and the GALNT enzymes, gives mucins their protective gel properties, and its failure is linked to tumoral calcinosis and epithelial barrier defects.

Sugars added to serine and threonine residues shape mucus, muscle attachment and developmental signalling, and the inherited defects grouped here are the congenital disorders of glycosylation that follow when O-linked chains are built incorrectly. Three branches are represented. Mucin-type GalNAc glycosylation, elaborated by the C1GALT1 galactosyltransferase with its obligate chaperone C1GALT1C1 and by GALNT enzymes, decorates the secreted and membrane mucins that protect epithelial surfaces; loss of GALNT3 activity causes hyperphosphatemic familial tumoral calcinosis. O-mannosylation initiated by the POMT1/POMT2 complex and extended by POMGNT1 and LARGE1 builds the matriglycan on dystroglycan that links muscle fibres to laminin, and its failure produces dystroglycanopathies with muscular dystrophy and brain malformation. Protein folding is the chaperone-assisted process by which newly synthesised polypeptides reach their native shape in a crowded cytosol where spontaneous folding would fail or aggregate. Without it cells cannot build a microtubule cytoskeleton, assemble signalling complexes, or clear misfolded species, and aggregation-prone proteins accumulate. The genes centre on the eukaryotic chaperonin TRiC/CCT, an ATP-driven double-ring cage that binds unfolded substrates and releases them through cycles of nucleotide hydrolysis, working with the prefoldin co-chaperone that captures nascent chains on the ribosome and delivers them to the cage. Its principal clients are actin and the alpha/beta tubulins, which are then matured by tubulin-specific cofactors into polymerisation-competent heterodimers, and the G-protein beta subunits, whose folding gates assembly of heterotrimeric G proteins for receptor signalling. Cell cycle regulators and ubiquitin ligases link folding capacity to quality control and protein turnover.

Newly synthesized polypeptides rarely reach their native shape unaided in the crowded cytosol; protein folding by molecular chaperones is what converts them into functional protein. The dominant machinery here is the eukaryotic chaperonin TRiC/CCT, a double-ring ATPase built from eight paralogous subunits, fed by the prefoldin co-chaperone that captures nascent chains at the ribosome and delivers them. Cycles of ATP-driven substrate binding and release stabilize productive intermediates rather than adding information. Two obligate clients dominate the substrate list: actin and the alpha/beta tubulins, whose folding is completed by tubulin-specific cofactors before heterodimer assembly, and the G protein beta subunits, which acquire their propeller fold on CCT before pairing with gamma subunits for receptor signalling. Consequently cytoskeletal dynamics, mitosis and heterotrimeric G protein signalling all depend on this chaperone capacity, and its overload contributes to protein misfolding and aggregation.

Prostanoid ligand receptors are the cell-surface G protein-coupled receptors through which prostaglandins and thromboxane act, converting locally released lipid mediators into changes in vascular tone, platelet behaviour, inflammation, pain sensitivity, fever and smooth muscle contraction. Arachidonic acid released from membranes is cyclised by cyclooxygenase to PGH2 and then tailored by tissue-specific synthases into PGD2, PGE2, PGF2alpha, prostacyclin and TXA2; the receptors named here read that output. DP1/DP2, the four EP subtypes, FP, IP and TP couple to different G proteins, so the same ligand family can raise or lower cAMP, mobilise calcium, and produce opposing effects such as prostacyclin-mediated vasodilation versus thromboxane-driven platelet aggregation. This branch explains why COX inhibitors relieve pain and inflammation yet perturb gastric protection, renal perfusion, uterine contraction and cardiovascular risk, and DP2 antagonism is exploited in allergic airway disease.

Prostanoids made downstream of cyclooxygenase — PGD2, PGE2, PGF2alpha, prostacyclin and thromboxane A2 — act on cells through a family of prostanoid ligand receptors, and these receptors are what convert local lipid mediator production into changes in vascular tone, platelet aggregation, pain sensitivity, fever, uterine contraction and inflammatory cell recruitment. They are G protein-coupled receptors with opposing outputs: the prostacyclin receptor and the EP2/EP4 subtypes raise cAMP to relax smooth muscle and restrain platelets, while the thromboxane receptor and FP and EP1 receptors mobilise calcium to constrict vessels and promote aggregation, so the balance between them sets haemostatic and vascular set points. Two DP receptors mediate PGD2 actions, with the second recruiting eosinophils, basophils and Th2 cells in allergic airway disease. This receptor layer explains the therapeutic effects of aspirin and NSAIDs, which act by removing their ligands.

Adrenaline signalling through Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor is the inhibitory arm of adrenergic control, the route by which adrenaline and noradrenaline damp rather than stimulate cellular activity. It sets the negative feedback that limits noradrenaline release at sympathetic nerve terminals, suppresses insulin secretion while promoting glucagon release, contracts gastrointestinal sphincters and vascular smooth muscle, and lowers the threshold for platelet aggregation. Because of the presynaptic autoreceptor function, agonists at these receptors are used clinically as antihypertensives, sedatives and analgesics. The three receptor subtypes are G protein-coupled receptors that preferentially engage Gi/Go heterotrimers; the released alpha subunit inhibits adenylate cyclase so that cAMP falls and protein kinase A activity declines, while liberated beta-gamma subunits act on potassium and calcium channels. The pathway therefore opposes beta-adrenergic signalling within the same catecholamine response.

Adrenaline acting on alpha-2 adrenergic receptors is the arm of catecholamine signalling that damps rather than drives cAMP production. The three receptor subtypes encoded here couple preferentially to Gi/Go heterotrimers, so agonist binding inhibits adenylate cyclase and lowers cyclic AMP, while the released G protein subunits also regulate potassium and calcium channels. The physiological consequences are broad: suppression of insulin secretion and promotion of glucagon release from pancreatic islets, contraction of gastrointestinal sphincters, platelet aggregation, and presynaptic autoinhibition of noradrenaline release at sympathetic and central synapses. That last negative feedback loop is why alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine and dexmedetomidine lower sympathetic outflow and blood pressure and produce sedation and analgesia, and why the subtypes differ in their vascular versus neuronal contributions to autonomic tone.

Metabolism of proteins spans the entire life of a polypeptide, from its synthesis on cytosolic and mitochondrial ribosomes through folding, covalent modification, trafficking and eventual destruction. It is the layer of cell biology that determines how much of each protein exists, where it sits, and what chemical decorations tune its activity, and its failure underlies congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies, neurodegenerative amyloid disease and cancers driven by defective degradation. The genes cover aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and initiation and elongation factors, chaperonin and prefoldin folding machinery, ER translocation and signal peptidase, N- and O-linked glycosylation, GPI anchoring, gamma-carboxylation, sulfation and methylation, RAB prenylation with COPI/COPII and exocyst transport, and the ubiquitin, SUMO and NEDD8 conjugation systems feeding cullin-RING ligases, deubiquitinases and the proteasome. Peptide hormone processing by furin and PCSK enzymes, surfactant secretion, and amyloid fibre formation are downstream outcomes of the same machinery.

This is the full life cycle of a cellular protein, from synthesis through maturation to destruction, and nearly every compartment contributes. Ribosomal subunits, initiation and elongation factors and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases translate mRNA in the cytosol, while a parallel mitochondrial apparatus of mitoribosomal proteins and mitochondrially encoded subunits supplies the respiratory chain. Chaperonins and prefoldin fold nascent chains; signal recognition particle, the signal peptidase and oligosaccharyltransferase route and glycosylate secretory proteins, with COPI/COPII, TRAPP, SNARE and RAB components moving them onward. Covalent modification is broadly represented: N- and O-glycosylation, GPI anchoring, gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, sulfation, methylation, ubiquitination by cullin-RING and other ligases, SUMOylation, neddylation, and reversal by deubiquitinases. Proprotein convertases liberate peptide hormones such as insulin and POMC products; misfolded substrates are cleared by ER-associated degradation and the proteasome. Failures here underlie congenital glycosylation disorders, surfactant deficiency, and amyloid diseases.

Rap1 signalling governs how cells stick to their surroundings and to each other, acting as the switch that converts intracellular second messengers into integrin activation, cadherin-based junction assembly and controlled cell adhesion. Its outputs matter for platelet aggregation, leukocyte arrest on endothelium, T cell contact with antigen-presenting cells and endothelial barrier integrity; loss of the hematopoietic exchange factor RASGRP2 causes a bleeding disorder from platelet integrin failure. Rap1A and Rap1B cycle between GDP- and GTP-bound states at endosomal and plasma membranes, loaded by cAMP-responsive exchange factors (RAPGEF3/4) and diacylglycerol- and calcium-sensitive RasGRPs, and switched off by RAP1GAP family GAPs and SIPA1. Protein kinase A and PKG feed directly into this circuit, linking hormonal and nitric oxide signalling to adhesion. Rap1 also modulates ERK output through RAF1, tuning proliferative signalling alongside its adhesive role.

Rap1 signalling controls how cells stick to their surroundings: the GTPases RAP1A and RAP1B, when loaded with GTP, recruit effectors that switch integrins to a high-affinity state, so this branch of Ras-superfamily signalling governs platelet aggregation, leukocyte adhesion and arrest on endothelium, cell junction integrity and cell shape. Activation is set by opposing regulators. Exchange factors load GTP in response to second messengers, with RAPGEF3 and RAPGEF4 acting as direct cAMP sensors and RASGRP1 and RASGRP2 responding to diacylglycerol and calcium downstream of antigen and collagen receptors; RAP1GAP, RAP1GAP2 and SIPA1 accelerate GTP hydrolysis and shut the switch off. PKA and cGMP-dependent kinase feed in from hormonal and nitric oxide inputs, phosphorylating regulators, while RAF1 and 14-3-3 proteins link Rap1 to ERK-directed growth signalling. Loss of RASGRP2 function causes a platelet adhesion bleeding disorder.

Muscle contraction covers how a rise in cytosolic calcium is converted into actin-myosin sliding and mechanical force in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle, together with the electrical events that time it. It underlies every heartbeat, voluntary movement, and the tone of blood vessels, airways and gut; its components are the genes mutated in cardiomyopathies, congenital myopathies and inherited arrhythmia syndromes such as long QT and Brugada. Depolarization through voltage-gated sodium and L-type calcium channels triggers ryanodine receptor-mediated release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, calcium binds troponin C or, in smooth muscle, calmodulin to activate myosin light chain kinase, and SERCA pumps, calsequestrin, phospholamban and sodium-calcium exchange terminate the signal. Potassium channels and their accessory subunits set resting potential and repolarization, while titin, dystrophin, actinins and costameric adhesion proteins transmit force to the sarcolemma. Natriuretic peptide and cGMP signalling provide relaxation and vasodilatory control.

Every heartbeat, breath and voluntary movement depends on calcium-triggered sliding of actin and myosin filaments, and this module covers that force generation across skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle together with the electrical signalling that times it. Depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels, calcium release channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum amplify the signal, and calcium binding to troponin relieves tropomyosin inhibition so that myosin heads engage actin; in smooth muscle, myosin light chain kinase phosphorylation of myosin sets tone instead. Relaxation follows from calcium pumps, phospholamban-regulated reuptake, sodium-calcium exchange and nitric oxide-cyclic GMP signalling. Sodium and potassium channels with their auxiliary subunits shape the cardiac action potential's depolarization, plateau and repolarization phases and its propagation. Mutations in these sarcomeric, cytoskeletal and channel components cause cardiomyopathies, arrhythmias including long QT syndrome, and muscular dystrophies.

Activation of AMPA receptors is the fast step of excitatory neurotransmission: glutamate released at a synapse binds AMPA-type ionotropic receptors and opens a cation channel within milliseconds, depolarising the postsynaptic membrane and setting the pace of nearly all excitatory signalling in the brain. Changes in the number and composition of these receptors at the synapse are the physical substrate of long-term potentiation and depression, and hence of learning and memory; their overactivation contributes to excitotoxic neuronal death. The four subunits GRIA1-GRIA4 assemble as homomeric or heteromeric tetramers whose properties are tuned post-transcriptionally. RNA editing of the GluR2 pore residue makes receptors calcium-impermeable, so glutamatergic neurons typically carry sodium-only channels while GABAergic interneurons carry calcium-permeable ones. Alternative splicing of cytoplasmic tails and flip/flop exons further sets desensitisation and closing kinetics, generating functionally distinct receptors across synapses.

Fast excitatory transmission at glutamatergic synapses depends on AMPA-type ionotropic glutamate receptors, and their activation by synaptically released glutamate produces the millisecond depolarization that carries most information flow in the brain. The four subunits GRIA1-GRIA4 assemble as homomeric or heteromeric tetramers whose properties are tuned by subunit composition, RNA editing and alternative splicing: an edited GluR2 subunit places arginine in the pore and renders the channel calcium-impermeable, so receptors lacking it pass calcium as well as sodium, as is typical of GABAergic interneurons. Flip/flop variants and long or short cytoplasmic tails set desensitization, resensitization and channel closing rates and govern trafficking. Regulated insertion and removal of these receptors underlies long-term potentiation and depression, and hence learning and memory; excessive calcium entry through GluR2-lacking receptors contributes to excitotoxic neuronal death, while subunit mutations cause intellectual disability and epilepsy.

Incretin synthesis, secretion, and inactivation describes how the small intestine converts a meal into a hormonal signal that primes the pancreas for the glucose about to arrive. GLP-1 from L cells and GIP from K cells amplify glucose-stimulated insulin release, and this gut-to-islet axis explains why oral glucose is far more insulinotropic than intravenous glucose; its loss contributes to type 2 diabetes, and it is the target of DPP4 inhibitors and GLP-1 mimetics. Preproglucagon and proGIP are made in enteroendocrine cells specified by transcription factors including PAX6, ISL1, CDX2 and TCF7L2, processed by signal peptidase and the prohormone convertase PCSK1, and released in response to fatty acids and phospholipids sensed through FFAR1, FFAR4 and GPR119 acting via heterotrimeric G proteins. Circulating peptides are then clipped within minutes by dipeptidyl peptidase IV, keeping the signal brief and meal-locked.

Gut endocrine cells sense a meal and release hormones that amplify insulin secretion before blood glucose has fully risen, and incretin synthesis, secretion and inactivation covers that whole life cycle. Proglucagon in intestinal L cells and GIP in K cells are made as precursors, cleaved by the signal peptidase complex and by the prohormone convertase PCSK1 to yield active GLP-1 and GIP; transcription factors including CDX2, PAX6, ISL1, GATA4 and TCF7L2, with beta-catenin, specify these cells and drive hormone gene expression. Secretion is triggered by nutrients acting through long- and medium-chain fatty acid receptors FFAR1 and FFAR4, the lipid sensor GPR119, taste-type G protein subunits, and by gastrin-releasing peptide and leptin. Circulating incretins are then truncated within minutes by dipeptidyl peptidase IV, the reason DPP4 inhibitors lower glucose in type 2 diabetes.

Sialic acid metabolism builds, activates, installs and recycles the negatively charged nine-carbon sugars that cap most cell-surface glycans. These terminal sialic acids determine how cells are recognised: they form the ligands for selectins and Siglecs, mask glycans from galectins and complement, carry the polysialic acid that lets developing neurons remodel their contacts, and serve as attachment sites for influenza and other pathogens. Synthesis begins with GNE and NANS generating N-acetylneuraminate, CMAS activates it to CMP-Neu5Ac in the nucleus, and SLC35A1 imports the donor into the Golgi, where a large family of ST3GAL, ST6GAL, ST6GALNAC and ST8SIA transferases attaches it in linkage-specific fashion. Turnover runs in reverse: neuraminidases NEU1-NEU4 release sialic acid in lysosomes and at the plasma membrane, SLC17A5 exports it, and NPL degrades it. Loss of these steps causes sialic acid storage disease, sialidosis and GNE myopathy, and altered sialylation accompanies tumour invasion and immune evasion.

Sialic acids cap the outer ends of glycan chains on cell-surface glycoproteins and glycolipids, and sialic acid metabolism covers how the most abundant human form, N-acetylneuraminate, is made, activated, attached, recycled and broken down. The resulting negatively charged termini govern cell-cell recognition, immune self-marking through Siglec binding, neural development via polysialylated adhesion molecules, and serve as attachment sites exploited by influenza virus and bacterial toxins. GNE and NANS commit UDP-GlcNAc to the pathway, CMAS activates the sugar as CMP-Neu5Ac in the nucleus, a dedicated transporter delivers it into the Golgi, and families of sialyltransferases transfer it in alpha2,3, alpha2,6 or alpha2,8 linkage, the last generating polysialic acid. Lysosomal sialidases and a sialic acid exporter return free sugar to the cytosol for reuse or degradation. Loss of these steps causes inclusion body myopathy, sialidosis and free sialic acid storage disease, and altered sialylation accompanies tumour metastasis.

G alpha (12/13) signalling events is the branch of G protein-coupled receptor signalling that reshapes the actin cytoskeleton, converting hormone and lipid mediator binding at the cell surface into changes in cell shape, adhesion and contractility. It drives platelet shape change and aggregation downstream of thromboxane receptors, smooth muscle tone downstream of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, and the migration and invasion programs co-opted by tumour cells, with GNA13 mutation a recurrent event in lymphoma. Activated GNA12 or GNA13 engages RhoGEFs such as ARHGEF1, ARHGEF11 and ARHGEF12, loading GTP onto RHOA, RHOB and RHOC; Rho-kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2 then promote stress fibre and focal adhesion assembly. Many additional exchange factors for Rho, Rac and Cdc42 are recruited through this hub, linking the pathway to axon guidance via plexin receptors, cytokinesis and cell proliferation. Receptors using this route generally also couple to Gq.

Some G protein-coupled receptors, including alpha-1 adrenergic and thromboxane A2 receptors, signal through the G alpha 12/13 family to reshape the actin cytoskeleton rather than to raise calcium or cyclic AMP. This route governs cell shape, stress fiber and focal adhesion formation, adhesion, migration and proliferation, and underlies platelet shape change, vascular smooth muscle tone, neurite retraction and the invasive behaviour of tumour cells. Activated GNA12 and GNA13, with released beta-gamma subunits, engage Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as ARHGEF1, ARHGEF11, ARHGEF12 and AKAP13, which load GTP onto RhoA, RhoB and RhoC; the Rho kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2 then drive actomyosin contractility. Many other exchange factors acting on Rac and Cdc42 broaden the output. Because G12/13-coupled receptors almost always also couple to Gq, Rho activation is the practical readout of this branch.

Nucleotide-like (purinergic) receptors are the cell-surface sensors for extracellular ATP, ADP, UTP, UDP-sugars and adenosine, molecules that leak or are released from stressed, dying and activated cells and so act as signals of tissue damage and metabolic state. Through them, purine and pyrimidine nucleotides control vascular tone, platelet aggregation, inflammatory cytokine secretion, nociception and apoptosis; P2RY12 is the target of antiplatelet drugs such as clopidogrel, and adenosine receptors mediate caffeine's stimulant action and adenosine's brake on cardiac conduction and immune activation.
