The genes here are the G protein-coupled arm of the family: P2Y receptors coupling to Gq and phospholipase C or to Gi, the four adenosine receptors tuning cyclic AMP up or down, and related orphan and lysophospholipid receptors of the same structural branch. Signalling converges on calcium release, cAMP and downstream regulation of secretion, chemotaxis and cell survival.

Extracellular ATP, ADP, UTP and adenosine act as signals reporting cell damage, stress and nucleotide release, and this family of nucleotide-like purinergic receptors is how cells read them. The set covers the G protein-coupled arm: four adenosine receptors that tune vascular tone, inflammation, neuronal excitability and cardiac rate, and the P2Y receptors that respond to nucleotides. Some couple through Gq to phospholipase C and calcium release, others through Gi to lower cyclic AMP, so a single nucleotide can produce opposing outcomes depending on which receptor a cell expresses. P2RY12 on platelets drives ADP-dependent aggregation and is the target of widely used antithrombotic drugs. Related orphan and lysophospholipid-responsive receptors are grouped here by sequence kinship. Collectively these receptors shape vascular reactivity, immune cytokine secretion, platelet activation and apoptotic responses to nucleotide release.

G beta:gamma signalling through PLC beta is the branch of G protein-coupled receptor signalling in which the released beta:gamma dimer, rather than the alpha subunit, directly stimulates phospholipase C beta to generate second messengers. It converts receptor occupancy into a rise in cytosolic calcium and protein kinase C activity, and it is the dominant route by which chemokine and chemoattractant receptors on leukocytes trigger chemotaxis, degranulation and the respiratory burst. Mechanistically, the beta:gamma dimer binds the pleckstrin homology domain of PLC beta and increases hydrolysis of PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, the latter opening ER calcium stores; PLCB3 responds most strongly, followed by PLCB2 and PLCB1. Combinatorial pairing of multiple beta and gamma subunits, including retinal transducin gamma subunits, gives tissue-specific tuning of this output, and loss of the neuronal GNB5 subunit causes intellectual disability with cardiac arrhythmia.

Free G protein beta:gamma dimers, released when a receptor-activated heterotrimeric G protein dissociates, act as signalling molecules in their own right, and one of their direct effectors is phospholipase C beta. Engagement of the enzyme's pleckstrin homology domain stimulates hydrolysis of the membrane lipid PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, so that IP3 releases calcium from intracellular stores while DAG recruits and activates protein kinase C. This gives Gi- and Go-coupled receptors, which do not stimulate PLC through their alpha subunits, a route to calcium mobilisation; it underlies chemokine-driven leukocyte activation, platelet responses and taste transduction, where the hematopoietic isoform PLCB2 and the gustatory gamma subunit GNG13 operate. The various beta and gamma subunits combine combinatorially, and the beta isoforms differ in sensitivity, with PLCB3 the most responsive and PLCB1 the least.

Reduction of cytosolic Ca++ levels is the clearance arm of calcium signalling: it returns free cytoplasmic Ca2+ to its resting nanomolar concentration after a signalling spike, which is what allows the next spike to be interpreted as information rather than noise. Sustained elevation instead triggers protease and phospholipase activation, mitochondrial overload and cell death, and in heart and muscle it manifests as impaired relaxation and arrhythmia. Two routes do the work: SERCA pumps (ATP2A1-3) pump Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic and endoplasmic reticulum for reuse, while plasma membrane Ca2+ ATPases (ATP2B1-4) and the Na+/Ca2+ exchangers (SLC8A1-3) extrude it across the cell surface, the exchangers trading the sodium gradient for high-capacity efflux. Calmodulin tunes pump activity to the calcium load, and sorcin modulates the release channels, coupling clearance to excitation-contraction cycling.

Calcium signals must be terminated as sharply as they are generated, and this pathway is how a cell clears calcium from its cytosol after a transient. Pumps of the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum family reload internal stores, plasma membrane calcium ATPases extrude calcium against its gradient using ATP, and sodium/calcium exchangers move it out in exchange for inbound sodium, a lower-affinity but high-capacity route that dominates in cardiac myocytes. Calmodulin senses the rising ion and stimulates the plasma membrane pumps, giving feedback control over the recovery phase; sorcin modulates calcium handling in excitable cells. Restoring resting calcium sets the rate of muscle relaxation, resets neuronal excitability and secretory cells for the next stimulus, and prevents the sustained overload that triggers protease and phospholipase activation and cell death. Failure contributes to heart failure, arrhythmia and hereditary deafness.

NCAM1 interactions describes the binding partnerships of the neural cell adhesion molecule, an immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptor that also transduces signals across the membrane. It governs how neurons and glia stick to each other and to matrix, how axons grow and are guided, and how synapses remodel, so it underpins neural development, learning-related synaptic plasticity, and regeneration after injury. NCAM1 engages in homophilic cis- and trans-binding and in heterophilic contacts with collagens and other extracellular matrix and proteoglycan components such as agrin and neurocan, with contactin and prion protein, and with the GDNF family ligands through GFRA co-receptors, making it an alternative signalling receptor for neurotrophic factors. Downstream, it couples to voltage-gated calcium channel subunits to influence neurite outgrowth. Polysialylation by ST8SIA2 and ST8SIA4 weakens adhesion and switches NCAM1 toward permitting migration and plasticity.

NCAM1 is a neural cell adhesion molecule that both glues cells together and signals, and its interactions shape how neurons and glia migrate, extend axons, and remodel synapses during development and learning. Homophilic binding between NCAM1 molecules on adjacent cells is tuned by polysialylation, added by the sialyltransferases ST8SIA2 and ST8SIA4, which bulks up the extracellular domain and weakens adhesion to favour plasticity and cell movement; loss of this modification stiffens circuits and has been linked to schizophrenia risk. Heterophilic partners broaden the output: fibrillar and basement membrane collagens and the proteoglycans agrin and neurocan tie NCAM1 to the extracellular matrix, GDNF family ligands with their GFRA co-receptors couple it to neurotrophic survival signalling, and voltage-gated calcium channel subunits link adhesion to excitability and transmitter release. Contactin-2 and prion protein complete a set of neuronal surface associations governing adhesion, proliferation, differentiation and neurite outgrowth.

Cell-cell junction organization builds and maintains the contacts that hold epithelial and endothelial sheets together, giving tissues mechanical integrity and a selective paracellular barrier. Adherens junctions initiate contact through classical cadherins such as CDH1 linked by catenins and vinculin to actin; claudins and JAM-A seal tight junctions that control passage of water, ions and small solutes; desmosomal plakoglobin ties the intermediate filament network between neighbouring cells. Nectins, CADMs and the PAR3-PAR6-aPKC and Crumbs-PALS1-PATJ modules position these junctions and set apical-basal polarity, with Rho-family GTPases and Src-family kinases remodelling them dynamically. Transcriptional repressors including SNAI1/2, ZEB1/2 and TWIST, along with miR-200 family regulation and ubiquitin-proteasome turnover of junctional components, dismantle adhesion during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Loss of this organization underlies barrier failure, disrupted morphogenesis and wound repair, and the invasive behaviour of carcinomas.

Epithelial sheets hold together through three adhesion systems — adherens junctions, tight junctions and desmosomes — and this pathway covers how they are built, remodelled and controlled. Junction organization sets the permeability barrier of skin, gut, kidney tubule and endothelium, establishes apical-basal polarity, and its loss underlies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, wound healing failure and invasive tumour spread. Classical cadherins and nectins nucleate contacts and link through catenins, vinculin and plakoglobin to actin, while claudins and junctional adhesion molecules create the paracellular seal and select which ions and small solutes pass. Polarity complexes containing PARD3, PARD6 and atypical PKC, together with Rho-family GTPases CDC42 and RAC1 and their exchange factors, position junctions correctly. Cadherin levels are further set by proteasomal turnover, N-glycosylation and signal peptide processing, and by transcriptional repressors such as SNAI1, SNAI2, ZEB1 and TWIST1 acting with histone-modifying and microRNA machinery.

Regulation of insulin secretion describes how pancreatic beta cells convert nutrient and hormonal signals into graded release of insulin, the master control on postprandial glucose disposal. Its failure, through loss of channel function or blunted incretin amplification, produces neonatal diabetes, hyperinsulinism, or the impaired first-phase secretion that marks type 2 diabetes. Glucose entering through GLUT transporters is catabolised to raise ATP, closing KATP channels built from KCNJ11 and ABCC8; the membrane depolarises, voltage-gated calcium channels open, and calcium triggers SNARE-dependent exocytosis of insulin granules via syntaxin, SNAP25, VAMP2 and the calcium sensor synaptotagmin V. Layered on this trigger are G protein-coupled modulators: GLP-1 and GIP receptors and muscarinic and fatty acid receptors raise cAMP or IP3 to amplify release through PKA, Epac and PKC, while adrenergic Gi signalling suppresses it. Voltage-gated potassium channels repolarise and terminate each burst.

Pancreatic beta cells set the amount of insulin released into blood, and the tuning of that release keeps postprandial glucose within narrow limits; its failure underlies type 2 diabetes, while mutations in the KATP channel subunits SUR1 and Kir6.2 cause congenital hyperinsulinism or neonatal diabetes. Glucose entering through GLUT transporters is catabolised to raise ATP, closing KATP channels so the membrane depolarises and L-, P/Q-, R- and T-type voltage-gated calcium channels admit calcium, which drives SNARE-mediated fusion of docked granules through syntaxin-1A, SNAP25, VAMP2 and the calcium sensor synaptotagmin V. On top of this trigger, amplifying and inhibitory inputs converge via G proteins: incretin and muscarinic receptors raise cAMP or generate IP3 for calcium release, acting through protein kinase A and the Epac exchange factors, while adrenergic alpha-2 receptors coupled to Gi suppress secretion. Free fatty acid sensing adds a further amplifying arm.

Axon guidance is how a growing neuron finds its target, and it is the process that builds the wiring diagram of the nervous system; when it fails, commissures fail to cross the midline, sensory and motor projections mistarget, and cortical layering is disrupted. Motile growth cones read attractive and repulsive cues in their environment through dedicated receptor families "netrins acting on DCC and UNC5, Slits on Robo, semaphorins on plexins and neuropilins, and ephrins on Eph kinases" together with adhesion molecules such as L1CAM, NCAM1 and contactins and with extracellular matrix laminins, collagens and integrins. Signals converge on Rho-family GTPases, PAK and ROCK kinases, cofilin, Ena/VASP and the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton to steer or collapse the growth cone. Local protein turnover by the proteasome, receptor endocytosis, and translational control tune responsiveness, and the same cues are redeployed in tumour cell migration and angiogenesis.

Wiring the nervous system depends on axon pathfinding: growth cones at the tips of extending axons read attractive and repulsive cues in their surroundings and translate them into directional cytoskeletal remodelling, so that projections reach their correct targets and form functional circuits. The canonical cue families are all represented — netrins acting through DCC and UNC5 receptors, Slits through Robo, semaphorins through plexins and neuropilins, and ephrins through Eph kinases — alongside adhesion molecules such as L1CAM, NCAM1 and contactins, Reelin signalling through VLDLR and DAB1, and extracellular matrix laminins, collagens and integrins. Downstream, Rho-family GTPases, PAK and ROCK kinases, LIM kinases, cofilin, profilin, Arp2/3 and tubulins execute actin and microtubule turnover, while proteasomal degradation, endocytic adaptors and local regulation of translation tune receptor levels. Failures produce commissural and cortical malformations, and the same cues are redeployed in tumour cell migration and angiogenesis.

Sodium-coupled phosphate cotransporters bring inorganic phosphate into cells against its electrochemical gradient, supplying the phosphate needed for ATP and nucleotide synthesis, membrane phospholipids, protein phosphorylation and skeletal mineralisation. They also set whole-body phosphate balance: the SLC34 members reclaim filtered phosphate in the renal proximal tubule and absorb it across the intestine and lung, so their loss causes hypophosphataemic rickets, nephrolithiasis and pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, while the ubiquitous SLC20 (PiT1/PiT2) transporters handle housekeeping uptake and, in vascular smooth muscle, drive calcification when phosphate is high; PiT2 mutations cause familial brain calcification. All are secondary-active symporters that couple phosphate influx to the inward sodium gradient maintained by the Na+/K+-ATPase, and their surface abundance is tuned by parathyroid hormone, FGF23 and vitamin D. A related SLC17 carrier mediates apical anion efflux in kidney and liver.

Phosphate is needed for bone mineral, nucleotides, phospholipids and every phosphorylation reaction, and cells cannot take up this charged anion without help. Sodium-coupled phosphate cotransporters supply that uptake, exploiting the inward sodium gradient maintained by the Na+/K+-ATPase to drive phosphate across the plasma membrane against its electrochemical gradient. The SLC34 members handle bulk transepithelial handling: NPT2a and NPT2c in the renal proximal tubule brush border set urinary phosphate excretion and are the target of PTH and FGF23 regulation, while NPT2b mediates dietary absorption in the small intestine and phosphate supply for surfactant in lung. The SLC20 pair, PiT1 and PiT2, are broadly expressed housekeeping importers serving cellular metabolism. Loss of function causes hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis, pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, and, for PiT2, familial brain calcification.

Proton/oligopeptide cotransporters are the SLC15 family carriers that move di- and tripeptides across membranes using an inward proton gradient, and they are how the body absorbs dietary protein after luminal digestion has reduced it to short peptides. PEPT1 in the small intestinal brush border, together with its kidney counterpart, accounts for the bulk of amino acid nitrogen uptake and reabsorption, and its broad substrate tolerance makes it the route by which beta-lactam antibiotics, ACE inhibitors and peptidomimetic prodrugs enter the body, a fact routinely exploited in drug design. The related PHT1 and PHT2 work instead on lysosomal and endosomal membranes of immune cells, where peptide and histidine transport delivers bacterial products such as muramyl dipeptide and shapes endosomal Toll-like receptor and NOD signalling; variants in this arm are linked to lupus and inflammatory disease susceptibility.

Dietary protein is absorbed largely as di- and tripeptides rather than free amino acids, and the proton-coupled oligopeptide cotransporters of the SLC15 family are what move those peptides across membranes. PEPT1 in the small intestinal brush border drives bulk uptake of digestion products using the inwardly directed proton gradient maintained by sodium/hydrogen exchange, and its broad substrate tolerance makes it the route by which beta-lactam antibiotics, ACE inhibitors and peptidomimetic prodrugs reach the bloodstream, a property exploited in oral drug design. The related PHT1 and PHT2 proteins sit in lysosomal and endosomal membranes of immune cells, where they export histidine and bacterial peptide fragments into the cytosol; this delivery of muramyl dipeptide and related ligands to NOD sensors, and the trafficking role of PHT1 in endosomal Toll-like receptor signalling, links peptide transport to innate immune activation and to lupus susceptibility.

Sphingolipid metabolism builds, remodels and degrades the sphingoid-based lipids that give membranes their structure and that double as signalling molecules controlling apoptosis, stress responses and lymphocyte trafficking. Cells depend almost entirely on de novo synthesis, beginning with serine palmitoyltransferase condensing serine and palmitoyl-CoA, followed by reduction, N-acylation by a family of ceramide synthases with distinct chain-length preferences, and desaturation to ceramide. Ceramide is then transferred from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi by CERT for conversion to sphingomyelin, or glucosylated by UGCG to seed glycosphingolipids and gangliosides. Sphingomyelinases, ceramidases and sphingosine kinases run the salvage arm, generating sphingosine 1-phosphate that is exported by transporters such as SPNS2 to establish the gradients guiding T cell egress. Lysosomal hydrolases and their saposin activators complete catabolism; their loss causes Gaucher, Fabry, Tay-Sachs and metachromatic leukodystrophy.

Sphingolipids are membrane lipids built on a long-chain amino alcohol backbone, and their metabolism covers both the making and the breaking of ceramide, sphingomyelin, glucosyl- and galactosylceramides, sulfatides and gangliosides. Beyond structure, intermediates of the route act as signals: ceramide promotes stress responses and apoptosis, while sphingosine 1-phosphate, made by sphingosine kinases and exported by transporters such as SPNS2 and MFSD2B, guides lymphocyte egress and vascular integrity. De novo synthesis starts with serine palmitoyltransferase subunits condensing serine with palmitoyl-CoA, is restrained by ORMDL proteins, and proceeds through ketodihydrosphingosine reduction, ceramide synthase acylation and desaturation; CERT1 with VAPA/VAPB then delivers ceramide to the Golgi for sphingomyelin synthase. Catabolism runs through sphingomyelinases, glycosidases, sulfatases and ceramidases in the lysosome with activator proteins, and loss of individual steps causes the sphingolipidoses, including Gaucher, Fabry, Tay-Sachs, Krabbe and Niemann-Pick disease.

Deadenylation-dependent mRNA decay is the normal end of an mRNA's life: after rounds of translation, the poly(A) tail is trimmed and the transcript is destroyed. This sets mRNA half-life and therefore how long a gene's message can be translated, making it the main route by which cells clear transcripts during differentiation, stress responses and immune activation. Tail shortening happens stepwise, first by PAN2-PAN3 and then by the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex or PARN, stripping the poly(A)-binding protein platform that protects the message. The stripped body is then degraded from either end: Lsm1-7 recruits the DCP1-DCP2 decapping enzyme so XRN1 can chew 5' to 3', or the exosome with its SKI helicase partners degrades 3' to 5', leaving a capped remnant cleared by the scavenger decapping enzyme. Decapping factors such as DDX6, EDC3 and PATL1 tie this decay to P-body assembly and translational repression.

Most cytoplasmic mRNAs are retired by deadenylation-dependent decay, the default route that ends a transcript's working life after rounds of translation and thereby sets mRNA half-life, message abundance and the speed with which a cell can change its expression programme. Shortening of the poly(A) tail begins with the PAN2-PAN3 pair and is completed by the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex, whose CNOT6/6L and CNOT7/8 nuclease modules, or by PARN, stripping the platform that poly(A)-binding protein and initiation factors use to keep the message stable and translatable. The trimmed body is then destroyed from either end: the Lsm1-7 ring and decapping factors DCP1-DCP2 with DDX6, EDC3 and EDC4 expose the 5' end to XRN1, or the exosome with its helicase-containing cofactors degrades 3' to 5', leaving a cap fragment cleared by DCPS. Much of this occurs in cytoplasmic granules, and its regulation underlies developmental and immune transcript turnover.

Deadenylation of mRNA is the first and usually rate-limiting step in mRNA decay: trimming the 3' poly(A) tail that, together with its bound poly(A)-binding protein and the cap-binding initiation complex, keeps a transcript stable and efficiently translated. Shortening the tail therefore both silences a message and commits it to degradation, which is how cells set transcript half-lives and dismantle regulatory programs after a signal ends. Trimming proceeds in two phases, with the PAN2-PAN3 complex shortening long tails and the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex or PARN completing the job to an oligo(A) stub. CCR4-NOT couples this to transcription and to microRNA- and RNA-binding-protein-directed repression, while terminal uridylyl transferases mark shortened tails for decapping and exonucleolytic destruction. Related deadenylases impose rhythmic control on gene expression, and PARN-type activity governs tail length and translational timing in oocytes.

Shortening of the poly(A) tail is the first and usually rate-limiting step in cytoplasmic mRNA turnover, and it sets how long a transcript remains translatable. Because the tail bound by poly(A)-binding protein cooperates with the cap-binding initiation machinery to promote translation, trimming it both silences a message and commits it to decay, making deadenylation of mRNA a general lever for controlling gene expression after transcription. Two exonuclease steps are represented: the PAN2-PAN3 complex performs initial trimming, then the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex, whose catalytic subunits are CNOT6/6L and CNOT7/8 assembled on the CNOT1 scaffold, or the separate PARN enzyme completes it. Terminal uridylyltransferases mark short-tailed transcripts for destruction. This machinery shapes responses to developmental and circadian cues, oocyte maturation, and the clearance of unstable regulatory transcripts.

mRNA decay by 3' to 5' exoribonuclease is one of the two main routes by which cells destroy messenger RNAs once they are deadenylated, setting transcript half-life and thus the duration of any gene's expression. It also clears aberrant and surplus transcripts, so its loss produces accumulation of defective RNA and is linked to cerebellar hypoplasia and multiple myeloma through mutations in exosome subunits and DIS3. The exosome, a barrel of nine EXOSC proteins capped by the processive ribonuclease DIS3, threads the oligoadenylated 3' end through its central channel and degrades it to mononucleotides; the cytoplasmic SKI complex with HBS1L feeds RNA into that channel, including messages stalled on ribosomes. What remains is a short capped fragment, which the scavenger decapping enzyme DCPS hydrolyses, releasing m7GMP for recycling by downstream nucleotidases.

Messenger RNAs that have been deadenylated must be destroyed, and one of the two routes for doing so chews the transcript inward from its 3' end. This keeps transcript levels matched to need, clears aberrant and no-longer-wanted mRNAs, and sets the lifetime of regulated messages such as those bearing destabilising elements. The nine-subunit exosome barrel provides the channel, with DIS3 supplying the hydrolytic exoribonuclease activity, while a cytoplasmic cofactor complex built from SKIC2, SKIC3 and SKIC8 together with the GTPase-like HBS1L feeds substrate RNA into it from ribosomes. Degradation stops short of the 5' end, leaving a capped oligonucleotide that the scavenger decapping enzyme DCPS hydrolyses to release 7-methylguanosine monophosphate for recycling. Loss of exosome subunits causes neurological and skeletal disease, reflecting how closely RNA turnover is tied to gene expression control.

Passive transport by Aquaporins is the family of membrane channels that let water, and in some cases small neutral solutes, cross cell membranes down an osmotic gradient far faster than simple diffusion permits. It sets the water permeability of epithelia and so underlies urine concentration in the kidney, cerebrospinal fluid production and brain fluid balance, secretion by salivary, lacrimal and airway glands, bile flow, and lens transparency; loss of individual members causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, cataract, and renal cyst formation. Each monomer forms a narrow pore whose asparagine-proline-alanine motifs enforce selectivity, and four monomers assemble into a tetramer. The aquaglyceroporins AQP3, AQP7, AQP9 and AQP10 additionally conduct glycerol and urea, linking this transport to lipolysis and hepatic gluconeogenesis, while AQP6 conducts anions and AQP8 ammonia. AQP2 trafficking to the apical membrane is the regulated step in vasopressin-driven water reabsorption.

Water crosses membranes far faster than lipid permeability allows because aquaporins provide dedicated channels for it, and this family of channels is how epithelia and other tissues move fluid down osmotic gradients without expending energy. Each subunit folds into six transmembrane helices whose two asparagine-proline-alanine motifs line a narrow pore that admits water while excluding protons and ions; four subunits assemble into a tetramer. Selectivity varies across the family: the aquaglyceroporins AQP3, AQP7, AQP9 and AQP10 also pass glycerol, some conduct urea, AQP8 passes ammonia, and AQP6 conducts anions such as nitrate. The consequences are physiological rather than metabolic: AQP1 and AQP2 underlie renal water reabsorption and vasopressin-responsive urine concentration, AQP4 governs brain water balance, AQP0 keeps lens fibre cells transparent, and loss of these channels produces cataract, diabetes insipidus or renal cyst formation.

Post NMDA receptor activation events describes what a glutamatergic synapse does with the calcium that floods through an activated NMDA receptor, and it is the molecular basis of long-term potentiation, learning and memory. Calcium entering the dendritic spine binds calmodulin and switches on CaMKII, CaMKIV and the CaMKK kinases, engages adenylate cyclases and PKA, and recruits Ras-GRF proteins to drive ERK signalling; these converge on phosphorylation of CREB1 at serine 133, so that a transient electrical event is converted into transcription of genes that stabilise the strengthened synapse. In parallel, scaffolding by PSD-95 family proteins, Rac1/GIT1 signalling and remodelling of tubulin and actin-associated cytoskeleton reshape the spine itself. Neuregulin-ErbB4 signalling modulates the response. Dysregulation of this cascade underlies excitotoxic neuronal death and contributes to cognitive and psychiatric disorders.

Calcium entering a dendritic spine through the NMDA receptor is the trigger that converts brief synaptic activity into lasting change, and the events downstream of NMDA receptor activation are how that calcium signal is decoded. They underlie long-term potentiation, and with it learning and memory; disturbance of these steps contributes to intellectual disability, epilepsy and neurodegeneration. Calmodulin-dependent kinases, adenylate cyclases with cAMP-dependent protein kinase, and the Ras-ERK route each converge on phosphorylation of CREB1 at serine 133, switching on transcription of genes that consolidate the synapse. In parallel, scaffolding proteins of the PSD-95 family anchor the receptor to signalling enzymes, AMPA receptor subunits are inserted and modified to strengthen transmission, and Rac1 with its regulators remodels the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton so the spine changes shape. Neuregulin-ERBB4 signalling tunes the process.

VEGFA-VEGFR2 Pathway is the principal driver of angiogenesis, the sprouting of new blood vessels from existing ones. Vascular endothelial growth factor A acting on the receptor tyrosine kinase VEGFR2 (KDR) makes endothelial cells proliferate, survive, migrate and become more permeable; loss of the receptor blocks blood island and endothelial development and is embryonic lethal, and the same axis is exploited by tumours to recruit their blood supply, which is why it is a major anti-angiogenic drug target. Receptor autophosphorylation recruits SRC, SHB and PLCG1 and branches into PI3K-AKT-mTOR survival signalling, eNOS activation and vasodilation, p38-MAPKAPK2 stress signalling, and Rho-family GTPase control of the actin cytoskeleton through WAVE complexes, PAK and ROCK. Integrin αvβ3, focal adhesion components and VE-cadherin junctional proteins couple this to adhesion, motility and barrier control.

New blood vessels sprout from existing ones under the control of vascular endothelial growth factor A acting on its endothelial receptor tyrosine kinase VEGFR2 (KDR), and this axis is the principal driver of angiogenesis in development, wound healing, tumour growth and diabetic retinopathy; loss of the receptor kills mouse embryos for lack of endothelial and blood island formation, while blocking the ligand is standard anti-angiogenic therapy. Ligand binding triggers receptor autophosphorylation and recruitment of adaptors such as SHB, NCK and SRC, feeding PLCG1-calcium-PKC signalling, RAS-p38 MAPK activation through MAPKAPK2 and HSPB1, and PI3K-AKT-mTOR survival signalling. Rho-family GTPases with WAVE complex and PAK/ROCK effectors remodel actin for endothelial migration and sprouting, focal adhesion and VE-cadherin junction components govern adhesion and permeability, and eNOS activation supplies nitric oxide for vasodilation.

RSK activation describes how the ribosomal S6 kinases are switched on at the end of the RAS-ERK cascade, converting growth factor and mitogen signals into phosphorylation of substrates that drive protein synthesis, cell growth, survival and transcription. It is the step that couples ERK activity to targets such as ribosomal protein S6 pathway components, CREB and pro-apoptotic BAD, and its loss in the brain matters: mutations in RSK2 cause Coffin-Lowry syndrome, with cognitive impairment and skeletal anomalies, consistent with high RSK expression in synaptically active brain regions. Activation is multi-step and mostly membrane-localised: ERK1/2 phosphorylate the C-terminal kinase domain and linker, enabling autophosphorylation, while PDK1 phosphorylates the N-terminal kinase domain to complete activation. The four human isoforms differ in behaviour, with RSK4 showing constitutive activity independent of growth factor stimulation.

RSK activation converts growth factor signalling through RAS and the ERK cascade into a kinase that acts on translation, transcription and survival machinery. The four human isoforms, RSK1-4, are switched on by a two-input mechanism: the ERK enzymes MAPK1 and MAPK3 phosphorylate sites in the C-terminal kinase domain and linker, which licenses autophosphorylation, while PDPK1 phosphorylates the activation loop of the N-terminal domain to give full catalytic output. Activation occurs mainly at the plasma membrane but also in cytoplasm and nucleus, and RSK4 is unusual in showing high basal activity even without growth factor stimulation. The output matters physiologically: RSK2 is abundant in synaptically active brain regions, and loss-of-function mutations in it cause Coffin-Lowry syndrome with cognitive impairment and skeletal abnormalities. Because RSKs sit downstream of RAS, their activity also contributes to proliferative signalling in tumours.

Smooth Muscle Contraction is the contractile program of the non-striated muscle that lines blood vessels, airways, gut, bladder and uterus, setting vascular tone, peristalsis and airway calibre; its dysregulation underlies hypertension, asthmatic bronchoconstriction and vasospasm. Contraction is triggered not by neural command alone but by hormones, paracrine mediators, local chemistry and mechanical load, all converging on a rise in cytosolic calcium. Calcium entering through T-type channels binds calmodulin, activating myosin light chain kinase, which phosphorylates the regulatory light chains of smooth muscle myosin and licenses cross-bridge cycling on actin; a parallel arm relieves caldesmon's block of the thin filament, analogous to troponin control in striated muscle. Because the filaments attach to dense bodies and focal adhesions rather than sarcomeres, sliding pulls talin, vinculin, paxillin and integrin anchorages inward, shortening the whole cell. Nitric oxide-driven soluble guanylate cyclase and phosphodiesterase-5 oppose this, providing relaxation.

Smooth muscle contraction generates the force that narrows blood vessels, moves food through the gut, and controls airway, bladder and uterine tone, responding to autonomic nerves, hormones, local mediators and stretch rather than to voluntary command. Calcium entry, here through low-voltage T-type channels, loads calmodulin, which activates myosin light chain kinase to phosphorylate the regulatory light chains of smooth muscle myosin and permit actin cross-bridge cycling; a parallel caldesmon-dependent arm modulates the actin filament in a manner analogous to troponin. Because the contractile apparatus is anchored not to sarcomeres but to dense bodies and focal adhesions built on talin, vinculin, paxillin and integrins, shortening squeezes the whole cell. Relaxation runs through nitric oxide-stimulated soluble guanylate cyclase and cGMP, the target of phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors. Dysregulation underlies hypertension, vasospasm, asthmatic bronchoconstriction and bowel dysmotility.

TAK1-dependent IKK and NF-kappa-B activation describes how innate immune and inflammatory receptor signals are converted into new gene expression, driving cytokine, chemokine and survival gene transcription. NF-kappa-B dimers such as RELA/NFKB1 are held inactive in the cytoplasm by IkB proteins; the IKK complex (CHUK, IKBKB, IKBKG) phosphorylates IkB, triggering its degradation and freeing NF-kappa-B to enter the nucleus. Upstream, receptor engagement builds non-degradative polyubiquitin chains via TRAF6 and the UBE2N/UBE2V1 pair, recruiting the MAP3K7 (TAK1)-TAB1/TAB2/TAB3 kinase module that activates IKK. Inputs include cytosolic NOD1/NOD2-RIPK2 sensing of bacterial peptidoglycan, IRAK-coupled Toll-like receptor signalling, and RAGE ligands such as HMGB1 and S100 proteins. Negative regulators including NKIRAS proteins, N4BP1, NLRX1 and deubiquitinases limit output, since sustained activation produces chronic inflammation and supports tumour cell survival.

Inflammatory and innate immune receptors converge on releasing NF-kappa-B from cytoplasmic restraint, and TAK1-dependent IKK and NF-kappa-B activation is the relay that does it. Resting cells keep NFKB1, NFKB2 and RELA bound to inhibitory IkB proteins such as NFKBIA and NFKBIB; the IKK complex of CHUK, IKBKB and the regulatory subunit IKBKG phosphorylates IkB, triggering its degradation so the dimers enter the nucleus and switch on cytokine, chemokine and survival genes. Upstream, receptor engagement — including intracellular bacterial sensing through NOD1, NOD2 and RIPK2, IRAK1-coupled receptors, and alarmins like HMGB1 and S100 proteins acting via AGER — builds non-degradative ubiquitin chains using TRAF6 and the UBE2N/UBE2V1 pair that recruit and activate MAP3K7 with its TAB adaptors. Ubiquitin precursors and deubiquitinases set the duration of the response. Overactivity drives chronic inflammation and autoinflammatory disease, while loss cripples host defence.

Interleukin-1 family signaling is the core alarm circuit of innate immunity: eleven related cytokines, including IL-1 dalpha/beta, IL-18, IL-33 and the IL-36 group, that announce infection, injury and cell death and drive fever, neutrophil recruitment, and downstream T helper responses. Its failure or over-activity underlies autoinflammatory fevers, gout, sepsis pathology, pustular psoriasis and asthma, and it is the target of anakinra and canakinumab. Most of these cytokines lack a secretion signal and are made as precursors, so activity is gated by inflammasome caspase-1 cleavage and gasdermin-D mediated release, and restrained by decoy receptors, antagonists such as IL1RN and IL18BP, and negative regulators including SIGIRR and IRAK3. Cytokine binding pairs a specific receptor with a shared accessory chain, assembling MyD88, IRAK kinases and TRAF6 to trigger ubiquitin-dependent IKK activation, proteasomal degradation of IκB, NF-κB transcription, and parallel p38, JNK and ERK output.

The interleukin-1 family drives the acute inflammatory response: fever, neutrophil recruitment, acute-phase protein production, and the alarm signalling that follows infection or tissue damage. Eleven related cytokines, including IL1A, IL1B, IL18, IL33 and the IL36 proteins, pair with heterodimeric receptors such as IL1R1, IL18R1 and IL1RL1 that share the IL1RAP co-receptor, while IL1RN, IL1R2, IL18BP and SIGIRR act as decoys or antagonists that keep the response bounded. IL1B and IL18 are made as inactive precursors and require inflammasome caspase-1 cleavage before release, linking this signalling to pyroptotic cell death through gasdermin D. Activated receptors recruit MYD88, IRAK kinases and TRAF6, and through TAK1 and the IKK complex trigger ubiquitin- and proteasome-dependent degradation of IkB, freeing NF-kB, alongside p38, JNK and ERK activation. Excessive output underlies autoinflammatory syndromes, gout and psoriasis, and is blocked therapeutically by receptor antagonism.

Cell junction organization builds and maintains the contacts that hold epithelia and other tissues together and anchor cells to their surrounding matrix. It is what makes an epithelial sheet a barrier: tight junctions seal the paracellular space and set apical-basal polarity, adherens junctions and nectin-based contacts couple neighbouring cells to their actin cytoskeletons, and hemidesmosomes rivet basal keratinocytes to the laminin-332 of the basement membrane. Loss of these links causes blistering skin disease, renal magnesium wasting, and the detachment and motility that accompany epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The genes span cadherins and catenins, claudins and junctional adhesion molecules, the PAR-Crumbs polarity modules, integrin α6β4 with plectin and collagen XVII, and integrin-linked kinase adhesomes, together with the transcriptional repressors SNAI1, ZEB1/2 and TWIST that dismantle junctions and the proteasomal and glycosylation machinery that controls junction protein turnover and maturation.

Epithelia and endothelia only work as barriers and coherent sheets because their cells are physically linked to one another and to the basement membrane, and cell junction organization is the assembly, remodelling and turnover of those links. Tight junctions built from claudins and JAM-A seal the paracellular space and set ion selectivity; classical cadherins with alpha- and beta-catenin, p120 and plakoglobin form adherens junctions; nectins and nectin-like adhesion molecules nucleate contacts; and integrin alpha6beta4 with collagen XVII, plectin, laminin-332 and keratins 5/14 anchors basal keratinocytes through type I hemidesmosomes, loss of which causes blistering skin disease. Integrin-linked kinase, kindlin, parvin, paxillin, vinculin and talin-associated adaptors couple adhesion to actin and to Rho-family GTPases, while Crumbs and Par polarity complexes position junctions apicobasally. Transcriptional repressors such as SNAI1/2, ZEB1/2 and TWIST dismantle this programme during epithelial-mesenchymal transition and tumour invasion.

Neurofascin interactions describes the adhesive contacts made by neurofascin, an L1-family immunoglobulin cell adhesion molecule that organizes the node of Ranvier and the paranodal junction and directs axonal subcellular targeting and synapse formation. These contacts hold the myelinating glial cell to the axon and cluster the machinery that makes saltatory conduction possible; their disruption slows nerve conduction and is a feature of demyelinating neuropathy and autoimmune attack on nodal antigens. The neuronal 186 kDa isoform partners with NrCAM and links through ankyrin to the axonal spectrin cytoskeleton, while the glial 155 kDa isoform engages the contactin-CASPR complex to build the paranode. A carboxy-terminal PDZ class I motif recruits syntenin-1, coupling adhesion to intracellular scaffolding, and the same adhesive signalling promotes neurite outgrowth and, with doublecortin, microtubule-dependent neuronal migration during development.

Neurofascin is an L1-family immunoglobulin adhesion molecule whose interactions organize specialized axonal membrane domains, and this adhesive biology is what allows nodes of Ranvier and axo-glial junctions to form and hold together so that saltatory conduction works. Distinct isoforms act on either side of the junction: the neuronal 186 kDa form clusters at nodes with NrCAM and is anchored to the spectrin-based cytoskeleton through ankyrin, while the glial 155 kDa form works with contactin and its associated protein CNTNAP1 to build the paranodal septate-like junction with the myelinating cell. A C-terminal class I PDZ-binding motif recruits syntenin-1, linking adhesion to intracellular scaffolding and trafficking, and the presence of doublecortin reflects the roles these contacts play in axon subcellular targeting, neurite outgrowth and synapse formation during neural development. Disruption of these contacts causes paranodal disorganization and conduction failure, and neurofascin is an autoantigen in inflammatory neuropathy.

Interleukin-1 processing converts inactive cytoplasmic precursors of the interleukin-1 family into mature, secreted cytokines, the step that licenses fever, neutrophil recruitment and the acute inflammatory response. Because pro-IL1B and pro-IL18 lack signal peptides, they bypass the ER-Golgi route and instead require proteolytic maturation by caspase-1 assembled on an inflammasome scaffold, with gasdermin D pores providing a conduit for release; alternative routes through secretory lysosomes, shed microvesicles and neutrophil proteases such as cathepsin G also contribute, and calpain-like activity processes pro-IL1A. Transcription of the precursors themselves depends on NF-kB subunits, so pathogen or damage sensing controls both substrate supply and its cleavage. This two-step control keeps a potent cytokine latent until warranted; its dysregulation drives the periodic fever syndromes and gout-like inflammation treated by IL-1 blockade.

Interleukin-1 processing is the step that converts an inactive cytoplasmic precursor into a released, receptor-competent inflammatory cytokine, and it sets the threshold for fever, neutrophil recruitment and the acute-phase response. Unlike most cytokines, pro-IL1B and pro-IL1A lack a signal peptide and cannot leave through the ER-Golgi route, so activation and export are coupled: inflammasome-activated caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL1B and pro-IL18 to their mature forms, and also cleaves gasdermin D, whose pore both releases the cytokines and can commit the cell to pyroptosis. Neutrophil cathepsin G offers a caspase-independent route to processing extracellularly, while NF-kB subunits supply the transcriptional arm that makes precursor available in the first place. Excessive flux through this pathway drives the autoinflammatory fevers and gout-like inflammation treated by IL-1 blockade.

Other interleukin signaling gathers the cytokine-receptor systems that regulate immune cell production and mucosal antiviral defence but fall outside the major interleukin families. Interleukins are small secreted proteins acting on nearby cells or on the cell that made them, and collectively they govern haematopoietic homeostasis, tissue growth and repair, and layered host defence against pathogens; loss of individual axes here produces specific immunodeficiencies. Two well-defined arms are represented: colony-stimulating factor signalling, in which CSF1 and IL34 act through CSF1R to specify macrophages and microglia while CSF3 drives neutrophil production, and interferon-lambda signalling through IFNLR1 with IL10RB, which restricts viral infection at epithelial barriers via JAK1 and TYK2. Also included is regulated secretion of cytokines and granule contents, using SNARE proteins such as VAMP2, STX3, STX4 and STXBP2, alongside CD4- and caspase-linked lymphocyte responses.

Interleukins are small secreted proteins that act on nearby or the same cell through surface receptors, coordinating tissue growth and repair, blood cell production and host defence; here the focus falls on interleukin-like cytokines handled outside the main receptor families. Colony-stimulating factors and their receptors drive myeloid output, with CSF1 and IL34 both acting through CSF1R to specify macrophage and microglial survival, while IL34 additionally engages PTPRZ1 and syndecan-1. CSF3 signalling through CSF3R sustains granulopoiesis. Interferon lambda uses a receptor pair of IFNLR1 with IL10RB and the JAK1/TYK2 kinases to protect epithelial barriers from viral infection. Also represented are IL16, released from its precursor by caspase-3 cleavage and binding CD4, and IL32, which lacks a defined receptor. The SNARE and syntaxin components indicate the regulated vesicle fusion required to release these cytokines.

JNK (c-Jun kinases) phosphorylation and activation mediated by activated human TAK1 is the stress- and inflammation-triggered arm of MAP kinase signalling that converts innate immune receptor engagement into changes in gene expression and cell fate. It decides whether a cell exposed to inflammatory cytokines, bacterial peptidoglycan sensed by NOD1/NOD2, UV or heat shock proliferates, survives, or undergoes apoptosis, and it drives the transcriptional programmes downstream of c-Jun and AP-1. Upstream adaptors such as IRAK1 and RIPK2 recruit TRAF6, which together with the UBE2N/UBE2V1 conjugating pair builds non-degradative polyubiquitin chains; these are read by the TAB1/TAB2/TAB3 subunits that activate the kinase TAK1. Activated TAK1 phosphorylates the dual-specificity kinases MKK4 and MKK7, which in turn activate JNK1, JNK2 and the largely neuronal JNK3. Isoform-specific substrate choice explains why the same module can promote either death or survival.

Stress and inflammatory signals are converted into a transcriptional response through the stress-activated JNK kinases, and this route describes their phosphorylation and activation downstream of active TAK1. The output determines whether a cell undergoes apoptosis, survives, or proliferates, and it drives AP-1-dependent cytokine production, so chronic engagement contributes to inflammatory disease while loss blunts innate immune responses. Upstream, pattern recognition by NOD1 and NOD2 recruits the kinase RIPK2, and interleukin-1/Toll-like receptor input through IRAK1 and IRAK2 converges on TRAF6, which together with the UBE2N/UBE2V1 conjugating pair builds non-degradative polyubiquitin chains. These are read by the TAB2 and TAB3 adaptors that, with TAB1, position TAK1 (MAP3K7) for autoactivation. TAK1 then phosphorylates the dual-specificity kinases MKK4 and MKK7, which activate JNK1, JNK2 and the largely neuronal JNK3 by dual phosphorylation of their activation loop.

Ionotropic activity of kainate receptors covers fast excitatory neurotransmission through one of the three families of glutamate-gated ion channels, distinct from AMPA and NMDA receptors in its slower kinetics and its prominent presynaptic role in tuning transmitter release and short-term plasticity. Tetramers assembled from GRIK1-GRIK5 subunits open a cation pore on glutamate binding; whether the channel passes Ca2+ depends on subunit composition and on RNA editing at the Q/R site of GluK1 and GluK2, so editing status directly sets calcium signalling in the postsynaptic spine. PDZ scaffolds of the DLG/PSD-95 family anchor the receptors at synapses, while calmodulin and neurocalcin provide calcium-sensor feedback onto channel behaviour. These receptors shape hippocampal mossy fibre transmission and interneuron excitability, and their dysregulation is linked to epilepsy and intellectual disability.

Kainate receptors are one of the three families of ionotropic glutamate receptors, and their ionotropic activity converts synaptic glutamate release into fast cation flux across the postsynaptic membrane. They shape excitatory transmission at a subset of synapses and also act presynaptically to modulate release, making them contributors to synaptic plasticity, network excitability and seizure susceptibility. Tetramers assemble from GRIK1-GRIK3 subunits combined with the high-affinity GRIK4 and GRIK5 subunits, and whether the resulting channel passes calcium as well as sodium depends on subunit composition and on RNA editing of the GluR5 and GluR6 subunits at the pore-lining Q/R site. Membrane-associated guanylate kinase scaffolds of the DLG family anchor the receptors within the postsynaptic density, while calmodulin and neurocalcin provide calcium-sensing regulation of channel behaviour and localisation.

Regulation of mitotic cell cycle covers the timed destruction of cell cycle proteins that makes mitosis irreversible and unidirectional. Its central actor is the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, a multisubunit ubiquitin ligase that, together with E2 enzymes and the 26S proteasome, degrades securin and mitotic cyclins so that sister chromatids separate, CDK1 activity collapses, and cells exit into G1. Substrate choice is dictated by the co-activators CDC20 and CDH1, and by inhibitors such as EMI1 and the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins MAD2, BUB3 and BUBR1, which hold the ligase off until every kinetochore is attached. Mitotic kinases including PLK1, Aurora A and Aurora B, and the SCF ligase acting on CDK inhibitors, feed into the same switch. Loss of this control produces chromosome missegregation, aneuploidy and the genomic instability characteristic of tumours.

Mitosis is timed by destruction rather than synthesis, and regulation of the mitotic cell cycle here centres on ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis that makes each transition irreversible. The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, a multisubunit ubiquitin ligase built from ANAPC and CDC16/23/27 subunits, works with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S and the 26S proteasome to degrade securin and the mitotic cyclins, thereby releasing separase to cleave cohesin, inactivating CDK1 and permitting sister chromatid separation and mitotic exit. Its two substrate adaptors act in sequence: CDC20 during metaphase, FZR1 from anaphase into G1, with the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins MAD2L1, BUB3 and BUB1B restraining CDC20 until all kinetochores are attached. Kinases including PLK1, AURKA and AURKB and the inhibitor FBXO5 tune the timing. Loss of this control produces premature separation, aneuploidy and chromosomal instability of the kind seen in tumours.

Mitotic G1 phase and G1/S transition covers the interval in which a cell decides whether to divide, and the commitment step that makes that decision irreversible once DNA replication begins. It sets the restriction point that mitogens act on, and its loss is among the most common events in cancer. In quiescent and early G1 cells the pocket proteins p130 and p107 with E2F4/5 and the MuvB core assemble repressive DREAM complexes that silence cell cycle genes, while RB1 restrains E2F1-3. Mitogen-driven D-type cyclins with CDK4/6, then cyclin E-CDK2, phosphorylate RB1 and release E2F-dependent transcription of replication factors -- MCM helicase subunits, ORC and CDC6/CDT1 licensing proteins, polymerases, PCNA and nucleotide-synthesis enzymes. INK4 and Cip/Kip inhibitors oppose these kinases, and SCF-proteasome degradation of p27 and CDT1 enforces the switch and prevents re-replication.

Between one division and the next, a cell spends G1 deciding whether to replicate its DNA at all, and this G1 phase and G1/S transition programme is where that commitment is made or deferred into quiescence. Mitogen-driven D-type cyclins with CDK4 and CDK6, followed by cyclin E-CDK2, phosphorylate the retinoblastoma protein and release E2F1-3 to switch on genes for nucleotide synthesis and replication, while pocket proteins p107 and p130 with E2F4/E2F5 and the MuvB subunits hold those promoters off in resting cells. INK4 and Cip/Kip inhibitors restrain the kinases, and ubiquitin-proteasome and SCF-mediated degradation makes the transition irreversible by clearing inhibitors and licensing factors. Downstream, origin recognition, CDC6, CDT1 and the MCM helicase license origins for firing. Loss of this restraint point, through RB1 inactivation, CDKN2A deletion or cyclin D and MYC amplification, is among the most common routes into cancer, and it is the target of CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy.

Thrombin signalling through proteinase activated receptors (PARs) is how the coagulation protease thrombin acts as a cell-signalling agonist rather than just a fibrin-generating enzyme, and it is the main route by which platelets are activated at a site of vascular injury. Loss or blockade of this route blunts platelet secretion, integrin activation and aggregation, which is why PAR1 is a target of antithrombotic drugs; excessive signalling contributes to thrombosis, inflammation and vascular remodelling. Thrombin cleaves the receptor N-terminus, and the tethered new terminus self-activates the receptor, which couples through Gq and G12/13 heterotrimers to phospholipase C beta, calcium mobilisation, protein kinase C and Rho-dependent shape change. Beta-gamma subunits engage lipid kinases and channels, while Src and ERK activation, partly via sheddase-released growth factor ligands, link thrombin to proliferation. Arrestins terminate and redirect the response.

Thrombin, the protease at the end of the coagulation cascade, also acts as a hormone-like signal by cleaving proteinase-activated receptors on the cell surface, and this route is how a clotting signal becomes a cellular response. In platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion, integrin activation and aggregation, making it central to haemostasis and to arterial thrombosis; the same receptors mediate thrombin's effects on endothelium, smooth muscle and inflammatory cells. Activation is irreversible and unusual: thrombin clips the receptor N-terminus, and the new tethered ligand folds back to activate the receptor, which then couples through Gq and G12/13 heterotrimers to phospholipase C beta, calcium mobilisation, protein kinase C and Rho-dependent cytoskeletal remodelling. Beta-arrestins terminate and redirect signalling, while Src and ERK link receptor activation to growth and differentiation responses. PAR1 is the dominant human thrombin receptor, with PAR4 contributing at higher concentrations.

Defective RFT1 causes CDG-1n describes what happens to protein N-glycosylation when the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor cannot be moved into the endoplasmic reticulum lumen. RFT1 is required for flipping Man5GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol from the cytosolic face of the ER membrane to the lumenal face, where the remaining mannose and glucose residues are added before the finished glycan is transferred to nascent polypeptides. Loss of this step stalls precursor maturation and leaves serum glycoproteins such as transferrin hypoglycosylated, the diagnostic hallmark of a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation. Affected individuals show early-onset developmental delay, dysmorphic features, hypotonia, seizures, sensorineural deafness, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency, reflecting how broadly secreted and membrane glycoproteins depend on an intact assembly line. The pathway sits at the interface of dolichol-linked sugar biosynthesis and ER quality control.

N-linked glycosylation begins on the cytosolic face of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, so the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor must be flipped into the ER lumen before the remaining sugars can be added and the finished glycan transferred to nascent proteins. RFT1 is required for this translocation step, though the mechanism by which the bulky dolichol-linked intermediate crosses the bilayer remains unsettled. Loss of RFT1 function stalls precursor maturation and yields a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation, in which serum glycoproteins such as transferrin are incompletely occupied by glycans. The resulting multi-system disease presents in infancy with developmental delay, dysmorphic features, hypotonia, seizures, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency, illustrating how broadly secreted and membrane protein function depends on this single early lipid-linked oligosaccharide flipping event in the secretory pathway.

Defective DPM1 causes DPM1-CDG describes the loss of dolichol-phosphate mannose synthesis and the multisystem congenital disorder of glycosylation that follows. The DPM complex supplies the single mannose donor used inside the endoplasmic reticulum for N-glycan precursor assembly, O-mannosylation of dystroglycan, C-mannosylation, and GPI anchor biosynthesis, so when it fails many unrelated glycoproteins are made incomplete at once. DPM1 is the catalytic subunit, transferring mannose from cytosolic GDP-mannose onto dolichyl phosphate, while DPM2 and DPM3 anchor and stabilise it in the ER membrane. Hypomorphic DPM1 mutations produce hypoglycosylated serum glycoproteins together with severe developmental delay, epilepsy, hypotonia and dysmorphism, a phenotype overlapping muscular dystrophy because dystroglycan glycosylation is also lost. The pathway sits at the junction of lipid-linked sugar donor supply and protein quality in the secretory route.

Dolichol-phosphate mannose is the mannose donor used inside the endoplasmic reticulum for N-linked glycan assembly, GPI anchor synthesis, C-mannosylation and O-mannosylation of proteins such as alpha-dystroglycan, and it is made by a three-subunit enzyme in the ER membrane. DPM1 is the catalytic subunit, transferring mannose from cytosolic GDP-mannose onto dolichyl phosphate, while DPM2 and DPM3 anchor and stabilise it in the membrane. Loss-of-function mutations in DPM1 starve all of these downstream glycosylation routes of their donor and produce a congenital disorder of glycosylation, recognisable as hypoglycosylated serum glycoproteins together with severe developmental delay, epilepsy, hypotonia and a muscular dystrophy-like picture. The pathway therefore links a single lipid-linked sugar intermediate to the quality and function of a large fraction of secreted and membrane proteins.

Defective DOLK causes DOLK-CDG describes what happens when cells cannot make dolichyl phosphate, the lipid carrier on which nearly all protein glycosylation is built. Dolichol kinase phosphorylates dolichol at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and the resulting dolichyl phosphate serves as the anchor for assembling the lipid-linked oligosaccharide used in N-glycosylation, as the mannose donor for O-mannosylation, and as a substrate in GPI anchor biosynthesis. Loss-of-function mutations therefore starve several glycosylation routes at once, producing a congenital disorder of glycosylation with hypoglycosylated serum glycoproteins, dilated cardiomyopathy, ichthyosis, seizures and often death in infancy. Because O-mannosylation of alpha-dystroglycan depends on the same lipid pool, some patients also show muscular dystrophy-like features, illustrating how a single lipid-modifying step upstream of the secretory pathway constrains protein maturation across many tissues.

Dolichol kinase converts dolichol to dolichyl phosphate in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, the lipid carrier on which the oligosaccharide precursor for N-linked glycosylation is built and which also supplies O-mannosylation and GPI anchor synthesis. When DOLK activity is lost, dolichyl phosphate becomes limiting and glycan transfer to nascent proteins fails across many substrates at once, producing the underglycosylated serum glycoproteins that define a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation. The resulting DOLK-CDG is a severe multisystem disease, with dilated cardiomyopathy, ichthyosis, seizures, hypotonia and developmental failure, and death frequently occurs in infancy. Because the affected step sits upstream of all dolichol-dependent glycosylation rather than within one glycan branch, the defect illustrates how a single lipid-activating kinase governs secretory protein maturation, membrane protein folding and cell surface anchoring throughout the body.

Defective DHDDS causes RP59 describes how loss of function in the first committed step of dolichol synthesis produces an inherited blinding retinal degeneration. Dolichol is the lipid carrier on which the N-linked glycan is built before transfer to nascent proteins, so cells that secrete or traffic heavily glycosylated membrane proteins depend on a steady supply; rod photoreceptors, which manufacture enormous amounts of rhodopsin, are especially vulnerable. The active enzyme is a heterodimer of the catalytic subunit DHDDS with the NUS1-encoded partner, working at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane to add isopentenyl pyrophosphate units head-to-tail onto farnesyl pyrophosphate until a polyprenyl chain of roughly 17-23 isoprene units is reached. Mutations that impair this cis-prenyltransferase activity cause retinitis pigmentosa 59, with night blindness, progressive loss of peripheral then central vision, and pigment deposits reflecting rod loss followed by cone loss.

Dolichol is the lipid carrier on which N-linked glycans are built before transfer to nascent glycoproteins, and the first committed step of its synthesis is carried out by a two-subunit cis-prenyltransferase at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, comprising the catalytic DHDDS subunit and the NUS1-encoded partner. Together they add isopentenyl pyrophosphate units head-to-tail onto farnesyl pyrophosphate to give polyprenyl pyrophosphate, the precursor of the 17-23 isoprene dolichols used in glycosylation. Loss-of-function mutation in the catalytic subunit underlies retinitis pigmentosa 59, an inherited pigment retinopathy in which rod photoreceptors degenerate first and cones follow, producing night blindness, progressive loss of mid-peripheral and then central vision, and pigment deposits in the fundus. Rhodopsin is among the glycoproteins dependent on adequate dolichol supply, linking a general biosynthetic lipid pathway to photoreceptor survival.

Chromatin organization is the packaging of genomic DNA with histones into nucleosomes and the continual remodelling of that packaging to control which sequences are readable. It sets the accessibility of DNA for transcription, replication and repair, and thereby defines cell identity; mutations in its components underlie many developmental syndromes and are among the most common lesions in cancer. The machinery falls into recognisable groups: core and variant histones themselves; writers and erasers of histone marks such as acetyltransferases, deacetylases, methyltransferases and demethylases; readers bearing bromo-, chromo- and PHD domains; and ATP-dependent remodellers of the SWI/SNF, CHD and NuRD families that slide, evict and exchange nucleosomes. Polycomb and Trithorax complexes impose heritable repression or activation, while histone chaperones and elongation factors keep chromatin restored behind polymerases. The output is epigenetic memory that persists through division and is reset during differentiation.

Genomic DNA in the nucleus is packaged with histones into nucleosomes, and chromatin organization is the set of activities that build, mark and move those nucleosomes so that DNA can be read, copied and repaired while remaining protected. Core histones of all four classes plus variants such as H2A.X and H3.3 provide the substrate; deposition is coupled to replication and to transcription-associated histone exchange. Writers and erasers of epigenetic marks set the accessibility state: acetyltransferases including EP300, CREBBP and KAT5-containing complexes, histone deacetylases with NuRD and NCoR corepressors, lysine methyltransferases such as KMT2A-D, EZH2 within Polycomb repressive complex 2, SUV39H enzymes and demethylases of the KDM families, alongside arginine methyltransferases and deiminases. ATP-dependent remodellers of the SWI/SNF, CHD and INO80-related families reposition nucleosomes. Mutations in these subunits are widespread in cancer and in developmental syndromes affecting growth and neural patterning.

O-glycosylation of TSR domain-containing proteins is the sugar modification that licenses secreted matrix and guidance proteins to fold and leave the cell. Proteins built from thrombospondin type 1 repeats — thrombospondins, the ADAMTS metalloproteases and ADAMTS-like proteins, F-spondin, properdin, semaphorins 5A/5B — depend on it for quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum, and its loss causes Peters plus syndrome, with eye, skeletal and craniofacial defects. POFUT2 recognises a CSX(S/T)CG consensus within folded TSR domains and attaches fucose to the conserved serine or threonine; B3GLCT then adds glucose to build the rare Glc-beta-1,3-Fuc disaccharide. Because the fucosyltransferase acts only on properly folded repeats, the modification doubles as a folding checkpoint that governs secretion. The client proteins in turn shape extracellular matrix assembly, procollagen processing, angiogenesis, complement activation, axon guidance and von Willebrand factor cleavage.

Secreted and matrix proteins built from thrombospondin type 1 repeats are sugar-modified inside the endoplasmic reticulum before they ever reach the extracellular space, and this O-glycosylation of TSR domain-containing proteins acts as a folding and secretion checkpoint. POFUT2 attaches fucose to a serine or threonine within the CSX(S/T)CG consensus of a properly folded repeat, and B3GLCT then adds glucose to build the rare Glc-beta1,3-Fuc disaccharide. Substrates include thrombospondins, properdin of the complement alternative pathway, spondins, several semaphorins, and the large ADAMTS metalloprotease and ADAMTSL families that process procollagen and proteoglycans. Because the modification stabilises the repeat, its loss leaves substrates retained and degraded rather than secreted; B3GLCT mutations cause Peters plus syndrome, with skeletal, eye and craniofacial defects that echo the connective-tissue roles of ADAMTS proteases in matrix assembly, angiogenesis and wound healing.

Mitophagy is the selective autophagic removal of mitochondria, the quality-control route that clears damaged or surplus organelles before they leak reactive oxygen species and pro-apoptotic factors. It also serves programmed elimination: paternal mitochondria after fertilisation, and the wholesale clearance of functional mitochondria during erythrocyte and lens fibre maturation. The best-defined arm depends on the kinase PINK1, which accumulates on depolarised outer membranes, phosphorylates ubiquitin and recruits the E3 ligase Parkin; ubiquitin chains built with UBE2D and UBE2N conjugating enzymes on TOM complex subunits, VDAC channels and mitofusins are then read by the receptors OPTN and SQSTM1, whose TBK1- and casein kinase 2-dependent phosphorylation strengthens LC3 binding. Hypoxia engages the receptor FUNDC1 instead. ULK1 and the ATG5-ATG12 conjugation machinery build the engulfing membrane. Loss of PINK1 or Parkin causes early-onset Parkinson disease.

Mitophagy is the selective clearance of mitochondria by autophagy, the route by which cells dispose of damaged or surplus organelles and keep the mitochondrial population functional. It matters for quality control in neurons, for programmed loss of mitochondria during erythrocyte and lens maturation, and for maternal inheritance of mitochondrial DNA through destruction of sperm-derived mitochondria; failure of the kinase PINK1 or the ubiquitin ligase PRKN causes recessive Parkinson disease. Loss of membrane potential stabilises PINK1 on the import channels, where it phosphorylates ubiquitin and recruits PRKN to ubiquitinate outer-membrane substrates including the translocase components, mitofusins and the porins. Ubiquitin-binding receptors such as OPTN and SQSTM1, assisted by TBK1 and casein kinase 2 phosphorylation, then link the tagged organelle to LC3 and the ATG5-ATG12 conjugation machinery, while the hypoxia-responsive receptor FUNDC1 provides a receptor-mediated alternative under low oxygen.

CASP8 activity is inhibited describes the switch that decides whether a cell receiving a death signal dies by apoptosis or by necroptosis. Caspase-8, recruited through FADD to ligated death receptors such as FAS and the TRAIL receptors, normally both drives the apoptotic protease cascade and cleaves RIPK1 and RIPK3, thereby suppressing regulated necrosis. When its proteolytic activity is blocked — by pan-caspase inhibitors, by the short FLIP isoform encoded by CFLAR, or by viral FLIP mimics — RIPK1 and RIPK3 survive intact, assemble a necrosome and kill the cell by membrane rupture instead. The distinction matters physiologically: apoptosis is immunologically quiet, whereas necroptosis spills contents and inflames tissue, and this route serves as a backup defence when viruses disable caspases. Loss of caspase-8 restraint underlies inflammatory tissue damage and embryonic lethality in animal models.

Death receptor engagement can end in either apoptosis or necroptosis, and the decision hinges on whether caspase-8 is allowed to work. When CASP8 activity is inhibited, the apoptotic route is closed and signalling is redirected toward RIPK1/RIPK3-dependent regulated necrosis, an inflammatory form of death that releases cellular contents rather than packaging them quietly. Ligands such as FASLG and TRAIL cluster their receptors, FAS and the TRAIL receptors, and recruit FADD or TRADD together with TRAF2 to assemble a platform where procaspase-8 dimerises. Catalytically inactive CFLAR (c-FLIP) short forms, viral FLIP mimics and pharmacological caspase inhibitors block full processing of the protease, so RIPK1 escapes the cleavage that would normally restrain it. This switch matters for antiviral defence, where pathogens suppress caspase-8 and provoke necroptosis instead, and for the inflammation seen when caspase-8 function is lost.

VEGFR2 mediated cell proliferation is the arm of vascular endothelial growth factor signalling that drives endothelial cells to divide, supplying the new cells needed for angiogenesis during development, wound healing and tumour vascularisation. VEGFA binding to KDR triggers autophosphorylation of Tyr1175, which recruits and activates phospholipase C gamma; the resulting diacylglycerol and IP3-mediated calcium release through ITPR channels activate protein kinase C isoforms. Rather than using the canonical GRB2-SOS route, this cascade reaches RAS by relieving GAP-mediated suppression, while PKC alpha can also phosphorylate RAF directly, feeding the MEK/ERK module that licenses S-phase entry. Calmodulin, PDPK1, SRC and sphingosine kinase shape the calcium and lipid second-messenger context. Because endothelial proliferation depends on this route, it is the target of anti-VEGF therapies in cancer and retinal disease, and its loss blocks vessel growth.

Endothelial cells divide in response to VEGF, and this is the branch of VEGFR2 signalling that drives that proliferation — the basis of angiogenesis in development, wound healing and tumour vascularisation, and the target of anti-VEGF drugs. VEGFA binding to the KDR receptor triggers Src-dependent phosphorylation of the receptor tail, which recruits and activates phospholipase C gamma; the resulting inositol trisphosphate opens IP3 receptor channels on the endoplasmic reticulum, releasing calcium that, with calmodulin, cooperates with diacylglycerol to activate conventional protein kinase C isoforms. PKC then feeds into the Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK cascade, either by phosphorylating Raf directly or by acting on Ras itself — here through relief of GTPase-activating protein restraint rather than exchange-factor recruitment. Sphingosine kinase and PDPK1 add further lipid and kinase input, linking the same receptor to survival as well as growth.

Myogenesis is the formation of skeletal muscle, in which proliferating myoblasts exit the cell cycle, commit to a muscle fate, and fuse into multinucleated myotubes; it builds muscle during development and rebuilds it from satellite cells after injury, so its failure underlies muscle hypoplasia and poor regeneration. The pathway is centred on the myogenic bHLH factors MyoD, Myf5, myogenin and MRF4, which heterodimerize with E proteins such as E12/E47, HEB and ITF-2 to occupy E boxes in muscle-specific promoters, acting combinatorially with MEF2 family MADS-box factors to drive the contractile gene program. Upstream, the transmembrane co-receptor CDO, together with Boc, neogenin and netrin-3, works within N- and M-cadherin adhesion complexes at myoblast contacts; through the scaffolds JLP and Bnip-2 it engages Cdc42 and p38 MAPK signalling, which hyperphosphorylates E proteins and potentiates bHLH heterodimer activity, coupling cell-cell adhesion to differentiation.

Skeletal muscle is built when proliferating myoblasts exit the cycle, switch on muscle-specific genes and fuse into multinucleated myotubes, and this account of myogenesis focuses on the co-receptor CDON and its partners as an entry point into that transition. Loss of this programme underlies failures of muscle formation and regeneration, and the same transcription factors are reactivated by satellite cells after injury. CDON acts with the related Boc, neogenin and its ligand netrin-3, and N-, R- and M-cadherins with catenins at sites of myoblast contact, linking adhesion to differentiation. Through the scaffolds BNIP2 and JLP it engages Cdc42 and the p38 MAPK cascade, which promotes heterodimer formation between the myogenic bHLH factors MyoD, myogenin, Myf5 and MRF4 and E proteins such as E12/E47 and HEB. These heterodimers act at E boxes together with MEF2 family factors to drive muscle gene expression.

Caspase activation via extrinsic apoptotic signalling pathway is the route by which a cell is instructed from outside to kill itself, allowing immune cells to eliminate infected or transformed targets and allowing tissues to remove cells that have lost their positional cues. Death ligands such as FasL and TRAIL cluster their receptors, which recruit adaptors including FADD and TRADD into a death-inducing complex that dimerises and activates the initiator caspases-8 and -10; these cleave executioner caspase-3 directly or cleave Bid to amplify the signal through mitochondria. FLIP and RIPK1 set the threshold, determining whether ligation instead yields survival or necroptotic signalling, and TLR4 adaptors feed into the same node. A second arm operates through dependence receptors such as DCC and UNC5, which trigger caspase activation when their netrin ligand is absent, coupling neuronal and epithelial survival to trophic supply and suppressing tumour growth.

Cells can be instructed to die by signals arriving from outside, and this extrinsic route converts receptor engagement at the plasma membrane into activation of the caspase proteases that dismantle the cell. It underlies immune killing of infected and transformed targets, deletion of autoreactive lymphocytes, and the sculpting of tissues by removing cells that lack trophic support; its failure permits tumour survival and autoimmunity, while excess drives tissue injury. Death ligands such as FasL and TRAIL cluster Fas or TRAIL receptors, which recruit FADD and TRADD together with RIPK1 and TRAF2, allowing procaspase-8 to dimerise and cleave executioner caspase-3, with FLIP acting as a competitive brake. Toll-like receptor 4 with its TRIF adaptors feeds into the same machinery. Dependence receptors including DCC and UNC5 homologues take the opposite logic, triggering apoptosis when their ligands are absent.

Signaling by Hedgehog is the morphogen pathway that patterns the developing embryo — limb buds, neural tube, skeleton — and later sustains stem cell compartments in adult tissues. Its loss causes congenital malformations such as holoprosencephaly and skeletal dysplasias, while inappropriate activation drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. The genes trace the full circuit: ligand maturation and release by palmitoylation and SCUBE2, reception by Patched and co-receptors GAS1, CDON and BOC, and relief of Patched's inhibition of Smoothened. Output converges on the GLI transcription factors, whose fate depends on PKA and CK1 phosphorylation, SUFU sequestration, and ubiquitin-proteasome processing to repressor or degraded forms. Much of this occurs in the primary cilium, explaining the presence of intraflagellar transport, kinesin, tubulin and ciliary base components — the reason many ciliopathies present as Hedgehog patterning defects.

Hedgehog signalling converts a secreted morphogen gradient into patterned gene expression, and it is what tells cells in the limb bud, neural tube and developing skeleton which position they occupy; in adults it maintains stem and progenitor compartments. Loss of output causes birth defects such as holoprosencephaly and polydactyly, while inappropriate reactivation drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. Ligands SHH, IHH and DHH are lipid-modified and released, then bind the receptor PTCH1, relieving its inhibition of Smoothened. Signalling is organised at the primary cilium, so intraflagellar transport components, the anterograde kinesin motor, retrograde dynein and tubulins are integral rather than incidental. In the off state, GPR161 raises cAMP and protein kinase A, GSK3 and casein kinase 1 prime GLI proteins for processing by the ubiquitin-proteasome system into repressors; SUFU sequesters them. Activation preserves full-length GLI activators, with SPOP, ITCH and SMURF ligases tuning the response.

Synthesis of diphthamide-EEF2 builds a modified histidine found on just one protein in the cell, elongation factor 2, the GTPase that drives ribosomal translocation during translation elongation. Without this modification translation elongation loses fidelity and speed, and loss of the pathway in humans causes developmental disorders with microcephaly and short stature; the same residue is the target that diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates to shut down protein synthesis and kill the cell. Four enzymatic steps are involved: an iron-sulfur radical-SAM-like complex of DPH1, DPH2, DPH3 and DNAJC24 transfers a 3-amino-3-carboxypropyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to histidine 715, DPH5 methylates it, DPH7 demethylates the carboxylate to give diphthine, and DPH6 amidates that carboxyl group.
