The pathway thus links one-carbon metabolism and iron-sulfur cofactor biology to the accuracy of ribosomal protein synthesis.

Translation elongation depends on a single unusual amino acid: histidine 715 of eukaryotic elongation factor 2 is rebuilt into diphthamide, and no other protein in the cell carries this modification. The pathway matters because EEF2 drives GTP-dependent translocation of tRNA and mRNA through the ribosome, and because the finished diphthamide is the residue that diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates to shut down protein synthesis and kill the cell. Construction proceeds in four committed steps: a radical-SAM complex built from DPH1 and DPH2, with the small iron-sulfur protein DPH3 and its partner DNAJC24, transfers a 3-amino-3-carboxypropyl group from S-adenosylmethionine; DPH5 methylates it; DPH7 removes a methyl group to yield diphthine; and DPH6 amidates the carboxylate. Loss of these enzymes impairs translational fidelity and causes developmental disorders with craniofacial and neurological features.

Mismatch Repair corrects single-base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops that escape the proofreading of DNA replication, and it is the main guardian of microsatellite stability. Loss of it produces the hypermutable, microsatellite-unstable tumours of Lynch syndrome, most characteristically colorectal and endometrial cancer, and also confers resistance to some thiopurine and alkylating agents. Recognition is by MutS complexes: MSH2 paired with MSH6 detects single mismatches and one- or two-base loops, while MSH2 with MSH3 handles larger loops. The activated sensor engages MLH1:PMS2 and the replication clamp PCNA, which marks the nascent strand; MLH1:PMS2 nicks it and EXO1 excises a tract around the error. RPA protects the resulting gap, DNA polymerase delta resynthesises, and LIG1 seals the nick. Expression and activity peak in S phase, tying the pathway directly to the replication fork.

Replication is accurate but not perfect, and mismatch repair is the system that removes the base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops that polymerases leave behind, raising replication fidelity by orders of magnitude. Loss of it produces microsatellite instability and a hypermutator phenotype; germline defects in MSH2, MSH6, MLH1 or PMS2 cause Lynch syndrome with its high risk of colorectal and endometrial cancer, and MMR status now guides immunotherapy decisions. Recognition is by MutS heterodimers, MSH2:MSH6 for single mismatches and short loops and MSH2:MSH3 for larger loops, which then engage MLH1:PMS2 and the replication clamp PCNA to nick the newly made strand. EXO1 excises a tract containing the error, RPA coats the gap, polymerase delta resynthesizes and LIG1 seals the nick, tying the repair directly to S-phase replication.

CTNNB1 S33 mutants aren't phosphorylated describes how cancer-associated substitutions at serine 33 of beta-catenin escape the destruction signal that normally limits WNT signalling. Serine 33 is one of the GSK3-beta target residues in the beta-catenin N-terminal degron; when it is mutated, the protein cannot be marked for ubiquitin-dependent turnover, so it accumulates, enters the nucleus and drives constitutive transcription of WNT target genes such as MYC and CCND1, promoting proliferation. The machinery involved is the axin-APC destruction complex, including AXIN1, AMER1, casein kinase 1 alpha, GSK3-beta and PP2A subunits that tune the phosphorylation state of the complex. Loss of this control point underlies tumours of the liver, endometrium, stomach and central nervous system, and makes this pathway a paradigm for oncogenic stabilisation of a transcriptional coactivator by degron mutation.

Beta-catenin levels are normally held down by a destruction complex that marks the protein for degradation, and mutation of serine 33 removes one of the phosphate acceptor sites that makes this possible. Because GSK3B cannot phosphorylate the altered residue, beta-catenin escapes recognition by its ubiquitin ligase, accumulates, and moves into the nucleus where it partners with TCF/LEF factors to drive a constitutive WNT transcriptional programme of proliferation and stem-like gene expression. The machinery that fails here is the scaffolded complex of APC, AXIN1 and AMER1 together with casein kinase 1 and protein phosphatase 2A subunits that tune its activity. Such stabilizing substitutions are recurrent driver events in hepatocellular carcinoma, medulloblastoma and other central nervous system tumours, endometrial and gastric cancers, illustrating how loss of a single phosphodegron site converts a regulated signal into an oncogenic one.

Mitochondrial translation is the organelle's own protein synthesis system, which makes just thirteen proteins — all hydrophobic core subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase — yet without it oxidative phosphorylation cannot be assembled and cells lose aerobic energy production. Everything else, including the ribosome itself, is nuclear-encoded and imported. Mitoribosomes are protein-rich 55S particles built from small and large subunit proteins around short mitochondrial rRNAs, and they work at the matrix face of the inner membrane, where OXA1L co-translationally inserts nascent chains into the bilayer. Initiation uses formylated methionyl-tRNA and dedicated factors, elongation cycles through TUFM, TSFM and GFM1, and termination and recycling require MTRF1L, MRRF and GFM2, with separate rescue factors clearing stalled or non-stop complexes. Mutations in ribosomal proteins, translation factors and the mitochondrial tRNAs cause encephalomyopathies, cardiomyopathy and other mitochondrial diseases.

Only thirteen human proteins are made inside mitochondria, and all of them are hydrophobic subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation complexes, so mitochondrial translation sets the ceiling on a cell's capacity for respiration and ATP synthesis. The machinery is bacterial in ancestry but heavily remodelled: a protein-rich 55S mitoribosome built from small and large subunit proteins around short rRNAs, the full set of mitochondrially encoded tRNAs, and dedicated factors for each step. Initiation requires formylation of methionyl-tRNA and the factors MTIF2 and MTIF3, elongation cycles through TUFM with GTP regenerated by TSFM and translocation by GFM1, and termination and recycling use MTRF1L with MRRF and GFM2. Nascent chains are inserted co-translationally into the inner membrane via OXA1L, and quality-control factors clear stalled peptidyl-tRNAs. Mutations in ribosomal proteins, tRNAs or translation factors cause mitochondrial disease with encephalopathy, cardiomyopathy and lactic acidosis.

Negative regulation of TCF-dependent signaling by DVL-interacting proteins is a brake on canonical WNT signalling that acts at the level of Dishevelled, the hub that relays receptor activation into stabilisation of beta-catenin and TCF/LEF-driven transcription. Restraining this step keeps proliferative and stem-cell programmes in check; unchecked beta-catenin output underlies colorectal and other cancers, while loss of the DVL-binding protein CCDC88C (Daple) causes congenital hydrocephalus, and CXXC4 (Idax) levels tune WNT responsiveness in development and tumours. Mechanistically, DVL1, DVL2 and DVL3 recruit AXIN away from the destruction complex after WNT stimulation; direct binding by CXXC4 through its DIX-interacting region and by CCDC88C sequesters DVL and blocks that recruitment, so the destruction complex continues to degrade beta-catenin. This sits alongside phosphorylation and regulated degradation as ways cells set the gain of WNT signalling.

Dishevelled proteins sit at the hub of WNT reception, and one way cells set the ceiling on WNT output is by sequestering them. This branch describes negative regulation of TCF-dependent signalling by DVL-interacting proteins: CXXC4 (Idax) and CCDC88C (DAPLE) bind DVL1, DVL2 and DVL3 directly and dampen their ability to relay signal from activated receptors, so less beta-catenin escapes destruction and fewer TCF/LEF target genes are switched on. Because WNT/beta-catenin activity governs stem cell renewal, body axis patterning and tissue growth, restraint at the DVL step matters as much as activation does; loss of CCDC88C causes congenital hydrocephalus, and unchecked TCF-dependent transcription is a hallmark of colorectal tumourigenesis. DVL is also the point where canonical and planar-cell-polarity WNT branches diverge, so its interactors influence which route a WNT signal takes.

Truncations of AMER1 destabilize the destruction complex describes how loss-of-function mutations in a scaffold of the beta-catenin destruction complex switch on Wnt signalling inappropriately. AMER1/WTX normally binds beta-catenin directly through its C-terminal half and helps assemble the complex with APC, AXIN1, CSNK1A1, GSK3B and PP2A subunits, which together phosphorylate beta-catenin and mark it for ubiquitin-dependent degradation. Nonsense and frameshift mutations that remove the beta-catenin-binding region leave a protein that can no longer support this turnover, so beta-catenin accumulates, enters the nucleus and drives TCF/LEF target gene transcription. Depleting AMER1 has the same effect, identifying it as a tumour suppressor. The clinical consequence is Wilms tumour, a paediatric kidney cancer in which AMER1 truncations are recurrent, placing this biology within Wnt-driven control of nephron progenitor proliferation and differentiation.

Beta-catenin is kept low in unstimulated cells by a cytoplasmic destruction complex built on APC and AXIN1, in which casein kinase 1 and GSK3B phosphorylate beta-catenin to mark it for ubiquitin-mediated degradation, with PP2A subunits acting as regulatory counterweights. AMER1/WTX is a membrane- and complex-associated scaffold that binds beta-catenin through its C-terminal half and helps hold this assembly together. Truncating nonsense and frameshift mutations remove that beta-catenin-binding region, destabilizing the destruction complex so that beta-catenin escapes turnover, enters the nucleus and drives TCF/LEF target gene expression. This is a loss of tumour suppressor function: AMER1 truncations recur in Wilms tumour, a paediatric kidney cancer, and illustrate how constitutive Wnt pathway output arises from scaffold failure rather than ligand stimulation.

XAV939 stabilizes AXIN describes the pharmacological brake that can be applied to Wnt/beta-catenin signalling by protecting the pathway's rate-limiting scaffold from destruction. AXIN1 and AXIN2 assemble the beta-catenin destruction complex with GSK3beta and APC, and their abundance sets how much beta-catenin escapes phosphorylation and degradation to drive transcription; because tumours with APC or beta-catenin lesions depend on that escape, restoring AXIN levels is an attractive way to shut down constitutive Wnt output in colorectal cancer. The poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases tankyrase 1 and 2 normally PARsylate AXIN, marking it for ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. XAV939 occupies their catalytic sites, so AXIN protein accumulates without any change in transcript levels, GSK3beta-AXIN complexes increase, beta-catenin is phosphorylated and cleared, and beta-catenin-dependent proliferation is suppressed.

AXIN proteins are the limiting scaffold of the destruction complex that phosphorylates beta-catenin and keeps Wnt target genes off, and their abundance is set by poly-ADP-ribosylation. The two tankyrases, TNKS and TNKS2, modify AXIN1 and AXIN2, marking them for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation and thereby raising the threshold for Wnt signalling. Blocking the tankyrase catalytic site with the small molecule XAV939 stabilizes AXIN without changing its transcription, restores GSK3beta-AXIN complexes, increases beta-catenin phosphorylation and lowers beta-catenin-dependent transcription. This is the rationale for targeting tankyrase in colorectal cancers driven by APC loss, where the pathway is constitutively active; growth of such cells is suppressed in culture. The biology illustrates how a post-translational modification controls the stability of a scaffold and so the output of a developmental signalling route.

Cardiac conduction is the ordered electrical activation of atria and ventricles that sets heart rate, rhythm, and the timing of contraction, and its failure produces long QT and Brugada syndromes, atrial fibrillation, conduction block, and sudden arrhythmic death. The cardiac action potential is built by sequential ion fluxes: voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN5A with their beta subunits and FGF-homologous factor modulators drive rapid depolarisation; L-type calcium channels sustain the plateau; and delayed rectifier and transient outward potassium channels, including KCNQ1/KCNE1 and KCNH2 with KCNIP-regulated Kv4 currents, restore the resting potential set by inward rectifiers and Na+/K+-ATPase. Coupled to this are the calcium handling proteins of excitation-contraction coupling -- ryanodine receptors, SERCA with phospholamban, calsequestrin, and sodium-calcium exchange -- plus CaMKII and PKA arms that adapt beat-to-beat behaviour to autonomic tone, and transcription factors such as NKX2-5 and TBX5 that specify the conduction system.

Each heartbeat begins as an electrical event, and cardiac conduction is the ordered generation and spread of the action potential that makes atria and ventricles contract in sequence and lets rate adjust to autonomic tone. Voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN5A with their beta subunits drive rapid depolarisation; L-type calcium channels sustain the plateau that supports contraction; delayed rectifier and transient outward potassium channels, including KCNQ1 with KCNE1 and KCNH2, restore the resting potential set largely by inward rectifiers and the sodium pump. Calcium handling by ryanodine receptors, SERCA pumps regulated by phospholamban, and sodium-calcium exchangers couples excitation to mechanical output, while calmodulin, CaMKII and PKA tune the response. Transcription factors including NKX2-5 and TBX5 specify the conduction system itself. Mutations in these channels underlie long QT and Brugada syndromes, conduction block, and sudden arrhythmic death.

Phase 2 - plateau phase is the long depolarized shoulder of the cardiac action potential, the interval that keeps ventricular myocytes contracting and sets the refractory period that protects the heart from re-excitation. It is held by a near balance between inward Ca2+ current through L-type channels and outward K+ current through the slow delayed rectifier. The L-type channel is a multi-subunit complex in which the CACNA1C pore is tuned by beta, alpha2delta and gamma subunits; the Ca2+ that enters triggers sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release and excitation-contraction coupling. On the repolarizing side, KCNQ1 requires KCNE accessory subunits to generate slow kinetics, and is anchored with kinase signaling by the scaffold AKAP9. Loss or gain of function in these channels lengthens or shortens the plateau, producing long QT and short QT syndromes and arrhythmic risk.

The long plateau that distinguishes cardiac from nerve action potentials comes from a near-balance between inward and outward current, and this phase 2 biology is what keeps ventricular myocytes depolarized long enough for calcium-induced calcium release to drive a full contraction and for the refractory period to prevent re-excitation. Depolarization is sustained by Ca2+ entry through L-type channels built around the CACNA1C pore-forming subunit with beta, alpha2delta and gamma accessory subunits that tune trafficking and gating, and it is opposed by the slow delayed rectifier carried by KCNQ1 in partnership with KCNE subunits that convert the channel's kinetics to the slow, non-inactivating current needed here. The scaffold AKAP9 anchors kinase signalling to KCNQ1 so that adrenergic stimulation shortens the plateau as heart rate rises. Mutations in these subunits underlie congenital long QT syndromes and arrhythmic sudden death.

Phase 1 - inactivation of fast Na+ channels is the brief early repolarization that follows the upstroke of the cardiac action potential, producing the characteristic notch before the plateau. It sets the height and duration of the plateau and thereby the timing of calcium entry and contraction; loss or excess of this current reshapes repolarization and predisposes to arrhythmias such as Brugada syndrome and to the electrical remodelling seen in heart failure. Once fast sodium channels inactivate, a transient net outward current dominated by potassium efflux briefly drives the membrane back toward negative potentials. The Kv4 family channels carry this fast transient outward current, and their kinetics, surface expression and recovery from inactivation are tuned by calcium-sensing KChIP accessory subunits, which also underlie the gradient of notch amplitude across the ventricular wall.

Immediately after the upstroke of the cardiac action potential, fast sodium channels inactivate and a brief net outward current produces the notch of early repolarization, known as phase 1. This transient outward current, carried largely by potassium with a chloride contribution, sets the height and duration of the plateau that follows and therefore shapes calcium entry and contractile force; its remodelling in hypertrophy and heart failure prolongs repolarization and predisposes to arrhythmia. The channels responsible here are the Kv4 family pore-forming subunits KCND1, KCND2 and KCND3, which open and inactivate rapidly at depolarized potentials. Their kinetics, trafficking and surface density are governed by the calcium-binding KChIP accessory proteins KCNIP1-4, whose association slows inactivation and speeds recovery. In pacemaker cells the equivalent phase reflects rapid potassium efflux together with closure of L-type calcium channels.

Ion homeostasis covers the pumps, exchangers and channels that set intracellular ion gradients in excitable cells, with the cardiac myocyte as the central case. Each heartbeat requires calcium to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, bind troponin, and then be cleared again within a fraction of a second, while sodium and potassium gradients are restored so the cell can repolarise and fire again. Ryanodine receptors and inositol trisphosphate receptors provide release, SERCA pumps with their regulators phospholamban and sarcolipin provide reuptake, calsequestrin and triadin buffer and gate the store, and the sodium-potassium ATPase together with sodium-calcium exchange and plasma membrane calcium pumps handles trans-sarcolemmal balance. Calmodulin, CaMKII and PKA tune these fluxes to sympathetic drive. Store-operated entry via STIM1 and ORAI refills depleted stores. Mutations here cause catecholaminergic arrhythmia, malignant hyperthermia and cardiomyopathy.

Cardiac muscle contracts and relaxes on a beat-to-beat cycle, and that requires the ion gradients underlying the action potential and the calcium transient to be restored after every excitation — the substance of ion homeostasis in cardiac conduction. Sodium/potassium ATPase subunits with their FXYD regulators maintain the transmembrane sodium and potassium gradients that set resting potential, while sodium/calcium exchangers, plasma membrane calcium pumps and the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPases clear cytosolic calcium after release through ryanodine receptors and inositol trisphosphate receptors. Calsequestrin, triadin and junctin organise the release complex; phospholamban and sarcolipin restrain SERCA until phosphorylation by protein kinase A or calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase II relieves them, and STIM–ORAI components refill stores. ATP-sensitive potassium channel subunits couple metabolic state to excitability. Disruption produces arrhythmia, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, and impaired relaxation in heart failure.

Defective TPMT causes TPMT deficiency describes what happens to thiopurine drug handling when the enzyme that inactivates these drugs is lost. Thiopurines such as 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine are mainstays of treatment for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia, inflammatory bowel disease and autoimmune conditions, and their safety depends on S-methylation by thiopurine methyltransferase, a cytosolic SAM-dependent methyltransferase that diverts drug away from conversion into cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides. Inherited variants that reduce or abolish TPMT activity shift metabolism toward those nucleotides, so a standard dose becomes an overdose and patients suffer profound myelosuppression. The trait is co-dominant: roughly one person in 300 has negligible activity and several percent are intermediate metabolisers, making TPMT genotyping one of the earliest and most widely adopted examples of pre-emptive pharmacogenetic dose adjustment in clinical practice.

Thiopurine drugs such as 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine, used against childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and in immunosuppression for inflammatory disease, are inactivated largely by S-methylation. The enzyme responsible, thiopurine methyltransferase, transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to the thiol sulfur, diverting the drug away from conversion into cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides. Loss-of-function variants produce TPMT deficiency, in which methylation capacity is reduced or absent and standard doses drive excessive accumulation of active metabolites in haematopoietic cells, causing severe myelosuppression. The trait is co-dominant: heterozygotes with intermediate activity need reduced doses, while rare homozygotes tolerate only a small fraction of the usual amount. This makes the pathway one of the clearest examples of pharmacogenetic variation guiding dose selection, and genotyping or enzyme assay before thiopurine treatment is standard practice.

Defective UGT1A1 causes hyperbilirubinemia describes what happens when the liver cannot glucuronidate bilirubin, the yellow end product of heme catabolism. UGT1A1 is the sole enzyme that attaches glucuronic acid to lipophilic unconjugated bilirubin, converting it into a water-soluble form that can be excreted in bile; without this step bilirubin accumulates in blood and, at high concentrations, crosses into the brain to cause kernicterus. Loss-of-function and promoter variants produce a graded spectrum of disease, from the benign, common Gilbert syndrome and transient neonatal jaundice through Crigler-Najjar type 2 to the type 1 form, which requires phototherapy or liver transplantation. Because the same enzyme conjugates drugs and other lipophilic xenobiotics, reduced activity also alters clearance of compounds such as irinotecan's active metabolite, linking bilirubin handling to pharmacogenetic toxicity risk.

Bilirubin, the lipophilic end product of heme catabolism, must be made water-soluble before the liver can excrete it into bile, and UGT1A1 is the only enzyme that performs this step. It transfers glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronic acid onto bilirubin in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum, converting it to mono- and diglucuronides that enter bile; the same enzyme conjugates various drugs and other lipophilic compounds as part of phase II xenobiotic clearance. When UGT1A1 activity is reduced or absent, unconjugated bilirubin accumulates in blood and tissues. The consequences scale with the severity of the defect, from the benign intermittent jaundice of Gilbert syndrome and transient neonatal hyperbilirubinemia through Crigler-Najjar type 2 to type 1, where near-total loss of conjugation causes kernicterus and neurological damage unless bilirubin is removed by phototherapy or transplantation.

Defective CYP4F22 causes ARCI5 describes what happens to the skin barrier when a single keratinocyte cytochrome P450 enzyme is lost. CYP4F22 acts in the 12(R)-lipoxygenase arm of arachidonic acid metabolism, omega-hydroxylating trioxilin A3 and related fatty acid derivatives, and it is also the omega-hydroxylase that generates the ultra-long-chain acylceramides needed to build the epidermal lipid lamellae. That lipid layer is what holds water in the stratum corneum, so mutations that inactivate the enzyme give autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis type 5, with scaling, hyperkeratosis and defective barrier function from birth. The same lipoxygenase route yields 12- and 15-HETE products that modulate keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, linking this metabolic step to proliferative skin disease more broadly and placing it within epidermal lipid biosynthesis and terminal keratinocyte maturation.

Loss-of-function mutations in the keratinocyte cytochrome P450 CYP4F22 cause autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis type 5, in which the skin barrier fails and newborns present with thick scaling and, in severe cases, a collodion membrane. The enzyme acts in the 12(R)-lipoxygenase branch of arachidonic acid metabolism, hydroxylating trioxilin A3 and related eicosanoid intermediates; it also contributes to synthesis of the ultra-long-chain fatty acid species that form acylceramides in the stratum corneum. Because these lipids create the water-impermeable lamellar membranes of the outer epidermis, defective CYP4F22 activity leaves the cornified envelope unable to retain hydration, and the resulting compensatory hyperproliferation links this oxidative lipid processing to proliferative skin disease more broadly. The biology sits at the junction of epidermal differentiation, lipid barrier assembly, and eicosanoid signalling in keratinocytes.

Defective CYP24A1 causes HCAI concerns the loss of the body's main off-switch for active vitamin D, and the calcium overload that follows. CYP24A1 is the mitochondrial cytochrome P450 that initiates catabolism of calcitriol by 24-hydroxylation, starting the route to calcitroic acid, a water-soluble metabolite cleared in bile; it is itself induced by calcitriol, forming a feedback loop that limits hormone action on intestinal calcium absorption and bone. When the enzyme is inactivated by mutation, calcitriol persists, calcium absorption runs unchecked, and affected infants present with hypercalcemia, suppressed parathyroid hormone, failure to thrive, vomiting, dehydration and nephrocalcinosis, sometimes with kidney stones later in life. The defect illustrates that vitamin D endocrine balance depends as much on timely degradation as on synthesis, and it sits within steroid and xenobiotic hydroxylation metabolism more broadly.

Active vitamin D must be destroyed as well as made, and the mitochondrial enzyme CYP24A1 begins that destruction by 24-hydroxylating calcitriol and its precursor, committing them to a side-chain oxidation route that ends in water-soluble calcitroic acid for biliary excretion. Because calcitriol drives intestinal calcium absorption, this catabolic step is the brake on vitamin D signalling and is itself induced by calcitriol, forming a negative feedback loop that limits hormone exposure. Loss-of-function mutations remove that brake and cause idiopathic infantile hypercalcemia, in which persistently elevated calcitriol produces excessive calcium uptake, suppressed parathyroid hormone, failure to thrive, vomiting, dehydration, nephrocalcinosis and kidney stones, sometimes unmasked by ordinary vitamin D supplementation. The pathway situates vitamin D turnover within calcium and phosphate homeostasis and within mitochondrial cytochrome P450 sterol metabolism.

Defective CYP11B1 causes AH4 describes the loss of the final hydroxylation step of adrenal cortisol synthesis and the disease that follows. Mitochondrial cytochrome P450 11B1 converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol in the adrenal zona fasciculata, so when the enzyme is inactivated the gland cannot complete glucocorticoid production; ACTH feedback is lost, the cortex becomes hyperplastic, and precursors are shunted into adrenal androgens. This is 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, the second most common form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia after 21-hydroxylase deficiency, inherited recessively and presenting with virilization of affected girls, precocious pseudopuberty in boys, and hypertension driven by accumulated 11-deoxycorticosterone acting on the mineralocorticoid receptor. The pathway situates steroid hormone biosynthesis within the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and explains why a single mitochondrial monooxygenase defect disturbs both salt balance and sexual development.

The final step of cortisol synthesis in the adrenal cortex is 11-beta-hydroxylation of 11-deoxycortisol, carried out by the mitochondrial cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP11B1. When this activity is lost, cortisol cannot be made, feedback restraint on pituitary ACTH is removed, and the adrenal cortex is driven to hyperplasia while steroid precursors are shunted into androgen production. The resulting disorder, adrenal hyperplasia 4, is a recessive form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia and the second most common after 21-hydroxylase deficiency, accounting for a small percentage of cases. Affected individuals show virilization from androgen excess together with hypertension, the latter reflecting accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone, which acts as a mineralocorticoid and promotes sodium retention. This places the defect within adrenal steroidogenesis and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis that governs it.

Defective CYP21A2 causes AH3 describes the loss of steroid 21-hydroxylase activity that underlies the commonest form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, accounting for more than nine in ten cases. The enzyme, a microsomal cytochrome P450 of the adrenal cortex, hydroxylates progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone at carbon 21, the committed step toward both aldosterone and cortisol. When it fails, cortisol output falls, negative feedback on the pituitary is lost, and rising ACTH drives adrenal hypertrophy and a backlog of precursors, chiefly 17-hydroxyprogesterone, which is shunted into androgen synthesis. The clinical consequences follow directly: virilization of affected females, salt wasting when mineralocorticoid synthesis is also lost, and in milder allelic forms later-onset hyperandrogenism. This places the defect within adrenal steroidogenesis and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis that regulates it, and makes 17-hydroxyprogesterone the basis of newborn screening.

Steroid 21-hydroxylase sits at a branch point of adrenal steroid synthesis, converting progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone into the precursors of aldosterone and cortisol. When the enzyme is defective, the resulting adrenal hyperplasia 3 accounts for the great majority of congenital adrenal hyperplasia: cortisol output falls, feedback restraint on pituitary ACTH is lost, and the adrenal cortex enlarges while precursors such as 17-hydroxyprogesterone accumulate. Because those precursors are shunted into androgen synthesis, affected females are virilized and both sexes may show accelerated growth and early puberty; severe alleles also impair mineralocorticoid production and present as salt-wasting adrenal crisis in infancy. Milder, partially active variants produce late-onset hyperandrogenism. The clinical spectrum tracks residual enzyme activity, which makes this a mutation-severity-graded microsomal cytochrome P450 defect in adrenal cortical hormone output.

Defective CYP27B1 causes VDDR1B describes the loss of vitamin D activation that produces vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1B, a hereditary failure to make the active hormone despite adequate vitamin D intake or sun exposure. Cholecalciferol made in skin is itself inert; it must be hydroxylated at carbon 25 in the liver by the microsomal cytochrome P450 CYP2R1 to give calcidiol, and then at the 1-alpha position to give calcitriol, the ligand for the nuclear vitamin D receptor. Through that receptor calcitriol drives intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, bone mineralisation, and programmes of cellular differentiation and proliferation. When the 25-hydroxylase step is crippled by mutation, circulating calcidiol is low, hormone-dependent gene expression is not engaged, and children develop hypocalcaemia and the skeletal deformities of rickets, correctable by supplying the hydroxylated metabolite.

Vitamin D3 made in skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol is inert until it is hydroxylated twice: at carbon 25 in the liver by the microsomal cytochrome P450 CYP2R1 to give calcidiol, and then at the 1-alpha position to give calcitriol, the hormone that binds the nuclear vitamin D receptor and drives intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, bone mineralisation, and programmes of cellular differentiation and proliferation. This pathway describes loss of that activation step, which produces vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1B. Because the substrate cannot be converted to the circulating 25-hydroxy form, patients have a selective deficiency of active hormone despite adequate vitamin D intake or sun exposure, with hypocalcaemia, defective growth plate and bone mineralisation, and the skeletal deformities of rickets; the defect is bypassed clinically by supplying hydroxylated vitamin D metabolites rather than cholecalciferol.

Organic anion transport by SLC22 transporters is the kidney's route for clearing small anionic waste products and drugs from the blood into the urine, and for reclaiming solutes the body needs to keep. It sets the plasma half-life of diuretics, NSAIDs, beta-lactam antibiotics, antivirals and methotrexate, and it governs urate handling: URAT1 (SLC22A12) reabsorbs uric acid at the proximal tubule brush border, and its variants shift serum urate and gout risk, while SLC22A11 (OAT4) contributes to the same balance. OAT1 and OAT3 (SLC22A6, SLC22A8) sit basolaterally and drive uptake from blood in exchange for intracellular dicarboxylates such as alpha-ketoglutarate, coupling secretion indirectly to the sodium gradient. Because these carriers are polyspecific and share substrates, they are a principal site of drug-drug interaction and of nephrotoxic accumulation, and they also export uremic toxins and hormone conjugates.

Renal handling of small anions depends on a family of polyspecific organic anion transporters in the SLC22 family, and this pathway describes the transport step by which they move endogenous metabolites and anionic drugs across kidney epithelial membranes. The carriers OAT1 and OAT3, encoded by SLC22A6 and SLC22A8, work at the basolateral membrane of the proximal tubule, exchanging intracellular dicarboxylate for organic anions to load substrates for secretion into urine; OAT4 and OAT7 handle further substrates, while URAT1 (SLC22A12) reabsorbs urate from the tubular lumen and sets serum uric acid levels, so its loss causes hypouricaemia and its overactivity contributes to gout. Because diuretics, NSAIDs, antivirals and beta-lactams are substrates, these transporters determine drug clearance, nephrotoxic accumulation and clinically important transporter-mediated drug interactions, and they are the point of action of uricosuric agents.

Degradation of GLI2 by the proteasome is the off-switch that keeps Hedgehog target genes silent when no ligand is present. GLI2 is the principal transcriptional activator of the pathway, and cells that fail to destroy it acquire constitutive Hedgehog output, a route to medulloblastoma, basal cell carcinoma and developmental patterning defects of the neural tube and limb. In unstimulated cells SUFU sequesters GLI2 while PKA primes a cluster of serines that CK1 and GSK3 then extend, creating a phosphodegron recognised by the SCF-beta-TrCP ubiquitin ligase built on CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1. Polyubiquitinated GLI2 is delivered to the 26S proteasome and largely destroyed outright, in contrast to the related GLI3, whose C-terminal processing determinant domain directs partial proteolysis to a repressor form. Pathway activation blocks this phosphorylation cascade and spares GLI2.

Hedgehog signalling depends on keeping its transcriptional activators silent until a ligand arrives, and this route is how the activator GLI2 is disposed of when no signal is present. Unlike GLI3, which is clipped to a stable repressor, most GLI2 is destroyed outright, so that basal target gene expression stays low and developmental patterning of the neural tube, limb and other Hedgehog-dependent tissues remains faithful; loss of this restraint contributes to tumours such as basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. Sequential phosphorylation by protein kinase A, casein kinase 1 and GSK3 creates a phosphodegron recognised by the beta-TrCP-containing SCF ubiquitin ligase, built on CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1, which polyubiquitinates GLI2 for complete proteolysis by the 26S proteasome. SUFU sequesters GLI2 in the cytoplasm and promotes its turnover, linking receptor state to activator abundance.

Defective SLC36A2 causes iminoglycinuria (IG) and hyperglycinuria (HG) describes the loss of a kidney amino acid reabsorption step, the event that lets glycine and the imino acids proline and hydroxyproline escape into urine. SLC36A2 encodes the proton-coupled amino acid transporter PAT2, which uses the inward proton gradient of the proximal tubule brush border to recover filtered glycine and proline with high affinity; it is also expressed in muscle. When the transporter is inactivated, reabsorption fails and patients present with iminoglycinuria, an autosomal recessive trait, or the milder hyperglycinuria in which only glycine is lost. Penetrance and the exact urinary profile depend on the accompanying activity of related tubular transporters SLC6A18, SLC6A19 and SLC6A20, so the phenotype behaves as a polygenic threshold rather than a simple single-gene defect. Both conditions are generally benign, illustrating the redundancy of renal amino acid transport.

Reabsorption of glycine, proline and hydroxyproline from the glomerular filtrate depends on proton-coupled amino acid transporter 2, encoded by SLC36A2, which works at the apical membrane of the proximal tubule and uses the inward proton gradient to drive high-affinity uptake of these small amino acids; the same transporter is also expressed in muscle. When the transporter is defective, these substrates escape recovery and appear in urine, producing iminoglycinuria, an autosomal recessive defect of renal imino acid and glycine transport, or the milder hyperglycinuria in which glycine alone is lost. Both conditions are generally benign, and their severity is shaped by co-inherited variants in partner transporters of the same reabsorptive system, so the phenotype behaves as a digenic or polygenic trait rather than a simple single-gene loss.

Defective RHAG causes regulator type Rh-null hemolytic anemia (RHN) describes what happens to red blood cells when the glycoprotein that organises the Rhesus antigen complex is lost. RHAG is an erythroid-specific member of the SLC42 ammonium transporter family and is required for cell-surface expression of the Rh polypeptides; without it the entire complex fails to assemble and the Rh-null phenotype results. Affected red cells are stomatocytic or spherocytic, leak cations, lose normal membrane phospholipid asymmetry, and are cleared prematurely, producing chronic hemolytic anemia of variable severity. RHAG itself is thought to move ammonium across the erythrocyte membrane, preventing toxic NH3/NH4+ accumulation and contributing to systemic nitrogen handling. The pathway therefore links a single transporter defect to red cell membrane architecture, blood group serology, and inherited hemolysis.

The Rh-associated glycoprotein is an erythroid membrane transporter of the Rhesus family that carries ammonium/ammonia across the red cell membrane and, just as importantly, acts as the chaperone required for surface assembly of the whole Rh antigen complex. Loss-of-function mutations in RHAG produce the regulator type of Rh-null disease, in which Rh antigens are absent or severely reduced from the erythrocyte surface even though the genes encoding them are intact. The resulting Rh-deficiency syndrome is a chronic hemolytic anemia: red cells become stomatocytic or spherocytic, show disturbed cation fluxes and abnormal membrane phospholipid asymmetry, and are cleared prematurely. The pathway links solute transport across the erythrocyte membrane to the structural integrity of the red cell, and explains why blood group antigen expression can fail through a defective accessory subunit rather than the antigen itself.

Defective SLC4A1 causes hereditary spherocytosis type 4 (HSP4), distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA) and dRTA with hemolytic anemia (dRTA-HA) covers the disease consequences of losing band 3, the chloride/bicarbonate exchanger that is the most abundant protein of the red cell membrane and the basolateral bicarbonate exit route of kidney alpha-intercalated cells. In erythrocytes it both carries CO2 as bicarbonate during gas exchange and anchors the spectrin-ankyrin cytoskeleton to the lipid bilayer; mutations that destabilise this link produce spherical, fragile cells that are cleared by the spleen, giving hereditary spherocytosis with haemolytic anaemia. In the collecting duct the same exchanger supports net acid secretion, so loss-of-function or mistrafficked variants leave the kidney unable to acidify urine, causing distal renal tubular acidosis with metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia and nephrocalcinosis, sometimes together with haemolysis. Normal sequence variation at this locus defines the Diego blood group.

Band 3, the erythrocyte anion exchanger encoded by SLC4A1, swaps chloride for bicarbonate across the membrane and is the most abundant protein of the red cell surface, where it also anchors the spectrin-based cytoskeleton and defines the Diego blood group. The same protein sits in the basolateral membrane of kidney collecting duct alpha-intercalated cells, exporting bicarbonate to blood as protons are pumped into urine. Loss-of-function or mistrafficked variants therefore produce two distinct clinical pictures: membrane destabilisation gives hereditary spherocytosis type 4, with rigid spherical erythrocytes and haemolytic anaemia, while defective renal handling causes distal renal tubular acidosis, an inability to acidify urine that leads to metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia, nephrocalcinosis and rickets or osteomalacia. Some alleles combine both, presenting as distal renal tubular acidosis with haemolytic anaemia, and inheritance may be dominant or recessive depending on the mutation.

Defective SLC9A9 causes autism 16 (AUTS16) describes what follows when the endosomal sodium/hydrogen exchanger NHE9 is lost or impaired, a defect linked to susceptibility to autism spectrum disorder with associated epilepsy and attention deficits. NHE9 sits in the membrane of late and recycling endosomes, where it leaks protons back out in exchange for sodium or potassium and so sets the luminal pH of that compartment. Because endosomal acidity governs how quickly cargo is sorted and returned to the cell surface, this housekeeping activity determines the surface residence of glutamate transporters and synaptic receptors in neurons and glia. Mutations that reduce exchange activity over-acidify endosomes, slow recycling, and alter excitatory synaptic signalling, connecting a general ion-homeostasis function to the reciprocal social interaction, communication, and stereotyped behaviour phenotypes that define the pervasive developmental disorders.

The endosomal sodium/hydrogen exchanger NHE9, encoded by SLC9A9, sets the luminal pH of recycling and late endosomes by trading luminal protons for cytosolic sodium or potassium, countering the acidification driven by the vacuolar ATPase. Because compartment pH governs how fast receptors and transporters are returned to the cell surface, this housekeeping activity has particular consequences in neurons and glia, where it influences surface levels of glutamate transporters and synaptic receptor recycling. Loss-of-function and truncating variants in the gene confer susceptibility to autism 16, a form of the prototypic pervasive developmental disorder marked by impaired reciprocal social interaction and communication, restricted and stereotyped interests, and developmental abnormalities evident before age three; the same locus has been linked to attention deficit and epilepsy phenotypes, illustrating how over-acidified endosomes disturb neurodevelopmental signalling.

Defective SLC2A10 causes arterial tortuosity syndrome (ATS) describes what happens when a cell loses GLUT10, a high-affinity glucose transporter of the class III facilitative carrier family, and why that loss is felt in the arterial wall rather than in metabolism. Loss-of-function mutations in SLC2A10 cause arterial tortuosity syndrome, an autosomal recessive connective tissue disorder in which the aorta and other large arteries become elongated, twisted, aneurysmal and prone to dissection, often with early death, alongside joint laxity and skin hyperextensibility. GLUT10 is expressed most strongly in liver and pancreas but present broadly, and is thought to supply dehydroascorbate to intracellular compartments; its absence disturbs redox balance and TGF-beta signalling in vascular smooth muscle, degrading elastic fibre assembly in the extracellular matrix. The pathway therefore links sugar transport to arterial structural integrity.

Arterial tortuosity syndrome follows loss of function of GLUT10, the high-affinity glucose transporter encoded by SLC2A10 and one of the class III facilitative sugar carriers. GLUT10 is most abundant in liver and pancreas but present at lower levels in most tissues, and its transport activity is thought to supply dehydroascorbate or glucose to intracellular compartments where redox balance and collagen and elastin processing depend on ascorbate. When both alleles are defective, the elastic fibre architecture of large arteries is abnormal and vessels become elongated and corkscrew-like, with aneurysm, stenosis and dissection; affected individuals also show joint laxity, skin hyperextensibility and craniofacial features, and death may occur early in life. The gene lies in a chromosomal interval linked to type 2 diabetes susceptibility, connecting sugar transport to connective tissue integrity and vascular wall mechanics.

Defective SLC24A1 causes congenital stationary night blindness 1D (CSNB1D) describes what happens to rod photoreceptors when they cannot expel calcium after light stimulation. SLC24A1 encodes NCKX1, a sodium/calcium-potassium exchanger enriched in rod outer segments that trades four Na+ for one Ca2+ and one K+, providing the calcium efflux arm of phototransduction. Light closes the cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, and continued exchange by NCKX1 lowers outer segment calcium, which resets guanylate cyclase and channel sensitivity so that rods recover and adapt to changing illumination. Loss-of-function mutations block this recalibration, and affected individuals inherit an autosomal recessive, non-progressive impairment of night vision with a Riggs-type electroretinogram reflecting reduced rod response amplitude. The condition illustrates how calcium homeostasis in a sensory cell, rather than the excitatory signal itself, sets the dynamic range of vision in dim light.

Rod photoreceptors recover from a flash of light by clearing calcium from the outer segment, and the exchanger encoded by SLC24A1 is what does that clearing. It carries one Ca2+ and one K+ out in exchange for four Na+ entering, using both the sodium and potassium gradients so that calcium can be extruded against a steep gradient; the resulting fall in cytosolic calcium resets cyclic nucleotide synthesis and channel sensitivity, which is the basis of light adaptation and of the rod's ability to respond to a second stimulus. Loss-of-function mutations cause congenital stationary night blindness 1D, an autosomal recessive, non-progressive condition in which patients see poorly in dim light and show a Riggs-type electroretinogram indicating that rod phototransduction itself is impaired rather than the downstream bipolar cell connection.

Defective SLCO2A1 causes primary, autosomal recessive hypertrophic osteoarthropathy 2 (PHOAR2) concerns loss of the prostaglandin transporter PGT, the carrier that moves prostaglandins across the plasma membrane and thereby terminates their signalling. SLCO2A1 is expressed nearly everywhere and handles PGD2, PGE1, PGE2 and PGF2A, taking up circulating prostaglandins for cytoplasmic degradation and contributing to release of newly synthesised mediators. When the transporter fails, PGE2 accumulates in tissue and plasma and its receptors are chronically stimulated, driving bone remodelling and soft tissue overgrowth. The result is primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, a rare recessive genodermatosis with thickened facial and limb skin, digital clubbing, periostosis and painful joint swelling, more severe in males. The condition illustrates that prostaglandin inactivation by transport is as much a control point in eicosanoid signalling as synthesis by cyclooxygenases, and explains why COX inhibitors relieve symptoms.

Prostaglandins act locally and must be cleared from tissue and circulation once they have signalled, and the prostaglandin transporter encoded by SLCO2A1 is the carrier that performs this uptake. It is broadly expressed and moves PGE1, PGE2, PGD2 and PGF2alpha across the plasma membrane, supporting both the release of newly synthesised prostaglandins and their delivery to intracellular degradation by 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase. Loss-of-function mutations block that uptake, so PGE2 accumulates and drives sustained signalling in skin, periosteum and vasculature. The result is primary autosomal recessive hypertrophic osteoarthropathy type 2, a rare genodermatosis with thickened facial skin, digital clubbing and periosteal new bone formation, more often symptomatic in males. The condition illustrates how eicosanoid signalling is terminated by transport rather than by receptor shutdown alone, and overlaps clinically with deficiency of the degrading enzyme itself.

Defective SLC2A2 causes Fanconi-Bickel syndrome (FBS) describes what happens when cells lose their bidirectional exit route for glucose, galactose and fructose. SLC2A2 (GLUT2) is a low-affinity facilitative hexose transporter placed at the basolateral membrane of intestinal and renal proximal tubule epithelium and in hepatocytes and pancreatic beta cells, where it lets dietary sugars taken up apically pass into the circulation, allows the liver to move glucose in either direction according to fed or fasting state, and lets beta cells sense ambient glucose before secreting insulin. Loss-of-function mutations produce Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, in which hepatic and renal glycogen accumulates, the proximal tubule leaks glucose, phosphate, amino acids and bicarbonate, and galactose and glucose utilisation is impaired, causing rickets, hepatomegaly and growth failure. The pathway thus links transepithelial sugar absorption to whole-body glucose homeostasis.

Fanconi-Bickel syndrome is what follows loss of the low-affinity hexose transporter GLUT2, encoded by SLC2A2, and it shows how much whole-body sugar handling depends on a single facilitative carrier. GLUT2 moves glucose, galactose and fructose bidirectionally across the plasma membrane down their concentration gradients, sitting basolaterally in intestinal and renal proximal tubule epithelium to release dietary and reabsorbed sugars into blood, allowing the liver to take up or export glucose as feeding state demands, and serving pancreatic beta cells as part of the glucose-sensing step that sets insulin release. When the transporter is defective, glucose is trapped intracellularly and stored as glycogen, giving hepatorenal glycogen accumulation, proximal tubular wasting, rickets and stunted growth with impaired glucose and galactose utilisation.

Defective SLCO1B1 causes hyperbilirubinemia, Rotor type (HBLRR) describes what happens to bilirubin handling when hepatocytes lose the transporter that takes it up from blood. SLCO1B1 (OATP1B1) sits on the sinusoidal, basolateral face of the hepatocyte and imports unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin along with bile acids, and it is the route by which conjugated bilirubin secreted into plasma is recaptured for biliary excretion. When it fails, together with its paralogue, that reuptake step is lost and conjugated bilirubin accumulates in the circulation, producing Rotor syndrome: an autosomal recessive, benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with mild jaundice appearing in infancy or childhood and no hemolysis. The same transporter clears many drugs, so its loss or reduced activity also alters statin and methotrexate pharmacokinetics, linking heme catabolite disposal to hepatic drug uptake more broadly.

Bilirubin generated by heme breakdown must be taken up from blood into hepatocytes before it can be conjugated and excreted in bile, and the organic anion transporter SLCO1B1 on the sinusoidal (basolateral) hepatocyte membrane performs that uptake, including the re-uptake of conjugated bilirubin that has leaked back into plasma. Loss of functional SLCO1B1 blocks this hepatic clearance step and produces Rotor-type hyperbilirubinaemia, an autosomal recessive conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in which mild jaundice appears after birth or during childhood without haemolysis and with otherwise normal liver histology. Because the same transporter carries statins, methotrexate and other anionic drugs across the sinusoidal membrane, its activity also sets hepatic first-pass drug uptake, and reduced-function variants raise systemic drug exposure. The pathway sits at the entry point of hepatobiliary elimination, upstream of glucuronidation and canalicular export.

Defective SLC20A2 causes idiopathic basal ganglia calcification 1 (IBGC1) concerns loss of a sodium-dependent inorganic phosphate transporter and the brain calcification that follows. SLC20A2 encodes PiT2, which co-transports two sodium ions with each phosphate and, together with the related PiT1, performs housekeeping phosphate uptake from interstitial fluid — a function that also shapes extracellular matrix, cartilage and vascular mineralisation. When PiT2 activity is reduced, phosphate is not cleared efficiently from the brain interstitium and cerebrospinal fluid, and calcium phosphate deposits accumulate in vessel walls and pericapillary spaces of the basal ganglia, thalamus and cerebellum. Inheritance is autosomal dominant; carriers range from wholly asymptomatic to presenting with parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance. The pathway links solute carrier–mediated phosphate homeostasis to neurodegeneration and to the broader biology of ectopic tissue calcification.

Cells take up inorganic phosphate from extracellular fluid through sodium-coupled cotransporters, and PiT2, encoded by SLC20A2, performs this housekeeping uptake with two sodium ions carried per phosphate. In the brain its activity keeps interstitial phosphate low enough that calcium phosphate does not precipitate around small vessels. Loss-of-function mutations cause idiopathic basal ganglia calcification type 1, an autosomal dominant condition in which mineral deposits accumulate in vascular and pericapillary spaces of the basal ganglia, thalamus and cerebellum. Carriers range from wholly asymptomatic to presenting with parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance, so the clinical picture is variable even within families. The same transporter family also contributes to matrix, cartilage and vascular calcification elsewhere in the body, placing this defect within the wider problem of phosphate handling and ectopic mineralisation.

VxPx cargo-targeting to cilium is the sorting route that delivers selected membrane proteins from the trans-Golgi network to the ciliary membrane, giving the cilium its distinct receptor and channel composition. It matters because the cilium cannot synthesize its own membrane proteins: photoreceptor outer segments depend on it to load rhodopsin and cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, and kidney epithelia depend on it for polycystin-1 and -2, so failure produces retinal degeneration and polycystic kidney disease. Cargo bearing a C-terminal VxPx-like motif is captured by ARF4 at the Golgi, together with ASAP1 and GBF1, and packaged into carriers whose delivery is controlled by a RAB11-RAB3IP-RAB8A cascade. Docking and fusion at the base of the cilium require the octameric exocyst complex, which tethers the vesicles at the periciliary membrane. The pathway thus links Golgi export and polarized vesicle traffic to ciliary signalling capacity.

Cilia and the outer segments of photoreceptors are built from membrane proteins made in the secretory pathway, and this route is how those proteins get there. Cargo bearing a short VxPx-type signal in its cytoplasmic tail is captured by the small GTPase ARF4 at the trans-Golgi network, together with an ARF GAP and a GEF, and packaged into carriers that are then handed off through a RAB11-to-RAB8 conversion mediated by the exchange factor Rabin8 and delivered at the ciliary base with help from the exocyst complex. The cargoes define why it matters: rhodopsin and cyclic nucleotide-gated channel subunits for phototransduction, polycystin-1 and -2 for renal tubule mechanosensing. Mislocalisation of rhodopsin underlies forms of retinitis pigmentosa, while polycystin trafficking failure causes polycystic kidney disease, linking this targeting step to ciliopathy in general.

TNFR1-mediated ceramide production is the lipid arm of tumour necrosis factor signalling: when TNF-alpha engages TNFR1, sphingomyelinases hydrolyse membrane sphingomyelin to ceramide, converting a cytokine signal into a second messenger that biases cells toward growth arrest, stress responses and apoptosis. This route contributes to inflammatory tissue injury and to the cytotoxicity of TNF, and it links receptor engagement directly to membrane composition rather than to transcription. Neutral sphingomyelinases such as SMPD2 and SMPD3 act at the plasma membrane and are recruited through the adaptor NSMAF, which bridges them to a dedicated activating region of the receptor, with RACK1 as a scaffolding partner; the receptor death domain and its adaptors instead drive caspase-dependent activation of the acidic, lysosomal enzyme. Downstream metabolism of ceramide to sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate reverses the signal, so the balance of these lipids sets whether a cell dies or survives.

Tumour necrosis factor does not only trigger caspase activation; it also remodels membrane lipids, and TNFR1-mediated ceramide production is the branch that converts receptor engagement into a sphingolipid signal. Sphingomyelinases hydrolyse sphingomyelin to ceramide, which acts as a second messenger favouring growth arrest and apoptosis, while its downstream conversion to sphingosine-1-phosphate has the opposite, pro-survival effect; the balance between these lipids helps set whether a TNF-stimulated cell dies or persists. Neutral, magnesium-dependent sphingomyelinases such as SMPD2 and SMPD3 act at the plasma membrane and are recruited to a dedicated cytoplasmic region of TNFR1 through the adaptor NSMAF, with RACK1 as a scaffolding partner; an acid, lysosomal sphingomyelinase is engaged instead via the death domain and caspase cleavage. The pathway links inflammatory cytokine signalling to lipid-mediated control of proliferation, stress responses and cell death.

Defective Mismatch Repair Associated With MSH2 describes what happens to genome maintenance when MSH2, the human counterpart of bacterial MutS, is lost or altered. MSH2 is the obligate partner in the mismatch-recognition heterodimers that scan newly replicated DNA: with MSH6 it detects base-base mispairs and small insertion-deletion loops, and with MSH3 it handles larger loops, after which downstream excision and resynthesis restore the correct sequence. Without functional MSH2 these lesions persist, replication errors accumulate at repetitive tracts, and tumours acquire the microsatellite instability and hypermutator phenotype used to diagnose them. Inherited heterozygous mutations cause hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, with related presentations including the sebaceous tumours of Muir-Torre syndrome and, in biallelic form, childhood-onset mismatch repair cancer syndrome. The same defect also removes a barrier to tolerating certain chemotherapeutics while sensitising tumours to immune checkpoint blockade.

Mismatch repair corrects base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops left behind by DNA replication, and MSH2 is the common subunit of the complexes that recognise them: it pairs with MSH6 to form MutSalpha, which handles single-base mismatches and short loops, and with MSH3 to form MutSbeta, which handles larger insertion-deletion heterologies. Loss of functional MSH2 therefore disables mismatch recognition altogether, the initiating step that licenses downstream excision and resynthesis. Cells with defective mismatch repair of this kind accumulate mutations and show microsatellite instability, particularly at repetitive sequences in coding regions. Inherited pathogenic MSH2 variants underlie Lynch syndrome, with high lifetime risk of colorectal and endometrial cancer, and the associated Muir-Torre and constitutional mismatch repair deficiency phenotypes. The resulting hypermutated, neoantigen-rich tumours are characteristically responsive to immune checkpoint blockade, making repair status a clinically actionable marker.

Fructose biosynthesis is the two-step polyol route that converts glucose to fructose through sorbitol, and it is the source of the fructose that dominates seminal fluid and fuels sperm motility. Aldose reductase reduces glucose to sorbitol using NADPH, and sorbitol dehydrogenase oxidises sorbitol to fructose using NAD+; the pathway therefore runs independently of insulin and accelerates whenever intracellular glucose rises. That property makes it a central mechanism of diabetic tissue injury: in lens epithelium, peripheral neurons, kidney and retina, flux through aldose reductase depletes NADPH needed for glutathione regeneration, traps osmotically active sorbitol, and shifts cytosolic redox balance, contributing to cataract, neuropathy and microvascular disease. The same enzymes are abundant in seminal vesicle and epididymal tissue, where the output is a physiological energy substrate rather than a hazard, and aldose reductase inhibition remains a therapeutic strategy in diabetic complications.

Fructose biosynthesis in human tissues runs through the two-step polyol pathway, in which aldose reductase reduces glucose to sorbitol using NADPH and sorbitol dehydrogenase then oxidizes sorbitol to fructose with NAD+. This route supplies the high fructose concentrations of seminal fluid, where it serves as an energy substrate for sperm, and it operates in epididymal and seminal vesicle tissue as well as in the eye lens, kidney, peripheral nerve and retina. Because the first enzyme is not insulin-regulated and has a low affinity for glucose, flux rises steeply in hyperglycaemia, consuming NADPH, depleting glutathione regeneration capacity and accumulating osmotically active sorbitol. This makes the pathway a recognized contributor to diabetic complications such as cataract, neuropathy, retinopathy and nephropathy, and a target of aldose reductase inhibitors. It also links glucose disposal to fructose metabolism and to cellular redox balance.

Vesicle-mediated transport is the cell's internal courier system: proteins, lipids and other cargo move between compartments and to and from the cell surface inside membrane-bounded carriers, either dissolved in the vesicle lumen or embedded in its membrane. It underlies secretion of hormones, antibodies and matrix proteins, uptake of lipoproteins and iron by scavenger and endocytic receptors, receptor downregulation, and delivery of hydrolases to lysosomes; its failure produces disorders of bleeding, pigmentation, cholesterol handling and neurodegeneration. Cargo selection and budding use coat complexes such as COPII at ER exit sites, COPI for retrograde traffic, and clathrin with AP adaptors at the plasma membrane and trans-Golgi; dynamin severs the neck, motors and cytoskeletal tracks move the carrier, and Rab GTPases with their GEFs and GAPs, tethers like TRAPP, COG and the exocyst, and SNARE-driven fusion complete delivery. ESCRT components route ubiquitinated receptors into multivesicular bodies.

Vesicle-mediated transport is the system by which cells move proteins, lipids and extracellular cargo between compartments inside membrane-bounded carriers, and it underlies secretion, receptor uptake, lysosomal delivery and the maintenance of organelle identity. Its failure blocks hormone and antibody secretion, leaves receptors such as LDLR, TFRC and EGFR uncleared from the surface, and causes storage and pigmentation disorders. The genes here cover the full itinerary: COPII components with SAR1B and the SEC23/24 subunits bud carriers from the ER, COPI and the Golgi-associated conserved oligomeric Golgi and TRAPP complexes handle intra-Golgi and retrograde steps, clathrin with AP-1 and AP-2 adaptors, dynamins and endophilins drive endocytosis, and ESCRT subunits with TSG101 and VPS4 sort ubiquitinated cargo into multivesicular bodies. Rab GTPases with their GEFs and TBC-domain GAPs specify identity, SNAREs and NSF execute fusion, and kinesin, dynein and myosin motors carry vesicles along cytoskeletal tracks.

Phospholipase C-mediated cascade: FGFR1 is the branch of fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 signalling that converts ligand binding into calcium and protein kinase C signals, shaping limb and skeletal patterning, neuronal and craniofacial development, and, through Klotho-dependent FGF23 responses, phosphate handling in the kidney. Loss or distortion of this output contributes to craniosynostosis syndromes, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and FGFR1-driven cancers. Mechanistically, one of the FGF ligands together with heparan sulfate dimerises FGFR1 and triggers trans-autophosphorylation; a specific phosphotyrosine in the receptor tail recruits PLCG1 via its SH2 domains, and the receptor kinase phosphorylates and activates it. Activated PLC-gamma hydrolyses PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, releasing stored calcium and engaging calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases and PKC. This arm runs in parallel with the FRS2-RAS-ERK and PI3K routes, allowing the same receptor to specify distinct cellular outcomes.

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR1 trigger receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation, and one of the branches that follows runs through phospholipase C-gamma. This arm converts growth factor binding at the cell surface into a calcium and lipid second-messenger signal, feeding the proliferation, migration and differentiation responses that FGF signalling drives in limb and skeletal development, neuronal patterning and wound repair. Phosphotyrosines on the activated receptor tail create docking sites read by the SH2 domains of PLCG1, which is then phosphorylated and activated in place; it cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, releasing calcium from intracellular stores and engaging protein kinase C and calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases. The ligand repertoire here spans classical paracrine FGFs and the endocrine FGF23, whose action on FGFR1 requires the co-receptor klotho and governs phosphate handling. Aberrant FGFR1 activity underlies skeletal dysplasias and several cancers.

Downstream signaling of activated FGFR4 describes what happens inside the cell once fibroblast growth factors bind and activate FGFR4, converting receptor autophosphorylation into proliferation, survival, migration and differentiation decisions. This particular receptor, partnered with the coreceptor beta-Klotho, transmits the hepatic FGF19 signal that suppresses bile acid synthesis, and its overactivity through amplification or activating mutation drives rhabdomyosarcoma and hepatocellular carcinoma. Mechanistically, phosphotyrosines on the receptor tail and the long juxtamembrane docking site recruit FRS2 and FRS3, which assemble GRB2, SOS1 and the phosphatase SHP2 to load RAS proteins with GTP and trigger the MAP kinase cascade; GAB1 recruitment engages PI3K and AKT-dependent survival signalling, while phospholipase C-gamma generates diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate for calcium and PKC responses. The same adaptor logic serves all FGF receptors, with ligand and coreceptor availability determining tissue-specific output.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 4 binds FGF ligands and, once its kinase is autophosphorylated, converts that event into the intracellular programmes that drive proliferation, survival, migration and differentiation. This receptor is also the metabolic arm of the family: with the coreceptor beta-Klotho it responds to endocrine FGFs such as FGF19 and FGF23 to control bile acid synthesis and phosphate handling, and its aberrant activation is implicated in hepatocellular and rhabdomyosarcoma tumours. Downstream signalling of activated FGFR4 proceeds through docking proteins FRS2 and FRS3, which recruit GRB2, the phosphatase SHP2 and GAB1, feeding the SOS1-RAS-ERK route and PI3K-AKT survival signalling; SHC1 provides a parallel adaptor link and phospholipase C-gamma generates diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate. Ligand identity, coreceptor availability and adaptor choice together determine which of these outputs dominates.

Signaling by FGFR1 describes how fibroblast growth factors, held in place by heparan sulfate proteoglycans, activate one particular receptor tyrosine kinase to direct cell fate, proliferation, migration and survival across development. It patterns the limb bud, skeleton and brain, and drives GnRH neuron migration, so loss-of-function mutations in the receptor or its partner anosmin cause Kallmann syndrome and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, while amplification and fusion of the receptor drive squamous lung cancer and other tumours. Ligand binding dimerises the receptor and autophosphorylates its tail, creating docking sites for FRS2, GRB2 and SHC1 that launch RAS-RAF-ERK output, alongside PI3K-AKT via GAB1 and PLCG1-mediated calcium signalling. Feedback through SPRY, SPRED, PTPN11 and CBL-mediated ubiquitination limits the response, and Klotho co-receptors redirect the same kinase toward endocrine FGF23 control of phosphate homeostasis.

FGFR1 is one of four fibroblast growth factor receptor tyrosine kinases, and signalling through it directs cell fate, proliferation, migration and survival during development and in tissue repair. It patterns limb and craniofacial structures, drives olfactory and GnRH neuron development — loss of FGFR1 or its partner anosmin causes Kallmann syndrome with hypogonadism and anosmia — and, with Klotho as co-receptor, transduces FGF23 signals that lower phosphate. Ligands such as FGF1, FGF2 and FGF8 act together with heparan sulfate to dimerise the receptor; autophosphorylated tyrosines then recruit FRS2, GRB2, SHC1, PTPN11 and GAB1, feeding into RAS–RAF–ERK, PI3K and PLC-gamma outputs. Sprouty and SPRED proteins, protein phosphatase 2A subunits, and CBL-mediated ubiquitination restrain the response, while adhesion molecules of the FLRT family provide ligand-independent activation on neuronal membranes. Amplification and activating fusions of FGFR1 occur in several cancers.

Termination of translesion DNA synthesis ends the emergency mode a replication fork enters when it meets a DNA lesion, and returns synthesis to the accurate replicative machinery. This matters because the Y-family polymerases that copy past damage — POLH, POLI, POLK and REV1 — are error-prone, so leaving them on the template beyond the lesion is a direct source of mutation and genome instability of the kind seen in cancer. Recruitment of these enzymes depends on monoubiquitinated PCNA at K164; deubiquitination by enzymes such as USP10 and USP43 strips that mark, evicts the bypass polymerase and licenses a switch back to polymerase delta or epsilon with RFC and RPA at the fork. ISG15 conjugation, driven by UBA7, TRIM25 and UBE2L6, provides a parallel brake, and PCLAF modulates polymerase access to PCNA. The pathway is thus the mutagenesis-limiting arm of DNA damage tolerance.

Translesion synthesis lets a replication fork copy past a damaged base, but the Y-family polymerases that do it are error-prone, so cells must switch back to accurate replication as soon as the lesion is passed. Terminating translesion DNA synthesis is that switch, and its failure raises the mutation burden carried forward into daughter cells, a route toward the mutational signatures seen in tumours. Monoubiquitinated PCNA recruits the bypass polymerases eta, iota, kappa and REV1; removing that ubiquitin mark, by deubiquitinases including USP10, evicts them and restores processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon loaded via replication factor C on RPA-coated template. An ISG15 arm, acting through UBA7, UBE2L6 and TRIM25, modifies PCNA and PCLAF to help disengage the bypass machinery, linking interferon-inducible conjugation to the fidelity of damage tolerance and to normal fork restart.

Defective amino acid transport by SLC7A9 causes cystinuria (CSNU) describes what happens in the kidney when the transporter that recovers cystine from urine stops working. Normally SLC7A9 pairs with the glycoprotein SLC3A1 to form a heterodimeric exchanger in the apical membrane of proximal tubule cells, taking up cystine and the dibasic amino acids lysine, arginine and ornithine in exchange for neutral amino acids, sodium-independently, so that these residues are reabsorbed rather than lost. When mutations disable the light subunit, cystine remains in the tubular fluid, and because oxidised cysteine is poorly soluble it precipitates into recurrent urinary stones, with obstruction, infection and occasionally renal failure. This is the type B form of an inherited aminoaciduria, mechanistically parallel to loss of the heavy subunit, and illustrates how epithelial solute retrieval sets urinary composition.

Cystine filtered by the glomerulus is normally recovered almost completely in the proximal tubule, and this reabsorption depends on a two-subunit transporter at the apical membrane: the light chain SLC7A9 (b(0,+)AT/BAT1) disulfide-linked to the heavy chain SLC3A1 (rBAT), which chaperones it to the surface. Together they carry out sodium-independent, high-affinity uptake of cystine and the dibasic amino acids lysine, arginine and ornithine in exchange for neutral amino acids. Loss-of-function mutations in SLC7A9 produce type B cystinuria, the counterpart of type A caused by SLC3A1 defects. Because cystine is poorly soluble in acidic urine, the unreabsorbed load precipitates as recurrent stones, leading to obstructive uropathy, pyelonephritis and, occasionally, chronic kidney damage. The pathway illustrates how epithelial solute recovery, rather than synthesis or catabolism, sets urinary amino acid composition.

Essential pentosuria is a harmless inherited metabolic quirk in which large amounts of the pentose sugar L-xylulose appear in the urine, historically one of the first recognised human biochemical variants and notable mainly because it can be mistaken for diabetes on older sugar-based urine tests. It arises when both copies of the gene for L-xylulose reductase, DCXR, are inactivated by loss-of-function mutations, as occurs at appreciable frequency in Ashkenazi Jewish and Lebanese populations. This NADPH-dependent enzyme normally reduces L-xylulose to xylitol as part of the glucuronate/xylulose pathway, a branch of sugar metabolism that disposes of glucuronate derived from UDP-glucuronic acid and feeds carbon back toward the pentose phosphate pool. Blocking the step leaves L-xylulose with no route onward, so it accumulates and is cleared renally without metabolic consequence, making this a benign trait rather than a disease.

Essential pentosuria is a harmless inherited condition in which large amounts of the pentose sugar L-xylulose appear in the urine, inherited recessively and found mainly in Ashkenazi Jewish and Lebanese families. It arises when L-xylulose reductase, encoded by DCXR, is inactivated by mutation, so the NADPH-dependent reduction of L-xylulose to xylitol cannot occur. That step belongs to the glucuronate–xylulose pathway, a branch of carbohydrate metabolism that disposes of glucuronate derived from UDP-glucuronic acid and feeds carbon back toward the pentose phosphate pool; blocking it causes the unused pentose to spill into urine rather than any metabolic crisis. The trait matters chiefly as an interpretive problem, since the urinary reducing sugar can be mistaken for glycosuria and prompt an unnecessary diagnosis of diabetes, and it illustrates how a metabolic dead end can be tolerated without disease.

Diseases of carbohydrate metabolism collects the inherited defects that break the route from dietary sugar to usable energy and to glycan turnover. It matters because each block produces a recognisable clinical syndrome: lactase or sucrase-isomaltase deficiency causes osmotic diarrhoea and carbohydrate intolerance; aldolase B or ketohexokinase loss underlies hereditary fructose intolerance and benign fructosuria; glucose-6-phosphatase and its transporter, glycogen synthase, branching enzyme and glycogenin failures give the glycogen storage diseases, with acid maltase deficiency causing Pompe disease; laforin and malin mutations produce Lafora body epilepsy. Pentose phosphate pathway defects in transaldolase and ribose-5-phosphate isomerase impair NADPH and nucleotide precursor supply, while loss of dicarbonyl reductase in glucuronate catabolism yields harmless pentosuria. Lysosomal sulfatases, glycosidases and hyaluronidase are included because failure to degrade glycosaminoglycans produces the mucopolysaccharidoses, with ubiquitin genes reflecting degradative quality control.

Inherited defects in carbohydrate handling span the whole route from a meal to usable energy, and this collection of diseases of carbohydrate metabolism covers failures at each step. Loss of intestinal brush-border enzymes such as lactase or sucrase-isomaltase leaves disaccharides undigested and causes osmotic diarrhoea, while ketohexokinase and aldolase B mutations produce benign fructosuria or the hepatotoxic, hypoglycaemic syndrome of hereditary fructose intolerance. Glycogen storage disorders arise when synthesis or mobilisation breaks down: glycogenin and glycogen synthase deficiencies, branching enzyme loss, acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency in Pompe disease, and failure of glucose-6-phosphatase or its transporter, which uncouples the liver from fasting glucose output. Laforin and malin mutations yield insoluble polyglucosan and progressive myoclonic epilepsy. Pentose phosphate pathway lesions in transaldolase and ribose-5-phosphate isomerase, lysosomal glycosaminoglycan degradation defects, and dicarbonyl reductase loss causing essential pentosuria complete the spectrum.

RHO GTPases Activate Rhotekin and Rhophilins covers one branch of RHOA/RHOB/RHOC signalling in which the activated GTPase engages scaffold effectors rather than kinases, linking RHO activity to actin organisation, cell polarity and membrane traffic.
