These effectors matter because they determine where RHO output is delivered: rhotekin binds GTP-loaded RHOA, RHOB and RHOC, restrains their GTPase activity, contributes to septin assembly and polarity establishment, drives SRF-dependent transcription, and can suppress apoptosis through NF-kappaB. A lymphocyte-restricted relative broadens the family into immune cells. Rhophilins pair an N-terminal RHO-binding domain with BRO1 and PDZ modules, so they couple RHO to protein kinase C signalling and, through PDZ partners such as TAX1BP3 and LIN7B, to junctional and polarity complexes; RHOB recruits rhophilin-2 onto endosomes, relevant to thyroid cell function. Together they shape cytoskeletal remodelling, motility and epithelial architecture.

Active RHOA, RHOB and RHOC do their work by recruiting effectors, and rhotekin and the rhophilins are one such set of GTP-dependent binding partners that link RHO signalling to the actin cytoskeleton, cell polarity and membrane traffic. Rhotekin binds the GTP-loaded forms of all three GTPases and dampens their hydrolysis, and has been tied to septin organization, serum response factor-driven transcription, and NF-kappaB-dependent survival; a lymphocyte-restricted relative remains poorly characterized. Rhophilin-1 and rhophilin-2 pair an N-terminal GTPase-binding region with a BRO1 domain and a C-terminal PDZ domain, the latter engaging PDZ-containing partners such as TAX1BP3 and the scaffold LIN7B, and RHOB recruits rhophilin-2 onto endosomes. Through these effectors RHO activity is translated into cell shape, motility and directed membrane organization rather than into a single enzymatic output.

RHO GTPases Activate NADPH Oxidases describes how the small GTPases RAC1 and RAC2, in their GTP-bound state, switch on membrane NADPH oxidase complexes to generate superoxide. This is the reaction behind the neutrophil respiratory burst that kills ingested bacteria and fungi — loss of the NOX2 subunits CYBB, CYBA or the cytosolic factors NCF1/NCF2 causes chronic granulomatous disease — and the same chemistry supplies superoxide as a second messenger downstream of VEGF receptor signalling in endothelial cells during angiogenesis. Assembly requires RAC:GTP to dock directly on the flavocytochrome and on NCF2, joined by NCF1 and NCF4 after priming by protein kinase C isoforms, p38 and ERK MAP kinases, phosphoinositide kinases and the S100A8/A9 arachidonate carrier. Related NOX1 and NOX3 complexes use NOXO1 and NOXA1 in place of the phagocyte factors, extending RAC-dependent reactive oxygen production to epithelia and the inner ear.

Superoxide is made deliberately by NADPH oxidase complexes, and small GTPases of the RHO family are the switch that turns them on. When RAC1 or RAC2 loaded with GTP docks onto the membrane flavocytochrome and its cytosolic partners, electrons pass from NADPH to oxygen and superoxide is released into a phagosome or across the plasma membrane. In neutrophils this burst is the chemistry that kills ingested bacteria and fungi; loss of the catalytic subunit or of the p47/p67/p40 assembly causes chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent infection and granuloma formation. In endothelium the same output acts as a second messenger that amplifies VEGF receptor signalling during angiogenesis. Assembly is licensed by phosphorylation, with kinases including protein kinase C isoforms and ERK/p38 MAP kinases modifying the cytosolic factors, and S100A8/A9 and PIN1 contributing to subunit handling. Related oxidases NOX1 and NOX3 are activated through homologous adaptors.

Constitutive Signaling by AKT1 E17K in Cancer describes how a single recurrent point mutation locks a central growth-and-survival kinase into the active state, driving tumours of the breast, bladder, ovary and endometrium independently of upstream receptor input. Substitution of glutamate 17 by lysine in the pleckstrin homology domain lets AKT1 bind PIP2 rather than requiring PI3K-generated PIP3, so the kinase sits constitutively at the plasma membrane where PDPK1 and the mTORC2 complex (MTOR, RICTOR, MLST8, MAPKAP1, PRR5) phosphorylate it. The consequence is unrestrained output through the normal AKT substrate repertoire: inhibition of the pro-apoptotic BAD and CASP9, phosphorylation and nuclear exclusion of FOXO transcription factors, stabilisation of MDM2 against p53, inactivation of GSK3 and TSC2 to unleash mTORC1-driven protein synthesis, and blockade of the CDK inhibitors p21 and p27. This bypass of PI3K shapes tumour responses to pathway-targeted inhibitors.

AKT sits at the centre of growth factor signalling, and a single glutamate-to-lysine change at position 17 of AKT1 turns that node on permanently, driving the survival and proliferation programmes that underlie breast, ovarian and other cancers. Normally AKT must wait for PI3K to generate PIP3 before its PH domain docks at the membrane; the E17K substitution lets the kinase bind the abundant lipid PIP2 instead, so membrane recruitment no longer reports on receptor activity. Once there it is phosphorylated by PDPK1 and by the rapamycin-insensitive mTOR complex containing RICTOR, MLST8 and MAPKAP1, and becomes constitutively active. The downstream consequences are the familiar ones: FOXO transcription factors and GSK3 are inactivated, BAD and caspase-9 are silenced to block apoptosis, MDM2 is activated against p53, TSC2 is relieved so mTORC1 drives translation, and CDKN1A and CDKN1B are held away from the cell cycle machinery.

Negative regulation of MAPK pathway is the braking system on RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signalling, setting how strongly and for how long growth factor cues are transmitted. Because the same inputs can drive proliferation, differentiation, or senescence depending on signal duration, these brakes determine cell fate, and their loss is a route to oncogenic ERK hyperactivation. Several mechanisms converge: ERK-dependent feedback phosphorylation of RAF and of MAP2K1 T292 dampens kinase output, PP2A and PP5 strip activating phosphates from the RAF activation loop and N-terminal acidic region, priming PKA/AKT-mediated rephosphorylation that restores 14-3-3 binding and the inactive conformation, and PEBP1 uncouples RAF1 from its MEK substrates. Nuclear and cytoplasmic dual-specificity phosphatases, themselves ERK-inducible, dephosphorylate ERK and stress-activated MAPKs, while GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis returns RAS to its GDP-bound state. Scaffolds, ubiquitin, and KSR1 tune complex assembly.

Growth factor signalling through RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK must be switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and negative regulation of the MAPK pathway is how the duration, amplitude and location of that signal are set. Without it, sustained ERK activity drives inappropriate proliferation and transformation, which is why many of these brakes are lost or bypassed in cancer. ERK itself feeds back onto RAF and onto MAP2K1 at T292, priming the PP2A holoenzyme and PP5 to strip activating phosphates from the RAF activation loop and N-terminal acidic region; subsequent phosphorylation restores 14-3-3 (YWHAB) binding and returns RAF to an autoinhibited state. PEBP1 sequesters RAF1 away from its MEK substrates, and scaffolds and modifiers such as KSR1, BRAP and PAQR3 constrain complex assembly and membrane localisation. Nuclear and cytoplasmic dual-specificity phosphatases, many of them ERK-induced, dephosphorylate ERK and stress-activated MAPKs, closing the loop.

NIK-->noncanonical NF-kB signaling is the slower, longer-lasting arm of NF-kB activation, here triggered downstream of the fungal-recognition receptor Dectin-1 and SYK, and it shapes which cytokines a dendritic cell or macrophage makes in response to a pathogen. Where canonical signalling is rapid and transient, this branch builds over hours and sustains transcription, inducing chemokines such as CCL17 and CCL22 while repressing IL12B and thereby biasing the ensuing T helper response. Mechanistically, stabilised NIK (MAP3K14) activates IKKalpha, which phosphorylates the NFKB2 p100 precursor; an SCF-betaTrCP ubiquitin ligase and the 26S proteasome then process p100 to mature p52, releasing p52:RELB dimers into the nucleus. The same axis governs lymphoid organogenesis and B cell survival, and its dysregulation drives lymphoid malignancy and immunodeficiency.

The noncanonical NF-kB route is the slower, longer-lasting arm of NF-kB signalling, and it controls transcription of chemokines and immune modulators that shape the character of an inflammatory response rather than simply switching it on. Downstream of receptors such as the fungal sensor Dectin-1 acting through SYK, and of several TNF receptor family members, stabilised NIK (MAP3K14) phosphorylates IKK-alpha (CHUK), which marks the NFKB2 p100 precursor for recognition by a SKP1-CUL1-beta-TrCP ubiquitin ligase. Instead of being destroyed, p100 is partially processed by the 26S proteasome to mature p52, releasing p52:RELB dimers into the nucleus where they induce genes such as CCL17 and CCL22 while repressing IL12B. Neddylation components and polyubiquitin precursors supply the conjugation chemistry. This pathway underlies lymphoid organ development, B cell survival, and dendritic cell polarisation of T helper responses; its constitutive activation drives multiple myeloma and lymphoma.

Protein repair reverses two kinds of spontaneous chemical damage to proteins that would otherwise accumulate with age, restoring function to already-folded polypeptides rather than degrading and replacing them. Reactive oxygen species oxidise methionine side chains to sulfoxides, altering enzyme activity and structure; the methionine sulfoxide reductases MSRA and MSRB1-3 reduce the S- and R-diastereomers respectively, using a catalytic cysteine, an internal disulfide intermediate, and regeneration by NADPH-dependent thioredoxin. Because each cycle consumes an oxidant equivalent, these enzymes double as catalytic antioxidants alongside peroxiredoxins and superoxide dismutases. Separately, PCMT1 methylates isoaspartyl residues formed by spontaneous asparagine deamidation, driving them back through a succinimide intermediate to normal aspartate linkages. Loss of these activities accelerates oxidative and age-related protein damage, with the selenoprotein MSRB1 linking the system to selenium status and immune redox control.

Proteins accumulate chemical damage simply from living in an oxidizing, aqueous environment, and a small set of enzymes reverses two of the commonest lesions rather than letting the damaged protein be degraded. Reactive oxygen species oxidize methionine side chains to methionine sulfoxide, altering folding and activity; the methionine sulfoxide reductases restore them, with MSRA acting on the S-diastereomer of free and protein-bound substrate and the MSRB enzymes on protein-bound R-sulfoxide in cytosol, mitochondria and secretory compartments. Each cycle consumes an oxidizing equivalent, so these reductases double as catalytic antioxidants, regenerated through thioredoxin and NADPH. Separately, spontaneous deamidation of asparagine creates isoaspartyl bonds that distort the backbone, and PCMT1 methylates them to drive conversion back to normal aspartate. Loss of such protein repair capacity contributes to the protein damage that accompanies oxidative stress, neurodegeneration and ageing.

Defective CFTR causes cystic fibrosis describes what happens to a misfolded chloride channel that never reaches the cell surface. CFTR normally conducts chloride across airway, pancreatic, intestinal and sweat gland epithelia, setting the hydration and salt content of secretions; when mutant forms such as F508del fail quality control, secretions become thick and poorly cleared, producing chronic lung infection, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, meconium ileus, male infertility and salty sweat. The genes trace the disposal route rather than the channel's function: lectin-like sensors and the SEL1L adaptor recognise the misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum, derlins and ERLIN proteins mark it for retrotranslocation, RNF5 and RNF185 ubiquitinate it, the VCP ATPase extracts it, and the 26S proteasome degrades it. This is endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation acting as the proximate cause of disease, and the target of corrector therapies.

CFTR is a cAMP-regulated chloride channel in the apical membrane of epithelia, and the chloride and bicarbonate it moves set the hydration and pH of airway, pancreatic, intestinal and biliary secretions. When mutation prevents the protein from folding, as with the common F508del allele, the channel never reaches the surface and cystic fibrosis follows: thick unclearable mucus and chronic lung infection, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, meconium ileus, biliary disease, salty sweat and male infertility. The genes here trace the fate of the misfolded protein rather than the channel's transport function — lectin-like ER quality control and retention factors such as OS9, ERLEC1 and the SEL1L complex, membrane ubiquitin ligases RNF5 and RNF185, the VCP ATPase and derlin channels that retrotranslocate the substrate, and the ubiquitin and 26S proteasome machinery that degrades it. Loss of function is thus a disposal problem imposed by endoplasmic-reticulum-associated degradation.

Defective ABCC8 can cause hypo- and hyper-glycemias concerns the pancreatic beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channel and the glucose-sensing function it performs. This channel, built from the sulfonylurea receptor ABCC8 together with the pore-forming subunit KCNJ11, couples metabolic state to membrane potential: as glucose oxidation raises the ATP:ADP ratio the channel closes, the beta cell depolarises, voltage-gated calcium entry follows, and insulin granules fuse with the plasma membrane. Because the channel sets the threshold for secretion, mutations shift glycemia in either direction. Loss-of-function alleles leave the cell chronically depolarised and secreting insulin regardless of glucose, producing familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and leucine-sensitive hypoglycemia; gain-of-function alleles hold the channel open and cause neonatal or transient neonatal diabetes and adult non-insulin-dependent diabetes. The same subunit is the binding site for sulfonylurea drugs used to stimulate insulin release.

Insulin release from pancreatic beta cells is timed by an ATP-sensitive potassium channel built from the sulfonylurea receptor ABCC8 and the pore-forming subunit KCNJ11. When glucose metabolism raises the ATP:ADP ratio, the channel closes, the membrane depolarises, voltage-gated calcium entry follows, and insulin granules fuse with the plasma membrane; when the ratio falls the channel opens and secretion is silenced. Mutations in ABCC8 break this coupling in either direction. Loss of channel function leaves beta cells persistently depolarised and secreting insulin regardless of blood glucose, producing familial hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia and leucine-sensitive hypoglycaemia of infancy. Gain of function holds the channel open, blunting depolarisation and insulin output, and underlies permanent and transient neonatal diabetes as well as susceptibility to non-insulin-dependent diabetes. The same channel is the target of sulfonylurea drugs and of diazoxide, so genotype guides treatment.

Defective ABCA3 causes SMDP3 describes what happens to the lung when a single lipid transporter fails. ABCA3 sits in the limiting membrane of lamellar bodies in alveolar type II cells and pumps phospholipids and cholesterol into them, so that surfactant lipids and the surfactant proteins can be packaged together and secreted into the airspace. That secreted film lowers surface tension at the air-liquid interface and keeps alveoli from collapsing at end-expiration. Loss-of-function mutations produce pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 3: lamellar bodies are absent or replaced by small vesicles with electron-dense inclusions, surfactant is not delivered, and lipoproteinaceous material accumulates in the alveoli. Newborns present with severe, usually fatal respiratory distress, and milder alleles underlie childhood interstitial lung disease. The biology places surfactant production within ABC-transporter-mediated lipid trafficking and lysosome-related organelle biogenesis.

Pulmonary surfactant lowers surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface and keeps the lungs from collapsing at end-expiration, and ABCA3 is the lipid transporter that loads the phospholipids and cholesterol needed to build it into lamellar bodies of alveolar type II cells. There, lipids and surfactant proteins are packaged into bilayer stacks for secretion into the airspace. When ABCA3 function is lost, normal lamellar bodies fail to form and are replaced by small vesicles with electron-dense inclusions, surfactant secretion collapses, and lipoproteinaceous material accumulates in the alveoli. The resulting disorder of surfactant metabolism, pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 3, presents as severe and usually fatal neonatal respiratory distress, with milder mutations underlying childhood interstitial lung disease. This links ABC-transporter-mediated lipid translocation directly to lung development and neonatal respiratory physiology.

HDR through MMEJ (alt-NHEJ) is a backup route for sealing DNA double-strand breaks that trades accuracy for speed, and it becomes the dominant repair choice when higher-fidelity options are saturated or genetically lost. It matters most in tumours: cells deficient in homologous recombination, such as BRCA-mutant cancers, depend on it to survive, which is why DNA polymerase theta is pursued as a drug target, and its error-prone action leaves a distinctive scar of deletions, base substitutions and translocations that drives genome instability. Mechanistically the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex with CtIP performs limited end resection without the CDK-dependent BRCA1 recruitment that would commit the break to recombination; PARP1 or PARP2 then load POLQ, which anneals short microhomologies in the 3' overhangs and extends them, while FEN1 trims displaced flaps and LIG3-XRCC1 ligates the remaining nicks. ATM activation suppresses this route.

Microhomology-mediated end joining, also called alternative nonhomologous end joining, is a mutagenic backup route for repairing DNA double-strand breaks that operates when high-fidelity repair is saturated or genetically compromised. It matters clinically because tumours deficient in homologous recombination, such as BRCA-mutant cancers, lean on it to survive, which is why polymerase theta and PARP are drug targets there. Repair begins with limited end resection by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease complex together with CtIP, generating 3' single-stranded overhangs that are not licensed for recombination. PARP1 or PARP2 and DNA polymerase theta then align the two ends through short microhomologous tracts, POLQ extends by strand-displacement synthesis, FEN1 trims the displaced 5' flaps, and LIG3 with XRCC1 seals the remaining nicks. The outcome is invariably a deletion spanning the sequence between microhomologies, plus frequent base substitutions and occasional chromosomal translocations.

Metalloprotease DUBs are the zinc-dependent deubiquitinases of the JAMM/MPN+ family, which strip ubiquitin from substrates rather than adding it, and so decide whether a ubiquitin signal is read or erased. They matter at three junctions: PSMD14 in the proteasome lid removes chains from doomed substrates so they can be threaded into the proteolytic chamber, STAMBP and STAMBPL1 act with STAM on endosomes to recycle ubiquitin from receptors destined for lysosomal degradation, and BRCC3 within the BRCA1-A complex, with ABRAXAS1, BABAM1/2 and UIMC1, trims K63 chains on histone H2A to control how DNA double-strand break repair factors are retained at damage sites. MYSM1 similarly deubiquitinates H2A to permit transcription. Catalysis uses a zinc-activated water and a conserved glutamate acting as general base. BRCC3 also licenses NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and loss of these enzymes causes microcephaly-associated neurodegeneration and defective genome maintenance.

Zinc-dependent JAMM/MPN-domain deubiquitinases remove ubiquitin from substrates, and this metalloprotease branch of the DUB superfamily handles most of the K63-linked chains that act as signals rather than degradation marks. Their activity decides whether a ubiquitinated protein is degraded, sorted to lysosomes, or used to recruit repair factors. PSMD14 sits in the proteasome 19S lid and strips chains from substrates as they are unfolded and fed into the core, recycling free ubiquitin. BRCC3 works within the BRCA1-A complex with ABRAXAS1, BABAM1/2 and UIMC1 to trim K63 chains on damaged chromatin, tuning the DNA double-strand break response; the same enzyme also acts on NLRP3 during inflammasome activation. STAMBP and STAMBPL1 deubiquitinate cargo at endosomes alongside STAM during receptor sorting, while MYSM1 removes monoubiquitin from histone H2A to permit transcription. Catalysis uses a zinc-activated water and a conserved glutamate general base.

Homologous DNA Pairing and Strand Exchange is the search-and-invasion step of homologous recombination, the error-free route for repairing DNA double-strand breaks and collapsed replication forks using an intact sister chromatid as template. Cells that cannot execute it accumulate chromosomal rearrangements, and inherited loss of BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 predisposes to breast, ovarian and pancreatic cancer while also conferring the sensitivity to PARP inhibitors exploited therapeutically. Mechanistically, MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP, EXO1 and DNA2 resect break ends to 3' single-stranded overhangs coated by RPA; BRCA2 and PALB2 then load RAD51 in place of RPA, and the resulting nucleofilament, stabilised by RAD51B-RAD51C-RAD51D-XRCC2 and stimulated by RAD51AP1, invades homologous duplex DNA to form a D-loop. ATM, ATR-ATRIP, TOPBP1 and the 9-1-1 clamp couple the process to checkpoint signalling, while BLM-TOP3A-RMI resolves the joint molecules formed.

Repairing a DNA double-strand break by homologous recombination requires the broken end to find its intact sister chromatid, and homologous DNA pairing and strand exchange is the search-and-invasion step that makes this possible. Without it, breaks are repaired by error-prone routes or not at all, producing the chromosomal instability and cancer predisposition seen when BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 are lost; the same dependency underlies the sensitivity of such tumours to PARP inhibition. Resected 3' single-stranded overhangs, generated by MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP, EXO1 and DNA2, are first coated by RPA; BRCA2 with PALB2 then replaces RPA with RAD51, whose nucleofilament is stabilised by RAD51B-RAD51C-RAD51D-XRCC2 and stimulated by RAD51AP1. Invasion of the homologous duplex forms a D-loop, engaged further by RAD51C-XRCC3 and by BLM-TOP3A-RMI helicase-topoisomerase activity. ATM, ATR-ATRIP, TOPBP1 and checkpoint clamp components couple the process to cell cycle arrest.

Nucleotide Excision Repair removes bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions — UV photoproducts such as cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and 6-4 photoproducts, and chemical adducts from agents like benzopyrene and aflatoxin — restoring template integrity for replication and transcription. Loss of it causes xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sunlight sensitivity and skin cancer, as well as Cockayne syndrome and trichothiodystrophy. Two branches feed a common core: global genome repair, where XPC-RAD23 and the DDB1-DDB2 ubiquitin ligase scan the whole genome, and transcription-coupled repair, where an RNA polymerase II stalled at damage recruits ERCC6, ERCC8 and UVSSA. The TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3 open the duplex, XPA and RPA verify and orient it, and ERCC1-ERCC4 with ERCC5 excise the damaged oligonucleotide before PCNA, RFC and replicative polymerases resynthesise and ligases seal the gap. Ubiquitin, SUMO and chromatin remodelling regulate throughout.

Bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions such as UV photoproducts and chemical adducts from benzopyrene or aflatoxin are removed by nucleotide excision repair, which cuts out a short damage-containing oligonucleotide and resynthesises the gap. Loss of this capacity underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer, as well as Cockayne syndrome and trichothiodystrophy, linking repair failure directly to mutation rate and tumour risk. Two branches share most machinery: global genome repair surveys the whole genome using XPC with RAD23 partners and the DDB1-DDB2 damage sensor, while transcription-coupled repair is triggered when RNA polymerase II stalls at a lesion and engages ERCC6, ERCC8 and UVSSA. The TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3 open the duplex, ERCC5 and the ERCC1-ERCC4 nuclease incise, and replicative polymerases with PCNA, RPA and ligases restore the strand. Ubiquitin, SUMO and CUL4-based ligases regulate factor turnover throughout.

Dual Incision in GG-NER is the cutting step of global genome nucleotide excision repair, the pathway that removes bulky helix-distorting DNA lesions such as UV-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers from anywhere in the genome. Its loss underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition. After damage recognition by the DDB2-containing cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase and XPA, and unwinding by the TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3, the lesion sits in an open bubble stabilised by RPA. ERCC1-ERCC4 cuts 5' to the damage first, allowing repair synthesis to begin, and ERCC5 then cuts 3', releasing a 27-30 nucleotide fragment. Gap filling uses PCNA loaded by replication factor C together with polymerases delta, epsilon or kappa, coupling lesion removal directly to restoration of an intact duplex.

Global genome nucleotide excision repair removes bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as UV photoproducts and chemical adducts from anywhere in the genome, and the dual incision step is the committed cut that releases them. Once the damage-verification factors XPA, RPA and the TFIIH helicases ERCC2/ERCC3 have opened a bubble around the lesion, the ERCC1-ERCC4 endonuclease cuts 5' to the damage and ERCC5 cuts 3', excising a roughly 27-30 nucleotide fragment. The resulting gap is immediately filled, so replication factor C, PCNA and DNA polymerases delta, epsilon and kappa are recruited as part of the same transaction. Damage recognition by the DDB1-DDB2 complex with cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase components, plus PARP1/PARP2, marks lesions in chromatin for this processing. Loss of these incision activities underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition.

Post-translational protein modification covers the covalent changes that convert newly synthesised polypeptides into functional, correctly located and appropriately short-lived proteins. Without it secreted and membrane proteins cannot fold or reach the cell surface, signalling cannot be switched off, and damaged or surplus proteins accumulate; congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies, coagulation defects and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria all arise from failures within it. One branch builds sugar chains in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi — dolichol-linked N-glycan assembly and transfer, mucin-type O-glycosylation, O-mannosylation of dystroglycan, sialylation — alongside GPI anchor synthesis, vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, sulfatase formylglycine activation and secretory-pathway kinases. Another branch attaches ubiquitin, SUMO or NEDD8 through E1, E2 and cullin-RING enzymes, reversed by deubiquitinases, to control proteasomal degradation, DNA damage responses and transcription. Further arms handle prenylation of RAB GTPases, tubulin polyglutamylation, hypusination of eIF5A, and non-histone methylation.

Most proteins only become functional after translation, when enzymes attach sugars, lipids, small chemical groups or other proteins to specific residues. This broad programme of post-translational protein modification determines where a protein goes, how long it lasts and what it can do. N- and O-linked glycosylation and GPI anchoring, built through the ALG, PIG, GALNT and sialyltransferase enzymes, mark secreted and membrane proteins and support quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum; geranylgeranylation licenses RAB GTPases for vesicle traffic; vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation by GGCX activates clotting factors; sulfatases are switched on by formylglycine generation; and tubulin is tailored by polyglutamylation, tyrosination and detyrosination. A large ubiquitin, SUMO and NEDD8 arm, including cullin-RING ligases, deubiquitinases and the proteasome, sets protein stability and signalling output. Defects cause congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies, bleeding disorders, lysosomal storage disease and cancer.

Highly calcium permeable nicotinic acetylcholine receptors describes the subset of nicotinic receptor assemblies that admit substantial Ca2+ along with Na+ when acetylcholine or nicotine binds, converting a fast ionotropic signal into a second-messenger event. This matters because Ca2+ entry through these channels drives presynaptic neurotransmitter release, activates calcium-dependent kinases and gene transcription, and supports neuronal survival and plasticity; the same receptors mediate nicotine reinforcement and are implicated in addiction, and in epilepsy and cognitive decline. Permeability is set by subunit composition: homopentamers of the alpha7 type are the most Ca2+-permeable, while heteromeric combinations of alpha3 with beta2 or beta4 that incorporate the accessory alpha5 subunit come next, and alpha4/beta2 receptors carry less. The pathway thus links cholinergic transmission in brain and autonomic ganglia to calcium signalling rather than to depolarisation alone.

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are ligand-gated cation channels, and certain subunit combinations pass enough calcium that acetylcholine acts less like a simple depolarizing signal and more like a second-messenger trigger. This matters at presynaptic terminals, where calcium entry through these channels promotes release of glutamate, dopamine and other transmitters, and in neurons where it engages calcium-dependent kinases, gene expression and synaptic plasticity. Permeability is set by composition: homomeric alpha7 receptors are the most calcium-permeable, while heteromers built from alpha3 with beta2 or beta4 plus the accessory alpha5 subunit come next, with alpha5 variants altering calcium flux and desensitization. The subunits here also form the receptors of autonomic ganglia and the muscle endplate. Because this calcium signalling underlies nicotine reinforcement and neuronal survival, these channels are studied in addiction, cognitive decline and inflammatory regulation.

Interleukin-6 family signaling transmits a group of structurally related cytokines — IL6, IL11, LIF, oncostatin M, CNTF, cardiotrophins and IL31 — into changes in gene expression that shape inflammation, acute-phase protein production by the liver, haematopoiesis, neuronal survival, bone remodelling and metabolic control. Chronic output from this route drives rheumatoid arthritis, cytokine storm and tumour-promoting inflammation, which is why IL6 and its receptor are antibody drug targets. Each cytokine binds a private receptor chain but most converge on the shared transducer gp130 (IL6ST), alone or paired with LIFR or OSMR, while IL31 instead uses IL31RA. Receptor assembly activates associated JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT3 and STAT1 for nuclear translocation and target gene transcription. SOCS3, the phosphatase PTPN11 and CBL-mediated receptor turnover restrain the response. Soluble IL6R permits trans-signalling on cells lacking IL6R, redirecting IL6 from regenerative toward pro-inflammatory outcomes.

Cytokines of the interleukin-6 family drive inflammation, hepatic acute-phase protein production, hematopoiesis, neuronal and glial survival, metabolic control and, when chronic, tumour promotion and autoimmune tissue damage; blocking IL6 or its receptor is now standard therapy in rheumatoid arthritis and cytokine storm. The family is unified by the shared signal-transducing subunit gp130 (IL6ST), which pairs with ligand-specific chains such as IL6R, IL11RA, CNTFR, LIFR or OSMR to read out IL6, IL11, LIF, oncostatin M, CNTF, cardiotrophin and cardiotrophin-like cytokine; IL31 is the exception, signalling through IL31RA. Receptor assembly activates associated Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, TYK2), which phosphorylate STAT3 and STAT1 for dimerisation, nuclear entry and target gene transcription. Shed or spliced soluble IL6R permits trans-signalling on gp130-bearing cells that lack IL6R, biasing responses toward inflammation, while SOCS3, PTPN11 and CBL impose negative feedback.

GDP-fucose biosynthesis supplies the activated sugar donor that all fucosyltransferases require, and so determines whether a cell can fucosylate its glycoproteins and glycolipids at all. Fucose caps on glycans build selectin ligands for leukocyte rolling, ABO and Lewis blood group antigens, and the O-fucose modifications that tune Notch receptor responsiveness, so loss of donor supply produces immunodeficiency with recurrent infection and developmental defects, as in congenital disorders of glycosylation. Most GDP-fucose is made de novo from GDP-mannose by a dehydratase and a bifunctional epimerase/reductase; a smaller salvage route recovers free fucose taken up or released by lysosomal turnover through a kinase and a pyrophosphorylase, with a mutarotase feeding the correct anomer in. A dedicated Golgi transporter then delivers the nucleotide sugar to the lumenal compartment where glycan assembly occurs, linking cytosolic metabolism to secretory pathway modification.

Fucose attached to glycoproteins and glycolipids underlies selectin-mediated leukocyte rolling, Notch signalling, ABO/Lewis blood group antigens and much of glycan-based cell recognition, and every fucosyltransferase that installs it depends on the activated sugar donor made here. GDP-fucose biosynthesis proceeds by two routes: a dominant de novo pathway in which GMDS dehydrates and GFUS epimerises and reduces GDP-mannose, and a minor salvage route in which free fucose taken up or released by glycan turnover is phosphorylated by FCSK and adenylyl/guanylyl-transferred by FPGT, with FUOM handling fucose anomer interconversion. The product must then reach the Golgi lumen, which is the job of the transporter SLC35C1; its loss causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency II, with recurrent infection, impaired neutrophil recruitment and developmental delay. The pathway thus links central sugar nucleotide metabolism to immune trafficking and developmental signalling.

rRNA modification in the nucleus and cytosol installs the roughly 200 chemical marks that turn newly transcribed ribosomal RNA into a functional ribosome. The modified nucleotides cluster in the peptidyl transferase A and P sites, the polypeptide exit tunnel and the subunit interface, so their loss degrades translational accuracy and ribosome assembly; mutations in the machinery cause ribosomopathies such as dyskeratosis congenita and are exploited by proliferating tumour cells. Two guide-RNA-directed systems dominate: box H/ACA particles containing DKC1, GAR1, NHP2 and NOP10 convert uridine to pseudouridine, while box C/D particles built around fibrillarin, NOP56, NOP58 and SNU13 add 2'-O-methyl groups, each snoRNA base-pairing with pre-rRNA to select its target. Stand-alone enzymes contribute base methylation and acetylation, including BUD23, NOP2, DIMT1, TSR3 and NAT10. Much of this occurs within the nucleolar small-subunit processome, coupling modification to pre-rRNA cleavage and ribosome biogenesis.

Newly transcribed ribosomal RNA is chemically decorated at roughly 200 positions before it can work, and this nucleolar and cytoplasmic modification programme installs those marks. They cluster in the functional heart of the ribosome s dash the peptidyl transferase A and P sites, the polypeptide exit tunnel, and the subunit interface dash so their loss degrades translational accuracy and ribosome assembly rather than any single metabolic route. The two dominant marks are pseudouridine, made by box H/ACA particles built around the DKC1 pseudouridine synthase with GAR1, NHP2 and NOP10, and 2'-O-methylation by box C/D particles containing the fibrillarin methyltransferase with NOP56 and NOP58; guide snoRNAs base-pair with pre-rRNA to select each target nucleotide. Base methylations and acetylation are added by standalone enzymes such as BUD23, DIMT1, NOP2 and NAT10. Many components sit in the small subunit processome alongside UTP and WDR proteins, linking modification to cleavage; mutations cause dyskeratosis congenita and other ribosomopathies.

Neutrophil degranulation is the effector step of innate antimicrobial defence: activated neutrophils fuse their storage granules with the plasma or phagosomal membrane, discharging antimicrobial and proteolytic cargo onto microbes and simultaneously delivering new receptors to the cell surface. It underlies bacterial and fungal killing at inflammatory sites, and its dysregulation drives tissue injury in sepsis, ARDS and chronic inflammatory disease, while loss of granule proteins or trafficking components causes congenital neutropenia and specific granule deficiency. The cargo spans azurophil enzymes such as myeloperoxidase, elanase, proteinase 3 and defensins, secondary and gelatinase granule proteins including lactoferrin, lipocalin-2 and MMP8/MMP9, and lysosomal hydrolases. Their release depends on Rab GTPases, SNAP/VAMP fusion machinery, RAB27A-UNC13D-dependent exocytosis and cytoskeletal remodelling. Mobilised membrane proteins such as integrins, Fc and formyl-peptide receptors and the NADPH oxidase subunits then reprogramme how the cell senses and responds to its environment.

Neutrophils are the most abundant circulating leukocytes and the first responders to bacterial and fungal infection; degranulation is how they deliver their arsenal, fusing preformed granules with the plasma or phagosomal membrane to release antimicrobial and proteolytic cargo and to display new receptors at the cell surface. Azurophil granules supply myeloperoxidase, elastase, cathepsin G, proteinase 3, azurocidin, defensins and bactericidal permeability-increasing protein; specific and gelatinase granules contribute lactoferrin, lipocalin-2, matrix metalloproteinases and components of the NADPH oxidase, while secretory vesicles bring integrins, complement and Fc receptors, formyl-peptide receptors and adhesion molecules that retune the cell to its surroundings. Rab GTPases, SNAREs and Munc13-4 with cytoskeletal and motor components drive the trafficking step. Excessive release damages host tissue in sepsis, vasculitis and chronic inflammatory lung disease, whereas defective granule biogenesis or oxidase assembly causes recurrent infection.

Antimicrobial peptides is the innate chemical defence that epithelia, neutrophils and secretions use to kill bacteria, fungi and enveloped viruses directly, without waiting for adaptive immunity. It keeps skin, gut, airway and reproductive surfaces colonised but not invaded, and its failure underlies conditions such as atopic dermatitis, Crohn's-like Paneth cell deficiency and recurrent skin infection. Most members are small cationic amphipathic peptides — alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin, histatins, dermcidin, RNase family peptides — that bind anionic microbial membranes electrostatically and disrupt the bilayer. Several are made as inactive precursors and require proteolysis by neutrophil serine proteases such as elastase, cathepsin G and proteinase 3 to become active. A second arm is nutritional immunity: calprotectin (S100A8/A9), lactoferrin, lipocalin-2 and copper transporters withhold or weaponise zinc, iron and copper at inflamed sites. Many of these peptides also act as chemoattractants, recruiting leukocytes and shaping the ensuing inflammatory response.

Antimicrobial peptides are the chemical arm of innate host defence at epithelial surfaces and inside phagocytes, killing bacteria, fungi and enveloped viruses directly and shaping the inflammatory response that follows. Most are small cationic amphipathic molecules "" defensins, cathelicidin, histatins, hepcidin-like LEAP2 "" that bind anionic microbial membranes electrostatically, insert into the bilayer and permeabilise it; others act enzymatically, as with lysozyme cleaving peptidoglycan, or by sequestering nutrients, as lactoferrin, lipocalin-2 and the calprotectin subunits S100A8/A9 starve microbes of iron, zinc and manganese while copper handling by ATP7A and ATOX1 supports metal-based killing in phagosomes. Several precursors, including dermcidin in sweat and cathelicidin, require proteolytic processing by neutrophil serine proteases or kallikreins to become active. Beyond direct lysis, these peptides recruit and modulate neutrophils, monocytes and T cells through chemokine receptors and Toll-like receptor engagement. Deficient or dysregulated production underlies skin infection, periodontal disease and altered gut barrier immunity.

TP53 Regulates Transcription of Genes Involved in G2 Cell Cycle Arrest describes how the p53 tumour suppressor halts cells at the G2/M boundary after genotoxic stress, buying time for DNA repair before mitosis and preventing damaged chromosomes from being segregated. Loss of this arm of the p53 response permits mitotic entry with unrepaired lesions, driving aneuploidy and tumorigenesis. p53 works in two directions: it activates GADD45A, with help from the acetyltransferase EP300 and the arginine methyltransferases PRMT1 and CARM1, and GADD45A then inhibits Aurora kinase A; and it induces SFN (14-3-3-sigma), aided by the target ZNF385A, which sequesters the CDK1-cyclin B1 complex outside the nucleus. In parallel, p53 acting with the repressor E2F4 and its DP and retinoblastoma-family partners shuts down CDC25C transcription, removing the phosphatase needed to activate CDK1. SFN additionally restrains BAX, coupling arrest to apoptosis avoidance.

When DNA damage is detected in the second gap phase, cells must hold off mitosis until repair is finished, and p53-driven transcription is one route to that arrest. The tumour suppressor switches on GADD45A and SFN (14-3-3-sigma) while shutting down CDC25C, the phosphatase that would otherwise dephosphorylate and activate the CDK1-cyclin B1 complex driving entry into mitosis. GADD45A binds and inhibits Aurora kinase A; SFN sequesters CDK1-cyclin B1 in the cytoplasm, and because it also binds BAX it can restrain apoptosis at the same time. Induction of GADD45A depends on coactivators and chromatin modifiers including EP300 and the arginine methyltransferases PRMT1 and CARM1, while repression of CDC25C involves E2F4 with pocket proteins RBL1/RBL2 and DP partners. Loss of this checkpoint permits division with unrepaired lesions, producing the aneuploidy and genomic instability typical of p53-mutant cancers.

Regulation of TP53 Degradation sets how much p53 protein a cell keeps, and therefore whether damaged or oncogene-stressed cells arrest, senesce or die. In unstressed cells p53 is held at low levels by continuous ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover, so that growth is not needlessly restrained; loss of this restraint is embryonic lethal, while its excess is a common route to tumours that retain wild-type p53. The E3 ligase MDM2, itself a p53 target gene, forms the core negative feedback loop and works with its partner MDM4, both also subject to auto- and cross-ubiquitination. Kinase inputs tune the loop: AKT and SGK1 downstream of mTORC2 promote MDM2 nuclear entry, CDK1/CDK2 and PP2A adjust its affinity, and ATM with CHEK2 uncouple MDM2 from p53 after double-strand breaks. ARF sequesters MDM2 during oncogenic stress, and USP2 and USP7 reverse ubiquitination.

The tumour suppressor p53 is kept at low levels in healthy, unstressed cells, and controlling its turnover is what allows the protein to be silent normally yet surge within minutes of damage. The E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2, itself induced by p53, ubiquitinates p53 for proteasomal destruction and acts with its partner MDM4 (MDMX) as a heterodimer; both ligases also ubiquitinate each other and themselves. Growth signalling through mTORC2, PDPK1, AKT and SGK1 promotes nuclear entry of MDM2, while CDK1/CDK2 phosphorylation weakens its grip on p53. DNA double-strand breaks activate ATM and CHEK2, which phosphorylate p53 to block MDM2 binding and mark MDM4 for degradation, stabilising p53. Counterweights include a PP2A complex recruited by cyclin G1, the deubiquitinases USP2 and USP7, and p14-ARF, which sequesters MDM2 under oncogenic stress. Loss of this balance underlies MDM2-amplified and ARF-deleted cancers with intact p53.

Regulation of TP53 Activity through Acetylation controls how strongly the p53 tumour suppressor turns on its target genes, and which of them it chooses. Acetylation is the switch that converts a stabilised p53 protein into an active transcription factor, so this layer of control decides whether a damaged cell arrests, dies, or shifts its metabolism, and its loss lets tumours tolerate p53 that is present but inert. EP300 acetylates lysine 382 with help from BRD7, enhancing promoter binding at CDKN1A, MDM2 and TIGAR; KAT6A acting with PML modifies the same residue plus lysine 120 in the DNA-binding domain, where MYST-family marks bias the arrest-versus-apoptosis decision. The NuRD complex, recruited through MTA2 and carrying HDAC1/2, reverses these marks and dampens p53 output. Acetylation in the DNA-binding domain also uncouples transactivation from repression and feeds into reactive oxygen species control and ferroptosis.

Whether p53 arrests a damaged cell or kills it depends heavily on which of its lysines are acetylated, and this is the branch of p53 regulation that sets that choice. Acetylation in the DNA-binding domain and at the C-terminal K382 strengthens promoter occupancy and drives targets such as the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A, the MDM2 feedback loop, and genes governing energy metabolism, reactive oxygen species and ferroptosis. EP300 acts with the bromodomain protein BRD7, while the MYST-family acetyltransferase KAT6A works together with PML and BRPF/ING/MEAF6 scaffolding subunits. The opposing reaction comes from the NuRD chromatin remodelling complex — CHD3/CHD4, MTA2, MBD3, RBBP4/7 and HDAC1/2 — which deacetylates p53 and damps its output. Loss of this tuning blunts tumour suppression after genotoxic stress.

Regulation of TP53 Activity through Methylation tunes the tumour suppressor p53 after it has been stabilised, deciding which of its target programmes -- cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, or none -- actually gets transcribed. This is a layer of control that determines whether a cell damaged by genotoxic stress pauses, dies, or continues dividing with mutations, and its subversion contributes to tumours that retain wild-type p53. Lysine and arginine methyltransferases write opposing marks on the p53 C-terminal regulatory region: SETD9 methylation at K372 stabilises and activates it, PRMT5 acting in an ATM-activated complex with TTC5, JMY and p300 biases output toward arrest genes, while SMYD2, the EHMT1-EHMT2 complex and KMT5A-directed recruitment of the chromatin compaction factor L3MBTL1 silence transcription. These marks interact with the parallel MDM2- and MDM4-driven ubiquitination route that controls p53 abundance, integrating damage signalling from ATM and CHEK2 into a graded response.

The tumour suppressor p53 decides whether a damaged cell arrests, repairs itself or dies, and methylation of its own lysine and arginine residues is one of the switches that sets which target genes it turns on. Because the marks can either stabilise and activate p53 or silence it, this layer of control helps determine whether DNA damage produces cell cycle arrest or is tolerated, and its subversion favours tumour growth. After ATM and CHEK2 sense damage, PRMT5 is recruited with TTC5, JMY and the acetyltransferase EP300 and methylates arginines that bias p53 toward arrest genes, while SETD9 methylation of K372 raises p53 stability and activity. Opposing marks placed by SMYD2 and by the EHMT1-EHMT2 complex repress transcription, and KMT5A-generated monomethylation recruits the chromatin compaction factor L3MBTL1. Ubiquitin and the MDM2-MDM4 axis link these marks to p53 turnover.

Keratinization is the differentiation programme that turns a living keratinocyte into the tough, dead, water-impermeable corneocyte of skin, hair, nail and other stratified epithelia. It builds the barrier that keeps water in and microbes and allergens out; its failure produces ichthyoses, palmoplantar keratodermas, epidermolysis bullosa simplex, monilethrix and hair-shaft defects, and Netherton syndrome. Type I and type II keratins pair as obligate heterodimers into 10 nm intermediate filaments whose bundles anchor at desmosomes through desmogleins, desmocollins, plakophilins, plakoglobin and desmoplakin, giving epithelial sheets mechanical continuity. In the granular layer, filaggrin, involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins and late cornified envelope proteins are cross-linked by transglutaminases beneath the plasma membrane, while kallikrein proteases restrained by SPINK inhibitors, plus caspase-14 and calpain, execute cornification and controlled desquamation. Hair-specific keratins and keratin-associated proteins form the disulfide-rich hair shaft.

Keratinization is the terminal differentiation programme that converts a living keratinocyte into a flattened, cross-linked corneocyte, giving skin, hair, nails and other stratified epithelia their mechanical strength and barrier function. Type I and type II keratins pair as heteropolymeric intermediate filaments that bundle into tonofilaments and anchor at desmosomes through desmogleins, desmocollins, plakophilins, plakoglobin, desmoplakin and the plakin family, distributing tension across the tissue. In the upper layers, filaggrin and trichohyalin aggregate filaments, while involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope proteins are cross-linked by transglutaminases into the cornified envelope; hair keratin-associated proteins supply the disulfide-rich matrix of the hair shaft. Kallikrein proteases, balanced by SPINK and cystatin inhibitors, and caspase-14 govern desquamation and filaggrin processing. Mutations in these components cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex, palmoplantar keratodermas, ichthyoses, Netherton syndrome, monilethrix and pemphigus-related blistering.

Negative regulation of MET activity is the brake on signalling by the hepatocyte growth factor receptor, terminating the proliferative, motility and survival programme that MET otherwise drives in epithelial cells. Its loss underlies sustained MET signalling in invasive carcinomas, and mutations that uncouple MET from these controls are transforming. Two mechanisms dominate. Phosphatases strip activating phosphates: PTPRJ removes the Y1349 docking site needed for GAB1 recruitment, while PTPN1 and PTPN2 dephosphorylate the kinase activation loop to blunt catalytic output. In parallel, the E3 ligase CBL, recruited with GRB2 and CIN85, ubiquitinates activated MET at the membrane or in early endosomes, committing it to ESCRT-dependent sorting through HGS, STAM and USP8 and lysosomal destruction; endophilins and EPS15 supply the endocytic step. LRIG1 drives degradation of unstimulated receptor, setting basal MET levels independently of ligand.

The HGF receptor MET drives proliferation, motility and epithelial morphogenesis, so signalling through it must be terminated once the ligand has been sensed; negative regulation of MET activity is how the cell sets the duration and amplitude of that response, and its loss underlies the sustained MET signalling seen in invasive and metastatic carcinomas. Two mechanisms dominate. Tyrosine phosphatases strip activating phosphates: PTPRJ acts on the site that docks the GAB1 adaptor, while PTPN1 and PTPN2 dephosphorylate the kinase activation loop to blunt catalytic output. In parallel, the E3 ubiquitin ligase CBL, recruited with GRB2 and SH3KBP1, ubiquitinates activated MET and commits it to clathrin- and endosome-dependent trafficking, with EPS15, endophilins, and the HGS-STAM sorting complex delivering it to lysosomal degradation; USP8 deubiquitination counterbalances this, and LRIG1 promotes turnover of unstimulated receptor.

Zymostenol biosynthesis via lathosterol (Kandutsch-Russell pathway) is one of the two alternative routes by which post-squalene intermediates are converted to cholesterol, and the one that predominates in skin. It differs from its counterpart only in timing: the side-chain double bond is reduced first, by DHCR24, so all subsequent steps proceed on saturated sterols. From there the standard sequence follows — CYP51A1 demethylation at C14, TM7SF2 reduction of the resulting Δ9(11) bond, and the MSMO1/NSDHL/HSD17B7 triad that removes the two C4 methyl groups — yielding zymostenol and then lathosterol. Because this branch generates 7-dehydrocholesterol in keratinocytes, it supplies the substrate for UV-driven vitamin D3 formation. Flux through both routes is set transcriptionally by SREBF1 and SREBF2 in response to sterol depletion, tying the pathway to membrane lipid homeostasis; loss of its enzymes causes skeletal and skin malformation syndromes.

Cholesterol can be built along two routes that differ only in when the side-chain double bond is reduced; the Kandutsch-Russell route reduces it first, so the sterol intermediates are saturated and pass through zymostenol and lathosterol rather than desmosterol. This branch predominates in skin, where it feeds 7-dehydrocholesterol, the precursor that ultraviolet light converts into vitamin D, and it supplies membrane cholesterol and the raw material for steroid and bile acid synthesis generally. The early reduction is carried out by DHCR24, after which the shared post-squalene enzymes act on the saturated series: CYP51A1 removes the C14 methyl, TM7SF2 reduces the resulting double bond, and MSMO1, NSDHL and HSD17B7 together strip the two C4 methyl groups. Output is set transcriptionally by the sterol-responsive regulators SREBF1 and SREBF2, and defects in these steps cause congenital skin and skeletal disorders.

Formation of the cornified envelope is the terminal differentiation programme by which epidermal keratinocytes convert themselves into flattened, dead corneocytes, building the water-impermeable, mechanically tough outer barrier of skin, hair and oral epithelium. Loss of it causes ichthyosis, peeling skin and Netherton syndrome, and leaves the body vulnerable to dehydration, infection and allergen entry. Transglutaminases crosslink loricrin, involucrin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope proteins into a rigid submembranous shell, to which keratin filaments and ceramide lipids are covalently anchored; filaggrin and trichohyalin aggregate the keratin cytoskeleton. Desmosomal cadherins, plakins and plakophilins are crosslinked into corneodesmosomes that glue cornified cells together, while kallikrein and other proteases, restrained by SPINK inhibitors, later dissolve those junctions for orderly desquamation. Caspase-14 and calpain drive the accompanying organelle and nuclear breakdown, a specialised, calcium-gradient-controlled form of programmed cell death.

The outermost skin barrier is built by a specialized form of programmed cell death in which upper-epidermal keratinocytes convert themselves into flattened corneocytes. Formation of the cornified envelope creates a heavily crosslinked protein shell coated with covalently bound lipids, giving the stratum corneum its rigidity and its resistance to water loss and microbial entry. Transglutaminases crosslink loricrin, involucrin, small proline-rich proteins and late cornified envelope proteins into that shell, while keratin filaments and filaggrin or trichohyalin aggregates fill the cell interior and anchor to it. Desmosomal cadherins, plakins and corneodesmosin are incorporated to hold cornified cells together, and kallikrein-family proteases balanced by SPINK inhibitors later dissolve those junctions to allow orderly shedding. Loss of individual components causes ichthyosis, palmoplantar keratoderma, Netherton syndrome and hair or nail defects, and barrier failure predisposes to atopic disease.

COPI-dependent Golgi-to-ER retrograde traffic is the return arm of the early secretory pathway, recycling membrane, cargo receptors and escaped resident proteins from the cis-Golgi back to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment and the ER. Without it the ER loses its chaperones and lipid and protein balance across the two organelles collapses, disrupting secretion and quality control. Vesicle formation begins with the ARF1 activator GBF1, which recruits the seven-subunit COPI coat; ARFGAP proteins and p24/TMED cargo receptors shape the coat and select cargo, while KDEL receptors capture escaped chaperones such as BiP for return. Carriers move along microtubules using kinesin motors and tubulin tracks, then are captured at the ER by the NRZ tethering complex (NBAS, RINT1, ZW10) working with ER SNAREs STX18, USE1, BNIP1 and SEC22B, with NSF and SNAPs recycling the fusion machinery. Rab1 GTPases coordinate tethering and fusion.

Secretory traffic leaks: ER residents such as chaperones escape forward to the Golgi, and the machinery that carries them back is COPI-dependent Golgi-to-ER retrograde transport. By recovering escaped proteins and recycling the membrane, receptors and SNAREs consumed by anterograde flow, it keeps the ER competent for folding and quality control and maintains the compartmental identity of the early secretory pathway. KDEL receptors capture the escaped chaperones at the cis-Golgi and concentrate them into vesicles whose coat is the heptameric COPI complex, recruited by ARF GTPases activated by GBF1 and disassembled with help from ARFGAP proteins; p24/TMED components and cargo receptors such as SURF4 contribute to sorting. Motor and microtubule components move the carriers, which are captured at the ER by the NRZ tethering complex with ZW10, RINT1 and NBAS acting alongside ER SNAREs STX18, USE1, BNIP1 and SEC22B, with NSF and SNAPs recycling the fusion machinery.

Assembly of the ORC complex at the origin of replication is the licensing step that marks where DNA replication will begin, and it determines that each origin fires once and only once per cell cycle. Without it cells cannot load the replicative helicase, and hypomorphic subunit mutations cause Meier-Gorlin syndrome with dwarfism and microcephaly. ORC1 acts first, recognising G-rich, largely nucleosome-free origin DNA near transcription start sites and reading the H4K20me2 mark on flanking nucleosomes; it then nucleates assembly by joining a preformed ORC2-ORC3-ORC5-ORC4 module, remodelling an autoinhibitory ORC2 winged-helix domain that otherwise blocks the central DNA channel, with ORC6 added last and loosely. Importin-mediated nuclear import brings subunits and histones to chromatin. ORC1 is degraded on S-phase entry, coupling origin choice to once-per-cycle control upstream of pre-replication complex formation.

Every round of DNA replication begins by marking where it will start, and the origin recognition complex is what does the marking. Loading ORC onto chromatin licenses origins for later firing, so that each stretch of the genome is copied once and only once; defects in its subunits cause the dwarfism and microcephaly of Meier-Gorlin syndrome, reflecting how tightly growth depends on faithful origin licensing. Assembly is ordered: an ORC2-ORC3 heterodimer recruits ORC5 and ORC4, ORC1 joins to relieve an autoinhibited conformation that otherwise blocks the DNA-binding channel, and ORC6 attaches weakly. ORC1 binds origin DNA on its own, favouring G-rich and guanine-quadruplex-forming sequences near transcription start sites, and reads neighbouring nucleosomes carrying dimethylated histone H4 lysine 20. Importins carry subunits into the nucleus, and ORC1 degradation at S phase entry prevents relicensing.

CDC6 association with the ORC:origin complex is the first committed step in licensing a replication origin: CDC6 loads onto the origin recognition complex bound at chromatin, creating the platform onto which MCM helicases are later deposited to form the pre-replicative complex. Without this step no origin can fire, and cells fail to duplicate their genome; conversely, unrestrained CDC6 loading permits re-licensing within a single cycle, causing re-replication, amplification and genomic instability of the kind seen in tumours. CDC6 acts as an AAA+ ATPase switch, working with the six-subunit ORC ring to sense and clamp origin DNA, with MCM8 among the helicase-family partners recruited. Cell cycle control is enforced on CDC6 itself, through E2F-driven expression in G1 and phosphorylation-triggered nuclear exclusion and ubiquitin-mediated degradation once S phase begins, restricting replication to once per division.

Loading of CDC6 onto origin-bound ORC is the licensing step that makes a replication origin competent to fire, and it is where the cell enforces the rule that each stretch of DNA replicates only once per cycle. The six-subunit origin recognition complex marks origins in chromatin; CDC6, an AAA+ ATPase related to the ORC subunits, joins it in late M and G1 to create the platform that subsequently recruits CDT1 and the MCM2-7 helicase, with ATP binding and hydrolysis acting as the switch that commits helicase loading. CDC6 abundance is set by E2F-driven transcription in G1 and curtailed after S-phase entry through phosphorylation, nuclear exclusion and ubiquitin-mediated degradation, so that reloading cannot occur. Loss of this control permits re-replication and gene amplification, linking origin licensing to genome stability and to proliferative control in cancer.

Assembly of the pre-replicative complex is the licensing step that marks replication origins for a single round of DNA synthesis, and it determines that each chromosome is copied exactly once per cell cycle. Loss of this control produces re-replication, amplification and genome instability, while insufficient licensing blocks S phase entry entirely. From late mitosis through G1, the origin recognition complex binds chromatin and, with CDC6 and CDT1, loads the MCM2-7 helicase as an inactive double hexamer around DNA. Timing is imposed from outside: the anaphase-promoting complex with its activator FZR1 and the ubiquitin-proteasome system degrade licensing inhibitors and the components themselves, geminin sequesters CDT1 after firing, and importins deliver factors into the nucleus. Nucleosome components reflect the chromatin context in which origins are selected, linking histone deposition to where replication begins.

Before a cell can replicate its DNA, every origin must be licensed exactly once, and assembly of the pre-replicative complex is that licensing step. It runs from late mitosis through G1, when the origin recognition complex (ORC1-6) marks chromosomal origins and CDC6 with CDT1 loads the MCM2-7 helicase as an inactive double hexamer; only at the G1/S transition is that helicase activated to unwind DNA. Restricting licensing to a window when CDK activity is low is what prevents re-replication, and loss of the restriction produces polyploidy and genome instability; germline ORC and CDT1 defects cause Meier-Gorlin syndrome. The controls are largely degradative and inhibitory: the anaphase-promoting complex with its activator FZR1, ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes and the 26S proteasome clear geminin and mitotic cyclins to open the window, while geminin itself sequesters CDT1 once S phase begins. Importin-mediated nuclear import and chromatin context complete the setting.

DNA replication initiation is the step that gets DNA synthesis started, solving the problem that no DNA polymerase can begin a chain from scratch. Every chromosome duplication in every dividing cell depends on it, and defects in these polymerases cause replication stress, genome instability, and developmental syndromes such as microcephalic primordial dwarfism. The primase subunits PRIM1 and PRIM2, held in complex with the POLA1 catalytic subunit and its POLA2 partner, lay down a short RNA primer and extend it with a stretch of DNA, creating a substrate that processive polymerases can take over. DNA polymerase epsilon, with its POLE2, POLE3 and POLE4 accessory subunits, then elongates the leading strand. The same priming activity is reused repeatedly on the lagging strand, linking initiation to Okazaki fragment synthesis and to S-phase progression.

Every new DNA strand has to be started, and DNA polymerases cannot begin one on bare template. Initiation of DNA replication solves this by laying down a short RNA primer that can then be extended, a step required at each origin and at the start of every Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand. The polymerase alpha-primase complex does both jobs: the primase subunits synthesize a few nucleotides of RNA, and the associated catalytic and accessory polymerase alpha subunits extend it with a short stretch of DNA before handover to a processive replicase. The polymerase epsilon subunits here carry out leading-strand synthesis once initiation has occurred. Because priming licenses S-phase DNA synthesis, defects in these subunits impair replication fidelity and proliferation, and mutations in them are linked to hypermutated tumours and developmental growth disorders.

Removal of the Flap Intermediate is the step in lagging-strand DNA replication that gets rid of the RNA-DNA initiator segment left by primase, so that adjacent Okazaki fragments can be joined into a continuous daughter strand. Without it, replication leaves nicks and unligated flaps that become double-strand breaks, and cells accumulate the genome instability and repeat-expansion mutations associated with loss of flap endonuclease activity. Strand-displacement synthesis by DNA polymerase delta, held on the template by the PCNA clamp, peels the primer made by DNA polymerase alpha-primase into a single-stranded flap. Short flaps are clipped directly by FEN1; longer ones become coated by replication protein A, which blocks FEN1 and instead recruits the DNA2 nuclease/helicase to trim the flap to a size FEN1 can finish. The nicked product is then sealed by ligase, completing Okazaki fragment maturation.

During lagging-strand replication, each Okazaki fragment begins as an RNA-DNA primer laid down by pol alpha-primase, and that primer must be displaced and cut away before the fragments can be joined into continuous DNA. Removal of the flap intermediate is that cutting step: strand-displacement synthesis by DNA polymerase delta on a PCNA-loaded primer-template generates a single-stranded 5' flap, which is trimmed by flap endonuclease 1 when short, or shortened first by the DNA2 nuclease/helicase when the flap grows long enough to be coated by replication protein A. RPA binding is what dictates the handoff between the two nucleases. Efficient flap processing keeps replication from leaving unligatable nicks and single-stranded gaps, so defects here feed genome instability, repeat expansion and replication-associated DNA damage; the same nucleases also serve long-patch base excision repair.

DNA strand elongation is the synthetic phase of genome duplication: the moving replication fork where template strands are unwound and copied, producing the two daughter genomes that mitosis will separate. Its fidelity determines whether cells inherit an intact genome, and stalling or collapse here is a principal source of the replication stress and chromosomal instability that drive cancer. Because polymerases work in one direction only on an antiparallel duplex, one strand is copied continuously and the other in short pieces. The MCM helicase with CDC45 and the GINS complex opens the duplex, RPA coats the exposed single strands, and primase-polymerase alpha lays down primers that RFC-loaded PCNA hands to polymerase delta for processive extension. Okazaki fragments are then matured by flap removal through FEN1 and DNA2 and sealed by ligase I.

Once a replication fork is established, the genome is copied by DNA strand elongation, the synthesis phase that must duplicate every base accurately and at speed before mitosis. Because the duplex is antiparallel and polymerases work in one direction only, the leading strand is extended continuously while the lagging strand is built as short fragments that are later joined. The machinery here covers each step: the MCM helicase with CDC45 and the GINS subunits unwinds the parental duplex, single-stranded DNA is protected by the RPA heterotrimer, primase lays RNA primers extended by polymerase alpha, and clamp loader RFC installs PCNA to make polymerase delta processive. Flap endonuclease FEN1 with the DNA2 nuclease/helicase trims displaced primer flaps and LIG1 seals the nicks. Errors or stalling here generate fork collapse, replication stress and the genome instability underlying cancer predisposition.

G1 Phase is the interval in which a cell decides whether to divide, and the point at which growth signals are converted into an irreversible commitment to replicate DNA. Its failure is the most common route into cancer: loss of the retinoblastoma protein or of the INK4 inhibitors, or amplification of D-type cyclins, removes the restriction point altogether. Mechanistically, cyclin D partners with CDK4 and CDK6 to begin phosphorylating Rb and its relatives p107 and p130, releasing E2F-DP heterodimers to transactivate the genes needed for S phase, including cyclin E. Cyclin E-CDK2 then completes Rb inactivation in a feedback loop. The pathway is tuned by CIP/KIP proteins p21, p27 and p57, by CDK-activating kinase and PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation, and by SKP1-CUL1-SKP2 ubiquitin ligase activity that degrades inhibitors once the decision is made.

G1 phase is the interval in which a cell decides whether to commit to another division, and this decision point is where growth signals, nutrient status and damage checks are integrated before DNA replication becomes irreversible. D-type cyclins partnered with CDK4 and CDK6, and later cyclin E with CDK2, progressively phosphorylate the retinoblastoma protein and its relatives p107 and p130, releasing E2F-DP transcription factor complexes to switch on the genes needed for S phase entry. Opposing this are the INK4 family inhibitors and the Cip/Kip proteins p21, p27 and p57, whose degradation through SKP1-CUL1-SKP2 ubiquitin ligase activity, together with CDK-activating kinase and phosphatase input, sets the timing of the transition. Loss of this restraint, by p16 deletion, cyclin D amplification or RB1 mutation, is among the most common events in human cancer.

Synthesis of DNA is the duplication of the genome during S phase, the step that gives each daughter cell a complete and accurate copy of its chromosomes. Its control determines whether cells proliferate on schedule or accumulate the re-replication and replication stress that drive genome instability and cancer. Origins licensed in late M and G1 by the origin recognition complex, CDC6 and CDT1 are loaded with MCM2-7 helicase, which CDC45 and the GINS proteins activate; primase and DNA polymerase alpha lay down primers, and polymerases delta and epsilon extend them with PCNA and the clamp loader RFC, while RPA coats single strands and FEN1 with DNA ligase I finish Okazaki fragment maturation. Cyclin E- and A-CDK2 activity, geminin, and ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis through SCF and the anaphase-promoting complex restrict firing to one round per cycle.

Duplication of the genome in S phase is what this pathway accomplishes: origins licensed in late mitosis and G1 are fired once, and once only, to copy every chromosome before division. Origin recognition complex proteins load CDC6 and CDT1, which deposit the MCM2-7 helicase; CDK2 paired with cyclin E and then cyclin A, together with CDC45 and the GINS tetramer, converts these into active replisomes. Primase and DNA polymerase alpha lay down primers, RFC loads the PCNA clamp for processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon, and FEN1 with LIG1 matures Okazaki fragments while RPA coats exposed single strands. Re-replication is prevented by geminin and by ubiquitin-proteasome destruction of licensing factors through SCF-SKP2 and the anaphase-promoting complex. Loss of this control produces endoreduplication, replication stress and the genome instability that underlies tumour development.

Cell Cycle, Mitotic is the complete program by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, the basis of tissue growth, renewal and development; its deregulation is the defining feature of cancer and its errors generate aneuploidy. Progression is timed by cyclin-dependent kinases paired with D, E, A and B cyclins, restrained by CDK inhibitors and the RB-E2F and DREAM transcriptional switches that decide whether a quiescent cell re-enters division. Downstream steps are represented in depth: licensing of origins by ORC, CDC6 and CDT1, MCM helicase loading and replisome-driven synthesis in S phase, WEE1/CDC25 control of CDK1 at G2/M, centrosome maturation and gamma-tubulin-nucleated spindle assembly, kinetochore and cohesin function under spindle checkpoint surveillance, nuclear envelope breakdown and reformation, and APC/C-driven ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of securin and cyclin B that triggers anaphase and cytokinesis.

The mitotic cell cycle is the ordered programme by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, passing through G1, S, G2 and M with quiescence as an alternative exit. Its fidelity determines tissue growth and renewal, and its deregulation through cyclin, CDK inhibitor and retinoblastoma-pathway lesions is a hallmark of cancer. Cyclin-dependent kinases paired with D, E, A and B cyclins drive the transitions, restrained by CDK inhibitors, WEE1 and phosphatases and reset by ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis through SCF and the anaphase-promoting complex with the proteasome. Origin licensing on ORC and MCM proteins commits cells to replication; centrosome maturation, gamma-tubulin nucleation, kinetochore assembly, cohesin and condensin, spindle checkpoint surveillance, nuclear envelope and Golgi breakdown, and ESCRT-dependent abscission complete division.</description>}

DNA Replication is the duplication of the genome that must happen once, and only once, before every cell division; its fidelity and its licensing controls are what keep cells from accumulating mutations or amplifying chromosome segments. Origin recognition complex subunits, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase onto origins, and CDK2- and CDC7/DBF4-dependent phosphorylation converts these licensed origins into active replisomes containing CDC45 and GINS. Elongation then requires RPA on single-stranded DNA, primase and polymerase alpha for priming, polymerases delta and epsilon with PCNA and the clamp loader RFC, and FEN1, DNA2 and ligase I for maturation of nascent strands. Re-replication is prevented by geminin and by ubiquitin-proteasome and APC/C-mediated destruction of licensing factors, tying replication directly to cell cycle progression; mitochondrial polymerase gamma and its accessory factors duplicate mtDNA in parallel.

Duplicating the genome once, and only once, per cell cycle is the task of DNA replication, and the fidelity of this process determines whether daughter cells inherit an intact genome or accumulate the mutations and rearrangements that drive cancer. Origin recognition complex subunits mark start sites, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase, and CDC7-DBF4 together with CDK2-cyclin E/A activate it; GINS and CDC45 convert it into the active replisome. Priming by DNA polymerase alpha-primase gives way to processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon on RPA-coated template, with PCNA and the clamp loader RFC coordinating elongation and FEN1, DNA2 and LIG1 finishing lagging-strand joins. Licensing is restricted to one round by geminin inhibition of CDT1 and by ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis through SCF and anaphase-promoting complex activity, while histones supply chromatin for the new strands. Mitochondrial polymerase gamma and TWNK extend the same logic to mitochondrial DNA.

Ubiquitin-Mediated Degradation of Phosphorylated Cdc25A removes the phosphatase that switches on CDK2, and so enforces the G1/S checkpoint after DNA damage or replication stress. CDC25A normally strips inhibitory phosphates from CDK2 to license S-phase entry; destroying it keeps CDK2 phosphorylated on Tyr15 and halts the cell cycle until damage is resolved. Failure of this route allows replication to proceed on a damaged template, and CDC25A stabilisation is oncogenic. Mechanistically, checkpoint kinases CHEK1 and CHEK2, together with GSK3B, PLK3 and stress-activated p38 kinases, prime CDC25A; NEK11 or casein kinase I then completes a phosphodegron recognised by the SCF complex through the F-box proteins BTRC or FBXW11, with CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1 building the ligase. Polyubiquitinated CDC25A is then destroyed by the 26S proteasome, linking damage sensing to proteolytic control of cell cycle progression.

CDC25A is the phosphatase that removes inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation from CDK2 to let cells enter S phase, and destroying it is how the DNA damage checkpoint imposes a G1/S arrest. When replication stress, ionizing radiation or UV activates CHEK1 and CHEK2, they phosphorylate CDC25A; priming phosphorylation by GSK3B, PLK3 or p38 kinases is followed by casein kinase I and NEK11 to complete a phosphodegron recognised by the beta-TrCP subunit of an SCF cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase built on CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1. Polyubiquitinated CDC25A is then dismantled by the 26S proteasome, whose core and regulatory subunits make up most of this route. Loss of this control lets cells replicate damaged DNA; CDC25A stabilisation or overexpression bypasses the arrest and is associated with genomic instability and tumour progression. The same degradation also operates in unstressed cycling and differentiating cells.

Glycolysis is the cytosolic route that breaks glucose 6-phosphate down to pyruvate, yielding ATP and NADH without any need for oxygen. It is the universal core of energy metabolism: red blood cells and other cells lacking mitochondria depend on it entirely, proliferating and tumour cells lean on it for biosynthetic carbon, and inherited defects in pyruvate kinase or phosphofructokinase cause haemolytic anaemia and exercise intolerance. Hexokinases and glucokinase trap glucose, phosphofructokinase-1 commits it in the pathway's irreversible flux-setting step, and aldolase, GAPDH, enolase and pyruvate kinase complete the split and payoff phases. Control is layered on top: PFKFB bifunctional kinases set fructose 2,6-bisphosphate levels, glucokinase regulatory protein sequesters GCK in the hepatocyte nucleus, and PKA and protein phosphatase 2A tune enzyme activity to hormonal state. Downstream, pyruvate feeds mitochondrial oxidation or lactate production.
