Glycolysis is the cytosolic route that breaks glucose 6-phosphate down to pyruvate, yielding ATP and NADH without oxygen and feeding carbon to mitochondrial oxidation, lactate production, or biosynthesis. It is the sole ATP source for erythrocytes and a dominant one in proliferating and tumour cells; inherited defects in pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase or triosephosphate isomerase cause haemolytic anaemia and exercise intolerance. Hexokinases and glucokinase commit glucose, phosphofructokinase-1 catalyses the irreversible control step, and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, phosphoglycerate kinase, enolase and pyruvate kinase complete the payoff phase, with several steps represented by tissue-specific isoforms. Flux is set by allosteric and hormonal control: the bifunctional PFKFB kinase/phosphatases govern fructose 2,6-bisphosphate levels, while PKA phosphorylation and protein phosphatase 2A subunits tune the enzymes, and glucokinase regulatory protein sequesters glucokinase. Nucleoporins and nuclear transport components appear alongside, reflecting regulated shuttling of these factors.

Glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) mobilises stored glucose, supplying muscle with fuel during contraction and liver with glucose for export to maintain blood sugar between meals. The chemistry is identical in all tissues but the isozymes differ, so liver and muscle glycogen serve different physiological ends: PYGL output feeds glucose release into the circulation, while PYGM output stays in the myocyte as glucose 6-phosphate for glycolysis. Phosphorylase clips glucose 1-phosphate from branch ends and is switched on by phosphorylase kinase, a calmodulin-containing complex of PHKA/PHKB/PHKG subunits that links hormonal and calcium signals to fuel release; debranching enzyme handles the residual four-residue stubs, and phosphoglucomutase converts the product to glucose 6-phosphate. A parallel lysosomal route uses acid alpha-glucosidase. Loss of individual steps causes the glycogen storage diseases, with hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly or exercise intolerance depending on the isozyme affected.

Glycogen is the cell's rapidly mobilizable glucose store, and glycogenolysis is how it is released: in liver to maintain blood glucose between meals, in muscle to fuel contraction locally. The chemistry is the same everywhere but the control is not, with tissue-restricted phosphorylase isoforms (liver PYGL, muscle PYGM, brain PYGB) and distinct phosphorylase kinase subunits linking hormonal and calcium signals, through calmodulin as the kinase's delta subunit, to distinct physiological outcomes. Phosphorylase cleaves glucose 1-phosphate from branch ends, the bifunctional debranching enzyme clears the last residues of each branch releasing one free glucose, and phosphoglucomutase converts glucose 1-phosphate to glucose 6-phosphate for glycolysis or export. A parallel lysosomal route degrades glycogen via acid alpha-glucosidase. Defects cause glycogen storage diseases, including Pompe, Cori and McArdle disease, with hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly or exercise intolerance.

Urea cycle is the liver's route for disposing of excess nitrogen, converting ammonia into urea for excretion in urine while also generating arginine. It is what keeps blood ammonia low, and inherited defects in any step cause hyperammonemia with encephalopathy, the classic urea cycle disorders presenting in neonates. The cycle spans two compartments: mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I condenses ammonia and bicarbonate, ornithine transcarbamylase makes citrulline, and dedicated ornithine/citrulline carriers of the inner membrane shuttle intermediates to the cytosol, where argininosuccinate synthase and lyase and finally arginase release urea and regenerate ornithine. Flux is set by N-acetylglutamate, an allosteric activator of the first enzyme whose synthesis rises with arginine, so abundant free amino acids drive their own nitrogen disposal. Acetylation control by SIRT5 adds a further layer, linking ureagenesis to fasting and dietary protein load.

Excess nitrogen from amino acid breakdown is toxic as ammonia, and the urea cycle is how the liver converts it into urea for renal excretion while regenerating arginine. Four core reactions span two compartments: mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I condenses ammonia and bicarbonate, ornithine transcarbamylase joins the product to ornithine to give citrulline, and cytosolic argininosuccinate synthase and lyase then build and cleave argininosuccinate to release arginine and fumarate, linking the cycle to the TCA cycle. Arginase completes the turn, yielding urea and ornithine, which is returned to the matrix by mitochondrial ornithine carriers. Flux is set allosterically by N-acetylglutamate, whose synthesis rises with arginine, so abundant amino acids accelerate ureagenesis; deacetylation by SIRT5 tunes carbamoyl phosphate synthetase activity. Inherited deficiency of any step causes hyperammonemia with encephalopathy, the classic urea cycle disorders.

mRNA 3'-end processing completes every protein-coding transcript: an extended primary RNA is cleaved at a site downstream of the stop codon and the upstream fragment receives a poly(A) tail of roughly 250 residues, giving the mRNA the stability, export competence and translational efficiency it needs in the cytoplasm. The cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor complex recognises the polyadenylation signal, CstF binds downstream sequences, symplekin scaffolds the machinery, and poly(A) polymerase with PABPN1 builds the tail; the downstream product is degraded by XRN2, which also drives transcription termination. Coupling to the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, to spliceosomal and hnRNP/SR factors, and to the TREX export complex explains why cleavage, last-intron splicing, termination and export are mutually dependent. Choice among alternative polyadenylation sites reshapes 3' UTRs and their regulation; major histone mRNAs are cleaved without polyadenylation.

Nearly every eukaryotic mRNA acquires its 3' end not by the polymerase stopping cleanly but by endonucleolytic cleavage of a longer transcript followed by addition of a poly(A) tail, and this processing determines transcript stability, export competence and translatability as well as which of several alternative last exons a gene uses. Recognition of the polyadenylation signal by the CPSF complex, with CPSF3 as the nuclease, is coordinated with downstream element binding by CSTF subunits, symplekin scaffolding, poly(A) polymerase and the nuclear poly(A)-binding protein that sets tail length. Coupling to the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, to spliceosomal snRNP and SR/hnRNP proteins, and to the exon junction and TREX export machinery ties 3'-end formation to splicing and mRNA release, while PCF11 and the XRN2 exonuclease drive transcription termination. Misregulated site choice shortens 3' UTRs and removes microRNA control in cancer.

tRNA processing turns raw polymerase transcripts into the mature, decoding-competent tRNAs that every ribosome depends on, in both the nucleus and the mitochondrial matrix. Precursors carry 5' leaders, 3' trailers and sometimes introns; RNase P (the RNA-based nuclear enzyme and the wholly proteinaceous mitochondrial PRORP/TRMT10C complex) removes the leader, ELAC2 trims the trailer, the TSEN endonuclease and RTCB-containing ligase excise and rejoin exons, and TRNT1 adds the untemplated CCA that permits aminoacylation. Dozens of enzymes then install methyl, pseudouridine, thiol, queuosine, wybutosine and threonylcarbamoyl marks, many at the anticodon, tuning decoding accuracy and speed. Nucleoporins and exportin XPOT with RAN move tRNAs between compartments, including retrograde return to the nucleus for quality control. Defects cause mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, microcephaly, pontocerebellar hypoplasia, sideroblastic anemia and altered type 2 diabetes risk, reflecting how tightly translational fidelity constrains tissue function.

Newly transcribed tRNAs are not usable until their ends are trimmed, introns removed, a CCA tail added, and dozens of nucleotides chemically modified; tRNA processing carries out that maturation for both nuclear and mitochondrially encoded tRNAs and so sets the fidelity and capacity of translation. RNase P complexes remove 5' leaders, ELAC2 or its mitochondrial counterpart cuts 3' trailers, the TSEN endonuclease and RTCB-containing ligase handle intron removal, and TRNT1 adds the untemplated CCA end. A large family of methyltransferases, pseudouridine synthases, deaminases, thiolases and queuosine or wybutosine enzymes then decorates the anticodon loop and body, tuning codon reading. Nucleoporins and exportin-t move tRNAs between nucleus and cytosol. Defects cause microcephaly, intellectual disability, anaemia and mitochondrial encephalomyopathy.

rRNA processing converts the long precursor transcripts of ribosomal RNA into the mature 18S, 5.8S and 28S species of the cytosolic ribosome, and the 12S and 16S species of the mitochondrial ribosome, so that ribosomal proteins can be assembled into functional subunits. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on protein synthesis and growth, this is one of the most energy-consuming activities of a proliferating cell, and its disruption triggers nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation; inherited defects cause ribosomopathies such as dyskeratosis congenita and Diamond-Blackfan anaemia. Work proceeds in the nucleolus through ordered endonucleolytic and exonucleolytic cleavages by the exosome, XRN2 and NOB1, guided assembly of small nucleolar ribonucleoproteins containing fibrillarin or dyskerin that direct 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation, and a large cohort of UTP and WD-repeat processome factors, with final maturation steps completed in the cytoplasm.

Ribosomes are built from rRNA that must be carved out of long precursor transcripts, chemically modified, and folded together with ribosomal proteins before a subunit can translate anything. In the nucleolus, a single 47S precursor is trimmed by endonucleases and exonucleases into the 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNAs, with snoRNP-guided pseudouridylation and 2'-O-methylation plus base methylation and acetylation installed as cleavage proceeds. Large assemblies of processing factors, RNA helicases and the exosome complex act on the precursor, while the ribosomal proteins of the 40S and 60S subunits join and final maturation steps occur in the cytoplasm. A parallel set of enzymes processes and modifies the 12S and 16S rRNAs cut from mitochondrial polycistronic transcripts, supporting mitochondrial translation. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on cell growth, defects in these factors cause ribosomopathies such as bone marrow failure and craniofacial syndromes, and the pathway is heavily exploited by proliferating tumour cells.

Formation of the ternary complex, and subsequently, the 43S complex is the first committed step of cap-dependent translation initiation, the point at which a cell decides how much protein it will make. Initiator methionyl-tRNA is loaded onto GTP-bound eIF2 to form the ternary complex, which then docks with the 40S small ribosomal subunit already carrying the multisubunit eIF3 scaffold and eIF1A, producing the 43S preinitiation complex that goes on to scan mRNA for the start codon. Because eIF2's alpha subunit is the substrate of stress-activated kinases, this step is the main throttle on global protein synthesis during amino acid deprivation, ER stress, heme deficiency and viral infection, and its regulation drives the integrated stress response. The ribosomal small subunit proteins listed here supply the platform on which assembly occurs.

Every round of cap-dependent translation begins by loading an initiator methionyl-tRNA onto the small ribosomal subunit, and this is the step that does it. The GTP-bound trimeric factor eIF2, made of its alpha, beta and gamma subunits, captures Met-tRNAi to form the ternary complex; that complex then joins a 40S subunit already carrying the multisubunit eIF3 scaffold and eIF1A, producing the 43S preinitiation complex that will later engage mRNA and scan for the start codon. Because eIF2 activity is the target of the integrated stress response, phosphorylation of its alpha subunit shuts ternary complex formation down and globally suppresses protein synthesis during amino acid deprivation, ER stress or viral infection. The abundant small-subunit ribosomal proteins listed here supply the 40S platform, and defects in them cause ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

GTP hydrolysis and joining of the 60S ribosomal subunit is the final commitment step of translation initiation, the point at which a scanning 43S complex parked on a start codon becomes an elongation-competent 80S ribosome. Everything a cell makes as protein depends on this handoff, and its regulation sets global protein synthesis rates during growth, stress and differentiation. Once the initiator methionyl-tRNA base-pairs with AUG, eIF5 triggers hydrolysis of eIF2-bound GTP, releasing phosphate and destabilising the initiation factors; eIF5B then catalyses docking of the large subunit and, on hydrolysing its own GTP, departs. The genes reflect this composite event: the eIF2 trimer and the multisubunit eIF3 scaffold, cap-binding and helicase components of eIF4F, and the full complement of 40S and 60S ribosomal proteins. Mutations in these ribosomal proteins underlie ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

This is the final step of translation initiation, the point at which a scanning 43S complex that has found its start codon is converted into an elongation-competent 80S ribosome. Once the initiator methionyl-tRNA is base-paired with AUG in the P site, eIF5 triggers hydrolysis of GTP bound to the eIF2 trimer, committing the site selection and releasing eIF2 and the other initiation factors, including the multisubunit eIF3 scaffold and the cap-binding eIF4F group. eIF5B then promotes joining of the 60S subunit and, after hydrolysing its own GTP, leaves the assembled ribosome. Because every protein made in the cytoplasm passes through this handover, it sets the rate of protein synthesis and growth; it is the step suppressed when eIF2 is phosphorylated during the integrated stress response, and mutations in the large and small subunit proteins involved cause ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

Translation is the decoding of mRNA into protein, the step at which genetic information becomes the working machinery of the cell, and it consumes a large share of cellular energy and biosynthetic capacity. Cytosolic ribosomal subunits, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and initiation, elongation and release factors carry out initiation at the start codon, cyclic peptide-bond formation, and stop-codon-triggered release and recycling; cap-binding and eIF2 regulation make this the main point at which growth signals and stress restrain protein output. Included are the co-translational branches: signal recognition particle capture of secretory and membrane proteins for insertion through the ER translocon and cleavage by signal peptidase, and a separate mitochondrial system in which bacterial-like mitoribosomes synthesise the thirteen respiratory chain subunits encoded by mtDNA. Quality-control components resolve stalled ribosomes and degrade aberrant nascent chains. Defects cause ribosomopathies, anaemias and mitochondrial disease.

Translation is the step where genetic information becomes protein, and this collection covers the whole of it: cytosolic initiation, elongation and termination, aminoacylation of tRNAs, co-translational targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum, and the separate translation system inside mitochondria. Cytosolic ribosomal subunits work with cap-binding and scaffolding initiation factors, the eIF2 complex and its guanine nucleotide exchange factor eIF2B, elongation factors eEF1A and eEF2, and release factor eRF1 with ABCE1 for recycling. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases exist as distinct cytosolic and mitochondrial enzymes, and mutations in either class cause neuropathies and mitochondrial disease. Signal recognition particle, its ER receptor, the Sec61 translocon and signal peptidase route secretory and membrane proteins into the ER. Mitoribosomal proteins, formylmethionine-tRNA machinery, TUFM and OXA1L build the thirteen hydrophobic respiratory chain subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Quality control components resolve stalled ribosomes and degrade aberrant nascent chains through ubiquitination and the proteasome.

Base Excision Repair removes and replaces individual damaged bases, and is the main defence against the most common forms of DNA damage a cell sustains: oxidised, deaminated and alkylated bases produced by mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, ionising radiation, lipid peroxidation and inflammatory oxidants. Loss of its components drives mutation accumulation and cancer predisposition, as with MUTYH-associated polyposis. A family of glycosylases each recognising particular lesions — OGG1, UNG, NTHL1, the NEIL enzymes, TDG, MPG — cleaves the glycosidic bond to leave an abasic site, which APEX1 incises. Repair then proceeds either as single-nucleotide replacement by polymerase beta with XRCC1 and LIG3, or as longer-patch synthesis using PCNA, replicative polymerases, RFC and FEN1. PARP1/PARP2 signal strand breaks and recruit repair factors, and end-processing by PNKP prepares ligatable termini. Repair also operates on damage arising in chromatin and at telomeres.

Base excision repair handles the most common everyday damage to DNA ": oxidized, deaminated and alkylated bases produced by mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, ionizing radiation, lipid peroxidation and inflammatory oxidants. Without it, mutation rates rise and lesions such as 8-oxoguanine are mispaired during replication; loss of MUTYH predisposes to colorectal adenomatous polyposis, and the route is also how uracil and thymine glycol are cleared from the genome. Repair begins with one of several damage-specific glycosylases ": UNG, OGG1, NTHL1, SMUG1, TDG, MPG and the NEIL enzymes ": which cleave the glycosidic bond and leave an abasic site. APEX1 and PNKP process the resulting ends, then either POLB with XRCC1 and LIG3 fills a single nucleotide, or PCNA, RFC, replicative polymerases, FEN1 and LIG1 replace a longer patch. PARP1 and PARP2 signal the strand break and recruit the scaffold, and chromatin and telomere-binding proteins set the context in which this repair occurs.

Chromosome Maintenance covers the specialised chromatin structures that keep linear chromosomes stable and functional across divisions: the centromere, which directs kinetochore assembly and accurate segregation, and the telomere, which caps chromosome ends so they are not read as broken DNA. Loss of either causes aneuploidy, end-to-end fusions, or replicative senescence, and mutations in these components underlie telomere biology disorders such as dyskeratosis congenita and premature ageing syndromes. Centromere identity is epigenetic rather than sequence-encoded: HJURP and the MIS18 complex deposit the histone H3 variant CENP-A outside S phase, seeding the constitutive centromere-associated network. At telomeres, shelterin proteins including TRF1, TRF2 and POT1 protect the repeat tract, telomerase with its dyskerin-containing RNP extends it, and the CST complex together with lagging-strand replication and helicase activities completes end processing.

Chromosome maintenance covers the two places on a chromosome that cannot be copied by ordinary replication alone: the centromere and the telomere. Both must be rebuilt every cycle or chromosomes missegregate and ends fuse or erode, outcomes that underlie aneuploidy, premature ageing syndromes and the immortalisation of tumour cells. At centromeres, replication-independent deposition of the histone H3 variant CENP-A by its chaperone HJURP, with the MIS18 complex and ATRX/DAXX-type remodellers, marks the site epigenetically and nucleates the constitutive centromere-associated network that builds the kinetochore. At telomeres, the shelterin proteins TRF1, TRF2, POT1, TPP1 and TIN2 cap the repeat tract and license the telomerase holoenzyme, whose RNA-binding partners include dyskerin, NOP10, NHP2 and GAR1; CST components plus lagging-strand polymerases, RPA, RFC-PCNA and helicases such as WRN and BLM finish the C-strand and resolve G-quadruplexes.

DNA Repair is the collective machinery that keeps the genome intact against damage from radiation, reactive metabolites, chemical adducts and errors of replication. Its failure drives mutation accumulation, cellular senescence and cancer, and inherited defects in its components underlie Fanconi anemia, xeroderma pigmentosum, ataxia-telangiectasia and Lynch syndrome; because dividing cells have little time to repair, the same machinery determines the response to DNA-damaging chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors. The genes span all the major routes: glycosylases and APEX1 with POLB and XRCC1-LIG3 in base excision repair, MSH2/MLH1/PMS2 mismatch correction of nascent strands, XPC-DDB2 and the TFIIH helicases in nucleotide excision repair, direct reversal by MGMT and ALKBH enzymes, FANC proteins unhooking interstrand crosslinks, translesion polymerases that permit damage bypass, and BRCA1/BRCA2-RAD51 recombination versus DNA-PK-mediated end joining at double-strand breaks. Overlaid are ATM/ATR checkpoint signalling, ubiquitin, SUMO and PARP marks, chromatin remodelling, and p53-directed arrest or apoptosis.

Genomes are damaged continuously by radiation, reactive metabolites, spontaneous base loss and replication errors, and DNA repair is the collection of enzyme systems that finds and mends those lesions so that genetic information is passed on intact. Its failure underlies cancer predisposition and premature ageing syndromes, and inherited defects in its components cause Fanconi anemia, xeroderma pigmentosum, Lynch syndrome and ataxia telangiectasia; its inhibition is also the basis of many chemotherapies. Distinct routes handle distinct damage: glycosylases such as OGG1 and UNG initiate base excision repair, XPC and the ERCC helicases excise bulky helix-distorting adducts, MSH2-MLH1 complexes correct replication mismatches, MGMT and AlkB-family enzymes reverse alkylation directly, BRCA1/2 with RAD51 drive homologous recombination while Ku and LIG4 mediate end joining, and FANC proteins unhook interstrand crosslinks. Damage sensing by ATM, ATR and TP53, ubiquitin and SUMO signalling on chromatin, and translesion polymerases coordinate repair with replication, checkpoints and apoptosis.

Depyrimidination is the first committed step of base excision repair for damaged pyrimidines: a lesion-specific DNA glycosylase cuts the glycosidic bond between an altered base and its deoxyribose, releasing the free base and leaving an abasic site for downstream AP endonuclease, polymerase and ligase action. This is how cells erase uracil from cytosine deamination or misincorporated dUTP, thymine glycol and other oxidised pyrimidines, and T:G mismatches at methylated CpGs; failure raises mutation rates and, in the case of MBD4 and TDG, disturbs epigenetic demethylation and predisposes to cancer. UNG, SMUG1, TDG, MBD4, NTHL1 and the NEIL enzymes each cover distinct lesion spectra. The reaction occurs on chromatin, so core histones frame the substrate, while shelterin components including TRF1, TRF2, POT1 and TIN2 mark telomeric DNA as a repair context requiring special handling.

The first step of base excision repair when the damaged base is a pyrimidine: a lesion-specific DNA glycosylase cuts the N-glycosidic bond linking the altered base to deoxyribose, releasing the free base and leaving an abasic site for downstream AP endonuclease, polymerase and ligase action. This depyrimidination step is how cells erase deaminated cytosine (uracil), thymine glycol, hydroxymethyl- and formyl-pyrimidines and mismatched thymine arising from spontaneous hydrolysis, oxidation and alkylation, preventing the mutations that would otherwise accumulate at every cell division. Uracil-directed glycosylases such as UNG, SMUG1, TDG and MBD4 act alongside the oxidative-damage enzymes NTHL1 and the NEIL family, while OGG1 overlaps with purine lesions. Histone components place the chemistry in chromatin, and the telomeric shelterin proteins mark telomeres as a site where such repair is specially controlled. Loss of these activities drives base substitution signatures and cancer predisposition.

Base-Excision Repair, AP Site Formation is the opening step of the repair route that removes small, non-bulky base damage from DNA: a glycosylase recognises an aberrant base, cleaves the bond linking it to deoxyribose, and leaves behind an abasic (AP) site that downstream incision, gap-filling and ligation steps resolve. This is how cells cope with the constant chemical erosion of their genome by oxidation, alkylation, deamination and spontaneous base loss, and losing it raises mutation rates; inherited MUTYH defects, for example, cause adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer, while UNG and TDG activities also serve programmed processes such as antibody diversification and DNA demethylation. Distinct glycosylases cover distinct lesions, from oxidised purines handled by OGG1 and the NEIL enzymes to uracil, thymine mismatches and alkylated bases. Damage recognition occurs in chromatin, and the accompanying histones and telomere-capping proteins mark where this scanning takes place and where it must be restrained.

Every day cells sustain thousands of small base lesions — oxidised guanine, deaminated cytosine, alkylated purines, uracil misincorporated during replication — and base excision repair removes them before they become mutations. The first step is the recognition and excision of the damaged base itself, generating the abasic (AP) site that downstream nucleases, polymerases and ligases then resolve. Dedicated DNA glycosylases each police a lesion class: UNG and SMUG1 remove uracil, TDG and MBD4 act on deaminated bases at CpG sites, MPG on alkylated purines, OGG1, NTHL1 and the NEIL enzymes on oxidised bases, and MUTYH excises adenine mispaired with 8-oxoguanine, a defence whose loss causes adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer. Repair occurs in chromatin, so histones are intrinsic to the substrate, and shelterin components including TERF1, TERF2, POT1 and TINF2 govern how this chemistry proceeds at telomeres.

RNA Polymerase III Transcription Termination is the final step in making the short, abundant non-coding RNAs that sustain protein synthesis and RNA processing — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and RNase P RNA. Ending each round cleanly matters because polymerase III transcribes very short genes at high rates; failure to release transcript and DNA would trap the enzyme and starve the cell of translational capacity. Termination is directed by a simple cis signal, a run of thymidines on the non-template strand, which destabilises the elongation complex without dedicated release factors, and the polymerase's own subunits, including POLR3A, POLR3B and the shared core shared with polymerases I and II, determine termination efficiency and recycling into reinitiation. The released transcript is bound by La protein (SSB), which protects the nascent 3' oligo(U) end and channels it into maturation.

RNA polymerase III makes the small structural RNAs a cell needs in bulk tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others and this step ends each round of synthesis, freeing the transcript and the DNA template so the enzyme can recycle onto a new gene. Termination is driven almost entirely by the polymerase itself: a run of thymidines on the non-template strand is enough to destabilise the elongation complex, without the dedicated release factors or extensive cis-elements that other polymerases require. The seventeen-subunit enzyme is represented here in full, including subunits shared with polymerases I and II and the alternative catalytic-region paralogues POLR3G and POLR3GL. Released nascent transcripts bearing 3' oligo-U are captured by the La protein SSB, which protects them from exonucleolytic trimming and guides folding and maturation. Output from this machinery sets the ceiling on translational capacity and cell growth.

Ketone body metabolism is the fasting fuel switch: the liver converts surplus acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation into water-soluble acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, exports them, and extrahepatic tissues burn them for energy. This spares glucose during prolonged fasting, exercise, or ketogenic diets and keeps the brain, which cannot oxidize fatty acids, supplied when carbohydrate is scarce. Synthesis runs through mitochondrial HMGCS2 and HMGCL, with BDH1 setting the acetoacetate/beta-hydroxybutyrate ratio according to mitochondrial redox state; acetone arises by spontaneous decarboxylation. Utilization requires OXCT1 (SCOT) and ACAT1 to regenerate acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle, and because liver lacks SCOT the hepatic route is effectively one-way. Cytosolic AACS and ACSS3 route ketone carbon into lipid synthesis instead. Inherited defects in these steps cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia or ketoacidotic crises, and uncontrolled flux underlies diabetic ketoacidosis.

During fasting, the liver converts fat-derived acetyl-CoA into water-soluble fuels that can circulate and spare glucose, and ketone body metabolism covers both their synthesis and their oxidation elsewhere. Hepatic mitochondria condense acetyl-CoA through a thiolase and the rate-setting HMG-CoA synthase HMGCS2, then HMGCL cleaves HMG-CoA to acetoacetate, which BDH1 reduces to beta-hydroxybutyrate; acetone arises by spontaneous decarboxylation. Because liver lacks the CoA transferase OXCT1, synthesis is effectively one-way, and the exported ketones are taken up by brain, heart and skeletal muscle, where OXCT1 and thiolase regenerate acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle. Cytosolic AACS instead activates acetoacetate for lipid synthesis. This fuel switch sustains the brain during starvation and on ketogenic diets; inherited defects in the synthesizing or utilizing enzymes cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia or recurrent ketoacidotic crises, and uncontrolled flux underlies diabetic ketoacidosis.

IRS activation is the first committed step downstream of the insulin receptor, converting hormone binding into a phosphotyrosine platform that the rest of insulin signalling docks onto. It is what allows insulin to lower blood glucose by driving glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid synthesis, and growth-promoting gene expression; loss or chronic inhibitory phosphorylation of IRS1 and IRS2 is a molecular basis of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, and IRS2 failure in particular compromises pancreatic beta cell mass. Mechanistically, insulin-bound receptor autophosphorylates, and IRS1 engages the juxtamembrane phosphotyrosine through its PTB domain while its PH domain grips membrane phospholipids. The receptor kinase then phosphorylates multiple IRS tyrosines, releasing the scaffold to recruit PI3K and Grb2-SOS and thereby branch into AKT and MAP kinase cascades. GRB10 binds the activated receptor as a negative regulator, tuning signal output.

Insulin's message gets past the receptor only through a docking protein, and IRS activation is that step: the activated insulin receptor recruits IRS1 or IRS2 and phosphorylates them on multiple tyrosines, converting them into membrane-associated scaffolds that assemble downstream effectors. This is what couples insulin binding to PI3K-dependent glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis, and to the Ras-MAP kinase arm controlling growth and gene expression. IRS1 engages the receptor's juxtamembrane phosphotyrosine through its PTB domain, with its PH domain anchoring it to membrane phospholipids, then releases once phosphorylated so that SH2-containing partners can bind. GRB10 competes at the receptor and dampens the output, one of several brakes on the pathway. Loss or serine-phosphorylation-driven inactivation of IRS proteins underlies insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, making this node the main site where metabolic signalling is tuned.

Signal attenuation is the shut-off phase of insulin action, the step that makes the hormonal signal transient and proportional to circulating insulin rather than self-sustaining. After the insulin receptor and its ligand are internalised, insulin is degraded in the endosomal lumen and endosome-associated protein tyrosine phosphatases dephosphorylate the receptor and its docking substrates, so that IRS1 and IRS2, SHC1, GRB2-SOS1 and the downstream ERK module can no longer be recruited and the assembled signalling complexes collapse. Adaptors such as GRB10 contribute by dampening receptor output. Termination matters because sustained receptor phosphorylation would uncouple glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid synthesis, and growth signalling from feeding; conversely, excessive or premature attenuation through phosphatase and adaptor activity contributes to insulin resistance. The pathway therefore sets signal duration and sensitivity in metabolic tissues and links receptor trafficking to endocrine control.

Insulin signalling must be switched off as well as on, and signal attenuation is the step that returns a stimulated cell to baseline after an insulin pulse. Once ligand and receptor dissociate inside the endosome and insulin is degraded in the endosomal lumen, endosome-associated protein tyrosine phosphatases strip phosphate from the activated insulin receptor and from its docking substrates. Dephosphorylation of IRS1 and IRS2 releases the adaptors and exchange factors they recruit — GRB2, SHC1 and SOS1 — so the complexes that feed the ERK arm through MAPK1 and MAPK3 fall apart, and the adaptor GRB10 contributes further negative regulation of the receptor. Loss of this shutdown leaves growth and metabolic signalling running without a hormonal cue, while excessive attenuation blunts insulin action and contributes to insulin resistance, making it part of how glucose homeostasis is kept responsive.

RNA Polymerase III Abortive And Retractive Initiation describes the false starts that precede productive synthesis of tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA and other short non-coding transcripts. Before Pol III commits to elongation it repeatedly makes and releases short oligonucleotides, and can retract the nascent RNA back into the active site, a proofreading-like cycle that sets how efficiently the polymerase clears its promoter and therefore how much translational and splicing capacity a cell builds. The machinery is the full Pol III enzyme with its shared and specific subunits, loaded by TFIIIB (TBP with BRF1 or BRF2 and BDP1), the six-subunit TFIIIC that reads internal A- and B-box promoters, TFIIIA for 5S genes, and the SNAPc complex with ZNF143 and POU2F1 at type 3 external promoters; La protein binds the released transcripts. Deregulated Pol III output accompanies growth signalling and oncogenic transformation.

RNA polymerase III makes the small structural RNAs a cell needs constantly — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others — so the rate at which it commits to productive synthesis sets the ceiling on protein synthesis and ribosome production. This step describes what happens immediately after the enzyme opens promoter DNA: the polymerase repeatedly synthesises and releases very short oligonucleotides, and can retract the nascent transcript, before it escapes the promoter and elongates processively. Promoter recognition upstream of this depends on distinct assembly factors for the different promoter classes — the multisubunit TFIIIC complex with TFIIIA at 5S genes, TBP-associated BRF1 and BDP1 at tRNA genes, and BRF2 with the SNAPc complex and ZNF143 at U6-type type 3 promoters. The La protein binds the uridylate-rich 3' ends of the released products. Deregulated Pol III output accompanies oncogenic growth, and mutations in its subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy.

mRNA Editing: A to I Conversion is the most common form of RNA editing in humans, in which adenosine deaminases acting on RNA convert adenosine to inosine within double-stranded regions of pre-mRNA. Because the ribosome and spliceosome read inosine as guanosine, editing recodes codons, alters splice sites, and diversifies the proteome beyond what the genome encodes. It is most active in brain, where recoding of the GluA2 AMPA receptor subunit at the Q/R site makes the receptor impermeable to calcium and protects neurons from excitotoxicity, and where editing of the 5-HT2C serotonin receptor tunes G-protein coupling. ADAR and ADARB1 carry out this chemistry through paired double-stranded RNA-binding domains and a catalytic deaminase domain, with duplex structure formed by intronic complementary sequences specifying which adenosines are targeted. Editing of endogenous duplexes also marks them as self, restraining innate immune sensing of cellular RNA.

Adenosine-to-inosine conversion is the most common form of RNA editing in humans, rewriting transcripts after they are made so that a single gene can yield proteins of different function. Because the ribosome reads inosine as guanosine, editing within coding sequence changes amino acids: the best-known case recodes a glutamine to arginine in the GluA2 AMPA receptor subunit, making the assembled receptor impermeable to calcium and protecting neurons from excitotoxic damage. Editing of serotonin 5-HT2C receptor transcripts similarly tunes G-protein coupling efficiency. The reaction is carried out by double-stranded RNA-specific adenosine deaminases, ADAR and ADARB1, which recognise duplex structure in pre-mRNA formed with complementary intronic sequence rather than a linear consensus. Activity is highest in brain, and beyond recoding, widespread editing of repetitive duplexes marks transcripts as self and restrains innate immune sensing of endogenous RNA.

TRAIL signaling is an extrinsic apoptosis route in which the TNF-family ligand TRAIL kills target cells by engaging death receptors on their surface. It matters because it preferentially destroys transformed and virus-infected cells while sparing most normal tissue, making it an arm of immune surveillance by NK cells and cytotoxic lymphocytes and a long-standing target for cancer therapeutics. Ligand binding clusters TNFRSF10A and TNFRSF10B, whose cytoplasmic death domains recruit the adaptor FADD and procaspase-8 and -10 into a death-inducing signalling complex; local dimerisation activates the initiator caspases, which then cleave effector caspases or BID to amplify the signal through mitochondria. Sensitivity is set by competing components: cFLIP occupies the complex without catalytic activity, and decoy receptors such as TNFRSF10D bind ligand without transmitting death, mechanisms tumours exploit to acquire resistance.

TRAIL signalling is one of the extrinsic routes to apoptosis, in which a TNF-family ligand kills a target cell from outside by engaging death receptors on its surface. It contributes to immune surveillance of tumour and virus-infected cells, and its selectivity for transformed cells over normal ones has made the pathway a template for cancer therapeutics. Ligand binding to the death receptors TRAIL-R1 and TRAIL-R2 clusters their cytoplasmic death domains, which recruit the adaptor FADD and, through it, procaspase-8 and procaspase-10 into a death-inducing signalling complex where the initiator caspases dimerise and self-cleave. The catalytically inactive homologue CFLAR competes for the same platform and blocks caspase activation, and a receptor lacking a functional death domain further buffers the response. Resistance at these checkpoints determines whether cells survive TRAIL exposure.

TNF signaling is the inflammatory response cells mount to tumor necrosis factor alpha, released by macrophages, T cells and many non-immune tissues after injury or infection. It decides whether a stimulated cell survives and inflames or dies, and its dysregulation drives rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis, which is why TNF blockade is a mainstay of therapy. Ligand binding to TNFR1 nucleates a complex of TRADD, TRAF2, RIPK1 and the ubiquitin ligases cIAP1/2 and LUBAC; the ubiquitin chains they build recruit the TAK1 and IKK complexes, activating NF-kappaB and MAP kinase programs that induce anti-apoptotic proteins and cytokines. Deubiquitinases such as CYLD, A20 and OTULIN restrain this output. When survival signalling is blocked, RIPK1 assembles with FADD and caspase-8 to trigger apoptosis, or with RIPK3 for necroptosis, while sphingomyelinase-derived ceramide adds a parallel pro-apoptotic arm.

TNF signaling decides, cell by cell, whether an inflammatory stimulus ends in survival or death. TNF-α released from immune and stromal cells engages TNFR1 (TNFRSF1A), and the receptor assembles TRADD, TRAF2 and RIPK1 with ubiquitin ligases including BIRC2/3 and the linear ubiquitin chain complex (RNF31, RBCK1, SHARPIN). Those chains recruit the TAK1–TAB and IKK complexes, which activate NF-κB and MAP kinase output, driving pro-inflammatory cytokine production and anti-apoptotic proteins such as cFLIP and XIAP. Deubiquitinases — CYLD with SPATA2, A20, OTULIN — restrain this, and when the survival arm fails, RIPK1 moves into a FADD:caspase-8 platform for apoptosis or the RIPK3 necrosome. Sphingomyelinase-derived ceramide adds a parallel pro-apoptotic signal. Dysregulation underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, the target of anti-TNF therapy.

Transcription from mitochondrial promoters produces all RNA made inside mitochondria: the 13 respiratory chain subunits, 2 rRNAs and 22 tRNAs encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Because the organelle cannot import these transcripts, this step sets how much oxidative phosphorylation machinery a cell can build, and its failure causes mitochondrial disease with lactic acidosis, myopathy and neurodegeneration. The system is minimal and bacteriophage-like rather than nuclear: a single-subunit RNA polymerase, POLRMT, is recruited to the light-strand and heavy-strand promoters in the non-coding control region by TFAM, which also packages the circular genome into nucleoids, and by the initiation factor TFB2M, which melts the promoter. Each strand is transcribed as a polycistronic precursor that is later cleaved into individual tRNAs and mRNAs. MTERF1 terminates transcription past the rRNA genes, helping explain why ribosomal RNAs accumulate far above mRNA levels. The same promoter region couples transcription to mitochondrial DNA replication priming.

Mitochondria carry their own genome and must transcribe it themselves, and transcription from mitochondrial promoters is how the thirteen respiratory chain subunits, two rRNAs and twenty-two tRNAs encoded there are expressed. Without it oxidative phosphorylation cannot be assembled, and defects in this machinery cause mitochondrial depletion and multisystem energy-failure disease. A dedicated single-subunit RNA polymerase, POLRMT, is recruited to the light- and heavy-strand promoters in the non-coding control region by TFAM, which bends and packages the DNA, together with the initiation factor TFB2M that melts the template. Each promoter yields a long polycistronic precursor that is later cleaved into individual mRNAs and tRNAs. MTERF1 binds near the tRNA-Leu gene and terminates the rRNA-containing unit, helping explain why ribosomal RNAs accumulate far above mRNA levels. The same factors couple transcription to mitochondrial DNA copy number and replication priming.

RNA Polymerase II Transcription Initiation is the moment at which a promoter-bound polymerase makes its first phosphodiester bond, committing the cell to synthesising a messenger RNA. Every protein-coding gene depends on it, and it is the step at which most regulatory signals converge, so defects in its components cause developmental and repair disorders — mutations in the TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3 underlie xeroderma pigmentosum and trichothiodystrophy. TBP and the TAFs of TFIID recognise the promoter, TFIIA, TFIIB and TFIIF position the twelve-subunit polymerase, and TFIIE with TFIIH melts the duplex using ATP hydrolysis to expose the template strand in the active site. The open complex is unstable and yields abortive dinucleotide products until escape succeeds; TFIIB then leaves, and the CDK7–cyclin H kinase module phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain to license promoter clearance and elongation.

Every protein-coding gene begins its expression here: RNA polymerase II, guided to a promoter by TBP and the TAF subunits of TFIID and by the general factors TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and TFIIH, melts the DNA duplex and makes the first phosphodiester bond. Opening the promoter places the template strand in the catalytic center, and the resulting open complex is unstable, reverting to the closed state and releasing short abortive transcripts until a stable elongating polymerase escapes; TFIIB leaves once synthesis starts. The helicase subunits ERCC2 and ERCC3 within TFIIH drive strand opening using ATP hydrolysis, while the CDK7-cyclin H-MNAT1 kinase module phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain to license the transition to elongation and capping. Because TFIIH is shared with nucleotide excision repair, mutations in its subunits cause xeroderma pigmentosum and trichothiodystrophy, and TAF defects give tissue-restricted developmental disease.

Synthesis of Ketone Bodies is the liver's route for converting fat-derived acetyl-CoA into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, water-soluble fuels that circulate to heart, skeletal muscle and brain when carbohydrate is scarce. It is what allows fasting, prolonged exercise and low-carbohydrate feeding to spare glucose for tissues that depend on it, and its loss causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy in infancy. Inside hepatocyte mitochondria, thiolase condenses two acetyl-CoA units, HMG-CoA synthase 2 adds a third, and HMG-CoA lyase cleaves the intermediate to acetoacetate, which BDH1 reduces to beta-hydroxybutyrate using the NADH generated by beta-oxidation. HMGCS2 is the rate-setting, hormonally controlled step, induced by fasting and repressed by insulin. Related activating enzymes allow acetoacetate and acetate to be recaptured for lipogenesis. Unrestrained flux through this route, as in untreated diabetes, produces ketoacidosis.

When carbohydrate is scarce, the liver converts acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation into ketone bodies that circulate as fuel, and this ketogenic route is what allows heart and skeletal muscle to burn acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate while the limited glucose supply is reserved for the brain. In hepatic mitochondria, a thiolase condenses two acetyl-CoA units to acetoacetyl-CoA, the mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase HMGCS2 adds a third to form HMG-CoA, HMG-CoA lyase cleaves it to acetoacetate, and BDH1 reduces that to beta-hydroxybutyrate; an acetoacetyl-CoA synthetase can also recapture ketone-derived carbon for lipid synthesis. Output rises during fasting, prolonged exercise and low-carbohydrate feeding. In untreated diabetes, unrestrained fatty acid oxidation drives production beyond peripheral oxidative capacity, acidifying the blood and impairing oxygen delivery, while inherited defects of the lyase or synthase cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemic crises.

SLBP Dependent Processing of Replication-Dependent Histone Pre-mRNAs generates the mature messages for the core histones needed during S phase, and it does so without polyadenylation: instead of a poly(A) tail, these transcripts end in a conserved stem-loop produced by a single endonucleolytic cleavage. This is how a dividing cell matches histone supply to the amount of DNA it is replicating, and coupling of the pathway to the cell cycle keeps free histone from accumulating outside S phase. Stem-loop binding protein occupies the hairpin on the nascent transcript, while the U7 snRNP — built on Sm proteins plus the U7-specific LSM10 and LSM11 — base-pairs with the downstream element; ZNF473 bridges the two to position the cleavage machinery, with the cap-binding complex marking the 5' end. Stem-loop binding protein then accompanies the mature mRNA to the cytoplasm and directs its rapid destruction when replication ends.

Replication-dependent histone mRNAs are the one major class of eukaryotic mRNA that is not polyadenylated; instead their 3' ends are made by a single endonucleolytic cleavage that leaves a conserved stem-loop, and this SLBP-dependent processing of histone pre-mRNAs is how that end is generated. Coupling histone supply to S phase depends on it, since the same stem-loop and its bound protein later control mRNA stability and translation, and failure to restrict histone synthesis to replication disrupts chromatin assembly. Stem-loop binding protein engages the nascent transcript, while the U7 snRNP base-pairs with a downstream element through its snRNA. That particle carries a distinctive core in which Lsm10 and Lsm11 replace two of the canonical Sm proteins, and the zinc-finger protein encoded by ZNF473 bridges Lsm11 to SLBP to recruit it. The nuclear cap-binding proteins link processing to transcription and export.

Interconversion of 2-oxoglutarate and 2-hydroxyglutarate clears a metabolite that cells must not allow to accumulate. Both stereoisomers of 2-hydroxyglutarate arise as low-level byproducts of other routes -- plausibly lysine breakdown or aminolevulinate metabolism -- and are oxidised back to 2-oxoglutarate in the mitochondrial matrix, returning the carbon to the citric acid cycle. Two FAD-dependent dehydrogenases handle this with strict stereospecificity, D2HGDH acting on the R enantiomer and L2HGDH on the S enantiomer, while ADHFE1 reversibly couples R-2-hydroxyglutarate with succinate semialdehyde to yield 4-hydroxybutyrate and 2-oxoglutarate. Inherited loss of either dehydrogenase produces D- or L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, with variable epilepsy, developmental delay and leukoencephalopathy. The accumulating acid inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, linking this small housekeeping route to chromatin demethylation and hypoxia signalling.

2-Hydroxyglutarate is a metabolic dead end that cells must clear, and this small mitochondrial route returns both of its stereoisomers to 2-oxoglutarate so the carbon can enter the citric acid cycle. Two FAD-dependent dehydrogenases do the oxidation with opposite stereospecificity: D2HGDH acts on the R(-) isomer and L2HGDH on the S(-) isomer. ADHFE1 provides a separate, reversible link, transferring reducing equivalents between R(-)-2-hydroxyglutarate and succinate semialdehyde to yield 4-hydroxybutyrate and 2-oxoglutarate, tying this chemistry to GABA-related metabolism. Inherited loss of either dehydrogenase causes D- or L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, with accumulation of the acid and variable encephalopathy, seizures and developmental delay. The interest in these reactions is broader than the rare diseases, since 2-hydroxyglutarate competitively inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases that control DNA and histone demethylation.

Synaptic adhesion-like molecules describes how the SALM/LRFN family of cell-surface adhesion proteins builds and matures excitatory synapses, determining where dendrites and axons contact each other and which receptors are held at the contact site. This is the final step of synapse assembly, and it sets the strength and composition of glutamatergic transmission that underlies learning; disruption of these adhesion systems is linked to autism spectrum and other neurodevelopmental disorders. Each SALM carries extracellular leucine-rich repeats, an Ig and fibronectin III domain, and in most members a cytoplasmic PDZ-binding tail that docks onto PSD-95 family scaffolds (DLG1/3/4). Through this link they cluster NMDA (GRIN1, GRIN2A-D) and AMPA (GRIA1-4) receptors in the postsynaptic density, while trans-synaptic binding to presynaptic receptor tyrosine phosphatases PTPRD, PTPRS and PTPRF drives synapse induction, neurite outgrowth and branching.

Excitatory synapses only work once glutamate receptors are concentrated opposite the presynaptic terminal, and the SALM/LRFN family of leucine-rich repeat adhesion proteins is one of the systems that puts them there. These single-pass transmembrane proteins span the synaptic cleft through extracellular leucine-rich repeats, an Ig-like domain and a fibronectin III domain, while most members end in a cytoplasmic motif that binds PSD-95 family scaffolds (DLG1, DLG3, DLG4), tethering AMPA-type (GRIA1, GRIA3/4) and NMDA-type (GRIN1 with GRIN2A-D) receptors to the postsynaptic density. Presynaptic receptor phosphatases of the PTPRD/PTPRF/PTPRS group act as their trans-synaptic partners, coupling adhesion to synapse assembly. Beyond receptor recruitment, these molecules shape neurite outgrowth, dendritic branching and synapse maturation, and variants in family members have been linked to autism spectrum and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

The role of GTSE1 in G2/M progression after G2 checkpoint describes how a cell that has arrested in G2 to repair DNA damage dismantles the arrest and commits to mitosis. This recovery step decides whether a damaged cell dies by p53-driven apoptosis or resumes proliferation, and its deregulation contributes to cancer cell survival, invasiveness and taxane resistance. GTSE1 is a microtubule-associated protein expressed maximally in G2; through binding tubulin and the plus-end tracking protein MAPRE1 it influences microtubule dynamics and cell migration, until CDK1-associated mitotic phosphorylation displaces it at prometaphase. PLK1 phosphorylation instead drives GTSE1 into the nucleus, where it binds TP53 and promotes its MDM2-dependent export and proteasomal destruction, lowering apoptotic and arrest gene output. Paradoxically GTSE1 also stabilises the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A together with an HSP90-FKBPL chaperone complex, linking checkpoint recovery to ubiquitin-proteasome protein turnover.

After DNA damage arrests cells in G2, they must eventually silence the arrest signal and re-enter mitosis, and GTSE1 is one route by which that recovery happens. GTSE1 is a microtubule-associated protein expressed maximally in G2; through binding tubulin and the plus-end tracker MAPRE1 (EB1) it decorates growing microtubule tips, an activity linked to cell migration and to the invasiveness of breast cancer lines that mis-express it in G1. PLK1 phosphorylation drives GTSE1 into the nucleus, where it binds TP53 and, with MDM2, promotes p53 export and proteasomal destruction, blunting apoptosis and arrest gene expression so that CDK1-cyclin B can fire. GTSE1 also binds CDKN1A (p21) together with HSP90 and FKBPL to extend its half-life, a combination implicated in paclitaxel resistance. Mitotic phosphorylation near the EB1-binding site releases GTSE1 from microtubule ends in prometaphase.

Signaling by MST1 describes the activation of macrophage-stimulating protein and its receptor RON, a growth factor axis that shapes how macrophages and epithelia respond to injury and infection. It tunes inflammation in two phases, first driving macrophage chemotaxis and phagocytosis and later damping their inflammatory output so tissue repair can proceed; the same receptor is overexpressed in epithelial cancers, where it promotes invasive growth. The ligand is secreted by the liver as an inactive single-chain precursor of the kringle family, related to hepatocyte growth factor and plasminogen, and must be cleaved by a membrane serine protease such as hepsin at sites of coagulation or inflammation. The HAI-type inhibitors SPINT1 and SPINT2 restrain that proteolysis, setting how much active ligand reaches the receptor. Receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation then create a docking site for GRB2, PI3K and SRC, coupling to survival, motility and wound-healing programmes.

Macrophage-stimulating protein (MST1), a kringle-domain relative of hepatocyte growth factor made by the liver, circulates as an inactive single-chain precursor until proteolysis converts it to the active dimer that engages its receptor tyrosine kinase RON (MST1R) on macrophages and epithelial cells. Signaling by MST1 shapes the inflammatory response to bacterial infection and tissue injury: it first drives macrophage chemotaxis and phagocytosis, then restrains further macrophage activation, so the pathway both starts and limits inflammation and contributes to wound healing and epithelial repair. Activation requires cleavage, here supplied by the membrane serine protease hepsin (HPN), whose activity is held in check by the Kunitz-type inhibitors SPINT1 and SPINT2; ligand binding then promotes receptor dimerisation, autophosphorylation and recruitment of SH2 adaptors. RON is overexpressed in many epithelial cancers, where this axis supports tumour progression and invasion.

Interleukin-20 family signaling is the axis by which immune cells instruct epithelial tissue, driving antimicrobial defence, barrier integrity and wound repair at skin, gut and lung surfaces. IL19, IL20, IL22, IL24 and IL26 belong to the broader IL10 family but share receptor subunits (IL20RA, IL20RB, IL22RA1 with IL10RB) that are expressed largely on epithelial and stromal cells rather than leukocytes, so these cytokines act outward from the immune system instead of within it. Binding activates JAK1/JAK2/TYK2 and predominantly STAT3, inducing antimicrobial peptides, mucins and proliferation, with SOCS3 and the soluble decoy IL22RA2 limiting the response. Excess signalling produces the keratinocyte hyperproliferation of psoriasis, while deficiency compromises mucosal healing and pathogen containment. The related interferon-lambda ligands and IFNLR1 use the shared IL10RB chain to drive STAT1/STAT2-dependent antiviral protection of the same epithelia.

The IL20 subfamily of cytokines "IL19, IL20, IL22, IL24 and IL26" lets leukocytes speak to epithelial cells, and signalling through this family is how barrier tissues mount antimicrobial defence and repair themselves after injury. Skin, gut and lung epithelium respond by producing defensins and mucins, proliferating and restoring barrier integrity; excessive IL22 or IL20 signalling instead drives keratinocyte hyperproliferation and the epidermal changes of psoriasis, while loss of IL22 responses leaves mucosal surfaces vulnerable to infection. Receptors are heterodimers built from shared chains including IL20RA, IL20RB, IL22RA1 and IL10RB, with the secreted decoy IL22RA2 sequestering IL22 to limit responses. Ligand binding activates receptor-associated JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT3 predominantly alongside STAT1 and STAT5, with SOCS3 imposing negative feedback. The closely related lambda interferons use IL10RB with IFNLR1 for antiviral epithelial protection.

Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is the principal route by which cells internalise plasma membrane proteins and the material bound to them, forming clathrin-coated vesicles that deliver cargo to early endosomes. It supplies cells with nutrients and lipids through receptors for transferrin, LDL and mannose-6-phosphate, recycles synaptic vesicle components after neurotransmitter release, and sets the surface levels of signalling receptors, so that internalisation of activated EGFR or beta-arrestin-bound GPCRs both attenuates and redirects their signalling from the membrane onto endosomes. Coat formation begins with adaptors that read PI(4,5)P2 and cytoplasmic sorting motifs — the AP-2 tetramer plus sorting proteins such as DAB2, PICALM and epsins — which recruit clathrin triskelia and bend the membrane through ENTH and BAR domains. Actin and dynamin GTPases drive constriction and scission, and HSPA8 with auxilin uncoats the vesicle, returning clathrin for reuse. Ubiquitination marks many cargoes for degradation rather than recycling.

Cells continually pull patches of plasma membrane inward as clathrin-coated vesicles, and this route is how they take up nutrients such as transferrin-bound iron and LDL cholesterol, retrieve synaptic vesicle components after exocytosis, and control how long activated receptors keep signalling. Ligand-bound receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR and G protein-coupled receptors are internalised through it, determining whether they are recycled or handed to the degradative endosomal machinery, so the pathway sets the amplitude and location of downstream signalling as much as it clears cargo. A coated pit begins with PI(4,5)P2-binding initiators and the AP-2 adaptor tetramer, which together with sorting adaptors like epsin, DAB2 and PICALM read cytoplasmic sorting motifs and couple cargo capture to clathrin lattice assembly. BAR-domain proteins and actin nucleation bend the neck, dynamin GTPases sever it, and HSPA8 with auxilin strips the coat for reuse.

VLDLR internalisation and degradation controls how many very low density lipoprotein receptors remain on the cell surface, and therefore how efficiently triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and remnant particles are cleared from blood. Because receptor number sets clearance capacity, the rate of this catabolic route influences circulating lipid levels and cardiovascular risk, and it is the same logic exploited therapeutically by antibodies against the secreted convertase PCSK9. Two destruction mechanisms converge: PCSK9 binds the receptor extracellularly and routes it, via clathrin- and AP-2-dependent endocytosis, to lysosomal degradation rather than recycling, while the LXR-induced E3 ubiquitin ligase IDOL (MYLIP) ubiquitinates the receptor's cytoplasmic tail to trigger its turnover. The nuclear receptors LXRα and LXRβ thus couple intracellular sterol abundance to receptor removal, making this a feedback arm of cholesterol and lipoprotein homeostasis alongside receptor-mediated lipid uptake in liver and other tissues.

The very low density lipoprotein receptor clears triglyceride-rich lipoproteins from plasma, and how quickly it is internalised and destroyed sets how much receptor is available at the cell surface — one of the determinants of circulating lipid levels. Two routes converge on the same outcome. The secreted convertase PCSK9 binds the receptor and, rather than cleaving it, escorts it through clathrin-coated pit endocytosis — clathrin heavy and light chains with the AP-2 adaptor complex — into lysosomal degradation. In parallel, the E3 ubiquitin ligase encoded by MYLIP (IDOL), induced by the sterol-sensing nuclear receptors LXRα and LXRβ, ubiquitinates the receptor's cytoplasmic tail and commits it for destruction, linking intracellular sterol abundance to receptor turnover. Loss of these controls raises receptor numbers and lowers plasma lipoproteins, which is why PCSK9 blockade is used therapeutically in hypercholesterolaemia.

Negative regulation of activity of TFAP2 (AP-2) family transcription factors describes how the AP-2 transcription factors are held in check, setting limits on programmes they drive in neural crest, craniofacial and limb development, epidermal differentiation, and breast epithelium. Losing this restraint matters: unopposed AP-2 activity contributes to tumour progression, and mutations in the inhibitor KCTD1 cause scalp-ear-nipple syndrome and renal defects, while KCTD15 restrains neural crest induction. Repression works at several levels. KCTD1 and KCTD15 bind the transactivation domain of AP-2 homo- and heterodimers and block transcription directly. SUMOylation by UBE2I with SUMO1 dampens the activity of TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C, linking their output to a reversible post-translational switch. The tumour suppressor WWOX sequesters TFAP2C in the cytoplasm, and transcription of TFAP2A itself can be repressed by CREB and E2F1.

AP-2 family transcription factors drive programmes of neural crest, craniofacial, limb, skin and mammary development, and their output must be restrained as well as switched on; this pathway covers the mechanisms that damp AP-2 activity. KCTD1 and KCTD15 bind the AP-2 transactivation domain and block transcriptional activation, a brake whose loss in KCTD1 mutation causes scalp-ear-nipple syndrome and renal defects. SUMO conjugation through the E2 enzyme UBE2I attaches SUMO1 to TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C, converting them into weaker activators and influencing epithelial differentiation and cancer stem cell traits in breast tumours. The tumour suppressor WWOX sequesters TFAP2C outside the nucleus, preventing it from reaching its targets. Together these controls set the dosage of AP-2 signalling, which matters because both excess and deficiency distort embryonic patterning and epithelial gene expression.

rRNA processing in the mitochondrion generates the 12S and 16S ribosomal RNAs that build the mitoribosome, the machine that translates the thirteen mitochondrially encoded subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase. Without it oxidative phosphorylation fails, and mutations in the responsible nuclear enzymes cause infantile mitochondrial disease with lactic acidosis and cardiomyopathy. Because the mitochondrial genome is transcribed as long polycistronic precursors, the rRNAs must first be excised: the tRNAs punctuating them are cleaved at their 5' ends by the proteinaceous RNase P complex and at their 3' ends by ELAC2, releasing the flanking rRNAs. Nucleus-encoded enzymes acting in the matrix then install a small set of methylated and pseudouridylated nucleotides, and MTERF4-NSUN4 and RCC1L-containing complexes couple modification to assembly of the large and small mitoribosomal subunits.

Mitochondria make their own ribosomes, and the 12S and 16S rRNAs at their core must first be cut out of a single long polycistronic transcript of the heavy strand and then chemically decorated. This rRNA processing in the mitochondrion sets the ceiling on how much respiratory chain protein a cell can synthesise, since the mitochondrial genome encodes core subunits of complexes I, III, IV and the ATP synthase. Endonucleolytic release depends on the RNase P-like complex of PRORP, TRMT10C and HSD17B10 acting at tRNA 5' ends and on ELAC2 at 3' ends, with FASTKD2 and RNA granule components aiding folding and maturation. Methyltransferases including TFB1M, NSUN4 and the MRM enzymes, plus pseudouridine synthases, install the handful of modifications needed for subunit assembly. Defects impair mitochondrial translation and cause infantile encephalomyopathy, cardiomyopathy and deafness.

RAB geranylgeranylation is the lipid modification step that licenses the RAB family of small GTPases to work on membranes, and so underpins essentially all vesicular traffic through the secretory and endolysosomal system. Newly made RABs are soluble and inert; attachment of one or two geranylgeranyl groups to C-terminal cysteines gives them the hydrophobic anchor needed to dock on target compartments, cycle on and off with GDI, and recruit sorting adaptors, tethers and motors. The reaction is carried out by a trimeric geranylgeranyltransferase in which RABGGTA and RABGGTB provide catalysis while the escort proteins CHM (REP1) or CHML present GDP-bound substrate and then chaperone the prenylated RAB to its membrane. Loss of CHM impairs prenylation of a subset of RABs and causes choroideremia, a progressive retinal degeneration, illustrating how one shared modification step supports compartment-specific trafficking across more than sixty RABs.

RAB GTPases only work on membranes, and geranylgeranylation is the lipid modification that puts them there. Newly made RABs are soluble and inert until one or two C-terminal cysteines receive twenty-carbon geranylgeranyl groups, after which they can dock on the endosomes, Golgi cisternae, secretory granules and autophagic membranes whose identity they define. The reaction is carried out by a trimeric prenyltransferase: the catalytic RABGGTA/RABGGTB heterodimer plus an escort protein, CHM or its paralogue CHML, which binds the GDP-loaded substrate, presents it for modification, and then delivers the prenylated GTPase to its target compartment. Once installed, the RAB cycles between GTP-bound membrane-associated and GDI-bound cytosolic states under GEF and GAP control, recruiting tethers, sorting adaptors and motors. Loss of CHM causes choroideremia, a progressive retinal degeneration, illustrating how underprenylation of particular RABs disables trafficking in specific tissues.

MET receptor recycling is the route by which the activated hepatocyte growth factor receptor is returned to the cell surface rather than degraded, sustaining the motility and survival signals that drive epithelial wound healing, tissue regeneration and, when deregulated, tumour invasion and metastasis. After HGF binding, MET is internalised and sorted by GGA3 through RAB4-positive early endosomes back to the plasma membrane, with ARF6 supporting the membrane trafficking step. Recycling does more than replenish surface receptor: MET continues to signal from endosomes through its GAB1, GRB2 and CRK/CRKL adaptor complex, and this endosomal phase is what converts a transient ligand encounter into prolonged ERK1/ERK2 and STAT3 activation. The balance between this recycling arm and ubiquitin-dependent degradative sorting sets how long and how strongly a cell responds to HGF, and oncogenic MET mutants that escape degradative sorting are shunted into this pathway.

After hepatocyte growth factor binds MET, the activated receptor is internalised rather than simply switched off, and its route through the endosomal system determines how long and how strongly it signals. Recycling of MET back to the plasma membrane sustains ERK1/ERK2 and STAT3 output, supporting the motility, scattering and invasive growth responses that HGF elicits in epithelial cells and that are hijacked in carcinoma progression. Endocytosed receptor is sorted by the adaptor GGA3 through RAB4A/RAB4B-marked early recycling endosomes and returned to the surface with help from ARF6, while adaptors GRB2, GAB1 and the CRK/CRKL pair remain bound and continue to relay signals from the endosome itself. Diverting MET toward degradation instead of recycling shortens the response, so this trafficking step acts as a control point on receptor tyrosine kinase signal duration.

Listeria monocytogenes entry into host cells describes how this food-borne bacterium hijacks normal receptor endocytosis to get inside non-phagocytic cells, the step that lets it cross the intestinal, placental and blood-brain barriers and cause meningoencephalitis or sepsis in newborns and immunocompromised adults. Two bacterial surface internalins do the work by mimicking host ligands: InlA engages E-cadherin, pulling on the junctional complex of beta-catenin and p120-catenin, while InlB engages the MET receptor tyrosine kinase and activates PI3K/AKT signalling. Both routes converge on the machinery that normally internalises these receptors — Src-family kinases, Cbl and CBLL1 ubiquitin ligases with polyubiquitin, GRB2 and CIN85 adaptors, the ESCRT-0 components HRS and STAM, endophilins and EPS15 — so clathrin-mediated uptake and actin remodelling deliver the bacterium into a vacuole. Subsequent filopod formation spreads it between cells while evading immune detection.

Listeria monocytogenes is a food-borne intracellular pathogen that invades non-phagocytic cells by hijacking host surface receptors, and this entry step is what lets it cross the intestinal, placental and blood-brain barriers to cause gastroenteritis in healthy adults and meningoencephalitis or sepsis in newborns and immunocompromised people. Two routes converge on the same host endocytic machinery: the bacterial surface protein InlA engages E-cadherin, pulling on the junctional complex with beta-catenin and p120-catenin, while InlB engages the MET receptor tyrosine kinase and switches on PI3K/AKT signalling. In both cases Src-family kinase activity, Cbl- and CBLL1-mediated ubiquitination of the receptor, and clathrin-associated adaptors such as EPS15, endophilins and the ESCRT-0 components HGS and STAM drive receptor internalisation, with the resulting membrane and actin remodelling engulfing the bacterium. The pathway is essentially receptor endocytosis and adherens-junction turnover subverted for bacterial uptake.

InlA-mediated entry of Listeria monocytogenes into host cells describes how a food-borne bacterium hijacks an adhesion receptor to get inside epithelial cells, the step that lets Listeria cross the intestinal barrier and reach the placenta and brain in listeriosis. The bacterial surface protein internalin binds E-cadherin on the host cell surface and mimics the signalling that normally follows cell-cell contact: SRC kinase is activated and phosphorylates E-cadherin and its bound catenins, creating docking sites for the ubiquitin ligase Hakai. Ubiquitination of the junctional complex drives clathrin- and caveolin-dependent endocytosis, and SRC-directed actin remodelling through cortactin and ARP2/3 pulls the bacterium in with the receptor. The same machinery governs physiological turnover of adherens junctions, so this route is subversion of normal junction endocytosis rather than a dedicated uptake system.

Listeria monocytogenes crosses the intestinal epithelium by exploiting a junctional adhesion receptor, and InlA-mediated entry describes how the bacterial surface protein internalin A binds host E-cadherin and turns adherens junction turnover into a route of invasion. This is the step that allows a food-borne organism to reach the bloodstream, placenta and central nervous system, causing listeriosis in pregnancy and in immunocompromised people. Engagement of E-cadherin activates SRC, which phosphorylates the cadherin and its associated beta-catenin and p120-catenin; the ubiquitin ligase CBLL1 (Hakai) then docks on the phosphorylated receptor and ubiquitinates it, marking the complex for clathrin- and caveolin-dependent endocytosis with accompanying actin remodelling. Because the same phosphorylation and ubiquitination steps operate during normal cadherin internalisation, the pathway doubles as a model for how junctional adhesion is dismantled and recycled in epithelia.

Protein methylation is the transfer of methyl groups onto lysine and arginine residues of proteins other than histones, a widespread post-translational mark that tunes protein activity, stability and partner binding rather than being a metabolic end in itself. Through it, cells modulate signal transduction outputs including MAPK, WNT, BMP, Hippo and JAK-STAT, and coordinate chromatin remodelling, transcription, translation and DNA repair; methylation frequently crosstalks with phosphorylation, ubiquitination and with histone marks. The enzymes here are dedicated methyltransferases acting on defined substrates: calmodulin is trimethylated by CAMKMT, the translation apparatus is marked on elongation factors eEF1A and eEF2 and on ribosomal protein RPS2, chaperones and the AAA-ATPase VCP are modified by METTL21A and VCPKMT, and mitochondrial electron transfer flavoprotein is methylated by ETFBKMT. Loss of individual enzymes, such as CAMKMT, causes developmental and neurological disease.

Methyl groups added to lysine and arginine side chains tune the behaviour of proteins well beyond histones, and protein methylation of non-histone substrates regulates signalling through routes such as MAPK, WNT, BMP, Hippo and JAK-STAT, as well as chromatin remodelling, transcription, translation and DNA repair. The enzymes here are largely seven-beta-strand methyltransferases acting on defined targets: a calmodulin-specific lysine methyltransferase modifies calmodulin, dedicated enzymes methylate elongation factors eEF1A and eEF2, another modifies the electron transfer flavoprotein beta subunit, and further members act on the AAA-ATPase VCP and on Hsp70-family chaperones, while an arginine methyltransferase modifies ribosomal protein S2. The pattern shows methylation being used to set the activity of the translational apparatus, chaperone and protein-quality-control machinery, calcium signalling and mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation, with crosstalk to other post-translational marks integrating these responses.

Vitamin E transport is the intracellular handling step that determines how much alpha-tocopherol, the body's principal vitamin E, reaches the circulation and peripheral tissues. Because tocopherols are lipophilic, they cannot diffuse freely through the cytosol and depend on dedicated carrier proteins; in hepatocytes this task falls to alpha-tocopherol transfer protein, which selectively binds alpha-tocopherol taken up from lipoproteins and directs it for secretion into nascent VLDL rather than degradation. This selectivity explains why alpha-tocopherol predominates in plasma over other dietary tocopherol forms. The pathway sustains the antioxidant protection of membrane lipids, particularly in neurons and erythrocytes, and its loss causes ataxia with isolated vitamin E deficiency, a progressive spinocerebellar degeneration with peripheral neuropathy and retinopathy that responds to high-dose supplementation. It belongs with the broader trafficking of fat-soluble vitamins and lipoprotein metabolism.

Alpha-tocopherol, the predominant and most biologically active form of vitamin E in humans, is a lipophilic antioxidant that cannot move freely through the aqueous cytosol and depends on a dedicated carrier to reach its destinations. This transport step occurs mainly in hepatocytes, where the alpha-tocopherol transfer protein binds tocopherol taken up from dietary lipoproteins and directs it toward secretion into circulating very low density lipoproteins, thereby setting plasma vitamin E levels and the supply available to peripheral tissues, including neurons. Selective retention of the alpha isoform over other tocopherols and tocotrienols explains why body stores are dominated by a single vitamer. Loss of this carrier causes ataxia with vitamin E deficiency, a progressive spinocerebellar and peripheral neuropathy attributable to unchecked lipid peroxidation in membranes, and it responds to high-dose tocopherol supplementation.

DAG1 core M3 glycosylations builds the sugar chain on alpha-dystroglycan that lets muscle and brain cells grip their basement membrane. Matriglycan is the actual binding site for laminin, agrin and perlecan, so this modification, not the protein alone, creates the mechanical link between the extracellular matrix and the cytoskeleton in skeletal muscle and at the pial surface of the developing brain. Assembly is strictly ordered: POMT1 and POMT2 transfer mannose to specific threonines, POMGNT2 adds beta-1,4-GlcNAc, B3GALNT2 completes the GalNAc-GlcNAc-Man linker, and POMK phosphorylates the mannose 6-position to license further elongation. Loss of any step abolishes ligand binding and produces dystroglycanopathy, ranging from limb-girdle muscular dystrophy to Walker-Warburg syndrome with cobblestone lissencephaly and eye malformations, illustrating that a glycan can be the functional unit of a receptor.

Alpha-dystroglycan must be sugar-coated before it can work, and the core M3 glycosylation route is how that coat is built on specific threonines of its mucin-like domain.
