Platelet-type 12-lipoxygenase (ALOX12) oxygenates DPAn-3 at carbon 14 to a 14(S)-hydroperoxy intermediate, which is then converted through further oxygenation, reduction and epoxide hydrolysis into the maresin series; 5-lipoxygenase (ALOX5) contributes related oxygenation chemistry from the same substrate pool. Products of this kind promote resolution of inflammation, macrophage clearance of debris and apoptotic cells, and repair of injured tissue, linking dietary omega-3 intake to the termination phase of the inflammatory response rather than its initiation.

Erythropoietin activates Phospholipase C gamma (PLCG) is one branch of the signalling that erythropoietin triggers in red cell progenitors, converting hormone binding into a calcium and protein kinase C response that supports erythroblast survival, proliferation and terminal maturation. Loss of erythropoietin signalling causes anaemia, while its overactivation drives erythrocytosis. Mechanistically, EPO dimerises its receptor and activates the receptor-associated kinase JAK2; the Src-family kinase LYN, recruited alongside adaptors such as IRS2, phosphorylates PLCG1 or PLCG2 docked on phosphotyrosines of the receptor tail. Activated phospholipase C gamma hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, releasing calcium from intracellular stores, and to diacylglycerol, which engages protein kinase C isoforms. This arm runs in parallel with STAT5, PI3K and RAS-MAPK outputs of the same receptor, adding calcium-dependent control to erythropoiesis.

Erythropoietin drives red cell production by keeping erythroid progenitors alive and proliferating, and one branch of that signal works through phospholipase C gamma. When erythropoietin binds its receptor, the receptor dimerizes and JAK2 is activated, creating phosphotyrosine docking sites; PLCG1 or PLCG2 is recruited to the activated receptor complex and phosphorylated by the Src-family kinase LYN, with IRS2 serving as an additional scaffold. Activated phospholipase C cleaves membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, which releases calcium from intracellular stores, and diacylglycerol, which activates protein kinase C. The resulting calcium and PKC signals feed into transcriptional and survival responses that expand the erythroid compartment during hypoxia or blood loss. Loss of erythropoietin or receptor signalling causes anaemia, while gain-of-function receptor and JAK2 lesions produce erythrocytosis and myeloproliferative disease.

NR1H2 & NR1H3 regulate gene expression to limit cholesterol uptake is the arm of sterol sensing that shuts off LDL import when a cell already has enough cholesterol. The liver X receptors LXRalpha and LXRbeta bind oxysterols generated from excess cholesterol and, as heterodimers with RXRA or RXRB, switch on a transcriptional program that lowers sterol load. Here the induced target is MYLIP (IDOL), an E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates the cytoplasmic tail of the LDL receptor and drives its lysosomal degradation, reducing lipoprotein uptake independently of the SREBP-2 route that controls LDLR transcription. This feedback complements LXR-driven cholesterol efflux and suppression of biosynthesis, and it sets circulating LDL levels, making the receptor-degradation step relevant to hypercholesterolaemia, atherosclerosis and the response to lipid-lowering therapy.

When cells accumulate sterols, oxysterols generated from excess cholesterol bind the liver X receptors NR1H3 and NR1H2, which then act with retinoid X receptor partners as heterodimeric transcription factors to shut down further cholesterol acquisition. This arm of the response limits cholesterol uptake by inducing MYLIP, also called IDOL, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates the cytoplasmic tail of the LDL receptor and consigns it to degradation, so fewer receptors remain at the surface to internalise LDL particles. The result is post-translational control of LDL receptor abundance that is independent of the sterol-regulated transcription of the receptor itself, and complementary to the other LXR outputs promoting cholesterol efflux and suppressing synthesis. Because LDL receptor levels set plasma LDL cholesterol, this circuit is of interest in atherosclerosis and in understanding variation in lipid-lowering responses.

NGF-stimulated transcription is the nuclear output of nerve growth factor signalling: the wave of gene expression that converts a transient kinase signal at the TrkA receptor into the lasting decision of a neuronal precursor to stop dividing and grow neurites. It supports sympathetic and sensory neuron differentiation and survival, and the same machinery underlies activity-dependent gene expression in mature neurons, so it links extracellular trophic cues to synaptic plasticity and memory. Sustained ERK signalling activates CREB, ELK1 and SRF, which drive immediate early genes including FOS, FOSB, JUNB and the EGR family; these encode transcription factors that in turn switch on delayed response genes such as VGF and TPH1, with EP300 and CHD4 shaping chromatin and REST and the ID proteins restraining neuronal programmes. CDK5 and its p35/p39 activators couple the response to cytoskeletal remodelling during neurite extension.

Nerve growth factor binding to its receptor ends in the nucleus, and NGF-stimulated transcription is the gene expression response that converts a trophic signal into a lasting change in neuronal identity — cell cycle exit, neurite outgrowth and survival of sympathetic and sensory neurons. The first wave is immediate early genes: FOS, FOSB, JUNB, EGR1-4 and ARC are switched on within minutes by pre-existing factors such as CREB1, ELK1, SRF, ATF1 and ATF2 acting with the p300 acetyltransferase, without any need for new protein synthesis. Many of these products are themselves transcription factors, so they impose a slower, delayed wave that includes neuropeptide and neurotransmitter enzymes such as VGF and tryptophan hydroxylase, the NAB corepressors that restrain EGR activity, ID proteins, and CDK5 with its neuronal activators. REST and ASCL1 set how permissive the neuronal programme is. This is the logic underlying activity-dependent plasticity as well as differentiation.

Peroxisomal protein import delivers the entire folded matrix proteome of the peroxisome from the cytosol across a single membrane, and so builds the organelle's capacity for fatty acid beta-oxidation, glyoxylate and D-amino acid detoxification, hydrogen peroxide breakdown by catalase, and ether-phospholipid synthesis. Its failure causes Zellweger spectrum disease, neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy and rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata, in which enzymes such as ACOX1, PHYH, AGXT and GNPAT are made but never reach their compartment. Cargo carries a C-terminal PTS1 read by PEX5 or an N-terminal PTS2 read by PEX7, and the loaded receptor docks at a membrane translocation module of PEX13, PEX14 and the RING proteins PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12. Uniquely, substrates cross without unfolding. Receptor recycling drives the cycle: PEX5 is mono-ubiquitinated on a cysteine, extracted by the PEX1-PEX6 AAA-ATPase with PEX26, then deubiquitinated by USP9X.

Peroxisomes carry out fatty acid beta-oxidation, glyoxylate detoxification, hydrogen peroxide breakdown and plasmalogen synthesis, but they make none of their own matrix enzymes; peroxisomal protein import is how roughly four dozen cargo proteins reach the lumen from the cytosol. Cargo need not unfold to cross, which is unusual among translocation systems. Cytosolic receptors recognise targeting motifs on cargo — PEX5 binding the common C-terminal signal, PEX7 the alternative signal found on a few enzymes such as phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase and thiolase — and dock at a membrane module built from PEX13, PEX14 and the RING proteins PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12. The receptor is then mono-ubiquitinated, extracted by the PEX1–PEX6 AAA-ATPase ring with PEX26, and deubiquitinated by USP9X for reuse. Loss of these steps causes Zellweger spectrum disease and rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata.

Blood group systems biosynthesis builds the surface antigens that determine transfusion compatibility. Mismatched donor red cells are attacked by recipient antibodies, so the products of this pathway dictate who can safely receive whose blood, and variation in them is linked to susceptibility to infection, thrombotic and cardiovascular risk, and tumour-associated carbohydrate changes. Most of these antigens are oligosaccharides added stepwise onto glycolipid and glycoprotein scaffolds: galactosyltransferases and sialyltransferases extend the core chains, the ABO transferase adds the A or B terminal sugar, and fucosyltransferases generate H, Secretor and Lewis structures, with FUT2 activity also determining whether antigens appear in saliva, milk and other secretions. Inactivating or altered alleles convert one antigen into another or abolish expression, as in the O phenotype. The Rhesus proteins contribute a protein-based antigen system central to haemolytic disease of the newborn.

Blood group antigens are the inherited surface markers that determine transfusion compatibility, and their biosynthesis is largely a matter of carbohydrate chemistry: glycosyltransferases add specific sugars in defined order to oligosaccharide chains carried on red cell glycoproteins and glycolipids. The ABO transferase transfers N-acetylgalactosamine or galactose to the H antigen made by fucosyltransferases, while other fucosyltransferases, beta-1,3-galactosyltransferases and sialyltransferases build Lewis, secretor and related structures that also appear in saliva, milk and other secretions. RHD and RHCE instead encode protein antigens, the basis of Rh incompatibility and haemolytic disease of the newborn. Inherited variation in these enzymes creates new antigens or abolishes expression, explaining why mismatched transfusion provokes immune destruction of donor cells, and why blood type associates with susceptibility to certain infections, cardiovascular and malignant disease.

RHOF GTPase cycle describes the activation state and downstream effectors of RHOF (RIF), a vertebrate-specific Rho-family GTPase that builds unbranched actin bundles. Its output is visible as filopodia, stress fibres, the microvilli that let lymphocytes scan endothelium, and dendritic spines in neurons, so it shapes how cells probe and adhere to their surroundings and how synapses are formed. Unusually, RHOF appears constitutively GTP-loaded, with no known exchange factor or dissociation inhibitor, so timing is set almost entirely by GTPase-activating proteins such as ARHGAP1, ARHGAP5 and ARHGAP21 and by effector availability. The principal effectors are the diaphanous formins DIAPH1-3, which nucleate and elongate linear filaments, together with BAIAP2L1/2 membrane-deforming adaptors, actin capping and crosslinking proteins, and PI3K regulatory subunits. The set thus links a small GTPase switch to filopodial protrusion, cell shape and immune cell surface architecture.

RHOF (RIF) is a vertebrate-specific Rho-family GTPase that drives actin remodelling, and its regulatory cycle determines how cells build finger-like filopodia and contractile stress fibres. This output shapes cell surface architecture: microvillar protrusions on lymphocytes, dendritic spines in neurons, and the exploratory protrusions used in migration and cell-cell contact. Unusually, RHOF appears to sit largely in the GTP-loaded active state without a known exchange factor and without dissociation inhibitors, so the balance is set mainly by GTPase-activating proteins such as ARHGAP1, ARHGAP5, ARHGAP21 and SRGAP2, together with effectors that execute the cytoskeletal change. Chief among these are the formins DIAPH1, DIAPH2 and DIAPH3, which nucleate and elongate unbranched actin filaments, alongside I-BAR proteins BAIAP2L1 and BAIAP2L2 that deform membrane into protrusions, plus actin crosslinking and capping components including ACTN1 and CAPZB.

Meiotic recombination exchanges DNA segments between homologous chromosomes during gamete formation, generating the genetic diversity of sexual reproduction and, just as importantly, the physical links that let homologs pair, synapse and segregate correctly. Failure produces aneuploid eggs and sperm, infertility and pregnancy loss. Programmed double-strand breaks are made by SPO11 at hotspots specified by the histone methyltransferase PRDM9, then resected by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease with ATM signalling and RPA coating the resulting 3' overhangs. RAD51 and the meiosis-specific recombinase DMC1, assisted by BRCA2 and the MND1-PSMC3IP complex, drive homology search and strand invasion; most intermediates resolve without crossover, while MSH4-MSH5 and MLH1-MLH3 channel a minority into chiasmata. FIGNL1-FIRRM restrains recombinase dynamics, and nucleosome remodelling with H2AX phosphorylation frames the chromatin context, including silencing of the unsynapsed X-Y body.

Meiotic recombination is how homologous chromosomes exchange DNA during gamete formation, shuffling alleles between parental chromosomes and, just as importantly, physically tethering each homolog pair so that the first meiotic division segregates them correctly. Without at least one crossover per bivalent, chromosomes missegregate, producing aneuploid eggs and sperm, infertility and pregnancy loss. The process begins with programmed double-strand breaks made by SPO11, whose covalent attachment to the DNA is removed nucleolytically before the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and its partner RBBP8 resect the ends. RPA-coated 3' overhangs are handed to the RecA-like strand exchange proteins RAD51 and DMC1, aided by MND1 and PSMC3IP, which invade the homolog. Most intermediates resolve without crossover; a minority mature through MSH4-MSH5 and MLH1-MLH3 into chiasmata. PRDM9 marks hotspots by methylating histones, targeting breaks to defined genomic positions.

Regulation of IFNA/IFNB signaling describes the brakes on type I interferon responses, the arm of innate immunity that arms cells against viral infection. Interferon alpha and beta signalling must be transient: sustained JAK-STAT output through IFNAR1/IFNAR2 drives inflammation, cytopenias and interferonopathy, and loss of these restraints underlies autoimmune disease and, in the case of USP18 or ISG15 deficiency, lethal interferon toxicity. Negative control operates at every tier of the cascade. The phosphatases PTPN6, PTPN11 and PTPN1 strip activating phosphates from JAK1, TYK2 and STAT1/STAT2; SOCS1 and SOCS3 bind and inhibit the receptor-associated kinases while targeting components for degradation; USP18 displaces JAK1 from IFNAR2, and nuclear inhibitors of activated STATs limit transcription. Because several of these regulators are themselves interferon-induced, the pathway forms a self-limiting feedback loop that sets the duration and amplitude of antiviral gene expression.

Type I interferon signalling must be shut down as promptly as it is switched on, and this is the braking system for it. Interferon alpha and beta binding to the IFNAR1/IFNAR2 receptor activates JAK1 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT2 to drive antiviral gene expression; the negative regulators here set how strong and how brief that response is. Tyrosine phosphatases including PTPN1, PTPN6 and PTPN11 dephosphorylate receptor-associated kinases and STATs, SOCS1 and SOCS3 suppress JAK activity, and USP18 binds IFNAR2 to block its engagement with JAK1 independently of its deubiquitinase activity. Loss of this restraint produces sustained interferon-stimulated gene expression, the basis of type I interferonopathies such as USP18-deficient pseudo-TORCH syndrome, while excessive damping permits viral replication.

Degradation of GABA clears the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter after it has acted, and recycles its carbon into the citric acid cycle. This two-step route sets the size of the GABA pool available for inhibitory synaptic transmission, so its failure produces neurological disease: loss of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase activity causes a rare inherited disorder marked by developmental delay, ataxia, hypotonia and seizures, with accumulation of GABA and of the abnormal metabolite gamma-hydroxybutyrate. Both reactions occur in the mitochondrial matrix of neurons and astrocytes. 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase transfers the amino group to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding succinic semialdehyde and glutamate, and ALDH5A1 oxidises the semialdehyde to succinate, which enters mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. The shunt therefore links neurotransmitter turnover directly to energy production, and the aminotransferase is the target of the antiepileptic drug vigabatrin.

The main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the central nervous system is cleared by catabolism as well as by reuptake, and GABA degradation is the route that disposes of it while feeding its carbon back into energy metabolism. In the mitochondrial matrix, 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase transfers the amino group of GABA to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding succinic semialdehyde and glutamate; succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase then oxidises the aldehyde to succinate, which enters the citric acid cycle. This short two-step shunt links neurotransmitter turnover to oxidative metabolism in neurons and astrocytes, and sets the size of the GABA pool available for inhibitory signalling. Loss of the dehydrogenase step causes succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency, in which the intermediate is diverted to gamma-hydroxybutyrate and patients present with developmental delay, hypotonia, ataxia and seizures; aminotransferase deficiency is likewise a severe infantile encephalopathy.

Activation of IRF3, IRF7 mediated by TBK1, IKKε (IKBKE) is the step that converts detection of viral double-stranded RNA or bacterial LPS into type I interferon production. Toll-like receptors 3 and 4 signal through the adaptor TRIF (TICAM1), with TICAM2, CD14 and MD-2 (LY96) supporting LPS recognition, and recruit TRAF3 and TANK to assemble a complex in which TBK1 and IKBKE phosphorylate the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7. Phosphorylation drives their dimerization and nuclear entry, where they switch on IFNβ and interferon-stimulated genes that restrict viral replication and shape antiviral and inflammatory responses. The two kinases act partly redundantly, and their output is tuned by negative and modulatory regulators such as SARM1, optineurin, SHP2 and polyubiquitin. Loss of this arm leaves cells unable to mount an interferon response and susceptible to viral infection, while persistent activation contributes to interferon-driven autoimmunity.

Detection of viral double-stranded RNA or bacterial lipopolysaccharide must be converted into type I interferon output, and this step is where that conversion happens. Signals from TLR3 and TLR4 pass through the adaptor TRIF (TICAM1), with TICAM2, CD14 and the LPS co-receptor MD-2 (LY96) serving the surface-receptor arm, to recruit TRAF3 and the related kinases TBK1 and IKKε (IKBKE). These kinases phosphorylate the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7, driving their dimerization and nuclear entry so that interferon-β and downstream antiviral genes are transcribed. The two kinases overlap in function, and only loss of both abolishes IRF3 activation. Scaffolds and regulators including TANK, optineurin, SARM1 and polyubiquitin tune the response, while excessive or deficient signalling leads respectively to interferon-driven inflammation or failure of innate antiviral defence.

Class I peroxisomal membrane protein import builds the peroxisomal membrane itself, delivering the transporters, docking receptors and division factors that make an otherwise empty vesicle a functioning organelle. Without it peroxisomes cannot import matrix enzymes or fatty acid substrates, and the result is the severe peroxisome biogenesis disorders of the Zellweger spectrum. Newly synthesised membrane proteins are captured in the cytosol by the chaperone-receptor PEX19, which recognises positively charged transmembrane segments, then dock at PEX3 on the peroxisomal surface and are inserted without ATP or GTP hydrolysis. PEX3 itself is handled differently, docking with PEX16, and both can enter the ER or mitochondrial outer membrane, from which pre-peroxisomal vesicles bud and fuse to seed new organelles. Cargoes include the ABCD fatty acid transporters, the PEX13/PEX14 matrix import docking complex, and PEX11B and FIS1 for peroxisome division, linking membrane assembly to beta-oxidation and ether lipid synthesis.

Peroxisomes cannot build themselves without first installing their membrane proteins, and class I peroxisomal membrane protein import is the route most of them take. The cytosolic chaperone-receptor PEX19 captures newly made membrane proteins, recognising signals within their transmembrane segments, and delivers them to PEX3 in the peroxisomal membrane, where insertion proceeds without ATP or GTP hydrolysis; PEX3 itself is handled by PEX19 together with PEX16, and both can enter the ER membrane co-translationally so that budded vesicles seed new peroxisomes. The cargoes placed this way define what the organelle can do: fatty acid transporters such as ABCD1 and ABCD3, small solute pores, division factors including PEX11B and FIS1, and the docking and ubiquitin-ligase components that import matrix enzymes. Loss of these steps yields peroxisome biogenesis disorders of the Zellweger spectrum, with failed β-oxidation and impaired ether lipid synthesis.

Negative regulation of NOTCH4 signaling restrains the output of a Notch receptor whose activity is concentrated in endothelium, where it shapes arterial-venous identity, sprouting and vessel remodeling; unchecked NOTCH4 activation disrupts vascular development and contributes to breast tumorigenesis, while loss of its brakes is embryonically lethal in mice. Control acts on the cleaved intracellular fragment rather than on ligand binding. AKT1 phosphorylates the fragment so that 14-3-3-zeta sequesters it in the cytosol, keeping it away from the transcriptional complexes it would otherwise coactivate. Phosphorylated fragment is also recognized by FBXW7 within an SCF complex built on SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1, ubiquitinated, and destroyed by the 26S proteasome, whose subunits make up the bulk of the machinery here. Additional inhibition comes from TACC3 binding and from MDM2-dependent degradation downstream of p53, tying Notch dosage to growth and stress signaling.

NOTCH4 is the endothelial-biased Notch receptor, and restraining its output keeps angiogenesis and vascular remodelling in check; loss of that restraint gives excess Notch activity, disordered vessel development and, in mammary and other epithelia, oncogenic transformation. Signalling is shut down after receptor cleavage, by preventing the released NOTCH4 intracellular domain from reaching the nucleus and by destroying it. AKT1-mediated phosphorylation creates a binding site for 14-3-3-zeta (YWHAZ), which sequesters the fragment in the cytosol, while the F-box protein FBXW7 within an SCF complex built on SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1 recognises the phosphorylated fragment and polyubiquitinates it for destruction by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits is represented here. Binding to the centrosomal coiled-coil protein TACC3 provides a further inhibitory interaction. This is ubiquitin-proteasome control of a developmental transcriptional switch.

Defective Base Excision Repair Associated with MUTYH describes what happens when the adenine DNA glycosylase MUTYH fails, removing a safeguard against oxidative mutagenesis and predisposing carriers to colorectal adenomas and cancer. Oxidation of guanine to 8-oxoguanine, or incorporation of 8-oxo-dGTP from the nucleotide pool, creates templates that direct misinsertion of adenine; MUTYH excises that mispaired adenine from the nascent strand so base excision repair can restore the correct cytosine. When its catalytic activity or its partnerships with other repair proteins are lost, the mispairs are fixed as G:C to T:A transversions, which accumulate in APC and KRAS and drive tumour formation. Biallelic germline mutations produce MUTYH-associated polyposis, a recessive syndrome resembling familial adenomatous polyposis but with later onset and fewer polyps, alongside duodenal, gastric and other extracolonic tumours. Distinct isoforms distribute the enzyme between nucleus and mitochondria.

Oxidative damage turns guanine into 8-oxoguanine, which pairs with adenine during replication and fixes G:C to T:A transversions into the genome unless the misincorporated adenine is removed. The adenine DNA glycosylase encoded by MUTYH performs that removal, excising adenine mispaired with guanine or 8-oxoguanine on the nascent strand and initiating base excision repair to restore the correct base. When this activity is lost through biallelic germline mutation, the mutational signature accumulates in genes such as APC and KRAS, producing MUTYH-associated polyposis: multiple colorectal adenomas and a high lifetime risk of colorectal cancer, with additional duodenal, gastric, skin and breast tumours reported. Defective repair arises both from missense changes that cripple glycosylase catalysis, including the recurrent Y165C and G382D substitutions, and from variants that leave catalysis intact but disturb partner interactions or subcellular targeting between nucleus and mitochondria.

Lipophagy is the selective autophagy of lipid droplets, the route by which cells mobilise stored triglyceride into free fatty acids for mitochondrial oxidation when nutrients are scarce. It supplies energy during fasting, keeps hepatocytes from accumulating fat, and its failure contributes to steatosis and the lipid overload seen in fatty liver disease and ageing tissues. Access to the droplet core is gated by its protein coat: perilipins PLIN2 and PLIN3 shield stored lipid, and their recognition by the chaperone HSPA8 and delivery to lysosomal degradation strips the surface so that autophagic membranes can engulf the droplet. The AMP-activated protein kinase subunits present here provide the nutrient sensor that triggers the process, coupling a falling energy charge to both autophagy initiation and lipolysis. Lipophagy therefore links autophagic membrane traffic to whole-body lipid and energy homeostasis.

Cells store neutral lipid in droplets and must mobilise it when nutrients run short; lipophagy is the autophagic route to that mobilisation, delivering droplet triglyceride to lysosomes for hydrolysis into free fatty acids that feed mitochondrial beta-oxidation. It matters most in hepatocytes, where failure of droplet turnover contributes to steatosis and fatty liver disease, and it links lipid stores to the cell's energy-sensing machinery. The droplet surface is coated by perilipins, and PLIN2 and PLIN3 must be removed before autophagic components can engage the droplet; the chaperone HSPA8 recognises these coat proteins and routes them for chaperone-mediated degradation. The AMP-activated protein kinase subunits present here provide the starvation signal: rising AMP activates the kinase, which promotes autophagy initiation and suppresses lipogenesis, coupling nutrient scarcity to breakdown of stored fat.

Chaperone Mediated Autophagy is the selective route by which single cytosolic proteins are delivered to the lysosome for degradation, one protein at a time rather than in bulk vesicles. It lets cells clear damaged, oxidised or misfolded proteins and remodel their proteome during nutrient stress, and its decline with age contributes to the accumulation of aggregation-prone proteins in neurodegeneration; PARK7, a Parkinson disease gene, is among its substrates. The cytosolic chaperone HSPA8, with HSP90 co-chaperones, recognises a KFERQ-like pentapeptide motif in target proteins and brings them to the lysosomal surface, where LAMP2A oligomerises to form a translocation channel and the substrate is unfolded and passed into the lumen. Lipid droplet proteins such as perilipins are removed this way to permit lipolysis, and cytoskeletal and ubiquitin components modulate lysosomal positioning and substrate flux.

Chaperone-mediated autophagy is the selective route by which single cytosolic proteins, rather than bulk cargo in vesicles, are delivered across the lysosomal membrane and degraded. It lets cells dispose of individual damaged or misfolded proteins and mobilise amino acids during nutrient stress, and its decline with age is linked to accumulation of aggregation-prone proteins in neurodegeneration. Substrates carrying a KFERQ-like recognition motif are bound by the cytosolic chaperone HSPA8 with HSP90 co-chaperones, brought to the lysosomal surface, and threaded through a translocation complex formed by the LAMP2A receptor, whose multimerisation is the rate-limiting step. Cytoskeletal and lipid-droplet proteins such as GFAP, vimentin and the perilipins regulate or populate the lysosomal membrane microenvironment, while PARK7 and centrosomal and ciliary proteins are among the substrates cleared, connecting this pathway to proteostasis, lipid mobilisation and organelle turnover.

FOXO-mediated transcription of oxidative stress, metabolic and neuronal genes is the transcriptional output of FOXO factors when insulin signalling is low, turning fasting and stress into coordinated changes in antioxidant defence, fuel supply, appetite and muscle mass. It matters because it keeps blood glucose steady between meals, protects neurons from reactive oxygen species, and, when chronically active, drives muscle wasting and contributes to insulin resistance and neurodegeneration. FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4 and FOXO6 bind insulin-responsive elements to induce mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and catalase, the gluconeogenic enzymes PCK1 and G6PC, and IGFBP1, while repressing glucokinase and SREBF1 through SIN3A-HDAC complexes to limit lipogenesis. In hypothalamic neurons they raise NPY and AGRP and silence POMC to stimulate feeding; in skeletal muscle they induce the atrophy ubiquitin ligases FBXO32 and TRIM63. Insulin-driven PI3K/AKT signalling shuts the programme off, with PPARGC1A, SIRT3 and SMAD partners tuning it.

FOXO transcription factors act as the nuclear output of insulin and growth factor signalling, and this branch covers their direct control of oxidative stress defence, fuel metabolism and neuronal gene programmes. When insulin is low, as in fasting, PI3K/AKT no longer restrains FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4 and FOXO6, which then drive hepatic gluconeogenesis through PCK1 and G6PC1 while repressing glucokinase via a SIN3A:HDAC corepressor complex and repressing SREBF1 to hold back lipogenesis; IGFBP1 and resistin further tune systemic insulin sensitivity. In hypothalamic neurons the same factors raise the orexigenic peptides NPY and AGRP and repress POMC, linking nutrient status to appetite. Antioxidant targets SOD2 and catalase, with contributions from cofactors such as PPARGC1A, SIRT3 and ataxin-3, limit superoxide and peroxide burden and support neuronal survival in neurodegeneration. FOXO6 also induces PLXNA4 during cortical radial glia migration, and FBXO32 and TRIM63 induction underlies starvation-induced muscle wasting.

Transcriptional regulation of granulopoiesis describes how a hematopoietic stem cell in the bone marrow is committed, step by step, to become a neutrophil or other granulocyte, the most abundant leukocytes in blood and the front line of antibacterial defence. Loss of this program produces neutropenia and recurrent infection, while its corruption by fusion proteins involving RUNX1, KMT2A or the retinoic acid receptor underlies myeloid leukemia. RUNX1 and its CBFB partner induce SPI1, which activates CEBPA; CEBPA then drives GFI1, KLF5, CSF3R and IL6R, autoregulates, and restrains proliferation by repressing MYC and by binding CDK2 and CDK4 so that progenitors differentiate rather than divide. CEBPE and SPI1 switch on the granule proteins used for microbial killing. During infection, G-CSF and GM-CSF signalling through STAT3 substitutes CEBPB for CEBPA, relieving MYC repression to expand progenitors in emergency granulopoiesis, with chromatin and histone-level changes accompanying commitment.

Neutrophils and the other granulocytes are the most abundant leukocytes in blood, and this transcriptional programme is how hematopoietic stem cells are routed through multipotent and common myeloid progenitors into granulocyte-monocyte progenitors and on to mature, granule-laden cells. RUNX1 with core binding factor induces SPI1 (PU.1), which turns on CEBPA; CEBPA then autoregulates and drives CEBPE, GFI1, KLF5 and the receptors CSF3R and IL6R, while simultaneously repressing MYC and binding CDK2 and CDK4 to curb proliferation so that differentiation can proceed. Under infection, G-CSF signalling through STAT3 favours CEBPB, relieving MYC repression and expanding progenitors in emergency granulopoiesis. Retinoic acid receptors, MYB, GATA2, TAL1, FLI1, EP300 and chromatin/histone components shape the underlying promoter landscape. Disruption of these factors underlies congenital neutropenia and the differentiation block of acute myeloid leukemia, including PML-RARA-driven disease.

NR1H2 & NR1H3 regulate gene expression to control bile acid homeostasis describes how the liver X receptors, sensors of cellular sterol excess, tune the synthesis, transport and disposal of bile acids. This matters because bile acids are both the route by which cholesterol leaves the body and detergents that damage hepatocytes and enterocytes when they accumulate; the pathway links sterol sensing to safe handling of that load. Activated by oxysterol ligands, NR1H2 and NR1H3 heterodimerise with retinoid X receptors on target promoters, exchanging NCOR1 and NCOR2 corepressor complexes for coactivators such as NCOA1. Among the induced genes are the ileal bile acid binding protein FABP6, which shuttles bile acids during enterohepatic recirculation, and UGT1A3, which glucuronidates hydrophobic bile acids into polar products cleared in urine. The pathway sits within nuclear receptor control of lipid metabolism and hepatic detoxification.

Liver X receptors, encoded by NR1H3 (LXR alpha) and NR1H2 (LXR beta), sense cellular oxysterols and reprogram transcription to unload excess sterol; one arm of that program tunes how bile acids are made, carried and disposed of. This matters because bile acids are both detergents needed for fat absorption and potentially cytotoxic molecules, so their levels must be held within a narrow range to avoid cholestatic liver injury. Ligand-bound LXRs heterodimerise with retinoid X receptors (RXRA, RXRB) and switch from corepressor complexes containing NCOR1 and NCOR2 to coactivators such as NCOA1, driving target genes including the glucuronosyltransferase UGT1A3, which conjugates hydrophobic bile acids into polar forms suitable for urinary excretion, and the ileal bile acid binding protein FABP6, which shuttles bile acids during enterohepatic recycling.

Defective Base Excision Repair Associated with NEIL3 describes what happens when the DNA glycosylase NEIL3 cannot excise oxidized bases, the first step of base excision repair. NEIL3 prefers single-stranded and quadruplex DNA and removes hydantoin lesions from oxidized guanine as well as thymine glycol, work that matters most at telomeres and ahead of replication forks, where unrepaired lesions block polymerases; it also unhooks psoralen- and abasic-site interstrand crosslinks independently of the Fanconi anemia route. A catalytically dead D132V variant leaves oxidative lesions in place and predisposes homozygous carriers to autoimmune disease, while loss of the enzyme causes telomere attrition, impaired proliferation of neural stem cells with learning and memory deficits, and worse outcomes after myocardial infarction and in atherosclerotic plaque, some of these through transcriptional rather than repair functions. The pathway thus links oxidative genome maintenance to stem cell renewal and vascular disease.

Oxidative attack on DNA leaves lesions that must be excised before they block replication or cause mutation, and the glycosylase NEIL3 is the enzyme that initiates that removal in a particular niche: single-stranded DNA, telomeric repeats, and replication forks. It cleaves hydantoin products of guanine oxidation and thymine glycol, and also unhooks certain interstrand crosslinks independently of the Fanconi anaemia route, so loss of activity leaves both oxidative base damage and crosslinks unresolved. Failure of this arm of base excision repair has consequences beyond mutagenesis: an inactivating variant predisposes to autoimmune disease, depletion accelerates telomere loss, and deficiency limits proliferation of neural stem cells and adult hippocampal neurogenesis, with learning and memory deficits. Expression rises in failing heart and atherosclerotic plaque, where its protective role appears only partly explained by DNA repair.

Protein hydroxylation is the enzymatic addition of hydroxyl groups to specific amino acid side chains, a modification that tunes how proteins fold, interact, and are read by the translation and transcription machinery. It matters because these oxygenases sense oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate directly: their activity links cellular metabolic and oxygen status to protein function, and losses cause defects ranging from impaired ribosome fidelity to abnormal blood clotting. Members of the JmjC and related 2-OG-dependent oxygenase family hydroxylate proline, lysine, asparagine, arginine, aspartate, and histidine residues on targets that include ribosomal proteins such as RPS23 and RPL8, translation factors, splicing factors, and developmentally regulated GTPases. Aspartyl/asparaginyl hydroxylase acts on EGF-like domains of secreted proteins including coagulation factor IX, while JMJD6 modification of splicing and elongation regulators couples this chemistry to gene expression control.

Protein hydroxylation adds a hydroxyl group to specific proline, lysine, asparagine, aspartate, arginine or histidine side chains, a modification made by 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases that consume oxygen and iron and so report on cellular oxygen and metabolite supply. Outside collagen maturation, which is handled separately, these marks tune the ribosome and the translational apparatus: ribosomal proteins such as RPS23, RPL8 and RPL27A are hydroxylated by enzymes including OGFOD1 and RIOX1/RIOX2, affecting translational fidelity and stop-codon readthrough, while JMJD4 hydroxylates the release factor ETF1 to promote efficient termination. Other members act on splicing and RNA-binding proteins such as U2AF2 and on the GTPases DRG1 and DRG2, and ASPH hydroxylates aspartate in EGF-like domains of secreted proteins including coagulation factor IX. Collectively the pathway links oxygen availability to gene expression, protein synthesis and cell growth, and several of these oxygenases are overexpressed in tumours.

Defective NTHL1 substrate binding describes the loss of a DNA glycosylase that normally initiates base excision repair of oxidised pyrimidines, and the tumour predisposition that follows. NTHL1 recognises lesions such as thymine glycol and 5-hydroxyuracil generated by reactive oxygen species, excises the damaged base, and leaves an abasic site for downstream APE1, polymerase beta and ligase steps to restore the sequence. Truncating germline mutations, exemplified by the Gln90 nonsense allele, remove the DNA-binding and glycosylase domains so that damaged bases are never engaged, leaving oxidative lesions to be misread during replication and producing a characteristic mutational signature of C-to-T transitions. Inherited biallelically, these alleles cause an autosomal recessive tumour syndrome with adenomatous polyposis, colorectal and breast cancer and multiple other neoplasms, placing this glycosylase step among the genome-stability caretakers whose failure permits mutation accumulation.

NTHL1 is the DNA glycosylase that initiates base excision repair of oxidized pyrimidines, recognizing lesions such as thymine glycol in duplex DNA and excising the damaged base so that downstream AP endonuclease, polymerase and ligase steps can restore the sequence. Loss of substrate binding by truncated NTHL1 protein removes that first recognition step: the germline nonsense and frameshift alleles found in patients delete the DNA-binding and glycosylase regions, leaving oxidative base damage unrepaired and driving a characteristic mutational signature of C>T transitions. Biallelic inheritance causes a tumour predisposition syndrome with adenomatous colorectal polyposis, colorectal and breast cancer, and a broad spread of other malignant and benign tumours. The biology situates oxidative genome maintenance upstream of cancer avoidance, and illustrates how a defect in lesion recognition, rather than in catalysis alone, is sufficient to abolish repair.

Evasion of Oxidative Stress Induced Senescence Due to Defective p16INK4A binding to CDK4 and CDK6 describes how tumour cells escape a barrier that normally halts proliferation permanently. Oxidative stress and other damaging signals induce p16INK4A, which clamps the CDK4 and CDK6 kinases, prevents RB phosphorylation, and locks cells out of S phase in a stable senescent state. Missense substitutions and truncations of CDKN2A abolish the physical interaction with these kinases, so the cyclin D-CDK4/6 module remains active and stressed cells keep dividing rather than withdrawing from the cycle. This loss underlies familial melanoma and is one of the most common events in sporadic cancers; the same mutations also relieve p16INK4A-mediated restraint of NF-kB signalling, adding an inflammatory component. The pathway sits at the interface of cell cycle control, redox stress responses, and tumour suppression, and explains the rationale for CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy.

Oxidative stress normally pushes cells into permanent cell cycle arrest, and p16INK4A is the brake that enforces it by binding CDK4 and CDK6 and blocking their phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein. Missense substitutions and truncations of CDKN2A that destroy this binding let the kinases remain active, so cells that have accumulated reactive oxygen damage continue to proliferate instead of entering senescence. This escape from a tumour-suppressive barrier is one reason CDKN2A is among the most frequently inactivated loci in human cancer, notably in familial melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma and glioma. Loss of p16INK4A function also relieves its restraint on NF-kB-dependent transcription, adding an inflammatory and survival-promoting component to the phenotype. The biology sits at the junction of redox stress sensing, G1/S checkpoint control and the senescence programme that limits the lifespan of damaged cells.

NEIL3-mediated resolution of ICLs is a repair route that removes interstrand crosslinks, the lesions that covalently tie the two strands of the double helix together and block both replication and transcription. Cells that cannot clear such crosslinks stall replication forks and accumulate chromosome breakage, the defect underlying Fanconi anemia and the basis for the cytotoxicity of psoralen and crosslinking chemotherapeutics. Here the glycosylase NEIL3 acts at a converged replication fork and cleaves the N-glycosyl bond of the crosslinked base directly, unhooking psoralen-induced and abasic-site-derived crosslinks without incising the phosphodiester backbone. Because no double-strand break is generated, this route bypasses the Fanconi anemia nuclease machinery and homologous recombination altogether, offering a faster, less mutagenic option. It represents a specialised extension of base excision repair into replication-coupled crosslink tolerance and genome maintenance.

Interstrand crosslinks covalently tie the two strands of the double helix together and block both replication and transcription until they are removed. This route unhooks certain crosslinks directly, using the DNA glycosylase NEIL3 to cleave one of the two glycosidic bonds holding the lesion in place, converting the crosslink into a pair of more tractable single-strand lesions that base excision repair and downstream replication can handle. It acts on psoralen-induced crosslinks and on those arising spontaneously from abasic sites reacting with an opposing base, and it does so without the Fanconi anaemia machinery, so it avoids the double-strand break intermediates and incisions that nuclease-dependent crosslink repair requires. Acting at stalled replication forks, it offers cells a rapid, low-risk first option for crosslink removal, with the Fanconi anaemia route as backup when the lesion resists unhooking.

Prevention of phagosomal-lysosomal fusion describes how Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside macrophages by arresting the maturation of the phagosome that engulfed it. Normally a phagosome acquires RAB5A and then RAB7A, gains phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate, recruits tethering and sorting factors such as HGS and VPS33B, and fuses with lysosomes to destroy its contents; blocking this step gives the bacterium a protected replicative niche and explains the chronic, latent character of tuberculosis. Shed lipoarabinomannan inserts into lipid rafts of the phagosomal membrane, mycobacterial phosphatases strip PI3P and so disable RAB5 effector recruitment, the actin-associated protein coronin-1A is subverted, and VPS33B-dependent fusion is inhibited, with ubiquitin contributing to turnover of the affected trafficking machinery. The result is a host-pathogen interface where innate antimicrobial killing and antigen delivery to degradative compartments both fail.

Intracellular pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis survive inside macrophages by arresting the phagosome before it can merge with lysosomes, and this blockade of phagosomal-lysosomal fusion is what lets the bacterium persist in the very cell meant to destroy it. Normally a phagosome matures by exchanging early markers for late ones, acquiring RAB5A and then RAB7A, recruiting tethering and sorting factors including HGS and the fusion mediator VPS33B, and finally delivering its contents to an acidic, hydrolase-rich lysosome. Shed bacterial cell wall lipoarabinomannan inserts into the phagosomal membrane and disrupts these steps, retaining the actin-associated protein coronin-1A, interfering with VPS33B, and depleting the phosphoinositide signal that RAB5A effectors require. Ubiquitin contributed here reflects the ubiquitin-dependent sorting and degradative control that accompanies phagosome maturation. The outcome is a non-fusogenic replicative niche and failed bacterial killing.

Manipulation of host energy metabolism describes how Mycobacterium tuberculosis rewires the glycolytic machinery of the macrophage it infects, turning an immune cell into a nutrient-rich niche. Secreted bacterial proteins stimulate the activity of host glycolytic enzymes, here represented by phosphoglycerate kinase and enolase, which together carry the payoff phase of glycolysis. The consequence is increased glucose uptake and, because flux through the pathway is unbalanced, accumulation of dihydroxyacetone phosphate, a precursor that feeds glycerolipid synthesis. The infected phagocyte therefore builds lipid, contributing to the foamy macrophage phenotype characteristic of tuberculous granulomas and supplying fatty acids that the bacillus uses as its preferred carbon source. This is host-pathogen metabolic subversion rather than signalling: by shifting central carbon metabolism, the bacterium secures nutrients and blunts effective macrophage killing, favouring persistence.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis does not simply survive inside a macrophage; it rewires the cell's metabolism to suit itself. Bacterial secreted proteins stimulate host glycolytic enzymes, and this manipulation of host energy metabolism raises glucose uptake and flux through the pathway, causing dihydroxyacetone phosphate to accumulate and feeding glycerolipid synthesis. The result is the lipid-laden foamy macrophage characteristic of tuberculous granulomas, a nutrient-rich niche in which the bacterium persists. The host enzymes affected, enolase and phosphoglycerate kinase, catalyse consecutive steps of the glycolytic payoff phase, converting 3-phosphoglycerate onward toward phosphoenolpyruvate and generating ATP; enolase also functions at the cell surface as a plasminogen receptor. This is an example of a pathogen redirecting central carbon metabolism of the immune cell that is meant to destroy it, and it links infection biology to macrophage lipid handling and immunometabolism.

Metal ion assimilation from the host describes how bacterial pathogens strip iron and other trace metals from human tissue in order to grow, and how the host tries to withhold them. Iron is scarce in the body because it is locked inside heme and carrier proteins, so enterobacteria secrete siderophores such as enterobactin, salmochelin, yersiniabactin and aerobactin to capture ferric ion at high affinity, take up the loaded complexes through dedicated outer-membrane receptors, and separately import ferrous iron under acidic or anaerobic conditions. Hemolysins lyse erythrocytes and free hemoglobin, whose alpha and beta globin chains yield heme that is imported and degraded to release the metal. Zinc, manganese, cobalt, nickel and copper are scavenged by analogous transporters. This nutritional tug-of-war is a determinant of virulence, and the host counters it with nutritional immunity through iron and manganese sequestration.

Bacterial pathogens colonising a mammalian host must extract iron and other transition metals from tissues in which those metals are deliberately kept scarce, and this metal ion assimilation from the host determines whether an infection can establish. Iron is the limiting nutrient: it circulates complexed in heme within hemoglobin, whose alpha and beta globin chains are represented here as the host-derived substrate. Hemolysins lyse erythrocytes and release hemoglobin, from which heme is captured, imported and degraded to liberate Fe2+, while free ferric iron is scavenged by high-affinity siderophores such as enterobactin, aerobactin, yersiniabactin and salmochelin and taken up as chelate complexes. Distinct transport systems handle zinc, manganese, cobalt, nickel and copper. Because host nutritional immunity works by sequestering exactly these ions, the acquisition machinery is concentrated in pathogenic strains and behaves as a virulence determinant.

Wax biosynthesis produces the esters of long-chain fatty alcohols and long-chain fatty acids that coat the skin surface, keeping it supple and resistant to water loss and abrasion. In humans this chemistry is concentrated in sebaceous glands and the meibomian glands of the eyelid, where wax esters dominate the secreted lipid film; loss of these lipids leaves skin dry and the tear film unstable. Two steps are defined enzymatically: peroxisomal fatty acyl-CoA reductases FAR1 and FAR2 reduce activated fatty acids to fatty alcohols, and the acyl-CoA wax alcohol acyltransferases AWAT1 and AWAT2 esterify those alcohols in the endoplasmic reticulum. An unidentified transport step must move alcohols between the two compartments, since co-expression of the reductases and transferases is sufficient to make non-sebaceous cells produce wax. FAR1 also supplies alcohols for ether lipid synthesis.

Wax esters are long-chain fatty alcohols esterified to long-chain fatty acids, and their synthesis supplies the sebaceous lipids that waterproof skin and hair and protect the surface from drying and abrasion. The route has two characterized enzymatic steps in humans. Fatty acyl-CoA reductases FAR1 and FAR2, anchored in the peroxisomal membrane, reduce activated fatty acids to fatty alcohols; the alcohols then reach the endoplasmic reticulum, where the acyltransferases AWAT1 and AWAT2 condense them with acyl-CoA to give the finished ester. How alcohols move between the two compartments is unresolved, but co-expression of a reductase with an acyltransferase is sufficient to make non-sebaceous cells produce wax, arguing the transfer step is not limiting. The same reductase activity also feeds ether lipid and plasmalogen synthesis, linking sebum production to peroxisomal lipid metabolism more broadly.

Aggrephagy is the selective autophagic clearance of protein aggregates that the proteasome cannot handle, and it is the cell's last defence against the accumulation of misfolded, insoluble protein. Its failure underlies inclusion-body diseases of neurons, where aggregated species persist and become toxic. Misfolded proteins are tagged with ubiquitin, recognised by HDAC6, and hauled along microtubules by the dynein motor complex to the microtubule-organizing centre, where centrosomal and intermediate filament components such as pericentrin and vimentin enclose them in a single aggresome that is then engulfed by autophagosomes. The pathway is coordinated with the heat shock response through HSF1 and HSP90, and draws in AAA-ATPase and E3 ligase activity via VCP and parkin, linking it to mitochondrial quality control. Substrates include misfolded CFTR and aggregation-prone neurodegeneration proteins, making this a central arm of cytoplasmic proteostasis.

When misfolded proteins outpace what the proteasome can handle, cells sequester them into a single perinuclear inclusion and clear it by autophagy — the route known as aggrephagy. This gives cells a disposal option for aggregation-prone species that cannot be threaded into a proteasome, and its failure underlies inclusion-body pathology in neurodegeneration and the retention of misfolded CFTR. Ubiquitin tags on the substrate, added and extended with the help of conjugating enzymes, are read by HDAC6, which links cargo to dynein motors that haul it along microtubules toward the centrosome; tubulins, pericentrin and centrin mark that destination. There the material is caged by vimentin intermediate filaments to form an aggresome. Chaperone and unfoldase activity from HSP90, VCP and the HSF1-driven stress response, together with PRKN and PARK7, feeds the inclusion into autophagic degradation, tying protein quality control to microtubule transport.

EML4 and NUDC in mitotic spindle formation describes how a microtubule-binding protein and its partner are handed off at mitotic entry to build a spindle capable of capturing chromosomes. It matters because accurate attachment of microtubule ends to kinetochores and alignment of chromosomes at the metaphase plate determine whether daughter cells inherit a correct genome; failure produces missegregation and aneuploidy. In interphase EML4 binds and stabilises microtubules, but phosphorylation by the NEK6/NEK7/NEK9 kinase module releases it, permitting the dynamic microtubule turnover a spindle requires. Through its WD40 repeats EML4 recruits NUDC to kinetochores, where it acts alongside the constitutive centromere proteins, the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes, the RZZ and spindle assembly checkpoint machinery, dynein with its LIS1/NDEL1 regulators, and Aurora B. The N-terminal region of EML4 is also the fusion partner that creates constitutively active ALK in a subset of non-small cell lung cancers.

Cells entering mitosis must convert a stable interphase microtubule array into a dynamic spindle that captures every chromosome, and EML4 together with NUDC is required for that switch, for attaching spindle microtubule ends to kinetochores, and for aligning chromosomes at the metaphase plate. EML4 is a WD40-repeat protein that binds and stabilizes interphase microtubules; phosphorylation by the NEK6 and NEK7 kinases at mitotic entry releases it from microtubules, while its WD40 repeats recruit NUDC to kinetochores. The surrounding machinery here is the kinetochore itself — centromeric CENP proteins, the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes, spindle assembly checkpoint components, depolymerizing kinesins, dynein with its NDE1/NDEL1 and LIS1 regulators, Aurora B and PP2A phosphatase modules, and α/β-tubulins. Errors produce misaligned chromosomes and aneuploidy; rearrangement fusing EML4 to ALK drives a recurrent subset of non-small cell lung cancer.

Response of EIF2AK1 (HRI) to heme deficiency is the arm of the integrated stress response that matches globin synthesis to heme supply during red cell formation. It matters because without it, developing erythroblasts keep translating globin they cannot fold, producing heme-free aggregates, ineffective erythropoiesis and anemia under iron deficiency; the same axis influences fetal hemoglobin levels and is of interest in hemoglobinopathies. HRI binds heme at two sites, and loss of heme from the kinase insert domain releases inhibition, allowing autophosphorylation and phosphorylation of eIF2-alpha. This dampens general translation, especially of ribosomal proteins, while selectively promoting translation of upstream-ORF mRNAs such as ATF4, ATF5 and DDIT3. ATF4 then drives amino acid and redox genes including ASNS and CHAC1, feedback regulators GADD34 and TRIB3, and GRB10 to restrain mTORC1; unresolved stress tips toward CHOP-dependent apoptosis. HRI is also activated by oxidative, heat and osmotic stress.

Developing red cells must make globin only as fast as heme is available, and this heme-sensing arm of the integrated stress response is how they match the two. EIF2AK1, the heme-regulated inhibitor, binds heme at two sites; when heme dissociates from the kinase insert domain the kinase autophosphorylates and phosphorylates the alpha subunit of eIF2, damping general translation while favouring mRNAs with upstream open reading frames. The result is induction of ATF4, ATF5 and DDIT3 together with partner factors CEBPB and CEBPG and targets such as ASNS, CHAC1 and TRIB3, plus GRB10 to restrain mTORC1 and PPP1R15A to reverse the phosphorylation and end the response. Losing this control leaves heme-free globin to aggregate, and in iron deficiency produces ineffective erythropoiesis and anemia; the same kinase also responds to oxidative, heat and osmotic stress and influences fetal hemoglobin levels.

Signaling by MAP2K mutants describes how activating mutations in MEK1 and MEK2 lock the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade into a constitutively active state, driving proliferation independently of upstream growth factor input. Such mutations appear at low frequency across many cancers, including melanoma, lung and colorectal tumours, and in the germline they cause developmental disorders of the RASopathy family such as Noonan and cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes, where dysregulated ERK output distorts craniofacial, cardiac and skin development. Mechanistically the mutant kinases escape the autoinhibitory constraints normally imposed by their regulatory helix and by RAF-dependent activation, so they phosphorylate ERK1 and ERK2 persistently, sustaining transcriptional programs for cell cycle entry and survival. Because these variants can also confer resistance to RAF-directed therapy, they matter clinically for the choice and sequencing of MAPK pathway inhibitors.

MEK1 and MEK2 are the kinases that sit between RAF and ERK, and mutations that lock them in an active state drive constitutive output through this arm of the RAS-ERK cascade. Signaling by MAP2K mutants describes that deregulated state: altered MAP2K1 or MAP2K2 phosphorylate the ERK1 and ERK2 kinases regardless of upstream input, sustaining proliferative and survival transcription programmes without growth factor stimulation. Such alleles arise somatically at low frequency across many tumour types, including melanoma, lung and colorectal cancer and histiocytic neoplasms, and also in the germline, where they produce Noonan and cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes and related RASopathies with their characteristic cardiac, craniofacial and skin features. Because mutations in the negative-regulatory and allosteric regions can bypass RAF dependence, they are a recognised route to resistance against RAF- and MEK-directed inhibitors, making the identity of the mutation clinically consequential.

Sensory processing of sound is hearing at the level of the cochlea: how mechanical vibration is converted into neural signals by the hair cells of the organ of Corti. It defines the inner and outer hair cell phenotypes, and mutations in its components are the commonest causes of inherited deafness, from Usher syndrome to auditory neuropathy. Stereocilia built on tightly regulated actin bundles are linked tip-to-tip by cadherin-23 and protocadherin-15; deflection tensions these links and gates a mechanotransduction channel formed with TMC1/TMC2, TMIE, LHFPL5 and CIB2, depolarising the cell. In inner hair cells, voltage-gated calcium entry triggers otoferlin-dependent glutamate release at ribbon synapses scaffolded by RIBEYE, bassoon and piccolo onto spiral ganglion afferents. Outer hair cells instead amplify motion through voltage-driven prestin conformational change, tuned by potassium channels and by cholinergic efferent feedback through the CHRNA9/CHRNA10 receptor. Noise overexposure damages these structures, causing temporary or permanent hearing loss.

Hearing begins when cochlear hair cells convert mechanical vibration into electrical signals, and this is the machinery that makes that conversion possible. Inner hair cells act as the sensory receptors that drive auditory nerve firing, while outer hair cells amplify motion of the organ of Corti; loss of either causes sensorineural deafness, and many of these genes are mutated in inherited hearing loss and Usher syndrome. Stereocilia built from actin, espin, and unconventional myosins are linked tip to tip by cadherin-23 and protocadherin-15, whose tension gates a mechanoelectrical transduction channel containing TMC1/TMC2 with TMIE, LHFPL5 and CIB2. Depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels at ribbon synapses, where otoferlin triggers glutamate release onto spiral ganglion neurons. Prestin drives voltage-dependent outer hair cell length changes, and potassium and calcium pumps plus cholinergic olivocochlear feedback restore and tune the resting state.

Defective DNA double strand break response due to BRCA1 loss of function describes what happens to genome maintenance when cancer-associated mutations disable BRCA1, the tumour suppressor whose germline loss underlies hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome and confers added risk of pancreatic, stomach, fallopian tube and prostate tumours. BRCA1 normally directs homology-directed repair of double-strand breaks, so cells lacking its function accumulate chromosomal rearrangements and genomic instability, and Brca1-null embryos die early. The mechanism turns on the N-terminal RING domain, which heterodimerises with BARD1 to stabilise BRCA1 and confer E3 ubiquitin ligase activity; mutations in this domain abolish BARD1 binding and exclude BRCA1 from the break response, though whether ligase activity itself is required for tumour suppression remains unsettled. The resulting repair deficiency defines the vulnerability exploited by PARP inhibition and platinum chemotherapy.

Loss of BRCA1 function cripples the cell's ability to repair DNA double-strand breaks by homologous recombination, and the consequence is the hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome: early-onset breast and ovarian tumours, with smaller excesses of pancreatic, gastric, prostate and fallopian tube cancer in carriers. BRCA1 acts at breaks as an obligate heterodimer with BARD1, an interaction made through its N-terminal RING domain that stabilises the protein and confers E3 ubiquitin ligase activity; its C-terminal BRCT repeats read phosphorylated partners in the damage response. Cancer-associated RING mutations abolish BARD1 binding, leaving BRCA1 unable to join the repair reaction. Cells then accumulate chromosomal rearrangements and copy-number change, the genomic instability that drives tumour initiation, and become dependent on alternative repair routes -- the basis for the sensitivity of such tumours to PARP inhibition and crosslinking agents.

FCGR3A-mediated IL10 synthesis describes how immune complexes of IgG engaging Fcγ receptors on macrophages drive production of interleukin-10, the principal brake on inflammation. This output limits and terminates inflammatory responses and shapes differentiation of several immune cell types, but the same circuit can be exploited by pathogens: IgG-opsonized Leishmania amastigotes trigger FcγR-dependent IL-10 that suppresses the killing capacity of phagocytes, favouring persistent cutaneous infection. Mechanistically, IgG heavy and light chain variable and constant regions form the ligand; receptor clustering activates Src-family kinases (LYN, FYN, HCK, FGR) and SYK, then phospholipase Cγ and inositol trisphosphate receptor-driven calcium release with calmodulin, alongside adenylate cyclase–cAMP–protein kinase A signalling that converges on CREB1 to transactivate the IL10 gene. It is a clear example of antibody-mediated feedback linking humoral immunity to myeloid anti-inflammatory programming.

IgG immune complexes engaging Fc gamma receptors on macrophages drive production of the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-10, an arm of Fc receptor signalling that restrains rather than amplifies inflammation. This output limits and terminates inflammatory responses and shapes differentiation of other immune cells, but it can be exploited: IgG-opsonized Leishmania amastigotes trigger it to suppress the killing machinery of phagocytes, favouring parasite survival in cutaneous leishmaniasis. Receptor crosslinking by immunoglobulin heavy and light chains recruits Src-family kinases and SYK, activating phospholipase C gamma and inositol trisphosphate receptor-mediated calcium release, while adenylate cyclases and protein kinase A raise cAMP and converge on CREB1 to transcribe IL10. The same circuitry operates alongside Toll-like receptor input, so the balance between activating and immunoregulatory signals determines whether a macrophage clears or harbours an opsonized pathogen.

Cell recruitment (pro-inflammatory response) is the arm of innate immunity that summons leukocytes to a site of infection and arms them for killing, illustrated here by macrophage encounters with Leishmania. A strong pro-inflammatory burst in acute infection limits parasite load, while a distorted chemokine and cytokine balance permits parasite persistence or drives immunopathology, so the same machinery sets both host defence and tissue damage. Mechanistically the genes centre on the inflammasome: NLRP3 with the adaptor PYCARD and caspase-1 matures IL-1β and IL-18 and cleaves gasdermin D for pyroptotic release, with TXNIP and pyrin among the sensors and modifiers. Extracellular ATP acting through P2RX7 and P2RX4, its hydrolysis by CD39 and CD73, and complement C3–C3AR1 signalling provide the upstream cues, converging on NF-κB-driven transcription of chemoattractant cytokines.

Pro-inflammatory cell recruitment is how an infected tissue calls in leukocytes that can kill intracellular pathogens, and it sets the balance that decides whether an infection such as Leishmania is contained or becomes chronic. A strong early response limits parasite load by bringing in cells with enhanced microbicidal capacity, while a distorted chemokine and cytokine network drives immunopathology or permits parasite survival. Much of the output here is inflammasome-driven: NLRP3 with the adaptor PYCARD and caspase-1 matures IL-1beta and IL-18, and gasdermin D executes the pore-forming, pyroptotic release step; TXNIP and pyrin add further activation inputs. Extracellular nucleotide signalling through P2RX7 and P2RX4 and its termination by ENTPD1 and NT5E tunes the threshold, alongside complement C3 acting on C3AR1 and NF-kB-dependent transcription of the cytokines themselves.</description>

Signaling by ERBB2 KD Mutants describes how point mutations and small insertions in the kinase domain of ERBB2 (HER2) convert a growth factor receptor into a constitutively active oncogenic driver. Such mutations are found in breast, lung, gastric and bladder cancers, often without gene amplification, and they define tumours that may respond to HER2-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors, while secondary mutations at the gatekeeper threonine cause acquired resistance. Mutant ERBB2 heterodimerizes more readily with EGFR and ERBB3 in the presence of neuregulins and EGF-family ligands, increasing autophosphorylation and prolonging recruitment of GRB2, SHC1, SOS1 and GAB1 to drive RAS-ERK signalling, and of PI3K subunits to drive PI3K-AKT survival signalling, with PLCG1 as an additional effector. Folding and stability of the mutant receptor still depend on the HSP90:CDC37 chaperone system, and ERBIN restrains its localization. The net output is ligand-hypersensitive proliferation and cellular transformation.

Point mutations and small insertions in the kinase domain of ERBB2 (HER2) make the receptor signal without normal restraint, and these variants drive breast, lung, gastric and bladder cancers even where the gene is not amplified. Substitutions such as L755S, V777L, D769H, V842I and L869R raise intrinsic kinase activity and favour heterodimerization with EGFR or ERBB3, so ligands of the EGF and neuregulin families feed more strongly into growth signalling. The activated dimers recruit GRB2, SHC1 and SOS1 to load RAS proteins and engage the MAP kinase route, and recruit GAB1 with PI3K subunits to activate PI3K-AKT signalling, with PLCG1 as an additional effector. HSP90 with CDC37 stabilizes the mutant kinase, and secondary gatekeeper changes at T798 confer resistance to HER2-directed inhibitors.

Pexophagy is the selective autophagic removal of peroxisomes, the organelles that break down branched and very-long-chain fatty acids and detoxify hydrogen peroxide. Because damaged peroxisomes leak reactive oxygen species rather than clearing them, their timely disposal sets the cell's oxidative tone and adjusts peroxisome number to shifting nutrient supply. Recognition depends on ubiquitination of peroxisomal membrane proteins, notably the import receptor PEX5, which is read by the autophagy receptors NBR1 and p62/SQSTM1; these tether the organelle to LC3 on the forming phagophore for delivery to the lysosome. The deubiquitinase USP30 opposes the tagging step and restrains turnover, while ATM signalling links oxidative and ROS-sensing cues, alongside hypoxic signalling through EPAS1, to the decision to degrade. Defective pexophagy leaves dysfunctional peroxisomes accumulating, with consequences for lipid catabolism, redox balance and metabolic adaptation.

Pexophagy is the selective autophagy route that clears surplus or damaged peroxisomes, keeping the organelle population matched to metabolic demand. Because peroxisomes both oxidise branched and very-long-chain fatty acids and generate and detoxify hydrogen peroxide, failure to remove dysfunctional ones allows reactive oxygen species to accumulate, while excessive turnover starves cells of lipid catabolism; the balance shifts with nutrient supply and oxidative stress. Targeting works through ubiquitination of peroxisomal membrane proteins, notably the import receptor PEX5, which recruits the autophagy receptors SQSTM1/p62 and NBR1; these bind LC3 on the forming autophagosome and deliver the organelle to the lysosome. The mitochondrial deubiquitinase USP30 opposes tagging by removing ubiquitin, and ATM signalling links oxidative and stress cues to receptor engagement, placing peroxisome quality control within the broader ubiquitin-dependent organelle turnover system.

Resistance of ERBB2 KD mutants to trastuzumab explains why some HER2-driven breast and gastric cancers fail to respond to the monoclonal antibody trastuzumab even though the receptor is the drug's intended target. Trastuzumab binds the extracellular domain of ERBB2 and blocks its dimerisation and downstream growth signalling, but activating point mutations in the receptor's kinase domain drive signalling from within the cell, where an extracellular antibody cannot reach, so proliferative signalling through the MAPK and PI3K routes continues unabated. Stability of the mutant receptor depends on the HSP90 chaperone system together with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37, which makes such tumours sensitive to HSP90 inhibition and to small-molecule kinase inhibitors instead; the scaffold ERBIN modulates receptor localisation and signal output. The pathway is a template for acquired and intrinsic targeted-therapy resistance.

Trastuzumab is a therapeutic antibody directed against the extracellular region of the HER2 receptor, and it works in breast and gastric cancers that overexpress the intact receptor. Mutations in the ERBB2 kinase domain, however, activate signalling from inside the cell and so blunt the benefit of an antibody that acts at the surface, making this a route to acquired or intrinsic drug resistance and a reason patients are stratified by mutation rather than by receptor level alone. The mutant receptor remains dependent on chaperone support, with HSP90 and its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37 stabilising the folded kinase domain, while ERBIN binds HER2 and constrains its localisation and output. The biology sits at the junction of receptor tyrosine kinase signalling, chaperone-dependent oncoprotein stability, and the rationale for kinase inhibitors or HSP90 blockade when antibody therapy fails.

Sunitinib-resistant KIT mutants describes forms of the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase that continue to signal despite treatment with sunitinib, the drug most often given when a KIT-driven cancer has already escaped imatinib. It matters because gastrointestinal stromal tumours and some mast cell and myeloid neoplasms depend on constitutively active KIT for growth and survival, and the sequence of mutations acquired in the kinase domain dictates which inhibitor still works. Sunitinib binds the inactive conformation of the kinase, so substitutions in the activation loop that favour the active state, and certain gatekeeper changes at the ATP pocket, abolish binding while leaving downstream signalling to PI3K-AKT and MAPK intact. This is clonal drug resistance in the classic sense: selection of pre-existing secondary mutations under therapy, driving the choice of later-line kinase inhibitors.

KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase for stem cell factor, and activating mutations in it drive gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis and some acute leukaemias. Such tumours are usually treated first with imatinib, and sunitinib is given second line when resistance emerges; this pathway captures the subset of KIT alleles that resist sunitinib as well. Resistance arises because substitutions in the kinase domain, particularly in the activation loop, reshape the pocket so the drug can no longer hold the receptor in the inactive conformation it requires, leaving the kinase constitutively autophosphorylated and signalling to proliferation and survival effectors without ligand. Clinically this defines the point at which second-line therapy fails and later-generation inhibitors with different conformational preferences are needed.

Inhibition of DNA recombination at telomere is the protective packaging that stops chromosome ends from being mistaken for double-strand breaks. Telomeres look like broken DNA, and unless they are capped they recruit break-repair machinery, triggering damage signalling, senescence, and end-to-end fusions by non-homologous or microhomology-mediated joining. The shelterin complex — TRF1, TRF2, RAP1, TIN2, TPP1 and POT1 — binds telomeric repeats and blocks both recombination and checkpoint activation, while the ATRX-DAXX chaperone deposits histone H3.3 to keep telomeric chromatin repressive and limit transcription by RNA polymerase II of telomeric RNA. Loss of this restraint, especially ATRX inactivation, permits homologous recombination between telomeres and drives alternative lengthening of telomeres, a telomerase-independent route to replicative immortality used by roughly 5-15% of cancers. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of chromosome-end maintenance, chromatin state, and tumour suppression.

Chromosome ends look like double-strand breaks, and this pathway is how cells stop them from being treated as such. Shelterin — TRF1, TRF2, RAP1, TIN2, TPP1 and POT1 — caps telomeric repeats, suppressing end-joining fusions and blocking homologous recombination between telomeres, while the ATRX-DAXX chaperone deposits histone H3.3 to keep telomeric chromatin repressive and limit transcription by RNA polymerase II through the repeats. When capping or chromatin organisation fails, damage signalling at short telomeres drives replicative senescence, uncapped ends fuse to produce dicentric chromosomes and genome instability, and recombination-based alternative lengthening of telomeres can be unleashed. ALT, common in ATRX- or DAXX-deficient tumours such as sarcomas and gliomas, gives cancer cells telomerase-independent immortality. The pathway therefore links chromatin state at chromosome ends to ageing, DNA repair choice and tumour suppression.

Defective F8 accelerates dissociation of the A2 domain describes a molecular mechanism of hemophilia A in which mutant coagulation factor VIII is secreted and activated normally but falls apart too quickly, shortening the burst of clotting activity needed to stop bleeding. Activated factor VIII is a non-covalent heterotrimer whose A2 subunit is held at the A1-A2 and A2-A3 interfaces by intersubunit hydrogen bonds; it serves as the cofactor for factor IXa in the intrinsic factor X-activating complex, amplifying thrombin generation on platelet surfaces. Missense substitutions at these interfaces, such as R550H, A303E, S308L and the R717 variants, weaken those contacts so A2 dissociates prematurely and factor VIIIa decays, collapsing factor Xase activity. Patients therefore show a mild to moderate bleeding phenotype with near-normal antigen levels but discordantly low functional clotting activity.

Activated factor VIII works only as long as it stays assembled: its A2 domain is held non-covalently against the A1 and A3 domains, and once A2 drifts away the cofactor is spent. Because factor VIIIa is the cofactor that lets factor IXa activate factor X on the platelet surface, its lifetime sets how much thrombin a wound can generate. Certain hemophilia A missense substitutions in F8 sit at the A1-A2 and A2-A3 contact surfaces and break the hydrogen bonds that keep the subunit docked; the protein is secreted and can be activated normally but decays far faster than wild type, so intrinsic pathway factor X activation collapses prematurely. The result is a bleeding disorder driven by cofactor instability rather than absent protein, a distinct molecular phenotype from null or secretion-defective mutations and one reason clotting activity can be low despite measurable antigen.

Defective F8 binding to the cell membrane describes a molecular lesion in blood coagulation: mutant factor VIII that can no longer dock onto phospholipid surfaces, and therefore cannot assemble the intrinsic clotting machinery where it is needed. Normally thrombin-activated FVIIIa binds phosphatidylserine exposed on activated platelets through its C1 and C2 discoidin domains, serving as the cofactor that concentrates factor IXa and accelerates factor X activation by orders of magnitude.
