Hemophilia A variants clustered in these membrane-binding domains, including substitutions and deletions such as A2220P and Q2330P, leave the protein expressed but functionally inert, so tenase complex formation fails and thrombin generation is inadequate. The clinical consequence is X-linked hemophilia A with spontaneous joint and soft-tissue bleeding, illustrating how coagulation depends on correct localisation of enzyme complexes to membranes rather than on enzyme activity alone.

Activated factor VIII works only when it is docked on a phospholipid surface, where it serves as the cofactor that accelerates factor IXa-mediated activation of factor X in the intrinsic clotting pathway. Membrane attachment is mediated by the C2 domain of factor VIII, which inserts hydrophobic loops into the exposed phosphatidylserine of activated platelets, concentrating the tenase complex at the site of injury. Missense and small deletion variants in this region, including changes at the C2 domain such as A2220P and Q2330P, leave a protein that can still be secreted and thrombin-cleaved but binds membranes poorly, so tenase assembly fails. The result is haemophilia A, an X-linked bleeding disorder with delayed, unstable clot formation, joint and soft-tissue haemorrhage, and a phenotype whose severity tracks how much residual cofactor function survives.

Defective F9 secretion describes the failure of coagulation factor IX to reach the bloodstream, one of the molecular routes to haemophilia B. Factor IX is a vitamin K-dependent serine protease made by hepatocytes and secreted into plasma, where activated factor IX together with factor VIII drives factor X activation in the intrinsic arm of coagulation; when circulating levels fall, thrombin generation is inadequate and patients suffer recurrent joint and soft-tissue bleeding. Mutations spread across the F9 gene can compromise not only catalytic activity but the earlier steps of protein biogenesis — folding, stability, and export through the secretory pathway — so that mutant protein is retained intracellularly and accumulates rather than being released. This links a bleeding disorder to quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum and secretory trafficking, and explains cases where antigen levels are low despite intact coding of the active site.

Coagulation factor IX is a vitamin K-dependent protease made by hepatocytes and released into plasma, where it works with factor VIII to activate factor X and sustain thrombin generation at a site of injury. Defective secretion of factor IX describes the situation in which mutant F9 protein is synthesised but fails to traverse the secretory pathway efficiently, so it accumulates intracellularly and circulating levels fall rather than the protein being simply inactive. The result is haemophilia B, an X-linked bleeding disorder whose severity tracks residual plasma factor IX activity, with joint and soft tissue haemorrhage in severe cases. Because the defect lies in folding, stability and export rather than catalysis, it connects the biology of blood clotting to quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum and to the post-translational modifications, including gamma-carboxylation and propeptide processing, that a secreted clotting factor must pass through.

Signaling by cytosolic PDGFRA and PDGFRB fusion proteins describes how chromosomal rearrangements convert platelet-derived growth factor receptors into constitutively active oncogenic kinases, driving myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia, chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia and related myeloproliferative disorders. Because these tumours respond dramatically to imatinib, recognising the fusion has direct therapeutic consequences. In each case the receptor's extracellular and transmembrane portions are lost and the cytosolic kinase domain is joined to the N-terminal oligomerisation region of an intracellular protein — the RNA 3' processing factor FIP1L1 in the case of PDGFRA, and coiled-coil or scaffold partners such as striatin for PDGFRB. Forced dimerisation activates the kinase without ligand, so growth factor control is bypassed and downstream RAS-MAPK, PI3K and STAT signalling runs continuously, producing autonomous proliferation and survival of haematopoietic progenitors rather than normal mesenchymal growth responses.

Chromosomal rearrangements can fuse the cytoplasmic kinase domain of the platelet-derived growth factor receptors PDGFRA or PDGFRB to the N-terminal region of an unrelated intracellular protein, and the resulting chimeras signal without ever binding ligand. Because the partner contributes an oligomerization surface, the kinase dimerizes constitutively and fires downstream growth and survival routes — RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT activation — driving proliferation independently of normal receptor control. Such fusions underlie myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia, chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia and related myeloproliferative disease; the FIP1L1 fusion to PDGFRA, in which an RNA 3'-end processing factor supplies the fusion partner, is the best characterised example, while PDGFRB recruits many rarer partners including striatin and WDR48. Clinically these tumours matter because the constitutive kinase remains sensitive to imatinib and related tyrosine kinase inhibitors, making fusion detection directly actionable.

Signaling by membrane-tethered fusions of PDGFRA or PDGFRB covers the oncogenic receptor tyrosine kinases created when chromosomal rearrangements join a dimerization-competent partner to a platelet-derived growth factor receptor that keeps its transmembrane anchor. These fusions drive myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia, as well as some gliomas and sarcomas, and they matter clinically because the resulting kinase is constitutively active yet remains sensitive to imatinib and related inhibitors. Partners such as ETV6, GOLGA4, KANK1, BIN2 and KDR contribute self-association domains that force the kinase domains together at the plasma membrane, bypassing the requirement for PDGF ligand and producing ligand-independent autophosphorylation. The downstream output is the normal PDGFR program -- PI3K/AKT, RAS-MAPK, PLCG and STAT signalling toward proliferation and survival -- but run continuously, converting a growth factor response into autonomous clonal expansion of the affected hematopoietic or mesenchymal cell.

Chromosomal rearrangements can fuse the kinase domain of the platelet-derived growth factor receptors PDGFRA or PDGFRB to an unrelated partner protein, producing constitutively active oncogenic kinases; a subset of these retain the receptor transmembrane segment and so remain anchored at the plasma membrane rather than becoming cytosolic. Partners such as ETV6, KANK1, GOLGA4, BIN2 and KDR contribute self-association domains that drive ligand-independent dimerization and autophosphorylation, switching on the downstream growth and survival routes normally used by PDGF receptors, including RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT signalling. The resulting unchecked proliferative signal underlies myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms, notably chronic eosinophilic leukaemia and myeloproliferative disease with eosinophilia, as well as some gliomas. Because the lesion is a driver kinase, these fusions are typically sensitive to imatinib and related tyrosine kinase inhibitors, making their detection clinically actionable.

Sunitinib-resistant PDGFR mutants describes forms of the platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha kinase that continue to signal despite treatment with sunitinib, the second-line inhibitor used when imatinib fails in PDGFR- and KIT-driven tumours. This matters clinically because gastrointestinal stromal tumours and related malignancies are driven by constitutively active PDGFRA, and sequential kinase inhibition is the mainstay of therapy; mutations that alter the ATP-binding pocket or the activation loop reduce drug affinity while leaving the receptor's ligand-independent kinase activity intact. The consequence is sustained autophosphorylation and downstream RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT signalling, driving proliferation and survival of tumour cells during therapy. Such alleles define acquired or primary resistance and dictate the choice of later-generation inhibitors, making this an example of oncogenic receptor tyrosine kinase signalling escaping pharmacological control.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumours and related cancers are frequently driven by activating mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase PDGFRA, and the small-molecule inhibitor sunitinib is given as second-line therapy when imatinib fails. This biology captures the subset of PDGFRA variants that remain active despite sunitinib binding, so that receptor autophosphorylation and downstream proliferative and survival signalling through RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT continue unchecked. Resistance typically arises from substitutions in the activation loop, notably at the D842 position, which stabilise the active kinase conformation that type II inhibitors such as sunitinib cannot engage; other changes alter the ATP pocket or gatekeeper contacts. Clinically this explains why genotyping the receptor, rather than tumour histology alone, determines which inhibitor is likely to work, and motivates conformation-selective agents for patients whose disease escapes both imatinib and sunitinib.

Potential therapeutics for SARS collects the molecular targets through which candidate drugs act against SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 infection, either by blocking viral entry and replication or by damping the destructive host inflammatory response that drives severe COVID-19. It matters because most agents repurposed during the pandemic were developed for other RNA viruses or for autoimmune disease, and their usefulness depends on which human proteins they hit. Targets here span the entry machinery, including ACE2, furin and clathrin-adaptor endocytosis; interferon and cytokine receptor signalling through JAK/TYK2 and STAT2; B cell receptor kinases such as BTK and SYK; nucleotide synthesis via IMPDH; and chromatin regulators including BRD4 and the NuRD and CoREST complexes. Also represented are off-target liabilities and the pharmacokinetic strategy of inhibiting cytochrome P450 enzymes to sustain antiviral plasma levels, as exploited in ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir therapy, plus neutralising antibody variable regions.

Drug candidates aimed at SARS coronavirus infection fall into two broad groups, and the protein targets here reflect both: machinery the virus needs to enter and mature, and host pathways whose overactivation causes the lung injury and cytokine storm of severe disease. Viral entry factors include the receptor ACE2, the protease FURIN that cleaves spike, and clathrin adaptor subunits used for endocytosis. On the host side, Janus kinases with interferon and interleukin-6 receptors, Bruton tyrosine kinase with B cell receptor adaptors, and kinases such as RIPK1 and ROCK1/2 are targeted by anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory agents, while HSP90, immunophilins, IMPDH nucleotide synthesis, and a NuRD/CoREST corepressor module represent off-target or repurposing interactions. Neutralizing antibody variable regions are also represented. Anticipated liabilities, including inhibition of unrelated essential proteins, are part of the same picture, as is deliberate cytochrome P450 blockade to extend antiviral half-life.

Virion Assembly and Release is the final step of the coronavirus replication cycle, in which newly made structural proteins and genomic RNA are packaged into infectious particles and exported from the cell; blocking it aborts spread even when replication itself proceeds normally. Assembly happens at the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment rather than the plasma membrane, and depends on the host secretory and retrieval machinery: retention signals in the cytoplasmic tails of the viral membrane and spike proteins engage COPI and related coats, so the proteins cycle between compartments and concentrate at the budding site. Homotypic interaction of M protein builds a lattice that bends the membrane and recruits E, S and the helical nucleocapsid, fixing a particle roughly 100 nm across with defined protein stoichiometry. Completed virions then traverse the secretory route for release, making membrane trafficking the effective bottleneck for viral egress.

The last step of a coronavirus replication cycle is building new particles and getting them out of the cell, and it happens not at the plasma membrane but on membranes of the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment. Structural proteins are concentrated there by retrieval signals in their cytoplasmic tails that engage host coat machinery such as COPI, so that repeated anterograde and retrograde trafficking keeps them at the budding site. Assembly begins with self-association of the membrane protein M into a lattice that bends the membrane and recruits the spike, envelope and nucleocapsid proteins, the latter delivering the helical ribonucleoprotein containing the genomic RNA. The result is a roughly 100 nm enveloped particle with spike trimers, abundant M, and packaged nucleocapsid, plus small amounts of accessory proteins, which then exits through the secretory route to infect new cells.

Maturation of protein E covers the post-translational processing of the small envelope protein of a coronavirus after its synthesis on host ribosomes, a step that determines whether virions can assemble and bud correctly from intracellular membranes. Protein E is palmitoylated and ubiquitinated, oligomerises into trimers with ion-channel or porin activity, and accumulates in the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment rather than the plasma membrane, where it contributes to membrane curvature during particle formation and to the ion permeability that shapes secretory-pathway pH. The host contribution here is ubiquitin itself, supplied by the polyubiquitin genes and by the ribosomal protein fusion precursors, illustrating how viruses conscript the ubiquitin system for the modification and turnover of their own structural proteins. Loss of E maturation yields poorly assembled, attenuated virus, which is why it is examined as an antiviral and vaccine-attenuation target.

Coronavirus envelope (E) protein is a small membrane protein that must be modified after synthesis before it can perform its role in virion assembly and budding, and the maturation of protein E covers those post-translational steps. Following translation, E is palmitoylated and ubiquitinated; the host ubiquitin precursors represented here, including the ribosomal fusion proteins RPS27A and UBA52 and the polyubiquitin products of UBB and UBC, supply the ubiquitin that is conjugated to it. Matured E oligomerises into trimers with ion-conducting porin-like activity and remains in internal membranes of the secretory pathway rather than reaching the plasma membrane, consistent with its function at the endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi intermediate compartment where particles bud. This illustrates how viral structural proteins are routed through host modification and ubiquitin systems, which also govern their turnover and immune detection.

Maturation of protein E covers the post-translational processing of the coronavirus envelope protein, a small membrane protein required for assembling and releasing infectious virions. After synthesis, E is palmitoylated on cysteine residues and modified by ubiquitin, steps that govern its stability, oligomerisation and retention in intracellular membranes; the mature protein forms trimeric ion-conducting channels with porin-like activity in the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment rather than reaching the plasma membrane. This viroporin activity alters ionic balance in the secretory pathway, supports virion budding and morphogenesis, and contributes to inflammatory activation during infection. The host contribution here is the ubiquitin supply itself, drawn from the polyubiquitin genes and the ribosomal protein-ubiquitin fusion precursors, illustrating how a virus recruits ordinary host protein-modification machinery to finish building its own structural components.

Maturation of the SARS-CoV-2 envelope (E) protein covers the post-translational modifications that convert the newly translated viral protein into its functional, membrane-associated form. E is a small hydrophobic protein that accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi and ERGIC membranes, where it contributes to virion assembly, budding and the ion-channel (porin-like) activity attributed to E trimers rather than trafficking to the plasma membrane. After synthesis the protein is palmitoylated on cysteines, which stabilises its membrane interaction, and is ubiquitinated using the host ubiquitin pool supplied by the ribosomal fusion precursors and polyubiquitin genes represented here. Because correctly matured E is required for efficient production of infectious particles and for the membrane remodelling that accompanies coronaviral egress, this step links host protein-modification machinery to the late stages of the viral replication cycle and to candidate antiviral targets.

SARS-CoV-2 Infection describes the full course of coronavirus replication in human cells and the host machinery it commandeers, the biology underlying COVID-19 and its progression from respiratory infection to systemic inflammation. Entry begins with spike binding to ACE2 and priming by host proteases such as TMPRSS2, furin and cathepsin L, followed by membrane fusion, uncoating, translation of the viral polyproteins and assembly of replication complexes on remodelled ER-derived double-membrane vesicles, with virion morphogenesis in the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment. The host contributions listed here are the systems the virus depends on or disables: oligosaccharyltransferase and glycan-processing enzymes that decorate spike, S-acyltransferases that palmitoylate it, COPII transport, ESCRT and HOPS membrane traffic, autophagy initiation, the small ribosomal subunit and LARP1-controlled translation, nucleoporins whose blockade traps STAT1, and RIG-I/MDA5-MAVS and TLR sensing that drives interferon induction, antigen presentation, and NLRP3 inflammasome activity.

The life cycle of SARS-CoV-2 in human cells, and the host machinery it commandeers, underlies COVID-19 and its progression from airway infection to systemic inflammation. Entry begins when spike engages ACE2 and is primed by host proteases such as TMPRSS2, furin and cathepsin L, with neuropilin-1 and heparan sulfate proteoglycans as attachment cofactors; fusion releases the genome for translation and replication on ER-derived double-membrane vesicles. Beyond replication, the module captures how viral proteins subvert the host: blunting RIG-I/MDA5-MAVS and STING-TBK1-IRF3 signalling and interferon-driven JAK-STAT responses, blocking nuclear pore transport, silencing MHC class I presentation, redirecting small ribosomal subunits and LARP1 to suppress host translation, disrupting autophagy and HOPS-dependent trafficking, and displacing PDZ scaffolds at epithelial tight junctions. Glycosylation, palmitoylation and COPII components shape virion maturation.

RND1 GTPase cycle describes the activity of an atypical Rho-family GTPase that breaks the usual rules: RND1 is constitutively GTP-bound, has no measurable hydrolytic activity, and is not controlled by exchange factors, GAPs or dissociation inhibitors. Instead it is regulated by expression level and by phosphorylation-driven 14-3-3 binding that pulls it off the plasma membrane into the cytosol. Its output is antagonism of RHOA signalling: through RhoGAPs such as ARHGAP35 and ARHGAP5 it lowers actomyosin contractility, dissolving stress fibres and focal adhesions and rounding the cell. Partners including plexin and Eph receptors, planar cell polarity components VANGL1/2, and cytoskeletal linkers place it in axon guidance, cell migration and adhesion remodelling. It shapes embryogenesis, neuronal development, uterine adaptation in pregnancy and angiogenesis, and is commonly silenced in tumours, where its loss favours invasive, contractile behaviour.

RND1 is an atypical Rho-family GTPase that stays GTP-loaded and, unlike classical switches, is not toggled by exchange factors or GTPase-activating proteins; its activity is set instead by expression level and by removal from the plasma membrane after phosphorylation-driven binding to 14-3-3 proteins. Its output is antagonism of RhoA signalling: actomyosin contractility falls, stress fibres and focal adhesions disassemble, and cells round up and lose adhesive traction. This restraint on cytoskeletal tension matters in embryogenesis, axon guidance and neurite remodelling, myometrial adaptation during pregnancy, and angiogenesis, and its loss is common in tumours, consistent with a tumour-suppressive role and links to therapy response. The associated proteins reflect that biology: RhoA-directed GAPs such as ARHGAP35 and ARHGAP5, plexin and Eph receptor guidance modules, caveolin and flotillin membrane scaffolds, planar polarity components, and PI3K regulatory subunits.

Drug resistance of ALK mutants describes how tumours driven by the ALK receptor tyrosine kinase escape the inhibitors designed to shut it down. Aberrant ALK activity, arising from gene fusions, activating point mutations, amplification or overexpression, drives anaplastic large cell lymphoma, a subset of non-small cell lung cancer, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumours and neuroblastoma, and these cancers initially respond well to crizotinib, ceritinib, brigatinib, alectinib or lorlatinib. Resistance nearly always follows. Secondary mutations in the kinase domain alter the ATP-binding pocket or the conformation the drug requires, so the inhibitor no longer binds while catalytic output and downstream RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and JAK-STAT signalling continue. Alternatively, bypass signalling through other receptor kinases restores those same growth and survival outputs without ALK. Understanding which substitution has arisen guides the choice of next-generation inhibitor in the clinic.

Anaplastic lymphoma kinase becomes an oncogenic driver when it is rearranged into fusion proteins, mutated, amplified or overexpressed, and tumours that depend on it — anaplastic large cell lymphoma, a subset of non-small cell lung cancer, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumours and neuroblastoma — respond initially to targeted kinase inhibitors such as crizotinib, ceritinib, brigatinib, alectinib and lorlatinib. Resistance is the reason those responses are usually temporary, and this pathway describes how it arises at the level of the kinase itself: secondary substitutions in the ALK kinase domain, including gatekeeper and solvent-front changes, reduce drug binding while preserving catalytic signalling through the RAS–MAPK, PI3K and JAK–STAT routes that sustain proliferation and survival. Tumours can also escape by activating bypass receptor signalling that removes dependence on ALK altogether, which is why inhibitor choice in the clinic is guided by the specific resistance mutation present.

STAT5 activation downstream of FLT3 ITD mutants describes the aberrant signalling that makes internal tandem duplication mutations of the FLT3 receptor tyrosine kinase one of the most common and prognostically adverse lesions in acute myeloid leukaemia. Unlike the wild-type receptor or kinase-domain mutants, ITD forms are retained in an immature intracellular compartment where they constitutively phosphorylate STAT5A and STAT5B, aided by the adaptors GRB2 and GAB2 and the phosphatase PTPN11. Dimerised STAT5 enters the nucleus and drives transcription of the survival factor BCL2L1, the kinase PIM1, and cell cycle regulators such as CDKN1A, while NOX4-derived reactive oxygen species sustain signalling by inactivating opposing phosphatases. The net effect is cytokine-independent proliferation and apoptosis resistance in myeloid progenitors, and this axis is the rationale for FLT3 inhibitor therapy.

Internal tandem duplications in the FLT3 receptor tyrosine kinase are among the most common lesions in acute myeloid leukaemia, and one reason they transform cells is that the mutant kinase, unlike the wild-type receptor, drives strong constitutive STAT5 activation. This gives leukaemic blasts a growth and survival signal that no longer requires ligand, and it is the arm of FLT3 signalling most closely tied to disease aggressiveness and to response or resistance to kinase inhibitors. The mislocalised, autophosphorylated receptor recruits GRB2 and the scaffold GAB2 together with the phosphatase PTPN11, phosphorylating STAT5A and STAT5B so they dimerise and enter the nucleus. There they induce targets that push proliferation and block death, including the anti-apoptotic BCL2L1 and the kinase PIM1, alongside altered CDKN1A control of the cell cycle and NOX4-derived reactive oxygen species that sustain the signal.

KW2449-resistant FLT3 mutants describes variant forms of the FLT3 receptor tyrosine kinase that continue to signal despite exposure to the type I inhibitor KW-2449, and so explain why targeted therapy fails in some acute myeloid leukemias. FLT3 normally drives proliferation and survival of hematopoietic progenitors; internal tandem duplications and kinase-domain point mutations lock it in a ligand-independent active state that sustains leukemic blast growth through RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT5. Inhibitors of this kinase are used to blunt that signal, but substitutions at gatekeeper and activation-loop residues alter the ATP pocket so the drug no longer binds effectively, restoring constitutive autophosphorylation and downstream output. Such resistance alleles are typically selected during treatment and underlie relapse, making the mutational spectrum of this receptor a determinant of which inhibitor is clinically useful.

Activating mutations in the FLT3 receptor tyrosine kinase drive proliferation and survival of myeloid blasts and are among the most common lesions in acute myeloid leukaemia, making the receptor a prime drug target. KW-2449 is a type I inhibitor that binds the active kinase conformation and blocks signalling through several mutant FLT3 alleles, including internal tandem duplications of the juxtamembrane region, but certain substitutions in the kinase domain and activation loop alter the ATP pocket so that the drug no longer engages productively. Cells carrying these KW-2449-resistant variants retain constitutive, ligand-independent FLT3 signalling to STAT5, RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT despite treatment, and such alleles account for relapse after targeted therapy. Cataloguing them matters for choosing between type I and type II inhibitors and for interpreting resistance mutations that emerge under selection.

Gilteritinib-resistant FLT3 mutants describes forms of the FLT3 receptor tyrosine kinase that continue to signal despite treatment with gilteritinib, a type I inhibitor used in FLT3-mutant acute myeloid leukaemia. This matters because relapse on FLT3-targeted therapy is common, and the mutations captured here explain why remissions are often short-lived and guide the choice of alternative inhibitors. FLT3 normally drives proliferation and survival of haematopoietic progenitors; internal tandem duplications and kinase-domain substitutions lock it into a ligand-independent active state that constitutively engages STAT5, RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT signalling. Secondary substitutions in the ATP-binding pocket and activation loop, or additional gatekeeper changes, reduce drug binding while preserving catalytic activity, so downstream signalling resumes under therapy. The biology sits at the intersection of growth factor receptor signalling, leukaemic clonal evolution and acquired pharmacological resistance.

Activating mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase FLT3 drive a large fraction of acute myeloid leukaemia, and gilteritinib is a type I inhibitor used to shut that signalling down. Clinical benefit is often lost when the receptor acquires secondary changes that no longer permit effective drug binding, and this grouping describes gilteritinib-resistant FLT3 mutants, which restore ligand-independent kinase activity and downstream proliferative and survival signalling through STAT5, RAS-MAPK and PI3K routes despite continued treatment. Because type I inhibitors engage the active kinase conformation, substitutions in the activation loop and kinase domain, as well as alternative resistance alleles arising on the background of internal tandem duplications, are the usual cause of relapse. Understanding which variants confer resistance guides the choice between inhibitor classes and explains the limited durability of single-agent FLT3-targeted therapy in myeloid leukaemia.

sorafenib-resistant FLT3 mutants describes variant forms of the FLT3 receptor tyrosine kinase that continue to signal despite treatment with sorafenib, a type II inhibitor that otherwise blocks the kinase by trapping it in an inactive conformation. FLT3 drives proliferation and survival of haematopoietic progenitors, and activating mutations -- internal tandem duplications in the juxtamembrane region and point mutations in the kinase domain -- make it constitutively active in acute myeloid leukaemia. Substitutions at gatekeeper and activation-loop residues, notably around D835 and F691, restore or preserve the active kinase conformation that type II drugs cannot bind, so downstream STAT5, RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT signalling continues unchecked. Such mutations typically emerge under therapy and underlie clinical relapse, which is why they guide the choice between type I and type II FLT3 inhibitors and motivate next-generation agents.

FLT3 is a receptor tyrosine kinase that drives proliferation and survival of hematopoietic progenitors, and activating mutations in it — most often internal tandem duplications in the juxtamembrane region — are among the most common lesions in acute myeloid leukemia, where they predict relapse. Sorafenib, a type II inhibitor that binds the inactive kinase conformation, suppresses such mutants and can produce responses in FLT3-mutant disease, but treatment selects for sorafenib-resistant FLT3 variants. Substitutions in the activation loop and at the gatekeeper position stabilize the active conformation or occlude the drug pocket, so the receptor continues to autophosphorylate and signal through STAT5, RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT despite drug exposure. This resistance underlies loss of response in the clinic and motivates type I and next-generation FLT3 inhibitors, illustrating how mutational escape within a single oncogenic kinase shapes targeted leukemia therapy.

sunitinib-resistant FLT3 mutants describes forms of the FLT3 receptor tyrosine kinase that continue to signal despite treatment with sunitinib, a type II multi-kinase inhibitor. FLT3 drives proliferation and survival of hematopoietic progenitors, and activating mutations in it are among the most common lesions in acute myeloid leukemia, making the receptor a principal drug target in that disease. Type II inhibitors bind only the inactive, DFG-out kinase conformation, so substitutions in the activation loop and kinase domain that stabilise the active state, or that alter the drug-binding pocket directly, abolish inhibition while leaving the receptor constitutively autophosphorylated and coupled to STAT5, RAS-MAPK and PI3K signalling. Such mutants explain relapse on kinase inhibitor therapy and the clinical logic for switching between inhibitor classes. The biology sits at the intersection of growth factor receptor signalling, leukemic transformation, and acquired pharmacological resistance.

FLT3 is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose activating mutations drive a large fraction of acute myeloid leukaemia, and inhibiting it is a mainstay of targeted therapy in that disease. Sunitinib, a type II inhibitor that binds the kinase only in its inactive conformation, blocks many FLT3 variants but not all: certain point mutations in the kinase domain, particularly at the activation loop and gatekeeper positions, stabilise the active conformation or occlude the drug pocket so that sunitinib-resistant FLT3 mutants continue to signal. The consequence is sustained ligand-independent autophosphorylation and downstream STAT5, RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT output, driving proliferation and blocking myeloid differentiation despite treatment. Such variants explain relapse on kinase inhibitor therapy and motivate the use of later-generation or type I inhibitors that engage the receptor differently.

Defective HDR through Homologous Recombination Repair (HRR) due to PALB2 loss of BRCA1 binding function describes what happens to error-free double-strand break repair when PALB2 can no longer be tethered to BRCA1. PALB2 is the physical bridge between BRCA1 and BRCA2, and through it RAD51 is loaded onto resected DNA ends to invade the sister chromatid; mutations in the PALB2 N-terminal coiled-coil break that bridge, so RAD51 foci fail to form and gene conversion is lost even though the mutant protein can still reach break sites. Cells fall back on mutagenic repair, become hypersensitive to interstrand crosslinkers such as mitomycin C and to PARP inhibitors, and carriers are predisposed to breast, ovarian and pancreatic cancer. The surrounding machinery—MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP for end resection, EXO1, DNA2 and BLM-TOP3A for extension, and the RAD51 paralogs—remains intact but unproductive. ATR phosphorylation of PALB2 normally reinforces the interaction.

Homologous recombination repair fixes DNA double-strand breaks accurately by copying an intact sister chromatid, and PALB2 is the physical link that brings BRCA2 and RAD51 to BRCA1 at the break. When mutations in PALB2's N-terminal coiled-coil region abolish BRCA1 binding, that bridge fails: the protein can still reach damage sites through other partners but cannot support efficient gene conversion, RAD51 filament assembly, or resolution of the break, so cells fall back on error-prone end joining and accumulate chromosomal rearrangements. The consequences are clinical — hereditary breast, ovarian and pancreatic cancer predisposition, hypersensitivity to crosslinking agents such as mitomycin C, and sensitivity to PARP inhibition, the basis of synthetic-lethal therapy. Surrounding steps remain intact in this defect: MRE11–RAD50–NBN with CtIP and EXO1/DNA2 resect ends, and BLM–TOP3A–RMI dissolves joint molecules, but the RAD51 loading step is lost.

RHOBTB3 ATPase cycle describes the activity of an atypical member of the Rho/Ras-like superfamily whose nucleotide-binding domain hydrolyses ATP rather than GTP, and which works at the interface of membrane traffic and targeted protein destruction. It supports retrograde transport of cargo from endosomes to the Golgi, acting with RAB9 on late endosomal membranes, and serves as a substrate adaptor for CUL3-based ubiquitin ligases through its tandem BTB and BACK domains. Substrates linked to this route include cyclin E, tying RHOBTB3 to cell cycle progression, and components of the hypoxic response, where it cooperates with VHL to shape HIF signalling. Prenylation via its CAAX motif anchors it to membranes. Expression is broad but highest in neural, cardiac and endocrine tissue, and is reduced in many tumours, consistent with a tumour-suppressive function.

RHOBTB3 looks like a small GTPase but behaves differently: its nucleotide-binding domain hydrolyses ATP rather than GTP, and the cycling of this atypical Rho-family protein drives membrane traffic and targeted protein degradation. It works on Golgi membranes and endosomes, where it cooperates with RAB9 to return cargo from late endosomes to the trans-Golgi network, and it is anchored by a C-terminal prenylation motif not found in its RHOBTB1 and RHOBTB2 relatives. Through its tandem BTB domains it serves as a substrate adaptor for CUL3-based ubiquitin ligases, delivering targets such as cyclin E for degradation and thereby restraining cell cycle progression; it also feeds into the hypoxic response alongside VHL. Loss of RHOBTB3 expression is common in tumours, consistent with a tumour-suppressive role linking vesicular transport, ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis and proliferative control.

RHOBTB GTPase Cycle covers the atypical RHOBTB branch of the Rho family, proteins that keep a GTPase-like fold but do not cycle between GTP- and GDP-bound states in the usual way; instead they act as substrate adaptors for ubiquitin ligases. RHOBTB2 bridges CUL3-based ubiquitination, working with COP9 signalosome subunits to control the turnover of its own partners, and its loss in tumours and in developmental epileptic encephalopathy shows how much depends on that degradation control. RHOBTB1 sits in a cascade governing smooth muscle tone, vascular function and blood pressure, in part through phosphodiesterase handling. Associated chaperones (HSP90, CCT subunits, CDC37) point to folding and complex assembly requirements, while actin and intermediate filament components, ROCK kinases and myosin VI tie the family to cytoskeletal organisation, membrane traffic and, unexpectedly, RNA-binding and splicing machinery.

RHOBTB1 and RHOBTB2 are atypical members of the Rho family: they carry BTB domains and lack the regulated GTP hydrolysis that defines conventional Rho GTPases, so their cycle is better understood as an adaptor function than as a nucleotide switch. Both serve as substrate-recognition subunits for cullin-3 ubiquitin ligase complexes, and their activity is itself tuned by COP9 signalosome subunits such as GPS1, COPS2 and COPS4, linking them to targeted protein degradation rather than classical effector activation. RHOBTB1 supports smooth muscle function and blood pressure control, in part through handling of phosphodiesterase PDE5A, while loss of RHOBTB2 is associated with tumour suppression failure and with developmental epileptic encephalopathy. Associated chaperone, cytoskeletal and RNA-binding partners, including HSP90, the CCT chaperonin, ROCK kinases, actin, vimentin and several hnRNPs, place this biology at the junction of protein quality control and cytoskeletal organisation.

Impaired BRCA2 binding to RAD51 describes what happens to homologous recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks when BRCA2 can no longer deliver RAD51 to resected DNA. BRCA2 normally uses its BRC repeats and a C-terminal TR2 site to nucleate RAD51 filaments on RPA-coated single-stranded DNA, the step that licenses strand invasion of a sister chromatid; cancer-associated mutations in these contact points leave the upstream machinery intact but the repair reaction unfinished. The accompanying genes trace that upstream arm: MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP and BLM/DNA2/EXO1 carry out end resection, RPA coats the resulting overhang, and ATM, ATR-ATRIP, TOPBP1 and the 9-1-1 clamp signal the damage and arrest the cycle. Loss of the final loading step forces breaks into mutagenic alternative repair, driving genomic instability, hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition, and sensitivity to PARP inhibition.

Homologous recombination repair of DNA double-strand breaks depends on BRCA2 loading RAD51 onto resected single-stranded DNA, and this describes what happens when that hand-off fails. BRCA2 contacts RAD51 through BRC repeats and a C-terminal TR2 region; cancer-associated missense changes in either interface leave the upstream steps intact but prevent nucleation of the RAD51 filament, so breaks cannot be repaired by strand invasion. The upstream machinery represented here is the break-sensing and end-resection apparatus: the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex with CtIP, BRCA1-BARD1, the EXO1, DNA2, BLM and WRN nucleases and helicases, RPA coating the resulting overhang, and ATM, ATR-ATRIP, TOPBP1 and the 9-1-1 clamp signalling checkpoint arrest. Loss of productive RAD51 loading forces error-prone repair, drives genomic instability, and underlies hereditary breast, ovarian and pancreatic cancer predisposition as well as sensitivity to PARP inhibitors and crosslinking agents.

Sensory Perception covers how the body detects light, odours, tastants and sound and turns each into a neural signal, the basis of vision, smell, flavour and hearing. Phototransduction runs from rhodopsin and cone opsins through transducin, PDE6 and cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, with the visual cycle enzymes (RPE65, LRAT, retinol dehydrogenases, retinoid-binding proteins) regenerating chromophore; mutations here cause retinitis pigmentosa and Stargardt disease. Olfaction uses hundreds of odorant receptors coupled through GNAL and adenylate cyclase 3 to CNGA2 and ANO2. Taste is read out by sweet/umami TAS1R and bitter TAS2R receptors via gustducin, PLCB2, TRPM5 and CALHM channels. Hair-cell mechanotransduction depends on stereocilia and tip-link proteins such as MYO7A, CDH23, PCDH15, USH1C, TMC1 and LHFPL5, plus prestin and otoferlin for amplification and transmitter release; their loss causes deafness and Usher syndrome.

Sensory perception is the conversion of external physical and chemical stimuli into neural signals, and this collection spans the four modalities for which the molecular steps are best defined: vision, olfaction, taste and hearing. Photoreception depends on opsins coupled through transducin to cGMP phosphodiesterase and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels, supported by retinoid supply and recycling enzymes such as RPE65, LRAT and the retinol dehydrogenases. Odorants act on the large odorant receptor repertoire signalling via adenylate cyclase 3 and CNGA2, while sweet, umami and bitter tastants act on TAS1R and TAS2R receptors feeding into PLCB2 and TRPM5. Mechanotransduction in hair cells uses tip-link cadherins, TMC channels, unconventional myosins and stereociliary actin regulators. Failure of these components produces retinal dystrophies, anosmia, taste loss and inherited deafness.

Cellular response to starvation is how cells detect that amino acids and other nutrients have run short and rebalance growth against survival, switching off biosynthesis and turning on stress-adaptive gene expression and autophagy. Two arms are represented. The kinase EIF2AK4 (GCN2), positioned on the ribosome with GCN1, senses uncharged tRNAs and phosphorylates the translation initiation factor EIF2S1, damping bulk protein synthesis while favouring translation of ATF4 and its partners CEBPB, DDIT3 and TRIB3, which reprogramme amino acid supply through transporters and enzymes such as ASNS. In parallel, mTORC1 activity is controlled at the lysosome, where the v-ATPase, the Ragulator (LAMTOR) subunits, Rag GTPases, GATOR/KICSTOR components and sensors including CASTOR1, SAMTOR, SESN2 and SLC38A9 determine whether RHEB can activate MTOR. Loss of this control underlies dysregulated growth in cancer and tuberous sclerosis-like syndromes, and shapes fasting physiology.

When amino acids run short, cells must stop building and start conserving, and this starvation response is how that switch is thrown. Two arms are represented. In one, the kinase EIF2AK4 (GCN2), aided by GCN1, detects uncharged tRNAs at the ribosome and phosphorylates the translation initiation factor subunit EIF2S1, damping bulk protein synthesis while favouring translation of ATF4; ATF4 with CEBPB, CEBPG, DDIT3, ATF3, TRIB3 and targets such as ASNS then rewires amino acid supply and, if stress persists, commits cells to death. In the other, amino acid sufficiency is read out at the lysosomal surface by SLC38A9, SAMTOR, the CASTOR sensors, the Rag GTPases and their Ragulator, GATOR and folliculin regulators, together with the vacuolar ATPase, controlling whether RHEB activates mTORC1 to drive growth, ribosome output and lipid synthesis or releases autophagy. Sestrins link this to stress. Chronic mis-setting underlies metabolic disease, tumour growth and tuberous sclerosis-like disorders.

Cellular response to chemical stress is the set of defences cells deploy when exposed to reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, electrophiles, heavy metals and xenobiotics, whether generated internally by mitochondria and NADPH oxidases or delivered from outside. It determines whether an insult is neutralised or leads to lipid peroxidation, DNA damage and apoptosis, and it is the reason chemotherapeutics that act through oxidative injury can be resisted by tumour cells. The core regulator is NFE2L2, held in check by KEAP1 and CUL3-dependent proteasomal turnover until oxidation of sensor cysteines allows it to partner with small MAF proteins and induce glutathione synthesis, NQO1, thioredoxin and peroxiredoxin systems, superoxide dismutases, cystine import and the pentose phosphate route that regenerates NADPH. Heme oxygenase 1 provides a parallel cytoprotective arm, its biliverdin and carbon monoxide products limiting further damage, alongside p62-linked autophagy, ATF4 and p21 responses.

Cells exposed to oxidants, heavy metals, electrophilic drugs and other chemical insults must neutralise the damage before it reaches lipids, DNA and protein; the cellular response to chemical stress is the coordinated programme that does this, and its output determines whether a cell survives an exposure, ages prematurely, or dies. Reactive oxygen and nitrogen species are the shared mediators, generated endogenously by mitochondrial respiration and NADPH oxidases and amplified by xenobiotics. Sensing converges on KEAP1, whose oxidation releases NFE2L2 to partner with small MAF proteins and drive transcription of heme oxygenase 1, NQO1, glutamate-cysteine ligase, thioredoxin and peroxiredoxin systems, the cystine transporter SLC7A11 and pentose phosphate enzymes that regenerate NADPH. Superoxide dismutases, catalase and glutathione peroxidases dispose of peroxides directly, while ubiquitin-proteasome components, p62-dependent autophagy and sestrins clear oxidised cargo. The same circuitry underlies tumour resistance to chemotherapy and inflammatory signalling through NF-κB and NLRP3.

Sensory perception of taste is how taste bud cells on the tongue detect sweet, umami, bitter, sour and salty chemicals and convert them into signals the gustatory nerves can read, guiding food selection, avoidance of toxins and the regulation of appetite. Sweet and umami are read by TAS1R heterodimers and bitter by the large TAS2R family, all coupling through gustducin and PLCB2 to IP3-mediated calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum; calcium opens TRPM5 and TRPM4, and voltage-gated sodium channels amplify the resulting depolarization until CALHM1:CALHM3 channels release ATP as the transmitter onto afferent fibres. Sour taste instead depends on proton entry through OTOP1 and block of KCNJ2 in a separate cell type, while low salt is sensed by epithelial sodium channel subunits. Variation in bitter receptors such as TAS2R38 underlies well-known individual differences in taste sensitivity.

Taste buds convert chemicals in food into neural signals, and the sensory perception of taste is what lets an animal seek calories and amino acids while rejecting acids and potential toxins; its loss flattens appetite and food choice. Sweet and umami detection uses TAS1R2:TAS1R3 and TAS1R1:TAS1R3 heterodimers, while a large family of TAS2R receptors covers bitter compounds, TAS2R38 variants explaining common differences in perceived bitterness. These receptors share one cascade: gustducin-containing G protein heterotrimers activate PLCB2, IP3 opens ITPR3 to release stored calcium, and calcium gates TRPM5 to depolarize the cell, with voltage-gated sodium channels amplifying the response and CALHM1:CALHM3 releasing ATP as transmitter to afferent fibres. Sour taste instead depends on proton entry through OTOP1 and inhibition of KCNJ2 in type III cells, and low-salt taste on epithelial sodium channel subunits.

Translation of Accessory Proteins covers the synthesis of the small, non-structural accessory proteins of SARS-CoV-2 from the subgenomic mRNAs produced late in the coronavirus replication cycle. These products — ORF6, ORF7a, ORF8 and ORF9b among them — are dispensable for making virus particles in culture, but they are a large part of why infection causes disease: they blunt interferon induction and signalling, interfere with antigen presentation and mitochondrial antiviral signalling, and shape inflammatory responses in the infected host. Their production depends on the nested set of 3'-coterminal subgenomic mRNAs generated by discontinuous transcription, with each message translated by host ribosomes at the endoplasmic reticulum; the bicistronic mRNA9b yields protein 9b from an internal open reading frame. This step therefore links viral gene expression to immune evasion and pathogenesis rather than to genome replication or assembly.

Coronaviruses devote the 3' third of their genome to accessory genes, and translation of accessory proteins is the step that produces them from the nested set of subgenomic mRNAs made during SARS-CoV-2 infection. Ribosomes on host endoplasmic reticulum translate mRNA6, mRNA7, mRNA8 and the bicistronic mRNA9b to yield ORF6, ORF7a, ORF8 and ORF9b, the last read from an internal start site within the nucleocapsid message. None of these products is required for replication or particle assembly in cell culture, so their significance lies in how the virus handles its host: accessory proteins of this family antagonise interferon induction and signalling, interfere with nuclear transport and antigen presentation, and modulate cell death, shaping pathogenesis and disease severity rather than viral growth per se. Their synthesis depends entirely on hijacked host translation machinery.

Sensory perception of sour taste is how the tongue detects acidity, the modality that warns against spoiled or unripe food and contributes to the flavour of fermented and citrus foods. It is the business of type III taste bud cells, a distinct population from those detecting sweet, bitter and umami. Acid is sensed as protons themselves: the proton-selective channel OTOP1 conducts extracellular H+ into the cytosol, while weak organic acids such as acetic and citric acid cross the membrane in their uncharged form and dissociate inside. The resulting cytosolic acidification blocks the inward-rectifier potassium channel KCNJ2, removing the resting potassium conductance and depolarizing the cell enough to fire action potentials. Transmitter release, including serotonin and GABA, then conveys the signal to gustatory afferent fibres, linking a chemical stimulus directly to intracellular pH.

Sour taste detection tells an animal that a food is acidic, guiding avoidance of spoiled or unripe material, and it is the one taste modality read out directly as protons rather than through a G protein-coupled receptor. The sensing cells are type III taste bud cells, which carry a proton-selective channel, OTOP1, that conducts extracellular H+ into the cytosol; weak organic acids such as acetic and citric acid can also cross the membrane in their uncharged protonated form and acidify the cell from within. Cytosolic acidification closes the inwardly rectifying potassium channel KCNJ2, removing a resting conductance so the cell depolarizes and fires action potentials, leading to release of serotonin and GABA onto gustatory afferents. Purinergic signalling contributes to onward transmission, linking proton flux to conscious perception of acidity.

MITF-M-regulated melanocyte development describes how a single lineage-specific transcription factor builds and maintains melanocytes, the pigment cells that arise from the neural crest and populate skin, hair follicles, iris and inner ear. Its output is melanin: melanosomes loaded with eumelanin and pheomelanin are handed to keratinocytes, shielding skin from UV damage and setting pigmentation. Loss of MITF function removes melanocytes altogether, causing pigmentary defects, sensorineural deafness and eye malformation, while its reactivation drives melanoma proliferation and phenotype switching. Upstream, SOX10, PAX3 and Wnt/beta-catenin-LEF1 inputs plus KIT and melanocortin receptor signalling through MC1R and CREB converge on the M-promoter; downstream, MITF turns on the pigment enzymes TYR, TYRP1 and DCT, melanosome structural and transport proteins including PMEL, MLANA, RAB27A and MYO5A, lysosomal V-ATPase subunits, and genes balancing proliferation against survival and differentiation, with SWI/SNF chromatin remodellers and p300/CBP as coactivators.

Pigment cells owe their identity to the melanocyte-specific M isoform of MITF, the transcription factor that commits neural crest-derived melanoblasts to the lineage and keeps mature melanocytes differentiated. Its output is the melanosome and its contents: MITF-M drives tyrosinase, TYRP1, DCT, PMEL and MLANA for melanin synthesis, plus RAB27A, MYO5A and melanophilin for transport of pigment granules toward keratinocytes, and a battery of vacuolar ATPase subunits that acidify the organelle. Upstream, KIT/KITLG, endothelin and MC1R-melanocortin signalling converge with SOX10, PAX3 and WNT/beta-catenin-LEF/TCF input on the melanocyte promoter, while SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complexes, CBP/p300 and SIN3A-HDAC1 shape target selection. MITF-M also balances proliferation against differentiation through CDKN1A, CDKN2A, CDK2 and cyclin D1. Loss of function produces Waardenburg-type pigmentary defects and deafness; dysregulated activity underlies melanoma phenotype switching.

Induction of Cell-Cell Fusion describes how an enveloped virus turns the machinery it uses to enter a cell into a means of merging neighbouring cells into multinucleated syncytia. In severe COVID-19 this is visible as fused pneumocytes in the lung, and syncytia are thought to help the virus replicate while shielding it from antibodies; they can also engulf and destroy lymphocytes, contributing to lymphopenia. The event begins when spike on an infected cell engages ACE2 on an uninfected one, forming finger-like projections and synapse-like contacts that mature into a fusion pore. Proteolytic priming of spike by TMPRSS2 and FURIN raises fusion efficiency, and scramblase activity of anoctamin family members, notably ANO6, exposes phosphatidylserine and lowers the barrier to lipid bilayer merger. Certain viral variants fuse more readily, linking this process to disease severity.

Late in infection by enveloped viruses, the same fusion machinery that mediates entry can merge neighbouring cells into multinucleated syncytia, and this describes that induction of cell-cell fusion. In SARS-CoV-2 infection, spike displayed on the surface of an infected cell engages ACE2 on a neighbour, generating synapse-like contacts that progress to a fusion pore and cytoplasmic continuity; infected syncytial pneumocytes are a hallmark of severe COVID-19 lung pathology. Proteolytic priming of spike by the cell-surface protease TMPRSS2 and by furin at the S1/S2 boundary raises fusion efficiency, and several variants fuse more readily. Anoctamin family members contribute as calcium-activated chloride channels and phospholipid scramblases, with ANO6-type scrambling exposing phosphatidylserine to destabilise the bilayer and permit lipid mixing. Syncytia are thought to aid replication, immune evasion, and internalisation of lymphocytes.

Defective APRT disrupts adenine salvage describes what happens when the single enzyme that recycles free adenine into AMP is lost. Adenine is released continuously as a by-product of metabolism, notably polyamine synthesis, and adenine phosphoribosyltransferase normally captures it in one step by transferring a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP, feeding it back into the purine nucleotide pool. With the enzyme inactive, adenine is instead oxidised by xanthine dehydrogenase to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, a compound so poorly soluble that it precipitates in the urinary tract. The consequence is not nucleotide shortage, since de novo synthesis compensates, but crystal nephropathy: recurrent stones, tubular injury and progressive renal failure, sometimes presenting only after transplant loss. This places purine salvage failure among the inherited crystalline kidney diseases, and explains why treatment targets the oxidising enzyme rather than the missing one.

Adenine released by polyamine synthesis and nucleic acid turnover is normally recycled rather than degraded, and adenine phosphoribosyltransferase performs that salvage step by transferring a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP onto free adenine to give AMP. When the enzyme is defective, this purine salvage route fails and adenine is instead oxidised by xanthine dehydrogenase to the highly insoluble metabolite 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which precipitates as crystals in urine and renal tissue. The clinical consequence is APRT deficiency: radiolucent kidney stones, crystalline nephropathy, and progressive renal failure that can recur after transplantation unless xanthine oxidoreductase is inhibited. The biology sits within purine metabolism, where salvage pathways spare the energetic cost of de novo nucleotide synthesis, and it illustrates how loss of a single recycling enzyme causes disease through toxic accumulation of the unsalvaged substrate rather than through nucleotide shortage.

Diseases of nucleotide metabolism covers the inherited enzyme deficiencies that break purine salvage and catabolism, showing what happens when cells must rely on de novo synthesis alone. Loss of adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase allows toxic deoxynucleosides to accumulate in lymphocytes, killing developing T cells and causing severe combined immunodeficiency; ADA deficiency was the first target of human gene therapy. Loss of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase diverts hypoxanthine and guanine to uric acid instead of recycling them into IMP and GMP, producing hyperuricaemia, gout and, when complete, the neurological and self-injurious features of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency leaves adenine to be oxidised to insoluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which precipitates as kidney stones. Together these reactions link nucleotide economy to immune development, urate handling and renal function.

Purine nucleotides are salvaged rather than built from scratch in most tissues, and inherited loss of the salvage and catabolic enzymes produces a recognisable group of diseases of nucleotide metabolism. Adenosine deaminase and purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiencies allow toxic deoxynucleotides to accumulate in lymphocytes, causing severe combined immunodeficiency with absent T, B and NK cell function. Loss of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, which recycles hypoxanthine and guanine onto ribose phosphate, diverts purines to uric acid and gives the hyperuricaemia, gout and self-injurious neurological disease of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency instead leaves adenine to be oxidised to insoluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which precipitates as kidney stones and can destroy renal function. Together these enzymes show how purine recycling supports immune cell development, uric acid balance and neuronal function.

Drug ADME describes what the body does to a drug rather than what the drug does to the body: its absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, the four stages that set circulating drug concentration, duration of action and dose requirements. This is the biology behind interindividual variation in drug response, drug-drug interactions and toxicity, and polymorphisms in these genes underlie clinical pharmacogenetics. Uptake transporters of the organic anion and cation families and nucleoside carriers move compounds into hepatocytes, enterocytes and renal tubule cells; cytochrome P450 monooxygenases and esterases perform oxidative and hydrolytic conversion; UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, sulfotransferases, glutathione S-transferases, N-acetyltransferases and thiopurine methyltransferase conjugate metabolites for elimination; and ATP-binding cassette efflux pumps export them into bile, urine and gut lumen. Plasma proteins such as albumin govern distribution, while purine salvage enzymes activate thiopurine and antimetabolite prodrugs.

The fate of a drug in the body — how it is absorbed, distributed, chemically transformed and excreted — determines its dose, duration of action and toxicity, and this collection of absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion steps is where that pharmacokinetic handling is carried out. Uptake transporters of the organic anion and organic cation families, together with nucleoside carriers, move compounds into hepatocytes and renal tubular cells, while ABC efflux pumps including ABCB1 and ABCG2 export them back to blood, bile or urine and set oral bioavailability and blood–brain barrier access. Between the two, cytochrome P450 oxidations and hydrolysis by carboxylesterases generate metabolites that UGT glucuronosyltransferases, sulfotransferases, glutathione S-transferases and N-acetyltransferases conjugate for elimination; thiopurine and purine-handling enzymes such as TPMT, HPRT1 and XDH activate or inactivate antimetabolite drugs. Common variants in these genes underlie much interindividual variation in drug response and adverse reactions.

Ribavirin ADME describes how the antiviral nucleoside analog ribavirin is taken up, activated and cleared in humans, which determines both its efficacy against hepatitis C, respiratory syncytial virus and viral haemorrhagic fevers and its dose-limiting toxicity. Because the drug is a prodrug, its activity depends entirely on host nucleoside handling: concentrative and equilibrative nucleoside transporters carry it across intestinal and hepatocyte membranes, adenosine kinase performs the first phosphorylation, and nucleoside diphosphate kinases complete conversion to the active triphosphate, while 5'-nucleotidase, purine nucleoside phosphorylase and adenosine deaminase run the competing catabolic route of dephosphorylation and de-ribosylation. Trapping of phosphorylated drug inside erythrocytes, which lack the enzymes to reverse it, gives the very long half-life and the characteristic haemolytic anaemia; ITPA variants that relieve accumulated triphosphate reduce that risk, making this pharmacogenetics as much as metabolism.

Ribavirin is a guanosine analogue prodrug used against hepatitis C, respiratory syncytial virus and some viral haemorrhagic fevers, and its absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination determine both its antiviral potency and its main toxicity. Because the drug must be phosphorylated to the triphosphate to act, it depends on host nucleoside salvage machinery rather than any viral enzyme. Concentrative and equilibrative nucleoside transporters carry it across intestinal and cell membranes, adenosine kinase performs the first phosphorylation, and nucleoside diphosphate kinases complete the conversion to the active triphosphate; 5'-nucleotidase, purine nucleoside phosphorylase, adenosine deaminase and the inosine triphosphatase ITPA oppose or divert this flux. Accumulation of phosphorylated drug in erythrocytes, which lack dephosphorylating capacity, explains the long body half-life and the dose-limiting haemolytic anaemia, and variation in ITPA modifies that risk.

N-glycan antennae elongation in the medial/trans-Golgi builds the branched, terminally decorated sugar chains that give secreted and cell-surface glycoproteins their mature identity, determining receptor half-life, cell adhesion, immune recognition and the clearance of circulating hormones. After a committed GlcNAc is added to the alpha1,3 branch, the pathway forks: a bisecting GlcNAc placed by MGAT3 blocks further mannose trimming and yields hybrid structures, while Golgi alpha-mannosidases with MGAT2 open the route to complex N-glycans. Additional branches from MGAT4 and MGAT5 enzymes are then extended by beta1,4-galactosyltransferases and capped by sialyltransferases such as ST6GAL1, with core fucosylation by FUT8 and sulfation adding further variation. The resulting diversity tunes lectin binding and growth-factor receptor signalling; loss of individual transferases causes congenital glycosylation disorders, and altered branching accompanies tumour invasion.

Glycoproteins leaving the Golgi carry branched N-linked sugars whose outer arms are built here, in the medial and trans compartments. This elaboration converts simple oligomannose structures into the hybrid and complex N-glycans that determine protein half-life, receptor clustering, cell adhesion and recognition by lectins of the immune system; loss of branching enzymes causes congenital glycosylation disorders, and altered branching is a hallmark of tumour cell surfaces. Alpha-mannosidase II enzymes trim mannose residues, after which GlcNAc transferases including MGAT2, MGAT4 family members and MGAT5 add antennae, MGAT3 adds a bisecting GlcNAc that blocks further branching, and FUT8 attaches core fucose. Beta-1,4-galactosyltransferases cap the branches, and sialyltransferases such as ST6GAL1 and ST3GAL4 terminate them with sialic acid, with sulfation and fucosylation generating further diversity. Glycoprotein hormone subunits are among the substrates matured this way.

Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) during gastrulation is the step that turns the epiblast into a body plan: cells in the primitive streak lose their epithelial character, detach from their neighbours and the basement membrane, and ingress to form mesoderm, while an incomplete version of the same program generates definitive endoderm. Without it no mesoderm forms and embryogenesis fails. FGF, WNT, NODAL and BMP signals converge on the posterior streak, where the transcription factors TBXT and EOMES switch on SNAI1; SNAI1 then represses E-cadherin, occludin and claudins, dismantling adherens and tight junctions so cells can move and adopt an N-cadherin mesenchymal program. Cytoskeletal and polarity regulators coordinate the actual ingression. The same transcriptional circuit is reactivated pathologically in carcinoma cells, where it underlies invasion and metastasis.

Gastrulation requires that epiblast cells in the primitive streak stop behaving as an epithelium and leave it, and this epithelial-mesenchymal transition is how mesoderm is generated; an incomplete version of the same programme delivers definitive endoderm. Posterior signals, prominently FGF acting through FGFR1 along with WNT, NODAL and BMP, converge on the primitive streak transcription factors EOMES and TBXT, which switch on SNAI1. SNAI1 then represses the genes that hold the epithelium together, including E-cadherin, occludin and claudins, so that junctions dissolve, cells detach from the basement membrane and ingress, and a mesenchymal expression programme with N-cadherin takes over. Without it the germ layers cannot be laid down. The same transcriptional switch is redeployed in carcinoma cells, where TGF-beta-driven loss of E-cadherin underlies invasion and metastasis, making this early developmental step a template for tumour cell dissemination.

Gastrulation is the step that turns a simple two-layered early embryo into a three-layered body plan, generating the mesoderm and endoderm alongside ectoderm and thereby specifying the founders of muscle, blood, gut, skin and nervous system. Failure at this stage is embryonic lethal, and its regulators reappear in birth defects and in tumour cell invasion. Epiblast cells at the posterior primitive streak, where NODAL/SMAD, BMP, FGF and WNT signals converge, switch on TBXT, EOMES and MIXL1 and undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, losing CDH1 and claudin/occludin junctions through SNAI1 and ZEB2 while endoderm-bound cells only partially do so before re-epithelialising as SOX17/FOXA2 gut progenitors. Notch-RBPJ with MESP2, TBX6 and HES7 times somitic mesoderm segmentation; SOX2, OTX2 and PAX genes pattern the retained ectoderm. Proteasome subunits enforce the rapid turnover of these transcription factors and signalling effectors that makes lineage switching irreversible.

Gastrulation converts the single-layered epiblast of the early embryo into the three germ layers "" ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm "" from which every tissue of the body is later built, and it establishes the anterior-posterior and medial-lateral coordinates along which those tissues are patterned. Epiblast cells ingress through the primitive streak, a posterior site specified by converging NODAL/SMAD, BMP, FGF and WNT signalling, and lose their epithelial character through an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition driven by SNAI1 and ZEB2 with loss of CDH1, claudin and occludin junctions. Streak cells switch on TBXT, EOMES and MIXL1 as pluripotency factors such as POU5F1 and NANOG are resolved into lineage programmes: SOX17 and FOXA2 for endoderm, TBX6 and MSGN1 for paraxial mesoderm, SOX2 and ZIC factors for neuroectoderm. Notch components with a segmentation clock, Hedgehog signals from axial mesoderm, Hippo effectors and proteasomal turnover of regulators shape the output. Failure produces embryonic lethality or axial and laterality malformations.

Regulation of Homotypic Cell-Cell Adhesion governs how much cadherin is present at a cell's surface to bind identical cadherins on its neighbours, and thereby sets the strength of adherens junctions holding an epithelium together. Loss of this control is the core of epithelial-mesenchymal transition: when E-cadherin expression falls, cells detach, become motile and invasive, a step central to development, wound healing and tumour metastasis. Cadherin ectodomains form calcium-dependent trans dimers across the intermembrane space, while their cytoplasmic tails recruit alpha-, beta- and p120-catenin, plakoglobin and vinculin to anchor the junction to actin. Regulation here is largely transcriptional and post-transcriptional: SNAI1/2, ZEB1/2 and TWIST repressors recruit HDAC1/2, LSD1 and Polycomb complexes to silence CDH1, microRNAs including miR-200c act through Argonaute complexes, and glycosylation, proprotein convertase processing, ubiquitin-proteasome degradation and Src/Fyn phosphorylation tune the mature protein.

Cells of the same type stick to one another through calcium-dependent cadherin dimers that bridge apposed membranes, and control over homotypic cell-cell adhesion determines whether an epithelium stays sealed or a cell detaches and migrates. E-cadherin and its relatives link through catenins -- beta-catenin, alpha-catenin, p120 and plakoglobin -- to actin and vinculin, so adhesion strength is read out as cytoskeletal tension at adherens junctions. Much of the regulation shown here is upstream of the junction itself: transcriptional repression of cadherin genes by SNAI1/SNAI2, ZEB1/ZEB2 and TWIST factors acting with histone deacetylases, LSD1 and Polycomb components, microRNA-mediated silencing through Argonaute complexes, plus biosynthetic maturation by N-glycosylation and signal peptidase machinery, proprotein convertase cleavage, cathepsin and ADAM-mediated shedding, and ubiquitin-proteasome turnover. Loss of this control underlies epithelial-mesenchymal transition, developmental patterning defects and carcinoma invasiveness.

Regulation of CDH11 gene transcription controls expression of OB-cadherin, the adhesion molecule that lets osteoblasts, fibroblasts and mesenchymal cells recognise and bind one another. Its output determines bone matrix formation, mesenchymal condensation during development, and the fibroblast-to-myofibroblast conversion that drives tissue fibrosis and synovial invasion in arthritis; loss of CDH11 weakens skeletal mineralisation and blunts fibrotic remodelling. Transcription is tissue-restricted, active in bone, heart, brain, lung and placenta but not kidney, liver or skeletal muscle, and is set by a small set of direct regulators: HOXC8 and FOXF1 acting in skeletal and mesenchymal patterning, the epithelial-mesenchymal transition factors ZEB2 and SNAI1, the Notch effector HEYL, ILF3, SP1, and the BHLHE22-PRDM8 repressor complex in neurons. Growth factors and hormones, TGF-beta in particular, feed into these factors, and CDH11 in turn modulates TGF-beta signalling as a feedback loop.

CDH11 encodes OB-cadherin, an adhesion molecule of osteoblasts, fibroblasts and mesenchymal tissues that also appears in heart, brain, placenta and lung, and its transcriptional control determines how much of this adhesive capacity a cell displays. The level matters: CDH11 induction accompanies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, fibroblast activation in fibrosis and synovial invasion in arthritis, and it participates in bone matrix formation. Direct activators include HOXC8, ZEB2, FOXF1, HEYL and the RNA/DNA-binding factor ILF3, with SP1 supplying basal promoter activity and SNAI1 linking expression to the EMT programme; BHLHE22 acts with its partner PRDM8 as a repressive complex in neural contexts. Growth factors and hormones, TGF-beta family ligands in particular, feed into these factors, and because CDH11 itself modulates TGF-beta responses the arrangement can form a self-reinforcing loop during tissue remodelling.

Regulation of Expression and Function of Type II Classical Cadherins controls where and when the type II classical cadherins are made and how they hold cells together, an adhesion code used mainly in the nervous system to sort neurons into circuits and to bundle motor axons, and in mesenchymal and endothelial tissues via CDH11 and VE-cadherin. These cadherins bind through strand swapping, in which conserved tryptophans in the first extracellular repeat dock into a partner's hydrophobic pocket, producing homotypic and selective heterotypic pairs whose binding preferences define distinct specificity subgroups. Adhesive strength depends on cytoplasmic partners such as beta-catenin, plakoglobin, p120 and alpha-catenin linking the complex to actin. Expression is set transcriptionally by factors including SOX10, SNAI1, ZEB2 and PRDM8, and post-transcriptionally by microRNAs acting through Argonaute-containing silencing complexes. Misregulation contributes to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, tumour invasion and defective neural wiring.

Type II classical cadherins are calcium-dependent adhesion receptors whose five-repeat ectodomains pair by strand swapping, docking conserved tryptophans from the first repeat into a partner's hydrophobic pocket via an intermediate X dimer. Because members bind selectively within defined specificity subgroups, both homotypically and heterotypically, they act as an adhesive code that sorts cells and wires neuronal circuits; CDH5 instead seals endothelial junctions, and CDH11 mediates mesenchymal and osteoblast adhesion. Regulation of their expression and function determines how much adhesive receptor reaches the surface and how long it stays there. Transcriptional control involves lineage and epithelial-mesenchymal factors such as SOX10, SNAI1, ZEB2, PRDM8 and BHLHE22, while microRNAs acting through Argonaute and TNRC6 silencing complexes tune transcript levels, and ADAM metalloproteinases shed ectodomains. Cytoplasmic tails couple to α-, β-, p120-catenin and plakoglobin, linking adhesion to the actin cytoskeleton and to junctional signalling that influences proliferation and tumour invasiveness.

Regulation of CDH1 Expression and Function governs how much E-cadherin an epithelial cell displays at its surface, and therefore whether that cell stays anchored to its neighbours in a polarized sheet. E-cadherin trans-dimers, linked through alpha-, beta- and p120-catenins to the actin cytoskeleton, build adherens junctions; losing them is a defining step of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and germline CDH1 loss underlies hereditary diffuse gastric cancer while sporadic silencing accompanies invasive carcinoma broadly. Control operates at every level: transcriptional repression by SNAI1/2, ZEB1/2 and TWIST factors recruiting HDAC, LSD1 and Polycomb complexes, microRNA-mediated silencing through Argonaute effectors, co-translational translocation, N-glycosylation and proprotein convertase cleavage in the secretory pathway, endocytic trafficking, and ubiquitin-proteasome and cathepsin-dependent degradation. Src- and CK2-mediated phosphorylation of the cytoplasmic tail tips this balance toward junction disassembly and motility.

E-cadherin (CDH1) is the adhesion receptor that holds polarized epithelial sheets together, and the control of its abundance and activity decides whether a cell stays epithelial or converts to a migratory mesenchymal state. Because loss of CDH1 permits invasion, this regulation underlies its behaviour as a tumour suppressor: germline loss-of-function mutations cause hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, and silencing accompanies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in many carcinomas. Transcription is repressed by SNAI1/SNAI2, ZEB1/ZEB2 and TWIST factors recruiting histone deacetylases, LSD1 and Polycomb components, while KLF4 and other factors favour expression; microRNAs and Argonaute-containing complexes add post-transcriptional control. The mature protein is made through signal peptide cleavage, N-glycosylation and proprotein convertase processing, then anchored to actin through beta-catenin, alpha-catenin, p120 and vinculin at adherens junctions. Kinases such as SRC and casein kinase 2, HECT-type ubiquitin ligase CBLL1, endocytosis, cathepsins and the proteasome drive its turnover.

Regulation of CDH1 mRNA translation by microRNAs describes how small RNAs silence E-cadherin, the adhesion molecule that holds epithelial sheets together and marks the epithelial state. Loss of E-cadherin loosens cell-cell junctions and is a defining step in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, invasion and metastasis, so post-transcriptional control of its message directly influences tumour behaviour. Mature miR-9 family members and miR-10b base-pair with the CDH1 transcript within an Argonaute-containing silencing complex, where TNRC6 scaffolding proteins and the helicase MOV10 enforce translational repression and decay. The MYC and MYCN oncoproteins drive transcription of the miR-9 genes, linking proliferative oncogenic signalling to dismantling of epithelial adhesion. Additional microRNAs, including miR-23b, miR-106a, miR-155 and miR-503, have been reported to target the same message, making CDH1 a convergence point for microRNA control of epithelial identity.

E-cadherin, encoded by CDH1, holds epithelial cells together at adherens junctions, and lowering its abundance is one of the decisive steps by which an epithelial cell becomes migratory and invasive. One route to that loss bypasses transcription entirely: microRNAs base-pair with the CDH1 message and silence it post-transcriptionally, with miR-9 family members and miR-10b the best supported examples. The silencing is carried out by the canonical machinery, in which an Argonaute protein loaded with the guide microRNA recruits a TNRC6 scaffold and associated factors such as the RNA helicase MOV10 to repress translation and destabilise the target. Because MYC and MYCN drive miR-9 expression, oncogenic transcription factor activity is linked to junctional dissolution, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and metastatic spread, making this a translational control node in tumour progression.

Degradation of CDH1 removes E-cadherin from the cell surface, dismantling the adherens junctions that hold epithelial sheets together.
