This post-translational loss of E-cadherin is one of the earliest steps in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, preceding transcriptional silencing of the gene, and it underlies the loss of cell-cell adhesion, apical-basal polarity and contact inhibition seen in invasive carcinoma. Two routes are described: MDM2 ubiquitinates E-cadherin for proteasomal destruction, while CBLL1 (Hakai) tags it for clathrin- and dynamin-dependent internalisation and cathepsin-mediated lysosomal breakdown. Src-family kinases including SRC and FYN phosphorylate the cadherin-catenin complex to license this ubiquitination, releasing alpha-, beta- and p120-catenin; freed beta-catenin can then feed into Wnt-responsive transcription. The pathway therefore links junction turnover to cell motility, wound repair and tumour progression.

E-cadherin holds epithelial cells to their neighbours, and its removal from the cell surface is one of the earliest steps by which an epithelium loosens and cells become migratory. Degradation of CDH1 describes the post-translational arm of that loss, preceding the transcriptional silencing seen later in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and it matters for wound healing, for morphogenesis, and for the invasive behaviour of carcinomas in which E-cadherin is lost. Two ubiquitin ligases are implicated: MDM2 routes E-cadherin to the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits is represented here, while CBLL1 promotes ubiquitin-dependent internalisation and lysosomal destruction involving clathrin machinery and cathepsins. Src-family kinase phosphorylation of the junctional complex — catenins, p120, plakoglobin — licenses this turnover, tying adherens junction stability to growth factor and kinase signalling.

Regulation of NPAS4 gene expression controls the level of an activity-dependent transcription factor that neurons use to translate electrical activity into lasting changes in synaptic wiring. NPAS4 is induced by Ca2+ entering through NMDA receptors and L-type channels, so its abundance tracks how strongly a neuron has been firing; the protein then shapes inhibitory input onto excitatory cells, supporting circuit plasticity, contextual memory formation and protection against neurodegenerative stress. Induction is opposed by repressors acting at the promoter, including REST and the Ca2+-binding regulator KCNIP3/DREAM, while SRF and glucocorticoid signalling through NR3C1 tie expression to activity and stress hormones. Argonaute proteins with TNRC6 scaffolds and the RNA helicase MOV10 impose miRNA-mediated control on the transcript. The same calcium-linked regulation operates in pancreatic beta cells, and chronic stress, isolation, ageing or viral infection lower expression.

NPAS4 is an activity-dependent transcription factor whose induction couples neuronal firing to changes in synaptic wiring, and the control of its expression is how calcium entry becomes a lasting change in circuit behaviour. Transcription rises within minutes of calcium influx through NMDA receptors and L-type channels, driven by factors including SRF and the calcium-sensitive repressor KCNIP3/DREAM, and is held down by REST in non-neuronal contexts; glucocorticoid signalling through NR3C1 links chronic stress to reduced hippocampal levels. Argonaute proteins with their TNRC6 scaffolds and the RNA helicase MOV10 place the transcript under microRNA-mediated post-transcriptional control as well. The output matters for excitatory-inhibitory balance, plasticity and contextual memory formation, and NPAS4 loss accompanies neurodegeneration and age-related memory impairment. The same calcium-driven regulation operates in pancreatic beta cells.

Defects of Coagulation cascade collects the inherited failures of blood clotting, the molecular basis of haemophilia, von Willebrand disease, afibrinogenaemia and the platelet disorder Bernard-Soulier syndrome, as well as gain-of-function variants of factors V and IX that tip the balance toward thrombosis. Normal haemostasis depends on a proteolytic relay in which factors VIII, IX, X and V assemble on activated platelet surfaces to generate thrombin, which converts fibrinogen into the fibrin mesh of a clot; von Willebrand factor and the GPIb-IX-V receptor complex tether platelets to injured vessel wall. Loss of any component gives spontaneous joint, mucosal or surgical bleeding, while loss of the protein C/protein S anticoagulant arm gives thrombophilia. Also represented are the post-translational steps clotting factors require, including vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation and tyrosine sulfation, and phospholipid scrambling by ANO6 that exposes the procoagulant membrane.

Blood clotting depends on a relay of plasma proteases and cofactors that converts fibrinogen to fibrin at a site of vessel injury, and this grouping collects the inherited defects of that cascade. Loss-of-function changes in factor VIII or factor IX cause haemophilia A and B, fibrinogen chain mutations give afibrinogenaemia and dysfibrinogenaemia, and von Willebrand factor defects impair platelet adhesion through the GPIb-IX-V receptor complex, whose subunits are themselves mutated in Bernard-Soulier syndrome. Failures of post-translational processing matter as much as the factors: vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation by GGCX licenses calcium-dependent membrane binding, and tyrosine sulfotransferases modify factor VIII and related substrates. The balance runs both ways, since protein C and protein S defects, and gain-of-activity variants of factor V and factor IX, tip the system toward thrombophilia rather than bleeding. Scrambling of membrane phospholipid by ANO6 supports procoagulant surface exposure on platelets.

Initiation of coagulation cascade is the trigger step of blood clotting: when injury or inflammation exposes tissue factor to plasma, a small burst of thrombin is generated on the surface of tissue factor-bearing cells such as fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells and pericytes, committing the system to clot formation. Without it bleeding goes unchecked, while inappropriate tissue factor exposure on activated macrophages, apoptotic cells, tumour cells or shed extracellular vesicles drives thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation in cancer and sepsis. Tissue factor is held in a cryptic state until phosphatidylserine exposure, sphingomyelin hydrolysis and thiol-disulfide exchange decrypt it; it then binds factor VII/VIIa with high affinity and the complex activates factors IX and X. Antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, protein S and cell-surface heparan sulfate proteoglycans including syndecans and glypicans restrain the reaction, keeping initiation local to damaged vessel wall.

Blood clotting begins when injury or inflammation exposes tissue factor to plasma, and this initiation phase produces the first small burst of thrombin that primes the rest of the cascade. Tissue factor (F3) sits on fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells and pericytes, normally held in a cryptic, low-activity state; phosphatidylserine exposure and thiol-disulfide rearrangement convert it to its procoagulant form, where it binds factor VII/VIIa with high affinity and the complex cleaves factors IX and X to their active proteases. Cofactors FV and FVIII, von Willebrand factor and prothrombin carry the signal forward, while TFPI, antithrombin and protein S restrain it, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans such as syndecans, glypicans and perlecan provide the surface on which inhibition is accelerated. Unrestrained or ectopic tissue factor activity, including on tumour- and sepsis-derived vesicles, drives thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation; deficiency of FVIII or FIX causes haemophilia.

Amplification and propagation of coagulation cascade is the explosive middle of blood clotting, in which trace thrombin made during tissue factor-dependent initiation feeds back to generate a burst of thrombin on the activated platelet surface and convert fibrinogen to a stable fibrin clot. Without it, haemostasis fails and bleeding disorders such as haemophilia A and B follow, while unrestrained activity produces thrombosis. Thrombin activates factors XI, VIII and V, assembling the tenase (FIXa:FVIIIa) and prothrombinase (FXa:FVa) complexes on phosphatidylserine exposed by scramblase activity, so that prothrombin cleavage accelerates enormously. Platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V and von Willebrand factor tether platelets to the injury site and support their procoagulant conversion. Counterbalancing anticoagulants -- antithrombin, heparin cofactor II, protein C with protein S, and protein C inhibitor -- confine the burst to the site of vessel damage.

Once tissue factor has generated a trace of thrombin at a wound, the amplification and propagation phases turn that trace into a burst large enough to clot blood. Thrombin feeds back to activate factors XI, VIII and V on the activated platelet surface, where the tenase complex (FIXa with FVIIIa) makes FXa and the prothrombinase complex (FXa with FVa) cleaves prothrombin, so fibrinogen is converted to cross-linked fibrin and the platelet plug is stabilised. Phosphatidylserine exposure, which requires the scramblase ANO6, and von Willebrand factor binding through the GPIb-IX-V receptor provide the procoagulant membranes and platelet adhesion. Antithrombin, heparin cofactor II and the protein C/protein S system restrain the burst; loss of factor VIII or IX causes haemophilia, while defective inhibition predisposes to thrombosis.

Serine metabolism supplies the L-serine that cells use as a precursor for nucleotides, phospholipids, sphingolipids and one-carbon units, and that the brain uses to make the neurotransmitters glycine and D-serine. Because serine crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly, neural tissue depends on local synthesis, and loss of the biosynthetic enzymes causes congenital microcephaly, seizures and psychomotor retardation that can be mitigated by early serine supplementation. The route branches from glycolysis at 3-phosphoglycerate, with PHGDH oxidising it, PSAT1 transferring an amino group from glutamate, and PSPH releasing free serine; serine dehydratase activity returns carbon to pyruvate when serine is in excess. Serine racemase generates D-serine, the co-agonist at NMDA receptors, while serine incorporators feed serine into sphingolipid and phosphatidylserine synthesis at the membrane, linking amino acid supply to lipid biogenesis and synaptic signalling.

Serine metabolism supplies the brain and dividing cells with L-serine, a precursor for nucleotides, phospholipids, sphingolipids and the neurotransmitters glycine and D-serine, and a donor of one-carbon units for folate-dependent methylation. Synthesis branches from glycolysis: 3-phosphoglycerate is oxidised by PHGDH, transaminated by PSAT1 using glutamate as the amino donor, and dephosphorylated by PSPH to release free serine. Serine racemase generates D-serine, the co-agonist at NMDA receptors, while serine dehydratase enzymes catabolise serine to pyruvate and ammonia and set the balance between supply and disposal. The SERINC proteins incorporate serine into membrane lipids during their synthesis. Loss of the biosynthetic enzymes causes congenital microcephaly, seizures and severe developmental delay that respond to dietary serine if begun early, and PHGDH is frequently amplified in tumours dependent on serine for growth.

Regulation of Complement cascade keeps an amplifying, self-sustaining immune proteolytic system aimed at pathogens and away from healthy tissue. Because C3 activation feeds back to generate more C3 convertase, and because the alternative pathway ticks over continuously through spontaneous C3 hydrolysis, host surfaces must be actively protected; loss of this control causes atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, C3 glomerulopathy and age-related macular degeneration. Regulators built from tandem complement control repeats — factor H, CD46, CD55 and CR1, with C4BP and the factor H-related proteins — act in two ways: accelerating decay of C3 and C5 convertases, and serving as cofactors for factor I cleavage of C3b and C4b. C1 inhibitor restrains the classical initiating proteases, carboxypeptidases inactivate the C3a and C5a chemoattractants, and CD59 blocks assembly of the membrane attack complex. Pathogens subvert this system by capturing plasma regulators onto their surfaces.

Complement is destructive by design and self-amplifying, so host tissue survives only because its activation is continuously restrained. This regulation keeps the inherent positive feedback of C3 cleavage and the constant low-grade tickover of the alternative pathway from turning on healthy cells, while still allowing opsonisation of pathogens and clearance of dead cells, debris and oxidative damage. Membrane-anchored and plasma regulators of complement activation work in two ways: they accelerate irreversible decay of the C3 and C5 convertases, as decay accelerating factor CD55 does, and they serve as cofactors for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b and C4b, the role of factor H, membrane cofactor protein CD46, complement receptor 1 and C4b-binding protein. C1 inhibitor blocks the classical pathway proteases and CD59 caps membrane attack complex assembly. Loss of these brakes underlies atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, macular degeneration and hereditary angioedema; many microbes evade attack by capturing host regulators.

Ciprofloxacin ADME traces how a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibiotic is absorbed, distributed, metabolised and excreted, which determines both its efficacy against susceptible urinary, respiratory, gastrointestinal and bone infections and its liability for tendon, nerve and CNS toxicity. Because the drug is neither highly soluble nor highly permeable at intestinal pH, its handling depends less on passive diffusion than on carrier proteins: organic cation and anion transporters mediate hepatic and renal tubular uptake, an organic anion transporting polypeptide contributes to intestinal and hepatic entry, and the efflux pump ABCG2 drives secretion back into the gut lumen and bile. Albumin binding sets the free fraction in plasma. Most of the dose leaves unchanged by the renal and biliary routes, with only a minor fraction oxidised or sulfated, so transporter competition and renal impairment dominate exposure and dosing decisions.

Ciprofloxacin, a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibiotic, is handled by the body largely through transport rather than metabolism, and this disposition route explains both its tissue concentrations and its drug interactions. Absorption occurs mainly in the upper small intestine, where the drug's poor permeability makes uptake and efflux carriers decisive; the remainder of a dose is excreted essentially unchanged by the kidney and, to a lesser extent, the intestine and bile, with only a minor fraction converted to oxo- and sulfo-metabolites. An organic anion transporting polypeptide mediates cellular uptake, organic cation and organic anion transporters of the solute carrier family move the drug across renal tubular and hepatic membranes, and the ATP-driven efflux pump ABCG2 exports it into gut lumen and bile. Albumin binding limits the free plasma fraction. Variation in these carriers shifts exposure and underlies the tendon, nerve and central nervous system toxicities that now restrict prescribing.

Formation of axial mesoderm is the early embryonic step that builds the notochord and its anterior derivatives from cells ingressing at the front of the primitive streak. It matters because the notochord is the embryo's midline organiser: it stiffens the body axis, patterns neural tube, somites and gut through Sonic Hedgehog and related signals, and later persists as the nuclei pulposi of the intervertebral discs, whose failure underlies disc degeneration and, in rare cases, chordoma. NODAL signalling through SMAD2/3 cooperates with the pioneer factor FOXH1, with TBXT expressed before streak formation, and with TEAD factors held in check by Hippo signalling via YAP1; together they activate FOXA2, which drives notochord-specific targets including NOTO and SHH. WNT input through beta-catenin with TCF/LEF partners contributes to axial specification, linking morphogen gradients to midline cell fate.

Early in gastrulation, cells ingressing at the anterior primitive streak form the axial mesoderm, or chordamesoderm, the midline tissue that becomes the prechordal plate, head process and notochord. This midline is the embryo's organizing rod: it stiffens the body axis, patterns neural tube and somites through secreted Sonic Hedgehog, and later persists as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc, whose degeneration underlies disc disease. NODAL signalling through SMAD2 and SMAD3 cooperates with the pioneer factor FOXH1, with TEAD factors and their coactivator YAP1 released from Hippo restraint, and with the mesodermal factor TBXT to switch on FOXA2, which in turn drives notochord genes such as NOTO and SHH. WNT input via CTNNB1 with LEF1 and TCF7 positions this programme along the axis, coupling germ layer specification to midline identity.

Assembly and release of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) virions is the final step of the RSV replication cycle, in which newly made genomes and viral proteins are packaged into filamentous virions that bud from the apical surface of ciliated airway epithelium and spread infection through the respiratory tract. Progeny virions form when the nucleoprotein-coated negative-sense genome, together with the L/P polymerase and the M2-1 processivity factor, is bridged to the matrix protein layer beneath a lipid envelope studded with the fusion, attachment, and small hydrophobic proteins; the last forms a pentameric ion channel that delays death of the infected cell. Budding depends on host membranes and cytoskeleton, and on the HSP90 chaperones, whose folding activity supports viral polymerase and glycoprotein maturation, making them a point at which host chaperone function can be targeted to limit virion production.

The final step of respiratory syncytial virus replication is the packaging of new genomes and the release of infectious particles from the infected cell. RSV assembles at the apical surface of ciliated airway epithelium, where viral filaments form: the negative-sense genome coated by nucleoprotein and bound by the polymerase and its phosphoprotein cofactor is bridged by M2-1 to a matrix layer that in turn supports an envelope carrying the fusion, attachment and small hydrophobic proteins. Budding depends on cooperation between these viral proteins, host membranes and the cytoskeleton, and the requirement here is for host cytosolic HSP90 chaperone activity, which supports folding and stability of the viral polymerase and structural proteins. Blocking this chaperone step limits production of progeny virions, making it a host-directed target in bronchiolitis and other severe RSV disease of infants and the elderly.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) genome replication, transcription and translation is the intracellular phase of infection by the leading cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants, in which the virus copies its negative-sense RNA genome and expresses its eleven proteins entirely from host resources. The viral polymerase complex, built from the large catalytic subunit and its phosphoprotein cofactor, reads a template that stays encapsidated by nucleoprotein, and switches between making mRNAs and making full-length antigenome depending on regulatory viral factors. Everything shown here is the host contribution the virus subverts: casein kinase 2 and protein phosphatase 1 set the phosphorylation state of the phosphoprotein that governs elongation, HSP90 and HSPA8 chaperone polymerase assembly, importin and exportin move viral proteins across the nuclear envelope, and signal peptidase and furin process the envelope glycoproteins. Blocking these steps is the basis of antiviral strategies against RSV.

Respiratory syncytial virus carries a negative-sense RNA genome that must be copied and expressed entirely by virally encoded machinery, and the host proteins gathered here are the ones that machinery borrows. RSV genome replication, transcription and translation depend on the viral polymerase large subunit and its phosphoprotein cofactor acting on nucleoprotein-coated RNA, with a processivity factor and a regulator that switches synthesis between mRNA and antigenome. Host casein kinase 2 subunits and protein phosphatase 1 catalytic subunits set the phosphorylation state of the phosphoprotein that licenses transcript elongation, HSP90 and HSPA8 chaperone polymerase assembly, and importin beta and exportin 1 move viral proteins in and out of the nucleus. Signal peptidase subunits and furin process the envelope glycoproteins, furin cleaving the fusion protein into its active form. This biology underlies bronchiolitis in infants and is where antiviral polymerase inhibitors act.

Somitogenesis is the periodic segmentation of the embryo's paraxial mesoderm into somites, the blocks of tissue that later give rise to vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis; its failure produces congenital vertebral malsegmentation such as spondylocostal dysostosis. Segment size and timing follow a clock-and-wavefront logic: an oscillator running in presomitic mesoderm cells intersects a slowly regressing determination front set by opposing WNT/FGF and retinoic acid gradients. The oscillator is built from Notch signalling with negative feedback, in which HES7 represses its own transcription and LFNG glycosylates Notch to damp DLL1/DLL3-dependent activation through RBPJ. Where the wave meets the front, TBX6 with MSGN1 licenses MESP2 expression, which sets rostrocaudal polarity, induces EPHA4 for boundary formation, and drives RIPPLY2 to extinguish TBX6 and reset the cycle. Rapid proteasomal turnover of these short-lived regulators keeps the oscillations sharp.

Somitogenesis is the periodic segmentation of the vertebrate embryo's paraxial mesoderm into somites, the blocks of mesenchyme that give rise to vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis; its failure produces congenital vertebral malformations such as spondylocostal dysostosis. Segment size and spacing arise from a clock-and-wavefront arrangement, in which a molecular oscillator in presomitic mesoderm meets gradients of WNT, FGF and retinoic acid signalling that set the determination front. The oscillator is built from Notch-pathway negative feedback: HES7 represses its own transcription, and the glycosyltransferase LFNG, induced through NOTCH1/RBPJ, feeds back to dampen Notch, with DLL1 and DLL3 ligands shaping the response. At the front, TBX6 and MSGN1 drive MESP2, which turns on EPHA4 for boundary formation and RIPPLY2 to extinguish TBX6. Rapid proteasomal turnover keeps these short-lived regulators oscillating.

Regulation of MITF-M-dependent genes involved in DNA replication, damage repair and senescence describes how the melanocyte master transcription factor MITF, beyond pigmentation, sustains the machinery that copies and protects the genome. This link explains why melanocytes and melanoma cells tolerate proliferation without accumulating lethal damage, and why lowering MITF levels drives replication stress, DNA damage and entry into senescence rather than simple growth arrest. MITF-M binds promoters of replication and repair genes including the MCM helicase subunits MCM2 and MCM5, the ligase LIG1, the homologous recombination factor BRCA1, and the telomerase catalytic subunit TERT, coupling lineage identity to S-phase competence and chromosome stability. The outcome of MITF loss depends on context: depletion accompanied by ATF4-driven translational reprogramming yields reversible arrest instead of senescence, a switch relevant to melanoma phenotype-switching and drug tolerance.

MITF-M is the melanocyte-specific master transcription factor, and beyond pigmentation it directs a set of target genes that keep proliferating melanocytes and melanoma cells genomically stable. Through this arm of its programme it drives replication and repair machinery, including the MCM2 and MCM5 subunits of the replicative helicase, the DNA ligase LIG1 that seals nicks during replication and repair, the homologous recombination and damage-response factor BRCA1, and the telomerase catalytic subunit TERT for chromosome end maintenance. Losing MITF by RNA interference allows DNA damage to accumulate and pushes cells into senescence, whereas MITF suppression driven by ATF4 and translational reprogramming produces a reversible cell cycle arrest without senescence. The pathway therefore links lineage identity to replication licensing, genome integrity and proliferative lifespan, and is central to how melanoma cells switch between proliferative and invasive, dedifferentiated states.

Nephron development builds the kidney's filtering unit -- glomerulus, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and connecting segment -- from mesenchymal progenitors, and sets the number of nephrons a person is born with, a count that is never increased and whose deficit predisposes to hypertension and chronic kidney disease. WNT9B from the ureteric bud tip induces progenitors to aggregate and switch on WNT4, driving a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition into renal vesicles, while SIX2-positive neighbours instead self-renew to keep the progenitor pool alive. The vesicle is polarised from the outset: WT1 marks the proximal pole and represses PAX2 to permit podocyte formation, whereas LHX1, POU3F3 and HNF1B pattern distal segments and switch on Notch ligands DLL1, JAG1 and LFNG, with HNF1B also activating IRX1/IRX2 in the intermediate limb. Mutations in HNF1B or PAX2 cause human renal hypodysplasia.

The nephron is the filtering and reabsorbing unit of the kidney, running from glomerulus through proximal tubule, loop of Henle and distal segments to the collecting duct, and its formation during fetal life sets the number of nephrons a person will ever have. Nephron development begins where ureteric bud tips meet metanephric mesenchyme: WNT9B from the bud induces progenitors to aggregate and express WNT4, driving a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition into renal vesicles, while a self-renewing progenitor pool is maintained in parallel. The vesicle is polarized from the outset, with WT1 acting proximally to repress PAX2 and permit podocyte formation, and LHX1 and POU3F3 specifying distal segments and loop elongation. HNF1B then activates Notch components DLL1, JAG1 and LFNG plus IRX1/IRX2 as the comma- and S-shaped bodies form, and HNF4A supports proximal tubule identity. Defective versions of this programme underlie congenital kidney malformation and reduced nephron endowment.

Formation of the posterior neural plate is the step in early embryogenesis that lays down the neuroepithelium destined to become hindbrain and anterior spinal cord, as distinct from the anterior neural plate that yields forebrain and midbrain. It matters because this sheet must be specified and then folded into a closed tube; incomplete closure produces neural tube defects such as spina bifida, the commonest congenital malformation of the central nervous system. Posterior neural fate arises largely from bipotent neuromesodermal progenitors near the primitive streak, in which WNT3A and FGF8 signalling drives SOX2 expression through a posterior-specific enhancer, while TBX6 diverts sister cells to paraxial mesoderm. Regional identity is then fixed by mutual repression between GBX2 posteriorly and OTX2 anteriorly, which sharpens the midbrain-hindbrain boundary, with SOX1, ZEB2, POU3F1 and ZNF521 accompanying commitment to neural progenitor character.

Early in development the dorsal epiblast thickens into the neural plate, the sheet that folds into the neural tube and becomes the entire central nervous system; incomplete closure produces neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Formation of the posterior neural plate specifies the caudal half of that sheet, which gives rise to the hindbrain and anterior spinal cord, and it is built differently from the anterior half: rather than arising directly from epiblast, its caudal portion derives from bipotent neuromesodermal progenitors in which WNT and FGF signalling, via WNT3A and FGF8, drive SOX2 through a dedicated posterior enhancer while TBX6 pulls sister cells toward paraxial mesoderm. Regional identity is then fixed by mutual transcriptional repression between GBX2 posteriorly and OTX2 anteriorly, setting the midbrain-hindbrain boundary, with SOX1, ZEB2 and POU3F1 accompanying commitment to neural fate.

Signaling by TGFBR3 describes how betaglycan, a transmembrane proteoglycan co-receptor without kinase activity of its own, shapes the cell's response to TGF-beta family ligands. It matters because betaglycan sets ligand sensitivity: it captures TGF-beta isoforms and presents them to TGFBR2 so that a signalling complex with TGFBR1 can form and activate SMAD3/SMAD4, while sequestering inhibin and modulating activin and BMP responses. It is abundant in normal tissue and lost in many carcinomas, where its downregulation removes a brake on invasion and marks it as a tumour suppressor; it also contributes to FGF2/FGFR co-receptor function. The pathway includes its own regulation, by myogenic and other transcription factors, by microRNA silencing through Argonaute-containing complexes, and by ectodomain shedding via matrix metalloproteinases and gamma-secretase, which converts membrane betaglycan into a soluble ligand trap.

Betaglycan, the type III TGF-beta receptor encoded by TGFBR3, is a transmembrane proteoglycan with no kinase activity that works as a co-receptor, capturing TGF-beta family ligands and presenting them to the signalling type II and type I receptors so that a SMAD2/3-SMAD4 transcriptional response can be mounted. It also binds activin and inhibin subunits and BMPs, and stabilises FGF2:FGFR complexes, so it can either promote or dampen a given ligand's output. Its abundance is set transcriptionally, by factors including SP1, myogenic regulators of the MyoD/myogenin family and E-protein partners, retinoid receptors with EP300, and post-transcriptionally by Argonaute-TNRC6 microRNA silencing; the ectodomain is shed by membrane metalloproteinases restrained by TIMPs, and gamma-secretase components process the remaining stub. Loss of TGFBR3 is common in carcinomas, where it behaves as a tumour suppressor, and it has been linked to inflammatory disease and Alzheimer's.

TGFBR3 expression governs how much betaglycan, the type III TGF-beta receptor, a cell displays, and thereby sets the sensitivity of that cell to TGF-beta, activin and BMP ligands. Betaglycan presents ligand to the signalling receptors and can also be shed to act as a soluble trap, so its abundance tunes growth inhibition, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cell migration; loss of expression is a recurrent feature of carcinoma progression. Control operates at two levels. Transcription is driven by Sp1 together with retinoic acid receptor heterodimers, SMAD3/SMAD4, and the myogenic program of MYOD1, MYF5, MYOG and E-protein partners, with EP300 as coactivator and HELLS, KLF16 and MYCN acting as repressive inputs. Post-transcriptionally, miR-23b, miR-27b and let-7 loaded into Argonaute-TNRC6 silencing complexes limit translation of the transcript, linking receptor levels to microRNA-mediated repression.

TGFBR3, or betaglycan, is the most abundant TGF-beta receptor on many cell surfaces; it presents ligand to the signalling type I/II receptor pair and, when shed, acts as a soluble ligand trap, so how much of it a cell makes sets the gain of TGF-beta family signalling. Control of TGFBR3 expression operates at two levels. Transcriptionally, Sp1 together with retinoic acid receptors RARA/RXRA, the myogenic bHLH factors MYOD1, MYF5, MYF6 and MYOG with their E-protein partners TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12, and SMAD3/SMAD4 acting with the EP300 coactivator converge on the promoter, while chromatin regulators such as the HELLS remodeller and the KLF16 zinc finger, and the oncoprotein MYCN, modulate output. Post-transcriptionally, miRNAs including miR-23b, miR-27b and let-7 direct Argonaute-TNRC6 silencing complexes to the transcript. Loss of betaglycan is a recurrent feature of carcinoma progression.

Signaling by LTK describes ligand activation of leukocyte tyrosine kinase, a receptor closely related to ALK and, like it, a receptor for the small secreted cytokines ALKAL1 and ALKAL2. The pathway supports neuronal differentiation and cell survival, promoting neurite outgrowth in responsive cells, and has been implicated in regulating secretory traffic between the ER and Golgi; oncogenic LTK fusions drive a subset of non-small cell lung cancers, making it a candidate kinase target. Ligand binding to the extracellular EGF-like and glycine-rich modules drives receptor dimerisation and trans-autophosphorylation, creating docking sites for SHC1, GRB2-SOS1, IRS1 and the p85 regulatory subunits of PI3K, so that RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT arms are engaged together. The kinase TNK2 and ubiquitin-mediated receptor downregulation shape the duration of the response.

Leukocyte tyrosine kinase is a receptor tyrosine kinase of the insulin receptor superfamily and the closest relative of ALK, with which it shares the small secreted cytokines ALKAL1 and ALKAL2 as activating ligands. Signalling through LTK has been linked to neurite outgrowth and cell survival, and to control of secretory traffic between the ER and Golgi; fusion proteins involving the kinase occur in non-small cell lung cancer, placing it alongside ALK as an oncogenic driver. Ligand binding to the extracellular glycine-rich and EGF-like modules drives trans-autophosphorylation of the cytoplasmic kinase domain, creating docking sites for SHC1, GRB2 and IRS1 and thereby engaging the SOS1-Ras-MAPK route, with recruitment of class IA PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits feeding the survival arm. TNK2 participates as an associated cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase in the downstream response.

Adipogenesis is the developmental program by which precursor cells become fat cells, generating the tissue that stores and releases energy for the whole body and, in its brown and beige forms, burns substrate to make heat. Its output determines fat mass distribution, insulin sensitivity and thermogenic capacity; when it fails or is misdirected, the result is lipodystrophy, ectopic lipid deposition and metabolic disease. Commitment runs through a transcriptional cascade in which C/EBP factors induce PPARG, which with RXRA drives the mature adipocyte program — lipid handling and secretion by FABP4, CD36, LPL, PLIN1, ADIPOQ and leptin. Brown and beige identity is imposed by PRDM16, EBF2 and PGC-1 coactivators, activating UCP1, CIDEA and DIO2. Much of the gene list is coregulatory machinery: the Mediator complex, p300/CBP and NCOA coactivators, and NuRD and NCOR/HDAC corepressors that keep the program off until BMP, TGF-beta and Wnt cues permit differentiation.

Adipogenesis is the differentiation of precursor cells into fat cells, the storage depot and endocrine organ that buffers systemic energy supply; when it fails or is overwhelmed, lipid spills into liver and muscle and insulin resistance follows, while its extremes produce lipodystrophy or obesity. The programme is transcriptional at heart: CEBPB and CEBPD initiate, then PPARG with its RXRA partner and CEBPA lock in the mature state, driving the lipid-handling machinery of white adipocytes such as FABP4, CD36, LPL, PLIN1, GLUT4 and the hormones leptin and adiponectin. Coactivators and Mediator subunits, acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300, and repressive NCOR/HDAC and NuRD complexes tune this output; WNT and TGF-beta signals restrain it. A parallel branch specified by PRDM16, EBF2 and PPARGC1A yields thermogenic brown and beige cells expressing UCP1, CIDEA and DIO2 for heat production.

Enhanced cleavage of VWF variant by ADAMTS13 describes a molecular basis of type 2A von Willebrand disease, in which mutant von Willebrand factor is destroyed too readily by its own regulatory protease and platelet plug formation fails. Normally the metalloprotease ADAMTS13 trims VWF multimers by cutting the Tyr1605-Met1606 bond in the A2 domain, a site exposed only when shear forces unfold that domain, so that ultra-large multimers are kept in check and microvascular thrombosis is avoided. Missense substitutions such as Y1584C, I1568N and G1579R destabilise the A2 fold and expose the scissile bond prematurely, accelerating proteolysis and depleting the high-molecular-weight multimers that tether platelets to exposed collagen I at sites of vessel injury. The result is a mucocutaneous bleeding phenotype, illustrating how haemostasis depends on balanced VWF multimer turnover.

Von Willebrand factor circulates as long multimers that capture platelets at sites of vessel injury, and their size is trimmed by the plasma metalloprotease ADAMTS13, which cuts a single Tyr-Met bond in the A2 domain only when shear force unfolds it. Certain von Willebrand disease missense variants, including Y1584C, I1568N, G1579R and G1631D, destabilise that domain so the scissile bond is exposed too readily; the resulting enhanced cleavage of the VWF variant strips high-molecular-weight multimers from plasma and produces a bleeding phenotype of the type 2A kind. The same protein also carries collagen-binding sites that tether it to subendothelial type I collagen, the step that presents VWF to flowing blood and generates the tension needed for proteolysis. This regulated degradation sets the balance between haemostasis and thrombosis, with loss of ADAMTS13 activity causing the opposite disorder, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

Regulation of MITF-M dependent genes involved in invasion describes how the melanocyte master transcription factor MITF controls whether a pigment cell stays put or moves, a switch that governs melanoblast migration in development and metastatic spread in melanoma. MITF-M, the melanocyte-specific isoform, activates targets that remodel adhesion and the actin cytoskeleton: the adhesion molecule CEACAM1, the formin DIAPH1 that drives actin filament elongation and a rounded, less invasive morphology, and GMPR, which lowers GTP available to Rho-family GTPases and thereby damps membrane protrusion. MITF also feeds into epithelial-mesenchymal transition programmes through factors such as SNAI2. The result is the phenotype-switching behaviour characteristic of melanoma, in which high MITF favours proliferation and differentiation while low MITF licenses an invasive, migratory state, linking transcriptional identity directly to cell motility and metastatic potential.

The melanocyte master transcription factor MITF, in its melanocyte-specific M isoform, does more than drive pigmentation: it sets how mobile and invasive a melanocytic cell is. Through targets such as the adhesion molecule CEACAM1, the actin-nucleating formin DIAPH1 and the purine-metabolic enzyme GMPR, MITF tunes cell-cell adhesion and the state of the actin cytoskeleton, and it also feeds into epithelial-mesenchymal-transition programmes via SNAI2. This matters most in melanoma, where cells switch between an MITF-high proliferative, differentiated state and an MITF-low invasive state; the level of MITF activity therefore helps determine whether tumour cells divide locally or migrate and metastasise, and it influences response to targeted therapy. The same transcriptional control underlies normal melanoblast migration during development, linking lineage identity to motility rather than treating them as separate programmes.

Cellular responses to mechanical stimuli describes how cells sense physical force — blood flow, tissue stretch, matrix stiffness, touch, skeletal loading — and convert it into chemical signalling that changes gene expression, growth and behaviour. It underlies endothelial adaptation to laminar versus turbulent shear stress and the nitric oxide production that sets vascular tone, osteocyte responses to mechanical load and bone remodelling, and tactile sensation in Merkel cells and Pacinian corpuscles; its failure contributes to atherosclerosis at branch points, hypertension, disuse bone loss and touch insensitivity. Force is detected by mechanically gated channels such as PIEZO1 and TRPV4, by integrins and their adhesion plaques with talin, vinculin and focal adhesion kinase, and by junctional and G protein-coupled receptors. Signals are then amplified through PI3K-AKT-mTOR, adenylate cyclase and PKA, NF-κB, purinergic ATP release via pannexin, and YAP-mediated transcription.

Cells continuously read the physical forces around them — blood flow shear, tissue stretch, matrix stiffness, touch — and convert them into chemical signals, and this conversion is what allows endothelium to align with laminar flow, osteocytes to remodel bone under load, and sensory structures to register mechanical contact. Force-gated channels such as PIEZO1 and TRPV4 admit calcium, while integrins (ITGA5, ITGAV, ITGB1) coupled through talin, vinculin and focal adhesion kinase transmit tension from fibronectin and the matrix into the cytoskeleton. Downstream, PI3K–AKT–mTOR complexes, adenylyl cyclase and PKA, NF-κB subunits, and the transcriptional coactivator YAP1 translate the stimulus into changes in gene expression, growth and survival; PECAM1, CDH5 and eNOS carry the endothelial arm toward vasodilation. Purinergic release through pannexin and P2 receptors amplifies the response, and NLRP3 links excessive force to inflammation. Disturbed mechanotransduction contributes to atherosclerosis at flow-disturbed sites, fibrosis and disuse bone loss.

Regulation of FXIIa and plasma kallikrein activity restrains the contact activation and kallikrein-kinin systems, the plasma proteolytic cascades that link surface-triggered coagulation to bradykinin release, complement activation and fibrinolysis. Restraint matters because unchecked activity produces bradykinin-driven swelling and pathological thrombosis: loss of C1 inhibitor, the serpin encoded by SERPING1, causes hereditary angioedema, and this same inhibitor accounts for the great majority of factor XIIa neutralisation in plasma. Alpha-2-macroglobulin traps plasma kallikrein by a distinct caging mechanism, and the two together dominate its inhibition; histidine-rich glycoprotein competes for the negatively charged surfaces that nucleate assembly. Factor XII, prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen form the reciprocal activation loop being controlled, assembled on endothelial and leukocyte receptors including gC1qR, cytokeratin 1 and the urokinase receptor, which localise the cascade to vessel walls and inflamed tissue.

The contact activation system generates factor XIIa and plasma kallikrein, proteases that link blood clotting to inflammation by cleaving kininogen to release bradykinin, feeding back to activate each other, and touching complement and fibrinolysis as well. Restraint of FXIIa and plasma kallikrein activity keeps this amplifying loop from running away: C1 inhibitor, encoded by SERPING1, is the dominant brake on FXIIa and a major inhibitor of kallikrein, alpha-2-macroglobulin traps kallikrein in a covalent complex, and histidine-rich glycoprotein limits assembly of the system. Loss of C1 inhibitor causes hereditary angioedema, in which unchecked kallikrein activity produces bradykinin-driven vascular leak and episodic swelling. Assembly is surface-dependent, with prekallikrein and factor XII delivered by high-molecular-weight kininogen to endothelial and cell-surface partners including the C1q-binding protein, cytokeratin 1 and the urokinase receptor.

Malate-aspartate shuttle moves reducing equivalents from the cytosol into mitochondria without moving NADH itself, regenerating the cytosolic NAD+ that glycolysis, serine synthesis and glutamate metabolism depend on while feeding electrons to the respiratory chain. Cytosolic malate dehydrogenase reduces oxaloacetate to malate, which enters via the oxoglutarate carrier in exchange for 2-oxoglutarate; matrix MDH2 regenerates NADH, and transamination by the GOT1/GOT2 pair exports aspartate through the calcium-sensitive aspartate-glutamate carriers AGC1 and AGC2. Because glutamate import is proton-coupled and effectively irreversible, the proton-motive force keeps the cycle running in one direction. The shuttle also sets aspartate availability for nucleotide and protein synthesis. Its failure starves the cytosol of NAD+ and the brain of aspartate and glutamate for neurotransmission, and mutations in the carriers and mitochondrial glutamate transporters cause early infantile epileptic encephalopathy and citrin deficiency.

Cytosolic NADH cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, so the malate-aspartate shuttle moves its reducing equivalents indirectly, keeping the cytosol oxidized enough for glycolysis to continue while delivering electrons to the respiratory chain. Cytosolic malate dehydrogenase reduces oxaloacetate to malate, which enters in exchange for 2-oxoglutarate via the dicarboxylate carrier SLC25A11; inside, MDH2 regenerates NADH. Transaminases GOT1 and GOT2 interconvert aspartate and glutamate on either side, and the aspartate-glutamate carriers SLC25A12 and SLC25A13 co-import a proton, making the cycle unidirectional and driven by the proton-motive force. Glutamate carriers SLC25A18 and SLC25A22 feed the amino acid arm. Loss of any step starves the cytosol of NAD+ and limits aspartate, serine and glutamate supply; in the brain this presents as early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, and carrier defects also cause citrin deficiency with hyperammonaemia.

Protein lipoylation builds the lipoyl cofactor inside mitochondria and attaches it to the handful of enzymes that cannot run without it: the E2 subunits of pyruvate, 2-oxoglutarate, 2-oxoadipate and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenases, plus the glycine cleavage system. It therefore sits upstream of oxidative energy metabolism, amino acid catabolism and one-carbon supply, and its failure produces severe lactic acidosis with combined dehydrogenase deficiency; loss of the carrier protein GCSH additionally causes hyperglycinemia and epileptic encephalopathy. Octanoyl groups from mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis, carried on the acyl carrier protein NDUFAB1, are transferred by LIPT2 onto GCSH; the radical-SAM enzyme LIAS then inserts two sulfurs using iron-sulfur clusters supplied through NFU1, with FDX1 providing electrons; LIPT1 finally relays the lipoyl group to the acceptor lysines of DLAT, DLST and DBT.

Five mitochondrial redox enzymes work only if one of their subunits carries a covalently attached lipoyl arm, and protein lipoylation is how that arm is built and installed. It supplies the pyruvate, 2-oxoglutarate, 2-oxoadipate and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes, linking glycolysis to the citric acid cycle and driving amino acid catabolism, and it equips the glycine cleavage system. Octanoate delivered by the acyl carrier protein NDUFAB1 is loaded onto the carrier GCSH by LIPT2, the radical-SAM enzyme LIAS inserts two sulfurs using iron-sulfur clusters supplied with help from FDX1 and NFU1, and LIPT1 transfers the finished lipoyl group to the E2 subunits DLAT, DLST and DBT. Loss of any step produces severe lactic acidosis with combined dehydrogenase deficiency, and GCSH defects additionally cause hyperglycinemia with epileptic encephalopathy.

SLC15A4:TASL-dependent IRF5 activation is the branch of endosomal Toll-like receptor signalling that turns nucleic acid sensing into type I interferon and pro-inflammatory cytokine transcription. It gives immune cells, particularly plasmacytoid dendritic cells and B cells, their interferon response to viral RNA and CpG DNA, and its overactivity by self nucleic acids drives systemic lupus erythematosus, making the transporter and its adaptor attractive drug targets. SLC15A4, a proton-coupled histidine and oligopeptide transporter, doubles as a scaffold on the endolysosomal membrane, docking TASL on the cytosolic face. After TLR7, TLR8 or TLR9 engagement, TASL is phosphorylated and its pLxIS motif recruits IRF5, which the IKK complex catalytic subunit IKKβ phosphorylates; IRF5 then homodimerises and enters the nucleus. This positions the pathway as a spatially restricted, lysosome-anchored counterpart to the STING and MAVS routes to interferon induction.

Endosomal Toll-like receptors that sense nucleic acids need a dedicated route to switch on interferon gene transcription, and this is it: a lysosomal transporter doubling as a signalling scaffold delivers IRF5 to the kinase that activates it. SLC15A4, a proton-coupled histidine and oligopeptide transporter, anchors the adaptor TASL on the cytosolic face of endolysosomes, where TASL is phosphorylated and captures IRF5 through a pLxIS motif. The IKK complex, with IKBKB as the relevant catalytic subunit, then phosphorylates IRF5, which homodimerizes and moves to the nucleus to drive type I interferon and pro-inflammatory cytokine genes. The output shapes plasmacytoid dendritic cell and B cell responses to viral RNA and DNA. When self nucleic acids trigger it, chronic interferon production follows, and both SLC15A4 and IRF5 are genetically linked to systemic lupus erythematosus, making the axis a drug target.

Response of endothelial cells to shear stress describes how the cells lining blood vessels sense the frictional force of flowing blood and translate it into vessel tone, cell shape, and inflammatory state. It explains why arterial regions of steady high flow stay atheroprotected while branch points and curvatures with disturbed or sluggish flow become sites of atherosclerotic plaque. All flow types open the mechanosensitive channel PIEZO1, admitting calcium that activates calpain-2 and remodels the submembrane cytoskeleton so cells elongate along the flow axis. Steady laminar flow additionally engages VEGFR2, purinergic P2RY2 and adrenomedullin signalling through PI3K-AKT to phosphorylate eNOS, raising nitric oxide and driving vasodilation. Disturbed flow instead works through integrin alpha5-beta1, PDE4D-mediated cAMP loss, PP2A-dependent YAP1 activation and FAK-driven NF-kB nuclear entry, switching on pro-inflammatory transcription and adhesion molecule expression.

Endothelial cells lining blood vessels continuously read the frictional drag of flowing blood, and how they respond to shear stress determines whether a vessel segment stays quiescent and dilated or turns inflamed and atherosclerosis-prone. Flow is sensed at the apical membrane and at junctional and adhesion complexes: the mechanosensitive cation channels PIEZO1 and TRPV4 admit calcium, activating the calpain-2 protease that remodels submembrane cytoskeleton so cells elongate and align with the flow axis. Steady high-volume laminar flow signals through VEGFR2, ATP-released P2RY2, and adrenomedullin acting on CALCRL/RAMP2 to raise cAMP and activate PI3K-AKT, which phosphorylates eNOS to generate nitric oxide and vasodilation. Disturbed or low flow instead engages integrin alpha5/beta1, PDE4D-mediated cAMP hydrolysis, focal adhesion kinase, and PP2A-dependent YAP1 activation, driving NF-kB-dependent inflammatory gene expression, inflammasome priming, and leukocyte recruitment at branch points and curvatures.

Loss-of-function mutations in DBT cause MSUD2 describes how defects in the dihydrolipoamide branched-chain transacylase subunit cripple the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex and produce maple syrup urine disease type 2. This complex performs the committed, irreversible step of leucine, isoleucine and valine catabolism, oxidatively decarboxylating their transaminated keto acids so that the carbon skeletons can enter the TCA cycle. DBT forms the E2 core to which the E1 heterotetramer of BCKDHA and BCKDHB and the shared E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase attach, and its lipoyl domain shuttles the acyl group between them; losing it destabilises the entire assembly. Branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids then accumulate in blood and brain, causing the characteristic sweet-smelling urine, encephalopathy, ketoacidotic crises and, untreated, neurological damage or death. It illustrates how one scaffold subunit determines the activity of a whole multienzyme complex.

The branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex commits leucine, isoleucine and valine to oxidative breakdown, and mutations that destroy the integrity of its E2 core subunit cause the maple syrup urine disease subtype known as MSUD2. The complex is built from E1 decarboxylase subunits, the dihydrolipoyl transacylase E2 component encoded by DBT, and the shared E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase; E2 carries the lipoyl groups that accept the acyl intermediate and pass reducing equivalents on, so loss of functional DBT stalls the whole complex regardless of intact E1. Branched-chain amino acids and their ketoacids then accumulate in blood, urine and brain, producing the characteristic sweet-smelling urine, encephalopathy, ketoacidosis and risk of cerebral oedema. Management relies on dietary restriction of these amino acids, placing this step at the centre of branched-chain amino acid catabolism and nitrogen handling.

Maple Syrup Urine Disease is the inborn error of metabolism that follows loss of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, which performs the oxidative decarboxylation step in catabolism of leucine, isoleucine and valine in the mitochondrial matrix and feeds acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA into the Krebs cycle. When this step fails, branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids accumulate, producing the characteristic sweet-smelling urine along with neonatal feeding failure, encephalopathy, seizures, coma and death unless dietary intervention follows newborn screening. The complex is built around a 24-mer transacylase core (DBT) decorated by the E1 decarboxylase tetramers of BCKDHA and BCKDHB and by DLD, the E3 dehydrogenase also shared with pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Flux is set by reversible phosphorylation of the E1 beta subunit, with PPM1K dephosphorylation activating the complex, linking amino acid disposal to nutrient state.

Maple syrup urine disease is the inborn error of metabolism that follows loss of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, the mitochondrial machine performing the second, committed step of leucine, isoleucine and valine catabolism. Without it, branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids accumulate in blood and urine, producing the characteristic sweet odour along with poor feeding, lethargy, encephalopathy, seizures, coma and death in the classic neonatal form; milder intermediate and stress-triggered intermittent forms reflect higher residual activity. The complex is built from an E1 decarboxylase made of BCKDHA and BCKDHB dimers, a DBT transacylase core, and the shared DLD dehydrogenase, and requires thiamine diphosphate, lipoamide, FAD and NAD+. Flux is set by reversible phosphorylation, with the phosphatase PPM1K activating the complex. Because DLD also serves pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, its loss causes broader, lethal lactic acidosis. Newborn screening enables dietary intervention.

Loss-of-function mutations in DLD cause MSUD3/DLDD describes an inherited metabolic disease in which the shared E3 subunit of several mitochondrial keto acid dehydrogenase complexes fails, blocking the oxidative decarboxylation steps that feed the citric acid cycle. DLD serves as dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase built from BCKDHA, BCKDHB and DBT, so its loss has pleiotropic consequences: lactic acidosis, accumulation of pyruvate, alpha-keto acids and plasma branched-chain amino acids, and progressive neurological deterioration, sometimes with liver involvement. Because branched-chain catabolism is impaired, the condition is grouped with maple syrup urine disease, but the phenotype is broader and reflects a general failure of mitochondrial fuel oxidation. Affected individuals are frequently compound heterozygotes, and residual enzyme activity measured in vitro predicts clinical severity poorly.

Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase is the shared E3 subunit of three mitochondrial alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes, so recessive loss-of-function mutations in it disable branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and pyruvate dehydrogenase at once. The resulting deficiency presents with lactic acidosis, accumulation of pyruvate, branched-chain amino acids and urinary alpha-keto acids, and progressive neurological deterioration, sometimes with liver involvement. Because the branched-chain complex is affected, the condition is classed with maple syrup urine disease, but its pleiotropic biochemistry sets it apart from defects in the complex's own catalytic subunits, the E1 alpha and beta chains and the E2 transacylase. Mechanistically the E3 component reoxidizes the lipoamide arm after decarboxylation, passing electrons to NAD+; without it, oxidative decarboxylation stalls and both amino acid catabolism and entry of carbon into the citric acid cycle fail. Compound heterozygosity is common and residual activity predicts severity poorly.

Proteasome assembly builds the cell's principal protein-destroying machine, the multisubunit complex that carries out ubiquitin-dependent regulatory and quality-control degradation. Without it, cyclins and transcription factors are not cleared on schedule, misfolded proteins accumulate, and antigenic peptides are not generated for MHC class I presentation. Dedicated chaperones (PSMG1-4, POMP) template the heteroheptameric alpha and beta rings of the barrel-shaped proteolytic core, whose catalytic beta subunits mature by autolytic propeptide removal; ATPase (PSMC) and non-ATPase (PSMD) subunits with ADRM1 and SEM1 then form the regulatory particle that recognises polyubiquitinated substrates, deubiquitinates them, and unfolds and threads them into the core. Subunit swapping generates tissue-specific variants: the immunoproteasome and thymoproteasome shape peptide repertoires for cytotoxic T cell recognition and thymic positive selection, while PSMA8-containing spermatoproteasomes serve spermatocyte differentiation. PSME activators and the inhibitor PSMF1 tune output, including stress-induced turnover of oxidised proteins.

Nearly all regulated protein destruction in the cytosol and nucleus passes through the proteasome, and building that machine correctly is what proteasome assembly accomplishes. Seven distinct alpha and seven distinct beta subunits must be placed in the right order into four stacked rings to form the barrel-shaped 20S proteolytic core, a task guided by dedicated chaperones (PSMG1-4) and the maturation factor POMP; the ATPase base and lid subunits then stack on as the 19S regulatory particle, which recognises ubiquitylated substrates, strips their chains and feeds unfolded polypeptides into the core. Alternative caps and subunit swaps generate specialised forms: the PSME1/PSME2 activator and the interferon-inducible beta subunits produce immunoproteasomes that shape peptides for MHC class I presentation, PSMB11 supports thymic positive selection, and PSMA8 with PSME4 serves spermatogenesis. PSMF1 restrains core activity. Defective assembly causes proteotoxic stress and inflammatory proteasome-associated syndromes.

Circadian clock is the cell-autonomous 24-hour timekeeper that schedules gene expression, metabolism, sleep-wake behaviour and cell division, with the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus entrained by light acting as master pacemaker over peripheral tissue clocks; its disruption underlies sleep phase disorders, metabolic syndrome and altered drug responses. Timing arises from a negative transcription-translation feedback loop: BMAL1 paired with CLOCK or NPAS2 drives E-box-dependent transcription of PER and CRY genes, whose protein products accumulate, are phosphorylated by casein kinase 1 delta/epsilon and CDK5, re-enter the nucleus and shut off their own activators. Overnight, SCF complexes using beta-TrCP, FBXL3 and FBXL21 direct PER and CRY to the proteasome, restarting the cycle. A reinforcing loop through RORA/RORC and REV-ERB tunes BMAL1 output, while coactivators, HDAC3/NCOR and SIRT1 couple the oscillator to lipid and NAD+ metabolism via PPARA, PGC-1alpha, NAMPT and SREBF1.

Nearly every tissue keeps its own 24-hour time, and this cell-autonomous oscillator is what sets the daily schedule for sleep and waking, hormone release, and fuel use; its disruption by shift work, mutation or mistimed feeding predisposes to metabolic syndrome, sleep phase disorders and altered drug responses. A transcription-translation feedback loop lies at the core: BMAL1 paired with CLOCK or NPAS2 drives E-box-dependent transcription of PER and CRY genes, whose protein products accumulate, are phosphorylated by casein kinase 1 delta and epsilon, re-enter the nucleus and shut off their own activators. Overnight, SCF-type ubiquitin ligases using BTRC or FBXL3 mark PER and CRY for proteasomal destruction, restarting the cycle. A reinforcing loop through ROR activators and the repressor NR1D1 tunes BMAL1 expression, while SIRT1, coactivators and corepressors couple the clock to NAD+ status and to lipid programmes via PPARA, CPT1A and SREBF1.

3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency is an inherited block in the breakdown of leucine, and the most common organic aciduria detected by newborn screening, at roughly one in fifty thousand births. The normal enzyme is a mitochondrial biotin-dependent carboxylase built from an alpha subunit encoded by MCCC1, which carries the covalent biotin needed for ATP-dependent carboxylation, and a beta subunit encoded by MCCC2, which supplies carboxyltransferase activity; together they convert 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA at the fourth step of leucine catabolism. Recessive mutations that destabilise either subunit or prevent its biotinylation stall the route, so 3-hydroxyvaleric acid and 3-methylcrotonylglycine accumulate and are excreted. Outcomes range widely, from lifelong absence of symptoms in most carriers of the biochemical phenotype to neonatal metabolic crisis with severe neurological damage in a small minority, linking amino acid catabolism to mitochondrial energy supply.

Leucine breakdown in mitochondria passes through a biotin-dependent carboxylation step, and loss of that step defines 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, the most common organic aciduria found by newborn screening at roughly one in 50,000 births. The enzyme converts 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA as the fourth reaction of leucine catabolism, and is built from an alpha subunit encoded by MCCC1, which carries a covalently attached biotin needed for ATP-dependent carboxylation, and a beta subunit encoded by MCCC2, which supplies carboxyltransferase activity. Recessive mutations in either subunit destabilise the complex, impair catalysis, or block biotinylation, so leucine-derived intermediates spill over into 3-hydroxyvaleric acid and 3-methylcrotonylglycine. Outcomes vary widely: most affected individuals remain mildly affected or asymptomatic, while a small fraction present in the neonatal period with metabolic decompensation and severe neurological injury.

Defective visual phototransduction due to OPN1SW loss of function describes the failure of the blue-sensitive cone photopigment and the loss of blue-yellow colour discrimination that follows. Human trichromacy depends on three cone opsins with distinct spectral peaks, and downstream retinal circuits compare their outputs to construct colour; when the short-wavelength pigment encoded by OPN1SW is disabled, the roughly 420 nm channel drops out and the perceptual comparison becomes impossible, producing tritanopia. Missense substitutions in this opsin are inherited dominantly and are thought to misfold or mistraffic the pigment in the cone outer segment, so that light absorption no longer activates the transducin-driven cascade that hyperpolarises the cell. The condition is rare relative to red-green defects, is not progressive in the way retinal degenerations are, and illustrates how a single G protein-coupled receptor defines an entire sensory channel.

Blue-cone opsin is the visual pigment that gives short-wavelength sensitivity to the eye, and its loss produces tritan colour vision deficiency, in which blue and yellow become hard to distinguish. Trichromatic vision depends on comparing the light captured by three cone classes with peak sensitivities near 420, 530 and 560 nm; the short-wavelength pigment supplies one of those channels, and downstream retinal circuits cannot reconstruct it when the pigment is faulty. Missense substitutions in OPN1SW misfold or destabilise the opsin so that it fails to initiate the phototransduction cascade in blue cones, and the resulting defect is inherited dominantly and is much rarer than the red-green deficiencies. The consequence is selective loss of blue spectral sensitivity rather than reduced acuity, since rod and long-wavelength cone phototransduction remain intact.

Defective visual phototransduction due to STRA6 loss of function describes what happens when cells can no longer take up circulating vitamin A, cutting off the supply of retinoid needed both to build the eye during development and to regenerate visual pigment afterwards. Retinol travels in blood bound to retinol-binding protein 4, stabilised as a complex with transthyretin, and STRA6 is the membrane receptor that recognises that complex and channels retinol into target cells for conversion to retinyl esters and ultimately 11-cis-retinal, the chromophore of rhodopsin. Loss of STRA6 function starves retinoic acid signalling in the developing embryo, producing syndromic microphthalmia (Matthew-Wood syndrome) with anophthalmia, cardiac, pulmonary and diaphragmatic malformations, and in surviving tissue leaves photoreceptors unable to sustain the visual cycle, causing blindness.

Vitamin A reaches the eye bound to retinol-binding protein 4, which circulates in complex with transthyretin, and cells take up that retinol through the membrane receptor STRA6. Loss of STRA6 function breaks this uptake step, and the retinoid supply needed both for embryonic patterning and for regenerating the visual chromophore 11-cis-retinal fails. The consequence is defective visual phototransduction together with a severe developmental syndrome: microphthalmia or anophthalmia with blindness, frequently accompanied by diaphragmatic, pulmonary and cardiac malformations, described as Matthew-Wood syndrome. The pathway therefore links plasma retinol transport to retinoic acid signalling in the developing eye and to the retinoid cycle that sustains rod and cone pigment. It illustrates how a single receptor-mediated transport event, rather than an enzymatic defect, can limit access to an essential dietary cofactor.

Dengue Virus-Host Interactions describes how dengue virus proteins, once made and processed in the cytosol, ER and ERGIC, spread to other cellular compartments and seize host machinery, and how that seizure produces the vascular leak and immune dysregulation of dengue fever and dengue hemorrhagic fever. Secreted NS1 circulates in blood, binds glycosaminoglycan-bearing proteoglycans, complement components and pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR4, and disrupts endothelial junctions before cells are even infected. Inside the cell, the capsid protein and NS5 enter the nucleus, where NS5 engages the spliceosome, the RNA polymerase II transcription and 3'-end processing apparatus and heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins, reshaping host mRNA output. The NS2B3 protease cleaves innate sensing adaptors including STING and MAVS to blunt interferon induction, while other viral proteins tune autophagy, mTOR complexes and apoptosis to favour replication.

Dengue virus encodes only ten proteins and must therefore borrow host machinery and disarm host defences, and this collection captures the physical and functional contacts it makes across compartments. The consequences are clinical: secreted NS1 circulating in blood engages complement components and pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR4 and CLEC5A, and together with nuclear NS5 it perturbs endothelial junction proteins including ZO-1, contributing to the vascular leak of dengue haemorrhagic fever. The viral NS2B3 protease and NS5 blunt innate sensing by acting on the STING/MAVS/RIG-I axis and on STAT2, so interferon induction and signalling both fail. Extensive interactions with spliceosomal, hnRNP, SR protein, RNA polymerase II and 3' end processing factors, and with autophagy and mTOR complex components, show how host gene expression, membrane remodelling and metabolism are redirected to support replication, while nuclear capsid and NS5 also modulate apoptosis.

SPOP-mediated proteasomal degradation of PD-L1(CD274) sets how much of the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1 a cell displays, and therefore how effectively tumour cells escape cytotoxic T cell attack. PD-L1 is a short-lived protein: the substrate adaptor SPOP delivers it to a CUL3-RBX1 cullin-RING ligase, which polyubiquitinates it for destruction by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core particle, ATPase and lid subunits together with ubiquitin executes the final step. The rate-limiting control is on SPOP itself. Cyclin D1-CDK4 phosphorylates SPOP at Ser-6, promoting binding by 14-3-3 gamma, which sequesters SPOP away from the ligase complex and stabilises PD-L1; casein kinase 2 contributes further phosphoregulation. This links cell cycle machinery directly to tumour immune evasion and explains why SPOP mutation or CDK4/6 inhibition alters checkpoint blockade responsiveness.

How much PD-L1 a tumour cell displays determines how effectively it silences cytotoxic T cells, and one route controlling that level is ubiquitin-dependent turnover of the protein by a cullin-RING ligase. SPOP acts as the substrate-recognition adaptor within a CUL3:RBX1 complex, marking PD-L1 for destruction by the 26S proteasome, whose core particle, regulatory ATPases and ubiquitin receptors are all represented here alongside ubiquitin itself. Cyclin D1:CDK4 opposes this by phosphorylating SPOP at Ser-6, creating a binding site for 14-3-3 gamma that sequesters SPOP away from the ligase; casein kinase 2 subunits contribute further phosphorylation input. Loss of SPOP function, common in prostate and endometrial cancer, stabilises PD-L1 and reduces tumour immune surveillance, which links cell cycle kinase activity and CDK4 inhibitor therapy to checkpoint blockade responsiveness.

PD-L1(CD274) glycosylation and translocation to plasma membrane describes how the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1 is matured and delivered to the cell surface, where it engages PD-1 on T cells and enforces immune tolerance. Tumours exploit this route to escape cytotoxic killing, and the modifications it installs determine how much PD-L1 a cell displays and how well checkpoint-blocking antibodies recognise it. In the endoplasmic reticulum the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, with catalytic STT3A or STT3B, attaches N-glycans at three asparagines; this shields PD-L1 from GSK3B-directed proteasomal turnover. IL-6-activated JAK1 both phosphorylates PD-L1 and promotes STT3A recruitment, linking inflammation to checkpoint output. In the Golgi, B3GNT3 extends the glycans and MIB2 adds K63-linked ubiquitin, after which PD-L1 reaches the plasma membrane. The pathway sits at the interface of secretory protein quality control and adaptive immune regulation.

PD-L1 can only restrain T cells if it reaches the cell surface in a stable, correctly modified form, and this route describes how the immune checkpoint ligand CD274 is glycosylated and translocated to the plasma membrane. Tumour cells exploit it to engage PD-1 on T cells and enforce immune tolerance, which is why the modifications here influence responses to checkpoint blockade. In the ER, the oligosaccharyltransferase complex — catalytic STT3A or STT3B with RPN1, RPN2, DDOST, DAD1 and accessory subunits — attaches N-glycans to asparagines in the PD-L1 extracellular domain, blocking GSK3B-directed proteasomal degradation. IL-6-activated JAK1 both phosphorylates PD-L1 and promotes recruitment of the glycosylation machinery. Further elongation by the Golgi glycosyltransferase B3GNT3 and K63-linked ubiquitination by the ligase MIB2 complete maturation before surface delivery, where PD-L1 and the related ligand PDCD1LG2 engage PD-1.

Expression of BMAL (ARNTL), CLOCK, and NPAS2 describes how the positive limb of the circadian clock is itself transcribed, setting the amplitude and phase of daily rhythms in sleep, feeding, hormone release and metabolism. The BMAL1:CLOCK heterodimer, with NPAS2 substituting for CLOCK, drives diurnal gene expression; loss of this arm flattens behavioural and metabolic rhythms and predisposes to metabolic disease. Their promoters carry ROR response elements contested by activating retinoid-related orphan receptors RORA/B/C and the repressive nuclear receptor NR1D1 (REV-ERBα). RORs recruit coactivators such as EP300, NCOA proteins and PPARGC1A, while heme-bound NR1D1 brings NCOR1, TBL1X and HDAC3 to silence the same sites. Because RORs sense oxysterols, NR1D1 senses heme, and SIRT1 and PPARα couple in nutrient status, this secondary feedback loop links the clock directly to cellular metabolism.

The positive limb of the mammalian circadian clock depends on transcription of the activators BMAL1 (ARNTL), CLOCK and its partial substitute NPAS2, whose heterodimers drive rhythmic daytime gene expression throughout the body. How much of these activators a cell makes sets the amplitude and phase of everything downstream, from sleep-wake behaviour to rhythms in glucose and lipid handling; loss of the loop flattens circadian output and is linked to metabolic disturbance. Their promoters carry ROR response elements contested by the retinoid-related orphan receptors RORA, RORB and RORC, which recruit coactivators such as EP300, NCOA1/2 and PPARGC1A to activate, and by REV-ERBα (NR1D1), which recruits NCOR1 with HDAC3 and the TBL1X adaptors to repress. Because the RORs bind oxysterols and NR1D1 binds heme, and because SIRT1 and CREB-regulated coactivators feed in, this secondary feedback loop ties clock gene expression to metabolic state.

Phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of BMAL1 (ARNTL) and CLOCK is the activation step that licenses the positive limb of the circadian clock, converting newly made transcription factors in the cytosol into a nuclear heterodimer competent to drive rhythmic gene expression. Everything downstream of the clock -- the daily cycling of period and cryptochrome genes, sleep-wake timing, feeding rhythms and the rhythmic control of hepatic and metabolic gene programmes -- depends on this dimer reaching chromatin on schedule. Casein kinase 2 phosphorylates BMAL1 while CDK5 modifies CLOCK; these marks promote heterodimerization and nuclear import, and they also set the tempo, since altering the phosphorylation sites lengthens or shortens period and can destabilize the proteins. NPAS2 substitutes for CLOCK as BMAL1's partner in some tissues. Such post-translational control links kinase activity and metabolic state to the phase of the clock.

The core positive limb of the circadian clock is built in the cytosol and must be phosphorylated before it can act in the nucleus. Newly made CLOCK is phosphorylated by CDK5, while casein kinase 2, through its catalytic CSNK2A1 subunit with the regulatory CSNK2B partner, phosphorylates BMAL1; the modified proteins then heterodimerize and move into the nucleoplasm, where the dimer drives transcription of period and cryptochrome genes and sets the pace of the roughly 24-hour feedback loop. NPAS2 can substitute for CLOCK in this partnership. Such modifications tune both the timing and amplitude of clock output and mark the proteins for eventual turnover, linking the oscillator to metabolic state. Disruption of this step flattens rhythmic gene expression and contributes to sleep, mood and metabolic disturbance.

Defective GALM causes GALAC4 describes the metabolic block that arises when galactose mutarotase loses function, producing type IV galactosemia. GALM is the cytosolic epimerase that interconverts beta-D-galactose and alpha-D-galactose, and only the alpha anomer can be phosphorylated by galactokinase, the first committed step of the Leloir pathway that funnels dietary galactose into glucose-1-phosphate and onward into glycolysis and glycoprotein synthesis. Without this anomeric conversion, galactose and its derivatives accumulate in blood and tissues. Affected individuals are usually mildly affected, with raised galactose levels, transient cholestasis and cataracts from lens galactitol accumulation, but severe cases extend to kidney, liver and brain injury. Because newborn screening detects elevated galactose, this defect is part of the differential diagnosis alongside classic galactosemia caused by loss of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase or the epimerase, and it is managed by dietary galactose restriction.

Dietary galactose enters catabolism only in its alpha anomer, and galactose mutarotase is the cytosolic epimerase that interconverts beta-D-galactose to alpha-D-galactose so that galactokinase can phosphorylate it, the first committed step of the Leloir pathway. Loss-of-function mutations in GALM cause type 4 galactosemia, the mildest and most recently recognised form of the disease: affected individuals typically show raised blood galactose with transient cholestasis and cataracts, the lens opacities reflecting accumulation of galactose and its reduction product galactitol, while severe cases extend to liver, kidney and brain injury. Because the defect sits upstream of galactokinase rather than at the classical galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase step, toxic galactose-1-phosphate accumulation is limited, which explains the comparatively benign course and the need to distinguish this condition from classic galactosemia in newborn screening.

NuRD complex assembly builds a chromatin remodeler that is unusual in coupling two activities in one machine: ATP-dependent nucleosome sliding by a CHD3, CHD4 or CHD5 ATPase, and histone deacetylation by HDAC1 or HDAC2. The resulting complex sets the accessibility and acetylation state of target promoters and enhancers, and through this controls lineage commitment, stem cell differentiation, DNA damage responses and metabolic gene programs such as hepatic gluconeogenesis. Assembly nucleates on a core of HDAC1/2 with MTA1/2/3 and the histone chaperones RBBP4/7, onto which MBD2 or MBD3, GATAD2A/B and CDK2AP1/2 are added; paralog choice generates compositionally distinct complexes with different targets. Recruitment to chromatin comes mainly from transcription factors, including Ikaros family and nuclear receptor partners, plus reader proteins such as ZMYND8 and PWWP2A. Originally viewed as purely repressive, NuRD also activates transcription, and its misregulation contributes to cancer and developmental disorders.
