Chromatin remodelling and histone deacetylation are usually separate jobs; the NuRD complex does both in one machine, sliding nucleosomes with a CHD3/CHD4/CHD5 ATPase while HDAC1 or HDAC2 strips acetyl groups from nearby histone tails. Assembly of this complex is what licenses that dual activity: a nucleating core of HDAC1/2 with MTA1/2/3 and the histone-binding WD40 proteins RBBP4/7 recruits MBD2 or MBD3, GATAD2A/B and CDK2AP1/2, and paralogue choice at each position generates complexes with distinct targets. Recruitment to genes comes largely through transcription factors and chromatin readers, including Ikaros-family zinc fingers, nuclear receptors, ZMYND8 and PWWP2 proteins, and can repress or activate transcription. The outputs shape stem cell differentiation, lymphoid and neural development, DNA damage responses and metabolic gene programmes such as gluconeogenic PCK1, FBP1 and G6PC1, and its subunits are recurrently mutated in cancer.

Affinity selection of immunoglobulins is the germinal centre reaction that converts a repertoire of randomly generated B cell receptors into high-affinity antibodies, and it is the reason vaccination and repeated infection yield progressively better protection. In the light zone, B cells test their receptors against antigen held as immune complexes on follicular dendritic cells via FCGR2B, CR1 and CR2, and high-affinity clones physically extract antigen using non-muscle myosin IIa and the actin and microtubule machinery, then process it through cathepsins and present peptides on MHC class II to follicular helper T cells. CD40L, IL4 and IL21 rescue those cells from apoptosis and return them to the dark zone, where BCL6, PAX5 and AICDA-driven somatic hypermutation, coupled to error-prone polymerases and mismatch repair, diversify the immunoglobulin variable regions for another round of selection. Failure distorts antibody quality and underlies immunodeficiency, autoantibody production and germinal-centre-derived lymphoma.

Antibody responses improve over days to weeks because germinal center B cells are repeatedly tested for how tightly their receptors bind antigen, and only the best binders survive. This affinity selection of immunoglobulins is what converts a low-affinity naive repertoire into high-affinity, class-switched antibody, and its failure underlies poor vaccine responses, immunodeficiency, and, when selection is subverted, autoantibodies and B cell lymphoma. Antigen held as immune complexes on follicular dendritic cells via complement receptors CR1/CR2 and FCGR2B is extracted by high-affinity receptors using non-muscle myosin IIa, then processed by cathepsins and presented on MHC class II to follicular helper T cells, whose CD40L, IL4 and IL21 grant survival. Selected cells cycle back for AICDA-driven hypermutation, requiring mismatch repair, translesion polymerases and BCL6-centred transcriptional control.

Loss of Function of KMT2D in MLL4 Complex Formation in Kabuki Syndrome describes how disease-causing mutations in the histone methyltransferase KMT2D break assembly of the MLL4 complex that deposits H3K4 methylation at enhancers. This modification licenses enhancer activity during development, so its loss disrupts transcriptional programs in neural, craniofacial, cardiac and immune tissues, producing the intellectual disability, distinctive facial features, heart defects and immunodeficiency of Kabuki syndrome. Catalysis requires KMT2D's C-terminal SET and adjacent WIN, FYRN/FYRC, PHD and zinc-finger modules to engage the four-subunit WRAD platform of WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30, which stimulates methyltransferase activity. Missense changes in this region weaken WRAD binding, while truncating alleles trigger nonsense-mediated decay of KMT2D mRNA and cause haploinsufficiency. Both routes converge on reduced enhancer H3K4 methylation, placing the disorder among chromatin-modifier developmental syndromes.

KMT2D is the histone H3 lysine 4 methyltransferase of the MLL4 complex, depositing the mono- and trimethyl marks that keep developmental enhancers and promoters poised for transcription. Its catalytic activity depends on assembly with the four-subunit WRAD module — WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30 — which docks onto the C-terminal region containing the WIN and SET domains; the SET domain alone is a poor enzyme without these partners. Missense changes in that region, found in people with Kabuki syndrome, weaken WRAD binding and so impair methyltransferase output, while truncating alleles trigger nonsense-mediated decay of the transcript and produce haploinsufficiency. The result is a congenital disorder of chromatin regulation marked by distinctive facial features, intellectual disability, growth delay, skeletal and cardiac anomalies, illustrating how quantitative loss of enhancer H3K4 methylation disrupts the transcriptional programmes of embryonic development.

MPS II - Hunter syndrome (CS/DS degradation) describes the lysosomal step that fails in Hunter syndrome, an X-linked disorder of glycosaminoglycan turnover that affects mainly boys. Iduronate-2-sulfatase removes the 2-sulfate group from L-iduronate residues in dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate and heparin, and this desulfation must occur before the downstream exoglycosidases can continue stepwise degradation of the chain. When the enzyme is deficient or absent, partially degraded glycosaminoglycans accumulate in lysosomes throughout the body and spill into urine. The consequences are systemic: hepatosplenomegaly, thickened heart valves and reduced cardiac function, airway obstruction, joint stiffness and skeletal deformity, and in severe forms progressive neurological deterioration and death in childhood. Milder forms preserve cognition and allow survival into adulthood. The pathway situates lysosomal catabolism of extracellular matrix polysaccharides within normal tissue remodelling.

Hunter syndrome is the X-linked lysosomal storage disease that results when the degradation of chondroitin/dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate stalls at a single sulfatase step. Iduronate-2-sulfatase normally removes the 2-sulfate group from L-iduronate residues in dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate and heparin, and this removal must happen before the downstream exoglycosidases and sulfatases can continue trimming the glycosaminoglycan chain. Loss of that one activity blocks the whole sequential pathway, so undegraded fragments accumulate in lysosomes throughout the body and spill into urine. The consequences are multisystem: hepatosplenomegaly, thickened cardiac valves, airway obstruction, joint stiffness and skeletal dysostosis, and in severe forms progressive neurological decline and death in childhood, while attenuated forms allow survival into adulthood. Because males carry a single copy of the gene, affected individuals are almost exclusively boys.

MPS VII - Sly syndrome (CS/DS degradation) describes the failure of lysosomal beta-glucuronidase and the block it imposes on stepwise breakdown of glycosaminoglycans. GUSB removes terminal glucuronic acid residues from chondroitin sulphate, dermatan sulphate and heparan sulphate as these long sugar chains are dismantled one sugar at a time by a relay of exoglycosidases and sulfatases; when the enzyme is absent, degradation stalls and partially digested chains accumulate in lysosomes throughout connective tissue, liver, spleen, bone and brain. The consequence is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease with a broad spectrum of severity, from non-immune hydrops fetalis and perinatal death to hepatosplenomegaly, dysostosis multiplex, coarse facial features and cognitive impairment in those surviving to adulthood. It illustrates how turnover of extracellular matrix proteoglycans depends on complete lysosomal catabolism, since a single missing step arrests the whole sequence.

Mucopolysaccharidosis VII, or Sly syndrome, is the lysosomal storage disease that follows loss of beta-glucuronidase activity during the stepwise breakdown of chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate. Glycosaminoglycan chains from turnover of extracellular matrix and cell surface proteoglycans are degraded inside the lysosome by sequential removal of terminal sugars and sulfate groups; GUSB performs the step that releases terminal glucuronic acid residues, and without it the partially digested chains accumulate in lysosomes of liver, spleen, bone, cartilage and brain. The consequences are strikingly variable, from non-immune hydrops fetalis and perinatal death to milder disease compatible with survival into adulthood, with hepatosplenomegaly, dysostosis and skeletal deformity, coarse facial features and differing degrees of cognitive impairment. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the defect illustrates how a single missing glycosidase can stall an entire catabolic route.

ARG1 variants cause hyperargininemia describes the loss-of-function mutations in arginase 1 that break the last step of the urea cycle and produce an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. Arginase 1 is a cytosolic, manganese-dependent enzyme most abundant in liver and present at lower levels in kidney, where it hydrolyses L-arginine to urea and L-ornithine, both disposing of waste nitrogen and regenerating the ornithine that keeps the cycle turning. When the enzyme is deficient, arginine accumulates in blood and tissues and patients develop spastic paraparesis, progressive neurological impairment and developmental delay; unlike other urea cycle defects, severe hyperammonemia is uncommon, so the phenotype is attributed largely to arginine and its guanidino derivatives. The pathway therefore links hepatic amino acid catabolism and nitrogen excretion to neurological health, and underlies dietary arginine restriction as treatment.

The final step of the urea cycle is carried out by cytosolic arginase 1, which hydrolyses L-arginine to urea and L-ornithine, completing nitrogen disposal and regenerating the ornithine that re-enters the cycle. The enzyme is most abundant in liver, with lower activity in kidney and red cells. Loss-of-function variants in ARG1 cause arginase 1 deficiency, or hyperargininemia, an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism in which plasma and cerebrospinal arginine accumulate. Affected children typically present after infancy with progressive spastic paraparesis, developmental regression, seizures and growth failure, a neurological course distinct from the other urea cycle disorders because severe hyperammonemia is uncommon. Treatment relies on protein restriction and nitrogen-scavenging agents. This biology links amino acid catabolism and ureagenesis to arginine availability for nitric oxide and polyamine synthesis.

SLC-mediated bile acid transport groups solute carrier proteins that move bile acids and related amphipathic solutes across membranes, activity that sustains the enterohepatic circulation by which conjugated bile acids are secreted, reabsorbed in the ileum and reclaimed by hepatocytes. Efficient recovery of this pool is what allows dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins to be emulsified and absorbed, and limits the accumulation of cytotoxic bile acids in liver and gut. The sodium-dependent carriers here are the same family that handles choline: SLC10A6 transports sulfated steroids and bile acid conjugates, while the SLC44 choline-like transporters and the high-affinity neuronal choline transporter SLC5A7 supply choline for phosphatidylcholine and acetylcholine synthesis. The shared theme is sodium-coupled uptake of small charged metabolites, linking bile salt handling to membrane lipid supply and cholinergic neurotransmission.

Bile acids and structurally related amphipathic solutes cross plasma and organelle membranes only with help from solute carriers, and this grouping collects the SLC-mediated bile acid transport steps together with the closely related choline-transporting members of the same superfamily. SLC10A6 belongs to the sodium/bile acid cotransporter family and imports sulfoconjugated steroids and bile acids into peripheral tissues, where local desulfation can regenerate active hormone, linking this transport to steroid availability rather than to hepatic bile flow alone. The SLC44 choline transporter-like proteins and the high-affinity, hemicholinium-sensitive carrier SLC5A7 move choline into cells; SLC5A7 supplies presynaptic cholinergic neurons with substrate for acetylcholine synthesis, and its loss causes congenital myasthenic syndrome with impaired neuromuscular transmission. Collectively these carriers set intracellular supply of bile acid conjugates and choline for membrane lipid synthesis, neurotransmission and enterohepatic and steroid handling.

Assembly of the 9+2 motile cilia builds the beating cilia that line the airways, brain ventricles, and reproductive tract, where their coordinated strokes clear mucus, circulate cerebrospinal fluid, and move gametes. Beyond the nine microtubule doublets and central pair, motile axonemes require dynein arms, radial spokes, and nexin links, and multiciliated cells must first amplify hundreds of centrioles through deuterosomes. The genes here represent the transcriptional and post-transcriptional program that licenses this fate: GMNC and MCIDAS relieve Geminin-mediated restraint and partner with E2F4/E2F5 and TFDP1 to drive centriole amplification through DEUP1 and CCNO, while FOXJ1, RFX2/RFX3, MYB, TP73, and Grainyhead factors switch on axonemal and motility genes. Notch signalling limits how many progenitors adopt this fate, and miR-34/449 families acting through Argonaute complexes reinforce the commitment. Failure produces primary ciliary dyskinesia, with chronic airway infection, laterality defects, and infertility.

Motile cilia of the 9+2 type — nine microtubule doublets around a central pair, equipped with dynein arms, radial spokes and nexin links — beat rhythmically to clear mucus from the airways, drive cerebrospinal fluid flow in the brain ventricles, and move eggs along the oviduct; when their assembly fails the result is primary ciliary dyskinesia, with chronic airway infection, situs defects and infertility. The genes here largely cover the front end of that programme: the transcriptional and centriole-amplification decisions that let a single epithelial cell build hundreds of cilia. GMNC and MCIDAS, acting with E2F4/E2F5 and TFDP1, license multiciliate differentiation and deuterosome-mediated centriole duplication via DEUP1 and CCNO, while FOXJ1, RFX2/RFX3, MYB, TP73 and Grainyhead factors drive axonemal and motility gene expression. Notch signalling restrains the fate, and miR-34/449 families with Argonaute and TNRC6 partners relieve that repression.
